If you are like me there are times you wish you had no responsibilities. You might wish you had only to devote yourself to something you love with no interruptions. Michelle Hodkin novels make me feel that way. Synopsis taken from Goodreads: Mara Dyer once believed she could run from her past. She can't. She used to think her problems were all in her head. They aren't. She couldn't imagine that after everything she's been through, the boy she loves would still be keeping secrets. She's wrong. In this gripping sequel to The Unbecoming of Mara Dyer, the truth evolves and choices prove deadly. What will become of Mara Dyer next? This second volume of the Mara Dyer trilogy takes the reader on a journey along with its characters that both frightens and exhilarates. Mystery and fear are exploited. Passionate love and familial bonds are tested. And the fine line between sanity and insanity is explored. The characters are fascinating in their complexities. As someone who has dealt with emotional and mental instabilities, I found some scenes eerily familiar. The story is great. The arc from the first book settles into the second, answering some questions then bouncing into another round of "what's going on?" It definitely makes the reader want more. I had a bit of a problem with the plot points. Had I not been so engrossed with the other elements of the book, the drawn out plot would have been too much. Tone, setting and atmosphere were superbly crafted. Those stolen moments between Mara and Noah sizzled with barely restrained desire, but their relationship didn't overshadow the overall story. Loved it. I've grown weary of the romance formula and the way Hodkin handles the bond between these two characters is very satisfying. The Evolution of Mara Dyer is a superb follow up to the first book in the trilogy. I give it four and a half stars. It doesn't get five because of I felt the plot could have been condensed, and my real-life experience with behavioral health facilities differs a bit from the character's. I highly recommend this book and it predecessor.

"Grave Secret" is the fourth book in Charlaine Harris's Harper Connelly series, and seems to wrap up so many of the continuing plot points that I can only imagine that it's the last in the series. Once again, Harper and devoted "brother" Tolliver locate the dead, get involved in nefarious dealings, and try to track down the loose ends of their disastrous childhood. The mystery elements came together nicely, but I was much more interested in the family secrets and resolutions than in the whodunnit pieces of the plot. As a devoted Sookie Stackhouse fan, the Harper Connelly series pales by comparison... but taken on its own merits, these books are fun, fast-paced, and full of the quirky characters that Harris writes so well.
I liked this a lot more than I liked the last several JW books I read. A very quick read and a nice break from the vast amount of political non-fiction I've been reading lately.

3.5 Stars Keeping this review shorter & simpler c: Maybe this book was a copy of another. Maybe not. Honestly, I'm not sure. But what matters to me is the quality and intensity of the plot, depth of the characters, and the fantastical world City of Bones builds. I love the world Cassandra Clare builds - she describes it remarkably and succeeds in drawing me in. Moreover, the world of the Downworlders and the Nephilim is intriguing, and unique in its own way. Same with the plot - from the first page, the plot is fast paced and interesting - I was never bored. There were many, many fight scenes - so many that sometimes you just knew something was going to go wrong because there has to be action. And finally, most of the characters had (at least a little) depth. Clary seemed a little weak and boring, although she does pull through to the end. Meanwhile, Jace seems more complicated - he's a bit of a jerk but is still fearless and kind, and his relationships with Clary, his half sister (who he obviously loves), and Valentine, his father supposed arch-nemesis . Overall, this book is great if you love fantasy with action and a bit of romance (especially if you're a teenage girl), if you don't mind the apparently large similarities with the Draco Trilogy/Harry Potter. It's enjoyable - just not remarkable.

"We cling to our fairy tales until the price for believing in them becomes too high." I want to give this book five stars so bad. But I just can't. :( Don't get me wrong... I loved it. But there are some things that got me confused and frustrated. As much as I hate to say this, some characters let me down... especially the peculiar children. *sigh* I wanted to know more about them. I crave for information- the things they like to do, their favorites, just anything. We simply know them by their names and their peculiarities. I wanted know about their lives back when they were still with their families. I'm not really looking for a chapter-length explanation, a few sentences could have been enough. I hated that I only got to know Emma because she's Jacob's 'love' interest (which is WEIRD, by the way). I loved Millard, though. *winks* One more flaw. I got excited about the ransack-the-town thingy. I thought there's a story behind it. Like maybe, sometimes they could be EXTREMELY dangerous or something. But I just got disappointed. Enemies were not really shocking at all. I expected a bigger revelation than what happened. "...so one day my mother sat me down and explained that I couldn't become an explorer because everything in the world had already been discovered. I'd been born in the wrong century, and I felt cheated." Hmm. Here comes the good things. I love Jacob. I know he seems a bit selfish for leaving his father all the time (and temporarily at the end)  , but I thought it was a brave thing to do! Oh yes, his grandfather is my favorite character. I got too emotional when he died! I don't know why- I just did. I loved how the grandfather (and not the father, too usual) who introduced him to the peculiar world. Having the adventure with Jacob, the peculiar children and Miss Peregrine was truly marvelous. As I was reading, I kept on wishing that I'm a peculiar too. Riggs' made me believe in fairy tales and fantasy for a while. It's like reading a fairy tale book... but with peculiarity. It's a strange book. Goodness, the book cover scared me! Ha-ha. But I promise you, it's worth the read. Though the characters are a bit dull, you'll enjoy it. MAYBE RIGGS WILL INCLUDE THE PECULIAR CHILDREN'S STORIES IN THE SECOND BOOK? I hope so! Best thing I liked about it: The photos. Do you want to know a secret? I didn't peek at the photos before reading the book. I wanted to surprise myself. Believe me when I say that I used my fast-reading abilities (am I peculiar now? hihi) just to get to the photos! Gaaah, it was a torture... But it was worth it. So, in case you still haven't read the book, don't peek at the photos before reading, okay? It'll be more exciting... and of course, peculiar. "I used to dream about escaping my ordinary life, but my life was never ordinary. I had simply failed to notice how extraordinary it was."

Read for the Idle Thumbs Book Club. It's the book for March. By Blood is about a professor who moves to San Francisco during the 1970s because he did something bad at the university and so is put on leave. There, he rents an office in a building with paper thin walls (literally, it is like their walls are made of rice paper) in the hopes that he can make a university comeback. While in that office, he becomes obsessed with the story of the patient of the next-door neighbour, an adopted lesbian who just doesn't feel like she belongs. Oh, boy. I don't think I can even fully divulge my feelings on this book. As you can tell, it too me a loooong time to read. The reason for this is because it's one hell of a boring book until you get the third part (the book is split into four sections). It also took me a while because I truly and without a doubt despise the protagonist. I understand that it's possible to like a book without liking a single character, let alone the protag, and there are some books for me where I've experienced that. However, this is not one of those books. We are stuck inside the protagonist's head as he recounts his creepy obsession with disturbing forced intimacy -- the patient is "[his] dear patient" always -- and not only is it frightening in a he's-definitely-a-stalker-who-will-murder-you-and-keep-your-corpse-forever way, but it's also trite as hell. It's great to know you're a creepy old man who immediately gets a boner when the patient describes her lesbian encounter (which wasn't even that sexually detailed! At least, not the first time he gets a boner). In fact, the protagonist as narrator and narrative frame for the actual story (the patient finding out her history and birth mother, etc.) didn't work. Ullman tries to make it work, but it doesn't and it can't simply because we get minimal to zero external details. The professor's entire existence revolves around this patient's story and it almost never seems like he does other things, or even work on his planned "comeback". Sure, we get a bit of reminiscence on Patty Heart's abduction and bank robbery case but only because it will later apply to the patient's story (which is really just to discuss Stockholm Syndrome as being a real thing). The professor doesn't shape to be an actual character, other than a creepy old man, because Ullman only uses him as a narrative frame. It might have worked for Conrad in Heart of Darkness, but it doesn't work here. The narrative would have flowed much easier and the story would have been more compelling if we had just gotten the professor out of the way. (I do realise that the professor was instrumental in helping the patient find her birth mother, but let's be honest, Ullman could've worked around that perfectly easily.) I raised my rating up to two stars because once we get into part three, it actually gets interesting. We get to hear part of the mystery unfold in a more clever frame: this time we get to hear (well, through the damn professor) the story out of a tape recording the patient brings. The mystery isn't that "mysterious" exactly, but it's kind of a fun (relative term) romp back into Nazi-infested Europe to see how the patient's mother survives. Obviously, still very sad, but we are a bit removed from that actual emotion because of the narrative frame. (Damn it, Ullman, why did you have to use the professor as a narrative device?) But, I have to disagree with the Lebensborn "twist". If it had been worked in earlier and not just tacked on to the end (I'm not kidding; it's around the last three chapters and these chapters are about 1-3 pages), then I can see it contributing to the narrative. As it stands, it just feels like Ullman found out about the Lebensborn project after she'd written most of the book and was like, "That's such an interesting bit of history! It'll be cool to put in my book about World War II!" It doesn't work, feels like an afterthought and becomes an unimpressive narrative decision. I also didn't like that the patient's lesbianism seemed only there so that the professor could be more interested and for Ullman to write a lesbian porn scene for the professor to get a boner to. Okay, it was also there so that she could have some contention with her super Catholic adoptive mother and so that she could say, "I'm not a typical lesbian; I work in the financial district and I'm not very political." Well, thanks for that. Ullman does have some decent writing chops and her prose can be quite lyrical at times. Sadly, she can also be on the opposite end and be very dry at times. Either way, once you muscle past parts one and two, By Blood becomes a bearable read that's mildly interesting. Unfortunately for Ullman, other people have tackled the Jewish situation in Europe under the Nazis and probably much better, too.

I can absolutely see how this would be a polarizing book. I am a fan of hard science fiction. I whine and moan when historical references are mangled and bang my head on the desk at space explosions. I read this book and I just didn't care. Do I think this is the likeliest result of the epic catastrophe of a slowing planet? Shouldn't the moon fall out of the sky and the planet's orbit skew with a thing like that? Wouldn't crime surge earlier and mass social movements bloom? Don't know. Don't care. I found Julia's story entrancing. I cared about her and her story. I wanted to know what it meant for her to come-of-age as the very notions of age and time were shifting. And this very microscopic look into her very small world was beautiful and meaningful and just enough. I would have stopped the book a chapter earlier, without the twenty-three-years-old-but-I-still-think-about-my-middle-school-boyfriend editorializing, but eh. And much as I was trying to remember what I knew about that whole pole magnet switching phenomenon in the early pages of the book and develop a working theory, I was actually, genuinely, honestly (for one of the first times in my reading history) pleased with Walker for not explaining the slowing with some pseudoscientific answer. Hmm, for bonus points, I recommend reading this in one sitting in a darkened basement without clocks at night and judging the effects of disoriented paranoia for yourself.

It's 1937. Jack Miller had hoped his escape from poverty would come through academia, but after that turned into a failure, he's stuck in an impoverished, depressing life. An offer to take part in an Arctic expedition as a wireless operator is not particularly tempting, but as the only way to change his life, Jack takes it. The group, mainly composed of upper class academics, aim to settle in Gruhuken, on a small island in the Barents Sea, and spend a year there. As they approach the site, though, it becomes clear the locals are very uneasy about it. A couple of the expedition members drop out before they even get to their destination. Only three of them make it to the camp, where Jack experiences some of the same discomfort the locals seemed to show. He even sees something, but convinces himself he must have been wrong. And then disaster strikes, and his two companions must leave. Jack can either go with them, allowing the expedition to fail, or stay on his own through the Arctic winter. He chooses to stay. And through his diary entries, we get to share his experiences. This is one of the best, most original and most terrifying ghost stories I've ever read. Everything about it is perfectly executed. One of the things that impressed me the most was how Paver used characterisation to justify what was the main suspension of disbelief issue: why Jack would decide to stay on on his own in Gruhuken, ignoring his unease. Jack's motivations were completely convincing. There's the class envy-based need to prove himself by keeping the expedition going, plus his hero-worship, maybe more, of Gus. It made complete sense that he would stay. After all, he doesn't know what's going to happen. What does happen after Jack is alone is something I'm not even going to hint at. All I'll say is that it's deliciously chilling, and that Paver relies on suggestion and psychological development, rather than on gruesomeness, to generate the growing sense of terror. The narration, through Jack's diary entries, is genius. The writing itself conveys Jack's state of mind much better than any description could. If you're even mildly interested in horror, you should read this. Just, maybe, wait until the summer. MY GRADE: An A-.

Storyline: One normal day all the adults 15 and over disappear. Before long more and more weird things start to evolve, kids start developing supernatural powers and then they wonder out far enough to realize they are trapped under a dome. Chaos breaks out as civilization crumbles and the children start to act more and more savage like. My Favorite Characters from Gone: Sam Temple: Sam is your typical hero type, he doesn't really want to be the hero but steps up and takes the job because there is no one else. He is already known for being a hero to most of the kids having the nickname School bus Sam. Him and his friends take it upon themselves to try and figure out what is going on in the dome. Sam is a very entertaining lead character during Gone. I enjoyed how vulnerable he was at times but also feeling very torn by all his responsibilities. Astrid Ellison (Astrid The Genius): She is pretty much the brains to Sam's bronze. She is the smartest person in the FAYZ. She is Sam's right hand and formulates all the plans and strategy in the FAYZ. I really liked Astrid in the first book, she was protective and loyal to Sam, but also so smart she clearly had the best grip on the FAYZ. Quinn Gaither: Quinn has always been Sam's best friend and even now during the FAYZ. He is a loyal best friend through the beginning of the book but as time plays on the FAYZ has its effect on a lot of the kids left under the dome and Quinn isn't any exception. Quinn is one of my favorite characters in all the books, I love reading his parts and love to watch him go through the stages of finding himself and stepping out of Sam's shadow. He was unreliable at times but I truly found him to be a believable fourteen year old boy just trying to adjust to surviving in this new environment. Lana Lazar (The Healer): Lana is trapped in a car accident at the beginning of the book along with her dog Patrick. She is one of the kids that develops a power and she has one of the most important powers in the FAYZ the ability to heal. She is a badass and very independent. She is my favorite female character throughout the entire series. Drake Merwin: Drake is the devil in the FAYZ. He is the most feared character in all the books, 2nd only to the darkness. He is Caine's right hand throughout the first book and in parts of the other books. He finds it fun to torture people and loves the FAYZ it's like his own little playground. I hate Drake but in an intriguing way. He is crazy and is just pure evil!! Diana Ladris: Diana is one of the Coates kids. She is Caine's right hand go to person, he doesn't make any decisions without Diana's approval. I like Diana, she is a bitch  and I find it pretty funny at times. I feel for Diana throughout the series, I really wish she wouldn't have had to live in the FAYZ because I know that the things she had to do to survive really hurt her more than she lets show. Caine Soren: Caine is the leader of the Coates kids, he has the telekinesis powers. He strives to gain power from the FAYZ and he is one of Sam's arch enemies in the FAYZ. I feel sorry for Caine throughout the series a lot of the time, I don't think he is completely evil but just trying to be valued. Little Pete: Little Pete is a very important character, I have a hard time picturing how he would look. He is autistic and Astrid's little brother. I like his character but at the same time in the first book he's just kind of there not too important but not unimportant either, I really find his character interesting in the rest of the series. The Powers: (sorry putting these in a spoiler because some aren't revealed until later in the book or maybe even later in the series) The powers are defined on a scale of bars like on a cell phone, really powerful characters are mostly 4 bars and weak or no powers are a 1 bar. Caine-Telekinesis 4 bars Sam- Fire Hands/Light from hands (he can also make balls of light) 4 bars Diana- Ability to read power level 2 or 3 Bug- Camouflage 2 bar Computer Jack- Superhuman Strength level 3 Little Pete: 7 bar you have to read entire series to know all Little Pete's powers. Astrid: Read someone's importance by light 2 bar There are a lot more important characters but I just don't remember if they are introduced in book 1 so those are the most important at the beginning of the series. Music: Believe by The Bravery This Is Not The End by The Bravery Endgame by Rise Against My Thoughts: This is my favorite series of all time, I must have read this first book at least six times. I first started reading it when I was in tenth grade and was obsessed with symbolism. I remember sitting at home writing notes in the margins of my book and highlighting parts. I found this book to be a lot like Lord of the Flies but with some awesome twist. I thought that the Coates Kids entrance was just like the Choir boys entrance in Lord of the Flies, and the way they always fear the darkness reminds me of the beastie the boys fear. If you have time to put into this series and you like supernatural dark fiction I would highly suggest you read this series. However if you don't have time to read the whole series I wouldn't suggest you try to just read the first book hoping to be satisfied, it doesn't answer a lot of questions and leaves you with a lot to think about. Happy Reading

Audio book performed by the author. Kingsolver tells the story of William Harrison Shepherd, a young man caught in the gaps (the lacunae) between two countries, two parents, two cultures, two lives (public and private). The novel unfolds as a series of diary entries, letters, and newspaper clippings, spanning the period from 1929 to 1954. Never quite at ease with his place in the world, Shepherd is an astute observer, who carefully considers what he witnesses and forms his own opinions. But he is not a man of action; he goes along for the ride, letting history unfold around him and never quite understanding how it has derailed his meager hopes. When he fails to play the media's game, he finds himself the object of increasingly outlandish stories; and, eventually, accusations taken as truths will destroy him. The lacuna that is most important here is the space between truth and a falsehood perceived as truth. I love how Kingsolver's luscious writing paints the landscape and time period. I could just about taste the sugary pan dulce or savory chalupas; was nearly deafened by the howler monkeys, the din of the marketplace or the shouts of demonstrators and riot police; I relished in the colors of the tropics and felt subdued by the grey of a mountain winter. I did eventually grow to appreciate Kingsolver's narration, though I really had a difficult time with her performance at the outset. I thought she was too "careful" with her words; it lacked emotion and "life." But she really shone, in my opinion, when she voiced Frida Kahlo and, especially later in the novel, Violet Brown. I think I am going to have to read this one again - this time in a text format.

Wow, didn't think I'd like this as much as I did. It took me awhile to get into the story, but once the flashbacks happened, the book really got good. The word I'd use to describe this book as a whole is 'entertaining'. Total book crack. This is good if you want a fun, light read and aren't in the mood for something complicated. The book starts with the main character Justina dumped on the side of the road the morning after prom. She spills her troubles to the cashier at a 7-Eleven and the events of the night slowly unravel. You get to find out the story behind every bump, bruise and stain. It was so much fun to see how out of control things got and all the crazy stuff that happened. I did like the scenes at the convenience store, but I was so hyped that I just wanted the story to continue so I could find out what the deal with Ian ditching her was. Justina was absolutely hilarious. I wasn't sure if I'd like her character at first, but the thoughts that went through her head were so amazingly funny that I warmed up to her fairly quick. I felt so freaking terrible for her!!! Justina is the type of person who has the worst luck of all time. The whole prom night was a series of bad events. I swear that a single thing didn't go right until the end of the book. If you're someone that gets aggravated by misunderstandings and characters missing each other by a second, prepare yourself because this book is chockfull of them. I personally was so annoyed with Ian the entire book. I thought their relationship was sort of cute, but after Ian ditched her at prom, I wanted to punch him. Sure, I understand that Justina was always jumping to conclusions and made things worse, but I don't blame her. I would be assuming the worst too if I was in her shoes. The problem could have been solved if Ian had told her before he left. It killed me to see all the phone calls missed by like a second and the texts from Ian that didn't explain anything. I kept thinking to myself, 'Jeez, give the main characters a break already'. I was so glad when Justina got her happy ending because she deserved one after all the crap that happened. I still think that Ian's reason for leaving was kind of lame. Not the dog finding thing  because that was kind of sweet, but the surprise pizza party thing . I was seriously like WTF? It was a bit random and weird to me.

It's not often that a book is capable of reducing me into a screaming, howling mess of emotions. I'm simply not the type to react violently to whatever I'm reading. Perhaps I was, when I was a teenager, but those days are well behind me and even then I wasn't the most reactionary of readers. The only book that could do that was Lord of the Rings. But then, just last year, I read the first book in Scott Lynch's Gentleman Bastards series, titled The Lies of Locke Lamora, and it left me swinging between laughing out loud and brief bursts of screaming in protest, depending on what was happening. The experience has left me a devoted reader of Lynch's series: after all, any book that makes me want to simultaneously hurl the book across the room and cradle it close to my chest at the same time, is a good book. I did not, however, expect to react the same way to another series - or if I did, it wouldn't come so soon after discovering Lynch's series. Except that's precisely what happened when I started reading Brandon Sanderson's Mistborn Trilogy, which was recommended to me by my friend Hope, and who in turn was recommended the book by Matthew, the DM for our weekend D&D games. The result has been heartbreak all around - the good kind, I hasten to add. But if I thought the first book, titled Mistborn: The Final Empire, was very emotional on its own, I was not prepared at all for the effect the second book, Mistborn: The Well of Ascension, would have on me. And again, I mean this in a very good way. The Well of Ascension continues almost right where The Final Empire left off. With Kelsier dead after the events in the first book, it's up to his crew to pick up the pieces and figure out a way to keep the Central Dominance stable from the city of Luthadel, once the home of the Lord Ruler, whom Kelsier's apprentice, a street urchin-turned-Mistborn named Vin, killed in the climax of The Final Empire. As it turns out, starting a revolution and killing a despotic ruler is one thing; dealing with the fallout from that event is another thing entirely. With the Lord Ruler gone, his realm has began to crumble, with powerful nobles breaking away and setting themselves up as kings in their own right. The few nobles who remained in Luthadel after the fall of the Lord Ruler have sworn nominal fealty to Elend Venture, whose idealistic perspective on politics might just mean he's the wrong kind of man for this situation. And with armies headed towards Luthadel, intent on taking the city - and the stash of atium the Lord Ruler has hidden somewhere in it - Vin, Elend, and the rest of Kelsier's crew will have to make some difficult decisions that will directly affect the direction their lives take hereon out. One of the most important story lines in this series is the one I mentioned earlier: the fact that a revolution has just occurred, and a despot has been overthrown. This event is everything that the first book was leading up to, with the Lord Ruler's downfall forming the climax of that novel. The series could have ended there, or the second book could have picked up some years after when the dust had settled, but what I appreciated most about Sanderson's series is that he's sensible enough of history to know that revolutions don't just end there, with everyone tired but happy and ready to rebuild. No: revolutions are messy things, both before, during, and after, and I really like the fact that Sanderson tackles the "after" part. Regime changes are part and parcel of so much of fantasy these days, but not a lot of them deal with the messy bit that comes immediately after. That period is a rich mine for drama and story, and Sanderson does a good job pulling up as much compelling story as he can, both as a plot and as a means of developing characters - in this case, Elend Venture and the original members of Kelsier's crew. It's clear that the situation, as it stands at the beginning of the novel, is tenuous, mostly because Luthadel's new leaders aren't exactly sure how to go about running a country now that they have control of it. It's a problem that's plagued every revolutionary government in history, so it makes sense that Elend and Kelsier's crew now have to find ways of making sure that the Kelsier's sacrifice is not in vain - Elend, especially, since he's the king. Such conflict, though, helps characters grow, and Elend definitely does that (with a little help from a new character who is introduced in this novel). He's not a flake, necessarily, but he's certainly not strong-willed enough to make a proper ruler in a time of crisis - ideals can only go so far, after all, in holding a kingdom together. Fortunately, Elend does grow, and while it's not a completely dramatic and sudden change in character, I really like the fact that it isn't. There's still one more book after all, which means there's still enough time for Elend to change and grow, depending on what happens further down the line. I mentioned in my review for The Final Empire that the magic system was the second major plot line in the series, and that prediction bore fruit in this one, in the form of a prophecy about the Hero of Ages. In the first novel, everyone assumed that the Hero of Ages was the Lord Ruler, but it turns out that this might not be the case. The story about the Hero of Ages, the Well of Ascension, and mysterious entity called the Deepness are further explored in The Well of Ascension, with Vin at the heart of it all. Just like Elend's having a hard time being king, Vin has a hard time trying to adjust to her new roles: Elend's beloved, Elend's personal Mistborn (and therefore assassin), Luthadel's resident Mistborn (and therefore to be treated in the same way a tactical nuke is treated), and Kelsier's Heir, a quasi-religious figure to the followers of the Church of the Survivor. While the first two roles she has to fulfill are interesting for the way they help in her character development (especially her relationship with Elend), it's her status as the Heir of the Survivor that I find most interesting. That Kelsier was deified after the Collapse is unsurprising, but watching how Vin deals with her new status is interesting to read about - as is the development of the Church of the Survivor into a perhaps-legitimate faith. Will it replace the religion of the Lord Ruler? That remains to be seen. And then there's Vin's link to the prophecy of the Hero of Ages. That entire storyline is a lesson in how prophecies are so often shaped by those who believe them, and the tragedies that can result - both in the Lord Ruler's case, and in Vin's. I really liked this take on the concept of prophecies, because so often in fantasy novels, prophecies are taken as absolute truth, and, often, turn out to be absolute truth. But what if they were subject to human fallacy - as anything humanity has ever tried to understand is subject to? What if in the reading of a prophecy, someone or a group of people made a mistake in the interpretation? This was a nice place to go with the concept of prophecies, and I'm glad Sanderson went there. As for personal relationships, they are front-and-center more in this novel than in the last one - and the primary reason for the emotional roller-coaster my heart went through while reading this. I won't say anything further in case I give away too much on that score (and I mean this: part of the pleasure of reading about how these relationships develop is to know as little about them as possible), but suffice to say that Sanderson certainly knows what he's doing when he writes about interpersonal relationships, romantic or otherwise, and I'm still metaphorically picking up the pieces of my broken heart even now, some days after I finished reading the book. Overall, Mistborn: The Well of Ascension is a novel that does more than just continue the story that began in Mistborn: The Final Empire: it stands on its own as a tale to match the first novel, and carries the plot forward in a manner that makes the reader excited to read the third novel. Unlike so very many other second books in trilogies, it does not suffer from middle-book syndrome, serving as more than just a bridge between the events of the first and third novels and standing on its own as an important moment in this trilogy's development. And, as a part of that development - and part of what makes this book so good - this novel feels more emotionally-charged than the last one, with lots of time and opportunity for the reader to get more invested in the established characters, and to develop a fondness for newly-introduced ones. But it is, as I mentioned, only the second book in a trilogy, and while it might be hard to imagine that there could be more after what happens in this novel, there is definitely more, in the novel Mistborn: Hero of Ages. Whether or not that book lives up to the setup done in the first two remains to be seen, but I definitely look forward to finding out - and I cross my fingers that the payoff is as grand and magnificent as I hope it to be.

Wow. This was one intense, I-can't-breathe-until-I-finish-this-book kind of read. I decided to read this book due to a glowing review by one of my friends (thanks Ashley! ), and I'm really glad I did. I don't know about the rest of you, but I've become a little tired of the dystopian fad. I mean, death and destruction and nearly certain defeat are great and all, but only after so many times. This book had all the classic mistreated, poor workers vs. extravagant, cruel high society cliches that we've been seeing so much of, and at the beginning, it just made me roll my eyes. But then, it departed from that and left the pack of Hunger Game wannabes behind. The Silvers' powers were really cool, and vaguely reminded me of the premise behind Steelheart by Brandon Sanderson. I enjoyed learning of the different powers and what they were called, which led of course to wondering what type I would fall into. (I'm convinced I would be a shadow-after all, most of the shadows described in the book are redheads. ;) ) I also was strongly reminded of The Roar by Emma Clayton. Same basic idea, but a totally new twist. If you haven't read it yet, I suggest you do so. The characters were very interesting. Mare was, of course, the typical tough, cynical female protagonist in YA lit, but I still found her interesting and related to her. I was not a super-fan of the love triangle/square, though. Pretty much from the beginning, I was Team Maven, so I was ready for Cal and Kilorn to take a hike. That is, until he BETRAYED everyone! I totally hate him. And to think I wanted him to end up with Mare! Ugh! THE SNEAKY LITTLE RAT! Okay, enough ranting. I suppose I'm Team Cal, now. *sob* The rest of the characters were all right in themselves, except for Farley. For some reason, I just hate Farley! She seems like a total cold-blooded killer, and even from the first time she stepped on page, I knew I didn't like her. Same with The Scarlet Guard. I was not happy when Mare joined The Scarlet Guard, especially as it seemed very impulsive, even for her. Also, I was not expecting Maven to join as well. I was expecting it to be it Cal. Maven and Cal were interesting to watch, but not as engrossing as Mare. The only characters besides Mare that I really cared about and wanted to see more of was Gisa and Shade. Especially Gisa, as I was sad we didn't see more of her in the book. I can only hope she features prominently in the sequels. The setting was interesting, but not as fleshed out as I would have like it to be. The only places I found myself able to picture vividly was Mare's village, and the arena at Queenstrial. I would have like to gain a better understanding of the world around Norta, and what was going on. (For a fantastic dystopian world, see Nadine Brandes' Out of Time trilogy.) Plot-wise, I enjoyed the twists it took after the generic dystopian set-up. Kind of The Selection meets Steelheart meets The Hunger Games. It definitely was non-stop action, and I give Aveyard kudos for that. The end, although rushed, was a very good set-up for the next book, and I am excited to see what happens to the characters. Including Shade. I was very sad to learn of his death, and excited when he miraculously returned. I can't wait to see what kind of character he is in coming books! The one content problem I had was the violence. Honestly, if it gets any worse in coming books, I may choose to skip them. This is about the limit of my tolerance for violence and graphicness. Overall, I was excited to find another popular (though secular) read that did not have any content issues that would require me to abandon it. The only other popular/secular books I have enjoyed wholeheartedly are the Matched trilogy by Ally Condie. (I will say though, Matched is still my favorite over Red Queen.) I look forward to reading Glass Sword, and if all goes well, King's Cage as well. Tally ho! Rating: 4 stars Recommendation: 15 and up. Language: 2/10 (Only a few curse words-pretty good for mainstream) Violence: 8/10 (There was a lot of graphic violence in this one. Torture, battles, attacks, etc. I managed alright with most of it, but it was not a pretty sight. Those sensitive to violence and/or graphic descriptions should steer clear of this one. Weak of stomach, beware! ) Sexual content: 2/10 (Didn't notice much here, and this is what I am typically most sensitive to. A few kisses.)

Overall, decent but not a stand out. I liked that  the guy who showed her love could be fun wasn't the "first(good) and last". Too often the previously wronged lady gets one guy who "shows her how it should be" and then that's it. You're locked to him forever. Just a slight variant on the Virgin to Bride trope. And while there were two love interests, it wasn't a traditional triangle thing. She had one while the other pined quietly in the background, then the second stepped up, the first showed he wasn't a long term guy, and she made a decision fairly quickly, or at least without any whining. Thank Goodness. The realistic way she had to worry about food was a good detail, and there were some tiny scenes where the fae were less bland, like trying to learn to garden the human way or dropping off rabbits. Not enough of these though. Also liked Ahern's story, but that could have started earlier and been more. Morag and the puppy were the two best parts. The Fae lands and the witches' magic were a little boring and stale, in the way I remember these stories being in the 80's and 90's. They felt like they had all the uniqueness and variety of a particularly uninspired term paper. In spite of that, I did enjoy it, and by the end I was hooked. Took awhile though, the beginning was not great.

This isn't science-fiction, it's the possibilities of what's to come inspired from what has already happened. Atwood here, is warning the human race. We think with all our advancements we're actually moving forward but we're not, we're going a 100 steps backwards to the 50 take forward. With our own actions and impulses we'll end up imprisoning ourselves. We think we're becoming liberated but we're only turning more barbaric and divided from within. She didn't write this book out of her imagination, she wrote it from observing the reality around her. She connected the dots and speculated a possible future. Edit: After 2016 US Elections, this book is even more relevant than ever. What a horrifyingly prophetic book this turned out to be, I'm stunned.

2.5 stars The Crown's Game by Evelyn Skye was a highly anticipated book for me back in 2016. However, I didn't pick it up until a year later which was fine with me. Now I don't have to wait to read the sequel since it will have been released already. Overall, this book didn't live up to my expectations. The main aspect of The Crown's Game that ruined the entirety of the story was the romance. The love triangle that develops between three of our main characters; Nikolai, Vika, and Pasha, is so unnecessary. I especially despise the "strong pull" of love attraction between Vika, our female protagonist and one of the enchanters in this game, and Nikolai, the other enchanter and our male protagonist. With my first initial read, their "feelings" for each other bordered on instalove. The Crown's game is a duel to determine who will be the Imperial Enchanter and who will be sentenced to death. With your life on the line, you (being Nikolai and Vika both) care more about how beautiful each other's face looks or dancing to each other's rhythm. Give me a break! *smh* While I cringe at the romance, I can pass off the pull that the two have for each other. Their magic is like two halves of a coin, opposites almost of each other. Peas from the same pod. Also, considering they are both channeling from the same source (Russia), just differently, I guess that explains the constant attraction between Nikolai's and Vika's magic. BUT THAT DOES NOT MEAN YOU FORGET ABOUT THE GAME YOU ARE SUPPOSE TO BE PLAYING. Which brings me to another disappointing aspect of the book. This book is titled The Crown's Game so as a reader, I expect a very intense and interesting game between these two enchanters with both pulling all the stops to defeat the other enchanter. No! The book shifts from the intense training the two enchanters go through in preparation for the game in the first couple of chapters to the game being nothing but a means of wooing the other enchanter and keeping both enchanters alive for the sake of living. The tension and anticipation you feel when reading a serious or important fight is honestly nonexistent. Also, I'm no expert on Russian history, folklore, or culture but this book didn't feel very Russian-inspired. The only Russian vibes I got were from the setting, nineteenth century Russia, with a couple Russian names or phrases thrown here or there. I would say Bardugo's Grisha books does a much better job of incorporating Russian elements into the story. The one thing I wished was explored more was Nikolai's family dynamics. I'm a sucker for well-written family relationships. Nikolai's mother, Aizhanna, really captured my attention with her backstory. I secretly wished she hadn't killed Nikolai's father, the Tsar, because I wanted to see interactions between him and Nikolai. So you can see why I would be greatly sadden when this specific plot line didn't go in the direction I wanted it to. It would have made the story much more darker and in my opinion, more interesting too. Overall, an underwhelming book. I have heard that the sequel does get a bit dirtier and darker so I might pick it up. However, with so many books to read, I wouldn't recommend unless you want a romance heavy, light fluffy fantasy read. Otherwise, you will be quite disappointed like I was.

So, what can I say about this book? There was plenty of it that I liked; the cosmic horrors, the magic-and-computers mixture (it was very clear computers is a thing Charles Stross knows very well), the ridiculous paperwork drenched Laundry, and the stakes were wonderfully high every time. That said, why only three stars? Short answer: microagressions. Long answer is full of spoilers and under this cut: For one, there was a lot of casual ableism in this book. A lot of people were referred to as "sociopaths" just based on shallow impressions, the main character's on-and-off girlfriend is labeled different kinds of mentally unwell throughout the book, which basically translated to "evil". While such relationships as depicted in this book definitely exist, Mahdi was a very one-note "evil girlfriend" character, who did nothing for the plot but be the Veronica to Mo's Betty. And that brings me to the "evil women" characters. I'm sure it wasn't intentional, but in The Atrocity Archives the only not-harpy female character is Mo (whose only function is to get kidnapped, twice so Bob can have someone to save) and a SWAT-team background character (only known woman on her team) mentioned twice. The rest? We have Bob's "crazy" on-and-off girlfriend, and then there's Harriet and her female minion, who're ineffective villains. That's right, there not just villains, they're ridiculously none threatening to boot. The Concrete Jungle ups Harriet to a somewhat actual threat (though her plan is shown to be utter bollocks and she's defeated within two pages). Mo is off having her own adventure somewhere, which is mentioned in two sentences. Josephine could have been a great addition, if she'd been allowed to contribute more. Sure, she took out that camera and shot some zombies, but the camera Bob could have fixed himself and the zombies just kept on going, so what did she really contribute to the plot? Also, could we please stop with the "you're a woman?!"-trope? It's used twice here and it's just as annoying both times. It could have worked with the "Mo" situation, if it hadn't been completely illogical for Bob's boss not to give him any information of his target other than their name + the clear "OMG SHE'S SO HOT AND FEMALE" reaction to Mo's appearance. And with Josephine it was such an obvious set up that I had to face-palm. You ask for the DI and someone comes out to meet you, why wouldn't you assume they're the DI? Oh yeah, because they're a woman. I think these instances were meant as "look, women can have powerful positions too!" moments, but both times it came off as "look, Bob is unable to imagine women in settings other than 'girlfriend' or 'harpy accountant'". Sort of made me like Bob less, just saying. I don't think the microagressions were intentional at all. I don't think this book is meant as any kind of "attack" on women or neuroatypical people. It's just yet another "straight neurotypical dude save the world all on his own" kind of book, written by someone who doesn't seem to have had to reflect on or experience much ableism or sexism. Read it for the wonderful cosmic horrors. Try and ignore the microagressions if you can.

I have been eager to read this book since I read the first one in the series. I loved the first book and was intrigued to see where Roth would take Tris next, now that the faction system was beginning to break down (following typical dystopian fiction fashion). I enjoyed being taken to the other areas of the city in this book and having them described in detail. It was also great to see how the other factions live and work as the first book really just focused on Abnegation and Dauntless, with a brief insight into Erudite. Insurgent took Tris to Amity, the factionless, Candor and deeper into Erudite. I feel I now have a better understanding of how their world works, just in time for it all to collapse. When they were heading back into the city and came across the factionless I guessed that it was going to be Tobias' mother that they were going to see, as soon as they said that someone had been looking for him. One thing that did irritate me was the up-and-down-y-ness of Tris and Tobias' relationship. But I guess considering what they were going through it is actually quite natural. Tris was being a bit reckless, but not really in a way that a Dauntless wouldn't normally be. They are there to defend the city after all. I like the fact that they seem to be sound by the end of the book and I hope that it stays that way in the next one. The reveal at the end of the book was a complete surprise. I had been trying to guess what the big secret was (who wouldn't?!) that the Abnegation wanted to share but the Erudite wanted to hide. However the final reveal showed it to be nothing like what I had considered. This makes me very intrigued as to where the story is going to go next considering the fact that the world everyone took for granted has actually only existed for a generation. Also I'd love to know how Tris' mother came to be the spokesperson and how the situation for the development of this community came about. Hopefully this will be revealed in the next book. This book was brilliant and receives five stars. I can't wait to read the final book in the trilogy.
