HEARTBREAKING. I was in between books during my commute to my work. I want to read something short. And this one was on my library for quite a while. So I tried it, and oh my! What a short this is! Benjamin and Teddy's affair was heartbreaking. I'm in almost tears while reading this during my commute. It's quite embarrassing. XD Their love for each other was pure and unadulterated. And I ached when I found out that they separated and Teddy died. I was very glad that this story ended well eventually. Marie Sexton is one of my favorite authors and her writing style is intact in this free read. I love that this free short is a really really good one. It can rival those full novels. A RECOMMENDED FREE SHORT! Just try to not read this in the morning. XD

I'm actually really pissed off. This book was bad. Really bad. But it's the kind of book that's bad but thinks it's good. Let's get started on why, shall we? Firstly: the book is 202 pages. And yet nothing at all happens until the last, what? If you're writing a book that's 202 pages I don't think you have any reason not to have something decent happening on every page. Secondly: the story is predictable as fuck. The second the character of Piggy turned up I knew he'd end up dead. With the first argument between Ralph and Jack I knew Jack would probably try to take over. The first time Roger threw some rocks at a kid I knew he was a little asshole that was going to kill someone - and it ended up being with a rock! Such a shock! Thirdly: it's so unrealistic. I don't care what kind of kids these are; there's not a child in the world that would find themself marooned on an empty island with no adults and not cry. Not one. Yet all of these kids seem to think it's all grand? Plus then they seem to have tonnes of easily reached fruit to eat that never runs out, and a bunch of untrained boys take off into a forest and manage to kill multiple pigs? Not even pigs, boars, with homemade throwing spears? A real boar would gut a fully grown adult with barely a problem. It's just. Ugh. And then for my last point: that ending??? Also stupidly predictable, and yet I hoped so bad that Golding wouldn't go there, but he did. The man that talks to them is obviously a fucking idiot if he looked at the state of those kids, heard that two had already died, and thought that they were "playing war". So yep they're all fine and dandy saved right when they're about to murder the main character and suddenly all these savages have a massive fit of remorse and start crying? And then of course a fade to black because who could be bothered with examining how any of these kids are going to live back in civilisation. I just really want to hit this book in its face.

There are two stories going on in this book: the 'whodunit' serial killer mystery and the relationship between two women bound together because of a tragic event that happened when they were kids. The author uses the former in order to examine the latter but I felt there were issues with this approach that ultimately undermined both stories. The reader gets caught up with the whodunit because the author spends a lot of time on this aspect of the book. You do learn about the lives of Amber and Kirsty as adults and, through a series of flashbacks, as kids Bel and Jade who share a tragic day that binds them together for the rest of their lives. However, the author keeps drawing the reader back to the victims and suspects of the mystery. So your mind turns away from Bel and Jade and gets to wondering about who the killer is, thinking that it will have far more impact on what the author wants to say and reveal about Bel and Jade than it actually does. In fact, once the killer is revealed, the entire storyline is dropped. The point of having what seems like a typical serial killer plotline turns out to be a very roundabout and overly complicated way of  providing the means by which Amber is ultimately recognized as being Bel: her partner, Vic, turns out to be the serial killer and because of this, she gets chased around by photographers and the press. The sister of the girl who died while in the care of Bel and Jade on that day when they were kids recognizes Amber's true identity goes public with the information. One bit about this that particularly irked me was  when Vic, already in police custody, confesses to being the killer, he calls Amber 'Bel' and tells her straight out that he's known for years who she really was - his victims have been his 'gifts' to her, thinking he and she shared some kind of psychopathic killer instinct and bond and that she would appreciate his actions. But nothing ever comes of that reveal: you'd think he'd then tell the police or use this in some way against her when it becomes clear that she is not a killer like he is. The flashback to the event he references as the moment when he knew who she was does not, in fact, appear to tell the reader how he came to know that: he witnesses Amber's caring response to a dying boy and somehow from this knows that she's Bel, although we're not told he thinks that at the time, nor does he seem to react in any way that reveals his own predilection towards killing. It's this event that ultimately throws the two women back together again but there's not a lot of book left with which to properly delve into the bond that is between them. The glimpses you get of it are fascinating and you do want to know how each of them must feel, to have that kind of connection born of an event that was so tragic and also misunderstood by the public. Their lives took radically different paths after that: the privileged girl receives a harsher punishment and ends up in a middle class life while the poor girl gets breaks and chances and (ironically) makes a much better life for herself than she probably would have otherwise. But you only get a little bit of what each feels about the other and what has happened to them. Ultimately, the author doesn't really commit to either story and this weakens the book as a whole, I thought. For me, the 'real' story was with Bel and Jade, and how their childhood tragedy affected the whole of their lives afterward. The serial killer thing turned out to be an irritating distraction. I thought the characters - and the reader - deserved better.

Somehow I think the title meant something else. This is a story of George and Lennie, both hardworking labourers, dreaming to own an acre of land and a shack. Where they can grow their own crops, has their own chicken run, pig pen, work whenever they want, be their own master. George has all planned out. Going to work for awhile at a ranch in the Salinas Valley, earn some money enough to buy the land. But things doesn't go quite as they planned. With Lennie around, things seem too much for George. Lennie is a big guy, but with the mind of a young child. He is a strong man, but he doesn't know that such strength can kill. When Lennie got himself into another trouble at the ranch, the dream they had meant nothing. I like the way the author potrayed each character, each with different traits and interesting characteristics. I think the themes here is significant. How one achieve one dreams (or in this case not achieving it). I really wish that George and Lennie get the their own ranch at the end. But the story is also about friendship - so I guess it should end the way it is. It's a 107 pages gripping story. You definitely want to finish it in one sitting. It's worth to read.

I had a lot of fun with this one, until the heroine did a wildly stupid thing. She received a note from her friend, who was being held captive by evil aliens, telling her to come to the evil aliens' lair, and said friend would sneak her in. OK. First of all, it was an obvious trap. Second, if the friend had the ability to sneak someone in, then why didn't she just sneak herself *out*? And then no one would have to break in to rescue her. Of course, heroine, who seemed until this point to be a fairly sensible person, went straight into the bad guys dungeon. And not only did she follow the instruction to come alone, she didn't even tell anyone about the note or that she was going. She's been on the planet for all of, what? A week? You know the evil aliens are super evil. You know they're famous for playing dirty. You don't think that talking to the people who've been dealing with them for years and making a plan is a reasonable response? And now that I think about it, it was never mentioned on page that she told the good guys about the major leak in their own security that allowed a servant from the bad guys camp to get into their base and out again unnoticed. That big ball of stupidity really brought this book down for me. I'm giving it a generous 3 stars.

This one took a few pages to really get into it. It starts out with the usual suspects of cute high school girl dating popular guy. Enter bad boy that makes good girl want to kiss him. Smell him. Yawn. Countdown begins and Evie has a birthday bash. She also spent some time in the loony bin last summer but nobody knows. She is tired of cute football star but he is pressuring her to give him her V card. Bad boy Cajun redneck is rude, crude, and inconsiderate. Apocolypse. Not many left and resources running dry, Cajun boy, ironically named for his always present flask, Jackson Daniels, drops by and he and Evie spend the next month together having adventures. What the book lacks in character depth and development is compensated plus some in world building and story telling. There are cryptic clues that don't make sense but dangle until the next chapter or two. Not being familiar with Tarot cards, I still understood the storyline perfectly and hadno problem following the plot and the revelation of what the Tarot cards represent. I honestly nearly give the book five stars because the storyline is so intriguing and revealed at a well planned pace. The reason I don't rate it higher is the simple fact that, even after reading 500 pages, I still didn't know enough about the characters. But. It is not over. Pertinent questions are answered yet the book ends on a good cliff hanger.

Reading another Vlad Taltos novel for me is like coming home. I've been reading Taltos books since the age 15, and the facts that all of them are a bit alike never bothered me - I actually like it, it brings back good memories. Iorich feels like going all the way back to Jhereg. Similar drilling down to the heart of the mystery, similar a bit complicated solution. The gathering of Taltos, Morollan, Norathar, Daymar, Kragar and Kiera felt painfully familiar. The implementation of the plan was a bit rushed and unsophisticated for me. It could be a bit more twisted. But nevertheless, fun read.

This is one of the books I rediscovered on my Google Play app, something I bought in 2011 or 2012 when the money would go to my indie bookstore (in this case, the University of Oregon Bookstore), before Kobo. I finally dug my way back through 2-factor authentication and text messages and security questions to see my list of books, and this is the third one I've now read. So, to the book itself: I think it's a solid 3 - beautiful writing mixed with an order that doesn't quite work and a confusing lot of unresolved anger and resentment toward various people who aren't fully fleshed out so that I'm not sure why the mom or the husband aren't satisfactory. That said, I learned a lot about Manhattan in the 1980s and Italy, or at least parts of Italy, in the 2000s - and the thread of parenting, mothering, being mothered, etc. did re-emerge at the end. If you're interested in cooking or memoir, this is not the worst choice. (As a non-meat-eater, I also wonder why the heck I chose something called Blood, Bones, and Butter? Who even knows ... it's lost to the mists of 2011.) Wikipedia tells me the chef is now married to another woman, her co-chef at Prune , and that seems like something that probably will work better for her, though I wonder about her Italian in-laws and how her kids interact with them. Anyway! Worth a read for sure. And now I sort of want to go to Prune's Sunday brunch someday.
Sooo sad this is the end! But I must say it was epic!

Wow. What a uniquely beautiful story! I am so glad I stumbled upon Melina Marchetta -- this has got to be one of my favourite books & she will no doubt quickly be added to my favourite authors! In ways, it reminded me a bit of Walk Two Moons -- another favourite of mine. But the writing -- the story? It is so different. So wonderous. I sobbed throughout the last half of the book. It rips at your emotions, your heart. It is devastatingly beautiful. The many characters are so engrossing -- the two intercepting stories throughout really add that special quality. This is about friendship, laughter, heartache, hate, loss, love.. but more than anything, it is about life. And life goes on.. I absolutely adored this & cannot wait to read more from this lovely Printz Award-Winning Australian author <3

Actual rating: 3.5 This was a tricky one to rate! Whilst I enjoyed reading this once I got into it, I can't get past how confused I was for the first 50-100 pages. And "confused" may be an understatement- for part of this I had very little clue what was going on. I was really disappointed with the world building in this book. The concept is really cool, but I just didn't get it a lot of the time. I had so many questions that weren't really answered. I wanted to know more about the history of the Witchlands, more about the politics of the world, more history of the characters, etc. All we really know is that a Twenty Year Truce is coming to an end and the "Great War" (I think that's what it's called) is going to begin again. We know there are tensions between the kingdoms, but we don't really find out why. We don't find out a lot about the Cahr Awen, just that they are extremely important for some reason. It was really frustrating reading about these great concepts and not getting any answers. I especially wanted to know the importance of the Cahr Awen after we found out that Safi & Iseult are the Cahr Awen. I really hope this is explored and explained more in the following books. I'm also a little disappointed we didn't learn more about the magic system. Everything was sort of thrown at us and we were expected to just know everything? At times it was hard to keep track and I think it could have been handled better if it was explored and explained more thoroughly. On a good note though, I liked the characters and their relationships. Safi was infuriating at times, and made some very stupid decisions just....because? I don't even know why. She grew on me as the book progressed though. Plus, I totally shipped Safi with Merik too, and knew from the moment they danced at the ball that Merik was the love interest and I was not disappointed. Iseult was an interesting character to read from, and I much preferred reading from her perspective than Safi's. Where Safi was hot-headed, irrational and impulsive, Iseult was smart and calm and organised. We also got to learn about Iseult's past a little which I found really interesting! I'm very interested to see where Dennard takes her character. Aeduan was also a very complex character I liked reading about. I disliked him at first (obviously) but he grew on me as the book progressed. I wonder if there's any Aeduan x Iseult shippers out there? The story itself was really interesting. I wasn't quite sure where it was heading at the beginning, but I was quite happy with the result. Dennard writes in a way that keeps her audience engaged when they're not confused about the world, and the plot was not too complicated that it would get confusing. I'd recommend this to anyone wanting to read it, and will say that it gets better after 50-100 pages!

I loved this book! It slowly and slowly got better for me, and somewhere toward the middle as I read faster and faster and became more and more caught up in the story, I found myself falling more and more in love with Isla and Josh. They were magnificent. I love how Stephanie Perkins captures how adorable and awkward high school love can be. Her characters are messy, but perfect. They have a history, but a glowing future in front of them. Her writing is amazing, and you need to read this trilogy.

I enjoyed reading this book so much it was so compelling, marvelous, cruel and fast-paced. I could relate, smile and suffer with the characters and be in awe with their journeys, mistakes and hopes. I could literally feel through the fantastic prose of Sabaa their emotions and get into their bodies, minds and hearts as if I were passing for these terrible, wonderful and miraculous situations, these gut-wrenching life/death, healing/breaking and boundary/visionary choices. And sooooooooooooo much love for the characters: for Elias and Laia in their imperfect perfection, their doubts, their faith, their beautiful humanity that made the book so incredible and heartwrenching. For Helene and her fierce love and badassery, Cook and her wisdom and grumpiness, Izzi and her kindness and friendship, Keenan and his loyalty, Elias's granfather and his ceaseless caring and sassiness and Spiro Teluman for his words: "There are two kinds of guilt: the kind that drowns you until you're useless, and the kind that fires your soul to purpose." I loved that Laia began the story as a coward and scared girl in a tragic situation where the choices that she could make were clouded by her survival instincts, Laia feels just like us readers: human. Laia had to grow beyond passive behavior for an active one, she had to leave this cocoon of fear, doubts and low self esteem to turn into someone who above all she was proud to be and someone who didn't want to be saved, someone who could save others, someone that had no idea how determined she could be or how fierce she was to aid the ones she loved, Laia story is one of self discovery and it was such a stunning one. Elias on the other hand lived in a world that he hated and couldn't be free but at the same time this toxic world of Briarcliff couldn't own him or break him, although he had to watch the greatest atrocities or had to be part of them he managed to preserve in his own manner his moral principles of right and wrong, his limits and guilts. Elias was brave, competent, skilled and the best fighter that the academy had ever seen, but he was powerless to change his surroundings and disagreed with everything his world valued, which makes him a great irony. However Elias trait that drew more of my attention was his noncompliance even when submitting, Elias is utterly indomitable. Independent of his creation as a warrior, the pretensions of his grandfather, the hatred of his mother, his Spartan world, and the steady reassurance that everything he thought wrong was right by this world, his stumbles and doubts he remained unbowed. Elias story is one of freedom of spirit that made me revere and respect him so much. Two of the best parts of the book for me were near the end when Laia showed how dear she held her brother, her priorities and how practical she had become. It was when she put a knife across Elias neck and made him promise that he would help her obviously she would not have killed him if he said no, but she needed his agreement to save her brother and needed it to be as sincere as possible, so she put aside any infatuation or attraction she began to feel for Elias in favor of thinking clearly and getting the best chances to save her brother (she knew Elias would be essential in her plan). So she saved Elias but she didn't only save him because she liked him and felt indebted to him but also because she needed him for her brother rescue, and that while it shocks us it also shows us that you have to balance your emcional and your rational side, that we need to be whole to be with another person. In contrast for me the other great moment was when Elias saved Laia and he didn't only do it because he cared or liked her, but because he wouldn't sold his soul to the empire and become like his mother, he had outlined a line of what he thought was right and what he thought was wrong and he wouldn't cross it for the sake of his own life or becoming the new emperor. This two scenes were so well writen and so significant I shudder with excitement just thinking about them, they show us that all the strength we need is within us. And what about the masks people???? They gave me the creeps, they are more terrifying than Keris (the commandant) and this is saying a lot. They have free will? they are controlled by the augurs? Everytime the masks were described I thought "what kind of sorcery is this?" and "Elias don't put that thing back". I always know that a book is really really remarkable when I can't stop myself from reading it and when I notice I got to the last fifties pages I can't stop procrastinating, because I don't want it to end. I don't want to get away from the bubble of awe and magic that the book has given me. And An Ember in the Ashes is one of this books Thank you for the amazing book Sabaa Tahir

- Finished re-reading this again, time to pick up Glass Sword! I really, really enjoyed it and didn't really expect to. There was so much hype and that all kind of put me of, and I wasn't really planning on buying or reading this as soon as I have at all. But this was really good! Yes, it reminded me of the selection a bit and had some elements of other books in it. I might even say that this was kind of what I would have hoped The selection series would be but wasn't. But honestly, if it's good, who cares? I enjoy books in this genre and as long as i'm not feeling like i'm reading the same story, as long as the plot twists can still surprise me and i'm still turning the pages at a high rate; who cares that it is similar to other books? I really loved most of the characters, the world building, the plot, it just really captured me. Some of my favourite things: - The romancy parts, because they weren't the thing driving the story forward, nor insta-lovey, nor simply unnecessary and annoying (which I find with a lot of love triangle situations in YA). - The main character, she was just very realistic is all I can say. - The plot twist at the end, probably if I re-read this I will see all the signs leading up to this moment, but I somehow didn't really expect it.. Kind of like the main character looking back thinking " I should have known". Full review will be on my blog! http://thebookdutchess.blogspot.nl/

I realize that I am almost a decade late in reading this series, but rather late than never. Right? So many people love this series and rave about it until this day. So I decided that it's time to read this series for myself. I don't know why, but I honestly thought The Mortal Instruments series was a trilogy. Big mistake. City of Bones is just the first of six books in the series, and I intend to read them all. As I said before people LOVE this series and after reading City of Bones I can start to see why. At first I was a bit apprehensive about the book and miss Clary Fray. Right at the start Clary does what I hate so much in YA books: Mom: "Clary! Do not come home under any circumstance!" Clary: "Did you mean come home right now?" Mom: "No! Stay away! It's super dangerous here!!!" Clary: "Okay Mom! I'm coming home right now!" Why must characters do this? Why? Gradually Clary did start to grow on me and I ended up actually liking her very much as a protagonist. Until in MANY YA books, Clary didn't instantly become a demon-hunting-ass-kicking heroin after finding out that she's a Shadowhunter. No. She reacted like most of us would... By not knowing what the freak to do. This made Clary relatable and I liked that. I noticed that unrequited love is quite a huge topic in City of Bones which makes for some good drama and tension! I feel like this is pointing out the obvious but... OMG! Jace!! This guy is just so very swoon worthy. He is funny and mysterious and just a total badass! Excluding the whole Jamie Lanister/Cercei Lanister situation, the relationship between Clary and Jace is so funny. This whole book is actually filled with funny conversations. Most of the other characters like Simon, Izzy and Alec were pretty cool. I didn't have too many problems with them and the really helped the story along. I felt that the whole plot where Simon turns into a rat and gets taken by Vampires, was just really boring. One of the biggest plot twists, I guessed quite early on in the book. I was about 17% into the book when I first thought that Valentine could possibly be Clary's father. Not long after I was proven to be correct It might just be me... But how similar is Lord Valentine to Lord Voldemort? I mean they are both baddies (obviously). They both want to rid the world of the "impure" people. They both had followers who betrayed them and others who stayed loyal to the very end. I'm not saying the similarities is a bad thing. I'm just saying that I took note of it and it's awesome. Does this mean I can expect a Battle of Hogwarts type end to The Mortal Instruments series? All in all, this book has great characters and a great plot and a some great (and awkward) plot twists. I really enjoyed City of Bones and I cannot wait to see what happens in the rest of the series. I really hope Jace and Clary aren't related X IVDB X

Together with the then Gentlemen Bastards, the tomfoolery was quite fun to read. The pacing was off. The first two books were much better in terms of this. Eventhough the book was thick, I felt it contains less content and it was more like a bridge from the 2nd book to the next. Also, the ending!!! I'm confused as ever. I waited so long for this book and had such high hopes for it and it definitely did not disappoint. In my opinion SJM is an amazing writer and this was the best book she has written so far. "It's a rare person to face who they are and not run from it - not be broken by it." I had absolutely no problems with this book. The writing was magical, even better than in her other books, it created this atmosphere that completely transported you to a different world. The plot was so faced paced, I could not put it down. So many things happened that I am happy for. For the first time we got to go to almost all the other courts and meet all the high lords. The battle scenes were amazing, not too brutal and at the same time realistic. "Only you can decide what breaks you, Cursebreaker. Only you." One of the things SJM handles well is the way she makes characters change. Because she explains it in a way that makes so much sense. She explains not just the circumstances and actions that changed them but their thoughts and emotions as well. Feyre is a beloved character, she began as a weak girl that craved pampering and is now such a powerful woman. A warrior. "The great joy and honor of my life has been to know you. To call you my family. And I am grateful - more than I can possibly say - that I was given this time with you all" Rhys also changes in this book and it was so emotional seeing him open himself up to people. The ending was so difficult to read. I just read that sentence "Rhys is dead" and I just closed it and wept for so long. So emotional, even the scene with Cassian and Nesta. I really want to see what SJM is going to write next in this series because I really am not ready to say goodbye to this magical world yet! "Leave this world... a better place than how you found it."

This book is American af and Margo Crane is a very memorable protagonist. The only things I didn't love about it: I wish she didn't love shooting animals so much and  I'm very over unplanned pregnancies as a plot point.

This was surprisingly good. The only complaint I have is the insta-love and the fact Cameron thought everyone was jealous of her. Oh, and I wasn't a huge fan of her constantly asking questions. I understand that this was a mysteryish type book, but still. I can't wait for the second one.

A "wasteland world" dystopia of desperate survivers scrabbling on the edge of survival in the ruins of what was left by the Wrecker civilization (spoiler alert: I think that's us) in the tradition of Mad Max, complete with cage fighting, centred around a girl whose natural ability for berserking rage makes her a survivor in this environment. The narration is strong, the action and pacing are good, and the settings and characters are really alive. The writing is all in a dialect of English that suggests the American South, which makes it very vivid and instantly makes more vivid the hardscrabble poverty that the novel opens in and runs with. I always find it a little annoying when an author decides to do without using quotation marks, but in this case it is worth putting up with it. I actually found the hellwurms distracting. I believed absolutely in the world of "hostile environment + warped twisted humans", but adding a herd of giant toothed scaly predators that come up to feed and have some kind of queen - scary only if you believe. They sound made-up to me, so the book seemed more made-up. And it was hard to believe that they didn't make sure their enemies were actually dead when the Desert Swan met its end: a "you had one job!" joke sort of popped into mind when the King cropped up again. And a man in a wasteland world like that leaving his cozy pub... forever? Otherwise, I believed absolutely in the world and characters she described. My vote: the book was brilliant and I'll be reading the next.

I read this book with my online book club. The following is the review I posted for my book club, and discusses some specific points in the book. 9 of my Goodreads friends have read this book, and not one of them has rated it less than 4 stars. I'm going to have to buck the trend, and admit that I was lukewarm about this one. I just looked through my notes, and guess what? Like most people, I have a list of things I'm afraid of. I'm afraid of syringes and IV needles, because of a traumatising experience I had the first time I was hospitalised for dengue (this was during the nineties; they required a lot more blood tests then than they do now). I'm also afraid of falling: this is distinct from a fear of heights, because I'm usually okay with heights as long as I'm relatively sure I won't fall. I also have a deep-seated fear of being alone: not in the sense of being physically alone, but in the sense that I will have no one to turn to when I need them. Another personal, deep-seated fear--one which I'm sure I share with a great many other people--is the fear of losing my mind. When I first found out that Alzheimer's disease was genetically heritable the first thing I did was check my family's history, to see if there was a chance I'd wind up with the same problem. The check revealed a tendency towards hypertension, diabetes, kidney and bladder stones, and cancer, but--thankfully--none towards Alzheimer's. I know that having a history of cancer on both sides of the family should be cause for concern, but cancer can be cured, if caught early enough--it can be "beaten", as so many of those who recuperate from cancer often say. I have not heard of anyone who has "beaten" Alzheimer's: only stories of people who learn to cope as they lose their loved ones slowly, one small piece at a time. To me, that is terrifying to me beyond belief, whether I am the loved one losing someone else to the disease, or I am the one sick with Alzheimer's and losing everything around me. Losing one's mind also happens to be a common trope in horror fiction--and, in my opinion, one that isn't used nearly often enough in contemporary horror. I suppose this is due to the influence of film and television: visual cues and carefully-timed music are enough to scare an audience, and some writers think that that's all they need (sans music) to scare readers, too. Perhaps that is all some readers need: after all, a reader's preferred flavour of horror depends entirely on what they think is scary, and for some, it's enough to read about a serial killer roaming around with an axe or a chainsaw to give them the shivers. But it takes more than that to genuinely impress me. Scaring me isn't difficult: I have a sufficiently active imagination that I can scare myself sometimes. But being able to say something deeper with a horror story, being able to use the genre's license to investigate humanity's darker facets: that's something that will impress me. Fortunately, there are no serial killers--chainsaw-wielding or otherwise--in Justin Evans' A Good and Happy Child. It focuses on the protagonist and narrator, George Davies, who has a major problem that's causing his marriage to fall apart: he can't bring himself to touch his child. In a desperate attempt to save his marriage, he seeks help from a psychologist, who gives him a stack of notebooks so he can explore a certain past event that appears to be the underlying cause for all his current problems. In these notebooks, George tells a tale that could either be the result of a deeply troubled mind--or the cry of a soul trapped in a battle between good and evil. The first thing about this novel that really made me sit up and take notice was the prose. It's been described as "reminiscent of Donna Tartt's The Secret History", and since I like The Secret History rather a lot, I figured anything with a similar quality of prose couldn't be a bad thing. I was, however, rather skeptical: plenty of blurbs will compare a novel with another, more popular counterpart, only for the comparison to apply only in the shallowest way possible. I'm pleased to note, however, that the comparison of Evans' prose in A Good and Happy Child to Tarrt's writing isn't entirely misplaced. Take a look at this example, which comes from very early in the novel: A woman in a black overcoat and fancy shoes clopped toward me. She carried a bulky shopping bag, and she brushed me as she passed so I was forced to catch my balance on the cast-iron rail. I opened by mouth to say something, but as she walked by, I realized I could not see her face, just a blur where a face should be, and my mouth hung open with the obnoxious Watch it stuck there. The street went quiet, the way it can in New York. I sank onto the stoop, with your notebooks in my hand, remembering rotten things. The above excerpt has echoes of Tartt's writing in The Secret History, but it shades much darker. Even in the most disturbing scenes of The Secret History Tartt's prose has a luminosity to it that casts gentler shadows on the characters and their role in the plot's darkest events. One could label the characters as wicked sybarites who do what they do just because they can, but it's hard to think of them that way; Tartt's prose limns them with a certain kind of fragility that engenders feelings of tenderness and pity. In short, it's hard to hate them, even though what they do is absolutely deplorable. Evans' prose is a rather different beast, even if it has a similar cadence and tendency towards a more poetic turn of phrase. Most notably, it has none of the gentle light that illumines Tartt's prose. Instead, Evans chooses to go for the shadows, and stay there, as this selection illustrates: What is the reaction a person should have, seeing a strange face staring at them in the shower? I knew what I was seeing was impossible. In retrospect I could say my brain went off the rails; I felt a sickening lurch as my senses heaved out of their tracks, and I trembled despite the fact that I was standing in a hot shower. I felt myself teeter. I turned and balanced myself on the cool tile. I closed my eyes and said to myself, "When you turn around, it will be gone." I opened my eye. The face continued to stare. My breath returned to my lungs. I let out a scream, and I fell. The scene above happens fairly early in the novel, and it sets the tone for other, similar scenes. However, this scene, and the others in the book like it, are not in and of themselves "scary" in the way a scene in a horror movie or TV show or even novel might be. They might create a certain tingling in the spine, but they don't exactly encourage the reader to put the book down and hide under the covers. No, what's really scary about this novel is the way it shows how adults think they "know better" than a child, and don't really listen to what that child is trying to tell them. Throughout most of the book, I was terrified for the child-George, because despite knowing he survived to adulthood, the things that were done to him, ostensibly for his own benefit, were frightening even to an adult such as myself. Before I go on, I must say that I have no experience with interacting with people who have such severe mental health issues that they actually hallucinate. I don't know what I would do if I had to care for such a person, what sort of actions it would drive me to. Therefore, I can't say that I completely sympathise or oppose what the various adults in this novel did to young George. What I do know is that everything they did was frightening. From psychiatrists who are overzealous with medicating their patients; to "therapy assistants" who don't really care one whit about their charges; to religious nutcases who think "a past life as a deacon" actually qualifies one to conduct an exorcism--I was constantly resisting the urge to yell at the book, because I kept thinking all these adults were idiots and didn't really care about George himself; they only cared about their own opinions and ideas. They might have listened to him when he told them about their problems, but they weren't really hearing what he was trying to say, and instead only heard what they wanted to hear. This wasn't about "religion vs. science", or "faith vs. fact": it was about adults not listening to a child because he is just a child. And that made me simultaneously very angry, and very scared. After all, such people exist in the world--how many children are out there, who, like George, just want someone to really hear them, and are not given the treatment or help they need because so many adults are essentially deaf to anything that comes out of the mouth of a child? In the meantime, George is forced to confront his troubles more or less on his own. He tries to make sense of what's happening to him, but because he's only eleven he latches onto the idea that makes the most sense to him, even if it doesn't make the most sense to everyone else. I can't say I blame him, either: after all, he's just a child--a precocious child, to be sure, but still just a child. It should have been the responsibility of the adults around him to do their best by him, to really listen to him and help him understand what's happening to him, but that's not what they do. Instead, they are blinded by their own preferred understanding of the world, and in the end damage George more deeply than they can possibly know. And yet I can't help but wonder if George actually is wrong after all, and if the adults are the ones in the right. It's easy for me to say that if the adults just listened to George, everything would be okay, but what if they were hearing what George was saying, and saw him for what he was? What if the psychiatrist was right, and he is a menace to society who needs to be shut away and medicated? What if the religious folk were right, and he is a child in the grip of a malevolent evil that's using him for its own ends? Does this make me, as a reader, deaf to George's true issues, or am I really seeing him for what he is? This grey space is an interesting one to me, though perhaps other readers might not like encountering such uncertainty. Certainty is comforting, to be sure, but it's not very interesting--and I'm the sort of reader who will happily sacrifice a little bit of comfort for the interesting, as long as it's done well, of course. Overall, A Good and Happy Child is the sort of horror novel that isn't necessarily about scaring the reader with eerie rustlings in the dark, or with scenes of body parts strewn all over a room; instead, it focuses on how the human mind remembers, how it identifies truth from fiction--and how it can fail at both. It shows how adults seem to forget to listen, really listen, to children, just because they are children, and such a scenario can spin out into something genuinely horrific. It shows that sometimes, there are things that neither science nor religion can fix, and that there are darker things out there--or in the human mind--than can ever be thought or dreamt of. But the real beauty--the real, terrifying beauty--of this novel is that Evans leaves it up to the reader to decide what is real and what isn't, what's right and what is wrong. It's not a comfortable place to be, for some readers, but others will find a special kind of magic in what Evans does, and will enjoy this novel because it offers them that dilemma.

View more content on my blog MUSINGS OF A BLOGDER DEFY is a high fantasy version of Mulan with a lot more romance. Yep, a lot... more. - Nova @ Musings of a Blogder I've been anticipating this book since I started stalking following the YA Valentines (A group of 2014 Debuts) on twitter and their site. One book, Defy caught my interest. Strong female leads in dangerous situations always catch my interest in an odd way. I had been doing my best to get Defy and finally, it happened! I received a copy and it did not disappoint. The main character, Alexa is strong, loyal and likeable. She's pretending to be a guy to fight for the king's army. It's that or... the breeding house. Basically, the world is one with inequality where women are shown to be used as birthing tools and not much else. I can see where Alexa's personality came from. It's either punch harder or get punched. Alexa's been pretending to be a guy for so long that about a quarter in, she's exposed as a girl. This is where the ___ hits the fan. Everyone was really accepting to her being a girl and somehow a lot of people already knew about it. I don't know if I like this or I don't. It kind of gave me weird feelings because it's a secret that we're told she's trying so hard to maintain and here's a couple people who've already known from the start. It takes away from Alexa's effort and I'm starting to doubt her acting skills. The world building was not there. As much as Sara's writing was amazing (which, it totally was), the world-building was just not there. I didn't know how their land looked like except for the fact that they were in a jungle. It took away from the story because the setting was very open and readers wouldn't know what to think. In my case, I thought it was a bit medieval but I wouldn't know if I was right because of the lack of world building. WRITING! Let's take a moment to appreciate Sara's writing. As much as some of the other points bugged me, Sara's writing really went the extra mile. Her dialogue, character descriptions and way of telling the story was en pointe! If the entire story was a pile of rubble (which I hope you really don't think that) the writing will, honestly, shine. When I was like "oh this book is so cool... fighting!" I expected that. What I got instead was a love triangle that (although, didn't bother me) was unnecessary. It didn't bug me like some of them do because Larson didn't take it too far in the "mush" department. My issue is that this story didn't need a love triangle. I mean this girl's been pretending to act like a dude. How is she jumping on the romance wagon so fast? It was cute to see Alexa and Damien together for a few scenes; took away the tension. But that was it: cute. And I don't see how it could've progressed with it anyway. Overall, it's a great debut novel that I hope you'll check out! Sara B. Larson can only get better from here and this book is very good for a debut novel! It's got everything (and some unneeded but extra) things in it so you'll never be bored. I know I was never bored or tired of this book!

I enjoyed this. A lot, for the most part. Because I think it was well-written, and I liked seeing Rachael and Ryan trying to work things out and figure out how to actually be in a relationship. In fact, had it been focused solely on that, this would've probably gotten 4 stars. Unfortunately, I really didn't like most of the subplots. Not the 'Thomas is suddenly interested in Rachael', not the 'author Rachael was trying to help out conveniently knows those other football players and Rachael is being bothered by one of them in a club', and definitely not anything involving Sophie. The way that storyline was handled here and how everything was seemingly 'resolved' just made me kind of angry. And by kind of, I mean extremely. It also took me awhile to warm up to this book, I didn't like it all that much until I reached the halfway point. I'm sure that what goes on at pro-athlete parties was probably depicted fairly accurately here, but that doesn't mean I ever want to read two characters meeting like that again. It was terrible and just made me cringe, as did the first sex scene and its aftermath. I wasn't convinced they even liked each other all that much (I like a good fight, but them continuously shouting hurtful things at each other started bothering me when it just kept happening). Aside from that, I really liked a lot of the romance aspect and the various friendships throughout. Rachael with the guys, with her roommate and her New York friends, with her high school group, etc. Her and Ryan trying to figure everything out and both not being good at the relationship thing; it was well done. Speaking of well done, for once I did not mind the 'famous person' angle this book had. I'm usually not too fond of that trope, but it was sort of low-key here and just a part of Ryan's life as opposed to this all-encompassing thing. Also, as long as it took me to get into this, I found it hard to put down from the start. So that counts for something. I just feel like I could've liked this a lot more had certain things been handled differently.

This book. Oh my gosh. It destroyed me, but in the best way. This series is super hyped, but I wasn't completely sold on the first two books. They just felt okay to me, but they weren't really favorites, especially after all of the fantasy I've read. Ruin and Rising changed everything for me. I love this book. So. Much. There were a lot of ways this trilogy could have ended, and I feel like it couldn't have ended better. This was exactly what I wanted for these characters and this incredible story. Now for a few specific thoughts... The Darkling: I have said from book one that I am not a huge fan of The Darkling. I certainly did not want Alina to end up with him (although it was what I expected...nice twist Leigh Bardugo). But, I am all for a good redemption story, and I would have been fine with that. But I think his ending was for the best. It just kind of had to happen that way, ya know? Nikolai: I did not realize how much I liked Nikolai until this book. In the last book, I found him kind of annoying to be honest. But this book really showed who he truly is, and I wouldn't have been completely unhappy had Alina ended up marrying him and becoming queen. But when The Darkling did that thing to him (still not totally sure if he became a volcra, a nichevo'ya, or something else), I was so mad, and so heartbroken! I am so glad that he healed when The Darkling died, and I'm glad that it gave him a new level of maturity. The Other Grisha: I came to love everyone so much! Even some of the characters I didn't really care for before (*cough* Zoya *cough*) became favorites of mine. Their loyalty to Alina and the love that they had for her was so beautiful, as was their continued friendship described in the epilogue. Alina: Ok, Alina is seriously one of my favorite heroines ever. She became so strong throughout her journey. That being said, I'm glad she lost her powers. I think it closed this adventure she had gone on perfectly. It was a chapter of her life, one that certainly shaped her, but it ended, as it should. Alina and Mal: My babies! Haha :) Alina and Mal were truly my OTP from the beginning, and the fact that they had a little fairytale ending of their own made me so happy. All of the conflict between them was resolved well, and that epilogue was just perfect. I just love them, ok? I honestly cannot recommend this series enough. I think there is something in it for everyone. Leigh Bardugo's writing is beautiful, and you will fall in love with these characters. Just prepare yourself for some emotional upheaval.

3.5 stars. Who doesn't want the idea of traveling and leaving everything behind, when life becomes too tough? A story on making mistakes and growing up. Of fear and its confrontation. Of distrust and forgiveness. Of losing hope and gaining it again. It's a young adult novel that aims at your heartstrings, amidst a sea of dystopia and saccharine. It doesn't depend on fantasy for it to be interesting. It doesn't beautify and falsify ideas; it tells the story the way it should be told. Admittedly, there are more profound stories out there, but "Wanderlove" holds its own as a young adult novel. I love that it's not too fluff-y or dramatic. The characters have burns and scars, which they hide beneath their armors, without broadcasting, "Woe is me". I also like how they established the relationship - slow and without that sudden "BAM", just the way that characters who are 'healing' should form relationships. I just can't happily give it 4 stars, though. Despite the fact that I liked the book, I still felt like there's an important piece missing. For me, it lacked that strong theme to hold the ideas together. While there had been many character-building on Bria and there had been enough on Rowan, it felt like they weren't enough, like there's too much but there's nothing that stuck out (even Rowan's unquestionable and unconditional reliability was scratched at the end. Fine, maybe he believed Bria could make the trip, but more than that, it felt like he was just running away, since he didn't even give her time to think about things) Also, since the book relied on the manipulation of one's heartstrings, I looked for characters that grow on you despite their flaws. While the characters had foundations, there's nothing that had me thinking, "She did that? Figures". Even in the end, after all the past I've learned about them, it seemed like I didn't know them at all. Although, okay, fine, I'll excuse that part, since they're supposedly finding themselves and changing. Whatever. I'll try to ignore the part that people still have a distinct trait no matter how lost they are and that they cannot change who they really are, entirely. But, the ending! Sometimes, what you love the most is what you have to fight the hardest to keep. Okay... But why, oh why, do you have to be tested by the other person that way? Isn't there also a saying that goes, "If you love a person, you'll do anything for him, but if heloves you back, he'll never ask you to"? So, okay, for the sake of Bria's growth, Rowan's have to be regressed? After having all that talk about moving forward and forgetting the past - all that really boils down to is you leave everything behind, because you can't face them? Isn't giving Bria space just an excuse when you didn't even give her time? Wanderlove invokes the the idea of starting everything a new, but while it has the potential to draw empathy, there were times in which the excessive attempt hits a mark way beyond the target.

Throwback review! Even my innocent thirteen-year-old self did not expect much from this novel. I was cynical, I thought, yeah, okay, the cover's pretty, but I don't trust pretty covers. Still don't. But wow, was this a pleasant surprise. Like The Mortal Instruments series, The Iron Fey is another series that I talked all my friends into reading (and loving). Unlike TMI, I still enjoy rereading the Iron Fey (my last reread of The Iron King was last December) and love it just as much as when I first read it. Consider that my thirteen-year-old self was doing A Midsummer Night's Dream in English Lit at the time I found this book. Although the Nevernever (aka Fairyland) is more elaborate than in Shakespeare, where we don't know much about it, it was nice to see Puck and Oberon and Titania - although Puck is watered-down here, we do see glimpses of the malicious faerie throughout the series. Anyway. What I loved about The Iron King. First off, Meghan. She's not one of those karate-kid-fighter-girl strong heroines (think Dru Anderson), but she's not the weepy helpless heroine either. Meghan manages to be something that a lot of YA heroines aim for and miss: a fairly normal person. She's smart ("I'm an otaku fairy"), she has a way with computers, she's loyal, and she'll do anything for her family. Another thing I loved? The writing. Julie Kagawa is excellent at weaving in descriptions, which is absolutely essential for a fairy book. Unless you give me gorgeous setting, I will not give you my readership, let alone my tears and a piece of my soul. Despite the fact that The Iron King is told in first person, the scenery is described perfectly, and you are actually transported to Nevernever with Meghan. And I'm not sure if this counts as something to love, but the series has a noticeable upward arc in terms of awesomeness. I promise you that you will feel increasingly stunned as you read (except maybe the second book). The secondary characters too are so lovable, from Puck himself, to moody, mysterious Winter prince Ash, to Grimalkin, their exasperated feline guide. In my head, Grimalkin sounds like Alan Rickman merged with Benedict Cumberbatch. WHAT MORE INCENTIVE DO YOU NEED? The one thing this book (and the series as a whole) didn't give me that I wanted was a little elaboration on Meghan's tech skills. In the first book we learn that she's good enough to tutor classmates, but I wish we'd had something more - if you think about it, tech skills are so important considering Meghan's connection to the Iron throne. I had really wanted more on that but... oh well.

The day this book first came out I rushed down to the store to buy it because of all the glowing reviews. Did I read it immediately? Nope. Should I have? Yes! Even though I had a few issues with it, I thoroughly enjoyed THE WINNER'S CURSE. I immediately fell into the world, reading the majority of the book in one sitting. It really grabs you, the writing flows easily but is descriptive and pretty without being tedious or boring. Speaking of the world, it's pretty basic. We are told about two cultures that are described but not super fleshed out. Kestrel gets some history lessons that are obviously for the reader's benefit but I still wished it had been developed further, especially as this is a fantasy. Still, I have to admit I was never bored with the story. "He knew the law of such things: people in brightly lit places cannot see into the dark." Although I knew to expect a romance going into THE WINNER'S CURSE, I had not prepared for one that would give me so many FEELS. My favorite type of romance depicts the classic slow burning journey, and this book delivered that. When things finally started to get a little more evident (still not in your face) I was downright giddy to see more development. However, the romance, the strongest point of the book for me, could also be considered its downfall. There's no doubt this relationship that the characters are slowing moving towards is the backbone of the book. I wanted more fantasy. An underlying plot finally comes into the picture towards the middle/end of the book that obviously sets up the next book so I hope more is done with the sequel. Kestrel wasn't my favorite character. I did like her, but I struggled to connect and relate to her and her actions in some situations. We see some of her bravery towards the end of the book and I hope she continues to develop in future books. One thing that did bother me with her was that she went back and forth with her feelings a lot and didn't seem to hold a lot of resentment towards those who killed and tortured her friends. The only one she was sad about was Jess. Overall, I liked the book. It has a lot of entertainment value and am excited to see how the sequel compares.

The first time I read this, I did not write a review because I was in such a hurry to take it back to the public library and get the next book in the series. I really liked the heroine, Amelia. She is a responsible, caring oldest sister to her orphaned siblings. She puts their needs before her own. She handles all the responsibilities thrust upon her without complaint. She has survived the betrayal by her first love. She even shows a wry sense of humor despite all the bad luck that befalls her. She deals with what happens, until what happens to her is... Cam Rohan, who we met in the Wallflowers series. This barely civilized half-gypsy manages St. Vincent's gambling establishment. I liked that he did not feel like he belonged in English society. He had plans to give up his post and return to the roving life until his feelings for Amelia blindsided him. Somebody needs to take care of his beloved, and he's not going to allow anyone else to do it, even if it means he has to become a pillar of respectability (horrors!) We get active participation in the story by some of the Wallflowers characters, and meet a whole new family of stories waiting to occur. Part of Kleypas' genius is that she gives us well-rounded secondary characters, it is not only the protagonists who matter in her books. It is both good and amusing that Amelia's sisters think better of her for giving up her iron control and living a little, even though she fears she may end up with another broken heart. The theme of this book seems to be two strong individuals coming to grips with what fate has dealt them. Cam has to accept that he is not losing his freedom by joining his life to another's, freedom is the belonging he feels when in her arms. Amelia has to learn that it doesn't mean she is anything less if she accepts that she needs a shoulder to lean upon. She has indomitable spirit: "Yes. Yes. I'll marry you. Although...I still can't promise to obey you." I'm so glad I found a secondhand copy of this for myself, now I can read it again whenever I feel like it.

So this was a fast read. Took me about four hours, and English isn't even my first language. This was... meh. This book could be used as the definition of YA novels. It has everything it needs: a corrupt governement, a special snowflake main character, a love triangle (with one boy good and the other evil! ), a rebel group, some insta love, pretty dresses... We really have here the epitome of YA. *Sigh* There are two things, however, that make the book more interesting, and raise my rating from a 2 stars to a 3. The first is the mental state of Juliette, the main character, in the first half. She is bordeline crazy, in isolation for almost a year and never being able to touch anyone. The writing style (which at first I found annoying, but then I realised how great it went with Juliette) reflects perfectly her almost insanity. This all fades (way to fast) the more the book goes on, and I was disappointed about that. The second kind of interesting thing, or person, is Warner. I like the villain being a sex offender. And by that, I don't mean that I like sex offenders. I mean that I like the villain being a sex offender. That aspect of him is very well written. Unfortunately, this doesn't save the book from being another recycled YA dystopia. Some aspects of it are so like The Hunger Games. Adam is basically a more manly Peeta. Really. Also, I'm so tired of the governments in dystopias that are evil for the sake of being evil. It is said that the Reestablishment actually have lots of riches and food and animals, but they keep them for themselves. Why the hell would you do that? How is it productive? Where will you take your workers from if everyone is dead? *Sigh* And then the X-Men happened. And I was certain I would not read the rest of the series. (Not that I don't love the X-Men. But I love well-done X-Men.) So if you want a brainless piece of YA literature to pass time, then read it. Otherwise...

The Burning Sky by Sherry Thomas book one of The Elemental Trilogy. Iolanthe Seabourne, an elemental mage who has been predicted to be the greatest elemental mage of all time. She is protected by prince Titus and together they are on a journey to defeat the evil Bane. The task is definitely not easy and the only thing guiding them are the prophecies of prince Titus's dead mother. Will they succeed? who knows as we have to read the complete trilogy to find out. At first the writing style was a bit difficult for me to get in to. The characters didn't come alive and they felt cold and distant if that makes sense. The book is written in very formal english. I almost want to say it's old english but it's not (can't think of a better description). The book had it's fast parts and it's slow parts. I loved the fact that she has to pretend she is a boy as those type of stories are always very funny and hard to put dow. Eventually, I really started to love the characters and I started to understand and react to all the emotions. I even had some LOL moments. Iolanthe is a teenage elemental mage uncovering her true potential and initially, she has difficulties coming to terms with her destiny. I loved her character and I loved everything she did. She is not your regular teenager. She is smart and level headed. Prince Titus, he is funny and sarcastic and he is carrying the weight of the world on his non-adult shoulders. He has taken on the task of protecting Iolanthe no matter what the cost. He is training her to access her full powers and pushes her to her limits. Initially, I was going to give the book 4 stars for the issue of me not really "feeling" the characters. And also because there were some very NECESSARY parts but they were slow. However, the last chapters and the ending completely earned that last star. If magic carpets, wands and dragons are your thing, then this book is definitely for you. And don't worry I didn't really see any similarities to Harry Potter (for those reviews that compared it to HP). So you won't have the annoying feeling of repetition. In the end, I really loved this book and I'm definitely starting book 2 as soon as possible.

Well, Bella is still as dense and melodramatic as ever. As an adult reader, it really irritates me. Remembering myself in high school, however, I can understand why so many teen girls relate. So, Bella cuts her finger at her vampire birthday party within the first two chapters, and it just goes downhill from there. She learns many valuable lessons on her birthday, such as "it is generally considered rude to bleed your tasty human blood in the house occupied by vampires", and "boys are likely to break up with you when they are concerned that their family tried to eat you". Rather than pick up on the fact that Edward pushes her away to protect her, she falls into her little comfortable pit of despair, convinced that she is just not pretty enough or good enough to hold Edward's attentions. As usual, she is stupidly and stubbornly wrong, yet bent on prolonging her perceived (self-inflicted) pain. Bella is being a drama queen, and feels that her chest is imploding, rendering her unable to breathe or feel her heart with Edward gone. She becomes Bella-zombie. Several pages only say the name of the month on them. Maybe Meyer was paid extra for that genius waste of trees. Her zombification drives everyone insane and nobody wants to be around her. We spend some time with Jacob, who is changing in weird ways, but makes Bella genuinely happy (without the depression on the side). Eventually he also seems to avoid Bella, but we later learn it's because he can't control exploding into a rather large scruffy dog that can't control it's temper. This seems to make Bella happy; it wasn't her fault, he was just another monster! This apparently makes him another possible mate. Bella is only compatible with monsters. Several wasted pages later, Alice comes to town and tells Bella (who has been hallucinating Edward's voice when she does reckless things, and has recently taken up motorcycle riding and cliff diving) that she had an incorrect vision of Bella dead, and now Edward's gone off to commit vampire suicide. Appalled (because how can she live if Edward's dead? Again...), Bella jets off to Italy with Alice to stop Edward from showing off his sparkly skin in the sun to a gathering of mortals pretending to be vampires for a holiday dedicated to a dead priest who is actually a really old vampire living among them as some sort of vampire royalty. Adrenaline rush for the next couple chapters: Bella saves Edward, Edward thinks he's dead, vampire thugs collect Edward, Bella, and Alice to take them to ancient vampire council who eventually let them go as long as Bella is turned into a vampire soon. Happily, Bella gets her wish to become undead, and drinks Cokes in the plane on the way home to stay awake and stare greedily and rather creepily at Edward as a sort of mini-celebration. At least this time she doesn't bleed on everything. Once home, she is grounded and Charlie (her dad) is mad at Edward for leaving Bella in the first place. Edward climbs through her window to stay with her for the night, and they have a very redundant conversation that lasts several more pages than necessary about his undying love for her with nauseating references to Romeo and Juliet. Honestly, Edward may have had better luck getting Bella to realize that he left her to protect her if he just said a few sentences. Words seem to confuse the poor girl. Jacob turns feral and territorial and rats out Bella's much earlier reckless behavior by bringing her motorcycle home to Charlie (who disapproves of cyclists anyway). He seems to think Edward has her under his control, thus preventing Bella from seeing Jacob after arriving home from Italy. Jacob, Edward, and Bella have a mini-showdown in the woods. Bella goes home, and then there is a preview for the next book in the series. It really isn't TERRIBLE, but it really isn't GOOD, either. It took me about a day to get through, and I found myself really wanting to know what would happen next. Of course, that always led to disappointment and eye-rolls. BUT, there's more to this series, so keep an eye out for the next sarcastic installment!

I admit I did not have any expectations going in but I was looking for a new series and the blurb on this one sounded intriguing. The beginning was somewhat jarring, since it goes back and forth in time, it almost seemed like I had walked into the middle of the story. So much so that I went back to look to make sure I had not started with Book 2. For me it was kind of a slow burn. Once I got past all the time flipping I found I liked it more and more. Even the time flipping became enjoyable since it moved the story along in a different way. The world is modern day but deals loosely with Greek/Egyptian mythology and has a unique take on the immortals and the 'Everneath". This is not the usual Fae, Angel, Vampire, Were, plot line. These are Everlivings and what they are and how they work is all part of the uniqueness of the world of this book. I was not always sure if I liked our heroine Nikki. In a way she is responsible for everything that happens here due to one rushed decision. Sometimes I wanted to smack her but she is a teen and what teen has not jumped to rash conclusions, so in the end I emphasized with her. Our boys Cole (bad) and Jack (good) do what is needed in these books. They are handsome, smart and both have feelings for her, but deal with them in different ways. I like that the relationships ( especially between Jack and Nikki ) are shown that they took time to develop. The instantaneous " I love you" like in so many of these books is not there. Jack and Nikki were childhood friends who became more. And Cole... well like most of the bad boys in these books, his actions and words don't match and his ultimate motives are never truly clear, which in this case for the series is a good thing. The end was kind of predictable but no less enjoyable. I am currently in the final book of the series so I can say the stories and character developments have kept me interested all along the way. On my personal YA Paranormal checklist : 16/17 year old clueless girl who finds out she is special. CHECK (but complicated ) Dead or absentee parent CHECK Clueless parent who is away/busy a lot. CHECK Perky best friend who is not one of the "special" people. CHECK Good boy. CHECK Bad boy. CHECK Bad boy who might be good CHECK Instant love. Not Really Love triangle. CHECK A mission only she can complete. CHECK but complicated A willingness to die for love CHECK CHECK CHECK A lovely book cover that has nothing to do with the actual story  CHECK Final opinion : Totally recommend to those who like the genre and are looking for something a bit outside the box.

Today I've got for you four stories that made me switch to the child mode :). There are magical, colorful, full of fantastic creatures and have the strong good vs evil factor. Sounds good, right? Well, let's get to details. One small warning - since I'll be writing about the whole series, each next story might start with a spoiler for the previous book. I'll try to avoid them, but it will be hard. First of all, I love the covers, you can already see it's going to be a fantastic journey for children. Just look at them! I admit I waited way too long to read these stories, even though I had the first three on my kindle for a long time. When the "Second Twin" came out I decided I finally need to read them and here we are. Sometimes it's not easy to switch to the kid-mode. Some of the books simply take you int the story and you've got nothing to say about it, but in this case, I had to "manually" change my way of thinking. It wasn't easy because even though these stories are magical they also have this cruel darkness lurking about, ready to grab the unsuspecting reader. What bothered me was the simple language in which it was written. And maybe the point of view - I never like the all-knowing narrator and it was especially annoying when connected with the dialogs. It felt like it was written for small kids, but I wouldn't want to read them a story like this simply because they would be too frightened. Luckily the author improves with each story - language, characters and events get better, more interesting and a bit more complicated. Elora of Stone The first story is supposed to introduce you to the world, main characters and interest you enough to keep reading the series, right? The thing is there's just too much introduction and jumping from character to character, going through years so fast that you don't really care what happened before and when you're half way though you're finally getting to the point where the book blurb came in. Seriously, when you'll check the Goodreads description it pretty much starts half way through the story, which isn't a big loss, but it's kind of strange. After this one, I thought I won't make it to the next book, especially since the ending might work as final (it's not, but it would do if needed). I have mixed feeling about this one - the story was rather slow in the first half and then it flashed through all the events till the end. But I guess I'd like it as a kid. Into Coraira The second story pulls you into the magical realm of Coraira which is way more fun than the simple village and some almost-magical tree. This is when the story really picks up and from now on each book ends with a definite "must continue reading" event. Yes the POV still annoyed me, but I've started getting used to it here and I could enjoy the story more. This time, there's no half-book introduction, we're heading straight into the action zone and we're going to stay there for the next few stories. Two kids (who finally became the main characters) are reunited and learning their newly acquired skills. But the evil that plans to destroy magic won't give them much time. I really like the magic of this new world, it looks like author's imagination really kicked in in this one. Teagan of Tomorrow We'll be moving to time-travel zone now and meeting a new important character - Teagan. Part of this story will take place in our times and I have to admit the twins reaction to our world was quite well described. They were clearly lost here and that's something that's usually missing from the stories in which characters move from ar-away-past to present days. Other than that it looks like even greater evil took over the magical lands and the whole future shaped itself accordingly and our heroes (new and old) have to try saving Coraira and their family and friends. This was my favorite part of the series. It's dynamic and it won't let you loose track on when and where the characters are. Second Twin If you thought you knew all about the characters by now check this story. It shows some of them in a completely different light switching your point of view and telling you not everyone is bad from the beginning and it might not be their own choice. This time, we're moving from place to place and between different time periods. It happens so fast that you might get lost if you'll loose concentration. In theory, each chapter begins with time and location, but at some point, it doesn't help much. Still, if you'll manage to track it all this is a rather good story, a worthy continuation with some new aspects to the character's past and the world's future. These stories will surely bring some enjoyment to kids. The author let loose her imagination and it's clear she gets better and better with each book. I might've been a bit rough with my ratings, but I was really annoyed with the narration. I was so relieved that the later parts have more dialog and less all-knowing narrator.
