"The book you hold in your hands is meant for peculiar eyes only. If by chance you are not among the ranks of the anomalous, then please put this book back where you found it at once and forget this ever happened." Luckily for me, I consider myself to be quite strange and carried on reading. This Grimm-inspired collection of fairytales is so inventive and enjoyable that I feel like I might have to go back and re-read Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children all over again. Not only has Riggs created several unique and heart-touching tales for this book (yeah, I almost cried a few times; SO WHAT), but a few of them are tied to actual historical events, making the Peculiar world seem all the more real. One of my favorite things in storytelling is when an author includes details from reality, allowing me to feel like maybe, just maaaaybe, the characters or places I'm reading about could actually exist. Or, in this case, that a group of human-hating pigeons caused The Great Fire of London in 1666 . I mean, that's completely plausible, right?

DNF at 12% I found this book to be harmful to me as a trans reader, so much that I DNF'd, particularly as I understand from other reviews by trans readers that it gets worse, not better. This book presents trans life as inexorable misery with no hope or allies, full of bullying, misgendering, and gender policing, where even your best friend who supposedly supports you and has your back as a trans guy, will still coerce you to paint your toenails pink and come out as trans when you don't want to. We are told that the trans MC is invested in surviving, but not shown where that resilience & investment is coming from, how it's found. If you are going to have readers sit in bleakness like that, you also really need to show the roots of hope. In depth. This feels like a performance of the misery of being a trans teenager, for cis readers. Who could think this is good for trans teen readers? My experiences of misery as a queer trans person have never been one-note like this. It doesn't feel real. We have complex lives, things intertwine and co-exist. Even when there's a pile-on in my life, I'm doing things to manage it, to survive, to find hope and connection, looking for pockets of comfort. Yes, being misgendered every day sucks and is awful. And there can be hope and joy and connection and escape ad fantasy in a life that contains misgendering and trans oppression. Telling stories full of inexorable bleakness are about evoking pity and distance and dehumanization and othering. They don't actually build empathy, which is the kindest read I have of the books intended purpose (which it does not achieve). I know it was written for cis people, but it is not good for cis readers either, to read this kind of depiction of trans lives. It's also boring, and not very well written. Gabe doesn't really come through. It's like a series of accounts about his gender but I don't witness him having feelings or thoughts or reactions to these situations and difficulties. It doesn't have a strong voice or good characterization. For example, we are told Gabe has a crush. But I don't feel it with him, don't get to witness his yearning or frustration or fear or embarrassment or despair or whatever he feels. I don't have a sense of him as a person. I worry that trans readers dream too small. That we take scraps and feel grateful because at least we are tossed something. At least someone acknowledges us. I want us to dream bigger. I want trans YA with compelling voice and riveting plot and no deadnaming and trans teen characters who have friends who actually have their backs. I want trans YA where trans teens know/meet other trans people and are connected to community and have complex arcs and are deeply characterized. This book fails to do any of this, and these things are essential. Trigger Warnings I cannot give full trigger warnings, as I DNF'd. persistent use of trans characters dead name, persistent misgendering. pressure to come out as trans, bullying, gender policing. I understand from reviews by trans reviewers that the character gets outed and is targeted by physical violence as a result, and is depicted as thanking the person who outed him.

Beach read (if you can call reading at a Cancun resort the beach). Quick, intense, sort of depressing, will definitely keep you guessing and play with your emotions. Thank you anonymous person who left the book at the hotel library!

"House of Shadows" is a really interesting book which keeps you focused on the action. It has many descriptive passages which may bore some of you but if you read it when you feel that you can focus, you can discover the "magic" of the book, these passages creating some really nice images in your mind! This story starts with eight sisters and their father. Misfortune strikes, leaving the eight girls all alone after their father dies. Since they have to survive, some of the sisters need to be "sacrificed". I liked the authors creation, the "keiso", which has its roots in the gheisa lives from Japan. The combination between the sisterhood and the hardship that the eight girls have to go through was really interesting. The action is even more complex since, as you read, more characters become involved. I don't know what my favorite character is but I think I would choose Nemienne. The names of the characters are not usual names, thing that makes the book even more rich in fantasy! High fantasy readers would like reading this book since the action is twirled and the author includes magic and even dragons in the story! Quotes: "The candlelight illuminated an area perhaps an arm's ;emght on each side of her, not enough to gain sense of the place in which she stood. The light she carried with her seemed to create, not a rival for the darkness, nor even a contrast to it, but only an accent that clarified its sweep and power. There was no sign, now, of the cat." "He said after a moment, not turning, "The sea goes out forever, doesn't it? Sweeps in with the tide and washes endlessly out again, iterations on a single unfathomable theme... One could imagine the setting sun drowning out there in the far west. The sea seems more powerful even than light..." "

"I hope you weren't out killing any of God's creatures." I shrugged at him again. Of course I was out killing things. How the hell am I supposed to get heads and bodies for the Poles and the Bunker if I don't kill things? There just aren't enough natural deaths. You can't explain that sort of thing to people, though. The Wasp Factory tells the story of 16 year old boy Frank, who lives with his father on a remote Scottish island and indulges in the ritualistic torture and killing of animals and the use of 'the wasp factory' - a device used by Frank to fortell the future based on the decisions of angry and confused wasps that he traps inside. Quite macabre, but I rather enjoyed it. It's not often you encounter a psychopath in a novel that you can actually feel sorry for, but Frank is definitely that. The narration is matter-of-fact, yet the content is murder and violence towards children and animals, making it all the more chilling. Recommended for fans of Lord Of The Flies, and We Need To Talk About Kevin, because it involves the whole nature/nurture debate. There's also some interesting ideas about religion (Frank's totems and rituals) and gender (My greatest enemies are women and the sea. These things I hate. Women because they are weak and stupid and live in the shadows of men and are nothing compared to them). Actually, I'd recommend it to anyone. It's a brilliant read.

Catalyst was an interesting prequel to Rogue One: A Star Wars Story but I don't think it is a "must read" as it is being marketed as. Catalyst wasn't as exciting to me as Claudia Gray's Bloodlines or Lost Stars. Catalyst takes place during the construction of the Death Star and is an introduction to the main character of Rogue One Jyn Erso and her parents. Galen Erso is a brilliant scientist working on applying crystals as an energy source. As the Clone Wars continues Galen and his wife Lyra take a neutral position and focus on their research and the upcoming birth of their daughter. But the Empire has different plans for Galen's research and his old friend Orson Krennic offers him a position with Celestial Power (codename for the Death Star weapon). As the years go by Galen becomes obsessed with his research and is blind to the possible use the Empire plans for his discovery. Lyra remains by his side but suspects Krennic is lying to them and voices her concerns to Galen. Overall I thought the main plot was predictable. Krennic is ambitious and will manipulate everyone to get what he wants. The side plots with Lyra, Jen and a smuggler Captain Has Obitt was the most interesting and exciting parts of this book. The first half of the book dealt with a lot of technical information to lay the grounds for understanding Galen's research and it slowed the pace of the story. Until I watch Rogue One I don't know if Catalyst will enhance my movie experience. Catalyst was good but not great. 4 Stars for Audiobook Performance Even though I had problems with the writing I did enjoy the narrator Jonathan Davis. He makes distinct voices for the characters which always enhances the audiobook experience for me. He brought life to the story, even though some parts dragged for me. I will definitely look for more of his work.

This book! Everyone should read it. Brittainy Cherry has such a phenomenal talent. This entire series has been so fabulous. Maggie May was one of the most sympathetic heroines I've ever read. Happy go lucky until tragedy literally stole her voice. She was so cute as a little kid. I love that books were such a big part of this book. I've always been such a voracious reader so it's nice to read about others who love to read as much as I do. For me, this book was all about Maggie's relationships. Her relationship with her Dad and Calvin are so great. I love how they never ever stopped supporting her. Her relationship with her mother was so heartbreaking. I'm glad she made up with her sister. I hate reading about sisters who do ugly things to each other. Her relationship with Mrs. Boone was great. I love the back and forth and that Mrs. Boone refused to let her wallow and always wanted her to do more. Her back story was so painful to read. And, of course, Maggie's relationship with Brooks. What can I say. It was one of the sweetest, tender relationships I've ever read about. It's nice to read about a hero who isn't an alpha male but still knows how to stand up for his girl. The tragedy that hit Brooks was horrible. Accidents can happen in such a split second and your life is forever changed. Watching Maggie help pull Brooks out of his depression was wonderful. The reveal of who was the cause of Maggie's childhood trauma was a bit anticlimactic. I knew who it was as soon as the person was reintroduced into the story. I'm sure it was obvious to most people. I'm so looking forward to the last in this series coming sometime in 2017.

This book is really weird. Bray tries a lot of ambitious things. Some of them she pulls off brilliantly. Some of them made me want to throw the book across the room. So a plane-full of Miss Teen Dream contestants crash on an island. Things are pretty creepy right off the bat. Something's definitely wrong with this island. Plus, these models are completely lost, so there's a lot of good satire about the beauty industry. It's funny and a little creepy. So far so good. Then everything just gets over-the-top. Alright, so... it's a spy/action adventure now? The genre switch caught me off guard. The writing holds up, but it just wasn't really what I wanted. Some of the jokes got old. Everything was so random, I didn't really care what happened anymore. That being said, it gains a star for being smart. The commentary is witty, even if the book itself is basically thoughtless YA. It's the kind of social meaning that you can understand without thinking about it too much. It doesn't try to be intellectual or pretentious. Plus, multiple instances of LGBT+ representation. If you're intrigued by the premise, I'd say go ahead and read this book. But if you're already a little wary, just put the book down. It's even weirder than it sounds.

Wow. It's been an unfortunately long time since I've been this drawn into a book that I stayed up reading until I fell asleep and woke up early the next morning just to read it, simultaneously wanting to reach the end and dreading it all being over. I also don't think I've ever read a better-executed love triangle. It wasn't easy to choose a "team," but instead you hurt and hoped along with all three characters because the love Tessa, Jem and Will all had for each other was so strong and beautiful that you wanted all of them to find happiness. I'm not quite sure what to think of the bittersweet ending just yet. I'm a little put off by Clare's need to pair all the characters off romantically -- seriously, are there any single people in her series? -- but it's also kind of nice in a precious way. Cecily and Gabriel  are probably my favorite outside the main trio just because they're funny, along with dear old Henry. Speaking of Henry, the scene where I thought he had died was terrible. We're talking Fred Weasley dying in Deathly Hallows, punch-to-the-gut, why-are-authors-all-heartless-people terrible. He's always reminded me a bit of one of my younger brothers, which may be why it hurt so bad. I had had Jem's fate spoiled for me before reading as well, but even knowing he was going to be Brother Zachariah, Clare's writing was powerful enough I still believed he was dead. It wasn't as sudden and unexpected as Henry or Jessamine, but still hurt. The Mortal Instruments series didn't give me much hope for Clare's stories. They were like fanfiction, good fanfiction, but still fanfiction, and didn't feel deep in the slightest. I didn't hurt for any of the characters, and while their stories were interesting, they weren't particularly involving. This series, though, was masterfully done. I'm a bit apprehensive about going on to read  City of Heavenly Fire next (at least it's the last one?) but am looking forward to Clare's future series.

I really felt this book put the reader's emotions right there along with the main characters. I started reading the second and third book though in the series, though, and I somehow feel the author should have modified the ending of this book just a little and made it a stand alone book.

It seems that wherever Flavia de Luce goes, she finds dead bodies. Ordinary people would perhaps stop going out, but Flavia delights in the mystery each new corpse presents. This book continues her adventures with another body and another mystery. The whole gang of usual characters can be found in their respective supporting roles, save one notable exception. This book is pretty dark in overall tone, especially at the end. The subject matter is grim and has a few twists, some of which even I saw coming. Still, I enjoyed the story. I like Jayne Entwistle's narration of the audiobooks. I like the relationship between Flavia and Gladys, and how the author captures the child in Flavia while still managing to make her very capable and independent in other ways. The end of the book was hard. I look forward to the next novel to see what is going to transpire, but my enthusiasm for it is dampened by what we are intended to assume. All in all, an enjoyable book. I like watching Flavia grow as a character while still retaining some of her innocence. She is straddling that fragile middle ground and Bradley does a very good job of keeping her there.

I felt pretty much as I felt when writing that during-reading update: there wasn't really much wrong with it, but I didn't feel very engaged and just didn't enjoy it. I also felt the tone wavered rather from younger-kid's adventure-in-faerie to much older teen dealing with typical YA concerns.

Review originally posted at Step Into Fiction This book blew my mind. There is no other way to explain this. I'm going to try but I am seriously and utterly in love with this book. I am asking myself why I've owned this book for almost a year now & yet I hadn't read it until now? Why, Jessica, why? I really have no good answer to this... I do believe I am in love with historical fiction but usually only if there is a paranormal twist to it. Obviously, this book is about faeries (what gave it away, right?) and it's taken place in the late 1800's AND it's in London. It's like three in a row, tic tac toe! I win! I really had no idea how much I was going to love this mainly because of how a friend described it to me. I blame her for putting it off for so long ;) She made it sound so historical and boring. Like the history of fae, which could be interesting but not how she described. Obviously, she needs to do a better job selling books to me which I'll work with her on that but oh my goodness! Tiki, our lovely and adorable heroine is absolutely phenomenal! Like, I absolutely adore her and just want to hug her and tell her how fantastic of a person she is. This girl deserves an award or something. She has such an enormous heart, such intelligence and just always willing to put those she cares most about first. She was orphaned, in a sense, on her own terms. Her parents both died when she was about 14 years old and was forced to live with her and Aunt and Uncle she hardly knew. Her Uncle was a drunk and would look at her in ways that made her uncomfortable and he would make advances toward her that made her hide when he got drunk. She ran away to find her mothers close friend to find out she had passed away and so, she became orphaned. She quickly found a new family with Fiona and Shamus with finding Toots and Clara shortly after that. What I love most about Tiki I think is her dedication and love for poor, sick four year old Clara. That girl is all sorts of adorable and Tiki feels responsible for her. Tiki's world revolves around making Clara better and giving her a life where picking pockets isn't necessary. I love the history of fae that is tied in with this story and how it involves Tiki. The entire story she is dragged in to a world she never truly believe existed and she's trying to figure out how involved she truly is, especially what the appeal is about unique birthmark on her wrist. Her run in with the fae are putting herself and those she cares about at risk, especially little Clara when she goes missing. The suspence and the desire to keep her family together is intense and emotional. Her relationship with Rieker is amazing. Rieker is an orphaned pocket picker, as well and he's had his eye on Tiki for quite some time. Especially since he found out she's actually a girl and not a boy she dresses up to be. There is such a great, steady build up on these two...and I'm not talking a romantic relationship but just even their friendship. In the beginning of the book they really aren't friends at all...just have run in to one another from time to time. But we see him more frequently as the book progresses and you and Tiki are trying to figure out how trustworthy this handsome orphan truly is. Then there's the Royal family. I am utterly in love with the fact that they play such a huge role in this story, and hopefully that role continues in The Torn Wing! Especially Prince Leo! He's dreamy, as a Prince is meant to be (right? ), and he's got his eye on Tiki! His relationship with his older brother, Arthur, is charming and gah - I just love them. They're so proper but yet...they're not. Royalty truly are some of the best actors out there... Now that I mentioned the characters, the story is based around this ring that has been entrusted to the Royal family for safe keeping. Leo 'loses' it and basically London just isn't the same. This extraordinary ring isn't just a beautiful piece of jewelry, it's a faerie ring. It's a truce. As long as the flame inside the ring burns/glows, the two worlds will remain apart but there are those in the UnSeelie court dying to get their hands on it to end the truce and kill all mortals in London. Who knew so many problems would come out of a piece of jewelry? If you love fantasy, you'll love this. If you love novels taken place in the nineteenth century, you'll love this. If you love London...well, you'll love this. Seriously. For any fae fan...this is one you don't want to miss! It's up there as a favorite behind Julie Kagawa's Iron Fey series.
Well. That was steamy as hell.

I don't know how to feel about this book. On the one hand, Rowling clearly spent a lot of time developing this mystery and really tried pushing it to a dark place. It is at its strongest when Robin and Strike follow leads to out of the way places and learn more about each of the suspects. On the other hand, far too much time is spent on the non-love triangle love triangle. While these relationships add depth to Strike's character, they serve to make Robin fall apart. It feels as though Rowling can't make up her mind about whether Robin should be a damsel in distress or strong, independent woman. I really hope the next one focuses more on sleuthing and less on this nonsense, though I doubt it will.

For more reviews, gifs, Cover Snark and more, visit A Reader of Fictions. 3.5 stars Continuing a streak of good middle grade novels, I picked up Monstrous, because I'd heard good things from Dahlia (author of Behind the Scenes/Last Will and Testament/Under the Lights). In a lot of ways, it's a strange book. It's surprisingly dark for a middle grade novel, which okay yes I do see that about most of the ones that I read, but those are the ones I like. Monstrous will appeal to those who love fairy tales and who love eerie middle grades. The opening of Monstrous is great. Kymera wakes up, a patchwork creature. This story is essentially a Frankenstein retelling that's been combined with fairy tales. Her father tells her of her creation; using science, he's put his daughter back together after many failed attempts, following her death at the hands of the evil wizard. Unfortunately, he could not save her memories. As a bonus, though, she's now better than human; she's part cat, part bird, and part snake too. What I love is that Kym is partly a monster. She's not a sweet human girl trapped in the guise of a monster, at least not entirely. Kym is sweet, but she's also got animal instincts coming from her animal parts. She's a predator, and can consume raw rabbit flesh. Annoyed by the family pet, a sparrow-dog combo, she considers eating it. Kym can kill and she's willing to, despite being a little girl. Connolly also does a really good job with the balance between Kym being a child and being almost a newborn. Kym has instincts and reasoning from her brain's previous learning, but, without her memories, she's also a babe in the woods. Everything she knows comes from reading fairy tales and from her what her father tells her. It's no wonder that, when she meets a cute boy, she immediately decides she's in love with him, since that's how fairy tales go, right? Monster did drag for me in the middle couple hundred pages. There's a very long stretch of time where I knew what the twist was, and I was just waiting for Kymera to figure it out. On the one hand, I think it was pretty realistic, because again she's days old on some levels, so it would be hard on her. Even so, this period lasted long enough that my attention began to wander. It felt like no narrative progress was really being made. The ending picked back up again, however, getting back to the dark roots. I didn't expect such a death toll from a middle grade. Connolly was not playing around. I think Kym is an interesting ethical figure, both lovable and, indeed, monstrous. I wish the ending had been less abrupt, because I would have liked to know more of what came after. Why put in all the middle grade romance only to not let the reader know the outcome? How dare. I'm really impressed with Connolly's debut and will be curious to try whatever she writes next. Dark fairy tales are pretty much always Christina bait, and Monstrous is no exception.

I loved this book! This whole series is just perfect! All characters are very dear to me and each and every one of the stories touches you in some way. But I wasn't expecting this book to be so dark. We still have those funny as hell moments when the gang is together but there were some pretty dark themes in this one. What we found out about the past... It wasn't pretty at all. I can't to this review without mentioning some specific moments, so here we go. The spoilers are hidden. I can't believe the way this book started. Daisy (Noel, Brandt, Caroline and Colton's mother) giving a  hand job to Brandt, her own son! But it didn't stop there. I wish it did, but it didn't. It was worse than this, but thank God Linda didn't write it. I wouldn't have the stomach to read it. I just couldn't believe it. I already knew that woman was a sad excuse for a human being... but this!? This is surreal. I literally had to stop reading for a few minutes just to calm down. Some pages later another revelation comes up. Mason's mother literally  sold her own son to Mrs. Garrison (their landlady). Yes, that Mrs. Garrison... the one that turned Mason into a gigolo. Apparently Mrs. Garrison told Mason's mother to stay away during one Saturday and she said yes. That day Mrs. Garrison convinced Mason to have sex with her for money so that he could pay the rent. I couldn't believe this shit! What kind of mothers are these! Oh my God Colton! I'm so used to thinking about him with 10 years old that when he showed up at the Forbidden Nightclub to talk to a 22 year old Brandt I was just dumbstruck! What happened to that lovely little boy? I'll tell you. He grew up, and is now 17 and is so freakin cocky and shameless that I can't even! He's worse than Ten! Still love him though. The next book about Colton is going to be epic! Can't wait! Oh! And he was so cute with Felicity! Since she helped him with his nightmares when he was 9 or 10 he connected with her. I'm glad he still has a special connection with her. I laughed so much when Colton was giving advices to Sarah about Brandt. Colton said Sarah should seduce Brandt and he would fold like a house of cards. The whole operation Bang-Brandt was hilarious! Colton was the mastermind behind this obviously. Caroline and Zoey helping Sarah to pick out some lingerie and then Ten telling Sarah she should use the red and black one! I laughed so much! I love these guys! But this operation didn't end here. When Colton told Brandt that Sarah had asked him to  sleep with her...   My only thought was: Oh my God! You have a death wish! Brandt is going to kill you! Although I have to say that Colton is a genius. His methods are not the best but he gets the job done. That little lie was enough to make Brandt do something about Sarah. I can't believe Daisy (Brandt, Noel, Colton and Caroline's mother) had the nerve to  show up at Noel's house! She wanted to make amends with them! For 9 years, since Noel took his brothers and sister from her, she's been AWOL! Not to mention that she didn't give a flying fuck about whether her kids had money to eat and clothes and school when they were with her! Noel had to take care of everything since he was 4! Yes, you read right! Four years old! She was just constantly high! And now she wants >spoiler> to make amends with them and meet her grandchildren! WTF!? Screw you! I agree with Ten, he had the exact same reaction I had when she  showed up at Noel's doorstep. Get fucking lost! As if this wasn't enough, she  caught Brandt alone in the kitchen and she admitted that she was high when she molested him. But guess what!? She doesn't even feel sorry for it! She had the nerve to be ogling her own son! Obviously Brandt was petrified when he saw her advancing towards him. He still can't forget and get over what she did to him. THANK GOD for Colton! If he hadn't shown I don't know what that bitch would have done to Brandt. Colton told her to get the fuck away from Brandt. Apparently Colton knows about what happened and he stood up for his brother. I loved it when Colton told Daisy that his mother was Aspen. Take that you selfish bitch! I know I'm cursing too much but I can't help it. This excuse for a human being brings the violence in me to the surface. Right away, Noel put their mother out of his house. And Colton let it slip that he would never forgive her because of what she did to Brandt. So the cat is out of the bag. God! Colton explaining to all of them (Noah, Caroline, Aspen, Ten and Sarah) what  their mother did to Brandt was...   I can't even... It was heartbreaking. I cried, I couldn't help it. Linda wrote it a way that really touched your heart and got you thinking how is it even possible for  a mother to do that to her own child. Brandt was 13 at the time...   Brandt was wrecked after this. Right now he hates Colton because he told them the truth but Colton did the right thing. Brandt needs help to get over this. And Sarah was the one to help him. Sarah had two bad seizures is a row after she  had sex with Brandt and she had to be rushed to the hospital. Brandt and Mason were both desperate... but Brandt was at a whole other level. He literally can't live without that girl. Thank God everything was ok with her. Let's talk about Ten getting punched by  Mason! I can't believe he still can't keep his mouth shut! Ok I can... Ten is like that, he has no filter. But that's why we all love him. :) I really need to do a list of who punched Ten in which book. I think he got punched every single book except the first one because he wasn't a character of the series yet. These punches are epic! It's like a tradition. I love it! And if you're asking yourself why the hell did he got punched, well... You'll have to read to know it. Linda did a fantastic job with Sarah and Brandt's story. We could feel the emotional connection these two shared as young kids and how it grew over the years. Sarah is Mason's little sister who has cerebral palsy and Linda didn't forget to show us how is it to live with CP. We were able to see the obstacles that Sarah faced on a daily basis. Since they met at 13, Brandt has been like a knight in shining armor for Sarah. He's always protecting her and would kick anyone's ass if they looked at her wrong. His love for Sarah is completely fierce! And Sarah loves him too. I'm glad they finally found their way to each other. It was a really sweet romance. And now is Colton's turn. I just knew Julianna was going to be the one for Colton since that conversation at the Forbidden Nightclub. I just hope Colton doesn't get hurt in the process since Julianna apparently has  a crush on Brandt. I can't wait to learn more about Colton and roll on the floor laughing because of him.
*Listened to the audiobook, but was able to pay attention. This was such a cute read/listen! Unexpectedly full of humor and little one-liners. Made my daily commute so much better.

The Good: The characters and setting (essentially the antagonist of the book, probably)  were very well written and the mood was dark without being cartoonish. I assume Heart of Darkness was intended to be a disturbing read and it was. The Bad: I found the book far too wordy for my taste. Also, for a story about a boat trip up a river, it seemed to mostly lack direction. Like if there was no boat and no river it would just have been about a bunch of guys waiting for another guy to do something. 'Friends' character the protagonist is most like: Within the needlessly clever frame of a story within a story, Marlow was the protagonist. He was verbose, observant and a bit of a loner. If they remade this book and set it on the Hudson in the late 90s they could cast the guy who played Chandler.

I was completely expecting this book to be boring. Or I was expecting it to be similar to The Selection. Yet, everyone on Instagram RAVES about this book. So, naturally I bough the whole trilogy before even reading the synopsis. I'm sorry, I have a Book Outlet addiction that is incredibly unhealthy. Anyways, this book seemed kind of lame when I first started it, then everything started happening. Kestrel isn't your typical YA heroine. She is not incredible at everything she does. Her beauty is not talked about every other paragraph. She is a terrible fighter in a community that being an excellent fighter is praised. Kestrel does not seem to care what everyone else thinks, she knows what she loves and she does just that. Playing the piano is her passion and that's supposed to be what servants do. She is ridiculed because of it. I LOVED having a character that was not absolutely amazing at everything she does. I loved reading this book and thoroughly enjoyed it and because of that I am not going to pick it apart. My main grievance with this book was how boring the first few chapters were. Another thing I loved was that this was not an insta-love "hey I just met you and this is crazy, endanger your life for me maybe?" romance. They didn't really want to be in love with each other and definitely seemed to slowly start to realize it over time. A nice slow burn romance.
Wasn't all that great, in my opinion. But I'll give the next one a shot when I get ahold of a copy.

This was a bit of a strange read for me. There were sentences scattered throughout the book that were so beautiful, I underlined them and marked them with post-its. There's no doubt that Brit Bennett is a fabulous writer; she's a master at depicting grief with quiet, subtle phrases that tug at your heart strings and evoke empathy. Unfortunately, while the writing was stellar, the story itself was kind of forgettable. The lyrical sentences Bennett crafted will stay with me far longer than the plot and characters.

It is a little weird how, as of page 171 Percy seems to have done nothing out of his own free will. He stumbles on trouble, gets led by others, gets onto boats, into taxis by acccident or by someone else telling him to and over all it feels like he's a pinball being pushed around. I suppose he chose a ship - Queen Anne's Revenge so that was almost his own action - but as it's described it feels yet again as something beyond his control. And yet the book is still an entertaining read. I'm a fan of Greek Myth and for that alone I'm willing to overlook a lot. There's a lot of action and I'm starting to accept that Rick Riordna just isn't that good or really inerested in describing slower scenes. He literally skips anything that could be seen as mundane with Percy giving it the shortest descriptopn possible 'I ate , I slept, I trained, I built a chariot' kind of things. Which isn't bad but it kind of creates this breathless feeling that there is no respite from action. And so the action starts to seem almost boring. First: I LOVE this cover. It's perfect. (And I have a thing for tall, dark, and blue eyes.) Anyway... So, the story starts us out with Kendras, an injured mercenary who has been sent away from the battle (so that the King doesn't have to pay the mercenaries for their service) and separated from his unit, the Scorpions. He runs across another man, a man with grey eyes named Steel, who sees an opportunity with Kendras and takes advantage of the poor situation to put Kendras in his debt. Steel doesn't exactly want a slave, but he does want Kendras to be indebted to him. Steel thinks that he can buy that indebtedness, but at the first opportunity, Kendras takes off to go look for his unit. (He did tell Steel he was going to. Steel just thought he could forbid it. That should've been his first clue.) Through a flashback, we learn about the Scorpions and "the officer" who leads them, and who first found Kendras and thought him fit to join the unit. We learn that the group is what is left of a legion from an Empire long since deceased. The officers of the unit have kept a "memory" written of the members and political machinations of many decades (centuries?) and they use that information to determine which side they will align with (even if the price is lower). The comrades will live and die for each other, and to Kendras it is unthinkable not to go back and find out what happened to his comrades and the officer. To shorten up the plot synopsis, the officer is a hostage and Kendras winds up embroiled in a political mess he never dreamed of while trying to rescue him. Even if they rescue the officer, it becomes clear before too long that the unit might not get the officer back, which troubles Kendras in a variety of ways. I think that's enough of a recap for me to be able to say what I want to say about the story. Kendras sort of bothered me because he seemed to waffle between weak and strong, or rather he was weak in some ways and strong in others (which a serious feat to accomplish so well in writing in the first place). Don't get me wrong: I like the character and love the story, but I was sort of left wondering if he really had what it takes in the end to be the new officer of the Scorpions once Adrastes, the officer who found Kendras, decided he needed to return to that which he'd run away from initially. I mean, let's face it, from the moment Kendras picks up the memory, you know that's what's coming at the end of this story . I began wondering if Kendras would have been strong enough to carry on if Adrastes had been killed, or if Kendras had had to leave the man behind instead of being offered the position as head of his Guard , or would he have given up, as he did a couple of other times in the story. Is he really the right person? Because he sure doubts himself a hell of a lot. (Then again, we don't see inside the officer's head, so we don't know how his insecurities compare to Kendras's own, so there's no telling. We see the officer through the rose-colored glasses that Kendras wears.) Aside from the feeling that Kendras seemed to be getting weaker in his sense of self as the story progressed because he was in WAY over his head politically and depended on the officer to guide them on the right path (and that kept me from feeling like Kendras belonged where he finally ended up), I thought the story was fantastic. The world was interesting and the main characters really had depth that I enjoyed. Oh, and while I talk about Kendras being over his head politically, the story is not a lot of thick court intrigue. I don't mean to give that impression. It's more action. I mean to say that Kendras just doesn't think along those lines. You can see Adrastes grooming him for it. Kendras was the last to realize it, too. He wasn't kidding when he mused to himself that his men understood things before he himself did, and it might keep him humble. More power to him if that actually works for him and he can maintain leadership that way. I thought that aspect of the story was well done because it didn't get bogged down in explanation of machinations. Because we're experiencing all this through the filter that is Kendras, it is much simplified. In the end, I'm not sure I entirely bought into where Kendras ended up, but I didn't see better options either, and that was as happy as things were going to get. Is it truly HEA? Not in my opinion, because the whole situation is temporary. There's a lot of room for interpretation there. But it's not bittersweet either. I guess I'm happy with it because Kendras still needs some training to get where he needs to be to fill the shoes he found himself in, and I can live with that. EDIT: After re-reading in Jan 2014, changing this from 4.5 to 5 stars. I'm looking forward to the forthcoming sequels to see how Kendras grows.

3.5 stars I'm a fan of Kasie West so reading Lucky in Love was a no-brainer for me. I wish I could say I loved it. The balance and build were off for me. I didn't strongly connect with either Maddie or Seth until the book was 75% done, and for me that's when the story took off in the way West's books normally do for me. By the end, I really liked Maddie and Seth. I wish I'd felt more of a spark between them from the get-go. One of the biggest sticking points for me was why Maddie didn't tell Seth about her lottery win straight away. Further into the story, when everyone--even her best friends--were treating her differently, her paranoia and fears about telling him and having things change between them made more sense. Also, I was angry with Maddie's parents for giving her pretty much zero guidance. As a mom, I would have made the appointment with the financial advisor, and I would have made it again and again until I got my child to go. So yeah, not my favourite Kasie West book, but still a cute read. Shout out to the swoon's Seth gave me for his over-the-top sweetness and thoughtfulness on his first date with Maddie. That and the book's strong finish--Maddie showed tremendous character growth--are the reasons I'm rounding to 4 stars.

Ellie Martin meets Gray Whitby while she's hiding in a church garden weeding (without permission). He's there to attend a wedding (also without the church in question's permission). They begin a whirlwind courtship. I enjoyed their relationship, and those aspects of the story, but Ellie's mother drove me crazy! She's the type of woman that Ellie had to "warn" that she had a boyfriend because she knew her mother would not take it well. After Ellie's dad left when Ellie was six, her mom has been cautioning her two daughters against the evils of the city and the sweet talking men that live there. They're only after one thing! Going against her mother's wishes, Ellie leaves home at 18 to move to Atlanta. Now she's afraid to even tell her mom about Gray because she knows her mom won't see how considerate and funny he is. She'll see his handsome face and decide that he's just like Ellie's "no-good sweet-talking father." And Ellie is right to be worried. Her mother is judgmental and rude when she meets Gray. Now Ellie is stuck trying to choose between a relationship her mother, and her growing love for Gray. How can she keep both of them happy? Should she? I was really bothered when Ellie's mom  cut off her sister for "putting the bed before wed." I believe in saving intimacy for marriage as well, but her daughter already feels bad about not waiting, and now her mother is making her feel unworthy of being married. It was also pretty hypocritical since the mom got married because she was pregnant. You would think that she could have been more understanding. I felt like the focus of the story was Ellie's relationship with her family, when I wanted more focus on her and Gray. We even saw her relationship in terms of, "I love you, but my Mama's going to say....about our relationship". If I was Gray, I would feel a little irritated too. If you can get past Ellie's mom, the story was sweet and delightful. Content: clean Disclosure: I received A May Bride through NetGalley.com in exchange for an honest review.

Below is my original review. I'm leaving it as it's still essentially how I feel still. I have however decided that the overall story of the book rates a higher rating than I originally gave (you'll see below). The biggest problem for me was that Katniss seemed to grow some throughout the first and the second book, yet slid back and forth/up and down throughout this. I just didn't think it was still Katniss in some ways. To each of course and I'd say try it yourself and see how you feel/what you think. Some spoilers in review as I do discuss some things about the conclusion of the book. ***************** Spoilers in Review below ******************* Okay, just us now...a lot of people loved this book. I'm not one of them. I liked the first book immensely, I also liked the second volume. I appreciate the inspiration behind the books. I considered 3 stars here, as there are times when some very good writing comes through. But in the end for me to say I really didn't like the book wouldn't fit with a 3 star rating. There were too many times I skimmed through this one, too many times I came very close to abandoning the read all together simply due to the story and it's telling. If you read my review of the second volume in this trilogy you know that one of the things that bothered me most was the immature and selfish character of Katniss. I observed at the close of that volume that this had probably been intentional on Ms.Collins' part and that Katniss seemed to be growing out of it after the hard and troubling events at the end of said volume. Well, Katniss had a relapse...big-time. Apparently in all the wars and all the revolutions and all the tragedies of all time NO ONE has suffered as she has. Am I the only one who got so tired of her constant bemoaning of her own fate...as the world is flying apart around her? She forces the rebels to take her back to her blasted and burned former home where she apparently wanders around saying things like "I brought this on you"... GOOD GRIEF. No Katniss, the people who dropped the bombs brought it on them...the people who ordered it brought it on...the people who have been forcing children to kill each other in arenas to hold the entire populace under their heel FOR GENERATIONS brought it on. The world didn't start when you were born Katniss. The book becomes, it seems to me very much of a one trick pony with Katniss constantly discovering more pain and more woe. It turns into a story where the rebels seem often to be as bad as the oppressive government they seek to overthrow. A book that comes very close to one of those pompous tomes (and for that matter movies, short stories etc.) that defined itself as "anti-war" as if people sometimes get together and say, "hey, let's have a war." War is nothing more than an assault or an armed robbery writ large. Very few actually "want war" it doesn't make one extra righteous to say "I'm taking a stand against war! ", just self-righteous. The choice in the story Ms. Collins wrote is the same as it has been often...war or enslavement. You can accept what your handed and live with it, let them take your goods... your children, or you can resist. The longer you wait to resist the worse it may be. Thus the 1 star rating. It seems to me Katniss is an annoying character who (I think) became badly one dimensional. There are a few bright spots and some good prose, but over all, I'm not taken with the book. For me one of the most telling moment in the book was in a conversation between Gale and Peeta (the boy named after pocket bread) when they are having a conversation about which of them Katniss will eventually "choose" and Gale hits it on the head. He says she'll pick the one She can't survive without. Of course from Katniss we get the obligatory self recrimination, "am I that bad", well I don't need either of them, internal monologue..but (when proverbial push comes to proverbial shove) that is exactly what she eventually does. In the end so far as I can tell after all that's happened, after all the death and loss the world still revolves around Katniss at least so far as Katniss is concerned. I found this an unsatisfying book and conclusion to what had been up to now a pretty good trilogy and if my children were still young I'd definitely discuss this one with them to see what they took away from it. Not my cup of tea, and puts my retention of the other two in my collection in question...I regret the money spent on this book and the time invested in it, a bad sign. The first book is a very good read, the second is pretty good, but this, the end volume is very, very weak. My opinion of course. Update: Sadly this volume ruined the entire set for me. I sold all 3.

I really enjoyed this! At first, I thought it was just going to be the typical woe is me bad-girl meets innocent good guy and they happily ever after but it exceeded my expectations. I think the thing I like most about this book was that it seemed realistic; yes, there were plot twists and events that happened but they didn't seem outside the realm of possibility like some of them do and it felt like everything flowed organically. You could relate to Rowen in a sense that she wasn't some perfect 18-year-old girl who has everything sorted and instead went out partying a bit too much and dabbled with drugs, a lot of alcohol and sleeping around who did ok at school but was being given an ultimatum by her mum to go to art school. Her relationship with her mum was believable and it was easy to understand how it got to that point and the twist about what happened also seemed believable although I do have to question what sort of parent you must be to just put your head in the sand over what happened to Rowen. It was nice to see the relationship grow between Jesse and Rowen instead of them being Insta-love / insta-together and yes maybe there was the insta-love there but it didn't automatically jump into the being in a relationship or together, it just progressed as expected over time and spending time around each other. I enjoyed the role that Garth played in it all and I also lied how Rowen couldn't stay away from him either as I expected that she would have with her internal monologue being "he's the normal type of guy I'd go for an I don't want that at all" etc so I'm glad that that avenue. Although I have to say the part where she is asleep/passed out and kisses her is all a bit weird and literally wasn't addressed again in the book - what he did wasn't ok and yet Rowen, who didn't care if she confronted people and it was awkward didn't even mention what Garth had done to Garth himself and address that it wasn't ok. There were a few annoying parts to the book; how did Rowen manage to jump on a horse and ride out in the middle of a massive storm after literally a month or two of just starting to ride and there seemed to be a big fuss made of how Rowen dressed and looked at the start of the book which just seemed to vanish into nothingness by the end. The whole art-school mess seemed to get sorted out a bit too easily and (maybe it's just me) but I would have liked to have seen that play out. I mean where is she living and how was it all sorted out so easily when she was relying so heavily on her mum to do it all for her in the first place but then again maybe that's just me. Overall I really enjoyed it and I'm looking forward to read the next book and seeing what happens!

Class conflict novels can be fresh but the struggle was ruined by a sad love triangle and silly drama. 2) Not enough world building! What world are we in? The black-and-white illustrations are detailed and realistic, and it takes talent to make some of the fantastic beings in Kin appear 'realistic'. I prefer color in my graphic novels, though the B/W works just fine here. The plot was interesting enough, and the characters were good. I liked it enough to request the sequel (Kith) from SuperSearch, but I wasn't excited enough to eagerly check the library every day for its arrival. This novel, based in part on the author's own experiences, focuses on Alex, a teenage girl who is date raped by a fellow student at her boarding school, Themis Academy. Rather than going to the police, Alex decides instead to go through an unofficial student justice system founded by her older sister. The organization - named the Mockingbirds, after To Kill a Mockingbird - investigates violations against students of the school that the administration insists do not occur. Though the Mockingbirds do not think of themselves as a secret society, they operate like one, and Alex soon learns just how much power and influence the group wields over the student body. The details of the rape are revealed slowly throughout the story, as Alex's memories of that night resurface. The writing in these parts is necessarily graphic, and honestly portrays what happens to Alex and how it makes her feel. While these passages were not the easiest to read, they were well-written and I think they were essential to the plot. Without understanding Alex's attack, the rest of her story wouldn't carry the same emotional weight. I did wonder briefly whether it was plausible for a school administration to be so clueless and insensitive to the needs of their students, but that question didn't really take away from my enjoyment of the book. I also worried that Alex's decision to take matters into her own hands and pursue justice outside the law would discourage girls who have been raped from reporting their attacks to law enforcement. I was pleased to see, though, that the author's note covered this, and the author actually shared her own experience and discussed the more official channels she used to seek justice on her own rapist. I hope that readers who finish the book will take the time to read that note as well. I really enjoyed this book, even more than I expected. The Boo Radley references were wonderful and made me want to re-read To Kill a Mockingbird for the first time since high school, and I'm really glad there is a sequel (Rivals, 2012) to explore further the ins and outs of The Mockingbirds as an organization. I'd recommend this book especially to teens who like courtroom dramas, boarding school settings, and secret societies.

This book is like salted caramel. Sweet and sugary with just enough salt to offset and make it yummy. Jill Shalvis does the typical Chick Lit thing here: she sets up characters in a "world" - in this case it's a town along the Washington coast - sets up the romance and goes from there. She follows the typical Chick Lit formula, but somehow managed to make it just a tiny bit different. This story was such fun. Maddie, our main character, is the middle child in a family of three sisters. They all have the same mom but different dads, so they were all raised differently. When Mom dies, they converge on a run-down B&B that Mom left behind in order to fix it up and sell it. The interaction between these three sisters is priceless. Dialogue is where Shalvis really shines in her writing and here it is witty and quick. Maddie's character begins to be revealed through these scenes, so we get a really good sense of who she is as an only child who avoids confrontation like the plague. She has just left a relationship with an abusive boyfriend, her biological clock is ticking and she's a bit neurotic. This makes her sympathetic rather than annoying; we see her slowly emerge from her emotional hiding place. Jax, the love interest, is the typical hunk. But he is mostly described that way thru the observations of others around him. While there's a lot of "he's so fine" there is also a fair amount of interaction with his brothers and best friend. Again, enough salt to offset the sugar and make him believable. His backstory is revealed slowly but it isn't nearly as interesting as Maddie's. He is much more of a typical stock character while Maddie and her sisters are more dimensional. It isn't that Jax is boring - he's just what you'd expect in a chick lit novel. The romance happens pretty much instantly, which might bother some. They've suddenly each met their soulmate, yada yada, whatever. The romance isn't the most interesting thing here. It's the character development that makes it good. On audio the book is narrated by Celeste Cuilla. While she is an excellent narrator I didn't find her a good match for this story. Her voices for the women were great - but her voices for the men sounded a bit too feminine. As a voice actor she wasn't able to distinguish them as decidedly male. Because of this, I set aside the audio and read it as an ebook. Once I did that, it was a wonderful book. I don't generally read Chick Lit; I instead opt for New Adult and all its angst. But in this case, the wit and banter between the characters made it just delightful. This is the first book in a long series, so OK Lucky Harbor - what else have you got?

** spoiler alert ** This is a tale about two misfits who find their place in the classroom, in the school hallway and in the crowded bus that carry students to and from school every Monday morning. A tale about first kisses, messy hair, comic books, cassette tapes, butterfingers, first love and awkward conversations set in the year of 1986. This book will let you know how it feels like to be young again. With a touch of stories about family dysfunction and painful first encounters, this book will strike you in a beautiful way you never imagine possible. This book is filled with social awkwardness and utterly moving confrontations. "He'd stopped trying to bring her back. She only came back when she felt like it, in dreams and lies and broken deja vu..." I knew the moment I read the first sentence in the very first chapter that I am going to like this young adult book. I don't want to form any bias since it was written by Rainbow Rowell and with all the hype around her books; I guess it was best to lower my expectation to start with. After finishing the book, the story exceeded my expectation. I suddenly realized I couldn't take my hands off of it because I was totally HOOKED! I loved the development of the story with its well-paced plot. I also have a particular interest for any stories set in the year of 1900's. Nineteen hundred brings childhood memories and classical love stories here in the present time just like sniffing pages of old books also brings old memories. I loved their cute love story. There had been no conversation between the two main characters yet it gave you the feels. No "I-fell-in-love-with-you-when-we-first-met." No "instalove." No "exchange of hi's and hello's." No "You've-got-me-head-over-heels." No putting hands inside the hem of his shirt. No ruining someone else's lipstick yet it was freaking good! What they did for the first few weeks since they met was to exchange comic books and cassette tapes. Period. Nothing more, nothing less. When Park held Eleanor's hand, he was holding it as if it was the most delicate thing he had ever touched. How their hands fit together; it feels so raw, so fresh and so unique. It was by far the most beautiful holding hands I've ever read. "Holding Eleanor's hand was like holding a butterfly. Or a heartbeat. Like holding something complete, and completely alive." It was the most adorable and most authentic portrayal of teenage love. You could just imagine how sweet it had been for the two of them. How they slowly noticing each other's existence without literally saying, "I'm rooting for you," as if saying the exact words will somehow spoil everything. "You can be Han Solo, and I'll be Boba Fett. I'll cross the sky for you." I loved how Rowell described the characters in a most relatable way. How every chapter evolved into a charismatic and enchanting love story with just the right amount of sweet ingredients. I liked all the awkwardness and disfigurements of the characters which made them more likable and genuine. I liked Park. I liked that he's half-Korean. I liked how he ignored the girl he's been with at the bus every morning. I liked how he shared his comic books because he didn't know how to approach her appropriately. I adore him for having an exact mixture of timidity and thoughtfulness. I liked all the subtleties in this story and its captivating romance. "Park was never going to love her more than he did on the last day they said goodbye." Those ending that finally gives you the feels; those comeback long after the silence; all of it makes you want to crave for more. Then you realized you've come across the last page and there's nothing left to read. Aghh. Anyway, the ending just keeps on bugging me: "just three long words." What the hell is that? I'm keeping my fingers crossed hoping it was something positive since something heavy and winged took off from Park's chest. I'm not sure if I'll request for a sequel because I like to keep it hanging and let my mind do the rest of the story as if continuing it might otherwise ruin the abstractedness of the novel. I like to keep it that way. More often than not, the sequels just ruined the beauty of the story. There are times wherein words aren't enough and things are better left unsaid. For you, what do you think are those "THREE LONG WORDS?" A. I Miss You B. I'm Han Solo C. Just stop, Park D. I Love You E. Nothing Ever Ends F.

This book is part of my TBR list for #AsianLitBingo. If you haven't heard of it, you can look at Shenwei's post here, and check out the rest of my TBR here. Jacket Copy: "For Tara Krishnan, navigating Brierly, the academically rigorous prep school she attends on scholarship, feels overwhelming and impossible. Her junior year begins in the wake of a startling discovery: A message from an alternate Earth, light years away, is intercepted by NASA. This means that on another planet, there is another version of Tara, a Tara who could be living better, burning brighter, because of tiny differences in her choices. As the world lights up with the knowledge of Terra Nova, the mirror planet, Tara's life on Earth begins to change. At first, small shifts happen, like attention from Nick Osterman, the most popular guy at Brierly, and her mother playing hooky from work to watch the news all day. But eventually, those small shifts swell, the discovery of Terra Nova like a black hole, bending all the light around it. As a new era of scientific history dawns and Tara's life at Brierly continues its orbit, only one thing is clear: Nothing on Earth--and for Tara--will ever be the same again." Review: There is so much to love about this book, and yet I'm sitting here so torn. Let's start with the good: The characters, and the specter of Terra Nova and the repercussions for its existence. While the book started out a little too slow for me, by the time I got to the fourth chapter I was hooked. I literally could not put the book down. The high school drama was interesting and reminded me of the good parts of Pretty Little Liars (I've only seen the show). Of course, there was nothing so drastic as a murder mystery in this. Tara navigates school as she is taken in by the popular group. While each of the popular kids seems like a stereotype at first, their layers slowly become apparent. They feel fleshed out, if still very larger than life. The idea of Terra Nova was interesting. The way the world reacts to each additional piece of news was a creative backdrop to the story. The slow build-up of reactions to the news from individual characters to whole cities and countries heightened the tension and lent a gravitas to the story in some cases, Michiko Natori's death is a great example , but ultimately it was in the periphery. Overall, it was so fun to read! The not bad, but not so great: The lack of Terra Nova, and the ending. While I understand that the discovery of Terra Nova is supposed to act as a catalyst for the changes every character experiences, and the overriding paranoia, it didn't seem all that neccessary, aside from giving Tara another conflict with her mother to up her stress level . In all honesty, even though I loved the premise, there was no need for a sci-fi element in this story. Occasionally there would be a line from Tara along the lines of "little did I know, things were about to change," that made me think something big was going to happen. Something "big" did happen, it just wasn't what I assumed. I assumed: GIANT ALTERNATE PLANET ADVENTURE! It was (enjoyable) high school drama for the most part, with an interesting coming of age message. But I was hoping at some part Terra Nova would be more than a symbol in the book. And that was disappointing for me. In addition to that, the ending was anti-climactic and predictable. As soon as they all left the beach without Halle, it was obvious she was going to die. And even though I saw it coming, I dreaded it. I actually liked all of the characters, and even when it got messy I still wanted them to be happy. Of course, after the "thing" happens, the story just fades out with its little message. In summation: I really liked this book! But being sci-fi, I expected more than a high school drama. It really didn't need the sci-fi backdrop in the end. That just might be my bias though. It just felt like an anti-climactic, missed opportunity. Basically, I would read a sequel but not when I'm in the mood for science fiction.

I flipped back to find the last book I read by Kristin Hannah, and it was Winter Garden, and I see the similarities between that book and The Nightingale. Both are about two sisters who are as different as night and day. One stays home while the other chases her dreams. The difference is that The Nightingale is historical fiction about the German invasion of France and the Holocaust. Two sisters who are always at odds with each other, while protecting their family. Vianne stays home in their small town while Isabelle joins the resistance against Germany, showing amazing daring and strength. Vianne plays it safe at first, but later discovers her own strength in protecting the children left behind in the war. All the while I was reading this book, I kept thinking of All the Light We Cannot See by Anthony Doerr, which also centers on the German invasion of France but from a different aspect. Both books were often painful to read. I was thankful for the bit of parallel story in Nightingale, as it left me with an unexpected bittersweet ending.

I will be continuing with this series as I can't wait to find out what happens with Chrissy's trouble making brother in Full Contact. Pre-order from Amazon here. The main plot was based on murky and fuzzy conversations between the couple. I skimmed a lot in the last half. Jaime was beat up by some thugs and is recovering psychologically and physically. She is an heiress but keeps her name and money a secret. She believes she is unattractive and that men are only attracted to her money. Dom slept with many beautiful women before Jaime. So Jaime compares herself to them and feels lacking. I wanted more plot. This was mostly internal angst about not feeling good enough for the other. EXAMPLES OF CONFLICTS: Jaime keeps her name and wealth a secret. After they are having a wonderful sexual relationship, she tells Dom she has money to live on if she needs it, but she doesn't say how much. Immediately he becomes angry thinking "She was some kind of privileged princess...Crawling in the muck (with him - slumming)." Jaime has a low self image and thinks "How could she ask him to stick himself with a woman who couldn't rise above anything?" Dom's father beat him and his mother. Dom fears he might become abusive like his father. He thinks he's not perfect enough for her. Dom says "I want you to promise never to leave me. But I won't believe you if you (promise)." Jaime says "I want you to promise never to let me go. But it's hard to believe I have the right." FOREIGN WORDS: I was annoyed with so many French words that I did not understand. I wish the author put translations in italics or parentheses after them. She did that occasionally, but not with most. The most frequent French word was Putain. I looked it up in Google translate which said whore or prostitute. That didn't make sense since Dom frequently used it with Jaime. That would be an insult. I think it must be like the f-word or a swear word - not the Google definition. Here's one of his sentences. "That sounds like a good place to start over. With only you. Putain, I would love to have a base like that." COVER PICTURE WRONG: Dom has shaggy rebel black hair. Dom felt bigger than most men, oversized and clumsy. His hands were giant, hard laborer's hands. The guy on the cover looks delicate and slim with neat short hair. DATA: Narrative mode: 3rd person. Story length: 290 pages. Swearing language: strong but not often used. Sexual language: mild. Number of sex scenes: about 5, a few long. Setting: current day Paris, France. Copyright: 2013. Genre: contemporary romance.

A beautiful book about a difficult subject: a child with cancer. Andrew Grey handled it magnificently. We see the reality of coping with a long, painful treatment program, and the sheer emotional damage of having to be strong for the child. Add to that when Ken, the adoptive father, loses his partner of two years, Mark, when Mark bales during a period of remission. It's amicable enough (as much as such things can be), but it leaves Ken alone and very vulnerable as Hanna gets ill again. The rest of the book follows Hanna's treatment and the entry of Ken's mute neighbour, Patrick, into the scene. Patrick himself has had his share of angst - he lost his voice after being injured in the throat. We later learn  that he was a professional singer, and lost not just his voice but his career and his first love: singing. This is a definite 5-star book, if only because of the way it touched me and had me in frequent floods of tears. If a book touches you like that, it's good. Thank you Andrew, for taking on such a difficult subject. A word about the cover: it was only as I read I realised the significance of the hat. What a great image and well handled by L.C. Chase, an artist I haven't seen a lot of at Dreamspinner, but one I often like.

The two most important key words here are "amusing" and "erotic" with a heavy emphasis on the amusing side, and really I would only categorize this as "light to mild eroticism." Yes, I enjoyed reading this! And no I am not ashamed! I still maintain that a lot of people take this book way too seriously. Here is what I liked: Ana is a very normal girl. Yes she's annoying. And yes she constantly changes her mind. However, like many girls/women she doesn't have a lot of sexual experience, she's self-conscious about her body and thoughts. And most importantly, she's afraid of disappointing and/or making men mad, which I think is a particularly strong cord to strike for a majority of modern women. In that respect, I commend E.L. James. Christian is not a normal guy and this works good as a contrast to Ana. He is, by his own immission "fifty shades of fucked up" and its hard to tell which aspect of his childhood effected him the most: his abusive crack-whore mother, or the unusually achieving family he was adopted into. I like how mercurial he came across as, and its clear James herself was a little bit in love with him. The play-up of power in the relationship - both Ana and Christian have equal power over the other, but neither of them really realizes it until the end. Speaking of the end: nicely done E.L. James! The theme of "what is right vs what is wrong" received a wonderful concerto here. This book started as Twilight fan fiction!??! Hmmm.... Okay I can see that. Though, this was also a negative because a few times I got distracted by noting the similarities, like, Mia is so the Alice of the piece. The sex. Things I didn't like: The insta-love! I wish the relationship had been a bit more gradual. Less lust/love at first sight and more character driven. I saw little hints of this, i.e. Christian "rescuing" Ana after she got too drunk and sleeping in the same bed with her, something that up until that time had never happened before, or Ana trying to understand his BDSM lifestyle. But still, this left me dissatisfied. The repetitiveness of the writing. Words like "Heady" and "Inwardly" something multiple times within the page, very distraction. The "Inner Goddess," though I liken this to Ally McBeal's dancing baby as internal psyche, and Ana's "subconscious" and/or "inner sub." I've never run across a character with so many conflicting inner monologues. All in all, it kept me reading, laughing, and enjoying, which for me is all that really counts. This was my second read through, and I've already finished the series, but I wanted to prepare myself for the film. [image error] I'm really excited for this one, though I worry that the sexuality of the book will get lost in the rating translation for the film. I would think something like HBO might do better justice to it.

This book was poetic in an unexpected way. I love the music tie-ins. I was that teenager who wrote poems and listened to music to try to find the perfect song with the perfect lyrics to describe how I was feeling. (Okay, okay, sometimes I still do this even though I'm in my mid 20s). This booked tapped into that by starting chapters with music lyrics and I LOVED that. And I related to that. I love the way the flashback stories are immersed in present-time. I also really love the guy POV, which I don't think I've read too often. Somehow this book made me sympathize with a guy who  slept around with groupies to numb his pain . I didn't think I could ever understand a guy's rationale for doing that.. but this book allowed me to see that perspective. I love seeing other's perspectives. So, win/win. I felt that I could really relate to the theme of loss in this book, although it didn't grip me enough to make me cry... And I cry over just about everything. lol So that's why its 4 stars instead of 5. That, and because I found some of the conversation pieces to be awkward and unrealistic. Had I read this at 16, I would have probably loved it more than I currently do. Overall: I really really liked it, and I would recommend it to fans of non-dystopian YA. I liked it a lot, but not enough to re-read it (but then again my to-read list is insanely long and continues to grow so I'm not sure this is saying much haha). And, I will most definitely be reading other works of Gayle Forman in the future!

While reading the final hundred pages of this book, there is one quote that came to mind: "All this has happened before, and all this will happen again." It's from my favourite tv-series Battlestar Galactica  but it could be a tagline on these series as well. I have to admit after book 1 and 2 I thought that these trilogy was really good, but I didn't fully understand the utter brilliance it supposedly had. Now after book 3, I get it. This last book is the culmination of so many things and shows some utter brilliance indeed. One of the things that makes this book so brilliant: Abercrombie gives you a few jaw-dropping electroshocks along the way: Jezal king? Quai actually being Tolomei? The bloody nine killing Tul? which distracts from the real nuclear bomb that has been dropped at the start and is slowly building to general destruction of everything you thought you knew. Of everything that was so carefully constructed in Book 1 when Abercrombie really took his time to build solid foundations for all his characters. Tolkien learnt us to trust the grumpy old wise wizard that lives in seclusion most of the time, but comes out of hiding and heads to court when things get tough. Bayaz seemed to fit that profile, he even got himself a fellowship of his own, but it becomes clear that he is in fact a huge manipulator, power-hungry and he does not care about the consequences of his actions. This book is so complex, so intriguing, so fabulously constructed. At the end you really start wondering whether you have been cheering for the 'bad side' all along. The cost of winning is just too high. Listening to Bayaz stories all of it did happen before, he constructed this world, he casted the characters, he wrote the script and he has been recycling that script for a few decades already. "All this has happened before, and all this will happen again" The book even ends how it began. With Logen jumping/falling off a cliff.

3.5 An almost-now futuristic fantasy/dystopia exploring the implications of our increasingly cyber-connected world. After a whirlwind romance with a coworker at Commspan, a mobile phone company, Briddey Flannigan agrees to undergo EED surgery with boyfriend Trent: implants that will allow them to sense one another's emotions. But when Briddey wakes up from the surgery, it is not Trent to whom she is connected, but Commspan's oddball tech guy, C. B. Schwartz. And it's not just this other person's emotions she's hearing, but his actual thoughts. And he can hear hers, too. Telepathy is real! Comedic mishaps tumble out one fast upon the next as Briddey tries to keep Trent, the EED doctor, her nosy co-workers at Commspan, and her even nosier family from discovering the mistake. And to figure out her increasingly confusing feelings for the fellow now inside her head. Willis has a real gift for fast-paced comedy; her prose reads so quickly, I felt as if I were on the Tilt-a-Whirl, thrilled and laughing because I was at the mercy of the crazy ride. It's definitely an enjoyable read, especially if you like zany comedy, with a lot of rushing around and rapid banter. I don't think, though, that it will stick with me for very long, because I did not find it satisfying either as a romance or as a strong critique of our cyber-connected culture. Briddey, through whom the story is focalized, isn't given much of a character, and she's reactive rather than active, existing to be pushed around by others and by the plot (she also seems largely to function as a way to validate the goodness of the fellow with whom she ends up connected). It's obvious right from the start that boyfriend Trent does not have the best of intentions, so it made it hard for me to feel sympathy for Briddey, who seems to have no clue of Trent's actual character. I also wondered why the fellow with whom she connects would fall for her (did he like her before they could communicate telepathically? Or only after? ), since she doesn't seem to have much of a personality besides damsel-in-distress. I know, I know, this isn't a straight romance, and Briddey as blank slate rather than as fully developed character could just be a function of the genre. But I found it rather unsatisfying. I also did not find the critique of current culture aspect of the dystopian story a very deep one. Willis says on her blog that she didn't think people really understood the downsides of telepathy or constant connection, and she does a good job of showing the potential horrors of being connected to everyone else's thoughts and feelings all the time. But the magical ending--Briddey's precocious niece, who is a natural telepath like C. B., somehow rewrites C. B. 's jamming-all-telepathy program so that only the "natural" (i.e., nice/good) telepaths can now communicate with one another --undercuts that message. Amusingly, our two lovers end up as mystically merged during sexual contact as any lovers in a traditional romance: "And they were both talking at once, their thoughts and feelings tangling together till it was impossible to tell which were whose" (493). A departure from my usual romance reading.
