I think the Cassie Clare comp in the blurb refers to the fact that there are some fleeting similarities between this and the Infernal Devices trilogy, but Dark Metropolis reminded me more of the Something Strange and Deadly series by Susan Dennard. If you enjoyed those books, definitely check this one out!

I really loved reading this book. After finishing, I can see why it won the Hugo - it's not really a novel, but an ode to science fiction and speculative fiction. It's for those lifelong readers who read their way through an awkward adolescence and can't imagine what that period of their life would have been like without books. Since I fall squarely into this category, this book hit home. I feel a little more sympathetic towards people who enjoyed the movie version of Hugo, which was astonishingly terrible but somehow managed to get nominated for all sorts of important awards. Hugo is about the JOY OF MOVIES, and Among Other is about the JOY OF BOOKS. Hugo still sucked, but I get it now, I guess. Among Others follows Morwenna Phelps, who is sent to school in England after her twin dies in an accident. Mori keeps a detailed diary that chronicles the next year in her life, her attempts to escape her mother's (literally) magical influence, and, of course, the books she reads. There are a lot of books. If you've read any of them, each reference is a wink, like when Mori decides to skip over I Capture the Castle because she's not in the mood to read about a siege. Mori's voice and the overall feel of this book make it a lovely, enchanting read. This is not a book that is concerned with conventional plot, and it somehow works. I actually found the "action sequences" of this book tiresome. I wanted to get back to Mori's book club! The reason I rated this four stars is all to do with SPOILERS, so: Around page 80, Mori's estranged father tries to sexually assault her, and Mori's response is something like, "I said no, but perhaps it wouldn't have been so bad!" On one hand, reading Mori's thoughts after that experience was interesting, and the author kept to her voice. On the other, this thoroughly shook me, so I came out of the story. I realized at this point that I was already almost a third of the way through the book and the plot had yet to materialize; it made me impatient and a little annoyed with the slow-moving pace and the tone of the book. I'm not sure if I would have felt the same if I hadn't been shocked by the events. Again, I did love the feel of this book, and the plot is really secondary to Mori's voice, but I hit a weird wall with this episode. From NPR: Librarian Nancy Pearl's Picks for the Omnivorous Reader.

The issue of date rape is a serious one and I thought Ms. Whitney did a good job conveying the confusion, the guilt, the fear, and the desire for normalcy that Alex felt following the incident. I also really liked how Alex's friends supported her and encouraged her. They were wonderful, and the book sends a powerful message that the support of friends can really help the victim of a crime this horrible to recover and feel empowered. But Carter & his friends were one-dimensional bad guys and not nearly as fleshed out. The Mockingbirds is a student group that describes itself as "...Boo Radley and Atticus Finch all rolled into one. And our mission is to make things right. We investigate and try crimes committed by students against their fellow students." The punishment inflicted upon the guilty is to take away what that person loves most. I found the existence of a group like the Mockingbirds very intriguing. The members of this group at the fictional Themis Academy decided they needed to stand up for the kids who suffer mistreatment at the hands of their fellow students. The idea that these students were inspired to stand up for what's right, to protect their classmates and actively work to create a school culture where everyone feels safe and protected, is a really good one. I can see how a group like the Mockingbirds could do a lot of good. But should the Mockingbirds take on a case of date rape? In the end, I say no. This crime is just way too serious to be left up to a student group. And I can't shake the feeling that the book sends a rather dangerous message that adults can't be trusted. Over and over it's stated or implied that adults don't get what the students are going through, that they don't understand them or that they won't take action to deal with problems. All the main characters in the book feel this way. This is a young adult book, and to send the message that you can't go to an adult when faced with a real crisis feels irresponsible.

A very solid mystery. Kind of a pastiche rather than trying to mimic Conan Doyle's style -- which I can totally understand, if Horowitz was aiming at a general audience who are used to different language and different style (e.g. if you look at the beginning of the Hound, the opening is slow and without action until we get to the story of the hound, whereas a modern mystery or thriller will generally open with an action scene). One of the most interesting things I found in here was the lavish use of description, which having just read a series with a distinct lack of description, was quite visceral at times and always pleasing. It's also fairly self-referential/metafictional; Horowitz is clearly trying to smooth over elements of the canon in terms of social mores, writing quirks, and the portrayal/treatment of particular characters, and at some points he chooses to bring this into the foreground. The final conclusion to the mystery works well with the statement at the beginning that the story would have shocked Victorian readers' sensibilities too much, and the inclusion of Moriarty in opposition to the House of Silk serves well to illuminate his character as an "honourable" criminal (although I do think naming him was too much -- surely any reader would have worked out who he was, and leaving him unnamed would have been more interesting).

** spoiler alert ** While I found this book to be a fun read... that's all it was. Things change drastically in this book and without warning. When I look back now, I can almost see where the authors were building in this change, but at the same time, I can see where the characters (Tobias and Noah mostly) weren't building up to this change. All along, the series is about Noah and Tobias getting together and working on BDSM things together, as a couple. It was Phan who couldn't deal with being apart from his Master. And that never changed. After all the hard work several people put into helping him, going back to his Master is the magic cure-all. Literally. And it all works out like magic. Didn't know this series featured a fantasy aspect did you? Yeah, it does. Noah didn't want Phan to come between him and Tobias. It was one of his fears. And then in the blink of an eye he lets Phan move in with them. Temporarily, sure, it might be a good thing, but it only served to turn the book into a threesome, when all along, we were lead to believe that the resulting couple in the end would be Noah and Tobias only. Someone commented on Amazon that Phan should have gotten his own book, and I agree! Perhaps even his own three book series. The current series could have ended nicely at the end of book three. Then let Phan have his own story, where he works hard to get better and find the right Master. Here, though, Phan doesn't have to do a damn thing to get better. What's up with that? Noah hardly works on his BDSM, going deeper and further. He has one scene with Tobias, who comments that they'll have to work more on his sensory deprivation. Do they? No. They never get to it. Instead, the book is filled with too much plain sex and a lot of boring conversations about the house, about therapy, about their jobs, Phan's role in the household... They never leave the house and all they do is talk and have sex. Speaking of issues, there were a lot of them. And all of them were HUGE issues. But the thing that bugged me was that they appear in one chapter and in the next they're gone, magically erased and everything is made better again by more sex and talk. I always had a problem with the lack of scenes about Noah's job in the first three books. I wanted to know more. I wanted to see him in uniform more, perhaps even get a call while at the house on the weekend. But there was almost nothing. We know he loves his job, a lot. And then, finally, this book has him in uniform a lot more, and we learn that everyone suddenly has a uniform fetish they didn't have before. When Noah's in a shootout and Carol is shot, his issues are huge, but are gone almost instantly. He goes back to work, but we never hear how that first day goes. Everything seems to be fine, until the day he shows up at home early and announces that he quit. What the fuck? Never saw that coming. Never. When you train to be a police officer, it's hard, it's rough as all hell, and you should know by the end whether or not you can handle the job. They weed you out as they train you, and you know full well that you'll be aiming your gun at people, threatening to use it, never mind knowing that at some point you'll have to shoot it for real. At people. How he got through all that still wanting to be a police officer, I don't know. Everyone fell in love with each other in the beginning and that alone solved all their problems. So... what's the point of the book? Yeah, there wasn't much. But, I will say it was entertaining, and I was laughing a few times, but by the end, I was sick and tired of the sex scenes. When I was looking for a good place to pause while I slept at night, I stopped mid-sex. That's not good. Half of what was mentioned on the back of the book doesn't happen until close to the end of the book... um... what's up with that? I don't get that at all. I kept waiting and waiting, and rereading the back to make sure it still said what I thought it had, because it sounded really interesting, what with more about Noah's job and all. *sigh* It really was a big letdown. I will say though, I LOVED the scene in the beginning when Phan's father shows up and Noah answers the door in full uniform. That was AWESOME. And when he offered to let Phan move in, I only thought it was temporary, so it was ok at that point in the book. I also loved the scenes where Tobias let Noah dominate him, although I felt both scenes were too close together and I started to worry that the dynamic of their relationship would change permanently to switch, which wouldn't be the same at all. But I liked the fact that Phan wasn't about the dominate Tobias, that it could only be Noah, which did help to cement them in a special relationship set apart from that of their relationships with Phan. Still, Phan should only have been a temporary guest. All in all, this book could have been so much better than it was.

What are the chances you'd ever meet someone like that? he wondered. Someone you could love forever, someone who would forever love you back? And what did you do when that person was born half a world away? The math seemed impossible. As I read this again, I thought to myself: what are the chances you'd ever read a book as precious like this? I want to say it isn't like any other. It made me feel a thousand different emotions. It made me feel alive. It made me feel like being in love. That's what this is all about--love. And I love reading books like this. You won't find two of them completely the same. And Eleanor and Park did a good job of being really unique and special and beautiful. I don't like you. Sometimes I think I live for you. I don't think I even breathe when we're not together. And I live for the pleasure of seeing made-up lives in my head; living and feeling everything with them. It makes me feel happy. It makes me feel sad. It makes me feel alive. This book makes me feel alive. And ecstatic. And heartsick. And sad. And giddy. And a lot more. Eleanor and Park just takes you to their world, which I can say, is almost real. People don't always fit in. You never know who you'll fall in love with. You never know when things are going to get better. But there is always hope; and love. And it keeps people going. And this is what I love about the book. Despite everyone and everything, people always get their happiness. Happiness doesn't always last and it isn't always at the last part. Pain and Happiness always go together but not necessarily in that order. So when I thought that after everything, their happiness is far done, I didn't think the book would end with: Eleanor hadn't written him a letter, it was a postcard. Just three words long. My heart just shattered and got back together in pure bliss. We never really know what those words could be, but I think every sane mind would think what I'm thinking right now. So maybe they still aren't done with their cycle of Pain and Happiness. Well, that's life. I think I could marry this book.

This book is wonderfully absurd. If that's not quite an oxymoron, it's pretty close, but still an apt description. For those of you who haven't had the pleasure of reading Dave Barry's other work, please stop what you're doing (yes, right now), and go read his entire collected works. Now, once your stomach has stopped aching from the uncontrollable laughter, come back and we will talk about this book. Done now? OK. The main reason I picked up Peter and the Starcatchers is because I wanted to listen to something else narrated by Jim Dale, the incomparable narrator of the Harry Potter books. When I stumbled across this series, written by one of my all-time favorite American humorists (alive, that is - don't worry Mr. Twain), I had to listen. Ridley Pearson who? Apparently, he's a famous writer too. Whatever. The premise of the book is simple; it is an attempt to lay out the story of how Peter Pan came to be forever young, with the power to fly and with his own personal fairy. The book is very well written, and highly enjoyable, if somewhat predictable (I mean, we already know how it ends. How shocking can it really be?). There are some genuine laugh-out-loud moments:  my favorite is when the special sail that the pirate Black Stache has crafted for his ship is revealed to be a giant brassiere. It's a great story for middle graders, and very family friendly. The plot is action-packed with never a dull moment. Lots of sword play, kidnappings, treasure, battles, and the like to keep the boys interested. Only a very little bit of violence (as we know - someone has to lose a hand at some point!). Overall, a great listen. There are a couple other books in the series, and I will definitely be listening to those too.

First read in German in April 2013, these are my thought after rereading it in January 2017. Alright, it's absolutely no secret that I love the Graceling Realm trilogy and this book in particular. Rereading this trilogy has been one of the greatest experiences ever because it made me realize just how much I love everything about these books. Bitterblue is especially wonderful because it brings together all of our beloved characters. It makes me so happy to see them all interact together, to see their strong bounds. In general I just love Bitterblue's relationships with her family, friends and also advisers. Especially how intimate some of her friendships with some men are, without ever implying anything romantic between them. We need more male/female friendships portrayed like that in YA. But also the romance in this book is so wonderful and subtle. It's so far from many other YA romances where it's the situation of "I'd die for you, I can't live without you, I'd give up anything for you." Neither of the characters included in the main romance ever forget their important tasks and that they are needed by other people. They get off track, they are sad or worried about the other person but they don't drop everything for their love interest. I think the use of basically no tropes (as far as I can tell) is what makes this book most wonderful to me. It's what makes the friendships, the romance, just the characters in general so great to read about. Never once am I annoyed at any of them for doing stupid, not understandable things. There's no love triangle, no pretty dresses trope, no insta-love, no chosen one and even the little instances of characters lying to each other make ACTUAL SENSE and are not used just to frustrate the reader! I even love the slow pacing in this book. This is a book of over 500 pages that I never, not on one single page, get tired of. I love all the little adventures Bitterblue has, the political intrigue, the mystery that takes so long to get solved. All the times Bitterblue spends in the library, the kitchen or anywhere else in her castle, simply to find out more about how the people around her live and work. The way Cashore portrays that Bitterblue is a queen that is kinda ignorant and oblivious to some of the things going on around her BUT throughout this books is open and willing to learn about all of it is wonderful. In general I love the way Bitterblue develops as a character. She had to grow up fast to be a queen and has always taken this responsibility very serious. She loves her kingdom and the people in it but she is so removed from the actual people living in her kingdom. The journey Bitterblue goes on in this book does not only make her a better, more understanding person but also a greater queen. One of the most interesting aspects of the book is the main villain of the story. I know many people find it weird that Leck, while being dead for over eight years, is still the main villain of the story. But I think it shows what a powerful and horrible King Leck really was. This book doesn't need a new villain. The old one is still present enough, haunting everyone and it makes sense. Introducing a new villain is in no way necessary, the few, "smaller" antagonists that we have throughout the story are more than enough to keep the story going. I think everything else would have undermined the power and influence Leck had on EVERYONE in his kingdom. The first two books are just not enough to even slightly grasp the power and influence Leck really had! I also love how Cashore includes diversity in this book in particular. There are two same sex couples in this book and it's never really mentioned as problematic, except for when it comes to royalty and heirs, although it is mentioned as something that's gonna be changed in the future (it's just that in the particular kingdom where this is an occurring situation, the current king is an asshole). Also Cashore always takes care of mentioning contraception in everyone of these books, which is also something we need more often in YA. Especially in Fantasy where there's no condoms or any other modern forms of contraception, authors like to act as if it's not an issue in these worlds. Cashore handles it subtly but as a reader you always know it's taken care of. I guess it's clear from all of this how much I love this trilogy and would recommend it to everyone. I will recommend it till the end of my life. I think there's no YA Fantasy that you can compare to this. It is one of a kind. Unique but so simplistic. This trilogy will forever have a huge place in my heart and I'm forever thankful for discovering it. Trigger warnings for rape, abuse, violence, self harm.

I received a copy of this title thru NetGalley for an honest review. Hakwins's latest story is the tale of Prince Alexsey of Oxenberg and Brownwyn. Alexsey is the brother of a previous Hawkins hero Wulf. Bronwyn is 24 and content with her life in Scotland. She helps her inventor father with his correspondence and patents and her stepmother with her step-sisters. Hawkins uses the framework from Cinderella, but instead of the traditional evil step relations, Bronwyn is very close with her step-sisters and gets along with her step-mother, Lady Malvenia. When a neighbor decides to open up his castle for a house party, Prince Alexsey is one of the guests. Like any ambitious mother, Malvenia is excited by the prospect of her daughter becoming a princess. I really enjoyed the interactions between the three siblings and how supportive they were of each other. I also enjoyed the development of Alexsey and Bronwyn's relationship. Alexsey at no time wanted Bronwyn to be anything other than she was and he appreciated her inner qualities as much as her outer beauty. I found this to be a quick, easy read that engaged my attention. There was a twist at the end that I appreciated and I always enjoy the interactions of Tata with her grandsons. I would recommend this to anyone looking for an engaging historical romance and am looking forward to the next entry in the Oxenburg series.
I know I'm a 22-year-old reading young adult books, but even so, the Percy Jackson series seems a bit juvenile to me.

This book was awesome; I didn't expect anything that happened in this book! It developed the VDF plot line, as well as the Baudelaire and Quagmire parallels in a really fun way. It was more of a mystery this time, with actual riddles  the poems Isadora sends to them   for the children to solve. The ending was most certainly not what I was expecting,  I thought the triplets would get caught   but I actually really enjoyed it. The villagers were crazy and loved to follow the rules they had set, which made the story both funnier and annoying. I just wanted them to shut up at points  and stop trying to BURN the children   but I think over all they were pretty funny. I've already started reading The Hostile Hospital and I can't wait to get through it.

Beth Flynn did it again, and she managed to create something outstanding again! It was as amazing as always! <3 I loved that it could bring the same feeling and atmosphere as the Nine Minutes trilogy and I loved meeting with the characters again. The thing that took a little piece of the full 5 star experience for me, that I found the base of the story too similar with Nine Minutes since the relationship between Anthony and Christy also started with an abduction, and I also didn't really love the insta-love in a kind of raw and dark story as this one. But I truly loved it and I highly recommend it! (And this breathtaking cover!! OMG! I wish the Nine Minutes trilogy would be re-released with a similar design!

Well, I certainly got what I asked for. Demonglass was a good sequel, and managed to hook me to the series. The parallel to Bloodline grows and grows and I suspect strongly, infact, that Sophie's mum is related to the Brannicks I hated the Cal angle, because honestly, this book DID not need the love triangle. It's 2am so I'm not writing a more detailed review, but let's just say this series has me hooked. 4/5 stars

I've let this one sit a little while, but I'm still not entirely sure what I think about it. On the one hand, this book REALLY appealed to my love of flawed characters. I think they might have gone a little TOO far with the flaws in our heroine, because for most of the first two thirds of the book I was kind of bothered by how much she seemed to hate everything about herself. And the hero's grumbledypants stoicism did very little for me either. But I loved the fact that they made mistakes and had poor judgement and dealt with consequences. I liked that it didn't always take the easy way in the plot. I loved the world of intrigue and deception we spend the middle third of the book in, even if I hate how many people are portrayed as utterly shallow. On the other hand, as much as I was enraptured by the writing and the world and the story, I finished reading and found the experience... unsatisfying? I don't need a bow tied on or anything, but I felt like some of what was wrapped up didn't need to be while some of what was left open would have been better off given a stronger direction. Strike this, I was unaware this was first in a series. But the writing - I can't even guess at what it was about the book, I sort of want to dissect it from a writing perspective and see if I can figure it out. Because I could not put this book down. I read it faster than I have almost any book this year, staying up late and waking early to get back into the story. I also liked that because of the pov, and the writing, I could totally understand how our heroine got drawn into the Darkling's web and got so ensnared. So many times, when a book like this comes across my desk it's eye-rollingly obvious that something's up with the mysterious stranger and that trusting him is a Very Bad Idea. But in this, I only got a few inklings before we got into the heart of stuff going wrong. I appreciated that. Definitely read this, if you love language and fantasy. You may not like it, but I think reading it is an experience worth giving yourself.

When I first started this book I was a skeptical that I would even finish it. However, after a couple chapters I really started to enjoy it. I know you shouldn't judge a book by its cover but seriously... this cover is just kind of weird... It doesn't do the book justice at all. As other people have said the book needs some editing. What I really liked about the book: *The whole idea of traveling dimensions and having secret powers is really cool *Also, I enjoyed the struggle to find Chloe's missing father and find the artifact. Things I couldn't stand: *How Chloe constantly flipped out over. every. little. thing. I get that she has a short temper, but after her freaking out over the smallest detail for the 4th time, I became annoyed. *The love triangle... nooo, please nooo. It is not necessary at all, but if you ask me I think she should be with Nightshade. Only because Slade is so boring. My favorite part of the book was when Chloe and Nightshade went on the road trip. *When Chloe is fighting with Jess in the library and Jess says, "Little girl, you have no idea who you're talking too." That is not how girls fight! Jess is described as a "Barbie" so she would probably be saying more along the lines of "Skank.." *When Chloe says "OMG." I'm sorry but I cannot picture a girl like her saying that... *Finally, at the end Chloe all of a sudden says she declared for the Society. What about her SKG powers? They were mentioned but never really addressed. All in all this was a good read and I will most likely read the next book in the series :)

For only being 'almost 18' this girl's been through a lot, having lost her parents and now her older brother, too. To honour her brother's last (joking) wish (he was killed in Iraq before this novel begins but wrote her a letter which reached her after the news) Honor decides to drive from Texas to California to see a 'Kyra Kelley' concert to tell the singer about her (late) brother. An ex-friend of her brother's turns up after the funeral and tags along for the ride, and the trip becomes a kind of modern 'pilgrimage'. Books like this do make you wonder. If you're going to make a point of writing a YA where they don't go further than a kiss, why make them so ready to strip down to their underwear as they're driving, simply because it's hot? It's just as well for these two that they're both drop dead gorgeous; this is not the book to help teens feel good about their body-image. There's also some (under-age) drinking, which induces some wild, all-over dancing, just after Honor finds out her brother's car was named after a porn star. A few superstitions pop into the narrative: rubbing St Rita soil at the beginning of the journey for good luck, psychics telling the future and 'the universe' making things work for her, and farewelling dearly departed ones with lanterns at the beach. It was sweet how much Honor's brother had done for her without her knowing, but in the context it all comes across a little too forced and cheesy.

Oh man. Where to start. Okay, here goes: I have mixed feelings about romance novels. I want to love them. Really, I do. But they can be so damn aggravating! Often it's the terrible writing, the failure to even pretend that there's more substance to the story than sex. Or it's the tropes that seem rife throughout the genre - the instalove, the dubious consent between the rake and the innocent virgin, etc. As you might already be able to tell, Cold-Hearted Rake falls into the latter category. We're introduced to Devon, the "rake," and his brother West, the "alcoholic rake," and Devon immediately clashes with Kathleen, the "proper widow." (Can I just say I totally called that the marriage was never consummated .) Devon is pretty much an asshole. He initially plans to kick Kathleen and her sisters-in-law out of the estate he's inherited, which technically is his prerogative, but then when Kathleen is understandably upset by this, he gets mad at her for daring to protest! Other highlights of his behavior include physically detaining her against her will and mocking her for being "frigid" in front of the estate's solicitors. Now, as I mentioned, the whole dubious consent thing is a very real trope in the romance genre, and while I personally can't stand it and I think it reinforces a lot of problematic beliefs about consent, other readers find it enjoyable. And for what it's worth, I don't think the author is trying to imply that Kathleen doesn't want Devon's attentions deep down. But seriously, every intimate scene between them starts with her saying no. And he ignores her every time until finally she says yes. (On one occasion, he magnanimously informs her that "You'll have the choice of whether we go to bed before the talk, or after.") Not cool in my book. Consent issues aside, Devon's "rakish" behavior is actually very unconvincing. We're repeatedly told he's a rake - he's slept with so many women! He brawls in public! He gambles! The "Ravenel temper"! etc. But apart from being an asshole to Kathleen, it takes him seemingly no time to abandon his former lifestyle and take on an estate he swore up and down only a couple of chapters ago that he wanted nothing to do with. And of course he's a fair and just estate owner who takes an immediate interest in the poor farmers, yada yada yada, and then later he saves a second-class baby! What a swell guy! West, Devon's brother, is equally unconvincing. We're told he's an alcoholic, to the point where it's noticeably affecting his physical appearance, but a few chapters into the story he decides to become sober and does so with only the inconvenience of a minor hangover. No relapses, no desire to hit the bottle again, not even the slightest hint of difficulty in breaking the habit. He then goes on to throw himself into the workings of the estate, and denounces his former London life as unsatisfying. All told, there's even less evidence of his "rakish" behavior in this book than with Devon. But back to Devon for a moment. After all the women he's supposedly had during his life as a "rake," setting aside the fact that he really isn't much of one, he falls for Kathleen because... um... you know, the author never really explains that. Like, she's beautiful? And something about her manner is pleasing? I read the entire book and I still have no idea what made Kathleen so special compared with all the other women. Like Devon and West, she suffers from being described in a certain way at the beginning of the novel (she'll never cry!) only to have that immediately undone (oh, just kidding, she's crying). She seems to have good intentions, but honestly there's not much to her character. Now for my last major gripe with the book: Winterborne was a fucking DICK and I was very glad when he and Helen ended their engagement... but then I read the epilogue and it looks like they're going to get back together in the sequel?! I suppose I should have known, considering the behavior this author's excused so far. I was beginning to think it hypocritical that Winterborne should be the villain for assaulting Helen and threatening to rape Kathleen (the threat was implicit but certainly there), when Devon was doing the exact same thing. But now it looks like Winterborne will have a chance to redeem himself. Why? Because fuck this shit, that's why. Oh, and of course there's a baby. Of course. So what did I enjoy about this book? It was well-written, and in spite of his failure to be properly "rakish" (or perhaps because of it) I liked West's character. I also liked Helen, Cassandra, and Pandora. I might read the summaries for the rest of the series to see what happens to everyone, but I think I'll give the books themselves a pass.
Of course I loved it. But...  there are still some things left unanswered. Where did Kell come from and how is it he ended up with the royal family? I really wanted/hoped that would be answered.

My feelings about this are so 50/50, they nearly cancel each other out. First, the good: the Russian-inspired world of Shadow and Bone is really the highlight of the book. Leigh Bargudo's world-building was a pleasure to get lost in, especially for an Imperial Russia fan like myself. I also loved that the book made a strong point about how women give away their power for the approval of men. And then there's the Darkling! I haven't had a crush on a character like this in ages, and then he's the bad guy! I wanted the girl to end up with the bad guy so much! I may be reading the rest of the series just to get more Darkling, because even though Grisha world is lush, the ending of the book was so cheesy and contradictory to itself that I actually laughed out loud. I'm going to try the next book because I know so many people who love this trilogy, and I really hope that it can redeem itself.
I did quite enjoy this book for the most part, but honestly the end kinda lost me a bit.

When I read who was the "hero" in this book, I though "here goes another Styxx". But man was I wrong! This books was just incredible, I love how we see this whole new side of the story! I love the fact that Jules just let go of the past and accepted his new family and made peace with his past. I can't wait for the next book on these series. I also remember all of the children in Devyn's book and now I understand who they came to be Tavali! Another great book by another great writer.

This was a very enjoyable collection of stories, the title story "Story of Your Life' being my personal favorite. Though I enjoyed all but one of the stories, many of these stories kind of reminded me of OTHER works I've read. Here are my brief thoughts on some of the stories: Tower of Babylon - a fun, almost parable-like story of some miners climbing the miles-high "Tower of Bablyon" in order to dig into the floor of the heavens, an apparent ceiling. However, it reminded me very much of the ending of Stephen King's Dark Tower. When Hillalum climbs out of the ceiling and finds himself back in the desert outside of Babylon, this reminded me very much of Roland ascending the Dark Tower and finding himself back in the desert chasing the Man in Black. Understand - an interesting if not overly-heady tale about someone who receives an experimental drug treatment for brain damage and develops super-human intelligence. Reminded me VERY much of a cross between Limitless with Bradley Cooper and Lucy. Division By Zero - An interesting story of someone who becomes distraught because they prove that everything the world knows about mathematical principles is founded on a flawed assumption. Odd story. Story of Your Life - A fascinating story about the results in a linguists life after a First Contact. This story is great and has some unexpected twists. Seventy-Two Letters - A fun premise and interesting story about a 19th-century world where animation of inanimate objects through written "naming" is a valid and thriving science. HOWEVER, the ending was extremely abrupt and seemed rushed. The Evolution of Human Science - What science might be like if some humans became so intelligent that they no longer operated on the same plane of existence as the rest of mankind... Hell is the Absence of God - What if angelic visitations were sort of like localized natural disasters? While an interesting premise, I really didn't like this story at all. I thought the overall message was extremely convoluted. It seemed the whole moral of the story is that God sucks and is unjust. I just didn't see the value in this story beyond the idea behind the disaster-producing visitations. Liking What You See - A very interesting social commentary about judging people based on their looks and what could happen if you could turn that natural tendency off. Loved it Overall, I may not have picked up this collection if not for the fact that it was September's book pick for the Sword and Laser Bookclub. I would really like to see a full-length novel from Ted Chiang. Four solid stars and highly recommended.

This series started out okay. I'm not a big fan of this series since the second and last book are basically a disgusting mess, but the first book was  okay . Honestly I can't say anything else other than that. Sorry Jenny Han, you tried, but you failed with this series. If you want to start reading this because of the oh-so-glorious review. Think again.

The Iron King started out intriguing and reminded me a bit of those scary movies in which innocent kids have hyperactive imaginations and call out 'mommy!'. Meghan's life seems normal. She attends high school like any other teenager. When her sixteenth birthday comes round, she begins to notice things that other people can't see and she discovers her brother Ethan has been replaced by a changeling. It is up to her to venture into the Nevernever and bring him back. The lead up to her 'quest' was a promising start. However once we enter Nevernever, things go wacko. I felt a complete change in the pacing. There was not a single moment where Meghan stopped to take a breath. Strange and stranger things are thrown her way and we are given bucket and bucket loads of descriptions. It was a lot to take in! I found Meghan to be idiotic and less likeable as I continued reading. When a Chimera charges at her, what does she do? She closes her eyes hoping her death would be quick and painless. When someone warns her not to eat too many summerpods/faerie food, what does she do? She eats the whole lot and faints. When she discovers a drop of rain burn through her pants, what does she do? She puts her arm out to verify that it's acid rain! Cringe-tastic! Meghan was frequently a damsel in distress and her knight in shiny armour (figuratively speaking because of the iron allergy thing) happened to be Ash, an Unseelie/Winter Fey. Ooh, so forbidden! Unfortunately I found their development to be lacking. I liked the concept of the Iron Fey (faeries of technology and progress) . It was a cool idea and that part felt original among the the other things which brought Alice in Wonderland and Narnia to mind. Overall, an okay read.

I read the Spiderwick Chronicles back when I was quite young, maybe eight or nine. My sister and I read the crap out these books (we must have read them 15 times, no joke) and I've been wanting to revist this series and the wonderful fantasy world that Holly and Tony created for awhile now but I've finally gotten around to it. The writing partnership of Holly Black and Tony DiTerlizzi is remarkable and this series is by far some of the most well written literature that I've ever read. The three main characters, Jared, Simon, and Mallory, are so relatable and realistic. I can relate to each of them in a different way and I think most readers will feel the same. I felt like The Seeing Stone had expanded a lot of the world that was created in this series. Readers get a lot of new information on new creatures and a new character is introduced. The Seeing Stone is a lot faster paced than the first book. I loved the illustrations and artwork a lot. There's wasn't really any descriptions on the creatures so I had to rely on the illustrations a lot. Overall, I loved this book and I highly recommend this series to readers of all ages. It's such a great fantasy series and it's amazingly well written. I can't wait to continue rereading this series.

Where has this series been all my life??? I'm not going to leave a long drawn out review because what else can I say that hasn't been said already? This is not typically a series I would read, simply because I love a HEA and I knew I wasn't really going to get the kind that I like here. Anyway, I had been reading a bunch of sugary sweet books recently and I needed something a bit edgier. So, Friday night I picked up The Siren and read straight through Monday night when I finished the series. WHAT A RIDE. What a wonderful story teller Ms. Reisz is! I didn't feel the story lagging at all. My only complaint:  I don't get why he would sleep with Grace unprotected....especially after Nora had been through so much. It just seemed disloyal because he said he's only slept with people he loves. And the whole baby thing is just weird. I wasn't a fan of that. Frankly, I don't even know why Grace was in this book. I wanted to skip through her parts.

I think the purpose of the 3 amplifiers was a good twist and made sense to the whole scheme of the stories. However, I did not understand how they are created in the first place and the ending...when  the Darkling died? I mean the way he died after all the hoo ha of how powerful people are difficult to kill? kind of changed my opinion of the plot, hence, 3 stars. Mal redeemed himself here. Finally, I can see how he is a plausible love interest, although my preference is for Nikolai (if only his feelings are true). Still, I did enjoy this book better than the previous 2.

The Wind Through the Keyhole was a very enjoyable listen, and Stephen King read it to me. He's not as good as his usual narrator, but he's still a pretty damn good storyteller (in the reading aloud sense, as well as the writing sense). With this 4.5 installment of The Dark Tower, King weaves a story inside a story inside a story, with each one drawing me in. This was a solid 5 star read almost all the way through. Working inwards out, the fable of Tim Stoutheart is near perfect  with the tiger turning into Merlin being a bit meh  . The Covenant Man is an incarnation of a familiar villain, and one that is sunning, sinister and far more enjoyable than his tittering version in other books. I'm not sure why, but the saddest part of this story for me was  when King describes the death of the dragon who had spared Tim's life after the boy jumped on his head; a dragon breathing fire to fight back a fierce ice storm in an ultimately futile effort just seems about the saddest thing I can think of... or at least want to think of; sadly poetic and very depressing Then there's the tale of Roland's youth, spent chasing the Skin Man with a rather bland character, Jaime De Curry. Perhaps trying to distinguish Jaime from Cuthbert and Alain, King gave the boy almost no personality. He didn't matter to me and so he didn't matter to the story, so I take no points off for that. I only take points off for the ending - after a good, strong build up and investigation, the anticipation great and the suspense nail-biting, the big reveal and rushed ending was a bit of a let down - good, but not King great. As for the main storyline, we don't get much beyond a stark blast, but it plays out well and gives more insight into the characters. Given that this book was written after the next book chronologically story-wise, I didn't expect much to happen in that regard. All in all, a darn good book that earns a ranking equal to its numbering: 4.5

I put off reading this after finding out Glenn dies  but eventually I decided to read it. While I'm really sad that my favorite character is dead, I still enjoy the comic and I am hoping for some glorious violent payback.

Great ending to this trilogy! I loved that Luis was more centred than his brothers when it came to getting involved in the Latino Blood. There was something there in the end that screamed "magic wand! ", but I decided to let it slide and just enjoy this book.

What a pleasant surprise! This is my first book that I've read from his author and I'm sure it won't be the last. When I saw the blurb for the story I thought 'That sounds like an interesting story, why not give it a go. ', and that's exactly what I did. So happy how the story turned out. There is basically almost no drama and what little it is it's done in a very good way with great emotional background. Also, I loved that the heroine, Trish, and the hero, Boone, didn't have moments of doubt about each other. That really added more to the story and I believed in their relationship more. Had one of them chosen a different path, I'm sure I wouldn't like the story as I do now. I'm not sure, if this is a slow burn romance story but to me it felt like the perfect pace. They didn't fall in bed with each other at first sight and that's what this story needed. They definitely became great friends and that's what both needed to happen first. I enjoyed both Trish and Boone's character. They are just such fun to read about. And the way they are with each other, yeah, they make a great team, professionally and personally. As the blurb says, they a re co-stars of a movie they are making and Boone has some real trouble diving into his character and making him come alive on the screen. He's making Trish and the crew some gray hairs and at the final decision of the director, he has ten days to make a brilliant performance or the movie whole is canceled. And that's where Trish, his co-star comes in. At first she wants to kill him for not taking the role seriously enough but as they spent more time together, just the two of them, she starts to see the real Boone, not the partying rock star that he makes everyone believe he is. Boone is an amazing person who cares for his family more than anything and that really comes to show as the story goes on. It's safe to say that I loved how the story progressed. Trish really knew how to be a first class actress but that's not all that she is. She loves her family, has a big heart, can be stubborn, sometimes a bit pushy and just knows how to handle Boone. She pushes his limits and helps him defeat some of his demons that are holding him back from shooting one particular scene in the movie. I can't tell you enough times how much I loved this story. Since this is a series we also get to see characters from previous books and I have to say that I really liked them all. Trish's brohers are so OTT protective, it's insane but that only makes them that more adorable and likable. Boone's family is super great, too! And don't even got me started on the cute little kitten that captured both Boone and Trish's hearts. Soooo cute!!! Just for that reason alone I would give this book a chance. I definitely recommed it! Safety:  Totally safe. The OW/OM drama that happened...I wouldn't even say that's drama or anything the like. It's such a brief thing, really... Apart from that, nothing happens that would be worth mentioning. As for ages, I'll be honest I forgot the numbers but they are not that far apart age-wise. Also, Boone is not a man-ho and he hasn't kissed or been with a woman for six months. ARC received in exchange for an honest review.

I was expecting some insight into obviously troubled young Dahmer's life, not some toolbag, who seems to have helped ostracize him, humblebragging about having been a minor acquaintance and classmate in high school.

Young adult contemporary books for someone my age are hard for me to like because I just don't feel like they are that original or interesting. I can't say this book was original, but I absolutely loved it. This book follows a girl named Andie whose father was recently involed in a scandal and therefore her summer plans are in complete disarray. It is such a simple concept, but the way Matson wrote this story made it powerful. What I loved about this story was that it was a strong character story. I loved the main character, Andie. I felt like I was reading about a real person, who had both strengths and weaknesses in her overall character. I loved that she made some mistakes and face setbacks but also used her resourcefulness and ambition to deal with those mistakes. I found her group of friends to be real and despite being more popular than my group of friends in high school were, I actually did relate to their group dynamic. The only one I did not like was Toby. I found her to whiny and selfish and got tired of her "drama" very quickly  I also hated her obsession with Wyatt and felt she was entitled to him, even when he told her he was not interested. I hated Toby so much I sided with Bri when she ended up getting together with Wyatt  . I also adored Andie's love interest Clark as he felt like a real person. I can see why Andie liked him, but I felt he had a personality outside of that. I loved that he was a fantasy writer despite his young age. I wonder if the pressure he faced in writing his third novel in the series was the same as many writers feel when writing new books  . But what I loved about this story was that the romance was balanced with other aspects of Andie's life from her friends, her father and her new dogwalking job. I really felt like I was reading a slice of life piece rather than a structured story because it felt real to me. The only aspect where it didn't was the climax, where I felt too much fell apart but I actually did like where we ended up. I felt that Andie's friends being mad at her for not telling them about Bri and Wyatt along with Clark and Andie no longer speaking and her father's job being in jeopardy was a bit too over the top for me. HoweverI did like in the end that Andie and Clark got together and Andie will be working towards being a vet. I also loved that Toby and Bri did not automatically become friends again and that their friendship did not survive that "betrayal"  . This is a very long contemporary book but in my opinion worth it as I found it reads very quickly. It is the best young adult contemporary I have ever read because I felt it did the best of balancing all aspects of Andie's life and was written in an interesting and fun way. I think this is the perfect summer contemporary and I am so happy that I have read this book because I absolutely loved it.

Well, that was a rather disappointing sequel to Bumped. It seems that the books spends ages to get from point A to point B - these being the only two points adressed in the whole novel. Basically, Harmony is pregnant with Jondoe's twins and about to give birth. Meanwhile, Melody is faking a pregnancy and waiting to come clean. (We're not quite sure why, since in my opinion the revolutionary "Mission" could easily have been completed without that prank ...) In the end, Harmony gives her twins away to the parents who were supposed to get Melody's twins , and everyone is happy. Oh my grace !

Not what I expected at all! But I enjoyed it more than I thought I would. I love that Beauty Queens turns everything on it's head. It takes practically every stereotype about girls and beauty and says "okay but here's how it really is." Libba Bray manages to take a concept that could have been ridiculous, make it even MORE ridiculous, but also say a lot. This is satire, so the reader does need to suspend disbelief and understand that yes, it is ridiculous. However, that outrageous humor leads to bold statements, especially all of the advertising bits. They were gold. I definitely recommend Beauty Queens, crazy evil dictator, bodacious pirates, sequins and all.
If you like books that complete take you out of your own experience, this is a good one.

This classic is actually quite a short novella. Here's a summary, and I won't worry about avoiding plot spoilers for something as short and famous as this. Santiago is an elderly Cuban fisherman who's considered bad luck because he's had no catch for 84 days. The parents of his young helper, Manolin, have ordered their son to join a luckier boat instead. One day out on the sea alone, the old man manages to hook a mighty, 18-foot long marlin who defies getting reeled in and drags him way out to sea. Neither man nor fish are willing to give in, but finally Santiago manages to kill the beast. On the way home with his prize, sharks pick up the scent and rip its bones clean. That's it, folk. I could get away with a one sentence review. 'What a bummer!' Naw, since this little tale won the Pulitzer Prize of 1953, I'll thresh it out a bit. Critics say you have to 'delve beneath the surface' to get the most from this book, which I guess is an apt analogy considering it's set on the sea. You'll find many educational websites attempting to convince us all how brilliantly multi-layered this story is. Smart people think it's a wonderful fable or allegory, where everything represents something deeper and more profound. But then I stumbled across a quote by Ernest Hemingway himself, claiming that this is a load of bunk. 'The sea is the sea, the old man is an old man, the sharks are all sharks, no better and no worse. All the symbolism that people say is s**t.' Okay, since he's the author, I'm more than happy to believe him. Maybe my main impressions were about other readers' impressions. I saw a lot of animosity on Goodreads reviews! A couple of people wrote something like, 'Just cut the line, why don't you? Put us all out of our misery.' Then angry fans ticked them off in the comments for being so flippant about such a magnificent book, yada, yada, yada. 'It's people like you who make the world such a shallow place' (Another sea analogy, whether or not they realised it). I understand the 'cut the line' mentality. In our times, we're saturated with messages to chase our dreams and refuse to settle for less than the very best. It causes a lot of prolonged stress and suffering when perhaps we really should give up. But cutting the line never once crossed Santiago's mind. He lived in a simple culture and had the fatalistic belief that he was born to be a fisherman, like most of his neighbours. Often we sense when to quit, but if passion or enthusiasm for anything still drives you, then Santiago proves that you may always have more reserves of strength up your sleeve than you think. But having said that, I'm happy to live in a place and time where we can decide to cut the line in our own ways without losing face or self-esteem. A few reviewers wrote, 'I was forced to read this for school. It sucked.' That makes me sad about educational curricula. Making teenagers read and write about characters whose mindsets are poles apart from their own often ends up stirring nothing but resentment. Sure, bureaucratic book choices are meant to encourage students to feel empathy for different people, but it often backfires and gives them the impression that they 'hate' a particular author, who they just weren't ready for. I clearly remember the 16-year-old I used to be, and know I would have hated this book too. Back then, I wanted to read about cheerful things like romance and relationships, and not the melancholy musings of lonely old men floating on the sea. I wanted to focus on ways we could find happiness and fulfillment. I didn't want to hear that adversity is the flip side of the coin and just as likely to be in store for us. Now that I'm middle-aged, I don't mind reading about people making peace with adversity, because I've experienced more ebbs and flows of life first hand (hey look, I made an unintentional sea analogy too). But boy, when I was 16, Santiago's story would have seemed like a waste of a couple of days, both for him and me. I think it's time we stopped trying to fire poor kids up about certain stories way before they're ready to hear them, and then adding insult to injury by abusing them for giving their honest impressions. Okay, now for my impressions about the actual book :) Since Hemingway himself said that symbolism was you-know-what, I won't go that way. The question of personal drive is interesting. At one stage, Santiago can't shake a niggling feeling that killing such a noble fish was a sin. Reason tells him that of course it wasn't, since it was his livelihood. He hoped to keep himself alive and feed several people. But he can't deny the part of him that did it for pride and to make a name for himself. Given that he came to love that plucky fish and consider him a brother, it seems particularly brutal. Can one single act, such as killing a fish, be a good or bad deed depending on the motivation? No matter how good we may look to others, we know deep in our own hearts what drives us to do things. Santiago sees the sea as a beloved feminine entity, capricious and beautiful in its apparently random giving and withholding of favours. He's old enough to have learned that although life doesn't always seem fair, grumbling about it is never, ever helpful. I think of several wise sages' advice to never let either adversity or good fortune sway our equilibrium. Keep your hearts on an even keel (hey, another one), because both good and bad come and go. Santiago suffers great exultation and great loss within the same fishing trip. If we remember that it's wise not to get too overjoyed or too depressed about our own changing times, we'll be doing well. Finally, I guess it shows you never know how any event will look from a broader perspective. No doubt when Santiago first got back to shore, those couple of days out at sea would have seemed like a write-off. and serious lapse of judgement. In the excitement of the chase, he wasn't thinking straight. Surely he'd been around long enough to guess that tugging a bleeding marlin behind his boat would be an instant shark magnet. But hey, his story won millions of fans and a major literary prize. It would be nice if we could look back at our own most face-palming moments in a better light someday, even if it's just a lesson we learned. Overall, it really is a quick and simple story, and anyone could be forgiven for thinking that Ernest Hemingway got an easy win, when you compare it to some of the other lofty Pulitzer Prize winners. Perhaps those fickle winds of fortune were blowing his way in 1953. But maybe he had the last word when his fellow author, William Faulkner said something disparaging about his simple style. I believe it went something like this. Faulkner: Poor Hemingway. He has never been known to use a word that might send a reader to the dictionary. Hemingway: Poor Faulkner. Does he really think big emotions come from big words? Touche! This story was made into a black and white movie in 1958, starring Spencer Tracy. Has anyone seen it? I can't imagine how they could drag this out to a movie length, and I don't think I want to find out :) For more book talk and reviews, visit my blog, http://vincereview.blogspot.com.au/

What can I say about this book? As a hardcore Peter Pan fan, I loved the idea of a story about Tiger Lily, who always seems like an after thought in most Peter Pan retellings. I expected a sad romance. A sad story about Tiger Lily's love for Peter Pan, who ends up falling for Wendy. However, that's only a tiny part of the story. It's so, so much more than a romance. Tiger Lily is lonely. That's really the best word for her. Not just lonely, but incredibly lonely. She's stuck in a village where everyone believes she's cursed, and she's betrothed to an abusive man three times her senior. The only two people in the world who truly care about her are her adoptive father Tick Tock, and her loyal friend Pine Sap. Then Tiger Lily meets Peter Pan. He's everything the villagers warned her about- he's a wild, dangerous boy, but also child-like and vulnerable. He's a cold blood killer who saved the lives of all his lost boys. He's a combination of light and darkness- but what is light and dark in this twisted Neverland? Readers get to dive into a dark, harsh Neverland filled to the brim with good and evil characters that are very different from the blissful paradise filled with happy characters that most people imagine. Captain Hook is a hateful alcoholic with dreams of immortality. Smee is a sociopath who kills the people he admires. Tiger Lily isn't a princess. The Lost Boys are just dirty orphans trying to live in the unforgiving terrain of Neverland. The only character who I really think improves is Tinker Bell. She is usually petty and jealous in most Peter Pan stories. In this version, Tinker Bell is a wise and thoughtful narrator. She's able to dive into people's minds and tell the real story in all its dark glory. The ending isn't a perfect fairytale ending. In fact, it's rather sad. However, I really think it ended how it should have. I particularly liked the part where Tink went to England to see Peter, but ended up only having the courage to see the back of his head, covered in grey hair. I also thought the letter from Peter to Tiger Lily was the perfect bittersweet touch to end the story

Where She Went was a lacklustre sequel to If I stay, this time told from Adam's perspective. Gayle Forman definitely wrote well as Adam but the plot was lacking and uninspiring. Three years after Mia recovered from her coma, Adam and Mia had gone their separate ways and lost contact. Adam made it big as a rock star in Shooting Star with a chart topping album Collateral Damage. Meanwhile, Mia became a successful cellist, playing at Carnegie Hall, which Adam happens to attend out of the blue at the present day. Before long, Adam is invited to meet Mia backstage and they embark on a late night New York tour and in the process, they iron out their past that had come to an abrupt end. The thing about Where She Went that really irked me was had Mia and Adam been honest with each other from the beginning, they wouldn't have wasted three years of their lives. Adam wouldn't have been constantly wondering why Mia had left him and fallen into a 'black hole'. The lack of communication was what the whole plot is based on. In addition to that, Bryn and Ernesto, who were meant to be potential rivals, were easily brushed aside. They had little to no significance toward the end and were simply thrown in to buff up the book. Adam just had to pick up the phone and dump Bryn to go back to Mia. I'm glad Where She Went had a happy ending and it gave me closure, but it was nothing special...

Nominally a Star Trek parody but ultimately something deeper, this book is told from the point of view of minor characters who accompany science fiction heroes on planetary excursions and are killed by alien creatures or plagues or falling rocks. It's a fun idea and the book is full of action and humor, but where the author really gets it right is when the book breaks the fourth wall and delves into metafictional territory. As they continue to die, the characters come to realize their identities as fictional throwaways, which leads to some pretty memorable scenes and a very weighty final epiphany by protagonist Ensign Dahl. It's impressive for a silly science fiction book to end on such a resonant, philosophical note, but it happens and works very well here. I'd recommend this for genre fans looking for something a little more a little more experimental. Bonus points for the three codas: short stories basically which add perspective from minor characters in the story. The first, a series of blog posts from a Hollywood writer suffering from writers block after realizing the characters he creates and kills exist in some parallel world, is overly snarky and overly long, but the second and third, which deal with grief, love and uncertainty from two different characters, are arguably better than the book itself. I would give this five stars but some of the dialogue, characterization and humor were awkward. I certainly enjoyed it enough and loved its take on the nature of reality and identity. A better book that deals with similar themes is Nick Harkaway's The Gone Away World. Regardless, I'll likely investigate some of Scalzi's other works. I like what he represents: a genre fiction writer unafraid to add some literary flourishes.

** spoiler alert ** My main complaint here was that the suspension of disbelief required for this book was a bit much. I enjoyed the story -- once I just decided to suck it up and suspend -- and the description of the famine that resulted from the Great Leap Forward was heartbreaking, but overall I just couldn't get past how ridiculously improbably the entire scenario was. Starting from pretty much the first page you have situations that just defy reason. The only real conclusion we're left to draw as readers is that Joy is just plain stupid, except clearly we're not supposed to think that. We're supposed to think she's just young and idealistic and so in love with Tao from the village and as a result has abandoned all logic. She makes a series of startlingly bad decisions (and she has help making these decisions. For some reason nothing/no one stops her!) and yet things still turn out a-ok. Lisa See ultimately spends so much time writing around this overseas returnee premise, piling unlikely scenario upon unlikely scenario, that it almost ruined the book for me. The other major flaw with this book is that if you haven't read Shanghai Girls it won't make any sense. I feel like Lisa See must have just been really attached to her characters and not ready to let them go, but this book would have been so much better if she's just written a new book about the Great Leap Forward with new characters and without the whole return to the motherland premise. The most interesting characters in the book are the villagers, they're the ones with a real story to tell, not the spoiled 19 year old who thinks it'll be fun to play at revolution for a few years and has the inevitable rude awakening.

Lovecraft meets Cabin in the Woods in this tale of survivors of various supernatural horrors who come together in a support group to try to heal. But they discover that the "various" are less varied than they imagined and they're all linked by their experiences and their therapist. We Are All Completely Fine is a short, relatively easy read, but there's a lot going on in it nevertheless. The narrative style is fascinating, as the primary narrative voice is first-person plural; "we" are a group, "we" are fine, "we" felt this way, as if the idea of the group itself is an entity speaking to the reader from the pages. As the story unfolds, the plural collective makes even more sense, as the characters learn about their metaphysical connections. As a scholar of literary theory, the most interesting section for me occurred late in the book when the characters are discussing the Hero's Journey, which then turns to a narrative discussion of horror theory, specifically the "Final Girl/Boy" and how that horror trope feeds into sequels and series. That Gregory is on familiar terms with some of these literary and pop cultural tropes is clear both from this specific section and from the overall approach to the book.

Re-read April 2016. It was 5 stars the first time I read it, so I'm leaving my rating as such, but I think it's more like a 4 star read for me now. It was still really good, but it didn't quite hold up the same way for me that other books have. I didn't find myself enjoying it more, which often happens upon a re-read for me if the book is that good. (For example, the Hunger Games, or recently Station Eleven) I find Tris & Four's relationship slightly problematic -  he's so cold to her, and then suddenly they're crushing on each other? Maybe not so much. And what do they even really know about each other? Nothing! "But oh, Tobias, I know our relationship is real and I know that your love for me is going to wake you up out of this mind control serum that has you wanting to kill me." Something new that bothered me since my last read of this book is Roth's portrayal of losing someone important and close to you. I know everyone grieves differently, but I get the impression that the author has never experienced any kind of loss in that way  because Tris doesn't seem to be very upset about the fact that in the span of a few hours both of her parents are killed, never mind that she shot one of her good friends. "Yes, all these people that I love died, but oh, Tobias is so hunky, ooooh we're riding off into the sunset together." Sorry, that just doesn't fly for me. Overall, though, this is still a solid player in the YA dystopian genre.

Today I was watching Rafael Nadal play (and annihilate -- sigh) my homeboy Milos Raonic in the Rogers Cup, and I found myself unable to stop contemplating his ass. The boy fits his shorts well, I tell you. Nummy. The rest of Rafa does not work for me, though. The headband, the hair, the nasally voice. In fact, I can't think of one tennis player who entirely does do it for me -- bits and pieces, yes, such as Rafa's ass, Roddick's legs, Djokovic's style, Federer's money... (This does make me a jerk. If I heard a guy saying this about women, I'd probably get in a fistfight.) Nope, only one that's appealed is Jonathan Rhys Meyers in Match Point. But J. Kenner (and apparently Woody Allen) gets the potential of tennis players -- what the combination of rock-hard calves, fierce determination, and millions of dollars in winnings can do to a girl. Hence Damien Stark, former tennis star, current billionaire, always gorgeous. This is the third and final instalment of Kenner's Stark trilogy. It begins with Damien on trial for his coach's murder well after the fact. Nikki is begging him to reveal his history with his coach, assuring him it will solve all his problems (not entirely sure how...), but Damien's adamant that he wants his past kept very, very private. The trial is destroying both of them. The rest of the book is, like the other two, basically just angst, sex, repeat. Lots of angst, tons o' sex. Like Sylvia Day's Crossfire series but with more sex, I swear to god. Normally I'm totally on board with that, but -- and I can't even believe I'm writing this -- I did get to a point where I said, "Geez, again? Really?" Although the sex stayed interesting, so I kind of got over that. The angst, not so much. Maybe I'm just tired of Nikki and Damien and all the bloody drama. (Once again, much as I am with the Crossfire series.) I've never been a huge fan of Nikki, although I've tried. I just don't understand how she gets anything done ever, nor Damien for that matter. And she's so judgy when it comes to her friends. Always judging. Damien's too much of an enigma for me, so I can't get into him either. Fans of the series will probably enjoy this, as will fans of lots and lots of sex. I was kind of the former, and I thought I was the latter, but I wasn't a huge fan of this book. (Also, I think I'm completely burnt out on first person.) It was okay, it wasn't exactly disappointing, but it felt a bit like work. Lila Reviewed from ARC. I'm finding it hard to describe my feelings towards this book. It had so many aspects that I just adored. It was interesting. Unique. Adventure. I was 100% in this book while I was reading it. Every time I put it down, I couldn't stop thinking about it. I started the first section, and then read the majority of the book throughout the span of a day. I was completely and entirely in Weep. This is my first Laini Taylor book, and I adored her writing. I understand that it's not for everyone, and some people probably found the first portion of the book slow. Not the case for me. I enjoyed Lazlo's upbringing, and all of the set up. Reading about Lazlo the librarian really just felt like a nod to readers. I loved all of the set up. I found myself thinking so much about this world. All of the characters felt unique and interesting. There were a few side characters that I just wish we got more of. I have two complaints about this otherwise beautiful book. First, I just want more of the beautiful queer romance. We got like, three sentences total and they were pure and made me smile but I want more. Second, the instalove. I understand that this is a story about gods and monsters and adventures and stories and it's supposed to be epic and the nature of their meeting in itself is grandiose, but I just wasn't feeling it. I don't need pages upon pages about how kissing feels. 15 year old Skylar might have enjoyed that, but I'm over it. I know there's no time for crushes when you're dealing with gods and war, but come on.

Clearly a classic, but was a bit slow for me. I get that du Maurier was trying to draw out the tension, but that didn't quite work for me  possibly because I already knew that Max killed Rebecca and Manderly burns down  .

... man. I don't get it. How in the world are there so many books about THIS world? I got through all 400-and-some-odd pages of the first novel with the same amount of joy I have at the dentist. Sure, it's nice to get a free toothbrush and I do enjoy the feeling of clean teeth, but the rest of the experience is uncomfortable. I felt like I was reading an extended fan fiction with a lot of inside jokes and soap opera-esque revelations. Also overly long. Was Clare paid by the word? We could've easily cut out 100 pages and had a complete experience here. Clary (oh, boy, I see where this name could've come from) seemed like a blank character for the insertion of female reader role-play fantasies. Jace was a tough one for me. Sure, he was appealing, but his mindless automaton act during his interactions with Valentine seemed so totally out of character. I guess a lifetime of trauma and abuse does weird things to your modus operandi. Simon is the obvious choice for shipping (and the obvious loser in this unrequited love triangle). The only person I really loved was Luke (who JUST SHOWED UP IN THE END). I doubt I'm going to be able to finish the rest of the series, so I just read a whole bunch of Wikipedia articles. I feel okay with this. And I'm very happy that incest isn't actually a real plot point in this love triangle. I was worried.

Cover Blurb: Yes or No? Post-apocalyptic-y (that should be an actual word), dark sky, fire, beat-up school bus - yeah, I like it well enough. It's intriguing. Characters: I am still not attached to anyone, except maybe Alex, Dean's younger brother. Dean just spends too much time pining after Astrid, and then he loses his honor (more on that later), so what small attachment I had for him kind of vanished. Astrid is just a bitch, and a bit of a two-player. Chloe desperately needed to be used as an alternative source of food; I wanted to smack her so badly. Sahalia actually gets a little better, but I still don't like her. Niko kind of becomes a broken-down wreck, which was just sad; I wanted to wrap him in a blanket, but not necessarily because I liked him. He was just that miserable. Alex is the intelligent one here; the one who actually keeps his cool and all that, so I guess I liked him. But I still didn't become super attached. The Romance: Dean still likes Astrid. Astrid is a pill; I don't know what he sees in her. Jake turns up again, and Astrid pretty much starts playing both of them. Seriously, Dean, just move on. Alex also starts developing a crush on Sahalia. What's with the guys falling all over themselves for slutty girls? Neither romances take up a ton of time. Plot: Most of the kids have left the superstore in Monument 14 and are now making their way to Denver Airport, where people are being evacuated to Alaska and Canada. Alex, Dean's brother, is among the kids. But Dean and Astrid have stayed behind, along with Chloe and the twins, because if they are exposed to the chemicals outside, they will turn into bloodthirsty killers. Dean decided it was safer for them to stay behind, and for the others to send out a rescue party once they reach Denver Airport. Outside, Alex's group faces a nightmarish landscape with hostiles everywhere and no food or clean water. And back at the superstore, De and Astrid struggle to survive, as the power is slowly drained, and other hostiles try to break in. Sky on Fire was a very short read; shorter than it probably should have been. A lot happens, but not as much as I was expecting. For the most part, the encounters Alex's group has with outsiders are pretty quick. Dean and Astrid continue to try and make the superstore safe, then it gets breached, and they have to fight them off, et cetera. I wasn't bored; the book was too short for that to happen. But I did feel like a lot more could have happened. Believability: No complaints. Writing Style: First person, present tense. The chapters alternate between Dean and Alex's narrations, and they both have a very distinctive voice. I didn't enjoy Dean's narration as much because fewer things happened beyond his pining for Astrid. But overall, I never found myself dreading a narration switch. Content: Astrid and Dean sleep together, but there are no details. Conclusion: In some ways, the setup for a third book felt a little forced. The Author could have made this one longer and put everything that no doubt will be in the third book in this one. But I'll stop complaining now. Sky on Fire was too short to drag, and this is a plot-driven book; not so much character-driven. With the kids split up, there is less high school drama, less whining. So overall, I did enjoy this installment more. Recommended Audience: Guy-read, eighteen-and-up, fans of post-apocalyptic.
