The "struggles" that a teenage couple faces are VERY different from those of a couple in their late 20's early 30's.

The last summer before Dade goes to college is a time when everything changes. And that's not a bad thing - he wouldn't mind a change from his closeted friend with benefits and hostile, homophobic peers and a way to get away from his parents' crumbling marriage. When he meets Alex Kincaid, he finds that he can and should be willing to expect more for himself. Nick Burd presents us with an incredibly well-written tale about Dade and the people in his life. This coming-of-age story is one that seems to capture what it means to grow up, to go from being a teenager to being an adult. There's no instant moment that it happens, but when it does, we change as people and we change how we see the world. And Dade is no exception. Content warning: mentions of suicide

[Initial reaction] Super fucking awesome, but if you don't LEGIT like dark romance, this is not the book for you. This is fucking old-school dark romance. It is only for people who can stomach darkness/anti-heroes in their books. If you have moral objections to dark romance as a genre, stay far away from this book. ------------Actual Review------------- So, this is my second five star book in about a week. I don't even know what to do with myself. Clearly this is a Christmas miracle! There are just some debts that cannot be forgiven. Man, where do I even begin? There's almost nothing I didn't love about this book. You know how sometimes you feel like a book was written just for you? For a good 80% of this book, that's how I felt. There were minor things that weren't for me...? But I'm not even going to mention them, because if I read a review mentioning them, it might make me hesitate to pick up the book, and that would be a giant mistake. The story here is great. I love it. The writing is strong. The character psychology is spot-on. If you like dark romance (this might be classed dark erotica...either way) with legitimately dark anti-heroes who actually do bad things, then you're going to want to read this. If you like "bad boys" who never actually do anything bad but they have tattoos (! ), then...maybe not so much. If you live by the principle "forgive and forget" you're probably going to have some fundamental issues with Tax. But that's not my problem, because Tax is fucking awesome. He's a broken, vengeful anti-hero whose wounds have been festering for roughly half his life. He does not let things go, that's for sure. (But hey, that shows dedication!) Overcoming a shitty, abusive childhood, he built himself into the perfect weapon to get his revenge over the people who wronged him in the past--physically built, successful, ruthless. He is not a half-ass anti-hero. He has done terrible things, and he isn't even sorry. After years of having to just take abuse and be treated like shit by everyone, he's become hard and unforgiving...and awesome. In case you missed that up there. I live off the misery of my violators. Tax does, however, have a tight-knit mini-family-unit: his twin sister, Jude, and Rex, a guy they met a lifetime ago on the streets and welcomed into their fold. Rex is pretty cool, loyal almost to a fault, but those pesky human emotions will get you sometimes. Jude is a destroyed, bitter woman who breathes vengeance. She's more vengeful than even Tax. She also doesn't let go of the past; instead, she curls up in it like her favorite blanket. Her whole life is about seeking revenge on the people who ruined her. She is a miracle: loving enough to care for an asshole like me, and yet she has dark urges of her own. Mia, our heroine, was my kind of heroine. Mostly because she's actually someone who would be able to make it with someone as difficult as Tax. I've said it before, when the psychology is so right, I can forgive almost anything else. These two have complementary personalities; where Tax is hard and ruthless and vengeful and, at times, cruel, Mia is kind, resilient, and understanding. She is not a doormat, though I'm sure she'll be accused of that from time to time. Her thoughts and feelings are very well explained (unnecessarily so for me, since I get it, but probably necessary for many) and she is just a loving person--and she's also successful and ambitious and as well-rounded as you would expect a human being to be. There was only one instance in the whole entire book where Mia rubbed me the wrong way, and that is a big spoiler, so don't click this if you haven't read it  when Tax finally told her what happened to him and Jude all those years ago, and she wasn't even as horrified as I was; she didn't feel guilty, her reaction was something like "Ugh, I can't believe I ever dated that guy." And I'm like, "That's it?!" For being as empathetic and understanding as Mia is, I expected her to feel A LOT worse than that when she heard what happened for the first time . But she's perfect for Tax. I totally connected with the couple. There is quite a bit of sex in this book. For the most part, it doesn't feel like too much though since sex is such a big part of their chemistry/connection, but toward the last 20%, I remember feeling like, "Okay, I don't need another sex scene here," which led to me noticing some of the phrases I was tired of (the meat of her tight ass, her fat tits...). The first sex scene though...that was intense. I would have finished this book in one day if I wouldn't have started reading it on Christmas Eve, so I just couldn't. I didn't want to put it down. Home. The word gave most people a sense of comfort, belonging. For me, it has always been foreboding. A place of fear, isolation, and anger. A place I longed to forget. Someone else remarked in their review that you probably have to be a little jaded to appreciate this story, and I would say that's probably accurate. If you've lived a sheltered life, loved and protected by all the people who are supposed to love and protect you, unacquainted with the darker side of humanity, you're going to have problems with this book. The moral code that exists in this book is specially crafted by injured people who want real justice--for themselves. Not just want it, they need it. They will hurt people to get it. An eye for an eye. And it's unflinchingly awesome, if you're into that sort of thing. Overall, I'd say Nina G. Jones is an author after my own heart! Write me more dark books, please!

And, the family's barn in particular -- it is pretty much the second-best barn in all of literature, after (of course), the Wilder family barn in Malone, NY. I was so sold on this barn. Ready to move in immediately. So, it was a brisk read. As I mentioned, it's not very long, but even on top of that, it's a quick read because the pace is tight and you want to find out what happened. I think everything else I have to say is getting into spoiler territory. This is a "sometimes life isn't fair" book, which, okay, that's a thing and it's not always my favorite thing. And in this case, I got the whole message behind life not being fair to Toby ... YET STILL I felt like the logistics maybe weren't quite meshing for me with the "life's not fair" part. It seemed like once you had two respected adult members of the community (the mother and father, who, btw, were awesome parents all-around), AND the teacher AND the sheriff (four adult people total) on board with the true story, it was harder for me to believe that they were so helpless to impact the events as they were unfolding. Back on the plus side, I'm glad Betty was left as more or less a bad seed. I was half suspecting there was going to be some poignant backstory about why she acted the way she did ... and I was impressed that it didn't end up that way.
Absolutely loved it despite a few slow sections. Cant wait for the spinoff novels, I hope the first one is about Nesta

I admit it--I don't much care for Dickens. I can see the brilliance in his characterization and all that, but he just natters on way too much for my tastes. And there were moments in this story that I just skimmed, descriptions where I was done well before he was. But. This is a classic for a reason, and that is that Dickens captures perfectly the character of Scrooge. If you've only ever seen a filmed version of A Christmas Carol, you haven't seen the true Scrooge, because he's usually portrayed as way more hard-nosed than he is in the story. Confronted with the evidence provided by the spirits of Christmas, Scrooge is actually quick to be moved by what he sees and quick(ish) to repent of his past mistakes. I loved his interaction with his former partner Marley and how reasonable his resistance there is. The edition I read (not the one linked to in this review) included illustrations from one of the Victorian editions, and I wish I could reproduce the one showing Marley, draped in chains made of the spectres of those he misused and betrayed in life. My favorite part is probably that of his encounter with his future. It's obvious Scrooge knows who the man everyone is talking about is, knows and dreads the knowledge, and he's terrified not by the prospect of his death--really, does anyone not know this story by now? , but by suffering a future belonging to the man he was before his three visitors helped him change. The beauty of this story is that even having seen the rotter Scrooge is at the beginning, I didn't want him to suffer by the end. I'll probably add this to my Christmas reading in future years, particularly if I can find a print version with the illustrations. And someday I may even enjoy the descriptions.

I was recently reminded by a goodreads friend that, despite being a Stephen King fan, I have never actually read The Shining. I have no proper justification of this. I've seen the movie before, and I guess I just didn't feel like reading 600+ pages of three people stuck in a hotel during the winter. The setting just didn't appeal that much... but as a Stephen King fan, I had to make myself read it eventually, so now was as good of a time as any. Now, before I continue on, I should stress this; I'm not new to King's novels. I've read through quite a few of them (and enjoyed almost everything I've read), and with zero exceptions, none of them bothered me. I did not once feel afraid because of his books, get goose bumps, paranoia or even a slight shudder. Yeah... you can guess where this is going. The Shining scared the living hell out of me. Seriously, King made a fire hose unnerve me. A freaking fire hose. Now, while I may call this King's scariest novel, I don't consider it his best novel. Nor is it the greatest haunted house novel (I would personally give that to The Haunting of Hill House by Shirley Jackson which also creeped me the hell out). King in my opinion has written better novels, but the sense of unease and creeping dread here really does stand out as a remarkable achievement. In terms of complaints, I would say that it is a bit overlong... but, eh, it's not that bad. It's a slow burner, yeah, but I don't feel that I should complain, as I loved the research aspect of Jack's storyline. The slow understanding of the hotel's history and how absolutely... wrong it is. There does seem to be some aspects of the haunting that could have been expanded upon perhaps, but the mysterious nature of the place add a bit of charm for it. Fairly small complaints when compared to all the good here. Jack is one of King's more interesting characters, and the alcoholism tie to the haunting is a stroke of pure genius. He's the heart of this story in my opinion; a struggle with inner demons in a place that is unaccommodating with composing oneself. The setting is great and despite my initial hesitation of a 600 page book involving 3 people pretty much stuck in one setting, the Overlook is so well designed that it didn't bother me in the slightest (also the fact that the first hundred pages take place outside for the most part help). As a side note, it was a bit surprising as someone who had seen the movie, how many of the iconic scenes are not even in the book. While I knew there was no "Here's Johnny" scene (as it's one of the more famous film ad-libs) I was surprised by the lack of twins in the corridor, no hedge maze or the famous "All work and no play make Jack a dull boy"... which is still written on the side of my paperback copy of the book. In closing, a solid King novel, creepy as hell, perhaps a bit too long, but well worth a read.

A lot of people tend to believe that there is a very large distinction between fantasy and science fiction: fantasy is all about magic and elves and dwarves; science fiction is about space ships and lasers and aliens. Lately, however, this has not held true, with the two genres overlapping in ways that can make some novels difficult to classify neatly into either genre. Some fantasy contains sci-fi elements, while some novels that appear to be sci-fi on the surface read a lot more like fantasy. This falls completely in line with Clarke's (as in Arthur C. Clarke, renowned sci-fi writer) Third Law: any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic. The fine line between magic and technology is something that many contemporary writers of both genres have played with, each in their own way, producing works that do not slot neatly into one genre or the other. This meeting of genres is, of course, not a problem in the least, since the potential of any story has always fallen, not on the conventions of the genre, but upon the writer doing the writing, and their skill in creating a world and characters and telling a story. And Martha Wells, author of The Cloud Roads, the first book in the Books of the Raksura series, certainly knows what she's doing. The Cloud Roads, and the rest of the books in the series, tend to be classified as science fiction, but this first novel reads like fantasy, and I suspect that the other books will, too. This is, of course, not a problem, as The Cloud Roads has turned out to be quite an enjoyable read - albeit without the same depth I rather hoped it would have, or the same level of memorability. The story takes place in a world known as the Three Worlds, inhabited by a diverse set of intelligent races and creatures, but none of which the reader would recognize as human. For instance, the main character, Moon, has scales instead of skin, and the people he's living with, the Cordans, have multicolored scales as well, instead of skin. But Moon is different: he's not quite Cordan, not really, because he can shape-shift into a creature with black scales, a tail, and wings. Unfortunately, this makes him look a lot like another group of creatures called the Fell, which are the enemies of many other races because the Fell prey upon everything else. When he's betrayed by one of the Cordans, he is rescued from certain death by another creature like him, who calls himself Stone. Stone says he is from a race called the Raksura, and that Moon is like him. This sets Moon on a journey of self-discovery - one that involves saving not just himself, but others, as well. One of the most notable things about this novel is the world-building. Wells does not get into in a very in-depth manner, but allows the reader to learn about the Three Worlds as we see it through Moon's eyes. This is something I can appreciate, as I am one of those readers who enjoys having to work a little to learn about a world, and while learning about the Three Worlds in The Cloud Roads was not as challenging as learning about the world of Umayma in Kameron Hurley's Bel Dame Apocrypha books, I still appreciate the fact that I did have to work a little to comprehend the world. And it is an intriguing world, indeed: wild and beautiful, with pockets of civilization in the form of tribes and racial groups that move across the Three Worlds in their own way: groundlings (races that can't fly) on foot, and other races that can fly on wings. There are hints of a super-advanced civilization whose existence once spread across the entirety of the Three Worlds, but nothing is left of this civilization other than scattered ruins and the occasional relic. This ancient civilization, however, only lingers in the backdrop, and while it did pique my interest, Wells does not get into it in this novel - something I hope changes in the other two novels that come after this one. As for Moon, I pretty much liked him almost from the get-go. He's wary of everything, and very careful - a result of a major, traumatizing event in his past that continues to haunt and hound him into the present of the novel. While the circumstances that created his personality are far from pretty, and I certainly would not wish them on anyone, I tend the kind of cautious, wary character that Moon is, since they tend to notice if things are wrong - or over-think things, too, which can be funny and frustrating in the best of ways. Both of these things happen with Moon, which really makes him such a delight to read. However, the same cannot be quite said about the other characters. I suppose it's because of the sheer volume of them, but while I enjoyed reading about them while I was reading the book, now that I've put it down, I find that I don't quite seem to care about them as much. I came to care about the clutch that Moon rescued at the end of the novel, but beyond them, Stone, Flower, Jade, Chime, Pearl, Niran and Selis, everyone else seemed a little lackluster and faded into the background. I suppose this is because all the other characters are technically minor and meant to be forgotten after a while, but I wonder why it was necessary to name all of them when they were, in the end, meant to fade in the background. I suppose they will make a comeback at another point in the series, but I am not so sure of that. As for the plot, it was pretty standard fare, and was fun while I was reading it, but on hindsight, feels rather simplistic. There was a sense of true, genuine threat to Moon's life towards the end of the novel, and there was some excitement to be had learning about the truth of the Fell's plans , but apart from that, it was not as exciting or as deep as I hoped it would be, considering all the praise this story has gotten from others. I was hoping for something truly absorbing, something I could turn over in my head a while, but I did not quite get that in this novel. Overall, The Cloud Roads is a great introduction to the characters and world of the Books of the Raksura - and that might be all it is: an introduction. While the main characters are intriguing enough and memorable enough to stick with the reader, a great many others are forgettable, and as for the plot, it's not quite as deep or as absorbing as I was hoping it would be, which is unfortunate due to the richness of the world Wells has created for her series. I suppose everything will fall into place in the later books, with a deeper, richer, more expansive plot and better character development, but that remains to be seen.

*Thanks to NetGalley & the author for providing me with a free copy of this book* Actual Rating: 1.5 Now that I've read both books, I feel I can finally rate them properly. I thought that I didn't enjoy the second book because I hadn't read the first before it, but that wasn't the case. If anything, I thought the second one was better. Now, onto the review for this book. While I liked how the book dealt with human trafficking and how seriously huge and widespread it is, I didn't like much else. Hope didn't impress me too much in this book either. Just when I thought I grasped her character, the author would turn around and say 'but now she does THIS' and it was disorientating. A shy, quiet girl who couldn't stand up to a loser kid bullying her on the bus was suddenly travelling across America to rescue a girl she met once and then she drives the getaway car 'weaving in & out of traffic'? I just felt lost. What has happened to provoke such a transformation? Don't get me wrong; I love when a shy, quiet girl becomes badass and dominating but there has to be a event that changes her. And it wasn't Michael kissing her and almost incinerating her. She was already in Las Vegas when that happened. As for Michael...ugh. I couldn't stand him. He alternates between 'kinda creepy' and 'complete jackass' throughout the book. He comments on Hope's eating habits to a bunch of other girls - if any guy did that to me he'd get an earful! Don't even start me on how weird it is that he 'loves' a 15 year-old! When he confessed his love to her, I actually did a double take and read the few paragraphs leading up to it again, convinced that I missed something. Nope, there it was. Just thrown out there, randomly, without any build-up. Hope eyeing his muscles doesn't count as build-up. Every straight, 15 year-old girl in the world would be eyeing the muscles of a hot man if they were flaunted around her. That's not love, that's lust. I don't even buy him as an archangel either. Leader of God's Army? 'He who is like God'? What's he doing faffing about with little kids in school then? But wait - it would actually make sense if God had ordered him to; had told him to track the bearer of the Key and protect them from the Fallen Ones. Ok so, cool. Later on then, Michael screws this assumption I had when he tells Hope that he had no idea that she was the bearer of the Key. What? Then why were you stalking her, Michael? 'Because I felt drawn to her' UGH. There was a part in the book where Hope is explaining her idea of what 'The Key' is because she has a dream of Cain killing Abel with a rock and then Michael goes: 'The rock!' And she says: 'you talk about it as if you were there', to which he says: 'I saw it all'. Why couldn't you have figured that out yourself, then?! Why would an archangel, old as time, need to wait for a human girl to decipher an obvious biblical riddle for him? Even Hope, who apparently has the Bible memorised, couldn't figure out what 'The Key perverted Brother against Brother' meant. It was obvious that was about Cain & Abel, even to someone like me who only knows what Supernatural has taught me about the Bible. I mean, if you're gonna make them smart, actually make them smart. The plot was also a bit weird. I had assumed that Hope was on the run with a group of angels because if she stayed with her mom or dad, they would be in danger. No. Michael just tells her that they have to find this Key that a Prophecy talks about and she...just goes with him? And stays away for about a week? At the end of the book, she's still not returning home - instead she's jetting off to Turkey with Micheal. What about her poor parents, no doubt sick with worry? We get to see all the grief she's caused in the chapters from her mother's POV. Why couldn't she stay at home and wait for a vision to come to her and then tell Michael? I understand that some drama needs to be made in order for the story to progress, but I can't stand unnecessary drama. If Hope had no other choice but to leave, then I would be fine with it. But it made no sense when nobody was in danger. The plot wasn't even resolved at the end. The bad guys weren't caught. It felt like we readers were cheated out of a full book and got an excerpt instead. Also, there were no pretty places in this book, unlike its sequel. So no pretty descriptions of streets and buildings, either. *tear*

God I am so back and forth on whether I like this book. So I loved pretty much 80% of it. Basically all of it until the end (I will talk about the ending later in the review, so if you don't want spoilers then don't read that section. It was written as a true crime story, so much so that after the first chapter I literally googled the names to be sure it wasn't based of real people. The author is a very talented writer, and that really shone through with the style she chose. This book is about 2 separate disappearances. Kind of. Its about the disappearance of Molly Metropolis, a famous pop singer. Cait Taer becomes obsessed with figuring out what happened to Molly, until she too disappears- presumed dead after a boat crash in a lake, with Gina and Nick the only witnesses to what happened to her. It was definitely an interesting read- there are tons of side tangents through out the book, about maps, the situationalists, and all these other elements that are seemingly unrelated but tie together in the end. There were a few problems with the writing, though. The information had a tendency to overshadow the plot, and there was a lot of repetition- readers aren't stupid, we can remember what you told us the chapter before without a recap. It made the book feel a lot longer than it had to be. Also, the ending. I honestly liked the first ending better than the second. The idea that the train came, and it was all just fake? that Molly disappeared because she was disappointed by it all? That there was no conspiracy, it was all just made up in Cait, Gina, and Nicks minds? In my opinion, that made a much better story than the real ending, where everything was a lie and it all really happened like a conspiracy theorist thought it would. That was more disappointing to me than if there was no utopia. The whole time I was reading the book I thought it was a relatively good book, but the ending made me question whether or not I would even want to reread it. I would recommend reading this, but only because I want to vent about the ending with someone without spoiling the book for those who have not read it.

"Grabbing a bite. With a twenty-year-old. From a boy band. Under what circumstance might that ever be construed as acceptable?" I. LOVED. THIS. BOOK. A sharp and insightful commentary on our modern culture and obsession with celebrity, 'The Idea of You' is also a fantastic, sexy romance. This book really did it for me. If this is Robinne Lee's first book, I cannot wait see what comes next! Solene is a sophisticated, 39 year old divorced working mom who finds herself swept up into an exciting and sexy relationship with the world-famous Hayes Campbell, the 20 year old member of a famous "boy band". She is an educated and successful gallerist who is divorced from her ex-husband, who has a younger girlfriend. The world does not take kindly to Solene's relationship with Hayes, mainly because of the 20 year age difference. I loved the commentary on ageism in our society today. The public will accept an older man with a younger girlfriend but frowns upon the older woman/younger man dynamic. Solene is acutely aware of the age difference but is enjoying an awakening of sorts with Hayes, Ah, the joys of a younger boyfriend! What starts out as "just lunch" soon becomes much, much more. "I just want to look at you for a moment." "You've been looking at me for over an hour." "Yeah, but before I was trying not to be obvious about it. Come here." He led me over to the daybed against the far wall and pulled me onto his lap. I could feel him through his pants. Oh, the wonders of twenty. Solene at first tries to hide her relationship with Hayes from her young daughter. I knew this was going to be a disaster and her daughter at first does not handle the news well at all. But doesn't Solene deserve to be happy? She struggles not only with her ex-husband's reaction to the news but also with her daughter's. The entire time Isabelle had been just across the hall on the phone with her friend, oblivious to her mother going down the rabbit hole. Face-first. One of the things I loved most about this book was the sharp look at our obsession with celebrity. Hayes could not go anywhere without being mobbed, and even a causal trip to the store to buy a shirt led to a mob scene. He was used to it; Solene was not. This story made me re-think every headline I read about celebrities. Hayes wanted Solene to know him, and NOT "the idea" of him. Hayes was tender, sweet, funny, sexy and much wiser than his 20 years. "You want to be kissed, Solene?" His hands were in my hair, pushing it off of my face, cradling my neck. "Yes." I nodded. "You think you can handle that?" "I'll see what I can do." Robinne Hill gets her locations right. From Miami, to Malibu, to Manhattan and Paris, I felt as if I was THERE, experiencing the cafes, the clubs, the chic art galleries and the screaming fans at the huge concerts. This book really checked all the boxes for me!! I simply cannot recommend it highly enough. I am having a hard time moving on from this book. Would I love a sequel? YES. But I would also gladly welcome another book from Ms. Hill. Grab 'The Idea of You' and enjoy a fabulous time with this perfect beach read. I adored it. Favorite quotes: "You're making me blush," he laughed, tipping his head back. His jawline from this angle was well-defined, exquisite, like art. His beauty, like a gift that kept revealing itself. "Love," she said, "was not always perfect, and not exactly how you expected it to be. But when it descended upon you, there was no controlling it." ARC provided by the publisher in return for an honest review.

This was the first book of Lora Leigh's that I read (I think or I just see it that way in my memory). It was a page turner from giddy up. Callon was so hot and Merinus was a formidable Alpha female to match his character. I reread this every few months when I need a Breed fix. The birth of the Breed series could not have had a better beginning.

This was short but oh did it grab my attention and kick up the heat. The story was original and I was immediately drawn in. At first when I read the synopsis the guy talking about his cocks appetite put me off, I figured cocky guy perspective that might annoy me. However, that wasn't the case. Does Andrew talk dirty a lot? Heck yeah but it didn't grate on my nerves and his commanding presence was intoxicating. I was immediately engrossed in the story and I wanted to get to the bottom of his past and what Alyssa was hiding. The story is well written and so captivating with wonderful twists and turns. You are constantly thrown back and forth between these two by dialogue and actions that you just can't put the book down and you can't wait to find what happens next. The ending has me itching for the next installment in this series because holy hell! How the tables are turned on Andrew and I so want to find out what he has to say now.

Despite the fact that I had a major problem with the premises of this book, as they made absolutely no logical sense, it was still fun and I mostly enjoyed it. A collection of my thoughts on the book: No one is going to believe some random video supposedly proving the existence of vampires on YouTube, no matter how well done. There have got to be tons of videos claiming that, and how many people actually believe in vampires? Not that many. And actually, having the government issue a statement would make me more suspicious, not less. I mean, how would you feel of the government said that no, supernatural creatures don't really exist? That sounds like an acknowledgment that the government cares enough to try to cover it up. (Or maybe I'm just naturally paranoid and a conspiracy theorist.) It's one thing when a pseudo-documentary (like that mermaid one) claims the Navy actually has captive mermaids and people believe it because it's presented in such a factual manner, so the Navy gives a statement that it's false, but this is a video on YouTube! Since when do people look to the government for confirmation/denial of YouTube video hoaxes? Anyway, the government is not the way to deal with YouTube. The way to deal with unwanted videos is to write a blog post giving "proof" that it's a hoax- shadows are wrong, CG mistakes, etc. (Doesn't even matter if they don't actually exist- it's enough to point them out. Most people don't actually know what's correct, but if they're told something was done incorrectly, they'll probably believe it.) People would be far more willing to believe the video's a hoax than to believe it's real. Then get popular websites to repost your article. And voila, suddenly no one believes in vampires anymore. Why is it so difficult to get these "magic" herbs from China? This is China. You really want me to believe that this herb with an obvious marketable value is not being sold by people somewhere, plus a half dozen different cheap knock-offs? If the herbs had traditionally believed medicinal properties, then they'd probably stock some in Chinese medicine shops. And if not, someone on eBay would sell them. (Not that I'd really want to buy mystery herbs from random Chinese people on eBay, which sounds like a recipe for trouble.) So I really don't see why it's such a big issue and the herbs so difficult to acquire. Yes, maybe the demon one is hard to get because of the demon/vampire protection, but why not the other two? And how did the heroine hear about them in the first place? Somehow, a 47-year-old vampire seems a lot weirder than a 470-year-old vampire. I don't know why. Apparently Phineas looks like the guy in the Old Spice commercials. Or at least I can't picture him any other way now. (Most) (white) Americans have no understanding of fish heads. Fish cheeks are the best part. 2nd generation Chinese people, like J.L., generally do not speak Chinese well enough to converse with people in remote villages with strong accents, and certainly not if they speak another dialect, unless they grew up hearing the accent. (I certainly can't understand most strong accents, although I consider myself to be fluent in Mandarin.) It would be kind of like an English-speaker trying to understand someone with a very strong brogue- occasionally you get a sense of what they're saying, but usually it's unintelligible, despite ostensibly being the same language. (And if it's a different dialect, then you have about as much a chance of understanding it as if they were speaking German. And China has lots of dialects.) The heroine did some rather dumb things in her pursuit of freedom. Yeah, yeah, it's an inalienable right and all that, but staying to watch a vampire fight when they offer to teleport you away seems rather unintelligent. Why didn't they teleport the demon herb to Japan when they had the chance? And why didn't any of the vampires go teleport back to the field, grab a sample, then teleport away, now that they know where the field is? Their teleporting abilities seem to be severely underutilized, a problem which often seems to pop up when teleporting abilities are present.

If you asked me why I loved this book so much, I'm not sure I could say. Is it the poetic writing, that makes me want to rip pages out of the book so I can hang their beautiful quotes on the wall? Is it the characters that leap out at me because they're just so real? Probably both of those. I did have some slight quibbles, but that's just a given when it comes to me. First off, I have no idea what the plot is at this point. Maybe it's because I read The Raven Boys last October and I always forget details (this is why I marathon series, btw). But... who are they looking for? Or what? Is it Glendower? Glendower and Greywaren are spelled really similar to my eye so I'm never quite sure... Also, why are they looking for Glendower/Greywaren? This isn't me being snarky, I'm genuinely curious. Is it because he pays them something? Or what? #confuzzled Additionally, I'm not sure how I feel about some ...things. I don't know. Okay, spoilers. So... I don't know how I feel about the Bluesey relationship? *HIDES* I knoooooow. I like the characters individually well enough, but I feel like it went like this: Beginning of Book: Blue: I could never love Gansey! Ugh! *they never spend any time with each other and barely see each other because Gansey is in Washington, D.C. for the middle* At the End: Blue: I love Gansey and he is my soulmate I feel so bad putting it like this, but that's how I felt about it! Maybe it was supposed to be a subtle romance and I was just focused on other things and didn't pick up on it buuuut So, I started liking characters I didn't even like in previous books! Namely Ronan and Noah. Noah is an adorable cinnamon roll who needs to be protected. Still feel like his friendship isn't as strong with the three boys as the three boys have with each other, though. I really like him and Ronan's friendship, though! Unexpectedly, I like Ronan a whole bunch. Ordinarily, his "bad boy with a good heart" character trope annoys me, but with Ronan it works. Also, waah Adam, you must be protected too! I love him so much and got so angry at Blue sometimes. Kavinsky is my least favorite of ever he should burn in a fire. Gah. I'm so glad he burned in a fire. I hated that guy so much!! I like Maggie Stiefvater's writing a lot. I think it's very flow-y. It moves well and has a sort of dry humor to it, which is oddly enough sort of what I get from The Hobbit when I read it. Funny without being too forward with it. Additionally, I like the dialogue of this book. The characters talk very naturally. Especially the teenagers, who talk as teenagers probably do talk. (The exception being Gansey but Gansey III is so often an exception to things.) Interested to see what goes down in the next couple of books! Really liked this one, and could not put it down. It also has a lovely cover, which never hurts.

A pretty good book that falls short with its ending. "Life After Life" tells the story of Ursula, who keeps dying in various ways and ages and being reborn over and over. Eventually Ursula begins to feel deja vu and anticipate at times that something horrible is about to happen, but it's mostly unclear how consciously aware Ursula is that she's living her life over and over. The strongest part of the book are the World War II scenes in England. Atkinson does a masterful job bringing to life the continuous terror of the Blitz and the horror it wrought upon civilians. She's also good at describing Ursula's (mostly) carefree childhood. But there are a number of areas where this book fell seriously short. Ursula is the narrator for most, but not all, of the sections. But frankly, she's not a terribly interesting character! She never seems to develop much as a character. In fact, I found her most interesting "life" to be when she was abused by her husband, because the character development there was the most stark. The rest of her lives don't seem to mesh all that well with her upbringing and interests. Why is she a spinster in so many lives? Her goals and character are never well fleshed out, odd considering how inside her head we are. Many of the other characters are more interesting than Ursula, but Atkinson only gives us the barest details. Why were Sylvie and Hugh so unhappy together? Why was Maurice such a nasty character? Would the family really be so accepting of Jimmy as a homosexual? What happened to Izzie's son when he's sent to Germany? There are so many interesting, unexplored stories, that Atkinson throws in but never takes up. Atkinson isn't really consistent with her time travel universe, mostly towards the end of the book. Other characters start changing, not just Ursula. I have no idea why Atkinson chose to do this, but I found it undermined the idea that pervades the book that Ursula controls her destiny. 4. There was no real ending! At least, the way I read it, Ursula will continue to die and be reborn. I had expected there to be some conclusion - some life that Ursula was meant to "get right" and live. But no, it seems like her lives will continue. I just don't understand what the purpose of the book was, if she'll continue to die and be reborn over and over. At the end she's conscious of this, so how will that continue to affect her lives? Why end there? I was very disappointed that Atkinson couldn't let Ursula live and die, period, at the end. I don't understand why her German lives had to involve her meeting Hitler, and then trying to kill him (and failing? Maybe? It's never made clear.) I thought the best part of her German life was when she was starving with her daughter at the end of the war, not the Hitler scenes. Her scenes with Hitler could be taken straight from history books - Atkinson's interpretation adds nothing to the plethora of literature about Hitler. Too. Many. Quotes. I don't understand why Atkinson decided Ursula had to constantly quote famous poets. It just made her more insufferable, and didn't keep my interest. Some of the book is very interesting, and I would recommend it to people who are interested in the London Blitz or literature involving time travel. Unfortunately, the book fell short of my expectations.

Book on CD read by Adina Verson In 1930, fifteen-year-old Thea Atwell is sent from her Florida home by her parents to a boarding school in the Blue Ridge Mountains, to remove her from a scandal that has rocked her family's foundations. It's the early part of the Great Depression, but the residents at Yonahlassee Riding Camp for Girls are from the kinds of wealthy families that will generally survive and even prosper during this time. Isolated from home, they form their own societal norms, and Thea struggles to find her place. The story is told in alternating time frames: the events leading up to the scandal, and the events at the school during Thea's year at Yonahlossee. The reader watches Thea grow from a tomboy to a curious pre-teen, to a sexually charged young woman. As she related what is happening and how she feels about everything, I found myself worried for this emotionally distant girl, who seemed unable to control her impulses or to recognize the potential consequences of her actions. One thing that bothers me: Does no one recognize the predatory nature of the men/boys involved? Both Georgie and Henry take advantage of Thea. Even though she is an apparently willing partner, she is vulnerable due to her age, isolation and lack of experience. Adina Verson does a fine job of voicing the audio book. Her detached, almost monotone, delivery really gives me a sense of Thea's loneliness and struggle.

This volume feels like...taking a breath. A lot of setup is taking place, getting characters where they need to be. Less action and plot development than previous volumes. I'll be interested in the payoff, especially what results from the introduction of Petrichor, who The Will is going to see (Sophie? Gwendolyn? ), or what Marko's mom is planning in prison. And also Alana's pregnant again!! Whaaat?! How is this gonna go? Well, I hope. I couldn't handle it if my favorite couple had any more serious adversity heaped upon them.

I'm not usually thrown off by tons of characters of POVs, and I managed to get through the other 3 books in the series relatively understanding everything going on, but I struggled with this one. The characters didn't interest me as much as previous novels. No Quick Ben, no Tool, no Lady Envy, Kruppe or Anomander Rake. Kalam didn't seem to have much interesting going on, and as much as I love Heboric, he didn't really do much either. I think I'm definitely in the minority, but I actually liked the first quarter of the novel best. I enjoyed Karsa Orlong's introduction. Oh well. I'll still definitely be picking up the next one.

I own up!!!!!! I hated NEW MOON when I first read it. Where was Edward???? How could he leave Bella/?? And Jacob....I wanted to wring his not yet turned werewolf's neck!!!! How dare he tried and take Edward's place in Bella's heart. I was so attached to Edward and I turned page after page - fast and furious- hoping to find him again. But only towards the end of the book does he appear again. Pain and anguish was what I felt not having him in this book!!!!! I was relieved when Bella and Edward got back together and loved meeting the Volturi gang. Okay, so Jacob was a good friend when Bella went through the painful period of Edward's absence in her life!! I skipped a lot of pages when I first read this book but consequently have reread it many times and enjoyed it a bit more. However, it still remains the book I like the least in the series. Here's some dialogue from this book that I like - "I love a happy ending. They are so rare", "I don't care!! You can have my soul. I don't want it without you - it's yours already", "If you believed as he did, could you take away his soul?" "You're the very best part of my life".

I enjoyed this far more than I had any right to. This is a YA romance version of the Island of Doctor Moreau, Juliet the eponymous character, choosing between the manly Montgomery and the gentlemanly-yet-mysterious Edward Prince while discovering the true nature of her father's work. So why was it so much fun then, when every element is pretty much guessable from the first page? In part because this is a pretty classic Gothic novel, and I have a great weakness for them. And I thought the Gothic elements were pretty well done, a balance between being torn between forbidden love, and running away from monsters in the jungle, and discovering Daddy's monstrosity. As well Sheperd writes well, clearly, consciously and with a gift for action sequences. Juliet is a strong heroine although I would suggest the fact that she is likewise one of her father's monstrous creations is probably over-telegraphed . There are very few red-herrings actually, and making the plot a little more complex perhaps would have made the mystery a little more engaging. But then again, why shouldn't Shepherd focus on her interests? In any case, a very good example of what it is. Recommended.

** spoiler alert ** This book gets two stars because the ending made me cry. I have a weakness for beautiful, lively characters being reduced to their internal biological clocks. I'm not going to be reading more of Cassandra's work. This book succeeded in reassuring me that this was the right choice to make. I am now going to detail for you my problems with this series, and the final book in particular. Victorian Era -If you are going to write something historical, then please commit to it. Don't do it because it looks good on paper and when you need to make a scene extra dramatic. You can't write about Victorian England and allow the teenagers to act like they are from modern times. I wish I could time travel and show someone from that time this book. I'm sure they'd have a heart attack at some of the language the gang used. -Honestly. Tessa makes one comment about not being used to pants, and insists on using Will's Christian name once or twice. Not to mention, she is unusually comfortable with getting around with lots of guys. Even if that was simply a part of her character, it would have been good to make it more explicit WHY she didn't care exactly. Maybe she wants to defy social norms. I don't know. Tessa is a fucking robot. -This whole issue became especially prevalent at the end of the book. The descriptions were stunningly beautiful, and very atmospheric, but this only served to show me how much they were lacking throughout the rest of the novel. And while I adore Magnus's character, I found there to be something wrong with his kiss scene with Will. Don't add a man on man kiss just to make the fangirls squeal. Wouldn't Magnus want to adhere to social customs of the time to avoid raised eyebrows? Shadowhunters are homophobic in the newest series, so why isn't Will, living in Victorian England, hyperventilating at the fact that he has just been kissed by another man? I don't know the rules of this world, so I'm left guessing. Poor Characterization -First, allow me to say that Clare CAN succeed in getting me invested in her characters. Magnus is still a genius invention, and Will was probably one of the most swoon worthy men in literature I've encountered. HOWEVER. -At the end of the third book, I still felt like Mortmain was there simply to be a villain. He existed for no other purpose other than to give the book more plot. Not to do damage or make the characters question themselves and grow. No, he was there because the book needed a villain. I find it quite pathetic that Clare had three books to develop a menacing villain, and couldn't do it. His motives were weak, and he worked incredibly slowly. I never feared OR admired him. And I LOVE villains. There were so many great evils of this time Clare could have used to inspire him, whether it be rampant gossip or classism or sexism...and at BEST Mortmain was a weak example of the latter. -What the hell happened to Charlotte's baby? Why was that even mentioned? If you're not going to use it in your book, then don't add it for fucking shock value. How was this ok'd by her publisher? -Why was Henry's disability not talked about more? All he needed was one profound scene, perhaps in which he gave advice to another character. Maybe Gabriel? That could have been a humbling experience for him, I feel. Make him a little less self pitying. -The Irish girl existed simply for ambiance and I found that very irritating. USE YOUR CREATIONS, FOR CHRIST'S SAKE! -Tessa was boring. 'I like books' is not a personality. I wanted more from a main character. I wanted her to be unsure. I wanted her to be selfish sometimes. I wanted FLAWS. Instead I got a cardboard cutout who I vaguely recognized as a brunette. -What happened to Mrs. Dark???? -Bringing Jem back was lazy writing. It was cheap, and it ruined his entire character. The entire POINT of James Carstairs, as I understood it, was that he was selfless. He was a self sacrificing hero who would have DIED for love, and instead he cops out at the last minute? Cassandra, of all the places to make your novel realistic, why here? I WANTED to cry over Jem. That was what made him a good character. He deserved so, so much better. Now that he has it, I'm simply bored. He doesn't even have his damn violin, now. -And, the greatest sin of this godforsaken novel: Jessamine. She had INFINITE potential, and she was killed off for no conceivable reason. Was Clare BORED with her? This was just lazy writing! Jessamine had so much potential to learn from Tessa, and to teach Tessa. There were infinite possibilities for Jess. She could have been a villain, she could have been a hero. Instead, she's a fucking ghost. Poor worldbuilding -I'm sick and tired of not understanding the Shadowhunter world. Why am I still finding places in the third book where characters are narrating to me their own version of the Wiki page for warlocks, or some shit? Is it that hard to establish the setting in the first book? -Instead of utilizing the universe she has created to move plot forward, Clare keeps inventing new things to dig herself out of plot holes. Again, lazy as hell. These were the biggest things I've noticed, though there are plenty more problems that interfered with my enjoyment of the book. Overall, I've made my diagnosis that Cassandra Clare is a lazy writer, too good at creating characters and too bad at putting them in a story. Maybe that will change in her next series about another special girl with a boy best friend. I don't know. I'm moving on to books that actually deserve my tears. PS: That is a polyamory pride flag. This whole book would have been a whole lot simpler if a little representation had been included. It would have added conflict, Magnus could have offered support, Jesus, I should have written these books. I mean seriously, "Most have one great love, but you have two", PLUS, Will and Jem already are parabatai? You literally had it in the palm of your hand, and you threw it away. Incredible. An incredible waste.

Two and a half stars. Generic, but a quick and entertaining read. For a fantasy world, it didn't immerse this reader. While I was pleasantly surprised that Bardugo nipped the love triangle in the bud, I wouldn't have minded seeing a conflicted Darkling. Maybe the healing power of love vs ambition, but I think I'd have liked to see more of his utter distaste for the remnants of his humanity (see his lust for Alina, which by the way GROSS, and the connection with his mother) that he can't quite shake it off and he absolutely HATES himself for that weakness.

Wow oh wow... this one is going to stay with me for awhile. This author wove together complete brilliance. As the title suggests, there are so many lies between the characters in this story. This was a 3-star book until the last hundred or so pages, where it really shined and Scalzi reminded us why he's one of the kings of modern science-fiction. Zoe's Tale (that's right, dear readers, I looked up that trema for you) is essentially a re-telling of The Last Colony from--you guessed it--Zoe's point of view, much in the same style as Ender's Shadow. But it's so much more than a simple regurgitation. Where The Last Colony replaced politics for The Ghost Brigades's action, Zoe's Tale is a story about emotions. Scalzi absolutely nails the teenager narration, though you'll have to take that statement with a grain of salt seeing as how neither the author nor myself have ever been teenage girls. At least he explains this wizardry in the acknowledgements. I have no ready excuse, but if I was a teenage girl, I would probably be like Zoe. That being said, sometimes it got a bit too teenager-y, which isn't a criticism so much as a reflection that it didn't particularly resonate with me being twenty-odd years old now. Much in the same way that reading Harry Potter for the first time right now wouldn't have the same impact as when I read them as a child. Like I said, the last few hundred pages make the whole book worthwhile, with a much bigger emotional hit when [spoiler for [book:The Last Colony|88071]]Enzo dies  and of the events overall. Once you get into the swing of the book, you'll hardly be able to put it down. It hit home in a way I didn't expect, so Mr. Scalzi, I offer you my sincerest and Dogeiest "wow."

I really liked this unusual fantasy novel about a child being brought up in a cemetery. It wasn't just whimsical. The characters felt true. Gaiman is telling us something about family and parenting through this book.

I'm not really sure how to describe this book...It's a bit of a love story, a bit of one of those Picoult-ish ethical issue books. It's a lot of great. Our protagonist is Louisa Clark -- she's just lost her job and instead of pole dancing, she decides to take the option of caregiver. Her new daily companion, Will, isn't the most pleasant of men, but he has his reasons for not being excited about his life. One of my favorite parts of reading this book were the occasional breaks we got from Louisa's POV. The Famous Five books are what got me into reading when I was a kid. I loved reading about the children's adventures; it felt like I was right there in the story with them, getting tied up in the same mysteries they got themselves involved in and eventually helped to solve. Nowadays, I don't often read children's books or mystery stories anymore, but this book showed me that nothing has changed from my primary school days. I loved every second of it. The Mysterious Benedict Society is a much more massive tome than any of the Famous Five books ever were, and it's this space that gives it the room to include far more detail about the characters, the setting and the action. Where the Five stories were a little rushed (or at least, that's how they feel now when my reading speed has improved drastically from when I was a kid), this book is able to fill us in on the backgrounds of the characters, their relationships with one another and their complex emotions as they infiltrate the Institute , all in the same lilting, musical tone of children's books that makes reading on so terribly enticing. Despite being for kids and about kids, the story is not at all shallow or superficial; on the contrary, its portrayal of the characters is mature, emotionally complex and quite realistic, while also easy to identify with. Of course, it does help that the main characters of this book are geniuses, and this actually makes for excellent pacing with a slightly older audience (ie. me). The dynamics between the characters were very believable and relatable, and I really liked how each had an important role to play in the mission. Strength of character aside, this was, overall, a great book with a fast-paced plot that kept me on the edge of my seat especially towards the second half. The premise of the story itself was exciting, and its execution flawless--every small victory had that wonderful lifting effect that made me want to sing or pump my fist into the air and let out a whoop. The plot twists at the end were so emotionally gripping and the last hundred pages simply flew by in a flurry; I don't know when I last read a book that made me feel so purely happy. Needless to say, the second book is already on my ASAP list and I'm excited to see what Trenton Lee Stewart has in store for us! A lot of things were revealed in this book already and it almost reads like a standalone (except for that one small thing at the end), but the word from my friend is that the rest of the series is equally good, and I absolutely cannot wait to get cracking.

I am unsure about how I feel about this book. I think there were scenes where I anticipated things becoming more interesting, but overall the pace was slow and the revelations were not interesting. Beta is the story of Elysia, a teen Beta, or testable human clone. The novel takes place in a sort-of dystopia, after an event called the Water Wars. Humans can either live on the Mainland in enclaves that are scientifically modified to support life (the rest of the world is desert) or, if they are fabulously wealthy and/or powerful, they live on the island of Demesne, where there's pretty much hedonism-lite. The air on Demesne is hyperoxygenated so that everyone is on a high, which makes the subsequent drug abuse we learn about sort of confusing. The world building here is weak; unlike the Hunger Games or Harry Potter's world, it's hard to connect these facts to the actions of Elysia's plot. Mostly, it's concerned with Elysia's social life. Elysia gets sold, like other clones, to be of service. But since she's a teen Beta with a beautiful body, she gets chosen for a slightly different reason other than manual service. She is chosen to be a companion clone, taking the place of the Bratton family's daughter who's now in college (Astrid, who is described by everyone as a killjoy interested in social justice. We never meet Astrid in this book). Elysia calls her buyer Mother, and is introduced to her new "family": a secretive drug-addicted/future military member brother Ivan, a creepy/clone-sexin' father (called the Governor), and bratty but somewhat innocent Liesel. Other clones of the household are Xanthe, who performs housework; and Tawny, the Governor's luxisstant (supposed to provide luxury/exercise to the Governor, but instead acts more like a Massage Parlor Girl). Clones in this world originate from dead people ("Firsts") who've had their souls removed from them. There's a lot to be said about the treatment of clones in this world. There are some implications that I wish Cohn got into; for example, Elysia is a thin, blonde, athletic beauty chosen to be a companion, while Miguel (clearly based on a Person of Color) is a laborer. Even the laws against clone-human relationships resemble anti-miscegenation laws from the past. Oddly, Elysia has information on some aspects of our modern history, but neglects these obvious connections. I'm left wondering if the lack of thematic emphasis has to do with showing Elysia's lack of understanding, or if those themes are left unexplored due to the author's white privilege. The romance writing is shaky--she instantly falls in love with Tahir, has this weird connection with her "swimming God", and an abusive, scary relationship with her brother Ivan. Ivan wavers between protectiveness (he tries to keep his dad from molesting Elysia) and possessiveness (doesn't like it when others have her attention, claims she is there to serve him, and forces himself on her, resulting in Elysia's pregnancy in the end ). I got confused as early on as Elysia's understanding of language wavers. At times, she is confused by idiomatic language, but in many other paragraphs she uses idiomatic English to a great degree. It's not really how I expect a clone to use language from how it's described. The reason I marked this as two stars rather than one is that I'm hoping the second novel irons out the kinks in Cohn's writing. I understand she cowrote Nick and Nora's Infinite Playlist, so I guess sci-fi/dystopia is new to her and I won't hold it against her too much (yet).

Lakshmi is one of the 12,000 Nepali girls who are sold into sex slavery each year. She leaves her mountain village believing that she is going into the city to work as a maid for a wealthy family. When she arrives at Happiness House, Lakshmi quickly realizes that something isn't right, and before long her horrible fate becomes clear - her stepfather has sold her into prostitution. Mumtaz, the proprietor of Happiness House, tells Lakshmi that she will have to pay 10,000 rupies - the amount Mumtaz claims to have paid for her - in order to regain her freedom. Though Lakshmi initially refuses to have sex with the customers, she eventually comes to believe that it is the only way she can earn the money to buy her freedom. Then one day she gets an American customer who offers to help her. Lakshmi has heard that American are deceptive, promising to help girls like Lakshmi only to leave them begging in the streets, but Lakshmi wonders if the chance of getting out of Happiness House is worth the risk. Written in verse, Sold is a quick read, but the subject matter is by no means easy. Lakshmi's situation is horrifying; however, McCormick is rarely graphic in her description of the treatment that Lakshmi endures. She focuses instead on Lakshmi's emotional state and the relationships that she forms with the other residents of Happiness House. Though she is at times on the brink hopelessness, Lakshmi maintains her determination to escape her circumstances and find a better life. Overall, this was a very worthwhile read. My only criticism is that the ending, though hopeful, may be a little unrealistic, and it left me wondering what lay ahead for Lakshmi.

This book is enormous, expansive, and surprising. It reminds me of about a half dozen other books while still somehow being very much it's own thing and unique. I'm not even sure how to begin summing up what I loved about it. It's not a perfect book and I'd likely have been tempted by a 4.5 rating if it were an option but I just couldn't bring myself to go as low as four stars in the end. The book can be very technical at times and gets into a lot of the mechanics and science behind the story being told, so it may come across as being a bit dry sometimes. To me it was endlessly fascinating. The Martian was more of a page turner for me but I found Seveneves found a similar way to make the minutiae of science and math and engineering into an exciting element of the storytelling. Although, unlike that book, I found myself drifting a little more from time to time with this one when technical details got a little too long-winded. But if you're looking for another book to fill a craving you've got for something like "The Martian", this will likely be my first rec from now on. (And vice versa, of course.) But while there are a lot of similarities on that level, this book is not that book. This book's scope is kind of hard to describe. There were times when I was just stunned by the enormity of the story being told. There's easily a few dozen diverse characters in this book that we form a connection to and there are so many point-of-view characters that even though this book is LONG, I still left wanting even more of their stories. (Perhaps that is a bit of a flaw as well, as there was not nearly as much attention paid to the details of the characters internal, emotional lives as there was to the technical details about orbits and the like. As much as I enjoyed a number of characters, they do sometimes take a backseat to the technology surrounding them.) I understood, from reading the description that... at some point the book was going to jump five thousand years into the future. While I was certainly excited to see what came next, I was definitely kind of dreading that moment as well. I became so attached to the Seven Eves that I wanted to spend more time with them especially. This book almost feels like multiple books with how much it encompasses but despite a slight preference for some earlier portions of the story, I'm very glad it was all one giant tale. One giant, epic fucking tale. There's a lot of science and philosophy I loved and hated and was fascinated by, but that's better left for spoiler filled discussions with those who have read it. I'll be absolutely shocked if this isn't my favourite scifi book published in 2015.

Listening to Mockingjay recently, I wasn't quite as enamored as I had been when I first read it a few years ago. I find so much dystopian fiction is appealing as it presents a new society, revealing how its terrifying construction is often the direct result of our current bad habits. In these series, certain characters may really seem admirable or inspiring or even detestable. However, the fight back against the prevailing leadership often fails to move me. I still enjoy this conclusion to the Hunger Games series, but I was doing less fist pumping than I had before. One thing stood out this time as particularly anti-climatic: the death of Prim. While we do see Katniss struggle afterwards, the moment it happens is so fast! And then it's over and on to the rest of the fighting. I didn't have time to register the loss as the audio plugged onward. I'd also not caught on before that going into the capital was like entering another arena. So each book in the series really is another arena fight. Missed that before!

Well it turned out to be one hell of a page-turner. Told from multiple character perspective (which has been a style offlate...), one cannot put it down once you pick it up for reading. Language is decent, not much harsh stuff or obscene prose (except in few instances where the situation demands), suitable for all ages. The story is told from the perspective of different characters in the plot, namely Rachel, Megan, Anna. Rachel is the 'girl' on the train or rather in the train who watches the houses along the tracks. especially the one near the signal where the train stops by everytime briefly, enabling Rachel to watch that particular house more closely. She becomes obsessed with the occupants of the house and also starts observing their activities and their daily routines. One day she notices that the girl has invited a stranger to her house and seems to her like she is having an affair. After a few days she is able to relate a news item concerning the disappearance of a girl, with this house that she observes from time. She also learns the actual names of the house occupants from the news article. From here the plots turns very interesting as Rachel tries to help the police to unravel the mystery of the missing girl. The police refuse to believe her due to her drinking habits, but she pursues further and tries to help Scott, who is the husband of the girl who went missing, Megan. Initially he belives her but gives up after sometime as Rachel is unable to remember everything that happened on the night of the disappearance of Megan, when she had also visited her ex-husband Tom's to patch up for her past mistakes. Meanwhile Rachel looses her job is takes up to drinking and parallely runs around trying to solve the mystery. Loved the ending when different narrators close in on the day of the murder and pin down the culprit. I recommend this book to anybody who loves a good who-dun-it Novel.

This review can also be found on A Thousand Lives Lived, check it out for more! All is Not Forgotten is a novel that I would normally want to pick up and devour instantly. It definitely is "my kind of read," especially because it is a psychological thriller slash mystery. There are so many good things about this genre that I usually am unable to imagine anything horrible about it. However, this time around, I feel pretty confused or mixed-feelings-like about this novel, and I feel quite upset over the fact that I am writing this review NOW, maybe seven months after I first read it. This was basically the best book gone wrong. I had so much hope for it because I expected a read that would be more about the actual mystery instead of the aftermath of this all. In a few words, I would describe this as a PTSD book. It's heartbreaking to read stories like these when you know that they have the capability of being so good or enjoyable. I honestly am not able to remember what this book is even about. What I can tell you is that it was readable--I was able to enjoy some of it and pick up on some of the important/captivating parts where I couldn't stop reading, but there were other points of time where I just felt like saying "meh." That is the best way to describe this whole book. This definitely incorporates some graphic violence so I would keep my eye out for that if you're not into stories that are really depressing and difficult to endure. All Is Not Forgotten is an average mystery novel that hits you a little, but leaves you shocked because you completely expected more. *A review copy was provided by the publisher via BookExpo America in exchange for a honest review. Thank you so much!

I did not read the summary of this before I bought it. I had heard that Colleen Hoover wrote fabulous contemporary teen romance/new adult, so I got it because it had her name on it. I try to read a book from this genre every once in a while, sprinkled in among the league of sci-fi/fantasy/paranormal books I read. I can't read too many of them in a row, because they are so often extremely depressing, regardless of how fabulous they are. This book is no exception. I was honestly convinced that there was something bizarre going on with Holder. I thought he had the big problem, that he was some sort of crazy, that this book was all about him. I don't know if I just missed some things along the way, but without getting too spoilery, let's just say that this book is DEFINITELY about Sky. Through and through. Her journey of self-discovery is painful, heartbreaking, and if it hadn't been for her relationship with Holder, this book wouldn't have been worth it for me. Holder. Oh Holder. I was worried there for a while that you were extremely messed up. So messed up that you would lose all your attractiveness. But you really pulled through man. Especially when EVERYTHING went to hell. And that's putting it nicely. Things really went down the drain. It felt like the hits just kept coming, and I wondered when they would stop. But even through all of it, I was so glad that Sky wasn't like: Yeah, she had a hard time dealing with the HORRIBLE things in her past. And when I say HORRIBLE, I mean it. This book was hard to read. I can't even begin to imagine having to go through some of what Sky went through. But she tried so hard to move on. There were awful moments where what she tried didn't work, and those choices brought about really crappy consequences. But Holder wins the best boyfriend ever award. He sticks by her through some really rough stuff. Not going to lie, I was dubious when Holder was the only guy Sky had ever felt anything with. But the explanation is pretty great. Extremely painful, but also beautiful; it makes their relationship even more meaningful. Sassy gay friend Breckin disappeared half-way through the book. Why? He was fun. And he was sweet. I mean, I certainly enjoyed that Holder dominated her time after a while, but I missed some interaction with other characters. Slut-best-friend Six was entertaining. I kind of started missing their conversations as well. The people at school, however, were totally uncool. I mean, come on people! LEARN HOW TO BE A HUMAN BEING. Stop tormenting people you don't know, who have done LITERALLY nothing to you, especially on their first day. I didn't go to public high school, so I didn't deal with some of the stuff that happened in this book; I always have a hard time believing things like that really happen. I do agree with some of the reviews that said that Sky should have been more freaked out by Holder at the beginning. I mean, he was pretty crazy when he first saw her at the grocery store and then he sort of had intermittent craziness that certainly would have concerned me. So, yeah, she probably should have stayed away. But once you get to the end, you're so glad she didn't. So while a lot of this book wasn't necessarily enjoyable, it was quite beautiful. All in all, I've been very impressed with all the New Adult books I've read. I'm glad this genre is expanding, and I'm thrilled publishers are taking the risk to make these excellent books widely available. Similar Books: Wait for You by Jennifer L. Armentrout, The Coincidence of Callie and Kayden by Jessica Sorensen See this review and others like it in a more awesome format at Ramblings On Readings

A short, surreal tale about a magician who accidentally makes an elephant appear. "I intended only lilies!" he keeps apologizing. "Please, I intended only a bouquet of lilies." The elephant is the talk of the town for a while after having crashed through the roof of the opera house in the European city of Baltese. Overnight it becomes an icon such that "if, for instance, a person was deeply surprised or moved, he or she would say, 'I was, you understand, in the presence of the elephant.'" People have fabulous arguments with each other including such zingers as "Your lack of understanding is as apparent as the elephant and is even more unlikely to disappear." Some clever philosophy student could get some mileage out of this.

3.75 stars I received an e-ARC copy of To Have and to Hold from the publisher and NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. Brooke Baldwin has just moved to New York to join Wedding Belles, a premier wedding planning company. She's eager to move on from the fiance that was arrested on their wedding day and a fresh start is just the way to do it. Her first client is a sweet hotel heiress Maya and her tempting brother Seth Tyler, the Tyler hotel group CEO. Seth is trying to keep it all together. After finding out that his father hid his heart condition from Seth until after his death, Seth is determined to not lose anyone else. If that means investigating his sister's fiance behind her back, so be it. Maya is engaged after only knowing the guy for three months and Seth finds that suspicious, also he's never met the man. So because he holds the purse strings, he will be involved in this wedding. Now if the wedding planner would just stop distracting him with how attracted he is to her. I liked Brooke and Seth a lot. They had great chemistry, the banter was hot and the together they felt right. There were lots of cute moments together in the book. I liked Maya and Grant and I really would have liked to see more of them. I have slightly mixed feelings about this book. Seth and Brooke both have a lot of baggage that didn't get addressed. Brooke is ignoring everything to do with her former fiance and she isn't dealing with it at all. There were parts where Seth and Brooke were having a moment and she would make a quip that would totally break the mood for me. It just seemed off. Then she would fly off the handle about things that just didn't make sense to me. Like the breakfast scene. Brooke did not handle that well. Then when they break up and Seth tries to contact her and she is ignoring him, eventually he stops and Brooke says that he didn't try hard enough. Really! Seth is a control freak and he admits that right up front. It ends up damaging his relationship with just about all the characters in the book. When he loses control he lashes out and usually it's pretty mean. The good thing is that he is aware, but he doesn't put much effort into trying to fix it, until the end. I feel like Brooke and Seth should have been able to work through their problems together. What I really wanted was for them to do that. So what I really wanted was a longer book. The ending was sweet and cute but I wanted them to work together and I don't think I got that. It was a good read and I enjoyed it. I am looking forward to Heather's book.

This book is dangerous! That I was still awake at midnight when my reader downloaded the book, was a coincidence - that I'm still awake 6 hours later (and mainlining coffee) is not. You have been warned. I absolutely loved it! (apart from one thing at the end) What I absolutely loved about Scottie (apart from him being him ;-) ) was the development he went through, from cold and apart to - well, I don't want to spoiler to much... While Sophie didn't change as much, to my mind, she didn't need to, because she treated the hero in the right way from the start. I really liked her verbal diarrhea and that she was someone he couldn't intimidate. The thing that impressed me the most, was that the book managed not only to be sweet, but hot and sexy even though they didn't even kiss until about waaaay into the story. You want to have an impression of the swoon-worthiness of this book? Just look at the following quotes: You are my greatest weakness because I have no defense when it comes to you or [...]my hear still fucking fluttering. I wouldn't be surprised if there are cartoon hearts in my eyes, and I don't bloody care The only thing I had a problem with was the 'big conflict' in the end, because I had a little bit the impression that it was mostly there to have a conflict and for the characters to face their feelings. I mean, after they spent the time together in Italy and have a moment where they share their feelings - maybe not verbally, but I had the impression that it was definitely recognizable to both of them - to have such a misunderstanding because they aren't sure of the feelings the other has? Really? And for her to run away instead of talking to him about it? Somehow that doesn't really fit with the image I had of her. Yes, her biggest fear is Never being good enough. Being used up and tossed aside. and that's something I can emphasize with, but the way she behaves throughout the book had me expecting her to at least confront him about being thrown out and the NDA thingy. Especially since I think Kristen Callihan is an author who is so good, that she doesn't have to resort to plot-tricks like miscommunication.

Another heartbreaking love story from Melanie Harlow. Just when you think she couldn't get any better, she does. She pushes the envelope on love. She makes you think outside the box. She makes you feel. And I felt. I felt happiness, sadness, loneliness, closeness, and everything in between. Hannah is a widow, left to raise her daughter on her own. She's doing everything she can to survive, but sometimes life is just too hard, too much. Wes is surviving his brother's death. After spending years overseas, he finally comes home to his family. While learning the ropes at the family practice, he's building and mending bridges with Hannah, his sister-in-law, and Abby, his niece. But what happens when you start to fall for the one person you should never have feelings for? What happens when others stick their noses in your business and think they know better than you do? What happens when it all blows up in your face and the very thing you've been fighting against is inevitable? Do you embrace it? Or just let it slip through your fingers?
