Bandits are attacking the villages around Moscow and Grand Prince Dmitrii and his loyal friend and cousin the monk, brother Alexander, must ride out to help save their people from the Tatar threat. Once again, this is a beautifully imagined story interweaving Russian folklore with what is also a very cleverly written modern adaptation, seamlessly continuing Vasya's story whilst transporting it and the Frost Demon, Morozko, away from the countryside and into a fight for Moscow itself. Let me preface this review with stating that I WANTED to like this trilogy... family and friends have recommended this series to me and I decided to give it a go. My review of the first book wasn't exactly favorable, and "Golden Son," like its predecessor failed to wow me like it has for other people. Like in "Red Rising" the world-building is the strongest aspect of "Golden Son," with the structure of the colored society in the distant future painting a vivid picture of opulence and oppression. However, even within the fantastic world-building, I'm often left with questions about why there haven't been other rebellions (though we do hear about a few) and how colored segregation by birth seems to be extremely inefficient in many ways (why not segregate based on proficiency like they do in the academy... oh wait, that would be too much like every OTHER dystopian novel that's out there these days...) The biggest pitfall this series suffers from (aside from the melodramatic and choppy writing) is telling instead of showing. We're always TOLD that Darrow is fantastic (by Darrow; good lord get a room for yourself, bro), but half the time he makes incompetent, poorly informed choices that either blow up in his face or he gets bailed out by one of his team members. I get that a lot of the political maneuverings are supposed to be difficult for Darrow, and that the Golds are all backstabbing liars, but anyone could have seen the ending to "Golden Son" coming from a mile away. I often felt like Darrow (and sometimes other characters) were required to hold the idiot ball (http://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php...) for the sole purpose of plot progression. If Darrow is so amazing and smart, why is he falling into a trap every other chapter? I spent far too much time rolling my eyes while reading this book, and continued to be angered at the continued casual misogyny and homophobia. Darrow himself becomes less and less likeable as he appears to be just as prejudiced and judgmental as his evil-Gold counterparts half the time. We're supposed to be rooting for Darrow and the lowerColors throughout the novel, but even Darrow views Pinks and Browns and other lowerColors with derision, and NOT when he's acting for other Golds (he uses "sniveling Pixie" as an insult in his narration more than once). Sevro, Mustang, and Roque were the only characters worth sticking around for, and Roque got little to no screen time, and I didn't like the turn the novel took at the end; even if I did see it coming from a mile away. Sevro was great as always (his speech about Mustang's Golden Pedestal was wonderful), but Mustang's storyline and attitude irritated me as I read. She's always being compared to a whore and other gendered slurs, but we never hear that kind of derision being slung at the male characters (unless they're being compared to women as an insult, naturally), even if they sleep around. The novel doesn't address this disparity, so it's not close to being any sort of commentary. Overall, this book was another big disappointment. I may or may not read the last installment when it comes out, as I am curious to see how Brown resolves all of this dangling plot threads, but the writing and women-hating is draining on my soul.

I wanted to read this because a fifteen year old Louise Brooks is an important character, but I was delighted to find out it is her mature- in- age chaperone Cora, who learns the important lessons. Cora is a Wichita, Kansas housewife, whose sons are about to go off the college, when she decides to chaperone young Louise Brooks to New York City where she will study with the Denishawn Dance Company over the summer. Cora, who seems to be all about propriety, isn't. She has all sorts of secrets: her handsome, wealthy lawyer husband is gay, her "brother" who lives with them, is her lover, her husband's lover doesn't live there, but he spends many nights dining with them at their home, she is an orphan, who came to Kansas on the orphan train. The last one is particularly hard for me to understand, but if one doesn't know who one's relatives were, then it is difficult for 'society' to gauge one's worth. The novel could have ended when Louise went off to become Louise Brooks, but the novel is much more concerned with how Cora learned to live, a bit, like Louise Brooks. I liked this book a lot. I'm going to have to get a hold of Lulu in Hollywood, Louise Brooks' autobiographical essays.

So, it turns out this is the third book in a season (news to me! ), but it works well as a stand alone. Definitely seems worth going back and getting a little more of the back story, but there's certainly enough to set the scene without the prior knowledge. The story follows 17 year old Rachel, a rich girl who is heavily into cars and lives in the shadow of her deceased sister, and Isaiah, a tattooed and pierced punk product of foster care with a penchant for the drag racing circuit. Their meeting is chance, as Rachel seeks a thrill an accepts the offer of a drag race. The cops bust it, and she won't leave him behind. Their story at times has nothing exceptionally new: teens, the good girl and the bad boy, tattoos used as a sign that he's bad news, and an undeniable connection despite all their differences, parents and brothers who just won't understand. And while that much very much falls in line with what you'd expect, their actual back stories prove interesting. Isaiah has friends as family and rebels against his care worker and mother, who has been released from prison; he's bad news for everyone, in his mind. Rachel's is much more loaded. Born after her family kept having kids to replace the daughter they lost to leukemia, she feels the lifelong pressure to keep her mother happy and try be the reincarnation of the sister she never knew. Her brothers are overprotective and her anxiety is triggered by much of the pressure that is put on her; she fears being weak, but ultimately proves to have strength in other ways. The crescendo (though the subsequent plot points may say otherwise) comes as Rachel stands to present a 20 minutes speech at the leukemia charity her mother works with, a turn for both the book in tone, and the understanding of her as a person by those around her. Crash Into You is not without its moments of head over heels love, but it's easy to see why teens would fall into. At that age, it's easy to relate to that level of attachment. But where many others in this genre have a couple with no real grit to their tale, this brings to interesting characters together. Where many plots veil a possessive ass under the veil of 'being protective', Isaiah genuinely is protective from the off, and all for the right reasons. Kind of refreshing after some of the books that have come this year, actually.

Rainbow Rowell: still the queen of cuteness. 4/5 stars. This review was originally posted on my book blog. This is the third full-length novel by Rainbow Rowell I've read, and I'm pleased to report I enjoyed it as much as Fangirl and Carry On. Told from the alternating first-person viewpoints of the titular characters, Rowell (once again) shows her skill in depicting those small moments in which very two different people gradually realise they have more in common than they thought and, hang on a minute, actually kinda like each other. This section of the book, in particular, is adorable and made me grin like an idiot. The 80s setting didn't hurt either and I loved that they were able to connect through the music of the time: lots of excellent nostalgia for a slightly more mature (*ahem*) reader like me. E&P is a fantastic depiction of teenage love and friendship, in its all-consuming, overwhelming glory. When the characters say they've missed each other, even though they've only been apart for a few hours, it brought back strong memories of high school, when we used to see each other all day and then "have" to spend half the evening on the phone chatting about nothing much. As you may have guessed from the blurb, this story doesn't have a typical "happy ever after" ending. To which I say, "good". They're sixteen, for goodness sake! Having them waltz off into the sunset would just be weird. Besides, the darker, sadder aspects of the story (mostly revolving around poor Eleanor's home life - I wanted to adopt her and all her siblings pretty much instantly) provided much needed balance to the fluffier parts of the narrative. Overall: Eleanor & Park is a touching portrayal of the beginnings of fuzzy young love, tempered by some harder reality. A great choice if you like romance stories which are cute, but not sickly sweet.

I enjoyed this look into another vampiric world. In Laurie London's books, vampires have learned (in the medieval times, I believe) that they can go weeks between feedings by just taking energy (skin-to-skin contact). However, a faction (called Darkbloods) prefer feeding from (and often killing by draining) humans and the more civilized faction (Guardians or the Agency) protect humans from them. A twist is that some humans have special blood that is apparently an extra treat and is called Sweetblood - that makes these humans hunted. The heroine of the story is a Sweetblood, although she has no clue that that is what has made her family cursed. Many family members over generations have just disappeared, so Mackenzie has just given up on planning for a future, assuming that someday the same thing will happen to her. When she unexpectedly stumbles upon an injured Guardian in a graveyard as she photographs it, events are set into motion that bring her into Dominic's world. When an accidental (and believed to be a fairy-tale) blood bond occurs between Dom and Mackenzie, he struggles between protecting her and following the rules, with an added side dish of running the risk of missing out on the revenge he has sought for years. I enjoyed the "will they, won't they" dance as the two characters fought against their mutual attraction. They definitely had fireworks! I also liked the secondary plotline with the mole in Pavlos' organization turning out to be Dom's brother that he thought was a traitor. (I look forward to reading his story, too.) All in all, an enjoyable vamp romance!

Wow. This was an exhausting read. Between the epilogue, the afterword 1986, the last chapter 1989, the update: twenty years later 2000, and a postscript penned by Rule's daughter, I thought I might never finish this. That said, it is considered by many to be the definitive work not only on Bundy the serial killer, but also on Bundy the charismatic, attractive, and promising law student. And really. What are the chances? You're a struggling single mom of four, eking out a living writing true crime articles for detective magazines and suddenly not only have you received a contract to write a book detailing a string of grizzly murders, but once the murderer is caught you find out he is a friend and previous coworker. Seriously. You can't make this stuff up. At times, I found Rule's narrative to be repetitive and overly introspective, but I guess given the circumstances, it was hard to avoid. And what the hell. She deserves to get it off her chest. Plus, eventually, she makes some valid observations, particularly with respect to Bundy's final interview in which he tries to "blame" his actions on violent pornography and detective magazines (ie true crime stories). I had actually watched the interview earlier on in the reading process and admit that he almost had me biting--hook, line, and sinker. However, after reading Rule's analysis, I think she was spot on. Which, I think is the point. A sociopath, Bundy was a master manipulator, incapable of empathy and lacking a conscience. He certainly wasn't able to fully appreciate his culpability. Pointing the finger at society seems consistent with his character. I personally found some of the add-ons to be of little value, with the exception of the afterword and the last chapter, which both document the remainder of Bundy's ordeal. All in all, a fascinating story told with competence, at least for the most part. If you happen to pick up a later printing like I did, consider skipping the epilogue, the update 2000 and the postscript. As an aside, though unintentional or not on the part of Rule, I think there is an interesting discussion of the death penalty. It took millions of dollars to put Bundy to death, far more than it would have cost to keep him alive. Furthermore, seeing that he represents a "diseased" brain, I wonder if "we" (society) missed an opportunity to better understand exactly what contributes to the making of a Bundy. I also wonder if as a society we need to redefine what constitutes sanity and insanity and the legal implications. I'm not sure men like Bundy have the power to stop themselves, just like I don't think most of us with normal functioning brains can understand how a Bundy couldn't stop himself. Anyone who does what he did has to be playing by a different set of rules, and it seems to me they are suffering from something that may be no more their fault than a man who is stricken with cancer. What does that mean legally? I'm not sure. But while putting men like Bundy to death "feels" right on some visceral level, it doesn't even begin to address the underlying problem. Of course, on the other hand, this is a man who escaped twice, murdering and/or brutally attacking a half-dozen victims before being recaptured. Had he the opportunity, he would have killed again. Anyway, lots of food for thought.

Sometimes I really do not understand YA ratings on this site. To All the Boys I've Loved Before, a book that was really fluffy and had some character development/consistency issues, has a 4.08. This book, with a fantastically developed protagonist, believable conflicts, and, honestly, a really fun writing style, has a 3.55! This book was way, way better than To All the Boys I've Loved Before. The good: The Spectacular Now is a truly impressive character study. I love books like this, because by the end I feel like I know the protagonist inside and out. Sutter is a funny guy, but he has a huge heart, both of which make the story enjoyable to read. He's also much more dependent on alcohol than he himself thinks. For that reason, the ending makes your heart ache, but I admire the author for creating a realistic ending instead of making Sutter change dramatically, because that would have felt a little cheap. It's a good reminder that even in YA, stories don't always have fairy tale endings. The bad: The end of this book left something to be desired, and I can't decide if it's because Sutter himself left so many loose ends or the author did. I think it's a little bit of both. I want to be clear, though, that I don't mean the actual ending itself- because I absolutely loved that- but more the fact that when the book came to an end, literally nothing had been resolved. I don't necessarily think that's a bad thing, but it's a book that won't give you a lot of closure. You're going to want to read more that isn't there. Also, some people will probably hate Sutter and think he comes off as a flippant hedonist. I personally adored him, but if you don't like the protagonist, you probably won't end up enjoying this book. Overall: This book is surprisingly deep and poignant for YA. Sutter is a truly memorable protagonist, and I loved being inside his head for the duration of The Spectacular Now.

Wow. Just wow. Brandon Mull is a god of fantasy - one of my top three favorite authors - and this book does not disappoint. It is a great conclusion to a phenomenal series. As usual, Mull's imagination knows no bounds. He fills his world with such creations, I simply don't know how he comes up with them. Among the more impressive things in this book was the Maumet and the way it was destroyed. But as well as a fantastically developed world, this book also had fantastic characters, and especially the two leads - Jason and Rachel. Jason is the one we'd aspire to be, Rachel is the one we relate to. Jason is one of the most heroic, brave, and selfless characters I've ever read about. Yet he never seems to be on a higher level than the reader - he's fond of sleeping, he's riddled with doubts, he thinks about impressing the pretty girl... he's human, in short. And he never gets that "I am THE hero and must save everyone and everything" complex. When Rachel tells him in one of the earlier scenes, "you're inspiring," and so forth, I couldn't help agreeing. Rachel is probably the one that most of us would end up acting like - she's pessimistic, always questioning and untrusting, and she does contemplate giving up. Yet she's also very resourceful and caring. The scene, early on where she gets everyone together for a group picture before they depart on separate quests, made me tear up quite a bit. It was just such a beautifully human moment - trying to preserve, however flimsily, a moment when everyone is together and happy. While I was blinking back tears in the end as well, it was this scene that affected me the most. My one minor complaint,  is how Rachel counteracted Maldor's command to set her on fire with seeming ease. I get that she's a very proficient magical adept, but seeing her overpower the omni-powerful wizard who's conquered a continent, and especially using a spell for the first time, was a touch implausible. But since my issue is just with that one line, it's just nitpicking. Moving on. Thank you, Brandon Mull, THANK YOU for not having  Jason and Rachel end up together. Thank you for showing that a teenage boy and girl can be very close friends and spend a lot of time together without any romantic feelings involved. I admit, I was leery of this happening, because it happens in every damn book ever, and I applaud Mr. Mull for pleasantly surprising me. Maldor is a very convincing villain. He does not suffer from Evil Overlord Syndrome - at no point did I feel that he was a melodramatic shmuck who couldn't possibly have conquered all of Lyrian. His downfall came through almost no fault of his own - in fact, major props to the author for all the creative ways he managed to have the heroes defeat Maldor without making Maldor weak. Maldor is one of the most compelling and intelligent villains I've had the pleasure of reading about. Other highlights include Ferrin's last scene with Tark, and the two surprises (and very emotional ending) regarding Nedwin. I did not see either surprise coming, and the second one is absolute GENIUS. I mean, damn, what a fakeout! I loved all the snappy dialogue - the jokes and sarcastic retorts. Not only did it make me laugh, it made the whole thing seem more real. Again, I refer to the original parting scene between Rachel and Jason (truly is the best one in the book), when Rachel pleads with him to be serious as they part, and Jason keeps joking as his way of coping. I just wanted to hug them both so hard in that moment. Also, Brandon Mull does not pull his punches - characters die. Lots of them. Sometimes brutally. And he doesn't pull a Paolini - his important characters are not immune, and some do die. Admittedly, the body count mostly comes from minor characters and a majority of the main ones survive (also, having the seedmen is almost cheating - Mull can write his deaths and kept the characters around too!). But it's clear that they are fighting a war at a terrible cost. As a wrap-up, I bow down to Brandon Mull. Both this series and Fablehaven are some of the best books I've read, and this was both a fantastic book and a very satisfying conclusion. Now all I can do is release a contented sigh, and hope to find a book half as compelling as this series was.

As much as I liked the story, I feel like there are a couple unforgivable shortcomings. There are so many proposed solutions to the mystery that I've lost track of what parts fit together to make up the truth. It might just be that it's easy for me to lose track of these things. The really big issue is the female characters. They're all mothers, sisters, objects of desire, victims, servants, or secondary to the plot. There was no strong female character in the story. Not one. It's something I noticed early on, but withheld judgment on hopes that it would change as the story evolved. But it was like a boy's club sausage fest. I can't really support a story that treats women this way. There could have at least been a female cop or something.

Oxygen is essential for most living things. For 2.5 billion years, it was the most abundant chemical element on Earth. Until the switch. Inhale. Exhale. Breathe. Breathe. Breathe... What happens when oxygen becomes the government owns the oxygen? In the Pod, breathing is a  privilege , not a  right . Only the wealthy get to breathe as freely as they want. The poor? They have to consciously manage their oxygen usage. One gasp too many and they will suffocate. Bea is an auxiliary hoping to pass her exams to become a premium. If she earns the right to the status, she no longer has to fight for her air. She can provide for her family. They can laugh together, kiss each other. Alina is what the government calls a "terrorist." She knows what the government is doing, how they're getting the people to be addicted to an abundance of air so they're always needed. And she wants it to stop. She will do anything to give the world its freedom back. Quinn is Bea's best friend and a premium. When he meets Alina, he is instantly swept off his feet. He will do anything to get her to notice him, even if that means using his premium status to help the rebels. **** 3.5 STARS for BREATHE **** I really enjoyed this book, ESPECIALLY the premise behind it. What Sarah Crossan did really well was the world building. I understood the side of the rebels, but I also understood the government's side. Neither side was completely full of power hungry jerks or peaceful, freedom fighter. Each side had its handful of people with good intentions and bad intentions. My only problem with  Breathe  was that its action scenes were really anti-climatic. The whole book built and built. It was fast paced and you could tell it was leading somewhere and then... It just dropped out. I think this problem will fix itself in the second book, though, because stakes are much, much higher. I'd recommend this to fans of dystopian and young adult. I am definitely going to buy the next book when it comes out!

Definitely not as good as the first, but Parker is such an enjoyable writer that I still give it four stars. Charlotte and Rothbury are a couple of characters we met in 'At the Bride Hunt Ball'. Charlotte is introduced as a mouse who doesn't wear her spectacles because she 'reinvents' herself to go with other people's supposed desires. Rothbury is introduced as a rake with no conscience whatsoever (although his actions belie the other characters' perceptions). So, I was very interested in the idea of the two of them getting together. It seems like the premise for a typical romance, right? Opposites attract. But the premise is actually better than that. It seems Rothbury -- the rake who cares nothing for the women with whom he involves himself -- has been secretly in love with mousie Charlotte for years. He's never made a move because she's always fancied herself in love with Tristan -- his best friend. In fact, his bad behavior is partially a result of his unrequited love. Although his upbringing by a seriously despicable father and uncles is the main reason, he apparently has been cultivating this bad image of himself to guard his own heart. Great setup. I love the idea. The execution -- not so much. It was disorganized. I knew how he felt about Charlotte because I was told that in the exposition. But I didn't see how that started or any of the interactions that led to his being smitten. This is years after the fact and all we get is a vague 'she was always nice, and never judged' kind of thing. Which is lovely, but a flashback would have helped set up the chemistry. My biggest problem with all of this was Charlotte's POV. She never thought anything about Rothbury except that she should stay away from him. Then suddenly she's forming an alliance in order to get a mild vengeance against Tristan and help Rothbury win Lady Rosalind's (Tristan's sister) heart. There was fertile ground in the premise but it just wasn't used, I thought. I didn't have any idea where things were going next because it just felt kind of jumbled. The stakes didn't feel all that high to me, either. And then, when there's actual danger, it felt like it was tacked on. Almost like an editor said 'we need something here.' So why do I give it four stars? Because my harsh criticism is in light of having just read the excellent 'At the Bride Hunt Ball'. You set the bar high and expectations will be what they will be. I was rooting for this couple. I loved Rothbury and Charlotte and thought they made a very fun couple. I guess one of my main problems was that we didn't get to see a real arc of their romance. We cut ahead three months at one point and there were interactions within that time that probably would have been delightful and founded their relationship in action rather than just exposition. I have high hopes for Olivia Parker's historical romances. This left me slightly unsatisfied, but she's still one of my newest auto-buys.

I loved this book! It is the story of a young girl growing up in Nazi Germany. Her brother dies on a train and her mother leaves her in foster care with a family in a small village. The story is told from the point of view of Death who comes to take various people during the story and has become interested in the person he calls "the book thief." The style of writing was very different and perfect for this story. While the time period is one of tension and tragedy, the book is not especially gloomy. The everyday life of Germans during the war is fascinating. The characters have depth and complexity and I find that I remember them in much the same way I remember Dickens' characters. I would recommend this book to anyone. I read this in 2010 and knew I would read it again. I think I've gotten even more from it this time. I appreciate the view of WWII from the ordinary German point of view. I know from talking to German friends that a lot of people were against Hitler, especially as he gained more and more power. On my second reading, I've paid more attention to the power of words in this book. Leisle understands the power of words even before she can read. The book also raises the point that Hitler came to power through his ability to use words. By the time many people understood his whole plan, he had so much power it was hard to object.

Out of the three books in this series, Mockingjay was my least favorite. I feel that the book itself fell a little short. The series lost it's luster in a way, even though I found myself still enthralled with the book. I think this is because of the attachment I had to Katniss. I wanted to finish the book to see what happened to her. I am glad that she ended up with Peeta, but I wish we would have learned more about Gale. I would have liked Gale's character to be a little bit more developed. Also, the book did raise some questions that I hoped would be answered at the end. For instance, we have a good idea that Gale was somewhat responsible for Prim's death but we never really know for sure. I feel like I was left hanging a little bit. Katniss was my favorite character in books one and two, but I began to not care as much about her in this one. I felt like I had to finish the book to know what happened to her. She was completely detached from almost everything in the plot. Rather than being the Mockingjay that sacrifices herself for the cause, she blacks out and hides through most of the battle. She was just a pawn for District 13's rebellion and I wanted her to be more than that. She exhibited such strength in the first book and somewhat in the second. I was disappointed. She doesn't even seem to care all that much that Prim died. But maybe this is just to show how a war can affect people. I'm not sure. The love triangle was poorly executed as well. Peeta essentially goes crazy, which did add some twist to the story. From the start I really liked Peeta. Actually it wasn't clear that Gale had any feelings for Katniss until she returns from the first Hunger Games. I think that is why I never really felt he had to be with Katniss, although I did not dislike Gale as a character. Even when Peeta is not fully himself, he tries to protect Katniss. Gale it seems just gives up and we hear nothing more of him other than he works in district 2. And at the end of the book I'm still not certain which guy Katniss really wanted to be with. She's with Peeta just because he's the one who goes back to district 12. Gale doesn't even try to keep her, which makes me question if he really wanted her at all. Overall, Mockingjay was a decent book that fell short of expectations for what should have been an epic conclusion to a great series.

I received an advance review copy of this book courtesy of Netgalley and Bookouture. Have you ever read a book that so incredibly good, you wanted to tell everyone you meet that they MUST read it? Well, allow me to introduce you to The Gift, because this is an experience you don't want to miss! Gripping, riveting, spellbinding, engrossing--whip out your thesaurus and pick any synonym you like--this fascinating psychological thriller will have you staying up way past your bedtime. But don't worry... it's well worth the book hangover. Jenna is nearing six months of recovery from a heart transplant. She's been having dreams and flashbacks of memories that are not her own, not to mention behaving in ways that are not like herself. In her quest to understand, she researches cellular memory--the theory that the cells in your body can store memories which can then be transferred to another person after receiving an organ transplant--and becomes convinced this is the cause of it all. Breaking the rules and going against the advice of everyone she knows, she contacts the family of the young woman whose heart now beats in her chest. The more she learns about Callie, and what happened the night of the accident that took her life, the more convinced she is that there is more to it than anyone knows. Determined to find out what really happened, she insinuates herself into the lives of the people who knew Callie best, and uncovers unsettling information that makes her believe Callie's "accident" was, in fact, murder. Risking her fragile health and, indeed, her own life, Jenna is willing to do whatever it takes to learn what really happened to Callie that night. But when the answer comes, it's far more insidious (and heartbreaking) than Jenna could ever have imagined. Jensen's writing throughout is superb. The attention to detail regarding Jenna's recovery, and the sensitivity in showing the emotions of Callie's family was excellent. The ominous sense of eminent danger had me on the edge of my seat from page one. Simply put, it's everything you could hope for in a psychological thriller, and then some.
Ah, I am excited for the second book. I like the characters a lot as well as the humor and the story in general. I really hope that I will see Archer again in the next book.

5+ stars - Contemporary Romance/Erotica/Menage/BDSM I loved this book for so many reasons, but mainly for its strong characters, unforgiving honesty, and heartfelt emotion. Stoic Seattle cop Todd is different in many ways from his free-spirited, rocker chic neighbor Erin, but one place they are totally in sync is in the bedroom. It seems Todd harbors a secret kinky, Dom streak, and lucky for him, Erin is more than willing to indulge his darkest desires, wildest fantasies, and kinky fetishes and to submit to his sexual control. They have a good thing going and are engaging in a hot affair, but Todd panics and isn't ready to embrace his true self. He comes from a rather normal, straight-laced family and thinks he needs a relationship and future with a 'nice' girl with more, shall we say, vanilla appetites, so Todd and Erin sadly part ways. Now, 10 years later, after a failed marriage and a job related injury in Boston, Todd is back in Seattle to start a private security consulting firm with his best friend Ben and best friend's brother. When Todd runs into Erin, who's also back in Seattle after a stint of living the rocker's dream life for a time in LA with her brother Adrian, and now running her own deli restaurant, the blast from the past comes with strong, overwhelming, and never forgotten feelings. But this time around, Todd is a man who has finally learned to accept his true nature, and he knows exactly who and what he wants, and that's Erin, back in his heart and his bed where she belongs, forever. Unfortunately, convincing Erin to open her heart and trust again won't be so easy because a traumatic event has left her shattered and emotionally scarred, and she's trying to rebuild her life one step at a time. Although Todd's Dom nature and protective instincts might be exactly what Erin needs to help her heal, she wants to stand on her own and rebukes his controlling tendencies. Things pick up where they left off, and the two quickly set the sheets on fire once again. What neither of them expected was the positive impact on their relationship or for such strong feelings to emerge by the sudden ease with which Todd's best friend Ben joins their duo. Todd, Erin, and Ben find themselves becoming a threesome based on friendship, longing, trust, respect, understanding, and of course, love with Erin at the heart and center, and although they might have trouble clearly defining and labeling it, they can't deny what they've found in each other. Of all the menage books that I've read, Laid Bare is one of the most realistic and honest in it's depiction of the reasons, emotions, and motives behind people engaging in an alternative relationship, lifestyle. None of them anticipated being in a threesome, and they didn't enter into it lightly, without thought of the hardships and consequences, or just for kinks and giggles. There's some rather wild, hot, D/s sex between Todd and Erin, and although heterosexual Todd and bisexual Ben's friendship develops into something deeper and more intimate, it's a tentative, gradual progression, especially since those feelings are centered around their sharing in their love for Erin. The emotional nature of the trio's relationship takes precedence in the story, rather than the carnal, sexual aspects of being in a menage as the primary focus, which was rather refreshing. It's a sexy, touching, thought provoking, and evocative story with characters to fall in love with that tugs the heartstrings, and it brought tears to my eyes a few times. Lauren Dane really knows how to write relatable characters who are survivors of past trauma, and Erin's emotional pain "laid bare" was palpable and heartbreaking. I think Todd, Erin, and Ben's relationship is a menage that has a realistic chance of lasting for the long haul. I just wish there had been more time in the story to see it develop even further. I can't wait for the sequel Coming Undone that's about Erin's older, nurturing, protective tattoo artist, biker brother Brody to come out in Jan'2010 because I adored him in this, so I'm super excited to read his story. Laid Bare is a fantastic read with scorching hot sex, raw emotion, brutal honesty, and lots of heart. Big 5 stars from this reader! (And I also love the beautiful, sexy cover!)

So I already reviewed the movie a few months back on my blog. Visually, I liked a lot of the elements, but plot-wise I felt it was weak and stumbling. I decided to read the book to see if any of the gaping holes in logic and continuity would be solved in the written version. I'm happy to say that at least the world makes a bit more sense now. SPOILER ALERT No, these child Shadowhunters are not the only hunters on earth, which was alluded to in the movie. There was no ridiculous attempt to take over the world with flying demonspawn/bat things. And the logic of Jace being Valentine's son held together a lot better with a lot more evidence. So in those aspects, I liked the book better. It's still pretty junky teenage angst and creepy things, but it's like candy--it tastes good for a moment then leaves you hungry afterwards. I like candy fiction now and again. I read another review which stated that this book was basically rewritten Harry Potter fanfic, which I can somewhat see, but I applaud Cassandra for moving beyond that starting point, if that was the starting point. (which it probably was.) There's enough interesting details in the world with the runes and scars and glamors that I enjoyed the tale. I caution the writer to avoid similes whenever possible. They are not her best talent. (his hair was like brass. REALLY?!) I'm also not crazy about the pseudo-incest or whatever you might call that, but it certainly creates tension. I caution here to stay away from the Mary Sue-like portrayal of her heroine, and either let her be ugly or just do away with the poor me I'm just not as pretty as ____ attitude. I'd also like to see her actually train to use a weapon before using one. It's not that easy. Really. I don't particularly like Clary, the main character, which isn't a good thing. But I sort of like Jace and all his conflicts. The best character by far was the warlock, because he was SUPPOSED to be cardboard and over the top. As others have said, we know next to nothing about Valentine which basically makes him a boring 2D villain. About the only reason I felt anything at all for him was because of Jonathan Rhys Meyers' portrayal of him in the movie, which speaks volumes about JRM's acting talent and nothing about Cassandra's writing ability. For now at least, I'm willing try the next book. Then we'll see if I like where this series are actually going. So for me, this earns a lukewarm 3 out of 5 stars. Sort of liked but didn't love it.

Review: Um....wow... I actually was surprised by how this story concluded, which takes a lot. I cannot really say too much because I do not want to give anything about the story away, but let me tell you, there are twists! Lots of them! and they are super good. Lucinda come into her own very well in this book and the story FINALLY comes together and makes sense. It did however take me a while to get into this one though. I was a little disappointed when book three ended, because I thought it was a trilogy and then it turned out there was going to be another book. When I began reading Rapture, I really wasn't into it. There seemed to be a lag for me, once I hit about the half way point, I flew through it and couldn't put it down. If you recently read the other three and knew there was going to be a fourth book, I think that this will read very well for you. It picks up right where 3 leaves off, and immediately thrusts the reading into the drama and mission. Rapture is enchanting, astounding, and beautiful in its ending to this series. LOVED, LOVED, LOVED IT!!! Seth is officially back and better than ever! The Return was my most anticipated book of 2015 and it didn't disappoint. The book picks up a year after the events at the end of Sentinel and although you don't need to read the Covenant series before this, as the events are summarised, it does give you a better insight on Seth-our tortured hero- and the world of the Hemotoi. I already had a crazy amount of love for Seth from the Covenant series so getting to be in his head in his own book (it's in dual POV) was amazing. Seth was dealing with a lot of regret and self-loathing due to his previous actions and it is so sad to see him be so hard on himself. "I killed people. Sometimes I didn't make it quick. Do you know what that makes me?[...] A monster. It makes me a monster." Fortunately Josie, a demmigod who has had her powers bound to appear mortal and to whom Seth has been tasked with protecting, sees a different side to Seth. Especially when Seth begins to let her in, something he's never really done with anyone before. Going into this book I was very intrigued but wary of Josie, she had to be good enough for our Seth! Luckily I ended up loving Josie! She was cute, funny and had an inner strength her that was put to the test when her world was turned upside down. Her and Seth were also hilarious together at times. "Does compulsion work on me? "It shouldn't. You're a demigod[...] I can give it a try. Take off your robe." "What the hell?" "Guess it doesn't work." "You're a pervert." Josie sees past the Apollyon (or 'Pollyanna' lol) to the guy that Seth is underneath-something Seth desperately needs- all the while bringing out feelings in Seth that he's never had for anyone before, letting us see a softer side to him. And it's ADORABLE! "Sucked today or not, nothing in the sky is shining brighter than you." The brilliant old cast is back, Marcas, Solos, Deacon, Luke and of course Apollo, who is his typical hilarious self, trying to out-snark Seth. With Josie being one of the six demigods now tasked with acquiring their powers to eventually fight and re-imprison the newly freed Titans the stakes are rising on who will survive the impending battles. And will Seth be able to cope with what's to come, when it so resembles a past that ended in death? 'Everything would not be okay in the end. Not for me. Not for her. She was just a tool, a last resort against the Titans...' I so can't wait for the second book in the Titan series to see what happens next!! Also I desperately need to see Alex and Aiden make a reappearance! Seth definitely needs to resolve some issues there to have any chance of finding any peace and Seth so needs his happily ever after!

It's a bit strange- I've rated all of Megan Shepherd's books so far with 3 stars, which is a respectable rating but not amazing, and yet one might notice that I've actually read all of her novels. To be honest, the fact that I've read all of them is surprising- I guess her premises are gripping enough that I want to give the books a go, and the series then continues to be just good enough that I want to keep reading. There's something about this series in particular that's oddly addicting, even if the plotlines aren't the most well thought out, and the world building is not that great and the romance is quite lacking. There's just this slight curiosity as to what will happen next, but that curiosity is enough to keep your interest going. The world building in this novel was slightly better than in the first book, but I'm not sure that I have a good grip on the world and how things work. It's hard not to compare novels, and I've just read so many scifi novels where the world building is so much better. The plot in this novel is much improved though, with much more going on. There are multiple points of view, but this actually turns out in the novel's favour as seeing from the different characters' viewpoints is pretty interesting. I actually couldn't tell you right at this moment whether I'll eventually finish the series. I'm not that invested in it and probably wouldn't be upset to not read the last novel, seeing as though I have about a billion other books that I would put higher on my TBR. But on the other hand, if I see the last book in the library I quite possibly might pick it up. Ratings Overall: 6/10 Plot: 3/5 Romance: 2.5/5 Writing: 3/5 World Building: 2/5 Characters: 3/5 Cover: 2/5

Okay, so when I started the book I wasn't sure that I was going to like it because it seemed very stereotypical and dull. I was expecting a boy and girl meet, they have undeniable chemistry, fall in love, face a challenge, overcome challenge and happily ever after. That isn't exactly what I got. There are so many twists and turns in the book. I read it on kindle and there were so many times where I thought "Okay that's it I'm almost done with this" Then I check my progress and I'm only 50% through or 70% through or whatever. I still have a long way to go and I'm thinking what more could happen and the story kept going but not necessarily in a long stretched out kind of way. There were a bunch of turning points and through all of them I found Jordan to be easy to relate to. I mean, no my dad is not a big shot NFL player and no I don't play football and I definitely don't have a lake named after me but other than that... I loved how the story progressed because it never seemed over the top or super dramatic. There wasn't a point where I was reading and then thought, "Sigh if only that happened to me... but what are the chances, cause life is just not that dramatic or coincidental." Everything that happened seemed believable and realistic. It moved at the right pace and there wasn't a ton going on all at once in the kind of way that could only happen in stories and not reality. Catching Jordan turned out to be better than I expected.

I spent the first 90 percent of this book bored and skimming, hoping it would get better, and the last 10 percent rolling my eyes and screaming at the characters. Honor and her dead brother's best friend Rusty are driving from Texas to California to see Taylor Swift's Kyra Kelley's last concert because that's the last thing her brother asked her to do. I think it's stupid, but I could get past that if the rest of the book was good. But it wasn't. Honor meets some people in the woods and looks at the sunrise. And then she meets Rusty's family and watches the sunrise. And then she gets totally judgmental about people who make out in bathrooms and then gets so drunk she doesn't remember what she did. And then they park in front of a no parking sign and lose the car that she didn't register. And then they miss the concert. And then she runs into Kyra Kelley at the airport, and of course she wants to hear about her brother. The plot is just so unbelievable. If it were entertaining, I'd be able to overlook that, but it wasn't. There were no interesting insights or even situations. The inevitable romance between her and Rusty felt forced at times and didn't leave me wanting either of them to end up together. I hated them both at various times, when I felt anything at all. And the big secret revealed at the end about the real reason her brother went to Iraq? Fucking stupid. He wanted to make sure she could go to her dream college, so he had to join so that he could have money. Because there are no other jobs in the world that would let him make money and not, you know, die. As if members of the armed forces make a lot of money that justifies the risk. I sort of understand joining because you feel patriotic - or even because you're poor and this is your one hope of doing something. Not because you need quick money so you can take care of your sister. Because let me tell you - you can take care of her better if you're not dead. I'm sorry I wasted so much time trying to finish this book. I should have just DNF'd it when I first wanted to.
It is good! But I'm getting a bit tired of all those brooding males, how come men can't act like a normal piece of the human species in romance book.
The story was a bit slow, BUT, Park is the sweetest kid ever (!!!) considering that Eleanor wasn't the most desirable girl. (kid? I suddenly feel old.) Good read!

I strongly believe that a short story should stand alone, an entity unto itself. I find few things more annoying than stories that are so immersed in the author's "universe" that they require paragraphs of back-story to understand, or that are clearly a prequel and therefore end up seriously lacking in content. Too many of the stories in this collection suffered from one of these flaws. I understand the market for such stories, but please, tuck them away into a collection of "stories from the xyz universe" and let the free-standing collections return to truly being free-standing. However, there were a few gems in here that make me want to search out more by these authors. Most note-worthy: Jackson Pearce's "Things About Love." Beautifully crafted, maybe two sentences of back-story, if that, and truly touching. Jeri Smith-Ready's "Bridge." Fantastic opening grabbed me with the first two sentences, beautifully skillful at telling a fundamentally sad story with lots of humor.

Okay, so I may have over hyped myself with this one but it was still a very enjoyable read. Jamie is our lovable red headed cop who is determined not to let anyone near his emotions and Gavin is our resident lover boy/party runner who knows everyone and something else. They seem to make a odd pairing at first with all the we're just having sex talk, but what I really loved this one for was how close it came to being something you expect to happen in the real world. It wasn't the overplayed 'I'm sleeping with you so now I have feelings ' gig. It was two men being unsure about what they wanted and fighting tooth and nail against figuring it out of fear they'll mess each other up. That's what made this book so great. It made them human. They never realized that they came to a point where they cared and even thought that they could. Its kinda funny seeing that soon enough, it looks like Jamie will end up right where he didn't want to be in Quinn's shoes. I have a feeling he'll get used to it and love it though.

Yay! I missed having Chloe as a narrator. I'm so glad that we got to go back and get some closure to the end of the series with this novella, because that was one of the problems that I had with The Reckoning. This novella tells the story of (spoiler for The Reckoning) Kit telling Tori that she is his daughter . The group is living together post-escape as a "blended family" made up of Kit, Lauren, Simon, Derek, Tori, and Chloe. It was nice to be able to experience a little more of Tori's story, especially because of all the things she went through throughout the series and after reading Disenchanted, the Darkest Powers #2.5 novella from her perspective. This novella also gives closure to what Chloe goes through in the final scene of the series, which I thought was very much lacking from The Reckoning and was really glad to finally see some of.

This book literally changed me. It unbelievably nailed on making me cry like no book would ever make. The first book that had me teared up, the first book I ever truthfully categorize as a tear jerker. Not even TFIOS could even make me cry like I cried reading this book, despite reading it twice already. Suicide is not something to not be taken seriously with. People need to be aware of the fact that being alive is a wonderful thing to be. A person could have missed a lot of things in just a day. There's so much a person could do or be beyond their imagination only with being alive. There's more in this life that you could learn and take inspirations from. Every single second counts. Life is Life. I just never thought that Finch would end his life despite Violet and despite everything they did together. It breaks my heart and it upsets me how his selflessness of leaving Violet without even saying goodbye when he was well-aware that she was just started getting over his sister's death. I mean, how could he?? Despite this, I give all the stars in the sky for this book, just like how Jennifer gave Nicola Yoon's Everything Everything, and it was as if I'm giving them back to her showing just how much I was blown away reading this book! This book faithfully opens my eyes to a whole new level of how suicide is such an intimidating and stupid thing to do and taught me how life is valuable. It's beautifully written, I can't even imagine how a writer could be this genius that she could inspire people this much with only words. It becomes crystal clear why this book won the best 2015 Young Adult Fiction last year. It's like Fault In Our Stars all over again, it's just better. Much better.

Actual rating: 1 1/2 (& that's being generous) I wasn't expecting to love this book. It just didn't seem like something that would really blow me away. However, this book was even worse than I expected. I guess the main reason for that is that this book had a lot of tropes that I hate. Let's start with the love triangle. One of the weirdest ones I've ever encountered in fact. We have Adam, a childhood "friend," whom pretends to be her friend as a part of his plan. It turns out that their feelings have stemmed from childhood, despite not speaking to one another at all. "It sounds crazy," he says finally, so quietly. "To think that I cared so much without ever talking to you." Not weird at all. There's a difference between having a crush on someone and being so obsessed with them that your every thought revolves around them. Then we have Warren. He wants to use Juliette, our heroine protagonist as a war machine. You see, everything Juliette touches dies. Well, not dies immediately. Their power is basically drained out of them. So, he's automatically an asshole. He only "loves" Juliette so that he can seduce her into his plan of using her as a tool for domination. And, he's really creepy to her. Really. Everything he said to her was not "cute" or "romantic" at all. Now I fear for all of the people that I follow on Tumblr that like these two. Maybe they get better throughout the series, but right now, it seems bleak. I mean, he begged her to touch him (kinky? ), knowing very well that touching people and hurting them made her very uncomfortable. Then, he says things that can be considered underhanded compliments, but just made me feel flat out disgusted. "You're absolutely delicious when you're angry." "You don't know it yet, Juliette, but you are a very bad girl," he says, clutching his heart. "Just my type." "I like watching you squirm. He makes you uncomfortable, doesn't he?" Both guys are not ones that I would root for. Obviously Adam is less of a sexual predator then Warren, but they both have their faults really. Moving on to the writing. The writing in this...Mafi is trying so hard to make her writing something that it's not. She's trying to pull a Markus Zusak at times. She's trying to put these mind-blowing similes and metaphors out of her head, but they're just not there. They don't add to the book or make it more beautiful. They make it feel awkward and disconnected. For example: And we stand like that until I'm too old to remember a world without his warmth. What? You aged during that time that much? Just a weird sentence. Not cute or touching at all. I'm an old creaky staircase when I wake up. I thought this said "I am on an old creaky staircase," because that makes sense more than what's above. My eyes are two windows cracked open. Yeah...so your eyes are open basically. You don't need to tell us. Okay enough of that. And another trope that made me hate many series before, one being the Throne of Glass (cue gasp). Prepare yourself. Every guy is attracted to Juliette. I'm not exaggerating. Every male that we get to know in this book is at least attracted to her. I can't call it a love pentagon, but let's call it a I-think-you're-hot pentagon. They don't even know her yet! They're just stunned by her beauty. Maybe Juliette is beautiful (her personality ruins that though), but it's not realistic that every guy she meets in this book can't stop talking about her beauty and can't keep their eyes off of her. It's frustrating. Another thing that annoyed that is technically a spoiler is this: Two of her love interests can touch her?????? That's so stupid and such a cop out on the author's part. The only thing I can say is that this book is very easy to fly through. I think I read like two hundred pages in one sitting because it just flies. The writing is simple and there's a lot of stuff that's crossed out, even though it doesn't help the plot at all. Sorry this review is very very negative, but I just can't believe that the author could shove so many tropes that I dislike into one 300 page book. I honestly want to continue this series just to read about more stupid things that Juliette says and to see what guy she dreadfully chooses. Maybe if I get them for a gift, but I don't think I'll be spending my own precious money on them.

3.5 stars "Just when she thought this situation sucked as hard as it possibly could, it started sucking just a little bit more." A funny, fast-paced, romantic novel about demonic possession. After being attacked by a serial killer, Eden becomes possessed by the demon Darrak who can take form during the day but returns to her body during the night. Usually to offer unhelpful, earnest and funny commentary on everything. " 'Darrak' - Rosa began, 'I say your true name in order to bind you.' 'You told her my name?' Darrak asked with annoyance. She frowned. 'Aren't you supposed to be... binded, or whatever, now?' 'Bound. And no. No so much.' Rosa's forehead creased. 'Does the malevolent presence not acknowledge his true name?' Eden shifted nervously in her seat. 'Doesn't seem to.' 'Darrak,' Rosa said again. 'I bind you, you filthy spirit.' 'See now she's just being a bitch about it,' Darrak said. Eden rolled her eyes 'this isn't working.' Very easy reading, more than a few cringe-worthy moments, Darrak being an asshole and having bad puns, Eden running around and screaming a lot. The two idiots finally working out they like each other and it was cute af. Eden was snarky, empathetic and that right balance between smart and dumb. Sometimes, I wanted to shake her and other times I wanted to nod my head approvingly. I loved her constant, sarcastic commentary on everything, especially when she was on her date with Ben and had to listen to Darrak roast the guy the entire time. That was hilarious. And then the waiter! "Antonio wasn't looking at her. 'It's the restaurants tradition for the man at the table to make the dinner selections.' She blinked with surprise. 'I knew the waiters were snotty,' Darrak growled, 'but this guy is a serious asshole. Kick him in the shins, Eden. Do it.' She wasn't afraid to be shit-scared when she had to be and wasn't afraid to recognise when a decision she'd made had gone wrong. Darrak was funny, hot and shyly protective. He also had a few terrible (great) one-liners that literally made me groan in pain. " 'Oh,' she said after it sunk in. 'So I guess we're really going to be like brother and sister now, aren't we?' Darrak nodded nodded, but drew his thumb over her bottom lip. 'If the brother had incredibly inappropriate thoughts about his sister every minute of the day.' He managed a small smile. 'It's not going to be easy, but I won't hurt you again no matter how hard it gets.' He cleared his throat. 'You know. Literally.' He was sincere but had his selfish, asshole moments too. Poor Darrak, he was so earnest about changing. At least that made me like him. Keen to read the rest of the series! Sex with a bad boy usually left one with a broken heart. Sex with a demon left you with a broken soul. She'd have to remember that important little fact for future reference.

** spoiler alert ** This is one of the most beautifully written books I've ever read, and also one of the most disturbing. I'm usually into more hopeful books, but this one is like a punch in the gut. It was hard to put down, but sometimes it got so sickening I had to. It's hard for me to read about bad things happening to children, so this book was probably not the best pick for me. But it was so beautiful at the beginning that I got sucked in, and then I had to keep reading even though it only got worse and worse. Fitch is an amazing writer with a unique and breathtaking use of language. But the subject matter--incest, child abuse, neglect, pedophilia, foster homes, violence, drug use, etc was very hard for me to read about, especially since all of it was from the point of view of the girl. It was one of the most depressing books I've ever read. And I'm sure someone will ream me for this, but the only thing I could compare it to is a VC Andrews novel written by a poet. It's horrific, but you know things like this really happen in life, and you can't stop reading because you keep hoping something will get better. It doesnt. And then the child starts repeating the same patterns as the mother, and you just want to scream at her and shake her for being such an idiot. Sadly, that's what happens to lots of kids from messed up families. Victims of abuse become abusers, etc. Astrid sees how her mother is with men, and she becomes the same. In the end, instead of hope, you just get a clear indicator that Astrid will follow in her mother's footsteps, leave the only decent guy who ever loved her, and follow along through a string of men, leaving them and becoming hard and cruel like her mother. Really, really, really depressing book. I'd recommend to those who like books that make them uncomfortable, although people who say that make me laugh. But people who say that would like this book. It didn't make me uncomfortable--I dont think any book ever has. It did make me feel like crawling in a hole and crying for several weeks straight.

Actual rating: 3.5 In a future where the world is ravaged by Aether storms, the humans are forced to split into two highly differing societies. The Outsiders -- who live off the land, are segregated into tribes and led by a Blood Lord. A few people who live under the Aether -- the never sky -- have special talents, an enhanced Sense of sound, smell or sight. Then there are the Dwellers, who are everything opposite to the Outsiders. There's no stress or worries. They live in domed pods and get to participate in virtual realities through their Smarteye -- a device that suctions to one's eye and lets them be in any Realm they wish (if I were a Dweller, I'd want to spend my life in a Cupcake Realm). Aria, who's lived her whole life in a pod in Reverie, gets banished to the outside world and is left to die. Perry, an Outsider gifted with duel Senses of sight and smell, discovers Aria and makes her his hostage. It is because of her that his nephew was kidnapped by Dwellers. But the more time they spend around each other, the more they realise that they are actually similar -- with each a goal to save a loved one. Their original loathing of the other disappears and is replaced with a tenderness and compassion. Can their love survive their battle for a safe haven? Under the Never Sky was bit slow and confusing in the beginning. There was all this information you had to digest about pods and Smarteyes and the Aether and figure out what it all meant. But about a quarter way in, things became easier to understand and by then, it had its hooks in me deep and I couldn't put it down. I found it thrilling and enchanting. Perry and Aria's love was slow-building but so believable and dizzyingly perfect. I'm eager to read the next book in the trilogy. Don't disappoint me Rossi!

Warbreaker is a stand-alone (yesss!) novel about Vivenna and Siri, two very different sisters who, in a way, switch fates. Hallandren is a powerful kingdom based on colors (even the alphabet is color-based) and the powers these colors can bestow. It is awash in people who can use colors to take other people's essence or manifest other powers, and even bring people back from the dead (even if that will result in pretty much a zombie). It is ruled by the 'Returned' - people who somehow came back from the dead and are treated as Gods and, above them all, is Susebron, the God King, someone who was never alive - who 'returned' from being a stillborn. And Hallandren has its eye on Idris, a poor, small neighbor kingdom. From childhood, the King of Idris' oldest daughter, Vivenna, was promised in marriage to the fearsome God King of a powerful neighboring kingdom as a way to avoid war. Vivenna is dutiful, poised, ladylike. She has been brought up to know the ins and outs of her future husband's kingdom. Siri, the youngest, is the polar opposite - never meant to be anyone of particular importance, Siri is bad at obedience, defies her father regularly, and loves flaunting colors - the ultimate sin in Idris, where it is believed that colors can invite people who will steal one's 'Breath' (a sort of hybrid soul and power concept). So when push comes to shove, and the King has to send his daughter to marriage and almost certain death (even if the reputedly monstrous God King will leave her alive, war is coming and then the princess becomes a hostage and eventually dead), he cannot bear to send his favorite Vivenna. He sends Siri instead. And then, the proper, prim Vivenna does something unthinkable - she disguises herself and sets off to the faraway Hallandren to rescue her sister. The novel follows multiple characters - Vivenna and her adventure quest plus her interactions with a bunch of rebels and a mysterious man who may or may not be the key in stopping the war. Meanwhile, Siri is navigating the dangerous waters of the court and coming to terms with the fact that she is married to a person whom she is not supposed to speak to or touch (well, touch to the minimum necessary to get an heir). Oh, and there is Lightsong, a resurrected God who questions just how divine he really is. I LOVE IT!!!! The worldbuilding is great, I adore both Vivenna and Siri (though confess to liking Siri just a smidge more), the plot is complicated and things are not always as they seem (let's just say that God King and the priests are not really what/how you think they are). And if you need an OTP, Siri/Susibron hit all my kinks, in a very very unexpected way. Let's just say that between the two of them, the princess in distress is not who you think it is.

3.5 stars I'm a huge Kasie West fan so I really wish I could say I loved this book but unfortunately, I didn't. I did like it and, actually, couldn't really put it down once I'd started it, but it just didn't really have the depth that I've come to expect from West's books. I feel like the main character's struggles were confronted but only briefly dealt with and then completely fixed. One meeting at the end with a financial adviser, which everyone said she should immediately do after winning, seemed to solve every problem she had. And we also don't get to see the LI nearly enough. It would have been nice to see him and them together more. I don't know. I have some more thinking I have to do with this one.
What a lovely, charming book!

Dirty Little Secrets was a story that made me want to run thru my house and start filling trash bags although I am not even close to being what could be considered a hoarder. I can't imagine having to live like Lucy did with her moms addiction. This book was great and was a story that definately needs to be told but ewwww it just made me feel plum nasty and gross. How a parent can be this irresponsible to their childrens happiness and health or how it gets so bad that a child is so ashamed of their home they wont even call for help when it's needed. I have went back and forth in my mind pondering what I would have done and I guess without having lived in that kind of shame and turmoil for all those years I have no clue if I would have handled things like Lucy did. I would like to sit here and say no way that I would have called 911 but I can also easily feel Lucy's pain and conflict and even sort of understand why she did as she did. A must read...
