Just when we thought things were wrapped up, another thing came up, I liked the mystery and the way it was written didn't drag, the pace was fluid, great developments, great book!

3.5 stars. This is sort of a hard book to review. It's so long and so much happens, without too much ever really happening. Bear with me. Diana Bishop is a witch who was raised by her aunt Sarah and her partner, Emily, after her parents were mysteriously killed in Nigeria when she was seven. She's now an historian with a Ph.D. who's tenured at Yale but spending a year doing research on alchemy at Oxford University. Though she doesn't practice witchcraft, this doesn't stop her aunt and other witches, including Gillian Chamberlain, part of the Oxford coven, from trying to get her into a coven and begin practicing in earnest. While working one night at the Bodleian Library, she calls up a manuscript, the Ashmole 782, that is initially difficult to open, yet once it is, Diana notices not only mistakes in the alchemical depictions, but when she turns a page and it catches the light just right, writing that seems to shift over the page. Sensing an odd magic surrounding it, she finishes up and sends it off to be returned to the stacks. Immediately after, she is approached by Matthew Clairmont, who she immediately recognizes as a vampire and who she quickly learns is a respected member of the staff at Oxford, despite the fact that he never teaches. Soon, it's not just Matthew and the ever present Gillian surrounding her, all creatures are watching her every move at the library, which threatens to attract the attention of humans, as when more than one non-human being is in one area, their otherworldliness cannot be denied. Diana eventually learns that the circumstances surrounding her parents death may be far different from what she's been led to believe and could possibly involve a surprising person or people. I like Matthew, I really do, he's an interesting character with an unbelievable history yet, he felt exactly like every other hot vampire that's come down the pike, just older and more scholarly. I do have a number of other things to complain about regarding the characters and plot. Why is it that every scholar has to listen to Bach, be a wine aficionado and eat stuff like oysters (which look like something you pull out of your drain), partridge and the like. And it's not being a vampire that makes Matthew a monster, it's serving veal. The passages which dealt with wine and food were very detailed and it was almost like you could taste the food and especially the wine from the descriptions. Yet, and call me an uneducated heathen if you wish, as someone who doesn't like wine, it all tastes the same to me, and is a vegan, these sections grew to be a bit tiresome. If there had been some inclusion of pastries, chocolate and some veggie dishes, it would've been, pardon the pun, more palatable for me. However, these sections were good as they brought this pair together with shared interests and during these get-togethers they spent hours talking and getting to know each other. What did not serve to bring them together, at least for me, were the unbelievably ridiculous pages devoted to Matthew stalking some poor buck and killing it while Diana watches. TALK about how stupid what she said is. Using the bathroom's natural and part of who he is but I don't want to read about him doing that either. I really had to roll my eyes at that part. And the snobbery continued throughout the book. For exercise, Diana, of course, rows. She does also ride horses, but of course Western would've been too pedestrian, so she rides English and used to ride dressage. And they both adore yoga. And Matthew's hot English accent, well that eventually backslides to his original French. Ugh. I mean, really, do none of these freaking vampires or witches sit down with take away from Chipotle and a diet pop to watch The Walking Dead or Hell on Wheels? I know asking them to kick back and watch Hamlet 2 or a ridiculous(ly funny!) TV show like The Inbetweeners (American version) would be too much, but come on! My eye also started twitching when I found out that the whole being reborn as a vampire thing meant that everyone you turn is now called your son or daughter I thought it was unbelievably goofy when at one point Diana said "No son of mine" about Marcus. First, she's known the guy for all of a week. Second, he's older than her chronologically and about the same age looks-wise. Third, uh, he's not your son, he's not even really Matthew's son!!!!!! . And I am by no stretch of the imagination a raging feminist. I've seen people bug about books that they think depict stalking or some form of crazy/deviant behavior in the guise of romance and yeah, in real life, if someone acted a certain way you may not put up with it but for some reason or another, it works in books, but a number of times I found Matthew's behavior to be so freaking misogynistic, I would've probably staked his ass. The whole this is not a democracy bullshit really ticked me off and Diana's falling in line so easily was annoying. And for supposedly being a strong witch, despite not knowing how to use her powers, and a smart, independent woman, she sure passed out, slept, at Matthew's prodding, cried and freaked out (needing Matthew to settle her, of course) a lot. A LOT. And don't get me started on the whole marriage thing. Seriously, saying I love you to each other means you're married?! I hate to tell Diana, who immediately begins calling him her husband, but you aren't married! , I found this as ridiculous as the ideas behind what being reborn means. As the book wore on, and I say wore because it really started to feel more like a romance novel to me, with the supernatural plotline, especially the one involving the Ashmole, taking a backseat to their romance, more things started to bother me I felt like the god awful plot from the last Twilight book was ripped off towards the end. Really, a baby will most likely be born to them and it's going to be gasp a hybrid? Ugh. So what started out as a mystery about a long lost and inaccessible manuscript has turned into a procreation book. Awesome. Well, that is assuming they ever actually sleep together!!! . I just wish the secrets of the Ashmole had just stuck to possibly being solely about The origin of all supernatural beings. Okay, so this isn't a major spoiler and something we find out pretty quickly, I just don't want to give anything away. instead. As for the other characters, I really liked Ysabeau and Marthe, as well as Marcus and Miriam, and I would love to see more of Baldwin, just as long as he doesn't end up falling for Diana. For professing so much hate for her, he went to admiring her pretty quickly simply because she survived an ass kicking, and he needs to retain his screw anyone but vampires attitude (figuratively, not literally), at least for a while and especially as far as Diana is concerned. There are also a number of antagonists in the book, some are super creepy, and I'm hoping we get to see more of them in future installments, as they'd definitely amp up the tension and take some of the focus off of Matthew and Diana's staid yet touchy-feely romance. Despite the many things I had problems with, I did enjoy this book, it did a great job at keeping my attention and moved quickly, despite the languorous pace of many chapters, and much of the world building regarding the creatures was interesting. Though I decided I wasn't chomping at the bit to read the next book, the last hundred or so pages, whenever it was that some other creatures showed up at Em's house, took some of the focus off their love story and how the book ended made me more interested in reading the sequel, Shadow of Night, though I'll most likely wait until it comes out in paperback before I consider picking it up, especially considering the ridiculous price for the hardcover.
One of the most adorable reads I've come across ! I loved the setting where technology didn't quite exist and people just had face-to-face interaction to keep in touch.

I think that maybe I wasn't the right audience for this book. I've read other reviews and most of them give it four or five stars and talk about the mastery of the writing and emotion behind it all. For me? Not so much. To be honest, I was bored for most of the story. While I certainly agree that the ending was a great surprise, it wasn't enough to make me like the book. I didn't like Bilodo (let's be honest here, the dude's a creeper) and I didn't really care what happened to him or his haiku. This is probably better suited to a reader who likes cerebral-type books with an emphasis on poetry and introspective thought. Thanks to the publisher and Netgalley for sending me a copy to review.
Great debut and some surprises at the end, which was a nice touch!

This was good as usual for Lucy Maud Montgomery but I really feel that it's one of her lesser novels. It mostly just seems like a collection of short stories built around a big family, and the themes in her short stories end up really predictable. Margaret's story was lovely, though, as was Gay and Roger's. It is really annoying that we don't know where the jug was supposed to end up though!

I almost didn't start this book. The series came highly recommended, but I was put off by the title (I don't really like ghost stories) and then the cover threw me for a loop. On one hand there was a horse, which is a point in the "Pro" column. But on the other hand . well, it just didn't strike me as the kind of cover a solid story would have. Which is judgmental but there you go. I'm sure someone worked very hard on it, and I'm sure lots of people like it. I'm really glad I picked up the book anyway. How many books do you know where the (large, very manly, heir to the kingdom) warrior hero names his horse Dumpling? The book nearly won my heart on that alone. Charming horses aside, this book was also full of well-written adventure, novel and well-rounded world-building, full-fleshed characters, and good dialog. To add to which, it was just chock full to bursting of wonderful story. It's set in a Mongolia/China steppes setting, which is refreshing. (It's nice that everything doesn't always have to be about white people in Europe. Not because of Political Correctness, but just because there are lots of people in the world, and it's fun to read about them, too.) It also had the highest number of pregnant characters I've ever encountered in a book, and some of the most refreshing approaches to female characters and feminine issues than I've read in a long time. Plus, did you hear what I said about the horse? It's just a good book, all the way around.
Somtimes you just need a sexy book ;)

I hesitated to read this book, afraid it would be mired with the tediousness of surviving the red planet, and with the main character stranded alone the plot would become one dimensional. But Andy Weir's protagonist, Mark, proved to be quite entertaining all on his own. The plethora of facts and details lend credibility to the story without slowing it down. Did anyone perform an exhaustive fact check? I am curious how far suspended from reality The Martian truly is :-). I also enjoyed the upbeat philosophical ending. Look forward to seeing the movie!

Unfortunately Jay Bell we can't be friends. Enemies would be more like it cause when I finished this book I wanted to punch you in the face with a chair. Though my anger/sadness/frustration that I felt while reading Something Like Summer has slowly changed into real appreciation for your writing talents. I love books that just put my emotions through the wringer and this is definitely a novel that did that. I cried (a lot - think I went through a weeks rent in kleenex), I laughed, I was extremely frustrated but looking back so satisfied. Truth be told though I don't think I can read the next books for a very longtime. Anyway, I surprisingly loved this one even though I hated both Tim and Ben. Tim was overbearing and kinda a douch throughout where as Ben was the nerdy awkward kid who never grew up and that annoyed me. Out of the two characters Tim is the only one I felt aged, maybe it was all the stuff he went through but his voice wasn't that of a child later. Do I think Ben and Tim should be together? Oh hell no. I don't think Tim ever learned to live apart from Ben. He lived off the fantasy that Ben would be his no matter what happened. I realize the next book is from Tim's perspective and it could prove me wrong but I still don't want to read it yet. Plus I don't think Ben is a strong enough characters to shoulder a burden like Tim, he is too dependent on people and how they make him feel. It's almost like he never learned to live alone. On the other hand; Jace. The love of my freakin' life! Now that was a guy I could stand behind and know he was going to do great things. Unfortunately he dies. Why? Did you have to kill him? Divorce is legal in this day and age. It almost seemed convenient that Jace suddenly (I mean suddenly) had to die for Ben and Tim to get together. It would have made more sense if Jace had been complaining about headaches or was having double vision every blue moon. Jace is lovely and I loved him. Also, the plot line about chicky's (only been 2 days and I can't remember her name) dad just seemed out of place. It really didn't help move the story forward and it definitely made the story long to read. Either way, I highly recommend this book to anyone looking for a good cry or a long term built romance. Some people put this under YA and it definitely isn't that though it isn't an adult novel either it kinda fits into the middle of both. I'm going with New Adult Contemporary since they are college age through a good portion of it.

"But I am scared." "You have every right to be. You are among the humans." It is about this alien visiting Earth - "planet where the most intelligent life form still has to drive its own cars" The beginning is a lot like that of movie PK except that he other world from where the unnamed narrator comes from is prejudices with very misanthropic views and that is why he sent to planet to hinder the technological progress of those primates. But to his peril, he starts loving humanity. Anyways here are some of the things he discovered: "Humans, as a rule, don't like mad people unless they are good at painting, and only then once they are dead. But the definition of mad, on Earth, seems to be very unclear and inconsistent. What is perfectly sane in one era turns out to be insane in another. The earliest humans walked around naked with no problem. Certain humans, in humid rainforests mainly, still do so. So, we must conclude that madness is sometimes a question of time, and sometimes of postcode." "Written human languages are preposterously simple, as they are made up almost entirely of words." "They die, and so they have impatience. " "That's what starts to happen, when you know it is possible for you to feel pain you have no control over. You become vulnerable. Because the possibility of pain is where love stems from." "On Earth, social networking generally involved sitting down at a non-sentient computer and typing words about needing a coffee and reading about other people needing a coffee, while forgetting to actually make a coffee." "Parks were the most common destination on dog walks. A piece of nature - grass, flowers, trees - that was not quite allowed to be truly natural. Just as dogs were thwarted wolves, parks were thwarted forests. Humans loved both, possibly because humans were, well, thwarted." "Humans were always doing things they didn't like doing. In fact, to my best estimate, at any one time only point three per cent of humans were actively doing something they liked doing, and even when they did so, they felt an intense amount of guilt about it and were fervently promising themselves they'd be back doing something horrendously unpleasant very shortly." "part of being human ..... was about knowing which lies to tell, and when to tell them. To love someone is to lie to them." " Oh, and let's not forget The Things They Do To Make Themselves Happy That Actually Make Them Miserable. This is an infinite list. It includes - shopping, watching TV, taking the better job, getting the bigger house, writing a semi-autobiographical novel, educating their young, making their skin look mildly less old, and harbouring a vague desire to believe there might be a meaning to it all." "Magazines are very popular, despite no human ever feeling better for having read them. Indeed, their chief purpose is to generate a sense of inferiority in the reader that consequently leads to them needing to buy something, which they do, and then feel even worse, and so need to buy another magazine to see what they can buy next. It is an eternal and unhappy spiral that goes by the name of capitalism and it is really quite popular." "love is about finding the right person to hurt you" "To hypnotise a human was easy because, out of any species in the universe, they seemed the one most desperate to believe. ' "one of the key problems humans had with numerical understanding - their nervous systems simply weren't up to it" And about dogs: "It was then I realised the one thing worse than having a dog hate you is having a dog love you. Seriously, if there was a needier species in the universe I had yet to meet it." "After a while, with a dog on your lap, you realise there is a necessity to stroke it. Don't ask me how this necessarily comes about. It clearly has something to do with the dimensions of the human upper body." And there is a lot of advice too like: "Be curious. Question everything. A present fact is just a future fiction." "Sometimes, to be yourself you will have to forget yourself and become something else. Your character is not a fixed thing. You will sometimes have to move to keep up with it "Tragedy is just comedy that hasn't come to fruition. One day we will laugh at this. We will laugh at everything." "Happiness is not out here. It is in there" "A paradox. The things you don't need to live - books, art, cinema, wine and so on - are the things you need to live." "At some point, bad things are going to happen. Have someone to hold on to." "If you are laughing, check that you don't really want to cry. And vice versa." "Don't ever be afraid of telling someone you love them. There are things wrong with your world, but an excess of love is not one." " If there is a sunset, stop and look at it. Knowledge is finite. Wonder is infinite."

Admittedly there were a couple of moments where the girls realised situations that A could hold over them and so they beat them to the punch, but still! I was lucky enough to receive an ARC of this book and wowzers, am I glad I did. I honestly was not sure what to expect going in, but it blew any of my expectations away rather quickly. Gaby has been living in a quiet ocean-side town for nine months after the death of her twin brother Jude. She was happy to leave her former life behind in exchange for the quiet & solitude Pan Beach brings. Her roommate and friend, Maggie, landed her a job at the local library while also giving her a place to call home. On one of her daily runs through the forest trails she begins to feel watched. She stops and catches movement out of the corner of her eye. Unable to track the cause for fleeting movement, she bursts into a sprint, leaving the forest ... Gaby has been having disturbing dreams involving hellbeasts, beheadings and a rather sexy guy with green eyes and smells like sandalwood. She writes a short story and submits it to an online site hoping to win a prize of $1,000. What she wins is her past, returning like a hurricane. When she & Maggie walk into their local bar that night, standing at the bar staring right at her is the guy from her dream. Rafael I would probably get a little hot if he were standing there staring at me too, shit. Anyway, he wants to talk to her about her brother, Jude, and how he died. He begins to tell her stories and show her pictures that do not line up with her memories. She begins to realize all is not as it appears to be. Perhaps someone wants her to believe they were backpacking for the past year .. maybe some nefarious is going on? On the way home from the bar, two mysterious strangers step from the shadows & begin accusing her of things she has no recollection of. She tries to convince them she does not remember, but the girl Taya obviously has some unresolved issues and proceeds to kick her ass. Slowly things begin to come to light, Gaby is not who she thinks she is. Both she and her brother Jude were deeply involved in some serious shit when they went missing. I don't want to give too much away so I will just give you a quick rundown of what happens and why this book is a MUST read: 1) Angels 2) Demons 3) Nephilim (this is a new 'take' on them, I love it) 4) Hot guys 5) Kissing, not too much, just enough 6) Sexual tension, again, not too much, just enough 7) Saving the world 8) Missing good guys 9) You just want to find out what happens !!! It ends with a cliffhanger! I want the 2nd one now please. Please? Now? How 'bout now?

Review: Jackson's Trust by Violet Duke March 14, 2016 by Mandi Leave a Comment (Edit) Jackson's Trust by Violet Duke (Fourth Down #1) Released: March 8, 2016 Contemporary Romance Loveswept Reviewed by Mandi I really wanted this to work for me because I love sports romance. This features a hero who is a sports analyst and a heroine who has a new job as a sports sideline reporter, both working for the same large sports network. But from the very beginning, this story never quite grabbed me. Leila is very well versed in sports, especially football, so when her new boss treats her like a dumb dumb, she holds in her frustration and smiles. She knows she can prove her intelligence once she gets started with her job, which she does very well. Leila is a good interviewer and very good at analyzing facts and statistics. As a side job, she runs a very popular fantasy football picks site. (I love fantasy football so this made me smile). Her first day on the job, on top of having to deal with her annoying boss, she meets her co-worker, Jackson. He takes an immediate, and I mean immediate, liking to her. His lust is overflowing and he starts to call her Sunshine and Leila does reciprocate this lust somewhat.. Let me take a quick break to say how annoying it was that Jackson called Leila "Sunshine" the first day on the job. I just found it unprofessional and a bit disrespectful. It's one thing if he has gotten to know her and they become friends and he thinks of a nickname, but she is a stranger to him and it rubbed me the wrong way that he started doing this. While they lust after each other, it was a little over the top for me. There was just so much lusting I got tired of it. Jackson also makes it clear that he only has no-strings sex - so that puts the brakes a bit on their eye humping. "So because of your secretly complicated life, you only date women who want..." "Sex." His eyes stayed glued to hers as he dropped the one word like a bomb. "Just sex. At their place, not mine. Occasionally, with lunch or dinner as well, but never breakfast." Wow. That was the definition of just sex, all right. Leila does impress everyone on with her work performance, earning much respect....until they find out she runs that Fantasy Football pick site, which she could be using insider information to make those picks. After we make it through that hurdle, we encounter another one. It's a secret, so I don't want to blurt it out - but I will put it under a spoiler (it's not a huge, horrible secret or anything) Jackson is a billionaire. A secret billionaire. He didn't want Leila to know. This changes the focus of the story from sports to the secret. Boo. And other things are introduced - some suspense type stuff - and I just didn't like how it all turned out. Leila and Jackson are sweet together - but they just didn't do a lot for me.

Naw, my first three star book for the year! D: Now, this book isn't actually bad, but there were elements I just didn't like that made me finish with a bit of a bad taste in my mouth, and with no desire to read any more in the series. If a book can't leave you wanting more, then that's me out. So firstly, I would have no reason with the whole Kieron/Lucky, Keiron/Liora thing if it were explained more. He says he sees them as one, but they don't see each other as one, and they are polar opposites. What is that attracts him to either of them? I need more explanation than insta love. Secondly, I guess I'm a little over new guy moves to town and girls go nuts because he is sooooo attractive. I want something fresh. The writing is really good though, especially in differentiating between Lucky and Liora when one is in charge. Corinne seems interesting, I enjoyed her scenes. So a bit of a mixed bag, there are things to like here but the bits I didn't enjoy stopped me from going with a higher rating. Try it yourself, you might like it more than I did :D

The Dream Thieves is even more dark and complex than The Raven Boys. It's brilliant and unique in a way I've never seen another YA novel try to be. The Dream Thieves explores even more of the characters than we saw in the Raven Boys and explores new plots and possibilities as well.

I really enjoyed this! There need to be more stories about girls with near-crippling bloodlust. I think that the hallmark of a good action novel is when I don't mind suspending disbelief for the sake of getting on with the story. Yes, I know there is no way that someone with zero mounted combat experience is going to be able to get up on a horse and accurately fire a crossbow, but I don't care. It was still fun. I'll admit that I was a little bit disappointed when the obvious love interest entered the story, but I grew to like Jack. Unfortunately it took Saba so long to stop being a hag around him that the book lost steam toward the end. I'm not sure that I enjoyed this enough to read the rest of the series, but I'm glad I got through this one. I liked it more than Divergent, but less than The Knife of Never Letting Go and The Hunger Games.

Monsters of Men is a tour de force. It is an epic conclusion to an awe-inspiring series, as exhilarating and thought-provoking as a shoot-out among philosophers. There is a natural progression in the series. The first book, The Knife of Never Letting Go, is from the young boy Todd's perspective. He has lived his whole life in a single village on a foreign planet, populated only by men, where he can hear everyone's thoughts and sends out his own. It is the definition of isolation and indoctrination, and it all gets shaken upside down when Viola crashlands on his planet. She is the first female he's ever seen (but definitely not the last). In the second book, The Ask and the Answer, the narrative switches between Todd's and Viola's POVs. The two get swept up in a rising tension between men, women, and the native/alien race the Spackle. In Monsters and Men, we get a third POV: Todd, Viola, and one of the Spackle, called The Return or 1017. The Return has an utterly different perspective, the icing on the trilogy cake. Through these three POVs, we meet Mayor Prentiss, the man who wants to rule the world. He's fighting both guerrilla forces, mostly women, who object to his tyranny, and also a gigantic army of Spackle who want to take back their planet and rescue their enslaved brethren. But Prentiss has surprising advantages. First, he's found a way to use Noise (the thoughts that spill out of the men's heads) as a weapon. Second, he is ruthless, either a sociopath or a man blinded by his own vision. Third, he has Todd. Todd tries to resist him, but his conflicted motivations struggle to hold up under Prentiss's pressure, and he is drawn to growing power. Add in betrayals, spies, death, disease, explosions, and love and you have everything you could want in a book. I love Todd and Viola. They are great together and also strong, flawed, and fearless individually. Adding 1017 as a narrator was perfect, but personally I found him very single-minded, particularly compared to Todd and Viola. I would have liked to see more depth to his character. The other characters are all solid, except for a few that tended towards idealistic. Overall I really liked seeing characters make deliberate, controversial choices and then live with those decisions. When the world is falling apart, you have to act. Sometimes that means endangering yourself. Sometimes it's siding with your enemy. Ultimately I feel like this book is about a question: as a man grows powerful, more powerful than the rest of humankind... does he choose to become a god or a devil? Can he choose? This is speculative fiction at its peak: not lasers and dragons but the creation of a world that allows us to explore arguments on how we live. (Also, the audiobooks for the whole series were incredible. Excellent for car rides or running long distances.)

You wouldn't think a book about bees would have such rich characters and dramatic plot points, but man, this book is good! It's like a dystopia in a bee hive, and Flora 717 is our brave heroine, fighting for equality! She's truly an awesome bee. I thoroughly enjoyed reading her story.
Amazing worldbuilding, touching romance. Changed my perspective of what the genre could do forever.

This was a really quick read--it reads more like YA than adult fiction. Beautiful writing isn't really its strong point, but it is definitely effective and doesn't distract from the story. And it is quite a good story about the immigrant experience. I liked a lot of the issues it touched on, from family bonds to choosing a path that's authentic to yourself to white/wealthy privilege and the squalid poverty and illegal conditions many immigrants must deal with. I didn't really feel like the pregnancy twist was fully necessary, but I understand why the author did it and I think it worked pretty well for that purpose. I really cared about the characters and overall it was a pretty satisfying story.

3.5 stars This is my first Kristen Callihan book so I wasn't sure what to expect. The cover and the synopsis drew me in and, well, it rang all my bells! I have a thing for witty banter and this story has it in spades. Low on angst, high on humor and sexy times. I appreciated all the little details woven into the story. I liked Killian and I liked Libby at first then she just sort of grated on me. I'm not sure about their emotional intimacy though. It felt like all they ever did was have sex in closets and bathrooms, so it looked like lust and not love. I enjoyed the story though I kinda wished they could've stayed in the farm a whole lot longer... without the spotlight and the world watching them. Their moments there felt intimate and... just theirs. I can't explain this clearly but I liked the first half more than the second. Also the whole thing with her becoming a star was weird. It happened way too easily, with no obstacles, and she left just as easily. Audiences loved her too fast and too easily as well--I know I would be weirded out if the most famous all-guy band suddenly turned up with a female in tow, singing with them, no matter how talented. The whole part of her becoming a star and actually performing, etc. was also glossed over, when it was kind of built up to be a big deal.
