There's good news and bad news. Which to start with?! I'll start with the good news, I suppose. The good news is that there is very little distinctively Christian content within Lady Maybe. Why is that good news? Well, you don't have to be unChristian to have disdain for "Christian romances." Some Christians avoid it perhaps for the reason that "Christian fiction" is "preachy." Some perhaps for the reason that "Christian fiction" rarely contains realistic content: characters that are actually, genuinely sinners--or so they say. I can honestly say that there is nothing within Lady Maybe that could be considered preachy. The first slight evidence of "Christian content" comes in at around three hundred pages. The main character, Hannah, prays or speaks of praying. And another character reminds her that Jesus forgives all who ask. I can also say that the characters are certainly sinners living in a sin-filled world. For example, the main character is a "fallen woman". Hannah, the heroine, is a fallen woman. During her employ, she was seduced by Sir John who was angry and hurt by his wife's cheating. He arranges another job for her so they do not continue to fall into sin. He's worried that so long as she's in the house--she'll be a constant temptation to him to commit adultery. He also chooses that time to move with his wife. Hannah keeps her pregnancy a secret, and has Sir John's child with him being no wiser for it. Hannah's sudden re-entry for their lives is a bit of a shock for him. But what can he say when his wife surprises him within two or three minutes of them getting into the carriage to leave for their new home?! Readers, of course, know nothing of their past. As I said, this is a secret-driven romance. The carriage tumbles off a cliff, and Sir John and a woman are recovered. Everyone assumes that the woman by his side is his wife. And she is, in fact, clutching a ring belonging to Lady Mayfield. As you might have guessed--as I guessed almost right away--Hannah is that woman. Sir John does recover, but, he finds it wonderfully fun to have a new "Lady Mayfield." And he's beyond thrilled to learn that he has a son, Danny. (Danny was brought to their home while Sir John was still in a coma.) He loves putting Hannah in tricky situations. Asking the doctor when he can start sleeping with his wife again. Insisting that she sleep by his side. But Sir John is not Hannah's only temptation. James, Sir John's solicitor, comes around. He is anxious to prove that Lady Mayfield is TROUBLE. But, he falls in love with her himself. It doesn't help that he ever-so-accidentally comes across a just-finished-bathing still-very-extremely-exposed Hannah. James becomes a little lust-driven to say the least. He learns her true identity, and, is relieved that she isn't Marianna after all. He has heard too many stories about her. The book has dozens of twists and turns, and, yes, I've spoiled a small number of them. It isn't so much the fact that Hannah is a "fallen woman" who has had a child out of wedlock that is objectionable. It is the amount of graphic detail involved in the storytelling--past and present. Now this "graphic detail" might be laughable compared to other SMUTTY ROMANCES published secularly. But for any reader who finds such content undesirable, it will be disappointing or frustrating. The characters subtly point to the message that forgiveness is offered to all by Christ. I say subtly because there is nothing preachy--nothing obvious--about this one. Now, the bad news. The bad news is that there is very little distinctively Christian content within Lady Maybe. It would be unfair for me to generalize that all readers of Christian romance read exclusively Christian romances, or, that Christian readers avoid secular romances. But some readers--at least--do exclusively read Christian romances, and, there is a reason for this. They want their romances to be clean, absent of graphic details, a high purity quality especially between unmarried characters, but lacking of intimate details even between married characters. (Some secular books are capable of this. Georgette Heyer, for example, comes to mind.) But sadly, more and more Christian romances are failing this standard. Some readers perhaps--like myself--have learned the hard way that reading "smutty books" is spiritually dangerous or unwise. Some readers hold themselves accountable to a higher standard, not caring what everyone else is reading, or what everyone else considers fine for reading. Lady Maybe is a Regency Romance set during 1819. Marianna and Sir John are unhappily married. She has had a lover since the very beginning. Sir John is aware of his wife's cheating, but, hopes that if he keeps on forgiving her that even if it takes three hundred or so chances, that their marriage might eventually work out. Hannah Rogers, the heroine, has been in and out of their lives. She was first hired to be a companion for Marianna, (Lady Mayfield). She left her job--suddenly--and then returned a year later asking for past wages. She ended up getting rehired as a companion for the Lady. The couple is--for better or worse--moving yet again. Sir John is trying to "hide" his wife from his lover and cut off all communication between the two. But an accident within the first few chapters of the book changes everything.... Lady Maybe is a secret-driven, surprise-heavy historical romance. The characters are well-drawn. Marianna. Hannah. James Lowden. Sir John. Becky (the wet nurse). Dr. Parrish. Mrs. Parrish. Mrs. Turrill, the housekeeper. I could go on. There were plenty of characters that I genuinely started to care about and/or got the chance to know. That is a strength, I won't deny it. I have read Christian romances where 90% of the characters are completely one-dimensional and essentially lifeless. That is not the case with Lady Maybe. Was it compelling? Yes. I admit that it was. But was it bordering on inappropriate for picky readers? Yes. I think it was.

I liked the premise of the book and it started off pretty well. But... The 5 dates' rule - broken Not enough angst tbh... The one "fight" (obstacle they faced) they did have, resolved within 12 hours Lack of mystery, on what the characters would do, choose - too obvious It was a quick read, however, so I suppose it's fine. I did like the book, but it had the capability of being loved and it somehow just didn't get there. I still recommend though if you're looking for something easy, fun and quick. Kind of like the characters/premise of this book: Easy - yes. Both of them are way too easy. Fun - they were cute, and the whole "no, not happening" was fun while it lasted (we could all see it disintegrating quickly though) Quick - just like the thoughts of keeping their dates "chaste"... right out the window

Bitterblue is the third and final installment in Kristin Cashore's Graceling Realm series. As a whole, I felt the series had a very strange flow. The first book Graceling is now in my favorite's list, but the second book Fire felt like a standalone versus a sequel. So after I reconciled this in my head and prepared myself that Bitterblue would likely feel like a standalone, BAM-it totally feels like a sequel to Graceling, albeit, set years ahead. However, the character Fire from Fire made an appearance in Bitterblue and I did feel that all three books finally tied together somehow, although this didn't happen until the end. Anyway, my review of Bitterblue is that it was very long but amazing! I enjoyed seeing Bitterblue as queen and I felt for her as she struggled to keep "in the loop" when it comes to her people and her kingdom. She has such a strong heart and wants to serve her people well. But there was a huge mystery that surrounded what she was being told about her kingdom's history, current happenings, and needs and what was actually truth. When Bitterblue discovered why her advisors were acting strange and keeping her minimally informed, I was devastated for them and all involved! It nearly brought me to tears. Bitterblue handled it beautifully and in the best interest of all affected. I loved Teddy, Saf, and the others, and I really enjoyed the romance element, although it was not at all a focal point. I was disappointed Bitterblue and Saf didn't work out in the end but he was a perfect "first" for her! My favorite part of this book was the inclusion of Katsa and Po again. Yay!! My favorite quote: "It has been a hard lesson to learn, that greatness requires suffering."

Like my friend said, "Marie Lu broke my heart, semi-mended it, then ended the book." I felt like Champion was the book of character and emotional development for all the characters. Which is fine, considering that there are still action-packed scenes. Day and June remained strong characters throughout not only this book but throughout the trilogy. The world-building of this book was also very well down and nicely paced. However, I can't say that this is my favorite of the series. Don't worry, Marie Lu. I still love you. It was a fantastic way (except the heartbreaking ending)  to end a wonderful trilogy. Looking forward to the next series, The Young Elites.

This is a hard book to review..... I won't bore you with a summary because you can read that above from Goodreads. I will start off first by saying, if this book were written for an older audience, I would have given it more stars. Unfortunately, it is being promoted as a children's book. Publishers are rating as an interest level grades 3rd - 6th. As an elementary librarian, I will not be promoting this to the majority of my students under 5th grade. Have publishers lost connection with children? What happened to the fun, lose yourself in the moment, happy ending books? IF this book were being promoted as a young adult book (the two main young characters in the story are 12 and 14) then I would rate it higher. It is beautifully written, with lots of figurative language throughout. The dark, cruel aspect of the book does make it a difficult read. Some of the concepts in this book are just too deep for elementary age students. While a large part of the book discusses bullying, it isn't ever resolved in the story. Problems with the Story We never really get the back story to many of the characters, such as Betty or Toby. We are not able to understand why they act the way they do. Betty, the bully in the story, is unbelievably cruel. Even at the end when she is rescued from the well, she still lies!! You would think that when someone comes near death, as she did, the truth would come out. I was very disapointed that the author decided to not resolve this issue. So much was left unanswered. Was anyone else bothered by this?? Where was Betty's father? Did Toby have a family? Why did Toby carry around the guns that weren't working? Why was Betty so heartless and cruel? Why didn't anyone just tell the truth and spare Toby his life? What the heck?? The heavy topics in the book are overdone, and in my opinion, children will not be able to relate to them. The ending. Nothing more to say. I hate giving less than 4 stars, especially since this book is really beautiully written, but can we please stop wanting children to grow up so fast!! Let's keep these issues and topics in the young adult books and let children continue to be just that, children.

A deeply creepy and lovely ghost story set in 1920s England, with a really strong romance subplot. If Susanna Kearsley wrote a ghost story, it might feel a bit like this. It also made me remember how much I used to love reading Barbara Michaels's ghost stories when I was a teen! I'll definitely be reading more Simone St. James novels, too. (My star system, btw, is completely personal and subjective; it's certainly 5 stars in terms of objective writing quality, I just gave it four stars because I really liked this book but didn't LOVE it.)

If you're going to read smut--which I condone--at least pick good smut. This is not. This is bad. Badly written, badly plotted, badly characterized, and just plain abusive. (Of both the reader and the character.) Some books I read just so I can be an asshole about telling everyone how horrible the book they love is. This is one of those books. Also, upon meeting someone recently, she found out I love to read and said, "Oh my god, did you read Fifty Shades of Grey?!? I thought it was SO GOOD! The writing was great!" And see, having read it saved me all the time of even vaguely trying to be that girl's friend.
Classic survival story. Quite an interesting read.

Where do I even start with this book? This was a roller coaster of: I like it. I hate it. I love it. There were points in this that I didn't think that I could actually finish it, but I thankfully pull through and was rewarded at the end. Because  that ending tho. It was just hit after hit after hit. I knew that things were going to go south fairly quickly after Ella, and the Royal gang left Reed home, while they all went to DC for dinner  and I was right! I obviously need Twisted Palace like right now. Thankfully, I only have to wait about one more month until it is released. Hopefully Twisted Palace has... -More of the Royal brothers not just Reed and Easton. I'm not complaining because I love them both, but I would like to see more Gideon and the twins, Sawyer and Sebastian. They were really over casted by the big personalities that both Reed and Easton have. -Also, less of Brooke and Dinah. I can't stand them, so they need to go bother another wealthy family. -Lastly, I hope that the trilogy wraps up well. There's a lot of loose ends, and I need them to be tied up. Maybe not in a pretty knot, but at least tied up. I did have my issues with this book. In my opinion Paper Princess is still my favorite, but I do have to say that this book still had the same addicting factor that the first book had. I'm hoping that the characters develop more in the next installment.

I like Penelope Douglas. She creates awesome chemistry between her characters and I loved Falling Away - it touched on many sensitive subjects and created awesome characters, especially the female MC. This time around though was a complete fail for me - from the characters, to the plot, to the relationship dynamics, to the complete logic fail at times. I skimmed 50% of the book and was left with a complete disbelief as to the dumbness of the book and its protagonists. First, I somewhat liked the female MC, Easton. She was strong, smart and self-sufficient. Sure, she had issues but those were justified and she had found coping mechanisms which made her believable and relatable on many levels. What I did not like was the relationship she established with the male MC. First, he called her a brat for running her mouth and often insulted her intelligence. I couldn't quite understand why we were supposed to believe she was standoffish and impulsive when she was always saying the truth, providing argumentation and giving a valid and reasonable opinion. Surely, in this day and age, this does not make her a "brat"? Second, I like nice depiction of sex and high level of steam but I did not find the chemistry between the main couple believable and the development of their relationship was very abrupt which did not really work for me. Hence, the sex scenes just came out of nowhere and were over the top. Honestly, sometimes less is more and I feel that the author was trying to push the boundaries for shock value. Finally, I was willing to give this book two stars because it was engaging and easy to read if unoriginal and a bit shallow. The characters did not feel fleshed out and some of their actions just did not make sense to me. Still, I found some of the bits about parent-children relationship valid and informative as well as the tips about teaching were really good. But at around 75% things went downhill fast. First, Easton has another woman kiss Tyler and he plays along. I found the whole scene idiotic and preposterous and it left me with a bad taste in my mouth. Then came the whole thing about Jack which was really out of nowhere and ruined the perfectly good brother-sister dynamic which was one of the highlights of the book I just stopped reading after, going to the end which was one big info dump and I really didn't feel anything but sense of waste of time when I could have been reading something much more worthwhile. I will be very wary of Ms Douglas' books in the future.

major trigger warning for rape other trigger warnings include: suicide, self harm, depression and anxiety and panic disorders, dissociation, body shaming, substance abuse, alcoholism (suggested), bullying, some suggestion of child abuse, sexual abuse and molestation, stalking, harassment, sexism, memory loss (sort of), and isolation heads up this book is a very difficult read. it is a challenging read. and it is also an important read. i have a feeling that writing this review is going to be one of the most difficult things i have done in a while. the book is told from the perspective of emma. i feel like we all know an emma like character, that one person who has to be the best, the prettiest, the funniest. we've all probably had a friend like emma. i certainly have - it remains one of the worst and most destructive relationships i've ever had and it's only with hindsight i can see how terrible it was. but that does not mean that what happened in this book is acceptable for anyone. nothing in this book is acceptable. there are so many people like emma out there in this world. the people who's lives start of as something, they have dreams and hopes, and then this is all ripped away from them. the thing that is most mentioned in this book that i found hard was what emma was doing, how she was destroying the town 'heros' lives. at no point does anyone suggest within the context that they destroyed hers. and frankly they did. as this book unfolds you realise how dark the world that we live in is. emma's perspective is brutal and dark but at the same time so important. and if you're wondering if you should read this book, the answer is yes. a thousand times yes. this book is important. this book is so important. it does not preach societies views. it does not tell you what is right and what is wrong. it simple shows you the impact that something like this can have. something like going to a party, drinking, taking something - anything, and wearing a short dress. and it can end up destroying your life, and others lives. but what i took out of this book was that we all need to be held equally responsible. nothing in this book was emma's fault, for her control was ripped away. and yet she is the character who is held most responsible, by everyone, her friends, her family, the local people, and the people she's never met. honestly the part where the priest judges emma and finds her wanting, despite the christian faith preaching forgiveness tore me up. this is someone who should be neutral. who must be neutral. who cannot judge and must forgive. that is their role in the community and honestly i cannot imagine how much that would hurt. i cried then, and i think that no matter what this sort of story must be discussed this book shows us what growing up a member of the google generation is like. and how it is honestly unlike anything the previous generations have faced. the rules, the laws, need to change to reflect this - we need to have more understanding and discussion within society. and yet we don't. this is something that no one wants to face up to, no one wants to discuss. and we should. and there's something else i want to say. the ending. the ending ripped my heart out, but i can understand where emma was coming from. and even at the end #teamemma
You can just never go wrong with a Jennifer Echols Romantic Comedy. I love Harper's story.

This book has a great fantasy setting that's fairly unique. I loved the concept of the Grisha and the tensions between the characters throughout the book. I thought it was interesting that Alina so readily gave up on her love for Mal when the Darkling showed interest in her, but that she realized she still loved him after they were away from the Grisha. I was a little surprised that Alina wasn't more skeptical of someone called the Darkling -- the name doesn't exactly inspire hope and happiness and cheer. I liked that Baghra, who just seemed miserly at first, ended up being a fairly strong character with an agenda of her own, and I also like that Genya's power to improve appearances was temporary. Too often magic is limitless in novels, and I like that the illusion of improved appearances was just an illusion. I thought it was interesting that Mal, even though he wasn't a Grisha, had some kind of super hunting/tracking power that connected him to the prey he hunted. I also liked that Alina's mercy toward the stag gave her at least as much control over the amplifier as the Darkling got from killing it. It was looking a little hopeless there for a while, and I was really upset that Mal was going to die. I was satisfied with the ending, but I wish the next book was already published so I could see what happens next!

I enjoyed listening to the audiobook. I think the story was interesting with the concept of one girl falling in love with two brothers or two brothers falling in love with her. Whatever. I thought the book was slow at some points. I love Conrad...he was described as the Edward Cullen type and that made me like him more. Overall, it was a great read.

This book was a delightful, witty, heartfelt, heartwarming, unorthodox, offbeat, irreverent, cooky, adorable coming of age story of a boy who is blessed, or cursed, with a gift of self-awareness and awareness of the world that most people don't have. A sharp wit and the occasional unorthodox reaction to a situation made this book fun to read, not to mention the cartoons that were fun and telling and really added to the depth of the story, unlike a lot of books with graphics. Loved it. You know, I was really disappointed when I finished the last of Jordan Sonnenblick's books, because I thought that was the end of it, but it turns out there are so many of these light-but-heartfelt contemporary heroes out there. Arnold Spirit and Ansty Bonano (by neal shusterman) are my favorites. I like the sass. All this stuff happens to these characters and they just snark through it all and my heart is breaking for them, but I'm also laughing so hard I can't breathe. So thank you , some girl in my Creative Writing class, because if you hadn't reccomended it in a report, I probably never would have gotten around to reading this. It's one of those books you hear about forever and I knew I would read it someday. Sidenote: Gordy's rant about knowledge is the best thing ever. If it weren't so not me, I would yell about my adoration of this excerpt a lot louder. "You should approach each book --you should approach life-- with the real possibility that you might get a metaphorical boner and any point." "A metaphorical boner!" I shouted. "What the heck is a metaphorical boner?" Gordy laughed. "When I say boner, I really mean joy," he said. "Then why didn't you say joy? You didn't have to say boner. Whenever I thingk about boners, I get confused" "Boner is funnier. And more joyful." He was an extremely weird dude.
3,5 Stars It's really hard to give this book a rating. I really liked it but I can't give it 4 stars cause there are other books that I gave 4 stars that are better.

** spoiler alert ** Even though it followed a different court, the emotions were the same from the first book. I love the dark look at the fey world that the author has created. And I also really like how everything is not all wrapped up in a pretty little bow - not everything ends in a happy ending. I didn't want to like Irial, but as the book went on, I found myself drawn to his misery. I wasn't completely surprised when he gave up his court in the end because I felt that was where his character was moving toward this whole time, especially after Leslie. I was however, surprised that he just gave it to Niall - even though looking back, I really shouldn't have been. I do believe that Niall will make a great king of the Dark Court. With Leslie, I went through many emotions. I felt bad for her in the beginning. Her life was horrible and she was just trying to survive. But as the book went on, I found myself wanting to smack her for the choices she was making - even though I know they weren't all her own. I felt that her character was made to be weak and not strong, which is what Leslie wanted when she got the tattoo. She was redeemed when she finally broke through Irial's haze and severed her ties to him. I wonder if she will frequent the series in later books. Now, I have to talk about Keenan for a moment. I loved him in the first book. Even though I wanted Ash with Seth, I adored Keenan's attitude. But in this book, his true colors came out. He has no emotion, no empathy, except for his court. Don't get me wrong, that's good when he's ruling his court, but the fact that he's withholding information and acting behind his queens back shows how deceitful he actually is, which is interesting considering he's from the Summer Court. I am very intrigued to see where this series goes. The snippet at the end shows more with Seth in the next book and I love Seth. Can't wait to read it!

There are winged horses that live in the mirrors of Briar Hill hospital... 4.5 stars. The Chronicles of Narnia meets The Secret Garden in this enchanting and deeply felt story of friendship, hope and courage. The Secret Horses of Briar Hill is everything a middle grade novel should be. Majestic, magical horses dwell the Briar Hill hospital. To its patients, they are invisible, but Emmaline sees them in the mirrors everywhere she goes... and now one has found her way in the sundial garden. But she needs help, for she is chased by a dark horse. Emmaline will do anything to help her new friend. With beautiful writing, Megan Shepherd creates a world where darkness can be defeated if one is brave enough to dare fight against it and have hope light will seep through. No one knows if the horses are truly there or if they're purely fabricated by Emmaline's imaginative mind - and that is where the magical realism comes in. It's a splendid tale set during World War II with a charming set of characters who learn from each other, from their experiences and even teach us a thing or two about living and believing. Megan Shepherd has a real talent for writing middle grade books. I hope this will not be her last. Blog | Youtube | Twitter | Instagram | Google+ | Bloglovin'

But that was the thing about grief, Bellamy knew. You couldn't expect anyone else to share your suffering. The 100 presents us with the lives of four characters, who are the ones telling the story from their different POVs,: Clarke, Bellamy, Glass and Wells. Each one of them has a story to tell about how was life like in the city-like spaceships humans are forced to live in and mainly how actions that took place in the past have an effect in the present, after they had been sent to the earth. I'm in two minds about this book, because I kinda liked it but there were some parts of it that were dull and completely boring. After having to read through Glass' unnecessary POV and Clarke forgiving Wells and then dumping him again  and her awkward relationship with Bellamy I just started to lose interest, which is something that happened very few times to me. There was a resemblance to "character development" but most of it was made by Bellamy and Clarke, who seem to overcome prejudice and the social differences between them. This last issue is one that is repeated throughout the book and it's mostly shown through Glass' POV. It was a little shocking to know that even though the mankind had almost become extinct, years and years from the present, there're still social barriers between people. Regarding to Clarke, I reckon she's a different type of strong lead female character. As many other so called "strong female" of books she has her moments when you just want to punch her in the face for acting so stupid, but most of the time she is someone I look up to. She uses her knowledge for good, and though sometimes it seems she is being selfish like when she's trying to save her only friend  ;she takes her job as a Healer very seriously and wishes to have had further training. Also, as a girl trapped with a bunch of guys trying to be Alpha dogs she doesn't let herself be bossed around and shows a firm personality. I found this book lacking in a lot of ways, but the idea was a good one so I'm giving the TV series a shot. Maybe when I'm not busy or if someone I trust recommends it I'll read the sequel.
Heartwarming story about friendship and family.

This was just basic. It had every cliche YA trope you can imagine pretty much. Underwhelming when you find out what's going on with her mouth and stuff and honestly the rape part was just... Idk. Weak. I feel like if you're gonna try and make a statement using rape culture then make it! Loud and proud. This just wasn't hit hard enough.. This made me roll my eyes quite a few times  but seriously? Out of no where and hardly even in the heat of a moment she uses a paperclip to make scratches (if you could call it self harm)? And they just touch on it. Like one page then it's all better. Ugh. Whatever.

My first and sadly only (until this one) novel by Gemma Burgess was A Girl Like You which was the absolute best and sent around my entire friendship group. So obviously, when I heard about this series I was super excited to read it. This book follows Pia and introduces us to the rest of the girls that will get their own individual books later in the series. All the girls are likable or have the potential to be likable, whether that's the content of the characters of Burgess's genius is a 50/50 guess but I'm going to go with genius. This book was entertaining and the characters were compelling and 75% of all featured characters showed flaws and strengths. This is a crappy review but this is not a crappy book

3.5 stars. I liked this book. It doesn't read as fast as 'The Couple Next Door' or books by BA Paris. Also because, as a non-native speaker, the English language is a bit harder to grasp. The suspense starts early on. Who is Beth? Why is Laura afraid of Beth? Who is Jamie? It took a while before I could answer those questions and that sort of annoyed me in the beginning. The eclipse-hunting I liked. Essentially, the book is about lies. What are you prepared to keep hidden. What are you willing to give up, to endure, to keep the situation as it is. I thought this was somewhat implausible at times. For years and years, lie to the person you love the most? The person you spend your life with?

Mmm I wasn't a super big fan of this one. The narration, split between two sisters who have the same bigamist father, was okay. Although basically the narration was the same between the two of them (as in, the style wasn't different or anything), I thought that it was interesting to see the different points of views of the sisters, one who knows that she is an illegitimate daughter and the other under the delusion that she is part of a whole legitimate family. The writing was also okay. Not great, just okay. Just didn't blow me away or anything. A great deal of the book definitely read as YA which is fine but there was something almost a little subtlely adult there that I couldn't put my finger on. There was a darkness to it that never really felt resolved. It gave me an uneasy feeling and while reading it I wasn't exactly sure at all how to feel. Of course, this was an uneasy topic. To write of bigamy is quite interesting, especially if it results in two daughters who share so much and so little in common. I think the parts that I enjoyed the most were those that discussed I guess what you would call colorism, and the self esteem issues a black girl can face if she doesn't have certain hair, skin color or slimness. I thought those things were interesting, as the "legit" daughter had the "whole" family but felt ugly for having none of the aforementioned good traits. On the other hand, her sister was illegitimate but was pretty, slim and was a "silver girl". The thing is about all that is none of that felt resolved. I guess my major problem with the book at large was that there was so much focus on the backstories of the parents (only one of which was interesting) that it left the daughters' in the book's present moment almost entirely unresolved. It did not feel in any way that I knew Dana well or Chaurisse. And there were also many characters in this book, as a bildungsroman goes that didn't seem to have much to do with the plot either. I also hated the epilogue. Overall, I thought this story dealt with an interesting topic but I guess for me the execution didn't have me moved. I wish that I had gotten more info about Dana and Chaurisse (and even Raleigh) because they definitely would have made the book more interesting.

2 1/2 stars really. This is not McGuire's best work. I count myself lucky that I've read her October Daye series, because I probably would never have picked up another book by her again if this had been the first book I'd read. That's not to say that this book is awful - it's just cliche from the yawn-worthy romance to the plot. Some of the world building was interesting, but there were moments when nothing 'rang true' so to speak, and I found myself rolling my eyes. I didn't like any of the characters enough (with the possible exception of the mice) to really want to visit this world again, which is a shame.

So. Much. Love. I literally spent the entire day reading this book. It was a bit...odd, because I actually listened to the first 6, but I fell into the reading groove easily. The story is beautifully written and flows quickly --the book looks HUGE, but it really only took me less than 12 hours (taking into account distractions and regular life). And... I am SO excited to see that there will be another series in this world! THANK YOU SO MUCH ANGIE SAGE! YOU HAVE NO IDEA HOW AWESOME YOU HAVE MADE MY LIFE!! Seriously though, I've been reading some really crap books since Harry Potter ended --this series did a great job at bringing magic (or Magyk even) back into my life. I was sad to see this series end, but I look forward to more of Sage's work.

As far as conclusions to trilogies go Shattered was a good one. Kyla is still wound up about what happened to Ben, and although I felt sorry for her I wasn't actually too bothered about Ben. Why? Because I wasn't emotionally invested in the romance between Ben and Kyla in book one. It was dull and so was Ben to be honest. For this reason, as harsh as it may sound to some, I didn't really care much about what happened to him. I was, however, pleased with the way Aiden and Kyla's relationship evolved. He was the guy I was rooting for as a love interest, and although Kyla was pretty much oblivious to his feelings until the very end I am glad that the book hinted at a future for the two of them. One thing I appreciated about Aiden was that he completely supported Kyla, without being pushy or condescending. In contrast to Ben, he was a fully developed character. Many of the long awaited answers to questions readers have dying to know are answered in this book. Kyla's journey of self discovery continues and she finally learns the truth about her past. If there was only one thing I could say about this book it would be that there is no lack of character development on the part of the mc. She grows and grows, coming out stronger in the end. Furthermore, Terry's writing style really adds to the horrors of what goes down in this book, adding tension and edge to the story. The freakiest thing about this trilogy is that it seems realistic, like the events that took place could actually happen. In an overcrowded genre, Slated is a unique dystopian trilogy. This review also appears on my blog, The Page Turner.

I liked this story a lot. The more I thought on it today, I needed to add another star. I like all of Sophie's stories. I just wish that the endings would match all the build up in the character development and build up of story. Don't miss understand me. The book is very well written, and the story is very good. I personally feel a little let down with the finally. I thought that there should have been more story line to the investigation and also to her time with Nate after they returned to each other. IMO!

After I finished the Hunger Games, this was the one book everyone kept telling me to read. They said it was just as good (some even thought it was better!) than the Hunger Games, so you can imagine how excited I was to start reading it. Once in a while you come across a book that sounds good in theory, but doesn't deliver when you actually read it cover to cover. The Maze Runner is that book. It has a well thought out plot, interesting scenery, but every single one of the characters fell flat. Thomas, the main character, was annoying and spent a good chunk of the book whining. And the rest of the characters are so generic that they are instantly forgettable. The pacing was so ridiculously slow that I found myself completely disinterested in the story until about 60 pages in. 60 pages! That is a heck of a lot of pages needed to grab the reader's attention! After about 75% into the book, suddenly (and quite unexpectedly) the book started to take off. The payoff at the end is also pretty decent and sets the pavement for a sequel.

It was the last 200 or so pages that really brought this book down to a one star for me. I had a lot of issues with the end and I ended up getting bored of the same tired lines and characters. Glokta was my favorite :) Still is. If there was a book just about him and none of those other twats I'd read it. Anyways here's a small list of things that brought this books down for me: I was so sick of wars. Northerners, Gurkish, Northerners again, Gurkish again. Plus the fight scenes for just one person lasted 3 or 4 pages which grated on me after awhile since most of them end with the person getting hurt and failing or turning into the Bloody-Nine and not remembering what happened and repeating "still alive". Shut the fuck up Jezal. Abercrombie seems to think of several ways to say something and likes them all. So instead of picking just one he likes to throw them all together into the book instead. Or he'll think of a nice adjective for someone and want to use them all in one sentence. That's how it ends? That's how it ends? It drags on forever. It could've ended a 100 pages back and I would've liked that ending better. Also around 200 pages I realized that nothing would change. It would be a pointless end to a pointless read because... nothing changed. Everyone is back to what they were and no one ever changes and Blah blah blah. **Spoiler** 6.The buildup to things was non existent. So Quai is actually Tolomei and then they fight but no wait they don't Bayaz runs away and locks Yulwei behind and we never know what happens. Yay. I think that maybe if Abercrombie had shortened some scenes, only put one sentence to explain simple things like "the cannons stopped" then he might've been able to explore certain plot points more such as the Feared, The Seed, etc. I probably won't read his stuff again. Which is sad since I really did like the first book, but it was all downhill from there.

I really enjoyed this book. I've kind been reading this series out of order but it is strong charcaters. Erin came from nothing, raised by an older brothers after the lost of her parents. She is very sure of herself and what she needs and wants. Todd at the beginning doesn't know how to reconcille what he needs and wants with what he believes that he should want. You see a strong relationship building. Todd wants to protect her from everything bad exspecially after all that she had been through, I liked how Erin didn't want that, she likes it and will accept it but she still wants to deal with it on her own. Now other the other hand there is Ben, I don't know about how it wasn't until half way through the story that he gets involved. In the end it worked but it was almost like it was an after thought on the writers part. I liked him in the end because he seems to satify something within Erin and Todd that they didn't know that they were missing but still it seemed like it was slightly odd to me the way he came into the relationship. It doesn't take away from the relationship or the book.

4.5 Undoubtful Stars Definitely my favorite book up so far , Sabin and Gwen make outstanding characters on their own , but together they were even more astonishing . Sabin , Keeper of Doubt , character that always intrigued me from earlier books , serious warrior that he his , Sabin leaves nothing to chance nor does he want to ever get emotionally attached to someone. While on a raid , Sabin and his friends discover some female prisoners that hunters were torturing and raping and amongst them is Gwen , our female protagonist. She had such a character developement going from Gwen the timid to Gwen the vicious harpy if you touch her man , her journey towards self acceptance and self embrace made my heart soar. The plot was equaly on fleek (plots can be on fleek too!lol) , too much action and adrenaline , amazing sidekicks and fucking EPIC banter , especially William , damn that boy but his book is a MUST for me. Highly recommendable series , I prefer it better to what I've read from the Black Dagger Brotherhood , as I know a lot of people compare the two.

I've seen the movies and loved them so I thought it was about time I saw where everything began for Percy, Grover and Annabeth. The Lightning Thief by Rick Riordan tells the story of how twelve year old Percy Jackson discovers he's a demigod. Son of Poseidon, Percy has never quite been like other kids. Hidden in the mortal world to protect him from those with grudges against his biological father, Percy has always known that he was different. When Zeus' lightning bolt is stolen, Percy's existence comes to light and his paternity is revealed. If Percy is to find the bolt (and consequentially save his mother and become a hero) - he needs to overcome monsters and battle gods. Not alone in his quest, his best friend Grover and one of Athena's daughters, Annabeth, tag along to give Percy the best chance against the powerful immortals. For the right audience, I believe this book would be perfect. There's action and adventure. A great take on classic mythology and characters I could fall in love with. The problem is - I'm not the right audience. I'm in my twenties and unlike a lot of other young adult and middle grade books I've read - this one made me feel old in a way no other book I've read before has. The characters, as entertaining as they are, read a little young. I liked that they are true to their character. I believe that Percy is twelve despite him having to try and take on challenges that would terrify people many times his age. And the author is consistent with the the trio's skill levels. I just think that I'm not the right person for this book. The mythology is amazing. I love how much Riordan packed in. There's all sorts of gods met and mentioned with places and stories being inserted into the plot all over the place. Journey wise - it didn't feel very planned all the time. Like the trio were sort of stumbling upon where they were supposed to go next. But in the end they got to where they were meant to be so it all worked out for the best I suppose. I'll still watch the movies (provided they make more! Fingers crossed!) but this series isn't for me.
A funny, cute little book with a witty heroine that makes for a run read.

THIS. BOOK. IS SO SO. AMAZING. UNF. Kagawa takes the readers on a fun adventure where imagination shines bright. A very talented writer who knows exactly how to plant images in the readers minds. To be honest, I wasn't expecting much from this book, mostly due to the whole faeries and magical creatures part. I was half expecting sparkles and glittery stuff and rainbows and magical beings with their pretty wings and wands. But heh, this book kicked my low expectations right in their faces screaming "OH PUHLEASE!" This book is like the stories from your childhood packed together in a more wicked and twisted way, retaining the uniqueness of itself. The flow of the writing, the way the words are weaved together is amazing. It usually takes me a few chapters to get hooked on but I KNEW I'd like it from the very beginning. I finished this in one sitting, without getting the usual "meh" feeling. Meghan is a quite interesting character who cares for her loved ones and I have a strong feeling she's going to develop into a remarkable and brave heroine. I like the way she handled everything when she was shown a whole new side to her life, I could have punched a wall if "OMG OMG NO I CANT DO DIS NO I WANT MY OLD LIFE OMG NO NO" drama was included. Meghan accepted her true self and that's wonderful. I liked Ash from the very beginning since he has got the perfect book boyfriend thing about him. I quite fancy myself an Ash... But with the nice and funny Puck around the corner I think I smell a brewing love triangle. -wrinkles nose- Something tells me Meghan is going to end up with Ash. They make a better pair. Grimalkin was....adorable. Honestly tho. I liked Grimalkin, partly because, well, Cheshire cat. And partly because he is interesting with the right amount of sassy! YOU GO CAT!
I love little Carl. Hershel kind of annoyed me in this one, whereas I really like him in the series. Andrea and Dale together is a freak-fest, but hey whatever floats your boat.

I didn't enjoy this as much as the first book. I didn't feel like I really got to know the main characters, Cas and Tolemek and I don't feel as if they even really got to know each other. There was a lot of banter in this book, between Cas and Tolemek, Cas and Goroth, Tolemek and Jaxi...but there were very few serious conversations, so I didn't feel attached to any one character's story arc at all.

Ahhhh, I'm so disappointed by this ending! I should have just stopped after Prodigy, that would have worked better. This finale picks up 8 months after the last book ends. Anden is making the expected changes to the Republic and he's somehow close to getting the Colonies to sign a peace treaty. Now there's a new problem, though. The virus the Republic created inside Eden has somehow ended up in the Colonies and now they're ready to go to war again. Except this time Africa will back them up. Which means the Republic is fucked unless they find a cure. And throughout all this, Day is fighting his cancer. The story of the war didn't work for me like the story of revolution and changing the republic did, but it was still interesting and I definitely wanted to see how it would turn out. I was impressed by the directions the first two books went in, so I had high hopes. And there were a bunch of fun and exciting scenes. As the story progressed, though, I got less and less confident that the resolution would be strong, because I simply couldn't think of a good way it could all work out. And I was right to worry, because in the end, the story line just wasn't very good. It was messy and unrealistic and convenient. Really, though, the ending focused pretty much entirely on the romance, brushing off the whole war in a few sentences Because they found the cure, Antarctica showed up. Everyone else shat their pants and ran. Peace ensued... Somehow. . I wasn't a fan of the romance in the previous two books and this one didn't do anything to change that. The relationship between June and Day was never really justified in my mind. Their love never made sense. To be honest, I was rooting for June to really fall in love with Anden. And Day should have died. It would have been a much better story. And, I mean, he had cancer AND he'd been shot. The effect of that death would have been much more interesting and emotional than this ending was. June and Day's romance was eh throughout this book, but the ending was the worst. Let's just say Chuck and Sarah handled this crappy situation a lot better. P.S. It turns out the reason I'm not bothered by the fact that these majorly impressive main characters are 15/16 is because my head pretends they're not. It works. A bunch of things make more sense when you pretend they're, like, 25-30.
I'm speechless. BEAUTIFUL story. 5++ stars Review to come.

So, I've condensed two book reviews into one - because I read them back to back in about 35 hours so to me they are one book. Lets just get this out of the way first up - I LOVE CORMORAN STRIKE. There is something about the way that Rowling writes people that I just love. She is so good at showing us what they are feeling without telling. There's so much depth to Cormoran and Robin and even all the secondary and third characters in these books - even the culprits are well thought out and layered. I know that Rowling sometimes goes a little over board with descriptions of physical places and physical people descriptions but I just think she does so well with displaying people's feelings in a subtle way. I love Cormoran and Robin's relationship. I can see its heading in a romantic direction and I WANT THAT TO HAPPEN. I am shipping them so badly. I've never been so attracted to a character that is constantly described as fat and ugly with pubes for hair. The crimes are always interesting and hard to guess - I actually spoiled Career of Evil for myself by reading about the plot and I actually still didn't guess it in the book. I love that Rowling changed up the formula for Career of Evil and also gave us some more insight into Cormoran and Robin's pasts. Basically, I am loving this series so much. Crime layered with interesting characters and a touching and slowly developing romance/friendship between partners. Can't get enough!

In the 19th century in England, magic is dead. It has been relegated to theoretical study. No one feels that acutally practicing magic is possible anymore. All of that changes when Gilbert Norrell enters the story. Norrell starts a one man revival of magic and wants to keep it all for himself. Before long a second magician appears in Jonathan Strange and this story is off to the races. Norrell and Strange have completely different styles and it is surprised that they even talk to each other. If fact after a while they do separate. This portion of the story was my least favorite. While Strange was in Italy, the momentum seems to leave the tale while waiting for the conclusion Clark has written an amazing story. The blend of Jane Austen style writing with a fantasy twist is fresh and inventive. The story is interesting, funny, and well paced most of the time. I have heard rumors of a sequel and the ending sets that up perfectly.

The Hunter by L.J. Smith tells the story of Jenny, who buys this game for her boyfriends birthday. This game is unique. They must face their darkest fears controlled by the shadow man, also known as Julian, a boy who is in love with Jenny. They must win the game. If they lose, the shadow man will take Jenny forever. CHARCTERS- I loved the cast of charcters! Jenny was so smart and I loved following her journey through the house. ...  She was such a badass when she kissed Julian at the end then ran up the house to escape. Julian was such an intriguing character. He might have been bad but I loved him..oops ROMANCE- The romance was deadly and fascinating. Julian obviously loved Jenny very much and the way he only smiled at her. Swoon worthy romance with great chemistry. PLOT- The plot was unique and very special. I've never read anything like it. It reminded me of the movie Zathura. ENDING- Such a ending! I need the second book NOW! Characters-10/10 Romance-10/10 Plot-10/10 Ending-10/10 Speed-10/10 (very fast paced)

Reader thoughts: I've always liked sea adventures less. Treasure Island and Dawn Treader come to mind. They just seem slower and less clean. So, I have that issue with this book (too much sea travel and sea monsters). But, other than that, it's amazing! (It's Percy Jackson, how could it not be amazing?) First, we learn about the prophecy. Just in passing. Woot! It's not just that the big three gods aren't having children to prevent a human war. They want to prevent a global god/giant/titan-level war. And Percy's caught in the middle. Next, Percy gets a brother. I love Tyson! The idea of him is a bit ick (having a half-brother who is technically a monster? ), but I love how loyal he is and that he is good with making things. Grover gets to be awesome and figures out why so many satyrs are dying in the Bermuda triangle. He's so tricky! Unraveling the cyclops wedding dress. Ha! Percy gets turned into a guinea pig and rescued by Annabeth, also awesome. The whole wind-in-a-canister idea is pretty cool. I also love that they lose control of it. Writer thoughts: Riordan brought Percy's mother back from the dead (almost literally) in book one. Now, he had to figure out a way to write Percy's adventures so it made sense that she wouldn't try to follow him around everywhere (as moms are wont to do). Besides, we find out in book 4 that she can see through the mist. Anyway, RR uses quests to get Percy to travel with friends to dangerous islands without adult supervision. The first book, Percy wanted to save his mom. The third, it's Annabeth. The second, it's Grover. So, RR does a nice job making sure Percy has personal stakes in the quests. I think he's just trying to save Camp Halfblood in the fourth book, and he's trying to save all of Manhattan Island in the fifth one. So, the stakes are raised everywhere except between books 1 and 2 (how can a best friend compete with a mom?). Maybe that's why this book is the shortest of all five.

This book was recommended to me a couple of times, so I decided to check it out. The author uses studies from various fields to support his idea that we have something in our unconscious that can help or harm us in decision-making. This is an interesting concept, but I didn't find it a particularly new idea. Some of the examples were interesting, but I didn't always agree that they are supporting the overall argument.

My plan for the day: run some errands, do some laundry, make dinner and etc. But I said to myself, I'll read a couple of pages of this book first. Its due back on Tuesday to the library. I read the first chapter. New plan for the day: Don't move until book is finished. And I didn't. I dislike Beth *intensely* and I hate that she was in the book for even 5 pages, but, whatever. Rachel and Isaiah however? Adorable. I love them to teeny pieces and then I love the pieces. I want to read about Logan! I hope there's a Logan book. I am not excited about Wests book. I wanted every member of Rachel's family to take a leisurely stroll off a short pier and drown to death. She'd have been better off  when Rachel's mother said at the end of the book that Rachel should have tried harder to make her (the mother) see her (Rachel) and not Colleen? I may have slammed the book down and said expletive, expletive, expletive how about its not her job you expletive! and then somewhat calmly finished the book.

I adored George!! No really I could picture us having a very A.D.D. conversation over tea and cakes...lol. She wasn't the demure damsel like in other stories, she was a strong character for a historical and she was happy with herself. She never went through that stupid I dont' deserve him phase that most historical characters go through (although Harry had more than a few of his own moments). The little sister Violet made me want to slap the shit outta her though. Seriously she made me loathe all teenage girls for about 5hrs...lol. Harry made my heart flutter every time he said "my lady" in that calm cool voice. Story - 3.25 narrator - 3 Moira's male voices leave something to be desired but overall awesome job.

Three stars! I didn't really fall for this couple but their scenes were STEAMY. Hoyt knows how to write fantastic sexy time scenes and great, layered characters. I liked Temperance and Lord Caire but I didn't get the feels from them. I do look forward to the other books a lot because Hoyt did a great job setting up some of the future plot points.

DNF. After hearing praises upon praises on this novel, I decided to pick it up. What could go wrong, I thought, with a 4.40 rating on Goodreads? (A lot of things could go wrong, my dear past self.) First attempt at reading: It was okay. I arrived at page 100 and dropped the book because I couldn't bring myself to care. Second attempt at reading: I actually got offended. This book is quite honestly... astonishing. It romanticizes behaviors that are not, I repeat, not good. Alexander is creepy, even abusive at times - if not physically, emotionally. With over 200 pages of boring sex scenes (which I skimmed), even the historical bits couldn't save the plot. Everything was so, so tedious and boring. I like historical fiction. I don't like useless repetition of useless details that could be edited out. Where was the editor in this, seriously? Tatiana was an unbelievable main character. Everything about her was exaggeratedly innocent and virginal, to the point Alexander's relationship with her (especially towards the second half of the novel) made me want to toss my book into the bin. How can a supposedly hot young soldier get excited about his girl being "untouched" and a "virgin" while having sex with her for the first time? This was the creepiest thing. Also, his behavior is quite horrible towards Tatiana's hobbies and passions - he only wants her to be with him, all the time. She is not allowed to have her "boring" things. Ugh. I hated this. I almost fell asleep, but I was too outraged. Needless to say, I do not recommend this.

I have to admit I'm frustrated with this series. The issues I had in the last one are not really being addressed. They're still 12 (probably 13 now), Sophie still has "creamy skin", someone still can't be ugly and a good person, someone can't be a good person and have bad thoughts (maybe that's a lie, but it wasn't acknowledged: Agatha did loads of things wrong and was still considered "good", whereas Sophie did similar things but was not), and never was it mentioned anywhere that someone can have a best friend and a boyfriend! Novel, I know. And there were weird gender binaries I had a problem with, but I'm glad one of the boys masqueraded as a girl the whole time because he liked it better over there. Also that Tedros got so confused that he kissed Philip, even if Philip was starting to look like Sophie again. I really wish the boys would have come to a realization that the insignificance they were feeling was a bit of a payback. But they didn't learn anything. Maybe it's coming. What I'd really like the book to talk about is that attraction isn't all emotional (they got the "love at first sight" thing): none of the boys seemed to want each other romantically, and none of the girls wanted each other either, despite never wanting to see another person of the opposite sex again. I also still find it problematic that Sophie's true love is hundreds of years old... gross. Also she didn't fight that she only got to see an image of her mother and not her actual mother. I still enjoyed the plot, and I'm hoping the next (last?) one in the series actually addresses all the binary cans of worms he opened...

Audio relisten 3/14 - Yeah, it's a 4. A lot better when I remembered what happened in the first one. Still loving Patton although I feel like he could do better with Calla, Ronan, and my homeboy Kavinsky. Everyone else is 100% perfect. Let's go #3, let's go. I loved, loved, loved The Raven Boys, and was so looking forward to reading this. Now I'm just kind of disappointed. It might have been because I read an ARC on my phone instead of listening to the audiobook like I did for the first book, but I just didn't feel the same magic. If I was going to use one word to describe The Dream Thieves, it would be "tangential." Or maybe "interstitial" is more accurate... The main plots of the first book - the quest for Glwyndower, the mystery of Cabeswater, Noah's past, the Blue-Gansey-Adam romance, the Adam-Gansey tension - are still there, but nothing huge happens with them. Instead, the Dream Thieves is very Ronan-centric, revealing how he is able to take things from his dreams and the mysteries of his family. While I liked finding out the secrets behind his belligerent facade, it didn't make for a very lively plot. Some of the book's revelations were pretty great  Ronan's dad dreamed his mother into existence! There are many Dream Thieves, but only one Greywaren, etc. /but even with them, Ronan's story felt too weak to be the main storyline. Luckily, the characterization was just as strong as in the first book. I even kind of liked the character of Kavinsky, despite never really buying him as the crazy villain he was supposed to be. I'm hoping this book was quiet and exposition-heavy because it's building up to a great third book. Something that brings all the disparate threads back together and makes you go, "Ohhhhh! Now I get it." It's also possible I just need to go back and read the first and second book back to back. But right now, it feels like a bit of a sophomore slump.

I'm not giving this book a rating because even though I've given up on it--usually an automatic one-star--I wouldn't have tried it in the first place (if it hadn't been for a book club). So my lack of interest might not be the novel's fault. I mean, this thing won a Nebula! People other than I adore it. The Windup Girl takes place on a post-apocalyptic Earth where food is scarce due to plagues and blights. The action happens in Thailand, which has somehow managed to keep from flooding and also from losing all of its seed banks. Other than that, I can't tell you much, though I got halfway through. There didn't seem to be much of a plot going and the zillion characters all seemed very unsympathetic. The novel's title refers to a Japanese clockwork girl, genetically engineered to be utterly awesome...but she's not doing so well in Thailand where she overheats, is used as a sex toy, and generally finds herself hated and debased at every turn. While she makes the most sympathetic character in the narrative, she'd only had two chapters devoted to her by the halfway mark, so I wasn't holding out much hope. If you're really into character-driven confusion with no discernible plot until its all coming together, this book is for you. (Hey, I know some people like that kind of thing.)

This review was originally published on my blog Girl With A Pretty Keyboard. The Quick is intended to be a Victorian Gothic/Horror novel. It's widely touted to be among the best written since the heyday of the Gothic genre. It's a first novel from a young writer. I feel somehow as though I'm not allowed to write a summary of what it's about because it seems to be a gigantic secret jealously guarded with all the force and might of the publisher. So, I won't. But, there were multiple plot developments in the first 100 or so pages where I found myself saying, "Well that was unexpected!" I thoroughly enjoyed the first 100 pages and the last 100 pages, but the middle of the book is long, wind-y, and sometimes gets lost. I found myself impatiently reading through long segues that seemed to lose the thread of the novel. The pacing is just ... off. I will say that much of the information held in sections of the book that initially seem unimportant and superfluous do return to the plot later, but the book still seems unnecessarily tangential. The book starts as if it were a Jane Austen love story, told from a male perspective. I liked it. Then, abruptly, the perspective and focus changes and our likeable protagonist is lost to us for what seems like ages. There are sections of the novel told in the epistolary form, but it's among the portions of the novel that drag on the longest. Almost all of the characters get a backstory chapter, some of which were very interesting but hardly apropos. If you enjoy Victorian Gothic reads, it's probably worth your time, but if I had known it was a vampire  book, I wouldn't have been nearly as excited to read it.

Beautiful book! I especially liked how Crenshaw compares imaginary friends to books: "Imaginary friends are like books. We're created, we're enjoyed, we're dog-eared and creased, and then we're tucked away until we're needed again."

When I started reading the story, I was under the impression that this was a book focused on books and how books possess the power to heal. It's set in Paris, and the bookshop is a floating barge on the Seine. The book seller considers books medicine for people who are suffering. He asks buyers questions to assess their mood, likes, dislikes, and then fits them with a prescription along with a "dosage" for how to take/read the books he prescribes. Amazing concept! However, this book is a very languid (just to be clear about the pace of this book, synonyms for languid include: relaxed, languorous, unhurried, slow) exploration of love and self-forgiveness. So I felt slightly deceived by the book's marketing. And it only gets worse when you learn about the main love story: a woman who is cheating on her husband with the main character. The main character, Jean, has wasted away for the past 20 years since his great love, Manon, left him... for her husband. It's hard to feel that deep connection of their love when the characters only reflect back on their time together when they're naked. Naked became the buzz word of the book. Do French people really just lay around naked all the time? It seems like no one in the country had jobs. Oh, but wait, there's more! Manon is in love with a Jean and a Luc! You know? As in Jean-Luc Picard? Star Trek TNG fan girl much? Okay, these are probably common Frenchman names, but it felt TNG to me. Lost in translation, perhaps? The author does not get to the point well, thus the plot felt very piecemeal. First Jean decides to leave Paris on his book barge because he wants to find Manon. Then he's obsessed with finding the author of a book he loves. Then he dances the tango. Wait... where are we now? Motivations were never clear. Sure, they can fluctuate, but the protagonist needs to have a clear goal. In terms of the characters, while I enjoyed the ever developing father-son-like relationship between Max Jordan (author) and Jean Perdu (book lover and peddler), the rest of the characters felt unrealistic. For instance, a woman jumps into a rapid-flowing and dangerous river during a torrential rain storm just because she is curious what it would be like? Then she falls in love with one of her rescuers? Oh, that's a totally believable love story. Plus, she's the mayor of a town! So the one person who has a job is jumping to her death because she's curious about what it would feel like. The characters are lacking in any sort of redeemable and relatable qualities. Plus, they all seem to follow the same train of thought and express their feelings using the same words, so it's hard to decipher who is speaking at times. And I got sick of reading about all the women characters being naked! There's that buzz word again! There is a lot of beauty to this book, and there is also a lot that does not make sense. There are lovely spaces of thought-provoking observations about life, but there are also many superfluous moments (i.e., what the point was of the scene involving the unsuccessful rescue of the deer?). Then there were some parts of the plot that were so incredibly obvious. When Jean is questioning the woman they rescued after her river jump about who the author of his favorite book is, I wanted to beat him over the head. ITS HER! This is not rocket science! The characters came off as clueless. Plus, no one was very honest which subsequently caused themselves and everyone around them additional grief and needless heartache. It got extremely frustrating. I wanted to yell, "Get over it!" The plot only progressed when there was new agony for the characters to suffer through. It wallowed in its emotionally saturated plotline and self-punishing characters. I will say, though, that the end of the book was very heartfelt as the characters finally released their grief. I began to feel something for them. The last scene with Jean sitting by Manon's grave, reading her diary, and (climax coming...) discovering where her spirit passed on to was lovely. However, it took way too long to get there. I did not understand the point the author was trying to make with this story. Erratic is a good word for the plot flow. I finished the book and felt relieved that I was finally done with it! Worst part: Reading Manon's travel diaries was very grating. It was always we did this... naked; then we did this... naked. And let me quote for you: "My pussy glistens when I feel desire." Isn't that charming? Can the literary apothecary start narrating instead? I did not like her voice at all. It might have been more interesting if the author had included part of her time with Luc just so we could see that other side of her. Despite the fact Luc seemed a more interesting and resourceful character (I would have loved more time spent at the winery learning the craft), the author makes him okay with the fact that for five years his wife would travel to Paris to be with Jean ??? I understand forgiveness, but his outlook was, I don't know, like he was okay being emotionally neglected by his wife? It seems that his personality was simplified for an easy fit in the narrative in that regard. Best part: I enjoyed the handy little guide of books to read at the end of the novel and how those books are a fast-acting cure a specific malady. There are also side effect warnings. Very charming. The book had some charm, however, it got lost too often. The author's focus and intent for this book were never clear.

Such and entertaining read. I loved the world building and Alex's family and their dynamic. Seeing the family and how they interact with each other and how close they are reminded me a lot about my family especially when they got together to celebrate. I wish there was more Rishi and Alex before we went on full magic adventure or at least there was more background story given throughout the book as I didn't feel too connectedto their relationship. I will definitely read the sequel, I hope it has more of Alex's family as I felt that was the strongest and most interesting part of the book.

I have very mixed feelings about this novel. On the one hand, I stayed up late to finish it and was found in the wee hours, in tears, because it brought me so far into life in occupied France. On the other hand, the writing is pretty bad. The cliches and unimaginative prose almost made me put the book down a few times. Character development was uneven and frustrating, and as the plot moved along there were no surprises. (Must every historical fiction novel have a future parallel storyline?) The story is about two adult sisters coping with Nazi occupation. One joins the French resistance early on, and the other one loses her husband to the draft and must raise her daughter alone while the Nazis move into her house. Her story was the most compelling to me as an ordinary person slow to catch on that things were changing in her quiet life in a drastic and nonnegotiable way. It made me wonder what I would do if my husband was imprisoned in a labor camp, or if the Nazis rolled up and requisitioned my furniture. I've heard people criticize France for their role in the war, but the citizens had it pretty bad to the point of starvation, freezing, no electricity, while the Nazis ate like kings. God help you if you were a Jew. Also featured as a supporting character is a German soldier who is confused and stressed out by being a Nazi. Those stories of regular people who are sucked into the Nazi machine by social pressure rather than heartfelt duty always interest me, the gradual horror at their own people and the roles they are playing, their little acts of defiance, the fear for their families if they are caught. I can see why people like this book so much, though it had a lot of problems.

Mieville's always been one of those names, you know? I'd heard of him, heard he was a bit of a Marmite guy, but everyone agrees he's an author that you have to try at least once in your life. So I bookmarked the guy, decided to pick up his latest story about a boy on a hill in a houseful of keys. I was excited to see if it was my cuppa tea. I'm sure Mieville knows by now that not everyone's going to appreciate his specific brand of weirdness, and I'm sure he doesn't care that I'm now adding my name to the list. I can't judge his other works because I'm not going to read them; This Census-Taker was just so relentlessly awful. Plot? Nah. Interesting characters? Fuck no. Stupid narrative and one semi-interesting feature that is never explained? OH YEAH. Plus 200 pages of boredom, oddities, stuff that wasn't really a story. It was irksome to read, like being stuck listening to the semi-coherent ramblings of the local drunk while you're waiting at the bus stop on a groggy Monday morning. And when I stumble upon something so rubbish, something that feels like such a waste of paper, I spend far too much time obsessing about the point of it all, and severely angering myself in the process. Honestly, this is a bit of a nothing book. A boring and personality-deficient boy's father maybe  murders his mother. The boy still has to live with him, while growing increasingly scared of him. Until a census-taker comes to call and, well if you don't mind me telling you, takes him away. It's quite plain to see that the theme of this novel is childhood trauma, a sliver of domestic abuse and some child neglect to spice it up. Except why write a story about such poignant themes when it fails so hard to make me care? This little boy, the main character, is dull as fuck. He has no depth, hardly any feelings. He's just there, narrating this story, switching between first, second and third person like an absolute ponce, not evoking any sort of reaction in me whatsoever. What do I care that he's scared of his dad? He's not a real person, his suggested existence just annoys me. I'm concentrating more on trying to figure out where the fuck this story is set, and what the hell is up with those keys? Why won't you explain the fucking keys, Mieville? You've got to be trying to make a point here, right Mieville? But for the life of me I cannot figure out what it is! Are you saying that childhood trauma turns you into a husk, a shell of your potential self with no feelings or personality? Because that's not true, is it? Is this one of those cop-out books where the reader had to "make their own mind up" about the true meaning of the story? Because if so, see above. Is this a pass at surrealism or something? Because I tell you, it was fucking weird and not in a good way. And I tell you, if given this book to read Salvador Dali would tear it to ribbons and feed it to his anteater. Artaud would give you one of his looks of absolute disgust and call you a poser. I don't know what to think anymore, apart from thinking about how annoyed I am. As much as I know that art and literature are subjective, I would never call this art, I would never say this was well-written. Art and literature have intent, and This Census-Taker had none. If it did, it would have to be a commentary on childhood trauma and how it turns you into a weirdo, incapable of emotions, incapable of making anyone care about you. That's all I got from this. That, and anger. Maybe I just didn't "get" it. Fair enough. But you know what else I won't be getting? Any more of China Mieville's books.

2.5-3 stars. When I was half-way through the book, I thought for sure I was going to rate it at least 3.5 stars. I'd liked the heroine so far, and after reading Once Upon a Winter's Night, I was pretty easily impressed by any rendition of this fairy-tale that didn't have the bear listening in on the girl as she peed. More detailed, spoiler-y review behind cut. However, once the lass gets a good look at the prince and the troll princess whisks him away, the book loses steam. The journey that should have been the bulk of the book felt rushed, and the eventual confrontation with the trolls anti-climatic and disappointing. I honestly felt like the book would have benefited from being longer, and the trolls...scarier? More menacing? Being ugly is all very well and good, but I wish it'd gone deeper...Maybe it's because the set-up of the castle, and the carvings made the trolls into these more...frightening creatures than they turned out to be, but I felt like they should have either stayed distant or close at hand (as in either stay a mysterious, veiled evil or be an evil that was much closer to home, if I'm getting my point across at all. I suspect that I'm probably not, so sorry about that). The relationship between the bear and the lass could have been more developed also. I get that JDG tried to make reader feel more attached to the bear by describing their (bear and girl) daily talks about literature and poetry, but in my opinion Robin Mckinley still did that better in Beauty, which is, granted, a different fairy tale, but frankly the concept of beast-to-man is similar enough that it shows that it can be done. So to sum it up: A pleasant enough read, quick and effortless. Could benefit from more plot or more pages, and started off as very, very promising but gradually lost steam as the novel progressed. Not the best fairy-tale retelling I've read, although I've only read two of East of the Sun, West of the Moon, and the first was so bad that anything else is almost guaranteed to be better.

I also found that Sofia and Gideon were much much more interesting characters than Jubliee and Flynn from the previous book and both had very strong, if not stronger, personalities than Lilac and Tarver from These Broken Stars. This made the eventual meet up and collaboration between all of these characters - which happened around halfway through the book - really exciting. The book overall is definitely not as good as the first book in the series, however I would consider it a worthy second. I have had minor problems with this series throughout but, as always, the fluid and very enjoyable storytelling that Kaufman and Spooner managed to achieve has made it a very worthwhile and electrifying read. I do want to mention that despite having finished this book, I still do not understand AT ALL why Gideon was trying to track Commander Towers around the galaxy throughout the first half of the book?! That whole thread in the story completely ended once we found out that he was actually tracking Sofia, and so the reason's for his obsession with finding her were never discussed and that really disturbed me once I finished the book. WHY, GIDEON?
