Kresley Cole did it again! This book is just amazing. I breeze through it. My favorite part? The ending. It's not a cliff-hanger, it's an Anticipation- for the second book that is. I've been a long time KC's fan. Basically anything she writes I'll read. Her IAD series is like a drug to me. I need to re-read it once in a while for every month while awaiting the next sequel. So when I heard she's venturing to YA, I am delighted and worried at the same time. There have been so many Adult Romance authors that tried to write YA and missed the mark. Well I'd say Miss Cole NAILED it. Though it is a young adult book and written in first person POV, KC's fan would definitely realize the stamp she has on her style all over this book. It is just so Kresley. Fans of IAD would notice the resemblance that Mel has with Regin, and Matthew would be this book's version of Nix. Also as Miss Cole is a romance author you do get a dose of that here. If you're not use to how romance hero act, all Alpha-male and caveman act, this can take a while to get use to. But it brings up the HOT factor a notch from the rest of the YA books. Did anyone notice Jack's fixation on providing food is sooo Kresley's type of Hero? I am swooned. I really like how this book is structured. The opening first chapter is essential to the rest of the book. The story within a story concept is just so brilliant that I doubted how real the story I've been reading by the end of it. I also like how this book is divided before and after the flash. By knowing what happened before you really get a sense of character development, especially for Evie. The World Building The world building is flawless. It is easy to imagine. Some scenes were really movie-like. The Arcana concept is really new. But I think to fit the current market Kresley (or the editor, who knows) kind of forcefully fit the dystopian concept. It works, but I can't help feeling it's really just to fit the trend. And the Bagman too, the zombie that craves water = blood and doesn't like the sun. However I do like the KC's version of this end of the world thing. It's more barren, more cruel and savage, which is how it is supposed to be. The human morality or the lack there of here feels real. And I like the description of the blue sky in the deteriorating world. Its juxtaposition gives a very sad feeling, like the sky is mocking you. The Arcana This concept is really cool. The 22 major Arcana from the Tarot card are actually real kids with real power. And every few centuries or so they have to battle out and there can only be one survivor. They have to make alliances, pact, the evil card and the good. They have to seek each other out to do battle. I like the way each card recognizes one another. They will see a tableau of the card each represented the first time they meet. And the concept that each card has an Arcana Call is cool. I really like The Empress' - Come, touch... but you'll pay a price. Characters Evie Evie our heroine is a typical popular crowd, cheerleader, pretty, blond and timid girl that you usually get in a young adult book except for the fact that she was just sent to a mental institution for delusion and hallucination. She was just trying to be normal not believing in any of the voices in her head when actually it was a warning for what's to come. Imagined the regret for not listening to the voices and the 'what ifs' that will always haunt her. But I do pity her mother more for not believing in her own daughter. Evie's character can be quite annoying at times, because of her sense of morality and naivety that she holds on to in the time of survival of the fittest. But don't worry she will evolve and truthfully I've seen worse for a female character. But I also do think it's realistic for Evie to act that way from the way she was brought up. And what I like about her is that she is willing to learn to adapt and she doesn't complain. I hate characters that are whiny. And I assure you once you've finished the book, you will just love her. On Jack That boy on the cover is Jack 100%. Except that my Jack would have been more rugged. Jackson is totally Kresley's typical male hero; Alpha-male, possessive, protective, stubborn, and wild. The accent is sexy but the translation after every French word he spoke can be a bit jarring. Coming from the Basin his life hardened him. He's like an injured lion that's wary of everything. For him survival is absolute. He doesn't do noble if it means he or whoever he's protecting gets to live. And that's what I like about dystopian novel. How far would a person do for a chance of survival? But though he doesn't really do noble he still has his own sets of value which he follows. He keeps his promises and he is loyal to what he considers his. *Spoiler* On Jack and Evie This is complicated. There's no insta-love (thank god) but there is insta-attraction... and hate. Coming from their respective background I do understand why they can't get along though. I think Jack really has a complex on where he's from - being the poor boy from the Basin. It's realistic to hate over-privileged brats. They probably don't have to work on anything to get what they want. And it's even more realistic to hate them if you're attracted to one of them. His inner voice probably say  "I'm supposed to hate her kind so why can't I get her out of my mind?". So both Evie and Jack started off from a bad start. After the flash, fate brought them together again. As female numbers dwindling to single digits, Jack has to protect Evie and also to fulfill his (vague) promise to Evie's mother to bring Evie to her granny's place. So they both have to learn to tolerate each other. On the journey Jack can be a little rough on Evie but I believe it's all to toughen her up. One of my favorite scenes of them would be when Evie's emotional dam burst at their first stop over at the dock. Jack who can't handle emotional stuff went out the room but then paced back again and sat guarding the door. Which then after a while he sets on teaching Evie on survival things just to distract her. How cute is that? There's a lot of miscommunication on both side, but I guess that just happens when both is as stubborn as a mule. And that does frustrate me a little. But hey we do need a bit of obstacle in the romance department, and the big one being Selena. On Others We've only got to see a little bit of Death. But he manages to grab all my attention. He's probably my most anticipated character in this series. I can't wait to see the relationship that Death has with the Empress. I am strumming with anticipation when I read these lines: "I hear him so clearly; he must be close. I now have nothing to lose, no reason to live in fear of him. Watch your six, Reaper, I'm on the hunt. A rasping chuckle. - Your Death awaits.-" Other than him, I just love Matthew. He's like Nix. It feels like he's ancient but a boy at the same time. Though Evie claims to be taking care of him, I feel that it is actually Matthew who looks out for her. The scene where his mother tried to kill him just breaks my heart. He doesn't usually make sense but the things he said will click into place when the event happens. Selena is full of mystery but I don't think I like her. Finn is funny enough and his power and personality kind of fits. I can't wait to see Gabriel and also that boy with lightning. It's all in the next book. Favorite Scenes -When Evie made up her mind to burn down the house. -The car crash scene. -Then ending. That scene where Evie embraces her power and the rest of the crowd is transfixed by her. Conclusion Even though romance is probably a big part of this book, it doesn't seem like it's the center stage (to me at least). I am actually more interested in the power that each Arcana kids has and how it will all play out. The battle that is to come between the Empress and Death excites me more than the story of Jack and Evie. I would sum up this book as a starting, a prologue or the calm before a storm. I do believe that the second book will be even more exciting and better than this one. First Reaction on hearing KC writing a YA book: Lovely cover! I've read the excerpt and WOW I just can't wait! I was actually wishing for the overlapping time-line style from IAD, but this time the story is in a first person narrative (which are usually the case for YA) so let's just see how it is when the book is out :) I also had to search on YouTube for male cajun accent (sadly I'm not from that part of the globe haha) Am I wrong to base my "research" on videos of Gambit? Let me know if I'm wrong >.< http://thearcanachronicles.com/

A little backstory on this book: I had the opportunity to read The Martian as an ARC on not only one occasion, but two, and I turned it down both times. One eARC and one physical ARC, and both times I decided not to go for it. Why?! I thought the damn book was about aliens on Mars for some reason. (Spoiler: It's not). So I went along my merry way as I saw beaming review after beaming review, and eventually started to wonder if I'd missed something. Then at book club we started talking about the movie, and IRONICALLY it ends up being the book picked for August (we all throw book titles into a bag and pick at random). So, knowing I prefer to read a book before seeing the movie, and knowing we were going to discuss in book club, AND knowing everyone else seemed to love the darn book, I FINALLY picked up the book at the store and took it to the beach with me. I was so NOT disappointed!! This is probably one of the best sci-fi books I've read in a good long while, and I think most of my book club would agree with me. I truly thought the writing was great. Did you know this book was originally a self-published ebook? I certainly didn't! And now the man has been on the bestseller list and there's a movie coming out! If that's not hope for perspective/current writers, I don't know what is. But honestly, this book was written to be a movie. It would have been a travesty to NOT make a movie out of it, in my opinion. The best part, for me, was Mark Watney's character. His sarcasm and good humor kept the story light when it could have been dark and depressing. His comments on duck tape were exceptionally amusing, at least to me! I loved how he thought things through logically, and even when there were moments of "Oh shit, I'm going to die", he never gave up until he figured out a solution to the current problem. I thought all the characters were well written however, and the feminist in me especially loved the female roles. As a soil scientist, I ESPECIALLY loved when he decides he's going to create his own potato farm . I was smiling at the entire endeavor, and totally EATING UP the science behind it  HA, how'd you like THAT pun?? :)  . I think though that overall Weir makes the science easy for the reader to understand, even if they aren't science-y people themselves. This is CRUCIAL for a science fiction novel to go mainstream - if the general public can't understand it, you just aren't going to sell it. All in all, this is a FANTASTIC science fiction read that you NEED to pick up before you see the movie. I'm really hoping Matt Damon doesn't screw it up, because I struggled with picturing him as Mark while I read the book. Also, NASA had a hand in the making of this movie, so you know a lot of the science behind it is going to be THE REAL THING! Stop ignoring it like I did and go pick up the darn book already! This review was originally posted on Books Are My Thing

What there was of reflection or philosophy seemed to boil down to "people suck" and "being good at your job is important even if the consequences are horrific". I admire Scalzi for the role he plays in the publishing industry and the stances he's taken. So this was disappointing in more ways than one.

OK so I loved Red Rising, like really really enjoyed it. And I really want to say that I enjoyed Golden Son as much as I did the first book. Really I do. But right now, I'm just meh. It was a great read (seriously there isn't enough good SciFi in the world) and I am super stoked to see where this story goes and I can't wait for the next one. But I guess this book was soooo hyped to me, that it just didn't live up to expectations. Ended on a nasty cliffhanger (very well done) but the whole story seemed to have that vibe of Darrow wins and succeeds and then immediately gets beaten up and fails utterly and catastrophically that it didn't hit me as hard as it would others. I wanted to see Darrow just own his rage and anger and embrace this world that created him. But that's not the point of the narration, so I'm just left with meh. These feelings may change as time passes but oh well. Final rating: 3.5 stars.

Rounding up to a 4 because I could not bear to give a Shalvis novel a 3. It wasn't bad by any means, there are always lots of things to love about her books, but it was just missing something and I didn't connect with the romance the whole way through. There were some great parts like that first scene, loved it! But otherwise it dragged or rushed too quickly if that makes any sense. Can't believe the next one is the last, wahhhh *I received this is an ARC from Netgalley in exchange for an honest review.

This review can also be found on Written Permission This was the first book of Scalzi's that I have read. And even though I wasn't really a huge fan of Star Trek when I was younger (nor am I now, for that matter) I still enjoyed the book. I think the key is to not take it too seriously. This might be easier said than done if you are a Scalzi fan, as I understand his work can be quite deep. But aside from some existential questions, this book is all fun and spoof. Scalzi is light on the descriptive prose, which makes the book very lightweight and streamlined, but it also makes it hard to follow at times. I lost track of which person was which at times, and had to go back and remind myself. We don't really get a sense of what any of the characters look like, nor what the environment looks like. It is a little unnerving, coming from a high fantasy background where everything is descriptions and backstory heavy to something so slick and streamlined. The narrative has a great voice, and there are a lot of tongue-in-cheek moments. The humor is relatable and at no time did it feel like it was being pushed too hard. Plot-wise, I know the very last chapter upset a lot of people, but honestly I thought it was great. The thing that made me the most upset was that Scalzi never seemed to take the time to get invested in his characters or his plot. Was this a product of the subject matter? Was it because the characters were supposed to be "expendable"? I don't know. But it lessened the reading experience. And I hate that nothing was really explained in the end. Scalzi is a good writer. This is illustrated exceptionally well in the second of the three codas, which are essentially epilogues. The second coda is written in second person. It is still an awkward way of writing, but it is the least awkward second-person prose I have ever read. Bravo, Mr. Scalzi. Bottom Line: A fun and fast read that is not to be taken too seriously. Very meta, and highly recommended for the Trekkies out there. More of a 3.5 for me, not because I didn't enjoy the book, but because I am not as huge a fan of the meta as some. Rounded up because the book WAS entertaining.

What a painful little story. I didn't know if I should rate it 1 or 2 stars. I decided to go with one. Because I truly don't like reading about how people are in pain and how they have lost their purpose of life. It's depressing. I also don't like reading about "two years later" etc. It's my fear - fear of aging, losing time. But it was definitely a better book than the first one, because this one actually had a story. The first book was like an introduction and the second one was the main story. Usually the introduction is few chapters, not a whole book. "Letting go. Everyone talks about it like it's the easiest thing. Unfurl your fingers one by one until your hand is open."

I've read all the books from the series so I'm going to review three in one. Belly spend every summer at Cousins Beach with her mother, Beck and her two boys, Conrad and Jeremiah. Her mother and Beck been best of friends way back so the three teens known each other like forever. Growing up entitled changes. Belly's beauty more noticeable same with Conrad and Jeremiah looking handsome. The two boys feel something for Belly. As they're trying to understand this feeling, problems just ready too break it. In It's Not Summer Without You, Beck's sick again. All was tense but trying to feel good for the sake of Beck. We see that Belly and Conrad together but it was ruined by Conrad being a jerk. He can't deal with his feelings. Beck died. Belly and Conrad done. All was grieving their loss of someone dear to them. Belly thought they wouldn't spend summer at beach house again but Conrad's missing. Belly and Jeremiah to the rescue found him at Cousins because their dad want to sell the house. With the help of Belly's mother, the house was off the hook. Belly finally gotten the closure between her and Conrad. He went away. In We'll always have Summer, Belly and Jeremiah become a couple for two years. They decided to get married after their almost break-up because of a Jeremiah hook-up with other girl. Everybody was against it because they're too young to get married. Now, Conrad is back. Belly and her mother gotten into fight because of the wedding. Belly went to live in the Cousins Beach only to find out that Conrad's actually lived there. Things get really fast. The next thing I know, Belly and Conrad was together and married. I liked the series and I enjoyed reading it! I actually cried from a scene or two. The series was narrated from past to present or vice versa. I just wish that the ending wasn't just like poof. A girl want details, ya know.

4.5 stars! This was literally me throughout the whole book. This book is mind-blowing and as I sit here trying to write this this review I honestly don't even know where to start. So much goes down in this book and I don't want to give anything away so I'll try to be as vague as possible. This is the final book in Lily and Lo's POV and while I've been anticipating this book for so long the moment I got it on my kindle, I hesitated. I was scared and sad. It's feels like I've been with these characters for years and not just months but I honestly feel like these characters are my friends. This series started with Lily and Lo, two lost and damaged characters who just needed someone to believe in them and now they've grown up and despite the ups and downs of life, they've made it to the other side. I was so scared this book wouldn't live up to my expectations and for the first few days, I kind of took my time reading. I kept telling myself I had other things to do just to prolong reading the book. But finally I just couldn't take it any longer and I jumped into this book, and I never looked back. I wish I could write this amazing review giving you a billion reasons of why I love this series so much but I'll never be able to do it justice. If you've been an avid fan you know how Krista & Becca's writing captures your attention from the start. Every emotion, every character, you feel it all and you love it all. Like all the other books in the series, all the characters play a very important part in the books. We get plenty of time with Rose, Connor, Daisy, Ryke and even some Sam and Poppy screen time! There are so many amazing moments involving these characters: some sad, most funny as hell. And there are plenty of OMFG moments in here to tide over everyone until the next book. I'm still reeling from the stuff we learn about them and I've had hours to process it. I feel like I could go on and on but for fear of spoiling it for anyone, I will stop here. This book got me right in the feels and while I don't ever want to fully let LiLo go, I'm more then satisfied with their ending. KB Ritchie are my go-to authors and I know I'll be reading this series over and over again to try and compensate for the fact that I have to wait months for the next book. For everyone who hasn't read this series (ahem, Nicole), READ IT!!! ** On a side note I want to mention something and I'm going to be so vague you're going to want to punch me but there's a little surprise at the end of the book and at first when I read it I was 100% against it, so much so I ranted with anyone who would listen for like 2 hours about how upset I was about it. But now that I've calmed down and let my emotions settle down...I'm actually kind of excited for it. Hesitant excitement, but it's there. I trust KB and I trust that they know what they're doing. Sorry if I'm confusing everyone but you'll understand once you read the book :) 1st reread: June 13-15th, 2017, these books honestly fill me with so many feels. I love that I'm rereading these before DLU because I'm remembering little details I forgot and honestly it's just making me more excited for DLU.

"The Play's the Thing." Thespians and Shakespeare aficionados might give this several more stars than I did. But I didn't like it even as well as Equal Rites. Reading a dozen Pratchett books in a row has me pining for some romance and this was particularly unsatisfying in that regard. Tomjohn and Carrot from Guards! Guards! are basically the same character. Really, much of the plot is the same as that book (which was 3 stars instead of 2). I'm getting the impression that Pratchett just rewrote the same few stories over and over until he got them really right in the later years. Now I'm worried that reading the early ones will spoil the latter. We'll see.

Rating: 3.5 stars. WTF WAS THAT?!?! DO YOU CALL THAT AN ENDING? ARE YOU FUCKING KIDDING ME!?!?! If I rated this as soon as I finished, I would have given it 2 stars. But thinking rationally about it, it was a good book. Then ending took care of just one star. I don't know what's gonna happen with this review, I don't know what I will say, what will happen until I reach the end, how I am going to put what I want to say into words and I just don't know. I'm confused. I'm hurt. And I'm mad. I am so extremely freaking mad. I would like to pick up stones and throw them in the air with as much strength as I can afford; I would like to uproot a tree; I would like to tear apart walls and jump of a cliff and shatter the ocean. That's how much mad I am. I mean, just tell me why, why, WHY? Everywhere I went I read that this was a great ending to the trilogy, that you couldn't have asked for more and everything was going so smooth and it was moving and full of actions and most of the time my heart was pumping in my chest so loud I almost could hear it and then... Then I get to the last twenty pages and it all changes. How could I have completely changed my mind over a book only because of its last twenty pages? I didn't think I could but it is possible, it really is. I was already a bit taken aback by the beginning. Eight months have passed? What happened during those months? Is it possible that Legend and Prodigy developed in almost one month and June and Day already loved each other and then eight months pass without them seeing each other? Without speaking to each other? But then the story picked up and I completely got lost in all the military tactics and the politics and the wider world building and the bargainings and I didn't have the time to stop to think. Republic and Colonies at war; the Republic had to find the cure the Colonies were asking for, or else. Day's little brother was his country's only chance but Day could have never afforded it and a lot happens. I already knew Day was running out of time. I knew that with each day passing by, he was a step closer to his death. But somehow I felt he would have survived, I wasn't worried. Then the time of war comes. And the fall begins. Day gets shot. He goes into a coma. He wakes up. He doesn't remember June. I couldn't believe it. After all they've been through he doesn't even remember her? After telling her he loved her? But that's not the worst part. June chooses not to tell him who she really is. She knows that if she tells him, his pain will come back as well. Because Day loves June but he can't stop blaming her for his family's death, and there's no way around it, it's something that he could have never forgotten. But now he has and June can give him the happiness he deserves even if this means giving up on him forever. She'd rather sacrifice herself a hundred times than letting him remember what she did, the way he cried over his family and over his incapacity of forgiving her. I loved June because of this, what she did was so sweet and moving and I was aching for her so much. And then they meet again. Ten years later. TEN YEARS LATER? ARE YOU FUCKING KIDDING ME?!? It's too much, definitely too much! How can she have last for 10 years? Dating Anden and doing whatever military things she did? How could she? They meet again and Day starts to remember and he says we would like to meet her all over again and he says: "Hi. I'm Daniel" and she says: "Hi. I'm June". And that's it. HOW CAN THAT BE IT? I hated this ending with every fiber of my being, I couldn't believe it. I was hoping there was another epilogue to tell me what happened. I have so many unanswered questions! Did Day actually remembered everything? Was he able to forgive June in the end? Will he kiss her on the night of her 27th birthday? Will they end up together? Will they be happy however it goes? I need closure. I hate open endings. I don't want to create my personal ending. I read books to read a story, not to imagine it or I would have written it myself! I just... I don't know, I was so disappointed. This ending ruined the book completely for me and that's why I hate it so much because I was so enjoying it and now I can't even believe what's happened and that it's really ended. I wish it had all been different. I wish they had their happy ending at a younger age, if they had it at all; I wish he still was Day and not Daniel, I wish their past was still haunting somehow their present. And I felt so sad for what it could have been but it hasn't. Because this ending, told only from June's point of view, was too painful and I would have like to see what Daniel was thinking and I really wanted all this reunion as soon as he felt better and not after all those years. I wanted something better for them, they would have deserved it. Though I have to add one last thing. My heart skipped a beat when I read the chapter where Thomas tells June how and why he killed her brother. I was so sad, I was almost about to cry. But I felt like Thomas owed it to June, just like Marie Lu owed it to her readers.

I found so much of this book disturbing;  the blood draining, before and after photographs of prison dead, rape, kidnapping. . I was immersed in the world of this book and it was not a good feeling, unsettling and haunting. Yet for all of the graphic details about repressive North Korean culture, the book felt half finished, like Johnson was writing his way to a plot. The characters felt like caricatures. Despite the interesting point of view shifts in the second half, I still found myself counting pages till the end. I also wondered about the accuracy or truth of this depiction of North Korean culture. Was this book itself a propaganda piece by an American? I don't want to go so far as to say Johnson isn't authorized to write about North Korea because he's American, but how much do we really know about that experience? I want to know if the details are from interviews, diaries, or his state sanctioned trip?

As readers we go through many books, some we enjoy for the moment, some stay with us forever.We love some books so much that they are completely relatable and utterly unforgettable. And at times we come across a rarity-a book which you might not agree with on a principle level, but they reel you in, make you think and remain unforgettable! And that is something very difficult to achieve. I've been a fan of Karina Halle for years beginning with the Experiment In Terror series(Dex & Perry-love em! ).The thing that I love about Halle's writing is that she is able to take up a difficult subject matter,one you might frown upon in reality and turn it into something wholly beautiful!Something that we begin to root for..(like with her book Love, In English) In Heat Wave, we have Veronica Locke-talented chef,always-ignored-second-daughter of her mother: the mayor.Her elder sister Juliet was always the perfect one-the one her mother loved,the one people gravitated towards,the one who always left her in that shadow..But Juliet is dead and Ronnie has arrived in Kauai to work for Logan Shephard-the man who could have been her "one" and her sister's widower. Ronnie lost her job in Chicago when her relationship with the head chef turned sour and when she was accused of setting fire to the kitchen.Due to this she might never get hired in the future.Her only option is to work in Kauai and gain some experience.The island is perfect with her co-workers being superfriendly and fun-loving.Her only problem is Logan- the hotel owner and her ex-brother-in-law.He infuriates her and gets under her skin like no other.She wants to hate him, but she can't.She has always been attracted to him, from the first moment that they met. But as they begin to spend more time in close quarters, she begins to realize that all the things that she believed about him might be wrong and there is something brewing between them which has been a long time coming.But will this fragile relationship survive her mother's wrath,society's preconceived motions and the memories of the past? The book had me hooked from the first line of the prologue. "I saw him first. It shamed me to think it then, it shames me to think it now." I really emphatised with Ronnie and was kind of irritated with Logan in the beginning.But he slowly grew on me.The descriptions of Kauai, emphasis on Ronnie's character development and well-fleshed out characters were honestly wonderful.The writing was the best part about the book!It flowed seamlessly and is so effortlessly vivid! And then we come to the relationship between Logan and Ronnie.I really had no issue with the fact that he was married to her sister initially.The thing that prickled me initially was the fact that he chose Juliet despite knowing Ronnie..And I was kinda unhappy about that.But he explains the whole thing in the most honest way and I understood his reasons, the same way Ronnie did. Sometimes life happens and we end up making decisions in fear or with misguided beliefs not realising that the thing you need has been in front of you all along. "I loved her. "His words are a fist to my gut. "But I didn't like her.Does that make sense?" "Perfect sense," I whisper. "Look," he says to me, leaning in so his nose is brushing against mine. "Sometimes you love someone but you don't actually like them as a person.Like family, right?" More than just a romance, this book is also about letting go.We build up people in our heads and think them to be perfect, but mostly they aren't.We learn to forgive ourselves and them for letting us down.Life goes on. In the end, do what makes you happy.Do it for yourself alone as long as it doesn't hurt anyone else.We live such short spans that are nothing when compared to the size of this galaxy and universe.Might as well enjoy it when we can! :D

Imagine all the fairytales are true. Cinderella, Snow White, Beauty and the Beast, all true! And you had access to see them, through something as mystical as a magic mirror. Would you go for it? Of course you would! But if your pesky little brother tags along, fun turns into horror. And this realm, the pretty little princesses and happy little stories aren't as happy anymore. This book had a really good premise and idea. I loved the idea, it was gothic enough and was relatable. Sadly, it did not live up to my expectations. It was good but if you have read Inkheart, Cornelia's other novel, you will see the huge difference. Maybe the writing changed or perhaps she had a different view. I don't know but I know I didn't enjoy it as much as I could. Overall an okay read.

Yes, I'm reading Chick-lit books again. I love Chick-lit. There is always something awesome and humorous about this genre. I find a nice niche here. But... Oh, this book is going to be a mess. Let's start from the beginning. Slow. Yawn. Boring. I ask myself whether or not I should skip a few pages here and a few pages there. I'm serious. The plot doesn't move very much. Sure, it has an awesome prologue. But then! It sinks right into a bunch of monologue and moaning about how singledom sucks after dumping (or being dumped? I forgot already.) a long-term boyfriend. Honestly, I can't wait for the plot to get started, and I swear that a lot of these pages could be cut out. I do not need to hear self-pity. The humor is pretty funny at some parts, but mostly, meh. Nothing really stuck out to me, but the book does carry me away from this world to A Girl Like You's world for an hour or so. So that isn't too bad. (Just remembering that it is painfully slow in the beginning. I was already waiting for Robert and Abigail to finally kiss or something. I hate and love "will they, won't they" couples. And Robert and Abigail proves to be no exception.) Abigail dates like a man. For like... five chapters? All I remember is that she plows through the mess of men like a player. Very harsh, but she does take a good note out of Robert's book. Perhaps too good. Way too good. She is too good of a pupil, unfortunately. Somewhere along the way, she finds out who she is meant to be with. And I'm sitting here... Annoyed that she took so long to figure out and wishing I just abandoned this book at the halfway point. (I admit I don't have a lot of time to read as I used to.) Robert. He barely appears in the book. Okay, compared to a certain other man, he doesn't appear AS MUCH as him. He ticks me off, but he does have some good moments. The ending is the most redeeming part of the book. Subtle, but important and catchy. It's the only part worth rereading. Pretty hilarious. So what do I think? Overall, A Girl Like You is humorous and entertaining. It is annoyingly boring and slow and dull at the beginning, and I wish I know more about Robert. (I swear I forgotten about him halfway in the book until he reappeared.) Ending's the best part, though. Rating: Two out of Five -ofpaperandwords.blogspot.com

Although this was one of my most anticipated new releases of 2013 - I basically preordered it the moment I heard about it - I approached it with a certain trepidation. You probably know the kind: you've loved an author's previous work (in this case, for me, this was Stroud's Bartimaeus series) so very much that you're not really even sure you want to try their new work because it cannot possibly measure up. Still, it sounded excellent, so I dove in predisposed to love it. And ... there was a lot to like about it. There really was. Lucy, for starters, is a very likeable protagonist; brave, sensible, yet impulsive and not numbed by her line of (very dangerous) work of ghost-busting. Her co-leads, Lockwood and George - Lockwood clearly designed to be likeable from the start, George less so but a character you grow to appreciate nevertheless. The atmosphere - spooky. The world-building - imaginative and intriguing, this world that is so much like ours and yet not (a trait this series shares with the Bartimaeus books, although this is a rather different take on our contemporary-yet-changed world). The writing - wonderful, with some really lovely turns of phrase. So... with all that said, why the three stars? I suppose it's more like three and a half, but I asked myself whether I liked this book or really liked this book, and came away with "well, liked, not really liked". I enjoyed it; it's a lot better than many other books I've rated worth three stars. On the other hand, there's the inevitable comparison not just with any other books but with my own expectations for Stroud's work, and this book just lacked that "wow" feeling that I had with the Bartimaeus books. Not only because it didn't have a character I could instantly adore, as likeable as the cast was, but also because it just... I don't know, maybe I'm too old and jaded for this particular kind of book? I got the feeling it relied heavily on the spookiness, and while I appreciated the writing, it didn't once actually evoke any deeper feeling in me. I didn't feel the horrors, I didn't feel the fear. I just read a story. A well-written, interesting story where I wanted to know what would happen next, but I didn't get immersed in it. I also wasn't quite convinced by the pacing: the book starts off with some excitement, which is then followed by a relatively lengthy flashback / backstory sequence, and only at about halfway into the book (i.e. over 200 pages in) did I start to get the feeling that now we're getting somewhere; that now the plot was starting to creep in (in hindsight, it had been there all along, or at least in that starting bits, but it didn't feel that way when reading). There was some excitement towards the end and a relatively decent mystery, at least. All that said, I'm more than willing to give the next book(s) in this series a go - I trust that there will be more character development and less world-building history in the next books, which might help.

The first two-thirds of the book was an exercise in eye-rolling, huffing and sighing, and restraining myself from throwing the book across the room. I understand the mechanics of the chick-lit genre, but I really can't stand it when the author strains the protagonist's credibility, (and the reader's patience), by making her delusional/psychotic/pathetic and someone you just can't relate to or don't EVER WANT TO BE. The characters weren't that likeable and about a quarter of the book could have been trimmed. The last third of the book was much better when the author focused more on the mystery, moral of the story (insert more eye-rolling) and (FINALLY!) romance. I used to love these kind of "fluff" books (shoot, I own most of the Shopoholic series), but I think I've outgrown it's use and now it's time to move on.

The Dresden Files series, by and large, is fun, but lately the books had gotten a little...heavy. (There was brooding...a lot of brooding.) I had started to feel like maybe Butcher was struggling to find realistically scary foes for his super-charged wizard to deal with, and all the gloom and doom was feeling oppressive. But not Skin Game. For this book, our friendly-ish neighborhood Chicago wizard gets back to some good old-fashioned problem solving, and it's a joy and a relief. After months of isolation on the jailhouse island, Dresden is antsy for action...and he's learned a few new skills (Parkour!). But the ability to leap tall objects in a single bound isn't really enough when it comes to stealing from Hades himself while trying to avoid being killed by an arch-nemesis-turned-temporary-coworker. With the help of old friends and a bit of divine intervention, Harry is up to the challenge. This book was a nice change of pace because several characters who had been on the bench for awhile finally got to come out and stretch. I still miss some of the original old gang, but for the most part, we got to revisit a lot of characters who had been unavailable or at least busy elsewhere. Butcher clearly put a lot of thought into the effects some of Harry's actions would have on even his closest friends, and it's good to see folks with their own distinctive character arcs. (It would have been all too easy to have everyone else stay the same--is is the (Harry) Dresden Files, after all.) This book reminded me what I liked about the Dresden Files, and I'm happy to be back on the bandwagon.

3.5 stars. A cute romance with lots to love. I just had issue with how unbelievable I felt the main character's background was. Not that I felt the circumstances between the love interests meeting were any different... but when you have a main character leaving her wedding where apparently she had no family OR friends? And she had only known the groom for 4 months with basically no physical relationship? And of course by doing so left her homeless and jobless? Yeah. Too much that didn't seem believable to me. Sometimes I can't overlook the scale of believability when there is so much written for convenience to move a story along in a certain direction. Make it hard. Make the characters have to work for change. Give me heartbreak! BUT on a whole I did love Lydia and Vaughan and the sparks they set off as well as some of the secondary characters.

*Received in exchange for an honest review* *Thank you, Orion* Not only is this one of my favourite books of 2014 so far, but it's also my favourite book cover so far this year! The image above does not do it justice. The book is absolutely gorgeous. It's bright, it's colourful and it echoes the hope that's displayed in this book. I love that the dark bike and the dark silhouette of the boy on the spine contrasts with the colourful background. It echoes the subject matter in this book so well. The Apple Tart of Hope is one of those reads that I'm glad was brought to my attention by Orion Books; it's stunning, it's emotional, it's so full of hope and I absolutely fell head over heels in love with it. Meg and Oscar are such lovable characters. I just wanted to bundle them up and hold them tight. They are both so adorable but so real. I love the friendship that they have; chatting to each other through their bedroom windows. There's something so sweet and so pure about their friendship. Things are turned quickly on their head when Meg has to move to New Zealand for half a year, and that is where The Apple Tart of Hope starts to get really interesting. As readers we get an insight into Oscar's school life without Meg, and Meg's life without Oscar. Things take a turn for the worst and this is where we end up at the beginning of the novel. Oscar is missing, presumably dead, and this novel shows the journey of Meg and Oscar's brother Stevie as they try to uncover the mystery of Oscar's disappearance. If I could I'd make everyone I know read this book. I fell in love with it from the first page to the last. I couldn't get enough and I wasn't ready to say bye to these characters. The world building is brilliant and the character development is perfect. I felt like I knew them and I found myself hoping for that happily ever after - get reading to find out if I got it! Oscar is such an unusual and rare breed of person; I loved him immediately, quirks and everything. Meg is the perfect partner in crime. Their personalities shone through the pages and it'll definitely be one of those books that I'll keep going back to. A brilliant read!

This book is indie published and, unfortunately, it shows. The cover is bad enough, but the editing... ouch. That said, the story was at least interesting and the setting has enough depth to be engaging. I'm a little conflicted about the main character. So much in UF depends on a strong viewpoint character and I don't so much mean physically (which is good because Harri isn't very tough). She's no wimp or anything, but physical confrontation really isn't her cuppa. But I'm torn because while she's brave and tenacious, her motivations seemed a touch opaque at times and once or twice I wondered why the heck she would bother with actions so muzzy-headed. Particularly at the end when she actually went alone to speak with Lyle just because he held her father and brother hostage. Personally, I'd have been fine if she just sent the police in and let them duke it out. It wasn't like her father hadn't more or less hired people to kill her already. They had made it perfectly clear that they wanted nothing to do with her so I didn't see why she'd put herself in that position. Personally, when someone wants to see me dead, I'm just as happy that they self-destruct before completing the task. My connection to the book wasn't helped by the little we discovered about her newly-arrived-on-the-scene ex, Kaij. Normally, I'd be pulling for some kind of reconcile there as he was hot as all get-out (and nobody else in the novel came close to possibly compatible with Harri). But what little we learn of the past really does put him beyond the pale, to me. I'm kind of glad that Arthur didn't try to sell him as a romantic possibility. The man who would do what he did in the past is not relationship material period, end of story. Not that there's no redemption possible, but he'd have to be proving how he was no longer that man (people can change in ten years, but that'd be something of a fundamental remake, really). All of which is random musing as he doesn't appear to have anything of the kind on his mind. Which is also part of the problem--the book had no viable relationship possibilities for Harri, making her a little one-dimensional (all work and no play). Add that Harri is something of a doormat with her neighbors and I found it hard to warm to her. The book ends up as a low three stars--particularly with how really bad the editing was. Seriously, if that kind of thing bothers you at all give this book a miss. Still, the setting and story were solid enough that I might pick up a sequel when it comes out (but only if I hear good things about it).
This was my first Sandra Brown, and I loved it. The suspense was palpable, and it kept me guessing until the end. Delicious!

3.5 stars. I was really excited to read this one. After introducing Ghost in the first book, he intrigued me. I was like, this is my type of man. Broody, mysterious and an all around bad boy. But as much as I like Ghost, some of the things he did just didn't sit well with me. The wanting to see his cum come out of Nat's vajayjay is NOT HOT. The choking part. A big NO NO for me! He did it to prove a point but still. NO! The sleeping around part bothered me too. He kind of reminds me of Knight and Hawk from Kristen Ashley's book. Both are douchebags btw. Sigh. Can't wait for Max's story and Trick's though!

A nice, quick read. This book is both a story about survival in the wild and a story about a girl dealing with bullying and lies told about her. The two parts of the story are really nicely combined and I really liked the main character. I feel like she was very realistic. Even though it was a little frustrating that she didn't stand up for herself and told someone the truth about what happened, it did feel like something that would happen in real life. Especially because the guy spreading the lies was very well liked and popular and she wasn't. While they're lost in the woods, Hallie, Jonah and Rachel help each other survive and they all grow closer in the meantime. Hallie and Jonah have a complicated past, and Rachel doesn't know either of them very well. The way they interact and the way their relationship grows is very nicely written. All three of them struggle to survive but they all help each other in their own way. The romance didn't need to be there for me personally, but it wasn't a huge part of the story and didn't take over the general plot. My one complaint is that the ending was a little bit sudden. I would have liked to see a little more about  the time after they've been rescued.
A really good read. I'd been putting of reading this series for ages, I dont know why. But I'm glad I finally decided to bite the bullet and pick the first book up. Onto number 2!

Jack and Pearl were not there most of the time, I missed them. The ending was unexpected. And Jack didn't even ask Pearl before he started performing the ancient wedding ritual and it did not sit well with me that they went to find the prodigies and upon their return they are together! Horrorstor is a parody-humor-horror novel about the hell that is working in retail. Designed like an Ikea catalogue, but for the fictional Ikea-knockoff Orsk, the physicality of the book really adds to the depth of satire and emulsion for the reader. The chapters each begin with a faux-Swedish but cleverly-named piece of furniture, complete with description meant to entice the buyer. After this description of a chair, I almost wanted one myself: Introduce your home self to your work self with the adjustable rolling HUGGA. Let the creativity you feel when you're at your most comfortable transform your workspace into a smartspace. The concept is simple: someone has been vandalizing the store after hours, so a group of employees (partners) stay overnight to investigate. After a series of weird events, what they find out is the store was built on an old alternative-methods prison that "comes alive" at night, the warden of which starts inflicting his punishments on the partners as they struggle to escape. The store gets inside their head, confuses them, twists them around, and tries to convince them to stay. I worked in retail on and off for almost a decade. My first job was a cashier at Kroger (where I was forced to stand behind the self check-out kiosk for hours on end, listening to the same computerized voice tell customers to "please place item in the bag"), then at Target, where I switched over the floor after a year. Next was an amusement park, where I worked in, you guessed, it: merchandise! Then came the college bookstore, etc... and this book's extended metaphor of "retail is hell and won't let you leave" is pretty accurate. Literally. (SPOILERS) Two of the characters are sucked into the walls (sort of) and cannot leave. Even the characters who escape, return, night after night (to try and free their lost colleagues/friends). As much as you try to escape working in retail (or even, hell, SHOPPING those giant stores), you can never, ever escape. Even now, I have a full time career as a teacher, with plenty of hobbies, and I've contemplated returning to work retail part-time for extra money. Then I remember that I was one of the lucky ones that got out, and the thought of returning chokes me. The parody and satire elements were spot on, though, and I really enjoyed the furniture descriptions that soon mutated into torture devices, still with appealing taglines and selling phrases. If this is a metaphor for the fact that putting together your own furniture from those massive retailers IS torture, then it is spot on, and I appreciate it so much. While parts of Horrorstor are gruesome, it wasn't as scary as I thought it would be/would have liked. I don't even like scary things, but I felt the ghost story side of things was a bit weak. I would've liked something a bit more creative, but I enjoyed it nonetheless.

Let me first of, start with saying that I am an ardent fan of the Gentleman Bastard books. My expectations were sky high for this book- I mean come on, after reading the previous book Red Seas Under Red Skies, which was very awesome, and ended with that major cliffhanger, I all but pounced on this book. My thoughts... Well, I did enjoy this book, but not as much as the other two. We finally get to see the fabled Sabetha here. Most of this book revolved around Locke/Sabetha/Jean in both the present and the past interludes. SPOILER ALERT! THIS REVIEW MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS FOR THE BOOKS TILL DATE This book starts where the previous book left off. Locke's poisoning so much worse. Locke and Jean sell their ship, and hole up in a hotel. With Locke's symptom getting worse every day, and all the physikers Jean tries to get to help Locke being unable to do anything to find cure, they are forced to accede to the the only possible solution- a highly powerful Bondsmagi offers to heal Locke. In exchange all she asks is that they represent her faction, the "Deep Roots" to win the coming Five Year Election. Seems simple, right? Well, the only problem- whom do you think the opposing faction has chosen to help them? Ya, you guessed it right. Sabetha And there is one more condition- they must not try to contact each other in any way other professionally acceptable- ya right, like that can ever happen. While this is supposed to be the main plot, it lacked certain... depth to it. I mean, the Magi's political ideas , and the whole point of it seemed like a farce. The whole thing about using Locke's feeling for her to fool him and send him packing in a ship... Not good, Sabetha. Not nice at all. But what was infuriating was that, Locke could finally accept what she did as.. necessary? Really???? The past interludes were synonymous to the story, and were a whole different plot in themselves. We get to spend some time with the Sanzas again. This interlude basically shows us more about Locke and Sabetha. Sabetha. Well, I did not like her at all.She is totally selfish, infuriating, jealous, and thinks she should be on top of everything. If she loses, she throws a tantrum, and mostly it is Locke who gets the end result of it. She is a perfect match for Locke in many ways though. She is strong, and likes to take decisions on her own, and not be pushed around. Her character was fun in many places, though I can't say she is the best of characters. Locke. Well, Locke is wonderful as ever. Except when he is around Sabetha, he becomes a spluttering, sputtering ninny. But otherwise, he is still great. I really can't see why he is so fixated in Sabetha. But, may be the next books will make that clear. Jean. Well, Jean has definitely grown on me since the first book. He is totally responsible, reliable, and a dependable friend to have around. He is there to lend a supporting hand to Locke when he needs it, to take care of Locke, when Locke himself is unable to do so, and to bring him to his senses when Locke strongly needs it. An excellent character indeed. I could certainly have done with a little less cussing. Almost every two pages, there is some crude swearing. But, hey, what else can we expect when we have the Sanza twins in our midst. And, man, these Magi are seriously twisted. You'll see what I mean when you come to the end of this book. All together, while I did not love it as much as the previous books, this book was enjoyable just the same. I just hope the next book The Thorn of Emberlain gets better than this. This book was provided by the courtesy of the publishers, through Net Galley in exchange for an honest review.

This Immortal is an unlikely hero tale with a SF premise. The premise, which is discovered gradually throughout the book, is interesting but the plot, characters, and especially the action all seem a little too silly without being funny. I don't care for action sequences when survival depends on a rescue appearing suddenly. This book is laced with Greek mythology and themes. Zelazny is ambitiously creative synthesizing mythology with SF but it doesn't work logically. Fortellings from dreams and beasts appearing on cue to do battle fulfilling a prophecy providing a ridiculous action sequence just doesn't lend itself well to believability. The holes in logic revovling around assassination attempts are troubling. For example, Hassan was about to kill Myshtigo with a shotgon. Conrad stops him then challenges Hassan to a duel. Then Conrad decides to go practice for the upcoming duel leaving Hassan with Myshtigo in camp. Now Hassan should be unopposed to assassinate Myshtigo. Indeed, Hassan is Myshtigo's body guard and has had countless opportunities to kill Myshtigo outright or discreetly but only makes an attempt when Conrad is involved. This is the first book I've read by Zelazny. I'll try something else of his if it doesn't look like it's another hero-adventurer with a flimsy plot tale.

First off, this book managed to keep me interested at every turn. A lot happened, but not too many that they blurred together. The blackout memories were really interesting, and I think that Dr. Kells being evil  was something I never could have seen coming. Talk about a good plot twist, man. Secondly, I really liked the scene where  Jamie, Noah, and Mara were breaking into Dr. Kells' office. My favorite line being, "teenagers are suppose to be sarcastic"  . I feel like mental illnesses aren't often discussed in most YA novels, so I found this to be very interesting. And lastly: the reason this book messed with my mind was mostly due to the unreliable narration. I wanted to believe 100% in Mara, but you just really couldn't all the time. I was suspicious of everything, and this made me feel a bit insane. However, characters like Daniel kept me steady while I read. I don't think anyone who reads this book will be disappointed. I know that I certainly can't wait until the last one comes out!

The stakes are definitely up and more and more people seem to be at risk. I can't wait to read the next installment and see where it leads Charley. 3.5 stars This was Heidi's pick for one of our Hidden Gem buddy reads in one of my goodreads groups. Honestly, I never would have picked this book up on my own, let alone finished it. The main character Marnie is nothing short of a special snowflake. She can do everything she sets her mind to and fails at nothing. Not only that, but the plot of the story was made just for her. I found this quite annoying, and normally would have marked this as a DNF, but I pressed on. I'm really glad I did. Raver is deaf, but since no one knows that, he is treated as insane, maybe even possessed by the devil himself. When Marnie comes along, she figures out that he is deaf and works to communicate with him by creating signs for them to use. This leads the townspeople to believe that she is a witch. I thought the author did a superb job of showing the misunderstandings that can come if people aren't educated about others and how difficult life is when someone is deaf. Her handling of a witch hunt was spot-on and again showed the prejudices people can have when we rely on our pre-conceived notions. The second half of the book was considerably stronger than the first. Although I still had some issues with it--mainly I didn't like the fact that Marnie married Raver (Raven). She made such a big deal about not wanting to get married and then magically the next day she is saying vows to Raver. Not only that, but she mothered him so much, so it didn't seem like it would be an equal marriage. All-in-all though, despite the issues, I applaud the author for tackling such hard topics and bringing real-life issues to a fiction book.

** spoiler alert ** The book is told in alternating chapters - Sarah Starzynski, her parents and younger brother in Paris and environs during WW 2, and Julia Jarmond Tezac, an American living in Paris in 2002. Sarah and her parents were rounded up in August 1942 by the French police on orders of the occupying Nazi regime. They were held for about a week at the velodrome stadium - without food, water, toilets, beds. They were then sent via train to a detention camp, and some time later divided. Her parents are sent directly to Auschwitz (where they will be gassed), but Sarah escapes the camp and finds refuge with an elderly farm couple. She's haunted by the fact that she left her younger brother locked in a closet - she believed she'd be back within a day or so. When she finally convinces Jules & Genevieve that she will go to Paris alone if necessary, they accompany her to her old home only to discover a new family living in the apartment, and Michel's decomposing body in the well-hidden secret cupboard. Meantime Julia Jarmond has been given an assignment to write about the Vel' d'Hiv' for the 60th anniversary commemoration. She's an American who has been in Paris for about 25 years, but has never heard of the event. She becomes obsessed with the story, and when she discovers that her husband's family moved to the apartment the day after Sarah's family "vacated" it, she doubles her efforts to find the truth. I was completely mesmerized by the story for the first 160 pages, because the chapters alternate between Julia's search for the truth, and what is happening to Sarah 60 years earlier. But after Sarah returns to the apartment we no longer hear from her. The rest of the book focuses on Julia, and frankly descends into a chick lit romance drama. I thought The True Story of Hansel and Gretel The Book Thief , and Suite Francaise were all much better books dealing with the Holocaust.

What a U-turn of a followup! What got me a bit about Book 1 is the lack of fun factor. Just way too world weary and cynical to really keep the pages turning. Book 2, though- I'm not saying the cynicism is gone, it just takes a back seat to the story. And the story is pretty cool. I have read a fair amount of fantasy, and let's be honest, you rarely read it for the surprise factor. There are so many series in recent years turning the typical genre cliches on their head, and this one targets the hero complex that is so central to this type of book. I liked how arbitrary justice was in Grossman's world. Not everything works out the way it should, and he embraces that. Another cool thing is that it did the surprise factor well. I had no idea what was coming for the entire last half of the book, from a Venetian palazzo, a trip to the underworld, which turns out to be the dullest of all possible school gyms, to a scene of the rape of Julia by a god and her subsequent immortality, to a journey to the end of the world... Was a bit bummed no Alice, though. This is still not the typical fantasy story even compared to other recent genre benders, though. If I could assign it a genre, I think I would call is psychological fantasy. It's all about being inside the head of someone who gets everything they want, in this case including supernatural abilities. Quentin, like so many of us, never appreciates what he has until it is gone. Even magic can't fix that particular road to unhappiness. There were still a few annoying things for me about the writing. You're either on board with the faux intellectualism of the whole cohort or you aren't, I guess, so I'll leave that alone. The time transitions seemed better this time (I liked the way Julia's story as a hedge witch was woven in with that of the Fillory adventures), but the new characters seemed so incompletely sketched to me. So much more could have been done with Benedict the budding mapmaker! He was an interesting character. The worst though were the Murs magicians. In the final scene I couldn't even remember who have the people were. Took a little away from the gravity of the situation. On to Book 3!

This turned out to be a rather extraordinary little book. I was expecting something lighter and frothier, but it was actually quite the serious philosophical journey, rife with good writing and some excellent quotes, and leavened with humor. I'm glad I bought my own copy--I will want to read this again.

I waited in line at my first BEA for this hardcover of Bitterblue. I was so excited to meet Kristin Cashore and to read the third book in one of my very favorite series. Yet, I didn't read it. Not until just now. The long wait for the third book turned my anticipation to levels that I knew the book couldn't possible meet, especially after the mixed reviews began to roll out. Partly, I also saved Bitterblue because I didn't want to run out of Cashore books, which turns out to be a somewhat valid concern. Still, the time finally came to give Bitterblue a try. This will be a review of Bitterblue but also somewhat about the series as a whole, which I just reread. Oddly enough, Graceling, which had been one of my favorite books for so long, the one I always thought was technically superior to Fire has ended up my least favorite of the three. Fire I think the strongest on many levels. Bitterblue falls in the middle, featuring all the things I love about Cashore's writing but also a bit messier than Fire. Bitterblue surprised me. I expected her to more greatly resemble the child she was in Graceling: hesitant, fearful, loath to trust. In the years since, however, she has grown into a kind, trusting, adventurous, and happy person. She has pain beneath the surface obviously, but there's a lightness in her spirit compared to either Katsa or Fire. The difference lies, I believe, in the fact that Bitterblue was rescued by good, reliable people and she had that decade to sort of recover. Also, she buried a lot of her pain, allowing her to carry on more easily. Of course, those things are going to be hers to face throughout the book. Bitterblue starts out rather lighthearted, with the young queen sneaking out of the castle to find out what her city is really like. She goes on adventures and meets a street rat thief named Sapphire, or Saf for short. (Cashore's great strength as an author does not lie in naming characters; the names are so ridiculous they're almost charming.) Bitterblue felt cooped up in the castle and disconnected from what life in her kingdom actually meant, so she wanted to see for herself. As one might predict, she befriends Saf and his good friends, the adorable Teddy and Saf and Teddy's sisters who are in love. She and Saf are totally shippable. I can see, though, why readers would be surprised by Bitterblue and potentially disappointed in the romance. The last book in the series fails to deliver an HEA for the main ship. Personally, I'm a fan of this because 1) these kids might work it out in time, inspired by the Dells where the king married a commoner 2) I wouldn't mind if she hooked up with Giddon instead and 3) Cashore really considers the practicalities of their relationship. Queens aren't always free to do what they wish and people don't always fall end up with their first love, so I feel like leaving it open adds a dash of realism. The plot is a bit of a mixed bag. Lots of things happened that blew my mind with their cleverness. Twists surprised me, like the fact that her advisers had been the ones actually inflicting most of the pain and that Hava was her sister . At the same time, though, I feel like the biggest mystery was really obvious. From the very beginning, I was suspicious and my suspicions proved correct. Obviously the people Leck worked closely with wouldn't be trustworthy, so I really question that Ror would have encouraged Bitterblue to keep them on as her advisers. It would have been better to start fresh. Sure, Bitterblue trusts them now because they've aided her for so long, but as a reader I was like OMG OBVIOUSLY THOSE GUYS WHO ARE SUPER FUCKED UP. Holt was the one surprise, but otherwise I didn't really believe they would have been kept as her advisers and thought it was obvious they were involved. That said, I do really like the way that Bitterblue handles the fall out. What I love most about the series as a whole is how aspirational this fantasy world is. Terrible rulers exist but good people are working to improve the world. There are powerful women working to ensure that women are treated equally. There's no double standard about sex and every culture the reader has encountered in these books is completely sex-positive. There remains some discomfort with homosexuality in certain kingdoms but that's obviously in the process of changing. Fantasy often reinforces medieval social constructs even though the worlds are fictional and don't need to be that way, so I admire Cashore so much for not doing that. I'm happy to report that I thought Bitterblue was wonderful. I adored getting to see my favorite characters from the first two books again, and I loved the new additions too. Now begins the torturous wait for more books from Kristin Cashore.

I liked it, but I didn't always buy the mythology of the Everliving. I did like the incorporation of the Greek myths. I liked Jack and while I didn't exactly like Nikki, I didn't hate her. She made some decisions I thought were dumb and I had a hard time believing how she went to Everneath. I think it might have been better if Cole outright forced her? Which he kind of did, but only after she went to him. Also I'm not sure if we're supposed to like Cole. I didn't. . Anyway, I thought this was a good paranormal YA. I'm not counting the days to the sequel, but I'll most likely read it.
Wow, this book was very depressing for most of it. Nothing happened until the end. I didn't love it.

Whilst tagging deer for a project, Milo Mitchell never expected to come across anyone in the woods. Let alone a gorgeous stranger dressed in a tuxedo... and perhaps shooting him with her dart gun by accident wasn't the best way to make a good first impression. To make things stranger - after having been shot, the well dressed stranger can't remember anything about himself - not even his name. Milo takes in the stranger and giving him a change of clothes, a new name - 'Nick' - and a place to stay till they figure out what to do next. The stranger appearance of Nick isn't the only weird thing happening in the small town of Golden. The electricity starts acting up and Nick finds himself knowing things that should be impossible to recall. Milo and Nick start a quest to find who he may have been before they met in the woods. But Milo and Nick aren't the only ones looking for answers... and things are not going to go well if they find Nick before he finds out who he is. I love the vibe of this novel. It's such a fun and quick read. Milo's a little lost in the world after he father died but she's keeping it together well. If you call hanging out in the woods tracking deer a good thing. She still manages to have a group of good friends, hobbies and a fairly healthy social life. She's responsible and I like the mixture of level-headedness mixed with romantic wonder that she has. She's brave and a great match for Nick. This book is mostly told from Milo's point of view but every now and then Ms. James switches things up and we get to see the world from Nick's perspective. It's an interesting way to show how things are not quite right for the boy - more than just some fairly extensive amnesia. Whilst I liked the look into him and his thoughts - I think I would have liked him more as a character had he been a bit more mysterious. Because we get to see him confused and vulnerable but only in short snippets - I didn't really find him a desirable male lead. He's not a bad boy nor is he the boy next door or any of those other categories that I like my leading men to fit into. He's just a little lost and for the most part a little bland. That said - I loved the action. This book is well paced with some characters that amused me and made me want to keep reading. Milo is sweet but a little damaged and I feel like Nick has potential to grow into someone who I really root for. This is a book I'd recommend for fans of Jennifer L Armentrout's Lux series and not just because of the scifi-ness they have in common. It's a well written exciting book and there is no doubt - I will definitely be reading the second book in the Here series.

Every single time I read one of Maggie Stiefvater's books, I sit there afterward and think, to myself, two things: How does she do it? She can't possible outdo that. There is just so much to love about this series as a whole - the romance (OMG, there is a KISS in this book. THAT KISS. ), the mystery, the originality. But it's the characters that really get to me - especially Ronan. He's so complex for a teenager and if you've read the last line of The Raven Boys, I know that you're dying (like I was) to read The Dream Thieves and learn more about Ronan (don't worry, because you definitely learn more about him). This series took a turn that I didn't really see coming (although I'm not entirely sure what I thought the direction would be) and I'm most interested to see how Ronan's story melds with the overall quest for Glendower (some was explained in this book but I want more!). And I'm also interested in how the other characters will factor in - and what their fates will be! More awesomeness from Jemisin. It took me a little while to get over one of the blurbs that said something to the effect that Jemisin's world has five seasons rather than four. After all, "seasons" are quite arbitrarily defined. But, as usual, the people who make the covers frequently have no idea what's actually in the book. The "fifth season" actually refers to periods of great turmoil in the planet's history, which can last anything from months to decades (or, likely, in the case of the Fifth Season of the book's title, a great deal longer--it's no spoiler to say that, as the first line of the book is "Let's start with the end of the world, why don't we? Once I got over that, all I had to deal with was a story told from three perspectives (one of them in second person--I hate second person!) in different time streams, and work out the connections between Damaya, Syenite and Essun. Strangely, I came to not even notice the second person... Damaya is a child who has just discovered she's an Orogene. Orogene's have a kind of Earth magic, and they can do anything that involves using the power of the Earth--in fact, building mountains is easier for them than many much smaller magics, as it's a matter of letting the power of fault-lines and magma streams do what they want. This, of course, makes an untrained Orogene very dangerous, and scary. So Damaya is taken away to school. Syenite is a trained (and captive) Orogene, forced to work (and breed--that's creepy without really advancing the story) on behalf of the Empire. Essun is a "wild" adult Orogene, living incognito at the time of the world-ending event that starts the book.

Taking it back home for feedings from its mom.... seems incredibly impractical lol. That part never really made sense to me. I guess I liked the whole bucking-misogynistic-tradition thing, but it might've had more impact and felt more realistic, less contrived, if she'd been more reluctant to do it at first. Instead she decides to take in a baby pretty much immediately, and there wasn't really a good plot reason for this, it should've been a much harder decision than it was. She leaves the baby alone for hours at a time! she's not feeding it in the middle of the night, as I recall! the baby never cries except when hungry pretty much! it should never have worked out as long as it did, and ultimately she gives the baby up not for these reasons but because she's afraid it'll get killed being around her while her life is this dangerous?? hmmm it just didn't make sense to me. I know I always do this, spend more time complaining than praising the books I actually really liked. But seriously I did like this one and if there's more in the series I'll read them. The romance in this one was super light but I'm quietly shipping Willinghouse  and Ang... don't ask me why I don't know. Anyways I'm hoping for more of that :P

I really, really like this series. I don't love it yet. But I'm on my way. "It is our choices, Harry, that show what we truly are, far more than our abilities. - Dumbledore, one of my favorite fictional mentors already. Time for my second informal Harry Potter review. Rowling continues Harry's quest to become the best wizard he can be at Hogwarts alongside his two best friends, Ron and Hermione. Great (though not beautiful or superbly sophisticated) writing, smart development of characters, and a clever plot with laud-worthy foreshadowing motivate me to give this second installment five stars. One aspect of the book I loved was how Rowling built Harry's numerous conflicts. There was internal conflict (which house does Harry really belong in? ), external conflict with other individuals (darn the Malfoy family and all of Slytherin) and external conflict with society (everyone suspecting Harry of being the heir of Slytherin). When all of these clashes are resolved by the end of the book it brings a strong feeling of satisfaction to those who empathize with Harry, the underdog from the start. Not to mention that I saw none of the plot twists coming - that shows how even adults can attain entertainment from this series, even if they have more foresight than I do. The quote I included above also exemplifies this book's appeal to all readers; it's a crosscutting theme amongst all ages that our actions make us who we are, not just what we're given by biology or God or whatever you believe in. Everyone tells me that these books get more and more enthralling as they progress. If so, Harry Potter may become one of my favorite series of all time. Better late than never, right?

I received a copy of this book via the publisher in exchange for an honest review. This does not affect my opinion in anyway nor does it change the outcome of my review. What an enchanting book this was! From the very first page, I was enthralled by the words and I never wanted to put it down, even for things like food and sleep. Dolamore has created the perfect mixture of whimsy and horror to make the perfect read. The book is set in a world much like our own was in 1930's -- except it is a world with magic. And zombies. I will say the two paired nicely together and reminded me of Cassandra Clare's Infernal Devices (which it is billed to be like). However, unlike ID, there are no Shadowhunters to save the city. The world was very dark and I kind of felt this fog-like quality hung over the story. It was definitely set the tone for what was to come. The world is actually meant to be post WW1 Germany, in an alternate universe. I think that is important knowledge going into the story -- we are seeing life post a war, trying to recover and reacclimate from ration lines and poverty. And in this world magic has been outlawed. I loved the idea of the bound-magic. The idea that you could choose not only to marry your spouse, but know where they are is such a romantic idea. Thea was a great, strong female lead. I normally dislike reading books from multiple POV's (I don't put books down when they are, I just don't like it because if not done well it is confusing), but this one was well done. I never got confused about who we were following and having it in third person kept it from being a confusing flit from one 'voice' to another. Even though it felt like Thea was our 'main' character in the beginning, Freddy and Nan's plots were both just as fascinating and center stage. I liked that they didn't seem like secondary characters, whose POVs were just thrown in to show parts of the story Thea couldn't tell. They were integral to the story. The romances in this book was light, and I liked that, because it gives room to build as the series continues. Plus, there was a lot of other things going on, so keeping the romance on the back burner to give way to the action was quite alright in my book. The mystery of the plot was what really kept driving me forward. I just had to know what happened to Nan and where she was. I had to know why Thea's mom was sure her father was alive when it seemed like he was dead. I can't wait to know more about this world and its magic. It's utterly addictive, this world Dolamore created. The end was rather neat, so I am curious to see where the author will go next. I hope to learn more about how this 'world' came to be, and some of the history that goes along with it. Overall, I found myself utterly charmed by this story. I didn't want it to end and I already can't wait to see where things go next. For this review and more, visit Such a Novel Idea.
