I didn't like this book as much as I thought I would. Mostly, as a member of a world that is post- third wave feminism, free-love, and putting the man on the moon, this book is an interesting historical read. Heinlein preaches free-love and the idea that every religion is right (Thou art God, you grok?) --which must have been incredibly incendiary when it was published. Otherwise, the preachyness was, well, a little too preachy for me. Don't get me wrong; Heinlein has some great things to say and some very interesting ideas, but many of them are old hat. The idea of couple sharing is quite prevalent today. The characters are lovable and compelling however and, even if the preaching gets boring, you still want to know what happens to the Man from Mars and his water brothers. The thing that annoyed me the most is that he spends the entire book explaining why some people need ideas wrapped in religion so that they can accept them then, at the end, he insults our intelligence by doing the same thing---wrapping his liberal (for the 60s!) ideas in a Judeo-Christian trope. Suddenly, we realize that Mike is actually the Archangel Michael and he was sent to Earth to deliver the Godly message of free-love and telekinesis. Snark.

This is Beautiful continues right where This is Dangerous left off. Throughout the book we see how Kayla and everyone in her life deals with the fallout of what happens to her. Without saying too much, this book was my favourite out of the series. If I was being forced to pick my one favourite thing that happens in This is Beautiful, I would pick the role reversal that happens. In This is Dangerous, and in some of the other books in the series, we see Kayla doing the chasing of Logan. Kayla tries her hardest to get him to see that they would be good together and tries to get him to lower his walls a bit. In This is Beautiful, we see Logan doing the chasing... not in a creepy, stalker way! I promise. Another thing I also loved was how supportive everyone was. We know the gang is close, but seeing them deal with the devastating situation head-on and as a group makes my heart melt. I can't believe we have reached the end of this series! It was an OK book. The thing about Quirk books is that they rock the presentation but that means that sometimes the content is not it-blew-my-mind awesome. If you are an habitual of Tumblr, have been fangirl for the past few years and are familiar with major fandoms like Star Wars, Harry Potter and Supernatural, there is nothing new for you here. For me, particularly, the bit about cons was the most useful one, since I intend to attend my first con next year (if the gods agree with my plan). But I think that's about it. Is not that this was a bad book, because it is not: the art is fantastic, there are little interviews, and the tone is fun and...well, quirky. I was just simply expecting something else. Also, the book is TINY! I mean, I was expecting a full-sized book, or at least paperback size, but this is really tiny. And I definitely didn't liked that.
This was just ok. It wasn't bad, and the idea was interesting, but it didn't really blow me away. Definitely my least favorite by this author by a large margin.

It's hard to say when my relationship to this novel began. But let's begin with the list. My most recent goodreads project (I always have a project), has been tagging all the books from Bookslut's 100 Best Books of the 20th century. I don't remember how it started -- perhaps a question on Facebook from Bloomsbury Review about how often one read current books versus classics. And now here I am, butting heads agains the Bookslut 100 yet again (Why, oh why, did we ever decide to include plays?). But why did I fixate on this novel in particular? Perhaps it was Michael Schaub's enthusiastic review, it was also partly a residual effect from all those hours I spent pouring over the Eighth Day Books catalog in my early twenties. Whatever the reasons, they were strong enough to send me on a very directed mission to the bookstore in a torrential downpour. This book did not disappoint. It's one of those books that I have a hard time writing about intelligently. It's just too good. From the very first page I had that sensation of trust that comes from relaxing into a book that has been written by a master of the form. As the narrator, who is also a novelist, sets up the story, it is obvious both that Greene understands people and understands novels. But of course, if he didn't, he wouldn't have the reputation that he does, no would his works appear on so many lists of modern classics. So, of course I don't aim to add to the scholarly discourse on this novel. My personal response: it was certainly interesting to read this story of religious conversion (and how religious love is entwined with romantic love) in the midst of my current estrangement from religion. Indeed, any moments of distance from this book I had were the result of trying to insert my current experience into the book to argue, which of course didn't work. Despite that small dissonance, I was still blown away by this novel. I want to go to Eighth Day books and buy Greene's complete works. Except I'm not allowed to buy any more books until 2014. Drat.

I was surprised when I know there's gonna be another book in this series. I thought the second one was the last one. Well, this one is better than the second one. All I remember from the second book is sex, sex...and more sex. So I'm glad this book focused a little more than just sex. Cassie and Jack finally got married, and Jack's attitude when he broke his hand was a shock. Thank god, his Grandma "slap" some senses into him, and told him that baseball is not everything. I guess, in the end everything ended well....ok...maybe a tad bit surprise at the end when the epilogue is actually Chance's (*their son's*) POV.

Can't say that I'm surprised, but I'm still surprised that this happened again. Lauren DeStefano creates great stories that immediately pulls you in, but this is the second time she's written a subpar second book despite the fact that the first one was so good. In Burning Kingdoms, Morgan and her band of merry men and women have escaped their magical island in the sky and landed on the ground. Before they have a chance to do anything noteworthy, they're immediately whisked away to a hotel. The hotel is owned by the King's Advisor and he lives there along with his...six? I want to say six kids. Everyone stays in the hotel and sometimes, when the girls are feeling rebellious, they sneak out and visit the city and or they just go out and drink alcohol. And that's pretty much what happens for the first two thirds of the book. Apparently there's a war on the ground over precious metals that when melted down can be used as fuel, but it's pretty much irrelevant until near the end. Burning Kingdom is a fast read, but all of the things I loved in Perfect Ruin are ruined here. The story was severely lacking. So much so that you start to find holes with this world. I mean, how is it possible that an entire island is just floating in the sky near the stratosphere and how was everyone able to adjust to the different gravitational level that the ground has compared to the island? How are they able to hand the different air pressure? On Internment, the citizens ate mostly vegetarian dishes but on the ground it's meat and meat and more meat. How are their stomachs able to handle such a change in diet? They also came during the winter and seemed to enjoy the snow and stuff, which is great. As a Canadian, I love snow too. But you know who hates it, my African parents and aunts and uncles and grandparents and cousins...basically most Africans who grew up in Africa. Despite living in this climate for years still can't get use to the cold. Even though they mentioned that they felt the cold straight to their bones, they didn't really show much I had way too many questions about the island and the world below it, but that's only because nothing happened in the plot. It isn't until the final third portion of the novel when the war starts to rear its ugly head. Unfortunately, I didn't really care. As for the characters, Pen's depression from being away from home was written well, but after awhile it seemed like every bad thing that could happen to her did. Morgan's relationship with Alice and Lex were a joy to read in the first novel, but here...well Alice and Lex are hardly around. The only time they make a proper appearance is so Morgan can get incredibly angry at Lex and say that she hates him. Which is fine, but her anger seemed hypocritical considering the amount of secrets that she's been harbouring from everyone. Even when she was having trouble, she would still go to him for some sort of advice and yet she doesn't do anything here. She hardly does anything, but everyone keeps lamenting about how great and wonderful she is. As for Thomas and Basil, they hardly make an impression in this book. Thomas worries after Pen, to the point where you wonder why he even likes her when she's constantly pushing him away and acting like he's not there. It does make some sense after her history with her father is revealed and we do see her soften around him when no one else is looking, but still...that poor guy is being lead around by the neck and no one seems to care. I liked Basil in the Perfect Ruin. He was a great boyfriend to Morgan who was supportive, sweet, and patient with her. And for the most part, he's still like that, but he's hardly in the novel and the only times he shows up is to say how wonderful Morgan is. There's nothing else to his character. It bored me. Judas also bored me, because he only showed up to make Morgan question her feelings for Basil. Unfortunately, he too hardly showed up in the novel so this whole love triangle was fairly pointless. Celeste was still amazing though. I liked how we got to see more from her and learn that she's actually pretty decent, despite the whole kidnapping thing. Despite her sheltered upbringing, she's seems like the most stable one out of everyone and keeps pushing forward hoping for the best. And Morgan...*sigh* Like I said before, I shouldn't be surprised because this is pretty much the same thing that happened in The Chemical Garden series. Wither was amazing, but Fever was a disappointment. Sever was just okay, so hopefully the last and final book in the Perfect Ruin series, Broken Crowns, doesn't follow suit and ends up being amazing.

This was the 5th Ann Patchett novel I've read, but the 2nd of those chronologically. It was...interesting. Within the first 50 pages or so, you know quite a few things about Sabine: *She's lived in Los Angeles most of her life. *She could have been an architect, but instead she makes architectural models. *She's been a magician's assistant for over 20 years. *She was in love with Parsifal, the gay magician (who was also quite wealthy from his successful rug stores). *Parsifal and his even more wealthy partner had AIDS. His partner died first, then Parsifal married Sabine so that she would inherit all his stuff. Then he suddenly died, actually not from AIDS-related complications at all. *Parsifal claimed that he was from the east coast and that his family was all killed in a car accident when he was in college. *Parsifal was actually named Guy, was from Nebraska, and his mother and two sisters are very much alive...and want to meet Sabine. that's not really a spoiler. So, boom. Where does Ms. Patchett go from there? There are still several secrets to be revealed, lots of family drama, and...there's Nebraska. And this is not Rainbow Rowell's quirky, but kind of hip Nebraska. This is small town, white bread, 1990s Nebraska, as seen from the point of view of an author and a main character who have spent their lives in LA. I'm not saying there's not some truth in the portrayal, but it sometimes feels condescending. Even without the "dreams" in which a ghost speaks to Sabine (sometimes foreshadowing things she doesn't even know yet), this book is odd. It kept me guessing, and the characters were intriguing, but the ending was too open for my taste. Will Sabine actually start living her own life? Is she going to hook up with Parsifal's look-alike sister?

Very good. It seemed like GGK's prose style has changed a little since River of Stars, or my memory of it has faded a little bit. While he still had a beautiful turn of phrase in many places, and characters that mused upon their place in an ongoing story, there were many fewer sentences that I would've been able to pick out as his after reading them in isolation. The story held my attention, with quite a lot of action and many sympathetic and interesting characters. I really enjoyed the setting and the politics of the area. I was on the verge of giving the book a five star rating until the end that I was dreading came about. Long-time readers will know what I'm talking about: the inevitable happy ending where everyone is paired (or tripled) up. Still, a must-read for GGK fans, and I'd recommend to almost anyone.

On her fifth wedding anniversary, beautiful, talented, amazing, perfect Amy Dunne is taken from her home. All signs point to foul play and it seems like Amy's husband Nick is behind it. Because this is a Gilian Flynn novel, all is not what it seems. It's much, much worse. Actually, as far as Gillian Flynn novels go, this is the most tame and most accessible of all her works. I'm not surprised that this is the one that took off in a major way and is getting the A-list actor treatment in the movie. Not that things don't get dark here, but they're not stomach-churningly, trigger warning dark. The first section of the book was very tense and stressful to me, when the cat and mouse game was in early stages and I was left wondering who was telling the truth and who was the liar or if both narrators weren't to be trusted at all. But I had guessed most of the major plot twists early on, so the second and third sections weren't as tense for me. The story did keep my interest, mostly because I was interested in seeing how deep the hole that Amy created actually was. What I really like about Flynn's works is her ability to show the dark side of women without making them a stereotypical bitch or a manipulative femme fatale. All of Flynn's women are bursting with power. They're conniving, they're dastardly, in many cases they're borderline evil... but they're also the smartest people in the room and they are filled with their own agency. Amy hoodwinks the world and even the people who know they've been hoodwinked have no way to escape her traps. I have a feeling, as the plot progresses, that I'm supposed to find Nick more and more sympathetic and likable, but I just didn't feel much for him. He uses women when they're convenient - his mother, his twin sister, his wife and his mistress - and is enraged when they act against what feels to be their proper behavior. He doesn't deserve to go to prison, but I also never rooted for him as the hero of the story.

*~~*ARC kindly provided by the author to me in exchange for an honest review *~~* I've read Leo loves Aries by the author and was flashed and with True Colors it wasn't different. What's different is the theme, the tempo as well as the topic. Where Leo loves Aries is sweet, slowburning this book is a story where former friends become "enemies" (it has a reason I write it in quotation marks). I really was captured by the way how the story was displayed. We get right into the story, right from the start you understand that something terrible happened to Marco. You understand for a short time not the grief of Marco, you have too many details left out but you are aware of other things and so - piece by piece - you get the whole picture. It realy hit you hard, to be honest, because it is - at least for me - understandable why Marco is rejecting Oscar. The tension is still there, Oscar is trying to connect with his old friend, but Marco has a lot - maybe too much - on his shoulders. I really loved how we got the insight of Marco, we see as a reader how he suffers, how he is torn. And the ending is so sweet you are so happy. It is hard to go the path with Marco but when other things are settled there is the other side displayed, too, the side by Oscar. I can only give this book also 5 out of 5 stars for its slow burning, former friends turn to enemies and reunited later story. Review originally posted on my blog with added content Mikku-chan / A world full of words

'The Fifth Season' is a unique and fabulous read! Unfortunately, it also left a lot of questions unanswered by the last page. Apparently the next installment in 'The Broken Earth' series will be published later this year (2016). Grrrrr. However, many of the important mysteries raised are explained so I am not completely frustrated. I do not normally read trilogies before they are finished, but I also do not like reading too much information about a book before I read it. Unfortunately, this policy of self-imposed ignorance means I occasionally pick up part one of an unfinished trilogy. This is a literary (although the author N. K. Jemisin used popular YA idioms and made-up words instead of $5 English Great Literature words) science-fiction novel placed on an unknown planet with a variety of humanoids and non-human races possessing various talents and technology. I read a lot, gentle reader, but never have I ever come across such talents as these characters possess! However, as usual in YA plots, and often in real life, those who are extremely talented and amazing are ostracized, dehumanized, enslaved and abused by a crowd of boringly mundane, ordinary, uneducated and no-talent 'normals' in this novel. Plain untalented plodding thick-headed ignorant normals sometimes think themselves better on moral grounds since they literally have nothing else with which to feel good about themselves. Lesson should be well-learned, by now, right? The continent called Stillness by the current civilization, the Sanzed Equatorial Affiliation, under the rule of Emperor Verishe Leadership Yumenes, has seen countless civilizations rise and fall; in fact so many different cultures and civilizations have risen and fallen that when mines are dug out the miners often find the detritus of dozens of ancient cities and peoples long forgotten or unknown. The soil is depleted, dry and worn out, as are the surviving remnants of previous civilizations, with pockets of greenery and forest maintained for wealthier classes. The current civilizations recognize five Seasons, and they are now in the fourth Season. The entire planet's various 'nationalities' of Antarctics, Equatorial, Eastern and Western Coastals, among other 'nations' with different ethno-racial characteristics, are expecting the onset of the Fifth Season - a season marked by complete destruction caused by cyclical geological disturbances. Earthquakes and volcanic eruptions which frequently rock entire regions usually become world-wide in the Fifth Season, devastating whatever civilizations have managed to gain a foothold, although current cities are hoarding and storing food in preparation. In the distant past, it is rumored cannibalism was prevalent in some villages and cities. The book opens on the raw grief of Essun, mother of Uche. Her husband, Jija, beat Uche to death. Why? Well, all I want to say is it is for an amazing reason. Next, we meet Damaya Strongback who is eight years old. She is being sold to Schaffa Guardian Warrant because she almost killed a boy at school with her talent of Orogeny. Her talent was previously undiscovered and she is now quite thoroughly despised by the ordinary villagers. She is lucky her parents, who now hate her guts, contacted the Fulcrum, to take her away for training. Many children who are discovered to be an oregene are immediately murdered. The problem with this ability is it makes earthquakes happen. By the time Book One is done, gentle reader, we have become knowledgeable about the cultures and beliefs of Stillness. Remarkably, the same ills which mar our own Earth civilizations also poison Stillness - lack of education, the substitution of mythology for science, social divisions based on class and ethnicity, tribal hatreds, politically-driven social divisions which are created intentionally to divide and demean potential rivals, withholding wonderful technologies from nearby 'comms' (communities) and having revised truncated histories about the past taught to schoolchildren in order to maintain power and groupthink cohesiveness. However, YA reader, and others, if your mouth is making that ewwww sound right now, stop it. These deep philosophical and sociological and political subjects are served up under a large dollop of the sweet sugar of an intelligent YA science fiction story. If you loved Ender's Game and the rest of the Ender series, this book will please you. Even better, the author Jemisin is, I think, liberal, so we get all kinds of sexual permutations common to humanity included in a quite matter-of-fact manner. (Frankly, gentle reader, I love this casual recognition and acceptance of sexuality variety.) The only thing which may delay comprehension and satisfaction in the book is a bewildering timeline. Hang in there, gentle reader! The reward of perseverance is an introduction to a tremendous and exciting new story about unusual characters and world-building that is certainly beyond anything I have ever read in science fiction!

While this is a time travel novel, it's not what I would call science fiction. It's a moving portrayal of a modern black woman thrown back in time to her white ancestor's plantation, where she's forced to save his life again and again to save her own family. Quite an accomplishment by Octavia E. Butler. The horrors of slavery come alive through believable, conflicted characters who are oppressed by evil. Highly recommended.

Last night I finished reading Eleanor & Park which means I now have read all of Rainbow Rowell's books until Landline will be released this summer. If you follow me on Twitter, you may have seen me tweet about my ambiguous feelings about this book. Yes, I'm not head over heels with this one but let me explain. In the beginning, everything was great. I had all the sympathy for Eleanor and liked the style of the book. Let's face it, Rainbow Rowell knows how to write; how to string words together into sentences that go down your brain ways like maple syrup but a book can't live on just that. It was a neat concept of having Eleanor and Parks points of view shift every so often and I really liked Park's character but after a while, that just wasn't enough for me anymore. The subject of growing up with negligent parents and domestic abuse is a heavy subject and I salute the author for writing about it but there was just something missing for me, towards the middle, I got quite annoyed with Eleanor and wanted to yell at her to USE YOUR WORDS! with Park because her keeping all of everything bottled up inside her was exhausting. I understand that Eleanor thinks she can't share it, and doesn't want to burden anyone else with it because she is not used to having people in her life she can rely on. I get it. I really, truly do but there was some plot development missing for me here. There are a LOT of words but plot wise, the story isn't big. By the end of it, I had more feelings for Park than for Eleanor which seems messed up to me. In my opinion, Rowell spent a little too much time on Eleanor and her problems. We don't get anywhere with Park and his issues with his father that are talked about but never really broached. It's all Eleanor all the time. Like I said above, I do have all kinds of sympathy and empathy for her. My childhood may not have been as bad as hers but my first memory is of my father hitting my mother repeatedly against the wall in his office. He used enough force to crack the plastering, like, really crack it. I must have been 4 or maybe 5 years old when I saw it. Most of the other stuff he did I never saw but my Grandma hints at some of it every now and then. Thankfully, I never lived in fear of getting hurt myself. I don't want to diminish Eleanor's struggles but there could have been a bit more going on because 300+ pages was too much and I lost interest in all of the middle of the book. I can't decide if Eleanor is meant to be so irritating or if she just feels like it to me or if it's meant as a character trait of hers. It makes me angry how little she shared with Park, always making him feel left out. He never got the full picture of her life until the very end and even then she doesn't even write, she doesn't answer his dozen letters and parcels and it makes me hurt for poor Park. It's not his fault Eleanor couldn't stay in town but would it have killed her to call him? I don't think so. All in all, this is my least favourite Rainbow Rowell book, sorry. I know there are lost of raving reviews out there and people who absolutely love this book but for me, it just isn't cutting it. The romance is cute at first but then it gets to the 'eye-rolling'-stage for me. Maybe I'm simply a cold hearted bitch, the verdict is still out on that one.

Overall I rate I 3.5 but I can't do that so four stars instead. First I'll start with the things I didn't like about it. First in my mind was the climax was way too long. I read this book twice and both times I got exasperated with impatience and started to speed read and skip passages and after that I still wasn't done the climax. I found that all the characters had the same vocabulary. Different voices, sure, but the same vocabulary and I find that really strange when some of them don't even know how to read. But this might be just me. Now, this is just a personal preference but I didn't like the ending. I'm not saying it wasn't a good ending; I actually think it was. It didn't end exactly how I was expecting and left an efficient opening for the second book. I just wasn't satisfied and not in that 'I want to read more' sort of way. I found it a bit too predictable in some cases. As soon as they mentioned Giles and knew immediately that they would suspect Finn was Giles. A certain amount of predictability is good, but I liked a little bit more mystery in this secret. Now for what I did like. I did like the book. I mean, I read it twice; mostly because I just bought the sequel and wanted a refresher, but liking it enough to read it more than once is a big deal for me. I liked the words and descriptions. Creating such a complex world and trying to describe it would be a difficult task. I'll admit that sometimes I was lost in them and couldn't picture the areas well, but she did a fairly good job. I think the whole idea surrounding it was very interesting. I liked the cast of characters. You could see their personal struggles, their personal changes; they didn't stay static but they grew and changed with the story. I like the excepts of letters, stories and songs at the beginning of each chapter. It gave a vague outlook into some of the story that might not have been revealed otherwise. Some of the poems and songs were quite catchy and/or beautiful. I liked this book. I am looking forward to reading the second installment.

That ending tho. (I read this series a long time ago and I'm just writing a review) Spoilers June and Day have been through a lot of crap. A. LOT. So, Day is dying (Of course. Marie Lu just had to make me cry harder), June is all I-can't-go-back-to-him-not-after-what-I-did-to-him-he'll-never-forgive-me-he's-better-off-with-out-me-ish right now. So, EVERYTHING'S GREAT! NOT. I don't know how to feel about the ending. I mean, I'm happy that they ended up together(REALLY happy), but maybe I just needed an extra chapter or something telling about how happy they are together and all that crap. I just wanted the ending to be a lot happier. Also, did you see the drawings of Day and June online? DAY IS GORGEOUS.

**SOME SPOILERS AHEAD** Having read the first book in this series (which I LOVED), I couldn't wait to get started on this one. Now I feel like if I could go back in time and just finish at the first book, I would. Unfortunately for me Very Wicked Things was a total letdown. Even though I read the book in a day, I feel like I really just persevered because I figured with all the drama going on, there was gonna be some major HEA action coming up and it'd all be worth the bad feelings I was experiencing as I read. And even though there was a HEA, I feel like it was too little too late. Too much drama had happened, so many shitty decisions had been made and certain friends were just so damn self-involved for me to forgive. Another thing that bummed me out was that Sebastian, one of my favourite characters from the first book, even he was dragged down in this story. I wanted so badly for him to remain the flirty, fun guy from the first book, and while he was for the majority of the story, now his journey has been darkened. If he ends up the father of that skank Emma's baby, I will never read his story. I've hated her since the first book, I don't care how tough or not her life has been if there's a back story. And Spider, another character I started out liking, even he turned into a douche. Yeah, he redeemed himself somewhat in the end, but what kind of friend demands you admit you love them (even though you don't) and then kicks you to the curb and out of his life when you refuse! The more I think about what I've just read, the more I'm starting to dislike this book. So on that note, I'm out.
I LOVED THIS SO MUCH IT HURTS. Before reading May 2014. May 2014. May 2014. I'm in a good mood. I just want you. Badly. *waits patiently*

3.5 - 3.75 stars. This was a good book! It was an original story line. I really liked the suspenseful, but romantic story. I liked Mallory and Alex. It was a little slow some times, but other than that I really liked it and look forward to reading more from this author.

Nope. I mentally debated giving this book two stars because there was some pretty good writing, but in the end, I just can't do it. Every time I remember reading this book, all I feel is some sort of unpleasant, annoyed sensation inside. First and foremost, Girl Through Glass turns out wildly different from what the description indicates. This can be totally fine - great, even! - as long as the actual narrative is an improvement upon what you expected. This one was not. In the 1970s is Mira, a young girl who's set on a track to become an amazing ballerina. In the present, there's Kate, a professor who has an affair with a student. Both of their lives spiral out of control. Both of them lack pretty much any interest whatsoever. I think it's pretty obvious from the beginning Mira and Kate are the same character, even if we don't know why she changed her name. I'm just putting this under a spoiler in case someone doesn't pick up on it and doesn't want the rest of this dull read spoiled for them. The thing that really gets me with this book is that it could have been interesting. It could've had an engrossing plot that made you want to learn how the story unfolded. Instead, the whole thing just felt dated, musty, and disjointed. When I say disjointed, it's easy to see from the writing what I mean. Scenes frequently remain unfinished, and while that raises a million questions, the way the answers are handled isn't satisfying. Mira takes forever to get into her dance school, and once she does, you see little of her there, so this really isn't a ballet book, either. It's just a book that uses aspects of ballet for plot points. Really, this is a book about a creepy relationship between a girl and an old man, as well as an inappropriate teacher-student affair. There's a lot of emotional distress, but never anything concrete or any enticing character traits that give you reason to truly care about what's happening. I finished this book, hoping with each new page things would improve stylistically and I would actually start to feel invested in some part of this story. Alas, it wasn't meant to be; in place of piqued curiosity, I just got irritation, boredom, and disgust. This is not the worst book I've ever read - not even close (I can name what the worst one was, and I hope it's rotting away, mysteriously falling off library shelves into trash cans, never to appear again). Even so, it felt like it was trying too hard to make clever narrative choices but always falling short. Where there should've been development, there was none. Where there should've been the possibility of emotional ties to the reader, there pretty much was none. Girl Through Glass is a demotivating read that I cannot recommend, simply because I feel I wasted precious hours of my life trying to like its uneven and uninspiring style and plot.
I loved this book. Sure it was predictable but the writing was quick paced and the characters were enjoyable.
I will write more here later but WHY IN THE WORLD DON'T PEOPLE PUT MORE EFFORT INTO THEIR ENDINGS. WHY. TELL ME. WHY.

"You drive me insane June. You're the scariest, most clever, bravest person I know, and sometimes I can't catch my breath because I'm trying so hard to keep up. There will never be another like you. You realize that, don't you? Billions of people will come and go in this world, but there will never be another like you." This book was  everything. It was one of those books where the pages just fly by and you finally take a breather to look up and two hours have passed. This book wasn't even 400 pages and  so much happened. All of the things I was wondering about were cleared up  Like what would have happened if June had chosen Anden! and everything the characters were doing, no matter how stressful to read about, felt realistic and authentic. Not only did they feel it, but as the reader, you felt it too. Every feel. All the feels. The emotional depth of this series was incredible. I think finishing an amazing trilogy is always bitter sweet and this one was no different. The ending of this one in particular could have gone so differently and for me, the last 30-50 pages of this book were so carefully written and were so essential to letting the reader ease out of this story with as much impact as possible, while still feeling content with the outcomes of each character. This is one of the best endings to a series I've read in a while and I'm definitely sad to see this story end. I loved it.

James Choke, a 12 year old boy friend London, has a rather unconventional childhood. his mom ran a shoplifting ring in the city, so he never wanted for anything that could be bought in his life. Emotionally, he longs for the days that his 9 year old sister Lauren's birth father wasn't in his life. Her father hates James, pinning him as a troublemaker, and allows his mother/lover to get drunk all the time even encouraging it. At the start of the book, a girl in James' class is teasing him about having an overweight mom and he slams her into the way, making her cut her face on a nail by accident. He is suspended from school, but when he runs away from the school to his mom to try to explain himself she is again too drunk to care although she is on prescription drugs. She dies in her sleep as a result of the alcohol on top of the drugs, and now James and his sister are put into foster care. James meets a friend named Kyle in foster care, but as he is just settling into the new lifestyle Lauren's birth father comes to adopt her permanently. However, since he is not obligated to take on James in any way, he leaves him in foster care and does not allow him to see his little sister. James struggles with the thought of being banned from seeing his sister, his mother's death, his stepfather's cruelty, and his new life as an orphan. He decides to go back to his mom's house and take all the money from her safe once he cracks the code, hiding it all around his room in the foster home so that his stepfather would only get the obvious bills even if he came to rob him. He wakes up in a strange place where no one will talk to him, but soon learns that he is in CHERUB. CHERUB is a kid spy organization that allows kids that are orphans and in foster care a chance to have a permanent place to stay and train to be spies for the government. After the events of the past few months, he could not pass up the opportunity, and decides to take the tests so that he will be accepted. After passing the tests with flying colors, and finding out that Kyle was also an agent that was sent to recruit a kid and chose him after the money trick, he moves into CHERUB headquarters. Before embarking on missions, he must learn to swim, go through basic training, one of the toughest tests an agent must face, and then if he passes both he must go on his first mission. He passes his basic training, making a potential love interest in his teammate Kerry, but then he must go on his first mission to stop hippies that may be planning a terrorist attack on a business meeting with oil companies. I liked the character growth of James throughout the book, and I really enjoyed the idea of kids being spy (huge spy kids movie fan). Some parts of the book I saw James acting more like a 16 or 17 year old instead of a 12 year old, and I could not tell if it was because of his job or because the author just wrote them too maturely. Also, I felt as if the book crammed a lot into one book, it felt like 2 stories in one, however the size of the book was just a bit over 300 pages long so it did not feel as if I was reading it forever. Altogether, I truly enjoyed this book, and I will be reading/reviewing the rest of the series shortly. Overall Rating: 4/5

No more than one day after complaining about reading a book with a cliff hanger (Never Never) and having to wait for the sequel, I go and do it again. I must be a glutton for punishment. This book grabbed my attention right away and kept it throughout. After reading the Fixed Series, it's nice to know more of the story behind Gwen's departure from Eighty-Eighth Floor. Mid-book, i was really annoyed at Gwen for allowing herself to get attached. Then I had to get over the whiplash that was JC's change of heart and personality once he admitted that he loved Gwen. I actually started to suspect that he might+ have split personality disorder because it wasn't the same guy at all. . Plus, what the hell kind of thing is it to say  I'll come for you...but don't wait for me? So where is the line between disliking the story and just feeling the annoyance that the author aims to draw from her readers?

The Ringmaster's Wife is a truly excellent book. There are certain books that come to your mind when you see quotes about "books taking you places", and this will be one from now on. The environments in this story were rich and engrossing, the characters relatable and more than just a cardboard cutout. I greatly enjoyed the backstory or John and Mable Ringling, as they are people in history I knew little-to-nothing about. It was so nice to travel to that other time, other place. Parts of this story are rather on the tragic side, especially what happened to Mrs. Ringling. Her dying from what is now a disease that can be managed was heartbreaking. Especially when I have that disease, myself. I loved the ending though, the last chapter, AND, the epilogue. Such sweetness. Rose and Colin had such a beautiful story, and a telling of it.

** spoiler alert ** The main character is a knight, sworn to protect the King. Most every chapter is its own short story about how a good friend of the knight's gets killed because the King is a jerk. After six or seven of these, he kills the King. I've seen several rave reviews of Dave Duncan but I frankly don't get it. After reading this terrible book, I'm reluctant to try anything else he's written.

What I liked: -Daniel. Once again, he was one of my favorite parts of this book. I like how consistent and how good he is, but most of all, I like his relationship with Harper. Daniel is a unique character, as he's the only one who is immune to the siren's song,  which makes him an asset to Gemma and Harper. Daniel was witty, brave, devoted, and caring, and I wish he had been the main character. -Concept. I still love the idea behind this series. The sirens, the Greek mythology, the watersong, the spell they hold over men...everything comes together to create a wonderful idea that captures my interest and keeps me reading. I wish there had been more about the sirens and less about Harper and her search for Gemma. I feel like we still don't really know what they're all capable of because Gemma--the only siren we can experience the story through--doesn't ever really utilize her abilities. She swims with her tail and forces herself not to sing but doesn't try to learn how to be a siren. What I disliked: -Pace. Not a lot happens in this book, and there were nearly unbearably long chunks where nothing happened other than Gemma or Harper complaining or laying around. The only interesting parts of the book were things that happened to Gemma while with the sirens, but these things never went into detail. When Gemma killed Jason Way, there was no freak out or crying or panicking. All she did was have "nightmares" after, which were never shown or elaborated on. It's almost like Gemma wasn't fazed at all by killing a man. -Harper. Once again, she annoyed me so much throughout the entire book. She does nothing but whine over her sister, push Daniel away while admitting her feelings for him, and she doesn't actually do much. Everyone else around her makes the plans and does the work, Harper just provides the older sister vibe. With perhaps the exception of Alex, Harper is probably the flattest character in the entire book. -The ending. I felt like the ending was a bit of a copout. The sirens just decided to back off and hang around Capri? That doesn't seem like it was in Penn, Thea, and Lexi's personalities. I know Penn has ulterior motives to doing so, but she did not present herself as the kind of girl that would just back off and let Gemma live after being so disrespected. She would have fought and killed them all. Overall, the sequel was an okay book, but it wasn't as good as the first part. The writing was okay, but the characters were a little boring and flat and there was almost no action and very little drama or suspense. I would recommend this book for diehard fans of mermaids, sirens, or Amanda Hocking.

Probably more like a 3.5 star book. There are spoilers from the first books in the series in this review. On her way home in the mortal world to see her family, Meghan is attacked by Iron fey and after fending them off she realizes that she can't truly go home until things are settled in the Nevernever. Although she offed one Iron King, the new false king is waging a war on the Seelie and Unseelie courts and encroaching on their lands, spreading poison in the wyldwood and beyond. Of course Meghan can't return home now and must return to Faery, but before she does anything, she needs to recover her memories of her human father before she attempts to rescue him from Leanansidhe who she must also ask for sanctuary while she figures out her next step, as she and Ash are now exiles. I found myself getting a bit sick of the constant "We'll never make it together, I'll get old, he'll stay young. We're doomed" bit. Yes, there's supposed to be tension and things against them to build up the tension and drama of their love but geez, if you'll never be together, don't torture yourself, move on and get over it! After bartering with Oberon, her biological father, and Mab, the Winter Queen and Ash's mother, eventually, Meghan agrees to venture into the Iron Realm so as to try and kill the Iron King, which will end the trio's exile, should they survive, because you just know that Ash and Puck will accompany Meghan on her quest. I loved the first two books in the series, and maybe it's just because I waited so long to read this one, but it wasn't a can't-put-down read for me. Ash came off as far too needy and Meghan was too angsty at times, and I love Puck but am sick of him mooning over someone who doesn't want him. And in reality, not a lot happened. I mean, there were battles and new lands were visited but still, the plot didn't advance too much until the end. Actually, the last thirty pages or so were the most interesting and I found the resolution to certain problems to be well thought out and believable with the exception of one thing I didn't get how Meghan had any powers left to feed into the tree and heal the land since she supposedly gave it all to the Iron King . It was a good read and I'm interested to see what happens in The Iron Knight but I just didn't get wrapped up in the story like I did with the previous books. I love Puck, I don't know what happens in the next book, but if he makes it and is alone, I'd love to read a spin-off with him. I know Kagawa has one coming out that focuses on Meghan's brother, Ethan, and it's set years after this trilogy (I know I haven't read the last book, but it'll be weird to see what's going on in the lives of Meghan and her friends in what I would imagine will be at least ten years later, though I guess they'll probably be about the same age since you age so slowly in Faery. Assuming they're not dead. Then not too much would be going on with them.) but I'm not sure how interesting of a character he'll be, at least compared to Puck. I was surprised to see that the next book will focus on Ash and, I'm assuming, Puck, and I'm not sure how much of a part Meghan will play in it, but I have to say I'm kind of hoping she won't be in it a lot because the angst is just getting to be a bit too much for me.

I was excited to read this book when I bought it. I had just discovered the New Adult genre (thanks to Crash by Nicole Williams) and was greedy to get my hands on this one. But when I went to read it (months later I might add), it took be awhile to get into. I think the main reason was that I didn't particularly care for Cassie. She irked me to no ends actually. Compared to other "heroines" of new adult reads, she has nothing on them. Most have a tragic past that really gripes you and explains why they have trust issues. But Cassie's problem? Her dad failed to get a concert for a high school dance and she was embarrassed-um, what?! After reading such heavy stories prior to this (I had just read Wait for You by J. Lynn), I felt this book was very juvenile in it's approach to Cassie's "damaged, mistrust" issues. Jack's reasons were totally acceptable in my opinion so I didn't mind him so much but Cassie really needed to get over her "daddy issues". As I said before, it took me a bit to get into but I eventually got there. It wasn't until halfway through the book that a plot twist grabbed my attention. After that happened, I started to enjoy the book more. I'm not sure why there is a sequel. I would have been more than happy to have the series end as it did and have another set of characters in the next one. I will probably read it for curiosity's sake but this wouldn't be my first pick for a New Adult Series to read. But if you enjoy athletes falling in love, then you might enjoy this one! (For more series reviews, check out my blog: http://seriesousbookreviews.wordpress...)

The heroine of this book is just so... clean. Seriously, in the first 24 hours of the story, she took one bath and two showers. -And it's not like she'd been exerting herself doing anything crazy or dirty to merit all that bathing: no, in those twenty-four hours, she slept (alone) on clean sheets and then sat around in a vineyard watching a photo shoot all day. However, bathing = being naked, which leads to imagining the hero naked, which leads to imagining other things, and imagination shortly leads to action, so as a plot device, I guess all that bathing served a purpose. I like romance series featuring families. Shannon Stacey's Kowalskis series is a contemporary favorite. Stephanie Laurens' Cynster books were a big part of my introduction to the romance genre (though, wow, is it well past time for Laurens to move on to another project). I picked up this first book of the Sullivans series because it features a family of eight kids, and I figured if it was good, the series would be likely to keep me busy for awhile. I liked Andre's writing style. The plot moves along, the characters are relatable, the Sullivan family seems like people I'd like to know better. I'll probably keep up with the series, but this book wasn't the strongest start. There just wasn't much to it. The entire book takes place over the course of four days, two and a half of which are pretty much sex-sex-sex-sex-sex. Which, you know, is fine: I like sex, and in a contemporary setting, I don't care if people hop right into bed together. We're all adults, here. The problem is that the dramatic conflict was a little ... lacking. When we meet Chloe, the heroine, she's got a bruised cheek and a busted car. It's clear someone hit her, probably her ex, but we're kept in the dark for two thirds of the book until she finally decides to trust the hero (who she's been banging for two days already) with the story: she left her husband six months ago, but he tracked her down at her new apartment and hit her. So, yeah, I get that someone who's just been battered would be a little gun shy about trusting someone else, except that Chloe really isn't: she keeps saying she needs to take things slowly, keep things light, whatevs, and then she... doesn't. Like I said, the ENTIRE romance takes four days. Also, as a domestic violence prosecutor, I cringed throughout the entire subplot having to do with Chloe's assault. She kept telling herself she needed to call the police, and then not doing it. While I understand the impulse to avoid an unpleasant experience, if you are a victim of a crime, your story seems less credible every minute that goes by and you don't report it. I kept thinking of how a defense attorney would tear her up on the witness stand if she ever had to testify: Question: You must've been on the way to the police station when you crashed your car, right? Answer: Uh, no. I'm not sure where I was going, actually. Question: But when you crashed, and Mr. Sullivan stopped to help you, you asked him to take you right to the police, yes? Answer: Um, no, actually. I asked him to take me to a cheap hotel. Question: And did he? Answer: Er, no. He took me to a fancy guesthouse at his brother's winery. Question: There must have been a phone there, right? Did you call the police then? Answer: Uh, actually, No. I mean, yes, there was a phone, but I didn't call police. Question: No? Well, what did you do? Answer: Well, I took a bubble bath. -And, I, er, kind of got distracted. <*witness is mumbling, blushes crimson, looks at her lap not at jury. That's some reasonable doubt, there, that is.

The creatures outside looked from pig to man, and from man to pig, and from pig to man again; but already it was impossible to say which was which. It's about time I read Animal Farm. My favorite booktuber of all time, Ariel Bissett, constantly reminds her subscribers that this is her favorite book of all time. I just never got around to finding a copy that I really liked. I actually picked up the one that has both 1984 and Animal Farm in it, but I wanted to review them separately. Anyway, it was pretty damn good. The balls on Orwell are impressive. To write a book calling out a dictator and pretty much everyone else in power at that time is super wild and interesting. I read an article explaining how each character is meant to represent a person in the Russian revolution. I love symbolism, and that pretty much describes this story to a T. If you don't know what Animal Farm is about, it's about a farm run by animals. Duh. Just kidding, but it is about a farm that gets overthrown by animals. At first, things are going smoothly. They have enough food and leisure, but then two pigs named Snowball and Napoleon grapple for power because after all, when has power ever been able to be shared? While some animals are distrustful and fearful of how things are going, they are all too scared to speak up (as they should be). Yeah, there's some murder. Orwell isn't trying to be super grandiose with this novel, which is a compliment. In the world of classics, many find themselves seated beside a dictionary or perked by their computer with Sparknotes open. It's short, the writing is relatively simple, and the story is kind of goofy. Most of the things the animals do like writing words, learning the alphabet, and building a windmill are totally unrealistic. However, he still manages to get his point across without using SAT words and theme upon theme upon theme. All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others. That is all.

Phenomenal. This deserves a second and third read and I am actually excited to do just that eventually. There is so much deliciousness here. Vonnegut's style and surprises do not disappoint in this one. Malachi Constant's story is dished out evenly across several planets and moons and states of mental clarity. Vonnegut is not afraid to disparage his main characters, in fact it is this complex human portrayal that makes reading this story so rich.

This book was close to get just two stars but I liked the story, it just took me ages to get through it. I only continued the book because I felt like reading and this was the only book I had near me. As said earlier it was really long drawn at the beginning; the details about Tom's sight when he first arrived the lighthouse bored me so much but I'm glad I finally got myself to end the book - it was worth it. I caught myself thinking what I would do in Isabel's situation, to have lost three fosters at involuntary abortion and one day, an infant floats up the shore in a boat alive with a dead dad, lost to an heart attack. The whole thing with Hannah and her family, Bluey, Ralph and Isabel's family is very well written!

I finished this novel so quickly; the perfect book for a train trip. I'm a fan of everything pirate and this novel included the basics but struggled to go beyond. I felt romance directed most of this plot. The sea monsters and end of the world talks which usually come with pirate novels/movies was missing. There was no adventure as they spent the entirety of the novel pretty much on the same boat, in the same room/jail cell. The siren aspects of the novel was the most interesting (alas I had already seen the title of the sequel before I began reading so I wasn't at all surprised!) and it is the only reason I'll keep reading the rest of the series. Hopefully the writer decides to focus on more than just kiss scenes and love-hate behaviours which are in every other YA novel.

I... have so many mixed feelings about this book. At first, I was swept away by the beauty of Bach's ideas, these moments of transcendence and inner peace reflected in the seemingly mundane life of a seagull. I won't ignore the loveliness there. Going past that, it started looking like another book that tells the story of yet another special snowflake who broke away from the mundane in order to find a higher existence. Somewhere between the beauty and the bunk, there is an enjoyable story. You just have to be in the mindset for alternative thinking and seagulls.

-2 stars- I have mixed feelings about the book but it was okay. I can say I liked it. *I didn't throw my e-reader against a wall or something like that* Well I didn't know what to expect from The Goddess Test. But it somehow didn't reach my imagination..at all. The tests. Hmmm. Yes I had a more survival of the fittest idea when it came to the tetst.. Something like the Hunger Games.. Fight for your survival.. But the 7 mentioned tests were just..Hmmm no words for it. Henry. Well I did have a little crush on him. Who doesn't want someone with eyes like the moonlight. Swoon! But one thing just shattered my crush in gazillion pieces: ''The angles of his face were too symmetrical to be normal, his smooth skin devoid of even a hint of stubble, the thick, jet-black hair - Ooh, this is going to the right direction. -  that hung an inch above his shoulders....'' -No. Nah. What(?) Hair that hung an inch above his shoulders...- No offense but I guess I am not the long-hair-guy-type. Still love his eyes! Kate. .. I don't know. Just Kate = confusing. I liked her determined character at the beginning but it kind of changed. Ava. No words. Most confusing of all. Confusing. How come everything in this book surprises me so much. I was caught off guard the entire time. Especially at the end how everything turns out. The members of the council.. and the rest Their love. Yes. I love(d) their interaction and their growing (unseen most of the time Henry's side) love for each other Anyways. The Goddess Test was interesting but still not interesting enough to give me that addiction-kick... that page-turner-flipper-thing. But I will continue read the books because it's worth it! Even though the ending left me confused and curious.. Kate and Henry all the way.

Shanghai Girls: This was disappointing. I had looked forward to it, having read "Peony in Love" recently. But this book read just like someone's diary. There seemed to be no up or down in the tone or emotion, even during what must have been traumatic times during the escape from China in 1937/38. The book only started to get emotionally absorbing at the end, with the rise of McCarthyism; then we are left with a cliffhanger ending. Very disappointing.

Hate to Love You. Oh Tijan... what you do to football/college romances. There was definitely some flashes of Sam/Mason here... I could see it if I closed my eyes tight enough, LOL! I struggled a little in the middle of this one, it kind of dragged a bit, but I was too hooked to give up and then it came back around and everything made sense. I do hope this really isn't the end and we will see these characters pop up somewhere again. My favorite line came super late... but wow, way to keep it real... "...isn't the bad guy here." "Really?" My tone was dry. "So, who is?" "No one. There are no bad guys. Everyone's bad. Everyone's good. Everyone changes and the whole situation can be flipped tomorrow." 4 stars!

Boricuan Bookworms- Book Reviews I picked up The Maze Runner because I was preparing myself for the movie that's coming out this same year.I can't believe I hadn't read it sooner! This is a dystopian that anyone could enjoy. There's secrets, conspiracies and betrayal around every turn. Since I can't seem to produce coherent words to express how I feel, I've decided to use GIF's as a way to review this book. After all, an image is worth a thousand words... First off, the characters were all so complex. I never met a single character who wasn't important in this story. Thomas was the protagonist, and he was so likable! But, he was also an unreliable character. (One of my favorite types of characters!). He didn't remember anyone or anything from his past, and yet being in the Maze reminded him of something, something bad. The "villains" in this story were mostly unseen, yet feared all the same. I couldn't help but feel despair and angst as much as the other boys did. It kind of felt like the villain was "Big Brother" from 1984. Unseen but terrifying! I also loved the fact that this book also introduced a paranormal aspect. That aspect definitely helped this story grow. I couldn't stand one thing, though and that was the made up swear words! It was so annoying! I mean, if you're going to swear just do it. Don't make up words for it. It makes me feel childish. The book also has a slow start, but once the "good things" start hapenning, you won't be able to put down the book. Reading Process: Rating: 4 stars.

This book gets a lot of crap for not being exactly like Graceling. and that's very true. Not even in plot, it's an entirely different genre to Kristin Cashore's previous work. I have mixed feelings about this, I was expecting another sweeping adventure epic because I could read a million of them so long as they're written by Kristin Cashore. But I was so pleasantly surprised by this book. I liked the author mixing things up. Everyone references her blog on green triangles. She makes an excellent point. So there was no epic quest halfway through this book. There was no mustache-twirling baddie. The Villain died ten years before the events of the story. Genre-wise, this is a loaded gun. Mystery, romance, political, healing, there is SO MUCH GOING ON. It's nearly flawlessly executed, with a few plotlines that could have been tightened a bit. When we last left Bitterblue, she was a recently orphaned- potentially molested- princess of a severely messed up nation. (she wasn't really molested, but with Leck, it's best to assume the worst) Now she's older, years after her coronation and still on a major learning curve, being separated from the people with her best interests at heart, Katsa and Po. So this is the new queen learning curve/investigation of her father's crimes. It is intense and compelling as all hell. I poured over this book, spent every second of free time reading it. It was so suspenseful and had such a great mystery element to it. Saf. I could punch that smug bastard, the kiss him, then slap him, like some demented Spanish soap opera. I loved him. I hated him. I loved to hate him. I hated to love him. Inner turmoil. When he was a basic love-interest when Bitterblue was sneaking out, he was at his strongest. Rogue-ish and sexy. Then he stole the crown and oh...the stupidity. That mess, that terrible mess of the crown subplot. I could live to see that cut out. It added nothing and tangled up so many other complicated parts. Their relationship had it's purpose though. While he could be an asshole, his disrespect, rudeness, and hard-headedness weren't directed at a queen. Bitterblue was given the freedom to have someone judge her as a person, not a queen. Sparks was very liberating for her. She needed that. And she sacrifices nothing. I'm sick of girls giving up power to be with a flawed, jackass boy. bitterblue doesn't. She and Saf have sex a couple times, he leaves her, she lets him go, easy peasy. It's Kristin Cashore, of course nobody gets married or compromises or makes any serious commitment. Katsa and Po are shoved into this as well, basically acting married while not really being married. I wish we had their POV or something instead of these awkward fly-on-the-wall moments with Bitterblue, because they are the greatest couple EVER. Unghh. Saf and Bitterblue consummate their hot burning love after witnessing a trusted adviser commit suicide in a blizzard. He was probably still drowning while they headed up to that tower. Not kidding. This is a Kristin Cashore novel. Casual sex! Then Saf has to go away and this is my favorite aspect of the book. Thank you, KC. You do not sacrifice for a guy like Saf. You sleep with him a couple times and look back on the relationship fondly. I like Saf as a jumping-off point, hopefully she'll hop into bed with Giddeon, who got totally redeemed this book. KC is always so character-driven, this book is no exception. These poor, broken advisers are so smartly written. Katsa, Po, Raffin and Bann light up every page they share. Bitterblue grows so much strength and wisdom. Saf and Teddy are a blast to sneak around at midnight with. It is dense with real, well written people and relationships. The reveals of this book hit like a fist, and the emotions and tragedy will have you reeling. The romance leaves you excited and swooning. so many great characters, and KC is never afraid to slow things down and just let them talk and develop. It's such a good read. It took me a while to appreciate how great this is, and I love it as it's own standalone book. yes, I missed all the elements of Fire and Graceling, but I love what made this different. With the right mindset, this book can not disappoint.

I am very angry at myself for not checking my feeling that this was the last book in the series because it is NOT and things did not get fully resolved in the way I hoped. I'm pleased there's more, though. Just displeased that evidently I have to wait. (Unfinished series problems). Also please to stop being silly and talk, Stephen and Rory? I was hoping you'd learned your lessons but then you went and forgot about the death-world.
I loveeeed it. So much ugly crying happened.

This was my favorite of the series so far and I think a large part of that is due to the hero, Ice. He is not in the same social class as the other Brethren and he always seems to the odd man out. Even in the last book you could see there was an attraction between Ice and Sabelle. Sabelle is always the good girl always doing what she should, not what she wants to do. This time around is not different, she knows that if she is alone with Ice things will happen and she tries to make sure that it never happens. Unfortunately after a battle she was forced to escape with him and her brother who had been in a spell induced coma for days, leaving her essentially alone with him. The more time they spend together neither can deny the attraction, after giving in they see there were unexpected consequences to their actions. While gathering info to pass on to others in their group, while the war escalates, they fight their feelings along with what the others think of them and past grudges.

Alive by Scot Sigler is one of the most confusing books I've ever read. I spent most of the book questioning what was going on, and even when I finished it there were a lot of unanswered questions. I was even questioning the genre - I assumed it was a dystopian, but then by the end I was questioning that as it had a lot of sci-fi elements. Overall I enjoyed this, the start and the end were especially good. The start, where the characters wake up in coffins, fully grown but thinking its their 12th birthday, was a really great start to the book. It pulled me in straight away. As the story went on it got a bit 'meh'. Not much really happened.We spent so many chapters just wandering corridors. There were so many elements that I just didn't understand, or seemed to have no meaning for the story  all the little god debates about Tlaloc (I think that was the name!) got on my nerves a bit. And also the stuff about different shapes/symbols on the foreheads was never really explained either The characters weren't amazing either. There were quite a few characters but we didn't really get to know many of them. There wasn't a lot of character development even for he main characters such as Em, O'Malley, or Bishop. Alive had an interesting ending so I do plan to read the next book, but I do hope its better than the first.

A roller-coaster of emotions! This series continues to deliver with plenty of gasps, humor, and heartfelt moments. Hazel and her grandmother are separated from Alana and Marcus, as they are prisoners on Alana's home planet. We catch up with Prince Robot is is living on a secluded planet with his son. The Will is drugged out and seeking revenge for the death of his sister. So glad the family is reunited, Marcus and Alana are feeling the romance and expecting another child. Read my non-spoilery review on Book Nerds Across America: http://www.booknerdsacrossamerica.com... Full review below: I lied, this isn't really a review so much as me rehashing all my feels! Switch is a new adult, dystopian story with a heavy romance element. From the start, there was a lot going on. This story offers multiple plots from multiple perspectives. I was a bit thrown off in the beginning; I was certain there would be a romance between Roman and X and then other characters entered and we are suddenly reading about two different romances and parallel stories. It's not a complaint, just unexpected. I noted that throughout the book much of what occurred was unexpected and kept me on my toes. This is refreshing after reading books where I feel I could tell someone what was going to happen after reading the first chapter. There were parts of the book that kept me glued and connected and there were parts that I gave up and just skimmed. However, overall I liked the story. It ends in suspense that can only be relieved after reading the next book so I have some motivation to continue the series. Favorite part: The suspenseful ending/cliffhanger involving Bridgette. Least favorite part: Pete kept referring to his father as "da"???? FYI: There is adult content in this book and is not for young readers.

There is great dialogue and I loved the Pleinsworth daughters, who Anne is governess too. I'm always impressed with how well Julia Quinn writes chaotic conversations with many characters and interruptions, yet still keep it clear who is talking. I think I liked Anne more than Daniel, who I didn't love. In the end, while I really liked the book, I found myself enjoying the scenes with all the secondary characters more than the ones with the leads alone. That means it wasn't the love story that hooked me in.

I would like to thank Nastassja for lending me this book after I told her I wanted to read it! she's the sweetest. A line to the freaking door for a glimpse, a taste, of magic. If declaring something criminal doesn't render it sexier, then I don't know what does. They should try doing that to this book, then, because it was anything but sexy. A Criminal Magic started off with such an interesting premise. Forbidden magic across America, the roaring 20s, gansgter wars and star-crossed lovers. What's not to love about that? Well, a lot of things, apparently, because despite all of those elements, this book was as dull as brick. It was seriously a pain to go through sometimes because it was so flat. The book starts with us meeting our two main characters, Joan and Alex. Joan is a barmaid at her uncle's shine room in a dead end town in Virginia. Her uncle is a drunk who got addicted to his own shine (some sort of magical drink that only lasts a day after it's brewed and who gives the high of a lifetime, apparently, cause everyone wants to get a taste) and not only she finds herself responsible for tending the bar, she also has to look out for her little sister and her cousin, and they're about to lose their house because they have no money. Alex is a former playboy/trust-fund baby whose father was a prominent pharmaceutic in town, but he's now lost nearly everything because daddy was mixed up in gangsta business and got busted by the Feds, and he's recently joined the police force in their Prohibition unit (the one that deals with magic-related cases) in an attempt to distance himself from his father's name. They both receive opportunities that could possibly change their lives, and that's where the story begins. So... it sounds pretty awesome, I know. I first heard about this book sometime late last year, and I added it to my tbr list without thinking twice because I was 100% sure I was going to love it. But it's very poorly executed. For starters, I felt the writing was very stiff. It's not bad writing, it's just emotionless. The author tries to describe what the characters are thinking and feeling, but it didn't convince me at all. The dialogue also felt forced? Maybe it's because I've read  The Diviners before, which is also set in the 20s, and it did a much better job at capturing the atmosphere the Roaring 20s are supposed to have. I get why the author chose to set this book in such a time, to go along with the prohibition theme and such, but there were no specific elements of that time period present in the book, which was such a let down. Then there's that awful romance. Maybe it was because I wasn't a huge fan of the characters (more on that in a bit), but Alex and Joan had no chemistry whatsoever. Apparently there were a bunch of secret meetings between them where they developed a deep, meaningful bond but the reader doesn't get to see any of it. We're just told it happened and supposed to go along with it. I hate romances that have no build-up. (Also, the only time this book made me think of  The Night Circus was after the main characters started to develop their little crush, because they were star-crossed lovers who did magic and shenaningans with each other, but that was it. While I wasn't the biggest fan of The Night Circus, it's undeniably a book that is very atmospheric and ethereal, and A Criminal Magic wasn't like that in any way. I hate when books have like, one element in common with some other book and suddenly they're being marketed as the same thing.) There's not really a lot of interesting magic going on, despite what the synopsis might make you believe. Nothing is really explained about the background of magic in America. The side characters were completely useless and undeveloped, and I think that's truly a shame because they would've definitely made the story more interesting. There were a couple of opportunities the author could have used to expand upon the story and introduce more storylines to get the plot fresher (like the whole incest-ish thing with Tommy and Rose, which was mentioned once and that was it. Seriously no one thought to go investigate that??? None of them were even slightly curious? UGH)  but they went by unmentioned, sadly. The characters were just soooo boring. Joan was dull. She had a huge hero complex, and it got on my nerves. She became slightly more interesting towards the ending, leaving her moral complexes aside to do whatever she needed to save her family (I love grey morals! ), but that lasted a total of two pages because then there was the romance thingie and all she could think about was Alex and how hot he is and ugh. No. Alex was more interesting, because he had a clear personality developed and didn't lose his mind every time the pretty girl smiled at him. He was kind of an ass at the beggining, but he managed to develop a lot throughout the story and, honestly, by the end of the book I was only looking forward to his chapters and his side of the story. Maybe it would've been better if I hadn't had such high expectations because of the great premise, but overall, this book was a huge disappointment.
