Alrighty. I'm slightly disappointed with this book, and slightly happy with this book. Part 1: Is spent taking us to Tamlin's land and luring him into a sense of Feyre being "herself". Little does he know he invited a wolf in sheep's clothing into his court. Tamlin for his part is a massive idiot. Seriously. He's really really dumb. Lucien though has some suspicions. Most of part one is spent doing nothing. Nothing really IMO with the nice send off book 2 left us at. I expected more. I expected more plotting and scheming and for Feyre to finally tell Tamlin off, to stop looking for the human girl he fell "in love" with. Tamlin doesn't really love her, not really when you see his actions in regards to her. Feyre for her part plays the part and lures Ianthe into thinking she's still that same girl. The one without powers or smarts. Inside Feyre is seething. I just didn't like this part I expected more, more strategy, more plotting, and more stuff. I was disappointed. Part 2: BORING AS HELL That's what part 2 should be called. While I enjoy seeing Rhys and Feyre together and their band of friends it was just utterly boring. They were planning for war to always be behind, setting things up to just not have them happen. Portions of this part got confusing sometimes. I just wanted more. Also as noted by  Emily May in her review the author did more telling vs showing. She did an excellent job of showing in the last book. But often times in this one it was almost told from a perspective of reflection, where Feyre (and the author) would say reflective comments as though whats occurring on the page happened in the past, but is being told in the present. It was annoying, I wanted to experience things with Feyre. This lacked the punch and the interest. I found myself wandering throughout reading this book. With Rhys and Feyre being together the book also lacked the sexual tension and the are they for each other or not for each other tension. I missed that, there was nothing driving my forward into this book. The threat of war was a major driving force of this book, but it imo didn't do enough for me to care. It didn't keep my interested. So I found myself missing those moments between Rhys and Feyre when she didn't know about him being her mate  and when he wore the ruthless ruler mask. I enjoy the side characters, a lot. But I still immensely dislike Nesta. I can't stand her. At all. I find myself trying to think about what Nesta will do next, and she never follows what I think she will. I suspect that she and  Cassian, might be mates  but it's neither confirmed or denied at this point. I find Nesta to be utterly cold before the events in book 2, and I find her to be cold more so now. I can't even believe after all Feyre did for her she was still an asshole to her. Elaine *sigh* Elaine is like a damsel in distress and is such a minuscule character to me that I didn't care that she was Lucian's new mate. Elaine is not to me a strong character yet, and while I understand her life has drastically changed I'm surprised she clung to Grayson so much. She knew how that was going to end up what with an iron engagement ring. I felt no pull to even care about her story, until the end. I don't care that she's supposedly Lucian's mate I expect there is going to be something between her and  Azriel, because that would be of interest to me. He seems to want to help her, and Elaine seems to respond to him. but that's all in part 3. Part 3: The war. This is the culmination of all the things that we were prepping and dealing with in part 2. This was the better part of the book. There was a lot here, and there were things here that punched me in the emotional gut. But I knew everything would turn out ok, so I didn't get too attached to the moment. Nothing blindsided me, not really, not like in the last 2 books. Well one thing did blindside me,  when Amren take's Feyre to the Cauldren and doesn't help her. I was like wtf, seriously WTF. I was blown away by it, but it was all explained away so I couldn't be angry with her. Still though I enjoyed the book to a degree. I will be checking out the next book (in 2018 *Shakes fist*) depending on where and who the story is about. I hope Maas doesn't continue to write in the tell vs show format. I loathe it. I like living with the characters and being blindsided with them. I am disappointed in the overall book though. Since parts 1-2 are a big majority of the book they could have been written much better.

A little bit about me: I love March Madness. I especially love the opening Thursday and Friday games...ahh the upsets! I enter multiple pools and cheer on random college teams that I know next to nothing about. Now how does this relate to The Girl on the Train. Well this past weekend was the opening weekend of March Madness...32 games within 2 days starting on Thursday. And how did I spend my Friday night...reading The Girl on the Train. That's right. During one of the greatest sporting events of the year, I was curled up on the couch reading Girl on the Train. I just couldn't put this book down! There was the mystery aspect that I really enjoyed, but the thriller part just hooked me. I figured out the mystery about half way through, but the ending and the tension just kept going and I couldn't tear myself away. The characters were flawed, but at times I just wanted to be friends with them and be there for them. Overall, I loved it. As a fan of thrillers, I would suggest this novel to those who love thrillers as well, especially Before I Go to Sleep.

While this was the darkest book in the series so far, I also think it was one of the best. The characters are all changing and growing, and their relationships keep growing and evolving in a way that feels very natural. I loved seeing that small but important change in the relationship between Meg and Simon at the end of the book. Their relationship is moving slow as hell, but that feels right for the characters, and at least it is moving! I also liked seeing the various ties developing between those in the courtyard and the "human pack". The one character I really wish we could have seen more from is Tess; She is one of my favorites, and it felt like she was almost an after thought this time around. I'd also like to see Hope's role continue to grow. While I did enjoy the portions involving Meg and her development of the Trailblazer deck, I did find her constant doubts a little bit frustrating. I understand that she was sheltered and all, but a little more growth in the confidence department wouldn't be unwelcome. It's a small nit-pick with an otherwise excellent book, however.

This was delightful. The sort of a book that leaves you with a smile when you finish it. Cosmo is not quite as much of a brat in the book as I had expected from the blurb, he really has a heart of gold and genuinely wants to please Alasdair (even without the D/s trappings of their relationship, I think he would). Alasdair is adorably clueless at times about what to do with Cosmo when it doesn't involve sex but he gets it eventually. There is a refreshing lack of angst in the book, again opposite to what I was expecting from the blurb (which doesn't quite fit the story I think) - sure, in the beginning Alasdair messes up a bit by not understanding what Cosmo needs but it's quite quickly resolved. There were wonderfully honest parts, like Alasdair's lack of a playroom and Cosmo and Nash's frienship talk but also a couple of bits that just didn't quite fit (like Roger's revelation at the end, just felt a bit tacked on - not really necessary). The BDSM elements were nice, fairly low-key - I liked not necessarily seeing every single thing described on the page and being allowed to imagine the rest. Still, enjoyable enough to get 4 stars.

He seems like a good match for Waverly and if I decide to continue the series I hope I read that they end up making a go at it at some point. One of my favorite supporting characters got killed off which was a bit disappointing. I am kinda interested in what will happen now so I might pick up book two but it wont be a priority for me.

So I never thought I'd give a war book - especially a Civil War book - five stars, but here it is. I started to read this book ahead of a visit to the battlefields at Gettysburg, hoping to get a better idea of what I'd see there. I never expected to encounter such a good book. This is a magnificently written book with language understandable yet steeped in its time. Shaara actually made me care about the people whose names I'd heard about and written down on exams in high school, whose images I see in museums. He made readers understand how something that seems so ridiculous and stupid (Pickett's Charge) could actually sound like a good idea, and why they did it although it was such a terrible blunder. You can also see, through the discourse in this book, how people could convince themselves to fight on the Confederate side, which is something I've always struggled to understand. I really enjoyed this book, and I think this should be required reading for anybody about to visit Gettysburg.

Actual Rating: 2.5 stars I started this book with great expectations, and they were crushed as of chapter 1. Getting to finish it wasn't so much of a pain, though it did involve a lot of eye rolling and anger management. Prophet and Tom are supposed to be complex characters, with lots of baggage and secrets (which annoying Tom reminds us of every 2 pages till you just wish you could punch his lights out). The truth? They're just bland. This was the worst character portrayal and development I've seen in quite a while. It's like the author grabbed many different ideas, threw them all in a blender and "Voila! Characters". Erm..no, just no. Prophet: He was ok, I guess. I don't have much to say about him, other than he's lethal (thanks Tom). We don't get to see much of his expertise in stuff, and that right there is pretty annoying. Instead of reading about Prophet using his oh-so-lethal skills, we just know about most of them through Tom (who really doesn't even know Prophet all that much either). We could say Prophet's not bad, but nothing to write home about either. Yeah, he's a tourtured hero, but we've all read this sorft of stuff a thousand times already, and I'm personally not impressed. Tom: Now this guy simply annoys the ever-living fuck out of me. Ever since he and Prophet met, I knew I wouldn't like him. Again, this was the author's fault. Half the time, whatever Tom was saying or thinking made no sense/was too intense with no apparent reason/was out of the blue. In the end, in my opinion, Tom comes through as a psycho. And emo. As for the interactions and relation between our heroes, it was a mess. The author kept trying to make them so mysterious, so conflicted, and so everything, that it ended up being ridiculous. Firstly, they were both constantly licking their wounds/suffering/awaiting inminent destruction. I can handle that, but give me a clue! You've got to give the reader something to keep him/her interested and seemingly aware of what's going on. We got to see some of Prophet's past  through his flashbacks  , but not Tom's, so his constant whining made no fucking sense. Like I said before, the "too much" went onto anything. 80% of the conversations between the characters were cryptic, and I'm pretty sure they made a lot of sense on the author's mind. Well, guess what? They didn't, at least not for me. Here's an example: "How'd you know about the breakfast food?" "You mumbled about it in your sleep." Come on now, is it really necessary to make a big deal out of everything? It's not exactly uncommon for someone to have breakfast. Pretty much all the conversations between them were like that. Annoying doesn't even begin to cover it. The action parts were the best, and I believe that was because our MCs couldn't afford to talk to each other all that much then. Thanks to the pace during those moments, I could keep on reading and eventually finished the book. Will I be reading the second one? Yes, I'll give it a try. Mainly because of the cliffhanger ending.

Farmhands George and Lennie decide to strike it out on their own - a decision George is sure to regret by the end of this novella, which touches on dark, dismal themes such as euthanasia, murder, and the treatment of women and the mentally handicapped; it is by no reason an easy read, thematically speaking. Steinbeck's prose is lovely and the story is compelling and realistic (sadly). I didn't love how Steinbeck treated Curley's wife. First off, she has no name. Her name is derived wholly from her husband. She has no identity without him. The novella shames her time and time again, calling her a tart, no good, trouble, etc. At every turn she's dehumanized. Maybe Steinbeck was sexist. Maybe he wanted his readers to draw parallels between the treatment of women and the treatment of mentally handicapped - though George does his best to look out for Lennie, he's constantly asked why he bothers to do so. Maybe there's a connection between the fact that both Lennie and Curley's wife end up dead? Perhaps this is worth a re-read for that reason alone.

There are two kind of vampires in the world: those who accept the new ways and those who wish to bring back the ways of old. The Darkbloods are vampires who believe human lives and blood are theirs for the taking. Especially those known as "sweetbloods." Humans with that special quality in their blood are especially sought after, so much so that Darkbloods sell vials of the stuff on the street like it's a drug. Dominic is one of the vampires who embraces a life lived side by side with humanity. He rarely partakes in human blood and when he does -it's never to kill. He works for a group known as the Agency. They are vampires who police the rest of their kind and fight the Darkbloods. It's just after he is gravely injured, that Mac stumbles across Dom's path. She is a sweetblood -and though he tries to resist her, the pull is too strong and he takes her blood. He takes so much, in fact, that he must give her some of his own to save her life. The exchange activates a blood bond between the two, a rare and binding tie, which allows them to sense each others emotions and even share thoughts. The story was easy to get into. The world-building easy to follow. And perhaps most importantly, the building sexual tension between the two main characters was played to perfection. However, there was a bit of predictability as the story arc played out. I think some of the foreshadowing was a little heavy handed and I would have liked to be surprised a little more. Also, I found some of the scenes cut off a bit more abruptly than I'd like -and we'd see days or weeks gone as we went into another scene without seeing immediate repurcussions of what happened immediately before. All that being said, I did enjoy it. It was an easy read, not to complex, with some hot sex. Almost 4 stars.

Mermaids! Not something that comes along all that often, 'coz I understand it makes things very, very complicated. It was okay here since the mermaids would automatically (although painfully) get legs once ashore, which obviously kills what's ususally the main problem. So what conflict to base this story on? Viciousness. Lore teaches us that mermaids were as beautiful as they were cruel, which is already awesome basics as such. Plus, here mermaids feed on the emotions they drain out of their victims, killing them in the process, which makes them kinda the water version of a vampire. I love the concept of that! Back to the vicisouness, and how it plays into the story: Merman Calder was, other than his three sisters, not born a mermaid, but made one after he almost drowned as a child. Later, his mermaid mother was killed, and now the sisters want vengeance. The man responsible owed his son's life to the Lake Superior merclan, and now that the man is dead and his son, now with a family of his own, moved back to the lake, it's payback time. To get the non-swimmer into the water, Calder is to use his daughter Lily -- any means necessary. If that plan does not earn the Viciousness Approval stamp from you, I can't help you. But having a plan, and carrying it out are two entirely different stories. Because Calder doesn't have his heart in it like his sisters. Of course he owed his mermaid mother a second chance at life, although with some alterations, but he's not hellbent on vengeance. He only wants his oldest sister to release him from the clan, so he would no longer have to migrate back to Lake Superior every year, but can be free and do as he pleases. Calder can have his freedom -- after the sisters got what is rightfully theirs. Okay, no biggie. Except that Calder makes the cardinal error to fall for Lily of all people. Now it's not just that he's a murderous fish while she is human what makes things complicated, it's also that Calder has to help kill her father in order to be freed. Adds a whole other taste of viciousness to it, doesn't it?? I loved it, the concept a lot more than the style or plot as it played out. But the characters were good, especially Lily. I think I liked her even more because she was the outside perspective instead of the inside, because this book is from Calder's POV. Male POV in YA is not common, but I very much hope to meet more of it soon! And of course I'm looking forward to the sequel. This was a sweet, feel-good read, which I was in desperate need of. I turn to these sort of books when I'm recovering from illness or surgery. You know, those books that are comfort food? This is one of them. Anna, along with other Russian nobility, finds herself among the working class of England after the fall of the Tsar. Czar? I always mix those up. Anyhow, she is uncomplaining and determined to be happy in her circumstances. Anna is wise enough to know that the answer to most anything can be found in a book, so she embarks upon her new housekeeping endeavor with The Domestic Servant's Compendium, by Selena Strickland, tucked into her bag. She references this massive, three volume tome often in regards to her duties as a maid, much to her below stairs companions' amusement and sometimes irritation. Now, I loved Anna immediately. Her fellow servants quickly grew to love her. Almost everyone came to adore Anna. Normally, this Mary Sue type business is nauseating for me. I can't quite figure out what makes Anna such an appealing heroine. She's alive and full of life, and her attitude is contagious. She brooks zero nonsense and isn't afraid to be frank about it, all the while being kind. Maybe traditional Mary Sue characters tend to lack passion? They also tend to be tragic, and Anna simply is not. The other displaced Russian characters and their similar perseverance and joy made me want to hang out at their club. I'd specifically like to spend more time with Prince Sergei, Anna's gorgeous cousin and now taxi driver! The downstairs servants were likewise enjoyable, but I have no desire to join their ranks. Proom, the butler, was my favorite! Such a sense of loyalty and family below stairs that extends to those living above. A few beautiful, yet ugly villains to despise. My hate for Murial was honed into something as sharp as I felt for Delores Umbridge! It's no surprise there's a love story in all this. While it's a central theme, it's danced around in the story very lightly. Things unfold gradually and are barely hinted at, never overtaking the story or becoming boring. My only disappointment was in Rupert. While I would've had him behave in a less noble and martyr-ish manner, my real beef was  that he gave up on Anna so easily. Proom had to scheme to get them into the same room. Come on! That is so NOT what a romantic hero does. He was supposed to give up his stupid pride & go after the girl! It all turned out in the end, but I feel an opportunity was missed for him to act the hero. 5 stars. Highly recommended. It made me happy.

But then everything fell apart when Rachel decided to go off into prairie with a man she secretly loved for 12 years instead of pursuing her academic career. I was honestly rooting for her to go to college. Love by the Letter is a prequel novella to Jagear's Unexpected Brides series. Maybe 3.5 stars... *Thank you to Netgalley, the publishers, and the author for a free copy of this book in exchange for a fair review. **Some unavoidable spoilers for book one. Brief Summary: It's been two months since Adam awoke Cabeswater. Adam is changing into a person he doesn't recognize. Ronan is still learning about how his ability to take things from his dreams works. Blue is still wondering where her feelings lie, with Gansey or with Adam. Gansey is more impatient then ever to find the magical Welsh king, Glendower. The Ley line's energy is acting strange and a hit man comes to town to investigate. Review: The world building in these books is unique, intriguing, and captivating. The same is true for all of Ms. Stiefvater's characterizations. With each description of Blue and the Aglionby boys, I felt like another layer was being added. This author is so good at enchanting you with her writing style and with her characters' mystique that you almost don't realize how slow the story is coming together. Almost. My major problem with this book was the pacing. I love not being able to predict the plot, and I love being presented with a fantasy book that is different from other's I've read, but I still want answers and meaningful action. After finishing this book, I feel like there are SOO many more questions than there are answers. Much of the action was at the end, and some of it felt like it came out of left field. I'm still stumped at how that cliff hanger ending came about! All the action with Kavinsky was fantastic, but I couldn't figure where all his hate emanated from. Did he have an unrequited crush on Ronan? The Grey Man was a charming enigma, but his actions didn't always read plausible. And the romance, or lack of romance, just left me shaking my head. I'm not going to deny it. I wanted a Blue and Adam romance. Adam's emotional vulnerability ,to me, makes him the more appealing love interest. There was very little romance in this book, and I never thought that what romance there was would center on Maura! Recommendation: If you love a slowly unfolding paranormal story with multi-dimensional characters, beautifully descriptive writing, and a hint of romance, then try this book. (You have to read book one first, though.) I look forward to reading the third book! My reviews at FictionSnoop

Poor baby! Don't cha just wanna love and protect this little guy? In Kim Dare's Duck!, Raynard, a Hawk in the Nest, sees Ori being mistreated and steps in. He also can't help but notice his submissiveness. He takes Ori under his wing (pun intended) and offers him a servant position in his home. Ori, believed to be a Duck though he has yet to experience his full shift, is used and abused by the members of Nest because Ducks are the lowest on the Avian totem pole. While he's unsure what will be expected of him in Raynard's care, he believes the Hawk will not mistreat him based on the way he scolded the bullies. Their life together starts off a little bumpy at first. Ori literally trips over himself to please his new Master. Raynard eventually approaches Ori with the suggestion that he become his sub. Ori jumps at the offer and the two begin the second part of their relationship as M/s. Throughout this time, Kim does a wonderful job of portraying the growth in both characters and their relationship. The day finally comes when Ori is ready to make is full shift. Raynard has explained to him the wants and needs of a Duck. He's also reassured him that, following his shift in front of the elders, he will return to his side and wear his collar once again. Only things don't happened as expected. Ori, disoriented from his shift and unsure what he looks like, awakes to everyone calling him "Sire". He's confused and realizes that Raynard has abandoned him. Ori discovers that instead of shifting into a Duck he is a Swan, the most cherished among the avian. He is thrust into a position he does not know how to control or survive in. He reaches out to Raynard only to be told Hawks and Swans do not belong together; Swans are not submissive. Raynard is also struggling with this realization. He feels terrible for having misjudged Ori's nature and for having trained him in the ways of a submissive when he is never to be one. Raynard returns to the Nest a month later to reassure himself that Ori has accepted his role within the Nest and doing well only to find him gaunt and devastated. Hamilton, one of the elders who I didn't particularly like initially, has spoken with Ori and learned his true desire to return to Raynard. He convinces Raynard to give Ori another chance and understand that not every avian fits a specific mold or stereotype. Each avian is different, with different needs, and Ori needs the control Raynard brought into his life. I loved this book and will definitely be reading more of Kim Dare's work.

My feelings on this one are.... Complicated. Hooey. On the one hand, some of my feelings from "Litany of Earth" haven't changed, such as being a little annoyed Ms. Emerys took the black and white approach by making the Deep Ones basically completely innocent victims of the 1920's raid rather than making these two cultures have legitimate gripes with one another. I forgive her a little of her softening the Deep Ones by having them actually show up though! Which was neat. Most people say they liked the "Litany of Earth" novella better than this book, and I can see why. This book does drag, and if you don't care for descriptions of esoteric books or the characters themselves, this book will be quite boring. The book oddly speeds up right at the very end, I think when the author realized she needed do something to wrap things up since nothing had really happened throughout the rest of the book. Ms. Emerys mentions how she had only planned on writing the original novella, and it shows in the book's pacing. The virtue signaling was quite grating in the beginning, with how often the main character has to point out how she doesn't subscribe to any of those nasty -isms. Oh, and if you are a white male, you are going to be antagonistic in some way: female students all have more potential than the male ones, female librarians are more helpful, male government agents are bullies, etc. You get the drift. The only males who are allies are blood relatives or gay. Not even kidding. But despite all of its problems, I enjoyed myself more with this than the novella. And I think it has to do with the prolonged time with the characters. Emerys was able to spend more time with a novel's worth of story to allow me to care about the characters, and allow me to get used to her vastly different interpretation of the Deep Ones. Though I found myself sometimes wishing the book would speed things along, I became invested in Aphra's journey to rebuild Innsmouth. Though I think Audrey is the most interesting character of the lot. Mad Ones ahoy! So despite my eye rolling at some of the heavy handedness of the 'political correcting' of the original "Shadow Over Innsmouth" and the erratic pace of the plot, I overall ended up liking the book. I don't know if I could recommend it to Lovecraft fans, as it has none of his atmosphere, themes or original creations; merely using names of his characters and setting for the author's political viewpoints. But I have come to care enough about the characters that I will be reading the sequel; not for the plot though, as I can't say there's really much of one to follow. Edit: Thinking on it some more made me dock 1 star off the rating. On top of the problems I mentioned before, the whole point of the book being to not believe in malicious unfounded rumors seems to fly out of the window when one of the characters is revealed to have a dark family history and everyone.... proceeds to view that character differently based on malicious unfounded rumors. And in this case it turns out to be true! So what was the point of making the Innsmouth people all flowers and rainbows when Ms.Emerys was just going to shift the authentic big bad boogeyman label to another group and have the resulting prejudice be justified...? Seems to undermine the whole purpose of this 'revisionism' to me.

Serena Barton was a governess but she was let go. And she knows who was at fault. Now, she sits in the square outside the city apartment of the Duke of Clermont for eight or nine hours a day. And she is prepared to wait him out. Hugo Marshall is the Duke's fixer and is so good at his job that he is called the Wolf of Clermont. He is told to get rid of Miss Barton. But his eventual solution is rather unconventional. Hugo often solves his problems by thinking out of the box. For example, he doesn't take a salary from the Duke. The man has no qualms about not paying people who do work for him, so Hugo frames his salary as a bet and a percentage of the profit. Gentlemen always pay their gambling debts. He might have been a boxer, but there is nothing wrong with his brain. He asks the Duke why this girl is trying to shame him and is told that he promised her the governess job for his unborn child; it's lies. The wolf offers her money, he pays people to sit on her bench, he pays the landlord to throw them out and he tries to talk sense into her. His reputation precedes him but Serena isn't frightened of him. And she isn't leaving. Eventually, he guesses the truth. The duke forced himself on her but Serena clings to the idea that she wasn't raped because she kept silent. Hugo has no such issues with definitions. She isn't sure what she wants other than a future education for the child she carries and she'll fight for it. But the one thing she won't be is silent any more. Hugo is furious. His personal rules are no swearing, no drinking and no hurting women. But he has a large payout waiting, 500 pounds, if the Duke can talk his wealthy pregnant wife into coming home. She has left after his last affair. A pregnant ex-governess would destroy the fragile remnants of the Duke's marriage and remove his income source. Her father made sure her fortune was paid out in instalments. Meanwhile, Serena sits outside of the house and with time, her predicament will be obvious to all. But what neither expected is that in matching wits they both feel a frisson of attraction. And with him, Serena feels safe. I see, she wrote slowly on the reverse of his letter. You've been watching me. If you'll look out your window now, I have a special surprise for you. She handed this to the butler and then stood by her bench, waiting. Her heart pounded. Her hands were clammy. God, Freddy had it right--she jumped into everything without thinking, and now look what-- Her breath caught. A figure appeared in a window on the second floor. She couldn't make out any features, just a dark silhouette. Still, he could probably see her in sunlit detail. Serena forced her lips to curve into a smile. The Wolf of Clermont raised his hand. Before she could lose her nerve, Serena made a fist and delivered an extremely rude gesture. He stood at the window, stock-still, before turning away. She received his note not two minutes later. She opened it, her heart pounding. But there were only two words on the paper. Marry me. She writes back... I was wondering when you would start threatening me with fates worse than death. Congratulations, Mr. Marshall. I am now officially frightened. (Kindle Locations 724-732) Bwahaha. I saw one comment that the leads are people who are damaged but not broken, and that's true but Serena is almost broken. She lives with her sister Freddy on a meagre fifteen pounds a year income, and is so hurt that she flinches when Hugo merely touches her hand. And Hugo's back story is heartbreaking. It's also different to read a Regency romance about two ordinary people. So the cover is wrong; just wrong... sighs. Can they work it out and be together? Is she worth more than 500 pounds to him? And the way he takes her to bed on their first time together is absolutely the best way to deal with a rape victim, and it's incredibly sexy, too. The two sons are the eponymous Brothers Sinister, named for their left handedness, and Robert (now Duke) is the hero in the Duchess War while Oliver is his right hand man. Or should that be left? 4 sinistral stars

I loved this book so much. It's my favorite kind of romance, where the romance is really a vehicle for personal growth. Yes, Willem is dreamy, yes the immediate spark between Allyson and Willem made me alternately hold my breath and sigh, but that all takes place in the first half of the book and the book is about so much more than that. Willem's abrupt disappearance breaks Allyson's heart and sends her on something of a downward spiral, but she never would have figured herself out without that loss as a catalyst. Even when she goes back to Europe to search for him, it's not really about him. It's about herself. She wants to find that girl she was when she was with him that day, to see if that was really her "true self". I thought I'd be disappointed that easily half the book had no Willem, but I was so caught up in Allyson's journey that I really didn't mind. Allyson had to do that on her own. If they'd been together from that day, I don't think she would have taken any of the steps she took on her own. I felt so proud of Allyson by the end. Her steps forward into a new version of herself weren't easy or perfect. She made mistakes, she doubted herself and what she was doing, but she kept going, and by the end I really felt she'd made peace with what she had with Willem, no matter how it ended up working out. She was able to go back and appreciate the experience and what it did for her without being simply crushed by losing him. Loved this book. I think I'm going to go back and immediately re-read, which I almost never do.

3.5 (I rounded up) This is my second (first) Collins & Rideout novel and once again the theme here is girl-who-complains-about-not-being-very-pretty and yet she manages to get ALL THE GUYS. It's completely baffling because it's not even as if she suddenly became more confident and therefore more guys start to sit up and take notice of her. I couldn't help but roll my eyes every time a new guy began flirting with her and/or asked her out because hey she was supposed to be mousy and nothing 'special'. And ** Do couples really give one week anniversary presents? That's a bit much to me, but that could just be because I don't really keep track of anniversaries. The other thing that really bothered me was the age of the girls. They were sophomores, Zahra was fifteen but they acted like they were juniors or seniors. It just didn't make sense to me that girls so young would have gone threw almost every single relationship problem one can experience in high school. I was really skeptical as to how well Kali's matchmaking formula worked that was the only part of the business that seemed highly implausible to me. Granted there are people who love to match make (hello Emma) but that doesn't mean they are always going to be good at it. Kali's system wasn't always perfect which I liked but it was a very vague process as to how exactly she calculated their compatibility. Surprisingly this was one book I didn't mind not having the perspectives of all the main characters. Zahra best describes the three girls' personalities "Kali bubbles over with options, so if she were in charge of mediation, no one would stay together long. She's a 'grass is always greener' type, I'm a 'look how green this grass is' type, and Syd's a 'torch the lawn' type. The balance works for us" (pg. 263), and they become fully vibrant characters through her narration. Syd and Kali's stories were fully explored, I finished the book feeling as though I fully understood each of the three girls as well as the minor characters. It's a long book and sometimes I would put it down and forget to pick it back up but I never felt lost upon resuming it and the pace was good. The story is highly entertaining, the methods of revenge are mostly realistic and quite impressive in how easily they could be replicated in real life as are the other aspects of the business except for the matchmaking. The meditation process made a lot of sense, sometimes all relationships need is a person in the middle to help bring them to their senses. And as harsh as the break up service seemed, sometimes it was handled better than what the other person might have done. Love, Inc is a diverting read that isn't sickeningly sick, instead it's the right mix of lighthearted fun combined with accessible, genuine lessons about crushes and relationships. A bonus was the fact that Zahra was half Pakistani but her heritage wasn't the center of the plot, instead it focused on her relationship business that she started with Syd and Kali. She does complain a lot about her Scottish red hair and not feeling like a fully fledged MOT (Member of the Tribe) but she worries that her mother's parents who are visiting from Pakistan want to keep her newly separated parents apart permanently. Therefore she does everything in her power to resist her grandparents efforts to make her fully embrace her heritage, she doesn't want it to seem like shes betraying her dad's heritage and giving up on their marriage. I also loved how the setting of Austin, Texas was like a fourth main character which I love especially because I know little about Texas. Austin sounds like a vibrant, entertaining and artful city. I definitely recommend this story for the summer, not too heavy but not too light and if you liked John Tucker Must Die, you will really like this book. PS This quote amused me and also gave me something to think about "'You're getting brainwashed and you don't even know it. Pretty soon they'll have you wrapped up in a sari and on a plane to Karachi. They'll marry you off to the first old guy who offers a decent dowry.' 'Zahra! You're like a racist or something.' [Saliyah-Zahra's sister] 'It's not racism when you're mocking your own culture'" (pg. Hmm is it or isn't it? I'm inclined to agree with her but I'm not 100% sure how I feel about mocking your own culture. Especially because someone will inevitably complain that that's 'not fair'.

I guess it was inevitable. In a shortlist containing 6 books, odds were that there would be one that I wouldn't really be that enthused about. While in last year's shortlist that happened to be Jim Crace's Harvest, this year that "honour" fell to Howard Jacobson's J. Jacobson is actually a previous Booker winner, with The Finkler Question, a book I have not picked up or even heard of before I started this year's J but which seems to have split the Goodreads reviewers right down the middle. J is touted as the kind of book that needs to be mentioned in the same breath as 1984 and Brave New World, according to my dust jacket. Hint: if there's one thing you just don't do with this year's list it's reading the cover/jacket. If they're not spoiling parts of the plot as in We Are All Completely Beside Ourselves, they're clearly trying to influence my opinion or reading of the book. Make no mistake: this is no way in the same league as Huxley or Orwell and to even suggest it is laughable at best. The story concerns Kevern (pronounced Key-vern) Cohen and Ailinn Solomons, living in a European country (which may or may not be England; all we're told is that is has a coastline) in the wake of WHAT HAPPENED, IF IT HAPPENED, an event of such unspeakable horror that people cannot talk about it. Throughout the book, there are small references to it, flashbacks to violence as people reminisce about it. Kevern is the son of "aphids", strangers in a small community. He creates lovespoons for the local shops and teaches a class at the local university, until he is pushed into Ailinn's arms. From the very first time, they don't know whether it's been a fortuitous thing or if there is something deeper. Fundamentally, they are broken people (Kevern's father unable to pronounce the letter J without putting two fingers on his lips) and Ailinn adopted from an orphanage, with no inkling of her past or parentage. The biggest issue is how fundamentally unlikeable these characters are. I mean all of them. In this dystopian future domestic violence is the norm. Characters are all incredibly misogynistic and I just couldn't get behind that at all. I can understand the reasons why, but in fairness a lot of it read like a "real life" version of the worst internet comments you could imagine. It's not that far away from the current reality so to be honest, I was neither shocked nor particularly appalled. The men are horrid, the women are mostly as background decoration, with a couple of exceptions; sounds all too familiar. Ultimately, I just didn't find anything about the book engaging. With the exception of Ailinn, who can still be annoying, everyone is basically a write-off. The language is far too flowery when there is no reason to, the world building is haphazard and not very well thought out and at its core, it is a book about the Holocaust . Once I had figured that out, everything seemed far less interesting. Not because the subject has now become passe somehow, but because it has been done before and better. Jacobson brings nothing to the table here, and I think it shows in how much of a struggle it was for me to go through it. I genuinely cannot see this winning the Prize this year, but I could be very wrong. I am honestly happy to be done with it for now. Perhaps, in future, I will be able to tackle more of his writing (I am intrigued by The Finkler Question, I will admit) but this time, it was just not to be.

Like, Darkness Before Dawn before it, Blood-Kissed Sky was the good with the bad. Overall, it felt like a stronger book than DBD, in large part for the lack of romantic wibbling, but it also felt much shorter and in many ways was less satisfying. Despite having a really nice twist (well, one of them. The main twist was eye-rollingly predictable and not that exciting), BKS feels like half a book. On the plus side, JA London developed the three things I was most intrigued by in DBD -- Ian Hightower, the Night Train and Los Angeles. My problem with all three is that BKS didn't spend enough time letting us take in/enjoy them -- BKS had a LOT of telling and forward action, not a lot of showing/time to enjoy the world build. One problem I had, which is a personal feeling that others may not share, is that BKS missed a great opportunity to expand its world and develop Dawn as a character. She's sent on a mission to Los Angeles to investigate the Thirst and thrown into the company of Ian Hightower, one of the series' most intriguing characters. But instead of developing new characters, showing us more about the world by Dawn's interaction with people and places outside of Denver, we get the easy story: Michael and Tegan go with Dawn and Richard and Faith show up. I would have been fine with Richard and Faith (well, more Richard, less Faith -- Faith is a massive Buffy knock-off/Vampire Sue), but I groaned out loud, twice, when they revealed that Michael was Dawn's guard and Tegan snuck abroad the train. Since neither character is much to write home about (and the Michael/Dawn "romantic tension," like in DBD, is non-existent), BKS becomes driven by inert, uninteresting characters. Dawn is still a nebulous character -- she's a bit ballsier in BKS, but still has no personality beyond "is forward sometimes." Victor is basically non-existent in this book, which didn't bother me that much (see: less romantic wibbling), but contributed to BKS feeling like a bridge book. I mourn the missed opportunity to have Dawn strike out on her own, have to make new allegiances and introduce some mundane dramatic tension. London is GREAT at sudden and big dramatic tension -- the "mini" twist that happens in L.A. is wonderful -- but there's no real sense of rising action/continual suspense throughout the rest of the book. It's inconsistent. I guessed the "big" twist about fifty pages in, maybe less. Basically as soon as Victor said her blood was different/intoxicating, I knew Dawn was "OMG SPECIAL" and then when she saw the symbol on the mountain/scroll? It was PAINFULLY OBVIOUS what the twist would be. The one time they describe what they do, yes, they sound terrible, but you're *telling* me something very general. If they had SHOWN the reader a grotesque, inhumane application of the V-system (major missed opportunity when Dawn is in L.A.! ), then maybe we could have been somewhat appalled. This is not a book I would have selected for myself. It was a birthday present from a close relative who enjoyed it so much she wanted to share it with me - and I'm glad she did. I'm also glad that I waited until the holidays to read it, because I'm not sure I would've followed the book's complex, multi-layered plot very well if I'd read it in spits and spurts. As it happened, I read the entire 500+ pages in 72 hours while on a camping trip, burning through the pages of lyrical prose, as desperate as Daniel to unravel the mysteries of The Shadow of the Wind. Zafon paints a rich portrait of Barcelona after the civil war, bringing to life a city and an era that I previously knew nothing about. I fell in love with many of the book's characters, particularly the eternally optimistic, slightly naive protagonist Daniel; the enigmatic subject of Daniel's fascination, Julian Carax; and Daniel's slightly crazy, lewd-but-loveable older friend Fermin. The plot contains two overarching stories - Daniel's and Julian's - which mirror each other and become increasingly intertwined as the book progresses. The cast of characters is quite huge, but each character plays an important part in the story. For me, The Shadow of the Wind is very much about loneliness, regret and the darker side of human nature, but is also laced with romance, kindness and love. It is also a book for book lovers. It captures the powerful relationship between a book and its reader beautifully, with passages such as: 'Under the warm light cast by the reading lamp, I was submerged into a new world of images and sensations peopled by characters who seemed as real to me as my surroundings. Page after page I let the spell of the story and its world take me over, until the breath of dawn touched my window and my tired eyes slid over the last page. I lay in the bluish half-light with the book on my chest and listened to the murmur of the sleeping city. My eyes began to close, but I resisted. I did not want to lose the story's spell or bid farewell to its characters just yet.' Oh, that wonderful feeling of having finished a good book. Show me a book lover who can't relate to that passage! But although I adored this book, I also found it immensely frustrating. I had a love/hate relationship with its descriptive prose, because for every heartbreakingly beautiful passage, there were countless others that (in my opinion) could have benefited from a good prune. My main issue with this book, though, relates to the narrative. Although the story is predominantly told in first person from Daniel's perspective, there are large chunks that involve others recounting their memory of past events to Daniel. These memories add depth and further the plot, however they contain insights that are impossible for the person recounting the memory to have. For example, if I was telling you a story about a man I met years ago and hadn't been in contact with since, it would seem odd if I told you exactly what he was doing and precisely what he was thinking months after our last meeting. The Shadow of the Wind was riddled with point-of-view errors of this nature, and they marred an otherwise amazing reading experience for me. Zafon is obviously a masterful story teller, so I don't understand why he couldn't have applied his skills to provide us with these insights through other means. Despite the issues I've highlighted, The Shadow of the Wind is definitely a powerful, worthwhile read. I recommend it to anyone who enjoys multi-layered gothic fiction or stories that explore the darker side of human nature.

This review is also posted on my blog, Mad Scibrarian N. K. Jemisin attended a NASA-funded workshop titled Launch Pad which was meant to help "media influencers" understand science. This then helps media influencers such as a Sci-Fi/Fantasy author to write about accurate science since much of the public's misconceptions about science is from the media. This was in the acknowledgements section of the book and I'm glad I have that piece of information to go off of while writing this review, though my lack of actual Earth Science is going to be apparent. What I would just like to say is that I think N. K. Jemisin wrote a well-researched piece of fiction that involves people with the ability to manipulate the Earth. I don't have the time to fully research all of the Earth Science used in the book, but from what I remember from my primary schooling, I believe the terminology used works well with the concepts. Now, it IS a piece of fantasy fiction, so I'm sure it is still left to the author's own whimsy, but if I wanted to learn more about Earth Science I think I would find some similarities. If I ever gauge enough interest/time to investigate it further, perhaps I will update this review. With that bit, I did spoil that there are people who can manipulate the Earth in the book, but that is where I will stop. I believe you should just go into this book blind. Mrs. Jemisin throws you into her world and you are left trying to figure it out. It takes a little time to grasp things, so you may be confused or find it slow at first. I definitely don't think I am "fluent" after reading just the first book, but part of reading a fantasy is the worldbuilding. It's good for a trilogy for more to be explored. Her world has many features including discrimination, repression, diversity, and more. I will leave it up to you to discover it all. One thing that prevented this book from getting 5 stars from me is that I was a little disappointed with __________. Yeah, I can't word it at all without spoilers. Here is the spoiler bracket: The fact that Essun, Damaya, and Syenite all end up being the same person. We start out following 3 points of view characters and each grow on me so much. I thoroughly enjoyed each person's point of view, and by the end when I find out they are all the same person, instead of liking that one character even more, I am saddened to find out that throughout the whole book there was only one character. Not to say none of the side characters are great, I love Alabaster and Tonkee and Hoa are interesting, but now I only know I get to follow this 1 super great main character in the next book instead of following 3 super great main characters. And isn't the more the merrier? And while Essun's point of view is 2nd person so it kinda gives hints to the timeline of the story, the fact that a lot of this could've been figured out by featuring a timeline at the beginning at each chapter is frustrating. It's literally the author leaving off that one piece of information that prevents giving it all away. It just feels like a cop-out or lack of creativity at the author's part. Also, Mrs. Jemisin uses the name changes THREE times to help with her trickery. Damaya changes her name to Seynite as she becomes a ringed orogene for the Fulcrum. Seynite changes her name to Essun as she tries to run from her past. Then we have Tonkee who ends up being Binof Leadership Yumenes from Damaya's past encounter while breaking into the chamber in the Fulcrum. It's the same trick on THREE separate occasions and who knows if she is done. Is it partially me being frustrated that I never saw it coming? Slightly, but at some point I did start thinking Syenite was also Essun because I didn't see how there could be ANOTHER free orogene that has been so clearly trained in her abilities. I just hope this trend of re-naming for the sake of a "twist" ends here. I do truly appreciate the opportunity to learn Essun's past this way; I'm just frustrated that leaving out just the time made me unable to piece it all together fully. With that said, names are pretty important in this world, with all of the above and the fact that people's use-castes (kind of like a born job or role into society that is recognized by officials) are a 2nd name. I will definitely be paying more attention to names as I continue the trilogy.

You can read the full review and more on my blog. The concept of this book fascinated me. I am familiar with the stories of Genesis like the story of my life, and have been educated thoroughly in the traditional commentary. Therefore, this book was scary to me - I didn't want it to besmirch the names that are holy to me. However, more than anything I found The Red Tent a beautiful story, and maybe a thought experiment on the people I'm descended from. The setting was one of the most incredible I've read - Dinah speaks to all the women of the generations, and tells us her story. She starts with that of her mothers' - with all the facts and all the feelings, and no anachronistic judgements to marr the picture. She describes the house of Jacob in such detail that you feel Cnaan in the late Bronze Age - feel the heat, see the views, smell the food cooking and the animals. Hear the children, play in the red tent with the women, feel the pain and joy of motherhood along with them. Truly, it was an experience to read. The climax in this story, the turning point, is also the only incident from which we hear of Dinah in the bible. This is also the place in which our story parts ways with the traditional narrative. It was beautiful, and happy and sad all at once. The dramatic bit itself was rushed - I found it hard to follow what was happening until later. The third part of the novel takes place in Egypt. This part was the saddest, but also the slowest and a little... boring. However, I found the existence of this storyline in which Dinah finds herself in Egypt very interesting, because there is a legend saying she did but no explanation was given. The full circle in which we come to in the end basically made me cry. Like the rest of the book, it was beautiful and tragic.

I did not enjoy reading this book very much. Overuse of the, like, teenage vernacular was, well, like, meg annoying. I understand that the author was just trying to make the character's narration realistic, but he could have avoided this problem by using a 3rd person narration instead of 1st person. (What is it with modern writers, especially those who write for YA audiences, and their insistence on writing everything in 1st person?) Also, I hate to admit this, but I just couldn't understand several key parts of the story, such as: what was with the skin lesions? Maybe I missed something somewhere, but I found that completely baffling. Also, I couldn't understand Anderson's portrayal of this futuristic world. Part of the time, things seemed to be artificial (the artificial sun, the fake beef "farms," etc), but other times there seemed to be real trees and natural elements. Were the suburb bubbles totally enclosed? I just couldn't figure out how his up-car was moving through the world, and what the world looked like. Of course, I understand that the main point of the story was to explore the implications of our electronic "wired-ness" and where it might all lead. These are worthy ideas and concerns and definitely worth exploring. I'm looking forward to the discussions in my local community this summer that will focus on Feed as our "One Great Read" but as a reading experience, I'd have to say this book was not a great one for me. (Note to SLM -- Still, I look forward to talking with you about this!)

Yes, this is a good book. You already know that. I liked the way jaunting seemed very important to the story at the beginning. It helped get me in to the setting. Once things picked up, I didn't think about jaunting any more. It's not that it wasn't utilized, just that I was so immersed in the world that it didn't seem notable. I wasn't there analyzing the way jaunting works. For this reason, I accepted it when the space-jaunting thing happened. It was fair within the laws of the world, so I believed it. The plot moves really fast. This is a quick read, but a lot happens. There was no slow beginning. No boring part in the middle. No long haven sequences of self-reflection. Characters are introduced and developed without taking away from the story. It's a perfect balance of action, character, and meaning. Bester did a good job of making women actual characters. At the same time, I'm not entirely pleased  with the sexual assault. No one thought this guy was good, it wasn't necessary to prove it. And it seemed somewhat minimized, only being mentioned once after. Still, I'd rather have that than have a likable female character completely destroyed for the rest of the book. I guess. The science was good too. It obviously isn't realistic, but it was explained in a way I accept and it didn't break its own rules. That's a huge win. Overall, this was a great book.

After looking forward to reading this series for almost a year, I was disappointed at the beginning of The Iron King. Julie Kagawa forces every cliche in the YA genre into the first part of her novel: the uncaring parents, the funny best friend, the dark and mysterious stranger. My disappointment stemmed mostly from Meghan's character. She is a sixteen year old girl who begins the book by bemoaning the poverty of her family and mooning over a football player. The mysterious disappearance of Meghan's brother finally starts the ball rolling - Meghan becomes a much more interesting character because of her love for her brother. However, she regularly forgets the reason she made the journey into the land of the Fey. One look from Prince Ash, and she's forgotten all about her brother! My gripes with Meghan aside, I must admit that the book got a lot better as the plot progressed, especially at Part III. I liked Prince Ash - mostly because he seemed like a genuinely good person. I never did understand exactly when Ash and Meghan fell in love, there seemed to be many glances and gasps, and suddenly, randomly, they were kissing. I felt sorry for Robbie (Puck), but usually the scenes he was in felt strained and awkward, especially when it became clear he was the third wheel in the romance. I loved the idea of using characters like King Oberon, Queen Tatiana and Puck from Shakespeare, the Summer Court is a lovely re-imagination of the play. I also liked the Iron Fey - fey are born from the aspirations of mortals, and the Iron Fey were created because of mankind's progress with technology. I feel I should point out that the book needs a little more editing. When someone says, three quarters of the way through the book, that it's the first time Prince Ash has taken Meghan's name, I immediately go back and check if that's true. And it wasn't, Prince Ash had spoken to her and taken her name before. I feel that Julie Kagawa has a lot of potential, and since the quality of this book improved by the end, I am going to read the rest of the series. At the moment, however, I don't feel like this series deserves the hype it gets.

I am so glad that I finally re-read this stunning book. Though my heart is also all kinds of broken. But mostly I feel happy. Because I have so much love for these books. For Gansey. For Blue. We also get to know the boy, Kavinsky, more. And ugh. I hated most of the things he said. So badly. But he helped Ronan. A little bit. But.. I didn't like this boy. Maybe a little bit. If he hadn't been broken beyond repair. I was really curious about him, though. Probably :D A very small, very selfish voice inside Gansey whispered, What if you left him here, what if you made him find his own way back; what if he had to call you and apologize for once? Not once have he apologized to Gansey. I don't like Adam at all. And I don't get why they are friends with him. Hoping he might change, though. There is so much about The Dream Thieves. There is so much about it that I love. And so much about it broke my heart. There isn't much romance. But there are feelings. And they are hurtful and honest and just all kinds of perfect. I just loved this book to pieces. And I need you all to read it. Because it is all kinds of awesome. The characters are amazing. The plot is stunning. The magic is perfect. I just loved everything about The Dream Thieves. About Gansey. I cannot wait to get started on book three next. I first read The Dream Thieves from August 26th to 27th 2013. More reviews at Rondo of a Possible World: YA Book Reviews I had taken a Humanities course last year in my high school with the topic pertaining to Modernism. My favorite part of the course when when we were subjected to the world of Graffiti. Going to Five Points in NYC and seeing all the art that they wish to tear down and having a graffiti artist make something before my class's very eyes was exciting and absolutely enchanting. It's not like witnessing a Picasso but it has that existential forthcoming about it. The story was enjoyable, cute, and mystic in itself. Characters you just smile at when they stand next to each other and talk because they are just too adorable to even describe and sounds like "eep!" becomes the definition. The book was good, but not read-it-a-second-time good. The plot was quaint, the revitalization of art and expansion into the subgenre of graffiti definitely made Graffiti Moon an enjoyable and unique read in Young Adult. The hunt for Shadow and Poet, the most adorable names for graffiti artists I must say, lead to eventful and disastrous encounters. Right off the bat you're told who Shadow and Poet are and I really didn't know how that sat with me during the entire novel. It worked with the story but I see protocols like this numerously in novels girl wants to find mysterious guy + boy you don't really like is "mysterious guy" = you know the rest. The graffiti aspects thrown into this novel proved to be a beautiful expansion from most contemporary novels today and that made Graffiti Moon an original contemporary romance in my eyes. Art lovers and romantics definitely should jump into the pages of this novel.

I just can't believe it's all over. Emma and Calisto stole my heart in May 2016 and it's honestly felt like I've been waiting for years for them to finally get their happily ever after (It's September 2016, I haven't). Thankfully with indie publishing (in general) the wait between books is no longer a torturous nine months to a year but, a pleasant few months that still feel like they last forever. I knew we were going to be getting a happily ever after but I honestly had no idea how it would come about. Emma and Calisto were in such a sticky and delicate situation it almost seemed like they would never get out, and certainly not alive. I once read an TV writers' interview where they said they like to leave themselves in a huge dilemma for season finales and they get to enjoy their summer wondering how on earth their characters are going to get out of it. Clearly, Bethany Kris is one of these writers. I was so happy that Calisto and Emma managed to weather through the storm but I'm a bit sad at one thing that I will mention again later. The high stakes involved in this book were amazing. We pick up after Calisto's accident where he no longer remembers the past two years which would be fine if a) two years ago he didn't love Affonso b) He knew that Emma existed two years ago. Calisto loving Alberto was painful to read but I thought it was a great literary device to take us back to a time that had been alluded to since the very first book without actually going back in time. Emma is obviously suffering because not only does she have a high risk pregnancy and is still married to Affonso, the one true friend she has doesn't remember her and doesn't even speak to her beyond polite conversation. Life is hard I guess. Thankfully, a hard won victory occurs and Emma and Calisto get their happily ever after with their family, plus a bonus connection to the families of The Chicago War however their was one aspect that upset me: **MAJOR SPOILERS** Cross can never and will never know who his father is, he will never know that Calisto loves him just as much as his sister and if he does find out, it could destroy him. That hurts my soul, but Bethany Kris is playing well within mafia rules, so fair play to her. I've loved this series, I felt like it had a different, edgier tone to her other books and it was an interesting direction to go in. Rating: 4.5 stars

In Anna and the French Kiss and Lola and the Boy Next Door, we got two very slow-building romances. In fact, one half of each couple was with someone else for the majority of each book. In Isla and the Happily Ever After, we start off with romance. Isla, hopped up on painkillers after getting her wisdom teeth removed, heads out to a cafe called Kismet, where she runs into Josh, her long-time crush. While Isla is normally very shy, the painkillers take away some of her inhibitions that night, and she ends up having a very fun night with Josh. Back at school, Isla and Josh's relationship unfolds beautifully and realistically... until it also implodes, also quite realistically. I read this book in one sitting on a Saturday afternoon. I am a big fan of Stephanie Perkins' work, but Isla really surprised me. Anna and Lola had a very similar structure, very similar themes of unrequited love and leaving the one you might be comfortable with, but who isn't necessarily right for you. Isla is very different in that it's about finding yourself and not letting your insecurities get the best of you. In that way, it's actually a very frustrating book to read, because it's clear that Isla and Josh are so good for each other. They balance each other out perfectly. But Isla's insecurities and her uncertainty about what her future might hold end up putting a strain on her relationship with Josh until she snaps and breaks it off. Break up with him before he realizes he can do better than you. It's heartbreaking, and I almost cried reading it, because it's just so realistic. In Anna and Lola we saw what it takes for two people to realize they're meant for each other. In Isla, the story was more about what it takes to make that relationship actually work. And I think that's a good thing for teens, the target audience of these books. Yes, it's great to find someone you love. It's all sunshine and roses at the beginning. But as that relationship goes on, you have to work at it. And that's not often shown in YA novels. But yes, couples fight, and past relationships can come back to haunt you, and there will be days where you're not sure that it's going to work out. And that doesn't mean that your relationship is bad, or that you should break up, or that there's something wrong with you. It means that your relationship is normal, and I have to give Stephanie Perkins a lot of credit for doing a great job at showing that. Isla is so different from its predecessors, but it's still a really great book. Highly recommended for fans of Stephanie Perkins' works.

Sagan's Cosmos is a lovely book. So lovely, in fact, that I regret not having read it when I was younger. I'm sure youngsters everywhere would find this book both fun and educational in so many ways. Even though one might think that the book solely deals with the universe, cosmic bodies and space travel, it's far more complex then that. I'd venture to say that the point of the book is to make the reader think about some fundamental questions like, "Who are we?" and "What is this world/universe? Sagan goes about that task in an interesting way, by crafting a tale about life and, later on, the quest for knowledge, just liberally peppered with information about the universe and new breakthroughs in space travel. Very cleverly, Sagan starts off ab ovo in multiple aspects. After talking about the motivation for the book and the early origins of it (and the tv series) in the first chapter, he then continues to discuss yet another topic from the very beginning - the molecular chemistry of life - perhaps not in minute detail, but in a clear and concise fashion. He continues in the similar vein in the third chapter, with the start of yet another important thing - the human interest for stargazing, for knowing the universe, for establishing some sort of structures in the form of calendars. As the story progresses, and as the reader meets important people who have shaped the way we view the world today - Kepler, Newton, Huygens, da Vinci, Einstein and the myriad of philosophers and/or scientists of old Greece (Thales, Anaximader, Empedocles, Democritus, Anaxagoras, Aristarchus and Hypatia, to name a few) - it immediately becomes apparent how the road to our current knowledge of the universe has been rocky and fraught with many dangers. From pseudoscience to good old barbarism, there has been many things working against the progress of humankind. And although today's situation is by far the best if we look at human history as a whole, it's far from ideal. In my opinion, that's the biggest strength of Cosmos - raising awareness about how fragile life (and both knowledge and dreams) is. The wealth of historical and scientific information is a wonderful aspect of the book, and works well in underlining the main theme of the book.

Dara and Nick are sisters. Like all sisters, they fight. They get jealous. They both love each other but they can never see or understand what the other is feeling because they are so wrapped up in themselves and they're own problems. From the synopsis Vanishing Girls (sound familiar? Something along the lines of Gone Girl, right? )is about a girl who's sister goes missing. Honestly I found that this was incredibly misleading to the point where it's ridiculous. The entire book was slower than I feel when I wake up at 6 in the morning, and that's saying something. Her sister didn't actually go 'missing' until around the last 100 pages of the book and even then I was unsure about what I was actually reading. I felt as if when Oliver was writing this she couldn't choose what she wanted to write about and kept changing her mind as she went along. Don't get me wrong, I have nothing against her. People I've talked to already know that I loved Before I Fall and I loved Delirium even more, but this book was honestly so disappointing. I definitely was not feeling the whole Parker-Dara-Nick thing. Not only was the love triangle unoriginal but it was also incredibly boring. Dara and Nick were both entertaining characters but Parker was basically the definition of a cliche'. Yes, you guys, I did just say that. I don't take it back. Sometimes I think I didn't really fall in love with Parker. Sometimes I think it was really all about Nick, and proving I could finally be her equal. With all of it's short-comings I still refrained from giving it one star because I must admit Oliver has a gift for being able to set a scene. Although this book is definitely on the wordy side, it did pull me in and it wasn't so bad that I wanted to quit reading it. Lauren shows so much potential for her writing, and has clearly demonstrated this in her previous novels and in some parts of this book. I know from reading other reviews that I'm not the only one who thinks this. Now, if only she read these reviews and took them into account for future writing she could totally rule the book universe. About that 'twist', I saw it coming from the very beginning. If you have ever read more than a couple of Thrillers you probably would have too. Through all of the boring words and confusing story lines and multiple plot holes I thought that it was going to all lead up to something epic, and definitely not what I predicted. When I predicted it it had been merely a fleeting thought, and I immediately dismissed it because I simply thought that it was unoriginal and wouldn't have been used. Not to mention, there were major parts in the story that showed that it literally wasn't possible. Basically the entire thing was hallucinations and all of the boring confusing words meant legit nothing. Her sister was dead the whole time and whenever the book was under her sisters POV it was really the main character taking her persona, thinking that she was her sister. She had PTSD and a dissociative disorder and ended up in a mental institution until later she's all better and totally fine and the book meant nothing. Memory is like that, too. We build careful bridges. But they're weaker than we think. And when they break, all our memories return to drown us. I felt like it was just a cheap knock-off of We Were Liars and that pissed me right the fuck off. I'm sure if you're new to Thrillers you would enjoy it, but if not I don't recommend wasting your time on this one.

I love all of Kelley Armstrong's books and while this may not be her best, I still really enjoyed it. It might have been a little slower than her previous books but it was still interesting and hooked me from the start. The premise of the story is very original, but she didn't really delve into world building as much as I would have liked. It was only at the end that we really got to see any information in that area. But that didn't take away from the story and it was easy enough to get past. I know this is really knit picky but at the beginning of the book, Ashyn's hound, Tova was separated from her when she entered the forest but we didn't get a scene of them meeting. I was worried for such a long time that something had happened to him and we never found out what had happened after he was taken away. Even Ashyn didn't seem at all worried about it. Then, randomly, we get a mention of him again. He was just beside her like nothing had happened. So did I miss something. Did I accidentally skip over a couple of pages? The characters were all really unique and by the end I felt really attached to them. Even though Ashyn was supposed to be the weaker one, the one who didn't know anything about fighting, I still felt as though she had her moments where she was really strong and she stood up for herself. She knew that she didn't know how to handle knives and swords so she made herself useful in other ways. On the other hand I started out not liking her sister, Moria, very much. She seemed very arrogant and full of herself-at least in my opinion. But throughout the book I started to like her more and more and by the end I was supporting her completely. Though I have to admit that I still like Ashyn better. Both their love interests seem to fit them really well. Moria and Gavril's relationship is based on bickering and while it can be a bit much sometimes, they do seem to have a really good connection. As for Ashyn and Ronan, they become a really cute couple by the end of it. They are very tentative towards one another.

Most of the romantic development was between Nova and Alex, and while I understand that Rishi and Alex have been friends for longer and there was brief foreshadowing, we didn't get to see much of the why they got together.
