Goddamn... this is one of my top fav fantasy series by now... god DAMN... so good. And that ending... shit I did not see that coming but holy hell that was really, really appropriate and well set up. And waaaaay better than what I was guessing would happen haha. I'm talking about the part where Mulaghesh rejects the Voortyashtani sentinels, saying they're not true soldiers. I honestly thought she was just gonna stab herself??? It's what a lesser writer may have done. Mulaghesh was a fantastic character who I liked a lot from the first book, so I was pleasantly surprised to see that she's the star of this one! She yells a lot and grumps all around town, I loved it. She makes a great hero--far from a perfect person, but she tries real hard to live up to her ideals and I admire that. Given her military background, it is appropriate that this book was depressing as hell with its fixation on the horrors of war. Shit gets pretty gruesome. The topic was unexpected since it wasn't a focus of the first book, but damn it was written well. Also there's plenty more fun times with the Divine in this book--something I loved from the first one, since I love pantheons of gods. It is a nice and lovely bonus that this book is chock-full of well written women, many of them women of color :) It passes the Bechdel Test with flying colors--something I was thinking about while reading. Honestly it must take conscious thought on the part of the author to include this number of women--there are a lot of female characters, major and minor ones, who just as easily could've been men without affecting the plot. I kept coming across new female characters and thinking "huh! if someone else were to write this, this person would be a man." Women are also underrepresented and frequently poorly represented in western media; related to this, people usually assume that male is default. So it makes me REALLY, REALLY HAPPY that the author chose to show that women exist, and that they do things in their worlds, and that the things they do are worth writing stories about. Because these are all facts and I'm a liiiiittle (read: EXTREMELY) fed up with writers who either don't fucking realize this or just choose to pretend it isn't true. He's certainly not the first content creator to figure this shit out but hey! This is a great step in the right direction, plus a damn good book regardless. Sounds like there'll be more to come from this series--I'm greatly looking forward to it :) In the meantime I think I'll just continually scream at the sky about how much I love this series

I am really torn about this book. Like, the characters are (usually) very real and well-drawn and the stakes are satisfyingly high but there were some parts of it that just...bugged me. A lot. I have no idea how much of this is 'I have a cold and some things are bothering me more than usual' versus 'man, this book has Issues'. At the beginning, I really thought Samir would grow to regret the way he treated the women he got involved with, but no. You see, the good women are the ones who are completely dependent on him (his employees) or related to him (his mother or his sister in law). Which makes Milli the One Good Woman and the book makes sure to tell you that Samir hasn't had sex with a virgin before!! And it's so special!! And the woman he treats badly at the beginning of the book turns out to be Way Worse Than You Thought because she lies about Samir abusing her, but Milli defends him!! Because he would never hit a woman!! How she decided this I don't know, especially considering she was supposed to have spent her career helping battered women leave their husbands. Funnily enough, domestic abusers look a lot like everybody else and they'd known each other a few weeks at that point. We meet the woman Samir was involved with at the beginning of the book later on and she not only falls short of Milli, but Samir seems contemptuous of her in a whole different way now. 'It isn't ok to treat woman like all they are is a place to stick your dick in' seems to be a better lesson to learn than 'the woman who I love is so much better than these whores I used to spend fuck' but the book is far more concerned that Samir was getting involved with the wrong women than that he treated those women like a glorified fleshlight. And then there's Samir's mother. I have friends who were adopted. Some of them want to meet their birth parents, some don't. But Milli takes the decision entirely out of his hands and, in one of the great cliches of these sorts of stories, Samir's birth mother turns out to be dying so of course that makes it ok that a) Milli contacted her in the first place, without asking Samir's opinion on the matter and b) she then forces him to go see his birth mother. It feels...wrong, somehow, that it all turned out ok. That it turned out fine because Milli Is Magic and can do no wrong. Honestly, I would have felt better about the whole thing if it had gone REALLY badly. Then, Milli finds out about the grand deception and it occurs, of course, the morning after she and Samir have sex for the first time. So Milli decides he'd done everything in order to get her to sign these papers that he hasn't even mentioned yet, that this man she was so certain was Good that she attacked someone with a magazine was actually bad and awful. How about she's just upset about the deception, instead of thinking he's actually a big old faking faker who doesn't care about her at all?

So she can remain a virgin and therefore "deserve" the prince and the happily ever after, while her friend is completely dehumanised and get to stay in the dirt. Ew! The only thing the book has going for it is the exotic setting (if you're into Japan and stuff), but as other reviewers has pointed out, don't expect anything to be accurate or even true

Adam is a Shooting Star Thank you to Smash for recommending this series! While I really liked If I Stay, I LOVED Where She Went. Adam is one of the best male characters I've read, and the author made an excellent decision to write the story from his point of view. *This review is spoilerish so if you haven't read If I Stay, you should stop now. Adam Wilde is a 21 year-old rock star sensation, living out his dream of becoming a wildly successful musician. However, he's jaded and morose. His fame and money mean nothing to him because he's missing the most important part of his life: Mia. Three years ago, Mia let their relationship end without a word why. Granted, she was messed up after losing her family in a horrible car crash, but I was angry with her for never providing an explanation to Adam. He was gutted after losing her family AND her. After holing up in his parents' basement for months, he wrote a heartbreaking CD for his band, which elevated Shooting Star to the stratosphere (think Britney Spears fame). What's your favorite breakup CD? I'm partial to Chris Isaak's Forever Blue, Alanis Morissette's Jagged Little Pill, and of course Adele's 21. Adam's lyrics were my favorite part of the story. Gorgeous and devastating all at once: I'll be your mess, you be mine That was the deal that we had signed I bought a hazmat suit to clean up your waste Gas masks, gloves, to keep us safe But now I'm alone in an empty room Staring down immaculate doom and There's a piece of lead where my heart should be Doctor said too dangerous to take out You'd better just leave it be Body grew back around it, a miracle, praise be, Now, if only I could get through airport security I want to buy this CD Collateral Damage! Some of my favorite psychotherapy clients are young adult/new adult men because they try so damn hard to be tough and strong but they have vulnerabilities just like the rest of us. It can be immensely cathartic for them to express those feelings, and this novel is like one big therapy session for Adam. Adam is so sweet--I just want to hug him--especially when he thinks things like this: Mia's grandfather just looked at me in that quiet sad way that made me inexplicably want to kneel at the foot of his chair and put my head in his lap. *sobs* You'll make it Adam, hang in there! This book is a tearjerker but in a touching, satisfying way. Highly recommended!

Plot Blurb: Follows the story of a girl, Meghan Chase, who is bored with her life (and honestly I found her life in the beginning pretty boring) and she has plans of her job for the summer and all sorts of craziness. She lives far away from school and isn't very popular, she really only has one friend named Robbie who is a little weird. Long story short, she comes home one day and her little brother, who she loves, has been replaced by a changeling. Her friend Robbie reveals he's really from the fairy kingdom and is in fact Puck from Shakespeare's Midsummer Night's Dream and he's been charged by Oberon (king of the seelie court of the fairies) to protect her. Turns out she's the daughter of a fairy king! So she goes there trying to find her brother but then realizes there's something huge that's attacking the fairy kingdom and it has kidnapped her brother too! Adventure ensures... yadda yadda yadda.... Oh yeah, and there's a hot prince that helps/is a dick to her along the way. My reaction: I honestly wasn't blown away by this story... The beginning was really slow, so much so that I almost put it down. But after she got to the land of the fairies, things sort of picked up. I love that Kagawa is true to the maliciousness of the fairies, because that's how they really are in legend. She's obviously done a lot of work on this to make it realistic (yes, in my world, fairies are realistic). Once we meet Ash, the unseelie court prince, it starts to pick up a bit. I never really liked Puck, he seemed fake. So I made my way through Meghan's story and it really had a lot going for it by the end. The plot was very imaginative and I really enjoyed the idea as a fantasy enthusiast. I like that Meghan really became a sort of kick ass chick and saved the world and all that, and the chemistry between her and Ash was well done. But by the end, I have to admit that I was resolved it wasn't good enough to read the rest of the series. But then I read a review from a guy that had similar tastes as me who said this series was his absolute favorite. What had I missed? Which is why I am now in the middle of The Iron Daughter (#2 in the series) and it is fabulous so far. I don't know what happened, but Kagawa suddenly understands her characters much better! So should you read it? Definitely! As I said, push through the beginning and it redeems itself. Besides, you need to get through this one to get to the awesomeness of the second book! Just like Lord of the Flies, but with girls. Except not. At all. About the only parallel with my recent reading (well, listening) of Lord of the Flies was incidental (well except for the stranded-on-a-desert-island thing). Both audiobooks were both read by the author. In contrast to the tedious reading by Golding, Libba Bray was amazing, infusing all the girls and other characters with distinct voices, accents, personalities. At one level, this book is silly. On another, it's beautiful and touching. And one of the funniest books I've read in a long time. I find it amazing that so many books can be written about being who you really are without treading the same ground. Some amazing wisdom: In the pageant of life a girl picks up fallen sequins and turns them into a brand-new dress of awesome. And good practical advice: Miss Montana, is that the way a Miss Team Dream sits? All slutty like that with her hoo-hoo showing? We need to focus like it's the final interview round and the questions are all about anorexia and current events. While it often seems a bit over the top, it tackles heavy subjects like gender roles (of course), race, ableism, and transexuality . Adina was an amazing character. But I think I'm in love with Miss Michigan. Great book in taking to task all of the ways in "girls are supposed to be". Highly, highly recommended.

Authors thoughts: So, there's this very popular book called Twilight, and then there's this other very popular book called Percy Jackson. I want my book to be popular as well, so let's just produce an unhealthy mix of those two. I have no idea how to put it nicely, so I'll be honest: Reading this book has been painful. I've read my fair share of books and I can't remember having read anything so poorly written. Maybe the Hush, Hush series, which has been another Twilight rip-off. I cringed at every plot hole, and there have been many. Even if  half of the story has been a set up   most events made no sense, reactions were too far fetched and don't get me even started on the mental capabilities of both the heroine, poor sad lonely emo Hades (who goes by the pet name "Henry", by the way) and the "best friend" Ava. I might be strict, but look for yourself: Henry: -Girl lies with an awful head wound, dying. Second girl tries to reanimate the first one, crying for help- What does Henry do? Run towards them, providing first aid? Call an ambulance? Tell the girl #2 that she's too late, there's nothing to be done? Oh, please. That would be too predictable. Henry slowly approaches and introduces himself. He asks the shocked girl what her name is and INTRODUCES HIMSELF. Ava: Lured girl into foreign property by walking across a river by stepping on stones. She decides to get back to her car and leave the girl on her own. Does she escape by taking the aforementioned stone path back, maybe kicking some off so that the girl can't follow and makes a run for it? Naw, we're in TGT country here. Ava escapes by taking off her clothes (it's October, mind you. Might have been September, didn't care enough to check afterwards.) and jumping head first into a river which must have been shallow enough to allow stones to be on the surface. Kate (the protagonist): Sorry, but I can't decide on an example. There have been just too many things she thought and did which made little to no sense at all. Her opinion changes constantly. A change of view might be a good thing. Not here. She's whimsical, throws unjustified tantrums, has most of the time no idea what's going on even though it's obvious to everyone but her. Let me sum it up in one nice quote: "..she was connected to more machines and monitors than I could count..." The scene takes place in a hospital room, not a rocket launch station. She has been mentioned to dislike calculus; we just never imagined how bad she'd actually be at it. The love story was non-existent. What we've got instead were some awkward moments, some out-of-the-place verbal hints, some aphrodisiac and the sudden realization that our "heroine" had suddenly fallen in love. You might think that the advantage of writing from first POV is to propel the reader inside the head of the protagonist, making them emotionally attached to your heroine, making them understand her better and become emotionally invested in your story. That didn't happen. The characters were cut out of cardboard, the story was predictable and any potential plot twist could be seen from afar. Had I been someone else, I would have stopped reading after page 10 or so. But I am me, so I had to read it through to the bitter end. And knowing myself, I will probably suffer through volume 2 and 3 of the series. To everyone else, let me say this: read at your own risk.

Guest Review Taken From Book Angel Booktopia BZRK... I'm not 100% sure how to describe this book as this is a ... well... a hard thing to explain. But here's my attempt. BZRK, the first in a new series, is about nanos and biots. Not sure what these are? These are nanobots and biots, the biological counterpart of nanos. And here, it seems the world is in danger from these. Or rather, the group known as AFGC, who want to "rewire" the most powerful minds of the world: the President of the United States and the British Prime Minister, to name two. But BZRK has to stop them. Enter Sadie and Noah, the teenagers with their private reasons to join. But with the stakes so high and failure meaning they might lose their sanity, losing isn't an option... Now, this is my first Michael Grant book (never read his Gone series, though I have been told I should loads of time in the past), I don't know what my reaction would be. And, I hate to say, I'm a bit "muh" over it. I didn't love it, but I didn't hate it. I'm just in the middle, not sure with myself if I like or not. Ok, let's talk about this book's good point. Once you got your head into this, it was a fast thriller that played out on two levels: in real life and in nano (or "down on the meat"). And with technology at the level it is at the present moment, you sometimes go "This could/might be possible..." But, there are problems with this book. The first problem I had was when the story or the action scene jumped for human to nano/biot. For the first half of the book, I sometimes had to reread paragraphs to go "OK. Where am I again?" so I didn't get confused. And near the end of the book, I suddenly started seeing the nanos and the biots like the robot-cookies from Despicable Me. Another problem I had was the characters. I'm sorry, but I want to be gripped by the characters very quickly. I want to read their story and want to rush back to the book because of them. And with these characters... it took a long time to warm to them or the situation. And the reason I feel for this was that I never felt like I had time to get to know the characters. I would have a chapter (at the most) with one character before it jumped to another character, whether they were the good guy or the bad guy. I never "clicked" with any of the characters. I'm still unsure on how I feel about BZRK. This wasn't my cup of tea. But I'm sure all the Gone fans will love this and am sure that some of you guys will enjoy it a lot more than me. So please, don't let me review put you off. If you want to read this book, READ IT!

Locke Lamora is a thief, an excellent con artist who runs his little brood of villains to relieve the nobility of its coins. A fantasy Robin Hood, if you will, but where Hood used his bow and arrow, Lamora relies exclusively on his wits. The underworld of Camorr is run by Capa. When a challenger, the Grey King, appears, Locke Lamora gets sucked into a power play he doesn't want to partake. The book begins with an elaborate con which paints Locke as an almost too witty character that plans everything in advance, is always one step ahead and does it all with a smile on his face. The story takes an abrupt turn to darker side when the power struggle between the Capa and the King begins in earnest. Locke finds himself mixed in both underground and elite politics, and it's really not a good place to be. While the story progresses, we are offered with bried glimpses of the history of both characters and the surrounding world. These flashes are short enough to keep the focus on the main story but they provide both necessary information and welcome introduction to various aspects of Gentleman Bastards universe. All in all, The Lies of Locke Lamora is an excellent read. Once the story got into full swing, it was hard to let go of the book. The main story ends in an obvious point to continue in next books (which already exist), and the multiple sidesteps, while not stealing the focus, still make me want to read a full novel, or at least a novelette, of the history of Camorr and the world beyond.

I think this book was fairly easier to understand than many other Murakami books, either this is the case or it I might be becoming more accepting of his style of writing and imagination. I found multiple "Zen" factors when reading the books, many parts about shedding the Self for the benefit of tranquility and happiness. But by the end of the novel, Murakami begins to view this in a negative light and to be unnatural. I think I understand why he would have that opinion and as it could be viewed to be against common world thinking. All in all, I absolutely loved the book and Murakami never disappoints. It is not my favorite Murakami novel, that still remains Kafka on the Shore, but it is well written, devoid of pretense, and speaks directly to your soul.

I love Molly Harper's Half Moon Hollow books. I love her witty voice, and the lighthearted tone to her romances. She also usually has a slightly different take on the paranormal genre that sets her apart. But. This one? I... I didn't like it. I barely finished it. There was little relationship development, I didn't quite understand the antagonists' motivations, and Lord, I do not like 'wandering the woods' books. I really wanted to love the heroine because, hello, rare book archivist heroine? Yes, please. But she was just too neurotic in the beginning. It wasn't until she sort of declared her independence that she got interesting. Coincidentally, that's also when the hero disappeared for a bit. Like I said, minimal relationship development. But I love Harper's books. So is it a personal preference thing? Is my loathing for a wilderness setting impacting my objectivity toward the book? In the end, though, I circle back around to the complete and utter lack of any evidence the hero and heroine make a good couple, and the fact that I'm still confused about what the antagonists wanted. It seemed clear to me that the book would be pretty dangerous in the wrong hands as it could effectively eliminate shifters. A lot of emphasis was placed on that, but the hill shifters (I don't even know what to properly call them) seem to want other generic information from the book. Something specific is never mentioned and I didn't fully understand the difference between these shifters and the ones from the previous Half Hollow Moon books. So, much to my great chagrin, I have to rate this two stars. Even that may be overly generous, but a bad book from Molly Harper is still better than others out there.

3.5 Stars Note: I received a free digital copy of this book from Netgalley in exchange for an honest review. This does not shape or change my opinion of the book. Thank you Sourcebooks Fire and Netgalley for the review copy! Synopsis (from Amazon) Nothing says Happy Birthday like summoning the spirits of your dead relatives. Alex is a bruja, the most powerful witch in a generation...and she hates magic. At her Deathday celebration, Alex performs a spell to rid herself of her power. But it backfires. Her whole family vanishes into thin air, leaving her alone with Nova, a brujo boy she can't trust. A boy whose intentions are as dark as the strange marks on his skin. The only way to get her family back is to travel with Nova to Los Lagos, a land in-between, as dark as Limbo and as strange as Wonderland... [image error] This book was a book of contrasts for me, which makes this review pretty difficult. However, overall, in the general sense, I enjoyed it! Here's what worked for me: The mysticism: My favorite part of this book was the interwoven mythology and stories, and the lushness of Los Lagos. Labyrinth was littered with fantastical places, beings, and imagery and I appreciated all of it. The stories within a story...the woven in myths, legends and histories added an element--a RICHNESS to the prose that had me just Eating. It. Up. The focus on family: I loved the element of unconditional love and family being the anchor...being the thing that binds you and holds you together. The thing you can fall back on no matter what. Alex's coming of age: I loved Alex's growth in Labyrinth. A girl who is unwilling to accept a part of herself, who admits to having a bit of a darkness to her, who is angry, confused, and ashamed of a part of who she is. "I can feel the secrets pushing against my veins, and in turn, I push right back-hiding them deep inside, where I hope one day even I wont be able to find them." "Sometimes I'm afraid I've put on so many masks that one day I won't be able to recognize who I am." Then there was the gradual acceptance of who and what she is and stands for, conquering her inner fears, relying on and trusting her family (and friends), learning about love and what is means, and that she IS loved...Yes I'll have that! The writing: Cardova excelled at descriptive prose and painted such vivid fantastic images of Los Lagos that I could see it in my head. I could see the lush, vibrant landscapes, the mystical creatures, the darkness, the desperation, and loved it. I mean, Lovers Lament- a river full of vengeful souls unwilling to let go...The Meadow-very Alice in Wonderland tea partyesque--yesssss. What I struggled with: (NOTE: I received and unedited advanced copy, so some or all of these may have been changed, or improved in the final copy) The writing. Yes, it was strong in its description and imagery, but at the same time the flow also felt disjointed and stunted in a lot areas. This is one of my notes I took while reading "There are times when the prose are so descriptive, they literally plant the image in my head, or I literally feel the feelings and emotions of the character and yet other times the writing feels stilted. VIVID imagery, yet choppy." I am a character person. I absolutely must connect to, relate to, and appreciate them on some capacity, and it took a really long time for this to happen for me. It was probably not until the start of the last third of the book, which left me not really caring about the characters or not really liking them outright for a large majority. A lot of the side characters were amazing, and kind of overshadowed the main characters in my opinion. HOWEVER, I was invested by the end and since this is a series, I can assume that I will be for the remainder, and they will continue to grow and become more complex and layered. So yay! I think this book and others like it that are rich and steeped with diversity and culture are SO SO important and it was one of my favorite things about Labyrinth. While it wasn't perfect for me, I think it is a solid start to a series with a lot of potential! The stunning cover and the amazing map certainly don't hurt either! I will be reading the next one!

** spoiler alert ** This book was fairly interesting. It kind of read like a parody because even though at the heart of the book there's a good message, there's all this humor and wit. I will admit this isn't the BEST book I've read this summer but it's definitely one I'd like to re-read in person (aka not a e-book but a plastic covered hardcover from a library). However, in the beginning I found it hard for me to get into it. I actually started this book weeks ago but the first couple of chapters bored me and were taking to long to get to the plot that I forgot all about it until last night. Not to mention the descriptions of the outfits people were wearing and other things were sooooo long. I started skipping those paragraphs so get the point of the scene. Not a good thing I know but still. Over-all I did mostly enjoy this book there were some plot holes. It's revealed that the Tom Kelly that Becky meets isn't exactly real. Or alive I mean. It turns out that he's her dad and he died before she was born from AIDS (I could be wrong about the disease but it was never stated by name). He really did love her mom and she made him promise to give her daughter beauty too. So I'm guessing that the reason no one saw him for the 20-ish years before Becky came to NYC is that he was dead. In the beginning I thought maybe he was the devil, and I wasn't the only one but the whole death thing and how he came back to life thing wasn't really touched on. So I don't get what happened. Just that after Becky got her happily ever after, he called her and said goodbye, her dead mom said she loved her and the call was over. I was/am so confused. Also I wasn't that invested in Greg and Becky's love story. I thought it was somewhat interesting the way they're conversations went and I think even if they loved each other, I don't think they were IN LOVE. But maybe that would happen in time. And at least it wasn't that "insta-Love" crap. I kind of wanted Becky-as-Rebecca to ask Greg if he could still love her if she didn't look the way she did. I mean, sure the end of the book answers this question but I'm curious to hear Greg's reaction to that especially considering his WTF reaction when she pulled off her veil at their wedding and was just Becky after that. Lol, although I don't know how she and Rocher managed to run away without the Brit police catching up to them. I really did enjoy Becky's best friend although she kind of annoyed me when she got into a fight with Lady Jessalyn (the one England actually wants Prince Greg to marry) and only Becky is implicated in the press for it. It was ridiculous. And I could not believe that neither one of them thought to save any of the Rebecca money she had to have made from her VOGUE shoot or the movie she did. But it did seem very dramatic that they became poor after that. It kind of reminded me of the end of Jane Eyre after Jane runs from Rochester and goes and lives with these other people. Anyway, over all this book is a interesting read. Although I think the writing and plot holes do give the reading a bit of a hard time (and I NEVER notice plot holes) I definitely think this book offers something to readers that other books similar to this don't...lol although I can't exactly describe what that is. 5- Fairytale- Stars http://veronikasreaderfeeder.com/kell... This book really surprised me. I was expecting a fluffy and cute Kelly Oram book, but this story has a really nice depth and some of it was really heartbreaking. Because of the weak book cover I didn't even think that this story covers some really important topics, like school bullying, family abandonment, suicide, gay marriage and divorce. But on the other hand there are a lot of smiles, a fairytale kind of love, and a Cinderella adaptation with a stepmother and an evil twin sister. The main character is Ellamara aka Ella who lives with her mom and her biggest passions are reading and blogging. She meets with Cinder on her book and movie review blog. After it turns out that they share their love for The Cinder Chronicles book series they start to chat a lot and they slowly become best friends and maybe a little bit more. After two years of texting and chatting with Cinder, a horrible thing happens. She gets into a terrible car accident in which she loses her mother. She has so major injuries that she has to stay at the hospital for eight months but some of her injuries and scars are permanent. When finally she can leave the hospital she is forced to stay with her father - who leaved them years ago - and with his new family. And in addition she has to attend to a new school with her step sisters, where everybody bullies her because of her crippling injuries. Ella has to start again her life so she decides that she has to return to the online world, too. She starts again her blog and she reconnects with Cinder who actually thought that she may have died. Cinder is a humorous, smart, nice guy and he has everything that makes Ella's heart to beat faster. But Ella doesn't know his real name and she definitely doesn't know that he is actually Brian Oliver, the Hollywood star. Ella's character is really inspiring. Her life is full of pain, disappointment and despair. She has to move to a new place with people who she doesn't know and who she doesn't like. Everybody hurts her emotionally and they don't accept her, but despite this she is a very strong, nice, humorous girl and she has a beautiful soul. The relationship with her father has a hard start but they slowly rebuild it. I loved Cinder, too. The banter between him and Ella was really sweet, and it made me smile a lot. :) Maybe he was a little too perfect, but I loved that he always choses Ella over anything else despite all the pressure. This book has the perfect balance of pain and seriousness, smile and fairytale, so I highly recommend it for everyone! 3.5 Stars - I had a tough time rating this book. A part of me says that it only deserves 3 stars but I wanted to give it 4 for excellent ideas. In the end, I compromise with a 3.5 stars. Zoe's been on the run for most of her life. Her Mom didn't explain exactly why they're on the run. She only knows that her father was mixed up in something bad and her Mom took her away when she was a baby to keep her safe. Most people get to live in one town or two while growing up. Zoe has grown up all over the U.S. and under several aliases. She gets ready to take off again but it's totally different situation now. Her Mom fails prey to cancer and leaves her with two commands before she dies. The most important: Don't let her father's family find her. The world that Dana Cameron weaves together is striking in its unique mix of legends, paranormal, shape-shifters and mythology. It's like looking at the world with cool shades. Everything is familiar and the same but everything has a layer of meaning that has been left unseen. What if all those pictographs and cave drawings of half man and half animal beings were true? What would the world be like then? The first book of the Fangborn introduces us to an unlikely group of characters. In the lead is Zoe, a socially awkward young woman who isn't comfortable in her own skin and used to a life of secrecy. She can count the number of real friends on one hand, but she's willing to leave them all behind to keep everyone safe. She's not just running away from an unknown danger that haunts her family. She's running away from everyone to hide from herself. The Beast. She can't control the Beast. What if the Beast takes over and she never turns into a human again? What if the Beast attacks the people she loves? She can't take the chance. She won't take that chance. It doesn't matter. Everything Zoe knows and believes in will be challenged. The very people she least expects to be a part of her insane journey across the world will be at her side. How does she know who is a friend or enemy? How will she know who to trust? What is this prophecy that stays she's the chosen one? With every step forward, there are two taken sideways. Instead of leaving town and starting a new life in a new city, Zoe finds herself stalked by those who bear a striking family resemblance. Danny, an old childhood friend, becomes bait to lure Zoe into a dangerous game with nefarious characters. With heart pounding and terror trapped in her throat, Zoe dives into the rabbit hole to save her friend. The story grabbed me full tilt at the beginning. I became confused when the pace slows down to a near crawl, and I felt like I was thrown into an info dump with long mental digressions into the past. I realize all of them are important for the story but I felt rather disappointed in the pacing. It's like starting a roller coaster ride. Instead of getting ready to go down that first hump into speedy reckless exhilaration, you find out that you need to ride around for a while, go up another few hills and THEN you get the adventurous yeehaw drop. I love everything about the Fangborn, the hints about where they're from, what they can do and how they are an integral part of society. Even if they're a hidden part of it. As a lover of history, mythology and relics, I find myself equally put off and attracted to the archaeological aspects of the story. Parts of it is really interesting and parts of it throws me out of the story. As a reader, I never came to terms with Zoe being an archaeologist. If Zoe was still a student and working as an intern, it would be easier to accept. Most of the time, I would forget she is one until the book reminds me that she is. The climax of the story is MOST EXCELLENT! I wanted to give the story 4 stars just for the climax. It was very well done! It wasn't exactly what I expected and the unusual mix of events was awesome! I may have jumped up and down a little in excitement during this part. Okay, it was really a sit down chair dance but it still counts. I want to preface my next comment with this: I'm definitely team Zoe & Will. I want them to work. However, the love making scenario felt really out of place. I'm glad they got together. I just think the description could have hinted more and said less. That small bit of the book felt really out of place in the way it was written. Not by that part happening but because of how it is written. It's not because I don't like explicit love scenes. I do. I just felt that this part was an odd duck out with the rest of the book. I would have liked more time to get to know the other characters and a little less time in Zoe's head. The bones of the story are great and I can't wait to see what story the second book will tell. I know I didn't give the book 4 stars. It doesn't matter. You should read this book. The reasons why I would mark a book down to a 3.5 stars may not be your reasons. This book is an excellent start to a new series and I am definitely going to be in line to read the next one. Read via NetGalley To read more reviews, check out SSV website: Silk Screen Views

Everneath has been on my to-read list since I first caught word of it sometime last year. It's always perplexing when you find a debut novel that every single one of your reading buddies enjoyed...at least it is for me. Because always at the back of my mind is, Will I be the one to loathe it, resulting in endless virtual flogging? I should not have worried. This is one debut novel that has guaranteed that I will pick up the 2nd book...and the third, and subsequent novels or spin-offs (or completely different series) if they come to fruition. I had an over-abundance of Audible credits, and this book was on my wishlist, so I snapped it up, planning to listen on my commute and making it last approximately a week or so. Nothin' doin'. Once I heard the passionate Amy Rubinate give voice to Nikki's dire situation, I knew there would be no pausing the audio until I'd heard the whole tragic story. If there's one way to guarantee that I'll at least give a retelling a chance, it's to make it mythology-based. Even better? Make it a retelling of the Persephone myth, one of my very favorite myths. I've seen so many variations of the original story, and each one is unique. Everneath might just be my favorite so far, though. That might just have something to do with the fact that it's character-driven, rather than being focused on the romantic aspects of the story. I also liked that the book worked as a countdown to Nikki's return to the tunnels, switching back and forth between the days leading up to her decision to go to the Everneath with Cole and now, as she tries to find a way to remain on the surface. The romance does play a large role in why this is all happening to Nikki in the first place but it never really overshadows eveything Nikki is learning and what she's doing in her attempt to stay in the land of the living. As I said, this novel doesn't focus primarily on the romantic relationship of the main character, which is a refreshing change for a YA novel. Instead, it focuses on all of Nikki's relationships and how everything has changed since she emerged from the Everneath. The book delves into the idea of having a choice and making the wrong one and into wreckless teenage impulsiveness and the repercussions, not just to oneself but to everyone involved. There's also a lesson in there somewhere about forgiveness. Oh, and sacrifice. There's always sacrificing in mythology, literal and metaphorical. It's not all after-school special, though. There's some serious potential for a love triangle, but as it stands now, Jack is just as broken as Nikki, and Cole, it seems, is using Nikki as the means to an end. Sure, it's clear he might have romantic feelings for Nikki, but with a guy who wants to carry you back to the Everneath caveman-style, you just never know. It is apparent, however, that although Jack was deeply hurt when Nikki disappeared six months ago, he never stopped loving her. He might be quite different from the Jack she knew before, but after the events that led up to her leaving all those months ago, you know Nikki's got to be wondering if she ever knew him at all. I love where this first novel ended and that it leaves the next book open for all kinds of questing: for the truth, for a solution, for life and love lost. And I sincerely hope that Everbound is just as emotionally-charged as Everneath. I can't wait to make it mine and find out! Favorite quotes: "If you're gonna leave, I wish you'd just leave. Why do you keep coming back if you're not going to stay? Because even when you're gone, you're never really gone... I won't get over it if you keep coming back. Losing you once was hard enough. And now you're here again and everything's coming back. I'm going to get screwed. And I can't do it again." "I dreamed of you every night. It felt so real. And when I'd wake up the next morning, it was like your disappearance was fresh. Like you'd left me all over again." "Tell me, friend. Is there more for us?" I looked into his eyes, "There is everything for us." This review can also be found at The Starry-Eyed Revue.

** spoiler alert ** While I can't say this particular story line was wholly original (aka love coming back from the dead after horrible happenings) , I can say I still immensely enjoyed this book. Despite the familiarity of the concept, it was still an intriguingly written take on it. It held true to the series... but I must admit that I hope this doesn't change Dmitri's characteristic ways. They are far too amusing :D Awesome read and I can't wait for the next one.

I am not generally a fan of horror, so reading this book was a bit unusual for me. I have to say, I quite enjoyed it, even if I wasn't particularly scared. Perhaps that was because it was obvious Meg would be safe until the end, since she was the POV character, and I didn't much care for the other characters. I did, however, have an issue with who the culprit turned out to be. I was absolutely convinced it was TJ. All the clues were there - he had more opportunity to kill the others than anyone, especially with Lori and Vivian. Moreover, I suspected him as soon as he said he couldn't find the bag of almonds - because the lack of evidence was contingent only on his word, which is an instant red flag. Even though it was not TJ, I also would have been fine with Minnie, or perhaps even Gunner. But the killer should have been someone with an emotional connection to Meg. Instead, it's this random guy, who then turns out to be the long-lost brother of someone we didn't know even had a brother. I do not recall a single mention of a brother of Claire's at any point in the book. Having Tomben be the killer seemed like the least interesting outcome, and that's what happened. Also, it was a small thing but a big irk - we get several shoutouts to how one should be PC! Commenting that the black dude dies first in horror movies leads to "OMG you racist!" Joking that a guy is defending his boyfriend when he defends a male friend - "OMG you homophobe!" Listen people: I've had the misfortune, like most people, to come across plenty of racism and homophobia in my life, and that's not what it looks like. I can really see no reason for its inclusion, other than attempted shorthand at telling us Nathan is a douche. I was really so annoyed I'm tempted to take off another star just for that. That said, there is much to recommend this book. Meg is a good protagonist, smart and resourceful. The cast of characters is very diverse. It's very atmospheric, and the murderer's style of murder is nicely creepy. It was a very fast read, one I'm glad I did to change it up a bit.

Anne Brown, I love your mermaids. Yep, your evil, soul-devouring, divinely beautiful mermaids. They are kick-ass. Just my type, y'know? I loved the concept of this story. I was glad to see some change in what we usually thought of mermaids as soft and sweet creatures, with flowing red hair and seashells as bras. Everyone always likes a dark tale, no? And this was exactly what I got in Lies Beneath. So that made me very happy. Calder was an interesting character. He's different from his ruthless sisters by controlling his human-eating habits, but unfortunately, that still didn't help me connect much with him. I could only tell what he was feeling because he told me. Of course, his feelings became better to interpret while he was with Lily, thanks to his actions (He stalked. Edward-style. O_O ), but other than that, Anne Brown's writing didn't really hold any emotion. Even the urgency near the end of the book wasn't felt very much by me. I absolutely adored Calder's sisters. They were much more sinister and creepier, with absolutely no conscience at all, and that made me love them. I think Brown did a good job with these three mermaids, like carving out their individual personalities and character. They were very realistic mythical creatures. The plot was very well done. It was original, with some major twists at the end. I can't wait for the second book now! 4 stars. Want more reviews? Check out my blog! [image error]

The sequel to Bumped left me satisfied. As fascinated as I was by the world McCafferty was presenting me in the first book, I just wasn't that in to Melody or Harmony. Harmony seemed completely whacked out, not because of her churchiness but because of the whole sleeping with Jondoe because he looked exactly how she imagined Jesus , which was creepy. I liked Melody more but wasn't crazy about her. She seemed to serve mostly as a device to offset McCafferty's more extreme examples of a world gone breedy, specifically Shoko and Malia. In Thumped, however, the girls felt more central to the story, probably because the necessary world-building had been taken care of in the first book and there was more time to focus on them. I waited too long after reading to write my review, so it isn't very detailed. Just know that the characters grow and mature organically; none of the situations they were presented with felt contrived. They are forced to make tough, adult decisions, choosing between what is good for themselves and those directly involved or what society wants them to do. They live in a future where teenagers are treated as grownups but have no rights, and I enjoyed watching the characters navigate that world.
I ... uh ... I don't know if I want to keep reading. But I might just to catch up.

So my 2017 is ruined. My beautiful co-worker (who designed the shiny, shiny U.S. cover) threw this at me, and by threw I mean stopped me in the hall and held me hostage until I'd agree to read it. With nothing but her recommendation--and I mean I didn't even read the flap copy here--I dug in, and I will continue this review in that spirit: THE LESS YOU KNOW ABOUT STRANGE THE DREAMER THE MORE YOU WILL ENJOY IT. There's something good fantasy reads do for me that I rarely feel reading anything else. It's the sensation that closing the book without having finished will leave a part of yourself inside. You stay tethered to it, a little keyed up all day until you can get back. Strange does this. It's thanks to Laini Taylor's skill, thanks to the very complete world she's built, the shades of gray in every character. And thanks to dear Lazlo who, at his core, is a lover of stories. If you love books that are about the love of books, please start here. I know a lot of people won't like the romance in the latter part of this book. That's fine. It is one of the few things that smacks strongly of YA--the majority of the content is heartbreakingly mature. So I say with great tenderness that Strange the Dreamer is exquisite, and I will happily place it alongside my other fantasy beloveds as my favorite read of the year so far.

I'm still not sure what I think about Bledsoe's use of Arthurian mythos here. It's a good retelling/interpretation of the stories, with some important twists that you really wish had been part of the original story. Arthur, geez, if you'd just stabbed Mordred in the heart, how much better would life have been? Sure, he's your son, but he's also sort of a psychopath, so why let sentimentality get in the way? On the other hand, it's more or less the King Arthur story with everyone's names changed, in some cases through goofy anagramming, and much as I like the idea of Mordred's (Medraut's) first name being Ted, there's something about it that leaves me a little itchy. Intellectually, I have no problem with it, but I wish I knew why it bugs me. Still, as Arthurian pastiche (sort of) it works really well. All the players are there, and there's plenty of misdirection as to who's really behind the framing of Queen Jenny. Though readers who know their Arthurian myth will realize who the Morgan Le Fay analogue is, Bledsoe confuses the issue enough that by the end I was suspecting everyone of being her. I didn't really care for the frame story, but it wasn't intrusive, so overall I liked the book a lot.

I'm rounding down because, with the exception of Simon (and sometimes Clary), I thought the characters were rather unpleasant. I did enjoy the world building and look forward to exploring it more deeply. The ick factor ending is disturbing, and quite frankly, unnecessary. LOVED it!! Judd and Brenna were an awesome, awesome couple!! They both had so much to overcome...his Silence and Protocol 1, and her demons of remembering what was done to her by Enrique. Both are so heartbreaking in their own right, but they knew that they belonged with each other, no matter the cost, no matter what anyone else said or thought, and they fought to get over those obstacles. Judd's character is so strong, so menacing, he just comes right off the page. He and Brenna were inexorably linked together ever since he helped save her from Enrique, and even though there wasn't anything to explain that link (at least at firstI think I just about cried when they discovered their bond...yay!!!! They deserve it! ), they were constantly drawn to each other even thought Judd tried to remain cold as ice. They formed a friendship of sorts, and as she looked to him for help, answers, and safety when things in her mind just didn't seem right, she truly chiseled away that icy exterior of his. He, while still trying to maintain his icy nature because it is what is needed to maintain his sanity and to keep him from killing on a whim, was always there for her, to listen, to help, and to provide support. It was beautiful watching their relationship grow from a friendship of sorts, one of support, to one of love and passion. And OMG, was there passion!!! When Judd did what he did to help Andrew, flamed out, then woke up still drained, but without dissonance...O.M.G.!!! That Ice Man has some SKIILLZ!!!!!! Oh, I loved how he didn't hold back...he explored, tempted, treated, and did so right by Brenna. i would LOVE for Singh to provide us w/ a novella of Judd's "research". ~~SWOON~~ This had to be my favorite line from that moment: "Can I bite you here, too?" **THUD, THUD, THUD** Even with Judd being so "cold," so Psy, he so often said some of the most beautiful things to Brenna. They were such a touching couple, even when they weren't able to physically do so. And when they were finally able to, look out! And YAY! for the epilogue!! Not only did we get another AMAZING sex scene, but another wonderful thing came from it, too! In addition to the main romance, I loved Singh's interplay of both the bad guy (who I did NOT guess) as well as the Ghost (who I cannot wait to discover) into the plot. She kept it very interesting, and kept me guessing, that's for sure. As always, Singh does a fabulous job of bringing so many other characters into the books. It's such a pleasure to continue revisiting past main characters (i.e., Sascha & Lucas; I also liked Vaughn's little special appearance and him watching over Brenna after she left SnowDancer territory to go get a little pampered), and exploring further the ones from the periphery (i.e., HAWKE **THUD**). She is setting up his book very well, and I am very, very anxious to get to it. It broke my heart, though, to hear about him losing his mate when he was so young; since changelings only have one true mate, I wonder how this will play out for him. All in all...a fabulous read, another amazing story in the series, and enough to keep me anxious to read more.

Noggin's synopsis really surprised me when I first heard about it: how often do you hear about the story of a teen whose head has been cryogenized and reattached to another body a couple of years later, allowing him to live a second life? At first, I found Travis to be a very likable character, a very realistic and mature guy but as the story progressed, I found he was kind of immature in certain situations, especially in the pones concerning Cate and his relationship with her, not accepting the fact that people had moved on for the majority of the book. I obviously get that he felt out of the place at the beginning but his constant attempts at "trying to get her back", just like she was in his possession, despite the fact that she had another boyfriend, really irritated me. Nearing the end of the book, I found myself wanting to scream at him: Stop living in the past ! , as his stubbornness led him to be selfish and to act stupidly. By the way, the "proposing scene" in the coffee shop was one of the most embarrassing I've ever read about, What did he have in mind ???? (p 308)   Apart from Travis, I really like all of the other characters, which felt flawed but realistic, fundamentally human, especially Kyle and Hatton. Their relationship with Travis was really great to witness, they all truly are supportive friends to another and I particularly enjoyed the sarcasm-filled dialogues between Travis and them (particularly Kyle). Despite these problems, I enjoyed my reading experience: John Corey Whaley is a very funny author and I especially like the pattern he created throughout the book: his way of finishing every chapter by a certain group of words and titling the following one the exact same group of words was really interesting, tying the story together. To me, it was a way to orientate the reader on a certain point of the story to then tackle it just after. This system was mostly based on sounds, and the best example was probably "meandering" / "me and a ring" (p 212-213). This book really emphasizes on the relationships between people, and the way they evolve through time. If we put aside the fact that Travis was technically dead for a certain period of time, his return and his every day feel very much like the ones of someone who's back home after a long period of time, not having changed much, but seeing that everyone and everything else actually have changed, having to witness so many differences with the past and to navigate in this foreign environment. Travis is trying to hard to be his old self again while everyone else had to grieve his death, they had to move on, to move one in order to live their own lives and not die with Travis. "Truth is, I was the past and I had to find a way to exist in the future." (p 171) "I was [...] wondering if entering would somehow set everything back on its proper course, if the past could become the present and I'd finally feel like I was standing in the right place." (p 222) The scene at the arcade was a good example for this constant thought of Travis', trying to be the one he was once again, to be the same once again. Finally, the scene at the cemetery with Jeremy Pratt's mother and sister was very nice, a good conclusion to the story. It felt like Travis had finally accepted the fact that his life was now this one, that he should make the most of it, for him, for his dearest ones, ... for Jeremy Pratt; he was finally ready to move on.

I won't be able to do too much of a review on this since it was so short and I don't want to give anything away but suffice to say, this was creepy and odd. First, twins creep me out, especially identical twins. I'm not sure why but they just make me uneasy- and have made me uneasy since I was a child (sometimes I wonder if subconsciously I remember absorbing my twin in the womb or something, these are late night thoughts, welcome to my brain). But this is a very powerful and well written story of the bond of twins and how fear affects a person. This had a sort of Edgar Allan Poe vibe to it with it's focus on psychological terror, which I enjoyed. It's a quick read and I definitely encourage anyone to give it a go.

Unlike earlier books in the series, which I've re-read many times (I used to re-read them while waiting for the later books to come out), this was the first time I'd revisited Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince since I finished the series. It's a very different experience, reading this book now that I know how the whole epic conflict with Voldemort works out, than my relatively-unspoiled first reading. (At the time, there were rumors that a major character died; I had my theories but scrupulously avoided any media where spoilers might lurk, and I read the whole book in two days on the day of release, so I got to enjoy, er, experience the surprise.) This second time through, knowing what's coming, it strikes me that Book Six is actually very bittersweet. Half-Blood Prince isn't as dark and brooding as the preceding book, Order of the Phoenix. Now that Dolores Umbridge is gone, Hogwarts is a bright, happy place again. Now that the O.W.Ls (standardized testing for wizard students) is behind them, Harry and his friends seem to enjoy their classes more; they are less pressured, more leisurely. They find time for romance, for quidditch, for weekends in Hogsmeade, for learning how to apparate. Harry, who was furious at being ignored by Dumbledore in Order of the Phoenix, is back on good terms with the headmaster again: he's even singled out for special one-on-one lessons aimed to help him defeat Voldemort when the time comes. Book Six is the calm before the storm. Outside of Hogwarts, terrible things are happening now that Voldemort is back -- the Daily Prophet is always full of stories of kidnappings, murders, and other tragedies that show the Dark Lord is gaining ground -- and Harry and the others are aware of these miseries but insulated from them. In these dark times more than every before, Hogwarts is a haven, a refuge, a bubble. Dumbledore is the only wizard Voldemort fears, and so Dumbledore's school is the safest place to be. Knowing now that this is Harry's last year at Hogwarts (rather than the anticipated 7th year), I think it's kind of lovely that it was generally such a nice one: that he got to be the Quidditch team captain, that he finally had a potions teacher he could stand, that Gryffindor won the Quidditch cup, and Harry and Ginny got to enjoy a few weeks of happiness. Of course that idyllic calm can't last, and the conclusion is meant to set up the final book, Deathly Hallows. While it's not a cliffhanger in the traditional sense, the end of Half-Blood Prince leaves a lot more open questions than the relatively self-contained plot of the other books in the series. Again, knowing what is coming changed my perspective on the ending. The first time I read it, I was stunned and horrified, not only by Dumbledore's death but also by Snape's apparent betrayal, but this time, I approached the final chapters with a strong sense of inevitability. Random Spoilery Thought: As I've been making my way through Litchick's Epic Harry Potter Group Read (which has now been going on since before Thanksgiving), I've been thinking all along that Snape is so horrible, more horrible than I remembered, so horrible that the big reveal at the end of Deathly Hallows falls flat because it isn't enough to redeem such a nasty character. I still kind of feel that way, but in retrospect I think the part of Half-Blood Prince where Snape gives Harry Saturday detentions after Harry and Malfoy duel is a bit of a give-away. Detention is a really lenient punishment for almost murdering someone, and I should have been much more suspicious of that at the time.

Moving contemporary fiction about personal responsibility, friendship, family, and love. Thought-provoking look at motherhood: what does it mean to be a mother? To not want to be a mother? How are we defined by our relationships with our mothers? Multifaceted characters facing difficult decisions make this an excellent choice for book group discussions.

4 stars Finally. I finally finished this trilogy! Praise be to God! You have no idea how much I've wanted to read the Legend trilogy for two and a half years. Two and a half years of just staring at it and not reading it. Until now. So. Champion. What did I think of it. Well, it was a good finale to a trilogy. I enjoyed it and the ending felt satisfying. Initially, I was worried about the ending being too rushed or if the ending didn't give closure. Thankfully it wasn't like that. So it was good. The stakes are high in Champion. So many things were happening. We've got conspiracies, a war going on, a virus, political intrigue, and EXPLOSIONS! June and Day are the two character that make this trilogy good. As mentioned before in my previous reviews of Legend and Prodigy, they are my favorite characters and I really loved seeing them grow and making tough decisions. They're human, they can't handle everything and sometimes have to do things they don't like. Which is why I like them. They're flawed but are believable. I mean, aside from the age thing, they're good characters. (Why couldn't Marie Lu make them 17 or 18 at the beginning of Legend? As for the political/military stuff, I enjoyed it! This is a dystopian novel where not everything is simple. We've got two countries who hate each other for a petty reason (if you've read Prodigy then you'll understand) and lots of tension and EXPLOSIONS! I'm not exaggerating, there are explosions. There are only two things that bugged me a bit, but not enough to completely annoy me. I'm still not a fan of the romance between June and Day. When they're together, I just don't feel the sparks between these two. It probably didn't help that their love was insta-love in Legend which was annoying if I'm being honest. I like them as individuals and when they work together to accomplish a goal but not together as a romantic couple. I mean, don't get me wrong, Day sounds like a hot guy, and I know June does care about him, but I can't buy into their romance. I wanted June and Anden to be together! I like their sort-of romance much better than when June and Day are together. I really hoped that they would've ended up together by the end but when I found out they didn't I was like: WHY?! I thought they would get together since Day lost his memory of June. But I guess we can't get everything we wanted. Verdict A satisfying conclusion to a trilogy. If you're not sure about starting the series, I highly recommend reading Legend since it is only 305 pages long. If you like it, check out Prodigy and Champion. I am really glad I got to experience the trilogy. Thanks for reading my review! -Cesar

Yes I admit it. I only read it because the series is out and I wanted to watch the series. It would be a waste if the story line is good and I didn't get to read about it first. And it was. I've had my shares reading crime novels and usually, it started with someone being killed. A little bit of background story and bam! Somebody died and here comes the backtracking. But not with this book! I think that's what so genius about this book. It's both at the same time. There's an excerpt of interview with people at every chapter and there's also the real story before the death. It makes you guess who's the dead one! And boy I was wrong. The author wanted you to believe it's those poor poor victim but it isn't. I'm glad it's not either of them. I really thought it would be Jane, giving all she had to face about her son and her past. And then I thought it would be Celeste because of the domestic violence she's facing. Madeline was my last guess. If it's her it would be an accident. But it's Celeste's husband! Perry! He died! OMIGOD! And he's the guy who slept with Jane and being all vile about it. He's Ziggy's father! I couldn't believe it. And he died not because of anything dramatic. Bonnie pushed him out of anger and he fell from the balcony. Bonnie didn't mean for him to fall but he fell and he died. It couldn't have been better. It was better for everybody. I was so scared for Celeste. She was all ready to run away and hide from Perry but Perry found out about the apartment she bought. Although, I'm guessing he would still find out about it and kill her afterwards. But Celeste is free! And Jane got her justice! Apparently, Bonnie's father was abusive towards her mother too. That's explain the sudden rage. And it's not Ziggy who bully Amabella. It's Max, Celeste's son. Because Max saw what Perry did to Celeste. It all make sense now. Everything make sense. I had a hunch that it was the twins who did the bullying but attention was given to Ziggy to begin with.

I have mixed feelings when it comes to this book. There are things I liked about it and things that I didn't. I've been wanting to read this book for months now, and I finally picked it up today and started reading it and I couldn't put it down until I finished it. So yes, this book is good enough to keep you entertained for a few hours, and gripping enough that I couldn't put it down, so there's a positive. Summer is a 16-year-old girl who is abducted by this man named Clover/Colin. He takes her in his white van and drives her to his house in the middle of nowhere where he lives with three other girls he abducted and he re-names her "Lily" and all the other girls also are named after flowers. This book had so much potential, and the idea of this book is intriguing. I have a fascination with books that involve kid-napping, if it's written really well then I think it's super intense and fast-paced and interesting. Summer is kind of an idiot. She spends most of this book crying and feeling completely hopeless (which is understandable under her circumstances) but it still got repetitive after a while. You really have to suspend your belief while reading this book - I find it hard to believe that four girls can't take on one guy. There were so many opportunities for them to escape - and I could think of so many things they didn't try. Also, the writing itself was pretty bad. I understand that this was originally published on wattpad, and it definitely shows. The vocabulary is very basic and there's never any real descriptions of what characters look like, or anything like that. Also, Colin really wasn't all that scary of a villain. His presence really wasn't that intimidating and even when he was acting out violently I never felt afraid of him. He was such a weak villain and his "reason" for being a psychopath is so cliche. The author tried way too hard to make this like Psycho and try and make Colin like Norman Bates. Also, the fact that Lewis, Summer's boyfriend (not the police) was able to figure out that Colin was the abductor like how??? Just because he "seemed suspicious" and he decided to go look in his house? It felt very set up. Also, the way Summer so easily recovered in the hospital and was able to get over everything so easily.. It felt so unrealistic. She was abducted for eight months, raped, and witnessed several murders and now she's fine after a few days? It's so unrealistic. Also, the ending felt very anti-climatic to me. All the build up towards Colin getting caught and then hat final scene was so.. lame. I don't know what I was expecting but I wanted there to be more happening at the end. Maybe since I read a lot of thrillers my expectations were too high for the ending? This book was okay. It was definitely good enough to keep me reading for hours and finish it in one sitting, but I'm not as impressed with this book as I thought I would be.

Rebecca is the pinnacle of gothic literature. While there's no true ghosts, the way that you'd think of. No spirits of white wisping in the corner. No creaks and groans that sound suspiciously like steps. Yet there is still an ominous presence--in the form of our narrator's constant reminder of who Rebecca was, and Mrs. Danvers the creepy old goon. Our narrator is extremely unsure of herself. She's an introvert, painfully shy, and assumes that everyone believes the worst of her. This is in stark contrast to Rebecca, the always-warm and personable first Mrs. de Winter. And Maxim's stern refusal to talk about Rebecca compounded with everyone else's desire to talk of nothing else makes the new Mrs. de Winter feel like an unwelcome outsider to Mandereley. There's many little things that build up--Maxim's obvious refusal to go near certain places because it reminds him of Rebecca. The servants who still pluck the flowers from the garden and arrange them the way Rebecca liked them, and who stand looking as if they don't hear when the narrator asks for something different. The constant reminders of those calling: "There were such splendid balls before!" Before: when Rebecca was alive. And of course as a result the narrator is entirely at a loss as to how she's supposed to act. It's sometimes painful, the situations she makes for herself. The costume she chose to wear at the party. Her accidentally breaking the cupid and stashing the broken pieces instead of owning up to it. Hiding her feelings from Maxim, which would have saved herself a lot of heartache. What I loved the most though was Rebecca. The imprint she left. I couldn't deny that I would have had the same obsession as our narrator had--the way everyone described Rebecca, she sounded unattainable. As though she were a legend, and not a person that had died a year previously. And when the narrator finally learns the secrets of Mandereley, I was duly impressed. I hadn't seen that ending coming. Rebecca very much reminded me of Amy from Gone Girl--and I can't help but think that maybe Gillian Flynn may have gotten her inspiration for Amy from Rebecca. They're so similar with their ability to deceive and manipulate, it seems logical.

I was entirely disappointed with this book. I loved the first one, the second was okay (no where near as good as the first, but I chalked it up to the "second-book curse"), and then I got to this one and basically suffered through. I just could not get into this book. It wasn't entertaining and it wasn't interesting. The events could have been, but I just couldn't get into it. I am giving this a 1 and not a 0 because there were a couple aspects I liked in it such as some of the character attitudes, but that's about all.

Okay. I just have to defend this book. Everybody is going crazy about how awful it is. Don't get turned off by these reviews. I loved it! It was exciting with a good writing style, with that little tiny nagging at the back of your mind that tells you something isn't quite right, until you finally learn the truth about what is happening. I would recommend this book to anybody who even slightly likes this genre, because it is way better than anybody else says it is. Also, for those of you that have read it, You are all comparing this to Twilight. I disagree. First of all, Daniel. True, he has his whole life and he stays in high school with 17 year old girls, blah, blah, blah. But this is different, in my opinion. No matter what he does, he always ends up finding Luce. I think that he was trying to never find her, because she'd die, so he did bad things in bad places, because she isn't a bad person. He then got sent to the reform school where she would obviously NEVER be. But the fire that killed Trevor was some kind of thing that righted the world or aligned their path or something, just so she'd get sent to the reform school. That's why he was so surprised. That's just my theory, it's not necessarily true. Also, it has a lot of interesting plot turns. Sure, two people are head over heels for her and she has to decide who to be with, but isn't that the same with most teen romances, not just twilight? I thought that this had unique plot twists that made it different and better from other teen romances either. Her past lives? The fact that her two 'lovers' were mortal enemies? Penn dying? Yeah. A lot of other things too. I think that people who complained about how awful it was just were looking for a fight. Note: If this book confuses you, the sequel makes everything make sense. :) Torment

I was pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed this book. It spoke to the internal contradictions and conflict within us all. Siddhartha's spiritual journey first draws him to a life of being a nomad, before realizing that he was running from himself. Then Siddhartha seeks a life of in the flesh before becoming ill from his absorption in material things I think everyone should set aside some time to read this book! There is so much to be learned from it. Hesse's style of writing engages you and draws you in, creatively expressing a variety of themes we can all learn from. I thoroughly enjoyed this book, finishing it in a single evening. There are few books which leave you with an tidbits of thought that leave a lasting impression on you. Siddhartha is one of those gems which is an enjoyable read which makes you think.

Well, I read this third even though it's the first book in this series, because it took a while to get to me from the library. In any case, I think I like it best out of them all so far. Percy's pretty entertaining, mainly because he and his friends get a lil snarky sometimes. And I like all the mythology stuff. It's very educational, actually. Original review at Gabic Reads. ARC received via Netgalley. Chelsea Fine is amazing. I love her novella Sophie & Cater, even though I yearned for a longer book. And I enjoyed her Archers of Avalon series, which I still need to finish. I fell in love with Pixie and Levi's story. It was heart-wrenching and sweet. Watching them heal together was amazing. Pixie wants to leave the place where too many memories lie. Levi knows he needs to make something more of his life than being a handyman at a rundown inn. The two can't bear to be near each other because it hurts too much. They both blame themselves for the accident, and think the other does too. There were so many scenes between them that were really emotional. Levi parents are separated and live in different states and he feels abandoned and to blame for everything that happened. I loved seeing him heal that relationship. And the end!! GAH!!! I thought he was going ot let her leave and I was sitting there thinking "NOOOO!!!!!" But it was all good in the end. I'm glad somebody came to their senses. Zack is such a character! I hope he gets his own book. I love this quote of his: "The best friendships are rooted in hatred and blackmail." I have a friendship like that <3 If you love novels that involve lots of healing, but also avoidance and blame, Best Kind of Broken is an awesome book!
