I can always count of my girl, Chima. This was a satisfying conclusion to an engaging series. As an aside, does anyone else think Dancer is the most powerful person in the book? And think he needs his own series?

EDIT: I originally rated it 4 stars but since then (and watching the movie) I've realized how much I enjoyed this book and I really want to reread it (the ultimate test), so I guess it does deserve its 5th star ! I added the Martian to my (already awfully long) TBR list quite some times ago. The concept sounded quite intriguing. And then each time I browsed my shelves, there was The Martian winking at me but I would think "Seriously the guy is stranded all alone on an entire planet... This could potentially be the most boring book ever" ... and I would find something more exciting to read. And then the Martian happened to be on my new book buddy TBR' list (love Coffee & Books Book Buddies!). So I finally got my ticket to Mars in spite of my initial doubts... And boy did I enjoy the trip! It's hard to pinpoint exactly what made this book such a great experience. Because honestly for the most part Watney spends his time doing the most boring things ever like watching 70's TV shows, moving dirt around, or shitting in a box... And yet the author manages to strike an almost perfect balance of (realistic sounding) scientific facts, McGyver-worthy tricks and witty storytelling to make Mark's routine a page-turner. Mark Watney is quite the charachter, honestly I probably couldn't stand him on Earth but on Mars, he is just perfect. Maybe just a bit too much because I should think someone alone on a dead rock of a planet would experience some emotional difficulties if only because he's missing his family/friends or his earthly comfort. Still I can't deny that I thoroughly enjoyed the (bumpy) ride and was sad to see it end. So the only reason i'm withdrawing a star (a half really) for now is that I'm curious to see how will it will pass the test of the reread....

I know this book was set in the 1980's, but it had a feeling of long ago, like the 1800's. Possibly because the story partly revolved around Eli, who was probably from that time. Possibly because the Swedish setting was cold and dark. Dark as in haunting and sad, and dark as in much of the story took place in the night time. Creepy, terrible things happen at night. Especially when you have to walk the paths through the forest to get anywhere. I couldn't help but imagine this whole story in black and white. Except the blood. That was vivid. And Eli's yellow dress. Those scenes were quite unsettling, disturbing. But as overall creepy, violent and dark as this book was, it was just as tender, touching and emotional at the same time. Loneliness, love, friendship, longing, devotion, hope were on every page, between almost every character. Sometimes it was beautiful, sometimes it was twisted and sick. As vividly detailed and descriptive as each scene was, I felt the end was just a little vague and seemingly rushed. It was a big flourished end, but I was so engrossed in the details up to then, that I really missed them in the final scenes. Because of that (the endings are always so important to me) I offer up 4 1/2 stars, but because GR doesn't allow that, I ultimately settled on 5. It was just that good.

** spoiler alert ** I couldn't recommend this book any higher than I already do. This was absolutely amazing. I was hooked right from the beginning and couldn't stop reading it. Finished it in 2 days and I would tell everyone to read this book. The author had me hooked from the first book, and then where there was the twist at the end, I was absolutely gob smacked. To start with, the first book reminded me too much of Pretty Little liars, but reading the second book has made me realise how different of a story it is from PLL. Absolutely fantastic. The characters were so addicting and you just felt like you wanted to more and more about their life as it went on. You wanted to keep reading to find out what had happened to Parker, and what Nolan had done to the girls. I always want to finish a chapter and then put the book down, but at the end of every chapter...I just wanted to keep reading more and more, it was absolutely amazing. This has just confirmed with me that I want to read more of Sara Shepard's books. Absolutely brilliant author and can't want to read more.

I really am a sucker for happy endings. This one was almost sweet enough to make me forget all the frustration I telt through most of the book. Not quite, though, because there was a bunch of non-communication and annoyingness that brought my enjoyment of this book down. Sisterhood Everlasting wasn't what I expected. Something huge and awful happens in these girls' lives and the rest of the book is them dealing with their feelings and finding a way to live with it. Most of it was dark and painful, but also insightful and well written. I'm not sure if I was enjoying it, exactly, but it was definitely good. After a while I started getting frustrated at some plot points. Why is Carmen with this asshole? Why can't Lena just fucking talk to Costos? Why is nobody talking to Brian? I guessed that Tibby had been sick and not suicidal  early on, and the fact that nobody was considering it pretty much confirmed it. With the end getting closer, we got more and more resolution and happiness and that was great. I like where the girls are at now, even though not everything was really resolved. I didn't mind the things that were a bit ridiculous (not the least of which being Lena's financial situation), the emotions seemed right and in the end I just really enjoyed seeing these girls happy and FINALLY together  again. And I LOVED that Tibby named her daughter after Bailey. She was one of the best parts of the original books, even though she was only in one, and this was a wonderful tribute to her.

A decent book that had me pretty hooked all the at up to right before the end. What really confused me were all the unique terms the characters used like pivot, inversion, Baroque event, and SRT . Although the author explained them all near the beginning, I still felt jumbled and confused when reading those words. Though I said I was hooked until the end, that is not completely true, for I thought the book as a whole was a bit dull and repetitive but each chapter and "movement" itself was kind of interesting. However, it eventually got old and even the climax itself fell a bit flat. Also the characters made me want to punch myself because they practically did and said the same things over and over again. Another thing: the relationships in the novel weren't working for me at all. Even through all this critique, I'd say I'm pretty neutral about this book since it has a wonderful plot line and great writing. Some things just confused me and/or agitated me while in the process.

** spoiler alert ** This is definitely the "darkest" book in the series. Mia struggles with depression after her breakup with Michael. Reading about Mia spending day after day in bed was tedious, but that behavior is exactly clinical depression and teen readers need to understand what it looks like. There were some plot issues I didn't "get:" Mia and Lana suddenly buds?? Well, her psychologist did tell Mia to do something scary and shopping with Lana seemed scary. I thought all along that Lana was behind the ihatemia website, but we later find out that's not true. I'm probably in the minority as I adore J.P. and don't care too much for Michael, but geez, J.P. is a girl's dream--cute and sensitive and caring!! I guess he's too perfect!! Oh, and Mia does finally shake her depression and drops a whammy on her country after discovering a long lost document!

Labyrinth Lost is a witchy coming-of-age story about Alejandra Mortiz, a sixteen-year-old Latina girl living in Brooklyn who just wants to go out to parties with her best friend Rishi like a normal teenager. Unfortunately for Alex, she comes from a long line of magic-wielding brujas and brujos, who all expect her to awaken her powers and formally embrace a magical life with the traditional Death Day ceremony. Her sisters Lula and Rose are both adept with their own magic and they try to get Alex interested in awakening hers. What they don't know is that Alex's powers have already awakened. She's just afraid to let them out again after what happened the first time.... Read my full review at The Gothic Library: http://www.thegothiclibrary.com/labyr... Also, for a spoilery bit that I couldn't include in my blog review: Hurray for queer representation! This book has the best portrayal of a queer love triangle I've ever seen. The set-up of this book makes you expect your usual heteronormative paranormal romance tropes: a dark brooding bad boy suddenly appears in Alex's life, and she seems somewhat drawn to him. But wait! There's also Alex's best friend Rishi, who she tends to stare at a little too long.... It can be difficult to break readers out of their heteronormative expectations without beating them over the head with gay, but Zoraida Cordova walks that thin line, the perfect balance of both subtle and hard-to-miss. And by the end of the novel, she has not only turned an over-worn trope on its head, but has also made an important stride in providing more visibility for bisexuality and for relationships between women in young adult fantasy.

It goes without saying that Book four was my absolute favorite installment in this series. And for good reason... here is a taste of the "sweet" Eric that made me swoon... as well as Sookie... (Eric to Sookie) "We could go back to your house. I can stay with you always. We can know each other's bodies in every way, night after night. I could love you." His nostrils flared, and he looked suddenly proud. "I could work. You would not be poor. I would help you." "Sounds like a marriage," I said... "Yes," he said. Does this sound "out of character" for our usually self-centered vampire viking?? Well, yes... it does. That's because this is the book where Eric temporarily loses his memory, thanks to a curse by a vengeful witch out to make a point against the vampires of Shreveport. Eric was found by Sookie one night wandering around Bon Temp lost and confused. She was asked to hide him and protect him from the witch coven. While she was taking care of him Sookie could not help but fall for this all of a sudden gentle, caring and oh so sweet gorgeous viking... she fell right into his charms. Who could blame her though?? I fell right along with her... I loved this Eric. But, would he stay this way? HHmmmmm... I'll let you read on your own to find out. There is also plenty of action in book four... Sookie's brother is missing and feared dead. We are introduced to more of the Were pack in Shreveport and we get more Alcide time. (The hunky werewolf we met in the last book.) We also find out that along with shifters, werewolves, witches and vampires there are also... were-panthers. When will it end?? haha... I'm beginning to think there are fewer humans in Bon Temps than we originally believed. We also meet Claudette... kind of a "fairy" godmother who swoops in and saves Sookie when she falls asleep at the wheel of her car and helps the supernatural community in their efforts to fight against the witch coven causing problems for everyone. And we learn that vampires have an unusual attraction to fairy blood. And as usual... every supernatural big wig has their romantic eyes set on Sookie. Her love life resembles that of a roller coaster... big ups and even bigger downs! Just walk away Sookie... just walk away! The good news is that for once Sookie did not end up in the hospital. But, even though she doesn't get beaten up physically... her heart certainly does take a beating this time around. This is the book that made me want to see Sookie get her happily ever after. She deserves one... Well, now I'm on to book five... "Dead as a Doornail"... as we continue on our Sookie Stackhouse countdown. Follow the Sookie countdown on our blog: http://ktbookreviews.blogspot.com/

This surprised me a lot like  The Winner's Curse  surprised me. I ended up enjoying it more than I thought I would. And that's where the comparison ends. At this point there's more questions than answers. I look forward to discovering what's up. I will also take alllll the Gideon and Gwyneth scenes to come. Just... get to know each other better before having the happiest ending ever, okay? Okay. It's delightful brain candy that I am glad I decided to read, if only to get me out of the reading slump caused by my previous read. Happy reading if you decide to do so!

Not as good as the first two but still amazing. I feel like the expectations I had going into it both helped and ruined the book. Most people said it was boring but the very end was really exciting. I, however, found the book great except the very end was kind of anti climatic and not that exciting. But overall, this is one of my new favourite series and I highly recommend it. I'm really excited to see how Argent and Nelson play into this next book. Nelson scares the heck out of me but I still find his role so interesting. Also Risa and Connor better have a happy ending together and same with Cam but not with Risa. Ok just realized all the characters who need to have their stories close in UnDivided and oh man I am excited.

I'm surprised to say I'm totally on the Stephenie Meyer bandwagon. I really didn't have an interest in these books, didn't know any of the story, but finally decided to see what the buzz was about. My inner 17 year old is in heaven. There's nothing like a new love, and Meyer is wonderful about capturing those feelings of hesitation and exultation at the start of the new relationship. In New Moon, we see the devastation with the loss of a relationship when Edward wants to protect Bella's soul. Meyers also does really put an interesting twist on the vampire legends, using some traditional myths, and completely discarding others.

Istyria book blog ~ B's world of enchanted books Because this is the second book in the series, I'm not going to write a full review. Same with the third and last book. I adore Zuzanna and Mik. Both of them. They're so cool and cute together. And I don't trust Thiago. I do like Ziri though. I even like Liraz and Hazael. OMG! I knew I should hate Thiago. Stupid ass. AND Issa is back! YAY! And oh no, Hazael died! That were the spoilers from this book I had to share. The short version.

** spoiler alert ** It has been a long time since I've read this book and I loved it all the same. Four and Tris as characters are really interesting to me and I really enjoy reading about them. Sometimes the writing seemed repetitive which could be a little jarring when the same descriptions are used so often you notice it. But other than that I had a good time diving back into the Divergent world.

Wow it took me so long to finish this book! It's my fault though. I've been distracted by some contemporaries. Oops. Even though it took me a long time to finish it, I did find this book to be really good. Is it better than the Tiger Saga, well in my opinion no, but it had the same feel. This book had lots of adventure and thrills that I really enjoyed. This author is just really good with writing books that never have a dull moment. Something is always happening! Liliana was minding her own business in a restricted part of the museum. She's rich and her parents donated a lot of money to the museum, so she was allowed there. Then her life starts getting crazy when she meets Amon for the first time. I know a lot of people were annoyed with Lily's character. They thought she was a snob. I didn't really think so. Whenever she brought up her abundance of wealth, I felt like she was just stating a fact, and not trying to act haughty. Amon did control and force her to come with him to Egypt. He really didn't give her a choice. I know, creepy, but he was trying to save the world. Can we all just remember that Amon was actually trying to save the world? He couldn't do it without Lily. She was just at the wrong place at the wrong time. Amon could've been bonded with anyone. It could've been the janitor, but where's the fun in that? The romance: Mmm it was underwhelming, because Lily was just moping about how Amon seemed to reciprocate her feelings one moment, and doesn't the next. The really romantic parts were at the end of the book, which was frustrating as hell considering the circumstances they were in. I loved Amon's brothers. I hope they would still play a big part in the next book! BLOG POST

Once again, this is a wonderfully presented book. The illustrations are lovely and inserted very well with the text. I found the story more interesting than the one in the first book, too. It was a lot darker (those poor cats and dogs!) and due to this there was a lot more at stake. I also enjoy how the siblings work together, but still have an appropriately tetchy relationship with each other a lot of the time.

Ehhhhhhhh. Some of this was really great. I loved the main bad guy, his MO, and basically how he came into being. I thought it was awesome. I also loved how Barbara's mobility is finally explained (not much of a spoiler--it's a neural implant). I don't remember that being mentioned pre-Burnside, and suddenly in Burnside it's known she has this neural implant to create her mind map, and I was like "that sounds really risky, I don't think she would do that." Turns out she would, for plausible reasons. I also loved, as always, the dynamic between her, Frankie, and Dinah. I hope that Frankie sticks around in Rebirth. There were two things I didn't like, and it was enough to make me just not like the arc. One, stop trying to make Barbara and Luke Fox happen. I feel like they don't have any chemistry, not to mention it's sort of weird that it's this little relationship that only exists in the continuity of Burnside Batgirl, and they sort of barely interact in the rest of the comic lines (unless they do interact in Batwing, which I have not read). Two,  uh...so wait...The Fugue planted a fake memory that Barbara had started a company, and then Barbara actually started this company to make up for it? Isn't grad school enough? Like what has she been doing at any point that would make it plausible for her to start a clean energy corporation? I mean, it's a cool idea in theory, but I felt like it majorly did not fit--with her character, with the rest of the series, with her being in grad school for something entirely unrelated. Glad to see Batgirl getting a rebirth, because I think she needs it.

This book is built on a fascinating idea - a competition for most popular and most innovative app in which our heroine is a brilliant programmer and contestant who came up with a boyfriend app. The first part revolved around the contest and the second part revealed a much deeper plot. I think Sise made some devastating mistakes that bumped my opinion of this book. Here's the mistakes: 1) The logic behind the boyfriend app (1.0 and 2.0) Boyfriend app 1.0 is realistic but too common to even stand competition and I believe that if this app were put into application, based on limited time for research, I doubt the app would have 1/10 the success rate as depicted in the book. The 2.0 version of the app is just way out of the realm of reality, pure fantasy. Even though sounds may trigger certain response to the brain, I seriously doubt an app would be powerful enough to cause people to temporarily fall in love at the flip of a button. I mean if that's even possible, hell, a lot of people would have taken advantage of that already. Also, I am surprised and horrified really to find that no one (in the book) would be disgusted by the fact that girls are using a mobile app to force boys to love them! This is totally criminal! If Audrey found out and used that advantage to get a scholarship for herself, she's absolutely evil. What was more disturbing is the fact that Audrey acted like she's on the good side and kinda heroic for not accepting the deal proposed to keep quiet. She hacked into another person's computer, she exploited the manipulative logic of the program to win a scholarship and acted like she was a victim later on! Then she wanted to fight and be heroic. I really need to be careful and probably will avoid books by Katie Sise in the future because frankly, she and I have very different moral standards, apparently.

So freaking good!! Melanie Moreland is a favorite author for me. There's not a story she writes that I don't enjoy, but seriously, The Contract is by far my favorite! Review to post June 1 for author's blog tour on Books and Fandom . Stop by to enter the giveaway too! ARC received with thanks from author in exchange for a fair review.

After a devastating STD makes the majority of women infertile, ultra conservative religious extremists get into power. Abortion is made illegal. The prison system is also reformed to account for the high numbers of inmates and the massive expenses. With the exception of criminals too dangerous or serious to release back into the public, people are chromed based on their crime. Every surface of their body becomes a rich and vibrant colour that matches their crime. Hannah Payne, who grew up in a very religious home and was a dedicated member of her church, wakes up red. She has been chromed for the crime of murder- for having an abortion. Her sentence is made longer by the fact that she will not reveal the name of the father or the person who performed it. Hannah's entire life is thrown upside down. She has become the lowest of society, reviled by everyone that sees her bright red skin, the colour of blood. The story goes back and forth from present to past, explaining how she fell in love with her pastor and how their relationship grew. As she struggles in her new life, she faces challenges that she never could have imagined. There are people who want to kill her for her crime, and her bright red skin makes her an easy target. Easy to spot, and easy to harm without anyone standing up for her. No one will hire chromes. No one will associate with chromes, especially not reds. Her only chance is a long shot, a dangerous journey with a girl that she befriended in a strict chistian halway house. A modern retelling of The Scarlet Letter, you see how much Hannah is victimized for the difficult circumstances that she came under, and how judgmental people can be. This is a story of awakening and finding strength that she never even knew she had. Last week, I was actually reading an article online about abortion. The question was that if it becomes illegal, would the pro-life supporters also support sentencing women for murder if they had an abortion. Its an interesting question. I liked how this book handled it.
Brilliant. Impressive. Smart. Funny. There is hope for the YA literary world after all.

This was a quick read that kept me hooked but, really, it was teetering on the verge of 2 stars until the last little bit. Once we finally found out what happened to our main character, Helena, and her husband and daughter, I was hit with such an emotional punch. I really enjoyed the way that Torre ended this book and that was where it's magic really resided. The build-up to that ending was kind of boring to me. So many chapters ended with really vague (or not so vague) statements and questions about what was going to be revealed and I was over it by the halfway point. I could only read things like (paraphrasing) "I killed my husband" or "I'm crazy and I'm gonna tell you why" so many times before I was like JUST TELL US. Also, like, a good chunk of this book takes place while a cow gives birth. Literally. That's it. Okay, anyways, I did enjoy this for the addictability and the ultimate payoff, but it was kind of silly along the way.

4 stars. Do you know when you start reading a book recommened from people whose taste you trust but doesn't really convince you? This was the case with Burning sky. When I started it, I really didn't care for it, I read the first 20 pages and I thought that I would be nice and give it 3 stars. And then there was the insta-love with rescuing in a silly and implausible way and a lot of nonsense and a lot eye rolling on my part. Around page 40 and I was ready to give it 2 stars and finish it only because I was buddy reading it. And then it got amazing. Really. At a certain point I was sure that I wouldhave given it 5 stars. There need to be more hype around this book, it's one of the best take on this kind of plot. Grate male character, strong heroine, many plot twist, good chamestry between the characters, interesting setting. I'm in love with the whole idea of the crucible( I won't tell you anything because I don't won't to spoil the surprise). I'm more than a little in love wih Titus. And with Iolanthe "I'm going to break your wand hand," she shouted. "And your skull, too. I love the fact that what had started as ista love with the young orphan maiden gets saved by prince charming on a white horse( literally) , the worst cliche ever, changes into : What kind of person are you, to live without honor or integrity?" His nails dug into his palm. "Obviously, the kind chosen for what others are too decent to do." He wanted to come across as flippant, but instead he sounded harsh and angry. She clenched her hand. "I liked you much, much better when I didn't know you. " Wih this I'm not saying that this book hasn't any flaws.It has many; the worls building it's very confusing and at some points you'll find yourself start to roll your eyes and the finale is terribly anticlimactic. But it is vasly entartaining and I would definetly recommend it to any lovers of the genre. And you need to meet Titus.

I can has the second book now? I'm really not looking forward to letting 30 other people at the library read it first. This is a supernatural teen romance with angels. It has a love triangle. It has a girl struggling to understand her gifts. But this one is awesome. I seriously thought about giving it 5 stars and would have, except for the last 10 pages or so sort of stole that away. I love that our main character, Clara, doesn't become an absolute idiot for either boy. She might not be as focused, but she doesn't do anything stupid. I love that there is mystery to the angels, the Black Wings, and the idea of purpose, but Cynthia Hand doesn't string us along with no resolution. Answers are given slowly, throughout the book and they make you want to keep reading. Tucker is a proper love interest for a book directed at teen girls - he's sweet, thoughtful, clever and funny and he treats her right. While the other bit of the love triangle - Christian - is pretty lame and lacks personality in Unearthly, you can tell that he's going to be a huge part of the next book. Also, both relationships grow slowly from the beginning of the book and evolve naturally. Really enjoyed this and I can't wait to get my hands on Hallowed.

The plot was unique and the dialogue was amusing. I thought the romance could have been improved a little. It needed a bit more reasoning, beyond finding each other attractive and proximity etc. Much like the first two wives. Seemed a bit like it wouldn't have mattered who they were married too because they would have loved them if they were attractive and reasonably kind (especially during the first two thirds of the book). It couldn't really be helped though since the children were such a focus they took up a lot of pages in the story. For that reason, I don't usually enjoy that type of plot but in the case of The Bride and the Beast, I did enjoy it. The kids were so cute and diabolical. Even so, I have to admit, being a stepmother/parent to so many children (and counting) seems a bit like a nightmare to me. I like kids but not to that degree. I can't imagine how draining it would be to have so many mischievous (flat out naughty in some cases) children to look after. Poor Willow will never have a time in her life where she isn't raising children. Side note: the author really won me when Bannor didn't have any children outside of marriage and instead was taking them in to save them. So nice.

** spoiler alert ** rating: 3.5 it was good the first 3/4 of it, but the last quarter just went downhill. morris was def my favorite character, so I'm happy he finally got a good job with clyde. but honestly I wanted emaline and luke to get back together. in my opinion theo was way too over the top and just annoying. but also for them to have a half-breakup and then never even talk again was stupid. i mean if you're going to have a couple break up at least let it be a full-blown break up and get it over with instead of dragging it on. overall decent book, but ending just ruined it.

This is very weird, it's a 3  rating but it has to be explained: > The beginning is strong, I loved it so much. It was heading somewhere > The protagonists had an amazing chemistry, right from the epilogue and until page 93. > But then the plot becomes a mess. It's so weird! It was going somewhere, things were established, there was (seemingly) a goal but it all got lost so fast. And it's a bit sad because I was so excited with the beginning, there were so many sparks - I kept wondering how come the rating wasn't all that great. So I got very disappointed. It was sweet, and ultimately there's a happy ending, but things are solved too easily; it's a bit anti-climatic. For example, the family conflict: It got solved OUT OF THE BLUE. I was happy because it meant happiness, but storywise? It was lazy writing. It was an easy way out. Then some relationships and character developments more ahead were rather... Unexpected. It all just became too much. There was too much happening and not enough context, not enough explanations, not enough backstory. This book tried to be at least three books. These characters could've grown a whole lot more if only they had more pages. I'm here just lingering on how good the first pages were.

Few books can make me laugh out loud: Bitterblue, however, easily had me laughing throughout. Kristin Cashore's dialogue is witty and deep. The best part is that not only is the overall story great, but every side story is just as developed and deep. Few writers can reach the point in their writing that Cashore has. Of course, this book is not just about love. If it was, I wouldn't have given it such a high rating. This story is about a psychopath. The more I learned about the psychopath who went by the name of Leck, the more I was revolted by him and others in the real world (sadly, they do exist) like him. Cashore did a great job helping me as a reader to understand what Leck did and thus understand the capacity for horrors humankind has. But she also provided me with characters full of goodness that proved that there is hope. Great book. Dark, sickening, horrifying, yes; but also beautiful. Update: I do love Bitterblue; how could I note, when it was written by Cashore, whose feminist fantasies have become such favorites of mine? I love the strong women, I love the open LGBTQ relationships, I love the disability that is actually well-represented in a world where that almost never happens (see "Me Before You" for proof--actually, nevermind, please don't, just know it's awful for the disability community). I love the masterfully crafted settings, the well-detailed characters who feel real and are almost always entirely consistent with the personalities Cashore originally gave them, and I love the dialogue that keeps what would otherwise be a dark hole of horror and sorrow into a sometimes laugh-out-loud funny work of fiction. However. There must always be a however, mustn't there? However. At the beginning of the book, after the prologue, I easily believed that Bitterblue was 18. Despite the fact that the novel's opening scene has her as a young child, the intro to the main book itself conveys her new age quite well. Unfortunately, for me at least, this became less true as the book progressed, so that I typically thought of her as no older than 16, and struggled to picture her as even that old. Somehow Cashore wrote her as too young at times, forgetting that 18 is closer to 20 than to 16 in maturity levels, a forgetting possibly a result of Cashore's other protagonists (Fire and Katsa) being closer to 20 themselves in their books. This made Bitterblue's relationship with Saf less real, less deep for me. I wish I had been able to feel their passion more and I believe the biggest reason I couldn't came from this odd cloudiness of Bitterblue's age. Additionally, though the rest of the book is extensive, containing marvelous definition and detail, Fire's appearance comes across as entirely abrupt. I wanted there to be so much more to this part. I mean, there was a whole book devoted to Fire's life; why can't we have at least a few pages to remind the reader what happened? And don't tell me that would make the book too long, it's already 500+ pages as it is, what's another 100 once you've reached half a thousand? Because this aspect of the story wasn't more drawn out, I felt lost and confused, especially since I couldn't remember Pikkia or many of the other things Fire offhandedly mentions. For such a major plot point, I was disappointed that it wasn't given further elaboration. Even so, I loved the book. It show's humanity at its weakest, it shows war-torn nations at their most ugly; and it shows the capacity for beauty and healing in spite of all that. What more could a person ask for, really, when all is said and done?

3 1/2 stars Rachel is a mess. A drunk, obsessive, borderline-stalker, self-pitying, self-loathing, self-destructive mess. She also holds the key to the disappearance of the young woman whose life she glimpses from the train...if only she could remember what happened the night she got blackout-drunk. The writing is absorbing, and the attention to the little details of life makes the story feel real, like something that could be happening in your neighborhood, to the people you pass everyday on your commute. But waiting for clues to the central mystery to be doled out can be an exercise in frustration, one compounded by the fact that every single character in the story is so unlikable. I appreciate Rachel's complexity and the way her character develops over the course of the story, but there were so many, many times I just wanted to reach into the book and shake some sense into her. The resolution of the mystery was pretty satisfying, and all the pieces seemed to fit, however it was so drawn out that what should have been the most exciting part of the story actually started to drag. I also wanted a little bit more of what became of the all the various characters, but the ending chose to focus on Rachel alone. Overall, an interesting story with a fantastic sense of atmosphere, but weighed down by pacing problems and lack of characters that didn't make me want to slap them.

Leigh Bardugo Ruin and Rising Henry Holt & Co Before I begin to rant about this book, can I complain how I loathe the new user interface of Goodreads. I know that modern layout tends to be more obtuse and rounded, but this whole new layout is so cluttered and atrocious. It==I quoted what my boss said word by word--dun make sense at all. Anyway, I think this will be my last book that I read this year, as all my books left unread are Dune--I cringe when I click the insert book/author feature, it's so fucking messy--and Inkworld series--which I'm not sure I'm able to finish one of them in remaining days of this year. But, yeah whatever. Let's talk about the ending of the original trilogy of The Grisha series--as we have more Grisha in Six of Crows. As I have uttered over and over, The Grisha has so much potential in Shadow and Bone. The Russian-insinuated high fantasy (even though Bardugo messes the Russian surname--according to some knowledgeable people--but I won't complain since it is high fantasy anyone so why we should follow the real Russian world anyone??? ), great characters with great sense of humor, an intriguing premise. The Grisha has all basic recipe to be a great trilogy after all. But, Bardugo mistakenly mixes the wrong ingredients. It all begins in the second book, while I begin to sense that the magic has lost. It starts to feel boring and all the excitement that I had when I read the first book all magically vanished. Bardugo tries to fix it on the third book which I really appreciate it. The only problem is that the the first half of the book particularly can be omitted. It feels like Bardugo wants to stretch this book till the climax where a twist is introduced which is really nice actually. When a final battle occurs, the quality of book begins to dwindle again. But, when it comes to the ending, she gives us such a sweet ending that it warms my cold heart. Ruin and Rising is really unstable for me. It's like a roller-coaster. The journey to the top has been tiring and exhausting and uninspiring, but when the roller-coaster starts to go down, it's an exhilarating and enjoyable ride. It's an okay ending for a trilogy that has so much potential.

I'm a bit conflicted because I absolutely flew through this (I read this in less than four hours). It made me cry, yet I can't say I love this story. I've read some reviews, trying to deduce my own feelings about this book, and many complain about Belly being annoying. While I agree that she has some maturing to do, let's cut her some slack. She is just turning 16. She's very much in the middle of figuring herself out, and I think this book does a good job depicting her struggle. Belly has her frustrating moments, but I can't say that really affected my enjoyment. I think my main issue was with Conrad. Without getting into spoilers, I don't really see what was appealing about him in the first place. Jeremiah always seemed to be the one having friendly interactions with Belly, and I found myself rooting for him throughout. I was disappointed when it didn't turn out to be the case. Conrad just comes off as an asshole 99.9% of the time. I finished reading this about an hour ago, and I can't really remember a single scene before the end where he and Belly share a solitary, meaningful interaction in which he's actually being a nice person. I feel like I'm being a bit of a hater, as I do understand his plight, but that's just how I felt. I liked the idea of Belly spending all her summers on Cousins Beach, as well as the incorporated flashbacks and her relationship with both her mom and Susannah. I could sense that ending from a mile away, but it didn't stop me from bawling like a baby when it finally hit. Overall, I would recommend this book if you like bad boys and a few tears with your summer romance.

This book presents a terrible representation of a trans woman. Rather than portray a trans experience, this portrays the experience of someone with dissociative identity disorder (which is barely a thing anyway). Worse than that, the source material is way more interesting than what is portrayed here. The artistic liberties the author took to flesh out the story were poorly thought out. How such an interesting story and vivid characters can be painted so flat is beyond me. This novel is a disservice to the gender and sexual minority spectrum.

I have mixed feelings about this book. The writing is excellent, but the story and the characters falter. The beginning is slow. Alina is hiding. She's lost the strength of character she developed over the first two books, never to fully regain her inner strength. The Apparat is hiding them and trying to control Alina. He's a weak antagonist. The Darkling and the world outside the caves is worse than ever, but that's off stage. Alina is going to hunt the firebird, but that adventure doesn't begin right away. When Nikolai returns to help her, the story begins in earnest, and he's charming, witty, and injected action back into the story. The later half of the book works better than the first half. For me, and I realize that many readers will find Mel a heartthrob, he doesn't live up to the potential I saw in the first book. The Darkling still has power over Alina, which ads some tension to the story. Alina's choices seem more like the middle book of a trilogy. The romance gets settled; however, there's a Deus ex Machina wrap up that left me unsatisfied. I felt Alina took the easy way out. In YA fantasy, romance is mandatory. I usually ignore that part of the YA genre because the outcome is always predictable with little variation. There's a pattern to these romances, and Ruin and Rising follows the safe path, which is a shame because the ending could have been much more powerful.

I don't know how to classify this one. It feels like the times are older, with newspapers and TV somehow. I didn't care for the plot. It should have been interesting, with children asked to infiltrate an evil school (like Point Blank or Nightmare Academy, I suppose), but I didn't really care. The stakes were high, but they didn't feel high. This makes it much less likely that I'll read the next ones in the series. The kids act their age (Constance! ), which can make them a bit annoying, but it makes them so real too. Their struggles are less adventurous and more spying and such. The bad guys seemed a tad too incompetent. A fun read that didn't make me think too hard.

Even though I was very picky, wore only designer clothes, and had a monthly allowance bigger than what most people my age earned in a year, I was by no means a snob. Firstly: this book is a stupid, racist piece of shit. Secondly, it is a grand accomplishment that I could hate a character within pages of meeting her. Right after starting the book, I found out that our main character is rich, adored, and perfect. She gets straight As. She has parental-approved freedom to do whatever she wants. She lives in a fa-bu-lous *snaps finger* Manhattan apartment that never feels like home (;_;) There were definite perks to living in Manhattan, and even more perks to living in a hotel--like maid service, room service at all hours, doormen, valets, access to the hotel pool, the steam room, and the gym. Still, it was hard for me to think of this residence as a home. She has the financial means to do whatever she wants (a fact of which she blissfully and frequently reminds us). She gets straight As. She wears designer clothes (a fact of which she, again, frequently reminds us). She has been accepted to every single university to which she has applied. She has the ability to wander around the Metropolitan Museum of Art at her own will because her parents are wealthy donors. She is bloody fucking perfect. Whoop-dee-fucking-doo. Meeting the most perfectest Mary Sue in the whole fucking world. This is surely a fantastic start to any story. So there's beautiful, wealthy, perfect-in-every-way Lily. She spends her afternoons just chilling in off-limits (to regular middle-class folks) areas of the Met. While chilling in a closed-off Egyptian exhibition, she hears a weird noise and then a weird guy emerges from the shadows, and surprise, surprise. He's an Ancient Egyptian. He's gorgeous! HE SPEAKS ENGLISH!!!!!!!! He has green eyes, because that's so fucking common in Egypt. Who are you? I wondered as I studied the person, who was not a man and yet not a teen. He seemed...timeless. Hooded hazel eyes, at that moment more green than brown, beneath a strong brow pinned me with a gaze that was both intelligent and almost predatory. I felt like a mouse looking up at a swooping falcon, knowing death loomed but utterly unable to look away from the beauty of it. And he's looking for...jars! And without the jars, he needs...her! Oh my god, she is the only one EVAR WHO CAN GIVE HIM WHAT HE NEEDS!!!!!! *cough*Mary Sue*cough* "You do not understand. Without my jars I must share your life force." Panicked, I spun and ran toward the curtain. But before I reached it, the lights went out and I banged my knee against the golden sarcophagus. Stumbling to catch my balance, I heard him coming toward me. "Come back, Young Lily," he groaned. "I need you." He needs her. He pursues her. He all but kidnaps her. Wait, he does kidnap her. But he's so....different, and Lily finds herself oddly attracted to him. I didn't go for dangerous guys, especially bald guys wearing skirts who I couldn't figure out. He was different from any guy I had ever met. This is called a no shit, Sherlock moment. He follows her. He stalks her. Gripping the balustrade, I closed my eyes, basking in the feeling and momentarily forgetting my surroundings until I heard an all-too-familiar voice. "The sun makes us feel strong, Young Lily. As I am bound to it, you are bound to me." Though it was definitely strange and all kinds of wrong to find him not only in the building I lived in but also on the same floor and just outside my room, I was surprised that I felt happy to see him, crazy stalker or not. Surely Amon is the model of a perfect YA love interest. Do I need to go on? This book is culturally insensitive. It has The Last Samurai syndrome in which a white person swoops in and saves a culture about which they know nothing. It doesn't display anything true about the culture (in this case, Egypt) that it purportedly portrays. The "Egyptian" characters are exoticized and more or less whitewashed to a Caucasian ideal of what a foreigner should be. The characters gorge themselves on American food. Egypt is restricted to an "exotic" ideal, without a single mention of the current, dangerous, and politically unstable condition that the country is currently experiencing. It is the story of a rich white girl who, more or less, plays tourist in a foreign country and sees nothing of that country beyond the boundaries of her 5-star hotel room. Do yourself a favor and don't waste your money.

I really like this first volume of Teen Titans (the New 52). It introduces all (or maybe most of) the members of Teen Titans. It is not entirely in-depth about everyone's histories, but certainly that will come later. There are several problem makers for the Teen Titans which make an appearance. I expect more will be seen of them in following volumes. The main villain that takes center stage in this volume is evil organization Project Nowhere. To combat this threat the Teen Titans are formed. The Titans consist are Red Robin, Wonder Girl, Solstice, Kid Flash, Skitter, Bunker, Superboy and a couple of other characters. There is also an appearance by Virgil Hawkins. I had not heard or seen him since the cartoon Static Shock. That got me a bit nostalgic. Later if he joins the Teen Titans as Static Shock it would be awesome. If not it's fine. I still love that he showed up. I think I have seen Red Robin in cartoons, but everyone else is new to me in Teen Titans. So I did some research. (Mainly when the characters first made an appearance. A lot of them are new and some have been around a bit longer. Anyway, didn't mean to go off topic. It's just all so interesting to me.) Already I have characters that I really like. They are Kid Flash and Solstice. The artwork and story of their meeting was my favorite part volume one. I will be anticipating subsequent volumes.

I'm going to be honest; when I read the description I had very middle of the road hopes for this book. I thought it would be ok, but had major reservations. Was it going to be another TFIOS? To set the record straight, I did love that book, but let's be honest it was unrealistic beyond belief. I was expecting another cast of totally ridiculous non-teenagers, characters that just didn't feel like they were real. I was wrong...and I am so, so thankful that I gave this book a chance. Yes, the main character is nerdy, but it's very believable. He isn't over the top, he still bitches and curses like any other teenager. I believed him; I knew who he was and I really connected with him on an emotional level. It's a romance, but so much more. I left this book thinking about our fundamental right to make decisions about our own body, even if it's not exactly what other people might want. I thought about how to value all the time I have with people, that love is beautiful and incredibly imperfect. But we have it, and more than anything that is what matters. Please, please give this book a chance. I alternated between laughing and being angry and incredibly sad. I was grateful that I could go on Charlie's journey with him, to witness him grow and change. All the characters had a place; I didn't feel like there was anyone who was thrown in just to move the plot along. Trust this book, if there's only one you're going to take a chance on this year make it this one...I'm so incredibly glad that I did. It's probably not for everyone, but if you enjoy romance, particularly YA, don't be put off by the simplicity of the description.

I'm not a huge fan of the romance genre and this book didn't change my mind, but it was fun. Things that I liked: > spunky positive protag without being annoying > blind love interest (mostly) > that blind love interest didn't get his sight back in the end > protag has a weasel as a pet (even if weasel had a dumb name) > even though protag is a virgin, she's not a prude when it comes to voicing what she wants sexually Things I rolled my eyes at: > protag is a virgin > love interest is an ex-womanizer > that the whole book culminated in marriage and bun in the oven - as a young woman who is not interested in marriage or birthing my own babies, why does this equal the ultimate "happy ending" in most romance novels? > romance went from like 0 to 100000 REAL quick - lil smooch then like shoving tongues down each other's throats and ripping bodices like I get it that's the genre but brooooo I enjoy a little bit more of a progression than 'hey I just met you and this is crazy but here's my castle so let's hump bby' > oh and when they would make out, bone, etc. blind love interest fumbled ZERO times ZEROOOOO he even managed to unbutton all her tiny little victorian dress buttons and the only reason it took him a while was because his hands were shaking LIKE BRO HOW DOES SHE HAVE MAGNETS ATTACHED TO ALL HER PINK PARTS THAT REACT TO YOUR HAND MAGNETS???? (that was a weird thing of me to say but you get the idea, right?) > sometimes love interest would say some borderline rape-y things > love interest's personality flip-flopped once he fell in love

Originally posted on my blog: Tangled Up In Books You know how sometimes in the movies someone is sitting down getting ready to do something they don't want to do and they're highly distracted by other things. Then there's a few minutes worth of a montage of them doing things like, oh I don't know for some bad examples let's say; playing with their hair, messing with things on their desk, stacking things, drumming their fingers. Just stupid stuff you know? Like anything but what they should be doing? That's me with this review. Sigh. The Impact of You was one of our #GwB weekend reads with: Jessica from Lovin' Los Libros, Danielle from What Danielle Did Next, Wendy from Book Scents, Tonya from lilybloombooks Trish from Between the Lines, Chelsea from Starbucks & Books Obsession and CeCe from CeCe's Steaming Mug of Books. To be honest I don't even think everyone finished or even started it. Some of us had a busy week and couldn't start right away and I think from the responses by the rest of the group sort of wrote it off. I was really excited to start this. People are always raving about Kendall's books and so I've been wanting to give one a read. Unfortunately, this one fell flat for me. I had a really hard time finding anything to like with either Avery or Jase. Avery was all over the place and couldn't seem to make up her mind one way or the other what she wanted. Jase and I are just friends! Oh I but I don't want any other chick around him! Oh am I jealous? No we're just friends! And for someone who's "big secret" had her untrusting and keeping guys out and whatnot she sure attached herself to Jase pretty freaking easy. She was a total contradiction from start to finish. And Jase. Oh Jeebus Jase. Seriously I'm all for bad boys. But there wasn't a single thing attractive about this guy. He was a complete douche! I mean had some "totally hot guy" that's slept with practically every chick on campus purpose to become my "life coach" I probably would have punched him in his arrogant face. I was almost ready to give him a chance up to right about then. And then it was all downhill from there. I mean he's supposed to like this girl and one of his "Lessons/Dares" is to tell her to go kiss some random guy at the frat party? What the hell is that?? And his complete inability to make his ex Stacia go adios, come on dude grow some balls! Oh and then the guy with the type of past he has, gets all judgmental on her when he finds out her secret. Yeah he wasn't very likable at all. I wanted to like this book, I really did. And maybe with a different set of characters who weren't so wishy-washy or irredeemable it could have had some great potential. I probably could have enjoyed it more. Because the secret had potential to make for some intriguing plot twists. Hopefully the next book of hers I read will turn me around because I haven't given up yet. E for effort, characters just got in the way.

For the most part, I really enjoyed this. I like the world Corey has built, and I like most of the main characters (I loved Bobbie and Avasarala, quite like Amos, and even Alex felt more flushed out. I still want to slap Holden most of the time, and Naomi felt very much like a trophy for this entire book, which... meh). I don't know if I'll keep going, though. I probably will? I mean, I have the next book on audio as well, so maybe I'll give it another shot to fix a couple of things that are really frustrating me. Those things being the freaking return of the vomit zombies, and how much I'm starting to notice the go-to insults of the characters are generally homophobic, and how very little queer content there actually is in this world Corey has built (like, two of Holden's dads seems to be the sum total, and maybe the Tycho mechanic?)
I knew what was coming, so it wasn't quite as good as I expected it to be. Very good characters though. I also really liked the little side chapters from other points of view.
this was the coolest book ever!

As someone who revels in post-apocalyptic worlds, this is unlike anything I've ever read. Dude. Mind-blown. You can't describe this book. You have to experience it. It's like trying to describe to you how a roller coaster feels.. You can use as many adjectives as you'd like, but the FEELING won't get across, because you will only understand if you've been through the experience. But I'll try. It's a wonderfully, horrific, beautifully, terrifying book! There's no warm up, no cool down, its head first into freezing water, and it relentlessly holds your head under; past the point where you can't breathe. Literally, I caught myself holding my breathe several times. It's wonderfully written. I was totally lost in this world. This terrifying world! A world where sight is forbidden! It could drive you mad! I will warn you though,  you don't find out what exactly it is at the end   and that's why I debated for a long time about giving it 5 stars. But then I thought, what's more terrifying then the UNKNOWN thing???? Your own personal fear???? Nothing!! Isn't in a way, the unseen much MUCH scarier then the seen?? That's the BEAUTY of this book! Incredible.

Personally, the new-adult ship has sailed for me and I just don't find the genre that enjoyable anymore. However, I like to check out titles from time to time because I have found a few gems for sure. I've seen Penny Reid's name around quite a bit lately so I thought I would check out one of her books. The first installment in her Elements of Chemistry series: Attraction was available via audio at my library so it was perfect timing! This short novel was pretty cute, with a storyline that kept my interest. It does end on a cliffhanger though...a very predictable cliffhanger in my opinion, but I thought it was worth mentioning. Overall, I liked Attraction but I didn't feel invested enough to continue the series. Nothing against the book, it's a "new adult" thing...we're just not compatible anymore. But, if you enjoy the new adult genre, then I would encourage you to give this series a chance. It's definitely got some originality. Check it out! My favorite quote: ""If I let another person's opinion matter then I was giving him control over me; I alone had complete control over my self-image."

When I first picked up The Unleashing, I was thrown a bit by the dynamic in the Crow house. All the women with their varying degrees of, lets face it, craziness took a bit for me to get used to. I was happy that I stuck the first book out, because once I understood the ebb and flow of the other women's personalities the humor of the situations really came to the forefront. That same humor flows into the second book The Undoing. I think just by understanding the writing style and the characters, I ended up enjoying The Undoing even more than the first book. I found the antics between the Crows even more funny. I loved the somewhat naive seriousness of The Protectors. Their love of books was charming and the way they thought themselves smarter than other clans was hilarious. Jace was a stand-out Crow for me in The Unleashing. Her penchant for hiding in seemingly random places was intriguing. I wondered what her deal was, in a good way I assure you. So I loved the The Undoing was her book. What I loved even more was that her quirkiness was not a result of her tragic past the lead to her becoming a Crow. That kind of closed off manner that she has is just the way she is, and I liked that the point of this book wasn't trying to "change" who Jace was. Yes, there are some characters who don't understand Jace and want to get her out of her shell, but the core group of people who matter to Jace and who care about Jace in turn would never think of changing her. Ski was a great love interest for Jace because he sought to understand her so he could fit into her life rather than trying to make him fit into hers. There was attraction between the two of them from the beginning but because of Jace's past experience with her ex she's hesitant to start anything with anyone. I loved that there was really no pressure on either side for something to happen, things just developed naturally. I'd say that it's probably wise to read the first book in the series before jumping into this one just because one of the main story arcs from the first book flows over to The Undoing. I think readers are well aware at the end of the first book that things are not yet taken care of, even if the characters aren't so aware yet. The same thing happens in this book. There are definite story threads that are dealt with yet no necessarily completely resolved but I will go so far as to say there's nothing cliffhanger-like about the ending by any means. Overall, this has started to be a series that I really look forward to. There's just the right amount of humor coupled with some very interesting Norse mythology. I liked seeing Kera and Vig from the first book still get a good amount of page time, yet we see them from Jace and Ski's points of view and it's always interesting kind of turning the tables in how a character is perceived. This series is highly recommended. Plus, there's a not-to-be-missed party at the Crow house!

From my blog Auntie Spinelli Reads Holy hell weasel, this book was just as good (if not better) than Hex Hall!! Hawkins really brings it in the second installment with even more twists, danger, and betrayal. There were so many things I never saw coming! Demonglass was riveting, particularly in the last quarter - and okay, I admit it, I got a little misty in certain parts. But it also made me giggle a lot, since Sophie's wit is back in full force. The romance, again, takes a backseat. But what little that existed was ohh so sweet! At the very start, you get a little piece of news that immediately made me think, Oh, Lord, there's going to be a love triangle. (And boy, do I hate love triangles.) And it was, in a way, true. There are a few moments where Sophie did look at Cal as potentially more than a friend. But those moments were fleeting. She stayed true to her heart, which belonged to Archer. Ohh, Archer. "This thing with us is the only real thing I've had in a long time. You're the only real thing." He raised our hands and kissed my knuckles. "And I'm done pretending I don't want you." I had read a lot about swooning in the romance novels Mom had tried to hide from me, but I'd never felt in danger of doing it until now. Which was why a snarky comment was definitely called for. "Wow, Cross. I think you missed your calling. Screw demon hunting: you should clearly be writing Hallmark cards." I think I fell in love with Rachel Hawkins right there (and Archer - even I was in danger of swooning). Say something totally cheesy, then have the lead ruin it with a sarcastic remark? That's my kind of book right there! (I hate spoilers, but this was my favorite part of the whole book so I had to share :p) It was interesting to see Sophie learn control of her demon powers. In addition to seeing more of the characters that I loved in Hex Hall, there were also some new ones. Daisy, Nick, and Sophie's dad were the biggest ones. I was quite surprised by how much I liked her dad - you get to see where she gets her snark from, and maybe that's why I liked him so much. :D I blew out a breath. "Dad, this is a total cluster...um, a mess." He flashed me a wry smile. "I think the word you were about to use is probably the best summation of the current situation." Awesomesauce, dude! Daisy and Nick creeped me out. Needless to say, I didn't care for them very much. (except for the part where Nick and Sophie get into a bit of a magic war - Nick in a purple prom dress, lawl!) Something else I wanted to mention was how much respect I gained for Cal. In the first book and through most of the second, he was just kind of there for me. Not that he isn't sweet, it's just that I'm team Archer all the way. But, towards the end he does something really amazing that made me want to give him a big ole' kiss on the mouth (okay, maybe just a hug would suffice). I can't imagine how much strength and courage (and self-sacrifice) it took to do that! That ending - argh!! Thank goodness I managed to snag Spell Bound from the library, because I'd be very unhappy if I had to wait more than a few hours to start the next book. My advice? Don't start Demonglass until you have Spell Bound, because the cliffhanger is KILLER. Favorite quotes: Yeah, except for that whole sleeping with the enemy part, I thought. Wait, not that I would actually be sleeping with...I mean, it's a metaphor. There would only be metaphorical sleeping. "It was my assignment." "From the Eye?" "No, from the Boy Scouts. That Witch Dating badge just kept eluding me." "Well, you must have at least three Total Douchebag badges by now, so that has to count for something." Favorite character: Gonna have to go with Archer on this one. I still love Jenna though! ASSESSMENT Plot: 4.5/5 Writing style: 4.5/5 Characters: 5/5 World-building: 4.5/5 Pace: 5/5 Cover: 4/5

The story has some nice and unique ideas, but for me it didn't really form a full story (on the level expected from a short story), and it also has some flaws. It has value, but didn't make me part of the fan group. Some of my problems, as spoilers follow. Experiencing free will has nothing to do with the world being deterministic or not. A chess program will make decision, but in practice, it will follow a deterministic path. (A curve in the memory phase space.) Consequently, the fact that we perceive free will says nothing about our world being non-deterministic. Similarly, a deterministic universe would not imply the existence of a 'Book of Ages' and create the kind of paradox described. A deterministic universe would obviously only exist if it didn't have an internal paradox and the 'Book of Ages' is one. The philosophical section related to the 'Book of Ages', only proves that there could be no Universe with free will AND a 'physically' existing 'Book of Ages'. Again, this is of no value to prove anything within the story. 'Variation' variations: The fact that the path of the light between two points can be found by means of variations, has nothing to do with the 'light knowing in advance where it will go'. Light will go where the laws of physics will take it. If you shoot a laser beam from point A, it will travel according to these rules even if it's vacuum all along, or you decide to push a prism into its path after it has left point A. I don't see the relationship between being able to 'get the hang of Heptapod B' and 'seeing the future'. Just because I understand an equation that describes the working of the Universe (let's call it Unified Equation), I won't automatically able to put in all existing information and process it. Just because you acquire the capability to read a book with a single glance (absorb the story at once), won't make you an Oracle, just a superfast reader... Not all human languages are completely linear either, but not everyone is a lottery winner.

*ARC provided by publisher in exchange for an honest review* Sigh. It hurts to write this and after reading other reviews I might be in the minority but Off the Record left me underwhelmed. Liz Dougherty, a journalist major at UNC, gets her first stab at reporting when she attends the political press conference of state Senator Brady Maxwell. There with her editor-in-chief and current crush, Hayden, Liz is determined to finally prove her worth as a reporter to Hayden and herself. When Brady selects Liz during the Q&A part of the press conference, Liz makes quite the impression when she throws Brady a hard hitting question that throws him off guard. But Liz's question not only impresses Hayden, but Brady as well. Brady then pursues Liz despite the harm a relationship could cause to his career as well as Liz's credibility as a reporter and the two of them decide to carry out a secret relationship. But the reality of their relationship leaves Liz constantly questioning Brady's motivations for secrecy and her own hang-ups with being his mistress. My biggest problems with Off the Record has to do with the characters and the lack of depth in Brady and Liz's relationship. Liz has no personality. I could not connect with her character and nor could I feel sympathy for her when it came to her feelings towards Brady. For someone that is so determined to be a serious reporter she seemed more than willing to throw away her credibility in order to prove that she was Brady's woman. Plus every male in a 5 foot radius wanted her. Brady, Hayden, some random guy at the bar, etc. Really? I also couldn't connect with Brady. I love men in power but I didn't find him that charming. Well, maybe I did when he first pursued Liz, but after I couldn't understand why Liz was so willing to ruin her reputation to be with him. He was cold and indifferent unless he was trying to get into Liz's pants. And the two of them together? Boring. I hate to say it but there was no depth between them. Liz and Brady basically just get together to have sex and that magically transforms into love. How or why I don't know. I didn't feel anything between them but their own lust for one another. Especially when Brady showed almost NO emotion towards Liz until the very end of the book. The only character I actually found charming was Hayden. He and Liz had a relationship that wasn't focused in the bedroom. There was actual development between them personally and professionally. If I was Liz, I would have dropped Brady in favor of Hayden who actually made her a priority in his life. On top of all that there is are a few secondary characters brought into this book that I cannot help but feel are reincarnated from the Avoiding series. For example, Liz's best friend, Victoria, reminds me of Chyna 2.0, the book smart version. As well as Clay, who reminds me of John. I wish I could have loved this. I really really do. K.A. Linde is a great writer and she definitely knows her stuff when it comes to the political portion of this book but I found myself getting bored and skimming the pages. I hope this is one of those "everyone loved but me" books and that I haven't turned any one off on what is a very promising series, but I just could not connect with these characters or this story. 2 stars*

On the other hand, she's not written with nearly the same deftness as Atticus. The passing of the Morrigan was more emotional than I had expected and part of me is sad that so much of her depth wasn't revealed until after her death. Oberon, as usual, is the star of the whole thing. He is legendary. on his behalf, I rate this book 4/5 pies

Wow, what an incredible, powerful read! I laughed, I cried. I was overjoyed, disgusted, stunned, excited. I smiled, I frowned. It was truly an amazing roller coaster ride for me. The story itself is very well-developed and the concept of this dystopian future comprised of five factions is interesting, creative, and effective for this book and the many sequels I hope will follow. The book starts with its female protagonist, Beatrice, who must make one choice that will transform her forever: at the Choosing Ceremony, all sixteen-year-old teenagers must choose the faction that will become their new family for life, their future--either Abnegation, Erudite, Dauntless, Amity, or Candor. Beatrice makes a decision that may surprise even herself, and it is nothing less than an act of bravery that lands her in Dauntless. There, she will make both friends and enemies, show strengths and weaknesses, face her fears, and possibly even find love along the way. The Dauntless training section of the book is pretty intense and often brutal, and it kind of took me off guard. But I enjoyed seeing Tris--her new Dauntless name to fit her new identity and her new life--grow into a powerful, badass heroine, and I got to be with her every step of the way. I love the variety of characters, most complicated in their own right. The chemistry between them, especially between Tris and Four ( a.k.a. Tobias ), is fantastically conveyed by Veronica Roth's language. All of the private scenes between Tris and Four felt very intimate, enlightening to their character, and extremely fun and enjoyable to read. I loved the two of them so much! I can't wait to see more of them in Insurgent. Finally, the ending of the book--really, the last 50 pages--completely took me off guard. There are great twists and turns throughout the book that kept me glued to the pages. I pretty much read this book in one sitting, which rarely happens for me. I neglected studying for exams and writing term papers for the day so I could read this book. Lol. 10/10--I wholly recommend this book and will probably reread it within the next month. Veronica Roth did such a grand job in creating a vivid, complex world that becomes real to the reader, as Tris immerses us in one faction and then another. I LOVED Divergent!

*Disclaimer: I received a copy of this book thanks to a Goodreads giveaway. I was not obliged to review, and all opinions are my own* Things I loved: - The varying perspectives. This was done soo well in An Ember in the Ashes and totally carries on here. Every character point of view has a unique voice, and seeing them through other character's eyes is also done very effectively. I loved the addition of Helene's perspective - Helene. She's delightfully nuanced, even more so in book 2 than book 1, and the emotional arc she goes on here is quite something to behold. - The realistic portrayal of conflict and compromise. Characters in this series don't just get what they want - they have to make genuinely hard decisions, and Sabar Tahir seems to be fairly expert at portraying that process and the character development it involves. - The politics. Of gender, of society, of race. this series has it all and it's thought-provoking without being heavy handed. - The secondary characters (and the villains for that matter). They're not two dimensional. Avitas is my new favourite. Things I didn't like so much - The plot suffered a little from *second book in the series syndrome*. It felt like not an awful lot happened for an awfully long time, and it wasn't really until the last third once Elias gets caught in Kauf  where I felt myself really sucked into what was going to happen. Much of the book felt like necessary (maybe) filler. - I don't know if it's just me, because I had the same problem with An Ember in the Ashes, but the plot twists were kinda predictable. The only one I didn't see coming a mile off was Avitas and Harper sharing a father . Everything else I could have told you well in advance of it coming to fruition. On the whole? Not as strong as book one, to be honest. But I'm still fully on the bandwagon of this series.
