Cover Blurb: Yes or No? I do like the cover, with the spooky shadows and ominous red coloring. Unfortunately, my love for the cover did not transfer over to the story itself. Characters: I don't have anything good to say in this department. Michael is too busy lying to everyone and hating himself for doing it to really be a good protagonist. There is also the huge fact that Michael is too much of a guy for me to like him on any level. Patrick, his five-year-old brother, is a major brat, not to mention the most dense child I have ever met. He seriously thought it was all a game? And really - he trusted a total stranger that quickly over his own big brother? A brother, I might add, he completely trusts and would follow to the ends of the earth. Stupid child! Jopek, I'll admit, was kind of a fun jerk to hate, but I cared so little about what happened to Michael and Patrick that it didn't really matter to me what Jopek did to them. I mostly wanted Jopek to die so I wouldn't have to put up with his obnoxious accent and ridiculously stupid G.I. Joe persona. The dude was so clichely military awesome that I wanted to groan out loud (actually, I did). The other characters lined up in the typical zombie-cast fashion: the jerk that everyone wants the zombies to eat, but of course ends up lasting for a long time (Jopek), the girl (Holly), the sweet religious, older lady who everyone likes and is therefore doomed to be eaten by zombies (Bobbie), and the young man who blindly follows the jerk and meets a sad end because of it (Hank). Their personalities are about as complex as your basic zombie characters, too: not very. And of course, besides the zombies, there is the fanatical group of crazy humans that have turned the zombies into God's judgment and sacrifice people to them. Rubon, their leader, was a lousy villain. Sure, he was crazy, but he was exactly like every other religious fanatic in zombie stories. The Romance: Like a typical guy book, not a whole lot of time is spent with romance (not complaining!). Michael notices that Holly is hot, and of course since Michael is a nerd, he doesn't think he'll have a chance with her. Blasting zombies to kingdom come overshadows the romance, so it boils down to a basic, kinda sweet teen crush, and doesn't go much further. So the romance really didn't bother me all that much. Plot: Oh dear. Well, first off, the official synopsis lies - big time. The "Game" and the "Game Master" are totally unimportant to the story, and last for only about forty pages of this 368-paged book. Michael just made up the whole Game and Game Master for his brother so Patrick wouldn't know that the zombies were real. I guessed this by page 10, and it's revealed by page 40; maybe sooner. What the synopsis also fails to mention is that this is a zombie novel. It conveniently doesn't really tell you what the Bellows are - just that they're creatures who prey on people at night. Nope; they're Class A zombies! Needless to say, when I found this out - which was page 5 - I felt totally cheated. Like Michael does to Patrick, this story tricked and lied to me, so that I would read it. What promised to be an interesting and bizarre story boiled down into nothing more than dodging zombies every other page, strung out emotions, and more zombie dodging. In short, there isn't a plot! Once Michael and Patrick meet up with the survivors in a no-longer Safe Zone, they tag along with Jopek every time he goes outside of the perimeter to blast Bellows (no pun intended), and after lots of moaning and muscle flexing and cheesy one-liners from Jopek (while standing astride a pile of rubble with a machine gun in each hand), they all go back behind the perimeter to explore one another's emotions. This mostly consists of Michael realizing just how much of a jerk Jopek really is, while trying to keep Patrick hoodwinked about what's really going on - and Patrick being a stupid child and not realizing the truth. There are some "tragic" losses to the little group (surprise, right? I mean, zombies never get to anyone in the main group), Michael stages a coup against Jopek, which doesn't go well because his other participants are totally unwilling, and then - gasp! There's a twist! Super zombies! Okay, that's not what they're called; they are eventually dubbed Shrieks, because they can literally shatter glass with their screams. Oh yes, and they climb walls, you can pump them full of lead with no effect, they're blood is black and oozing, and for some inexplicable reason, they're shedding their human skin to expose nothing but bone and sinew - and still they somehow manage to climb around. Did I also mention their cliche unhinging jaws? To top all of this silly zombie zone gore, Michael and Patrick have personal issues that, yes, crop up. Patrick is constantly on the verge of a tremendous mental breakdown - the sort that you don't recover from. If he becomes too rattled, he'll disappear into himself and never return. This, of course, leads to a lot of temper tantrums that are supposed to be emotional breakdowns, but quite honestly, it just made Patrick seem like a brat. Why couldn't a zombie eat him? And then Michael is a compulsive liar, blames himself for everything, and has a sob story to constantly break into the narration as flashbacks. Question: why are zombie stories so fixated on emotional trauma? Believability: It's a zombie book. I shouldn't be looking for believability at all. But I'm going to, because there were two things that really bothered me. One: even if Patrick doesn't think that everything that's going on is real, the kid would still be super traumatized. He's seeing people getting killed in gristly ways! Two: the supposed cure. If the virus is mutating, the original cure would more than likely no longer work. Writing Style: Third person, past tense. The flashbacks, however, are in present tense, and often interrupt the narration in wholly untimely moments. The writing style was terribly difficult to follow. It is almost like the Author wanted the feel of a first-person narration without actually putting it in first person. As a result, Michael's personal thoughts are constantly being interjected, and these are written like stream-of-consciousness. They leap here and there, the words are often run together (like this: ohmygoshIcan'tbelievethisishappeningrunrunrun), and sometimes Michael will be arguing with himself inside his head, and the Author won't tell the Reader! So we get a series of thought processes that are going back and forth between each other, and the Reader begins to wonder if Michael is losing his mind. The general narration was also just plain convoluted, disjointed, movie-ish, and bad. Content: 31 s-words, 22 g--damns. The f-word is never actually used, but the derivative "fuggin" is a constant and far too close to the actual word for my liking. The violence is, surprisingly, not nearly as detailed as I thought it might be, but it's still got the classic zombie gore. Conclusion: Why do I get the awful feeling that this might have a sequel? Because it ended on a "this isn't finished" note. In a series of disjointed events, Michael is forced to face down the Raptures - the fanatic religious group that worships the Bellows. This somehow leads to a totally ridiculous explanation to where the virus that created the Bellows and the Shrieks came from, and that leads to a classic zombie horde - complete with a zombie boss. And then . poof! Michael defeats them in a totally spur-of-the-moment, what-a-coincidence manner that left me rolling my eyes and shaking my head. Ah, but are they really defeated? Of course not! Because someone out there is going to urge the Author to write a sequel, and nowadays sequels simply must be written (apparently). I really cannot express the depth of my disappointment with The End Games. When I first read the synopsis, I was so excited to read it, because it sounded awesome and weird and possibly a bit like The Maze Runner and The Hunger Games combined. And then I opened it, eagerly scanning the first two pages, and . I realized that I had been tricked. It is only because of my dear Readers that I finished the book at all: because I wanted to let you guys know what I thought of it. And now you know. Recommended Audience: Guy-read, eighteen-and-up, zombie fans!

Review also posted on Sab The Book Eater It's quite scary going through all the ratings and reviews of this book on Goodreads. You won't find a lot of low ratings. That's why writing this review is kind of scary for me. I feel like I'm stepping on a minefield when I say that Hopeless is just okay for me. I think the main reason why I'm not that much into this book is the pacing. The first half of the book was confusing for me. Sky meets Holder early on and right off the bat you know something's wrong with him. The guy has a bad temper but of course Sky would look past that because she's curious of the hot guy who may or may not be a stalker. I was mildly annoyed but I have to admit I was hooked because of the mystery that surrounds Holder. I wanted to know what was making him tick. So yeah, I got a bit of feels when they were getting cozy. There were plenty of lines that were sweet albeit cheesy but what the heck, right? That was still entertaining. Then it got to the core of the story and the big plot twist and... woah, woah, woah, woah, woah! (woah!) I knew some kind of big revelation would happen but I wasn't expecting something this big! And this is where the pacing becomes problematic for me. The book was going slow in the first half and I didn't quite see where it was going, then we're given this chunk of information that was just too much to digest! I feel like I wasn't prepared for any of it. It was a shocker and I like the twist but as a whole, it didn't quite work out for me. After everything that happened, it was surprising how Holder and Sky were able to joke about their sex life. It was uncomfortable for me to read that, even if it was kind of a funny moment between them, because the book deals with sexual abuse. It didn't make sense to me how easy it was for them to joke about it. Furthermore, I didn't like how both of them handled Sky's shock upon learning the truth. I may not be an expert on the matter but I'm pretty sure having sex with your boyfriend for the first time would erase the emotional pain from childhood sexual abuse. One other thing I didn't like, and this is just a teeny tiny rant, was how mature 6 year old Holder was. I have vivid memories from when I was in kindergarten but I don't remember being so... wise. Holder told Sky some pretty deep stuff about stars and friendship (I think. I can't remember much anymore) that it sounded way off. Am I supposed to believe a six year old came up with that sort of wisdom? I know kids say the most grown up things sometimes but young Holder didn't sound believable to me. Holder getting hung up on finding the girl he lost when he was six is believable because it was something traumatic so it definitely left a mark in his memory. But Holder sounding so profound at age six? Nope, I don't buy it. It's sad rating this below 3 stars considering I stayed up all night (I went to bed around 6 a.m.) finishing this book. I guess I had trouble liking the whole of it. I liked it in parts but as a whole I think it wasn't all that. Had the pacing been smoother I think I would've enjoyed it more. Maybe I should've started with some other Colleen Hoover book because Hopeless clearly wasn't for me. (Copy from NetGalley. This review is based solely on my opinion.)

My boyfriend and I read this book together, and we both agree - everyone in this book is fucking crazy except Cathy. TEAM CATHY, YO. You have the stars of this screwed up festival of misery: Rachel, the pining, pathetic barren drunk;  Anna, the self-absorbed and more than slightly psychotic bitch;  and Megan, the cheating and depressed accidental baby killer . Then there are the guys: Tom, Rachel's ex-husband and Anna's current husband, a violent and manipulative man who defines "abusive,"  and Scott, Megan's distrustful and controlling ass of a  husband. Add all of these toxic personalities together, and what do you get? Well, poison, of course. Well-written, compelling, attention-grabbing poison that you just can't seem to stop drinking into your brain, because who can look away from a train wreck?

I loved this book. Unlike the last two Megan really changed as a character in a good way. She became more powerful and no longer a bystander. And the Romance. I  LOVED  Ash in this book. In the other two I didn't like Ash or Megan and Ash's romance. It became a whole lot better in this book. And when Ash became Megan't knight I was sold for good. But Puck. You will always be my favorite character in this series. I read the book of eden series first and I must ask. WHY JULIE! Why must you allways rip out our hearts once upon a time style and crush then in front of us.

It's rare that I rate a book 4 stars when I actually had to fight my way through to the end. I was close to giving up on it so many times, but it somehow always kept me interested at the last second. For me Catch-22 is most brilliant in its understanding of the human character. Yes, most depictions were stereotypes, not fully fledged out people, but it showed how every single decision and consequence in life is firstly decided by how people think and act. Even people who we think have to be professional act on their emotions. Soldiers under the command of one person, have to suffer because of that person's insecurities, etc. War (and the military) were made to look like one huge chaos (which I guess is the most accurate depiction there is), no one really knew what they were doing, it was all senseless, hopeless. Most characters were really only looking out for themselves, not even listening to others. At least that's what I got from the book. It was mostly told in a comedic tone, though, which somehow made it all even more tragic. The writing could be tiring at times, switching POV's in the middle of a paragraph, repetitive style of conversations, WAY too many characters to really remember. But the humour made it alright again. I might have even laughed out loud at one or two sentences. It is a somewhat difficult read that needs a little bit of patience, but it really pays off in the end.
Cute and funny, but wow. Can't believe her best friend never even noticed that her boobs went flat to a size D over night! I mean, really. When the entire school is gossiping about it?
Another Wendy Higgins book? Yes! And it's based on a fairy tale? Sign me up! [image error]

This one had so much potential, but fell flat in the end. It started off strong; great dialogue, sweet premise, and well-written characters. However, the plot/pacing derailed after 65%. In short, there was enough conflict and resolution to span over a multiple book series. There was so much back-and-forth after 50%, that it contradicted the integrity of the character development. It just didn't make sense; the additional "issues" felt contrite. It was almost like this book had everything and the kitchen sink, plot-wise. Second-chance romance? Check. Friends-to-lovers romance? Check. Hero loves heroine, but has commitment issues? Check. Heroine emotionally scarred by physically abusive, drug-addicted ex? Check. Hero with Mommy issues? Check. Romance story with not one, not two, but THREE (plus more) break-ups within one book? Check. I could go on and on. Just know that even though I'm being super critical about this book, that somewhere within all the mess, there was a decent story. But it was just trying to do too much all at once. If this story were told over a couple of books (where the first half was book 1, and the second half was book 2), I think I would've been comfortable giving this 3.5-4 stars. But alas, it was not so, therefore I am giving it a solid 2.5 stars. Mainly because I was compelled to keep reading, even through the unnecessary added (and overall contrite) conflicts in the last 35-50% of the book.

Great book! What an unusual setting. It reads like a historical romance for the most part, but it is also futuristic with some of it taking place on a spaceship. The planet Regelence is all gay men. Aiden is one of 5 sons of a gay couple. (I can't wait to read about Aiden's brothers.) I loved Nate! Dominant Alpha male...yum! And I especially loved  his Prince Albert piercing! So sexy! I have already started the next book in the series The Englor Affair. While I have this setting and all of the characters fresh in my mind, I want to keep reading.

This was a cute twist on soul mates. What do you do when you find out you are the perfect match to someone in every single way... yet they aren't who you thought they were at all? Or are they really? Joe! Big, bearded, and SEXY! I really enjoyed how this one started... a case of mistaken identity. I loved the playful banter between these two. Joe with his quiet and unassuming ways... until he wasn't all that quiet after all. Joe was a naughty one, he was! rawr But he was also kind, caring, and totally lovable. And Alex was a hilariously goofy chick. She was eighty percent sarcasm and twenty percent Little Miss Fucking Sunshine! The story was cute, funny and sweet. There was an OMG moment that had me teary-eyed, and then there was some WTF ones that, to be honest, left me a little bit pissy! In the end, I'm happy to have been able to not only get lumberJoe's story, but a little reunion with both the Dive Bar folks and Stage Dive as well! Looking forward to more Eric in Chaser! *ARC provided by author in exchange for an honest review

Finally!!! Now that's what I'm talking about! This one's all Stefano and Silvio, yay!!! The temperature in the room just goes up if these two are in the same vicinity as each other. *shivers* Mama likey! While Silvio and Franco are out causing havoc on the Russians everything's not candy and cupcakes on the home front for Stefano. His number two is getting restless and starting to question his authority in front of his other capo's. Not to mention of course that Donata's decided he has a mistress. She's noticed he's changed and things aren't quite how they use to be. When Silvio and Franco return though Stefano is drawn to Silvio like the moth to the flame. He just can't resist the man any longer. God Donata almost killed me in this one. Her response to Stefano asking her what she wanted him to do, my brain just can't handle it. "Own up to it. I can live with a cheater, but not with a coward." I'm the evil one that'd be more likely to cut your dick off for cheating on me while I dump your ass. Then again that's not the culture she was raised to be a part of. As long as Stefano's top dog, head honcho, alpha she's happy. Still I have yet to figure out how this is all going to get resolved without hurting someone devastatingly. Silvio, Silvio, Silvio...oh my poor damaged boy. Honey, it really is ok to open your heart up to someone, I promise. A part of me feels like I missed something huge here not knowing exactly what went on between Franco and Silvio while they were out destroying the Russians. Franco's disappearing act was devastating to Silvio whether he wants to openly admit it or not. Their fucked up parents should have been put out of their misery before they ever thought of having kids. It's so sad to see two men who could be so amazing believing they have little value anywhere. They're two sides of the same coin, fire and ice, polar opposites but yet the same f*d up core. Silvio turns to hedonism and the adrenaline rush to cope, Franco shuts down and doesn't allow anyone close, not even the comfort of a normal human touch. So sad!!! They absolutely need saving. Stefano my dear, I do not approve of you cheating mind you, but THANK YOU!!! Finally you let yourself go and indulge in the man you're desperate for. Yummy, yummy hotness! I love the fact that he tracked Silvio down after the conversation with Donata, unable to stay away. I'm terrified to find out what his ultimate decision is going to be and see how this all resolves, but I'm game. I'm going to boldly go foraging ahead hoping for the best. All in all my favorite of the books so far. Thoroughly enjoyable and I'm completely invested in this story. The pieces holding up this mountain though are so precarious. I know it's going to take just one little thing to have it all coming down. The trains are racing full speed ahead! Collision coming soon...it's inevitable.

Now I'm hooked, I'll have to read the whole series. This hero is adorable when clueless. I liked that the heroine is the one who has to figure out how to make this big macho vampire destroyer have a happy ending.

First, the good: An entertaining narrator, very funny and plucky. Very funny, well-paced writing. A good plot, particularly exploring the difficulties of being on the reservation and trying to step out of the cycle of problems there. It felt very real. I've read about the pervasive pain of really systemic alcoholism for some reservations, but this did a good job of making it and other problems personal. There is this awful, painful part where Junior is supposed to attend the funeral of someone who died in a fire because she was passed-out drunk. And even though everyone knows she died because she was drunk, everyone at the funeral is still sitting around and getting drunk. And it makes Junior so mad that he won't stay there. It makes me mad too. Even though I can understand it (and so does Junior), it still makes me mad. To me, that was probably the strongest moment in the book. So why the low rating? Frankly because I can't recommend it for moral reasons. Junior is very open about his masturbating habits, etc., etc., and it just feels like he goes on and on about it. Since I believe this is not acceptable behavior, I got really tired of it. (Note to anyone out there who reads this review and disagrees with me: You're entitled to your opinion, but I'm also entitled to mine. So please don't comment and rant about what a close-minded person I am.) Also, there was a looooot of swearing. I still may have rated it higher, simply because it's good for the sake of awareness of other people, but I just didn't feel like its flaws overcame its shortcomings. Rating: PG-13 at least, for abovementioned.

I was worried when I picked this one up. There was so much hype about it and I'd heard so many good things...and a pretty large handful of bad things. But this book didn't let me down. No matter what anyone else says, I loved this book. Wither's opening scene pulled me right in a Rhine described being in the van, not knowing up from down, then being unloaded, chosen, and herded into a limo while the other girls are killed. It was the kind of opening that kept me turning the page. As the story unfolds, I found myself diving right into this future world and getting lost in its complications and twists and turns. Why did someone kill Rhine's parents? If they cured cancer, why can't they stop this life-ending disease? I hated Housemaster Vaughn so much, but I still wanted him to find the darn cure! Rhine was a great character for me. So many YA novels that I've read lately have had these clumsy, oblivious female leads and while I've still enjoyed some of those novels, I have craved strong females who try to get something done (hence, my love for Gaia in Birthmarked and Katniss in the Hunger Games). Rhine falls into this category of strong female. She knows what she wants (to escape and find her brother) and what she'll need to do to get it (deceive her husband to win favor). I loved that she sometimes forgot that she was "pretending" to be in love with Linden because that sort of questioning of her feelings made her more human. Linden was a character that struck such conflict in me while I was reading. I wanted to hate him--I really, really did. However, as his oblivion is slowly revealed bit-by-bit (and you realize that everything is Vaughn running the show), I couldn't help but feel sorry for the guy. He was no less a pawn in his father's game than the girls. There were definitely points in the book where I was rooting for him to steal Rhine's heart and I would catch myself and be like "What about Gabriel?!" There were some things about this story that were difficult to believe. For one, the emphasis on procreation (especially by the young men_ when there doesn't seem to be any kind of push/brainwashing by the "first generations" to convince the younger generations. If this type of emphasis was being pushed, then these girls would ALL be like Cecily with her desire for a husband and children...but they aren't. Also, killing teenage girls when they are apparently vital to the next generation? Especially ordered dead by a man desperate for the cure? Despite any minor qualms I may have had with this book, my opinion remains: I loved this book and I cannot wait for the next one. (When does it come out?! What is it called?! I want to know so bad!)

3.5 stars I struggled with how to rate this one because there are a lot of pros and cons. Ever since I first heard about this book - which was forever ago, at least a year - I've been anticipating it. Even though I've only read one of Perkins' other books (Anna), I remember really enjoying and I was intrigued by how different this genre was for an author that usually writes such fluffy romantic stuff. I'm not good with horror. I avoid it like the plague, especially the movies. Books I have a slightly higher tolerance, but it's still not really my thing. I had heard beforehand that this one wasn't scary so much as it was bloody and filled with gore. I have to agree with that. I can't say that the story ever truly freaked me out, but that doesn't mean that the story itself wasn't thoroughly entertaining. Perkins has a knack for creating endearing characters, and her writing is certainly a pleasure to read and easy to follow. I finished There's Someone Inside Your House in two days, which is unusual for me as of late, as I haven't been reading as much as normal and when I do it takes me much longer to finish despite being a quick reader. I enjoyed following along with Makani and her friends, and I can definitely appreciate the diversity of the cast. As for the romance, I wasn't incredibly crazy about it, but it was definitely very sweet. I was surprised by how early on the identity of the killer was revealed. It seemed like there was still about a quarter of the book to go when we find out. And the reveal wasn't super satisfying as it turned out to be a very non memorable character that I couldn't for the life of me remember reading about before it was revealed. I wasn't thrilled with the reveal of Makani's big secret that she hints at throughout the whole story. She cuts off her best friend's hair. Said friend almost drowns afterward, it's true, but honestly I was very underwhelmed because her crime really wasn't that bad at all. I did like that Perkins killed off a semi main character, Alex, because at least not everyone got away unscathed. I know it kind of sounds like I'm harping on all the negatives about the novel but overall I really did enjoy reading it and would definitely recommend checking it out if you're a fan of the author's other books.

This is another dystopian novel because I enjoy them so much. The first thing that I thought when I reached the end was that it differs from other dystopian novels in that there is no uprising or rebelling within the first novel of the series, not on a large scale anyway. It does however set it up nicely for this to occur in the next book. I found the society presented in Matched to be very interesting. It is incredibly controlled; every little thing is decided for every person and everything is carefully monitored. One very interesting thing was that they had decided that the world was too cluttered and therefore just chose the 100 best of everything to keep and destroyed the rest. So they only ever had 100 poems, 100 songs, 100 films etc. It all seems to work fairly well, except for Cassia's longing to create something that's limited by the fact that she doesn't know how to create anything. Of course there has to be a love triangle, because most YA books these days can't be written without one (I am a little fed up of them, although it works well in this book and is the whole premise of the story). Cassia is Matched with Xander, her childhood friend which is a rare occurrence, normally the girls do not know the boy they are Matched with. What is even more surprising is that when Ky's data is added to the matching pool as an experiment he is also Matched with Cassia. Personally I prefer Ky, because he is a bit mysterious and clearly has more knowledge of the world they live in due to his past. He also knows things such as how to write by hand and is willing to stretch the rules. Xander is also a really nice guy, but very obviously written to be the guy-friend. I liked the fact that Cassia is a strong character that has never had to resort to using her green pill to calm herself down. I also liked her grandfather, who rebelled in his own small ways and gave Cassia little bits of knowledge and the strength to also rebel. It is interesting that thee red pills do not work on either Xander or Ky, which I reckon might be important in the rest of the story. It was also mentioned that there has only been one other time that Cassia's community were all told to take the red pill and only Xander can remember what happened. He refused to tell Cassia what it was, but I think that it will probably be important for her to find out at some point. I would be intrigued to know what happens to Cassia and Xander's relationship now that her family has been moved away. They are still Matched and presumably still have to get married in three years, therefore should still be having their chaperoned meetings. However, I get the feeling that Cassia is probably going to run away to find Ky before she sees Xander again. I really enjoyed this book and am looking forward to the rest of the trilogy.

THANK GOODNESS THIS DIDN'T END WITH A CLIFFHANGER! *phew* I'm starting to LOVE this series! I don't know about you, but I ship Anna and Nick. Yes, Sam is darn fine, but I just don't feel the chemistry between him and Anna.

I'm a huge fan of historical fiction and when you add mystery and romance into the mix, it's an automatic yes please for me. After reading the synopsis for 'Til Death Do Us Part I knew I had to get myself a copy (thank you Indigo for putting it up on sale ;)). Ms. Quick's writing brought out the creepy atmosphere of the story really well. Talks of tear catchers and coffin bells really took the story to another level of eerie. Aside from the tone of the story, each bite-size chapter renewed my curiosity and held my attention. The mystery wasn't overwhelmingly complex making the alternating POVs easy to follow. I was completely invested in the wellbeing of the characters. 'Til Death Do Us Part was a really fast story due to the nature of the mystery. It needed to be solved asap. I enjoyed the fast pacing a lot. No plot points were dragged out. Ms. Quick efficiently gave us the whole story along with the background to our lead characters. I'm amazed at how she manages to smoothly fit it all in. Calista, Trent and their siblings (basically their sidekicks) were pretty awesome. They're most always calm and collected while investigating the threat against Calista. I am especially a fan of Trent's logic: "...I am convinced that a truth only makes sense when it is revealed in the form of a story. Without that context it is simply a random event with no meaning. It cannot teach us anything and it cannot be used for any purpose..." (p. During the worst of situations, each characters' quick thinking got them out alive. They made a great team! As I said before, the story moved quickly. Hence, the romance played out quickly too. Normally I loved a slow burn but in the case with Calista and Trent, I was excited to see their attraction acted upon. They're both adults and knew what they wanted. Seeing them willing to share personal things with each other made me happy. I love how close and intimate their relationship became in such a short period of time. I was expecting a bigger challenge identifying Calista's obsessor so honestly I was a bit disappointed. I'm proud that my gut feeling proved me right but the mystery was a tricky one to place. It doesn't quite just give you the killer and be done with it. Is it really a mystery when the killer you're looking for doesn't get identified until after the mystery is solved? This puzzled me since I was trying to figure out his identity from the very beginning when really... there wasn't a way to correctly guess at all. While the mystery in 'Til Death Do Us Part left me desiring more, everything else about the story was on point. It's an excellent historical fiction with a tight plot, bold characters and an ominous world.

I was really excited to read Eona, and I wasn't disappointed at all. Again, I seem to be reading only "monster" books lately that seem intimidatingly thick, but Eona flew by. I found myself going back to it again and again until the whole entire story unfolded. There are just so many things I love about Eona. The copious amount of description that accompanies all of Eona's energy world-entering and dragon-uniting can get tedious at times, but the whole style and story seem to have this strong East Asian vibe that I love. I've always been very drawn to the stories and all things associated with ancient East Asian culture. The story is reminiscent (in a good way) of the traditional stories of heroes and warriors, folktales and people who sacrifice everything. There are so many plot twists and surprises, and Alison Goodman keeps the reader guessing until the end. With most novels you get the feeling that there will be a happy ending of some sort. Too few authors are willing to take the risk of an unhappy ending, but with Eona, nothing is certain. The emotions are raw and powerful and they seem to jump off the page or just drag you in. Even though I'm finished, I'm still left breathless. MASSIVE SPOILER ALERT! I'm glad that Eona finishes off with a "happy ending." Happy in the sense that Kygo survives and he and Eona are together. For a moment, I thought that Kygo would actually die. And in a way, I think I would be okay with it. It would be a tearjerker worthy of conversion into a sad, sappy Korean drama, but in a way, it would work as an ending. Of course, there would probably be a huge uproar and I would probably get really mad, but I'd also accept it. Nevertheless, I'm glad Eona is able to find a happy end to her long, sad tale. I'm sad that the beautiful world of the Empire of the Celestial Dragons has come to a conclusion with Eona, but I'm also glad that the story is finally resolved and it isn't dragged out into another sequel as so many fantasy authors seem fond of doing. I would certainly look forward to another novel set in the same world (but not a true sequel or continuation of Eona's ordeal; more of something like how Tamora Pierce has several series set in the Tortall Universe), but the tale of the world seems to have a rather set conclusion at the end of Eona and I don't think Alison Goodman has any plans to extend the story. Eona is exciting, absorbing, and a welcome break from reality.

The full review can be found on my Blog. As with Anthony Ryan's first book, Blood Song, there's much criticism hurled at Tower Lord. Shortly after the book came out I noticed many readers expressing their disappointment with the book. While I (again) do agree that the criticism isn't just taken from empty air and some things definitely don't work as well as in Blood Song, the overall enjoyment of the series is not hampered by this second book. I liked it as much as the first book and while some things I enjoyed reading about are obviously missing, other's add some depths to the story. Instead of staying with Vaelin as the only POV character, the narrative gets split across a few more important characters, many of whom were not in the first book and make their first appearance at the beginning of Tower Lord. Not all of them are as enjoyable to follow as Vaelin's POV, but I think they were needed. Why? Because the setting gets much larger and we finally get a better view at what Vaelin and his comrades are fighting against. The introduction of a large empire that makes a play at world domination came out of nowhere for me and I'd have liked some more foreshadowing to its appearance in the first book. As it is, they are introduced like a hammer on the head, screaming "Here we are and now you're doomed!". That's especially a problem because of the intermissions. We know these from the first book, but this time I found them especially jarring. Not only because they introduce the enemy empire in a way that made me question what I'd missed in the last book, but mainly because they spoiler interesting twists for a siege in the last part of this book. The siege is one of the best parts of Tower Lord and could have taken great advantage of the twist mentioned if it had not been spoilered on the very beginning of the book. Overall, the story is not quite as good as the one of Blood Song, which I attribute to Vaelin's part. It's lacking for most of the book, as he seems to be the wise warrior tired of fighting. The warrior that can't even draw his sword anymore and simply does the bidding of his weak king. Only in the last third does his story step up again, when he's become the Tower Lord and has to deal with invasions. There, his newfound wisdom comes as a blessing and makes him a much more dangerous opponent, one of strategical and tactical awareness. What I found the biggest weakness of the second book of the Raven's Shadow series is actually Vaelin's Blood Song, which seems overpowered. The Blood Song basically tells Vaelin what to do perfectly and Vaelin follows its bidding to the letter. That means his storyline lacks tension, as it's obvious very early on that his ability will always tell him what best to do to deal with the growing danger and even makes him into a deadly warrior that can kill hundreds. No, that's not a wrong number, not even much exaggerated. The ending is solid, holding surprises and defangs some of the criticism. It makes you want for more, too. This book is just the beginning of a great war, with the main characters finally in their designated positions. They might have grown in experience, but experience often comes at a price. For some, that price is very high. Anthony Ryan builds the story up and stops at a great place, with the factions poised to pounce on each other and all-out war only a book away. Concluding: Despite all the criticism, I loved it as much as Blood Song. And that's much more of a compliment than one might think. The series is shaping up to become something established for the fantasy genre that will be recommended for years to come. If the next book(s) can hold the quality. I'm not really worried about that though, as Anthony Ryan has shown he's able to repeat with Tower Lord what he started with Blood Song.
The ending made me so glad. I feel so enlightened right now. I didn't really like the twist though, I felt that there weren't enough hints leading to it.

This book was a quick read for me. I really liked the plotline, though you should be warned that it does turn a little young-adult-romance midway through. Still though, the pace is very good and I didn't feel bored at any point. By the end, I wanted to find out what happened next, so I will give the next book in this series a try when it comes out. My primary negative comment on this book is that Ember, our main character, is too stupid to live and really has no self-preservation instinct until the end of the book. I had real trouble midway though when  Chase almost killed a man to protect her, and then she was mad at him. He was going to kill you! Would you rather have died? Also, Chase didn't even actually kill the dude! CMON!! . The author did make up for this nearing the end of the book, when Ember hardened and grew up a little. Overall, a nice quick read, if a little bit formula dystopia.

What a gorgeous story! Poe's writing is just as potent in this day and age. I loved the descriptions of Lady Liegia, even if the narrator is not fully reliable he speaks of he so amazingly fond of her making it a pleasure to read in trying to envision what this wonderful woman would have been like. What makes this story interesting is you have to wonder what is going on with the narrator when  Lady Rowena dies. Does she really come back to life or is he succumbed to opium and grief which truly starts to take his toll?

(7/10) The most remarkable part of Zeitoun comes in its second half, where it goes from being a hagiography of its titular character paddling around a flooded New Orleans saving people and kittens stuck up trees to the nightmarish story of him being lost in an ad-hoc Kafkan prison system that springs up like some kind of terrifying pocket dimension. At that point it becomes a remarkable story of survival in a Kafkan beauraucracy. Eggers is pretty restrained here, avoiding all of the quirkiness he's known for and restricting his "writerly writing" to the opening and closing passages, a depressing trend in mainstream fiction. The NPR liberalism does grate a bit -- the Zeitouns are made out to be the ideal hard-working immigrants, hewing close to the capitalist idea of success and conformity, and this is supposed to make them relatable. (Eggers also goes to some pains to obscure the family's true wealth.) And I can't fight the sense that it's more of a New Yorker article than a book proper. But it's an important story, if not a particularly well-told one.

The U.S. Federal Bureau of Reformation has enacted five moral statutes or articles. Article 1: The United States has the Church of America as it's official religion. Article 2: Literature and other media considered immoral are banned. Article 3: Whole Families are one man, one women and children. Article 4: Traditional male and female roles shall be observed. Article 5: You are only a valid citizen if you are born in wedlock. America in the future has been attacked. We went to war and when the war was over a new America was created, a "reformed" America, with stricter rules and laws that force its citizens to follow a very strict moral code. So let me ask you, what would you give up for your safety? Would you give you your religion, your freedom, your rights? Ember did. She lives in the new reformed America. Yes, sometimes it is annoying that there is a curfew. Yes, she and her mother desperately miss comic books and romance novels, but if it means you live in a safer America, well then, it's all ok. But all this changes when Ember finds out she is actually breaking one of the Articles, Article 5, she was born out of wedlock. Suddenly, Ember's safety is no longer important to the Government. Ember is torn from her home, her family and friends, separated from her mother, thrown in prison and tortured. And the worse part of all of this is the man they sent to get her, to rip her from her family and her home, is none other than her ex-boyfriend Chase.

Impressive Start! I've waited quite a while to start reading this, as I didn't really want to read it as a serial. On the one hand, having it broken up would nicely break up the tension that I can see slowly building already, but I just don't trust myself. I'll want to read it all and who knows what my crazy mind will be in the mood to read one month from now, not to mention more. So I waited, and I'm glad I did because I'm about to dive into Servant of the Crossed Arrows and I'm SO EXCITED! I'm a new reader to Ginn Hale. I've bought all of her books (I'm bad about buying things I never get around to reading). I know they're great -- too many readers I trust have told me what a wonderful author she is. So not only was this big, unfolding story set before me but I'd yet to become acquainted with her writing, her style, anything. She does many, many things well, at least from this small perspective of her work, but what I love most is how balanced her writing is. There seems to a lot of great care in her writing, which could also come from the editing of Nicole Kimberling as well. Still, it works for me. Now, to this first very brief introduction into a much longer story. With The Shattered Gates we're getting a very small bit of the story. I confess that I read quite a few reviews when this first installment was published last year and I can now understand the difficulty it must be for everyone to really take this fragment and consider it on its own and as one tenth of a long novel. It could have very easily fallen into the world-building trap, or really fallen either way into a trap of extremes. What Ginn Hale did correctly was open the story to us in a setting that we slowly understand and only then start to build on it. Even then, I must say that by the end I was lost out of my mind. I'm not a huge puzzler as a reader. My mind just doesn't work that way. I tend to get wrapped up in the present tense of the story, right there with the characters, and I never guess anything that will happen (one reason I'm not big on whodunits, or mysteries of any kind, really). But, I have faith. Maybe that's why this works so well as a serial. Maybe it's just me -- even though I will read these all back to back, I just know it, my mind knows where to pause for a bit of a time out. So, while I don't have much to say on the story, and writing ten long reviews (long for me anyway) for each installment of this story will probably be too much, I can't wait to see what happens next and I can't wait to actually have something to say about the plot!

Falling somewhere between offbeat/quirky and silly/juvenile, Secondhand Souls was actually a much more enjoyable read than I anticipated. Clearly I've missed something by diving into the second book of a series, butChristopher Moore recaps previous events well (and often . a tad too often), so I don't really feel like I've missed anything. What you have here is a world where people are 'chosen' to become Grim Reapers - yes, plural Grim Reapers, because it really is too big a job for one person. Charlie was a recipient of theBig Book of the Dead last around, had the recommended kitty calendar, carried around a #2 pencil, and ultimately sacrificed himself to stop a Celtic banshee from destroying San Francisco. Or, at least that's what the world believes. In reality, his Buddist nun girlfriend saved him from that fate, cobbling together a new body out of lunch meat and animal parts - a 14 inch body, with a 10 inch penis. Yup, and we're just getting started. There's also a seven-year-old daughter, who used to be princess of the Underworld, but whose powers have deserted her along with the hellhounds who protected her. Suffice to say, since his replacement couldn't be bothered to actually collect any of the souls that came so conveniently penciled in on his kitty calendar, it falls to Charlie to save the world. Fortunately, he's not alone - aiding him in this insanity are the aforementioned horny Buddist nun and profanity-charged daughter, along with a tiny crocodile wizard, a gang of Squirrel People, a retired cop, a bridge painter, the weirdly eccentric Emperor of San Francisco, and a Goth girl turned inappropriate suicide hotline counselor . whose best line for getting a guy not to jump is to offer him a blowjob. The plot itself is pretty basic, with your requisite dark powers trying to take over the world, but it's really secondary to the characters and the comedy. To be honest, I think we were halfway through the story before the villain even stepped onto the stage. It's a book that bordered on tedious or repetitive at times, but the frantic swing between satire and slapsitck, not to mention irreverence and (political) incorrectness, keeps you on your toes. Secondhand Soulsis a book that certainly owes a debt to Pratchett and Gaiman, but which seems tailored more for a Hangover or Neighbors generation. Funny, funny stuff, with scenes that will stick with you long after you forget what it was really about. This has been on my tbr shelf for a few years now, one of those books I'd been wanting interested in but for some reason never got around to, so finally I said to myself for god's sake woman just do it already, so I did, and... It was kind of a letdown. I want to keep it short and simply put what went wrong for me. In large part, I never felt any attachment toward any of the characters. No one's personality stuck out to me, I never got the sense of truly knowing any of these people, and everything kind of flew too fast to really grab at me. And while I know she wasn't the focus, Allison's lack of development beyond being Ben's best friend with a stereotypically tyrannical father was somewhat bothersome. And with Tim and Ben as a couple? I have to be honest and say I was left with no reason to root for them. Sure I hoped that, as teenagers, they would be able to really explore the same kind of trial and error as any other young couples in love for the first time, but life happened and it couldn't be. As time passed and they met up again, I felt nothing. Ben was in a healthy relationship with a kind, albeit too perfect man, Jace, and Tim with his stalker-ish tendencies and disrespect toward his ex-boyfriends current relationship, followed by a particularly messed up, manipulative move? Ha, no. It would be one thing if this was supposed to be a fucked up, unhealthy love story, but unfortunately I don't think that was the intent. So, yawn, the second half basically turned into a trite love triangle that was inevitably "solved" with an all-too convenient plot device and I was simply left feeling empty. I am happy that there is a lgbtqa+ novel geared toward young adults and one that has gained so much popularity, even turned or turning into a movie, I think that's great. But after all that time wanting to read this, it ended up falling flat for me. It could have been so much more.

Wow! The poetic prose is beautiful and reminded me of Lauren Oliver. Lauren DeStefano creates a creepy, beautiful world. She immediately pulled me into Rhine's struggle. Her memories. Her nightmares. This place where she's trapped is haunting. Her world is dying, and the author never lets you forget it. I liked how her relationship with her sister wives develops. Things take a while, but I think that's realistic. It's not like things would click into place all at once. By the end, I really liked both Cecily and Jenna, and I wanted happier endings for them. I know we might see one in future books, perhaps with a happier fate. I also liked her relationship with the boys, Gabriel and Linden. Both of them were really likable, and I found myself even rooting for her and Linden, even though it was obvious it wouldn't work out. I liked that Rhine never strayed form her mission. She never loses her determination, even when she gets caught up in the world of the mansion. This story was half in the past, half in the present, and I liked that. Since Rhine doesn't have much of a future and since she's in captivity, it's realistic that she would think of her family and what she was torn from. I just loved the author's way of writing, and I loved getting lost in that world. I read this book over the weekend while I was sick, and it was a perfect way for me to forget my sinus headache. There two big things keeping me from giving this 5 stars instead of 4. 1. Why didn't she tell Linden that they were forcibly kidnapped?? What benefit was there in keeping him in the dark? I realize she's afraid of Vaughn, but I think Linden would have been a valuable asset. He could have helped them escape. I think if it was only Rhine's fear of Vaughn that kept her quiet, the author should have made that clearer, because I kept thinking, 'Why don't you tell him his father MURDERED Jenna's sisters??' Unfortunately, that's a direction of the story that will never be explored. As I look back to Rhine's escape, I realize she didn't do anything. Jenna starts the fire so she can find Gabriel. Jenna talks Linden into giving hr the house key. Cecily sends down the servant to let them out of the gate. I know this is supposed to show us how close they all were, how Rhine needed both of them and she lost them, but I wanted to see Rhine do something. I wanted to see her actively go for it just a little bit more. Other than those two things, I loved this book. Can't wait for the sequel!

"Everyone has some evil inside them, and the first step to loving anyone is to recognise the same evil in ourselves, so we're able to forgive them.'' Allegiant is the final book in the Divergent trilogy. We follow Tris and Four as they travel past the city, where they've spent their whole lives. They have to face new truths, new lies, while struggling to make a better life for themselves and for the people they've left behind in Chicago. I loved this book. It is generally quite slow paced, since the protagonists spend most of their time in an old airport- as weird as that sounds. But they finally discover the truth that lies behind the faction system and the Divergents, and as their perception of what is real and what is right falls apart, they have to make tough choices, which will scar them forever. I can't really say a lot about this book without spoiling it, although I have to admit that I feel very grateful for accidentally spoiling it for myself, because if I hadn't known what was coming, I wouldn't have been able to stop crying after THAT ending; and bear in mind that I don't easily cry over a book. The thing I enjoyed most in Roth's trilogy was the characters. I liked almost everyone throughout the series, and even the bad guys had their own reasons for doing the things they did. Tris and Four are the protagonists but they have their flaws, they make mistakes and they suffer from them. They grow and change, they become more mature in every book. The relationship between them isn't perfect, nor is any other relationship in these books. Friends fight, siblings drift apart and sometimes help comes from the people you least expect it to come from, people who are considered as enemies. But isn't this what happens in real life as well? People are bound to hurt you, willingly on not. One of the most prominent topics in Roth's books is bravery, and nothing is braver than finding the courage to forgive the ones who let you down, to heal yourself and move on. The only reason why I deducted one star is that the explanations we finally get about the dystopian aspect of the story seem too simple and rushed. Some things are actually never really justified, for example  why do the serums work on some people and not on some others, even if they're not Divergents? And telling me that it all comes down to some genetic anomaly is way too simplistic. Furthermore, the way the final conflict is resolved fell a little flat. It seemed too easy a solution to be realistic, like Roth couldn't come up with something more compelling. I secretly wish that I could combine the world building of the Hunger Games and the characters of Divergent; what a great story that would be. But all in all I thoroughly enjoyed the series, and I'm sad that it is now over. Well done Ms. Roth, it was a wild ride.

3.5 stars I felt somewhat detached from The Epidemic, by Suzanne Young, for a good deal of the book. A continuation of The Remedy, the story follows Quinlan McKee as she tries to figure out who she was before Arthur Pritchard erased her memories and her life. Deacon is there by her side but he's got secrets of his own. Young did a superb job layering doubt into the plot so you never knew who to trust in a very unsettling way. I think part of the problem for me was that while I felt bad for everything Quinn had to go through, I didn't genuinely admire her until late in the story. What kept me reading was the bond she shared with Deacon. I liked the evolution of Deacon's character very much, as well as Quinn's. I liked Reed though I admit I was confused by him, by his familiarity. Marie pissed me off something fierce, despite her good intentions . Love, love, loved Aaron. I liked that he came to help when he was free and clear of the program. I liked that he never hid his emotions or lied about things. At the end of the day, books 0.5 and 0.6 of The Program series didn't pull me in like books 1 and 2 did. I felt different levels of detachment from the characters--or lacked that deep attachment that I felt for James and Sloane in the first 2 books, if that's a better way to put it. I was more moved by their story. Here, I was pleased by the ending but I still had questions and lingering doubt/confusion. Someday I'll go back and read them all in a row and see if some of the blanks are filled in.

A wonderful conclusion to a great series. I only have one major complaint, it had to end. I have a feeling this will not be the end we shall see of the characters, however, at this time their are no further announcements for future sequel/companion series. Beyond this story being cut short, the only other flaws were the slower pace in the beginning and not enough of my favorite character. To each its own. The series as a whole is a solid 4.5 stars out of 5 and the same can be said about this final novel. Awesome world, awesome characters, awesome concepts and great execution. SPOILER WARNING< if you have not read previous novel, do not read the following! The Story Basic premise, Clara, Angela and Christian head to Standford to begin school and decipher Angela's visions, as well as the new visions for Clara and Christian. Relationships grow and change, our main characters learn who they are and want to be, and we finally understand the motives and actions of the black wings towards are lead characters. For the conflict set up prior, this story lives up to expectations. This book ends at a good emotional conclusion for most characters. However, there is a lot left to be covered and a few moments where the author introduced what appears to be set up of a future novel. I want to see more, but as of the moment, there is no news on future novels. There is a possibility it may never happen. Its so unnerving. Either way, the conclusion is enough to stand alone on its own. Its still an awesome novel as is. The Characters The author really steps up her game in the developments of the characters during this novel. As most of our main characters start to define who they are. The only complaint is since the setting of the book is mostly at Standard, there isn't a lot of coverage for those who did not follow. I found myself missing a couple characters. Everyone is still present, just some more than others. Its excusable, just a bit disappointing. The Writing Still, quite comfortable writing style. Only issue is the flow. There were times when the story seemed to be quite slow and others that went by so fast I felt like I missed something. I think is is due to the fact that the climax is very intense and nonstop for a long time. We needed the lighter approach in the beginning. To ground us back into the setting and give us the "cuter" or "fun" moments we had seen in previous novels. Overall Awesome book, could stop the last third. Ended up staying up until 3 am to finish. Then, couldn't sleep because I was so caught up in the adrenaline and giddy excitement that end gave to me. I spent an hour just theorizing what will potentially happen next if another series was to begin. Boundless definitely did its job! MAJOR SPOILERS WARNING!!!!! Fan girl moment ;-) Okay... Yes! Tucker! I am so happy he was chosen in the end! I am now very curious if they will go into further details of his new role in another novel/novella. It left me hanging to want to understand more. Plus, Jeffery was barely focused on in the conclusion. He was no longer confused, but now what? Christian, where does he go? I mean, he doesn't get the girl, and must leave so he won't torture himself. Not exactly a happy ending for him. I am pretty well convinced their will be another book/series, and it will be on either Jeffery, Christian, or Tucker. So yeah... there better be a sequel/companion book/novella. This is definitely not fully finished yet.

Borrowed from Tongue Hanging Delicious on Amazon This was my second Lauren Dane story. I read Sway a story featured in the anthology Cherished. I fell in love with how Dane writes when I read that, and I'm still in love with how she tells a story in Tart. Her writing has humor and a freshness is added to the dialogue. When you're introduced to the people in the delicious group you get a total picture and understanding of who they are. I could even see and hear them as they talked because that's just how good the dialogue was and the setting was written. I loved the chemistry between Gideon, Juliet, and Calvin. Even though we don't see a triad relationship in our every day life that doesn't mean that the reader can't relate to what they are going through, the issues that rise, and the love they share. It's a complete love story in the sense that the reader for the most part really gets to watch their every day life for 3 months; skip a few days or weeks give or take, here and there. There is the interaction with each other but also with everyone involved in their lives, so it's not just sex scene and after sex scene. It's more like the sex scenes are placed around what's important in their lives and the sex is just one of the many other things that is a part of their normal lives. The sex is hot but it's also very tasteful and so is the menage relationship. Lauren Dane's writing made me feel like a fly on the wall sitting on a tart eves dropping on everything happening. I wasn't just reading a book. Buy it and you'll enjoy the release of stress you'll feel and the lightness on your shoulders from everthing else going on in your life. Don't forget to have some dessert and tea on hand while you read. The complete experience will be well worth it.

Actual rating - 3.25 This was an okay read, But it felt really long. I liked Opal most of the time, but she annoyed me a couple of times. Damn. This time I'm gonna wait a few days to write a coherent review. So apparently I waited more than just a few days to write a review lol. But the good thing is that I just finished re-reading it, my own copy that (thank god) was available in the local bookshop and I had to buy it. Carol, Carol, Carol. To start I'm gonna say that I was not remotely familiar with Patricia Highsmith. I had watched Strangers on a train and loved it, and heard of Mr. Ripley movies but I outrageously didn't know about her. And this is such a peculiar book to start with... I was so surprised when, reading around and reading reviews, I came to find that Carol -mainly for the roadtip- inspired Lolita and the movie Thelma and Louise, two of favorite things of mine. Then, I knew that this was the only romantic novel that Highsmith wrote. Wow. It makes the book kind of special, and I have to thank this one for getting me into Highsmith literature, and the thing about writing this review after months I first read it, is that I got to read other books by her and getting acquainted with her style. Jesus, I was really mad (sometimes I think about it and rage a little) that it was public knowledge that the ending of the novel was happy. I read it here, on the cover, and even Patricia Highsmith talked about it on the prologue (magnificent one nevertheless.) It seems a stupid thing to get mad at but I don't know, I guess I've 'accidentally' or deliberately spoiled myself so many times in the past, that I felt being spoiled once again, even by the author. And lol I can't be certain about if I read the thing about Lolita's inspiration before or after... I think after, because I would've been even more disappointed in thinking that as a spoiler. So thank goodness for that. Even though I "knew" the ending, when I read the last pages I began to doubt about it, as if it indeed could be a nice ending but not the one I thought like... they said it was a happy ending because it didn't condemned homosexuality... I mean, Carol did kind of lost her daughter but she was socially alright, and Therese could've start again... and I swore I thought she was going to end with that british actress she met at the end. But hehe nothing of that. but no worries, it was alright, I loved the ending, I wish Patricia's words were trees so I could hug them for hours. It was brilliant brilliant and ohhh since there's going to be a movie, I hope they make it as beautiful as I visualize it. Honestly, one of my favorite book endings. About the plot. Sublte, charming, chaotic, with good persecution, defiant for its period, well-written and complex characters with development. Certainly the most notable character development comes from Therese. To read it all in her POV proves it. It was a great journey and also a kind of coming out of age story. It was curious and kind of alarming how sometimes it was literal how she only had eyes for Carol, and wanted to be with her alone all the times etc. At times it was cute and lol, I guess another reason I Love this book is because I empathize with her character a bit too much in some of her thoughts. I've been far away from a situation like hers but I let my imagination wander and wander, wonder how it'd be and I think I'd be some sort of Therese. The brief break-up they had towards the end of the book helped Therese a lot in her development, and in her realizations. She began to see Carol not just in an idyllic and ideal way, but for a woman that did love her after all, and like she said, was the one with most things to lose, and in fact did kind of lost her daugher FOR her. That's why their last conversation in the book is great. It's just that Therese was feeling betrayed, hurt, etc, and hadn't thought things properly. And Carol overcame herself. She still had that air of an indiferent person, but with a new impatience. That's sum up when Carold asks her if she wants to live with her. The before-Therese would have answered yes right away... but now she was hurt. And even though deep inside she wanted to say yes, and even doubted, she said no. And Carol understood her, and like Therese thought, she knew she would come back and that's pretty much the happy ending. Therese wanted to be with Carol not just because she was Carol since the first time she saw her, but because she has known her and started loving the Carol she was, the person. She wanted it and she did it. Period. And Carol's development was fascinating as well. At first I admit I may have liked Carol just because Therese liked her so much, and because of all the things she thought about her. But I knew she was going to be nice the moment she called to thank Therese for the christmas card, and started their friendship. At first it didn't seem that Carol was really inerested in Therese in a romantic way, but there were subtle things, actions and words, and right before the roadtrip her feelings seemingly grew and grew stronger. The roadtrip. Oh! the roadtrip... probably the most emblematic part of the novel, and I dare to say more than the ending, and I can't argue with that. It's here where they finally engage in romantic ways... it's like they were waiting for the another to start, to say something. And yep it was finally Therese who did it, it was great, more character development. Seems like Carol could finally breathe and make amends to Therese. Therese only didn't say anything because she was afraid Carol would mock her or tell her to go away. It's not like she was afraid, afraid like Carol was, -and the reason she didn't start it- afraid that this couldn't happen to her again; plus, she had more things to lose. However, the roadtrip was the perfect excuse to start it and finally let go. only if they knew they were being chased  And they finally filed in the blank spaces, especially Carol, and I think at first I was surprised whenever Carol acted lovingly towards Therese or tell her sweet things, because before that she didn't show her affect as much and in such ways. So thank you Therese, for being brave and finally speaking your feelings out yay! Yeah, the roadtrip was definitely the best part, and it's where the lady of suspense could put down the mystery and danger into the book. No need to say how the psychological study of things and actions, and inner speech per se typical in her books was as amazing as in any other of her thriller books. I loved Highsmith's Prologue and Epilogue. Such great insight of the novel and her thoughts. I found it subtle and fascinating that the idea of it all was a real life experience, in a situation like Therese. How much I'd like to thank that woman who inspired Carol (character). The struggles of the publishment, and the feedback of the people who read the novel. Whenever I read that she was considered a misogynist I'm like D: if it was true I doubt she could have written Carol in the first place, or the prologue; plus, wasn't she openly lesbian? I do know and have read some articles talking about this. There was a really nice one in spanish, that talked about her two faces... how people mostly assume that she was an asshole, hated everybody, never smiled etc... but then I read about some candid interviews she made and how nice she was... so basically it talked about the two sides of Patricia, and if she did that deliberately or not? and why? Well, complicated stuff to be honest... just like her characters. But still, it's known that she was a conflicted woman, has serious problems, felt terrible about her lesbianism, considered a misanthropist... and on top of that a misogynist... give me a break! In some spanish article I read they asked "if it was possible to be a lesbian and a mysogynist? Absolutely! I know cases." It wouldn't be rare if two mutually exclusive things coexist... but in this case I've always doubted it, and I am talking about serious stuff. Patricia Highsmith was, in the most trivial word, troubled. Such a shame but these things happen. (Also she may have been considered like that because I assume -I haven't read all of her novels- that all her books were written in a man pov, except Carol. And read in another spanish article how she said/wrote she preferred writing in men pov and found them more interesting, and not so dull. Well if that makes her a woman-hater... sometimes I think that she just hated her condition, and that's a whole another story so.) I'm gonna leave here an amazing article I read that talks about her issues, and this fantastic quote: "I am troubled by a sense of being several people (nobody you know). There is an ever more acute difference -- and an intolerableness -- between my inner self which I know is the real me, and various faces of the outside world." http://thisrecording.com/today/2011/8... Well that's it! I finally got to write my review and thoughts for this awesome book.

If there was a single theme that I can pick from 2013 that I fell in love with it was definitely parallel worlds. They absolutely INTRIGUE me, and I cannot get enough of these stories so needless to say when I seen Dissonance on Edelweiss I jumped at the opportunity to read this one. Surprisingly none of the characters really took hold on me except for one. I liked Delancy and Simon, they were definitely interesting and I liked how there feelings spread across the multiverse but it wasn't until nearly the end of the story that I truly cared about what happened to them. The character that I did love immediately though, was Monty, Del's grandfather. I just adored him from the second he came into the story. He has a lovely relationship with Del and I really can't wait to see what happens with him in the second book (because SERIOUSLY?! there has to be more there!! Despite the characters not wowing me, what really makes the whole book is the world building. It's absolutely PHENOMENAL. The way it's explained is fascinating and I love that it's compared to music. It's very different from any other parallel world novel that I read and I couldn't get enough of the echos. I think it just fascinates me because it's infinite... there are so many Echo's that you could cross to. And the cleaving, the inversions, the tuning... it was all remarkable and explained so, so well. Often in science fiction, the world building is confusing and is dumped upon you but that's not the case at all in Dissonance. It's a wonderfully crafted and well thought out world and has you nearly itching to be a part of it. The ending shocked me, the story went down a whole different road than I thought it was going. I'm not entirely sure what to make of one of the plot points and I'm sure there is more there but it's a given that I will be continuing this series. I'm actually really sad upon finishing this book and I had tears in my eyes during the last few paragraphs. It's going to be a looooooooong wait for the second book!

I read some of the reviews before reading the book, so I went into it a bit wary of what I would find. And after the first couple of chapters, I was thinking this book was going to be an enormous let-down. I mean, come on ladies, get your acts together! You're nearly thirty, for heaven's sake! And then... WHAM. I cried for about 150 pages. I thought Ann Brashares did a great job of describing the process of grief, and making it different for every person. As horrifying as it is to lose a major character, I don't think these women could have made such strides in pulling themselves together, or in learning about themselves, without it. And that's one reason I took off a star, because while death does that to you in real life, it makes for a clunky plot device when written down. And the other reason I took off a star is because of Bee & Eric's behaviour. I've always related to Bee more than any other character, but taking off for five months and living wherever? And expecting your boyfriend to hand around waiting while you don't bother communicating with him? Eric's willingness to go along with whatever made Bee happy, regardless of his own feelings, made me a little bit crazy. What did he do while she was gone? Just sit around and hope she was okay? I think I would have liked her storyline better if she was at least communicating with Eric, and seeing his reaction to her choices would have been nice. Despite misgivings and annoyances, I still really enjoyed this book overall. It was great to catch up with the girls again.

I couldn't put this down! I pretty much loved everything about this book. The passion for sports, the focus on family, the personal growth, the development of relationships. Sometimes there is only one aspect of a book that you enjoy, the love interest or the family or where the plot is going. I just adored it all here! I was not bored for a single second. "One thing I learned a long time ago is that even if you think you're meant to be with someone, that doesn't necessarily mean you get to be with them." Nothing went quite as expected, if you read the blurb and get into the book you expect everything to work out 100% for our herione and she gets everything her little heart desires, right? Not quite what happened here! And I love it when that happens. Unexpected twists come up. I love how the romance went in this book. She never makes us fall for Ty and then suddenly dislike him as some authors do. I was wary of him all along andthought it was a bit too insta. And the tiny clues from Henry just built it up and when I realised it I was like YES!! PLEASE! !I also like that Jordan broke up with Ty without knowing for sure that Henry would be with her, because you shouldn't stay with the wrong person just so that you're not alone. I will most definitely be looking into Ms Kenneally's other work!

So let me preface this by saying I did not hate this ending. It was your run-of-the-mill, simple, happy ending. I don't always mind that. I'm happy the characters are happy. Despite my dislike for the Mal/Alina pairing, I can get on board with how things went down, and I can safely say I'm satisfied with how the trilogy was wrapped up. That being said, here are a few ways I wish the books would have ended: 1) Mal stays dead, Alina defeats the Darkling with her amplified powers, she becomes Nikolai's queen, and the reader is left with hints that the power is going to Alina's head, that she's slowly going mad with it all, that she's a new Darkling in the making, etc. 2) Mal stays dead but otherwise things go down the way they did in the book with Alina losing her powers and killing the Darkling, but afterwards she becomes a hermit. 3) Alina manages to steal the Darkling's powers Aang-style but keeps him alive, and in the process loses her own powers as well (they cancel each other out maybe?). They begin a toxic relationship, as they are still two of a kind. (This is my shipper heart talking). But I guess I'll take the basic happy ending with a bittersweet twinge.
