This was kind of dumb. The thing is, it was a 4 star read until around the 80% mark, or I would've dropped this like a hot potato a lot sooner. And I say this as someone who liked Gone Girl and Sharp Objects; I gave both those books a solid 3 star rating. This, though...I don't even know. It's similar to the other two books in that it's cleverly crafted, but unfortunately at some point it all kind of went to hell. (Almost literally.) Gillian Flynn is so great at building suspense, which is not all that easy in a book where you already know the outcome. We know from page 1 (well, from the summary, really) that Patty, Michelle and Debby Day are murdered. They don't survive and yet, through the chapters that are written from Patty's POV from that day, you can still feel the suspense building as the hours of the chapters slowly tick away and you know her end is near. Unfortunately, there is just too much information being withheld from the reader and no one likes a carrot dangling in front of their nose for too long. Actually, I probably wouldn't mind the dangling carrot too much if it led to a great, mind-blowing revelation of the mystery at the end. Needless to say, that didn't happen here. The resolution was convoluted, completely unrealistic and just stupid. There are far too many coincidences popping up left and right as well. Especially when it comes to incriminating evidence against Ben. I was already scoffing at many things that turned up, but I honestly drew the line at the fact the "molested" girls said they'd had to give Ben their underpants (which was not true) and then children's clothes were found under his bed later that day (because he'd bought secondhand clothes for the baby he was expecting with his girlfriend). Too many of those things happened, it just made me roll my eyes. Not to mention that I find a lot of the violence and sex in Flynn's books gratuitous. It's like she needs to reach a certain quota or something. Anyway. Having said all of this, she still has a knack for writing pageturners that will keep you up all night if you're not careful. Just like writing unlikeable characters is clearly her thing. Libby - as the only surviving girl of the Kinnakee massacre - is a fantastic main character, like only Flynn can write them. She's kind of despicable and does some horrible stuff, but because she's just so damaged you can't help but root for her to find out what actually happened the night of the murders. Sorry that what actually happened was really dumb, Libby. You and I both deserved a better explanation.

The concept of a Martian - a human being by birth, but in essence, a Martian - rehabilitated on Earth is an arresting idea, and a great canvas. In Heinlein's work, this canvas is mainly coloured through lens of social commentary and a new moral philosophy that became a manifesto for the counter cultural movements of the 60s. Although divided in 5 main parts, the novel can really be said to be composed of halves. The first half is where the narration is the focus, the story keeps moving and there is a real sense of 'happening.' The second half lags in terms of action but brings out the core concepts and ideas of the novel in full, successively developing from satire, taking on government and civilisation, to the formulation of a new philosophy which underlined the beginning of the Free Love movement that came in later in the decade. Typically, Heinlein employs the use of two main characters as the main propogator's of his thought and ideas. They are, of course, Jubal Harshaw and Mike himself. Sex The core of Heinlein's philosophy lies in sex, and how sex is perceived and ought to be perceived amongst humanity. When Mike, the man from Mars discovers that human beings share something that has no equivalent in the Martian culture, he is fascinated. On Mars, there is no distinction of 'male' and 'female' as such. The female equivalents are mere 'nymphs', who, by any accounts, do not figure into much prominence. However, as Mike discovers, things are different on Earth. Men and women co-exist. The male and the female are distinct, yet harmonise with each other. Sex is the basis for this harmony, the basis for all humanity. Sex is important. Sex is good. This is where Heinlein goes a step further for his time; his attitude towards sex in belief and practice were radically different from existing social norms for his time. To Heinlein, and consequently Mike, sex is not a commodity, to be hoarded and practised in the privacy of two individuals behind closed doors. Instead, sex is shared goodness, to be given and taken and exchanged at large. Where Mike comes from, jealousy as a concept does not exist. This lack of jealousy, lack of possessiveness manifest themselves in his attitude towards sex. Because jealousy doesn't exist, polygamy is no problem. Jubal explains Mike philosophy in contrast with religious indictments. The Bible declares: Though shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife. But this, as Jubal wryly observes, is a natural impossibility. As long as men continue to live, they continue to be subject to their desires, whether physical or otherwise. Mike and his philosophy are exactly opposite. What the Church is saying is don't eye your neighbour's wife, full stop. What Mike is saying is: You want to covet my wife? Take her! And have some good rocking sex while you're at it. For Mike, sex isn't off-hands and restricted between two people. Love and sex, intertwined as they are, deserve to be shared among people, their goodness shared across all people in the Nest. Far from something to be ashamed of or to be guilty about, sex was a goodness, to be cherished and enjoyed and shared. Of course, this is almost a line-by-line blue print of the hippie movement that came in later during the 60s. This book was published much before it happened, and was there just at the right time when it did. The Free Love movement of the 1960s underscores Mike's philosophy. Heinlein's thesis of religion While everyone was busy having orgies, it did not escape Heinlein to incorporate commentary on religion as well. This he does through the portrayal of the religious order, the Fosterites, who are of the Christian denomination but differ widely in essentials. While Christians unnecessarily torment themselves with original sin, Fosterites embrace it, accept it, and get ready to put it behind themselves. The ultimate aim of life according to Fosterites is to be happy. Heinlein criticises Christianity's doublespeak. Christianity and Islam are quick to mete out judgement to their followers, to dictate moral, social, political and sexual rules and judgments to their followers. Yet, at the same time, their scriptures are full of inconsistencies and sexual deviance. A case in point in Lot's offering of his two virgin daughters to a mob banging on his door. Lot trades his young daughters so as to have 'the mob stop banging on the door.' This is the God who complies with such an act, who rewards this morality while simultaneously frowning upon a million other things. Such a God is a hypocrite. Fosterism then, as a religion seeks to eliminate this bias, to do away once and for all with the doublespeak and hypocrisy of religion. However, their unabashed glorying in happiness and hedonistic pleasure is initially disquieting to Jubal and Jill. Conclusion I can see why Stranger in a Strange land became such a landmark novel when it was published. It must have provoked and outraged and shocked people of its time - it still does today, in certain places and among certain people. However, any hope of life on Mars, our direct neighbour, let alone a civilisation as highly advanced as the one portrayed in the novel, in light of successive Martian expeditions over the decades is rendered unrealistic at best. There are also some major flaws with the book, most particularly Heinlein's portrayal of women. Women are either shown as passive and 'go-along-with-what-he's-saying-and-doing', like Miriam, Dorcas and Anne, or manipulative and controlling, like Mrs. Douglas and Patty and, to some extent, Jill. My main gripe with Heinlein was Jill saying, 'Nine out of ten times, when a woman gets raped, it's her own fault.' However, all these things considered, the redeeming hallmarks of Stranger are its social commentary and its original ideas about religion and civilisation, which, in the post-60s, post-hippiedom world might strike us as tired and tested, but which were strikingly original and timely for the time it was published in. If you can put aside the 50s-60s attitudinal drawbacks behind, this is a quintessential science fiction read.

Claire, a nurse who recently served at the war-front, is enjoying the peace post World War II with her husband. While in Scotland studying his family tree the couple discover a standing stone ring. When Claire visits it later on her own she is sucked through the stones and thrown back in time 200 years. stuck in the past Claire is embroiled in political intrigue as well as at risk of physical harm, some of which is aimed at her by her husband's 8x grandfather. I like Claire, she has a lot of strength, intelligence and adaptability, but she isn't a snob. I do think she took a little too long to figure out she was in the past though. I get you wouldn't just meet one person, snap your fingers and go 'that's it! ', but it took a while. Jamie was a bit like a Game of Thrones character to me, not out of any similarity between the books but in the way you liked his character, then you hated him, then you liked him, but you were wary, because after all, he did *that thing* and you weren't sure you could trust him. And you could forget and really like his character sometimes, but then you'd remember oh that's right, he's screwing his twin sister and pushed poor Bran out a window - oops wrong Jamie. Same feeling though. He did something, and you'd forget about it, and like him, but then occasionally remember what he did and think, no, no I shouldn't like you, you're a jerk. The historical setting is well researched and wonderfully real. The descriptions didn't get too long, but you felt well grounded and were given pretty much all the information you needed. The story had a good flow and impetus to it, it kept me reading even through the less riveting parts. If you aren't a fan of corporal punishment and spanking your children this book is not for you. There are repeated floggings, and there are MANY discussions about how when they were children they were beaten by their parents in the pursuit of discipline. These conversations are mostly used to sway anti-physical punishment Claire to a pro-physical view. Jamie repeatedly recollects with fondness having the living daylights throttled out of him and discusses how it made him such an upstanding man. Yeah... who was willing to flog his own wife. Sure. My personal stand point accepts that there *may* be points in time, for specific children, depending on circumstance when such discipline is required, but only a spank, not a thorough beating such as what was described. One thing that bugged me with the ending was  they disposed of such an excellent antagonist as Captain Randall. He was horrid, but as a villain magnificent. And his disposal was highly unsatisfying. He was ran over, off stage, by cattle. No grand confrontation where he was suitably trounced. Very unsatisfying. And to follow that point up, Claire took notice that since he'd been killed before he was supposed to, she'd changed history, thus proving she actually could alter history. And then she barely considers and doesn't react AT ALL to the thought she basically just wiped her 1945 husband out of existence. She really doesn't bat an eyelid over it. I know she's chosen Jamie and all, but really? So little care for your first husband? It's not like he cheated on you and left you for the younger model. That was you. I really hope it's a red herring death, and it wasn't actually Randall but someone else who died and he's going to plague them further. The story ended on an interesting note, clearly with much more to come. I'm not desperate for the next volume (as proven by starting a totally different book ;p ) but I am interested to read on, maybe later in the year. I think I'm just not ready to commit to another epic series so soon after reading the entire Wheel of Time. A richly detailed historical romance with speculative fiction elements that should be a hit with romance fans, fans of cross dimensional fantasy, and historical novel fans. I also recommend it to anyone with a penchant for Scotland.

UH...WHY DO I FEEL LIKE I AM THE ONE THAT JUST GOT DUMPED? That's how good this book it. The feelings that Min felt, all her thoughts, her emotions, just rushed out of the pages and poured at me. I felt everything she did-every smile, every laugh, every bitter frown, and all the love and hate for Ed. Ed...that asshole. I think everyone can agree that: sometimes in life we are Min and sometimes we are Ed, but if we are lucky, we wouldn't be either. At first, I had to admit, I thought this story was pretty weird. Min isn't your typical cookie cutter YA character, even if Ed sometimes is. She's quirky, strange, but at the same time witty and adorable. Still, it was hard to relate to her-her sense of humor, her interests, even her friends but soon she started to grow on me and all was lost after that. What I love most about this story is the undeniable fact-and this is written in the back of the book so I cannot take credit for such a great line-every breakup starts with a love story-it's just so simple but nonetheless undoubtedly true. I didn't relate to Min and Ed isn't the kind of guy I would fall for, but I understood her and I understood their love story. Just two people getting to know each other, falling in love, and along the way life happens and everything that used to be rock solid starts to liquify. I just appreciate how honest this book is, from start to finish. I like how Min saw all the signs but chose to ignore them because the good outweighs the bad, I love how she fell hard for Ed and didn't stop because that's how first love is and should always be, I love their little banters and how well they understood each other, I love how they made sacrifices for one another, and lastly I love how Min can't hate Ed without remembering why she loved him, and that my friend, is true with any and all relationships.

I am beginning to get more and more used to hearing Ramses' perspective, and I definitely appreciate it. The mystery in this particular novel was rather confusing - part of it was centered on this parchment the kids got their hands on, but then it was more about them being abducted. And then you add it the fuss about Akhenaten/Tiya's tomb and the horrible Mr. Davis, and at times it was hard to figure out what the focus was. So here are some things I did and didn't like from this book: Nefret was horrifyingly annoying - she was being so bossy with Amelia, demanding that she and Emerson tell the kids everything about their past, everything that they had or will be doing. I understand where Nefret is coming from -- there are some things that it's important to share, so everyone can guard against them -- but it seemed especially hypocritical when the kids had been hiding such big things from them most of the book, first the parchment and fight in Cairo, and then David & Lia's relationship. Add to that her oblivion in regards to Ramses' feelings for her, and I just can't handle that much of her anymore. My annoyance with Nefret was counterbalanced with my delight at the reappearance with Sethos. As much as I love Emerson, and think he and Amelia are perfect for each other, I can't help but like and admire Sethos as well, for his love and respect for Amelia. He's so dashing, in a James-Bond-secret-spy sort of way. His rescue of her from Bertha's grasp was so romantic and sweet, and I loved their farewell at the train station . I'm so glad that we haven't seen the last of him. Ramses: He needs to be honest with Nefret about his feelings. Pining away for her isn't doing either of them any favors. I love his depth of emotions, but I'm worried that his constant suppression of those feelings is going to effect him permanently. Lastly, Abdallah. What a heartbreak. Clearly, they've been foreshadowing at least his retirement for a while, but I wasn't expecting his death, especially is such a manner. If he had to die, this is the way he would want it, protecting Amelia and the family he loves so dearly. But did Abdallah need to die? Who knows. His funeral was quite touching, and he was more of a true father to Amelia than her birth father ever was. He will truly be missed. . P.S. I am editing this review to add, if you are reading these books in order, I would recommend you skip out of order and read #16, Guardian of the Horizon next, as it is set the next winter after this one. That is all.

I wrote this (or at least part of it) at midnight on the plane to Sydney, after devouring the entire book whilst everyone else was sleeping around me. I couldn't sleep, I was restless, and all I could think about was Fateful. Fateful had consumed my mind, my thoughts and the story replayed intermittently like a movie inside my head. I've always been fascinated by the Titanic, although I have to admit this fascination only started after I watched the movie, and it was what initially drew me to Fateful. I don't know about you, but whilst reading Fateful, I could not help but compare it to the marvellous award-winning 1997 movie Titanic, which I might add is without a doubt my favourite movie. With every page, I was constantly thinking of a similar scene from. I mean, they weren't all that different: star-crossed lovers who, under normal circumstances would never have set eyes on each other, somehow fatefully meet and fall in love, only to be met with a doomed fate. But comparing Fateful to Titanic was not all that bad; since I loved Titanic, it also meant I was in love with Fateful. The romance.Alex. Tessa.The delicious, yet heart-breaking romance. It was the sort of romance that was so real , so heart-warming yet heart-breaking and I loved it. There was also a part of me thinking about how falling in love within a mere week just seemed...too fast. But then I had to remind myself, we're talking about true love and the Titanic. Under normal circumstances I would probably roll my eyes and the scream in annoyance, but there was a certain realness about their romance that captured my heart and won my full support. Alex and Tess were consistently fighting on the verge of life and death for each other, and as a bonus, this took place on the Titanic. (Yes, I'm contradicting myself, but that's just how my brain works!) Oh, how can I forget? Werewolves.The whole concept of werewolves and the Brotherhood intent on recruiting- or should I say stalking Alex was all extremely interesting. I've never been much of a werewolf girl (blame the vampires for stealing all my attention! ), but I thought the Brotherhood was described and explained reasonably well in one novel alone. This may not appeal to everyone, but definitely try it if you are, like me, extremely interested in the Titanic. I'm actually still debating whether I would have preferred an alternative ending since the twist at the end was so unpredictable, but it felt both good and bad. Overall, this was a beautifully crafted historical romance, with a paranormal twist. If you like a novel that can evoke a strong emotional response from the reader, then this is perfect for you! Highly recommeded to everyone!

This is the second half of A Dance of Dragons, which catches up to the timeline set by A Feast for Crows and then breezes past it, bringing back characters from that book as well as continuing to follow characters from this one. Unfortunately, I was spoiled for one of the major plot points of this book (Jon Snow's death ), so instead of the gut punch it should have been, it fell kind of flat. That's what I get for lagging behind in my reading whilst the HBO show races on, I suppose. People can't resist posting their reactions on Facebook! But still, you know, there were a lot of things I hadn't been spoiled for, and for that I am grateful. There was still plenty of plot in this book to keep me entertained. You can tell that Martin struggled with the Dany/Meereen plotline, as her chapters feel mired in names and politics, dragging out her time there so that the author can get all the major characters into place around her. Not that it wasn't an enjoyable read (and believable in that Dany kept trying to do the right thing, but that the right thing was having not very good consequences), but Martin's struggle really did show in the writing. The last Daenerys chapter makes me hopeful that he has emerged on the other side of that mire, and hopefully stronger for it. I love the way that Martin writes. One day, I would love to do a reread of the whole of A Song of Ice and Fire series, probably when all the books have been published, and really take my time and enjoy the language. I am a lover of words, and Martin's prose is full of gems (though he does have a few words he likes to overuse to the point of it being noticeable). I can see why people don't like Feast and Dance as much as the previous three books, but I find much to admire about them in their own way. Sure, they're slow in a lot of places, with a lot of walking and a lot of talking, but all the important plot threads are still moved forward (and some introduced). Looking at all of the threads that have been built up over these two books, I feel as though the books are a breather, in a way. The calm before the storm. If Martin wants to wrap up the story in only two more books, the next books are going to have to be quite full on. I don't have much more to say about this one, other than I was not disappointed. I have a lot of thoughts, but I can't quite articulate them right now - I'll add some stuff when I do an indepth reread at some other point. I really am looking forward to when the next book comes out. I think that, even though the HBO television series is now ahead of the books and some of the mysteries will be solved on television before they are on the page, it will still be well worth the read. This is definitely up amongst my all-time favourite series, even though it's taken me so long to read all the currently-published books. I'm relieved to finally be able to join the wait for the next book!

The choice of Death as the narrator of this story was a bold one, and definitely risky. Zusak was mostly able to pull it off in my opinion, but there were a few stumbles along the way. The sentence structure got a little clunky at times when he was trying too hard to be eloquent and philosophical. The first few chapters were almost too much, with the over-the-top ruminations on colors and weather. I did enjoy Death's random side notes. These quirky asides were a unique perspective, and gave more depth to the character than any of the more poetic ramblings. I have a bit of a love-hate for all the foreshadowing, if you can even call it that. It was very unsubtle, but I liked Death's reasoning for that - he's giving away the story to help prepare himself for telling it. Perhaps the most unique part of Zusak's structure are the hand-drawn sections of Max's books. I think these bits turned out extremely well, and managed to be inventive without being cheesy. As likely any story about Nazi Germany attempts, The Book Thief is exceedingly emotional. Sometimes the writing comes off as almost manipulative because of this. The scene, for instance, when  Liesel repeats Max's words to him as he's marching to a concentration camp  is a bit heavy-handed and unrealistic, and it felt out of place. For the most part though, the relationships are honestly crafted and moving. I might not have rated it so high if it weren't for the fact that it did succeed in making me emotional. Even though manipulative storytelling like that gets annoying sometimes, I can definitely concede when it is effective.

In 'Til Death Do Us Part, Amanda Quick returns to historical romance with the story of Calista Langley, who operates an "introductions" salon in the grand mansion that she inherited from her rather cranky grandmother. Since all of the money they inherited had to be spent on renovating the house, Calista and her younger brother are dependent on the income from their business. When a mysterious man starts stalking Calista and leaving rather nasty gifts (memento mori to be precise), she's determined to find out who it is before they make good on the implied threat. When a reclusive author named Trent Hastings offers to help, Calista teams up with him to track down her unwanted admirer. I probably just need to stop reading Amanda Quick/Jayne Ann Krentz' stuff. It's not that it's bad. After having been a fan for years and devouring everything I could find that she'd written though, I found myself getting bored very quickly with this one. I'm honestly not even sure what it was exactly. Mostly just seems like all of her characters feel the same after awhile. All of the men are martially skilled detective sorts and all of the women are sensible and independent. None of this is bad inherently, but when it's always the same, it's difficult to care about what happens to them. She also made the choice to reveal pretty early on who the villain is which was an interesting tactic but not entirely it paid off. It made me suspect that there was another person in play so the ending was less of a surprise than I'm thinking was intended. I ended up skimming through the last bit just to see if I was right about how it ended. It's not terrible, but if you've read an Amanda Quick book before, you may get a bit bored with this one.

In her author's note Colleen Hoover says she writes "strictly to entertain and not to education, inform, or persuade" but that this book was her exception to that rule. And what a fantastic exception it is. Her skills as a new adult romance author make her uniquely qualified to put us in the position of a woman who finds herself  in an abusive relationship. She makes Ryle so funny, charming, and handsome it is DEVASTATING when he first hits Lily because you feel so much for both of them at the point it happens. This book along with Leslie Morgan Steiner's TED Talk "Why domestic violence victims don't leave" really helped me understand why a person would stay in this type of unhealthy relationship. Some of the book is predictable and the tacked on happy ending feels like an attempt to let us down easy after such a whirlwind, but that doesn't change the illuminating and engaging story Hoover has crafted. I really respect her for tackling this novel and topic without coming across as preachy or like a Lifetime Movie.

I've been wanting to read one of Elliot Wake's books for ages. I've got Unteachable, Black Iris & Cam Girl sitting on my shelf, and I've just been waiting for the perfect time to dive in. So I was looking for a new read (I can never pick a book so I just read the first pages until one really grabs my attention) and Unteachable did just that. I knew from the start that I was going to absolutely love Maise O'Malley. She's confident in herself, she knows what she wants, and she isn't afraid to get it (unless it means getting on the first car on a roller-coaster because everyone else on the coaster is a savage). She's the perfect heroine, because I love girls who are confident, because I can live my life through them, because I am so not. Unteachable is just one of those books that drags you in, until you literally sit and read it until you're finished and that's what I did. Maise's story is fantastic, and her relationship with Evan is completely intense. It sucks you in and doesn't let you go, and because of the nature of their relationship, and the whole teacher-student thing, you're never quite sure if you should be cheering or not, which is hard considering I'm a hopeless romantic, no matter who it's between. I just love a happy ending. But watching Maise and Evan was a bit like watching a car crash, it was too intense, too much, too fast, and I was kind of wanting to read it through eyes hidden by my hands because I couldn't help wondering if it was all going to implode in their faces. What actually sets this book apart from other books, is not only the intoxicating romance, duh, but the writing. This is one of the best written New Adult books I've ever read - in fact, it's just one of the best written books, ever. So lyrical, there were even words used that I had no idea what they meant, so I had to look them up, but it added to how amazing the book was, because Wake really has a way with words. It makes me want to go and dive into the other two books immediately, because I need that kind of book in my life, it lets me just dive away into a different world for a few hours, and forget my own life and that's hard to do. Not a lot of authors can do that. I loved this book, and I'm not sure my words could ever do it justice. Unteachable is one of those books that doesn't let you go until the very last page, and even then there's a part of me that would absolutely love a sequel. I need more of Maise O'Malley in my life. And Wesley! I kinda liked him, I kinda feel like he has a story to be told, too. And Evan was kinda dreamy. I KNOW. You need to read this book, if you like the New Adult genre you will love this, and if you just like a well written book, this is for you. It's hard to believe this is a debut novel, but it is and it was amazing.

First of all, I LOVED THIS BOOK. I have not found a contemporary romance so compelling in a long while. The characters are complex, but the author slowly builds a layered picture of all thier underlying motivations, even the unconscious ones that compete with what they know they should do. Not to mention that the relationship between Etienne and Anna is sexy and realistic and full of delicious tension. Even apart from the romantic aspects though, this story was just so well-written. Paris was more than just a romantic backdrop, it was a character. My one hick-up with this was it's title--Anna and the French Kiss--it makes it sound so fluffy and kinda cheesy, but this book was so much more than that! Paris was a real place, full of culture, and landmarks and, I don't know how to describe it other than to say it had a real sense of place. Perkins made it come alive instead of doing what so many others have done with location-based novels. It's great the way Anna gets to know the city slowly, the culture shock she goes through, and the way she slowly develops a relationship with Paris itself. So, so good. It's the first book I've read in 2010, and I think that it's one that will stick with me and end up in next year's top ten list! Four stars!

There were a lot of things I didn't really like about this book... our world Penny seemed like a fake person, the whole chapter with "John" being in charge, the overly complicated climactic scene... and some other stuff. But somehow I still overlooked all that stuff and enjoyed the read. There were parts that got slow, but then it'd pick up again. The short chapters definitely helped keep me engaged and the writing, although occasionally scientific-sounding, was often dialogue heavy and flowed easily. There was even some insightful stuff that hit home a bit: "When someone dies they get very cold and very still. That probably sounds obvious, but when it's your mother it doesn't feel obvious - it feels shocking... the sentimental gesture of kissing her forehead makes you recoil because the moment your lips touch her skin you realize just how cold and just how still she is, just how permanent that coldness and stillness feel. Your body lurches like it's been plunged into boiling water and for the first time in your life you understand death as a biological state, an organism ceasing to function. Unless you've touched a corpse before, you can't comprehend the visceral wrongness of inert flush wrapped around an inanimate object that wears your mother's face. You feel sick with guilt and regret and sadness about every time you rolled your eyes in annoyance or brushed off a needy request or let your mind wander when she told some inconsequential anecdote. You can't remember anything thoughtful or sweet or tender that you ever did even though logically you know you must have. All you can recall is how often you were small and petty and false. She was your mother and she loved you in a way nobody else ever has and nobody else ever will and now she's gone." I'm not sure why, but I think my favorite part was him being frozen going backwards for 50 years.

3.5 stars Liked it. Interesting world/universe, interesting factions, interesting back stories, interesting power dynamics. Looking forward to reading more of this world/universe and hoping there's more in the work. One rather huge caveat though: I'm disappointed they didn't kill each other. There was so much history between these two that needed airing out, and the only way to do that was, imho, a battle to the death. At the very least. I mean, all that build up and yet no blood? Not even a serious injury or permanent damage? I expected more of Meli. Someone with her skill set and talent should have put them to good use. At the very least I would have liked to see her follow through on the "assignment." The thing I can't get past, even months later, is how she was literally raised to serve him and then he derailed her whole life and ruined all chances and prospects for her, yet her way of getting back at him was to play a well thought out mind game that ultimately did NOT end in his death and/or ruination? All that suffering she went through was for naught, you see. I'm very disappointed, Meli. Then again, I suppose a successful assassination wouldn't sit well with the Ilona Andrews' fanbase/intended audience, what with this book being a romance and all. The death and/or serious maiming of the leading man would have been too traumatic...for the reader. Full review at https://covers2covers.wordpress.com/2...

I rarely rate a book at only 1 star, but Invitation to a Beheading proved an awful reading experience for me. It took me about two months to finish this novel, although it has merely 223 pages. However, my mindset towards reading is that I finish a book no matter how much I dislike it, because I am well aware of the hard work an author puts into writing. Aside from Invitation to a Beheading, the only novel written by Nabokov that I have read is obviously Lolita, his masterpiece, which I enjoyed it to a higher degree compared to Invitation to a Beheading. Maybe my disappointment with this book derives from the fact that it seemed to me that it was poorly translated into Romanian and now and then I wasn't even sure what was actually going on. I figured out that through his main character, Cincinnatus, and the couple of days he spent in jail ahead of his execution, the author wanted to reflect certain profound ideas but it simply didn't work out for me. In my opinion, even though this novel is relatively short, it is a difficult read and requires a lot of attention. I noticed that there is a significant number of people who have enoyed this book written by Nabokov, therefore I am probably the one having a problem.

This book had a lot of things going for it. It is a coming-of-age story (among other things), which I tend to have a soft spot for. It references literature and films with which I am familiar; sure, it gets rather pretentious, but it's the type of pretension I have no problem getting behind. It is fairly humorous - not laugh-out-loud funny, but dry and amusing in a way I enjoy. And the middle of the book was quite a page-turner. Unfortunately, there were a number of problems with the novel as well. The sheer volume of metaphors quickly became tiresome. The dialogue is noticeably unnatural. The "fascinating" Hannah is actually pretty boring. And pretty much everything after Hannah's death is a letdown. I'm not going to say it's not worth reading, because I did enjoy it. It just had the potential to be a lot more than it was, and that was frustrating.
Hummm. I felt like the boys were really uncomfortable sharing Lily, among other things. Wierd. LOL.

Didn't like this one quite as well as its sequel - too much advancement of plot via misunderstandings/lack of communication. Still a quick, easy read, and I'll add other books from the series to my rainy day fund of mindless comfort reading.

This book dragged in the middle. The author always takes a risk when you remove the characters from the setting (and supporting cast) you know, and in this case, I'm not sure Ms. Banks succeeded (especially since our leading man and lady spent a fair portion of the book apart). The ending was rather ho-hum. We don't find out what happens with the Archives (though it seemed to work out given the epilogue) and the stuff with Kennedy gets resolved off page and we get a couple of sentences worth of an explanation from Milligan. It sort of feels like she got tired of writing so she just stopped or she thought writing the political debate stuff would get boring so she didn't do it. If that's the case, that's her own fault for setting the world up as she did. There could have been a war or something if she wanted more action . Three stars is being generous. It's more like 2.5.

Such a pretty cover! I borrowed You're Never Weird on the Internet (Almost) because I like Day -- well, I like her persona, I guess. I don't do YouTube as much as my kid does, so I didn't know how big Geek & Sundry was until I read Day's memoir, which is probably kind of backwards, but I knew her from lots of smaller roles and The Guild (watched it on Netflix, not in real time). Day's writing voice is a LOT like her speaking voice. I am a person who enjoys using capslock in her own writing, so I liked it, but I am clearly biased. Never Weird is a memoir, and it does go into Day's childhood and how she became so situationally recognizable, but it doesn't hit on some of the things I was interested in; Day explains her struggles to do acting beyond commercials in depth, and then moves from that into writing a pilot that eventually became The Guild, and later she just drops a mention of her role on Buffy the Vampire Slayer in there without much explanation about how she landed the gig. I mean, at some point she cracked the code, since she's been on multiple sci-fi-ish shows (playing characters other than "the secretary") since her commercial days. I don't know if some stuff didn't get mentioned because Day is still in ~the biz~, if she didn't want to feel like she was mining her current work relationships for book material . it seemed strange to me. Maybe there just wasn't space. I think I liked this more than I might have otherwise because Day completely nails her descriptions of certain anxieties that I've run up against, too. Just wish my middle-of-the-night realization of my own mortality ended with some sort of life-altering resolution. I knew it was missing something! (three-and-a-half stars)

Slightly better than Lola and the Boy Next Door. Though I do not get why they have to be so hormonal at, what, 18 years old? Who am I to become without him? WHOA GIRL, BETTER PUT A BRAKE ON IT. And please, why is Perkins so fixated with gays? There's Meredith, and Lola has two dads, while Isla has a bisexual sister. It serves no purpose to the stories--maybe except to highlight that Perkins is very supportive of LGBT rights? I am, but you don't see me talking about it with strangers. So gee lady, thanks for throwing that in so casually without back stories and all. But whatever right? Her books, her rules.

The plot of this book was good, it kept me reading despite all the annoyances in it. Although I did skim over some of it. Everything seemed to happen to fast. Harlow "Princess" did everything she said she would never do within a day of being released from prison. She went from being single and never hooking up with a brother to being an old lady to a complete stranger immediately. The relationship between Harlow and Cooper was completely forced, the child went from not knowing her to calling her mommy almost immediately. There was a lot of public shootings in this book with very little police involvement. And it ended with a cliffhanger. It also drove me crazy that everyone called Harlow Princess all the time and she apparently didn't care even after stating that she didn't like it. Overall, it was okay. I'll read he next one with the hope that it will be better.

Likes: a fairly compelling plot. Like when you know a train is going to wreck and you don't want to but you kinda want to see what's going to happen. For all the eye-rolling I did while reading, I couldn't put the thing down either. dislikes: each and every single character is so shallow and self-absorbed, there's not one in the entire book that I liked or wanted to root for. The possible exception is Claire, one of the servants, but as she gets practically nil development, eh. This had shown up on my radar a few times and so I gave it a try. I can imagine reading the sequels if they ever go on sale on my kindle, but otherwise probably not. When the best thing about a book is it's cover, that's not a good thing!
Im not a big fan on these kind of novels, but this is good.

The Fiery Heart was good - but it wasn't great. I think it is the weakest link in the series thus far - and that has nothing to do with its place in the overall series arc, and everything to do with the fact that it didn't have enough interior plot or story. It was like it suffered from middle-of-trilogy syndrome without actually being in the middle of a trilogy - it was all a bridge to the next step in the series-wide plot arc, and didn't have anything that was its own. Series Continuation Points: - Further development of Sydrian (which is a fantastic relationship. I love them together. I love them even more than I loved Rose and Dimitri, which is saying something). - Further development on the Strigoi-vaccination front. - Further development on the Alchemist re-edcuation plot. - Further development on the relationship dynamics between the whole Palm Springs crew. - Introduction of Adrian's POV, but only because we're going to need it in the next book Because Sydney, our usual narrator, seems to be out of commission . - Fantastic cliffhanger lead-in to the next book. All of that was really good. But what kept this book from being as good as the previous two (for me, I'm sure others have totally different and totally valid opinions on it) is that it didn't have any distinct plot for this book that wasn't just a build up for something that will happen in a later book. Bloodlines had Keith and Lee and the tattoo plot. The Golden Lily had the Warriors of Light. The Indigo Spell had the evil witch. But The Fiery Heart had nothing that was its own. And, for me, that made it a weaker book. I do, however, have high hopes for the next book. Re-Education, while awful for Sydney, is bound to make for an intersting story .

First off, there isn't a lot of similarity with the movie script. Other than the basic premise that a child is born and ages backwards. Let's not deal with the fact that he is born a cigar smoking adult sized septuagenarian. His poor mother... ouch. Amusingly it is seen as improper in the social sense. His father worries. How he will walk down the street with his son? What will the people say? How will he buy him clothes? It is unacceptable. As if poor Benjamin can do anything about it. He lives a remarkably normal life. As people get older, they often wish to live their life over again; especially if they retain the knowledge acquired with age, but poor Benjamin doesn't get to do that either. He is old when he is young and vice versa. He doesn't fit anywhere and that makes the story kind of sad. His own son tells him he needs to stop it now; as if he can?

This book picks up right where book one end. I loved it that this book has Jay's POV, I was able to connect much more with him and I really enjoy the way Jay becomes Noah and how he reacts to life. And of course Lily was the same badass girl from the first book :) And as much as I loved the epilogue, I wish it wasn't so far in the future. I would loved to have much more story about the characters that we abandon them in the bank: Arianna, Vault/Ben, Harriet and Charlie. I feel like there's more with these characters and their untold story.

Again, as in the case of  Simple Genius, this is the reason I don't read more fiction. Even the historical fiction nature of the book, (Germany wins WWII, it's a different world, yada, yada, yada--you can read more of the storyline in the reviews others have written) couldn't save it for me. I thought that both this book and  Simple Genius had excellent premises but the stories failed to draw me in like a good  Dean Koontz book. Oh, and I am very literal. The book ends sort of like the movie Field of Dreams where they went into the cornfield and that was it. What? So what happened? Don't leave me guessing. I hate that. All in all, the book was just a'ite, but based upon the raving reviews here, at Amazon, and Audible.com, my expectations were so much higher. I appear to be a definite minority in my opinion but had to voice it anyway.

What I find the most interesting about this book is that everybody who rates it less than 5 stars always has to start with a disclaimer. "I feel bad giving this 3 stars, but..." Well, I'm not going to start with a disclaimer. It's okay to hate a book even if the main character is an endearing boy with congenital abnormalities. That is one of the problems with books about touchy or sad topics. Everyone feels like they have to love it. There were many good parts to this book. The characters were good, and the way the author made each character have a unique voice was awesome. The problem with this book was the ending. This ended the way every tween book has to end: Happily ever after. At the end, August gets an award basically for being ugly. And he's so happy about that. Well, I'm not. I don't think that's what he would have wanted. What he says he wanted throughout the whole book is to be just like everyone else. And with the exception of beauty queens (an entirely different problem), people don't get awards just because of the way they look. Many of the people in the book also seem to baby him, which is not doing him any favors. But the way the author writes it, it feels like that's what should be done. While I think this book was meant to say, "Be nice to everyone" what it ended up saying was, "give people who are different special treatment even though they just want to be normal." It was a bit frustrating.
Not as good as the first couple, but I still liked it a lot.

Continuing my Harry Potter re-read, I've come to Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, which is apparently the most popular book in the series. This has never really made sense to me. I think it's because people absolutely love Remus Lupin (he is pretty cool) and adore Sirius Black (which, I mean, he's not bad, but really?). But even re-reading this, with knowledge of the whole series in my head, I couldn't get past the feeling that, once we get to the beginning of the climactic events, the story feels very cobbled together and everything just goes on for way too long. This is, of course, the story of Harry's third year at school and it's also the only book of the series where there is not some sort of direct confrontation with Lord Voldemort or his minions! (Peter Pettigrew doesn't really DO anything in this book and so I am convinced he does not count.) After a confrontation that involves him unwillingly using magic, Harry runs away from the Dursleys and, through a roundabout series of events, ends up spending the rest of his summer at the Leaky Cauldron where he eventually finds out that an escaped convict from Azkaban Prison is probably out to kill him. This rather puts a damper on the start of the school year, but Harry promises to not go looking for Sirius Black, because why would he? Well, of course he's eventually goaded into doing stupid things, and also gets caught up in some rather random events involving time-travel and a couple of different varieties of shapeshifters. While many people love this book, I think it has more problems than the others in the series. Part of it is that Rowling essentially wrote herself into a corner--if your characters can time-travel to solve problems, what's keeping them from doing that to solve things for the rest of the series? She does try to set limits on it, but clearly recognized that this was something that was not sustainable long-term, as she tried to correct it in the fifth book by destroying the devices used to ravel through time. Except, apparently, one that pops up in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child but let's not get into that because it's kind of widely acknowledged to be a train wreck in comparison to the main series. My other two problems with this book is that it falls victim to a long info-dump of exposition right in the middle of some climactic events while the group is at the Shrieking Shack, with everyone going on and on about what's really going on when it kind of seems like they should be, I don't know, doing something about it. And then there's the thing about the climax itself just going on way too long. It basically starts with the group going off to the Shrieking Shack and lasts basically until the very end, which is a decent portion of the book. Keeping suspense going that long, especially with a big info-dumping monologue in the middle of it, is hard, and I don't think Rowling really managed it well. Honestly, to me, this book has always felt like the one that was most "off in the weeds" and didn't seem like Rowling had a really good idea of where she wanted to go with the series plot as a whole in it. Things like the Weasley twins not noticing that the Marauder's Map showed there was a guy named Peter Pettigrew hanging out in their brother's bed for several years come across as big plot holes that just weren't thought out, and the whole thing felt more cobbled together than the other volumes in the series. Professor Lupin is obviously a big draw here, but Sirius Black doesn't honestly have a big enough role to appeal to me and clearly is not qualified as a guardian for Harry so I don't know why people always tout him as such. (Honestly, Hagrid is a far better father figure for Harry than Sirius ever is. Sirius' appeal to Harry is entirely built up in Harry's own head rather than being based on anything concrete.) This is probably my least-favorite book in the series, after Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix, though we'll have to see if that changes after my OotP re-read. 3 stars out of 5.
Holiday comfort re-reading.

Grim but compelling - had a hard time putting this down. My only complaint is that I often sped through the futuristic chapters because the time-travel character and her story was so intense, leaving the place and characters of the future a bit dull in comparison.

This plot was like if someone combined a drunken Las Vegas wedding with a historical romance and tossed in 'The Hangover'. This was honestly super entertaining. The heroine and hero didn't even have a scene together for the first 30% of the book and it was basically all about them dealing with the aftermath of that crazy night. I wanted so desperately for Georgette and James run into each other again, but I just had so much fun just seeing them wandering around town and trying to put the pieces together. There were so many instances where I found myself laughing my ass off because of whatever new piece of information they'd stumbled upon. Once they finally met face to face, the hilarity continued. I liked how Georgette was relieved to finally find him and James was full of all these crazy notions that she was this con-woman that had stolen his money and tried multiple times to kill him . The fact that James happened upon the scene as Georgette and Elsie were breaking into his office  probably didn't help his opinion of her. As a reader, you knew that she hadn't done all those terrible things, but given the evidence up until that point, you couldn't blame him for coming to those conclusions. The dynamic between Georgette and James was cute and I really liked all the misunderstandings that continued to be heaped upon them. As much as I loved the beginning, I did feel like the plot got a bit weird in the latter half of the book. I was such a fan of the 'what the hell did we do last night?' storyline that I lost some interest once that came to a close. I thought the scenarios with Georgette's weird cousin and the murder attempts  to be a little silly and over-the-top. I just wasn't a fan. Also, it wasn't a huge deal, but the 'I love you's' between Georgette and James seemed kind of rushed to me. The book itself was so fast paced that it was easy to forget that it all took place over the course of a day. That said, I was completely won back over though at that final conversation they had in bed and I didn't care anymore about how sudden I'd previously thought their relationship was. It was pretty sweet of James to say that he'd uproot and move to London for her after he saved up enough money. He was hoping that life in Scotland with him would be enough for now until he could afford to give her a better life, the whole time not knowing that Georgette was rich . I'm not even sure why it was such a big deal to me, but hearing him say those things made me feel all warm and fuzzy inside.

Subtle misogyny aside, I can't help but picture every character flouncing around dramatically like a young William Shatner. This is turning unintentionally satirical rather quickly. lol Unfortunately, any humor that I found in this book melted away pretty quickly. This book lost that value when it introduced some rather rapey elements. Though I now that the author didn't intend it that way, there was a lot of manhandling that neither the leading lady nor I appreciated. I don't completely condemn it because I understand the author's intentions, but I felt pretty ostracized and I couldn't commit to the story. I ended up skimming the rest without much interest. I didn't particularly like the writing style, either. It was a little clunky, like the author was straining to hit her marks. Plus, there were all of these sudden changes in mood that were awkwardly expressed and didn't make any sense. The characters were unoriginal and yet inconsistent. The story line was also unoriginal and inconsistent. Everything that I found unexpected, was unexpected in a bad way. Oh, and I hated those characters. I don't care what plan you might be hatching, it is never okay to sell your daughter as a sex toy. Twice. And to top it all off, the story was kinda uncouth. I have nothing against vulgarity, and to be honest, this story wasn't even that heavy with it, but what it did display was just... I don't know, uncomfortable. Despite everything, I don't hate this book. I liked the occasional sarcastic jabs and sharp-tongued comments. Unlike some books that just make me mad, I enjoyed finding its faults. It had good intentions.
Good, but deeply anticlimactic in many ways.

Well, I thought this was wonderful. Hilarious. Honest. And I'm a little bit disgusted that other reviewers are fixating on random moments such as Grace, Lena's sister, pushing pebbles into her vagina when she was a toddler. I don't view this as "abuse" this is called growing up. Deal with it!!

This book made people remember what going to museums was all about. The land that was once filled with dinosaurs that roamed the earth. Must a scientist play "god" and resurrect such ancient creatures from long ago? That becomes John Hammond's dream, a choice that will quickly fall apart on him and the other people who check out the park before its opening day! The dinosaurs are being controlled with a strict diet and are engineered in such a way that they cannot mate. But even when that seems to be going so well, why is everything going out of hand...? And how are they breeding even though they all were made sure to be female? Sorry if I gave too many spoilers away with the "synopsis" but I felt all of that was what made this book so much fun. I absolutely loved this book so much when I had to read it for school and had to hand it in before the summer, I searched out in the stores for an old copy and read the rest of it during my own time. This book is that important. The story is fun (though, I admit, impossible when you really think about it) and I think anyone that wants a copy should get on board. Go on the ride with these guys as they take the helicopter to Jurassic Park. Just be careful along the way...

Rose spent over 14 years being terrorized by her abusive husband Norman. A single drop of blood on her bed prompts an unplanned-for run to freedom. Rose takes nothing with her from her married life except her purse and Norman's bank card. Rose quickly finds a community of women who have also been through abusive relationships. She finds a new job, she meets an interesting man and she stumbles across a painting that speaks to her. But Norman is not willing to let Rose get away from him. He's after her and he's willing to kill - horrifically - to find out where she is. If I were to focus on this solely as a novel about the violence done to women, Rose Madder would rate four or even five stars from me. Stephen King creates a real picture of an abusive relationship; the entitlement, need for power and misogyny that men experience and the hopelessness, shame and resignation that women go through. And the healing that can take place, the support systems that can exist for victims of abuse and the ability to recover a good life. Norman was a terrifying character. He was ruthless, driven, insane and (unfortunately) most women have met shadows of him in their real lives. But when the supernatural elements were brought into the story - the painting and the Christian/Greek mythology elements - I was less excited. Norman didn't need to be a mythical bull to be a monster; Rose didn't need to meet a decomposing goddess to find strength to fight him. I usually enjoy the fantastical elements of Stephen King's stories and find that they enhance the more mundane conflicts, but it just didn't work for me in this book.

2 stars Oh my god that was sooooooooooooo boringggggggggggggggggggggggggg. I can't even. How. How is this book so boring. It's Neil Gaiman. It should be magical and fantastical and absorbing and compelling. And I was bored out of my mind. Like, I get the idea of it, I guess. What happens to the gods over time, how do they move and manifest themselves in new areas on the earth, how are humans changing in their beliefs over time -- there are nice ideas there to explore. But it was long, slow, and completely emotionless. Shadow is such a snoozefest. He's not surprised by basically anything he comes across in the book, and there's some really disturbing, weird stuff. He just accepts it all and is like, "Yep, gods walk the earth. Yep, my wife came back to life as a zombie. Yep, I'll just follow you around, Wednesday, and do whatever you please without thinking. Yep, dude, I'm going to let you kill me at the end of all this, that's cool." Seriously, I wanted to smack him across the head. I switched to the audiobook after 50 pages because reading wasn't working for me, but listening was almost as painful - if not more so. I would get distracted or even doze off and not even care to rewind because it seemed like so much of the book was pointless and not going anywhere. Sigh. I am disappointed. But yeah, this was a massive waste of my time.

Last Kiss is the concluding novel in what has been such thrilling series to read. When we last left these characters, Amber was found to be alive. Emily and Reeve had finally reached a point in their relationship where they can actually call it one when Amber comes back to shake things up. Last Kiss mainly revolves around piecing together what happened to the Wicked Witch, Emily pushing Reeve away when she really wants him, and the Wicked Witch manipulating Emily. When reading First Touch, I kept Reeve at arms length. Was he dangerous? Was he the reason why two ex-girlfriends disappeared? So many questions. I commend Laurelin Paige for firmly putting this doubt in my mind because I felt what Emily felt. Reeve turns out to be the complete opposite. As you read, Laurelin peels back the layers of his character. "But I'm not going to manipulate you into choosing things that will make you unhappy. I'm not going to allow you to stop being a woman who can think and decide for herself. If that's what you get off on, then you're right, we need to be over." I love that he didn't push Emily into anything RE: her feelings for him. He wasn't going to convince her of anything. He wanted Emily to be able to make such decisions on her own and be able to think for herself. As for Emily, I've seen some complaints that she does a complete turn around from this strong minded female character to how she's portrayed in Last Kiss. In First Touch, besides flashbacks, we don't actually see Amber and Emily interacting in the present. While Emily is actively looking into her disappearance, Amber is not around to influence her in any way. Emily was allowed to be this character without Amber, who obviously has had a negative impact on Emily's psyche. Towards the end of Last Kiss, without giving away any spoilers, Emily breaks out of her hold. Letting her go? Emily finally realizes that Amber consciously manipulates Emily because she knows Emily needs that authoritative figure in her life. That was an awakening for Emily. There's much I want to say about Last Kiss but I don't want to spoil for anybody. This books does tie up loose ends and I think it ended quite nicely. It didn't match the pace of the first book but it is worth the read! I'll definitely be reading this book again to wrap my mind around certain things! Can Laurelin Paige just do us all a favor and release the second book earlier? Perhaps tomorrow? Also, I do not need a love triangle! FOR THE LOVE OF BOOKS PLEASE DO NOT INCLUDE A LOVE TRIANGLE

Why is it that dystopian YA featuring boys always seems to read like a Lord of the Flies rehash? I mean, come on, these dystopian worlds had William Golding, right? So why would they ever think it was a good idea to throw a whole bunch of boys together? Okay, okay, so these boys actually do quite well with their keep calm and carry on attitude about the Glade and the Maze, but still... This is a fairly solid piece of YA set up for a tidy little franchise, but let's face it: Thomas is no Katniss Everdeen - and don't even get me started on bloody Teresa with her big baby blues, perfect legs and feeble protests that, hey, she's really smart and tough too. Show, don't tell, Dashner. And it's okay for Thomas to be in love with a girl whose legs are not perfect and smooth. I know I sound bitter, but she really was the most poorly drawn character in the book. I hope she gets a chance at better development in the future instalments. Half a star came off for that and for the insanely predictable fate of one of the characters. Sigh. Nevertheless, The Maze Runner does a fairly good job of hooking you in and getting the heart pounding at times. Plus there's that little cliffhanger that leaves you saying, "What you mean, there's a Group B ?!"

Man, this book is sweet. Tightly coiled and perfectly executed. From today's standpoint, or at least from mine, this book has some interesting things to say about terrorism. : because that's what Pyle is, isn't it? He's a terrorist. I'm looking forward to reading more Greene. If this is the kind of thing he does, he's going to be one of my favorites.
Really great read for those of us who are into the dark and disturbing. I loved the movie when I saw it years ago, and I'm so glad I decided to read the book.

This was actually at least a 3.5 for me but I docked it a half star for taking the most well worn route in YA fiction: the love triangle . I docked it another half star, because this particular love triangle felt incredibly forced. Talk about an unsympathetic love interest . Other than that, I really enjoyed the setting and the idea of the dragons, and the role of the dragoneye. I zoned out on a lot of the energy world stuff (yeah, yeah, tidal forces of energy, streaming hua, points of power, yada yada), but I still enjoyed the mystery of the black folio and the history of Kinra and the imperial pearl. The characters were interesting (even that particularly unsympathetic one). As usual, the book would have been much shorter if there had been some better communicators in the cast of characters, but hey, I'd still recommend it to friends who read YA.
Simply amazing. A phenomenal series with such awesome characters and a thrilling plot.

When Maggie Stiefvater's writing and ideas are good, they're really, really good. She can come up with inventive imagery and sympathetic characters, and she's pulling in a lot of intriguing themes. The fact that she could make me give a shit about Ronan Lynch in this book speaks to her abilities--and to my weakness for interesting Catholic characters in fiction. But when things aren't so good? My God, does this book get tedious. This book is like one of those necklaces strung with only a few pearls, with an inch or two of chain between each one. There are great moments, and then you're stuck in a tepid, not-nearly-as-clever-as-it-thinks-it-is slog until you reach the next little gem. Near the end of the book, things get interesting and stay interesting, enough so that I'm halfway considering reading the next one, but getting to that "wow, things have picked up" moment is often boring and annoying. If I wasn't reading it for school, I wouldn't have finished it.

The third book in the series. This one is set up as a journey wedged between the plot-heavy books 2 and 4. I really like how this one deals with serious issues in a unique way - drug abuse, slavery, tyranny. When we see these issues in mg lit, they can be a bit predictable. Not in this book! Well done, Flanagan.

It's the third time I read this book I think, so you can guess I love it;) I don't even know what to write, it was awesome to read this again. 4.5 stars. Let me first say that this series is one of my all-time favorites. I think each and every book has received 5 stars from me, and I have loved each one equally. I was very sad to learn that this book is Lily and Lo's final book, from their points of view (but luckily we will still get to see them in the next two Calloway Sisters books). So, this final Lilo book was bittersweet. First of all, I didn't like it as much as the other Lilo books (or even as much as Rose and Daisy's books). This book didn't have the same build, arc and finale that the others shared. I feel like we were just sort of floating through their lives, watching this group live their lives, share experiences and learn to grow. There is nothing wrong with that, and the writing was still wonderful as ever - but it was enough for me to not award my normal 5 stars to this installment. Now, what did I love about this book? Soooo many things! Lily and Lo really grow up in this installment. I guess that's what having a child does for some people. The interactions between Lily, Lo and their sweet baby (no spoilers here) were so wonderful and precious. Not only the protection that Lo had for his child, but the clear love and affection that he showed towards the baby was so satisfying. Similarly, with Rose and Connor having a child of their own, they both changed with the birth of their child. Particularly Rose. Wow, her transformation tugged at the heart strings,, amazingly beautiful. And, I'm very curious to see how that plays out in the next Calloway Sisters book, where Rose and Connor are front and center. Also, AAA hinted at what may be to come with regards to Connor in FTF. I was also on the edge of my seat with regards to Ryke and Daisy's relationship. Without giving anything away, I was almost as concerned as Lily about Raisy. But, it appears that, at least for now, #RaisyLives! All in all, I thank the Ritchie sisters for this story (and the stories to come). This book was certainly Lilo's time to shine. Loved it!

ok this is more of a 2.5- 2.75 It would have been a much better book, if the author would havetaken the time to explain some things, like more about Claudia's world and the "era" and more about Incarceron and what exactly was going on in there. But the fact that she left it to where you had to guess kinda threw me off from the book. But I kept at it and after a while I understood it more, but the appeal of the book was lost. It got way better near the end of course but still the ending wasnt' able to raise my opinion of this book. It kinda reminded me of a bizarrer version of "The Princess Bride" the way it kept bouncing back between worlds, and in some ways it was confusing. I don't know if I will read Sapphique, it's up for debate, but I kinda want to know what happens because they did leave it as a cliffhanger.

This play affected me far more from what i've expected. At first, when I just saw it from our textbook and read some of its synopsis, it seemed impossible that something like this could move me. Maybe because my choice of reading varies from novels, short stories, and up to poetries. Never have I ever been amused by reading deep classic plays, like this one. Despite these impressions, I have to admit that I did read some articles about William Shakespeare and his works because he really is someone to look up to. Besides, as I was storming through the parts of this play, I struggled to interpret the lines and found it hard to fathom their deeper meanings. I had to read them again and again just to fully comprehend them. It did not fail to make me laugh and giggle as I read through the humorous parts. Plus, those with Puck's and Bottom's lines on it make me laugh the most. And as I stumble upon the young Athenian lovers' stories, I felt realized how troublesome being disobedient could be. I even became suddenly conscious of unrequited love cases and how heartbroken they could even possibly drive people. Anyway, I still believe that happy endings exist and that they just take time to be turned into real life. I was even amused by how playful King Oberon and how whimsy Puck could be. They weren't supposed to butt in and play with the lovers' lives at all, they were just so naughty that even their existence in the forest became one of their toys during play time. At some parts, I did take in several lessons like "wait for your turn. ", like what Helena experienced when Puck was tasked to put the magic juice on Demetrius' eyes and then he fell in love with Helana upon seeing her first afterwards. In addition to that, I have also learned that we should not take for granted those people who stay by our sides and never leave. Just like Helena, she got what she deserved at the end because she worked for it, she never ever stopped, too. It just made me sad that Demetrius just fell for her only because of the magic juice. I can't imagine how bad would that feel if I were Helena. It is possible that this play is really meant for teenagers like us to read because we are on the verge of falling in love and getting our hopes and hearts crushed later on. (c) My Literary Analysis' - Implication Part.

Most definitely my favorite book in the series so far. It was so good! I really wanted to break Seth's pretty face a few times while reading. He was such a stupid, naive asshat! But Aiden was especially amazing in this one, so that totally makes up for dealing with Seth's mega douchery. And that ending!!!!!!! I loved it

To be honest with you, this book dragged in it's pace and ended in a way that made it feel like the end of a TV season - leaving you questioning what happens next. That sort of ending has always frustrated me in books. With nothing truly resolved, you have to read the next book to see how things go. It's very episodic in that way. I feel it would make for a good children's show, perhaps for Netflix or something. Don't get me wrong - it's still a fun read. I recommend it if you're reading a chapter or two a night to your middle schooler. It's a good book, but it lacks depth for me. The characters are solid, albeit a bit samey, and the world is creative, but it really does drag. The supporting characters come in two distinct flavors: old and knowledgeable and weird or young and fighting the power after meeting Jason. It's actually a little irritating. Rachel and Jason often feel like very much the same character most of the time, just with talents in different areas. She's a runner, he's a pitcher. She rides horses, he knows animals. The differences are minuscule and their personalities are almost the same, which makes for some pretty dull interactions until you throw in supporting characters. My favorite character so far is Ferrin, simply because he's more in the grey area when it comes to personalities. He works for the bad guy but he's also loyal to those who he considers friends. Especially at the end, he really sticks his neck out for Jason. He also happens to be the only character who seems to have experienced any discrimination in his life out of any of the characters, making him infinitely more interesting. (It isn't ever directly stated, but Jason and Rachel are both more than likely white.) I will probably read the next book just to see how things go from there, but it won't be super high on my priority list.
