Going into reading this book, I had high expectations. I had heard great things about it, but my core group of "reader friends" hadn't hit it hard yet, so I'm not certain why I had my expectations set so high. But I was not disappointed. I don't know how to express my feelings about this book without spoiler alerts everywhere. I will start with the writing style. This writing style really speaks to me. I was instantly pulled into the worlds of Eleanor and Park. I use the word "worlds" because with the perspective changes, you can tell they see the world in a very different way. I didn't even feel like I had to keep track of who knew what; it was simple enough to follow along without filing specific details away. I love that there are chapters, but within a chapter the PoV switches often. In particular, when Eleanor and Park are both simultaneously reflecting on a moment and the PoV switches back and forth after short sentences. I also really enjoy how love is portrayed throughout this book. Annnd... There are many different types of love and variations of love portrayed throughout the book. There is so much love. Eleanor and Park are obvious. But there is also: * Eleanor and her siblings * Eleanor and her mother * Mother and Richie * Richie and Eleanor (<>) * Park and John * Park and Steve * Park and Tina * Eleanor and Tina * Park and his Mom * Park and his Dad * Park's Parents * Park's Grandparents And each of these relationships has it's own form of love-- both subtle and not. The most compelling relationships to me are Eleanor and Park, Eleanor and her mother, and Park's parents. Eleanor and Park experience the extreme emotion of first love. They are lucky that their first love it together; often with high schoolers it's not. I can relate to the extreme emotional spectrum they are experiencing and how they flip between forever and not. Eleanor and her mother are also fascinating. They are incredibly similar. Both of them live in fear for the rest of their family. Each of them are trying to keep the other happy and is willing to make sacrifices to help the other achieve that. But, they are terrible at communication, so they don't see themselves in the other. It's both inspiring and heartbreaking. Park's parents are incredible. They really love each other. I love seeing their interactions. The constant making out and visible signs of affection are something I hope to keep in the future. I am also most impressed with how they talk to each other. They allow each other the space to be upset, but they also won't back down on what the right thing to do is. It's amazing. All in all, this book is incredible. I would recommend this novel to anyone who has ever been in love, is looking for some light reading with a deep message, or who is into YA.

More like 3.5 stars, I think. This is the first book in Bella Andre's series about the Sullivan family. It is the story of Chase Sullivan, a fashion photographer, and Chloe, who is on the run from her ex-husband. When Chase finds her crashed at the side of the road, he persuades her to stay in the guest house in his brother's winery (where he's doing a shoot), and things go from there. So, this is more romance than erotica, but there's a lot of sex so I'm going to shelve it as both. There is a weird blurry line between the two genres, I think. I was initially attracted to this series because of the whole family thing. In each book, one of the siblings will find love, and their Happily Ever Afters (I'm assuming). I like this formula. I like when characters I've met in one book are then the focus of the next book, and so on and so forth. And so, I stumbled across this on Goodreads, skimmed a couple of reviews, and decided to give it a try. At first, I wasn't too enamoured with this book. The scene with Chloe in the bath was just too... creepy for me. It wasn't okay. I didn't understand how someone who was so scared of trusting a man could possibly stay in that house after that. Is it just me? After that, the book got better. I mean, there are some problems with it. The fact it takes place over like, four days, and there's this whole insta-love thing going on, for one thing. I mean, that kind of comes with the genre but hey, these two moved way too fast for my liking. Especially with Chloe's trust issues. I don't know, it just didn't quite hold together for me that way. And he proposed at the end, I mean, really? However, like I said, the book did get better. I loved Chase, as a character (aside from the bath scene). He was so sweet and gentlemanly and always tried to do his best to make Chloe feel safe and comfortable. It was like he didn't have a bad bone in his body. I really liked how much his family meant to him as well - you could really tell that he was worried about Marcus (his brother, the winery owner), and that he would do anything to help and protect said family. Chloe was a good character too, though I felt she healed emotionally too fast. I really liked the fact that her hobby was quilting, and she had some less than conventional desires. It was nice to see that sort of thing crop up in a romance novel, I think. The plot was a little lacklustre, but I still found myself enjoying it immensely. It was just... I don't know, simple, and easy to read, and filled me with little warm fuzzies. But it did lack tension and drama, excepting the final confrontation at the end . I just feel that it didn't really live up to its full potential. The writing was nice to read. It wasn't beautiful, lyrical prose, but it was written in a way that allowed me to get swept up in the story. And really, this is the kind of book you read when you just want to lose yourself in romance, and happily every afters, and warm fuzzies. So the writing style fit it perfectly. And I loved that Chase's word for Chloe was 'lovely'. I feel like that word doesn't get nearly enough love. I don't know. The tone I imagine it being said is just undeniably sexy. The epilogue at the end, from Marcus's point of view, was nice touch. A bit of a teaser for the next book. I liked that, and it serves its purpose well. Offering a tantilising glimpse of the next book so we, as readers, want to go out and buy it. And, you know what? Despite its shortcomings, I still enjoyed this book, and I'm definitely going to pick up the next one. I want to know what is going on with Marcus, and how on earth he's going to find his happily ever after. I'm just a sucker for happy, feel good books, I guess. Especially when they're as sweet as this one. (As long as you ignore that bath scene. Ack.)

Kara was summoned against her will into the Demon world and now has to fight for her life, all while trying to figure out who to trust. I hated this book. Hated. I really enjoyed the other books in the series so my disappointment with this one was fairly epic. The aspect that appealed to me most about the first several books in the series was the supernatural cop angle - that gets completely thrown out in this one. Moreover I just wanted to slap Kara so many times. She's a mostly passive, wishy-washy, whiny victim who allows herself to be manipulated and abused. She'll basically screw anything with legs and has the self-preservation instincts of a suicidal lemming. I forced myself to finish the book, praying it would get better. It didn't. The plot was painfully slow and tiresome. The big reveals (of which there were few) were tepid at best and not enough to keep my interest. I've always had a problem with Kara being interested in Ryan and yet perfectly willing to screw a demon at the same time. I'm all for female empowerment but I'd be just as thoroughly disgusted with a male character who did this. If you are in love with someone, or falling in love with someone, you don't have a F***-buddy(a term freely used in the series) on the side. It's like a huge moral black-hole. Moreover- initially Mzatal is set up as a persecutor, then he flips heavily into a father-figure. That relationship is definitely painted that way, but wait no - because in the end Kara has to screw Mzatal as well and it's all good because hey Ryan would understand if he was in his demon lord guise. Arghhhhhh! I hate this so much. Female empowerment is not synonymous with becoming a slut. That, more than all the other crap in this book, pissed me off the most. Complete sub-genre shift aside (goodbye Urban Fantasy, hello High Fantasy) the main characters fell apart and the plot went to hell. I am done with this series and won't read any future books.

one of the oddest repeating themes in the current trend of YA dystopian/post-apocalyptic lit is for the heroine to be an ordinary teenager, wandering through this brave new world of awful with only a vague sense of "huh." horrors pass before her eyes with barely a shrugged shoulder, because "that's the way it's always been," making her inevitable participation in rebellion later in the book that much more inexplicable. so mad bonus points to Griffin for writing a tale where most all of the characters have been actually impacted by the world being destroyed. Araby Worth, an inventor's daughter, has lived with a population-slaughtering plague since earliest childhood. she's lost both family and way of life, and she's rather shell-shocked, drugging herself into oblivion and wishing for something to change. the apocalypse here is real and visceral and immediate, not some distant "before times" memory, with touches of actual horror instead of gratuitous gore. there are occasional brilliant tiny "what if?" moments ("we'd been wearing masks for so long that i read a smile by looking at someone's eyes") that add wonderful depth to this slim story. if all that weren't enough, Griffin should be teaching a master class in how to do the de rigueur angsty love triangle properly: both male characters are interesting, well-developed, and differ by a lot more than just the color of their hair. so why only 3 stars? the end, my dears, is a trainwreck. after clipping along as a solid 4-star read throughout, the last 10% or so just thoroughly derails. we're subjected to several chapters of aimless running for our lives, in which Araby's innate passivity (the world acts on her far more often than she charts her own course) finally crosses over into annoying. both boys feel the need to display their "rightness" so that we're left with back-to-back moments of true love with the other guy. and worst of all, the book ends so abruptly that if i'd been reading it as an e-book, i would have assumed the file was incomplete. the story would have been nicely self-contained, yet i can only assume it's being stretched out into a sequel/series.

I am a little surprised at the reception this ending has received from many. Perhaps its because I have not been a teenager for a long time or perhaps its that I have learned that things don't always happen the way you want them to happen. Or perhaps I just understand that in life some wounds need time to heal and it makes sense that the author would write the ending that she did because in truth that is the reality of things. For all of you who have read the conclusion of the Legend series, you know what I mean. Yes, the ending was indeed sad, but I loved that Marie Lu ended it in a hopeful way. That there are always new beginnings. It is the truth people are able to withstand things and live on. Take it this way would you want to be with the person that participated in the destruction of your family. Sure maybe they were mislead which is what happened to June, but it does not take into account that they were a participant. You can love them but every time you would look at them you would wonder, what if this person was not here, would my family still be alive? Would or could it have made a difference? For that I understand and love the ending because it ended with a possibility of a fresh start. In reference to the writing in this book, it was clear and had good pacing of the events. There was never a dull moment. The story as a whole was really great. The explanation of what was happening, politically and such, was understandable, clear and not so far fetched as I have seen in other stories (I am looking at you Divergent series.) The characters were likable and nothing changed in my opinion of them from beginning to end. You can say the characters of June and Day developed a lot from the first book to the last book but their personalities were consistent. I started liking Tess again, Eden was adorable and Anden was also a solid character. I am very satisfied with this ending. I even have to say that it might be even as good as the Hunger Games, that is if we are comparing dystopian stories. For me it was much better than the Divergent series, much better written. I felt closure and that is something I really need in the story.

No more cliff hangers. Can't a book wrap it for me.

What intrigued me: I recently finished book 2 of the World-walker series, and I was excited to find she had another completed series. I hate waiting! What I liked: This was a fun series, that was a very quick read. Morpheus was by far my favorite character and I would love to read a whole book about him. I liked the spin on myths as well. What I didn't like: Well, with a series called Star-crossed I don't know what I was expecting, but it took way too long for them to figure out they weren't cousins. If Lucas is so clever the age differences should have jumped out at him fairly quickly. There was too much angst, and we were in on the secret far too early. Favorite quote: "You and I are way to fabulous to be ordinary."

I feel a little bad about the two-star rating, because I don't want to give the wrong impression. This wasn't a bad book. This was, in fact, a fairly good book put into the hands of someone who just probably wasn't ever going to enjoy it. So, I didn't enjoy it. But that's okay. That doesn't always mean it's not a good book. I'll admit that some things are good for other people while still just not being my taste. Like spicey foods, or maybe skydiving. Things I Liked - Pretty good portrayal of depression. (The loss-of-identity, feeling kind of adrift, not knowing if the people you love are getting it part. Not the Oh-No-Willem-Left-Me part). - That scene about falling-in-love vs. being-in-love. Cool sentiment. Good scene. - Ms. Foley is awesome. Things I Didn't Like - Willem. At all. I actually really hated him. I didn't find him charming when he showed up, he didn't grow on me, I didn't understand why Allyson was so attached to the idea of him. - Allyson, most of the time, although she had her moments. Part of my problem was that a lot of her motivation was Willem-based, and I didn't like him. - I didn't think the day Allyson and Willem spent together was romantic. I thought it was full of weird bouts of jealousy and bad decisions (like getting lost in a foreign country). - The whole "Lulu" thing. I felt like I would've been more on-board had she chosen to lie about her name, but instead Willem just never asked for it. Which leads to more confusion about how she thought it would be more than a one-night stand, when he wasn't interested in knowing her name. - The whole tracking-Willem-down plot. I'm not opposed to plots about tracking down a lost almost-love you've only ever spent a day with - Serendipity is one of my all-time favorite movies. But I think the difference is that that was two-sided and always honest about being kind of absurd - and this was neither of those things. - On that note: the one-sided-ness of the whole thing. I've got nothing against unrequited-love plots when the object of offection is at least likable, and they have some kind of relationship with the person who is in love with them. Willem is about 90% an asshole, and he and Allyson had an international one-night stand. Obsessing over him isn't love - it's obsession. - Allyson's lack of ability to get along with any of the women around her. Hating one woman? Fine. Hating every single other woman in the book? Um, not okay. Even her supposed best-friend gets mostly hate. I don't get it. Anyway, I wasn't a fan. But this was a well-written book, and I still love Gayle Forman's If I Stay and Where She Went, so I'm bound to pick up the next book of hers that doesn't include Allyson and Willem.

Actual rating: 3.5 stars Every book we read is a journey. Either short or long, difficult or easy, it might challenge our views of the world or confirm them. Any way the journey takes us we leave each book changed in some way, even if we reject its ideas. The Alchemist is one of those books that has the potential to speak to people powerfully, because in it we can find our own meaning. There is a simple, untainted truth to Cohelos book. It has the rhythm and repetition of ancient parables, mixed with modern ideas about individualism and the quest for self expression and fulfillment. I was fascinated to read in the intro to my special 25th anniversary edition that Choelo rereads the novel often, for its truth, and its honest expression of himself. Never have I heard of an author rereading their own work, except for public readings or audiobook recordings. To me there has always been a separation between reader and writer, where the former can only hope to guess at the true intent in each word or sentence, and reads their own experience between the lines on the page. But perhaps writers and readers are one and the same, even when it comes to their own work. But I come to reflect on the novel itself I was disappointed by the second half. Perhaps I am not in the right place for this book right now, I didn't need yet another voice to tell me to follow my heart and seek fulfillment in all that I do, because I am already telling myself that story. And though I enjoyed the 'ancient parable' feel, it became a bit tiresome in the second half. I can see why this is a word-of-mouth book. It is one that can so easily be recommended to those in our lives who need an extra boost of confidence to find their own way. Though for me, today, this is a 3.5 star book, one day that may be different when I am a different, future, self.

Maybe a 3.5. Much better than McNeil's other book, Relic. Ultimately not much to write home about, but a fun little thriller that ended up not being too predictable, I did actually find myself surprised at the killer's reveal, although if I were more familiar with And Then There Were None it seems like I wouldn't have been. The book did try overly hard to drop hints and make you suspect that a particular character was the murderer, to the point where it was obvious they weren't, which wasn't great. The teens did often find themselves more caught up in petty relationship drama than they were in the murders happening around them, but that was easy to get past.

It was good. An acceptable end to the Lirael plot. I didn't feel any wonder like in Sabriel's introduction to the Old Kingdom or Lirael's exploration of the Clayr's glacier and library. This was a march to the finish line. This book wrapped things up. (Of course, Nix wrote another unnecessary Lirael book ten years later. We shall see about that.) If I have to nitpick, I do have one complaint. For a book about keeping the dead down, a lot of the main characters refuse to die. We get fake-out deaths for Touchstone, Sabriel, and Nick, we are told Lirael has to die to kill the big bad, but she doesn't. None of them die. The Dog dies, but the Dog is an immortal rule breaker magic being so I didn't feel like I lost a character. I'm hard pressed to name a real main character who actually died, apart from doomed bad guy Hedge. (who was a very one-dimensional doomed bad guy, hardly a character at all) The most emotion I felt in the entire book was when Lirael recognized the dead soldier from the glacier. She remembered he had asked for a kiss. And she couldn't even remember his name at first. That was a great moment. Every other death in the book was nameless cannon fodder, which is weird. Is the author afraid to kill characters in a book that deals so much with death? This book is called Abhorsen, after the folk who keep the dead down. This book doesn't do it's job properly. That is my one main complaint. also, I liked Sam and Nick a lot more in this book. Once he gave up the mantle of Abhorsen-in-waiting, Sam stopped acting like a whiny coward and became rather helpful. It was easier to like Nick once he realized he was being controlled by evil magic.

Narrator Sophie Mercer 16 will summer in England with her father, Head of the Prodigium (magical beings), at his family mansion, Thorne Abbey, with 5/12 Council survivors after their London Headquarters was "burned .. to the ground two months ago" p163. A demon himself, he wants to teach her how to control her powers, not undergo the potentially fatal Removal process. She fears the inner demon going wild, like great-grandmother Alice, who killed fellow Hecate Hall student Elodie, and other murders within her family. The best part is the fun. Demon teen Nick interrupts Sophie before she can answer a question about him by splashing into a fountain, drenching the girls, then magically clothing them in silly and revealing outfits, the Easter Bunny, then a bikini, then showgirl. Sophie retaliates with a snowsuit, then "a particularly poofy purple prom dress" p 176, then scuba suit. She had first turned the fountain water pink, also without usual drastic overkill effects. Why? Her best friend lesbian vampire Jenna feels superfluous, added for gratuitous smooch p172 when her gal pal Vix visits. Why does the costuming duel send Jenna right into "Remember" "the night before the All Hallow's Eve ball .. you turned all the mashed potatoes into ice cream sundaes .. beets into maraschino cherries"? Sophie goes gushy "hours before the kitchen raid .. on cellar duty with Archer .. hands overlapping" p178. Her heart belongs to crush Archer Cross, a fellow student disclosed to be an enemy agent of The Eye, but kindly healer Cal (Alexander Callahan) 19 is her official fiance. Quibbles Too much current YA has two suitors for the heroine, a tired cliche. The series is called Hex Hall, but the nickname does not appear till later in the book, and keeps switching (cell phones "weren't allowed at Hex Hall" p37). Why the title? "A puckered scar ran across my palm" p 12 of Sophie's right hand from demonglass, shards blow out of a bomb later, but otherwise no relevance. How could headquarters destruction be kept secret? Sophie/ author spends so much time in the past, I never feel present. All back story, confusing. Even while she runs, fights, or kisses, she's steeped in memories. What is otherwise a fun fast read stumbles, slows, interrupts, stops dead (no pun). Suddenly, in a fight with ghouls, we learn she has necromancy abilities. Ghosts are supposed to be tied to a place, and unable to communicate. But Elodie appears in her bedroom, and warns her of trouble. Why do the villains have to reveal this binding? Councillor Lara Casnoff is the sister of Hall head Mrs Casnoff, never given any first name. Casnoffs keep their maiden names, an indication of their family's significance. "Their father used to be the head" p268 of the Council. Teens Daisy and Nick have no memory of their lives before recent forced transformation to demons. Finding who creates demons, where and when, exposes the villains. Someone tore out the demon creation ritual page from a guarded grimoire. Archer shows Sophie the site of demon creation, the Hall island. Students have vanished from the school, and heavy spells laid around to hide the disappearances. Graymalkin Island is the domain of Mrs Casnoff. The Casnoff family have been the villains for generations. Sophie's excuse is unneeded, and does not wash "if I could just turn around and try to hide, I would know who was behind all this. But I couldn't risk it. The best plan right now was to get back to Thorne and tell Dad what was going on." p277. The final cliff-hanger has the good guys powerless and trapped. Should not the Council Head have allies to call on? How can he be taken down so quickly and easily? Too much coincidence, unexplained, woo-woo. Obviously Mom and Dad love each other. Why should her Dad's confession be a big deal? Sophie is powerless, her Dad permanently so (the Removal) and trapped with Archer. Jenna's bloodstone necklace lies crushed. Only then do we learn that the bloodstone keeps vampires from burning alive during the day. Why does Lara take blame ""It was time to clean house, in more ways than one" p350, not demons, the Eye, or accident? Councillor Kristopher barely gets a name before "a silver dagger .. squarely in the chest .. his eyes staring at nothing" p351. Similarly, demon Daisy, Nick's sweetie, was a throwaway, example, runs amok, attacks Sophie. Even then the text harks backward, to Alice's ""violet-red" eyes p299. Nick kills "nearly twenty people .. in just a few minutes" p347. Daisy and Nick both can reappear in a sequel. All too conveniently, Elodie directs Sophie through a hidden passageway outside to Cal. How did he get Archer's protective necklace? Why leave it at the Iteneris? How did he know he would find Sophie? Cal rushes toward blazing Thorne to rescue prisoners. He sends her via Iteneris (like itinerary = route, the only sensible of too many impossible spelling choices) teleport doorway to her mother, hiding with Aislinn Brannick, leader of (weak?) white witches. His kiss "Goodbye" sounds final. Her "psychic impulse .. Hope" p359 only includes Archer. I dislike premonitions and omens, sloppy devices, lazy fiction.

We are, in the end, a sum of our parts, and when the body fails, all the virtues we hold dear go with it. A penetrating memoir about how fragile our lives are. The author did a very good job at painting a complete picture of what happened and how it affected her. We get to see the build up to her sickness, her uncertainty of how to deal with all the changes in her personality. Through the eyes/memories of her loved ones we get to experience her lowest points, as she can't remember any of this. But most revealing for me she explains to us how her ordeal has changed her emotionally, and why. The Story: When twenty-four-year-old Susannah Cahalan woke up alone in a hospital room, strapped to her bed and unable to move or speak, she had no memory of how she'd gotten there. Days earlier, she had been on the threshold of a new, adult life: at the beginning of her first serious relationship and a promising career at a major New York newspaper. Now she was labeled violent, psychotic, a flight risk. What happened?

This book divided into seasons is chock-full of my favorite kinds of poems--super short imagistic ones. They are mostly just a few lines, and they are like small bits of beautiful candy. You pop one in and can't help but move on to the next. All feature keen observation; many evoke a certain mood; and a few lead me on to thoughts of bigger implications/themes. Each uses accessible language, but each also stands alone as a tiny vacation from my everyday thoughts. There are so many gorgeous ones, both contemporary and not. Here's one of my favorites, a cinquain by Adelaide Crapsey (who invented the form): November Night Listen... With faint dry sound, Like steps of passing ghosts, The leaves, frost-crisp'd, break from the trees And fall. Sigh. An excellent anthology from Paul Janeczko, beautifully illustrated by Melissa Sweet. I'll be buying my own copy of this one.

I'm disappointed because I love Lauren Oliver, stories about sisters, and mysteries, but I found this to be a frustrating, confusing, and slow read. I don't even know how to review it, because everything up to the last 80 or so pages and everything after it felt like two different books. I had trouble connecting with the characters, and I think it's because Nick and Dara fell too easily into the good-girl with a party-girl sister stereotype. I wanted them to be more complex than that. I also never got a sense of who Parker was, making it hard to care about the love triangle; he felt like a plot-point more than a character. As for the ending...We Were Liars did it better. I was frustrated by the twist because of all the holes it leaves in the story. Also, everything with Andre came out of nowhere, and seemed to leave just as quickly? That storyline could've been so much more interesting.

I started to read this book because I heard that Ki Hong Lee was going to play Minho. SDKJHGSKJDGH >u< I heard many people praise this series, but after reading it I realized that... You either really loved it, or hated it. PROS - Interesting plot with the maze and the world - Certain relationships established well : Chuck x Thomas // Alby x Newt - Good action sequences CONS - Took too long to FINALLY get some questions answered - Characters were not as developed as I liked - Grievers were super creepy and scary - Not as creative as I would have liked (e.g. code words just led to a computer?! No significance really...)

Hyperion is The Canterbury Tales crossed with Aliens. It works. Yet it is so much more than that. Simmons is extremely well read, and the references in this book draw heavily from English literaure, in particular the Romanitics, and especially John Keats. The story concerns seven pilgrims who are making thier pilgramage in the midst of what might be the beginnings of a interseller war. Along the way, the pilgrims each tell the story of why they are making this journey. Like Chaucer's tales, the stories range in subject matter. There is romance, old fashioned sci-fi adventure, humor. Each one is different in style and tone. There is even horror of the old fashioned type; who doesn't get a thrill of terror when the words vagina dentata appear. (There is apparently an anti-rape device that works in the same way). The most affecting story is that of Sol Weintraub. Heartbreaking. The characters are well and compassionately drawn. I actually enjoyed Lamia (note the Keats reference) the best. She must be the love child of the Wife of Bath and Miss Piggy.

One of the best heroes ever. I can't imagine any female who wouldn't fall for Vane. What I enjoyed: * Vane. He is amazing. Tall, built, rich, powerful, loyal and puts Bride first. He is actually almost too perfect. * Bride. Other than being insecure over her weight, she is confident and protective of those she loves. I love it when she kicks Bryani's a$$ * Fury. I really want to read his story. * It was great seeing more of the Sanctuary and the bear clan. * Good to see more of Kyrian and Amanda What could have been better: * Wouldn't have minded more of Nick and Simi (I love her). * I still don't like Valerius. Re-read and still absolutely love this book.

I could barely make it through this book, and found myself skimming large amounts of text just to get to the end of the thing. I almost gave up on it numerous times, and still don't know why I finished it. No new twist on the vampire legend here (even for a book from the late 80's). The writing was weak, with metaphors that were groan-inducing. The end literally had the hand of god defeating the vampires.

One of the most interesting things to me in this series is the question of sainthood and where the line is drawn between someone holy and someone with extraordinary magical skills. Seeing Alina become mythologized in her own lifetime was fascinating. I have to give credit to Bardugo- when she makes things hopeless, they feel Truly Hopeless. Especially when  Nikolai is cursed- you realize he'd been the glue that held everything together and losing him looks like losing the entire game. And it was nice to spend more time with my favorite secondary characters Genya, David, and Tamar. Tamar's queer relationship not being treated like a taboo and having a happy ending? Neither lesbian died? Amazing. Thank you. David's speech to Genya made me sob. Stripping away Genya's beauty and letting us see that she has a terrific mind for inventions and chemicals? Be still my heart. GenyaxDavid over AlinaxMal any day. (I apologize for stooping to shipping in my review, but I care so much.) I will grudgingly let Mal back into my good graces, but damn Alina, how could you say no to Nikolai's proposal even after you'd lost your powers? No matter how much you protest, he cares about you. The ending was good. Not perfect, but satisfying.

When I first read Twilight in early 2008, it wasn't as popular as it is now. I mean, when I went to go check out the book at the library there was a wait list, and I had to wait about two months to get my hands on it..but still-there wasn't much talk about it. There wasn't as much hate around this series either. I really enjoyed this book, and the charming little town of Forks, Washington. I've always been a fan of cold, overcast, rainy weather so I didn't find the setting too depressing-in fact, it sounded very beautiful since there was lush vegetation everywhere. I live in Southern California, so it's hard to find acres of untouched land. I really liked Bella as a narrator-she's funny, witty, sarcastic, and brave. I don't know if I could be as...accepting if the cute guy in my Bio class was a vampire. That would take-some getting used to. Edward was pretty hot, as hot as fictional character can get I mean. He is just as sarcastic-if not more than Bella-and I appreciate that since most people find sarcasm annoying and not at all funny. He's dark, and humorous. I know a lot of people didn't like Stephenie's "recreation" of a vampire, but I thought it was pretty different. The fact that they don't sleep, and the special powers that Alice and Edward have were interesting to read about. I'm glad that she created this new type of vampire, since writing is all about evolving and putting one own's opinions to existing literature. Honestly, don't judge this book based on people's hatred of it. Give it a try, and decide for yourself. I have friends who never liked to read, and flew through this series. Twilight was the reason why they started to pick up a book, and if anything, that is what is really important-to encourage reading.

A young reporter is enjoying an upper-class British house party when abruptly, someone is found dead! I can't say I enjoyed this. There's an entire subplot concerning a Bolshevic satanic cult (?!) that goes nowhere, and isn't even an effective red herring. This is the first Inspector Alleyn book, and it's clear that Marsh isn't sure how to write him yet. His personality is all over the place: one moment he's burbling Bright Young Things slang, the next he's cold and remote, the next he's romantically morose. It doesn't read like a complex character so much as one without any fixed characterization. The mystery itself is very frustrating, because there's no way it should have worked. The murderer springs out of the bath, pulls on gloves, slides down a bannister face-first, yoinks a dagger conveniently nearby, and stabs his victim who just so happens to be standing with his back directly in front of the bannister? No one on earth would plan a murder that way! And there's no way that Alleyn figured out that the murderer did it that way, when his only evidence was that the murderer wore a glove! How does that prove that someone slid down the bannister face-first, let alone which person did it? Ridiculous! I'll try one more Marsh book, by virtue of her reputation, and then I think I'll call it quits.

As far as books assigned for class goes, this book is my favorite. I love how many lives get intersected from a simple series of events. IT really shows how one same ripple can change the world, or, at least, a good portion of it. If anyone is interested in how a few people can affect a nation, this is the book for you. If anyone wants to read a book about the trials and abuse of slavery, this is the book for you. In short, this novel appeals to a large audience and just could be the book for everyone to read.

How to review this larger-than-life story? At times I felt like I was reading an epic story comparable to Lord of the rings, other times it was more classic Midsummer Night's Dream. This series is about walking the line between old school fantasy and current day science fiction. And don't get me wrong I don't like sci-fi too much. Whenever it got too technical with machines in the Iron Realm, you would have Puck saying something old school like: "Great. The false king's fortress is a giant rabbit hole." So yeah, I enjoyed The Iron fey series more then I enjoyed any series recently. And like I said during my review of The Iron King: best fae series. I haven't read tons, but Julie Kagawa beats the crap out of Melissa Marr and Aprilynne Pike. This volume was a bit slower to start then the previous two. I confess I was a bit annoyed at the useless quest for a Token at first. But my patience was rewarded at the end for Paul's teaching to Meghan about his music. The key to the whole salvation of the realm and all. That's what I have learned to love about Julie Kagawa's writing. Nothing is written for nothing, which is something that is taught in writing classes but hey, that not every author chooses to apply. Oh and way before I forget: gorgeous covers for the three books. Oh Prince Ash. *sigh* What a complex character and oh yeah dreamy. All I need to say is: "My name is Ashallyn'darkmyr Tallyn, third son of the Unseelie Court...Let it be known--from this day forth, I vow to protect Meghan Chase, daughter of the Summer King, with my sword, my honor, and my life. Her desires are mine. Her wishes are mine. Should even the world stand against her, my blade will be at her side. And should it fail to protect her, let my own existence be forfeit. This I swear, on my honor, my True Name, and my life. From this day on..." His voice went even softer, but I still heard it as though he whispered it into my ear. "I am yours." Drool I also quite enjoyed Grimalkin's character. "Please attempt to use the brain I know is hidden somewhere in that head. [...] The light bulb finally comes on." Don't you want to hug him and pet him at the same time? There are two things however that still bugs me. I am not complaining since this is so going on my favorite shelf but here are two questions for the universe: (there might be spoilers here so beware) 1- If the power of Machina went to Meghan because she killed him and he chose to give her his power, how did Machina get Ferrum's power in the first place? 2- How did Meghan's power get unbound again? Oh that's right we don't know. Only Mab or Oberon could do it. They certainly didn't do it while they were exiling Meg and Ash so yeah I am confused.

On the whole, I think Romancing the Duke is a lot of fun, and I'm glad I had a chance to read it. It's cute and often funny, with a lot of likeable characters--including a rather charming female friendship. Dare could have made our heroine's companion, Abigail Pelham, the mean bitch out to get the hero for herself. Instead, she's a friend to Izzy, and they support each other over the course of the story. I loved that a lot. It only gets three stars, however, because the historical details seemed a little wavery at times. I couldn't tell what year this was supposed to take place--the best I can tell is "sometime soonish after the Napoleonic Wars"--and that was frustrating. It's definitely categorized as a Regency romance on Amazon, and since the time period appears to be "at some point after 1815," that's appropriate. That said, such an early setting means that a few things don't quite fit for me. The Goodnight Tales, the Tennyson-like stories of romance and derring-do, seemed a bit anachronistic to me. (It only occurs to me now that they weren't meant to be seen as children's literature, but they absolutely sounded like it to me. They'd be absolutely anachronistic there, since they fall far closer to the "delight" end of the spectrum than to the "didactic" end--but it's hardly Dare's fault that I'm used to everything being kidlit, lol.) The stories' devotees sound a little like Holmesians, who are still decades into the future at this point in time. (LARPers and Rennies, with whom they share many more qualities, are even further away from the setting.) Fictional Moranglia as the backdrop for romantic adventures reminds me strongly of Ruritania, which first appears in 1896's The Prisoner of Zenda. Meanwhile, the way "little Izzy Goodnight" is portrayed in the stories seems like it also belongs pretty firmly in the realm of the Victorian era, as is the expectation that the real Izzy Goodnight must be perpetually childlike. The concept of the idyllic childhood is something still in the process of creation at this point in time--it's ultimately a Victorian idea itself--and since this story presumably predates "Angel of the House" rhetoric, I found it a little jarring that Izzy was under pressure to play up this preadolescent persona. (Plus, the whole "constrained by my father's writing!" concept even if they aren't actually her father's stories  draws to mind no one so clearly as the children of A. A. Milne and Kenneth Grahame. Those children postdate Izzy Goodnight as well--their fathers' stories were published during the first half of the twentieth century.) There's also a corset scene that's very reminiscent of tight-lacing, which is a subject best left to the Victorian era; the metal eyelet that made tight-lacing possible wasn't invented until the late 1820s. While it's implied that they're tightening up Izzy's corset so she can fit into a slightly-too-small dress, someone unfamiliar with the history of undergarments might read Izzy sucked in her breath as Miss Pelham gave her corset laces a firm tug. and assume that it's tight-lacing that's being described. Anyway, as you can see, the nebulous time period bugged me, probably way more than I should have let it, lol. I also found Ransom, our hero, a little too possessive at times, though I thought he was all right on the whole. That said, I loved Dare's passionate defense of stories, whether high- or low-brow, and romance. I thought it was well-put and absolutely worth quoting: "You don't have to admire my father's stories," she said. "But don't disparage the readers, or the notion of romance. Cressida and Ulric are just characters. Moranglia is entirely made up. But love does exist. It's all around us." Wonderful. Anyway, all this to say that I'd pick up more of Tessa Dare's books, but I wasn't as wowed by this one as I thought I'd be when I finished the first chapter.

I'm afraid I was prejudiced against The Fifth Season from the start because of several stylistic ticks that put me off. Firstly, it's all in the present tense. Secondly, many chapters are in the 2nd person, which is never justified (no, not even now that I've finished the trilogy and know why). Other niggles include neologistic curses such as: 'What the rust?' or 'You're rusting useless'. The book also makes liberal use of profanity, such as 'Rusting fuck!' or 'You fucking ruster!' The people of The Stillness are a potty-mouthed lot. Fake-cursing always sounds lame and forced to me, even when it does turn out to be relevant to the world building. It surprised me at first, because usually the only reason to make up your own swears is if you're avoiding the real ones to maintain a PC rating. This book does not attempt to maintain a PC rating. It is grimdark through and through. It opens with a grieving mother standing over the corpse of her infant son, recently beaten to death by his father, and it just goes downhill from there. Every other child in the book seems to be the victim of some awful sexual or physical abuse. Part of the reason why I find grimdark fantasy so tedious is that the horrors are either gratuitous, implausible or - worst of all - not as bad as they would be if the story actually followed the remorseless logic of bad incentives instead of just being edgy. To give some examples, our heroes discover that children with the magical power of orogeny (the power to quell natural disasters) are being kept prisoner and sedated for life, so that while they are unconscious their magical powers work automatically, protecting the surrounding area from the constant quakes and volcanoes that plague the region. So far, so interesting, so grimdark. Should one innocent child be sacrificed so that whole towns can live in safety? But then it transpires that the unconscious children are also being pimped out to local dignitaries. When one child awakens in the middle of a rape, he reacts instinctively nearly causing an earth shattering cataclysm to defend himself, only some quick thinking from our heroes prevents the disaster. I do not find this even remotely plausible. If magical children have the ability - and the instinct - to destroy the earth in their own self-defence then nobody would ever be allowed to rape them for small change. It's not about being evil, it's about having some basic sense of self-preservation. It's as stupid and dangerous as allowing someone to jack-off against the nuclear launch button. In a later incident, a young orogene child is being brought into a magical academy where she will be trained in the use of her magic. Her new guardian, in order to test her self-control, breaks her hand. The scene is wonderfully well-written. The tension mounts palpably as the guardian increases the pressure, and the poor innocent child trusts and loves him and doesn't understand why or what he's doing until her bones snap. It's horrifying, but it's not horrifying enough. The whole world over humans put youngsters (most often boys) through terrible and dangerous initiation rites to earn a place in a tribe. Broken bones are the least of it and invariably children are eager to participate and show themselves worthy. If the guardians of The Stillness were even half as evil as most ordinary humans they would be indoctrinating those kids until the kids, eager to prove their courage and self-control, were smashing their own hands to pieces and proud to do it! Well, it's not the fault of this book that grimdark annoys me. And The Fifth Season has many excellent qualities: new and inventive world-building, some very well written scenes and set-pieces. It's lucky that the mystery of the world-building was drawing me in, because I would have abandoned the book if it was down to the characters. None of the characters have any sense of humour, and the main character in particular, Damaya/Syenite/Essun, is a terrible person: sullen, spiteful and a mass-murderer. When she briefly takes up piracy her unthinking use of orogeny means that all of the witnesses must be killed to protect her secret. Literally hours after causing all those unnecessary deaths by revealing her power, she does it again, bringing the guardians down on them and causing the death of everyone at Meov as well as her first child. How stupid can one woman be? Finally, in Tirimo, she kills out of spite. She deliberately kills Rask, the man risking himself to save her life, and countless others. People she knew intimately: friends and colleagues; and all out of rage that her husband has killed her child. Essun makes a revolting attempt to justify this to herself. After all, her husband was one of these people. His hatred of orogenes came from their society. That hatred drove him to kill her son, therefore they are all responsible for her child's death. This is ridiculous and hypocritical. Nobody is responsible for killing her child except the man who did it. Her husband. The man she chose to marry and breed with, without telling him her secret although she knew how he would've felt if he'd known he was husband and father to orogenes. She did far more to create the situation than any other member of the town did. That's not the end of her hypocrisy though. A moment's thought would show that if people are all held personally responsible (paying with their lives!) for the prejudices of their society then she is exactly as responsible as the rest of them, being a member of that society. She also did nothing to change or challenge the hate. If she'd really believed that people deserved to die for bringing about the death of her child then she should've started by killing herself. So, an unrepentant hypocritical mass-murderer. But also a cowardly and petty one. When Essun and Alabaster discover the poor dead, raped child they don't report it. Even though there's an obvious and compelling obligation to report the rape, both to protect the children from rape and to protect the world from natural disaster, they chose not to and it isn't even clearly explained why except that they are slaves, nothing more than useful tools, and so it's not even worth thinking about fighting back and they will probably be in a lot of unspecified trouble if they do. Except a chapter later when they arrive at their destination they engage in a two day battle of wills with the local dignitary. When she isn't sufficiently respectful they actually refuse to start work until they get a proper greeting from the Mayor and a cup of tea. Where's the fear of unspecified punishment now? In the contrast of these two incidents, as well as others, I can't help but feel that the rape, torture, slavery and abuse are all set-dressing, while the real visceral oppression is here in the social snubs, slights and slurs. In the world of The Fifth Season rape is quotidien but being called rogga is unforgivable.

Have you ever read something that just changed you? That challenged your perception of the world and everything it contained? And most fundamentally, of what you thought you knew about yourself? This story, Soldiers, didn't quite do that for me. No, I loved every spectacular word contained in its pages, but I didn't feel the world tilt off its axis. Oh no. That honour goes to Mercenary Part I and by extension, the rest of the series. The verdict at the moment being: Will. NOT. Read. Let me start from the very beginning. Dan and Vadim were two enemy soldiers that met under the worst possible circumstances and against all possible odds, found respect, and love in each others arms. Spanning nine harrowing years, these two managed to find their will to survive and their way through the darkest moments of war by following the beacon of light that was one another. Their story was. An. Epic. That's all I am willing to say on that matter. And to be honest, in my mind and heart and soul, their story ended here. With Soldiers. With one last night together on the streets of Kabul. Now, I am reading Mercenary Part I. And quasi-spoiler alert, I'm barely plowing along while looking for a light at the end of the tunnel in the remaining books. And will post a separate review rant on there as to the details. But quick warning here for all those innocents who wish to read the whole tale, it gets dark. And not in the good way you've come to expect from Soldiers. I mean their relationship takes a dark turn that I can't come to terms with even now. Here's the heart of the problem. Dan being in a polygamy with several people. And... it's explicit. Not like in Soldiers where it's all very technical and mentioned in passing and therefore, unimportant. Oh no. It's all in your face unadulterated... well... it feels like adultery after everything they'd gone through in Soldiers. Regardless of the justifications, it never stopped feeling utterly wrong to me.

This book started off with some promise. It was by no means a tough read but it was fast paced and enjoyable. It was something light after finishing the mind-bending "The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle" by Haruki Murakami and that made it refreshing. I enjoyed the initial plot twist and continued through the book wanting to know how it ended... but then I hit that ending and everything was ruined. The best way to describe it was that I was cheated of a decent ending by an author who loved her characters too much. She spent so much time writing her characters into an impossible situation, one where the only way out was to kill off one of them, and then found she couldn't bear to choose which of them would die and so hit the problem with the metaphorical bus. Problem "solved", no loss of character needed. Cop out ending achieved. I've rated this two stars because up until the ending, I did enjoy the book, however, I'm the kind of person that truly believes that a book is only as good as it's weakest section, and in this case, it was a terribly written ending that undermined the whole book.

Translation by: Norman Denny (Penguin) Number of pages: 1232 Finished reading in: 1 month and 1 week. The book Les Miserables written by a French author Victor Hugo is about not giving up on being a good person even when it seems the hardest. Jean Valjean, the protagonist, has the habit of silent contemplation. The inner turmoil of emotions and thoughts make him a character of mind and heart. The decisions he make are against his own happiness, but he does justice to the bishop who gave him the two silver candlesticks to improve his life when the rest of society rejected him. The light from the candles in the candlesticks light his path throughout, metaphorically, making him lead a life of clear conscience. The mentions of Cain and Abel, the two biblical brothers remind us to part with anger and revenge. It is a fine line and a tough decision between being the evil one or the one who would be redeemed. The author compares Jean Valjean to Sisyphus in the last book. His every conscious act, from revealing his identity in court to saving Marius and letting him marry Cosette can be compared to that of Camus' quintessential absurd hero. He does a good deed, only to do it again, without ever any expectation of his own happiness. Each moments of decision-making in Valjean's life is similar to that moment, that pause, that return in Sisyphus' life when he watches the stone rush down which he'll have to push up again towards the summit. As Camus says, "We must imagine Sisyphus happy," Valjean would never have been happy having lived any other way, immoral and with a guilty conscience. His only desire in life, to be with Cosette, is fulfilled, though too late. He receives redemption through death. Les Miserables open the eyes of happy, rich and lucky men to the miseries and needs of their fellowmen. The title, The Miserable Ones, describe the people whose minds and hearts open to the vast reality around them. Becoming aware of a world outside the one that he has lived in throughout his life, Javert becomes one such wretched character during the end of the book. As to Thenardier, he is the character whom Hugo calls "incurable", and whom we should all try not to be. Gavroche and his two little brothers are the description of what happens when young ones are left to nature. Gavroche shows the true nature of a street urchin, fearless and free. The character of Eponine is what brings sadness to read- a young girl left to bad parenting; an innocence gone waste; a love unrequited. The book is written on a larger than life, epic scale. Every kind of emotion and feeling is dealt with, and comments from the tiniest to the major issues in society and governance and law are made. When the story starts to get interesting, the writer dwells in length on one or the other political issue of the time, leaving the story hanging mid-way. Also, the condescending nature of the preacher in Hugo acts like an irritant in an otherwise morally-valuable tale. The author seems to care more about the message of the story, than about the fictional tale delivering the message on its own. Despite some very intriguing parts in the novel, few of the subplots were poorly constructed. For example, contriving the character of a nun who wanted to be buried inside the convent, only to provide a solution for Valjean's problem of getting out of there unseen. A good book, but the expectations on reading reviews calling it "the best book ever," fell short a little.

This was a pretty decent book. I just did not like the pacing and that is why it took me so long to read. There was no real climax for me and no real point where I couldn't put it down. Evie had to go to a new school because her mom died, her dad is in the service, and her grandma (who has taken care of her since her mom died) got sicker. Evie got into the school because her dad was in the service and she also received a scholarship. On her first day at the school, Evie finds out that the only reason that she got into the school was because a spot because available. The spot became available because a girl died. The girl's cousin was angry and made Evie's life unbearable. Evie makes a few friends and comes across a boy. The only problem is the boy isn't really alive.. Why can she see him if he isn't alive? This school has a major problem.. the high mistress has a secret job. What is the job? Why does the cover of this book have a necklace? You will have to find that out by reading this book.

So, so good! I'm so happy I decided to read this after my indifference to the first book, there is such an improvement! Unlike Eon, this is action packed with rarely a slow moment. Everything about Eona was better; the characters, the relationships, the plot and the world building. It took me days to read the first book, I read this in half a day. I honestly couldn't put it down (even though I should be doing my uni work! ), I had to know how everything was going to work out. I related a lot more to Eona this time, she was much more fully formed and actually had a personality, rather than just worrying constantly about others. It was also very easy to sympathise with her when the majority of the other characters were treating her so horribly (Ryko was the worst) for completely unfair reasons. I also enjoyed the love triangle, it was understandable why Eona would be torn between both Lord Ido and Emperor Kygo. Even though Ido was terrible in Eon, he totally redeemed himself to me and I actually found myself rooting for him. Whilst Kygo was nice, I always prefer the sarcastic underdog! There were lots of exciting plot twists, no one trusts each other which made it fun trying to work out who was genuine and who wasn't. The story felt very high stakes compared to the first book and everything paid off in the end,  although I obviously wish Ido had a happier ending! If like me you were underwhelmed by Eon, please give Eona a chance! From the first chapter I was gripped and by the last I was so pleased I stuck with it. This is one of the best written fantasy stories I have read in a while.
addictive. After reading the "Six of Crows" duology, and now this...Bardugo is quickly becoming my favorite YA fantasy novelist!

Even though I've really enjoyed Kimberly Derting's other novels, The Taking ended up being a middle of the road read for me. Even though the premise sounded like something that would be perfect for me, there were little things about the characters and their reactions that really put a damper on things. That said, the ending was strong enough that I am very curious about where the story will go and will probably read the next one for that reason. While I'd love to say it took a while, The Taking went sideways on me almost immediately. Kyra gets into a fight with her father and insists that he let her out of the car in the middle of a highway. And he complies. What? Who is the authority figure in this relationship? If I was throwing a tantrum, 18 or not, my parents would never have let me out on the side of a highway. I don't know anyone else whose parents would have either. It just started the novel out on the complete wrong foot for me. Then, almost immediately after this fight when Kyra wakes up 5 years later, she ends up falling for her now ex-boyfriend's little brother. Most of you probably know how I feel about sibling triangles. HATE. Hate, hate, hate. And then when you consider that from Kyra's perspective, she was dating her ex-boyfriend just yesterday that makes it so much worse. She was convinced she was going to marry him, and while high school relationships hardly ever last, even though she is upset that he's gone she moves on pretty quickly with HIS BROTHER. Ew. Aside from the issues I had relating to the character's actions, I did really like the plot. The mystery behind Kyra's disappearance was interesting, and I wan't expecting it to work out the way it did. Can't say that much more about it without ruining the plot, but it definitely saved the book for me. Even though I was really frustrated with the characters throughout the entire novel, the plot did a pretty good job of redeeming the novel. I'll be able to look past my frustrations and pick up the next book because I'm genuinely curious about what will happen next.

This book was NOT as good as the first one. There are only two parts that I truly enjoyed, one happy, and one sad. Let's start with the sad one. When Mia tells Adam she hates him. It broke me to pieces. Especially after hearing him suffer for so long. I wanted to shout at her, to scream. NOW YOU TELL HIM? NOW! SERIOUSLY!! You are such a @#$&% Mia. I felt so bad for Adam. For waiting. For wasting all this time, for just hoping that one day, he might find her, and she might want him again. The happy one. When they decided to stay together. To be exact when the drummer keeps saying "Mia, Mia? Mia MIA Mia?!" I don't hate Adam. He reminds me too much of myself. The hurt in his eyes...Wait I can't actually see his eyes. I wish I could. It would be nice to meet him. I would like to hug him for a while. Omg. I can't believe I'm crying right now! I would recommend it still though. It's not a bad book, it's just not for me, not right now, anyways.

3.75-4 stars The first novel I've read of Sarah Alderson was Hunting Lila and I enjoyed it so much. I was really amazed on how she wrote the story and she instantly became one of my favorite authors then. So when I read a featured excerpt of Fated by the end of Hunting Lila I was instantly hooked up. I had it on my to-read list right away and had become one of my most anticipated reads for 2012. And finally I've read it! Although I did notice some flaws in this book I still find this really gorgeous. With all its awesome characters, exciting twists, and unique paranormal plot I really did have a lot of fun reading this! This was written in third person, narrating both Evie and Lucas point of views. I really loved reading a book in multiple POV. Having both perspective made it easier to connect with them and understand the situation. I adore Evie. She could be really whinny and naive at times and sometimes it could be really annoying but with all she'd been through I think it was pretty understandable. She still was a kick ass heroine. Although she had not known the truth about her family until she was attacked by the Unhumans and nearly died, she was able to handle and accept it boldly. She's strong, determined and wasn't afraid to say things and her thoughts. Well, Lucas, from the first time you heard his thoughts you would instantly know he was different. He was nothing like the Unhuman he was supposed to be. The way he thinks and acts - when he first time he saw the picture of Evie, when he realized what he feels and want to do, when he became so determined on protecting Evie, when he was so willing to sacrifice himself - you would really fall hard for him (though I must say I fell harder for Alex in Hunting Lila). And aside from that, of course he was a total mind candy. He was absolutely hot and drool worthy. I loved how Lucas and Evie's relationship developed. It wasn't at all an insta-love but there was an insta-attraction that both characters tried to fight and rationalize the first time they felt it and until they can't keep it anymore. We weren't rewarded with a kiss scene right away but when it came... oh boy was it steaming hot! The paranormal plot here was also interesting. The Unhumans (demons) were Lucas belongs were creatures from other realms - scorpio demons, mixen, thirsters, psych, shapeshifters and shadow warriors - which I really enjoyed learning about. The Hunters, were Evie belongs were the one who hunt and kill the Unhumans preventing them to spread out and take over the human realm. There wasn't really a good and bad side here. I kinda figured that out during the last parts. Both sides have their own wrong and incorrect ways. So were left not to side with anyone but only to Evie who made a choice to stop it - not siding with anyone and not as a Hunter. One thing I so noticed Anderson was so good about was writing an action scene. She did it in Hunting Lila that I seriously felt like I was watching and action-packed movie. The whole time I was tensed and excited. And she did it here again. The way she wrote it would make you imagine it so vividly and you'll absolutely be engrossed. Alright, you might wonder why I gave it a rating like 3.75 leaning to 4 when all I've said about it were positive. I was actually a little torn. As I have said earlier I think there were little flaws I noticed in this book. Well, maybe it was just me but there were parts that I think were pretty obvious that Evie should have figured it out already or at least doubted it. But she didn't and she was like really clueless. And also the when Lucas told Jocelyn how he felt for Evie and that he would betray the brotherhood for her, Jocelyn believed him right away, which I think was pretty fast since she was a hunter. Yet when Evie thought Lucas betrayed her Jocelyn didn't defend him. I guess they had a deal since Lucas believed that Evie should hold on to anger than on numbness and with that she'll continue to fight. I was a little confused though before realizing that. but the entirety of the book was really good that I can over see those little flaws and still love the book. Overall, this was a really fun and thrilling read! Anderson did a really good job again. This was a lot different from Hunting Lila but Anderson's captivating writing stayed the same and still as good as in Hunting Lila. Looking forward for the next book and more books from this great author. This review is also posted at Book Overdose

This book destroyed me. But sometimes that's a good thing. I won't say that I thought it was perfect, or that I didn't have any issues with the book as a whole, but I loved reading it. I think if you've come this far, you're already pretty hooked on Gemma's story and just want to know what's going to happen. That, or you're hooked on Kartik, like I was. Damn writers and their ability to make you fall in love with fictional characters! I'm not going to rehash what happens with them (because spoilers) but I will say that there is no shortage of Kartik in this installment. The friendships in this last book, in my opinion, still leave something to be desired. On the one hand, you hope that by now Ann and Felicity would start behaving better. On the other hand, maybe it's more realistic that they don't. So while I'm not a huge fan of these characters at times, I can appreciate that their flaws and shortcomings and poor decision-making abilities make them almost painfully believable. In the end, the book is not perfect. But if you love reading it, that's what really matters. And I loved reading. Even though I'm still f**king crying over the ending.

** spoiler alert ** I loved this book! It was my first read by Miranda Kenneally (and I'm just now getting around to reviewing it), and it did not disappoint! Jordan Woods is a female football player (aside: I actually thought she was a guy when I was reading the first chapter, though I knew she was a girl because of the synopsis on the back of the book) and has always been "one of the guys". (Aside: Not all authors can make this tomboy vantage point work, but Miranda Kenneally absolutely sells it!) She longs for her father's support and approval of her football love, though she has plenty of friends who don't care that she's a girl and are glad to have her on the team as starting quarterback. Even though she doesn't have guys throwing themselves at her feet, she doesn't mind, quoting football as her only love. Enter Ty Green, a boy from Texas with a family tragedy staring him in the face as he's slapped with a new school, new maybe-friends, and a new team. Playing the same position as Jordan leaves him at a bit of a disadvantage since she's been the starting QB since forever, but he gets his chance. Despite being sort-of rivals on the field, off the field Jordan and Ty are more than friendly. There's just something (and someone) standing in their way... Warning you now: THIS IS A SPOILER. IF YOU WANT TO KEEP GUESSING THROUGH THE BOOK WHO SHE WILL END UP WITH, DO NOT READ! Sam Henry has played on a team with Jordan since their house league days, when Jordan was a cheerleader up until she showed off her football-throwing prowess. He's her best friend, the guy she shares everything with, and she's never thought - or considered - more. But Sam has. Romantic intrigue ensues... The Main Players: Jordan Woods (Starting QB) Jordan is the epitome of female awesomeness. She has an amazing group of guy friends who are ready to defend her at the drop of a hat, is comfortable in her role on the team, and is an amazing team captain - fair, considerate, and firm. (We'll contrast with Ty later.) She's a great friend (if a little dense:  COME ON JORDAN, YOU COULDN'T TELL THAT SAM BROKE UP WITH HER TO BE WITH YOU?!?!?!?! ). I love how she's not girly, but it's not like she wouldn't like to have a boyfriend - if only she could find one that's taller than her, is okay with her playing football, and will stand by her side ( SAM HENRY!!! ). She's funny, sweet, and sure of her place. You gotta love confidence. Getting a look inside her head, though, we see that she has more aspirations (that she finds throughout the book) besides football - such as creative writing (her free verse poems are hilarious). This is such a heartfelt look at stereotypical jocks and girls and writing to break the mold. Ty Green (Other Starting QB - Or Would He Be Second String?) Ty is... Well, I don't really know what's amazing about Ty. I suppose we could start with looks. Yes, looks are good. Jordan describes him as looking like Chace Crawford's twin (that's good, right? I mean, just look at him in "What to Expect When You're Expecting". Yes, the movie.). I liked him at the beginning. He seemed really sweet and nice, kind of cliche, but how isn't that adorable? Later on in the book, though... Personality: He thinks he's amazing. Which, you know, isn't bad when you're sort-of-joking-sort-of-not. It's funny then. But, at least in my opinion, he thinks a little too much of himself, which I understand (considering he led his team to state in Texas, that says a lot). Most of his personality seemed small and a little broken just because of what happened to his parents, but it wasn't. It was cocky and arrogant once he got more comfortable in his role at the school and as backup QB. He's a very protective boyfriend, which, don't get me wrong, can be great and really good in a romance, but not in this one. He's a little too protective - for one thing, he seems more affected by Jordan's knee injury than she is. There's Sam, all strong and silent, holding her hand and waiting for her to be okay, giving space when she needs and smothering her when she needs it, and then there's Ty (my highly exaggerated impression): "OMG Jordan, please be okay 'cause I can't lose another person or I might go mental, OMG I bought you roses, so don't die. OMG Jordan you almost DIED, I can't lose you, OMG you need to stop playing football and leave it to the boys who don't hurt..." and on and on. Versus: Sam - "I'm here, Jordan. Squeeze as hard as you need, 'cause I'll never leave you or keep you from what you love." Now, you tell me which one is better. Yeah, I thought so too. Ty really is a great guy - for another girl who isn't Jordan. Sam Henry (Starting Wide Receiver) Sigh... Why can't all guys be like Sam? I believe that I will borrow a page from the movie "Major League": Wild Thing! You make my heart sing! Wild Thing! Now, Sam Henry isn't tall, dark and handsome with a broody and dangerous edge like Charlie Sheen. (Honestly, he's better.) To start off (because you always see the physical stuff first): he has the abs, and the shoulders, and the winning smile. You're literally drooling before you even get a full glimpse at him. To spoil the angel image (just a little), he has a player streak, mainly after breaking up with Jordan's best girl friend. ( Reason he is the way he is is because he is IN LOVE WITH JORDAN! What would YOU do if your best friend was dating another guy and only thought of you as a friend, even though everyone knew you loved her (it's painfully obvious)? I think I'd want to get away from her or at least wash my brain of them. But I digress. ) I <3 Sam very much, in case you couldn't tell. He's so funny and sensitive and wonderful, I just... Ugh. Where have all the good men gone...? Just watching him and Jordan throughout the book, you're kind of like... "Come on guys! You're just like an old married couple, get together already!" And at the end... Well, I won't ruin it, although I kind of already have. If you want to know explicitly, click here:  JORDAN AND SAM END UP TOGETHER!!! . PLOT: I found the entire plot was well paced and easy to read. Miranda Kenneally is excellent at writing hot, steamy moments in order to balance to balance out the parts where not a lot happens or where the OTP's aren't together. I really loved how action-packed this book was, though it seemed to level off a lot once Jordan found out that Alabama wasn't all that she wanted it to be, and the day count after Sam and her fight. That part was sad, because they totally wanted to be together but couldn't. Oh dear. I just spoiled it for you. That's okay, I'll make the entire review a spoiler since you can't really review a book without giving SOMETHING away. Anyway... I would definitely recommend this book for ANYONE who likes/loves/doesn't know anything about football, who loves strong yet sensitive tomboy heroines, and puddle-inducing heroes (because you WILL melt into a puddle after meeting Sam Henry). Read It!! "Long Live the BOOKS!"

Another great new seires from Jordan L. Hawk! As with msot of her series the two lead charcaters start off at opposite ends. Even more so than her other series they actually are completely at odds with each other. While they are both gay and can admit attraction, it is not something they act on as they rather positively hate each other. Henry believes that spirits should be dealt with through science and has the machines to do it, but no interest in them. He needs to win the competition to get the recognition for his work as well as the money to help him with production. Victor is a medium who lost his mentor and hasn't been working since then. He needs to win the competition to ensure that mediums can keep their livelihood instead of being replaced by machines, and he needs the money to save his and his partner's business. This puts the two firmly on opposite sides of each other and any initial flirting is used as a weapon rather than in any interest. Learning the history of the characters through this was a true delight. Not only are Henry and Victor important, but their respective partners has their own stories and weight within the story. Learning the motivations of everyone involved builds up such an amazing story that is also even more inclusive than Hawk's other stories, dealing with issues of sexuality, race, and gender. Mix in the misunderstandings of economic standing along with difficult pasts and the world created for this series is fantastic and wonderfully believable. It was endearing how Henry was so hopeful and naive, but also willing to acknowledge his faults. Victor was gentle and caring, as well as surprisingly open when the world had thrown everything at him to make him cynical. I loved watching them interact and find each other, and figuring out the haunting and the how to survive it was awesome. I can't wait to see what adventures will greet these characters moving forward!
