There are few things in the world of reading that I love more than an author who has done her homework. I am a history major with a religious focus, and let me tell you, Gretchen McNeil has done her homework. That satiates the nerd in me. The very real characters, unexpected murder mystery, exceptional world building, and amazing storytelling makes my inner-bibliophile a very happy camper. I was slow reading this at first because nothing scares the crap out of me more than demons. I was raised Southern Baptist, so we don't have exorcisms. Basically, if we get possessed, we're up the creek without a paddle. That being said, I was only reading it during my short daylight hours after work. Last night, it started getting so good that I read it until nearly 11 pm! Alone! When I woke up this morning, I read it straight through my beloved morning nap. In short (or long, whatever), this book is completely amazing. It is a great supernatural thriller for the teen crowd that has left me very anxious for more. And a little something extra that I wrote after reviewing that I hope to add to each review from now on. Drum roll please! ...Possess Haiku! Gorgeous Bridget Liu Banishes demons with ease Her great strengths unknown

Even before meeting each other, their lives have been tied up already ... Not in a good way, though. This book has so much going on. From Delaney's past, Adrian's past and from what they both have at the moment. I'm not complaining, 'cause those back stories made this book even better. Delaney Cross, I love how strong she is and persistent to make everything that surrounds her okay. Her being nice is over flowing. Her character is in a really hard situation. Then it turns into a harder situation as the story progresses. Delaney's in between of the truth and her feelings. She feels like telling the truth  (the truth - which you'll only know, when read this book) but then keeps on stalling 'cause she knows that it will create a strain in her relationship with Adrian. So, more than half of the book we see her struggle that. But once she drops that bomb on Adrian and tells him the truth ... Another bomb drops immediately. And seriously, it rendered me speechless. Complete with my mouth wide open  (good thing there weren't any flies around -_-) . But gahhh she's so strong! I love her character for that, she manages to stand up from that downfall and even face another problem head-on. Adrian Westfall  (Dagnabit! This guy has a very swoon worthy name! *swoons*)  Let's start with the light and fun parts about his character: I died with your freakin' awesome ramblings - poems that is. Those bits and pieces of his writings just makes you feel close to his character, it's so wonderful to read what Adrian's character is feeling at the particular moment. It maybe sort of haunting topics but how he translates it into words are just so beautiful. (Great job, Nyrae!) But who would've thought that, that guy from Charade is going through a very tough time. I never would've guess. Well, yeah. He maybe that intellectual and sort of all-knowing guy from that book but I didn't expect that he's suffering and going through that kind of pain. To know more about him and his life, better read this! FYI. This book made me cried a lot. Seriouly. I cried during that moment when Laney already revealed everything to Adrian and Adrian has this comeback of a revelation, as well. I cried when Laney went to her mom and talk to her. I cried when Maddox talked to Adrian. I cried when Adrian was having those thoughts/dreams about Ash. I cried when Laney and Adrian got to talk and patch up things between them. And I cried at the scene in the cemetery. See? I cried freakin' a lot. Those scenes were just so sooooooo good. Painful. A certain tear jerker. You can just feel your heart clenching while reading those scenes. I just wanna hug both of these characters  (hugs my pillow instead). This book tells us, readers, that being with someone is not that easy and always filled with rainbows and unicorns. Some people have to put up a tough fight or go through hell for them to be together. But in the end, everything that they do to push through it - is worth it. Okay. No more of that painful moments. I also love the cameo parts of Colt in this book. Knocking some sense into Adrian's mind and trying to console him about losing someone important in his life. Now, they found this same experience, like a platform in which they can  bond together  or be able to go through together without hiding any emotion. Feels like they're going to be closer than ever. Random thought: Is there going to be a story that will focus on Maddox? (Please, say yes)  I think, it'll be cool to know more about him and his take on their family problems. On how he's going to be able to deal with it and find his own happiness. Just imagining what could be his story, makes me want to sigh and sigh and sigh. Anyways, before wishing and day dreaming of Maddy's story - pick this book up and read it! It's a must read! Ha, also read Charade, the first book of the Games series by Nyrae Dawn!

Captivating, Intriguing and Suspenseful Glass House (The Morganville Vampires 1), by Rachel Caine is a very intriguing story that pulls you in from the very beginning. I was captivated by all the twists and turns the story took - it keeps you guessing all the way to the end! Glass House is about Claire, a very mature and smart 16-year old who is in her freshman year at college in a small town called Morganville, TX. She's picked on by the popular (and gorgeous) girls in her dorm, so much that she's seriously scared for her life. Scared enough to call about a Roommate Wanted Ad in the paper. "Gone with the Wind meets The Munsters." Upon meeting Michael, Shane, and Eve she forms an instant easy-going friendship with the three and fall into a regular routine. Until a certain vampire targets her and all hell breaks loose for the inhabitants of the Glass House. "Then you're stupid. Can't save an idiot." "I could have looked all heroic and caught you or something." "I know. It's not your fault. It might have been a dumb idea, but at least it was a sweet one." "I need shock and awe, man - come running. You know why." "Do they sell stakes at Home Depot here?" I'm torn between liking this book and loving it. I rounded up to 4-stars to give it the benefit of the doubt. I have to remind myself it is a true YA (PG-13) novel. I enjoyed the storyline, the idea was fascinating. I felt the characters could have been more developed. Honestly, I am upset because I think the dynamic between Claire and Michael could have been more interesting and further developed into a natural romantic relationship. While I liked all the characters, I felt Eve and Shane could have had a better connection, leaving Claire and Shane to have a big/little sister relationship. I am still torn because I really wanted Claire and Michael to end up together. I felt these two characters could have had a vibrant relationship full of depth and emotions. Several occasions presented itself to allow her (and him) to opened up and create a "closer" insight into each character, especially after she shared his secret. Their personalities seemed (to me) to be a better match for each other than how it ended up. All in all I enjoy the book; I am intrigued and (at some point) I will continue the series, though it won't be my next read. The ending was satisfying, it did end in a (wanna-be) cliff hanger, however it isn't intriguing enough to make me pick up the next book and start reading it immediately.

Rating: Did I read a different book than everyone else? I quite enjoyed Carve the Mark which lets me question my sanity or my capability as a critical, thoughtful reader. Sooooo many people seemed to hate this book. But why? Sure this was a sci-fi book and it's hard to write a sci-fi book without being compared to the classics, but this story didn't focus much on the sci-fi aspects, which was fine with me. The setting could have been a medieval fantasy world - it wouldn't really change anything. Cyra was the most 'real', 3 dimensional character due to her morally grey zone. I enjoyed reading from Akos persepctive very much. Ryzek was so interesting as well. I hate when we get a villain who's super evil, but hasn't much motivation other than 'I want to rule, I want all the power'. No child is born evil. But his motivation was quite sound. The cast of side characters was vast, so vast and with so many different names that I made a dramatis personae for myself. I wished Veronica Roth would have provided us with that, other than just the glossary (which I never used tbh...). But they all had a role to play in the story, they weren't all good or evil, which I appreciated. The world building was fine with me, we got some back story, but I see why it is not soooo relevant to the story. As I said, the setting was quite irrelevant, because the story could've happened anywhere. Because the actual story was character driven, which isn't a real problem for me. The concept of the gifts, the fate-favoured and the struggle for power in this galaxy were interesting and compelling. Onto the more controversial part: And I don't see the accusations of racism ... the characters are rather skin colour neutral, and just because one family wants to rule over the others doesn't mean it's white surpremacy - it's dictatorship. But I see that some people who suffer from chronic desease might be offended by the depiction of pain (in Cyra's case.) I for myself am disabled and have to suffer a constant pain in my right leg which makes walking really hard for me. But I don't see a problem in finding meaning in pain. I find it rather beautiful. Some days my pain sucks, other days it drives me onward. So yeah, I liked this book and I am not ashamed. But I give it 'only' 4 stars because the romance felt a bit rushed and was kinda insta lovely. I am really looking forward for the next (and final) book, because some twists at the end I didn't see coming (others were a bit obvious ...)!

Attempting this one again, mostly because I think R. Lee Smith is a pretty fantastic writer but also because I love alien/human sexy times. Oh, and I think I should add this disclaimer: she writes some pretty brutal stuff. This is not, I repeat, this is not a sweet alien love story.

I really hate to rate things as low as 1 star when it's not horribly written. It's just horribly conceptualized and executed. Not sure if you get what I mean. Writing style? It's not bad. I like it. It's for the young-adult group. I don't understand a whole lot about the new generation's type of speech but it's fiction. Author can create it however they want. I'm cool with that. Probably 4/5? The abstract or description? I wish I read it. Let me say that. It's accurate enough to say that it's not lying. But it's also vague enough to have some hope for it. And I fell for it. For example, I quote, "This fresh, geeky/cool novel includes online chats and exciting gaming, and features Maddy?s Mangastyle artwork." Whether it's 'fresh' or 'geeky' or 'cool' is debatable. If you ask me, who is a nerd/geek type of person, I would deny all of it. But maybe some do. The 'online chats' part is true. Admittedly, it was presented in a way that there's like no difference between an 'online chat' in a mmorpg and an 'online chat' room. I seriously don't think the 'exciting gaming' part is accurate at all. It is underwhelming and disappointing. I mean, for someone that doesn't like to play games, I guess they can call it 'exciting'. Lastly, the Manga-style artwork is cool. Unfortunately, the cover isn't drawn in Manga-style but it looks nice. It's a freaking trap but it looks nice. The other half of the description is more accurate. I do admit that. I don't like it, but this description is fairly well written. It's a trap but still. Probably 4/5? The plot? I don't know how to say it. I've read novels that is a smash up of cliches but they can be good too. Regrettably, this isn't one of those. Plots with a lot of cliches are generally poorly received. A girl with family issues. Okay. A girl moved into a new 'crappy' environment resulting in more issues. Okay. A girl's grandparent is being a grandparent and embarrassing them. Okay Most schools don't actually have cocky bastards that are the most popular and well loved group. But fine. A girl being bullied. Fine. A girl's old friends decides to forget about her because she moved. Okay. A girl dives into the gaming world to escape reality. Cool. A selfish dad. Whatever. An annoying little sister. I'll live. A mother who can't support the two kids and resulting in financial problems. Sure. Meeting a 'gallant knight' in the mmorpg instead of a douche or an old pervert. How lucky. I'll live. Okay I'll stop soon. One more. A happy ending. I can live with that. As to what I can't live with, The mmorpg makes no sense. The author is insulting the gaming world. What kind of 'amazing' game would only have three freaking class? You need a bare minimum of four with advancements. They only had a warrior/knight, priest and a wizard/mage. No rogue or archer. Then there's the inherent game mechanic that prevents players to help power level others. Apparently, it doesn't exist. So, the 'gallant knight' is capable of partying and helping out a level 1 wizard. If it's helping, I can accept. But partying? No way. The knight was supposedly playing the game at least a few weeks before the girl joined. And the girl was able to get to level 15 in a few weeks. So, them partying and stuff I can force myself to accept. But within a few months, the girl's father who is level 80 ore higher joins the party. And the girl's father started playing over a year ago. And he's a hardcore player too. Makes no sense. The manga club is stupid. I can accept that she's a talented artist. I can accept that she can teach the other club members how to draw. But I cannot accept that they are miraculously able to produce artwork of similar quality over a weekend. There's two ways to go about this. Either all the members are naturally talented and they don't know about it. So they can cram altogether within a weekend. Or they used a light table to copy it. But the girl claimed that her work was praised for being about to incorporate many different styles of drawing. Neither reasoning actually makes sense. I shall stop now. But last point, the plot that the girl made is horrific in manga standards and I read a lot. In conclusion, I feel that the author is insulting both the gaming and manga world. I also forgot the novel writing world too. Cliches are fine. A story fill and made up of cliches is also acceptable if properly conceptualized and executed. But she did not. After writing this 'review', which is more like a rant (my apologies), there are more things that do not make any sense than things that made sense. Exaggeration intended. In order to force it back to 1/5, probably -5/5. Overall, (4 + 4 + -5) / 3 = 1 stars out of 5! Wasted 3ish hours. Extra bonus review on Mari Mancusi: Do not read her work. I read the first two chapters of another two novels. It's just as excellent as this one, as in bad.

Trigger Warnings:  Suicide and Rape One word to describe this would be  Disappointing. This has a solid premise for a young adult book involving suicide. Someone's best friend supposedly kills herself, through burning herself. But her friend June is shocked by her death and believes it to be not her doing. June was an okay character and for the most part I liked her, than the book went down hill and so did her character for me. Her "best friend" Delia is  obnoxious! Not only is she a character full of tropes but her lines are usually offensive and concerning. She does a great job at portraying unhealthy relationships with everyone she meets. Just this is a quote from Delia involving abortion, "I sure as hell would kill that baby though" Which her buddy responds with, "It wouldn't be a baby yet... I mean not at first... It would be goo" Those quotes basically explain the girls relationship. They truthfully brings out the absolute  worst  in one another. Not only does Delia drag June along like a puppy but gets her in serious trouble. "Junnie opens and closes her sweet mouth like a fish. I want to shove my fingers in there, to stick therm all the way down her throat until I reach her heart" Like is she okayyy??????? Not only was this a disappointment, the first quarter was decent. I mean I read this in a day! But this went in a direction that was just not good. Like this book is full of bad relationships, drugs and smoking, and sex. With trying to be a dark book talking about suicide, it was not that.

3.5 stars for "Swift and the Black Dog" by Ginn Hale 4 stars for "Everyone's Afraid of Clowns" by Jordan Castillo Price because it's a Psycop story and I miss Victor and his endearing quirks I don't know how to rate this anthology. How do people rate anthologies when they read only two stories all the way through and sample the rest? 3 stars? Seems kinda harsh since I did really like those two stories. Both are great, and I got this anthology just for them. Worth it even if the rest of the anthology falls into writing exercise territory. Prose-wise they fall short of GH and JCP, but story-wise, they don't seem that bad, with one exception--the one that reads like fanfic. That aside, a few have interesting settings and world building, or rather interesting enough that I might come back to finish them later on, but the rest needs a more thorough edit to smooth out awkward clunky prose. Another thing is it's not clear if these stories are stand-alones or part of a series. Since I wasn't that invested, I didn't bother looking them up. So for now this is a DNF, but I might return later. Maybe. I really hope the haunted theater will play a part in the next Psycop book. It would be awesome to see Vic and Jacob renovate another old building.

The third of J.K. Rowling's mysteries written under the pseudonym of Robert Galbraith begins with a macabre package delivered to private detective Cormoran Strike's office, addressed to his assistant Robin Ellacott. Its contents: A woman's severed leg. Strike quickly comes up with four potential suspects, all men from his past with a history of violence and a grudge against him. With the police promptly focussing on the one person on his list that Strike is almost sure can be ruled out, it is up to him and Robin to investigate the other three in what may be their most dangerous case yet. A solid thriller with a number of unexpected twists and plenty of suspense, although I have to admit I didn't enjoy it quite as much as the two previous ones. Mostly I just got very, very impatient with Robin and her personal drama. How can you actually marry that jackass, you idiot?! *argh*  But well... let's see where that goes in the next book.

After reading the author's previous book, THE UGLY DUCHESS, where we are introduced to Griffin Barry, I was eagerly awaiting his story. I loved how the former pirate was reunited with his wife "Poppy"...who's real name was actually Phoebe. LOL Though the story takes place in a matter of days, the epilogue allows for a fit ending to this fairy tale. Eloisa James is an auto-buy for me!

As a fellow agoraphobic, this was a must read for me. Pros: + Soloman. He might be my favourite character in a novel. He is a lovable character because he has a really funny sense of humor and he is a nerd. He is determined, caring, utterly adorable and seemed like a good human being in general. So I basically fell in love with him. + I know I mentioned Sol, but another lovable, believable character that I adored was Grandma. She's hip. + I think the scenarios and the story in general was accurate (at least in my own personal experiences). I found myself nodding to a lot of what Solomon was saying or what he experienced. + friendships were formed and they actually felt real Cons: - Length. The novel was fairly short, but "shortness" wasn't necessarily the downfall. I feel like areas needed more detail or needed to be fleshed out more, so to speak. - Pertaining to the last point: the ending. Now, I liked the ending but I didn't like how it was delivered. More depth, more explanation and more character development (Lisa, I'm looking at you) would have been well advised and totally would have made this book so much better! - Certain Characters. Lisa and Clark. Clark was just...there. I felt like he really wasn't needed and would have preferred if he wasn't actually a character in the novel. Why? Well for one, I can't remember any huge redeeming (read: interesting) qualities that he had. He was a nerd, very nice and helpful but I felt like he wasn't really necessary. He was basically just "Lisa's boyfriend" and that's all I really viewed him as. Actually, I feel like he was only in on this so sol could confess he was gay, then to have a weird love-triangle go terrible? As for Lisa, she didn't really strike-up a good vibe in me when I started reading. She basically uses someone for their own benefit  and I really don't think she learned her lesson in the ending. Yes, she wrote that essay but it didn't feel real. Almost like she wanted to write the essay about Sol, but her boyfriend was telling her not to and she didn't want to disappoint him/couldn't make up her mind what the right thing to do was, so she just chose not to.

I must have enjoyed this book because I stayed up way too late last night to finish it. Meghan Chase is sort of an outsider, she lives in a rural area with a goofy, prankster guy as her best friend. She is picked on by the popular cheerleaders..... Okay, I wasn't impressed with the beginning of the book or the essence of Meggie (as her younger brother, Ethan, calls her), but I kept reading and found myself drawn in once they entered the Fae realm to rescue her little brother and bring him home. Kagawa's writing was easy to read, the dialogue was pretty good (most of the time), and I didn't feel like wringing Meghan's neck too often for stupid decisions or not responding to a situation in the most obvious way. Meghan was fairly self sufficient,  though at the end her inner dialogue and her hesitation annoyed me. Could she really be that self centered that she would consider joining the Iron King so that she could be on top for once? . I also liked the idea that our over-indulgence in technology could create a new kind of Fae. One that would eventually overcome the traditional ones - and they are still around only because people 'remember' the stories. But, I didn't understand how Meghan would be allowed to be enslaved while she was in the Summer Court's realm and her father (King Oberon) did nothing about it? Over all, I will read the next book in the series, I'm just trying to decide whether I want to wait to get the hard copy or if I want to get it right now with the e-book version.

I'm glad that the second book continued with the same characters and expounded on Nina's storyline. But, I didn't like this as much as The Accidental Werewolf. Nina's personality was too different from how she was portrayed in the first book. She spent too much time whining. I hope that the story for Wanda is back up to the same caliber as the first one. Even though I was a little disappointed with this story, I am still looking forward to the next book in the series.
Really loved this book, reading the second one very soon!

When the new Mrs. de Winter arrives at Manderley, she finds herself living in the shadow of the first Mrs. de Winter, the beautiful and well-loved Rebecca. The servants find her lacking, and now that they've returned home Max seems cold and distant. As Mrs. de Winter attempts to take Rebecca's place, more details about Rebecca's death emerge, and she finds that nothing at Manderley is what it seems. I think I've heard so much about this book, and always thought it was a horror classic about a haunting, that I expected too much from it. There are no ghosts except in Mrs. de Winter's imagination, it's more about how she projects her own insecurities and feelings to Rebecca (and in turn to her husband and to Mrs. Danvers, Rebecca's maid). I felt that the truth of what happened (that Mr. de Winter killed Rebecca ) was fairly obvious from very early on in the book, almost immediately after they arrived in Manderley. However, the building of the atmosphere was quite good and kept me going through the story even when very little happens. The way the narrator is not named does give an added aspect to the story, as she attempts to take Rebecca's place.

The final book in a series always seems to be the most difficult to review. They tend to be a mixed bag of emotions. Happiness because the ending truly does the series justice, combined with the touch of sadness because it has come to end. Or disappointment, combined with a dash of anger if the less than stellar final book has tarnished the memory of earlier, better books. Kingdom of the Gods falls somewhere near the middle of this spectrum for me, but leans more towards the former. It has many of the same qualities I loved in the first two of the series, great writing and compelling characters, but it lacks some of the magic, especially when compared to The Hundred Thousand Kingdoms. In Kingdom of the Gods we get a story from the perspective of the oldest godling Sieh, god of childhood and mischief. Without giving too much away, I can say that the plot revolves around Sieh befriending two mortal children. Two Arameri mortal children, descendants of those who kept him enslaved for centuries. This friendship ends up of having a ripple effect across both the god's realm and the mortal world, as well as irrevocably changing Sieh. Sieh was a favorite character of mine from the first book, so it was fun reading a story told from his perspective. Shahar and Deka, the aforementioned children, are interesting as the strong willed sister who vows to be a good ruler and the quiet, kind hearted brother who must learn to protect himself. Though they could have been developed a little further, especially Deka. These three provide the sexy undertones that we've come to expect after the first two novels of the series. The best part of this novel however, is the way it brings the series full circle. The mythology of the world is explored more deeply, and there is a recreation of several elements from the first two novels, which is a joy to see played out. The plot does drag a bit more than the previous installments of the series and there are some bits towards the end that are slightly convoluted, but N.K. Jemisin's writing is so lovely, and the world she has created so magnificent, that these faults can be easily overlooked. All in all, the final installment of The Inheritance Trilogy left me feeling quite satisfied. And I would certainly recommend the series as a whole to fantasy fans, lovers of great writing, and anyone who likes their stories a tad sexy.

I'm really not sure what people enjoy about this series, unless it gets significantly better and everyone just back-scores this one highly. There's nothing particularly interesting here. We spend a lot of time in characters' heads, but there's surprisingly little character-building. It's all tell, little show. There are a lot of info dumps about past events with a lot of names thrown around, but I can't feel a real connection to any of it, which makes it hard to bother keeping track of who's who. The narrators are potentially interesting, I just wish their internal monologues were less cumbersome. I nearly gave up on this one several times, but I get the impression the author has somewhere he's going with it that might be cool -- this really feels like he has a story he wants to tell, but had to go and write all this backstory for it to work. Things seemed to setting in motion at the end, so hopefully we've hit the story he's been wanting to tell and the next one will be better. I'm just curious enough to keep going.

Daughter of Smoke and Bone. I've been lusting after this book, stalking it, staring at it out of my peripheral vision for a long time. And I finally read it. And what can I say? I actually liked it. This book is about a girl named Karou who is a talented art student (yay!) living in Prague (what? awesome!) with her best friend. She's the daughter of a monstrous beast name Brimstone, and has a bunch of friends who are equally beastly. She has a rather strange job: she collects teeth for some strange purpose and reports to Brimstone with her bounty. One day, Karou finds sinister handprints have sprang up on portals to Brimstone's workshop, and the seraphim descend. These aren't biblical seraphim, however... Characters First! So. Karou. She's pretty cool! That's rare for me to like a female protagonist. She was cool, believable, independent, curious, a little feisty, careful, and adventurous. Not to mention artistic, of course. She made all in all smart choices for her age. Then there's her friend Zuzana. She's your typical perky caffeinated bestie. I liked her. Then there's Akiva. Akiva Akiva Akiva. A winged man of impossible beauty (heard that before) and a countenance that could freeze hell (and that too.) What sets him apart is that he's believable, actually, as one of these types of people. However,  like all love interests of his ilk, he devolves into a blubbering quivering mass of emotions and sobs eventually. A shame. I simply covered those parts with my fingers and screamed at the book until they went away. Problem solved! What a handsome specimen. I was pleased by his leonine eyes. The scarier the better! Brimstone. Wow. I really grew to love his character so much. He began as a monstrous, scary creature of mystery, but eventually I found there was so much more to him. I cannot expound for fear of spoiling his character. The Story It was exciting! After coming off Delirium, this is prose done right. However Taylor really goes crazy with all the metaphors! Too many. So many that I had to gloss over whole sections just to get back on tract! But anyhow, the story was interesting. I was completely devoted to the romance between Karou and Akiva until the big reveal of the book. It totally punched me in the gut and told me to step aside. Lemme explain, but if you don't want things spoiled, sorry. Karou turns out to be Akiva's lost love, Madrigal, some kinda chimaera with horns. So she ain't human after all. Okay. I don't like those types of deals. I don't want to hear about this whole other life Karou had/has. I've grown invested in Karou's life, and she's my vehicle into this other realm. But now I find out she's not "one of us." It made me step back a little. I felt like I didn't belong anymore. Call me crazy but having a relatable character keeps me in the story. When they "change" into something, it makes me recoil. After the reveal, I was still interested, but not to the same degree. I admit, I skipped bits here and there during a few flashbacks I didn't feel like reading. The end totally made me pissed. But Karou was pissed too, so that was expected. It was the good kind of pissed. I simply didn't expect Akiva to go from what he started as to what he devolved into. BOTTOM LINE? TL;DR It was a good book with good characters and a believable romance. I was invested up to a point, where a big twist caused me to recoil and detach from the story a bit. Not fatal damage, but severe for my tastes. Cost a star. Great book though! I will read the next!

Overall, this is a truly amazing book. I read this classic so long ago that I remember barely anything about it, so I decided to include it in my summer reading project ("classic books"). Honestly, it's even more inspired than I remember (I did also have one problem with it that I didn't have as a kid reading it -- I'll get into that at the end of the review though). Meg Murry is a "problem child" -- smart in a way unfitted to school life, with a missing father that her peers whisper has run away with another woman. Meg is a classic fish-out-of-water character: not special at first glance, not pretty, not confident, too different to fit in. She has an odd and mysterious younger brother named Charles Wallace, who people assume is stupid, but who actually understands the universe in a way few others do. Mrs. Whatsit, Mrs. Who, and Mrs. Which come into the lives of these two children, along with their friend Calvin (a boy who successfully feigns fitting in with his peers -- he's popular and good at sports, but only feels at home after entering Meg and Charles' lives). They embark on a mission across time and space and dimensions to find their father, who was a physicist experimenting with the fifth dimension of space, and to rescue him from the evil that has him imprisoned, and that threatens the entire universe. This book does so many great things. First, it introduces kids to complex science in an interesting way. This was the only part of the book I remember. This is the book's great strength to me: it doesn't let kids sit back and plod through it; the ideas in it actively challenge them and their imaginations. Second, it introduces the idea that you can be a super smart kid and still struggle in school. Just because a student has a bit of trouble in school doesn't mean they're dumb. Meg and Charles don't fit in at school because their minds work a little differently than normal, but they're actually two of the smartest kids in the school. Third, every character has glaring strengths and glaring weaknesses. Often, the Christ-child Archetype (in this book, Charles) can do absolutely no wrong. Such is not the case here. Charles gets into more trouble than almost any other character, in spite of his Special Child status. Conversely, Meg -- the plain, not special one -- has a strength that winds up saving the day. So this book does a really good job subverting genre expectations and balancing characters. Now, the one critique I had was how Meg was always taking the hands of the boys. Calvin is told explicitly that his task is to go along to protect Meg (the only girl through most of the story). True, this is subverted a tiny bit at the end, but the reality is that for much of what precedes the climax of the story, Meg clings to Calvin's hand to be led through things. I wish this one aspect of the book was stronger. Girls get enough of this message elsewhere: that they need to be meek or follow a boy's lead or turn to a boy to be stronger or braver than her. That is not the case, and Meg does eventually prove that isn't the case, but I'd have much rather had a strong, take-charge girl from page one.

I was quite annoyed with Ellie at first and all the little things that happen to Alex to have her lose stuff. I was up until the end expecting Tom to show up again, not sure if the author would go there or not. I kind of though this was a complete novel, but it ends on a cliffhanger and is only the first of a trilogy, as it turns out. I'm definitely reading the second one. But. There were things that annoyed me in the second half. The change of pace and mood - it's a bit like a different book, with a much less 'take charge' heroine. The almost Mormon vibes - I did not like but OK, I wasn't supposed to like Rule much, still, it slowed down my reading pace. The first part is a little more engaging. Hopefully the next book goes back to that. I liked it. I enjoyed the writing style, the characters (though not all of them right from their introduction), the over all plot - with some bumps. I think it has potential to be better though, hopefully. I didn't expect to like a book about zombies, not my favorite subject, but this was very good. The Change happens in a way that's not cheesy and the descriptions are pretty creepy. The protagonist deals with it all in a pretty realistic way, too. I loved how self sufficient and take charge she was right from the get go. I'm curious about Ellie and Tom and Chris and definitely reading the next one.

This book was really interesting. The premise was a little far fetched, but I was able to let that go. (As a side note, the audio had a very annoying typing sound that played during the comments segments.) There was one thing that really bothered me. So that one girl is killed by the infected squirrel in the kitchen. If small mammals are infected, it's pretty safe to assume so are big mammals. So does that mean that there are zombie cows running around? Zombie cougars? Zombie bats? Why was that one squirrel the only infected animal they ran into. Surely something else was infected?! It also makes taking in the dog, a very big risk. He could be bitten at any time and turned. Of course, I would have taken him in too, since it seems more cruel to leave him to become zombie food. This book had everything a good zombie book needs. Drama, action, and lots of dead people. The interesting parts were the characters. They were dynamic. You fall in love with them and watch them die.

I will have to admit that I feel a little sadness ending this series. Now, for many of you, this series wasn't your favorite. I on the other hand, enjoyed this series from the very beginning. So when I went into this last book, I tried to drag it on for as long as possible. The whole book felt kinda slow-paced. The action parts got right to the point and ended almost as quickly as they started. I liked that, although it wasn't as "on the edge of your seat" excitment as most are, the 2 bigger twists  made up for it. The ending... I don't even want to get into spoilers on this one. We all know that this was the novel where it would all end. Would Luce and Daniel finally have their "Happily Ever After?" Lets just say it was....trying to find the right word.....bittersweet? I don't even know at this point if that's the right word for it either. But I will stick with that for now. It honestly ended as best as it could. Although, I felt a little dissapointed in a way? Not to say that thousands of years depended on this ending, but I dunno I felt a little let down. I wanted to give this book 3 stars, but the last 5 chapters are what really turned it around for me. Do we finally go back to the beginning and learn exactly how the curse came into play? How Luce and Daniel first met? How everything led them to this? Absolutely. I couldn't be anymore freaking happy about it either. It was perfect. It was exactly how I wanted to picture all the pieces coming together. It was beautiful, shocking, sad, and over-all breathtaking. Who woulda thunk-it!? So I will conclude that it ended almost as perfectly as it probably could. All the answers that I wanted were met, all the puzzle pieces were put together and everyone except Gabbe and Molly :( *tear*  had the happy ending we were all hoping for. My insides are warm and fuzzy, yet a little sad. But it was a great series. One that I will have to admit may read again...one day ;)

I would describe this book in a few words as: Tear jerker Character development is good and right at the start I could really sympathise with the female protagonist for the pain she was going through. And anger for her that it ever happened. The author gives us characters who lingers in my head long after I finished reading the book... The author also weaves a very convincing world where ghosts feels so real to the reader. I would give the "suspension of disbelief" a 4.5 out of 5. The story itself though does not seem to have any clear structure where there is a central conflict and a climax. The story? I'd give it a 1.5 out of 5. The book feels like a simple retelling of events. I didn't want a history class, I want a story with a beginning, a middle and an end. The end therefore did not sufficiently close the story because there was not much of a story dilemma to close with. And it was sort of a cliffhanger, I would give the ending a 2 out of 5. The whole book reads like it is a first chapter of a bigger book. The author knows how to play emotional manipulation with the reader though and I cried at about the last three quarters of the book. But this does not compensate for the fact that the story lacks a strong dilemma centrepoint. I would give the story-telling quality a 3.5 out of 5. I found this book to be a quick read and the pace to be nice and steady until you get towards the end where it gets quicker and quicker, which I like and is a definite plus. I enjoyed this book and would say the book has an overall entertainment value of 3.5 out of 5.

What I Liked I am about ten years older than the intended audience, but this book was amazing. I know for sure that this would have been one of my favorite books when I was that age. Regular kids finding out about magic in our world was my preferred genre in my youth - and probably the reason I dig urban fantasy so much now. It reminded me of the Magic Shop books by Bruce Coville, who was my favorite author growing up. The characters are realistic, the world is interesting, and the magic is cool. What I Didn't Like Not much, but the ending did have a bit of a deus ex machina, although as a kids book I suppose it makes sense. It also added something that could be developed upon in later books in the series.

And just decided to change the rating to 5 stars! Just can't stop thinking about it. I looooved this book! I have to admit that I wasn't into it from the beginning, but as I kept reading I was taken to a wonderfully disastrous world. What really did it for me were the characters. I really liked everybody in this book and I think that's what made me continue to read. The setting is futuristic, where scientists have discovered a way to make genetically perfect humans. These people do not really get sick, especially with anything serious like cancer. However, when they reproduced, it created a virus. The result of this is that women do not live older than 20 years old, and men die at 25 years old. The heroin of this story is Rhine, a 16 year old girl. Her parents, former scientists, died when she was younger and she now lives with her twin brother, simply trying to survive a broken world. However, she gets kidnapped and is chosen by a young man to be one of his wives. She wakes up in this incredible mansion where she feels traps and all she wants to do is escape. She gets to know her other sister wives (the other women who married the same man) and really begins to like them. Rose, her husband's first wife, was his real love. But now that she turned twenty, she is dying. Rhine gets to know her along with her other two sister wives: Jenna and Cecily. She has no affection for her husband, Linden, but her goal is to get close to him in order to escape and find her brother. She also has sort of a thing with Gabriel, one of the servants. Finally, Linden's father, a doctor, is convinced he is going to find the cure and Rhine soon discovers that he has strange ways of going about that. I really love the characters of this book. Cecily, even though she was mostly a bitch, really grew on me, and so did Rhine and Jenna, and of course Rose! I even liked Linden! I lost it when Jenna died at 19 instead of 20. This book was full of surprises, had a very interesting setting and lovable characters. I just love it when the beginning, middle and ending of a book is so great. I definitely recommend this one!

Rating: 4 This book made me laugh so much it surprised me. I wasn't sure what to expect going in, but I'd heard good things, so I picked it up. This book truly covers all the reasons why people don't pursue their dreams. It also talks about why you should go for what you want and what to do if you fail or succeed. I've read a few books on writing, and this stood out. It seemed to have a broader focus, and as such it seemed more focused. ** spoiler alert ** Oh god... this book. So many thoughts, emotions, and feelings. I am a survivor so this book hits very close to home. It was beautifully written and I'm so very happy that I read it. *CAUTION* SPOILERS SPRINKLED BELOW* I wasn't sure if I wanted to write a review on CoHo's latest masterpiece, but I came to the decision that I had many thoughts and feelings about this book that I needed to get off of my chest ... so ... here we go. When this story opens, Lily has just buried her father... her abusive father. He never hurt her directly, but she witnessed what happened to her mother. Unable to do anything about this abuse as a child, Lily endured years of hearing it happen to a mother who refused to end it. Trying to hold on to the belief that there is good in the world, she befriends a homeless teen that is living in the vacant house next to hers - Atlas. They become fast friends and she tries to help him out the best she can. They spend time together and after some time, once she turns 16, she and Atlas take their friendship to more than friendship. Atlas was Lily's first kiss, first love, first everything. Suddenly, Atlas disappears and Lily never sees him again. Flash forward to current day and Lily is now living in Boston... happy. She befriends a handsome man, Ryle, and the two begin a rather unconventional relationship. Things are going very, very well for Ryle and Lily, until one night a simple accident turns into something incredibly serious. Lily is flashed back to her childhood and she battles her emotions to make sense of it. Lily suddenly finds herself in her mother's situtation and she now realizes that making the decision to end everything is not as black and white as she first thought it was. I'm going to be very, very frank and honest in this review so prepare yourself. I am a survivor of domestic abuse. Not sure I've ever typed those words before... but it is part of what made me who I am today. With that said, reading this story was so incredibly hard for me. It felt as if Colleen was writing a part of my history, as if she found a way into my memories. I didn't suffer as much of the physical as Lily's character did, but everything else felt as if I was reading my own story (minus the being pregnant part). The emotional, the psychological, the mental abuse were all there. That is why I felt so deeply connected to Lily and her story. I'm just laying the ground work for why I felt so deeply for this story. I was connected to Lily's character from page one. I just had to know how this story was going to end. This was nothing short of a non-stop emotional roller coaster ride. I felt all of the ups and downs as if I was right in the story with Lily. I wanted to desperately to take her hands and try to talk some sense in to her, but like real life sometimes, you have to let it play out. I loved how real this story felt (for me, at least). The raw emotions that came across on page were intense. I commend Colleen for being so brave and putting this story into the world. It is needed so much. Colleen does state at the end that parts of this story are taken from her own personal life. That's brave. That's hardcore. That's amazing. To be willing to share a part of yourself that is so personal in such a way is mind blowing. This book is simply sad, painful, brutally honest, and damn smart. The way she portrays notion that everyone has of being in and dealing with an abusive relationship is right on the money. Those relationships are deep, complex, and anything but just black and white. I believe she has finally been able to explain this situation in a way that actually makes sense to everyone. The other thing that stuck with me about this story is the power of female friendship. Thankfully the MC had a wonderful best friend that she could rely on no matter what. Allysa was well written and I just loved her. I want to be best friend with her in real life. I know I am going to be bias about this book for reasons above, but I have every right to be. I am not ashamed of what I went through because like the MC in this story, it made me a better, stronger person. I went into this book blind and I wish everyone would as well. Although... that might be difficult to do if you have read my review. Ooops... but I hope you give it a try. It is a powerful read that everyone should have on their TBR.

(This may contain SPOILERS, though I'll try to be vague) Hmm... I've been wanting to read this one for so long because of how good everyone said it was. Despite that I wasn't really sure what to expect. I liked it well enough to keep going (it held my interest), but I was definitely really underwhelmed. The one big thing that stuck out in this book was destiny/fate versus choice. I was really uncomfortable for a lot of the book because Charlotte is being forced to do all these things she doesn't want to do. She has to do certain things or else she's in immense amounts of pain and she can't function. Not only that, but all of this is leading her to give up on life and be forgotten. She's supposed to be this glorious being who has a Higher Purpose, but it really just made me uncomfortable. Yes, sometimes in life we have to make choices that are incredibly difficult but end up being for the best, but this was an odd way of telling that type of story. I really dislike books where it seems like the character has no free will or choice. In a weird way I can't decide if this is one of those books, or if Suzanne Young, in the end, was writing a story about free will. However I can't really buy it when the "choice" is between giving up yourself and being forgotten by everyone you love, or staying and being completely corrupted by evil. I feel like the story was really repetitive, which did it a disservice. Understandably, Charlotte is confused, upset, and grief-stricken at everything that is happening to her. However, this doesn't mean we need to hear it over and over again. I feel like the book could be summarized like this: Charlotte is confused, Charlotte has to fulfill a Need, Charlotte doesn't want to, Charlotte ends up going to fulfill the Need, has to lie to Harlin, Charlotte has a sad. Rinse, wash, and repeat, etc. I guess I did expect something really moving and emotional from this book after everyone's reactions, but there were only a couple of parts where I really felt emotionally connected (minus the overarching sense that the whole story wasn't fair -- see above re: free will, choice, etc). I have to admit that the ending made me curious about Book 2, but by reading the description I knew I couldn't sit through another whole book. I ended up reading the ending, and I'm glad I didn't.

It seems that the second book is going to be just as hard to review as the first. At times I wanted to give this book 3 stars, but ultimately I went with four. I liked it, much better than the first even, which is why I'm having such trouble with a review... I don't want to say I was disappointed, but I do have to admit that the last third made me restless and annoyed. The first two-thirds of the book are, in my opinion, excellent. It continued easily with the momentum of the first book, introduced new and beneficial plot points, had really great character development, and overall was just plain good old fashioned fantasy fun. The Felurian bit seemed to grind everything to a halt. I see the importance of it, of course, for a number of reasons. However, it was too long. In a way, I wish most of it had been summarized the way the shipwreck was summarized. I felt that way towards the Adem parts as well. I just wanted Kvothe to go back to the Maer so those story lines could be tied up, or rather, so that the major story plot could continue on as Kvothe needed the Maer to help with his quest--which effectively gets cut short thanks to an incident which I feel wasn't really needed... Okay, to be plain... While Kvothe is with Felurian, the Cthaeh tells Kvothe that being near the Maer will help his Chandrian quest. Then after, we go to the Adem for a long period of time where Kvothe trains and learns things... but only at the end does he learn things about the Chandrian. SO, now we want Kvothe to go back to the Maer and finally push forward in the Chandrian plot... only, first he rescues some girls, a worthy event that unfortunately bites him in the butt later after the Maer has to get rid of him. And that was immensely frustrating. Now, this could lead to all sorts of postulating as to why the event happened, why Kvothe was sent away from the Maer... was it the Cthaeh? Was it only harming Kvothe more? Is this going to cause issues with the Maer and his lady love? Does it lead to anything more fruitfull than just "now I have a reason to send Kvothe back to the University and write a third book"? I'm hoping so... In any case, I felt slightly jipped by how things turned out. By the end of the book, I felt like I hadn't really gone anywhere. We learned only a few new things about the Chandrian and made no real advancement towards finding them... Kvothe developed as a person, but unfortunately Kvothe developed a sex life that became quite annoying... Denna seemed to function better within the plot of the story, but still... There's a lot to wrap up in the last book. Many plot points that we keep getting references to still have not appeared, which makes me wonder how thick and wirlwind-ish this "third day" is going to be... But to end with the positives (which were persistant throughout the book thankfully): --What wonderful world development this book had! Absolutely great. I love the full cast of characters, the attention to detail within each city and social group, the way Kvothe gets confused and messes up... I could really feel Rothfuss' devotion and care towards his world. And that always makes me happy. --Did I mention that I actually LIKED Kvothe in this book? And I mean, like, quite a bit. Didn't think it was going to happen, but he really has grown on me. Especially as he matures. --The magic system continues to impress and delight. Not only because the mechanics behind it are so intricate, but also because this book seemed to illuminate the whimsy of magic. Elodin, in particular, helps with this, but also the Adem do. And in a way, the people of Vintas, with the superstition, help show the more mystical side of magic. And that's what I really like about Rothfuss' system. It's not all precise magic with formulas and steps and ingredients. There's still some mystery. Overall, great book. Liked it more than the first which is always a good sign. And I'd still recommend it to anyone who's really wanting some intense high fantasy.

It is unfortunate that the first time I heard of Iain Banks was when he released a press statement saying that he had terminal cancer, and that the next book he releases will in fact be his last. It was through this, and the recommendation of a dear friend, I came to read The Wasp Factory. I've heard this described as horror and to an extent can understand why. Though there is very little linear progression throughout the story each chapter, through its mix of horrific events retold and mundane day to day musings, a sense of suspense is almost effortlessly created. Questions constantly plagued me throughout; who is Frank, what is the Wasp Factory, why did he kill the people he did, who were those people to him...the list goes on and on. It is a book built on the inquisitiveness of the reader and your own psyche creates the tension, the slow build up to whatever event the ominousness seems to be hinting... Reading as borderline psychopathic Frank (he probably is in fact actually fully, over the line, psychopathic but after reading from his point of view I find it hard to commit to that verdict) is uncomfortable. That's the best way I can describe it - there are times when, seeing events unfold through his eyes, you feel empathy, horror, hatred and occasionally genuine affection for Frank. These moments of light were made almost grotesque to me when compared to the dark and there were several passages, describing Frank's offhanded approach to killing or maiming, which made me feel distinctly unclean for ever feeling any empathy for him at all. I found the end surprising. There was no chance, absolutely none, that I'd have ever seen it coming. After using the entire book to build up to what I assumed would be a certain ending, that conclusion is blown out of the water swiftly and without ceremony. I admired that, myself, being fooled by the author after being given all the clues is something I think only great writers can do. And Iain Banks is great. His style, his plot, his characters...there is originality and darkness there which, combined with flares of humanity, make The Wasp Factory an incredibly absorbing read. I am deeply saddened that the literary world is being robbed of such a man, to have written something so very memorable. Though despite the tragedy of his situation his work will, I have no doubt, live on in immense and brilliant tribute.

The passion between Miranda and Colin sizzle from the start and continues on until the last page, Tessa Dare delivers a spicy romance you won't want to put down. She spins a tale of two people who couldn't be more opposite from one another, but who fall in love despite themselves. They try to fight the attraction but ultimately; they finally realize they were made for each other. Minerva is your typical bluestocking girl, who is outshined by her beautiful sister. She is somewhat of an outcast, her own mother talks about her, even when she is in front of her! Minerva is seeking acceptance, maybe not from her family but from those who share her love of geology. It seems our Minerva has uncovered a footprint of what appears to be a prehistoric reptile, which she named 'Francine'. She plans on traveling to Scotland to present her findings at a geology symposium. But she is smart enough to know she can't travel alone, now can she just convince Lord Payne to accompany her... Colin is exactly the kind of man every woman would fall in love with! He is sexy and slightly scandalous. Colin sees another part of Minerva that surprises him and sparks his interest. He sees the beauty in her curious mind and her independent spirit. From the start you knew that Colin loved teasing her, it was also cute how he called her every name except Minerva... "I must say, Melinda. This is rather a surprise." "My name's Minerva." "Yes, of course." He cocked his head. "I didn't recognize your face without the book in front of it." She exhaled, letting her patience stretch. And stretch. "I'll admit," he said, "this is hardly the first time I've answered the door in the middle of night and found a woman waiting on the other side. But you're certainly the least expected one yet." A midnight seductress she was not. "This isn't that kind of visit." "Give me a moment to absorb the disappointment." I couldn't help but chuckle over their banter, and you don't want to miss their "tit for tat" discussion, it was hilarious. You will love the great improvising of Colin, as he spins his own tales to those they meet while traveling. There were some wonderful secondary characters which added to this storyline. I liked Kate Taylor; she seemed like someone who begged to have her story told... Through their journey Minerva and Colin heal each other, more specifically they "complete each other". I was very satisfied with this wonderful, touching, beautifully written story about two people, giving each other hope, acceptance, happiness and the freedom to love. You will not be disappointed with this book if you love a romantic story of two seemly opposite people who bring out the best in each other. You simply must get this book!! Tessa, I look forward to reading more of your books. I received this ARC in exchange for an honest review.

Wither by Lauren DeStefano (3*) I kept shifting between giving this novel three or four stars. On one hand, I greatly enjoyed this book. The protagonist's, Rhine's, voice was easy to fall into. The writing flowed nicely. I readily slipped into the story and followed Rhine as she moved through this tale. Rhine's loyalty to her twin brother and to her sister wives (Rhine is in a polygamous marriage) endeared me to her. As for the beginning, the premise intrigued me and then, while the first few sentences felt awkward, the opening chapter pulled me into the story. A bunch of girls trapped in the back of a van, only to be released somewhere unknown, examined and separated into two groups? Yeah, I'm curious to know what is going on. Many of the scenes and language were beautiful. I could picture Rhine relaxing on her satin bed sheets, while she languidly ate candy. (Though, she hated the situation she was in and desperately wanted to escape. Guess you have to make the best of a bad situation...I probably would have eaten candy too, while I bided my time, and kept an eye out for the right opportunity.) Soon, the attractive language and questions from the opening chapter weren't enough to completely hold my attention. My curiosity dwindled. I found myself rather bored for sections of the novel. My tediousness didn't stem from the unbelievable premise: All women die at twenty years old, while all men die at twenty-five from some illness/defect/something...no one knows what, only that people are dying because previous generations experimented with vaccinations and "test-tube" babies to create genetically perfect children (which then somehow resulted in these "first generations'" offspring dying at the previously stated ages). Or that the world building was sketchy at best. It was a stretch to suspend my disbelief, because when North America, and I mean all of North America, is somehow the only survivor of a world war (all other continents were destroyed and are now tiny, lifeless islands amid a vast ocean...even the polar icecaps were obliterated), you'd think that at least some cities, like New York, and some states, like Florida, would be underwater. Or, better yet, New York having been bombed during the war...let's face it, The Big Apple is a hefty target for enemies. I started losing interest when I began to feel that nothing really new was introduced. Beneath all the surface information was the same young adult story line: a teenage girl with something unique about her catches the eye of a hot/wealthy boy, this unique factor will somehow do more than make previously stated boy fall in love with her In this story's case, I'm betting Rhine's heterochromia (different colored eyes) will make it so that she doesn't die at twenty. This special quirk of Rhine's was mentioned too readily and early on for it not to play a larger role later in the series. Also, Rhine's a twin, which seemed to be a dominant fact within the story as well, and, usually, within fiction twins tend to mean special exception. , said boy ends up not being such a jerk, there's another boy involved, the true villain emerges, etc. But mostly, my loss of interest came from the story not being gritty enough. Rhine was forced into a polygamous marriage so that she'd get pregnant. Her children would effectively be experiments in an attempt to find a cure for whatever is killing off the population. This premise sets up for one heck of a dramatic and heart-wrenching thrill ride! Yet, Rhine's marriage to her husband Linden wasn't horrible. In fact, Linden ends up being clueless about how Rhine and her sister wives came to be with him. Linden's father Vaughn is the master manipulator. It's a bit difficult to swallow that Linden was so incredibly ignorant and naive. And though I understand how Linden would be completely reprehensible if he'd been aware of what was going on in the world around him and did what he did, I have trouble liking and caring about him because he was so uninformed. It wasn't until near the end that I began to see any true threat to Rhine, and what I did see what frightening. However, the intensity didn't continue, but instead petered off, so that what was supposed to be the climax was dissatisfying and muted. I wanted to feel terrified for Rhine. I didn't. But I did get frustrated, and I could no longer suspend my disbelief. The author DeStefano spent the entire novel hinting at how horrible, manipulative, and controlling Linden's father Vaughn was. Therefore, when the ending came about, I was not amused. Anyone who is running away from a monster like Vaughn, and who knows that she'll be murdered and her corpse dissected and studied in the supposed search for an antidote, doesn't stop at a movie theater that's located only a few miles from her captures, with the servant boy she's escaping with, and watch a marathon of zombie movies. How can readers feel tension, or sense any sort of real threat, when the protagonist doesn't seem to be all that afraid? Also, Rhine's got a key card, given to her by Linden, which she can use to get off the wives' floor and go outside. With Vaughn already suspecting that she tried to escape, and knowing that she has a thing for the servant boy, you'd think he'd have an alert go off every time Rhine used her key card. This again speaks to the question of why isn't Rhine more afraid, or at the very least more motivated to get as far away from her captures as soon as possible? Where dystopia is concerned, something major must be at risk. This includes more than what's obviously stated. There must be something underlying--I have to feel the danger. And I didn't really for this novel. After such an enticing premise, I was left wishing this book had lived up to its potential.

Okay. I did it. I finished the series. While it is better written from a technical standpoint than Fifty Shades of Grey, Fifty Shades Freed is probably the most boring of the trilogy. It took me 12 days to read this book. It would've taken longer but it's an ebook I borrowed through my library and it automatically "returns" after two weeks, so I made myself finish. Even once I resolved to finish it, I ended up skipping about thirty pages. I think I developed Stockholm Syndrome while reading this series. The first two books I was completely livid with E L James for creating this monstrous character and some stupid bint who just knew her love could transform him. I was annoyed with every woman who swooned over Christian Grey and told me she wished he was real. I knew I would never understand how anyone could think, "Hey, he's not so bad." Why would anyone perpetuate such dangerous ideas regarding relationships and mental health? I direct you to this article on 31 Ways to Know You're in the Right Relationship; they display 10 of the 15 things you shouldn't during the course of the series. I maintained these opinions for the first two days of reading Freed. My rage lasted throughout the first three or four chapters, which were peppered with inane flashbacks, like the one about him being angry at her for wanting to keep her job after their wedding  and them fighting about her refusing to vow to obey him . I was indignant when he referred to her as an asset that needed rebranding and said he liked to make random appearances at SIP because "it keeps management on their toes, wives in their place." And of course he decided not to tell Ana important things that could save her life, and then one time he left cuff marks on her and then bought her jewelry to cover them up partly because he couldn't stand to see them , and then another time he made her safe-word when he got mad at her and decided to sensually torture her and not let her orgasm as punishment . Which, you know, world's tiniest violin, lady. But still. Kind of a jerk move. But then I think I just went numb from the predictability of the plot and my overall boredom with the characters. Because even when he completely lost his rag over her being pregnant  (which I've spoilered-out even though it was the most predictable aspect of the book), I found myself thinking, Well, who cares. People fight. You'll both get over it. Meh. I guess "meh" could probably be my entire review, honestly. I'm not sure if this is in the print edition, but my ebook edition had some extra stories at the end: "Fifty's First Christmas" and then one about his interview with Ana from his POV. I didn't really read those but I did read his file on Ana and YIKES. This was when they had just met, mind you, and he had a file which included her bank account number, bank balance, social security number, mother's maiden name and husbands, etc. And at some point in the second or third book Ana read that file and didn't run screaming in the opposite direction. In conclusion, can we please get away from the irritating and senseless trend of giving unborn children dumb nicknames in novels? "Little Blip" isn't even a tiny bit cute, especially when you have to read it approximately 45 times in so many pages. And now I move on with my life.

Anyway, I'd call it straight up fantasy (though one of those fantasies without magic). Which is great! More of those in YA, please. I thought it did a fairly good job of showing a different kind of strong female character, too. She's not gifted at physical fighting and knows and mostly doesn't mind that, outside of maybe feeling a little like she's a disappointment to her father. Anyway, what she is good at is strategy and I think the book did a good job of showing us how true this is. (Still not very interested in traditionally feminine things, though I didn't feel like those were dismissed.) I've seen the romance in this described as slow burn and it is, but I actually needed it to be a little slower, I think. Or to see more scenes between the two of them. Given the power dynamics between them throughout the book, I just needed to see more of the connection. And those power dynamics . I don't know. I'm a little torn. The book made an attempt at exploring the moral issues there, but I'm not sure I got enough of that, either. What made Kestrel all along view things like slavery a little differently? Later, she says she sees the cause of the enslaved is just, but I didn't really see how she came to believe that. (Well, and, actually, I didn't see her as originally having the opposite belief, of their cause NOT being just, either. Actually, I don't really know what her original view of slavery was. There were hints it was different than most people's, but I don't really know what that all means.) (Sorry if this is confusing--I am confused!) But four stars because I did overall like it and it sucked me in and I read it fairly straight through. Really, the worst part about this book is that it's the first one in the trilogy. This book wrapped up just about everything and I don't think I'm interested in reading more. We'll see.

I've chosen not to rate this book because I don't feel like I've gotten the full sense of it. To put it simply, I can't think because of all the feelings. I'm not even sure if I'm ready to talk about this book, but I really want to get all this out, so here goes: First of all, I was not expecting anything that this book threw at me. From the synopsis, I expected it to be like an action-packed revolution against consumerism. To me, it seemed like a dystopian A Walk To Remember meets Inception, only better, only worse. Worse in a good way. I can't explain it. It has something to do with the sheer brutality of all the feelings. I'm not going to say I understood this book entirely, because I didn't. I still don't understand some of the words (fugue?) and I don't get what lesions are supposed to allude to, if they're supposed to allude to anything at all. My best bet is plastic surgery. Part of the reason I didn't expect anything that came at me is because I spent the whole first part ('Moon') trying to understand what the hell was happening. And after that, I was still expecting Violet to revolt or something and I thought her stint at the mall was just the beginning, but apparently, that was it. I don't know what I was thinking during the middle parts but by 'Slumberland,' I felt like I was being shot. In a good way. The narrative takes on this eerie atmosphere that only happens when you know someone's dying. To me, this book wasn't about consumerism or media. Well, it was, but it wasn't the main thing. I think it's really a love story. At its heart, it's about two people in the middle of all this crap, trying to make it work. Isn't that what love stories are? I do get the satire (it made me laugh at the most inappropriate times) and it did make me think about our dependency on technology and what the future holds, but really, the heart-wrenching thing is that these characters, despite how weird they are, are still human. I think that's what held me back, because it took me a long time to get around their weirdness. You'd expect Violet to be purely human and Titus and his friends to be out there, but I love that Violet is still a product of her era which means that she still talks weird and Titus is what's considered normal. I love that the two main characters don't fit into the cookie-cutters. They were both so alive even if Titus sounded so mechanical. I think that's what makes it succeed as a YA novel, that the characters are teenagers and they want to fit in and they want to be cool, and any teenager can relate to that. I've read some of MT Anderson's work before (a short story in Geektastic and I started Octavian Nothing but never finished it] and I noticed he has this weird insensitivity. His imagery is so clear and direct and downright brutal, there is no softening of the blow whatsoever. You get the full impact of everything. I swear, by the end of this book, I was literally sobbing. I wanted to sit on my bed and cry it all out, but I couldn't because it was time for dinner so I went downstairs for dinner, which was pointless because I didn't eat anything. The fights between the characters, oh my god. Also, the last page will tear you to pieces. Like I said, I only really got into this book at the last part and I'm writing this right after I finished it, so I can't be sure if my feelings are for the whole of the book or just for 'Slumberland,' which is why I think I need to read it again. tl;dr: Everything caught me off guard. I felt everything. Read this book.

I received this through a first-reads book giveaway. It's a novel in verse about three women in their late thirties/early forties who are all friends and mothers. One is married to a decent guy but craves erotic adventure, another is a divorced single mother, and a third is married to a largely absent husband who is totally unhelpful as she struggles to care for a disabled toddler daughter and gay teenage son. This was an absorbing, if sometimes soap-operatic story, and the verse format didn't make it any less gripping. In fact, I never imagined I could enjoy a novel in the form of poems this much. I was often so oblivious to the fact that I was reading poetry that it's difficult for me even to tell whether I thought the poetry was good poetry or not. For that very reason, I don't think it could count as great poetry for the ages. However, I found myself in awe of the author's ambitiousness in choosing this form for her novel and how well she pulled it off. When I did notice the poetry, I was often impressed with the author's interesting word choices and verse structures. As a single mom to a pre-schooler and woman of a certain age, I definitely felt like the storylines in the book were ones I could relate to. The portions dealing with the disabled child were especially heartrending. One of the characters reconnects with her spirituality in part of the book, but to my relief it was mostly presented in a literary way, as one possible choice a person could make for her life among many others, rather than as covert sermonizing. Some parts of the book get fairly steamy, so that it reads a bit like a Harlequin romanice in spots. (It amused me because one characters joins a writing group and, wow, I'll just say, her writing group is whole lot more interesting than any I've ever gone to ...) I also found some of the steamy parts unrealistic (e.g., there's a scene where a character goes to a sex club and engages in some kinky stuff there ... I've never been to a sex club myself, but I've heard enough first-hand accounts to be fairly certain that they tend to involve a lot more old, fat, funny-looking people then the book's idealized scene would lead you to believe ). (Content warning for my LDS reader friends: besides the aforementioned steaminess, there is also a girl-on-girl sex scene !) On the whole, it was a worthwhile and enjoyable read, and something new and out of the ordinary as well.
