I finished American Gods last night, and highly recommend it for anyone looking for a deep, dark, soulful, well-written novel. And I mean novel, not book. Not many books I've read lately can, in good conscience, be called novels in the strictest sense of the word -- especially not novels that are so well-sculpted. American Gods is easily among the best three novels I've read in the past decade, or more. It's no wonder it won so many awards (including the Stoker, for those of you who read a lot of horror etc). My only (very minor) complaint is that the conflict resolution, from the climax to shortly before the end (but not including the end, which was superb), seemed a little bit rushed. Not terribly so, however. It was still very, very well-crafted. So it's only a minor complaint. I hid this criticism in spoiler brackets because I don't want it to negatively impact or prejudice any potential readers. There is also a good chance that my mood while reading that part, totally separate from what was happening in the book at the time, was the cause of my feeling that it was slightly rushed. Because honestly, I didn't want the story to end . By the way, I'm glad I read the 2013 edition; after much contemplation, the author went back and rewrote large sections of it, added bits in and took bits out, and says this is the edition of which he is most proud. He seems to be quite a deep thinker, and I trust his judgement. Oh, there's also an "American Gods novella" tacked on to the end of this particular edition of the book, in the appendix -- and honestly, it's more like an epilogue than a completely separate tale. The novella is a continuation of the story that is more than worth a read. I cannot praise American Gods highly enough. Truly. What a refreshing gem.

3.5 stars I am a terrible procrastinator. Why does that matter for this review? Well, I read this book several weeks ago and never wrote a review of it. I do this far too often so I've made a deal with myself that now, before I start a new book, I need to review what I finished. And it's worked well, but it doesn't work so well for this situation where there's a book I really liked, but my memory is fuzzy. That said, I took some notes while I was reading so I'm going to do kind of a deconstructed review based on those. Angie, the main character is super relatable I was really worried that Angie would just be really odd. I mean, she's been missing for three years and some terrible things happened to her (which is pretty obvious from the beginning). But I liked her immediately. She was just a really normal girl and she wanted to go back to being a normal girl. The "alters," the personalities she created to deal with captivity, were very different and sometimes disturbing, but they didn't make the story as strange as I expected. There's not too much religion. This was actually a big concern of mine. I knew this was loosely based on the Elizabeth Smart case and I know she's pretty religious. I am personally not a religious person and I have a very different time relating to very religious characters. But Angie wasn't at all religious and I definitely appreciated that. There is some light romance, which was kind of a surprise given the trauma that Angie experienced. I honestly, at this point, don't remember anything about the romance, so it must not have been that big a part of the story. There is a storyline with Angie's boyfriend before she disappeared that really highlights the differences in Angie's alters, which I found interesting. My only criticism of the book is that there were a lot of coincidences. I won't go into them, because they're all pretty big spoilers, but the fact that someone with Angie's background was the one kidnapped which ultimately allowed her to develop these alters seems like a pretty big coincidence. And a lot of the relationships and interconnectivity of the book just seemed too contrived for me. I also thought the way the storyline with her parents wrapped up was too convenient and a little unrealistic. There are two big secrets in the book that comprise the bulk of the book. I actually managed to guess both of them pretty early on, but they were still disturbing, shocking, and painful to read about. Bottom Line: This is not an easy book to read. There are depictions of physical, mental, and sexual abuse of children. However, Liz Cooley handled these difficult situations very well and I never felt like she was exploiting these situations to sensationalize the story. Angie's recovery, including the depiction of the alters, was fascinating and although I can't say anything to to accuracy of the complicated psychological situations in the book, I never felt like I had to suspend disbelief about any of those. I definitely suspended disbelief about some of the coincidences, but despite that I would still recommend picking this one up.

Toppled by the weight of its own ideas, this is. We're in a Mievillean London, but William Burroughs or someone also slipped in. There are 80 weird things going on where 20 would have been plenty. It became clear quite early that any kind of explanation for this was going to involve some major hand-waving, smoke and mirrors - and sure enough it did. Our antihero drifts from event to event, becoming less and less relevant and rarely having a choice in what happens next. People have scrolls that tell their future, and this may or may not be related to why London has gone weird. Meanwhile we are supposed to believe that the rest if the world is still watching "Survivor" and going to Walmart as usual, just watching with concern as London turns into an LSD trip made real. The ending, such as it was, dragged on, and eventually became just a version of having the audience clap to save TInkerbell. Ptui. What's the Daddio? Explained with nonsense. What's with the foul-mouthed little girl? Never explained. What's at the top of the tower? No spoiler here, because if I told you you'd laugh anyway (hint: think of Pratchett's Hex) And so on. There seem to be some smart people involved, even a few who actually understand what's going on. But they are kept offstage, or appear to discuss something far more trivial. Perhaps because James is too dim to understand anyway. Interesting ideas here, enough for a series. But they're all jammed into one book and it just doesn't work. Your mileage may vary.

I honestly don't know what to make of this book. I mean, I sort of get that there's some things about change and continuity and growing up but I don't really see what the big point was. I didn't understand why there needed to be so much romance and the ending was... confusing, even though it was nice that she eventually got together with Conrad . On the other hand, though Belly was kind of annoying at times I felt like I kind of understood her in some ways, which was interesting because I hadn't realised that I wasn't the only one (even if this person was fictional). Some things could've been better wrapped up though, like Cam and Mr Fisher. All in all, this book was pleasant, but I don't understand the big deal about it.

** spoiler alert ** Really, three and a half stars. Having read and really enjoyed Bel Canto, I was looking forward to reading more of Patchett's lovely prose and excellent character profiles. And I knew The Magician's Assistant would probably make me weep a little bit and who doesn't like a bit of catharsis on a blustery winter's day? In all ways, my expectations were met. And in all ways, I was a little disappointed as well. Sabine, the titular magician's assistant, has spent her life placing her own ambitions, desires, and dreams on the back burner, happy to follow her life-mate-but-not-lover's path. After his death, she discovers that the past he told her about didn't exist. That the family that died in an accident decades ago is actually alive and well in Nebraska. Sabine discovers that the life she gave up everything to be apart of... may have been a lie. An interesting and beautiful premise and Sabine takes a difficult journey to discover the truth about Guy and herself. But the disappointment comes at the end, when Sabine has decided to start living life for herself but we as readers only see the barest glimpse of this new journey. We're left with mostly insubstantial hopes.

i love nora. i love her writing style - the beautiful prose, the great characters, even the predictable plots. and this book was no exception - i loved all of that. i especially loved Abigail, with whom i cried more than once. sadly, i felt like nora wrote herself into a bit of a corner on this one. usually there is a climactic moment where the good guys have to suffer a bit of heart-pounding panic before everything works out in the end. but in this book, the characters were developed such that it would have really been impossible to make that happen. so no big climax. just a nicely wrapped up package, and a promise of happily ever after. so only four stars this time.

*3.5 stars Josephine is an orphan whose life was destroyed by a careless driver when she was nine years old. Now, sixteen years later, she's barely living in a crappy apartment, working at a decent bookstore that she enjoys. Then she meets Damon, a rich entrepeneur, and her life pretty much turns upside down from there. This is a story of the bad/tough girl with a troubled past who meets the rich, sexy man who ends up taking care of her. Typical? Yeah, it's a typical story, but it reads in a gripping and passionate way. Damon was sexy! He's got the whole alpha thing going on, and he gives his woman whatever she needs or wnts (even though she is constantly refusing and denying the pleasures). But boy, does he spoil her! And it's so cute, and I was happy that Jo got to experience the pleasures of life, finally, since her life really was terrible and distraught. Jo also has the whole tough attitude going on. She's rude and cusses a lot. She's blunt and doesn't waste time glossing over details. I liked that about her, and fianlly, with Damon, she lets out her vulnerable side and he lets her in. There's lots of sex, lots of hot scenes between these two, and boy, is Damon hot! Whew. Seriously. I really did love the story. Not as much as I was expecting, but what put me off was the writing. The characters were likable, but I feel like they're not the memorable kind. Also, the writing felt a little contrived, and there were a few errors that distracted me. I just minor pet peeves based on the way the writing is, but don't let that stop you from reading the story. The ending, though? What was that? I'm kind of confused about this cliffhanger. And I don't know why, but as much as I loved Damon, that ending kind of made me see him differently than I beleived...Ok, I get that he loves Jo so much that he couldn't live without her, but to go and try to kill yourself? That is what he did, right? It just makes him seem like such a coward, when the whole book I fell in love with his whole protective and being there thing. It just seemed off for me. But, oh, it was sad to see Jo in such a mess over the possible death of him, though I won't for a second believe that's how it will end. Jo and Damon really do deserve their happiness, despite the shitty way they were thrown together.

At some point during this book, David Mitchell uses a Matryoshka doll as a metaphor. I had to smile, because I was already thinking of the novel in those terms. Have you ever seen them for sale? You know how they're all lined up, from biggest to smallest? If you buy one, the shopkeeper opens them up, one by one, then places the smallest into the next smallest, and so on: back up to the biggest doll. That's the structure of this novel. The author has set himself the dazzlingly ambitious task of writing the biography of a soul: as such, time is revealed not to be a linear measure. Each soul has its own story and each is nested into the next - time does not repeat itself but there are echoes: deja vu, half-memories and always the discovery of the record of a past-life (but never recognised for what it is). At the half-way point of the book, the stories begin to lift back out into the ones that preceded them (hence the Russian doll metaphor). Each of these stories inhabits its own time and space: from the 19th century pacific islands all the way through future Korea to post-apocalypse USA(?). Each of these stories is told utterly convincingly in a unique voice. That Mitchell can inhabit these disparate voices in one novel is a technical marvel. The thing is, a suspension bridge is a technical marvel and I don't much care about that either. It's ironic that a book about souls should be so utterly devoid of one. The first half of the book is as frustrating as it is dull. The second, after the author reveals his cards, is painfully heavy-handed. Capitalism and consumerism are driving us all to the collapse of society and environmental catastrophe because people are selfish. We know. A parable has to do more than simply moralise if it is to succeed. As if that wasn't bad enough, the author's heavy handedness often takes a smug do-you-get-it approach which sees him sign-post everything (e.g. the doll analogy above) which suggests he doesn't believe his readers are intelligent enough to understand his point. So, all in all: dull, frustrating, patronising and an unoriginal message presented as original. Only the language and the structure save this from being a one-star read.

SERIES REVIEW I take back every time I called a book an emotional rollercoaster. They have nothing on Ruining You and Ruining Me. These books will catch you by your hair and throw you repeatedly against the wall till you can't move. There are many plot points similar to those in other books but none of that matters because it is uniquely its' own. Think Captive in the Dark minus the torture and kidnapping, Taking Chances  and  Thoughtless without the cheating love-affair and Find You in the Dark without an emotionally unstable male lead, rather, here it is our protagonist named Jay. And since I forgot to mention it, both these books blew me away and in the most amazingly-delicious way. They were phenomenal and even with all the yelling and LOL moments I was taken for a ride. When we first meet Jay we know something awful happened to her. As much as readers want to know, it takes awhile before the truth is revealed, and boy was it a doozy. Jay is lost. Something horrific happened to her and the only way she saw to deal with it was to push everyone and everything away. Being underage and in high school does not stop her from having random sex or hanging out at a local bar. It is there she meets Kane who is as amazing as a tin of cookie dough. However, Kane and Jay do not jump right into things and in fact she continues to push him away. There is no insta-love here though the two are clearly attracted to one another. This poor girl is so tortured by the past it is hard to see how she even functions. Between pushing everyone close to her away and facing her demons/nightmares alone she proves how utterly brave she really is even if she makes a few bad decisions when things get tough. "Satan wasn't ugly. I had always been taught in church that he was the most beautiful angel, and even in my dreams, I realize this. "-Jay I was so totally thrown by the pace of this book at times. Just when you are getting excited about Kane and her, something else or should I say someone else happens. But then wham! before that too has a chance to percolate we are thrown the mother of all curveballs. It's hard to not give anything away but the emotions this book evokes is amazing. One minute your left wondering what the hell Jay is doing and why. You know something happened to here and though we don't fully understand it's reasonable to see why she falls back into old patterns. But then her choices are ripped away and she loses someone close to her at the same time her truths are revealed to everyone. She is so stuck on blaming herself that she forgets to point the finger at the one responsible. It takes her awhile to gather the courage to fight but thankfully she does and takes away all the power from her attacker. "My sins were supposed to kill me. "-Jay The pain is awful as if you are Jay yourself. I doubt I would have survived without immediately picking up Ruining You after finishing Ruining Me. By the time Ruining You comes around you want to sleep life away and hope that those last few chapters were only in your imagination. But as much as they suck, they also rock. The ending, threw me across Crazy Town. I loved how unexpected it was. Surely, a big showdown moment was on its way but the Who is what threw me. That was one of the things I loved about this book. It takes traditional and throws it out the window. What you expect is so not what you are going to get. With the truth out in the open Jay has her hardest challenge yet. Testify or not to testify. Thank God this book is in first person because being in her mind is so eye-opening and not only because as females we are able to understand her position but because it again just shows how alone yet brave she really is. This is a very sensitive issue, especially for victims of abuse. In Jays' case she was attacked by someone she should have been able to trust and before the truth came out she was still being harassed on a daily basis. It's so hard not to feel for her. She is so ashamed of what happened to her, she would rather leave the Earth than have the world know. She blames herself and makes excuses when none are justifiable. Poor Jay is like a bird in the wind without wings or directions. She just floats waiting for the lightning to strike her down so she can say 'I told you so.' Even with her 'giving up' attitude. She doesn't give up. It takes the death of someone close to push her to that level. It's so sad because her pain is a live tangible thing and you just wish she didn't push everyone away so she wouldn't be alone. "Sometimes the bad things that happen in our lives put us directly on the path to the most wonderful things that will happen to us." Kane is great and I really fell for him. Even with all Jay's hang-ups and obvious drama he was a rock. Giving in when he should have walked away, and just being ridiculously supportive of Jay even though her pain hurt him as well. At times these two would drive me crazy with the half-truths and subtly, as if speaking their feelings would be so bad. (Luckily, Jay's mom is a take charge woman and sets them both in their place). At one point Jay calls her relationship with Kane doomed. It was scary and sad at the same time because you want them together but you realize that Jay is both rash and afraid. The truth may be out, but she hides behind it and lets it linger, hindering her life. Kane really comes through for her and is more patient than she deserves. He helps her LIVE and break free from the shell she's hid under for the past two years. I was thrown by all the guys that seemed to be following her around. However, it helped add another layer of conflict to an already conflicted story. And in their own way, each guy helped Jay deal. Rhye was more of a buffer that she used to help separate from reality and I was sad to see this bad-boy bare his heart and still be strong enough to walk away. JT was a blast from the past, one she literally let go but emotionally they were wrapped all over one another. I was so thankful everything worked out for Jay and her friends. Though time may have past, the bonds of friendship were still strong and unhindered by the actions of others. My favorite line was when they were at the club and said, "It's Brittney BITCH." Priceless, since my friends and I do the same thing. It was at this point the book brings out an air of relief, like the air is clearing and you can breathe. Hope for Jay overcoming her issues is at the forefront and watching her reawaken to life is invigorating. Overall I abso-freakin-lutely loved these books and would highly recommend them. Though the story-line takes on a very serious and emotional tone, the characters will suck you in and throw you against a wall- leave you forgetting the pain but wanting more. Every chapter was remarkable, not because they were all great and happy but because each one, hell each page, invokes a different emotion that leaves you a bumbling mess. Pure genius. This is a story for any girl who has every suffered and arisen from the dust stronger than before. I just want to wrap my arms around these books and not let go!

I zoomed through the first two thirds of Red Queen. First Third: I enjoyed, and was contemplating a 3.5-4 star rating. The dystopian society with its unequal social tiers reminded me of The Hunger Games, although the world building was not as intricate, and the society was not as dower. At this point, I liked the main character, Mare, because she had an interesting mixture of characteristics. She was brave, but not stupid. She was arrogant, but sought approval from her parents. This quickly went away once she left her home. Second Third: The book turned into a weird royal Bachelor-type competition but with... X-Men abilities? I don't know. This section lowered the book to 3 stars. The characters of the royal court were interesting on the surface because of their abilities, but they had nothing to them. The Royal Court itself, while trying to be this blood-thirsty, trust-no one arena full of pseudo super heroes, was just boring. At this stage I also found it hard to follow what was going on in the plot. Final Third: Worst part of the book for me, and brought my rating down to 2 stars. I just stopped caring here and wanted the book to end. The Red Guard's revolution was completely useless, and given how easily all the revolutionaries failed, I don't know why they thought they could have any influence in the first place. I don't know how they were able to achieve anything in the middle of the book. I hated the love triangle, because no one in it seemed to actually like anyone else, let alone have strong feelings of love. Mason turning into a power-hungry throne-seeker who tricked Mare and tried to kill his brother just didn't feel believable to me.

In my last round of book speed dating, I included this book. I knew within the first few pages that I would go on to finish it! "Hannah was well aware of her own rebellious nature. Her parents had scolded her for it all her life ... Most often, it was for voicing the questions that cropped up so insistently in her mind: 'Why is it immodest for girls not to wear shirts but not for boys?' "Why does God let innocent people suffer?' 'If Jesus turned water into wine, why is it wrong for people to drink it?' These questions exasperated her parents, especially her mother, who would make her sit in silence for hours and reflect on her presumption. Good girls, Hannah came to understand, did not ask why. They did not even wonder it in their most private thoughts." With this description of Hannah, I knew I had found a kindred spirit. The world of When She Woke is a dystopian future where a virus has made it impossible for almost every woman to reproduce. Texas Republicans used this as an opportunity to enact laws making abortion murder, with the rest of the country quickly following suit. Somewhere along the line, criminals are grouped by type of crime and chromed, ie: their skin is injected with a permanent shading. Murderers are chromed red, and abortion is murder. The novel starts with Hannah in jail and newly chromed for her conviction. I loved the beginning. Except for the chroming which is an obvious shout-out to The Scarlet Letter in a futuristic way, the setting is not that impossible to imagine based on recent moves in some state governments to limit female reproductive rights. How much would some of those politicians love it if they could identify women who had had abortions by their skin? Slut shaming would be so much easier! The world is scary and not just for how criminals are treated. Hannah's sister is in an abusive relationship because she has been taught to be obedient. Hannah is taken advantage of by a religious leader for the same reason. Women throughout the society have zero control over their own lives. But any criminal is suffering the same way. Prison time is short, thirty days, but chroming is forever. The second half of the novel was less successful to me, lots of kidnappings and random groups of people, an interesting resistance/underground movement, but I never felt that Hannah took control of her own life! I wanted her to be stronger. I wanted her to make something change. But maybe that is what true dystopia is - either you escape or you play along. Either you are chromed or you are beaten. Nothing changes. And that may be the most chilling moral of this story.

A Flavia de Luce ebook short story. In this instance, the boy was not the killer, for the secretly ill housemaster suffered a heart attack and also slowly poisoned himself over time, but he did try to make the death scene seem much more complicated to implicate his fellow classmates so the blame wasn't focused on him as the discoverer (he and the housemaster had a blazing row shortly before this, so he felt suspicion may have easily fallen on him). A sort of abrupt Flavia story. I snapped it up quickly because I love Flavia so, but I much prefer Bradley's novels to this short piece.

Review: Protagonists: So this book focuses on two protagonists, Annie and Wes, starting with Wes. Wes is a film student taking summer course at NYU. He wants to go to school there full time, but unfortunately doesn't know if he's cut out for it, he also isn't quite sure how his family will feel about him being so far away. I liked the character of Wes, he's kind of a generic male protagonist who over the course of the book grows and develops into a much more unique and interesting point-of-view. Annie Van Sinderen is a bit of a rebel. She know she's supposed to be a proper lady, but constantly sneaks out to be with a boy her parents wouldn't approve of given his social standing. After waking up with a strange feeling of de ja vu and thing constantly and quite literally changing around her she doesn't know what's going on and the only person who could help her out is Wes. I liked Annie a lot more than Wes, she was a much more interesting character from the start and she just got better as the book went on. **There is a minor spoiler mentioned fairly frequently from here on out, proceed with caution! Romance: So there is a love triangle in this book, and with it being a standalone I was a bit apprehensive, but it was alright in the end. The thing is though I couldn't take the love triangle seriously. Annie is a ghost, there's no way they could end up together. If Annie and Wes were just friends in this book and Wes focused most of his attentions on Maddie instead the romance would have made a lot more sense. I felt that although the love triangle, under more normal circumstances, would have been one of the better ones I've read, in this situation it just kind of fell flat and the situation just kind of resolved itself without much payoff. World-Building: So the gimmick of this book is that it's a ghost story that doesn't use the word "ghost." At first I thought this was a great idea, possibly leaving some room for ambiguity and readers to interpret the book in different ways, however, the gimmick fell very, very flat. The word "ghost" never appears in this story, instead the author uses synonyms to make up for it, sometimes using spirit but most often using the term "Rip Van Winkle" that Annie came up with to avoid using said g-word, trust me it makes more sense in context. The thing is, if the author actually used the word "ghost" the story would still be the same and I don't think I would have liked it any less, in fact I may have actually liked it more since the author wouldn't have been tip-toeing around the word that everyone is thinking and driving me a tad crazy. Predictability: For the most part this book is pretty easy to figure out. The foreshadowing is pretty heavy handed and things just click together very easily. I have to say though that as the story came to a close there were a few things that I didn't expect, and things that I thought would get resolved that were left up in the air, but I'll get to that later. Anyway, I was never annoyed with the blatant foreshadowing and the twists were still fun and easy to enjoy even when things seemed a tad too convenient. Ending: So the ending leaves much open to interpretation and there were quite a few things left hanging, just not enough for a sequel. It's pretty easy to figure out why things were the way they were more or less, even though I'm still very confused about a few things. Even though I wish there was a more conclusive and wrapped up ending to this story, I did enjoy how everything came together in the end. Rating: So I did really like this book. The ghost story is more Casper than 13 Ghosts, but it's still an enjoyable read nonetheless. There were a few things that weren't for me but they didn't hinder the multi-layered and magnificent story that unfolded all that much.

This is a fun little title that's thankfully an improvement of the very lack-luster Wolverine and Wolverines of recent years. Taylor does a good job of characterizing Laura as someone really trying to find her way in the world, repeating some of Logan's character beats from the '80s, but still managing to feel original. The story itself is interesting too, as Laura tries to figure out how to deal with her own clones. It's a nice extension of Laura's own backstory, but feels innovative at the same time. My only complaint is that the big reveal at the end fell flat for me because I don't remember the minor character in question. Not an amazing comic, but an enjoyable one that I want to see more of.

Not unenjoyable, but nothing really new here. I like how Marcus is handled, there's a bit more insight in him. I'm somewhat appalled to find something to scratch my head about in such a short work, but that 1. it had been a decade since the last Abnegation-Dauntless transfer since Tobias, 2. Amar had become an instructor three years prior to Tobias's Choosing, 3. Amar states in Allegiant that he's noticed a trend of Abnegation->Dauntless being soldiers, and of course 4. Nobody talks about their transferred faction supposedly  doesn't add up. It seems like an oversight made so that a character could make their pithy observation in Allegiant, but at this point in an author's career, is there really an excuse for such irreverence to one's own plotting? ah well, it was a short read anyway.

A standing ovation for this final volume of the series! I was on pins and needles about Bobby and Buddy and no only breathed a sigh of relief, but almost teared up. Who knew a little woodchuck human hybrid could be such a heartwarming character. I don't want to spoil anything, so I will just say that your questions will be answered and you'll say goodbye to some good characters. Yet you'll also be hopeful, and you will be reminded of the bonds of friendship and family. DNA has nothing to do with it. Be respectful of nature. Oh, and one more thing: don't make ancient gods angry .

I liked this, but I kind of wanted the plot to be different! I was looking forward to seeing what these super-ghosts were all about! And I didn't like that Gregor (was that his name?) was evil. I thought it would've been cooler if he'd been someone with powers who didn't really know about them.
Fun and interesting. A bit rough and boyish.

This is going to be a shorter review, because I'm already so anxious to start Book Six. Trapped is a return to form for the series by far. Gone are the days of Coyote, or the invincible slayer of demons, and we're brought back to the Atticus that we knew at the beginning of the series. Vulnerable, worrisome, and candid. I was skeptical at first of the bringing up of his apprentice. It's something you could see coming from a mile away, but you wanted it so bad the whole time. On that other hand though, you didn't want it to happen, because you know exactly where it leads.... To excitement, that's where. Spoilers ahead! The way that Bacchus got kicked into the portal to the River of Time felt easy, too much of a gimmie, but at the same time, I'm glad they were able to get rid of him in that way. One can only hope that whoever is working with the Fae don't know of that transgression. While I would have liked more time in Hel at the end of the book, reading it I felt that anticipation and fear that Atticus and co. must have felt leading up to the final 'boss fight'. The only plot hole I could really come up with was...well...why didn't Hel just send Garm after Atticus once more? It happened once, why not again? Sans that minor point, the book was a great return to the fun, modern fantasy action drama that we were treated to earlier in the series. Hearne finally hit a stride on this book, and keeps on running, literally , into the next. Now, if you'll excuse me, I'm off to follow them down the rabbit hole.

Not sure if I want to give this 3.5 or 4 stars. I enjoyed it. I liked Rue from the beginning... I also enjoyed the inclusion of certain characters from Timeless. I am not certain, however, of the ending. In this case, it seems as though intentionally left with the story not wrapped up to get you to read the following novel - yet with the absence of a cliffhanger. It's rather annoying. However I really did enjoy and appreciate the slow burn of Quesnel and Rue's relationship. A bit surprised Percy didn't put up more of a fight. All the quipping between the three (Rue and Quesnel especially) was amusing. A few other characters I would have liked to see more of, from the previous generation... Like Lyall. And seeing Biffy in charge. Maybe in Imprudence? One can only hope. I suppose I'm leaning more towards 3.5 stars after all, all things considered. Even though I found it difficult to tear myself away from this book these last few days. I suppose what I wish most of all, is that it were longer...

After Emma's first 16 days of impersonating her long lost dead twin Sutton, she has shone light on memorize from the past that people wish would have stayed there. Now that Emma has a list of suspects that fit the role of Sutton's murderer, she finds out that many of her suspects have alibi's for August 31st, which was the day Sutton died. But when Emma starts to get close to some interesting facts from Sutton's past she is putting her and her partner, Ethan's life at risk. But when one of her decisions has a fatal consequence what will Emma do?

DNF First of all I have to say that I am a huge fan of Brittainy Cherry. Her 'The Air He Breathes' is one of my all time favorites and I really loved 'Loving Mr. Daniels'. I was loving this a lot during the first half. Aria and Levi were just too sweet. The book was making me smile like an idiot one minute and cry the next minute. I adored Levi so much! !He was perfect. He is for sure one of the sweetest and best heros ever! My favorite part of the book for sure<3 :) I loved the supporting characters Simon and Abigail too!Brittainy Cherry's style of writing is always so unique and heartfelt.But the twist ruined the book for me and I couldn't continue after this point. I just skimmed the rest to read some important scenes till the endAria decided to give up her baby :(( The whole Keira-Paul not being able to have a baby was too much of a coincidence and also it reminded me too much of Juno. Also I get it that Aria wanted the best for the baby and she wanted to help Keira and Paul but I still couldn't understand or feel for her anymore. The beginning dragged on a bit. It took me a little time to actually get into it but once I did (at about 30%), I really enjoyed it. There were some parts for me that were a little repetitive but it didn't lose my interest.
Story could've been great if they didn't skip so much details.

I've been Reading the Man Booker shortlist. I gave up on How To Be Both, by Ali Smith and J, by Howard Jacobson for the same reason, even though they are seemingly very different. J is set in a dystopian future, after an event referred to by the characters as "what happened, if it happened". It's a totalitarian world, in which the approach taken to ensure that event is not repeated is to force people to forget about it and deny what's happened, rather than our world's "never forget". Both are very much novels of ideas, which is something I usually like. In particular, I thought the ideas explored in the Jacobson were really intriguing (the way I've heard him describe it is what happens when you actually succeed in annihilating 'the enemy', and there's no one to attack but yourself). But in both books the characters created to explore those ideas just weren't up to it. They didn't behave in ways I felt made any sense or recognised as human. It might be that I'm a failure as a reader of serious literature by insisting on characters with internal coherence and with something in them that feels true, but if that's the case, so be it.

This book was a "I have remotely enjoyed watching the movies based on this and am in need of a cleanse" kind of book. I enjoyed the character Melody, who isn't in the movies at all, but she also was my least favorite character which is strange.

I really enjoyed The Magicians, but this one didn't really do it for me. I'm not sure what it was. It seemed to drag and jump about and left red herrings (Janet, The Order, Penny). Grossman used too many words, I think, and that diluted the potential punch of the story. There were some parts that were clearly supposed to be really poignant, but they were obscured by so much internal monologue on the part of the characters that I just didn't feel the impact. I expected to be bludgeoned (emotionally speaking) and instead got whacked with a foam mallet. "Quentin had always felt that way but now he felt this way. It pained him to feel this way. Frankly, he felt pissed. But, that's what he signed up for..." That kind of thing. That's not a direct quote, just my paraphrasing. Grossman's writing isn't that bad (it's not bad at all, really...it's just not as awesome as it was in the first book), but that's kind of the feeling I got while reading. I don't mean for this to be a negative review, and there were parts I enjoyed. It's possible, too, that I picked this one up too soon after Gaiman's American Gods and Jemisin's The Hundred Thousand Kingdoms, both of which dealt with similar issues of mortals interacting with gods and attaining "god" status themselves. Maybe if I'd read this one first, it would have held a little more oomph for me. As it was, though, I'm just kind of glad to be done with it. Now I need to take it back to the library so Lev Grossman's author photo on the book jacket stops looking at me reproachfully. I'm sorry! I just didn't really like it! I don't like Curtis Sittenfeld's books either, if that's any consolation.

A sneak peak for those who wants to know slightly about BDSM.. Plus the emotional connection of it. And though I failed to concentrate any further of the last 100 pages, I find the story worth a finish, for so many people are raving about the twist of the plot(and no, the end is quite seemingly predictable). I must say that beyond all the repetitive vocabs (i.e : murmurs, holy...,etc) and phrases (i.e : taking no prisoner,etc) I have just a tiny part of myself to reconsider on buying the next sequel. The Cover : Honestly if my reading group had not choosen Finding Sky as part of it monthly read I might not have otherwise have read it. Now don't misunderstand me, the art decoration is so simple... well not simple...elegant is a better word to use. The vine used with what looks like ribbon to intertwine a heart gives no indication as to what lies beneath the cover other that a possible romance of some kind. The Characters : Every book has them, heck without them the story would not have made it print. Well then again, it might have but I would not be interested in reading it. So, moving on we dive into the charming and some possibly not so charming characters of "Finding Sky". Guard your hearts ladies first up is the male lead!! Why you ask?? It's simple, because it's important to see if "Zed" is book boyfriend material. Why else? And the verdict is a solid yes. What girl, American or British can pass up a bad boy on a motorcycle? And to make him even yummier we find out that he has a heart of gold. Yes, ladies break out the fans because this is one bad boy we want our bad boys to reflect. Don't worry my fair gents, I didn't forget you, I'm sure you want to know if Sky Bright is girlfriend material. Being that well, umm.... I'm not a guy or into girls; I would still hand the verdict down as a solid yes. Yes she may seem weak and withdrawn at times, but who wouldn't with the shit she has suffered through. But when it comes down to protecting the ones she loves I think she has what it takes. Speaking of delicious characters and whether they are bf/gf material believe it or not "Finding Sky" has other characters besides Zed & Sky. The thing is if you really want to know if they bring the goods you are just going to have to read it.... after all I did. But I will give you a quick rundown. I have to start with Nelson: Sky human super hero... He is the kind of guy you want as your bff in high school. He's always ready to take the stand for a woman's honor. I was so glad the author found him love. I would have been disappointed had he not been rewarded. Tina: Tina is a first person to friend sky and become part of a side line story that is interesting. I was disappointed that it didn't dig deeper. And last but not least The Benedict Brothers : Yes you heard me....plural-- BROTHERS!! There are six other and I have a feeling they are all going to be yummy. Though we only get a peek at few of them as they play important roles in the story line. I can't wait as the series continues and we get a chance to get up close and personal as they find their soul finders. If you were to ask me, "Lissa did you like the book?" I would have to respond.... Did I like the book??? Are you completely mad??? I absolutely loved the book Zed turns out to b absolutely delicious I put my own order for a copy of Zed. I'm a bit disappointed he hasn't showed up yet. With my luck it was the answering machine I got and the message was deleted. My recommendation: Okay woman of all ages and guys who can handle a little chic lit.... run-- don't walk to your computer and log on to Amazon or B&N accounts and pick up your copy today.... Paperback, Nook or kindle no matter your vice they have pretty much anything. Remember be kind "like" my review before leave!
HP re-read 2015. This is one of my faves in the series. And still brings me to tears.
Love!!! on to the next one...xD

Justina didn't really care about going to Prom, until her best guy friend Ian convinced her to go with him. Ever since he wore that one shirt, she can't help but imagine how their first kiss would go. Justine has been in self-imposed non-kissing mode since that one party last summer which started all the rumors. But she knows if she's going to break her rule, Ian is the guy to do it with. Now only if she knew if he wanted to kiss her... Right off the bat Prom day doesn't go well. Her dress is not good, her shoes are even worse. Her mom gets involved, she starts getting random stains on her dress immediately, Alison keeps trying to mack on Ian, Ian keeps disappearing.... and then she wakes up in a ditch the next morning, DITCHED! This book was so Ehh for me. Just not what I was expecting at all. I LOVE books about prom and popularity and trying to get the guy to like you. LOVE that stuff when it's done right. This book just didn't get there for me at all. So you have Justina who shows up at a convenience store in her prom dress and proceeds to tell the middle-aged clerk and another self-proclaimed Cougar the story of her night... stain by stain. Like these women care! And then not only do the women care, they totally relate and agree that kissing moves Heaven and Earth. KISSING! Maybe I'm just too old, but kissing is not a big deal. Here's the good part: Justina goes on some crazy-amazing adventures during her prom night- and those I loved. The adventures were funny, silly, and the only part of the book I liked. There are these 2 stoner guys Mike and Mike and their dates who take Justina under their wing... and honestly I wish the book was about them! They were funny and endearing. I didn't like Justina... she's so dense, judgemental, and unlikable. In the end Ian DID ditch her... even if there is a reason, it's not good enough to leave your prom date and not let her know what you are doing. and like Justina didn't know Ian liked her... he basically tells her he does straight away so what's the mystery? The writing in this book isn't bad, it's the implausibility of the story that got me. Sorry if this sounded awful, the book is totally read-able. It flows good and I think there is an audience out there for it. I think that audience is middle-grade though. More @ http://pinkpolkadotbookblog.blogspot.com

*Listened to the Audio-book. I didn't expect to like this book, but I really enjoyed it. I am a person that loves organizing and getting rid of things or donating them, and I guess this is the reason why I love this book and want to follow her style of organizing "KonMari method". She discussed how to organize everything in your house; clothes, books, food, etc.. I liked everything about it except for the part she said that she ripped the pages she loved in the books she is didn't enjoy and wanted to get rid of it. This is not right! You can donate the book so another person can read it and may enjoy it more than you did. This part hurt me so badly. I also liked that the author respected the reader's emotions towards the things she wanted to convince him to give up. It felt like a friend was talking to me. "Imagine yourself living in a space that contains only things that spark joy. Isn't this the lifestyle you dream of? Keep only those things that speak to your heart. Then take the plunge and discard all the rest. By doing this you can reset your life and embark on a new lifestyle." Now, I want to see if the things I have spark joy or not. I am still not sure about it but I will give it a try!

Romance novels are not typically my thing... but this isn't your typical romance novel. This was a beautifully heartbreaking book that was written with so much intensity that I felt like I was living the story with Louisa and Will. I was honestly surprised at how many times I laughed while reading this. I absolutely loved all the sarcastic wit. When it comes to the ending, I am definitely disappointed. I wanted Will to choose to live so badly! I wanted Louisa to be enough for him, and to find out that she wasn't was excruciatingly heartbreaking. I was sobbing my eyes out by the end as I sure many other people were. I just kept thinking about what if something happened to my husband and he decided that this life was no longer worth living. Could I help him end his life? Could I be there for him when he decided it was time for it to be over? I don't know that I could take it. I don't normally rate books that I don't like the ending of 5 stars, but even with Will dying in the end... this is still a 5 star story. I'm really looking forward to reading After You, but I do have to admit that I am a bit scared.

Cash, Cash, Cash. What more can I say about Cash? He's the dudebro everyone wants to bang, and the adorable mush who had the ability to melt even my tar black heart. It takes a certain amount of skill to write a character who is so nuanced (he's a horny sweetheart and kind of a goofball, but he can also be ethnocentric and is self-aware enough to check himself because he is 100% aware of his own shortcomings) and have him read so damn real. Cash is a one-of-a-kind character, and one of my favorite of all time. He's just super fuckab--likable, and his voice is everything I imagined and all I wanted. There were also times when I related so strongly to things Cash thought or felt that I was like "damn, I feel you man". Steph and Cash are two side characters from Off Campus who were multifaceted enough to need their own story, and this is definitely the story they deserved. They both have their own hopes and dreams, their own fears and struggles, and I often found myself rooting for them or yelling at them in frustration because they were so real and their experiences resonated with me a lot. As a pairing, they were larger than life and bypassed Tom and Reese as my favorite couple in this universe (although I was thrilled that they had cameos). Oh and did I mention the sex was smoking hot? Because the sex was smoking hot. Not just because Amy Jo Cousins writes bomb ass sex scenes, but because Cash would pretty much do anything to please Steph. And he's very open-minded. Very VERY open-minded. *mysterious smirk* Never fear strictly M/M readers. There may be something in here for you yet.

Rebecca is one of those books I was always assumed I had read. I knew the basics of the plot, and of course the famous opening line, "Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again." When I realized I'd somehow missed reading it, I picked it up. It's the perfect book to curl up with on a rainy Sunday with a cup of tea. While I didn't love it as much as everyone else seems to, I certainly enjoyed it. While working as the companion to a rich woman on vacation in Monte Carlo, our unnamed protagonist meets wealthy widower Maximillian de Winter. After knowing each other only a few weeks, the pair decides to marry. After their honeymoon, the couple goes to de Winter's estate, Manderly. Our narrator, never full of self-confidence to begin with, is a bundle of nerves, as she becomes certain that her husband and everyone around her are comparing her unfavorably to her predecessor, Rebecca. Ah Rebecca. Beautiful, brilliant, lively, adventurous, perfect Rebecca, who accidently drowned a year before. The servants and the villagers seem to prefer her to our narrator. She sailed boats, threw wild parties, and was good at all the things rich wives should be good at. And everyone she meets falls over themselves to remind her of this. While wandering the halls of her new home, a servant informs her that Rebecca would spend this part of the day in the library, and so should she. Any attempt at change would be stymied with the proclamation that Rebecca had wanted it that way. Our girl, never particularly strong to begin with, wilts under the pressure. She's easily manipulated, especially by Mrs. Danvers, a maid who loved Rebecca. Her husband's kind of a dick, ignoring her if she displeases him, petting her head like a dog if she's done well. All that matters to her is making sure her husband is happy, and if something upsets him (like the freaking wind changes direction) it's obviously her fault. The setup of this book reminded me a lot of Jane Eyre. Both feature poor woman in love with the rich man. The rich man has a terrible secret regarding his first wife. Both couples are constrained by social norms (divorce is a truly great thing, y'all). I'm only bringing this up because I spent a lot of Rebecca annoyed with our weak-willed protagonist, begging her to grow a damn spine. Then I'd remind myself that she was from a different time, and it wasn't fair to impose my own values on her. Then I remember that Jane Eyre was published nearly a century beforehand, and Jane would NOT have tolerated this fuckery (Mr. Rochester was also a dickbag, but still). Our narrator is right. Maxim is keeping a secret from her. But it isn't that he loved his Rebecca. It's that he killed Rebecca. And instead of being horrified, our girl is thrilled! Because he hated Rebecca! And he loves her! Whoopee! Seriously, she doesn't even blink when he comes clean. Instead, she starts to develop confidence in herself because if her husband loves her, then she must be great. Girl, you should be a little concerned. Honestly, I had higher expectations for this book considering its long-term popularity. But I still enjoyed reading it. It kept my interest the whole time, and the prose was beautiful. It's the perfect book for a beach read or a long car trip. Just don't get your hopes up.

The thing that stands out the most, in my opinion, is the beautiful writing. It is written in such an innocent and gorgeous way that sometimes I felt like crying over the words. And then, the story is so powerful... the relationships between the characters is what makes the book. I personally loved the relationship between Liesel and Max (my favourite without a doubt) and Liesel and Hans. Obviously, as it is set in Nazi Germany during WWII, you know that it will not be a happy ending. When Liesel finds the bodies of all her loved ones at the end... it is a very tragic, sad and beautiful scene (the writing makes everything beautiful, even the war!)

In my opinion, this was the best Cal Leandros so far. Cal has a lot of much needed character growth, which I think will make future books better. He has amnesia (which Rob handled better than I expected) allowing him to look at himself objectively. He realizes Cal isn't such a nice guy and wasn't happy. You see a lot of his loyalty to Niko and his bravery. Overall, I thought Cal's self discovery quest was moving. Of course, the action is good, as always, and he is still your favorite smart @ss.

This is a cute book. It's written as letters between two cousins right after the Napoleonic Wars in Britain. It's fantasy both of the Jane Austen sort (everybody finds their True Love, gets married and never has any disagreements) and the magic sort. Charming and fun, but light.
A perfectly woven tale within a tale within a tale.

I have to say this, even though I will come back to it later in the review: I knew nothing about this trilogy, no spoilers and I am still good, but the one thing I kept hearing about was Kestral, whom I love, but no one speaks about Arin. I will get back to it. And you will see why I am surprise. This entire book took me by suprise. The world. The characters. The plot. The romance. The plot twist not so much, because I realise I knew it, but in my mind this was happening in book two. I will leave the characters in the end, because I really want to talk about them in spoilers and details. The world and the world building are so beautifully crafted. Given the fact that this is fantasy, with no magic, at least form what I know and read, the way the world works is still pretty intricate. I love how we see things from Kestrel's perspective, which after a while made me think why was she seeing all this like normality. Because to her it was. That was the society and she couldn't change that. Nor, from what I saw in the beginning thought of such a thing. Like I said, the world building is amazing (and *screams with joy* I've seen a map in book two), because Kestral is a strategist and sees things from a political point of view, thus showing how and why this came to be. The plot is not that straight forward. It suprised me where I was where I ended this book. Even though there are hints, because we see from third person's perspective, the plot is shaped into the actual plot (I am confusing everyone, I know) I think somewhere towards the half point. As for the action, I can say the first half is pretty slow, but that helps build the momentum, not to mention helps you know the characters and the world. So I say it is well deserved. The characters. I loved both main characters, and even though I really really liked Kestrel's way of doing things I was taken by surprise by Arin, because I never heard things about him. The focus with this trilogy always seems to be on Kestral, and is well deserved, because I love political plots and she helps with it, and I love intelligent characters that are not necessarily assasins. Plus I saw character development in her, which was big, by the way. But Arin, I never heard about his intelligence and funny remarks. About his strength and motivation. And I can't talk about him without spoilers, so sorry, but just letting you know he is an awesome character. Based on how the society works in this book: having Valorians and Herrani, one being the conquerer, the other being the conquered, thus slaves. The thing is that at some point is was hard to choose sides, because there was killing on both of them, but thinking about it, the Herrani had all the right to strike back. Let's remember the time Kestral was put by Cheat to wash his feet, yes he did exagerate with everything, but that does not mean on the Valorian side people like him did not existed. Arin, who was not strong enough to resist Kestrel, who let her go, even though it meant he might kill his people. This Arin was a surprise to me. Seeing him hurt when he let her go, made me stop for a second. He had tried everything to make her not see him as a threat. In the end giving up and letting her go. He is that one character who has been through a lot and shit keeps coming at him. I like that even though Kestral did a mistake she took it back, by agreeing to the emperor, which is one straight forward dude :'I have a son' - no way? Really? I conclusion, I really, highly recommend The Winner's Curse, for its characters, in the first place, for the world and plot and the romance, which I have not talk about, but it's beautiful and forbidden. And I think book two is going to torture me. Can't wait. And for the beautiful writing style. If I could give more than 5 stars I would, this was just amazing.

NEED. SEQUEL. NOW! I am blown away by this book. There is so much hype surrounding this novel that I was scared I wouldn't like it as much, but I have to say it completely lives up to the hype. It was action-packed, thrilling, and just all around fantastic. The characters were amazing and even the villains are written so beautifully that you can't help but be completely drawn into this world. I am so invested in this story now and can't wait to read more. I have to say that Elias Veturius is definitely my favorite character right now. I felt so much sympathy for him! He deals with one of the biggest internal struggles I have seen. He desperately wants to break his chains that the Empire holds on him. I can't wait to see him be completely free and happy because my heart breaks for this guy. His chapters were definitely my favorite because he so much going on between the Trials and his confusion over his relationship with Helene, plus his drawing attention to Laia. His journey is one to watch. Laia, was another delight. Her chapters weren't as entertaining because she spent most of her time just trying to survive being a slave to one of the most disgusting villains I've read since Levana (The Lunar Chronicles). Laia has her own internal struggle as she sees herself as the biggest coward because she didn't stay to save her brother. Her motivation to save her brother is what drives her and it's her loyalty that makes her so likeable. I can't wait to see her just turn completely bad@ss! This book had some pretty awesome secondary characters. I really enjoyed Izzi and Keenan and surprisingly Helene too. I hear so many mixed reviews on Helene but I didn't mind her. I could feel how strained her relationship with Elias had gotten and how confusing this was for her. My heart was breaking for their friendship at the end because they have been friends for years and I just felt like it's going to hurt for them to reunite in the future and be on opposite sides. I feel it.Keenan was okay. I liked him, but I wish I would have been able to see more of him to get a better grasp on him. But, the Commandant! Oh my god this woman was awful! You have to hand it to Tahir for writing one of the most awful persons in YA. Her relationship with her son and the way she sees him is heartbreaking! She really gives me the creeps. The plot was a little slow at times and felt like nothing was really happening, but the characters are so fantastic that I hardly even noticed. You really get to know the characters and what they are going through. The world-building was fantastic and it will be interesting to see more in the coming novels. The writing made it really easy to get into and see everything enfold perfectly. I was hooked from page one. What was a little funny was how we basically got a love square. I've seen people hate the romance in this book and it killed it for them, but to me it was so far in the background. Yes there is a lot of attraction that Laia and Elias keep thinking about, but it didn't overshadow everything going. At least not in my opinion. Overall, I absolutely loved this book. The wait fo rthe sequel is going to be unbearable and I sympathize those who have been waiting since last year. If you have not read this book yet, READ IT!

The orphans go to the town of V.F.D. where the entire village is the guardian of the children. They work and live with Hector, the handyman. Of course, Count Olaf (and the Quagmire triplets) are near and the Baudelaires have to figure out how to save them. Both Kaus and Sunny grow here. It's nice to see that they don't stay the same age/life cycle throughout the series.
This was a quick, fun read.

** spoiler alert ** Reading this story and my first time reading any books by this author, I noticed she always tend to go to a flashback almost all the time and continue with the current situation... if you get what I mean. I like that It was funny and the moral behind it plus the story it told and the characters that was in it (favorite character was Bengi), but I felt like it was unnecessary to keep going back and forth like that.... had me wondering what she was saying. I got and understood right away when Emaline would put "my father vs. my dad" and didn't really like the fact that Emaline moved so fast with another person after her and Luke been together for three years THREE YEARS I TELL YOU, but its all good I guess she wanted something different and Theo was most differently different, annoying, and rude. ughhh I hated him.
A nice retelling of Pride and Prejudice in a present-day setting? I say yes, and it was actually good to read. Not the best book but I quite enjoyed it.
Jac Jemc is a wickedly talented writer. review to come.

When I finished this book, I sat back and said, "Wow." That's how much I loved it. This story was funny, entertaining, and sweet with wonderful characters who I fell in love with. Here's an example of what I found funny (and this isn't even the snarky sarcastic stuff that comes later):Dani, how is it possible you're already dirty?" Jules sighed and led Dani to the sink. "Where did this come from? We were washing hands with the doorbell rang, and there's nothing sticky between here and there. "(Not to worry, the kids are only at the beginning and end.) It was great how he was a bit of a diva and didn't even know it and how shocked he was when he realized it. There was serious character growth which I really loved. I also appreciated how Reg's ego didn't get in the way. He was willing to have his job being working for JJ taking care of his needs  and doesn't have to have a separate career. The Gay For You was addressed, too, and in a way that I really liked and explained why I don't generally like GFY books:"People don't appreciate being mocked or--- "Nobody is mocking anyone," Reggie barked. Ignoring him, Bill continued, his voice louder. "Or having someone send a message that people can suddenly choose to be gay." He took a deep breath. "Think this through, Reggie. "If you can choose to be gay, you can choose to be straight, and I'm sure you can understand how problematic that concept is..."I had only one nitpick: You can never be sure you get every copy of something electronic. Never Seduce a Scot is a historical romance novel about a man and a woman from two feuding families who are brought together by an unexpected circumstance that changed their lives forever. Graeme Montgomery, laird of his clan, and Eveline Armstrong, daughter of the laird of Armstrong clan, have been decreed by the king of Scotland to marry. It would have been an auspicious prospect for both parties except for the fact that these two clans are archenemies and have been sharing bad blood with for years. But it was in the king's interest to join the two powerful clans through marriage all along so as to stop any future bloodshed between them and further strengthen his hold to his kingdom. Both clans are wise enough to avoid an altercation with the king and comply to his command, however bitterly. Graeme is naturally indignant with the idea of having to accept a truce from his family's most hated enemy and marrying a woman who everyone believes is daft and "touched". Eveline, on the other hand, is afraid to leave the family who accepts and loves her for who she is but recognizes that it is her noble duty as the daughter's laird to submit to the marriage bargain. Also, she holds a secret about herself that is central to the story. Eveline loses her hearing from a grave riding accident years back and learns to lip-read in order to understand the thoughts of others. She refuses to speak, being unable to gauge the proper timbre of her voice. Her family and clan, unaware of her true condition, begin to accept that she may not be mentally sound after periodically failing to respond to people (although she just couldn't hear them). For Eveline, though, her 'condition' proves to be convenient because it has prevented her from marrying the evil and manipulative Ian McHugh, to whom she was first betrothed. With the royal decree on hand and both clans incapable of repudiating the king's will, Graeme and Eveline marry and live...not happily ever after just yet. While Graeme is tolerant of Eveline and does not blame her for the 'sins' of her kin, his people (especially the women of his clan) do not share the same righteous sentiment and make it a point to disparage her at every turn. She mostly brushes off the maltreatment and tries to prove herself worthy to the clan, which Graeme finds admirable. Soon, Graeme finds himself liking and caring for his wife, who is beautiful, kind and astute in every way. Eveline feels the same way for Graeme and eventually trusts him with her secret. But there are clan members who still remain unhappy with Graeme's marriage to the daughter of a foe and help create a tension in the story that will eventually give us a virtual front seat view to the medieval way of rescuing a damsel in distress and a love that is forthcoming. The story is not the typical romance read that trivializes women's role in the society and gorges on a lot of detailed sex. Eveline as a woman and a person with disability is not rendered weak and small-minded. She is brave, competent and often sidesteps around difficult situations with grace. Graeme is a real charmer--he is kind, considerate and patient. Though feudal in most ways, he often allows Eveline to air out her thoughts and leaves room for her well-being. He also doesn't turn caveman at the sight of a beautiful woman at every turn, which seems to be the gruesome pattern of most novels I've read under this genre. While both of them enjoy intimacy, they are not too self-gratifying or needy--their 'lust' for each other is just right to remind us that what we are reading is a romance story, after all. And as I haven't read a lot of stories involving physically-challenged characters, it is very insightful of the author to draw one and add a personal touch to it, she being married to a man who has hearing impairment. Overall, I enjoyed this read. I think this is even my favorite Scottish historical romance novel to date.

This story is of Safiya and Iseult, two friends who are witches and live in Witchland.- Not very original, I know! Safiya is a Truthwitch (which is apparently rare) and is hiding this as she does not want to be a pawn in the war between different kingdoms. Iseult is a Threadwitch. The concept of threads is not explained but my guess its the essence and emotion of a person. The concept is really good but the execution not so much. Firstly, the book starts with a lot of information dump. I felt I am reading the 2nd book in the series because from the start I felt I am in middle of an ongoing story and should have been aware of the types of witches, their power and the land they hail from. There are different kingdoms about to go on war. No history or dynamics of these kingdoms is explained. Currently there is a 20 year peace treaty which is going to end- this is the only part which was clear to me. There are Monks ( which in simple terms are assassins- why the hell are they called Monks??) are pledged to guard Cahr Awen- what the hell is Cahr Awen is never fully explained! Safiya and Iseult are hinted to be the Cahr Awen in this book There are Guildmasters- who I think are like lords that serve the king but with special powers as they are witches. There is an interesting concept of Origin Wells- again not explained in detail and some sect known as Void Witches again too much is unknown about them There is something called Cleaving- Not Explained, why it happens? what triggers it? As you might have understood from the above rant that my main issue with this book is that the world building sucked. Safiya even though is the main protagonist is made up of NO substance and her romance with Merik did not interest me at all. So why not a 1 star? Iseult and the Bloodwitch made me keep on reading this even though I did not have any interest in the other parts of this story. The puppeteer is an interesting concept. I am not sure if I will read the next book in the series. It all depends on the reviews it gets once it's released.

I really loved this book. This is the first book that Jackson Pearce ever published, and I have to say that this was a great story. What would you wish for if you had a Jinn? At first, I thought, "I'd wish to be whatever body size I wanted, I'd want to find financial success an emotional reward in my work, and I'd like to never have to deal with depression again." Of course, my wishes were incredibly shallow, but if I could have something magical to correct the things in my life I'm not happy with, would I take them? That's the issue that Viola has to face. She's unhappy with her life ever since her boyfriend Lawrence came out to her. I think I loved the message of this book the most:  Only you can make you happy, not your significant other, not your friends, not your family. I thought that was an incredibly powerful message, one I've been waiting on all my life to hear. It's amazing all the things that you miss when you don't read. I really encourage others to read this book, especially young girls like I was at age thirteen. I wish I had this message when I was younger. Jackson has done vlogs about why book banning is wrong. Why should one person dictate you what to read? Shouldn't what you read be personal to you? We don't understand why a certain person wants to read what they read. I hate to think that this book could ever get banned quietly because I really want everybody to read this book!!

This did not work for me at all, though I can imagine that others by the author might be much more enjoyable, as I liked the touches of humour a lot. Lost for a few reasons: 1) the push-me-pull-you of the romance itself was much too thin to be credible. I could see Hugo's attraction to Serena because of her sheer stubborn courage in standing up to his attempts to break her. I could almost see Serena's having super-extra-insightful-vision enough to see beyond the ruthless and callous behaviour Hugo was famed for. Well, maybe not even 'almost'. But that he'd marry her and then after a riotous night of safely-wedded sex, send her off to her lavender farm in the country, vowing to have nothing more to do with her? Not so much. 2) there wasn't even the smallest attempt to make this historical (just pre-Victorian era) in anything more than the ways it suited the story: Serena has to be a governess, the historical period dictates that they're pretty powerless, like most servants, so when it's "proven" that she's had sex with someone, she's tossed out on her ear - a fallen woman, and that's the end of her chances of any kind of life. That suited the story, so it stayed. But then Hugo and Serena's language is not in keeping with this historical setting, so it just punctured the illusion of any serious attempt to make this read like 1830s. 3) YOU HAVE GOT TO BE KIDDING ME about what Serena wants from the Duke. Given that she's just had an extremely painful crash-course lesson in how people of her class are treated by the upper crust, she wants to torture her child by having the Duke send him to Eton -- ETON -- or pay for her to have a Season -- again, a Season -- why?? 4) The Duke's wife seems to be treated just as a handy plot point: nothing suggests that Hugo gave a damn about whatever poor (rich) girl he sent the Duke off to marry to save his fortune, but he shows great irritation at the Duke for not actually being faithful to this handy source-of-finance. And at the very end, Hugo gets revenge on the Duke by showing his confession to the Duchess - without the slightest consideration for how it might hurt her. 5) Story is too light to deal with a rape, especially as it was worse than it might have been because Serena was raped and led to blame herself for it. And the resolution of the scars it left her might have been sweet if it had been something much less devastating than a rape that had caused the scars.
