Enjoyed this book! Eveline might be playing "dumb" (literally) and allowing others to think her daft, but she's anything but... I like her spunk. It's interesting to see her try to extricate herself from the web that she innocently spun around her by her lies of omission. And I really hated that her father didn't believe her!!! And that even her brothers were deceived enough to take another "warrior's" word above their own, so-called beloved sister. Another reminder that in most of history, regardless of how obedient and dutiful women were, they were still not the voice that most men listened to first. Graeme is a romantic at heart, despite being a tough laird. He's loyal and determined to honor his promise to Eveline, despite her being the daughter of his most-hated adversary and enemy. I admired his commanding his clan to respect her and take care of Eveline. And I appreciated the fine line he had to walk when his own clan treated her so poorly. BECAUSE Graeme was so loyal and loving with Eveline, she was willing to do whatever it took to become part of his clan. And I flinched when she was taken advantage of. I was especially exasperated, disgusted, and disappointed with Nora. The story shows how strong and yet stupid in-bred hatred is. It's so easy to hate a name or a specific face... and to hate all those connected with that name/face (etc) simply because they're related or associated. Cruelty and separatist "we're better than they are because..." attitudes only breed ignorance and more hatred, which leads to unhappiness for all. Rorie is a treat! And I look forward to getting to know her better in future books. Especially because it seems likely that Rorie will end up falling madly in love with an "enemy"; just my own speculation, based on this book. (Either that or the Father who's teaching her to read and write!) I was a bit surprised at the ending... I guess being female kept Kiersten from being hanged, as she rightly should have been. Simply turning her out wasn't going to solve the problem; in fact, I think we'll see more of her in future books. Now she has even more reason to turn against the Montgomery and Armstrong clans. Looking forward to book #2.

2.5 stars I had a lot of trouble getting into this book. There were certain details that I found jarring and those details cropped up a lot. First of all, the magic users in theis book were called Grisha. Grisha is a diminutive of Grigoriy. So whenever the magic users were mentioned it was like reading about the great and wonderful powers of the Greg. Also, getting drunk on kvas would be like getting drink on root beer. There were some other things that bugged me but those were the main ones. Those who who aren't aware of these details might not be bothered by them, but to me they really stood out and bugged me every time they showed up. Especially the Grisha since they're mentioned a lot. While the supporting characters and villain were complex and well written, Alina felt flat. For the most part things just happened to her and she would either pout or mope about them. It wasn't until the mother of the villain shook her and told her what she needed to do that she actually did anything, but by that point I really didn't care about her anymore and was mainly reading for the supporting cast. The villain was really fantastic. He was manipulative and had reasons for what he did. From his point of view, what he was doing was for the greater good which was a nice change from all the mustache twirlers I've been running across lately. Alina's best friend Mal was also a fairly interesting character. He was able to avoid holding the idiot ball though most of the story where others in his position would be hording it. The problem was that in addition to Alina being bland, the plot was rather bland as well. It started out promising with armies and monsters, but then once Alina's power was discovered it immediately turned into the usual makeover and magic lessons which were just plain boring and lasted too long. Had there been intrigue or much world building it might have been more interesting, but instead we had Alina complaining about how bad she was at magic and barely trying to actually learn anything. The escape and chase that happened later were interesting enough to get me to the end, but in some ways came far to late and was over too quickly. Overall the book is okay. It really doesn't stand out among it's peers, but it's not badly written and the supporting cast was interesting enough. You can do worse, but you can also do much better.

If you've never read a book by Brittainy Cherry, you don't know what you're missing. You don't know about her writing that is most poetic, or the beautifully flawed and broken characters she brings to life, or the voice she gives to their heartbreaking stories. I could go on and on, but really, I just hope that you will read her books and fall in love with her like I have. The Silent Waters is the emotional, heartbreaking story about Maggie and Brooks. Maggie was so outgoing and loud until a monster literally took her voice and her freedom from her. Brooks became Maggie's anchor and never let her drown in her fear. When Brooks needed her to return the favor, she didn't let him drown, either. Their love was strong enough to bring them through the darkest of days. I know I am being dramatic and it reads like a fairy tale, but that's because the story felt that way to me. Maggie and Brooks fall in love when they are children, but circumstances keep them apart for many years. Their strength and determination, both together and separately when the other needed the support, was what I loved most about this book. Their intelligence, both emotionally and mentally, their kind and loving words, and their magnetic pull make this book magical. Ok, enough gushing about Ms Cherry and her book. I hope you will read The Silent Waters and love it as much as I did. I can't wait to see what she has in store for us in the last book of the Elements series. Firefly meets Heinlein juvenile. I've been wanting to read this for a year and finally got my copy. A rag tag crew take a lucrative job when they are chosen to open the first space-tunnel near a new member to the galactic community. We follow their spaceship on the year-long journey to get to the job and see how it all turns out. (That's the Firefly part.) It was a light, enjoyable read for the most part, especially with the imaginative species and worlds we encounter. It was an old school, straight forward, science fiction adventure tale. (That's the Heinlein juvenile part.) However, it was flawed in a few ways that kept me from really loving it. The author loves her characters so much that she seemed unwilling to have anything really bad happen to them. It soon fell into the pattern of the crew or a person being in peril and then, hey presto, an easy solution is pulled out of the hat. Everyone can go on their merry way. I almost never felt a bit of interest or worry about how something would be resolved for that reason. The one exception to this was Corbin, who seemed unlovable in every way. Perhaps that is why his story was the most interesting, albeit too brief, and his decisions the most moving. Also, the author's personal philosophy is visible like a gloss of shiny varnish. I can live with that but in a book this length, with very little action for the most part, it does get old after a while. And, that brings me to the third problem. The "Long Way" becomes even longer when most of it is spent on the relationships of the crew rather than anything else. When combined with conflicts that aren't allowed to be truly menacing, as mentioned previously, this leads to a trip that eventually becomes boring. This author can write compelling action and engrossing conflict. That is made abundantly clear in the last quarter of the book, which was very well handled. I rounded my 2-1/2 stars up to 3 because this is a first book. I enjoyed the authorial style and voice and hope that the future will see a better balance in the story telling. This made me want to reread a superior version of road-trip sf: Lord Valentine's Castle by Robert Silverberg. I'd also point you toward Earthrise by M.C.A. Hogarth, Hellspark by Janet Kagan, Citizen of the Galaxy by Robert Heinlein, or the Firefly tv series from Joss Whedon.

3.5 stars Anytime any book has Jane Austen in it, you know I'd be reading it (except, you know, if it also comes with zombies). I'm a sucker for anything Pride & Prejudice-esque, so I knew I had to read it. It took some reflection, but there were some Pride & Prejudice parallels. -Ezra was Darcy: the strong, silent type, whose first impressions were often misconstrued as being aloof and mean. -There was that scene where Ezra emerges from the pool, though not as gracefully, as Darcy did from the lake in P & P. -Ezra wrote a letter explaining things, just as Darcy did. -Devon was Lizzy: though witty and personable, she makes quick judgment on people and was quite oblivious to things around her For a character who had qualms about how Austen writes about first kiss, hers was lackluster -- I felt robbed! Still, my heart swooned at the dialogue between the two leads leading up to the kiss. There were minor characters that were very likeable but we didn't get too much of them. Foster, Lindsay, Jordan, Marabelle were all great, but I would have liked to have seen them developed more. Some I thought were just thrown in there, like Alex and Sophie, and Grace and Gwin, but they were inconsequential to the plot. Jordan was awesome but who was it that he was pining for? Who is the father of Marabelle's baby? Some closure is needed too: what did Devon end up writing her college essay on? What did she select as her major? Did she triumph over mediocrity? Did she get into Reeding? Will she be roommates with Lindsay? What about Cas? Did he end up with Lindsay? I loved seeing how Foster and Devon's relationship grew as they bonded and came to accept and embrace each other as family. Though I wished the story and the characters were developed more to achieve closure, it was a cute story and the characters were easy to love, and I loved it even more that it drew on Austen's works.

A short read takes you through Antony's life from school to retirement. The story takes you through decisions made and consequences. Friends and partners come and go, children grow up. A look at how events are viewed differently by different people and from different times in your own life. This book reminded me of Donna Tartt's Secret History, I think it was the way the main characters were able to look at their own lives in a detached way and perhaps the way the two main characters struggled with intimate relationships.

It's easy to see why Emma Donoghue has become a break-out author. A great story, wonderful writing, and especially fantastic characters. Some of the sex is quite graphic, which may turn off (ha!) some readers, but Donoghue's novel goes beyond simply telling the reader over and over about love and obsession to instead really working through why these characters might have had complicated relationships with each other.

The Good: Well it was very, very clever, and covered some interesting ideas. There were a couple of genuinely funny moments (THE MAGIC SCIENCE BOX GOES 'PING' WHEN IT'S READY! BWAHAHA)  and the end was touching. The Bad: The main characters were very flat, though I'm not certain they weren't meant to be that way - some peripheral characters that might not have been so peripheral  seemed more real. This is illustrative of Redshirts in general - it was so insanely meta I think it could almost be classed as fantasy or even philosophy. Despite sprinkles of funny, most of the humour is that condescending I'll-be-patient-but-you're-an-idiot nerdlike sarcasm that gets tired very quickly, and makes all the characters sound the same. 'Friends' character the protagonist is most like: Not only the protagonist but every other sarcastic wise-cracker in the book proved once and for all that there can be too much Chandler Bing.

Rating 3.5 stars By all indications I should not have liked this book, but I kinda did, yeah the sex was over the top and so was the hero with his possessiveness, plus the heroine did a TSTL thing at the end but despite that you sometimes have to enjoy the crazy ride and that is what I did.

This was deeply emotional and gorgeously written. I finished it with my eyes welling up, for so many motives but specially for  Ellie's last moments, for her life taken like that from her, for her very body being taken, her daughter, her happiness, her freedom, her being. I have been reading Lisa Jewell's novels for a while now and seeing how much she's been growing as an author. It's beautiful to see the evolution, how each new novel reads better, has an increase in its prose, in the plots, in character development. This one, in particular, made me so pleasantly surprised because it reminded me of a Ruth Rendell's standalone. This is the highest praise I can give any novel, since I have Rendell as one of the best writers of all times. I could feel her vibe here, in the way the story is presented, the way the separate parts are woven together, the way the characters' inner thoughts are introduced. A wonderful book, but one that will for sure break your heart.

I read this for a book club, otherwise I would never have read this at all. I'm completely averse to the romance genre because of its stigma of being completely and incredibly awful, and this book was no exception. I took great issue with the relationship between Holder and Sky, and how Sky's entire history seemed like a plot device just so she and Holder could have sex . I'm not sure when "stalking is romantic" became such a huge thing, but it's completely repulsive. Also, if I never again see the words "panty-dropping grin," it will be too soon. This was like reading a horrible fan fiction. The writing was juvenile, the plot was contrived and the dialogue was unrealistic. This could have been an amazing coming-of-age novel about self discovery and dealing with abuse , but instead it comes across as incredibly shallow.

I thought The Leavers was really well done, and I found myself reaching out to friends to talk about it. I just had so many feels! I believe this is Lisa Ko's debut novel, and boy does she show promise of crafting complex characters who are unflinchingly flawed. In The Leavers, the character choices are often frustrating but usually understandable. The plot itself revolves around Polly, a single mother and undocumented Chinese immigrant, who goes missing one day in New York. Polly and her son, Deming, are then both at the mercy of systems beyond their control. And Ko's story does a great (unsettling, fascinating) job of unmooring both characters, making me feel both may never feel at home anywhere, ever again.

By all accounts, I should have really loved this book. It's not to say I didn't - I enjoyed many things about it, including the writing, the Arabian-inspired fantasy setting, the interpretation of the famous 1,001 Nights story, the descriptions of food (my eyes were hearts and my mouth watering throughout), and the well-developed and interesting (mainly secondary) characters. Despina was especially wonderful and reminded me very much of Genya from the Grisha trilogy. However, this story is first and foremost a love story between Shahrzad and Khalid and that's where I failed to love it. It just happens too quickly. Shahrzad volunteers herself as tribute for a very specific reason: to seek revenge for her best friend's death at the hand of the boy ruler, Caliph Khalid. This seems to last about a day. After he lets her live, he starts calling her by intimate nicknames and once they kiss, it seems all hope is lost for them both. I just can't get my head around why Khalid took to Shazi so suddenly, that he was willing to endanger his country  for someone that he has only known for a few days. On the flip side, I also don't know why Shazi broke her resolve so easily. She struck me as a willful and smart character, who wouldn't let anything get in the way of her revenge, especially as she knew so little of him or his motives for killing his other wives. In this instance, the 'insta-love' or 'love conquers all' trope really didn't work for me. Basically, this love story is the opposite of everything I loved about The Winner's series - the choices Khalid and Shazi made were for selfish, childish reasons, as opposed to making sacrifices for the good of their country or cause. I also don't understand all the hate towards Tariq, because honestly, he's the only one whose motives clearly back up his actions in the whole book. I'll see what the reviews say about the sequel before continuing further with this series. I'm still deeply disappointed and I'm still desperately looking for an Arabic myth inspired book to love.

I was a bit skeptical when I read the first three chapters because of the way the chapters were presented. In contrast of the first book of the trilogy, Matched, Crossed was written in both Ky and Cassia's point of view and the chapters alternate between the two POVs. So the writing was a bit inconsistent in comparison of the first book. I do enjoy this particular style in literature, but it only works efficiently if the two POVs is completely different in ideals (for example Flipped by Wendelin Van Draanen). For the first couple of chapters, I got lost in which POV that I am currently reading, so have to flipped back to the beginning of the chapter to look. However, I did get used to it after five chapters or so and I am super glad that the author made the chapters the way they were as they elaborate Ky's character. Crossed picked up where Matched left off, where Cassia is sent to a camp so the Society can finalize her future and that Ky is sent of to Outer Provinces as a pawn of the Society. Cassia met a girl named, Indie, in which she befriended and escape with to find Ky. In Ky's POV, the audience learned that he is able to find friendship in Vick, whom he met at his work camp and Eli, whom remind him of Cassia brother. I really like the new characters, especially Vick and Eli and was sadden of what happened to Vick. Also, perhaps just me, I felt that Cassia's and Ky's reunion was a bit...forced in the way Ally Condie portrayed. Indie, however, I felt like she is starting a love-square in some ways. Although Cassia and Ky's POVs were interesting to read. I didn't enjoy both character as I did in the first book. I felt that the confrontation part was a bit later in the novel and the climax did not do justice. In addition, both character development was intriguing until the very end, they were still clueless about what they really want. I felt that the important decision that they have to make was a bit rushed. However, I like how Xander was put back in the story even though there was a brief appearance of him in the beginning but he wasn't lost at all in Crossed. Flashbacks of him were pretty much all over the book. I have hoped to know more about his character and his intention which I was not disapointed but I felt there were more things about Xander that should be put in the book (he wasn't a big focus in Matched either). Overall, I hope to find answers to the question in Reached (sigh...6 more months....). After reading Crossed, I understood Ky's character more since he was pretty much an enigma in Matched. Overall, Crossed was beautifully written. I especially enjoy how Ally Condie used poetry to tie everything together. The cliffhanger in the end was definitely intriguing, even more so than in Matched. I look forward reading Reached when it comes out.

What a phenomenally unique, interesting, and exciting book! The Palace Job is essentially Ocean's Eleven in a fantasy world, complete with humor and just slight hints of ridiculousness. The book starts out with Loch and her friend in a maximum security prison. To avoid spoilers, I will gloss over the plot, but essentially a team of thieves and miscreants must be assembled to steal an artifact. The series of chapters that describe said assemblage are just wickedly fun. The setting, magic, bits of steampunk, and plot are all awesome. I'm finding it difficult to go into more detail without giving away spoilers, so I will leave it at that.

For more reviews, Cover Snark and more, visit A Reader of Fictions. Actual Rating: 4.5 stars. My persistence with Stephanie Perkins totally paid off. I was so afraid I would be the black sheep on everything, but apparently Anna and the French Kiss is the only one for which I have mixed feelings. Lola and the Boy Next Door was adorbs in so many ways. Isla and the French Kiss was the perfect fluffiness and purest pain pretty much the whole way through. I'm hard-pressed to say which one was my favorite, because Isla definitely gave me the most emotions but I actually think Lola was a better novel. Make of this what you will. Isla's narrative voice was one of those that captured me immediately. Though she's probably the least overtly vivacious of Perkins' heroines, underneath Isla's as lively as any of them. Not only is Isla shy but she's introverted. Part of her journey is the realization that it might not hurt to let a couple more people in because friendship is really nice. As an introvert, much as you love your closest friends, it's sometimes hard to find the motivation to try to make more friends, but that can really screw you over if your friends move or there's drama or something. Much like Cath of Fangirl, I suspect some extroverts may have trouble relating to some of Isla's choices, but I totally felt along with her the whole way. As I mentioned in my post on instalove on Thursday, I do think that Josh and Isla are a case of instalove, BUT I don't think that's a bad thing. Josh and Isla fall in love over the course of about a month, which is pretty quick but not necessarily instalove levels. However, both swear they've been in love from the very beginning which is instalove and, likely, retconning. Despite the fact that I've been pretty vocal about my abhorrence for instalove, Perkins has done it right. With Josh and Isla, I can see their connection unfolding and I can feel the passion they have for one another. In this case, I actually think these two crazy kids stand a chance of lasting, perhaps not forever but for a good while. They are one of the cutest couples. In fact, they would be nauseatingly sincere were it not for their awkward moments and light banter. Perkins strikes the balance between these things perfectly, so that even a grump like me can read Isla and be charmed rather than annoyed. Either that or I'm softening in my old age (I'm 27 now, guys, so maybe I'm different). The other aspect of the instalove between Josh and Isla that makes it work in this instance is that you see them having to adjust. They were in love with what they knew initially for sure, but what they'd previously observed wasn't the whole person. Isla didn't know Josh's past or he Isla's. They were in love with the surface-level things and they need to deal with the rest. Everything is not perfect between Josh and Isla. They have issues they have to work through. I like how Perkins shows that they're in love but that have to get to know each other and that the instalove might not be enough. It also helps, I think, that they've both been in relationships before and have something to compare their current feelings to. Actually, I love books about characters that get together at the beginning because it happens so rarely. Much as I love my genderbending and hate to love romance tropes, they tend to have the couple getting together at the very end and you never really get to see them together and dealing with the reality and difficulties of an actual relationship. Though it might seem highly dramatic, it's wonderful to watch Josh and Isla work through her insecurities in the relationship and the trouble that Josh's past causes logistically. The barriers to their relationship are largely internal and all completely believable. On top of the romance, I loved the lessons about friendship wholeheartedly. It's highly powerful that Isla's just about as jealous of Josh's friend group as she is of his relationship with Rashmi. I love Isla so much for her friendship with Kurt and how much she values it. I love too that Perkins made Kurt a real, non-stereotypical character. Watching Isla's relationship with her sister Hattie grow gave me all the feels, as did her discussion with Sanjita, though those feels were bittersweet. The romance is the main part of the book, but the bits about friends and family are strong and touching. They give the book additional depth and power. Unfortunately, I wasn't a huge fan of the last four chapters or so of the book. I thought I would be rating Isla and the Happily Ever After five stars, but then the ending happened. I'm going to have to go into spoiler tags for details, but the short version is that it's cheesy and feels imbalanced, losing the awkwardness and banter and going full-on schmaltz. First, St. Clair and Anna get engaged, which, seriously, BARF. They are NINETEEN and have been dating for less than a year. Not fucking necessary, kids. I really try to not hate them and they make it impossible. All I want is to see them going through a divorce or not going through with their engagemnt in a later Perkins novel, much as that will make me unpopular. THEN Josh and Isla disappoint me. She gives him some good literary criticism on his graphic novel as well as hurt girlfriend feels. He edits it and gives her the new version to show that he still loves her and makes it ALL ABOUT THEIR ROMANCE. He even tells her how she's supposed to respond. It's vomitous. The graphic novel sounds SO much worse. It's retconning to the max and I cannot even with how it starts: "There's the page that I've seen before of him racing home to draw me, but then there's a new full-page illustration of me with the garden-rose halo. I glow on the page like something sacred. Josh is on his knees at the bottom of the illustration, looking up at me, weeping, his hands clasped. The word Salvation pours from his lips." THIS SERIOUSLY FUCKING HAPPENED (on page 321 of the ARC). I was SO on board this ship and now I kind of want to get off, because why the fuck is Isla Jesus now? Then Isla's all "I like it more not because I'm in it so much now but because it's better." Lies, girl. LIES. So yeah, the ending was upsetting. However the rest was all so good that I'm going to try to forgive the book for that. Isla and the Happily Ever After is where the adorable and sexy and painful feels live. It's the best example of instalove in contemporary YA perhaps. It's also a bit obnoxious at the end, but, hey, nobody's perfect.

This book makes me really glad that I live in America. Listening to Lakshmi's mother describe what to expect out of life once she is married made my heart hurt, and made me insanely grateful that I do not live in a country like that, and that I do live in a country that allowes me the freedom to choose, and to be who and however I can make myself. I can't imagine living in a world where a man who does not and cannot work, who gambles away everything you work hard for, and who is, for all intents and purposes, useless, but is still desireable to living without any man at all. I would not wish that life on anyone. The true horror of the story hadn't even happened yet, and already my heart hurt for this young girl's life. The heart of the story doesn't start until her worthless stepfather sells her into slavery. I hope that he believes he is sending her off into the city to become a maid, but I have a really hard time believing that most of the men who sell these young girls (fathers, brothers, uncles etc) know nothing about where they are going to end up. I have a horrid suspicion that they know exactly where they are going. It makes me sick, it makes me angry, mad, and, it breaks my heart. I felt for poor Lakshmi. What a horrible life to find yourself suddenly shoved into. Nothing in her quiet life could possibly have prepared her for that. It disgusts me that this is such a large part of our world. I do feel that the ending was perhaps a tad unrealistic, but at the same time, you need some ray of hope for this suffering child. And, some of them do get free. I feel that a line from Lakshmi in the middle of the story sums up my feelings her fairly well. After she watches Mumtaz bribe the police man, she says "I don't understand this city. It is full of so many bad people. Even the people who are supposed to be good." What a horrible place to find yourself in, when you can't even trust in the people who are supposed to be there to keep you safe.

Rating: 5 stars - This was an amazing book! This book was everything I wanted: a badass heroine, a solid plot, and a surprise twist at the end. The story is about Alosa, the daughter of the Pirate King who intentionally lets herself be captured onto an enemy ship to look for a treasure map. Although this book wasn't the thrilling kind that had me on the edge of my seat, I was hooked onto it from the first page, sharing Alosa's frustration and problems throughout the book. I also felt that the book set up and explained the various plot devices well - Alosa's Siren powers and both her comfort and aversion to the sea  - and yet left enough loose ends for us to anticipate the next book. Things I Liked: ALOSA. She was easily my favourite part of the book, and the biggest reason why this book was so enjoyable for me. Alosa was an amazing heroine full of sass and general badass-ery. She was confident of her own skills, and wholly unapologetic of her independence in the pirate business. She might have sounded a little overconfident at the start of the book, but the introduction of her powers added a whole different dimension of humanity to her character. Her constant struggle to maintain her own humanity led to her refusal to rely on her powers and to use her wits and skills instead. I also liked that she wasn't whiny about the brutal training she went through under her father, and instead viewed it as a strength and a testament to her confidence in her own skills. The loyalty of Alosa's own crew which was made up of - gasp! - mostly women! I loved their concern for their captain and the bond between them, and that Alosa put the welfare of her crew first. Each crew member was also a badass in their own right, with their own set of skills and are able to hold their own in a fight with men. The twist at the end. I totally saw it coming that Theris was going to be a betrayer, but I totally did not expect him to be the pirate lord Vordan himself! Things I Didn't Like: Riden. I didn't really dislike him, but he was just meh as a character/love interest for me. I wasn't as invested in his character as most of the time I didn't know how he was trying to help Alosa - I think a little more explanation from him would have been better. The love between them was also not as developed as I would have liked it, but maybe this development is reserved for the next book. And that's about it. There wasn't much for me to dislike about this book, except maybe the coldness of the Pirate King himself - although I guess you'd have to be cold and ruthless to be the ruler of the seas. Overall, this was a great book with a great main character and I am eagerly anticipating the next book!

"Tell the truth. Write the story." Tree Grows in Brooklyn feels autobiographical, and in fact it is. Betty Smith grew up in Williamsburg with an alcoholic father and a mother who favored her son. She worked at an artificial flower factory and as a press clipper. Some elements of the story are made up: most obviously, of course, Smith's omniscient narrator frequently dips into other characters' heads, and those bits - frequently, as with the sketch of the lonely saloon owner Mr. McGarrity, among the wisest sections of the book - were surely invented. Most oddly, the from-nowhere incident of the predator, shot in the dick by Frances' mother,  both feels and probably was made up, or anyway transposed from neighborhood legend into Frances' story. But most of it is based on her own life. "Brooklyn's better." "It hasn't got skyscrapers like New York, has it?" "No. But there's a feeling about it - oh, I can't explain it. You've got to live in Brooklyn to know." And very specifically based, too: Smith is Balzacian in her attention to detail. Her characters don't just buy an apple. They go to a specific, real corner, like Bogart and Moore in East Williamsburg, where they buy something else because an apple costs a dime and you can get a potato for free and here are the other things you can get for a dime. It's like an instruction manual on how to be poor in Brooklyn in the early 1900s. This precision is my favorite thing about the book. "Brooklyn. It's a magic city and it isn't real." Less successful is its sentimentality. It veers into corny territory with abandon. This is essentially ye old up-by-the-bootstraps story: it's probably not coincidental that Frances' father shares a name with a character from a Horatio Alger book. Fine as a novel; brilliant as a portrait of a specific place in a specific time.

I really can't figure out why but having said that she is far from unknown on this site. And rightly so. This book had a terrific plot and was written very well. It was unique enough to separate itself from the heavy crime thriller genre...oooo, until the end... It was so disappointing that Marsons chose to climax the near end of this novel with the all too familiar and stupid trope of: the killer having the detective at his mercy, and instead of killing her right away, he decides to calmly profess his manifesto: confessing to all his crimes, explaining why, and giving ample time for the cavalry to show up for the big rescue. I almost one-starred this novel just for that. And the all too convenience of Kim Stone also being a former ward of orphanages (or homes for unwanted kids, whatever you want to call them), investigating murders of wards of similar institutions, and she's also a twin, and her mother was also a drug addict...guh. Way too manufactured here to match this case. Oh well. I see the rest of the books in the series are ranked higher than this one so I trust they do in fact improve. But I will say that there was a lot to like about this one for the first 80%, really. So three stars seems fair to me.

I received this book as an ARC from netgalley.com So I went into this book thinking it would be all fluff and a quick read. I'm not usually a contemporary lit fan. The very next day, she went to her grandmother's house to empty it out because her Grandma just moved into a "swanky retirement community". This was a very enjoyable read and a lovely noir Urban Fantasy. The setup and world are grim without being grimdark and the plot and characters are layered in shades of gray with a story that is loaded with lots of really bad options and a choice to be made. The main character is key to enjoying this kind of story and Schaefer nailed that with Daniel Faust. A magician and sometimes con, Daniel does his best with what he has at any given time. He does mostly odd-jobs, including investigations for others, often using his magic (both kinds) to do so. It was interesting to see him blend real magic with sleight of hand depending on the needs of the situation (including using a non-magical trick for the final resolution and defeat of the bad guy Indeed, the magic in the book is a fantastically eclectic mixture of styles and capabilities. If you take Jim Butcher's magic that works through personal interpretation and dial that up to "weird", this is about where you'd end up. A system where Creole Voodoo is as valid and potent as astral projection or hermeneutical ritual or what have you. Schaefer pulls out some serious weirdness with both the good guys and the bad and I really enjoyed both the creativity and the interactions that deeply individualized system entailed (without being a simple free-for-all with anything legal and/or allowed). The theology (with demons and angels but no god or devil) is a bit loosey goosey but that's not really a bad thing and avoids stepping on the toes of the faithful, so no harm no foul. And I even liked Caitlin, though her character tended to morph situationally--as you might expect of a demon, though not in a bad way. She can go from retribution to uncertainty in the blink of an eye, but always in ways that made sense without breaking her character into mere whim or authorial intrusion. With one exception I'll get to. The book really shines in the pacing and plot, though. Yeah, I was totally with Daniel and happy to see him wage his private war against scum and villainy in a colorful (if somewhat dark) world of magic and demons but the plot hit fast and never let go and I mean that in the best possible way. Schaefer does a fantastic job of giving us everything we need to know without ever bogging things down. He does cheat once or twice withholding things Daniel knew for the impact to hit at a more dramatic time, but the delay is never long or unreasonable and I was able to catch one or two as they unfolded and felt clever doing so. So nice work. The only place the novel didn't really work for me was in the relationship between Daniel and Caitlin. They go from zero to sixty awful dang fast and I just didn't buy it. It didn't explicitly claim instalove or anything, but it wasn't much slower than that. You can kind of justify it if you squint real hard because he meets her while she's bound/enslaved and we've established how that draws his emotions out. Total white knight complex. And you can see that she's intrigued by his rescuing her without trying to bargain or enslave her just because he considered it the right thing to do--and in spite of the high probability that she'd be more likely to push his face in that thank him for it . I can see that as a start of a relationship, maybe, but Schaefer seems to consider that more like enough in and of itself and once they decide to be together it feels like a relationship that's way more mature than it has any right to be. Rolling with that was disconcerting, but I liked them and their relationship well enough that it didn't take long for me to just sit back and enjoy. At least some of that was Schaefer's fun having Caitlin pull a lot of stunts that are jarring for being gender-reversed. Like Caitlin ordering food for him without thinking about it. Other instances are more subtle, but Schaefer seems to like playing with gender roles and he does it well enough that I was delighted to go along. Anyway, this was a fantastic find and I'm delighted to have a new series to enjoy. I hope the next live up to the promise of this first. A note about Steamy: Really light steam, really. Especially considering one of the characters is a succubus. There are a pair of explicit sex scenes but Schaefer doesn't linger or dwell on them much. Like the romance, Schaefer gets through them with a minimum of fuss and moves on with the story. Not a bad thing, I didn't think, but if you're looking for romance, this isn't that book.

I was really not expecting to, but I LOVED this book! I'd heard some pretty "eh" things before I started it, and I'm not normally into science fiction, and wow is the (hardcover) cover ugly, but Soulprint totally blew me away! It did have a few minor problems that stopped me from rating it higher, but I think that, in general, it's definitely underrated and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it to YA readers. "This is what a belief can do to you. It can drive you, without reason, without cause. It drives you more than law, more than love. It drives you until you are the belief. Until your very soul becomes imprisoned by it." My favorite part about this book was how entertaining it was and how hard it was to put down. I pretty much read this book in one sitting, because I just couldn't wait to see what was going to happen! Right from the beginning, I was completely hooked and the pacing was so on point that I never got bored or felt like it was dragging even a little bit. I also really enjoyed each of the characters. Alina was so relatable for me. I loved how she was really unassuming and shy at first, but over the course of the novel grew bolder, more confident, and just became a complete badass. And the other characters in the book were just as likable. I thought that the author did a good job of incorporating a believable romance that really added to the story without pulling too much focus away from the science fiction part of the plot. "But I know that's impossible. Souls have no memory. But I wonder, for the first time, if they can still be drawn to each other. If we wander restlessly until we find one another again. If some of us are full of yearning, driving us to keep moving, searching for something we can't quite name." The author also succeeded in creating a future world that was completely plausible and easy to understand for a newbie science fiction reader like me, but also (at least, I think) detailed enough to intrigue somebody who is looking for a bit more world-building than your typical YA fantasy/science fiction/dystopian. I wouldn't say that it has a ton of world-building, but the author does make it seem like Soulprint isn't set too far in the future, so I don't think a large amount is needed. It was actually kind of creepy to think of how easy it would be for our world to turn into one where a "soulprint" could actually be a thing! It's not really that crazy when you think about all of the DNA/genetics discoveries we've made over the past century. Overall, this book was just a really great read. Megan Miranda has definitely proven herself to me as an author, and I can't wait for her to come out with more books! Please consider overlooking the weird title and bad cover design and giving this one a shot! It totally exceeded the expectations I had for it.

I love the idea of each of the characters being representative of one of the major arcana. Its absolutely fascinating. I really think that with all these brilliant ideas to work on, it has the potential to become a really good book.

When I first started this book, the premise was just a little bit too boring, the characters were a little too meh, and the story-line was dragging. Yes, it was. I was supremely bored, and more than a little unhappy that I'd accepted this book's pitch. Then, when I was about 50 pages in, it suddenly just all came together. The character's became more developed, the story-line sky-rocketed to terrific, and best of all, the premise suddenly became amazing. Because of one simple reason: It suddenly became an epic fantasy. Dystopian was just not working for this book. When I was sent the review request, that's what I chalked it up to. A simple dystopian, just like the hundreds of others that have been released recently. Was I ever wrong. The book was clearly fantasy, and I can't believe that I missed it before. Honestly, I am so blind. But I'm glad I am, because after a certain dragon book, (I'm sure you can guess which one) I completely backed off fantasy. It just wasn't my thing, after that one book ruined it for me. And that was that. So, in retrospect, I never would have picked this book up if I thought it was fantasy. On one hand, I can see the dystopian elements, but it reads so much like a fantasy! Moving on, because I've spent a little too much time rambling about fantasy. While the characters weren't exactly phenomenal, they were more than enough to keep me entertained, and I really wanted to know what happened to them. Nathaniel, our lead character, was extremely brave, honest, and he just wanted to be a hero. Nathaniel was a dreamer, and I love that. We very rarely get to see dreamers anymore, because of the contemporary craze. Orah and Thomas were every bit as good as Nathaniel, but they lacked the leadership that Nathaniel ignites. The rebellion, and other spoilerish content, would not have began without Nathaniel. He's a born leader. And he deserves every bit of praise he gets. All in all, There Comes a Prophet was a fantasy of epic proportions, that kept me reading until the very end. Favorite Quote: "Ideas combined with Courage can change the world."

T. M. Frazier is the definitive creator of art of the Dark Romance and her King series is a wickedly sinful Star. "Preppy" features the ultimate Tragic Hero a knight in tarnished armor rescuing a Damaged Heroine, a troubled princess, who is literally falling off of her tower. Preppy is a well dressed demon with a heart of gold or a cold black heart if you cross him. This angelic looking rogue can easily, and quickly, go from a curse word spewing artisan to a cookie loving charmer of old ladies. (Who knew he was such a swoony letter writer???) He is a chameleon. He's a Savior and Evil Incarnate. Dre is tired and as much as she wants her next hit of heroin she doesn't want it more. She's been traveling with two "friends" one of which feels as though she deserves whatever bad things befall her. He and his friend are two bad things - they emotionally abuse her, keep her addicted, and constantly rape and beat her. Despite this she helps them in their illegal endeavors including robbing her own grandmother. Little do they realize that they are stealing product that belongs to a very dangerous man and now he's out for blood. Andrea, Dre/Doc, meets Preppy when she and the guys were robbing her senile grandmother but she is actually a caring and devoted granddaughter to the elderly woman in a very bad situation. Dre/Doc, surprises and fascinates Preppy at every turn so he is very much drawn to her. He saves her life and still allows her two favors. Again the favors are not what he expects. The first is to use his phone to call home saying that she's coming back, the second request is asking Preppy to spare the life of one of the guys who has been, essentially torturing her. The most dangerous and cruelest of the two men - a promise Preppy has no intention of keeping. For some reason Dre/Doc curbs Preppy's more dangerous sexual tastes. He still likes his sex dark, dangerous, and rough but he attempts to hold himself back from Doc for as long as he can. But he has an extremely difficult time not pouncing on her and taking her every chance he gets until their attraction to each other finally snaps. The longer Preppy and Dre/Doc spend time together the closer they become. The timeline mainly takes place before all of the previously published books in the King series. The timeframe occurs mainly during the time King is in prison. Bear is a prominent character in "Preppy". This book provides answers to questions you didn't know you had and then blindsides you with gut wrenching revelations about Preppy. Reading "Preppy" is like a gripping addiction. The action is thrilling, some of the revelations will make you gasp on a smile, and of course Preppy's own brand of irreverent, profane conversation enhancers which often riddle his cheeky running commentary. But then T. M. Frazier turns on a dime and takes out her rusty jagged little melon baller and guts you with a poignant scene that will having you shedding tears and haunt you long after you read it. As with all of the King series books heroes and heroines, Preppy and Dre take part in a seemingly ruthless yet romantic pas de deux. They waltz through a minefield of what they want - the easy and happiness filled route and the what they should do - the painful and callous path they end up having to travel. The scenes that take place in the present day are brutal and yet Preppy is at his audacious best. Although all of the books in the King series are fantastic - I never thought I'd like romances this dark - "Preppy" is, at least to me, the most meaty, weighty, and substantial book since it pulls so many puzzle piece together that you didn't realize were scattered. The breadth of emotion: fear, vulnerability, confidence, lust, love, and heartbreak, that is covered in "Preppy" along with the brutality of the action juxtaposed with the romance and passion, and finally T. M. Frazier lets loose a destruction of long held assumptions which makes this book incredible and an absolute necessity to be read for a more vivid and complete picture of the "King" world. Actual rating: 3.5. I'm bummed I didn't love this. I'm embarrassed to say that a reason I didn't love it is that I found the main character, Molly, extremely annoying. The embarrassing part is she annoyed me because she reminded me of myself at that age! I so remember the pain of being 17 and never having a boyfriend. Like Molly, I was convinced that I was the only 17-year-old girl in the world who was still a virgin and had never been in a relationship. Now that I'm older and wiser and have worked with teenagers for twenty-five years, I know that the Mollys are the norm. When you want a boyfriend SO BAD (or anything) it's easy to feel like you're the only one missing out. So all those icky insecure feelings swarmed around me while I was listening to this book. On a non-personal note, it also bothered me that Molly didn't find her worth until  the end of the book when she finally got a boyfriend. <\spoiler> I should also mention that I did not love the audiobook so that may have also affected my feelings about the book. What I did like: tons of diversity and lots of positive female friendships.

We takes the form of the diary of D-503, a mathematical engineer responsible for building the 'Integral', a space craft designed to carry the political dominance of the One State beyond the limits of Earth. His deep loyalty to the State is briefly threatened by an illicit love affair with the enigmatic E-330, who takes him beyond the Green Wall of the One State's domain D-503 is a well-chosen narrator, because he is not a rebel, but an intelligent servant of the state seduced by a rebel. His glacial style can be clunky and distant, but in some ways this adds to the power of the work. I felt that there was a certain predictability to some elements which in the end were fuzzily, unsatisfactorily resolved, but it is easy to be critical with the benefit of having read Orwell's response to We. It is an original, terrifying vision, throwing the deep anxieties of its era into sharp relief.

"Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde" by Robert Louis Stevenson [4/5] I read this novella because I am in love the musical adaptation of this by Frank Wildhorn and because I remembered the book is different than the musical. I read this book a long time ago in German but I couldn't remember much of it, so I thought a re-read might be a good idea. I re-read it in English because I want my English to improve and what is a better way than reading books written in English in the not translated version? It was more difficult than I thought though. This book has many words I needed to look up in a dictionary but I think this is due to English not being my native language. And there are really good reference pages in my edition that helped me to understand words that have another meaning now. But even if it was not easy to read, the language was fantastic. The atmosphere he created was outstanding and it was easy to imagine myself being part of this historical London. I hope Stevenson's other books are this amazing in choice of words and atmosphere. The story is different than the story of the musical, way different. But I already suspected this because even if it was a long time ago I had read this for the first time I remembered the characters of Lucy (a prostitute in the musical) or Lisa (Jekyll's wife in the musical) are not in the book. But I also love the story of the book. Utterson seems to be a nice guy and a good friend to Jekyll. I like him and his voice and even he is sometimes not easy to relate to (because of the time period this book was written in) he is a compelling character. I think it is sad, that we never see his reaction to Jekyll being Hyde  at the end of the novel. I think many people might be irritated by the lack of Jekyll and Hyde in the novella because most of the modern media adaptations have Jekyll and Hyde as the main characters and the poor Utterson is only a minor character (yes, I am looking at you musical adaptation). The novella keeps an interesting pace, not too slow but not as fast you might expect when you have seen some adaptations in modern media. Everything is told from Utterson's perspective or the perspective of people who tell Utterson about their encounter with Jekyll and/or Hyde. We don't get to know how cruel Hyde is actually we get only the feelings of other people on him. I think some people might be disappointed by this because many readers may expect a fast pace thriller and not kind of a detective story where Utterson wants to know who Hyde is because Jekyll makes him the heir to everything if he disappears. I think many of the magic of this book is ruined to modern day readers because most of the readers already know the solution of the strange case but Utterson only gets to know about it in the last part of the novella. I think the book is more enjoyable if you never ever heard of Doctor Jekyll and Mister Hyde but with a look to modern media (an upcoming movie starring Chris Evans; the BBC series; Penny Dreadful and other adaptations like the musical by Frank Wildhorn) this is nearly impossible. I recommend this book to people who are interested in the original story after meeting this character in other media!

I obtained this ARC at BEA14, in exchange for an honest review. Robin Trainer knows that being a popular television host is a precarious position- she has already fallen once, and had a long struggle to get back on top so she is adamant that nothing is going to throw her off the peak again. Unfortunately, her resolution is challenged when a malicious stalker seems to be watching her every move. The terror quickly escalates and goes from vague threats to more harmful actions as Robin struggles to reveal her enemy before the tricks turn deadly. Kate White's latest standalone is a great read- the breathless first person narrative is appealing, it's cleverly plotted and fast paced, and readers will not know whom to trust. I only had one minor complaint when I was done the love interest in the end had a stalkerish moment himself, with his conveniently mentioned volunteer work that was pushed aside when it wasn't convenient. Are we supposed to ignore that? Was it a hint that he's not to be trusted as well? Am I over-reading? I'm probably over-reading.

I really liked this story. A lot. Yes, there were issues, a few parts where editing missed some mistakes, and instances where the characters drove me crazy, but I like it. Jackie was a good character. I did struggle with her a bit as I felt she was too much in her own head. I felt like she was looking for every reason she could to be unhappy and I really wish she had allowed herself even a peak of happiness during the story because for as great as she and Will were together, she held back so much and it made so sad. I understand her ex really damaged her ability to trust and rely on others. But in so many ways, it felt like she was using him a crutch so she didn't have to feel things. Jeff hurt me, the world isn't pretty, I can't move on from it. But at least she figured it out and didn't let the fear win. Because honestly, her self-sabotaging ways were starting to weigh a little. Maybe part of it is due to her age. Her whole world changed drastically at 18, I wonder if, for all that she has gone through, a part of her became frozen at that age until something came along to help her grow. I loved Will. I see that seems to be a popular sentiment. But he is really wonderful. And I love how he's older. Older than me at least. So many H's are young and alpha and studs and stereotypes. But not Will. He was a man and a set one at that. He didn't have anything to prove to anyone because he had grown beyond those games. The way he was, in work, in friendship, and in love was wonderful. I really need to read more books with mature (older than 20's) H's because they are wonderful. Especially as I age. Even with what he went through with his ex, he still believed in love in the end. He still accepted it and his heart was just so beautiful. Karina Halle has given me another H to swoon over for this year. The side characters...we never meet Jeff but that's good because he was a douche. Casey was creepy. Can I say I felt bad for Mona being put on the spot like she was? That was mean, even if a point was trying to be made. Poor woman didn't know what was going on. Sasha was a piece of work. And I'm honestly trying to figure out how she got her way the way she did when she was in the wrong. But whatever. It just proves how great Will was. I loved Ty. He seemed very sweet and his interactions with Jackie felt real. His interactions with Will were positively lovely. So very sweet. I wish there were more, to be honest. I wish we could have met Will's mom but beggars can't be choosers. The office characters were fun, Alyssa and Tiffany, and even Patty at the end. Wish we could see more Emmett. I'm undecided about Jackie's parents. Well, more so her father, since it seems her mother was trying. Her dad...he left me hot and cold. First there was the way he treated her. I understand she made mistakes, left home without a word at 18 but at 18 she was an adult. Allowed to do what she did. It's not like she ran away at 16. He seemed very intent on making sure she knew all the ways she'd messed up. And I think Will was right; sometimes Ted was more childish than he accused Jackie of being. Because even though it was probably all out of hurt, he was supposed to be the parent, deal with it maturely and he didn't. Add in throwing Mona at Will and then in front of Jackie just made him very smarmy to me. I mean there is no mention of how he felt finding out his only child had been beaten and was terrified. It just felt like he needed to grovel. Even if he did redeem himself slightly at the end. The ending was pretty good. I'll admit to wanting more future. A glimpse of longer jump. But what we do get is pretty great. I love that there is a real future mapped out for Will and Jackie (and Ty) and it's not just a few months jump without any growth. I wish there was more. I loved reading about these characters.

The story or rather the battle continues as I ride the journey of what was to come between Claire and Anthony's lives. Literally a game of Chess~ Review is full of SPOILERS sorry! More unanswered questions awaits within these pages. Different POV I come across with, Anton's past, Burke's lives (these POV I still didn't find their significance in the story) and the present situation of Anthony and Claire. Claire was released early than what is expected, she didn't believe that someone is willing to set her free despite what was being accused of her. Then I saw Claire who struggles to experience the freedom she longed for, it was kind of short while, before she and Tony finally saw each other after a long time, yet she experienced getting access to the world, buying her own stuff, getting her own IDs, and proving that she can be independent. People appeared in her new life, such as Amber and Harry who helped her to have her new life. The entrance of Harry in the scene also made the story much more interesting. Despite Claire's resolve to get her revenge, she cannot stop the feeling that she's still longing for Anthony, that deep down in her heart, his stares or his touch still get into her skin. That despite there is someone who already cared about her, she still think of Tony. It was ridiculous but she's aware that she still have feelings for her ex-captor and ex-husband. "I have missed your voice, your strength, your smile, and mostly your eyes. My god, Claire, you have the most amazing eyes!" I don't know how could this guy can find the guts to say these words after all what humiliation he did to Claire. I admit that I do hate Anthony but as pages turn I can't wait to see his appearance. And I don't know why, I am guarded with the words he say and yet I look forward to his appearance again. "First, you're sorry for invading my privacy for years, years before I even knew you existed. Second, you're sorry for kidnapping me, isolating, controlling me, and manipulating me. Third, you're sorry for lying to me, pretending you cared and oh yeah, marrying me. Fourth, listen carefully Tony, this is a big one... you're sorry for framing me for attempted murder, resulting in incarceration in a federal penitentiary." Tenderly he closed his fingers encasing her petite hand. "I am deeply sorry for one and four." He rubbed the top of her hand with his thumb. "I did provide you with an alternative destination for number four." Claire exhaled audibly, Tony continued, "I am not proud of two, but three would never have happened without it." His tone deepened and slowed, "I am not, and never will be sorry for three. And, for the record, I never lied about or pretended to love you. I didn't realize it at first, but I have loved you since before you knew my name." "And, you forgot our divorce. I am sincerely sorry for that also. Had I known you would be released so soon, we could still be married." He placed her left hand on her knee, and stroked her empty fourth finger. "You could still officially be mine." In the entire statement of that, I literally raised my left eyebrow, as in! I can't believe it! I mean is he really serious? But above all that, Claire didn't give in easily, when Tony said those words to her, she didn't crumble to him like a love-sick puppy, instead she held her ground and face Tony's dark eyes. Between passing chapters, I got a glimpse of the Rawl's family, their past life and secrets. I still am trying to seek for what these events in the past that could connect how these affect Anthony's life. Aside from these I could see how Claire can move on to another man but then still cannot define what she and Harry is to one another. I could say Harry is a good guy and exactly different from Tony, yet I admit I'm not comfortable, I should be giggling how perfect timing this guy came into Claire's life There are really vague scenes in the past and the search of the answers that lead to who gave box full of secrets about Anthony's life still gets on my nerves, I think this is the first time that I read a story that I'm so into knowing the mystery and yet as the pages turn I'm still wondering what I really am looking for. I still am confused who is Sophia Burke, I'm already halfway and yet I don't understand her significance, aside from she is a good artist and painted Claire's wedding picture, which she received a generous amount. In their figurative game of chess, Anthony Rawlings had Claire in check. Every move she made, he countered. I am surely as hell hate Anthony with all of my heart and that's a fact! I was certain that his evilness cannot be crash and anyone couldn't surpass this manipulative bastard. He perfectly timed and counter all circumstances that can jeopardize his perfect appearance. No matter how many times he convey his feelings to Claire, I cannot see the rationale of what he is doing to Claire's life. I CANNOT FORM A GOOD RATIONALE OF WHAT HE IS DOING!!!! But he made this story so interesting I'm shaking from the awesomeness of this! In the few months since her pardon, Claire had rekindled relationships with friends and family, as well as forged new ones. Who did Tony have? In that sense, I was also in deep thought, and felt pity for Anthony's life, he may be the best and successful billionaire in the world but who did he have to share this success? He bent down, their noses nearly touched. "I'll accept friends with benefits, for now. Not forever." His lips brushed hers. OMG! Harry!! Claire is so lucky these two guys willing to take the risk for her! Everything in their power to keep her in their arms! I'm shocked by Harry's willingness to accept whatever there is when it comes to being with Claire. My mind is already going crazy with all these revelations about Nathaniel Rawls and Catherine Marie, somehow their romance life got the key of Anthony's past and why he's doing everything he can to control Claire's life. And then there's Sophia Burke. Plus Claire missing her period! (OMG I can't believe I'm being affected with everything here!) and I'm even nervous when she's waiting for the pregnancy test! Tony -- his magnetism, his control, his dominance -- was erotic. Claire also wanted freedoms and liberties. She wanted a non-monitored telephone, the ability to come and go, and freedoms... and him. I finally understand why even I cannot believe that even though I hate Tony's actions, his evilness at the end I'm still rooting for him hoping and looking for that good side, and he amaze me, with his actions he really did try to change and I'm happy but I'm still guarding my perception of him, but little by little I can see his change of heart. "I have made some bad decisions...and done some things I regret in my life... but without a doubt... what I regret the most... is divorcing you." His penetrating gaze held her emerald eyes captive. "If you tell me there is hope, that one day you'll be Mrs. Rawlings again, I will wait." HE GOT ME! HE TOTALLY GOT ME NOW!!!! OMG Tony! Can you be forever this perfect right now? I'll erase all my past hard feelings for you, just to be this sincere forever! This is, I guess the best thing that ever happened between Consequences and Truth. When things do come in good times, there is something that will really hinders that, now Claire experienced another tragic accident that added to her past physical aches. This time in order to be safe she needs to be in Rawlings estate in Iowa, as much as the people around her hating her with the decision especially knowing Anthony and her is kind of having a certain understanding, she cannot jeopardize and Anthony wouldn't let anything again that can hurt Claire. I stayed up all night just to finish this! And it gave me a cliff-hanger I'll never gonna get over with. I literally got a headache trying to understand all the clues hidden between these pages. And it literally slapped me with the revelations. I think I finally understand what this is all about, t's not about Anthony and Claire but it's about a dark past that leads to these unfortunate events that was a Consequence of such vengeance that leads to finding the Truth of all these actions that cause harm and death of people. I can't believe that I'm reading a long story about a past that was made by people who are stupid to accept the reality that life is harsh. inally got around to reading Moonraker, the third James Bond novel, after a several month hiatus. As seen on Impression Blend In the near future, a highly contagious virus sweeps through the world. The lucky ones experience flu-like symptoms and move on with their lives. The less lucky ones face stage two--meningitis, which can cause serious damage. Stage three hits a very small percentage of the victims, and it's my personal idea of hell: being fully conscious and aware, but unable to move or respond to any kind of stimulus--lock in. Thanks to the advances in technology there are a couple of options for those locked in: they can either use an integrator (control another human's body and experience the world that way), or use an android (referred to as a "threep") to continue interacting with the outside world. Our main character, Chris Shane, is an FBI agent investigating a peculiar crime scene, but he is also locked in and using a threep. This was my first foray into John Scalzi's work, and I have to say I'm off to a very good start. This novel grew on me the further in I got, and the writing style is very smart and intelligent. There are a lot of details, and definitely some very interesting ideas. For instance, Lock In presents a very interesting argument as far as cure vs. adjustment goes. On one hand, you have people advocating for a "cure", thinking those who are locked in want to be brought back. But many of the afflicted (referred to as "Hadens") are actually pretty comfortable in their own community: they have ways to access the world, but they can also spend time in this virtual reality world, free from any bounds. To them, there isn't much to "come back" to. I also thought the choice of a threep for a body was an interesting one. They are made to look like C3PO (and that's where the term comes from), which is reminiscent of a human body, but also much more durable and provide the used with certain technological advantages useful in everyday life. At the same time any crime against a threep is treated the same way as a crime against a human. There are legal and social details, which I'm not going to get into, that make this futuristic world seem real. When it comes to the integrators (the humans who allow themselves to be controlled by a Haden) there are psychological and physical implications to consider. My main complaint about the novel has to do with the characters themselves--it took me a while to really care about anybody. Sure, the crime investigation was interesting to follow, and I was invested in the story lines, but with the exception of Shane's parter (whom I warmed up to eventually) I never really felt connected to anyone. The only other issue I had was with the ending--I thought it was a little too neat. This is a minor problem though, since I did like the way everything wrapped up. Something you may want to know about is that there is a companion novella called Unlocked: An Oral History of Haden's Syndrome. I read this after I read Lock In and immediately wished I read it first. As you can imagine, this is a short background for the virus told through multiple perspectives. The thing is, I found myself a bit confused for about a third of Lock In, and most of my confusion had to do with details about Haden's Syndrome--all of my questions would have been answered if I read the novella first. It's definitely not something you absolutely NEED to read, but if you're the type of person who likes to know as much as possible I would actually recommend reading the novella first. Overall, I really enjoyed Lock In and John Scalzi's writing style. I would definitely read more of his work, and I'm curious about a couple of his other novels. Suggestions are very welcome!

Author Neil Richard MacKinnon Gaiman born Neil Richard Gaiman; 10 November 1960)is an English author of short fiction, novels, comic books, graphic novels, audio theatre and films. His notable works include the comic book series The Sandman and novels Stardust, American Gods, Coraline, and The Graveyard Book. He has won numerous awards, including the Hugo, Nebula, and Bram Stoker awards, as well as the Newbery and Carnegie medals. He is the first author to win both the Newbery and the Carnegie medals for the same work, The Graveyard Book (2008). Review I read a lot of the children's books by Neil Gaiman and have been eying his adult books for a while already. I first picked up Ocean at the End of the Lane earlier this year when I heard Gaiman was visiting my country to give a talk about that book but it did give me a good reason to put some of his other books higher upon my "To Be Read" pile too, starting with American Gods. With every Gaiman book I read I get the same feeling in the first pages. I really need to switch a logic button on my panel to be able to accept the world and situations Gaiman is setting in his books. The beginning of American Gods does help a bit because it still seems quite normal and slowly pulls you into the maybe not so normal. I really enjoyed the developments in the story and the flow. The pace of the story is pleasant and kept me captivated. There was enough information on all the things happening that it was possible to wonder along with Shadow about what was actually going on which is something I love to do in a book. On the character side it was a bit busy. There are obviously a lot of Gods and they have a lot of people going around. The main character Shadow was not someone I could easily connect to. He felt distant and even though there are many things happening to him I never really got an idea that he realized it. On the other hand I noticed that did not really bother me which is pretty weird as I usually love to hook myself up to one of the main characters in a story. I did enjoy the character of Mr. Wednesday a lot. The dishonesty was pouring trough the pages and it was easy to feel that he was so charming that everybody fell for it anyway. I really liked Mr. Nancy and Mr. Ibis too and would not have mind more of them in the story. Though I really enjoyed this book and will probably read it again at some point it is not an "easy" read. I felt I really had to pay attention to what was happening and there are many background stories and little explanations about the gods to give the reader an idea about their influence and strength which are important to know if you want to place them on the right spot in the story. If you are planning on reading this do take your time, it is worth it.

I don't know if I even reviewed the first book, but this one was just as good if not better. AH MAZ ING. I have been a long time fan of Maggie Stiefvater simply because her writing is beautiful. It's elegant. The words grip you and you find yourself rereading a passage because it was so well written. Add to that a killer plot and some living, breathing characters...this book is five stars all the way. This book is about Ronan and his family history, the relationship with his brothers, mother, and most importantly his father, while continuing the plot from the previous novel; the hunt for red october Glendower. Looking at Ronan from everyone else's POV, it's easy to think he's made of barbwire, but Stiefvater is a master at showing you who he is and why he is and who he wants to be. I'm going to be honest, I fell in love with Ronan in this book though I totally ship Adam and Ronan. I felt so dumb when I realized how he feels about him; the signs were all there. This is why I'm alone . We also learn a lot about Adam and that sacrifice, which wasn't exactly what I thought it was. The book has many twists and turns, a ton of fated love and unrequited love and forbidden love, but thank the Lord Almighty it is NOT a love triangle. Give me a rhombus or pentagon any day, or just a good old fashioned  straight line .

** spoiler alert ** Wow, okay I am really disappointed with this novel. I don't know any other way to put it. I was so bored, constantly rolling my eyes, and was constantly waiting for it to just be over. I think this is literally my first one star on Goodreads, which is saying something. There were a lot of things that were done poorly which resulted in this book being a no no. Don't get me wrong, the magic was kind of interesting and all, but the bad really really outweighed the good. -There was not ANY worldbuilding Basically all I knew was that we were in another world called Algid, but beyond that there wasn't much for me to go off of. We jumped around from place to place, but I had no idea where we were. But of course our special character Snow knew exactly where she was because her scars were a map. Obviously. That made things way too easy and gave an excuse for no worldbuilding. Who needs worldbuilding when our character knows where she's going right? -BOR-ING The whole freakin time I was so bored. I just wanted to be done. It was 425 pages of yawn. I didn't want to read, and I can say I'm very glad I'm finish. Sadly, now I'm in a reading slump. Not the oh-my-gosh-this-book-is-amazing reading slump, but a I've-put-this-book-off-so-much-that-I-don't-feel-like-reading-at-all kind of reading slump. -NOW INTRODUCING THE FREAKING MOST SPECIAL SNOWFLAKE OF EVER This whole book was one big eye roller because of how special and chosen oney the main character Snow was. I MEAN HER NAME IS LITERALLY SNOW! The book went something like this: Hello my name is Snow and I was locked up in a mental asylum my whole life, and I escaped! Woohoo! Now I found out I have these powers and I'm the chosen one and the only one who can save these people in this kingdom I don't care about! And want to know the best part? I am instantly amazing at using these powers I never knew about in ONE DAY! Isn't that great! Plus, she was in a mental asylum for her whole life but she's not crazy. Awesome. Obviously she is perfect. Seriously, though, not representation. -I really just disliked Snow She was so whiny and ungrateful and lackluster that I basically wanted to strangle her 99.99% of the time. I did not sympathize with her at. all. She literally went to another world to save the person she loved and she was so unfaithful. There were three teenage male characters in this story (yes only three) and she kissed or had feelings for EVERY. SINGLE. ONE. Uggg. not cool. -The tropes. The tropes. Okay warning-- SPOILERS! Her mom isn't the loving parent. No just kidding, both of her parents are out to kill her. Cool. Oh, yeah, and the person she came to Algid for is evil. No kidding. And she has a twin. Of course. -Mess. The different parts of the story didn't seem to fit. It went from training to heists. The transitions were confusing. The concept was there but the writing was not. Overall: Basically, I am a sad snowflake. The idea of a Snow Queen retelling and magic was interesting, and I was excited, but it did not deliver. I'm disappointed because I really enjoyed Page's other book Dorothy Must Die. I was just confused the whole time and constantly rolling my eyes because of how filled with tropes and how predictable it was. Not to mention boring. I didn't like Snow's character, which is a major turnoff for the book.
