Finnikin has dreams from gods he may or may not believe in and when he was nine years old did silly nine-year-old things that everyone is convinced has affected THE DESTINY OF EVERYONE, although there's not a lot of evidence this is true. There are nameless evil people doing evil things, but a girl with whose parents were obviously illiterate ("Evanjalin") manipulates everyone she comes in contact with to fix them, dragging Finn and other unwitting accomplices along. Then everyone pretends it all makes sense. I got the impression that the author was trying to stick to the adage of "show, don't tell," but in the process forgot that books aren't actually a visual medium and you show by telling. I was frequently flipping back pages to figure out what one character was referencing...and discovering the apparent event didn't exist, or that what the characters had perceived was clearly different (or deeper) than what was actually written. Explanations of and in this fantasy world were few and far-between. The kingdoms, the places, the religion, the magic...it's fine to reference things before explaining them, but not when those things are key to the story and aren't explained for more than 200 pages. Also, the second-most-important character is a jerk, by which I am not referring to someone who cuts in line, but someone who cares for no one but herself and doesn't care who she hurts in the process of getting what she wants and there are probably a few more choice descriptives that would fit better, if you cared to use such language. Evanjalin manipulative and rarely talks straight. This is a recurring event: Evanjalin: My dreams say to do this. Everyone else: That sounds weird, but okay. *Events happen that were clearly not part of the plan* Everyone else: You lied to us! We're going to kill you! Evanjalin: My actions have caused large amounts of physical, emotional, and/or mental damage, but it accomplished an obscure goal of mine. Everyone else: Grrrrrrr Evanjalin: Also, you can't do this next thing without me, suckas. And a few things didn't sit right. Number 1: the thief boy. He's kidnapped, sold, stolen back, and basically develops Stockholm Syndrome for Evanjalin. Yes, there was the attempted rape, but that felt so much like a plot device, it didn't seem like it was something he'd actually do. Number 2: Romance. You mean there's supposed to be romance in here? Sure go ahead and tell us it's not Evanjalin being manipulative for the umpteenth time, because that would being totally beneath her, right? Well, sure, I guess if you just tell us that they're falling it love, it makes up for the lack of reason or evidence! Number 3: Sex. Superfluous, like the author was like, "what else should I add to add tension or realism? Young men like sex, right?" And really, taking a prostitute seemed to be beneath Finn. He really didn't seem like he (or his father) would be the type to do so. Perhaps the author's goal was to write a gritty, semi-realistic fantasy. But the reasons behind everything are so convoluted and the characters so unlikeable it doesn't work.

I think that I am in the minority that does not understand Rainbow Rowell novels. People everywhere seem to rave about these books, yet I could not finish 'Landline' and I have really struggled to read 'Eleanor and Park'. There was just no real plot, at least not one that I could fathom. The whole novel was just Park and Eleanor seeing each other and just being. At first glance there seemed so much within the novel that could offer drama; Eleanor's home life, Park's parents, the kids at school, the brief experimental period with eyeliner... yet actually all of these storylines just fizzled out, or were resolved happily. Even the ending didn't manage to be dramatic. I felt that for a kid like Park, who clearly knew what it felt like to be the odd one in a group, to judge Eleanor was just hypocritical. Not only did he judge her early on in the novel, but even into the later stages of the book he was making comments about her that to me seemed negative. To me, it felt that Park liked Eleanor and thought himself weird for it. I didn't see any development from either Park or Eleanor. The only one who seemed to change were Park's parents, whose experiences in the novel developed them as characters. I don't think I will venture into the Rainbow Rowell world again.

Because of Miss Bridgerton is set in a different branch of the Bridgerton family (to be honest, I'm not entirely sure of how exactly they're connected to the other Bridgertons), in the countryside of England. Sybilla, known to almost all as Billie, Bridgerton is a country miss who has exactly zero interest in the intrigue, gossip and parties of London life. She's quite content to help manage the Bridgerton estate with her father until her younger brother comes of age and can take over. The Bridgertons have been neighbors with the Rokesby family for centuries and as a child, Billie ran around with the Rokesby boys getting into all kinds of trouble. It has long been expected that Billie would marry one of the Rokesby sons but with two off at war and the other involved in running the estate, she hasn't really bothered to consider the matter. The one Rokesby that Billie finds impossible to get along with is the eldest brother, George. When circumstances throw them together, George and Billie find their mutual annoyance with each other turning into something else entirely. I've been a huge fan of Julia Quinn since the very first Bridgerton book (which I think I read in high school, strangely enough). The humor and cleverness of her writing has nearly always won me over, even if it's a story that feels very familiar. The mutual hate turning to love trope is one that I admittedly love to pieces. Not sure what it is about the war of the sexes that I find so enjoyable but if it's done with the right humor and competitiveness, I'm pretty much guaranteed to enjoy it. Such was certainly the case with this one. Between that and my love for Quinn's writing style, I enjoyed this one from beginning to end and had a hell of a time putting it down. Billie is reckless but she's exactly the kind of tomboyish character that I've always loved and I couldn't help wanting her to succeed in everything she touched. If you enjoy Quinn's style or even just humor and interesting characters in your historical romances, I'd highly recommend this one!

One of my favorite books so far this year - amazing! The story is about a girl, Mercy, who is learning to live life as a Succubus. This proves to be very challenging since her mother won't teach her a thing. The only thing she knows for sure is that if she kisses someone, they could die - her best friend Paul had a personal experience with this. I have to say that I've only ever read about Succubui & Incubui from the Beautiful Creatures Series but even through them I didn't learn a lot. We, along with Mercy, learn quit a bit about their nature here and I can tell there's even more to learn! This book is long, very long (I'm guessing about 600 pages) and I read the whole thing in 2 days it was so good! You can preview the first 5 chapters online and when you do you'll probably get sucked in just as I did. Since Mercy doesn't know a lot about controlling herself yet, it's really fun to watch her try. She literally has an inner demon who seems to control her life at some points, which makes situations bad for her but interesting for us. Particularly when it comes to the men. And there's A LOT of different men in her life. One thing I really enjoyed about this book was that there wasn't a love triangle or even two people working towards one love. Mercy was exploring her teenage inhibitions and with all the hot men running around it definitely kept me interested. I must admit that I have a soft spot in my heart for Luke, even though I understand they aren't really right for each other. This isn't really a spoiler unless you don't want to know much about the other guys but some ppl might want to read the whole book before I say why I wouldn't choose the others: Flynn is too fickle for me and what he did at the end I thought was awful (why try to break up something good? and to your best friend! ), also the bad boy thing is done too much. We don't know enough about Sebastian (even though I can't wait to learn more!) and Paul well, I like him but I just don't think he's right for her. I do want to say that at first I couldn't believe she was getting so many guys. It was a bit unrealistic to me, but then I thought about the raging teenage hormones and it made a little more sense. I wasn't sure what to make of this series at first; it ended up being nothing like I expected from reading the blurb on the cover of the first book. The first thing that struck me was Luce's complete ignorance and naivety. It felt like the author needed to give the audience and her main character a little more credit. She takes way too long to figure anything out. It always felt like you are missing half the story; even when things are revealed. Most of the climactic scenes are very half-hearted or barely witnessed, which meant there was never any real feeling of threat or danger, especially within the final battle of the first book, which Luce, and by default the reader doesn't even get to witness. Even the serious things like Penn's death or Todd's death are never really dealt with or dealt with very half-heartedly. Even though she constantly thinks back to Penn's death, it ends up seeming insignificant. We never actually find out why Trevor died or why she could kiss Miles without him bursting into flames. Again things like her family and other friends like Callie which seem so important at times end up insignificant. I felt like much time was spent describing certain actions and activities  especially when kissing Daniel. Pages are filled with long winded descriptions in parts with little explanation in others, by the last third of the 4th book I was losing interest. We were no closer to finding out the great mysteries hidden from Luce and instead were yet again treated to a description of how indescribable her love for Daniel was. Despite spending the 3rd book travelling through her past lives we never fully get to know why these two love each other so much. Even at the end, when their first meeting is finally revealed the moment of them falling in love feels like it's brushed over. Basically here's this guy who is nice to her and suddenly she understands love and that he is truly meant for her. For me that's a pretty weak basis for a millennia old love story. I think one of the worst examples was just a quarter of the way through the 4th book. "Kissing Daniel was somewhere between exhilaratingly new and unmistakably familiar, like a childhood memory that felt dream like until photographic evidence was found in an old box in the attic. Luce felt as if a hanger full of monumental photographs had been discovered, and all those buried moments had been released from their captivity into the recesses of her soul. She was kissing him now, but strangely she was kissing him then. She could almost touch the history of their love, taste the essence on her tongue. Her lips traced not just Daniel's, but another kiss they'd shared, an older kiss, a kiss like this one, with her mouth just there and his arms around her waist lie that." It goes on but what we end up with is 2 whole paragraphs describing something that was summed up in the first sentence. It was long winded and felt unnecessary; I didn't feel like such a lengthy description really added anything to the characters or my connection (as the reader) to their story. I did like the first book in this series but as it went on I liked the books less. You may ask why I continued reading if I so obviously lost interest. I love reading and I hate to leave a book unfinished; especially when it's a series. If I've read 3 in a series of 4, of course I'm going to read the last one. Overall I found the ending predictable at best. Regardless of the fact that Lucifer loved Luce and that this was the cause of his great rebellion we know as readers that the world wasn't going to end like that. This is a romance novel so of course, we will have our happily ever after; it is obvious from book one that we aren't dealing with a Romeo and Juliet situation. So overall, an interesting idea for a standalone novel but 4 books felt like a stretch; I'm disappointed I didn't enjoy it more.

Storyline: 2/5 Characters: 4/5 Writing Style: 3/5 World: 4/5 I liked the series first, Red Mars. A lot. Thus I feel something of an apostate in admitting that I struggled to enjoy and finish this one. In Red Mars the experience could have gone either way, up or down. The hail of geographical proper nouns could have been received as dry and technical, but I chose to accept it as exotic and informative. Similarly, the hard science fiction descriptions of chemistry and climatology could have been pedantic and unnecessary where I willed myself to take them as character-relevant and integral. Many readers undoubtedly found the discussions on alternative economics and political organization didactic, but I resolved to treat them as thoughtful and essential for the plot. The first in the Mars Trilogy, for me, then, was exotic, informative, character-driven, thoughtful, and full of minor details that compounded for a complex plot. My problem with this second Mars Trilogy book is that I wasn't as ready to will myself to the positive side of these antipodes. Green Mars was the account of the characters and parties whom were unhappy with the ending of book one, then it was 624 pages of their doing over again everything that had occurred in Red Mars, but with more planning and purpose. It was much more difficult to retain the enthusiasm and goodwill when so very little was new. One of the aspects I liked most about book one was the broad view of intellectual and personal motivations. Red Mars was not a ringing endorsement of a specific academic theory or political ideology. In fact, it presented the competing motivations of the original 100 as a mish-mash mess of ideas and programs for action that were under-coordinated and incompatible. This description of colonization resonated with me as I could see something like this happening, and I enjoyed the frustratingly complicated picture of a situation that was beyond any single person's (or party's or organization's or government's) control. Robinson does the same thing here except that he zooms in on the revolution-leaning side of the spectrum and explores the ideological expanse within even that half of the divide. Thus it is the same technique but refocused and magnified. This is the story that Robinson wanted to tell all along, I think. Personally, I liked the wider focused and more neutrally observant view of the first better. Robinson's political preferences, even within the revolutionary left, were more evident here, and I was bothered by the lack of sympathy he had toward some of the factions. Even though intellectually, religiously, and politically I disagreed with Ann Clayborn's radical conservationism - where rocks and basins had rights over people - Robinson made me sympathetic to her and her cause in book one. I felt Ann's pain and sense of loss at what was being done to Mars, and I mourned with her. Here there is no sympathy for Ann. She is a menace to the more conservative revolutionaries, and Nadia threatens and cajoles Ann and the militant Reds in ways that were reminiscent of the methods of the multinats. I think Robinson was aware of the antagonisms and contradictions and this was perhaps an honest account of what would be required of a revolution. I give Robinson credit for making it a murky, ethically compromised, coercive, unpredictable, dangerous, violent, two-faced enterprise. Yet Robinson did not give as fair of a view of the non-central characters as he had in book one. There were character perspectives I really enjoyed  Nirgal's childhood and everything with Sax . There were also gems of ideas scattered throughout that suggested a much richer and deep world human speciation, the green and the white, memory, the effects on a younger generation when their parents never die and pass on the mantle, hero-worship, charismatic leaders, historicity . Unfortunately not a single one of these promising ideas were developed or brought to completion. This was a guide to revolution, entertainingly set in a scientifically accurate description of Mars. This was far inferior as a novel, however. The characters did not serve ideas as well, and pointed tutorials replaced the wonder of uncertainty. My personal preferences, too, might have made this a less enjoyable experience. I am always ready to move on to new ideas, always on the look out for creativity. This was for fans of the first who wanted more of the same.

4.5 stars! Such an adorable read! Review to come. OMG I JUST REALISED I HAVEN'T POSTED MY REVIEW FOR THIS ON GR LOLOL. I actually posted this review on my blog in March. Firstly, thanks to Random House UK/Ebury Publishing for this NetGalley <3 "We want what we can't have. It's human nature." I was extremely hesitant to read this book as the premise seemed to be that being a virgin in college was a bad thing. There is nothing wrong with being a virgin while in college - if you're not ready and you haven't found the right person then why would you give away something you can't take back? But the amount of hype and positive reviews surrounding this broke my resolve and I just had to check it out. And I'm really glad I did because this was such a cute book (I think a LOT of people have labelled this cute) that I couldn't stop reading until the last page. What I really liked about Losing It was that it addressed one of my issues immediately - the whole reason why Bliss left that delectable, British specimen, NAKED in her own apartment was because she wasn't ready. Points to Bliss for actually having sense! The course of the book then shows Bliss' growth and understanding that just because she doesn't want to be a virgin, doesn't mean she's ready for sex. I loved how she came to realise she wasn't ready until she was in love. Also, I absolutely loved Bliss' insanely awkward personality. She was a bit of a control-freak, overanalysing every situation and so paranoid - her thoughts were so relatable and funny, I liked her instantly! "Like a complete psycho, I leaned my face into the pillow and sniffed like girls in books and movies always do to see if I could still catch his scent. I couldn't. And I felt super creepy." Now, aforementioned delectable British specimen. It would be a crime to explain him in such a manner and then leave y'all hanging as I talk about other things. SO. Garrick Taylor. WOOOOOAH *SWOONS* gorgeous accent, soft blonde hair, bright blue eyes that turned dark when staring into Bliss' and washboard abs! I was a goner from the first mention. Gah can he be any more perfect? He was so sweet, caring, understanding and undeniably sexy I just wanted to hug him all to myself. I think Garrick's one of the most constant book boyfriends I've ever read. And when I mean constant, I mean he was always there for Bliss, never hurting her, holding her up figuratively and literally. "The world fell over, bent sideways, broken. And it cradled me, taking me with it, but instead of dying, I fell into the warmth, solid and strong." OhmysweetGOODNESS the romance! Let me get the bad out of the way first. I felt there was a bit of insta-like bordering on insta-love. Carmack tried to dispel the insta-like/love but I felt she fell short of achieving this. Despite Bliss saying she wasn't falling in love, I could still see things moving too fast and her feelings developing in a matter of short chapters. However, the romance was so SWEET and it made me feel so warm and fuzzy I think I was floating half the time. Carmack doesn't hold back on the steaminess and man can she create sexual tension! I think I paused a couple of times to fan myself because dang was it HOT! Garrick was sexy as hell and so seductive - yet adorable at the same time... is that even possible? I DON'T CARE BECAUSE IT'S TRUE. "His tongue slid against mine, and my hand beneath his shirt came back to life, curling around his side, pulling closer until my pelvis pressed into his hip. The kiss was leisurely and divine, but too slow, slow, slow." I'm not really sure how I felt about the supporting characters. I really disliked Bliss' best friend Kelsey - she was trying to improve Bliss' moods when she was down, but it was in a really selfish way and I just wasn't convinced. Cade on the other hand, oh sweet Cade. Fell in love with him instantly! He was sort of the boy next door and I couldn't help but think of him as wounded puppy at times. I'm super excited to read his story in Faking It! Not an overly big issue, but I felt that there could have been more depth to the characters at times - especially Garrick. In particular situations it was like he was there only for making out purposes and his back story was a bit lacking too. Other than being a teacher, I wanted him to have a purpose too. But like I said, no biggy and the main plot of Bliss trying to sort out things with Garrick smoothed over this minor detail. On the other hand, I admired Bliss' independence. There may have been an insanely hot and sexy teacher who was smitten with her but she wasn't about to let him control her life! "And Garrick can be cool or not with it; he doesn't decide what I do." I really liked the writing style Carmack employed. Her descriptions were detailed and I loved the techniques she weaved into Bliss' hilarious thoughts (always a good sign when a debut author can show). The physical descriptions were especially a great read and it really allowed me to take in Bliss' surroundings and feel what she felt. "Each step felt like a nail gun had been taken to my heels, my knees, my hips." "Shampoo became the villain of my story, stinging my eyes and exhausting me as I tried to rub it in and rinse it out. It felt like hours before the water ran clear enough for me to open my eyes with them burning. And then I couldn't convince myself to do it again with conditioner." This was such a feel good book I'm definitely buying the paperback when it comes out to get some more Garrick! I feel all peaceful and content just writing the review. Re-reading bits to find quotes had me biting my lip and smiling hehe. "It was the sun, and it held me in its arms, called me by name, touched me from forehead to toes. I fell asleep cradled in the sky in the arms of a star."

After reading so many positive reviews from friends, I had to check this one out. It's the story of Nobody Owens, Bod for short, a boy who narrowly escapes death when his family is murdered and winds up being raised by ghosts in an old graveyard. The keepers of the graveyard impart some gifts of the dead onto Bod so he is able to move through solid objects, "Fade" out of sight etc. The man who murdered Bod's family is still looking for him so the outside world is still unsafe. As Bod grows older he learns various lessons from the ghosts and other beings who live in the graveyard and learns about his own history. Eventually it becomes clear to all that he needs to face the danger that exists in the outside world. Fast paced and creative, another winner from Gaiman.

So I have to say, I really loved this book! I was just totally immersed in the world, the stories and how they intertwined were just endlessly entertaining! You know the writing is good when you're shedding tears eighteen pages in! So obviously, I felt invested in these characters, and that makes or breaks a book for me. Laia was an awesome character and I enjoyed watching her growth as the story progressed. I was glad that she started out as someone who was normal, scared, ashamed, naive. Her flaws made her growth more profitable in my mind. I liked reading about her mother and how she felt like she would never be that strong, yet she knew that her brother's life depended on her, and so she was brave to save him. Her decisions affected her and helped her learn. Elias was a fabulous character too, I couldn't help but feel for him. Feeling like an outsider when everyone around him was bloodthirsty. Wanting to honor life rather than cause pain, death, and destruction. I felt his pain for wanting his freedom, I felt his love for Helene, I felt for the his lack of family. I mean, when your own mother harbors nothing but cold resentment and hatred for you, it can't be easy. I especially appreciated his POV after the third trial, his pain and anguish really got me. And then when he and Laia were together, those scenes were kind of magical; well minus the "rape" scene. I also liked his backstory and how his past life shaped him. And Helene, I really came to love her! I didn't think I would at first, but once I understood her, well how can you not love her? The love she has for Elias is palpable, and it was heartbreaking how their story unfolded. The Augurs were awesome! I enjoyed how their prophecies came to pass, how they annoyed Elias, and I even felt their pain at being unable to ever earn the freedom that Elias was seeking. I also liked how the mystical creatures (wraiths, jinn, etc.) were incorporated, although I'd certainly like to know more about the Nightbringer... Some questions I still have, who is Cook? What's the truth of her story? How did the Lioness betray her, and why is she still at Blackcliff? Who is Elias' father? Why is the Comandant such a stone cold bitch?? Why did everyone completely brush under the rug the fact that Hel saved Laia's life? Where is Darin and will he ever be saved? What will happen to Sana?? How was the Comandant blocking the Augurs from her mind? Why did the Augurs save Laia? What fresh hell will Marcus unleash as Emperor?! Poor Helene... Anyway, I read some negative reviews that said this book was slow... I don't know what book they were reading, but for me, I felt like there was a twist or turn on every third page! Definitely not lacking in action here. The fight scenes were epic, heads roll before you can even blink an eye! The Trials were one crazy twist after another, even Laia's trips to the market were chock full of action! The dread of being caught by the Commandant was enough to keep me biting my lip through most of Laia's narration. There is also a darkness and cruelty evident in the story that just underscores how terrible the world has become under Militia rule. Now obviously from Cook's story we know that Scholar rule wasn't necessarily better, but come on man, can't we all just be friends?? Lol... So overall, just a fabulous read that kept me engrossed the whole way through and deep into every night!

What worked: I ended up very disappointed with Shatter Me, despite my blogging friends who loved it. The only parts I enjoyed were the flirty Kenji Kishimoto and Adam's relationship with his little brother, James. It was so adorable that I felt myself smiling throughout their scenes. What irked: Shatter Me is very unusual indeed. At first, all of the crossed lines piqued my curiosity. Then I realised that it's very much like Marmite. You either love the writing style or hate it. Unfortunately for me, I definitely wasn't the former. The run on sentences, the myriad of metaphors and the weird things that Juliette came up with didn't endear the book to me. I understand that it's supposed to reflect her fragile state of mind but the way she uses numbers to emphasise something didn't sit well. It's a bit too over dramatic and I don't feel comfortable reading it. What else....The other characters didn't blow me away. The plot. What plot? It didn't feel like there was a whole lot actually happening in Shatter Me and the little that did was over in a flash. Overall, it was a bit of a disaster to me.

Despite its heavy, controversial themes, Me Before You still maintained a certain charm and humor. Unfortunately, that charm was missing from After You. I giggled a couple of times, but only genuinely laughed out loud once. I loved Sam (who cooked pasta for almost every meal! ), but most of the other new characters weren't that important to me. The Moving On Circle was made up of characters that were neither memorable nor distinctive. I couldn't even name two of them by the end of the book, except for Jake. Lou was more frustrating than anything else. I couldn't believe that a job in NYC basically landed in her lap (she wasn't actively looking for a job, the interview didn't go that great, and she still miraculously got an offer) and she said no! I was cheering on Trina when she chewed her out over the phone. Lou needed to hear everything Trina said. And when Lily showed up, I was surprised by Lou's willingness to just let Lily basically take over her life. Luckily--luck is the only way to explain it--it all worked out for her in the end. It seems that Moyes is possibly setting this up to be a series, so I wouldn't be surprised if a third book about Louisa Clarke is announced. Just a final note about the narration. Anna Acton replaced Susan Lyons as narrator. And I liked Acton much better than Lyons. Except Acton's American accent was dreadful. She'll need to improve on that if there is a third book and if she's narrating it.

I read many of the Sherlock stories as a teenager and am now revisiting them. I am reading them in an annotated version, one which gives explanations of the times, English phrases, the difference between broughams, hansoms and landaus, etc. It's an interesting read as well as a fascinating quick one. All the elements are there, Watson and his piquant observations of the even more-piquant Holmes, his strengths, his eccentricities, his ability to uniquely deduce the most minute of characteristics of a person at first meeting. There are errors here and there, though, as that annotated version points out - and wow, do Holmesian scholars pour over every word, every nuance, every tiny historical and geographical detail! - but the story was well worth it. I simply love the language, dialogue, settings themselves. This story involves a king being blackmailed by a vengeful woman, and the woman is Irene Adler, whom Holmes ever-after refers to as 'the woman.' This is supposedly the only tale in which Holmes does not win and is outwitted by someone else - and she's a woman! Holmes takes on the case to help the king and gain back the photograph and using subterfuge, an array of disguises and his keen intellect almost succeeds. A great story, worth reading on a gloomy night with a glass of wine and a roaring fire.

I really liked this book, and if this were my blog, it would have gotten an 4.5, and the missing .5 I will explain. But there were many aspects that were remarkably intriguing to me, and it was well written, entertaining, and fast-paced. First off, I love the personification and/or anthropomorphism of nature and other non-human/animal things. This book's spirit magic did a lot of that, and I thought that was awesome. I loved Eli's way with it, and how the whole spirit magic thing worked. It was great. Anyone who knows me well enough could guess I liked Josef best. He's no Bloody Nine, but he had enough of that barbarian side to make me happy. The dynamic of Eli, Josef and Nico was also great and fascinating. I really enjoyed it. Miranda was a good female character, I though. Might have annoyed me at times, but three-dimensional and strong. Always good. What was really interesting to me about this book was that there was a notable lack of character back story and world-building, which is typically a staple of your epic fantasy. There was just enough of the latter to explain what happened in the book, and very little of the former. This set it apart from your average fantasy, but the characters were engaging enough and the plot compelling enough to carry you right along. I liked the uniqueness of this succinct storytelling, but it's also where it loses the chance at the five star rating. Because lacking the back story, you don't get *into* the characters as much as you would otherwise, and being really involved in the characters is what gives a book its full power. For me at least, so while I liked it, it was also a slight hindrance over all. The final note I'll make is that there was a lot less Eli than I expected! The writing spends more time in the perspectives of many other characters than him, which was interesting. It was a new way to learn a "main" character. Not that we were entirely without his PoV, but there was much less than I anticipated. Perhaps, though, that's why the omnibus is called "the legend" of Eli Monpress: we see it through others more than through him. Which I found...I hate to use the same words over again, but I found it very interesting. Still, it was very enjoyable and I'll definitely be reading the second book. I actually have the omnibus (3-in-1) but am rating each one separately on here, to determine singly if I want to go on, but I think after this, I'll be finishing the next two. I hope that we do get to learn more about the stories behind the stories in latter installments, though. Still, a lot of fun.

I've looked at a bunch of the reviews of this book. My personal read? I liked this book. This is a good book. Let me start my review, however, by clearing one thing up: the narrator is not what I'd consider "subversive," as she is described on the book blurb. The term is misleading because Daisy is definitely not trying to subvert the system for any other reason than because it's pissing her off personally. Her character is too immature to think of the wider picture and the people around her, and she doesn't gain the capability to be truly subversive until later on when she ceases to view the world as something that's actively trying to ruin her life. Until that point, she's an unhappy, angry, often whiny teenager who hurts herself for the sole purpose of punishing others. And it's fitting that she should behave this way. She was often irritating to the point that I was rolling my eyes as I read. The thing is, the story progresses subtly and beautifully through a true coming of age. Daisy matures very clearly through her experiences, and the entire tone of the narrative alters to fit this. Gone is the infuriated impotent of the book's first third, replaced by a young woman who has learned to think of others before herself, who sacrifices to protect those she loves and yearns quietly after those she misses. Daisy becomes a person who is now aware of a much larger world. Now, the relationship she has with her cousin Edmond: It disturbs me, as it disturbs many reviewers. But I agree that it's not the main point of the narrative. The story has a real thread of magical realism running through it, and the entire situation becomes a little fantastical and floaty; there's the sense that in this time and place, rules are subjective and anything goes. I make no moral judgment here on the actions of the characters. Instead, I offer a literary judgment: that this book is interesting, and the story is unique. The constant capitalization of Important Words got on my nerves stylistically, but that's just another thing that changes, subdued by Daisy's new-found growth. An intriguing book told in a voice I could feel maturing as I read. Impressive.

This was easily a four star book up until around the 75% mark and then my brain put the puzzle pieces together, (without my permission), and I realized where exactly the author was leading the reader and after that I lost a lot of my enthusiasm for the book. Up until that point I absolutely loved almost everything about Strange the Dreamer. The writing style was beautiful. It was descriptive, poetic and Laini Taylor has a real ability to evoke stunning imagery. This was used to good effect especially in all the dream scenes, where anything the characters could imagine were possible and the reader was dragged along for the ride. The world building was extremely well done as well. The reader is drawn into the story and provided with information when needed so that you are never drawn out of the action because of large chunks of description. Lani Taylor also withheld information brilliantly and then uses it to dramatic effect. You don't even realize you're missing information until she tells you and it virtually slams you in the face, The citadel... need I say more . The main character Lazlo was a really likeable and relatable character. I loved a lot of the characters actually, but because this is a spoiler free review I can't really say anything about them as I don't want to spoil anything. "This life is not always what we think it will be," Cain says. "You are an ember in the ashes, Elias Veturius. You will spark and burn, ravage and destroy. You cannot change it. You cannot stop it." "You are full, Laia. Full of life and dark and strength and spirit. You are in our dreams. You will burn, for you are an ember in the ashes. That is your destiny." I was really looking forward to this book, and I wasn't disappointed (much). It's been on my reading list since the beginning of the year after it was already getting media buzz. Paramount has also already bought the movie rights. So, I wanted to discover what the hubbub was all about. An Ember in the Ashes is gripping while being surprisingly slow-paced. I guess there hasn't been word of sequel to the book yet. If it's a stand-alone, readers will be sorely disappointed. If it becomes a series, Ember... is one thrilling launching pad to the story. It was one of those books I couldn't put down. I stayed up way to late to finish it. I have few complaints, except for a complicated love quadrangle? I get tired just thinking about it... The Martial Empire is a dark place--threat of death, rape, and severe beatings are real, which makes the story that more urgent and compelling. When Laia is sneaking around Blackcliff Military Academy, I was continually gripped with horror at the consequences if she is caught. Neither of our main characters walk away unscathed. I liked both characters, but I particularly enjoyed Laia's development. She comes into herself towards the end of the book. They're from different social worlds, but Elias and Laia both long for their freedom. Elias wants to escape his future of dealing death and swearing fealty to an unjust Empire. Laia wants freedom for her imprisoned brother. Their journeys are wrought with difficulties and they will be tested to their breaking points, but through each other they might find deliverance. Would I let my teen read this book? Some of the themes of this book reminded me of Hunger Games--war and rebellion and fighting to the death. Martial Empire is worse than the Capital though. Children are beaten in the military academy, and the Masks (who graduate from the academy) are expected to rape and kill without remorse. Though you feel this threat, especially for the women of this story, there is no graphic sexual violence. The Commandant is a cold, frightening character that dishes much of the abuse. She's ruthless, tyrant of the academy. There are some sexual references, but no sex scenes. There are two kissing scenes with some mention of longing, but are relatively short. The soldiers especially talk about sleeping with women and whores. And several times Elias thinks about his love interests without clothing and in intimate embraces. Magic also has a part in this story, which plays out as devilry and is associated with dark figures. An Ember in the Ashes is a more mature young adult book. I'd save this one until high school, at least. I wouldn't recommend it for kids younger than 14. Age recommendation: 15 Language-- No common swearing Drugs & Alcohol-- References to getting drunk Sex--2 kissing scenes; Women slaves are treated as property to be used; Whore is regularly mentioned, along with references to the brothel; References to the soldiers having multiple sexual affairs. Laia is threatened with rape twice Violence--Sword and hand-to-hand combat; Character's are stabbed in battle; Throats are slit; A ten-year-old boy is whipped to death for deserting; Commandant physically maims slaves as punishments; Laia is nearly beaten to death Read more of my reviews on FickleLit.

I am on the fence about Scored. It has a strong dystopian premise, a decent MC and romance, and McLaughlin's writing is both vivid and brisk. I breezed through Scored in less than a day, certainly on the "edge of my seat" for much of it, eager to reach the conclusion. Unfortunately, the conclusion is a let-down. At just a bit over 200 pages, one has to wonder why Scored wasn't longer -- many YA novels are 400+ nowadays. And Scored could have been twice the length and twice as satisfying. Because the issue is that Scored feels incomplete. It stops right in the middle of rising action -- the revolution/tipping point in the dystopia's downfall -- and there doesn't appear to be a planned sequel in sight. Scored is a story that begs for a sequel: what are the results of Imani's actions? What happened to Sheryl Potter? What's going on outside of her Massachusetts town, and what will happen now? But we don't get any of that. Instead, we get a tacked on epilogue of sorts, a letter from the Otis Foundation saying she and Diego have won the scholarship, as if knowing that Imani gets to go to college equals a happy, satisfying ending to the dystopia. It's not. It feels slap-dash. Up until the last fourth of the book, Scored has all the elements of a good dystopia/YA novel: class disparity/availability of a college education "fixed" by technology (interesting and creepy! ), all-seeing/knowing "eyeballs" with safe zones and blind spots (suspense, check), something crazy unfair happening to the MC that makes you feel sick to your stomach and root for her (imagine having a free ride to college and the next day that's gone and your best option is the military -- you're not even qualified to work in retail), a compelling romantic interest with lots of layers (though most of them are tragically under explored in this book) and a nice conspiracy theory. I just wish there were more of all of the above -- some additional scenes between Imani and Diego, more discoveries about the conspiracy, and obviously, more book after the school meeting scene. Some specific things I liked: -- racial and ethnic diversity. Imani is mixed (black father, white mother) and actually reminded me of my mixed friend from a small town in Massachusetts. Loved that. Some of the other diversity we only really get through names, but despite the last name Landis, one has to assume Diego has Latin heritage, and Imani's "score mate" Anil is clearly South Asian. Usually white is the default in YA, but in Scored, it was not. -- teen realism. I was genuinely surprised when Cady had a sex tape scandal . Maybe this shows that I'm An Old, but "back in my day" you would NOT see something of that nature in a YA book. I felt really bad for Cady, but it definitely made it seem like a cut-throat, technologically advanced school of the future. Some things I didn't like/found lacking: -- Imani's family felt perfunctory. I would have liked a bit more interaction between her and her mother, and her and her sibling. (there was enough of dad) -- more about the world outside Somerset/beyond college. What long term effects had Scoring had on the professional sector? On poverty? How wide-spread is the Score? There's a brief mention of the military and "peacekeeping" which indicates a wider dystopia -- but it's never touched on again. (seriously, how is there no sequel?) I've checked the author's website, Twitter, Google, Random House and Amazon and there's no sign of a sequel. In the world of "trilogies where each installment rolls out a year after the first" and the one year anniversary of this book's release coming up, it does not bode well that there is no signs of a 2nd book. I hope that will change, because I would read more from this universe and I could forgive some of the issues with the book (mostly that there wasn't enough of it!) were there a meaty sequel. However, I worry that the letter tacked on at the end was a "neat" way of ending things, in lieu of a second book :(

Having being "blown away" by the first two books in this series, http://www.goodreads.com/book/show/16... and http://www.goodreads.com/book/show/16... , I knew that Edible was going to be another fantastic read....and I was so right!! Edible is a brilliant, beautifully written love story, filled with emotion, love, pain, romance, humor, sexy and hot love scenes and believable, quirky and lovable characters that you just can't help falling in love with. Rachel and Cole were a perfect fit for me. There was so much more to them than what we first thought. Underneath that quirky (I loved her style), strong, smiling, in control exterior, Rachel is more broken than she realizes. She feels disconnected and lonely. Cole ...wow what can I say about this man??? Confident, domineering with the well-put together look of a professional but he has a side that is hot and sexy...very very sexy. Piercings tattoos...a delicious wicked side that I so understand Rachel not being able to resist. The man is too f***ing much--cocky, arrogant, sexy, and bad. Oh yeah, and it didn't help that he look in his eyes and the tone in his voice screamed all the bad things he wanted to do to her. Oh Rachel, I so totally agree!! Their chemistry is intense and they have an incredibly deep emotional connection that jumps right off the pages. I loved seeing their relationship evolve, the sharing and the trust that grows between them. Great dialogue. I loved the witty and passionate banter between Rachel and Cole. And the interaction between Rachel's family and these two was so hilarious and sweet. Lena & Shelley are so totally "wicked".....i love those two...there's never a dull moment when they're around!!! The understanding he showed as Rachel begins to open up to him was so incredible. For some explainable reason, Rachel felt tears welling in her eyes. What the hell is going on? He was making her think about things she had long left behind. He was making her want things she had decided weren't for her. As he stood before her, showing her an even softer side to a man she wasn't sure she fully understood, she took a chance. She gave herself completely over to him. "I'm scared." "Of me?" he questioned cautiously. Shaking her head, she closed her eyes as she admitted, "I'm scared of how you make me feel." As her confession left her lips, he reached out both hands to cup her face, and he leaned down to press a firm kiss to her mouth. His kindness and the tenderness and care he shows Rachel...... "I don't know what to say," she finally replied. Cole continued to stroke her naked back, running his fingertips over her mantra--Pride, Strength, Hope, Love--and for the second time tonight, he thought that this woman needed to be his permanently. "Just start at the beginning and tell me what happened. Nothing you say will make me think any less of you, and nothing you did will make me look at you any differently. But maybe if you tell me what he did to you, you will see me differently and realize that you are safe here. I am not him, and you do not need to be scared when you close your eyes at night." Resting one hand on the curve of her hip with the other in her thick hair, Cole squeezed gently and pressed his lips to her head. "Let me in, Rachel. Let down that final wall." Cole realizing the depth of his feelings for Rachel pulled my heartstrings. Turning his face slightly, he took a deep breath and inhaled her intoxicating scent, and then he noticed her hair for the first time. It was pulled back into a high top-notch bun, showing off her elegant neck and the perfect tattoos decorating her spine. That wasn't what held his attention though. Her hair didn't have any bright color in it. It was sleek, shiny, and jet-black. When she turned her face toward him, those fascinating blue eyes locked with his, and Cole knew it was all over for him. This is where the search stopped. This is the woman. His heart was now in complete agreement with his head. She was unlike anyone he had met before. One minute, she was fearless and sexy, and the next, she was almost childlike in her joy and exuberance. In that moment, Cole knew without a doubt that he loved her. The scene where Rachel and Cole visit his mother had me almost in tears. As Rachel continued, Cole's mother beamed and began to hum along with her, occasionally slipping into the lyrics. Amazing. Songs seem to live in the soul even when everything else leaves, Rachel mused with a heavy heart, thinking of all the wonderful memories this woman had lost of her son. I LOVED THIS QUOTE.............. "It's beating hard because it wants the one it loves to feel it." No words, Rachel thought as she wrapped her legs around Cole's waist. He's left me with no words. This is what makes me read romance books. The love. The happiness. It's what makes my world go round. "I, Cole James Madison, ask you, Rachel Catherine Langley, to stand beside me through the toughest battles and harshest critics, namely your brother, and to lie beside me through the calmest of nights. I ask you to continue being the exact person you are today and to never be anyone but the woman who turned me into this impulsive man who stands before you here today." Cole squeezed her fingers in his, and his gaze stayed locked onto hers. He was intent on only one thing, and that was the woman in front of him. "I was not expecting you, and that's what makes me so sure. Nothing this perfect could be anything other than right. So, Rachel Catherine Langley, will you be my wife? I loved the characters from the previous books that were woven into this story. Mason and Lena, Josh and Shelley and did I love the teaser for the next upcoming book!!!!!!!! Logan sounds so delicious and I can't wait for his story.........I know it's going to be another book by Ella Frank that I will LOVE too.

4 stars This review will contain spoilers from Perfect Ruin. You have been warned. Also some minor spoilers for Burning Kingdoms You know, when a series is beginning to expand in the world building and exploring new places and new people, it can make a series much better. It all depends if the author manages to create a unique world with interesting characters. For some, it's either a hit or miss. I've read some books where the world building is great! And other times I've read some books where the world building is complete shit. And like I said, it all depends if the author can manage to do it right. So does the same apply to Burning Kingdoms? Well, yes and no. At the end of Perfect Ruin, Morgan and her friends have left Internment and are on the ground. They are in a new world with no knowledge of where they are. Things are going to be different for them and they have to adjust to their new environment. This in itself sounds intriguing based on the idea of exploration and adaptation. Morgan came from a floating sky city and is now on the ground. So, it sounds promising. And to an extent, it is, but I can see how some people have some issues about it. Myself included. Before I get into the world building aspect, let me start off with my initial review of Burning Kingdoms. Short answer: I liked it. Long answer: I thought it was a good sequel, we get to see new places and people and the character development is great. Though, I did have a few issues with the world. Lauren DeStefano has a way with words and writing good characters. Once again, the writing style is done beautifully to the point where I want her and Lauren Oliver to collaborate and write a book together. (IT NEEDS TO HAPPEN!!!) And her characters are so, so great! Morgan is a favorite character of mine and the others are good. Aside from Morgan, I also like Pen based on her development from the first book and where she is now in Burning Kingdoms. We get to see them adapt to being on the ground and having conflicting thoughts on what is safe and what isn't safe. Is the ground better than Internment? Or is it vice-versa? What is home to some people? And if it's possible to go back home, even if it isn't perfect? These questions are what made me like the plot even more! The plot and characters: Great. Now, let's talk about the world building. If you've read my review on Perfect Ruin, you would know I said the world was leaning a bit to the sci-fi/dystopian genre. As it turns out, I was completely wrong. And no, it isn't a fantasy. At least I don't think so. Turns out, it is, in my opinion, a re-imagining of the 1920s of the United States. Technically, it isn't the United States, but there are silent movies, speakeasies, and even one of the characters said jake. Basically, 1920s in America. Except, like I mentioned, it isn't America. Instead, it's a world with different countries that are living in the 1920s. That's pretty much what I gathered from what I read. Also, there are mythical creatures. Not mythical, but animals that aren't common in the real world. There are also mermaids. Yes, mermaids. And to top it all off, the country Morgan landed on is at war with another country. Why they are at war is explained so at least we get some background about it. As much as I liked Burning Kingdoms, the world building isn't what I quite expected. It was good, but I wish there was more of an explanation about the world. And I for God's sake, why isn't there a freaking map! It's the same compliant I had for Perfect Ruin and it's the same for Burning Kingdoms. A map would've made things better. I keep expecting the Map from Dora the Explorer to pop up out of nowhere and show me a map of both Internment and the ground. Still, I enjoyed my time reading the book. Verdict Burning Kingdoms is a good sequel with vague world building but with great characters and plot. Definitely good. Thanks for reading my review! -Cesar

Blah. This story was so unoriginal (reminded me so much of The Handmaid's Tale by Margaret Atwood which was so much better) and also rather unbelievable and full of plot holes. One thing I thought of right away - if men only live to 25 and women only to 20, who are all these medical labs staffed by? You're telling me a man or a woman can complete medical school to search for an antidote before they're 20/25? I mean the older generation has to die off at some point right? The next thing that really irritated me: This book is geared to a younger reading audience, yet it's basically telling the story of sexual slavery and harem life - WITHOUT SEX! Yeah, it's totally realistic that a rich dude would spend a load of money buying a beautiful bride/concubine and then be perfectly content with just holding her hand, and being perfectly content to settle for a single kiss after six months. Of course a young, horny man in a relationship of basically captor and captive would NEVER think to expect his bride to have sex with him, willing or not. Especially not from his First Wife, when he basically bought her to breed a new generation! I guess staring into her eyes was enough for him. Yeah, very believable. If you're going to write a book about harem life, but then the main character somehow remains a virgin - it's just a bit much to take. I don't understand this prudish mentality with young adult fiction - it's ok to write about what is essentially sexual slavery, but it is taboo for our protagonist to be anything but a virgin or to describe sexual relationships beyond timid kisses here and there. It's just ridiculous. Another thing that didn't add up was the obvious wealth of the household. Somehow, 2 men who don't even seem to spend very much time at work (the husband even took a break from working all together apparently sobbing over the loss of his last wife) can live in a vast mansion and support 3 wives, a whole host of house staff, and ever luxury imaginable, with grounds that seem to go on for miles and miles. Not to mention that the husband at 20 years old seems to be a thriving and gifted architect - I guess he must have started going to school for architecture and attained his degree when he was what - 14 years old?? It's absurd. I just felt the whole world to be entirely unbelievable. Why do men die at 25 and women at 20? Why the age difference and why do they die at all? How would a society even function? The answer is, it wouldn't - this was my main problem with the whole book. It also was extremely slow and nothing ever happened until the end when somehow some servant just opens a gate and off they go. It seemed too simple. I would have given it only 1 star, but it did provide some entertainment for me for one day, so I gave it 2. If you want to read this book, make sure to turn your brain off first.

A love story set in a classic YA dystopian world. If you'd told me before I read this book that I would end up really enjoying it then I might not have believed you. Young Adult Dystopian is a genre bursting at the seams. I wouldn't say this book was entirely original but it was a step in the right direction. The world of Delirium is a world where love is a disease and humanity have the cure. The plot of this book was fairly simplistic and yet it still worked wonderfully. One of my favourite things about this book was the passage of time. Weeks, even months, passed and it all felt natural. The plot-twists did have me gasping at parts "Lena, I think your mother is alive." and the ending was unexpected Aleeeeeex! . The characters were interesting, although I never really felt a connection to them. It was a shame that the friendship between Lena and Hana was so unimportant. I know the basis of the story is love so I was expecting the romantic plotline to be the main focus and yet I still felt disappointed when Hana was really only used as an excuse for Lena to meet up with Alex. I really enjoyed the quotes at the beginning of each chapter, my favourite being the Mama, Mama poem at the beginning of chapter 6. They gave a bit more of an insight into the world. In the end I settled of giving this book 4 star. My head was considering giving this book a 5 star and not my heart. I still enjoyed this book and am going to start to sequel straight away.
Drax is great as a villain ; in my opinion this is where the series has really begun to hit its stride.

I want to like Pynchon; I wanted to really like this book. After all, all the signs indicated it should be a cracking read. I enjoyed the nostalgic techie details: I'm in that industry and was in it at the time all those years ago in 2001, so I appreciated the references to tarballs, UTSL, Dilbert, the distaste for Microsoft. Been there. Bought most of the T-shirts. But I didn't warm to any of the characters. I didn't care about them. Some died. Some didn't. And I didn't mind much either way. What clinched it was something that happened in the strip club which seemed like self-indulgent wishful thinking on the part of the author rather than something the character would realistically do. "You want me, a smart professional fraud investigator, to wear these skimpy clothes right here, right now? Sure, why not?" "You want me to dance around this pole in front of the customers? Sure, why not? I can scan the crowd while I'm up there and then I'll be doing my day-job at the same time, or something." "You want a foot-job while I'm dressed like this? Sure, why not?" "What? It undermines my credibility as a character? (giggle) And it felt like reading a play: there's a lot of sharp, snappy dialog, present-tense narrative so terse it's little more than stage directions. The writing isn't beautiful in a way that would make me want to read it again, but merely functional. Maybe it works better for US readers, or for New Yorkers, but in places it felt like a sharp and stylish TV detective show that I'm only half-watching. I thought the story sagged in the middle. It picked up later, but not in a way that brought me much joy. I kept reading because I thought there was some great bombshell waiting - it never really came. In the end I'm glad I've read it. The look back at millennial IT trends is enjoyable. As a love-letter to New York, it works well. But for me, just some limey in the North of England, it wasn't very immersive.

El Deafo chronicles author Cece Bell's childhood. At the age of four, Cece lost her hearing. Her first school is a special school where all the students were hearing-impaired. Eventually, however, the family moves to a small town where education options for students with special needs were far more limited. Cece now has to wear a Phonic Ear, a large box-like hearing aid that is worn strapped to one's chest. Cece prefers to wear the box under her shirt so that no one can see it, but the wires going from the box to her ears are a lot more difficult to hide. The Phonic Ear comes with a microphone that the teacher must wear around their neck in order for the student to hear. Cece quickly discovers that her teacher never turned off the microphone as she moved about the building, so Cece can hear whatever's going on anywhere her teacher happens to go. She decides that this is kind of a secret superpower and creates her imaginary alter-ego "El Deafo" as a means to combat the loneliness of being different from all the other kids. El Deafo can handle anything, but she could also really use a sidekick. Graphic memoirs are probably my favorite type of memoir and this particular memoir is charming and accessible. Kids (or teens...or adults, for that matter) will find Cece's narrative both enlightening and relatable. Cece's approach to coming to terms with her disability is both heart-warming, humorous and poignant. El Deafo was a 2015 Newbery Honor book.

I'm sobbing. sobbing. sobbing. more sobbing. and more sobbing. HOW CAN YOU END THE BOOK LIKE THE MARIe? Okay. First things first. I loved the dual perspectives, and it really helped for this final book of the trilogy. Overall the book is very moving, packed with action and a mixture of emotion combined with it. Day is a character in whom I loved ever since the first time we were introduced to him in Legend. His gentle nature in conjunction with his gorgeous looks made him a beautiful character, and I cannot be more happy with how Lu developed his character. His major weakness is his family, followed by June, and it made me crumple to see him in so much pain. June somehow pissed me off in the beginning of the series, but I learned to love her throughout the trilogy. She is the ideal representation of a girl who strives to her fullest, and I admire her for following her brother's steps. She is so amazing, and I fully ship her and Day. Their natures, as a mix, are perfect and I could not stress how much I love their relationship. ... Throughout the novel, through the rollercoaster ride of emotion, I literally could not stop crying. Their reunion, and swap of romantic words made me torn up in my heart, but with joy, because of how much they seem to click into each other, despite their obvious differences. But the ending of the book, a bittersweet ending, to me it was a sad ending. I could not stop sobbing at the fact that they lost almost all romantic connections, only the slightest trace remained. That small sliver of a memory of June from Day, since he could not recall her, made me completely shattered. I was hoping for a happy ending for them, but no, Marie just had to shove it into my face. But at the end, I was crying, but no tears came. I guess that reflects my feelings. It's worth crying for, but not completely worth it. I will miss June and Day so much, and I'll never get to see them in action again. I may reread the trilogy, but nothing will repair me from what happened to the pair. Champion has to be my favourite book in the series, and could not be more complex in Marie's cauldron of strong emotions.

Full Review Here: http://likeakidinabookstore.tumblr.co... Real Rating: 3/5 I thought Maze Runner was a pretty decent and enjoyable distopian. However, if you were looking for a distopian with a love story like Divergent or Shatter Me, you'll definitely be disappointed. This book is much more world-building focused. Which made for interesting and believable world, but little else. Additionally, there was something in the lack-luster way this novel was narrated that kept me from getting completely engrossed. Like I said, I enjoyed the world building. The mystery aspect of their wiped memories and the puzzle of the maze made for an interesting brain teaser. But the way the novel is written means that the reader spends most their time being extremely confused. The world is never fully explained and the reader only gets a brief glimpse of it at the very end. But the maze and the glade and how everything seemed to fit together was still well thought out and believable. But, It was also slow and repetitive at points. The first 50 or so pages are spent learning what's written in the description of the book, making it terribly boring. No one in the glade seems to ever want to share information which seems kind of stupid if they're all trying to solve a puzzle together. The narrator also likes to repeat certain things about how confused or strange it is to have only certain memories. Thanks Dashner. Got it the first three times you said it. And, yet there were also many things that were still left unexplained. The changing is still a mystery to me even after we saw our main character experience it. Also the grievers were kind of random. And the grief serum. These things didn't seem unreasonable to me. But they needed more explanation on motives and just how they work which I'm hoping will be in the next books. I enjoyed most of the characters. I thought Thomas was a brave, strong main character, although maybe a little too special. But I loved Minho and Newt. I liked that Chuck was weaker and not perfect, but I didn't really feel the connection between him and Thomas. I liked him, but I feel like I was meant to like him much more than I actually did. I liked Teresa's dialogue, although I felt a lot of the descriptions of her were kind of one-dimensional. I don't really know how I feel about Alby or Gally. I still don't know quite enough about the changing or what WICKED did to their minds to fully understand these characters or their motives. This is also something I wish was explained further. But, the "romance" aspect was severely lacking. I mean I wouldn't have minded if it was completely absent. The world and mystery of the maze was enough to carry the book. But Dashner tried to add a romance between Thomas and Teresa which was booth too little and too much at the same time. I got tired of hearing just how much Thomas wanted to randomly touch her. I kind of wish he'd just have left it out completely. Also, the super special telepathy was also a little over the top. However, I think what bothered me the most was the stiff emotionless narration. There are things that happen in this book that should have made me feel, brought me to tears even, but I never came close. It was all so detached. It made it impossible for me to truly love or lose myself in the book. In fact, I think my favorite part of the book might have been the epilogue, which was done in a completely different style. It was exciting and crazy and made me super excited to read The Scorch Trials. It gave me hope that Dashner could write a more engaging story than Maze Runner had been. Overall, Maze Runner was a pretty good distopian, but its confusing pacing and detached narration keep it from being anywhere near one of my favorites.

3.5 stars , on the low end Red Queen was not exactly what I had expected. Going into it, I was expecting more of a medieval-style fantasy world. Instead, I got a semi-futuristic setting... not to say that that is inherently bad. It's just that it felt familiar - too familiar. In fact, Aveyard's debut is chocked full of plot elements and even character types used and overused by other popular YA novels, especially the one that started it all - The Hunger Games. Now, I have no problem with using common tropes in writing; it comes with the genre, but when it overshadows any sort of uniqueness, well, then there is a problem. The setting itself is very derivative of The Hunger Games in that the people in power, the Silvers, have vastly superior technology and power to those that they rule, the Reds, and they live in a big shining capital city that few Reds ever see in a land that is obviously the northeastern United States. Sound familiar, yet? There's more. Our female main protagonist, Mare Barrow, has a very close male friend in her hometown who eventually joins a rebel group . At least his name isn't some synonym of gale. Of course, this story would not be complete without a rebel group that secretly recruits the protagonist. To top it all off, there is a love triangle involved, though it's not as insufferable as most YA love triangles. Honestly, I thought it was relatively well done when compared to the rest. What keeps this book from being a complete rip-off of The Hunger Games is the powers, well, abilities, that Silvers, and *gasp* Mare Barrow, a Red, possess. The idea is strong, and can lead in interesting directions, but Aveyard chooses the mundane in this story, on the macro scale. The book is also much heavier on politics, lies, and betrayal than The Hunger Games. However, for a book that focuses on lies, it's extremely surprising that the main lie, the one that the entire plot hinges on, is faulty. In order to keep the fact that Mare is a Red blood with powers a secret, the king decides to tell everyone that she was actually a lost Silver baby who was raised by Reds, never learning her actual heritage and powers. Wait a minute. So you're telling me that this person never once drew blood in her ENTIRE life, which would instantly alert her of her parentage. Not possible. I mean, unless she was kept completely secluded from the outside world, never meeting another person besides adoptive parents, she would have learned about herself and realized she was Silver and different. Now, that's the bad with this book. Let's talk about the good. The writing is good, if not exceptional, and the dialogue is just the same. By the second half of the book, it starts to form a more unique identity, despite the fact that its start is very derivative of others. In fact, I particularly enjoyed the last half with its lies and betrayals, and the fallout of the choices made earlier. The plot moves at a good pace and never really gets bogged down. This book is definitely enjoyable, even if it is not the masterpiece it is hyped up to be, and I will be continuing to read the series, hoping to see something that really sets it apart from the rest of the pack.

It would be impossible to write a review about this novel without mentioning the non-traditional format in which it is written, so I'll just get that out of the way first; The author uses diaries, letters, audio and video recording transcripts, and snippets of books and newspaper articles to piece together the narrative. While this may sound gimmicky -- it is gimmicky -- it faded to the background very quickly to me. This surprised me as I thought it would be tough to read something in this format, especially because the novel literally starts in the middle of a sentence. But it genuinely works for this story, so let's move on. The story that is told is a new-weird/horror/mystery amalgam that hooked me very early and delivered through the end. Despite being set in 1995 Virginia, a gothic mood palpable, and as is often the case, the spooky Axton House almost becomes a character itself. There are very few actual characters other than protagonists A. and his "companion" Niamh, and very little is learned about these characters either, other than the fact they like The X-Files, so anyone seeking a character study can look elsewhere. But the mystery is compelling, as is the cryptography mentioned that A. and Niamh employ to discover what exactly is going on in the recently inherited estate. I won't say more about the plot, but will say that anyone that liked Mr. Penumbra's 24-Hour Bookstore will almost definitely also like this book, as they share similarities on multiple levels.

Bran is biting the bullet and thinking of the 3 millions dollars he has been promised. Jonathan is a rich jerk, Bran is a whore. It doesn't feel like a love story. There is nothing between them. At least, I didn't feel there was anything but a contract between them. The thing is, the story is good, I liked the writing very much. And if it had ended  when Bran finally got out of the situation, I think I would have loved the book. Two guys falling in the wrong relationship, making mistakes etc. But Bran comes back to Jonathan. If that was for the money, I could understand, but it's not entirely for the money. And since I had the feeling it was more of a brainwashing than a romance... It didn't sit well with me. I want to believe that their newfound resolutions will make for a better relationship but I'm not sure I'll buy the second book when it comes out 'cause I'm not sure I won't feel a brainwashing instead of a romance between the characters. I'm giving it a 2 but, I feel bad about that... I don't want to be unfair but it was not really my cup of tea. I probably would have liked more if Jonathan was more nurturing with Bran. He found him and his ideas interesting at the start of the book and then he made him a slave 24/7 which I can't help but find a bit of a waste of talents. Bran has ambitions, skills and he is reduced to a naked sex slave which doesn't make him happy at all - if Bran had been happy about it, it would have been different, but he isn't. I would have liked the past of Bran and his relationship with his father to be explored as well...

This falls squarely in the "OK" range for me. Nothing horrible, nothing exceptional. I finished it a few weeks ago, and already the memory of it is a bit hazy. My main complaint is that I really didn't feel any heat between the two main characters. They seemed more like friends than lovers. The author kept telling me how attracted they were to one another, but I never felt convinced. The heroine is a bit childish at times. She had no problem writing a story about vampires when she knows everyone in London thinks her husband is one? Really? How naive. It's not an over-the-top TSTL way, she just seemed too young and naive at times. I think she would have been more suited to a YA novel than an adult romance.

This is certainly the funniest horror story I've ever read. Howard's wit is very British-dry, my favourite. Zarenyia is a superb creation, as unsubtle as possible while Horst and Johannes are subtly changing. The action scenes are quite credible considering the impossibility of most of the characters. I agree with others that the Hell scene dragged a bit. I'm OK with the end ending, not so much with the Ninuka part. All that build-up, an obvious trap to get Cabal aboard, an epic showdown ... and she says "so shoot me already" and he's all "meh, OK" and that's it? All that Trial stuff led us to THIS? If it was indeed her work, what was the Trial supposed to demonstrate or determine? It's easy to make the case that the Trial forced J & H to develop, but why would Ninuka want that?

I had trouble connecting with the characters. There were some plot holes and it was very hard to believe. I didn't like it. It was an okay read for me. As always, what I may not like could be the opposite for you.

This is one of these books that just don't give you the ending you really wanted, but was enough so that it doesn't leave you with a bad taste in your mouth. I just don't feel like such an intense and emotional last few chapters was done justice. I didn't get enough closure, and although it's not like I hated the ending, it just wasn't what I expected, or really, really wanted to happen. That being said, it was alright (if not a little unrealistic). I mean I know she saved his life, but I don't think it's so easy for someone to just accept he'll have a ghost living inside him for the rest of his life. Could he ever get married? What happens when he dies? Do they both go to heaven (or wherever the fireflies go) when he dies? Does she comment on everything going on in his life or is she just quiet all the time? What about the fact that it would be really frustrating to never have true peace and quiet because someone else is always there? I know that if I'm not left alone after awhile, shit's gonna hit the fan. Is she inside him all the time, or also outside him sometimes (that thing with him holding her arm... I don't get it)? I don't know, it all just seemed very sudden. This was a book that was at times hard to put down, but still possible, which made it a very good read during school because I could pull it out on the bus or in between classes knowing I'd probably be able to put it down when I needed to. This kind of makes it sound like a bad thing, like it wasn't compelling enough or something, but that's not what I mean at all. It was simply not filled with suspense, but still managed to be accurately labelled as a thriller. I don't know how, but it did. Very talented book :) I loved the writing style in this book, there was no use of conjunctions (it was all "I am", "He is", "She will") and I think that added a lot to the story, as well as made it more realistic. I mean seeing as she is 300 years old, it's not appropriate for her to be shouting "Ohhhhhhh man, that's so ratchet!! But that homie's got swag, see him tryna twerk all up on there?!?" I apologize to all of you. I am obviously not a gangster; I like my stuffed bunny and chocolate chip cookies with smiley faces on them instead (note sarcasm).

Good? Yes. Satisfying? Not quite. But while the ending may leave you tearing your hair out in frustration the journey there is still pretty darn good. The main characters are as entertaining as they always have been and you get some good POV chapters from some of the supporting cast (I particularly enjoyed the perspectives of Barristan Selmy and Victerion Greyjoy). Plus this book overtakes the events of 'Feast for Crows' and we get a few chapters that provide news about events back in Westeros. Anyway(The Winds of) Winter is coming, we just have to be patient.
