Read for the second time on audiobook July/August 2017. First read review: THIS BOOK MAKES ME SO CONFUSED!! Aline is an apprentice map-maker until the day she crosses the Shadow Fold with the army of Ravka and sets loose a powerful stream of light to ward away the monsters trying to kill her and her friends. It turns out that Alina is a Grisha, the word for magician in Ravka, and her power is something that could save everybody. Now Alina needs to learn how to use her power while trying to trust The Darkling, the most powerful Grisha, and also sort out her own feelings for her childhood friend Mal. I've heard so much about this trilogy so I was afraid of going into it and being disappointed but I wasn't at all in the end. Once I got into the story, it took a few chapters for me to get my hear around the Russian-style words and the 'ki' at the end of everything, I was hooked. I love the magic system of the Grishas (reminds me a bit of Trudi Canavan's The Black Magician trilogy and how they're separated into their skills by colour) and I'm definitely guilty of falling in love with The Darkling. He's so addicting and I just wanted more him and more sexy time between him and Alina and then he went and ruined everything. And even though he's a total tyrant, I STILL LOVE HIM. His whole aura reminds me of The Dragon from Uprooted, plus a bit of Akkarin from The Black Magician trilogy AND Valek from Poison Study (and okay, a bit of Voldemort's cray-cray) and apart from Voldy, I love all those characters so much so The Darkling is bae, okay? I wish I could Mal just as much but I don't really right now. He's alright, he just doesn't set me on fire. I'm looking forward to seeing Nikolai in Siege and Storm because I've heard him mentioned a lot too. I love Alina's character development. She starts off being a confused, scrawny girl with no idea where her place in the world is and she grew so much in strength and confidence. I can't wait to see where she goes in the next books and how she grows even more. Onward to Siege and Storm (claps hands and descends into darkness).

What a great book, even if only a third of it is dedicated to feminism. Roxane Gray also talks about racism, sexuality, politics and gender. Her essay "The Careless Language of Sexual Violence" was powerful and brutally honest. All of her essays are wonderfully written. Even when I didn't necessarily agree with what she was saying, I still loved reading the book because I was in love with her writing. Great book - highly recommended.
I loved this book! The characters were interesting and the storyline kept me turning pages. I am looking forward to reading the next book in the series!
Really fun Lord of the Flies type adventure. A GREAT choice for boys who are reluctant readers.

This is an overall review for all three volumes of Junji Ito's Uzumaki. The story is set in a town of Kurozu-cho on the coast of Japan, and follows a teenage girl Kirie Goshima and her boyfriend Shiuichi Saito. The town they live in is cursed by a pattern - the spiral (uzumaki) - the most hypnotic shape of the world that manifests itself in every possible way - seashells, whirlwinds in air, on people bodies (as marks for example) or can drive them insane. The story opens with the insanity of Shuichi's father, who was obsessed with the spiral shape. He was pulled so deep in his fascination in spirals that it literally put him in grave. Following that event, his wife became paranoid and soon also 'got killed by spirals'. Each chapter follows the story of other people living in Kurozo-cho and the ways the mysterious spiral affected their lives. The episodes might seem unrelated to each other but after all they bind up and conclude the story. Some of the stories were quite good but some of them I found bit ridiculous and they made me laugh even though they shouldn't have. like they blood-sucker pregnant women. What the hell even, I have seen nothing more ridiculous for a long time. I also have issues with the final. It was just... I can't even find coherent words to describe my feelings towards the final chapter. I don't know... I probably expected some epic ending where Kirie and Shuichi somehow defeat the core of the spirals and break curse, and I didn't get one. The ending implies though that the story going to repeat itself sometime soon. But on the other hand the ending satisfied me somehow. Art itself is very important in the manga and the style used in this manga fit the story well. I liked how detailed it could get, especially in that whole spiral aspect and made them more disturbing. Overall it was a great story to read, and I would recommend it to everyone, mainly if you are a manga person it's one of these must-read mangas. But if you seek for something that might creeps you out I am not sure if it's a right choice. As far as I am concerned it was more of a psychological than a horrorish.

I'm in the minority here with this one but the ending just left me with an icky feeling. Ben and Tim's relationship in the beginning might be stereotypical in the closest jock and nerdy gay kid but I honestly have no sympathy for either one of them. I can't see why Ben was into Tim beyond his good looks and Tim really didn't have too many good qualities. The two star rating is only because of the middle of the book, otherwise I would rate it zero. Although Jace has more patience than most men I liked how their relationship developed and dealt with the Tim. What I really disliked about this book was the ending I hated the convenient death of Jace at the last moment. Really! Kill him off in the last couple of chapter so Ben and Tim can get together. Even though Tim did so many horrible things as a teenager and then trying to break Ben and Jace up the HEA end with Tim and Ben together is just way too much for me.
Ahhh!! So good. New favorite? Yes, I believe so. Review to come!

All the while the discworld continues to spin it's usual mayhem, causing problems left and right. A bit of an excursion from the previous novels, but definitely worth the read.

I went back and forth on this basically the whole time I was reading it. I feel like "talky" is really the best way to describe it. I mean, it's cute enough, but good lord does Connie Willis need a savage editor! I always like her books, but also I feel like I'd like them even better if they were a hundred (or two) pages shorter. For instance, in The Doomsday Book, there are multiple interminable sequences wherein one character tries to reach another by phone. Pages and pages of attempted calls. But then like 3 characters die of some terrible flu and it's just referenced in passing (never mind the fact that poor Kivrin's just living through the Black Death, but by all means, tell me more about how the professor in the present can't make a phone call). The same thing happens with those nonsensical theatrical rehearsals in All Clear, when the bomb shelter people decide to distract themselves with Shakespeare. Again, pages upon pages of droning about rehearsing a play, when these time travelers may or may not be trapped in the past forever! Here, there is no time travel, and we're probably a bit in the future. Briddey has just agreed to have an EED procedure with her boyfriend Trent. It's some brain surgery that allows "emotionally bonded" couples to read each others' feelings. Briddey also comes from a meddling Irish family (although I think this is set in Silicon Valley? Or somewhere similar). And said meddling family is the source of the ridiculous amount of talking, and talking in circles, and not figuring out things you should have known 300 pages ago, but let's logic it out for 5 more pages just to be sure. With some massive cutting, this could have been a cute romantic comedy, but it just got bogged down under the weight of So. Much. Talking. Basically, Briddey has the procedure without telling anyone, because her pushy boyfriend talks her into it. They don't "connect" right away, but she instead starts hearing someone else's voice: CB, the schlubby guy who works in the basement lab (they're all employed by the same company). After they argue for a million pages about whether or not he's blocking Trent, or doing something to Briddey on purpose, she finally figures out that she's a telepath. Which means she can hear pretty much anyone and it's exactly as awful as it sounds. But just when it seems like this will be a cute non traditional love story about CB teaching her to keep the voices at bay, she starts hearing Trent. Turns out the procedure woke up some dormant gene in him. And also he was using her the whole time because he wanted to create a smartphone that would let people hear each other's thoughts. Because that's not terrifying. Blah blah blah research, neuron mapping, blah. Oh and also Briddey's entire family is psychic too and those Irish heritage meetings her aunt has been trying to drag her to are just like psychic conclaves. And then CB invents some jammer to stop the voices, but somehow Briddey's 9 year old niece makes it better because she's able to "keep the nice parts" of being telepathic. Apparently it's just that easy. This was really the point where Willis lost me. CB has been telepathic since he was 13 and has spent his whole adult life working on a way to jam the voices, and this kid figures it out in like a day? And the best explanation we get is she "kept the nice parts"?! What. The. Fuck. I mean, explain your science or don't, but I feel like the whole telepathy thing was better left a mystery. Like, I don't really care *how* "the net" in Willis's time travel series works. It works, it's the thing which sends you back in time. Fine, now let's have adventures! So...yeah. With some massive edits (or just lots of skimming) there's a cute and interesting story in here somewhere!

Okay, I liked this book. However, it was just to short. This book seems more like a first draft that needs a lot more flushing out. There were so many great concepts! So many! This is a fairly enjoyable series. I like this group of friends and I like that each member has their own story (though there are times where I have to say "Really? Everyone is special in their own particularly magical way?") but who knows. Maybe it's just the way of things in Henrietta. Or maybe that's what draws them all together in the first place, whether or not they were aware of that. Moments of disbelief aside, I appreciate some of the struggles that these characters have. Struggles for independence or class awareness or searching for life's larger meaning. I also appreciate that book 2 really held it's own, both furthering overarching storylines but introducing and completing some of it's own. I'm hoping book 3 keeps on the same track.

I don't know how to properly explain but Panic by Lauren Oliver is somewhat unclear to me. It does have that typical dystopian set-up but the story and how the characters moved along with it made it different to me. In a glance, it sounded like other YA Dystopia novels out there being the game as an important piece of the story. But the game itself is not really the most substantial part, it was the characters and how they played the game. To be totally honest, I found the entire idea kinda fuzzy. And while it did explain the origin (although in itself admitted that no one knew or when Panic had begun) and the mechanics of the game, I still felt something lacking. It was at first hard for me to grasp on why they did what they did. Yes, they, the story have four integral characters, Heather, Bishop, Nat & Dodge, with being Heather & Dodge as the main focus. I always encounter problem dealing with too many characters in one book. I'm the type of reader who concentrates in one story at a time. And while I think that it did help me see things beyond, I still would have preferred if it focused with only one (but that's just me). So that's what I did, I concentrate on just one character. Heather failed to capture my attention from the very start. She was sort of scattered for me and her motivations as well as her stance on the whole matter didn't really look solid to me. Honestly, I found her action, reckless and a bit contrived. Dodge on the other hand, was quite unclear at first. I kept questioning his motivations and actions. But also, I wanted to know the reason why he was doing it. He wanted to win the game. He was doing it for someone. He was going to play the game for revenge. And that got me totally hooked on his side of the story. What I liked about him is that he was very aware that his objective was somewhat futile in the grand scheme of things. He cannot take back what he lost just by winning. He knew that but still he was firmed about it. I guess, even though I didn't agree on his entire intention, I somehow I understood why he was doing it. He wanted to inflict it to the people who had hurt him in order to have an equal footing. I think the aspect that made this book stands out is the ambiguity of it. Like I mentioned before, it does sound like dytopian book but in all honesty, what I saw was more of the internal conflicts of the characters. It's not about the system, it's not really about the bigger things. For me, it's more about them. It's about themselves and the reason why they were willing to play Panic. I've read all of Colleen Hoovers books now, and every single one of them I loved. I do believe that she is making her way up to my top favorite author. This book? Oh...where to start? I can't tell you what I'd give for Dean to come out of the pages and tell me he fell in love with me as a reader, and is gunna stay in real life and give me nonkisses all the time. I'm 100% in love with him. I don't fall in love with characters of books often, hazards of being a book worm with speed reading tendencies. But Dean..oh.. yeah. I need someone like him. Someone to share my forevers with, not just the firsts. I love how the author didn't do the typical change of POV like disaster #2 did, where it was like she just opened her word processing thing, and switched all the Her's to His's. I like the letters to his sister, I like the new things, the pro's and cons's lists. It gave me more of an insight to the drama inside of Dean's mind, in hopeless he always seemed so confident, in this book it let me know that he had no idea. I was never sure how he just seemed to know why she freaked out, but in this book it was clear that he really didn't know. Even though I read Hopeless, I still ended up staying up late bawling my eyes out, even though I knew what'd happened, I still cried, and cried and cried. The only thing I wish, was the end showed  the downward fall of the father, I wish all the people who didn't believe his sister were shamed but I understand why they couldn't

After a 5 year wait, the book should have been way better than what we got. To make a long story short, I feel as though this book was incredibly predictable and missed a lot of emotional notes that it was obviously trying to hit. I do have some questions and concerns: Merry is being worshiped. Soldiers are worshiping her. This automatically breaks the treaty that the fae made with Jefferson because not only are they praying to her and worshiping her as a goddess, but they're going around and spreading this legend/practice around in the middle east. Isn't that... illegal? Will this be addressed in a later book? Is Maeve polysexual and into ladies? Because that was a bit confusing. The fae baby development is confusing and it feels inaccurate. Babies wouldn't develop like that. They're developing too fast. If they live so long and x years in sidhe years is akin to y years in human, they need to be developing slower. A 2 month old baby (no matter what) should not be sitting up. A 13 month old baby should not be speaking in full sentences and walking/running perfectly. She needs to sit down and talk to experts on development because it's unrealistic in a way handwaving it away by saying "well it's magic" won't cover. Babies just don't work like the way they do in this book no matter how magical they are. I am a baby expert. I know this stuff. And she has a child who was once a baby, she should know enough to modify the rate of development accordingly. I cant explain why, but this was my biggest issue with the book I think. I did like how there was more development of the relationships between the characters. They were interacting and stuff and that was great. I feel though, that the Merry Gentry would be so much better in third person (possibly with alternating POVs) because there's so much going on that Merry can't relay but that needs to be relayed to the audience. I'm not saying that anyone has to feel the same way that I do, but I was expecting a lot from this book that I feel we just didn't get. I've been reading LKH's stuff since I was seriously wee and I think she's in need of a second golden age or something because I know she can do better, but I'm not really feeling what she's putting out.

Actual rating: 2.5 What kind of three hundred year old vampire listens to Jay-z? Most people stop listening to that when they're about twelve. There's an ancient order of vampire assassins in this book. They have the most rediculous names you can imagine. It's worse than things like; raven, daimon,etc. They're called Rhage, Thorment, Vishous, Zsadist(however that's supposed to be pronounced), the main character who's called Wrath(I swear) and oh,.. Darius. I have to assume that the author ran out of stupid names at assassin number six and just went with darius. Of course, because she wouldn't want to be reminded of that particular bit of creative bankruptcy, she went ahead and killed off right at the beginning of the book. This was really entertaining, though. For about seventy or so pages. Then it started going around in circles. This type of book has to be where all those new adult books developed from. At least here, there's a bit of mythology going on. These vampires don't sound at all like vampires, tbh. Not when they start every sentence off with "Man,.." The main character Beth has to be the stupidest person in the history of ever. and I actually had some high hopes for her after she  fought off a rapist and reported him to the police She follows up on that by sleeping with a guy who broke into her house, looks like a murderer and is carrying about 30 pounds of concealed weapons on his person at all times. Not only that, but she actually goes with him to his freaking house! and has dinner with him after he reveals that he's killed "thousands". Her stunning explanation for this affront to women kind everywhere is that she's "going with her gut." Even after he revealed that he's of the fanged persuasion and that she's going to become a vampire as well, her response was ridiculously watered down. I can't help thinking if someone came up to me and told me that vampires were real and showed me a set of fangs, I'd sooner believe that he'd had some fanboy elective surgery done than be persuaded that vampires were real. I picked this up because I wanted to read something with adult characters for a while. but urban fantasy/PNR just keep disappointing me with all the cliches. *Major Sigh*

3.5 stars This is exactly what I needed. I don't know, school is kicking my ass this semester. I feel like I haven't been able to sit down and read a book in months. And I probably won't read another one for another few weeks. This book was by no means perfect. The instalove was real and sometimes the relationship angst got to be a bit much. But overall I really adored these characters and I thought they were very realistically portrayed. Vivi and her mom just moved to Vera Cova, a small town in California, when she meets Jonah. (This is where the instalove comes in.) Jonah recently lost his father and is trying to take care of his siblings and mother, who is struggling with depression. "To the deepest, most cellular level of my being, I resent people who believe that depression is the same as weakness, that "sad" people must be coddled..." Vivi Alexander is vivacious, high on life, and she has a bipolar disorder. She's got this artistic soul, she can be selfish, immature, and so I can understand why some people don't like her or can't sympathize with her. But I do think Vivi is an amazing portrayal of a teenage girl living with bipolar disorder. Then we have Jonah Daniels. I adored him and his family. Jonah has five siblings and I loved how each of them had their own distinct personalities and their dynamic with each other. I also enjoyed how loud they were and their love for food. Lord managed to paint this vivid portrayal of mental illness and I liked how it was talked about so openly (because this needs to be talked about). We got to see two different sides of it. Someone living with it firsthand and someone living with it through a loved one. I also thought the ending was so perfect for the characters. I am so glad they didn't end up together. Throughout the story I felt like their relationship could lean towards toxic and if they had stayed together this book would be so much worse and would have done a disservice to their growth throughout the story. Honestly though, I think this book would have been damn near perfect if they were just friends throughout all this. Filled with vivid characters and one of the best depictions of mental illness, this book can get frustrating at times, but it's honest and I recommend it. "That's the thing they never tell you about love stories. Just because one ends, that doesn't mean it failed. A cherry pie isn't a failure just because you eat it all. It's perfect for what it is, and then it's gone."

This was good but wasn't the greatness I was expecting. I know, I know, I shouldn't expect my absolute devotion to Meadow's first series, Incarnate, to overflow into this new one. But I did. And I think that is what hurt my chances for really getting into this book. Because I spent half the book wondering what was wrong with me for not getting into this one. And there were SO many people telling me how amazing it was. So I got caught up in the hype and then took six months to finish. SIX. MONTHS. WTF. I have never spent that long on a book. All this makes it sound like the book was bad. It wasn't. It was really interesting and the last several chapters were finally reeling me in. But there were too many questions I had, even with all the information we'd been given. Two parts stood out to me: Wil's trip to the wraithland, alone to the lake and back and her interaction with James in the jail cell. Both of these were amazingly done; one a completely magical mystery which I have come to love from Jodi Meadows and the other a fiery protagonist not afraid to stand firm in who she is. Of course, I knew who Black Knife was from the first moment we met him in the city after the girls arrived. It wasn't a shock, but that didn't make me like him any less. So, overall, I liked it, but it took far too long to get into the story. Now that I'm invested, I'm excited to read The Mirror King. My hope is that it will start where this one left off in terms of my attention span and not let up until it is over.
I knew it was a novella, and I should judge it so, but the reason I'm giving this 4 out of 5 stars is because I wanted it to be longer. I'm kind of Courtney Milan's bitch.

5 stars! This is what humans do. Marked in Flesh is another amazing installment in the wonderful and unique The Others series. The stakes are the highest they have ever been, and Bishop delivers a story that's powerful, dark, and utterly brilliant. This is a story that sinks its claws into you and does not let go. Anne Bishop proves time and time again how great of a writer she is. Marked in Flesh shows just that, with its steady pace, action-packed twists, and predictable but still complex plot. Anyone who has been reading the series knows what is coming when they pick up this book. Still, this is a story that sinks its claws into you and does not let go. This is the culmination of everything that has been established so far. As said above, we all know what's coming. The humans want the world for themselves, and the terra indigene care about saving what's theirs by right. Even so, the writing is so well-executed that even though you know what is going to happen, you're still on the edge of your seat, unable to look away. And what a journey it is, oh my god. I love this series. The characters just get more and more developed as the story progresses. It's so satisfying to read a book where every characters grows and changes and transforms. No one is static in this series, which only enriches the story and the plot. Even the new faces that are introduced in this installment are great and interesting, all with unique voices and traits. One of the highlights, at least for me, is seeing the Courtyard humans and the terra indigene work together. This is a relationship that has been building since the first installment, and it is so gratifying to see it work. It shows how things have changed, and how much of a difference Meg made in this world and the people who live in it. Also, because I can't not say anything about it: Simon and Meg. This series continues to have zero steamy scenes! Its focus is on survival, human greed, and learning how to live with people's differences, but there is still a little romance to go around. Meg and Simon's relationship gets even more development in this book, and I have to say their final scene together is probably one of the sweetest things I've ever read. So once again, Anne Bishop has given readers a fantastic and unique Urban Fantasy book. Fans of her writing will love this, and Fantasy fans who still haven't read this: what are you doing? Series: #4 in The Others series. Beings: Werewolves, vampires, other shapeshifters, elementals, etc. POV: Told mainly from Meg, Simon, and Monty's POVs. Content Warnings: Self-harm! Steam: No steam! Cliffhanger: No! HEA: I'd say yes. Up Next: the final book, Etched in Bone!

Unbearably haunting and frighteningly possible, Lauren DeStefano has crafted a very possible future in Wither where mankind is dying at younger and younger ages and young teenage girls are forced into polygamous marriages to keep the human race from dying out. This book may be hard for some readers to stomach, eternal optimists or those who feel the future holds such promise, but take out the dystopian setting and what are we left with? A young girl who will do anything, who will escape a lavish household, who will leave behind a loving husband she was forced to marry, to search for her twin brother. What if you knew you exactly when you would die? This single sentence is massively powerful, and it's part of the synopsis to hook readers. It's freakishly dismal and depressing, knowing that once you hit 20, or 25, that you'd be overtaken by a terrible genetic twist of fate and die. Most people barely start living at 20 or 25. Early buzz for this book called it The Handmaid's Tale for this new generation. I can't stand that book, but enjoyed this one, which is interesting. Both give me that same "is this really what the world might turn into in the next 50/100 years and will younger and younger girls be used as brood mares to make sure the human race won't die out" weird squidgy feeling. It's books like this that make me realize I'm somewhat of an optimist when it comes to the future. Rhine was an interesting character, full of unexpected resilience and hope and determination, even when faced with kidnapping and a forced marriage and a husband and an extremely creepy father-in-law. I'm not sure what else I can say about this book without giving it away or turning readers away, so I'll leave you with this. This is one of those books that should not be read at night. It pulls at you, drawing your expectations from you, leaving you huddled, gasping, drained, emotions raw and exposed to a chill wind. The possible realism is shocking, and I hope if the world we know now does turn into Rhine's world, if we are stricken by a genetic ticking time-bomb, I hope I'm not around to live in it.

What could be more magical than an emotional and fiery love story set in the tropical surroundings of Hawaii? I couldn't ask for anything more, as Karina Halle transports us to the beautiful, sun-filled beaches during the day and steams up the nights with the sizzling romance between Logan and Veronica. Veronica is the disappointing daughter of the deputy mayor of Chicago, is a disgraced chef, and has appointed herself as the black sheep of her prestigious family. She's always lived in the shadow of her perfect sister, Juliet. While attending yet another party for her mother, Ronnie meets Logan, the enigmatic man with a delicious accent. She feels an immediate and undeniable connection with him. She's sure of it...until he meets her sister. Logan always wonders "what if" after marrying Juliet and losing touch with Ronnie. Several years later, Logan finds himself a widower, very alone and extremely grumpy. After Ronnie's unceremonious dismissal from her job in Chicago, she winds up becoming his employee at his hotel in Hawaii. Sparks fly from the moment Logan comes face to face with Ronnie again and a burn-down-the-house combustible relationship follows. This book had me feeling all of the things! I loved Ronnie and Logan's tumultuous relationship from the very first page. Even from the prologue, you know that things are about to get very interesting. I felt bad for both Ronnie and Logan and their situation--betrayal and guilt run deep on both sides. They are like oil and water, and it makes for a delicious, explosive, somewhat forbidden, somewhat enemies-to-lovers, somewhat second-chance romance. I really liked Logan when he was gruff and grumpy, but I really loved him when he was talking dirty and being all sweet and mushy. (The fact that he's a younger version of Hugh Jackman certainly doesn't hurt, either!) Ronnie is so strong, but she never measures up to her sister, and her mother never lets her forget. I loved watching her work through her insecurities and discover just how brave she truly is. Heat Wave is a captivating read and will envelop all of your senses. The beautiful atmosphere, the mouthwatering food, the gorgeous water are all depicted perfectly. Everything comes together with the brilliant writing and a fantastic cast to make a gorgeous story. Whoever approved that blurb should be fired for advertising different thing that what they're really selling. The whole book is one giant waste of time. - Does that blurb look interesting enough to you to buy this book? DON'T. The disappearances from the blurb/past DO NOT get solved. - The author drops a ton of tantalizing clues about this past crime that the current one is nearly forgotten. Doesn't help that the current one is as boring as it gets, and completely overshadowed by the Great Mystery from the Past. - When the author isn't wagging the stick with past mystery carrot on it, she's flooding the pages with WALLS of descriptions of every single f****** thing, mundane, ordinary, slice of life things that we all know and that we don't need described in so many words when one familiar one would do. The power of creating vivid setting doesn't come with the amount of words used and how many paragraphs can be crammed together without breaking them with dialogue, but from succinct, apt descriptions and fitting metaphors. You don't need to explain 2+2=4. - Main character devolves into unlikable jerk halfway through. I didn't mind, I don't need to like the main character (even though it helps in boring first person narratives, which I hate), but the whole situation turns into some cheap unprofessional disaster. While it was okay - not every mystery needs to be solved 100% and not every story ends with proper redemption and happy ending towards the sunset... I was NOT okay with the author basically selling the reader a big Tale of Whatever under the guise of thrilling semi-paranormal mystery. tl;dr Liked the blurb? Don't read the book.

I know many people love Stiefvater's Mercy Falls trilogy, but I have to say that I am glad she has come out with these brilliant plot-focused teen books. They stray away from the wishy-washy (and lovey-dovey) nature of the Mercy Falls trilogy and become more about the characters and the story that needs to be told. I am a huge fan of The Scorpio Races, and now The Raven Boys. Seriously, Maggie, this shit is golden. The funny thing about this first installment is that it actually is about its namesake. Four raven boys, all tousled, scarred and touched in different ways by a girl named Blue and this quest for something magical, and bigger than them. In some ways, Maggie's storytelling reminds me of the late DWJ, which I highly recommended she take as a compliment (don't even ask how much money I have spent gathering up her original UK firsts). DWJ would include romance, to be sure, but it wasn't straightforward, and it wasn't about creating a love triangle. It was a story that flowed out from somewhere deep. And my literary-god, do I love my damaged characters. Especially when I am so unfamiliar with their situation, but somehow the writing makes me feel enough compassion to actually be hurt when those characters are hurt. I know that is a lot of emotion, but I just feel like there is something about Maggie's writing (mostly) that gets me and what I want to read. I don't think this will be true of most people. I just think that everyone has some author's writing that they connect with instantly, especially at a certain point in their life. Mine has always been DWJ and Neil Gaiman, but occasionally someone else will come along, and practically have me on a lead. Now it sounds like a raving review (haha) for ONLY a four-star rating, but that's only because I like to be honest (not usually, lol). I really, really love Maggie's writing and the idea of this story, but I was not entirely satisfied with this book. But that's okay, I suspect this trilogy will wow me in ways those damn wolves couldn't. Ravens, ftw! Also the ending was very reminiscent of Nevermore by Kelly Creagh with the whole creating Chainsaw  bsns.

I was slightly prejudiced against this book before I started it, as I was imagining it to be some sort of glamorous, somewhat saucy popular novel. Luckily, the reading proved these expectation wrong: I found it very honest, intimate, at times cruel but altogether tactful. The book is a fictional autobiography of a geisha of Kyoto in the middle of the XX century, an eventful period which drastically changed Japan and the world. I loved the language, I found the prose enchanting with its rhetorical devices and undertones. Although many here have argued that the nature comparisons sound forced and unnatural, kind of "Japanese kitch", I found them on the contrary very beautiful and I went back to reread some phrases many times, finding them very poetic. Just one of the many examples: << Wherever he was taking us, I preferred it to being cast out alone into that great expanse of streets and buildings, as foreign to me as the bottom of the sea. I must admit that I found the reading at places disturbing and hard to put up with. The first years of Chiyo/Sayuri's life seemed to me like an endless stream of cruelty and oppression, where not a single soul around the protagonist could be defined kind or at least sympathetic toward her suffering. Furthermore, reading of the customary rape of a child by an old man is for me just as bad as it sounds. And yet, my concern was mostly for the events described, by no mean for the language used, that always stays within the boundaries of tasteful. I found it easy to sympathize with the main character because her feelings and thoughts are described in the most neutral and non-manipulative way. I had a more difficult time with the other characters, probably because the story is an autobiography and therefore it is told by a single point of view. With few exceptions, these other characters lack the necessary depth, and physically are described either as "beautiful" or "monstrous", with little middle way. This is particularly evident in the description of many rich and powerful male characters whose deformities are in stark contrast with the beauty of the geisha entertaining them. I believe the narrating voice is using this device as an implicit judgement of the subjugation these women were forced in, deprived of any real choice or agency. The length and pace of the story are just about perfect for my taste: they kept me intrigued in the plot and gave the right amount of information without dragging along of being too elusive. The only part that bothered me was the last chapter, that sounded a little too much like the "lived-happily-ever-after" sort of conclusion. Many interwoven stories run through the book and concur to its development: as for instance, the historical occurrences, the rivalry between geisha, the story of the friendship between Sayuri and Pumpkin and the romance. I liked the recurring theme of destiny and the narrator's point of view on one's life fate, though I do not completely agree with this philosophy. I am in no position to evaluate the book from the point of view of historical or cultural accuracy, but being so far unfamiliar with Japanese history and tradition, I found enjoyable the insights that it gave me about the lifestyle and education of a geisha. To me, this book was extremely charming despite its flaws and I am sure it will leave a long lasting memory years from now.

Whenever I pick up a YA book I try and change my mentality going into it. I know that grown-ups are the primary readers of YA but they are written and published for the 14-18 crowd. Let's face it, I am brilliant at acting like I'm 14 again. So with that in mind I opened this book, but quickly got sucked into the story not caring about whether I am in my 30's or pretending to to be in my teens. I met Pin man and Pencil boy, or Jordy and Owen. From the first page I fell in love with these two boys. Owen is steadfast, dependable, a good friend, loving , affectionate and no matter what always there for Jordy. When I think about Jordy I think of a vibrant young man bursting with ideas and colors. He was a perfect counterpoint to Owen. I loved how he created a comic book for the two of them, and dressed all crazy to cheer Owen on at his wrestling matches. Constant support. Constant friend. Come on, wrestling, superheros, and best friends, it makes for a brilliant story. There were some tense times. Not everything is roses in their relationship. Between the sexual exploration, the coming out in high school, and pressures on both of them to be something to their families. The story of Pin man and Pencil boy had more than a few wrinkles. But I'm glad to have read them all. I do have to mention there is quite a lot of sexual exploration and if you are a young person and you don't feel comfortable reading more graphic scenes, or a parent looking for a book for your young adult, know there are some on page sexual scenes. I truly enjoyed this book. I liked the way the story was laid out and the characters made me feel invested in their lives. There will be laughter and tears as you read. When it's done you will feel a sigh of satisfaction for that beautiful moment when you finish a good book. Reviewed by Beans

3.5 Stars Overall Opinion:  This was a cute, and relatively light read. I wanted exactly this type of story after reading a darker series. We get some drama, but not that much -- we get some sexy and sweet times -- AND we get a pretty easy ending. While I did like it for what it was, I don't think it'll go down as one of my favorites or be all that memorable in the long run. It didn't get that deep into the characters, or even really tap into my emotions. Even though I'm giving it 3.5 stars, I'm sure lots of people will love this! Brief Summary of the Storyline:  This is Katherine and Brady's story. They meet when Brady heads down to Texas to take care of things at his brothers farm after hearing the news of his brother and wife dying in a car accident. Brady is shocked to find out that their baby wasn't with them, and that he has a niece that now needs him to take care of her. Luckily Katherine, his brother's wife's best friend and nanny, was there to help him out. With the whirlwind of dealing with the painful deaths, they end up leaning on each other in ways that strongly bond them. Even though they both know that their time is limited, they eventually start up a relationship and fall in love. There is some financial issues, some ex and family drama, some sexy times, and some sweet moments...and they get their HFN ending. POV: This alternated between Katherine and Brady's POV. Overall Pace of Story:  Good for the most part. There were times that I got a little distracted by other things because I was a little bored waiting for things to happen (but it was not that much of the book that this happened). Otherwise it flowed well, and I never actually skimmed. Instalove: Kind of. They move really quickly, but they spend 24/7 together at first so this might be the reason. I didn't get annoyed with this type of instalove though. H rating: 4.5 stars. Brady. I loved how he was loyal and caring for his family. He worked himself to the bone for others, and he was hot too ;). My only complaint is that I wanted him to communicate better at times. I also loved how he was with Izzy! h rating: 3.5 stars. Katherine. I liked her up until the end when she ticked me off (see separation spoiler below). She was a cute character otherwise. Sadness level: Low. No tissues needed. Push/Pull: Yes  They are instantly attracted when they meet, but both of them are hesitant to act on it due to their circumstances and that the H is only going to be there temporarily. The H and h both push away at different points, but the H does most of the pursuing. Heat level: Moderate. They have some hot chemistry and scenes. Descriptive sex: Yes Safe sex: Yes. Condoms are used as well as birth control. Std status is mentioned. They do go without condoms a few times, but both mention that they've never been without before. OW/OM drama: Mild The h's ex shows up and wants her back and causes some drama, and there is a OW that the H had pined for in the past that causes some jealousy. Sex scene with OW or OM: No Cheating: No Separation: Yes  The h gets upset with the H when he asks her what her plans are and what she thinks about him selling the farm, she tells him to sell it and takes off to her family in another town. The H comes after her, and confesses his love. There are no OW/OM during the separation. Possible Triggers: Mild Loss of a brother and best friend. Closure: This had a cute epilogue, but I would still call it a HFN ending. There is some commitment, but not enough for me to call it a HEA (but others might). They get engaged, and are living at the farm. How I got it: I paid the $0.99 on Amazon. Safety: Safe with exception - Does Not have cheating - Does Not have a descriptive sex scene with OW/OM -  Does have the H and h pushing away -  Does have a short separation between the h and H -  Does Not have abuse -  Does Not have OTT sad parts - Does Not have a HEA ending IMO, but others might call it one (see closure section)

I am glad I finally made I through the series, if for no other reason than to get closure. I was starting to seriously doubt Scott's ability to wrap things up well, but he managed to bring things to a somewhat satisfying conclusion and make the events epic enough to warrant all of the build up. Granted, he had to backtrack some and change the rules up a bit, which was disappointing, but it was better than letting everything fall apart. I really thought it might come to that after the fifth book in the series. I have two main gripes. The first is the same as with the previous book - everything is supposed to be so mysterious and powerful and deadly that you stop caring. After the umpteenth time of having none of the history or power or awesomeness of items or places explained, you just kind of skip over the next so you can get back to the actual plot. It's sad. My second main gripe is that I feel like Scott had to change the rules of the game substantially to bring things to a conclusion, as well as abandon a lot of secondary storylines that readers were already well invested in. It made me think that the series as a whole hadn't been fully thought out (let alone planned) when he began, so that when he finally came up with the ending, it didn't quite fit the beginning as originally written. For example, Tsagaglalal is supposed to have watched over Josh and Sophie's family for generations, awaiting their arrival. But then we find out their parents aren't even human and they aren't even twins. How is that possible? And the whole using-up-your-aura-and-spontaneously-combusting thing really annoyed me. It never happened in the first three books or so. The danger was that you would run out and thus be weakened and defeated, not that you would simply die. Then suddenly everyone is running out of aura left and right by just doing things like scrying. It seems like a cheap way to up the ante on the proceedings for the sake of drama. But like I said, the fact that Scott could pull off this undertaking at all and provide a couple of nice moments (like Aoife and her father) and semi-decent plot twists (Josh's fate) is what made me give it three stars instead of two.

I can't imagine a person wanting to read a book that's mixed a childhood favourite tale with modern politics. It must be one of the worst combinations of genre I have ever read. I think I'm not the only one who picked up this book believing that 1) There would an interesting retelling of the original Oz story or 2) This was somehow connected to the popularity of the Wicked musical. This book failed to deliver either of those expectations. Granted, the musical was inspired by this book, I expected to see a good and interesting retelling of the first Oz book. But this was all about politics and religion! Change the names of the characters, and this could easily have been a story about some other place besides Oz. Plus, I couldn't sympathize with ANY character. Elphaba was so incredibly screwed up - she believed in nothing, and when she did fight for something, I didn't even know why. The entire book was about how sorry she felt about herself (That may be an exaggeration - alot of the book didn't really focus on her anyway) and she never develops into a character I could relate to or like. She decided she cared about Fiyero and Nor, but I didn't know why. Plus, she was completely batshit by the end of the book and I didn't know what to make of that. Glinda was a bimbo in the beginning and the end - I didn't see much evidence of her changing. There were so many superfluous characters examined - Nanny, Alma Clutch, Liir - that they cluttered up the plot. I'm sorry to say that I finished this book without really understanding anything about it. What the heck was with the mechanical dragon? What the hell were unionists and why the hell did they not get along with the other people who believed in the fairy Lurlina? Why on earth did Elphaba decide to let people call her the Wicked Witch of the West (the explanation behind that seemed so easy and dumb - "Oh, I'll just let them do that. That's cute.")? The Adepts, Dr. Dillamond's murder, Fiyero, Boq's crush, the weird sex scenes - it seemed more like Maguire wanted to shock people into turning a rated G children's book into a fucked up rated R story, full of sex, politics, and murder. What the heck was I supposed to take from this book - that Elphaba was good and everyone else wasn't? Dorothy certainly didn't seem terrible, the wizard hardly seemed that tyrannous, and Elphaba was unfeeling, unchanging, and eventually batshit. Sure, she was revolutionary, but why teach that lesson with a fairy tale retelling? It really didn't work. I'm sorry I wasted my time with this book...

In this volume, a creature is set loose in Hogwarts that preys on the children of muggle - or non-magical - parents, known as "mudbloods." As more students are found petrified, Harry goes searching for a secret chamber rumoured to have been built by the original founder of House Slytherin. The main theme of this volume seems to be identity, and whether it is something a person is given or something they must construct for themselves. Hermione, for example, is targeted because of her status as a "mudblood," and yet she is clearly the most gifted witch in her class. Harry finds out that he somehow absorbed a part of Voldemort when his parents were killed - a part that the Sorting Hat had identified when it had tried to put him into Slytherin in The Philosopher's Stone - but that he doesn't have to let this define him. The series is written for children, but the scene in which Harry&co. find Mrs Norris made me realize that this didn't mean that Rowling would be pulling her punches. This was a truly scary scene and, while Mrs Norris turned out not to be dead, it helped to prepare me for some of the tragedies to come in later volumes. The Chamber of Secrets is full of themes that are artfully set up for parents to discuss with their kids. The issue of racism, of course, is central to the book. Also, the idea of not simply accepting what one reads as fact even if it's labelled as such. Lockheart's books, while supposedly of his exploits, turn out to be lies. And, of course, Tom Riddle's diary serves as a great lesson in net safety. I didn't think it would happen, but I can feel myself turning into one of those "Potter-heads" I've spent the last couple years making fun of!

3 STARS FOR "THE MADMAN'S DAUGHTER" BY MEGAN SHEPHERD This review has minor spoilers due to character discussion. The newspapers had called him a brilliant criminal, but they'd never mentioned the little girl he'd abandoned. As far as the world was concerned, Dr. Henri Moreau was a collection of research papers and a grisly story. Non-spoilery Synopsis: Megan Shepherd revisits Dr. Moreau's island in this first installment of the trilogy, opting to let the readers experience it through the eyes of the scientists abandoned daughter instead of the shipwrecked Edward Prendick. Following her fathers disappearance to escape the scandal that left Juliet alone and working as a maid, Juliet becomes determined to get the answers to her questions. Travelling via ship to the remote tropical island her father lives on, Juliet begins to fall for her old childhood friend, Montgomery, just as a new boy, Edward, enters her life. Caught between the two boys, Juliet is also exposed to the horrors of her fathers island, brilliance, and madness. While I cannot exactly call this book "original" considering it's a retelling of the source material,  The Island of Dr. Moreau, I do have to commend Megan Shepherd for her choice of inspiration. I haven't read it, but the idea is so fascinating and creepy. I really do love retellings just because it introduces newer generations to all of the classics they may have missed out on. Such science wasn't meant to exist. We weren't meant to rival God. The book is  not fast-paced. You must know this before going into it. There are some action scenes, that of course mean life or death for certain characters, but it is much more a psychological horror. It focuses on her fathers insanity, the creations that stemmed from this, and the foreboding sense that the apple doesn't quite fall far from the tree. There is also a lot of focus put on the love triangle between Juliet, Montgomery, and Edward. Up until the last 20% of the book, the pacing is pretty slow. You're introduced to a lot of characters, and you watch as Juliet's perception of her dad evolves. I wasn't sure what I was going to rate the book, but the last 20% was so good I had to give it at least 3 stars. Not to spoil the ending, but it was definitely bittersweet. From what I understand, the author originally pitched this as a standalone. It's been extended to three books, but I honestly wouldn't have minded if it had ended here. It's open enough that the story could continue, but also gives each character their own personal ending if this had been the one and only in the series. Themes of human interference with nature, loyalty, human responsibility, and distinction between man and animal are excellently woven into Shepherd's tale. Edward didn't care that I was a little mad, that I could slip and slide away from reason. Just as I didn't care what he had done that made him flee England. We both had ghosts in our pasts that let us understand each other on a deep level - a level Montgomery never could. Montgomery might be capable of wicked things, but he wasn't wicked, not at the core. No matter how much Father had twisted him, he would always be that hardworking, kindhearted boy couldn't tell a believable lie if his life depended on it. Edward and I were cut from different cloth. Maybe we weren't wicked, but there was something stained, something torn, in the fabric of our beings. I will admit... I was very, very scared to start this book because I've developed a hatred for love triangles. So many are written so poorly, so one-sided that it would be better if they just cut out one of the love interests. While I'm not sure of how I feel about Edward, I can appreciate how he aided and helped in the development of Juliet. Montgomery and Edward represented two different lives for our heroine: a life tied to her father, with a boy who knows her better than anyone else; or a life away from her father, with someone who understands not just her fathers darkness, but hers. I liked what Shepherd did with Montgomery, in making him both an accomplice and victim of Juliet's father. He was taken in at such young age by him, so he has a really strong loyalty to him. The doctor is technically, aside from his creations, the only thing he has by his side. His only company and family. His only escape was the solace he received were his occasional trips to London. Montgomery was lonely, and the doctor absolutely took advantage of that. Neither Montgomery nor Edward were perfect. They both had dark sides and secrets that were hidden from Juliet for a lot of the book. Montgomery created Alice, and Edward himself was created by Juliet's father The rabbit's screams pierced my skull. I slammed my hands against the table, the paper falling to the side. "End this," I cried. "It's in pain!" That was me everytime I read certain scenes. As an animal lover, parts of this book were really tough to stomach. There's a lot of animal cruelty and scenes involving cutting them open. I understood this choice, since duh this how her father makes his creations, but it was really sad, guys. ++ One thing I will add, before I end this review, is that I really liked how the Father named everything after Shakespearean characters. It was such a small thing, but I actually liked how one particular play ties into one character.

"There are only two reasons a non-seer would see a spirit on St. Mark's Eve. Either you're his true love...or you killed him" Every year, Blue Sargent stands next to her clairvoyant mother as the soon-to-be dead walk past. Blue never sees them--until this year, when a boy emerges from the dark and speaks to her. His name is Gansey, and he's a rich student at Aglionby, the local private school. Blue has a policy of staying away from Aglionby boys. Known as Raven Boys, they can only mean trouble. But Blue is drawn to Gansey, in a way she can't entirely explain. He is on a quest that has encompassed three other Raven Boys: Adam, the scholarship student who resents the privilege around him; Ronan, the fierce soul whose emotions range from anger to despair; and Noah, the taciturn watcher who notices many things but says very little. For as long as she can remember, Blue has been warned that she will cause her true love to die. She doesn't believe in true love and never thought this would be a problem. But as her life becomes caught up in the strange and sinister world of the Raven Boys, she's not so sure anymore. This was a book that I've had on my shelf for a while. I've really been meaning to read it, and when paired with everything surrounding The Raven King, I figured it was time for me to read it. And I'm really kind of excited that I got started, NGL. This was a great start to this series. It was filled with possibilities for a romance, some pretty awesome snark/banter, mystery (and murder) and Welsh mythology. The concept felt as unique as the characters. This was my first introduction to Maggie's work, and she blew me away. I loved the way her style just worked with all the magic, ghosts, mythology and just plain unusual that filled these pages. She also does a wonderful job of putting snark in in just the right amounts as well as at the right times. Blue was a great character. She was sassy and independent and her aunts were pretty hilarious. She was also willing to take any and all weirdness in stride (of course, considering what her mother does, if she didn't take it in stride, there would have been serious problems), which probably made it easier to accept what Gansey was doing than most people. Gansey was interesting as well. He's smart, rich and seems to be used to getting his way. On top of that, he looks like he's smart, rich and used to getting his way. Yet as the book progressed and you get to know him, you start to see that most of that is a mask. He's doing his best to not be the guy used to getting his way, yet it's clear he's not really sure how to "turn it off" for lack of a better term. His quest for Glendower was intriguing, especially when you find out what turned him onto this quest. I really liked how he really cared for each of the boys and how he did his best to make sure that things were ok. Yes, he would often end up putting his foot in his mouth because, again, I'm not entirely sure he was exactly sure how to turn off his smart/rich/used-to-getting-what-he-wants, but he truly did care for his friends. And he even grew to care for Blue as they all spent more time together. Also, I'm all over the #SaveGansey program and I really, really hope that Blue changes her mind about relationships and stuff, and that she does it ASAP! Ronan was certainly an enigma. He presents with the tough guy front (fighting, skipping/slacking in classes, acting out at the reading), yet it's clear there's a slight tenderness to him. Just look at his actions regarding Chainsaw, I mean, he finds this raven and he's willing to be up feeding her every two hours and taking care of her. Then he turns around any time Declan shows up and that devolves into a brawl. So he's definitely got multiple aspects to who he is. Yet deep down, he also really cares for his friends. I mean, he jumps in to defend Adam (even though it's not what Adam wants) and he's willing to take the consequences because that's who he is (and also because he was defending Adam). Adam was kind of the outcast. In a way, I guess. He's the trailer park scholarship student who sort of resents everyone at Aglionby, yet he strives to do his best to prove he belongs. He's the kind of person who's always wanted everything done on their terms and they're going to do their best in order to make sure that happens. Unfortunately, Adam doesn't exactly get his wish and then things may have just gotten worse with his actions at Cabeswater. I'm not saying that Whelk didn't deserve to die, but at the same time, he really needed to face the consequences of what he did to Noah. And granted, by jumping into the circle, Adam probably saved all their lives, I'm still not sure that things are going to change for the better Then there's Noah. He's the quiet character and there's not really much that he's involved in. At least not directly. Of course, when you find out that he's actually a GHOST, that sort of explains pretty much everything Anyway, I really enjoyed this book and I can't wait to read the rest of the series!

I liked this one well enough, I suppose, but I just didn't feel that connected to it like a lot of other people seem to be. See, a self-medicated heroine isn't really my cup of tea. I really hated how Araby refused to experience things her brother wouldn't experience. It just felt so weak, and I hated her lack of will. I understand that this was part of her character progression, but I also hated that it took a boy for her to see her worth. Another thing that was a bit difficult with this book is that so much was going on. There was the old plague, the new plague, the clubs, political conspiracy, etc... there was so much all at once and it all kind of flowed together. I also felt like the characters were poorly defined. They also flowed together, in that it felt like they had different personalities at different times. There was also a lack of motivation going on with the prince. He was psycho and power hungry, wanting to control everything, even treating his family in a terrible way, but why? I didn't see any reason beyond the fact that he's the big bad. Despite these complaints I didn't mind this book for the most part. It had a great visceral setting that I thought was one of the main strong points. In the end, though, I found it a bit forgettable, and not really for me. I'd definitely recommend you check out some other reviews, though, because a lot of people seem to be in love with this one.

This book was awesome! It starts out a few days after Elysia "emerged" or was created, and we learn about the island of Demesne as Elysia does, through new eyes and the chip implant that allows her to research information. As a clone, it is her job to serve the humans of the island, and is supposed to be otherwise unfeeling. But Elysia isn't like that; she has tastes, and desires. The interactions between Elysia and the family that purchased her are incredibly hilarious. It really does show how the meaning of our words is very often implied or connotative, and how it can be interpreted when Elysia takes every word literally. On Demesne, the entire focus is on ataraxia; the human inhabitants strive to be in pure bliss every moment of their lives. Elysia's "brother", Ivan, and his gang of friends achieve ataraxia by chemically inducing it, using a drug nicknamed 'raxia. The drug pretty much just leaves the humans super mellow (but it must have other effects too because usually someone ends up topless or their "endowment" is mentioned). When Elysia meets Tahir, she instantly likes him and when she later  finds out Tahir is also a clone, constructed to look like his First, the human who died and he was made to look like  , Elysia finds him even more attractive. Then they both take 'raxia and are "awakened", to where they can finally feel and experience virtually everything a normal human can. They also make out a lot. Elysia grows discontent with her life the more time she spends with Tahir, and they decide they want to run away together, but on the night of the Governor's Ball, Tahir is exposed and his parents immediately fly him off the island and back to the mainland to keep his secret safe. Elysia then decides she wants to be free, and she tells Ivan that she is a Defect, or a clone that can feel and experience emotions. The whole book is filled with very controversial issues that I found extremely intriguing, such as: cloning, rape, and drug use. I give props to the author for diving into these issues and not tiptoeing around them. Eylsia was an very real character, one that I could relate to as she began to question where she belonged in her society. As she grew more human and expressed discontent for her situation, I rallied behind her. I can't wait for the second book, so bring it on, Rachel Cohn!

It's also nice that Charles' character is not completely transformed because *love* happens to him. Definitely eager to read more Heyer.

So many died: Quinn  - :( *Sevro* Tactus  -but I really thought that he redeemed himself before he died. Much more after. Fitchner  -He was Ares and he died. Red Queen Review 2.5 Stars I'll be honest after the first half of this novel I really just forced myself to read on. I think it really depends when in your "YA Dystopian reading history" you read this book. If this is one of the first YA Dystopian books you read then this book will definitely capture your attention and (hopefully) make you fall in love with YA. However to those of us who've read multiple YA Dystopian's including Divergent, The Hunger Games, and The Selection this novel simply seems like a repetition of old ideas. I'm giving this series a try though only because I have hope for it (and also I want to see them take down Maven  and tear him into shreds :D ).

The idea of this book is interesting but there were so many things left unexplained or that didn't make sense that it really took away from my enjoyment of the book. Why would the government send 100 teens to earth? I get that it's a risk but teens? Really? Also, how did these people survive in spaceships for hundreds of years? How are they able to store that much oxygen and food and such? There wasn't enough explanation to make this seem believable to me. There were 4 POV's and I think that was too many. I don't really think all of them were necessary and I didn't really feel like they all had distinct voices. They all started to run together. Some of the descriptions were wonderful - particularly of the first days on earth - but overall, I think the book lacked description that gave me a full picture of the settings. I was expecting a sort of Survivor meets Lord of the Flies but this was not that at all. It focused much more on romance and relationship problems than on survival. On the bright side, I didn't hate it and I think it could make a great TV show (I understand the CW network has optioned it). I suspect teens will like this much more than I did.

Wow. What a page turner this turned out to be! Was a bit of a slow start but about a hundred pages in things started to pick up and the book became hard to put down! Captivating plot, with enough mystery to keep you guessing, and a diverse range of characters, though mostly stereotypes ( I mention stereotypes a lot, I know- they're becoming a pet hate). The writing itself was not particularly special, and I think it probably needed one last, fine-toothed-comb edit to pull out all the unnecessary words and thoughts, as there was a bit of repetition and a large amount of superfluous detail. I think the author could have let us work out the feelings a little more ourselves through actions instead of spelling out Thomas's constant streams of consciousness. I also found it hard to gain a clear picture at times as the emotions seemed to jump around a bit. There were a few continuity issues I had (they eat a lot of sandwiches, but if they grow their own food, where does the bread come from?) and some sloppy loose ends that I can only hope will be tied up in further books ( though I doubt it) and that ending was just a terrible spot to leave things. I understand that the story continues in the next book but there were too many questions left unanswered that left this ending feeling unsatisfactory. It's for this reason I am hesitant to read the sequel. Still, a captivating novel and a great, original story.

This is a weird book. I really enjoyed The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time by this same author, so this book went onto my TBR quite some time ago. But the reviews kept coming in and weren't great, causing it to be a lower priority for me. And then a challenge wanted me to read a book with "bad reviews". Well, I can definitely understand the bad reviews and why so many people gave up on this book without reading much of it. The style was initially really offputting. While I often like stories that have multiple perspectives, those stories normally switch perspectives at the chapter level, which are at least a few pages long. This book instead switches perspectives all over the place. The longest sections are a page or two, more often it switches after a paragraph or a few sentences. It was kind of disorienting at first, and difficult to form a connection with any of the characters in such short spurts. But as I kept reading, I got to know the characters better. I ended up liking Dominic and Richard and Daisy, and even Melissa though I would have hated her if I were one of her peers. And Benjy! He was great. I never did warm up to Alex or Angela though. Or ... Melissa's mom, I can't even remember her name. I of course liked the parts with running. I wish more had been resolved between the family members, and that there was a conclusion to Angela's behavior. I mean, does she have the beginnings of Alzheimer's or not?! But I guess that can't be resolved in a week. I think they should have at least scheduled an appointment to get her checked out though! Anyway, the book wasn't great. But it did grow on me. If you can get past the weird style, you might actually find you like it by the end.

It's interesting to me that so many people liked this book a little less than the first three, because it features Cynna and Cullen instead of Lily and Rule. I think that's actually why I liked it more. It's not that I dislike the original lead characters; it's just that their romance was a bit lacking -at least for me. They're mates. They really have no choice but to be together. It's different with Cynna and Cullen. There is no physical imperative for them to be a couple. Their relationship isn't a given, it's a journey. And what a ride it is. As the story begins, Cynna is still struggling to accept the fact that she is pregnant. It wasn't anything she planned or thought that she wanted. But the fact is, it's real, and in her heart, there is no other option but to have the baby. Her turmoil over it quickly takes a backseat, however, when a group of beings show up from another realm, seeking her Finding skills. The details are murky, but when the chips fall, she is in their home dimension with Cullen and a handful of others, seeking the mysterious medallion. If you read "Inhuman," you'll be familiar with Kai and Nathan. She's a human telepath on a mission from the Winter Queen. He is the hellhound in human form, who loves her. Here, Kai's mission overlaps with our group from Earth, but it's not clear how right away. I really enjoyed Kai and Nathan's short story, so I liked seeing them again here and learning what became of them. But to those who skipped their short, these two may feel disjointed to the main story. Most of the book is in Cynna's POV, which I liked. She has some real issues and vulnerability, thanks to her difficult childhood. And I enjoyed watching Cullen work to break down her walls. I really appreciated his earnestness, especially since he has always been so mercurial before now. The world has changed for both of them so completely, the evolution of their relationship really works to ground them. Outside of the romance, there is a great adventure. Since we leave earth, this installment feels a bit more high fantasy than urban fantasy in some ways. The worldbuilding is solid, but what's cool is that it's built in more seamlessly than in other books of the series. The pacing moves much better; there were no slow pockets. I was excited to keep reading from beginning to end. The only question that niggles me is why/ how Cullen is able to slough off the very nature of lupi culture to choose monogamy. The mate bond settles that issue for Rule... but that doesn't apply here. He can't be the first lupus to fall in love and definitely not the first to get a woman pregnant -so why is this situation different? Don't get me wrong, I need that to buy into a HEA, but it feels a little convenient. Regardless, this is easily my favorite in the series. And I am excited to see where it goes next. Rating: B+

This book disappointed me. I'll just say it, get that out of the way right off the bat, because (a) I was incredibly excited about Isla finally finally coming out and I guess I had high hopes that weren't met. But also, (b) I did like the book. Just... not as much as I wanted to. A normal amount, which is kind of sad. Isla and Josh (but mostly Josh) were characters in Anna and the French Kiss, which is a neat little connection between the books and a good part of the reason I was so excited for the book. Essentially the plot is this: Isla has had a crush on Josh for THREE YEARS and then finally, in her Senior year, he notices her, too. Something happens between them and soon starry-eyed romantic Isla and slacker-boy-artist Josh are together. And they're in love. But the happy-ever-after doesn't last long after  Josh's habitual rule-breaking catches up to him and he gets kicked out of school and sent back home to the United States . Isla and Josh's love story has a fair bit of drama and most of it feels contrived. But that's not the main problem with the book. The main problem is this: Josh, and especially Isla, don't feel real. By the end of the book, after being immersed in Isla's love life for over a year, I still felt like I didn't have a solid idea of who she was. She's just... a girl... who likes a boy. A cardboard girl who likes a mostly-cardboard boy. I didn't not like her; I just didn't know her. The last fifty or so pages of the book really tried to remedy this problem as conversations with Isla's family and friends shined (shone?) more light on her character and personality. But for me it was a case of "too little, too late." There are some cute scenes here and I loved the easygoing banter between Isla and Josh -- it was obvious they were comfortable around each other -- but overall the cuteness couldn't make up for the lack of depth. So why did I like it in spite of all this? Because it was cute. Because Stephanie Perkins writes such quick and romantic stories; I couldn't stop reading. And because the ending -- it wasn't perfect, but it was cute and fitting and at one point all three couples were together. (You know, ISLA, LOLA, ANNA. It was great.)

I've had this book since Christmas and I finally decided to pick it up. I've heard many mixed things about this novel, but I am happy to say I am on the side that likes it. I can imagine plenty of young readers falling in love with this story. I almost did myself. The characters are remarkable and all have hidden depth to them, which I loved. Call's story tugged on my heartstrings, and I almost teared up a few times hearing about his struggles with his leg and how much he longed to change it. His development throughout the book really made it for me. I also delighted in the unexpected turns that take place over the course of the tale. Okay, I have to mention it: there has been a lot of talk about The Iron Trial being too close to Harry Potter. Were there similarities there? Of course - the book is about a school for young magic users! Does this make it a "rip-off"? No! Although [I do find the fact that Call is supposed to actually be holding the soul of The Enemy of Death a teensy bit close for comfort, and this is unfortunately reflected in my rating of the book, as it did affect my enjoyment. There was also the scene at the end where Call is in the infirmary and Master Rufus is talking to him and I couldn't help comparing it to the end of The Philosopher's Stone - and I am so mad at myself for judging the book by these things!] I enjoyed the underground cavern setting, as it gave the story a darker, more mysterious vibe. I find the magic system itself intriguing, and I can't wait to see it further explored in future books. My absolute favourite part of the novel has to be the tales of friendship and seeing bonds form between all the young apprentices at the Magisterium. I'm excited to see where this series goes.

Title: Existence Series: Existence Trilogy, #1 Author: Abbi Glines Cliffhanger: Yes Rating: 4 Stars "You're my existence. I'm yours" This wasn't my first Abbi's book and to be honest, I have no idea how I missed this one, though I had it in my TBR pile for some time now. And as usual, I was not disappointed. Abbi Glines is one of my favorite authors and just as I expected - this book was pretty damn good. What I really wished, while reading Existence was that I wouldn't have read the description and known what Dank was. Knowing, made the whole reading experience less intriguing. While Pagan tried to find out who, or what, Dank was, I knew everything from the first page and it bothered me because it seemed rather silly that Pagan couldn't figure it out, with the clues right in front of her, until a lot later. "My beautiful soul," he murmured and caressed my cheek. "When you have the ultimate selfless sacrifice it paid my wrong. You proved to be worthy of my devotion. Of Death's... love." The characters were pretty likable though I found some flaws in most of them. However there are always exceptions like.... Dank Walker aka Death. I fell in love with him. I knew I would but he was just so captivating, witty and loving that it was hard not to. I enjoyed how, since he was Death, his true nature was to be cold, calculating and unattached but when it came to Pagan - he was kind, loving and protective.
