4 to 4.5 stars. I enjoyed rereading this sexy, romantic story. Christina Lauren is a clever pair of authors, and I have enjoyed all of the books in this series, some more than others. This one is the story of Sara Dillon, a young woman who moves to NYC to take a new job, and to leave her old life behind. She has really only ever had one boyfriend/partner, whom she was with for a number of years. But Sara was too young/naive/inexperienced at the time to realise that he was using her/cheating on her. It took her a long time, but she has finally decided she needs to move on. And now she's in New York celebrating at a club with her girlfriends, when she meets a sexy guy with whom she has a wild, out-of-character (for Sara) fling. It's actually a fantastic opening scene for the book. Max is a high-powered, high-flying businessman in the world of venture capitalism. He is also a well-known player whom the paparazzi like to focus on. Max is a sexy Englishman living in New York, but although he loves women, his social life isn't quite as wild as the press likes to make out. He is attracted to Sara, and after their fling he can't forget her. And so they begin to build a relationship. At first it's mainly about sex, or so both of them think, but it's clear they are both quickly developing real feelings for each other. Their hookups have a little exhibitionist kink to them, and they meet up in some very unusual places. It's not the sort of thing I'd normally like to read about actually, but the authors have written some very real characters. You can see what drives them, and they are beautiful together. The sex scenes are actually very tastefully done (and very sexy!) There is an interesting cast of secondary characters, some of whom feature in other books in the series (e.g. Max's business partner, the gorgeous Will Sumner who is the H of my fav book of the series, Beautiful Player.) The NYC setting is done very convincingly as well, with the world of business and the arts, as well as the social side of things all creating a great background to the story. My only reservation with this well-written book was that I felt the scenes in the  sex club  just pushed things a little too far for me. I was able to accept the way Max and Sara both had a little exhibitionist side to them, but for me that just carried it a bit too far. But otherwise, a lovely, sexy romance with believable characters. Very enjoyable book.

You might like this book if: You enjoy Watership Down You are curious about bees and their way of life You want to read something bizarre and different You are looking for a book with an original dystopian society (not another Hunger Games/Divergent copycat) The Bees  is a surprisingly 1. original, 2. action-packed and 3. emotional! For the first half of the book, I kept asking myself - why do I keep reading this? It's the weirdest, most bizarre thing I've ever had my hands on and it doesn't even have a human logic to it! Seriously, the whole book is written from the perspective of a worker bee, trying to fit in a strict, fanatic society, survive the calamities that befall her hive and guard her ultimate secret -  her ability to lay eggs. I went into this book without knowing much about this particular insect and its way of life, but by the 60%, I had the strong, unbearable urge to watch Bee documentaries! There are some pretty good ones actually... Of course, apart from the fact that worker bees are supposed to die after they sting, the author really knows her stuff! Ok, but that's not even the point! The world-building is amazing - the psychology and structure of a bee society is already interesting and weird enough, but add a little bit of dystopia, interaction with other species and real-life ecological issues and I cannot complain. The character development is superb - the protagonist starts of as any other weak-minded, rule-obeying worker and she gradually becomes a strong and independent leader to her people. Her journey is truly fascinating, but I had a real problem with her being so brainwashed in the beginning. The conclusion was epic! There is a lot of action and fights in this book (makes you feel sorry for the real bees), yet, the ending was also surprisingly emotional. Thank you, Laline Paull, for bringing us a remarkable, highly-original and emotional story!

** spoiler alert ** I liked Martha Wells The Cloud Roads and decided that some day I would read her past books. Khat the main character is an outsider in the city of Charisat,his people the krismen were created/genetically engineenered to survive in the harsh desert called the Waste. This causes him to be treated like a second class citizen by many,luckily he has enough survival skills for people who wish him harm to think twice before they try anything. But other people seek him out because of his skill as a relic hunter of the Ancients artifacts. One day he accepts an assignment to escort a Warden (a magic user) across the waste to one of the Ancients ruins.On the way they are assaulted by pirates,people who have been driven out of Charisat and turned to The Warden is hurt and after removing the veil that most upperclass people wear Khat discovers that he is a she.She reveals her name to be Elen,apprentice to the Master Warden. After they are joined by other wardens and travels back to Charisat,Khat is tasked by the Master Warden with finding two very important relics with the help of Elen. Seems simple enough...if it werent for the fact that other people also want them... I recognized many themes from the Raksura series and at times Khat reminded me of Moon in personality. The author seems to be fond of the matriarchial society (used in the Raksura series) Here its just mentioned as being one of the reasons Khat left his fellow krismen. Another thing I couldnt help but make a comparison with the Raksura series was how the author incorporated an agressive female,in a way to reverse gender roles maybe? Khat is even taken advantage of a female character  not so much rape as he just lies back and let he have her way with him.Its not described in great detail. I was a bit disgusted by this...but it doesnt seem to be such a big deal with Khat.It just threw me off. I also wish that Khats relatives had gotten more than a walk on appearance,by the end of the book their relationship is still unresolved. And even though the end was fitting I hated to see him leave Elen :( City of Bones is a standalone book so there isnt even the hope of a sequel,so i guess I have to be philisophical about it. I didnt love this book but while I was reading it I was immersed in it,and the world building is pretty impressive. Just because of that it deserves a three star rating.

2.5 stars As a romantic-suspense well-known lover, I found this entertaining and nothing more. After reading Breaking Point and Striking Distance from Pamela Clare's I-Team series -no, I haven't read the first four books, though I have been spoiled a lot, as you can imagine- I can say that this lady knows how to write the action parts. The pacing is perfect and she seems to have a very in-depth knowledge of military/law enforcement terminology, operations, weaponry, missions and general warfare. In what the suspense parts are concerned, her stories are very close to the espionage thrillers I used to read a while back, and given the fact she is a romance author, I am highly impressed. But sadly, this is where my admiration ends. I thought the romance lacked almost in every aspect, the characters were boring and unrealistic, the chemistry non-existent and the overflowing sex was exasperating. I found myself skimming through the pages and pages and pages of graphic hand/oral/normal/vibrator sex just to the get to the good parts -which were NOT about Javier in his splendid nakedness, but Javier doing his job and being a badass. What he actually was till a certain point in the story, when, facing the almighty power of the vagina, he becomes a total wuss. Breaking Point deja-vu all the way from here. A fabulous start, a wonderful exposition of romantic-suspense know-how, and then baaam, all turns to crappy cheese. I strongly believe that if the real military operatives would be so easily distracted by the power of love, nobody would be sleeping peacefully at night. Though the romance between Javier and Laura was presented in the sappiest of ways, I still didn't feel it properly, and for that I blame the sex. Too much sex in a story kills the real chemistry between the characters -which, in theory, is supposed to be about deeper stuff than the earth-shattering sex marathons- and turns lovemaking into pure porn. Since the beginning -and by that I mean First Strike, a 70 pages length erotica novella about how Javier and Laura fucked their brains out at their first date- I didn't feel their relationship to be anything more than sex. Don't get me wrong, I am completely ok with the relationships based on sex, they are rather fun to get into, but don't sugarcoat it, don't talk about feeeelings and don't call it love. It is not love. It is lust, and it is a completely different thing. The story itself was good, perfectly paced and mostly believable -except that part about Javier getting Laura's baby out from Afghanistan Chuck Norris style, which had a very B action movie vibe to it and only made me laugh out loud . The epilogues were both eye-rolling material and absolutely unnecessary, and I really disliked that the PTSD problem was so rushed -  PTSD suddenly cured by the powers of magic vagina, as my friend Ash cleverly pointed out in her review. But to end on a positive note, lighter on the schmaltz and on the sex, Pamela Clare is a romantic-suspense author I could really get into.

Actual rating: 4.25 Update review When I originally read this book, it was the beginning of the school year and I began to get loads of work, so I didn't give this book the quality reading time it deserved. Now that I really had a chance to read this book in-depth, I think I enjoyed it much more. Meghan Chase is an average teenage girl--until the day that she discovers she's half-fey. Everything Meghan thought she knew begins to fall apart. Suddenly, she finds herself thrown into an unknown world, desperate to reclaim a loved one. However, she gets more than she bargains for as she finds herself in the middle of an ancient feud, and turns out to be the only person who can save the fey from an unknown and dangerous enemy. The characters in this novel are memorable ones. Meghan, Puck, Ash--they're all cleverly written. At the start of this novel I really hated Meghan's parents, until I learned why everyone forgot about her often. So if you're considering putting down this book because you think that's so unrealistic (I know I did), keep on reading. Meghan, although not physically very strong, is clever and a solid character. I didn't find many face-palm moments where she does something incredibly stupid (except maybe when she forgave Scott Waldron so easily for calling her a bitch and believed that he wanted to be friends with her. I mean, come on ). Puck seems like a very honest character, and the type of friend I've always wanted to have. Ash, although a bit scary and evil at the start, is fiercely devoted to those he cares about. That alone will make you fall in love with him. He's willing to risk everything for the people he cares about. I've read a few Fey books before, but none have interested me so much. I love the idea of a new race of fairies being created because that's what humans are believing in present day. The plot is well-paced and the relationships are very believeable. No insta-love here. After finishing this book, I desperately wanted to know more. Overall, this book is highly entertaining and one I'd definitely recommend. If you're looking for for a new favorite book, here it is!

Kendall Ryan never sees to amaze her readers with her writing. You honestly can never know what to expect, but you sure as hell should know to expect something hot and steamy that will make your panties melt, especially with this new British standalone hottie! Sterlin Quinn is the ultimate bachelor who treats women with respect, and acknowledges the fact they can drop to their knees in an instant just to please him. Yup! He is that type of persona. One that I freaking ADORE! As a divorce attorney, his opinion about a happily-ever-after and "love" is outspoken a lot in this story because he does not believe in those feelings. However, those opinions change the second his uncle tells him about the inheritance Sterlin's grandfather left him before he past away, and the rules regulated that need to be followed to obtain that inheritance- get hitched (does that sound familiar? Yes! That's because this is sort of a sequel to the Hitched Volume Series by Kendall as well.) That's when Camryn pops in the picture. She is a stunning businesswoman who works for the personal communications department in Olivia and Noah's company. They have both asked Camryn to assist Sterlin in finding the ideal woman for him to call his "wife." What they did not realize is that they would soon fall for each other... Camryn tries not to break the walls of keeping things professional, but with Sterlin's charms and trying to woo her she seems to fail at keeping a distance. Their "friendship" evolved at a quick pace that I would have found rather disturbing to read, but instead I ended up finding it quite well written. When they both finally open up for each other, their chemistry is off the charts! Sterlin can never seem to keep his hands off of Camryn and she never minds it. Except that in the back of her mind she is always thinking about finding him the ideal "wife". Sterlin on the other hand, tries to convince her that he is the ideal man for her. This was a beautiful love story that I enjoyed so much! With a cliche but at the same time refreshing ending/epilogue, Kendall Ryan has achieved yet again to woo her readers in this new NA Romance. Now, after reading the small excerpt she wrote at the finale of this book about The Room Mate (coming next year) I cannot wait to get my hands on that one! My least favourite Brandon Sanderson Novella to date. The ending fell a bit flat for me  possibly because the relationship between the two detectives wasn't developed enough for Davis planning to kill Chaz to have enough emotional impact. and the beginning was repetitive in its world building. It was extremely unlike Brandon Sanderson to keep on repeating the same information in different contexts, such as how expensive the technology was or that the city had been forced to buy it. It wasn't even particularly important information and certainly didn't need to be emphasised more than once. That being said, it is still a great short story, a very cool concept and an interesting read. It is Brandon Sanderson after all and quality is pretty much guaranteed, it's just in scaling it to his other works that this falls a little short. Weirdly, what I enjoyed most than all was reading the postscript note about how various elements of the story came to be. It's fascinating to go behind the writer's brain and see how he viewed the story. I wish this was a requirement for every work of fiction, I feel like I learned more about writing by reading that than by completing a number of university courses.

I laughed, I cried and I even clapped out loud and I'm not a clapper while reading, or so I thought. I loved this book! I can't believe how much this series just keeps getting better and better. Summer and Winter were supposed to be enemies. We were not supposed to cooperate, we were not supposed to go on quests together and, most important, we were not supposed to fall in love. Meghan and Ash have been exiled from the Nevernever. They chose love over their loyalty to their courts and because of this they have been banished to the mortal realm. While they are returning to Meghan's home, to see her family, the Iron fae intervene. They try to capture Meghan to bring her back to the false king of the Iron Kingdom. Meghan realizes she can't sacrifice her family's safety and that she will never truly be free until she faces the false Iron king. She becomes resonate that she needs to destroy the false king so she can finally start to live her life. The journey they embark on is even more eventful then their other journeys in the past. The faery fates lay in Meghan's hands and regardless of what happens nothing will ever be the same again. He sighed, framing my face with his hands. "My life...everything I am...belongs to you." It's hard to imagine I know BUT Ash is even more magnificent in this book. Meghan has fully melted his ice facade and we get to see ALL of him. He's sarcastic, heartfelt, protective, loyal, trust worthy and he knows in his heart that his world and future are Meghan. Ash's heart still bleeds from past events but with the help of Meghan's love he is trying to overcome it. Despite everything I felt and the crazy emotions churning inside me, it all came back to him. Meghan grows up so much in this book. She realizes what her duties are and she gives her all and then some. She speaks her mind and doesn't allow anyone, no matter their rank, to walk over herself or the ones she loves. She is strong, determined, and a force to be reckoned with. She is the epitome of who you want to read about if you love a take charge, kick-butt female lead! Gods forgive me if I was being selfish, but I wanted nothing more than to stay with him forever. One of things that I love about this series is that each character we know and are introduced to is so unique. Their personalities, their words and their actions are SO each their own. Each one stands out by themselves and each one ads so much to the book. I thoroughly enjoyed the constant reappearance of Grim and I enjoyed two newcomers that really stood out, Razor and Glitch. I understood. This was my fate, my destiny. I knew what had to be done. I always know that I've fallen for a book when I think about the characters long after the book is over. I'm shocked that this series will now be lumped in with my favorite books especially since the first book was so mundane. Now on to finding out what happens next! "This is the story of a girl who fooled a thousand boys, a boy who fooled an entire country, a partnership that would change the fate of realms, and a power to challenge the greatest tyrant the world had ever known. Fantasy, fairy tales and magic. A magical realm and Victorian London. One girl and one boy. The girl: Iolanthe Seabourne has been told that she's the greatest elemental mage of her generation. She doesn't really believe it. But after she powerfully displays her ability to the world, and ends up being hunted by for what she can do, she figures out that she needs to take herself seriously. Iolanthe has never known her parents and she's practically had to raise herself. She's smart, resourceful and highly adaptable, but doesn't trust easily. Iolanthe does a few things at the beginning of this story that bugged me, but knowing her past, I can't really blame her. I grew to understand her better as the story progressed. The boy: Prince Titus of Eberon (one of the magical realms) has spent his life preparing to train and protect Iolanthe. Because of his royal status and young age, he is constantly watched and monitored. As a necessity for survival, Titus is always deceiving and out maneuvering those around him. He's also willing to do nearly anything to succeed - lie, betray even kill if he has to. Titus is my favorite character in this book. I wasn't sure about him at one point early on, but I love how the author was able to alter my feelings about him throughout the course of this story. girl + boy: I really enjoyed watching Iolanthe and Titus get to know each other, especially the ways they surprised and challenged the other. The nature of Iolanthe and Titus's deception means that they can't trust anyone and must keep everyone at arms length. I think that's why none of the other characters stood out as much as they did, even though there are a lot of secondaries. I do think this started to change some at the end of the book, and hope that they are able to gain a bit more trust from others in the future installments. Inevitably, there is also a romance brewing between Iolanthe and Titus. It's an important part of this series, but these characters are strong individually and aren't spending all their time mooning over each other (thank goodness). I'm really interested to see how their relationship progresses through the series. While I enjoyed this romance, I'm hoping that it becomes more epic as the series continues. Settings: One third of The Burning Sky takes place in a land of magic where children are regularly born with the ability to control the elements (called mages), a third of the book takes place in the Crucible (read the book to find out about that) and the other third takes place in Victorian London, with its rain and trains and boys boarding schools. One of these schools is exactly the place that Titus hides Iolanthe. Dressed as a boy named Arthur Fairfax, Iolanthe gets to attend the illustrious Eton College, where royalty still educates its sons. She drinks tea, plays cricket and recites Latin, while secretly training to overtake the magical authorities who are advancing on her. Themes: I really enjoyed the contrast between the elemental world and the industrial one, and how Iolanthe talks about magic use changing because of the modernization of the world. I also liked the questions raised about fate and free will. Does a seer witness the future or help to create it? Is it possible to contradict a vision? I hope both of these themes come more into play in the next books. Conclusion: The Burning Sky introduces three unique worlds, each with their own set of rules, and I still feel like I've only scratched the surface of them. Also, to me it seemed like the magical rules conveniently (or inconveniently) changed occasionally, as needed in the story. Or at the very least, I feel as if I've still not mastered all the rules for all the locations and I can already tell I'm going to need to re-read this book before the next one comes out! Although it took me a little bit of time to warm up to these characters and immerse myself in this complex world, The Burning Sky is a great beginning to what I'm hoping is going to be a really exciting trilogy. It's been eight years since I've read this this, and the message of this book still might be one of the most moral repugnant I've ever seen. What's saddest is that A Mango Shaped Space could be a great book, were it not for the terrible moral of the story. So. A Mango Shaped Space is about a girl who begins a journey to learn who she is and accept her own synesthesia. Along the way, she makes friends at conventions for people with synesthesia. She even learns that acupuncture feels really good for people with synesthesia (which is really cool and something I didn't know). This is where everything about this book goes wrong. Along the way, she starts to abandon her family. Her new friends turn out to be false. And then she forgets to close the door because she was distracted by learning about her synesthesia, causing her cat to die. All of these things are portrayed as direct results of her synesthesia. It's even weirder when you consider that she starts talking to her family less because they didn't accept her synesthesia, even though it was their choice to not accept her synesthesia, not hers. The message that comes out, intentionally or not, indicates that learning who you are is a bad thing. The narrative punishes the main character for 1) being different, 2) liking the things that make her different, and 3) wanting to know who she is. That's a really messed-up narrative. That was the message I took from this book is sixth grade or so. And that wasn't a good message for me to internalize, or for any kid to internalize. The author also does not have synesthesia herself, and there are several other reviews on this page talking about how that negatively affected the book. Wendy Maas overexaggerates the issues that come along with synesthesia, making it seem like a blessing that makes the protagonist better than everyone else. Not only does this book have a fucked-up narrative around our differences, A Mango-Shaped Space doesn't even portray that difference correctly. So. I can't recommend this book, no matter how much I enjoy the writing style or the characters. I just can't. This is a really messed-up narrative and I can't believe anyone has the nerve to sell this to kids.

I find it difficult to give a dispassionate opinion on Never Let Me Go. Overall it is a very pleasantly fluent book to read, that at the same time appropriately conveys the unsettling feeling that you would expect from an alternative present/dystopian novel. The concept is touching: the story of these clones who grow insufficiently aware that their destiny is to donate organs until their bodies are disposed of and the politically engaged attempts to give these creatures a pleasant life, whilst not changing their future  is profoundly uncanny, so near to humanhood, yet so incredibly distant they partake somehow of Agamben's sacerta. The creation of an alternative jargon to refer only to the protagonists of the story is crucial, and adds to the overall unpleasantness of the environment. Clones do not die, they 'complete' (supposedly the cycle of donations, clones do not fear death, they hope to complete at their fourth donation, without having to linger as paralysed yet conscious bodies at the mercy of their future donations, clones do not live, they are reared, etc. Yet the writing is pedantic and it seems that at times you are watching a bad episode of How I Met Your Mother. Evidently interesting and plot-advancing events are hinted to one chapter before they are actually unravelled and the first person narrator all too often uses devices such as: 'but for you to understand this I have to go back to another' usually insignificant event. In spite of the unsettling environment, the plot line is in the end the growing up of the protagonists, which is remarkably similar to that of normal human beings  were it not for the setting. A YA novel framed in a very unsettling environment. As readers we are too often roller-coastered through not completely useful flashback and flash forwards, so many times that it looks like the author is purposefully trying to delay/defer the moment of the final 'spiegone', as we would say in Italian, the ultimate uber-explanation of all that you have always wondered but were too afraid to ask, a spiegone that inevitably arrives in the penultimate chapter. Pity, a good book that falls into too many established cliches and that fails to overcome them. Nevertheless, as a reading experience, it is very pleasant a part from the rather perverse deferral of the final explanation, which is not subtle enough and more often than not results annoying.

For some reason, I don't read very many gothic novels, even though when I do read them I love them. Is it that there aren't many of them written? Are they just not flashy enough to compete with their dystopian brethren? Or do I just not keep them high enough on my radar? This gothic beauty has been languishing on my TBR for a long time, and I'm kicking myself for not getting to it sooner. Immortal had everything going for it - sweeping romance, eerie moors, haunting ghosts. In the first 100 pages, I was enthralled. Evie arrives at Wyldcliffe, only to be nearly run over by a dark, mysterious, and handsome (naturally) boy on a horse. It was a scene ripped from Jane Eyre, that gothic novel to end all gothic novels. I was anticipating the love story to come and finding the secrets hidden in the passageways of the boarding school. Around the midpoint of the book I realized that I needed to adjust my expectations. Evie isn't really haunted so much as she experiences visions. She has odd dreams and keeps seeing a girl who looks like her lurking around the school, but she's never really frightened by any of it. This means, of course, that I was never scared as a reader, either. It took a lot of the fun out of Evie's trips down musty passageways and out onto the moor to meet up with Sebastian. Sebastian, the boy from the horse, runs into her again late one night after Evie has snuck out to get some air. They begin to meet up nightly, and Evie falls in love. I guess. Well, she says she falls in love, but I certainly didn't get swoony over it. This was one romance that just wasn't for me. You see, the book intersperses Evie's story with excerpts from Lady Agnes Templeton's diary from 1882 to 1884. Agnes, the daughter of the owners of Wyldcliffe manor, writes about her friend "S." who introduces her to the Mysticke Way. "S" is kind of a jerk, and as they unlock their mystical powers (witchcraft, though no one in this book wants to call it that), he gets worse. SPOILER ALERT! (I think, though it seemed pretty obvious to me.) I mean, clearly, "S" is Sebastian, right? So I'm reading all about this douche from the past who treated Lady Agnes like complete garbage...and then I'm supposed to be happy that Evie is falling for him? Nope. Not going to happen. (Carry on.) The witchcraft bit doesn't really come in to play for Evie's story until late in the book, at which point she has to rush to understand her role in the history of Wyldcliffe much too quickly for my taste. Once Evie finally starts to put together the pieces of the large and obvious clues in front of her, there are only a few chapters left. She has so much to learn and do, which gets rushed into a couple of scenes, only to build to a climax that is resolved so quickly and lacks so much (or any) confrontation that it feels too easy. Instead of wrapping things up with a genuine conflict between Evie and some badass witches in this story, it seems like the author left that for the next in the series. What a letdown! I would have liked to have seen more of Evie developing her own powers and working with her friends. I would have liked to have seen her then use those powers in a manner that actually accomplished something instead of seeming to delay the conflict for a bit. Still, I'm only really complaining because overall I really enjoyed the book. I liked the mystery of Lady Agnes and "S" and how it all tied in with Evie. I loved the setting (boarding school!) and the isolation of this old manor on the moor. I tore through this book - devoured it - to find out what would happen next. It was thoroughly engaging, even if it didn't turn out to be quite the book I wanted it to be.

She is also doomed, if she kisses her true love he will die. So who is her true love? Is it one of the Raven Boys? Adam, Gansey or Ronan, it can't be Noah, he is already dead. And what will the quest for the Glendower reveal? I really wanted to love this book. But it left me feeling exactly the same as the first book, unsatisfied. And I just can't put my finger on why. I really like Blue as a character. She is so grounded and practical, she isn't perfect, but she makes realistic and understandable decisions. And I liked the relationship between the boys, and between the boys and Blue, and also between the individual characters finding out who they were. It all feels real, and the book is well written and atmospheric. It just never hooked me, never got up under my skin like The Scorpio Races did. Actually that isn't totally true, because every now and then some parts of the book would come alive, but then poof, it was gone, and I was back to reading a perfectly adequate and entertaining book. Urgh, that is such a horrible thing to say about a book, utterly damning in a way that I don't want to. Because I liked this book, I like this series, and I will read the final book in the series when it comes out next year1 . I just wanted more feeling from it, and I didn't get it. Although part of the problem may have been that I didn't reread the first book, and it has been a year so details have definitely escaped my memory. A refresher probably would have helped. In her review of The Raven Boys Renay mentioned similarities with Susan Cooper's The Dark is Rising series. At first reading that didn't quite gel with me, but I've just finished a reread of that series so it is fresh in my mind, and after a seconds-worth of thought it makes sense. Both deal contemporary times but also with the whole notion of time and what is happening now affecting the past as well as the other way around, and of course Owain Glynd?r. But also the fact that they revolve around a group of children/teenagers, and that they are both so grounded in the landscape. That was one thing that really stood out in my reread of The Dark is Rising, the descriptions of the Thames region and Wales were so vivid. I'm not quite sure that Stiefvater got quite that same level of vividness across, but she came close in her descriptions of people within their landscape. Hmmm, talking about The Dream Thieves now makes me think that I actually got a lot more out of the book that I had initially thought :)

Despite randomly jumping into book 7 of the series, the Bridgerton family and other members of the extended cast (particularly Lady Danbury) grew on me really quickly, Quinn's writing style was easy and humorous without being overwrought and Hyacinth and Gareth's bickering friendship was promising. Ironically, what let down this historical romance was the actual romance. There was very little romantic happening for the better part of the novel, to put it mildly. I'm all for gradual development, but for the longest time I couldn't even see how Hyacinth and Gareth were going to make it past the acquaintance stage, or no further than tenuous friendship, anyway. Gareth makes his lack of interest in Hyacinth clear, and does so repeatedly. Cliche as it may be, I wanted them to slowly realize their attraction for each other, but on Gareth's end there was little more than passing curiosity, perhaps a mixture of amusement and quite a lot of exasperation, but nothing that convinced me he'd fall in love. I put up with it to this point, but what really tipped this over the line into "absolutely unromantic and not really forgiveable" was the way Gareth soured any chance of this being a lovely romance through his calculating and manipulative behaviour. Right up until his father made mocking comments about Gareth never being able to marry someone out of his league like Hyacinth Bridgerton, there was no indication that he'd seriously considered her romantically - in fact, he'd made it clear a few times that it was rather horrifying an idea to be tied down thus. Then out of nowhere, literally on a whim (and obviously motivated by his father's words), Gareth decides that he likes her and it'd be a spiffing idea to propose to her. What's worse, he then determines the best course of action is to ruin her so that she wouldn't be able to back out of the engagement when she inevitably found out about his family secret. This was apparently fine in his eyes, since he likes her anyway and this is partially done out of a desire to make sure she won't leave him. Romantic, right? It was so despicable that I nearly dropped the book right then and there; I simply didn't see how it was redeemable. And ultimately, it wasn't, really. Hyacinth didn't make him work hard enough to win her back, and I was never convinced that Gareth truly saw the error of his ways. The final third did a lot to restore my enjoyment of the book (after it took me weeks to force myself to finish it, mind you), but in the end, even if his feelings were genuine later, it was a case of too little, too late. I'm afraid that Lady Bridgerton was incorrect about "his kiss" being how one could determine whether a man loves them - it's in his actions. And nothing about Gareth's actions (not just regarding the way he made a disaster out of the proposal/marriage issue, but also the demeaning way he used a confused and uninformed Hyacinth to gain leverage during his petty verbal battles with his father on at least one occasion ) suggested that this was a man who truly loved her. It's truly odd that I liked just about everything about this book except for the romance, considering the genre. I'm curious as to whether it's worth trying another one of Quinn's books or whether I might run into similar snags.

**You can see this full review and more at Book Briefs: https://bookbriefs.net** NA Review My Thoughts Beauty of the Beast is the first book in the new adult Fairy Tale retellings series by Rachel Demeter. I loved Beauty of the Beast. Totally and completely loved this book. I have been really into retellings lately, and this is a great one. The blurb claims it is "Perfect for fans of Beauty and the Beast and The Phantom of the Opera" and I can totally see that! This is a dark and gothic retelling, so it is not going to be light and fluffy, but it is so heartbreakingly romantic. I just loved seeing Isabelle and Adam. Isabelle is taking care of her sick father and Adam is a Prince and also the sole survivor of a raid on his castle when he was younger. He now lives in seculsion and when Isabelle and her father happen upon his castle she trades herself to save her father and that is really where our story starts. This story made me super emotional. Both happy and sad emotions. There are two events that took place that really gutted me. When Isabelle's father dies at the start of the story! At the start! and when the dog stranger was shot. I'm sorry, but there is never any reason to kill a dog! It is a testament to how much I loved the rest of the story if I still gave it five stars when a dog died. That is normally the kiss of death for me. #isthatweird  But still, I loved the writing and the characters and the rest of the story so much that I still gave this book five stars! Which is really big for me if you know what one of the things was. That is normally a huge no-no for me in books/tv shows/movies. But Beauty of the Beast was good enough that I made an exception in this case. I'm not sure who was more wounded and who I felt for more in the story. Adam and Isabelle really are kindred souls. Adam with his obvious hardship and past and Isabelle with her awful fiance and dealing with family issues. Watching them come together and form a slow friendship and even slower romance was so sweet and satisfying. I really loved the slow burn romance in Beauty of the Beast. If you like retellings that take the bones of the tale and tell a really strong story with the basic plot, you will love Beauty of the Beast. Rachel doesn't do anything too radical with the storyline and it feels pretty true to the original but she does do a really cool mash up beauty and the beast and the phantom of the opera. The end result is a great slow burn romance with a tortured hero and a really likable heroine. I devoured this story in one sitting! This is a fantastic retelling. I can't wait to read more from Rachel. This is a book you do not want to miss, and it is one sale right now for preorders! This review was originally posted on Book Briefs

I received a free copy of this book in exchange for an honest review. Optical Illusion is a novel that works overall but falls aparts in the details, one of which is so fundamental to the plot's coherence that it threatens its success as a work of fiction. It starts off by introducing the two main characters before they actually meet, which was a good decision as it allows the reader to come to terms with their personalities before they affect each other. Jase is the stoical kind, a military man who got disabled in a suicide bombing and thus forced to retire. He is also very deep in the closet. Chris is a very spastic, flamboyantly gay young man with a chaotic lifestyle that includes homelessness and trading sex for occasional board and bed. Right away they are very different people so one is to expect plenty of conflict. They only become acquainted because it turns out Chris is the half-brother of Matt, Jase's very one-sided crush and very straight childhood friend. The story is structured in chapters alternating the points of view of this three characters, the focus shifting entirely cancelling out Matt as it progresses. Exposing the reader to the mental states of its cast can help give a greater depth but in this case it becomes almost irrelevant. If the titles of the chapters were scrambled around, there would be little to no difference to the functionality of the narrative. This is not to say that Optical Illusion does not do a good job at getting into the heads of its characters. Chris, in particular, is rendered beautifully. Suffering from extreme ADHD and unable to sleep, with a wreck of a childhood riddled with poverty and a truly toxic environment where drugs addicts and traffickers were the norm, he is a complex person whose inner contradictions seem very true to life. Both highly independent and clearly unable to function on his own, his often crass innuendo and joyful attitude are something of a breath of fresh air. For someone who has been so obviously let down by the system, and knows it too, he manages to cope with his issues better than one might think. Perhaps the most interesting aspect in his psychological life is his view on sex. For Chris, sex is a commodity to be traded and the notion of consent and abuse seems almost absent from his thinking. The very low self-esteem has him craving attention and the rush he gets from being wanted has him doing some very questionable choices. The intense hyperactivity leads him to be overly sexual as it is one of the few things that sends him to sleep. All this makes him a very vibrant and highly flawed yet still likable character. His ADHD in particular is conveyed through highly expressive language, the out-of-control and frantic feelings of spinning wildly being the highlights of the novel. As for Jase, his character is more wooden and not as big of a challenge. There are issues in him as well, a peculiar tendency not to vocalize emotions and not having come to terms with the implications of his accident, but it tends to fade in comparision with everything that Chris is. As for their relationship, it is as rocky as it to be expected and in a sense its inception seems rather unlikely. The novel is at its best when it realizes that no amount of love can solve deep rooted problems and that a relationship, particularly one between such different people, is a constant re-negotiation of limits and prospects. The greatest flaw in the novel, apart from the technical ones that will be addressed later, must be bracketed in spoilers given how central it is for later developments: At some point Chris gets kidnapped by a group of human traffickers in order to put pressure on Matt. They want Matt to use his lorries to transport some people across the Channel and threaten to kill Chris is he disobeys. The story nearly jumps the shark when it reaches this portion. Not only does the kidnapping happen in the parking car of a loaded club, as the kidnappers show their faces and let Chris find their names. After keeping him on a heroin induced trance for two whole weeks, then gang-raping him and sharing the footage with Matt and co., they proceed to release him. It makes absolutely no sense. Given that he has seen their faces and even has an idea of the inner geography of the place where he was kept, releasing Chris is a truly stupid move. The main kidnapper remarks that he would rather deliver his victims with an addictions then actually kill them but that also does not add up. Why would such a violent gang incur such a risk? It is made doubly bad since Matt was not able to keep his side of the bargain. This entire sub-plot could have been ommitted and probably should have been so. Its reasons for being seems to be connected to injecting greater drama, even more so given how phobic Chris is over heroine, and to serve as a catalyst to propel Jase into pushing for a relationship. It also entails a secondary character who acts with an annoying dose of omniscience as tends to happen with fictional characters crafted to orbit around the main ones and provide insight in lieu of the narrator. Nate, said character, also borders on Deus ex Machina given his wealth and medical knowledge, especially with dealing with addiction to drugs. Which is a shame as Nate has the potential for being a very interesting character and hopefully the rest of the series will develop him further. The before mentioned technical problems include occasional error of syntax and/or grammar and actual inconsistencies in the plot, especially when it comes to dates and the passage of time. Pay close attention and see how the time that has elapsed since Jase and Chris met, seems to contract or stretch. These are not fatal mistakes, though, and some editing and proofreading would fix them very easily. Overall, Optical Illusion manages to keep the reader engaged and even achieves greatness when it tackles the highs and lows of ADHD. It is unfortunate that it cannot reach that level throughout the entire narrative. It remains readable and worth taking a chance on.

I'm not usually a reader of Sci-fi. I was first drawn to this book by the cover. I work at my University's bookstore and we have two different editions of this book on the shelf. I definitely enjoyed this book (I finished it in about 2 days). For the most part, it read like an (unobjective) anthropologist's journal. World building was detailed but also very heavy-handed. I liked that the characters were all deep and complex. I would have liked to see more of a romance between Genry and Theren . I would have also liked more of a concrete explanation of what happened between Arek and Theren . I probably won't read the other books in this series, just because they don't really appeal to me, but I did enjoy this one!
Adorable Lovely Perfect Sweet Romantic Funny Satisfying Did I mention perfect?

This book was a really interesting exploration of grief, trauma, and friendship, and it was written very well. I was pleasantly surprised, because when I read the synopsis I totally thought it was going to be your straight-up romance with Otis falling in love with Meg and blah blah happily ever after, but that wasn't the case. The writing was gorgeous, and the characters really stood out - all of them were very well-written. I especially liked Dara, Otis's one-armed swim coach. She had a really big character presence and I really enjoyed her and Otis's friendship. Meg was nice too, and it was really interesting seeing this web of relationships. One thing I really appreciated is that the book seemed to value friendship over romance, as Otis constantly chooses Dara over Meg. It's not something you usually see in YA.

Oh the feelings I have about this book... TW (book & review): teen pregnancy, unplanned pregnancy, discussion of abortion, ableism, forced alien impregnation, infertility  (I'm really not sure this should be YA, actually.) Starting with the positive! Elvie was, for the most part, an enjoyable main character. She is smart and kicks butt at some things without being a complete Mary Sue. The concept - a space yacht full of pregnant teenagers turns out to be run by aliens - was certainly original. Our teenage female protag actually has a decent relationship with her father. I really like Ducky. The plot consistently managed to do something interesting a couple pages before I had planned to put it down. If you're looking for some fluffy summer reading with a different premise than your average YA novel, or for a book to snarkily discuss with the friends who roped you into this nonsense (ahem), here you go. However, and this is a big however, there is a LOT that is not good about this book. Writing: It varies from such breathtaking inanity as, "So yeah... that happens," to absolute gold, like, "Captain Bob looks at me with the sort of blank stare you'd give an opossum you just found out could play the ukulele." This may have something to do with which co-author wrote what. [Side note: Hey Goodreads, y u no credit female co-author?] There is also copious (to me) amounts of fake futuristic teenager slang. I was especially bothered by "chromers," which I had parsed as "people not with what's new and hip," but which turned out to be an in-universe ableist slur. Seriously, it's a reference to a chronic genetic disorder. Travel to LEO has become blase, but we're still making fun of physical/mental disabilities? Pregnancy: I'm making this a whole topic, because I'm not convinced the writers actually know what being pregnant entails. Lemme just say these girls can handle IMPRESSIVE AMOUNTS of physical exertion for the third trimester. The hangar scene. So much suspension of disbelief required for the hangar scene. Also bad physics. Additionally, the whole thing is just not handled very well. I felt like every few pages, the authors went, "Oh right, she's pregnant! Time to crave some hilariously nasty food combination and whine about her belly!" The TW I spoiler tagged: There's no good way to discuss this without spoilers, but I think it's important to note. The girls, once impregnated by the aliens, usually without their knowledge or consent, will be rendered infertile after carrying to term. This is NOT hinted at early in the book, and pops up as a huge nasty surprise halfway through. Obviously, this is wildly problematic and will be very potentially triggering for some readers. I will give the book credit for at least voicing Elvie's quite righteous anger about this. Cole: I hates him. Don't care how pretty he is. No. *haaaaaate* SO! If you managed to slog through all of the above and are thinking, "Seriously, she's whining about this? It's just a book..." you'll probably enjoy it. If you read all of the above and think "I MUST CONSUME THIS MONSTROSITY" you'll probably also enjoy it. Everyone else, I have no idea. Aliens. (I still hate Cole.)

3 Stars Well, what can I say? This book is Fifty Shades of Grey, Mr. President, and A Table for Three rolled into one. I have to say this was so out of my comfort zone but I was able to successfully finish it because the story was a lot more interesting than I could have ever expected. I knew what I was signing for when I started American Queen. Knew that it has some kind of strange and complicated love story about three characters and it has a menage and BDSM content. I have read quite a number of books with these themes but this was sure to be my first read that has M-M romance. I loved the fact that the story centered around the political world. Our two heroes namely Mexen Ashley "Ash" Colchester and Embry Moore are best friends and they happen to be politicians (Maxen is the United States' President while Embry is the Vice President). The heroine Greer Galloway also comes from Political roots as her grandfather is an ex-Vice President. In a way, I found the political aspect quite refreshing and full of sense which managed to fill the story with substance. There were lots and lots of kinky scenes here (if you know what I mean) and my inner goddess rejoiced lol. I loved that the author didn't shy away from making all those scenes a bit graphic for the readers. However, I didn't like how the relationship between the three characters eventually appeared to be manipulative. Ash was manipulative and selfish. I didn't like the way he made sure all things work in his favor. I mean, a relationship should have a give and take process on all sides. In this case, Ash was the one who always took but didn't give. I couldn't even get the reason why Greer and Embry allowed it. Was it because Ash is the President? And oh, don't even get me started on his romance with Jenny. I also have an issue with Greer. I understood her recklessness in her decisions when she was still 16. But as she grew, there was no character development that happened. She turned out to be such a weak heroine all throughout the book, easily forgiving Ash and letting him control her decisions. Although this book suffered quite a number of flaws, this was still a well-written adult fiction erotica book. This was my first Sierra Simone read and I can say that her writing, her choice of words, and the way she delivered the plot and those toe-curling sexy scenes absolutely drew me in. For fans of erotica, MM romance, and menage, you might love this.

4 stars. I really liked this book. When it was first released, I didn't really pay attention to it as much since at the time, I wasn't into fantasy. Of course, when The Winner's Kiss was released and everyone was practically calling it a great end to a trilogy, I decided to check them out. Plus, I was really getting more interested into fantasy. So, I ordered the trilogy (also another trilogy: The Powder Mage trilogy) and began reading The Winner's Curse. So what did I think of it? Well, as I mentioned, I liked it. But there were a few problems I had with it. Luckily, the positives outweighed the negatives. For starters, I really liked the world building and learning more about the history between the Valorians and the Herranis, not to mention the political aspects of each country. Lately, I'm really liking how some fantasies are playing with politics and how choices matter in starting wars, ending them, and how a country is supposed to be run. Fantasy politics are much more interesting than real life politics. We are introduced to Kestrel and Arin. Kestrel is the daughter of a very powerful general. So she has a lot to live up to. She has to decide whether to enlist in the army or marry by the time she reaches twenty. Of course, she doesn't want any of that. She wants to decide what is best for her. Kestrel is quick with her thoughts and a good strategists. It's shown how she observes people and saying the right (or sometimes wrong) words and can trick people. I like that about her character. Arin is the slave who seems to know a lot more than what a Herrani is supposed to know. And he has a goal in mind. And that goal could be... problematic. Arin was on the same level of wit with Kestrel because like her, he has to do a few things in order to accomplish that goal. But while doing so, he didn't want Kestrel to be involved in it. It showed how dedicated he was to his goal while not wanting Kestrel to get hurt. Then we get to the second half to the book. WOAH! I was really hooked from then on. I never knew I could get through a book so quickly. And that ending... Now, it's time to address the negatives. For one thing, the story, while interesting from the beginning, took a while for things to get developing. But I saw how it was slowly building up to what would happen in the middle so it wasn't that bad. The other would have to be how much planning there was yet it took a while for that plan to take into fruition. Of course, they would go through with the plan but it took a while. So other than that, there wasn't that many flaws. Overall, a good start to a fantasy series. And from what I heard, it gets better in book 2 and 3. Thanks for reading my review! -Cesar.

Buddy Read with Robin, Athena, Alexa, Jessica, Kat, Ashley, Eon What makes high fantasy so enjoyable to me is also what makes it difficult to review. It's so dense, and so much happens, yet, as others have pointed out, so little happens. This novel is no different in that it doesn't have a central plot (other than the overarching threat of war between each kingdom) so much as it has lesser, character-driven plots that eventually converge into the whole. In the background we have political intrigue and war, but the foreground introduces the characters, whose stories eventually begin to converge near the end. Because of this structure, the plot itself is still shrouded in some mystery. You might wonder, for instance, what Jezal's chapter about the poker game has to do with the plot. Well, it doesn't. But it serves to provide a detailed introduction into the type of person he is and what motivates him. Abercrombie's strength, which I first noticed when I broke my Abercrombie cherry on Half a King, is characterization. His skill in writing multiple POVs, each with a distinct voice, is flawless. I did not find that any of the voices blended together. In fact, so skilled is he that there was a moment in which I was reading a chapter written from Jezal's POV and another character entered the scene. That character was not named or described, but I immediately knew who she was when she spoke because each character's voice is so strong. He introduces a motley bunch here, most of which defy categorization. The murderous and notorious Northman. The pompous, pampered, womanizing nobleman seeking to advance his career with the contest. The commoner who rose above his station, but is still judged for his common roots. The mysterious, strict, but wise, magi (by far my favorite of the lot). The tortured who becomes the torturer. The clever, bawdy woman who doesn't play by society's rules and doesn't care what you think of her. The former slave who seeks to impose vengeance on the world for what they have stolen from her. But they all have more depth than my simple labels can give them. Just when you think you have a character figured out, they do, say, or think something that makes you question your notions of who they are. Everyone is a shade of grey, everyone has flaws. Dark characters have some good, and good characters have some bad. What I really liked is how many of the "bad" characters (Glotka, Jezal, Logen) were striving to be better. And good characters, like West, had moments of weakness that almost completely changed how I viewed them. So strong, and so ambiguous are his characters that some I didn't think I would like for anything other than their brutality were winning me over by the end of the book. As with Half a King, Abercrombie writes women who are in every way equal to the men, be it in wit, strength, or just will. They are equally flawed, as well. Ardee perhaps drinks a little too much, and though she has a clever mind and wit, she sometimes does not know when to stay silent. Oddly, she also doesn't know when to speak up, either. I was surprised that after her confrontation with her brother, she was not honest with Glotka about what happened to her. Of course, he isn't stupid, so he knew exactly what happened, but her excuses seemed like a moment of weakness to me. Ferro, my least favorite character, is strong, like a machine, but she is so blinded by her need for vengeance that she just doesn't think, and she blindly walks into dangerous situations that threaten her plans. Then there was the band of Named Men, still somewhat enigmatic. I enjoyed their chapters the least, but I think that's because I was already attached to other characters when they were finally introduced. I imagine their story will converge with many others in Book 2. However, one of the most touching moments in the book for me came in one of their chapters, when they paid tribute to a fallen comrade. They are nothing if not loyal to each other. Their chapters, along with Glotka's, introduced a theme I noticed here and in Half a King: how friendship can warm an icy heart and melt away the bitterness of the world. With an author this accomplished, it's almost pointless to mention the world-building, which, as expected, is top notch. Unlike some novels, my copy contained no map, but it's no matter. I built one in my head based on the descriptions provided in the book; that is, the novel is detailed enough that I have a good idea of where every land is relative to the other, the types of people who inhabit that land, and even what its terrain looks like. As with any good fantasy, many aspects of this world mirror our own. It contains castes, cliques, a commentary about the link between money and power, and even racism and nationalism. He doesn't present these themes in a polemic way, however; rather, these themes occur organically within the context of a character's individual chapter. For instance, Ferro, a dark-skinned character, refers to others as "Pinks," a word she delivers with such disdain and venom, it's clear the word is meant as an epithet. Abercrombie is known, at this point, as lord of the grimdark novel, so I was expecting something much darker, bloodier, and violent. It had bloody and violent moments, don't get me wrong, but it was not nearly as bad as I was expecting. But it isn't all dark! There were many moments of unexpected humor and sarcasm. In all, a very worthwhile read and I'm excited to see how the plot develops.

I've read all Lisa Gardner's books and I do like her as a writer but I had a few issues with this one. Yes, the pace was great, the details on people and places very good - though I did feel some of the characters were very shallow - part of the problem of having a cast who were on stage most of the time. In fact, I got confused with the police- FBI ones. But the story rattled on at a rate of knots. There was lots of suspense but part of my trouble was we were continually told - why could this have happened, why take a whole family etc and I got tired of it. For so called professional kidnappers- there was something that didn't ring true. It made it obvious who was behind the whole thing almost from the start and that spoiled it for me. I didn't guess quite all of it, but enough. So although it was a read I didn't want to put down - I wish the plot had been a little different and I wish I could have cared more about the family. They were a living breathing cliche. drug addict mum, pregnant teenage daughter, philandering husband.

This wasn't a particularly new type of story but I literally couldn't put it down. I found the story so compelling- both parts equally, the scenes from Craig's childhood and those from his relationship with Raina. The only thing I wish was that the child abuse scenes> were more explicitly explored, because I felt like there was a lot of opportunity to discuss them in either the context of Craig and Raina's physical relationship and his eventual break with his religious upbringing>. Unless I'm reading those scenes completely and utterly wrong, in which case I'm really sorry and thoroughly embarrassed.

Review: Protagonist: Snow has lived most of her life in a mental institution. She's not crazy, though, not really but day after day she tries to stay out of trouble and not let the other patients get a rise out of her. She had a friend, or maybe more, in a boy named Bale, but after their first kiss something happened and he went violent and they were separated. Then a strange new orderly appears in the middle of the night telling her that she needs to escape and find Algid, her true home, and so after Bale gets pulled through a mirror she sets off for Algid hoping that once she gets there she can find and rescue Bale, but once there she discovers that she's smack dab in the middle of all this world's problems. I really liked Snow, even though she has power over ice and snow, she has a fiery spirit and sardonic wit that bring a sense of excitement in me while reading from her perspective. Her reaction to all this fantasy stuff was very well done and I felt the author did a fantastic job at creating a very compelling and realistic character in our heroine caught between the light and the dark. Romance: Argh! I wanted to be on board with the romance(s) in this book, I really did, and for a time I was but three love interests all introduced in the first installment is more than I can handle. At first, I was on board with a possible love triangle. There was Bale the childhood friend and eventual romantic interest for Snow. We don't see much of Bale, but the little we do see makes it obvious that he's a love interest to take seriously. Then we have Kai, who we meet shortly after Snow makes it to Algid. Kai and Snow have a combative relationship at first, undercut by romantic and sexual tension, and again I'm all on board for this possible love triangle. Then we have Jagger who we meet early on in the story but isn't revealed to be a romantic interest until much later. By the time Jagger is revealed to be a love interest I've hit my breaking point, and it doesn't help that he embodies a romantic trope I hate, the alluring boy who is so annoyingly cocky. Since I have a feeling I'm supposed to take all these love interests seriously I'm really annoyed, two at a time I can handle, but three love interests, who are really the only guys in this book around Snow's age that we see and all have feelings for her is very annoying. World Building: The saving grace of this book, the thing that pushed me forward even when my head was about to explode with how aggravating the romance is, is the world building. As I'm sure a lot of you have picked up on by now, I love fairy tales and fairy tale retellings. Especially when they are of lesser known fairy tales such as The Snow Queen, like this one is. What I found so interesting about this story is that while it seems to promise a prequel to The Snow Queen and her rise to power, it also serves as a retelling of the classic tale as well. Not only that but there are elements of many fairy tales spread throughout this story and this land. My one annoyance though comes from the fact that there are inconsistencies between the eARC that I read and the synopsis, inconsistencies so large that I'm wondering if it was shoddy synopsis work or if the finished copy has larger changes than there usually are between ARCs and finished copies. That wondering is really annoying because if there really are changes they could be very large and change my entire feeling of this story. Predictability: Looking back on this story it was very hard to pinpoint where things were going to go. There were no easy paths that made sense and things shifted so smoothly from time to time that it was never easy to see what was coming next. That made for a very unpredictable story. I want to say that there were things I easily picked up on, things that the author wanted to leave a mystery but I can't. I have theories on certain things sure, but nothing that was revealed in this story was something I easily caught onto. Ending: My God this ending was insane. I tried to find a better adjective for it, but I still haven't fully processed it yet. So going into the final climax there was a lot of book still left to cover, more than usual at least, and I was extremely pleased with this drawn out, beautifully and terrifyingly described final climax. What I didn't expect however was the twist, the giant twist that I did not see coming that lead to a huge snowball effect that either made this book all the more awesome or completely ruined everything. Again, I'm still processing this ending and since I don't think it'll be fully processed for a while, for the first time I'm actually happy for the wait between books and I'm glad I have some time before the next installment to fully process everything. Rating: For once I'm truly at a loss for what to rate this book, and so while it does say four stars up there that may just as easily change once I've fully processed this book. There's a lot to love about this story but even after I've fully processed it I don't see this book getting five stars, mainly because of the clusterf*** of a romance.

Rereading (listerning to) this book for my book club was fun. I think I've finally made peace with some of my issues from the first few times I read it,  but I'm still curious as to why Katniss would vote for a final Hunger Games. Most of the time I've convinced myself that it was her way to lend false support to Coin, but then I wonder why Katniss never lets us in on her plan (she is the narrator of course). But other times I wonder if it wasn't some result of her PTSD and she really did inted for another Hunger Games to take place. I still really did enjoy the book and even the very end still moved me.

Damn it I LOVED this book. And there he whispered, "Mama." That one word tore through me like a blade. AND my favorite scene----- "Fell in love with you when I opened my eyes in Vegas, turned in bed and saw you put my bouquet in a vase." Fuck him. Fuck...him. "Shut it, mama." He was still whispering. "At the pool, when you showed, my day started." His arms now gave her a warning squeeze. "Shut it," he growled. "Sitting at the breakfast table, seeing your wedding ring, being able to really look at it on your finger up close for the first time, I had to touch it so I could remind myself I was the one who tot to put it there." Fuck. Him. "Shut it." This time, it was a rumble. "The next morning, when you didn't show at the pool, I had to find you so I could start my day." He rolled and shifted until he was top of her and he repeated, "Shut it." "Six weeks without you, I'd wake up and hours later go to sleep and not once did my day dawn." "Baby, shut...it." "You took the shadow off my world."

OMG, Aislinn Brannick is Sophie's mum... Or her sister or someone from this family, at least. That's why she and her dad couldn't be together. That's why Sophie is having premonitions or dreams. Rachel!! PLEASE!!! I want more, not just one more book, mooooorrrreeeeee, more Sophie, more Archer, more James, more magic, more everything...

Tony was having a great couple of days so of course everything went to shit. Even though I kind of like Savoy, I don't like that he's training Olive. I hope Olive and her Dad work out their problems sometime. Also, annoyed that no one was really looking for Tony. Colby and Toni were busy, yes, but I was a bit disappointed in them. Amelia was the only one looking, but she tracked him down and was pretty awesome. Also, Poyo is pretty awesome, but I'd be terrified of having him as a partner.

I borrowed the book from a certain someone and I was ready to start it because it's so tiny and it seems like the kind of book you read quickly. But, as my parents love doing, my mom just took it and she goes "Oh a book, I WILL BE HAVING THIS BOOK NOW". Luckily, she finished it in a day so I got it back. And in the end she was like "It isn't that good, but I will read the second, because I NEED TO KNOW WHAT HAPPENS. Tell your friend to buy the second one." Okay. But I second that. Please, bby, buy the other book :3 So where do we start. It wasn't unpleasant, it wasn't anything special, but it's idea was a fresh breath of air. First the bad things. Badly written characters. Gwen(ew) is just so plain and so ordinary, the usual YA main heroine. Urgh. Her friends, family, everyone is someone you've already seen in another book, nothing special, nothing unseen before. And Gideon, seriously. He's literally perfect. And not in a good way. One does not simply write perfect characters, such things shouldn't exist in the same way perfect people don't exist. Perfect to someone, yes. But in general. NO.NO.NO. The plot is predictable, but yet entertaining. It's easy to read, you can finish it in a day and still crave for more, but this will never be one of your favorite books, or a bestseller. And putting it in the same category as some YA masterpieces doesn't do justice to neither. Something I liked-London. Finally a book that's set in London and not in the States. And for me,that's a reason enough to read the book. And finish the series. Don't get me wrong, it wasn't that bad. I've read much worse. It was nothing special, but the idea is different and it's nice to take a break from witches and demons and vampires and dystopic worlds. I would recommend it if you want a light YA read and if you don't want to get your heart broken. Because I highly doubt that anyone is dying anytime soon.

I love stories set in Victorian London and this was no exception. Tiki was a great heroine. She's tough and loyal to her family of street children and willing to do anything to protect them and guarantee their survival - including picking pockets. Reiker was a great counterpart to her. And I loved Leo as well. Great start to a new series. Can't wait to read more about Tiki, 1800s London, and her connection to the Faerie world. A note on predictability: I have two complaints about this book regarding Reiker. I never understood Tiki's distrust of Reiker. He didn't do anything that seemed untrustworthy to me. In fact, everything he did showed how much he cares about her. Thus Tiki's worry that he only wanted to steal the ring seemed contrived to me. I wish the author had done more to make us question him through his behavior. Also, I figured out that he was Wills (love that nickname!) almost immediately, but had to wait for Tiki to clue herself into the truth. Even so, this was an enjoyable story.

I loved this. I bought it when it came out and for some reason I didn't read it. (I also bought all the books in the series that came after it, but couldn't read them because I have to read books in order.) Now I've read it, I have no idea why it took me so long to get around to it. I've been on a Nalini Singh binge since reading Rock Addiction, and it's now several days since I read this (in a day, which is totally unusual for me these days), so I didn't store up a lot of things to write down here, I just thought "Nalini is awesome and so is this series, why did I get so behind?" and rushed on to the next book. In the first books of the series, I wasn't as sold on this world as I was on the one in the Psy-Changeling books, which I think was a factor. Now, I've read enough of the books, and I'm far along enough in the developing story, to be equally fascinated with this universe. It's got a very different kind of sharp and very dangerous edge from the Psy-Changeling world and both are very, very well executed. Nalini creates complicated, faceted universes where the world-building and the developing story match beautifully with equally complicated, usually broken characters who discover healing and love, slowly and with difficulty. Having just read a bunch of her books in a row, I did notice that all the main characters have terrible, damaging traumas in their pasts, but how they disclose and begin to heal that is a needed part of the story. This is a world that creates great trauma and it's the kind of books she's writing, so I'm okay with that. It was lovely to see hard, cold Dmitri rediscover parts of himself he thought had been lost a thousand years ago, and (while thankfully I have to personal experience to compare) I felt the way Honor dealt with her past, sometimes succeeding and sometimes failing, was very well done. They are a lovely couple and I loved their story. I've talked more about the world than the romance, but that is both because they are intricately linked, and because I come to the book as a fantasy reader who likes romance in a story rather than the other way around. I would like to first say, the ending to this book was so amazingingly brilliant that I honestly felt the charactors pain. But unfortunatley you just got stuck with the country bumpkin :( Again I understand her story is important to the whole thing, BUT she's just so damn annoying with her aweful country "twang". It just makes for hard reading to me. Even my fiance took a peak at the book and happend to come across a Stevie Ray chapter, and asked, what is this crap? How can you stand to read something that is written so poorly? I had to then explain to him that the author was just trying to portray the charactors accent and such, but he still though the writing of this book was just aweful. Which I agree to an extent that the writting can seriously be a huge headache. So of course this book left me extremly excited to jump into the next one, I have a feeling my fiance will be making his own dinner tonight as I will be nose deep in the next book of this series! Yet i'm not really "excited" per say, more along the lines of I am eager to see if the author has corrected the aweful way she left this book. Not saying the book itself is aweful, it just broke my heart and i'm hoping the next book will right the wrong that has been made in this book. Again my heart breaks for the end of this book, oh I could just break down crying (if I wasn't at work at the moment) over the way this books ending has left me feeling. Seriously heart broken. Ok enough of my nonsense. All in all READ THE BOOK, if you like the others in this series there is no reason for you not to like this book. Unless you are just super judgemental and like to find every flaw you possibly can with the books you read. Personally I know this book has flaws, and major annoying aspects and parts to it (Zoey's lack of cussing and how far the author(s) go to stress the point of her non-cussing being an example) but honestly the story is good, the plot is good, the charactors for the most part are pretty awesome, the lust or shall I say "bloodlust" is amazing (and that's with out even haveing to make the charactors actually have sex with a bunch of people! )the series in general is just honestly captivating!
