This was a celebration of fandom, which I really appreciated. I liked the way it was told - through messages and emails and blog posts. I've been in fandom for several years and I recognize the style of how fic is written, I recognize the slang used - it's all very authentic. It's clear that the authors have had the same experience in fandom and it made me very happy to see fandom and the good - and the bad - that comes with it. Gena and Finn were very real characters in the way that they communicated with each other. The messages felt like they'd been ripped out of actual chat logs and they were both well-rounded characters. It validates internet friendships, which is nice, and problems show up that don't consume the story - the book revolves around the relationship between Gena and Finn. Finn and her relationship with Charlie was nice to see because it's a struggle I guess a lot of young adults have, and so is Gena's mental illness. It felt very much like two people with hectic lives trying to live it out the best they could. It's so cool, in fact, that you get a sense of all these characters from just online correspondences. I didn't like Charlie at first, but he got better and I became more sympathetic towards him. It was funny how they always talked about TylerGirl93 because, yeah, that happens in fandom too. I just wish we got more of the backstory about Zack because it seemed really shallow. I also didn't like how sudden it was that the accident happened and Zack died. I felt like that was a totally unprecedented plot twist and I really wish that it went on with a happy ending to fandom because that was really kind of disappointing. I enjoyed the book up until then; after that, it got fuzzy about Gena and Finn's relationship. A lot of other things could have been cleared up - why didn't Gena's parents care more about her, why exactly was Charlie so jealous of Gena. I feel like this book could have gone another way or been longer, because I feel like I was left hanging. I also wish that we got more about the fandom itself - look, I don't dabble in TV fandom but Fangirl had a fandom that was clearly based off something and I think how a fictional fandom was shown could have been dealt with better.

This book had gotten some buzz around awards time - receiving a Newbery honor award and the CYBILS award for best audiobook. I picked up the audiobook and gave it a listen and I think the awards are well deserved. This stands out as a unique offering in the world of children's literature. The basic story is this: 3 children living in Medieval France, each with a special sort of power, find each other and find their powers challenged and tested along the way. It ultimately leads up to a series of adventures that result in the King of France looking to track them down - and kill them. The format of this book is one of the things that makes it really different. I know other people who read it and didn't care for this type of telling, but I really liked it. The narrator basically knows from the beginning the summary I just shared, but we don't know what happened or why the King is after these children. While conversing in a pub with a number of people, it turns out that many of the people in the pub know a little bit of the story and have encountered the children before, and each take turns sharing their part of the story. We get "The Nun's Tale," "The Innkeeper's Tale," "The Chronicler's Tale," etc., and combined with the setting in Medieval Europe it has a bit of a Canterbury Tales feel to it in that sense. It was fun to collect bits and pieces of the story at a time, all leading up to the ending and explanation. There was even a twist I didn't really see coming, though I will admit I wasn't 100% satisfied with how that part ended. The narrator had been so interested in the children's story and I was really getting the vibe that he cared about them in some way. So I was surprised when it turned out he was sent to kill them. But the almost immediate dropping of the knife, admitting that because he knew so much about them that he cared for them, etc., felt just a little too sudden and cliche. There is a strong theme focusing on religious persecution. Again, something I don't see written much about in children's fiction, but in today's world I think this is still (sadly) an important topic. The overall themes of acceptance despite differences are also always pertinent no matter what the situation - be it religion, skin color, gender, etc. In some ways this book feels more like something adults would enjoy than children, but I spoke to at least one 6th grader who really enjoyed it. There are some bits of the story that definitely feel more "kid friendly" and I think would be enjoyable for them. The story of the farting dragon for instance, or a number of jokes made when Williams talks about his donkey/ass. As I mentioned I listened to this one on audio. And while the hard copy has some lovely illustrations, the audio is so strong I definitely think this is the way to go. Each tale is told by a different person, and so is narrated by a different person. It really adds to the feel of being in the pub with them and listening to different people share their tales. The narrator's part is done by the author of the book, Adam Gidwitz, and I loved his narration style too. I'd highly recommend this to any of my middle school students who show any inclination for appreciating more of classic literature or historical fiction.

All this madness with playboy falls for oh-so-different girl who thinks she is so above all the girls he's been with it's just getting old. Avery always behaved like she was too good for this earth, and she was annoying at all times. Josh seemed to be trying too hard to become book-boyfriend and he just seemed desperate. I've find a recurring theme in McGuire's books where the male characters JUST NEED TO GET MARRIED, and their will must be imposed over anything, because god forbid a man wants to get married and the woman doesn't (yes, I'm talking about America and Shepley and the rest of the characters from Jamie's books). While the Beautiful/ The Maddox Brothers series were awesome and I loved the main characters a lot, especially Travis and Trent, this one doesn't differ from all the new adult books out there. It always annoys the hell out of me when main character (here, Avery) just thinks all the other girls are sluts just for looking at wannabe-perfect-book-boyfriend, and she is just so above all the "sluts" who slept with him before. Ugh. Seriously. The only reason I've rated this 2.5 is because I was so surprised at the end. I did think it strange when Avery woke up from the accident and rolled with it like nothing happened, and now I'm kind of confused about this ending, because I did not see it coming, although I was rooting for one of them (please, Avery) to die. So my interpretation of all this mess is that both of them had the same *fucked-up* dream while in comma, and then when they woke up, they remembered it. Still. Why?

The book is essentially part of my new required reading packet for The Fandom, but I'm glad it is! There's one part that left me ruffled, but that's more because of fans than the book itself. More on that later... The Grisha Trilogy is loosely based off Tzarist Russia, noted most heavily in the extreme poverty gap and slight changes in the vernacular. Either you're a poverty-stricken laborer, like Alina Starkov, or a member of an elite class consisting of royals and The Grisha-- members of society with special talents that allow them to manipulate the world around them in one specific fashion. Forced to transverse the deadly, monster-ridden territory separating the two sides of her country on a military mission, Alina discovers something shocking: Not only is she a Grisha, she is a unique type. One that may be quite useful in helping save her war-ravaged country, if she could only get a grip on her power. This is the first book of a trilogy that takes place in a foreign fantasy land, so there some set up there. Thankfully, it's punctuated with some action and not completely overdone. Alina is a great narrator, but I wish we got to see a little more of her disposition. As she gained power, it would've been nice to see her gain some more inner-strength as well and actually speak some the spunky thoughts running through her head aloud. From the little we see of Mal, I like his loyalty and confidence and how he isn't afraid to stand up to anyone, even his oldest friend. Genya is fascinating, in a strange way. I'm guessing there's more to her power than meets the eye, there's no telling which side she's on for sure, and I want to find out more about her! Now, back to my fan-caused issue: The Darkling. I knew very little about this series except that ladies LOOOOOOOVED The Darkling. While not as bad as people loving Warner from the Shatter Me series (which I still use as the ultimate example of the fucked up female psyche), this is pretty ridiculous. The Darkling charms the hell out of Alina, but he does so because he's using her. He relishes in the fact that he was almost able to seduce her before she discovered he was THE WHOLE REASON THE COUNTRY WAS SHOT TO HELL. He's obsessed with her, but only because he believes he has ownership of her and her abilities. HOW IS THAT ATTRACTIVE? C'mon ladies, I expect better from you!

You may have noticed that my ratings for the Beyond series have moved up since book 1. I find that I am enjoying these books much more than I originally thought when I read book 1. With that said, Beyond Pain is definitely the best one so far. Don't get me wrong, Dallas and Lex's story was good (and holy crap..HOT) but I found myself enjoying Bren and Six's story a bit more...maybe because these are two pretty broken people who have been doing whatever they can to survive and in the midst of it all, they find something that makes them happy, wanted and needed. Amidst the erotica in these books you get a dystopian story that involves gangs, politics, and family. The O'Kane's really are a family and they take care of their own. It just so happens that Six has become one of them...despite the fact that she doesn't always feel like that is the case. In book 2 she wasn't sure what to make of them mostly because of the life she had prior to coming to Sector 4. The one thing she is sure of is Bren. She has come to trust him and knows he will protect her which leads to the beginning of their relationship. Bren....YIKES. He is one possessive male and I loved it. Honestly, all of the O'Kane guys are something else but there was something about Bren throughout this book that made me love him. He is honest and clearly one of the most dangerous guys but he was always careful around Six and aware of what she needed. He also has a history and that is what is blended into the rest of the book. On top of all the relationship stuff, The O'Kane's are working to clean up Sector 3. Six has some relationships with people in that sector that allow her to help a bit. We also get more insight into what really was going on in Sector 3 and I won't spoil anything here but I am glad we got more backstory on these characters. It helped move the story along well. One of the things that Kit Rocha does well is weave all these stories together. There are so many characters here but they all have a purpose and while the majority of this book is about Six and Bren, we still get chapters from Ace and Cruz, about Lex and Dallas, and we still get to see the interaction with the rest of the O'Kane's. Now, don't get confused...this is erotica. There is sex...a lot of it so if that isn't what you like to read, you have been warned. If you do enjoy that, definitely check this series out. I have been pleasantly surprised as it is well written and has a great story. I will freely admit that I am really looking forward to the next book...I mean, it's Ace and Cruz...come on!

Wow. This was a very good book. Comparing this to Fire and Graceling is quite a job. It was different. It wasn't so packed with real action or romance or power or world-changing as the others were. There was lots of slow, character building happenings. Loyalties were changing around. People were unstable. We weren't sure who to trust, and there was lots of politics. But I liked it. I really did. It wasso different from the other two, yet kept some of the same winning traits. Yet it didn't have some of the same qualities. Bitterblue was noticeably younger and less mature, more sheltered than the other two protagonists. She had a naivete about her that was more unfortunate than it was endearing. But she wanted to do the right thing, she just went about it in silly ways sometimes. This wasn't your typical girl-sneaks-out-in-boys-clothes story at all. The people she met really learned about what kind of person she was, even if they didn't know who she was. She learned what she had set out to learn, mostly. Usually I become frustrated with all the loyalty switches and spies for who and who to trust nonsense. But it was okay in this book. This book had all the potential to be atrociously boring. And it totally wasn't. I really enjoyed it. PS. Do it like Lynzee did on accident and read them Fire, Graceling then Bitterblue. That is the logical, actual chronological order of them, then you aren't so confused with the suddenly older characters when they crop up out of nowhere (avoiding the spoilers). All you'll lose out on is a little bit of dramatic irony when we meet a certain character whom we already know the fate of. I loved the way all the books connected at the end with more than the one weakfish character connection they had before. These are very complicated, long books. I usually avoid reading connected books within a couple of months of eachother, but it wouldn't hurt with these. You get more out of Bitterblue if you remember specific details about Fire and Graceling. I thought it was awkwardly executed how Bitterblue had been queen for eight years before this book started, yet they had done nothing. It was an awkward, not very well planned screwup of chronology. Cashore wanted Graceling to end happy, with Bitterblue as queen. Now she wants to wrote a book about Bitterblue, but B has to be of a reasonable age to be the star of a mature-YA novel. So eight years pass in oblivion. Relationships are in the exact same state, politics hasn't changed enormously, she still has not grown as a leader, and, unfortunately, we are left with only a memory of her as a ten year old that we just can't shake because she hasn't changed that much. Personally, I think Bitterblue was sixteen in this book. Katsa, Po, Giddon, Raffin we are left to belive are the same vague age they were before-and not showing any signs of taking on a different kind of lifestyle. All the Monarchs are the same etc etc etc. It was mildly annoying. Cashore could have avoided this by making her 13, stunted to a small size by hunger and mental fatigue. Cashore could have stopped mentioning how small Katsa was, made her mildly burly to make it feasible that she could carry a 13 year old girl. Well, maybe 12. Twelve is better. Then three years could have passed between Graceling and Bitterblue and it would have been much more seamless and believable. But she would have had to  scale back things with Saf, considering B was a little younger. But not a ton. It would have been fine. A person can be comforted by someone they love without any seabane being in order. Look at Katniss and Peeta. Plus, it was only one time she would have had to/should scale back. NBD. Have I mentioned how good Cashore is at naming her characters?! Because she is one of the best. I would hire her to name my characters. Heck, I would hire her to name my children. Even her kingdoms are perfect. Nander, Midluns, Lienid. She is so amazing at crafting this world that I just want to read book after book. Even if there are no plot twists or anything cool. Just those amazing characters with those classy names running around in this vivid world. Awesome. She is so talented. (excepting the occasional slipup of Fire, Po, and Bitterblue, as mentioned in reviews for Graceling and Fire. Although I have come to terms with Po's name since Graceling, in case you were wondering. It still had such potential though. Fat Chinese men. Sad really.) Another note of how well executed and amazingly creative the Monster concept and Graceling concept are. Real winners. Although it seems like the Gracelings are more numerous than Cashore intended them to be. There really were more graced characters than non-graced, so it seemed to be less than rare. She had so many ideas, she just needed to control herself. A lot of those minor characters didn't need to be graced to be effective. Although I am glad she refrained from gracing Bitterblue. That would have been too much. But really, the world was fantastic, and the graces and monsters added just enough magic to make it a little fantastical, just enough to attract the fantasy lovers like me.

Today many books try to hook the reader with frenetic pace and plenty of action, while everything else is mostly secondary. This isn't the case for The Fifth Season, which was for me a very refreshing change of... pace (hehe). It's by no means a slow book, it's simply, for lack of a better world, a "calmer" one. I can think of Robin Hobb in the same genre who does the same, taking their time with the world, characters, thoughts and intriguing you by combining the mundane with the exceptional and the exceptional with the mundane. In fact, I believe only twice there were actually fights. The storytelling takes precedence over action here. The planet where the story passes is full of potential cataclysms just lurking around. When a big one happens, they usually trigger a Season (the fifth) where humanity pretty much runs the risk of going extinct. Thus the blurb or opening line with "This is when the world ends... for the last time". Basically everyone creates cities and work just to prepare to survive another Fifth Season. People with magical powers (orogones - though there are other types) are sent to a magical school. Orogones can feel, manipulate and use mainly the earth to a lot of things, like prevent (or cause) earthquakes, tsunamis, volcano eruptions, etc. Because of their power (and lore of the world) they are widely feared and despised by the population and are controlled by a tight leash by the Fulcrum, the magical organization. A somewhat similar experience can be found in Dragon Age, with the Mage's Circles and view on mages on that world, and also has a little bit in common with the X-Men (the overall theme, not superheroes!) People with powers that normal people (the majority) don't have. Like in those two works, discrimination and prejudice are also explored here, perhaps even a little better. Also, be prepared as the book doesn't shy away from very bleak and dark moments. I guessed the "major revelation" pretty early (but by no means it looks something predictable or intended to shock, but simply looks like a natural progression if you paid attention to all the signs, and specially was willing to take a leap of faith in assuming it could be what it is.) That the three characters were the same person, though I also believed Essun's children were Alabaster's. Minor complaint: for all the journey and how Essun was broken and found happiness, I thought Essun didn't think as much as she should about her daughter or even husband... yes, she crosses the world after them, but what I mean is the daily life with them, specially again, considering how that allowed her to gain happiness after everything she went through. It would also establish some character for the daughter and husband, as important to Essun as they were, they remained faceless for the entire story and not even being sure the husband did what she thought he did left me a little disappointed as I couldn't fear for the daughter or despise the husband (assuming he really did what he did). I think the author preferred to go for the mysterious route and intended to explore this on another book, but I felt some glimpses wouldn't have hurt. It also has a very creative structure when dealing with things that possibly haunt many authors  "I have a very interesting past for my character as a child/teen/young person, but the big stuff really happens when they're much older. What do I do?" Well, Jemisin simply told those stories in different timelines in the same book. Damaya and the things that molded her personality, essential to understand how the other two also came to be, Syenite as a more matured, but still keeping something of Damaya and finally Essun, a culmination of the experiences in her life. Yes, it's possible the author could just go chronologically and have the first book with Damaya, the second with Syenite and the third with Essun... but it really wouldn't be the same book. Maybe these questions passed through her mind and she simply asked "Why not?" and she just decided to tell tell parts of their stories that mattered for the first book. And it worked for me. Minor complaint:  Near the end it's revealed that Hoa is actually the one narrating the chapters in second person. This was extremely distracting. First, because if he was the one narrating, unless stone-eaters develop some kind of telephatic bond with a person, there's no way he could have know a lot of things that were passing through Essun's mind. On the other hand, stone-eaters are portrayed and effectively used in the story as alien entities (meaning almost incomprehensible to humans, not a non-human creature with human feelings/tendencies/etc), so Hoa referring to Essun as "you" and to himself as "he" or "the boy" would actually be in character. But that would still leave how he can "read" her mind. But since I could not get a clear answer if it was just that paragraph that was Hoa speaking or all of Essun's, and whether he could or couldn't see inside Essun's mind, that revelation felt more distracting than intriguing. Another complaint would be some of Essun's chapters where she is baffled by some uses of orogeny. This romance was ... not to my particular tastes. This was something of a surprise given that it is chock-full of tropes I usually love: things based on Beauty and the Beast, virgin!heroes, spunky, sexually aggressive ladies, and (while this can sometimes be troubling) when my romantic leads are trapped together in a snowstorm / car during a snowstorm / creepy mansion following the abandonment of their car during a snowstorm. Marriages of convenience + forced togetherness = these things are my JAM, but only if they're written in a way that (1) deals explicitly with issues around consent and (2) doesn't involve Our Hero being a totally creepy puppetmaster who has engineered the entire situation to get in the heroine's pants. And this is where Beauty and the Billionaire failed for me. Here's the basic plot: Hunter Buchanan is a recluse who, following some crazy sad childhood trauma, believes that no woman will ever love him on account of his significant facial and bodily scarring. Fair enough. So one day he's in his house when he sees these two women who are totally foxy. One of them captivates his attention utterly: our heroine, Gretchen, is (a) super spunky (b) has a rockin' bod and (c) insists that she's not superficial and cares about things like character and personality. Hunter is predictably into this. Not so predictably, he decides at that moment that she is his and starts creepily thinking of her as "his Gretchen." How to make her his? That's easy. While it's convenient that he already has social connections in place that he could easily use to get to know Gretchen, this is not the path that Hunter pursues. Instead, he uses his billions of dollars and gold bars to stage an elaborate production where he starts a publishing company, buys some old letters, puts them in his mansion, and insists that Gretchen (a ghost-writer by trade) transcribe these old letters for a forthcoming book. He'll pay her lots of money and she just has to live in the house with him for a month. I could probably have gotten over this. I knew this was an aspect of the plot in advance. What I did NOT care for was that Hunter continued to use his money to manipulate Gretchen instead of say, having a conversation with her. Here are some examples: He wants to do something nice for her. So he makes sure that she becomes a best-selling author! This would all be well and good except that Gretchen hates her career as a writer and feels trapped by the idea of having to write more space-pulp for the masses. And it's possible that he would have known this if he'd ever bothered to talk to her about her work. BUT NO. Another one: Gretchen nears the end of her project, and to prevent her from leaving, Hunter has his butler thwart her. He destroys her laptop and all her backups. So she loses all her work and has to stay with him EVEN LONGER. At this point, they are already boning and having feelings for each other, but because Hunter doesn't trust Gretchen, he can't sit down and have a normal conversation with her where he, like, asks her to date him or something. Instead he traps her into staying. And then uses this situation as an opportunity to comfort / bone Gretchen. AUGH. . As a romance novel reader, one of the things I enjoy is how romance novels stress good communication over chemistry. And I never felt like Gretchen and Hunter got there. I also felt like the conflict between the two was unfair - when all is revealed, they're both upset: (a) Gretchen, because she realizes the Hunter has staged the whole thing and (b) Hunter, because he "realizes" that Gretchen is only after him for his money. But these things aren't equal! Hunter has ACTUALLY staged the whole thing and manipulated Gretchen. Who has been fairly explicit about her very strong desire to bone Hunter all over that goddamned mansion but has, not once, expressed any interest in his billions. They both apologize, but I feel like only one of these is actually a real offense, and it's not Gretchen's. Additionally, after they've both apologized and it seems like all will be well, there's another argument. Here's what happens:  Hunter's having a ball! Gretchen is totally invited! Will it be like that scene in Beauty and the Beast where they dance to "Tale As Old As Time" while Mrs. Potts and the other furniture watch? WHO KNOWS! So, Hunter asks Gretchen to go with him, and she responds, "Oh, you just want me to be your date because I put out," and Hunter gets PISSED and Gretchen realizes it's all her fault! And I'm like ... wtf, man! It should be ok for her to joke about this given that you just spent the last 20-30 pages implying that she was a gold-digger who whored herself out for your money! And it really upset me that the final reconciliation scene in the novel is characterized as one in which GRETCHEN needs to make amends. I just couldn't. After writing this, I think the real issue here is that, for some reason, I didn't think Hunter was going to be an alphole, and then he was, and I was mad because I felt like Gretchen could have done better. We know she hates writing misogynist space pulp about Astronaut Bill and his buxom space maidens! And while she does choose Hunter freely at the end - and forgives him for the shit he's done - I didn't really understand why she does this. While he's made baby-steps towards becoming a person who is not a jerk, he's still ... kind of a jerk. For someone who's interested in personality more than a pretty face, as she says at the beginning of the novel, Gretchen's choice of Hunter seems to be more about the raw animal passion they share. Which I think brings her closer to the the pulp fiction she despises than anything else.

When I finished reading this book, I was overwhelmed with a terrible sense of sadness. Not necessarily the kind that makes you bawl, although believe me, I came close. Instead, it was as if the tragedy of the Jeannette's fate had finally set in. I'd heard about the Jeannette before while reading that Holy Grail of Arctic exploration overviews, The Arctic Grail: The Quest for the Northwest Passage and the North Pole, 1818-1909. I remembered it being described briefly as a failure, and an ill-informed one at that. I did not find that voyage particularly intriguing or inspiring so I ignored it. Sides' book changed the way I'll forever think of the Jeannette from just a "mere failure" to a tragedy of the highest level. Sides has a gift for characterization and scene. I found it extremely easy to keep people apart, even on the ship. That's a rare feat--normally the main players get more development (and that still holds true here) but everyone else fades into the background so when they pop up again, you have to keep referencing the handy crew roster at the front of the book. Not so here. Everyone was well-drawn, from the eccentric, wealthy Charles Gordon Bennett Jr. (who I never even realized was the namesake "GORDON BENNETT!" exclamation, which I've heard my father use many a time) to the pun-loving Irishman Collins. My favourite was Melville, the skillful engineer who found ways out of the darkest and most impossible places. The fact that I had a favourite beyond the captain--well, I think that's neat. Sides also does well to emphasize and elevate the tragedy in this book. Captain De Long and his men went up to the Arctic based on incredibly inaccurate information as provided by August Petermann, the "Sage of Gotha." He believed there was an Open Polar Sea and that there might be currents to take you up there. He also believed there were a multitude of regularly-inhabited settlements in Siberia's Lena Delta, which proved not to be true. The tragic thing is that, had De Long waited a few more weeks, maybe a month or two, he would have seen the scientific climate change. The Open Polar Sea began to be doubted as a legitimate theory, and scientists moved onto other things. It was an exceptional case of bad timing, so you know the voyage is doomed from the start. The suffering in this book is also palpable. Frostbite, starvation--all par for the course with Arctic expeditions, but the way Sides writes them makes it visceral and real. (Here there be historical spoilers, although if you prefer not to know about who dies going in, avoid this paragraph.) I knew De Long didn't make it, because I knew his wife edited his journals. Having said that, I did not expect the recreation of his crew's deaths to be so moving. When Melville returns in the spring to find De Long, I knew there was no chance of them having survived much beyond having sent Niedermann and Noros out to go get help in October. Siberian winter is a cruel thing if you have no shelter and no food. But the overwhelming sadness kicked in--I didn't want De Long or Ambler or Alexey or the rest to die. Their deaths were needless and tragic. Had they had a bit more information, maybe they would have taken different routes--maybe they would have survived. It was poignant and struck an unexpected chord. All in all, this is a fascinating, gripping, well-researched historical read. I don't just recommend this to polar exploration aficionados (like me), but anyone interested in Gilded Age America, tales of survival, and good writing in general.

This book was a Whispersync purchase for one of my book clubs. I attempted the audio first as I was still working on another ebook. It did not go well for me. As usual with me, it takes a while for me to acclimate to a new narrator. I switched to the ebook. By about 40% in, I was ready for the book to be over. The witches could produce some fun magic, but I did not find anything spectacular about it. I also didn't understand the whole ancestry thing. Who came from who and how did Branna and Connor end up brother and sister but Iona as a cousin? Why were Branna and Connor's names so similar to the original children's but Iona's was so far off? At least the witches familiar's or "guides" as they are referred to here, were not cats. I definitely would have done more eye rolling. I found the romance in this book minimal. The main couple were not together romantically a whole lot. He didn't want to acknowledge his feelings, but yet would suddenly grab her off her feet for a kiss. Then they just move into the prologue where the minuscule amount of romance gives way to the HEA. I didn't get the connection in the romance at all. Iona I found downright annoying. She talked way too much. In fact, I thought there were way more words than necessary in all the dialogue, even the spells. The major conflict at the end of the story was disappointing. I know this is a trilogy so some things have to continue on, but that scene just totally lacked the excitement I was expecting after a whole book of build up. I did give the book points for the animals. I loved the connection that the witches had with their guides and other animals. The personalities of the horses came through and I really enjoyed that. If you are expecting a good romance, you are not likely to get it here. If you are looking for a good paranormal, you are probably not going to get it here. I think if you are a die hard fan of Nora Roberts and are familiar with her Irish heritage writing then maybe you would be better off with this book than I was.

This review and more can be found on my blog, The Library Canary. I've been meaning to read this series forever and now I finally have and my god, you guys were right. They are amazing. My favorite thing about these books is easily the characters. We've got our main character, Alina, who is a bit unsure of herself, doesn't really know where she fits in/belongs. But Alina is strong from the start. She grew up an orphan and it's given her a strength and resilience like no other that shines through in each and every book, but especially in this one when she's thrown into a whole new life. Alina is brave through some of the scariest things I can imagine. She never gives up, never backs down even when her situation seems completely hopeless. She grows so much throughout the series and becomes such an incredible woman along the way. Definitely a role model for young girls to look up to. Then there's Mal, sweet Mal. Alina's childhood and present day best friend, Mal was amazing, although a bit dense in the first book. I wanted to knock him upside the head and scream for him to just see Alina. At times he seemed completely oblivious of her and I knew they were meant for each other. But as the series went on, I just fell more and more in love with Mal. I loved watching him try to find his place in the new world he's thrown into. He's always fit in everywhere else, but now he has to figure out where he fits into Alina's new life, if he fits in at all. I loved his character arc and thought that Leigh did a great job of bringing him to life. And then there's the Darkling, the villain of our series. You know what the best thing about the Darkling is? The fact that Leigh Bardugo totally mind-fucks us with the first book. She lets us slowly fall in love with him, showing us that he's not a monster, that he genuinely cares about Alina and then she rips it all away leaving us crushed holding the pieces of our shattered hearts. Or was that just me? I fell for the Darkling hardcore just like I knew I would. And then I struggled to reconcile the character I fell in love with with the one I came to know. Oh Leigh Bardugo, you evil genius. I loved that he had multiple sides to him and that I was able to sympathize and even at times want to root for him. The Darkling is the best kind of villain, one that has a purpose for what he's doing that the reader can understand. A villain that's human. And of course, this review wouldn't be complete without talking about Sturmhond who we meet in the second book. A swoony pirate he is. Snarky, arrogant and devilishly handsome, Sturmhond reminded me a lot of Captain Carswell Thorne from the Lunar Chronicles and I fell in love with him. I loved how brilliant he was, how he knew just how to act in every situation. But through all his snark and charm, I also loved how big his heart was. There was a lot of depth to his character and I loved getting to know every side of him. In fact, there was a lot of depth to every single one of these characters. Even the minor, secondary characters like Tolya, Tamar, Zoya, and Genya came to life on these pages. I felt something for each and every one of them and an author that can do that is very talented. I also fell in love with this world of Grisha and humans. I loved the magic that the Grisha could yield and I loved hearing about the politics and structure of the country of Ravka. The world-building is fantastic, enough that I had a solid grasp on the world, but not too much to make it feel like information overload. It was a perfect balance and I never really questioned how anything worked. And the plot was breathtaking. Kept me on the edge of my seat the whole time reading. I read all three books in two days because I just could not put them down. I loved that Leigh didn't make things easy for her characters. She put them through trial after trial and just when I would think they were safe, something else would happen. I loved that her characters had to work so hard to achieve their goals because it made them that much more relatable and it made me want to root for them that much more. Overall, I can say that I absolutely loved these books and can't wait for more from her spin-off series. I'm currently reading Six of Crows and am sure I'm going to fall in love with a whole new set of kick-ass characters.

"There's a fine line between hate and love." That phrase was pretty much applicable in this book with the hot and cold relationship between the h/h. It was an okay read. Both characters and storyline are well-developed. There were angst and anger in the beginning. Jane Sherwood was a strong character. Behind her cold facade lies a very vulnerable, soft hearted, loyal to the bone and kind woman. Ryan Blair was our usual hero. Strong, ruthless businessman, possessive, used to getting what he wants, gorgeous and oozing with self confidence. And because of what Jane did, Ryan was hell bent to take revenge. I enjoyed the verbal war between them. But I think what Ryan did in the hotel was too much. I lost interest in him after than, it was below the belt. (he gave an impression to his client that Jane was a prostitute. He reserved a room, paid her and all. He was acting like a pimp just to humiliate her. And to his utter surprised Jane accepted it. Huh! Way to go girl. Give that guy the dose of his own medicine.) And after the scorching night she'd spent in the arms of her enemy, she left. Because she knew that if she stay with him he will learn the truth about the love she felt for him. That she was madly, deeply and irrevocably in love with him for years. I couldn't relax until I knew how she was going to get her happy ever after. Mistress of the Groom is a novel with all the elements that will surely make you love it. Highly recommended to those who loves ruthless and yet endearing and swoon worthy heroes. Very classic.

An epic novel, both in size and in narrative scale. Jacob de Zoet, a stubbornly honorable clerk, is at the center of the story, as he tries to acquaint himself with Japan of the year 1799. It's an exotic land, both geographically and psychologically. Jacob is surrounded by an unsavory lot of fellow tradesman, a group of sycophantic Japanese interpreters and the beguiling burned midwife Orito. The first third of the book was a struggle for me. It focused on ordinary life in the extra-ordinary world of Dejima, the Dutch trading town separated from Japan-proper. Unless a reader is really, really interested in the minutiae of copper quotas and herbs (and, I admit, I am not), the first section of Thousand Autumns can feel like an unrewarding trial. The second third of the book goes in the complete opposite direction, the story seemingly transcribed from a Mifune samurai film from the 1960s. Orito is whisked away to a mountain monastery, where the monks there are actually members of a crazy baby-killing cult. The story clips along quickly here, is exciting and interesting, but still somehow feels tremendously over-the-top. The final third of the book combines the researched realism of the first section with the excitement of the second. The British have Dejima under attack and de Zoet must fight them off. But a quick description of the plot(s) doesn't do The Thousand Autumns of Jacob de Zoet justice. Mitchell's writing is beautiful, flowing. His exhaustive research into 18th century Holland and Japan is so well integrated into his book that there are no glaring "Exposition Time!" moments. He is a true craftsman.
Another great volume! And that ending, wow!

There was a lot of broo-ha-ha this year about whether this book is sexist or feminist, and it turns out I don't really care about any of that because for me it was just boring. I put it on our Mock Printz list and maybe some book clubbers will really like it, but the story didn't grip me and I found all of the characters mildly annoying. I really didn't care for how the Girls talked. The sections told in first person plural were just awkward, like the author couldn't decide to make them poetic or chant-like or political or sarcastic so he mixed them all up. But then this is actually how the Girls talk in the rest of the book too; they say one thing, then take it back, then say it again but modify it, then pretend they don't have an opinion at all. Case in point, Kristle right before she dies/returns to the sea . And anyway, the story and mythology got really convoluted by the end. There wasn't so much a reveal as like maybe some of the characters got it figured out and they aren't going to tell you. Or maybe they will. Maybe they already did. Maybe the sea. There are a few references in the book that both were funny and took me out of the story, for example, this particular The Little Mermaid reference: "'Look at this stuff,' DeeDee said. 'Isn't it neat?'" And the Kelly/Brenda stuff I assume is a shout-out to 90210. In conclusion, this wasn't a terrible book (and I don't think it's sexist, or rather, where it's sexist it is on purpose because it's trying to make a point) but it's not my style.

This is an incredible book. That's just hands down true. The analog of the Holocaust/blind people is very well done. The writing is fantastic, and I think this is Jose Saramago's best book out of the three I've read. It deals with very heavy, complex issues and I think it does a great job of teasing those apart and breaking them down through the narrative. However, I did find it heavy going. It's depressing, heavy, sometimes difficult to follow. I had to read it in chunks. Read other things and come back to it to get through it. It was a challenge to finish it, but I'm glad I did. It was worth it.

Take the story of Cinderella. Add some more magic. Throw in a few werewolves. And, you have yourself this amazing book! Before Midnight was a fantastic romance. I absolutely loved it! Loupe was a wonderful heroine. She hasn't had the best life. She's not just forced to be a servant. She's also abused by her stepmother and forced to hide her nature as a werewolf because, should her stepmother find out, she would be killed. The fact that she endures all this and still manages to move on shows that she's a strong character. I thought she was very likable. She was a lovely character. Etienne was also amazing. He was easy to adore. He was immediately a sympathetic character, with his despair at the possibility of losing his werewolf. And he continues to be a wonderful character. He was very sweet, determined, and devoted to protecting his people. I thought he was brilliant and I adored him. The romance was well done. It was very sweet, with how they fell in love, despite each thinking that they can't be with the other. And, there were definitely sparks between these two that were hot. They were a delightful couple. The plot was fast paced. I was hooked the entire way through. Despite know how the story was going to go, this version of Cinderella still kept me guessing. It was darker and full of surprises and I loved it! The ending was brilliant and I can't wait to read the next book in this series. A fantastic new take on an old tale, Before Midnight was an amazing read. I loved every part of it and, now, I'm anxiously awaiting the next book in the Blood Prince series, One Bite. Romance lovers, if you're looking for a great read, then look no further, because this book is brilliant! *I received a free copy in exchange for an honest review

While I'm still not going to say this is a strong series, its definitely improving with every volume. This one not only got an emotional reaction out of me at one point, it also managed to be really exciting for the last hundred pages or so. There's action, and some truly surprising twists that suggest the author is starting to truly move away from the predictability of deus ex of the earlier books. Which is not to say there isn't still some deus ex. When it was mentioned our heroine has a comar brother, and then they immediately introduce us to a comar, my first thought was, that's got to be him. And guess what? It is, hooray!Or how they need to sneak into a vampire party and Dominic just HAPPENS to have a potion to change their appearance. Its sort of silly, in an endearing sort of way. Doc and Fiona's story manages to continue being more interesting and dynamic to me than our leads. The mayor's story on the other hand... ugh, I found myself wanting to throw the book during most of her sections, she's REALLY irritating by the end of this book. Creek also has an interesting story, but it feels somewhat detached from everything else. In fact, it was almost like there were three completely different books going on at the same time here. So, I'm looking forward to seeing how everything works out in the final volume, as there were some genuine unexpected things in the last 40 pages or so. Definitely worth the read for me.

Well, I finally got my wish - an Eric book. That is enough reason to make me give this 5 stars because come on! It's Eric! In this story, Charlaine Harris expounds more of the paranormal by introducing the presence of witches, other weres, shapeshifters, and fairies (although there's only one mentioned). I'm so glad Bill is finally out of the picture, and Sookie wasn't beaten up. She's stronger than ever and never failed to show her human side, even though she did kill in this, but not happily. So where to start the proper review? Ah yes, the story. It was great, the only thing missing is the un-cursed Eric and his one-liners, but the amnesiac still tugged at my heartstrings. In here one could see how old he really is by his way of thinking, and the terms he used (make love instead of fuck) and I was really happy to see Sookie and Eric got together. Be that as it may, I'm still hoping for the curse-free Eric (the Viking vampire) and Sookie to get together, but enough of that. Wow, who would've thought Jason could land himself in an even deeper heap of trouble? Things would get more interesting from here and I can't wait to read the next.

3.5/5 - Full review at emileereads: http://emileereads.com/blog/2017/3/14... Overall, The Nightingale was a thought provoking book even if I did wish for more depth in parts. It was a 3.5 out of 5 for me and I would happily try some of Hannah's other novels in the future. The sisters and their relationship were the highlight of the novel. Isabelle was immature at first, but as she aged she grew up and I came to love her. She was brave, determined, and a hero. (By the end, it seemed like every character - not just Isabelle - was undercover against the Nazis, which is nice to imagine, but not factual or realistic. Readers more knowledgeable on the time period than me have pointed out plenty of the historical inaccuracies on Goodreads.) Vianne, throughout most of the story, was understandably focused on her daughter and keeping her safe. She believed she couldn't risk her family for Isabelle's ideals, and their alternating convictions kept them at odds in spite of a clear love for each other. Isabelle, the secret hero, was the more interesting sister. I was disappointed with how little we saw of Isabelle's treks across the mountain range. The first time she made the journey with the downed pilots was my favorite part of the book. She was so determined to do something! All her life she'd been forced to sit and be ladylike, and she finally was able to fight. It was a huge triumph of hers, and the most dramatic action of the novel, and yet it was such a short section. Instead, there were way too many explanations of the various days standing in line for food. This book was very realistic when it came to the women's emotions and relationships. Vianne and Isabelle fought like all sisters do but loved each other deeply, even from a distance. The modern day chapters brought the story full circle and showed the power of a fighter's convictions, decades later. This was a worthwhile book because of the women, and I would recommend it to fiction readers for that reason.

Find this review and more at Ramblings From This Chick I am absolutely loving the Gridiron series from Jen Frederick. Jockblocked is the second standalone novel in the series, and I really enjoyed it! These characters are so much fun to read about, and I find myself getting lost in their world and not wanting to leave. If you are looking for a great football NA series, you have got to read these books! Jen Frederick is a great writer, and I cannot wait for the next book in this series. Lucy is used to living her life by avoiding anything that poses a risk to her. She has one goal this year, and that is to win the championship with her mock trial team. But when she meets sexy football star Matt Iverson, she is shocked by the connection she feels to him right away especially considering he is known to be a player on and off the field. But even if she wanted to take a chance on something, she has an agreement with her best friend that she won't date any of his teammates. Matt has just been handed the opportunity to be team captain if he can get the QB to step down and take another position instead. So when Matt finds out that Lucy is Ace's best friend, he immediately thinks he has found his way in. When things between them start to get serious though and Lucy finds out about his plan to help her convince Ace to step down, Matt will have to work harder than ever to show her that things between them are real and not just a plan to help him get his spot as captain. I really loved Lucy and Matt. Matt was so much more than I ever expected. He was sweet and thoughtful, and charming in a totally endearing way. He was impossible not to fall for and it was easy to see how great of a guy he was. Lucy was loyal and strong, and I loved that she wouldn't be pushed around. She had some insecurities and wasn't great at taking risks, yet she also didn't back down when she was put on the spot. These two together were fantastic! They had a great connection and the chemistry between them was smoking hot! I saw the spark between them from the very first meeting and it just continued to grow as the book progressed. I honestly couldn't get enough of them, and I really just loved their relationship. It was so easy and open, and I really loved how they just fit together. They had a lot of drama surrounding them, and yet I felt like these two were able to handle it together and in a mature way. Overall, I really enjoyed this book. I loved Lucy and Matty together and I really liked seeing more of the guys from the team. It was also great to see Ellie and Knox again from Sacked. I will say that Ace drove me nuts at times here, and he was my least favorite part of this book. While I felt bad for him, there were so many times that his actions made it really hard for me to like him. I didn't like how he treated Lucy here, and it was hard to see how their friendship had survived for so long if that was the norm for their relationship. But this was a great book and luckily Lucy and Matt were able to keep me invested from the very first page, and the few criticisms I had with Ace were easily forgotten with how much I was enjoying this story. I highly recommend this series for NA and sports romance fans. I think it has the perfect balance of humor, steam, sports and romance to keep readers turning the pages and wanting more. **ARC Provided by Bocci PR**

YES yes YeS! what a truly entertaining, enjoyable piece of loveliness! Really I just *holds back tears* what an amazing, truly wonderful sequel. Great Job Dude (so I feel about 75% uncomfortable referring to the author as "dude"... but hey! I wrote it and I didn't want to delete it.) 2.This is just a fun an entertaining book that happens to also address the importance of free will. It was sweet and poignant, and probably my favourite relationship in this book just after Denton and Paolo. I LOVED it when Denton realized that his stepmom was his real mom. I just live for relationships like this. I was just THE BEST! -I just also want to address the importance of Denton and Paolo's relationship. I truly love them. they are just sooooo ADORABLE! Denton grew so much during both these books and really I just loved getting to know him as a characters. I will miss him. and also what a GREAT SUPER ENTERTAINING BOOK! I wish more people knew about this "duology?" I'm not sure... Nitpicking... but maybe not So there were a few unprobably thing that you need to just not pay too much attention to. Suspend your disbelief... just let it go. You'll enjoy this book a lot more if you don't go into logistics. I never liked Cheryl aka Denton's "real mom" therefore I never really wanted her to succeed. She used Denton as a pawn for her own personal agenda and I never really believed that she cared for him, even when she said she did. I honestly loathed Cheryl. I cared zilch about her movement or anything she said. I had a hard time accepting that Denton understood and accepted her opinions, and even adopted some of them as his own. So this is 100% bias, but I was just rooting against her so hard! I was even willing to accept that the government - who were clearly being shady- was trying to help Denton. She was just so... clinical and kind of creepy... I was super dissapointed with the lack of development between Denton and Felix, because I saw the potential when I read the first book. But he really was just more interested in his relationship with Cheryl than in developing any type of bong with Denton (I AM DISSAPOINT!). Filial relationships are a weakness of mine and I had SO MUCH HOPE. So did Denton need 2 love interests? is one not enough? WHY? IT WAS SO UNNECESSARY. That said, they were both really great! They were both fleshed-out and just complex lovely people. There was not clear winner and I really loved that. Just tell me when Lance Rubin has another book out. Because I WILL be reading it.

Wolf Hollow is a tragedy about the unfairness of life and the complications of lying. In the autumn of 1943, young Annabelle is bullied by Betty, a troubled new girl at her school. Betty doesn't tease Annabelle, she threatens her. She beats her with a stick. She throws a rock, which misses and takes another girl's eye out . She tries to harm Annabelle's younger brothers by sharpening a wire and tying it between two trees at neck height . At one point, the strange but harmless wanderer of Wolf Hollow, Toby, intervenes to save Annabelle and all but tell Betty to GTFO. Toby's warnings ricochet off Betty's carapace. She continues causing trouble, now trying to blame it on the weird man. When Betty goes missing, the whole town is trapped in her web of lies. They believe Toby has kidnapped the girl, and a dual search-and-rescue/manhunt begins. Annabelle's family is friendly to Toby. Mom bakes him hickory nut pie. She lets him take the family's camera and they develop his beautiful pictures for him. Judgemental Aunt Lily, however, quickly succumbs to the town's mob mentality and brands him a kidnapper, or worse. What the family isn't aware of is that Annabelle has hidden Toby in the family barn. Annabelle understands how easy adults are manipulated by the lies of children. They all believe Betty at face value! So she must dissolve the madness with lies of her own. Although this book is set during WWII, it is not Holocaust tale. Yet it has echoes of a person hiding another and lying about it in order to protect him. Sanctimonious Aunt Lily is the type of person who would have turned Anne Frank in. It's satisfying to see her little bubble popped in the book's denouement. I looked on the back of the book expecting to find the word "evocative" in the blurbs. Yep. It's right there, thanks to Linda Sue Park. Two blurbers also credit the "honesty" of the book. I think they've pinned the novel's brilliant irony: Lies can destroy. But so can the truth. Wolf Hollow is about learning that the right choice is often whichever is harder to do. "If my life was to be just a single note in an endless symphony, how could I not sound it out for as long as a loudly as I could?"

I read all P&P retellings with a small degree of apprehension, and this one wiped it away almost instantly. Smartly written with careful divergences from the original. Mr. Bennett's quips were hysterical and made reading this even more fun. Despite my, ahem, many (many, many) readings of the original, this one caught me off guard several times. (For example, I missed Kathy de Bourgh's significance until her name was mentioned several times, and who can forget Catherine De Bourgh?!) I enjoyed the liberties because they were thoughtfully done and felt true to life. It's a hard book to stop reading, for sure. This was my first Sittenfeld book and I'll be reading more of her work in the future. She's a grade A writer. What may not please everyone : --> Liz and Darcy are the definition of instalove, due to the careful plot device of having them primarily together through "hate sex," so there's not a lot to make the romance believable. Austen's love story runs rings around this one. But who could _ever_ compete with Jane in the Lizzie-Darcy department? And this one is still quite fun. --> The wrap up feels a little quick and not as satisfying as it could be. --> I'm not sure how I feel about Sittenfeld's approach to diverse characters. Mrs. Bennet's prejudices are too gently portrayed and Liz's awareness of this is handled in the blinded manner of white privilege. (Thinking you're great because you have an open mind, when really, you connect on a superficial level and lift yourself up because of your generous-but-not-truly heart.) An excellent post about this, way more articulate than I was: http://therumpus.net/2016/09/literatu... -->ARGH. The spiders. My skin is still crawling. I didn't think brown recluses could invade a home since they're pretty solitary dudes and dudettes, but I will not fact check because of the pictures. Bleh.

Oh okay, Darcy takes a good look at her and decides she's beautiful and he loves to dance now?! Too late, buddy! Their mother sounds awful, totally uncaring for her daughter's health and just set on marrying them to the most wealthy man she can find. At least Elizabeth has a good heart and cares about her. Then their father's cousin wants to marry Jane or Elizabeth?! I'm so glad that Elizabeth's father won't let her marry him because it's gross and he looks awful! He's basically saying he really doesn't want to do this but he can't shake her from his mind so they might as well get married! It's good that he's written her a letter and is actually explaining what is going on but now she's really regretting how cruel she was to him but she can't tell Jane any of this! And then Elizabeth and Darcy had this epic moment in the rain and they finally admitted all their feelings to each other! It was a perfect happy ending.

This is a gorgeous and well researched piece of historical fiction. I was familiar with many of the major events, people, and places seen in [i]Shanghai Girls[/i] from an academic perspective, but See really brings these pieces of history to life through her descriptions of the lives of sisters Pearl and May. Writing the previous sentence just now, I actually typed 'the life of sisters Pearl and May'... and that would actually not have been an unjust description of this book. The sisters' lives are so intertwined that it can be hard to see where one ends and the other begins. We follow them from their home in Shanghai on a journey that brings Pearl and May to Los Angeles, which also allows us a view of the effects of major events in both the world and in the respective countries that the story takes place in: the Japanese invasion of China, the treatment of Chinese immigrants to the US, World War II and the Red Scare. Very well executed. I look forward to picking up the sequel.

** spoiler alert ** Really enjoyed this book, and the characters. I'm sure I'd seen the movie long ago, but didn't remember much of it. Picturing Matthew McConaughey as Jake, Donals Sutherland as Lucien, and Samuel L Jackson as Carl Lee, certainly added more dimensions to my perceptions of the characters. Lucien and Harry Rex very likable, as was Jake, and makes me want to read more about these lovable lushes. Loved Claude's diner scenes. I had been reading some Michael Connelly recently, and it's interesting how the styles are different... Connelly is much more into the legal theatrics, whereas Grisham seems more into the character- and plot- and case-building outside of court. At least, that was my point of view. Spoiler alert I was disappointed that the crimes by the KKK were never pursued, much less, resolved, by the end of the book. The K just kept on doing bad stuff, and no one ever looked into it, or reported any arrests, or conspiracies with someone back at the courthouse. Seemed like the K had some inside information to know details of Carl Lee's defenders, and the jury's whereabouts. Also, how did Mickey Mouse get found out? Why was MM sympathetic to protecting the good guys? Also, what happens to the good guys with respect to the K after the trial? Grisham said the K left town and mostly never returned, but that seems implausible... They tried to do harm during the trial, but once the trial was almost over, they gave up. Maybe it was due to all the thousands of blacks who were in town protesting by then. I just felt like... Ok now Carl Lee is free today... He's going to get harassed or killed starting tomorrow.

Still Alice is a very personal read. I felt so much sympathy for Alice right away, and I could only see her getting worse. Time and finality are some of the underlying themes of this book about a disease that only has one outcome. Some of Alice's family choose to focus on the present and Alice's current wants and desires. Some want to focus on the future and the inevitable. ("She won't know what she wants in a year.") Choice is also a central theme. Some family members say that Alice would never have wanted her disease to burden their lives. Some say she's their mother, and she'd never be a burden, Alzheimer's or not. There are no easy answers, and Lisa Genova provides none. I don't often put myself in the place of fictional characters, but I think everyone who reads this book wonders what it would be like to have early-onset Alzheimer's. Still Alice isn't fancy nor is its plot complicated. Its an "easy read." Yet it hits home for its themes about aging, disease, and death. Recommended to anyone who's been impacted by degenerative disease and anyone who's felt isolated due to mental illness.

'I've made my decision and sure, my heart is broken, but it's the good kind of broken. The kind that leaves you branded, so you never forget, and heals over time, so you can see how far you've come. It's the best kind of broken.' As fierce and beautiful as a midnight storm, Best Kind of Broken is the kind of novel you just can't put down. The story of Pixie & Levi is one that will make you consider that decades-old question: how do we, as humans, begin to heal? And, more importantly, how do we fix what we can't see? Death is a part of life. So is grief. But you don't have to face it alone. Best Kind of Broken will have readers captivated by the contrasting yet complementing characters of Pixie & Levi - and their undeniable chemistry - as well as the finesse with which Chelsea Fine has created what can only be described as a work of art. Emotions, layered like colours on a canvas, shine through the story and make it a NA read you don't want to miss. If you want something bad enough, you have to fight for it. Can Pixie & Levi find a way to let go of the past? To find out, be sure to grab your copy of Best Kind of Broken when it comes out :)

I couldn't sleep so I picked this up and ended up finishing The Summer I Turned Pretty at 2:30 in the morning. This book is about the main character Belly and her family who always go to her mom's best friend's beach house every summer. I hope that made sense. Belly's mom's best friend has two sons that Belly has known since forever, and things get complicated. This book reminds me of the anime Peach Girl... a lot. I also predict that this will have the same ending, romace-wise. I had really low expectations at the start of this book because I heard that people liked it, but then I heard that some other people didn't like it, so that was the negative impression I was left with. Either way this book had a rocky start. Because of my unenthusiasm, I never really sat down and read the book. I always just read for 5 minutes waiting for the microwave, or 7 minutes waiting for my brother to come watch tv. This being said, I was still getting through a considerable amount of pages in this fashion because it's a super quick read. The story is written in a bunch of really short chapters--some not even spanning two pages long--that alternate between the current summer and a mariad of past summers. It gives you the feeling as if you're just seeing a bunch of quick snippets into Belly's life, and I haven't read something like this in a while. As the story progresses the chapters do get longer, and it starts to focus more on the present summer. Another thing I haven't read much of is the writing style. It's reminiscent of The Catcher in the Rye in that you're really inside Belly's head. We get to read the story throuh Belly's thoughts as she thinks them which means the writing isn't very sophisticated. Though it's not quite like The Catcher in the Rye, I feel it's similar in that this can be very hit-and-miss. In the beginning the writing did kind of annoy me, but as I kept reading I got used to it. All this was in the first 36% of the book. ((/r/theydidthemath.)) Then, as I stated in my first sentence, I couldn't sleep and then I just didn't want to. I picked it up thinking, "Oh I'll just read a bit and I'll get tired after like 20 pages." WRONG. I don't know if that was when the story picked up, or it was because I was being more focused on it or what, but I couldn't put it down. It also helped that I was speeding through it and ended up finishing the book before I knew it. The story was your average contemporary summer read with boys and parties and annoying parents and all that. What made this book pretty good was the characters. I didn't even realize it, but I really grew to care about a number of characters in the span of these 276 pages. It was the weirdest thing when near the end of the book, and I don't know if this is a spoiler but, I started tearing up! I haven't ever cried at a book before (slight lie--I've cried... ONCE....), but I came darn close this time! Tears pooled at the edges of my eyes but they never like ran down my cheeks or anything dramatic like that. It was really weird and surprising and it happened twice in close succession. SO YEAH. THE CHARACTERS. AHEM, YES. They were uh, good. I liked them. Specifically the brothers, which for some reason I wasn't expecting to like. And Susannah... :,( Read this if you like summer contemporaries, and maybe not if you're super into high action or fantasy because it's very.... life. No action whatsoever. Maybe a smidgen dull at a point or two, but for contemporary fans it shouldn't be a problem. It is now 3:27 am, what is life. I feel like this is a book that gets creepier (and better) on a reread. After only reading it once, though, for me the book cultivates an unsettling atmosphere but it's nothing super frightening. It's a quick read, though, and pretty thought provoking. I will admit that I was more intrigued about the title meaning something other than suicide, since that was the first thing I thought of when I picked up the book - playing with all the ways someone can "end things" - and was a little let-down that it ends with a suicide. Like it felt predictable in a way I wasn't expecting from a book touted as innovative and surprising. Hopefully someday I'll revisit it.

I can't believe I've never read this. The Twits are the worst. They are ugly, smelly, hairy, mean and vindictive. They play tricks on each other like glass eyes in beer, making the other person think they are shrinking, and worms in spaghetti. Mr Twit keeps monkeys and wants to train them to be the worlds only upside down monkey circus. He is also fond of making pies out of birds. The monkeys try and warn the birds there is sticky stuff on the tree that will make them catchable but the monkeys only speak African. One day an African bird visits on vacation and warns all the other birds. The monkeys then exact their revenge. The birds let them out and with their help the put everything in the Twits house upside down so they think they are wrong way up. The birds gently put sticky stuff on their heads and the Twits stand on their heads so they are right side up and begin to shrink into themselves until they are nothing. The bird helps fly the monkeys home to Africa. A clever, funny story that reads a lot like a small collection of Essays on the Twits. It'd be the perfect book to read a kid before bedtime because most of the chapters feel stand alone but collect together to a larger story. Super fun.

A cute fun read filled with all your favorite classic YA tropes, guaranteed to get you out of a reading slump. Things I Liked -Evie & Edmund. Friends to lovers, how can it go wrong. It's so cliche, but I am such a sucker for it. Evie and Edmund share a lot of cute moments, and some not so cute moments as well, but I buy that they genuinely care for each other. They actually talk to each other when they have issues and don't leave problems unresolved. -FUN. This was a fun book. There's drama, romance, and a bit of mystery. This story is full of YA tropes, but it is so entertaining. You fly through the story and root for the characters. It's a really good book to get you out of a slump. -Evie. I liked Evie. She was a sarcastic and a little mouthy, but endearing. I loved that she was smart. She suspected where her mom's quest was leading her (even if it was a bit obvious) and she trusted in herself when she figured out the truth to be able to make some difficult decisions. I liked that she trusted her relationship with Edmund when Jax was being so manipulative. She was easy an easy character to follow, and it made the book really quick. Things I Didn't Like -Quest. I loved the idea of the quest from Evie's mom, but I wish it played a bigger part. Because the revelation was so obvious and Evie correctly assumed the intention, they letters and quests really served no purpose. -Suzy's subplot. I don't need any student/teacher plots in my stories. I've had enough of them and they can go away. This one was so minor it was basically nonexistent, so I really could have just gone without. -Tagline. I just did not understand what Edmund's part of the tagline referred to. What or who is he secretly loyal to? This is a really quick contemporary read perfect for fans of Anna and the French Kiss.

originally posted at http://booksaremylovers.tumblr.com/po... THE GOOD Devil is the type of hero you will definitely fall in love with. As a Duke and leader of his clan, he's reliable, powerful and intelligent. He is the type of man you will want to be a husband because he will protect you with his life. With him, any woman he chooses will be assured of her safety. And he's sensual but in a respectable way. Yes, respectable, because he never forced Honoria. Sure he steals kisses and caresses, but that was his way of convincing Honoria to marry him, since it was obvious she's attracted to him but just being hardheaded and haughty. I find it fascinating that Devil never attempted to lure Honoria to his bed until she told him she will marry him. Devil certainly is the reason why I gave this book three stars. THE BAD As much as I like Devil and his cousins, I find the story too long for its own good. The only major conflict, aside from Honoria's hardheadedness and haughtiness, was their search for their cousin's murderer. However, I have already discovered the murderer since the day of their cousin's funeral while it took them months before they realized who he was. As a reader, it should have gripped me more if I didn't know from the start who the killer was. Or maybe the author should have tried to mislead me just to spice up the story. But she didn't. It became dragging for me. Even their sensual scenes bored me eventually. I continued reading because I really adore Devil and his cousins. As for Honoria, I liked her at first. She's strong, intelligent and independent. But as the story goes, I just thought her strong character turned to plain hardheadedness. She doesn't want to succumb to Devil and she gave him a hard time. So maybe that was one of the reasons why Devil fell for her. But most of the time, I find it too much. And I was shocked when her character suddenly changed at the second part of the book, when she finally succumbed to Devil's seduction. It was out of her original character. Unfortunately, it turned me off.
