Lou Clark, recently unemployed, is looking for just about anything to tide her and her family over. So when a vacancy for a carer comes up, she doesn't think twice. Enter Will Traynor. Due to a tragic accident, Will is left paralysed and unable to do anything for himself, needing constant round the clock care. At first, Will and Lou do not get along. Will is temperamental and doesn't care for Lou whom he believes will only be temporary. Lou finds Will arrogant and disarming. Over time however, they begin to see a different side to one another and form a bond that nobody can break. This book had me yearning for the next page each time I completed one. It was funny at times, sad at others. It raises important questions about assisted suicide and the impact that this can have on those around you. I started this book on the journey home from Tenerife and got about halfway through it in that same day. Judging this as a book solely (I will not make any comparisons to its film adaptation), this was an absolutely fantastic read, I really cannot fault it. All the characters within this book are completely three-dimensional and independent. Though I suspect you know how the ending goes it was still sad when it came. You grow attached to Will and you end up caring for him as if you were right there alongside him in his struggles. Lou faces a morally controversial decision about whether to assist him or not and in the end decides to go for it. I found myself willing her to go, knowing if she didn't she would probably regret it for the rest of her life. If there are two thing this book taught me, they are: A) Not everything is black and white, there's a whole area of grey B) Seize life with everything you have because it could be over for you anytime. Go read this book!

The Crown's Game is an ancient dual that showcases magical skill - this time between two teenagers, Vika and Nikolai. Vika, a girl from the small island of Ovchinin, is eager to prove herself and show her skills while Nikolai, an orphan, wants to show he belongs. One will succeed to be the Imperial Enchanter and one will die. Vika and Nikolai never imagined having to compete in such a dual, or that they might have to kill someone in order to become the Enchanter. No one else knows what it's like to have magic and they find that they're drawn to each other. Things get complicated when Vika catches the attention of Pasha, Nikolai's best friend and the heir to the throne. With each round, the stakes get higher and it becomes clear that losing the Crown's Game is not an option. This book was high on my list of anticipated releases for 2016 and, going into it, I was worried it wouldn't live up to expectations since they were quite high. If it lived up to expectations, it might end up being my favourite read of 2016, already. So I'm extremely relieved and happy to say I not only liked it, I loved it. The book was told in alternating POVs of Vika and Nikolai, which not only worked well with how the crown's game was set up but also made me care about both of them. They were both good people and had their own reasons for wanting to win. I didn't want to see either of them die. I got attached to both of them quite quickly and the more I was hoping there would be some way no one would have to die. I liked Vika's spunky personality and it contrasted nicely with Nikolai's quiet one. They were both interesting characters, complete opposites, but they worked so well both against each other and together. Pasha was another interesting character and I was worried, at first, that I might dislike him if he seemed like a third wheel but he was charming and adorable and sucked me right in. I loved his friendship with Nikolai and the fact that he hated being the prince when it meant he was always watched, never free unless he snuck out. I also enjoyed his fascination with Vika. It was written in a way that didn't make it seem like a love triangle but really, just two friends whose attention had been caught by the same girl and everyone trying to figure out their feelings without hurting anyone. The Crown's Game part of the book was so much more than I expected. I loved that it wasn't just about powerful fighting and attack spells but it really was more of a game. They took turns and the spells weren't always destructive but showcased their talents. It was still dangerous and either could have died at any time but the fact that it wasn't an all-out arena-style dual made me enjoy it even more. I couldn't wait to find out what each of them would do for their next turn, how they would one-up the already impressive series of magical events that was showcased. I also loved how the general public, oblivious to magic, would come up with explanations to what was really behind the magical events - no matter how extreme they could be. Because it wasn't a magical fight-to-the-death dual, the pacing was slower than I expected but that just gave me more time to lose myself in the world. It wasn't slow to read, there was still always something going on, just slower with the action parts than if it had been a bloody dual. I was tense and holding my breath so many times throughout the book even with it being more of a game than a dual so I'm not sure I would have made it through a dual. I know that this is one book where, once I get the finished copy in hands, all the emotions I felt while reading it will come rushing back and my thoughts will echo what they were when I finished the ARC: I need the next book now! *I received a copy of this book from the publisher in exchange for an honest review.

It ended really abruptly just when things were starting to get intense both professionally and personally for the men. I would have loved to see at least one more chapter to see how things worked out for them.

**This book was given to me in a goodreads giveaway contest** 4 Stars Overall Opinion: This was an enjoyable, different read. I enjoyed the different storyline where sometimes these stories about an abused woman on the run tend to be similar. I do want to warn readers that this ends on a cliffhanger. I wasn't aware it did, so I was in for a shock! Storyline: This is Annie and Dylan's story. Annie is on the run from her abusive husband, and she moves into a trailer park in Cherokee, NC. When first moving into a furnished even/trailer she hears a phone ringing and finds it in the cushion of one of the chairs. She answers it and (kind of) meets Dylan. They have a conversation, and she learns that he paid the previous owners of the trailer to spy on another resident of the trailer park. She gives him a fake name, because she is paranoid of her husband finding her. Dylan is taken back by her kindness, and both of them go into instalust with each other...but Annie disconnects when she gets spooked. After some time they eventually start talking again, and start to steam things up with some phone sex and Dyan giving Annie some assignments to do wild things. There is some drama with other residents, some hot times, some deeper feelings developing, and then they finally meet face to face. Once they do meet, it has a beauty and the beast likeness (at least with Dylan). We learn he was burned in a race car accident, and has scars on his face and body. He has bought a mountain that he rarely leaves, and he has kind of a beastly attitude most of the time. Annie is in for a shock, they steam things up even more, both have some secrets being revealed, and then we have the cliffhanger (with a few things in between). POV: This alternated between Annie and Dylan's POV. Overall Pace of Story: Good. It was a quick read, and I would say it was instalust but not instalove. H rating: 4 stars. Dylan. He is the mysterious, sexy alpha that I love in books. h rating: 4 stars. I loved how innocent but eager she was, as well as how she was a hard of a worker. Sadness level: Low. I didn't shed any tears, but it does have some heavy subjects. Heat level: Moderate/high. This definitely had the story as primary and the sex scenes secondary, but there was a good bit of sex (mostly over the phone). Descriptive sex: Yes Sex scene with OW or OM: No Cheating:  Technically, yes. Annie is on the run from her abusive husband, and is still married to him. Possible Triggers:  Abuse - mentions but not experienced. Closure: This ended on a cliffhanger. I am looking forward to the next book, The Truth About Him! Worth the $? :  It was free for me with the giveaway, but I would say it was worth the $ otherwise.

I thought the concept of this story was very interesting! It was such a unique idea. Unfortunately, with that being said, I DESPISED the main character of this novel, Katla. She is OBSESSED with fashion, brand names and Starbucks. She favours cookie cutter malls over a historical downtown and judges people based on where they shop and what they wear. I found her to be very shallow. She also needs frequent rescuing. I would have rather the novel focused on the school's queen bee, Monique. At least she seems more layered. I wish the novel focused more on Katla's "gifts" and I have sooooo many questions about them..  Are there storks all over the world helping souls find Mothers or just in their town? What happens in the case of abortion? For example, in the case of Monique's pregnancy, what if she chose to abort the fetus? How are there so many unfit parents in the world if a special team of storks is choosing each 'vessel'? I found Katla's romance to be bizarre - I liked her romantic interest but wish he were more flawed to make him more realistic. He is nice and all but he seems to have no interests outside of farming and barely any personality. I understand that they have a special connection but their relationship feels too instant to me. I would like to read the sequel to this novel, but don't know if I can tolerate much more of Katla.

WOW! This was so refreshing different! I loved that, Hugo, the male protagonist was such an atypical hero, being neither a nobleman nor the devastataingly handsome and charming rake. The heroine was also an underdog to root for, a woman who had been wronged and was determined to set things right, heedless of the personal sacrifice. I loved how the chemistry built between Hugo and Serena. It was wonderfully and believably done. My only quibble with the story was  how so little was made of her pregnancy. It seemed like it should have surfaced in some manner either before or during their love scene. Rather the repercussion that Hugo would raise the despised duke's bastard son as his own appears not to have even entered either Hugo's or Serena's mind. It just seems like this should have been at least an internal debate with Hugo before he offered marriage, even if he and Serena didn't discuss it with one another. I guess I had a hard time believing what a non-issue it was in their relationship. Overall, however, it was a great story and I look forward to the series that will follow.

The end of Olivia and Noah's journey has come, but Sterling and Camryn will get a book! It's hard to be sad when you know you will see the characters again. The epilogue was amazing and sweet. As you know Noah thought about doing something terrible in the end of volume two. I wasn't as hard as to him as I should have been mostly because I know it's fiction and that no matter how desperate he was, he wouldn't do it. Olivia doesn't forgive him easily and it dragged a little bit more than I would have liked.For me there were 100 things that could have been this books focus. For me, the last chapter in Noah and Olivia's story was a little disappointing. I expected to see more things happening. What Noah said and did in the end were super sweet and made me swoon. I must admit that I didn't see some of the events coming and I liked that. I was hoping for a twist to make things better, but it never came and it was for the best. I believe the turn the events took are the best and most fitting for our characters. I might not have liked this book as much as the other two, but this book is still good and a great way to end Olivia and Noah's story. I can't wait for Sterling and Camryn's book!.

Debt by Nina G Jones 4.5 stars! "Don't convince yourself that you can play mind games with me, because you will lose. Every. Single. Fucking. Time." This is one of those books that while you are reading you think to yourself "I really should not be enjoying this!!" This book is dark in places and has triggers for some but personally I felt that it was all in done in keeping with the plot and the story as it developed. The plot was so totally and utterly captivating and compelling that I could not help but page turn furiously. The writing flowed easily, it was atmospheric, it had intensity, it was emotional and it was thrilling. Exactly what you want in a dark and suspenseful read. The thing that I loved the most about this book was that although you shouldn't have loved Tax, I couldn't help but love him and despite everything, I felt that these two belonged together and I was rooting for them from the beginning. The chemistry between these two was sizzling, the emotion that Nina Jones conveyed through her words had me in tears at times, so all in all the book felt perfectly balanced. It had a touch of everything. The following quote just about sums this book up perfectly. "Reckless. Irresponsible. Dirty. Dangerous. Exhilarating. Erotic. Wild. Euphoric. How can one thing be all of those? How can peering into the gutter of my soul feel like I just touched heaven?" Mia was your stereotypical "nice" girl. She was a work-a-holic who was high up in a sex toy company and working around sex toys all day only made her realise all the more how sorely lacking her own sex life was. She was quite happy though being who she was, she had worked hard to get where she was and her job was her "baby." Mia's best friend was the bright and bubbly gregarious one and Mia was always holding onto her coat tails when she was in her company, but she always brought out the wild side to Mia. She badly wanted Mia to see some action and so relays to her the name of a website that can act out your fantasies for you and this was one fantasy that they had both talked about previously together. While on her own Mia pondered the idea, ruminating the decision around and around, until she decided to be brave and go for it. She entered her details onto the site and waited... This is where the story kicks off and be prepared because this is one crazy train, but the good, addicting, mind bending, out of your comfort zone kind of crazy. As I said above, I really should not have liked this book, I should have been disgusted, but hell I wasn't and I really don't know whether I should be worried or not. Even as I am sitting here contemplating what I should say I have so many scenes flitting through my mind, I cannot stop thinking about this story and that is kudos to the author because this story certainly made an impression. "I will suck her dry, I will fuck the life out of her, I will ravage her until she is hollow and used, and then when she thinks things can't get any lower I will..." This is where Mia meets Tax, Mia thinking that this was all part of the fantasy that she had asked for on "the site" goes with the flow on their first encounter, despite something that should have been a warning that all was not as it seems. Mia thinks she has gotten what she had paid for but this was just the beginning. Tax was not her "fantasy man," Tax was a debt collector and Mia was the last debtor in a long list of people that had already paid. Mia had the biggest debt to pay because this was personal, very, very, personal. "I know you want someone to dirty you up. I'll make you fucking filthy. Now, show me." Tax was the antithesis of Mia, he was tall, he was dark, he was deadly, he was disturbed and he wanted revenge. He was drop dead gorgeous, tatted and f**ked like an animal, Mia was instantly taken by him. Despite having had her fantasy come to life she could not stop thinking about him and it seems that the feelings were mutual. Tax has an ulterior motive though, but slowly but surely this changes. "I want to swallow you. I want to consume you. I want to possess you. I want you." I cannot say anything about the plot; this is where you really need to go in blind. The blurb is all you need to read, apart from the book of course!! There are twists and turns galore, your stomach will clench, you may even feel a bit sick, you will be on the edge of your seat and flying by the seat of your pants but I doubt you will be able to put this book down. Even as you digest what you are reading, you will probably question your sanity. "Her touch singes those spots. Boots. Buckles. Shards of glass." This book is written in dual first person POV with flashbacks to the past and it is these flashbacks that only intensify this story and go a long way into explaining the man that Tax has become. They also show how Tax and Mia's paths have crossed before and how she has come to be a "debtor." One of these scenes was particularly harrowing and had me in tears. I must admit the tears flowed freely while reading this; it certainly hit the spot with me. This is the first book that I have read by Nina G Jones but it certainly won't be the last. If you like your dark reads, dirty and you don't have triggers, then this is the book for you. It is not all dark, as I said there is an underlying love story too albeit unconventional. But it is this love story that will have you on edge, wanting them to succeed, wanting them to both get their HEA, after all they deserve it, but you will just have to wait and see. I loved The Bone Clocks, and was excited to read "Jacob de Zoet," as I knew a couple of the characters (Marinus, Oshima) would pop up. Plus I love historical fiction (Shogun is one of my very favorite books), and "De Zoet" seemed like a great combo. Unfortunately, I was disappointed. "Jacob de Zoet" has its moments, but it's definitely inferior to "The Bone Clocks" (and "Shogun," which does a much better job of portraying the Dutch in early modern Japan). I had a few issues with "De Zoet." Pacing/editing. The first section, after de Zoet's arrival on Dejima, went on for far too long. I also thought the sections at the end with the British were overlong. I think Mitchell could have cut a fair amount from the book and still had it be effective. Orito is by far the most intriguing character. My favorite section was her POV at the Shrine. Yet she disappears for most of the rest of the book. I think Mitchell does an amazing job writing female characters - Orito, Holly in "The Bone Clocks" - and I think the book would have been stronger had it focused more on her rather than the rather boring/stereotypically principled de Zoet. This is obviously an early work of Mitchell's, and he hasn't quite honed his style yet. I got really sick of his overuse of ellipses. Mitchell makes a point of trying to show how people speaking foreign languages would sound. The Japanese interpreters don't speak Dutch very well, so many of those sentences are grammatically incorrect. That's totally fine. But when de Zoet speaks Japanese, it reads fluently. That seemed like an odd decision to make - no way for de Zoet to speak fluent Japanese after only a year of snatched study. Despite these flaws, there were a lot of things about the book that I liked a lot. Enomoto was a fantastic villain. It was fun seeing Marinus again after "The Bone Clocks," and Mitchell does a great job developing the sinister atmosphere at the Shiranui shrine. I liked the ending, with Shiroyama poisoning and punishing Enomoto - although I don't understand how Oshima fits in. In "The Bone Clocks," Oshima tells Marinus that he Suasioned Shiroyama to poison Enomoto - but in "de Zoet" Shiroyama has plenty of logical reasons to kill Enomoto. I wish Mitchell showed where Oshima came in, because I'm still confused about that. "De Zoet" is a fun book to read after (or before) "The Bone Clocks," to see how the worlds connect. I just wish "De Zoet" was a little more polished.

Ehhhhhhhhhhhhhhhh........................ So, I definitely love pirates. And I definitely think there should be more YA books about pirates, and of the fantasy variety rather than the historical fiction variety, if that makes sense. But this one is kinda weak. Okay, first of all, the whole brothers-with-three-parts-of-a-map thing is so totally Cutthroat Island, which is an amazingly bad movie that I absolutely adore--Geena Davis! Matthew Modine! Terrible acting! A cheeky monkey! Lines like, "See? I took your balls." Seriously, you should do yourself a favor and watch that mess sometime. I'll bring the mac and cheese! Anyway, there's also the whole map hunt pirate sexy time thing going on here that's part Romancing the Stone as well, and then the rest of it just feels like your typical YA paranormal romance stuff to me. In addition, the character development and plot set up felt kind of half-assed. There's not a lot of chemistry between the main characters. We know Alosa's hunting for this map, but we're not really given any reason to care whether she actually finds it or not. It all ended up feeling like a poorly disguised excuse for the romance, you know? What's your motivation, Alosa? Besides not wanting to upset your dad and keeping your dumb fiery red hair? *shrug* I dunno. I was actually kinda bored until around three-fourths of the way through, when a bunch of weird coincidences happen all at once and things get kind of crazy, but mostly in a rushed and unsatisfying way. All in all, there just didn't seem to be anything really new or compelling here, and I'm not really interested enough to read more in the series. I like my pirate books fun, and this just...wasn't. But it did make me want to watch Cutthroat Island again for like the five millionth time. Who's with me?? Anyone? Heh...

I am a fan of everything Eli Easton writes, but I was still surprised at how wonderful this novel was. It shot right up to being not only my favorite Eli Easton novel, but one of my all-time favorite gay novels. The romance was handled beautifully, with a very slow escalation from friendship to falling in love, and David's coming to terms with his sexuality was handled very carefully and realistically. It reminded me so much of how I felt as a fundamentalist Christian coming to terms with my own sexuality, though thankfully I was able to do so when I was young. As someone who grew up in rural areas, I loved the setting. I just wish David and Christie had been able to remain on the farm. I did think the ending could have been expanded a bit, but not by more than one or two scenes. Everything is resolved in a way that makes sense and leaves no doubt about the happy future for David, Christie, and everyone else. Additionally, I found the scenes with Christie preparing exotic dishes and setting the scene with music and pictures to be incredibly romantic. Like David, I used to collect pictures of other countries and fantasize about traveling to them. The dinner in Bora Bora was amazing! I can't recommend this book enough.

"Shadowhunters: Looking Better in Black Than the Widows of our Enemies Since 1234." I read City of Bones for the first time 5 years ago. I still remember that day. The sun was shining, the birds were singing It was during my first semester in Law School and I had to study History of Law, which was a complete waste of time because seriously, who is ever going to ask me whether women in Byzantium could get a divorce? (In case you are wondering, they could only if the husband was impotent or possessed). Aaanyway, I wanted a break and I grabbed this beautiful book and started reading until I finished it, bleary-eyed, disoriented and obsessed. A typical day in Kat-verse. So what's the story? Shadowhunters (ninja warriors with angel blood) fight demons and co-exist with vampires, werewolves, fae and warlocks while a former Shadowhunter with nazi tendencies threatens to destroy them. City of Bones is a fast-paced, action-packed paranormal book that keeps you invested in the story and the characters since page 1. A nerd, a heartbreaker, a jealous friend, a warlock who loves glitter, a werewolf, an artist and a gorgeous warrior introduce you to a world of magic, where nightmares come true, truths are revealed and decisions have to be made. Diving into this world is easy, effortless and so, so enjoyable. "Is this the part where you start tearing off strips of your shirt to bind my wounds?" "If you wanted me to rip my clothes off, you should have just asked." Humour and sassiness are all over the place and witty banters crack you up. But mind that there is also drama, plot twists and shocking moments that make you question the writer's humanity (and maybe sanity). Cassandra Clare has a unique ability, her writing can heal and stab your poor heart. "The boy never cried again, and he never forgot what he'd learned: that to love is to destroy, and that to be loved is to be the one destroyed." I need to warn you about Jace. He is the kind of bad boy who makes rude gestures to nuns and loves weapons and treats everything like a joke and is a total badass. You will fall in love with him and swoon and want to have his babies but you're in for disappointment. Because he is mine. So that's the general awesomeness of the Mortal Instruments. Title: The Problem with Forever Series: Standalone Author: Jennifer L. Armentrout Cliffhanger: No HEA: Yes Rating: 3.75 Stars "Forever was something we all took for granted, but the problem with forever was that it really didn't exist. Jennifer L. Armentrout is one of my all time favorite authors and so I didn't hesitate to pick up The Problem with Forever. And even though I didn't give it 4 Stars or more, it doesn't mean I didn't enjoy it. Quite the opposite, actually. The book was original, well researched and inspirational, but it just wasn't it for me. The main heroine, Mallory aka Mouse, was amazing. I didn't just like her, I loved her. At the beginning, Mallory was this timid and lost girl, scarred by her traumatic past but she grew so much throughout the book. Mallory became stronger and bolder while still remaining honest and compassionate. And she was really damn adorkable! "There! I did it. I spoke. Take that, everyone! Words were totally my bitch." "I was in speech class. I was here. I'd done it. I was going to throw myself a freaking party when I got home. Like an eat-fudge-icing-straight-out-of-the-freaking-can kind of party. Hardcore." "Was she inviting me to lunch? Oh my God, Paige and her Katniss braid could suck it. This was major. Like a huge step in the right direction" "When the bell rang, signaling the end of class, I wanted to jump and thrust my fist into the air, Breakfast Club style." As for Rider's character, he was complicated. Rider was loving and sweet but it wasn't easy that he didn't think he was worth a damn or even saw a future for himself. He looked out for the people he cared about, whilst forgetting himself. "This whole time I've thought I was the one who walked away from that damn house damaged and screwed up. I thought it was me." My voice broke as I backed away. "And it wasn't. It was you. It's always been you." And so the story captivated me and it was awe-inspiring. It was obvious that the author put a lot of thought and work into it by researching and talking to certain people. I believe she did a great job and her effort is visible and worth it.

"I'm looking into his eyes and he's looking into mine and I wonder if maybe it wasn't coincidence that brought me to him that night in front of the pool house. Maybe it was fate that guided me there so I could save him and he could save me and then it could lead us here to this moment where we are both completely content and free and glad we're alive." Alright, there is so much to say about this book. This is the follow-up book of  The Coincidence of Callie & Kayden and it was just as painful as the first. It's still highlights the personal effects that each and every character goes through after their traumatic events. These books do a great job at allowing you to feel how the characters feel through all their pain and suffering. By the end of this book I felt emotionally exhausted. "I'm just here,existing at the surface of the water,not quite drowning but not quite able to breathe." In The Coincidence of Callie & Kayden, Callie was saved by Kayden Owens. Now it's Kayden who needs help keeping his head above water. After Callie finds Kayden the way she did on that stormy night, she worries about him. She wants to see him, make sure he's okay, and make sure that what she thinks happened, happened. Once Callie goes a month without seeing him, she begins to feel like everything that happened was her completely her fault. "Just tell me what you need to make you happy." She looks me in the eye with tears streaming down her cheeks. "You." While Kayden was recovering, his mom ran the show, with his dad's disappearing act, his mom is adding pressure to keep his lips sealed and leave his father out of it. Kayden doesn't care what happens. He begins to feel like he isn't worth people's love and affection anymore. "I can't really do anything with you right now." Its the stupidest thing that's ever left my lips, but it needs to be said. She deserves better than the broken piece of shit that I am." Throughout this whole book, Callie is trying to show Kayden that he is worth saving and that he is worth her love. Callie will spend her whole life trying to make it up to Kayden, considering what he did for her could potentially ruin his life. The only problem is that Callie doesn't know the first thing to do to help Kayden. The only thing Callie and Kayden can both agree to do to save him from his dark future is to let the skeletons out of their closets and not run from the demons that come pouring out. The thing I loved most about this book is Callie's self-discovery process. She doesn't want to be the local freak that everyone thinks she is anymore. She knows that this has to end. She has to tell someone what happened to her six years ago, but will they believe her after all the time that has past? The one scene that I loved with Callie the most in this book is when she walked in on Kayden about to put blade to his skin, again, and made him stop. Even though he yelled at her to walk away she didn't leave him. I found it so admirable that she wouldn't leave him because she felt he wouldn't leave her if he caught her throwing up. "Kayden can't love me because he doesn't understand love. He understands pain and hurt and disappointment, but not love. I know right then that I can't tell him how I'm feeling, but I can show him." Kayden had so much growing to do in this book. He was definitely way in over his head. I'm so glad that he eventually knew what had to be done and followed through with it. We all know that he never could have done any of it without Callie, but it still felt so good to see that. He never had a family before, at least one that showed him how to love, and now that he is developing one...it shows such courage. It also couldn't be done without Seth and Luke to help both Callie and Kayden keep their sanity. Seth and Luke aren't completely sane themselves. They also have a lot of growing up to do and are faced with their own sets of problems. This book has been a roller-coaster to read, just like the first one. I don't regret a moment of it. All the heart break and awe-filled moments were completely worth it. This book definitely brought to light the feelings of all kinds of abuse that people are burdened with and it did a good job at helping me to understand how that feels and how they must feel like they've hit rock bottom. I definitely recommend this book though! It was an eye opener. (The perfect song for this book is Cry with you by: Hunter Hayes)

This book snuck up on me. Initially I was not overly impressed with it. Moriarty throws a lot of characters at you at once that seem superficially similar to each other. However, once I got past the first 50 pages or so I realized I was totally under this book's spell. I could not put this book down once I got into it. The characterizations deepen, the plot is expertly constructed, and Moriarty handles some very heavy emotional material well. The treatment of domestic violence in particular is fantastic. I read Moriarty's The Husband's Secret and enjoyed it with some reservation. In that work I liked her prose and her characterizations I found the plot structurally ungainly. Here I was impressed by how well her mystery plot hangs together  with one exception, I wasn't crazy about the "Perry is Saxon Banks" twist. This just seemed unnecessary and overly coincidental   as well as by the quality of her writing and her character development. Highly recommended.

I'm a sucker for celebrity-regular people romances, and was really excited to read BEHIND THE SECENS. While it's not my favorite of the category, I liked it nonetheless. I enjoyed watching the beginning of Liam and Ally's relationship. I liked their banter, and could definitely see a connection between them. It was fun watching their relationship develop, especially as they began to open up to each other. I also loved the friendship between Ally and Vanessa, as well as the book's commentary on the limited amount of roles for non-white people in Hollywood (Van is Korean). Ally even has a great relationship with her parents, though her family is in upheaval with her dad facing stage IV melanoma. That is actually the reason Ally starts working for her best friend Van and meets Liam - to make some money for college, because her parents' funds are going into her dad's cancer treatment. I could understand Ally's struggles and insecurities about dating a celebrity. Especially when Liam and Van have to start fake dating in the public to boost interest in their new show. But Ally eventfully lost a lot of my sympathy and got on my nerves. Liam wasn't perfect, but it is Ally who drove me crazy. I can only do so many contemporaries at a time, because I start getting very irritated by the repetitive plot flow. The 'obligatory' breakup/angst fest around 75% really grates on me, especially when it's accompanied by the MCs (in this case Ally) acting like idiots. The Nate storyline was especially annoying. I still don't fully understand who he was really interested in, or even his motives. But Ally was a complete moron for going to prom with him. I know she realized that, but it took her too long, especially after she was warned repeatedly. Overall, BEHIND THE SECNES was a fun and swoony romance, with some deeper and relatable themes imbedded. I just wish the storyline in the second half hadn't been quite so conventional in its descent into drama before everything is fixed at the end. I feel bad picking on this book specifically, because it is an issue I have with most contemporaries. But I struggle with having everything break down in the last 1/4 of the book leading to what can be a several month break between the characters - sometimes longer , only to wrap up quickly and happily in the last 5%. It wreaks havoc on my emotions (not in a good way), and usually I've barely recovered when the book is over. It also just feels like authors are trying to follow some sort of unwritten rules about how their stories are supposed to develop. Love Triangle Factor: None. Mild in action. What I loved: -The relationship. I was skeptical at first, but the dynamic between these characters ended up really working for me. Gideon is a hacker and Sofia is a con-artist and both of them are thrust together when their plans of infiltrating LaRoux industries go wrong. They have major trust issues, and lie for a living, so what happens when they have to rely on each other? You might think that the new main characters of this installment would take a back seat, but their character development did not suffer. The first half was so focused on the two of them that I felt like I really got to know them. Additionally, they both have ties to the other characters so it felt like they fit right in. -The examination of humanity. Once again, I love how the beings in this series have dropped truth bombs about what it means to be human. What I didn't love: -This is due to the format I read. I listened to the audiobook of this one, but had read the print version of the previous two books. While I LOVED the voice actors and they really made me fall for these characters, there was a lot of action toward the end of the book and I had to back track a couple of times to catch some things. The story definitely impacted me more in books two and three when I read the text and was able to sit with certain sections longer before moving on.

2.5 stars Romantic Heat:   Stepping into a tepid bath Pacing:   You know the speed limit is 70 not 50, right? Promising POV You should see a therapist for all that self-loathing Will I Read Your Next Book? Meh... Dark and twisty, this novel had tons of potential. The dark magic of the "forestborn" is fascinating and the Sun King-era France setting is magical in its own right, but ultimately the book is let down by its main character, Rachelle. While she should be (and sometimes is) complex, most of the time, she is repressing her potential for complex, multi-layered, morally ambiguous thought and action under an aggressively one-noted desire to do the right thing. This story often favors the right thing over the interesting thing, which I suppose could be viewed as a commentary on social moral codes, but is less gratifying. The act of reading this book offers a kind of parallel into the main character's mind in someways. We are given glimpses of brief, delicious romance and power that then get pushed away in favor of bland good guy love-interests and good-girl decisions. Much the same way that Rachelle rejects the intoxicating darkness of the forestborn in favor of what she perceives to be morally correct. The novel perpetually subverted the things I wanted to happen, giving me a taste of a more exciting, darker story and then pulling it out from underneath me, so that ultimately, even though all the right things happen in the book -- Rachelle and her good-guy love interest are saved and end up together, the kingdom is saved from the threatening darkness, the evil rulers (supernatural and human) are deposed --those "right things" provide little satisfaction.
Good story, would have been better if  he'd put his asshole brother in the hospital.

I've read a lot of time travel stories and this is by far the most unique. The first time Danny doubles back, I actually blinked in surprise. This isn't how it's supposed to work! I told the book. The book answered me by telling me pretty much exactly how it could work. And work, and work. The paradox is something every time travel novel has to deal with and Gerrold's treatment isn't just brilliant, it's pretty much the premise of the entire book. Without it, this story couldn't exist. The story itself is unexpectedly beautiful. I don't feel I can say much more without spoiling it. It's one of those things you really need to go into blind. I will say that I loved the author's commentary on sexuality and love. It was so poignant and made this book more than just a fascinating time experiment. This is definitely going on the keeper shelf and I will be reading more.

** spoiler alert ** Nikki Bennett has just spent a hundred years as a Forfeit in the Everneath, feeding her emotions and memories to Cole. She survives due to never letting go of one image, her boyfriend Jack's face, and she's able to return to the surface for six months before the Tunnels will come for her. Or she could choose to go with Cole and rule the Everneath as its queen. But Nikki has no interest in feeding off humans and participating in the feed. She just wants to find a way to fix the mess she left behind when she left, and hopefully find a way to stay instead of returning to the Everneath. The action in the book doesn't pick up until after the halfway mark. There's a lot of built up and because of that, it was too easy to set the book aside and do something else for a bit before coming back to it. But once the action does pick up, the pages fly by and suddenly the book's finished. Nikki's a strong character who doesn't blame anyone else for her decision to go with Cole to the Everneath. She takes the responsibility and the consequences for her actions and does her best to set things right with the people she's hurt. She's not ready to just give up and be a victim, no matter how dire her situation gets, and she doesn't try to make excuses for her addiction to Cole's ability to take away her pain. She knows it's wrong when she asks and when he does it. Jack's devotion to Nikki is sweet and heartwarming. He could have given up on her a lot of times during the book but even when he says he's done, he can't stay away because he loves her. That love comes into play in a huge way at the end of the book. Cole's hard to figure out. He's not clearly a bad guy. He does seem to care about Nikki and what happens to her, but he's extremely guarded and that makes it hard to trust him. He's a master manipulator so even when his actions seem sincere, it's hard to forget that he could be lying. It's a good start to what should be a really good series. Looking forward to the next book.

In the middle of the night, a baby wanders to the graveyard as his entire family is simultaneously murdered. The man, Jack, though he searches, cannot find the baby to finish the deed. This book was so profound and had such a deep impact on me that I couldn't write about it. Coinciding with all the nonsense of the past several weeks, I couldn't - and wouldn't - write about it at all. So, this is my last review on goodreads - and it's not really on goodreads. It's on booklikes here. I realize this is a rather inelegant solution to the problem, but for me it illustrates that reading and reviewing, no matter how off-topic or tangential the content is, are inextricably entwined. I simply can't, and won't here on goodreads, review Beloved without talking about why it's so hard to review Beloved. Goodreads offers me data to understand that reading/reviewing pattern, btw. Thirty-six of my friends have read it. Thirty-two have rated it four or five stars. Only four have reviewed it (and that's well before people started pulling their reviews). As goodreads continues to devolve, that data is going to start to dry up. These books are so life-changing, and the act of writing about them and talking about them with others has come to be so important to me, that I can't continue to do it under the circumstances that goodreads has created. How these books connect to our life; why they resonate the way they do; what meaning they create and compassion they inspire: that is what writing about them allows the reader to know. For me - perhaps for you? - books are not fully understood until they are written about. Which is why I often can't move on to a new book until I write even just a sentence or two, which may be unhelpful in a commercial sense, and indeed, off-topic or irrelevant in goodreads Terms of Service/Review Guidelines sense. And which is why reviews of the type that goodreaders have so generously given over the past six-plus years are so valuable, and mean so much to me - to all of us. They've provided insights, inspired thoughts and feeling, expanded the scope of books I read, and my understanding and ability to read and write myself. Most of all: they've created connections - in the full sense of the term - that add much-valued and much-appreciated layers to the joy and companionship that books themselves provide. This - this socialization of reading - is something that clearly goodreads does not understand or appreciate, and is no longer interested in fostering. For all of you who have rated and reviewed and built this place into the thing it was, I thank you. For all of you who are leaving now to places where your thoughts, writings and creativity can continue to flourish, I support you and will follow you. I will likely be using goodreads solely for its database and whatever ongoing socializing might occur here, but like many others, I'll no longer contribute substantive content of my own until and unless goodreads clarifies its review guidelines/ToS and desists in its policy of censoring reviews. You can instead find me at: http://eccentricmuse.booklikes.com/

As an album, Clockwork Angels took me a few listens to really appreciate. It just didn't grab me like the first two pre-released tracks did. It took me all of 30 seconds to adore Halo Effect, a song with a tenderness from Alex that recalls moments of Snakes and Arrows, but which steps into uncharted waters for Rush, lyrically speaking. But as for the rest of it, I just never fell into the hugeness that the album was trying to convey, story-wise. For me, the literary underpinnings of 2112 were always just...there. Obvious. But I couldn't quite dig down into Clockwork Angels as deeply as I felt like Neil wanted me to. So I can't say I was surprised when I heard the album was being novelized. He'd spent such time building his universe, how could he be satisfied with the stories he only half told? And that's exactly what Clockwork Angels the novel accomplishes. It paints between the lines of the lyrics, sketching us a more detailed understanding of the story, with all its philosophy, allegory and symbolism. I'm not sure it's possible to fairly evaluate the novel's literary merit without having read Voltaire's Candide. I'm fortunate enough to have read and studied Candide in French, and once you understand the links there (a scathing condemnation of the "best of all possible worlds" theory, an examination of a hero who is naive and optimistic to a fault, and how the things that hero was taught hold up as he encounters a series of progressively uglier and more violent realities, for starters) it really helps Clockwork Angels click into place as a companion volume to Voltaire, rather than pioneering any philosophical assertions itself. (Even such details as the appearance of Candide's maitre Pangloss, and the somewhat inverted journey to El Dorado--presented by Anderson/Peart as extreme poverty rather than extreme wealth--nod to Voltaire.) The rest of the nodding is done to Rush lyrics. Now I'm an avid Rush fan, whose hardest decision of the day is sometimes which album to listen to on the drive to work. But while I appreciate the spirit of the "find the Rush lyric" scavenger hunt sprawled through the pages of Clockwork Angels, I've got to say that sometimes the reach was just too far. Certain instances--a clown "rolling the bones", a tarot reading pulled straight from Peaceable Kingdom, the lake between sun and moon of legend, a subtle reference to a tide running red--were excellent, contextualized, and subtle. Others, though...the cries of "Presto!" at the carnival, Owen feeling "a pounding in his temples and a surge of adrenaline" and his later assertion "I'm nobody's hero", and oh so many of the lyrics from Clockwork Angels the album, were so awkwardly placed that they rang with the mental groan of an anticipated yet painful pun. In the best case, these out-of-placers jolted you right out of the story to hum a few verses to yourself before trying to get your head back into the book. At the worst, it felt as though Anderson compromised his narrative flow and tone of his writing, just to make a hundred-and-fiftieth "hidden" Rush reference. Aww, Watchmaker! Did you have to say "Wheels within wheels"? There's nobody in the room with you! Who are you talking to? Unfortunately, the out-of-placers completely got in my way of appreciating or even really caring too much about the story. It was simultaneously too short and too long (a feeling, ironically, that I also have about Candide)--jumping from continent to continent with reckless abandon, while hanging itself up far too much on re-restating that Owen's doing something outside the norm. I did really like certain details that had nothing to do with Rush or Voltaire:  I think that the Watchmaker's character was very well-executed. Rather than pushing him towards a Big Brother, Red Star-like oppression to choke-hold the masses, I really got the feeling that he thought it his duty to hold the Stability and make people genuinely happy and life genuinely better. And his longing for the companionship of poor re-animated Martin was surprisingly poignant. I also thought the eponymous clockwork angels and the worship of the clearly opiate-seduced crowd were excellently written. As the punky little brother of Candide, Clockwork Angels is a slam-dunk. As a furthering of stories and themes the album only had time to brush, it's quite effective. As a stand-alone story and minefield for Rush lyrics from five decades, it belly-flopped a little. Three stars.

Anya Whitson is a cold woman. She has never loved her daughters, or so they believe. Meredith and Nina are devastated when their beloved father dies, leaving them with the unwelcome task of caring for their aged, withdrawn and disapproving mother. Yet one thing intrigues Nina: their father's deathbed plea for Anya to continue the fairy tale story she began to tell her daughters long ago, the story of a peasant girl who loves a prince, long ago in the magical Snow Kingdom where a Dark Knight threatens to destroy all that is good. As the plot unfolds, it is apparent that Anya's fairy tale is anything but fiction. For Meredith and Nina, it holds clues to their mother's past in war-torn Soviet Russia, where she was caught in the siege of Leningrad. This is obvious to the reader from the start, but I anticipated when the daughters would realize the truth and wondered how the two women would react when they learn the truth of their mother's tragic background. (Anticipation is often better than surprise, Roger Rosenblatt claims, and here is a great example.) I've read several novels about the siege of Leningrad, and Anya's story rings true: the coldest winter on record for the city, the thousands of people who starve to death, the rumors of sausages made of human body parts being sold in the market. Her descriptions of pre-war Leningrad seem accurate, too: the fear of speaking one's mind, the knowledge that anyone might betray you, the disappearance of the free-thinkers and poets and intellectuals. One thing I particularly enjoyed was the dynamics between Meredith and Nina and their arguments over the what-to-do-about-mom question. When Anya breaks her ankle and seems to be losing her mind, Meredith, the one who stayed at home to run the family business, thinks that putting their mother in a nursing home will ease the burden of her overloaded life. Nina has left town long ago to pursue her passion--photojournalism--and rarely takes a break from shooting war zones, tribal people in Africa, and other places in order to return home. She of course doesn't have to care for mom on a daily basis and is horrified by Meredith's decision. I never had siblings, so the relationship between sisters fascinates me; the conflict over caring for an aged parent gave me insight into my own family as my mother and her siblings decide how to care for my grandfather. There are a few discrepancies in the story, but mostly minor things about Meredith's past. Did she get married because she was pregnant, or had she and Jeff married young and then she unexpectedly became pregnant? I seemed to get both impressions at different points in the novel. Tiny quibble. Some of the writing could have been better (not so many adjectives or adverbs, that sort of thing). But the family dynamics are just as intriguing and true to life as Anya's story of her tragic life in the brutal war. Definitely worth reading. For my more conservative readers: there is some cursing and implied sexual content. Considering the subject matter, the violence is surprisingly low-key.

This review is also available on my blog, Bows & Bullets Reviews Dean Holder will never forgive himself for walking away from Hope. That moment alter his life in ways his childhood self couldn't even imagine. Now, many years later, after facing tragedy and completely giving up on ever finding Hope, he is just making his way through life....until he runs into Sky. Sky looks so much like Hope that he seriously thinks she's lying when she says otherwise. Then she shows him her license and that's something you can't argue with. But he is filled with the desperate need to know her anyway. The more he learns about her, the more he hopes his first impressions were wrong. Please, don't let this girl be Hope. It will ruin her life and she likes her life. But all of us who have read Hopeless (and you should really read that first), already know where this is going and all we really want is to see how Holder takes it. Just prepare yourself because it's everything you imagined...and more. What is there to say about Dean Holder? I'm already in love with they guy before this novel started. Holder stole my heart in Hopeless. He's devotion to Sky was heart-breakingly awesome. That's the only term to describe this set of novels, heartbreaking. Colleen gives us what we want, we get a couple so in love that gets to have that happily ever after that all girls dream about, but she rips us apart along the way. Holder's perspective is just as devastating as Sky's was. The things he learns, especially about his sister just rip you in two. I found myself crying along with him as he learns about Sky's past and why Karen took her and the whole thing with Les. The whole thing brought on deep, body wracking sobs. But, getting behind his eyes just made me love him more. As much as his love for Sky shines through in Hopeless, here, we get to experience it first hand. We get to see how he felt that day when he saw Sky wearing Les' bracelet and his emotions over getting back with Sky after that break. He's perfect, in that amazing imperfect way. Obviously, we get more of Sky, but I don't have much to say about that. She's the same as she was in Hopeless, so there is nothing new to say. I will say that I officially love Daniel. That boy is hilariously awesome and I want to see more of him. I was a little sad once we start picking back up on the Hopeless timeline because we didn't get nearly enough from goofy Daniel. He's need to give everyone nicknames cracked me up on more than one occasion. I will be finding any possible way to squeeze Finding Cinderella into my reading list soon because I need more of him. I actually really love novels like this, where you get the same story via a different perspective. Actually, what I love is novels told in dual perspectives, but beyond that, this is the next best thing. It might be better because you still get all the mystery in book one with not knowing what the other person is thinking and then everything is laid out in book 2. You get to see your favorite scenes over again in a new light and it's awesome. I honestly don't understand people who complain about them because they are "the same book." Dude, the description tells you that. You know exactly what you are going to get when you go in, so if that's not your thing, WHY THE HELL ARE YOU READING IT? Sure, new scenes will be added, but it will be the same scenes and dialogue over again. I really love that. I love getting in Holder's head and understanding his thoughts. I don't think I loved it more than Hopeless because...well, there is no logical reason, but Hopeless broke me. Hopeless was that novel that just spoke to me and made me fall in love with Colleen Hoover. Sure, I really liked Slammed. I would even go so far as to say that I loved Slammed, but Hopeless was better and it has a special place in my heart. This is a close second to that. I adored it and I'm so glad that I have that pretty hardcover special edition now (::cough:: signed by Colleen and Griffin (if you don't know who Griffin is, fix that! Audio Notes: I really thought I had listened to something else by Kirby, but I've perused his whole list on Audible and the only other thing I've read by him was This Girl and I read an e-ARC of that, so I know I didn't listen to it. He does a pretty amazing job. He's voice is nice and he has great pacing. He doesn't hold back on the emotion. This book contains some difficult subject matter and he does a great job letting that emotion shine through. I definitely enjoyed him and I look forward to listening to more of his work.

I'm not sure what to say to do justice to this book. Kay is a master of creating worlds just inches from our own, drawing on real history and then twisting it to his own ends. With several protagonists, and a prose style that leaps from one to another, sometimes within a single scene, this could have been overdone. But it isn't. I loved the different voices and characters and was never bored or impatient to get back to one or the other. Kay plays with time and space in a way that bound all of them together, choosing his narrators carefully--even the ones who are only there to narrate their deaths. If I had a complaint, it's one I think I had with River of Stars, and that's the seemingly random choice to have one of the characters' scenes be in third person present tense. It didn't make that character more interesting (Marin is already plenty interesting on his own) and I don't think it added any immediacy to those sections. If I were going to make a critical analysis here, I'd say it indicates Marin's always living in the now--but I wouldn't take myself seriously. More interesting to me is the way the narrative gets tossed between characters, at some points even overlapping, and in one key scene revealing the difference between perception and reality. I found the whole thing fascinating and tension-building. I'm not as certain how I feel about the third person omniscient passages, though they're usually used to reveal the future and are satisfying in that way. They did tend to drag me out of the story, and I think I accepted them mainly because I did want to know what happened to the characters in the long run. For much of the book I was so, so grateful to live in a more civilized time and place, one where women's power isn't so dependent on their ability to please men. This is a brutal time, where honor killings are acceptable if you've got enough gold to pay the victim's family off, where men and women are vulnerable to the vicissitudes of climate and weather, where a father can condemn a wayward daughter to a lifetime shut up in a religious retreat because she fell in love with the wrong man. And yet there's great beauty here as well, people showing love and kindness even when it doesn't benefit them. Beauty, and courage in all its guises. The contrast gives the book great power. I love that Kay is a romantic and that everyone who deserves it gets a happily ever after. I love that in this story, the miracles that exist feel natural, part of the world. I love that Danica's voice speaks to her granddaughter after her death, just as Danica's grandfather spoke to her. It's just the tiniest stroke of magic that makes the whole thing feel otherworldly. It's a marvelous book, and one I'm sure I'll revisit.

Made it 65% into this book. It actually wasn't awful, up to that point. It wasn't good, but it wasn't awful. But there's only so much stupidity I can handle. And there were many issues. SO MANY ISSUES. Pretty girl takes priority over important mission. Trying to blend in as a slave-- constantly talking back to his "mistress" in public places. How did he survive ten years?!?! The duel. He would have gotten whipped. I think he would have preferred that. Drawing attention to both of you like that was beyond stupid and unnecessary. It's not like you were saving his LIFE. You were risking yours and became injured yourself to avoid having him receive lashings. Now, I've never been lashed. I was rarely spanked. So I feel kind of like a jerk for being so "oh, he would just be punished a little" about it. BUT it was still a very stupid move on her part. How the issue of slavery was handled. Number four is the biggest one. I just... I can't. First of all, they try to make Kestrel seem "different." It is implied that she is better than all those other slave owners. 'cause it all makes her a little uncomfortable. She freed her former caregiver slave. She feels bad for her impulse slave buy. So, you know. Yeah. Except that she is 100% a privileged brat. And when the Herrani revolt, she doesn't seem to ONCE stop and say... Huh. This is totally what we did to them, except OUR reason was that they were wealthy and we were jealous. They just want their homes back-- we just wanted to conquer. Hmmmm. It made me so angry. I mean, yes. She was brought up with the idea that she is entitled to this. But we are supposed to believe that she is somehow different. That she might be smarter than all that. Instead, I hear all about what monsters these people are and HOW DARE THEY NOT BE CONTENT TO KEEP BEING SLAVES IN THEIR OWN FORMER COUNTRY/CITY/HOMES!!! Arin SO TOTALLY BETRAYED HER and how could he when SHE LOVES HIM and they could totally have had an ILLICIT LOVE AFFAIR while she went off and married someone else or something. I mean, seriously?! She is shocked and betrayed and completely has no clue why these people would do these things until (I skimmed) some random point later in the book she randomly, randomly mentions that the cause is just. But she still is going to work against them. Arin keeps apologizing. "I'm so sorry for freeing my people. I hope you can forgive me. I mean, it's not like you were 80% fine with BUYING me and having me serve as a slave. As well as having a whole household that your barely even noticed. The fact that I am pretending to claim you as mine to protect your life is just the worst thing ever, I AM AWFUL! I'M SO SORRY!" Here is this lovely gem: "Fetch a basket," Kestrel said, "or a trunk." Sarsine glared, because they both knew she would have to do just that. There were too many things in the suite that could become weapons in the right hands. Kestrel hated to see them leave, but was glad that when they did, at least it would feel as if she had given an order and Sarsine had obeyed. Basically, Arin asks his cousin, Sarsine, to remove any object from the room that Kestrel could use to kill herself. Or as a weapon. Kestrel uses the opportunity to pretend to be the boss again because she just really needs that little thrill. It's a slave owner thing. Kestrel is stupid. I wouldn't care that she likes to gossip or wear pretty clothes or things like that. Or that she doesn't want to join the military. Totally fine. But the decisions she makes are incomprehensible and senseless. She just doesn't think things through, but I'm supposed to believe she is a brilliant strategist. For example, I kind of feel like, instead of betraying a whole ship full of trained sailors, she could have let the rebellion end right there. Apparently, Arin and Cheat had planned out everything perfectly, except for this one detail that Kestrel OF COURSE knows about. The were just going to try to sail up and take it over... Or something. They probably would have failed, and the ship would have sailed off and let the empire know. Or even killed Arin, one of the main leaders, and caused a lot of disarray. AND THEN gone off and let the empire know. Either way, assuming that she was the only one possibly capable of sailing off and letting the empire know was a little egotistical. But, hey. I was rooting for the Herrani anyways. A shame, really. I actually thought the flow/pacing of the book were pretty good.

She was perky, friendly, and annoyingly positive. Her past sounded just as tragic as the assassin's, so bonding was sure to ensue. Ilias was the Silent Master's son and oh. Em. Gee! From moment one he had his eyes on the prize (Celaena) and although he didn't speak, there was something about him. Sadly, Celaena began to realize she missed Sam... and probably actually liked him. Her training in the desert was brutal, but it gave her new skills, too. She also managed to open up and make friends. But, the assassins were being attacked by the nearby lord, and all goes to Hell one day after a huge betrayal. Celaena received what she went for, and more. I also hope to see a number of these characters in the future.

SOA Reading Challenge 2012 Surprise Me by Quarter: Quarter 2 Choice #3 - Rounding Out the Family - Listen to a romance where a child (under 18) or pet plays a significant role. (Fuzz, the dust bunny) SFR Reading Challenge 2012 2.5* rounded up to 3* Grade C+ Mildly entertaining futuristic suspense novel hampered by clunky writing and too much telling. I generally enjoy JAK in all her permutations, but this isn't one of her best. Lydia and Emmett skirted around actually talking about their true feelings for most of the book. That's a cliched romance novel trope, but it could've been used to create a little angst and distant between them, which could potentially have set the stage for an emotional confrontation/discussion. Instead, the tension basically was allowed to fizzle in one half-hearted conversation. The suspense plot was decent, but convoluted, and there were too many plot holes. Like why hadn't anyone found the secret chamber before? Lydia got out once through a series of tunnels not involving the big trap, is it reasonable that someone hadn't stumbled on the chamber from that direction before?

So I've only been waiting for this book for ages, and as soon as it was available for pre-order, I jumped on that and waited. And I waited. And I kept waiting. Eventually the wait was over and I finally had the book in my hands. I obviously can't go into the plot of the story so much, but there are basically new baddies, new goodies, and old buddies. Maybe it was the long wait, maybe it was the expectations, or maybe it was the mind-blowing cliffhanger of the last book, but to me, I felt as though this book didn't quite live up to my expectations. I mean, I still enjoyed it, and read it fairly quickly, but I wanted more from the book. Much much more. I'm not exactly sure in what areas I thought it lacking, but I wanted more. There was something almost hurried about the plot, and the new revelations seemed to be pulled out of nowhere. Having said that, I anticipate that this book - with its multitudes of new revelations and information - is a good setup for the book it come, because there is a book to come, in the far future...(please Maureen, please.) I still enjoyed Rory's character. As much as I wanted to smack her sometimes, I still enjoyed her. I would like to go into the Stephen stuff, but obviously. I will say though that I felt as though Stephen kind of lost a little bit of his Stephen-ness, especially following the events of the night before his death and the change in dynamics between him and Rory. He seemed like a different character all together. Yes, dying and not dying can do that, but I missed the unattainable, mysterious Stephen. I did like that we got to see him more on a personal level and see a different side to him. I especially liked Thorpe's character in this book, and would like to find out more about him because that dude's got some depth in him, let me tell you! The focus was shifted away a bit from Callum and Boo, and I would have liked to see the team be more team-like, but again, considering the situation...Freddie's supposed to be the new girl in the group, who's nice and trustworthy, but I felt as uncomfortable about her as Rory felt at times. STOP TRYING TO FIT IN EVEN THOUGH STEPHEN VETTED YOU. I don't know, she just annoyed me. All in all, a fun read, but I sure as hell waited forever and a day for this, and thus didn't feel as though it met my expectations completely. Not to detract anything from the book, but man, I was expecting a whole lot more.

This sexy, brooding bad boy just got a personality makeover and it made him hotter to the nth degree! Yes, Bad Romeo still lies in there somewhere, but oh man! When my kindle reached the 100% mark and there was no more story, I was like, "Nooooooooooooooo!" I think I called her every curse word in the book too. #SorryNotSorry. Catherine Fisher, you wrote an amazing book. Thank you so much. Why was this book so amazing? The plot was engaging, exciting, and interesting. The setting was super neat. The prison was especially fascinating. And the world outside. It's a weakness of mine, but I really adore books about monarchy intrigues, backstabbing, and kingdomness. Makes me feel all happy and bubbly inside. Also, the characters. Fleshed out, not (too) stereotypical, and even lovable! (some of them. Maybe not Gildas. Definitely not.) Have I mentioned the prison yet? Incarceron? It's awesome! I mean, I get that it could never work and the science/magic behind it is never explained, but I don't really care. I loved it. As in A Face Like Glass the world and setting itself is a character, and I like what that adds to the story. Really, the only thing I was disappointed with was how confused the ending left me. If I could give this book 10 stars, I would. If I could have every middle school child read this book, every teacher, every parent, I would. I have never cried so much throughout a novel, that through ABSOLUTELY ALMOST. Don't let that deter you. I was so deeply moved, so touched by what Albie experienced that my heart just couldn't hold it. There are Albies EVERYWHERE. In every classroom. Different parents, different circumstances, but the same. It's obvious that fifth-grader Albie has some learning issues, specifically what, we don't know. But he's called a dummy, a moron, and even worse. His parents aren't perfect. They don't know how to deal with him some times. But does he have a huge heart. He is kind and bright in his way. There are characters that will reach deep into your soul and have you remembering them: Calista, Albie's not-so-perfect but AMAZING nanny, Hugo, the owner of the bodega, Mr. Clifton, the math club teacher. I hope we all could be blessed with people like these in our lives. It's not fair to compare any book to another, but I think this will touch people the way WONDER touched readers. I can't rave about this enough. I hope that teachers will read it to their students. I hope librarians will book-talk it. I hope parents will read it their kids. I hope kids will read it themselves. This is a book that will CHANGE YOU! It's the kind of book I wish I could buy a hundred copies and distribute to a hundred different people. Don't miss it!

I received this book from Netgalley for my honest review. A very, very good thriller. Anna is the daughter of an ex-con who stole one million dollars but has always claimed that he's innocent. When her father has been arrested hers and her other's life has been destroyed. Her mother re-married after a short while. Anna was raped by her step-brother and never told a soul about it. Anna become very closed, very prim and proper, very repressed person. When her father discovers that his employees are stealing money, he knows that nobody will believe him. He transfers the money and tries to run to the FBI. He sends the printout of where he transferred it, and leaves a voice message to Anna to run. Unfortunately he never makes it and the goons kill him making it appear like a suicide after the theft. When Anna is notified of his death and hears the message, she obeys and run to the only friend of her father's - an ex-con Brent. Brent was convicted as a teenager for having killed his father and have passed 15 years in jail part of that time with Anna's father as cell-mate. He's bitter, dark and broody. He's estranged from everybody. He's guilt ridden. His only love is painting and he's a very successful and rich. When Anna arrived at his secluded house she's terrified by him, but she doesn't have anybody else. Brent is very annoyed, but for her father's sake decides to help her. Both of them have no idea who you're against, how to prove her father's innocence, how to prove that his death is not a suicide, where her father has sent the proof of the theft. Meanwhile the villains are looking for Anna and are trying to find out where the proof has been sent. They're ruthless and very determined. The story revolves around all of this: Anna secrets, her inability to have contact with men, her anger with her father for having stolen, her anger for her mother for having abandoned her. Brent has his problems too: he's convinced that his bad luck and death threat to all the people who love him; he's angry to the system for having him convicted for murder when he was only defending his brother; he feels guilty about the death of his ex-girlfriend. Anna mother also is part of the story: her marriage to Ed starts feeling stiffening. She's angry with her dead ex-husband for ruining her life and pushing her towards Ed. We also see inside the head of the main killer: his utter depravity, his lack of any humanity, his ego-mania. He think he has the right to do anything, kill, rape, torture, in order to get "his" money back! It's chilling! The writing style is very good and the story flows without problems, smoothly and thrilling. The actions of each character are coherent and logical - just what I would have done in their shoes (apart from one single action of the heroine near the end which was bordering on TSTL!!! Even if there're no doubts about who is the good and who are the bad guys, the book kept my attention till the end! And I loved the twist at the end - excellent and unexpected! :D I loved Brent and Anna. They were perfect for each other. Their damaged souls were meant to heal each other. The way they fell in love was just right! First there come the trust, then the attraction and after that love. Obviously, being both of them damaged in the emotional department, there was a lot of angst and desire to negate the feeling, but it was done in such a way that it fit their personalities perfectly! Great book! :D

I loved this book. I was debating myself between 4 and 5 stars because I loved it so much. Park is everything. He is so perfect, so sweet and generous and in love. He is quiet and strong, but he has his faults: he tries to be invisible because he doesn't want to stand out, and because he's afraid of being picked on. He has low self-esteem and feels like his father and society view him as feminine, unattractive and week. Eleanor is great. She is strong but weak at the same time. She wants to be accepted and loved and is scared of what others think, but because of her situation, she is treated as a freak. She uses old used clothes that don't fit her (because she doesn't have money to buy herself anything) and is scared of everyone finding out she doesn't even own a toothbrush. But Park and his music and comics are an escape to that. What I liked is that the story is about their love. Is not about his o her life, but about their relationship exclusively. So we see bits of their life creeping in into their story, and eventually  ending it. We learn more about Park's conflict with his father, and how it develops, and how he feels about himself, but it's bits and pieces. And Eleanor's home story is told, but as the book progresses you start to realize it is getting dangerous. To be honest I assumed his stepfather hit her mom, and I think it was suggested with bruisses she had seen. But I had a sick feeling about him when he had Masie sitting on his lap. Luckily they all slept together, so he couldn't touch the girls without everyone knowing, but at the end we realize it was only a matter of time I liked the other characters, Park's parents and grandparents, Eleanor brother's Ben and Mouse and her sister Maisie. I didn't like her mom, I couldn't understand why she didn't reach for help, but it happens every day in abusive relationships. It was hard to understand since we only got glimpses, but it paints the picture. I loved and hated the ending. It was bittersweet, no real closure. But like the author said at the end, at 17 life isn't about endings, it's about beginnings. We may not get the sweet ending that we hoped for. But not many 17-year-old couples do. I was happy that Eleanor's aunt and uncle took them in. It seems that the whole family got away, and that is the bigger happy ending one could hope for. What I hated was that she wouldn't write to him. He deserved better. So why 4 stars? It was a love story. It wasn't as deep as I would have wanted it to be. Most of the book is them thinking about how much they love each other, how perfect and beautiful and soft and amazing they are and how they make their life worth living. And while it's sweet and wonderful to remember being young and in love like that, it's also a bit flat. But I did love the book and teared up a little at the end.

4.5 Stars I'm so emotional right now. Pardon me as I take a huge breath and gather up my feels before I write this review. This book was unlike anything I have ever read. It wasn't just the story, but everything was put together so uniquely it was profound. This book had such a diverse cast of characters, and I could not love it more because of it. It was not your typical protagonists, it was real. That's why I loved this book so much. The people were real. They actually had flaws, which real people have. They weren't all white with white friends, other races actually existed in this world! Another reason why I loved this book was because of the events that occurred with it. It spoke about people living within a poor neighborhood. It spoke about abuse, both physical and emotional. It spoke about the effects of having addictions. Again, it was utterly REAL. I was completely amazed how the reality of life did not take away from this wonderfully crafted story. I almost had no problems with this book. But I started panicking when I realized there were about three pages left, and I wanted there to be more. I felt like the ending was sort of-- weak. It was a great ending, but so vague, with so many things left unsaid. I wanted to know what happened to Eleanor's family. Since they were such an important role in the novel, I can't imagine why Rainbow Rowell would leave that unclear at the end. I also, of course, wanted to know where things with Eleanor and Park had gone in the future. It wasn't enough. It was enough-- but my stomach still feels empty after a full meal. Still, I would recommend this novel to anyone who wants a quick fun novel with hints of the dark aspects of life!!! I flew right threw this book, and I wish I had slowed down.
