Every once in awhile, I just need to feed the geek inside by sinking into a sci-fi or a fantasy romance. When I saw the synopsis to Dark Alpha's Claim I thought this would be the perfect food for my geek soul. We've seen this kind of plot before. A Group of heroes who fight for their people, but who are forbidden to fall in love or have any kind of relationship. Baylon is a Reaper. One of seven fae who are tasked by Death to be the judge, jury, and executioner of the Fae who have done wrong whether they are dark or light. No fae must ever be given the knowledge of who they are, and if someone finds out, they must die. Tasked with stopping the Dark Fae's massacre of humans all through Scotland, the Reapers find out that someone knows who they are, and is targeting them or possibly even death. The Dark Fae are also targeting any human with fae blood, and brutally killing all who they come across. Baylon comes upon Jordyn, obviously half fae, and he is completely floored by her. Despite knowing that he can't have a relationship, he feels a need and a connection to Jordyn that he cannot deny. Jordyn is in grave danger from the dark fae and in order to protect her, Baylon may have to turn his back on his vows to Death which means death will come for him. I loved Baylon and Jordyn. Baylon was, I wouldn't call it damaged, but he'd been betrayed. He was definitely alpha, and badass, and so completely torn between duty and what he felt for Jordyn. Jordyn just wanted to do what was right and had to decide what she was willing to put on the line, not only for people like her, but for Baylon. The chemistry between these two was smoking hot, but I would have loved to have seen more relationship building. Once they got together, there was so much action going on of the fighting kind, it was hard to see the relationship coming together. There was a lot of world building since this is the first in the series, but it was apparent that this is a spin-off from at least one or more series. At times, I was kind of lost when the Dragon Kings and their war was mentioned. I still liked the book but wish I had read the other series first. You can definitely read this book without reading the other related series, but I think I may have enjoyed it more if I had read those first. There was action galore in this book with lots of sword fighting and heads rolling. With all the talk about the Reapers being judge, jury, and executioner, we never really see them doing that. They were mostly on defense against the dark fae. I would have liked to see them doing their actual jobs before all hell broke loose with the dark fae. The ending felt extremely rushed which was disappointing. The issues facing the couple which seemed so overwhelming and impossible just seemed to conveniently be fixed. I wanted more. Overall, I enjoyed this book and want to see what happens with the rest of the Reapers. I was all set to give this 4 stars by the time I hit the last third. I liked it overall, but there were some things that bugged me. I'll get them out of the way, get it out of my system, and then be able to distill why it's a 5 star. Firstly, I was super irritated with the French people speaking French, and then speaking...more French? I understand that the author is trying to create the environment and remind English readers that these characters are French, but this bugs the hell out of me: "Merci, Isabelle," Levy said. Or scores of Merdes and Oui. It threw me out every single time, because I've already accepted/understand they are speaking French. So when I see a French, italicized word in a sentence that is already--essentially--spoken in French, my brain tries to figure out what the hell. I know that's OCD perhaps, but it makes no sense. Are they speaking MORE French? Were they really not speaking French all along? I don't get it. I mean, I GET it, but it's completely unnecessary and chucks me out of the story every single time. Another thing that bugged me was some of the contrivances; plot events that were far too convenient. I found it extremely unbelievable that Vianne would take a train to Girot and be there right at the exact precise moment to see Isabelle hauled off to a camp. The precision timing was just too implausible. There were several instances like that felt like that: rushed and added for pushing the plot on instead of organically serving the story. Therefore, I was ready to 4 star. And then I hit the end. I WOKE UP thinking about this book. That means something. I woke up pissed off to no end at a certain villain, and saddened by certain events. though why the hell did Isabelle leave the hospital in Paris when she was so sick? That makes no sense. It was the emotional impact of the events of the story, rather than the actual novel, that makes me give this 5 stars. I've never had this happen before but I feel like the historical impact of stories like this: the sacrifice, and horror, terror and pain, of war--especially WWII where so many atrocities were committed--are so worth telling. The emotional impact I'm left with wasn't because I was super sad about Vianne or Isabelle, but because of the countless women they represented. Their struggles and pain were not fictional. These characters, to me, were avatars for the real women who endured the unthinkable in war time and this is their story. As a novel, The Nightingale was a solid 4 star read for me as far as the mechanics, the craft, the voice...etc.. But the lives and stories of women such as Vianne and Isabelle in wartime need to be heard. The impact of this book is bringing me closer to them, more appreciative of their sacrifices, more grateful of what I have and my children who will hopefully never know that kind of terror. For that, Kristin Hannah deserves all the accolades in the world for giving these women, via Vianne and Isabelle, a voice and a story on such a huge, far-reaching platform. And, of course, the endurance of love through horror is a message that resonates very deeply for me. Even amid death and war, love always wins.

When I used to read books as a kid that covered racism, like Iggie's House, I believed that racism was done, that the people who said "go back where you came from" had vanished after the 1960s, and we lived in the world that Sesame Street represented. Then I grew up, and the past year happened. Glory Be was a hard book for me to read because of its optimism contrasted with the stark reality that it portrays, a reality in the Deep South where the swimming pools are segregated and even get closed when integration comes to town. Glory, the title character, is upset when the pool closes before her birthday on July 4th, and becomes even more so as she realizes the reasons for said closure. Her best friend Frankie is a nice kid under the thumb of his prejudiced jerk of an older brother J.T., and her new friend Laura gets targeted with her mother opening up a clinic to help the poor. This is an important book to read, especially when as an adult you realize that the racist culture discussed in this book, and the people like J.T. don't get punished and are even celebrated in this day and age. Last year schools in Ferguson, Missouri got closed because of police protests and riots, so that many kids wouldn't get access to free lunches or to an education. The Baltimore riots happened and were publicized, but there was no justice for Freddie Gray despite the weeks of peaceful protests that went unnoticed. Quite a few passages felt triggering knowing that we haven't moved past the 60s, and more than a thousand people are stuck in that era. Now let's get to Frankie. Frankie is many things: a sweet kid, a bullied victim, an enabler to racist behavior, and in Glory's mind a  traitor  who takes a long time to apologize for his actions. Glory refuses to speak to him as he starts parroting his father and uncle's words, eventually pulling off a dirty trick under his brother's coercion that nearly destroys their friendship. He takes a lot of time to grow up, but the ending leaves the choice up to Glory if she wants to forgive him. I hope that Augusta Scattergood writes more books, about the contrast of optimism and reality. She did a great job portraying one town's internal conflict that eventually bubbles over.

A Temptation of Angels by Michelle Zink Release Date: On Shelves NOW! ARC received from Michelle Zink and Dial Books Reviewed by: Middle Sis Jenn The Sisters Say: Alluring and Charismatic 3.5 Stars Thank you to Michelle Zink and Dial books for my copy! I absolutely love the cover--he eyes are gorgeous and draw you right in! Before I had my baby boy, I taught 8th grade Literature and all the students had to read novel outside of class each six weeks. It was supposed to be something they would enjoy, and I found, that like me, many of my female students loved paranormal romance novels and they always wanted to know what book they should read next. However, middle school libraries are very strict with what books they will purchase; so many of the ones I had read would not have been found in our library. But A Temptation of Angels would have been perfect for them as it was more middle grade than YA. Michelle Zink creates a fun paranormal world, full of good and evil, angels and demons, love and betrayal. So...I'll start with what I enjoyed. I was sucked in from Chapter 1 when Helen's parents are killed and she is sent to Griffin and Darius. I loved the mystery surrounding the murder and the mystique surrounding both of the brothers. (I do wish I would have known how old everyone was--somehow that was left out and I felt like it should have been a big deal). I really loved how Griffin became attached to Helen-wanting to protect her. Their relationship was probably the best part of the book. I love the small innuendoes that Griffin would put out there about wanting to be closer to her an enjoying their bodies flushed up against each other. While I wanted more romance (and far more details), I will say that the romance was perfect for a middle grade book (like I had mentioned earlier). I was sweet and subtle, with many romantic kisses, but nothing beyond that. I do hope that the next books step up a bit on the steamy romance, though. The blurb talks about Helen being caught between Griffin and Raum (the childhood friend), and that was something that really drew to want to read the book. I love books where there is a good "bad guy." There was so much potential here, and I did like Raum, but I wish there would have been more of him. I wanted to find myself screaming, "Who should she choose??" But, I found myself strictly in the Team Griffin territory because there wasn't enough intensity between Helen and Raum. I'm crossing my fingers that there will be in the next installment. I enjoyed the world that Michelle set up, although I wish there would have been more details about the world and less about Helen's normal, everyday actions. I found myself wondering about the time period--it was obviously in the far past (like the 1800s) because it was inappropriate for Helen to be seen holding hands with Griffin. Plus, she had to take a bath in a basin in her room. But, beyond that, there wasn't much detail about the world. I would have loved to have seen more into the reality around Helen. On the other hand, there were too many details about Helen's simple actions--walking from place to place, hiding in corners, etc. I felt that the book could have easily been 50 pages shorter without all the extra simple details. Overall, this was a fun and quick read that I know the younger YA crowd would enjoy. Personally, I like more steam and more fierce action that what was there, but I still enjoyed the relationships and idea of the world. I would recommend this book to anyone who has a younger teenage girl who enjoys paranormal romance books.

All Detroit/Michigan lovers - this is an exciting thriller for you. It is a book on the edge of nearly every genre, and definitely solidifies Beukes literary voice. I enjoyed it while reading it, but the quick jump  to random supernatural explanations   left me a little chilled. Mostly I was reading it so to throw out references to my Michigan-born husband, who kept trying to wrest the book away from me. Since he read it in three days, I guess he enjoyed it more than I. This review was originally posted on IrisjeXx MORE RUSSIAN INSPIRED FANTASY! YAY! I think that was my very first reaction when I heard about The Crown's Game. It is no secret that I am a huge lover of the Grisha-verse and one of the main reasons I love it so much has a lot to do with the amazingly intriguing setting. So I was most definitely down for any book set in Russia! And boy, this book did not disappoint! First things first, The Crown's Game wasn't what I thought it would be! Which actually didn't turn out to be a bad thing (yay! ), I just had to adjust a bit. When I read the synopsis of the book I pictured glorious battles, fighting, stuff blowing up (aka violent things) and that's definitely not what The Crown's Game turned out to be. It became clear pretty early on that it was all about "impressing the Tsar with epic magic skills" rather then bloody fights. This made that the story moved quite slow, and not as fast paced as I expected it to be. However, I didn't find myself minding it as much as I thought I would've. It was a fun read, because it wasn't as stressful as a story full of fights would've been. Instead it all felt quite magical to me. The Crown's Game is super atmospheric, with amazing world-building! I don't know too much about 1825 Russia, but Evelyn Skye definitely did her homework! She intricately weaved history into her story, which made it so very beautiful to read. The setting is so incredibly detailed and written beautifully! The plot, or rather The Crown's Game itself, was unpredictable to me. Even though it wasn't really fast paced, the course of the game thrilled me and kept me on the edge of my seat. The friendship between Nikolai and Pasha was top-notch. One of my favorite things about The Crown's Game without a doubt! I love a well-fleshed out friendship in my books, and I got just that from Nikolai and Pasha's friendship. It kinda sucks a girl kinda comes between that, but hey, we'll let that slide fot the story's sake  . I'm not too sure about the romance though. There's a love-triangle... which I actually didn't actually mind it that much. But there was just something a bit off about the romance. It felt a bit underdeveloped to me, as did the characters. Both the romance and the characters could've used a little more complexity in my opinion. I think this is what kept me from fully connecting with the characters . All and all I think The Crown's Game made for a really solid debut and first instalment in a VERY promising series! Beautiful writing and aboslutely mind-numbingly awesome world-building and SO MUCH MAGIC! I'm really looking forward to seeing how the story will progress and mature in the books to come! As I am a part of Harper Collin's The Crown's Game blog tour I am including a little something extra in this review: a playlist inspired by the book! I handpicked 10 songs that reminded me of certain moments in the story, hope you enjoy!

When Albert's father sells his son's beloved horse Joey to the Cavalry, Albert promises he'll find him again. Meanwhile, Joey is plunged into the beginning of World War I with Captain Nicholls. In the first encounter with the enemy Nicholls is killed. His friend Captain Stewart gives charge of Joey to Trooper Warren. At first Warren is wary of Joey because his own horse was shot under him in battle and he's afraid to ride again; but he warms up. Warren and Stewart are captured by the Germans and Joey is put to work pulling an ambulance cart full of wounded German solders back and forth from the lines with Topthorn, Captain Stewart's steed; Topthorn is source of strength and encouragement to Joey throughout the book. After much turmoil, Joey eventually gets back to the British lines, where he is reunited with Albert, who joined the veterinary corp in hopes of finding his horse. War Horse is an easy read, and I enjoyed it. It's written from Joey's perspective; a horse's thoughts and feelings on what was happening were interesting. Joey's loyalty to and fondness for Topthorn reminded me of Black Beauty and Ginger from Black Beauty. At first it seemed like Joey always landed into good hands, and was going to be merrily passed from good owner to good owner, but it proved to be more realistic later on. Overall, it was a very good read.

Ramblings. Yes, I'm still in my "prolonging The Redemption of Callie & Kayden" phase. It's such a good day today and it'll be such a waste for my mood and energy to just be sucked right into the depressing and sad story of that book. That's why I decided to read this one. The summary of this book got my attention starting from: "Indy Savage, cop's daughter, rock chick and used bookstore owner, has been in love with Lee Nightingale, once bad boy, now the man behind Nightingale Investigations, since she was five years old." Yep, pretty much the start of its blurb. Immediate thought after reading this book. Is it just me or this book is really loooooooong? Rock Chick was definitely a very long roller coaster ride (I may or may not have this urge to get off the ride already in some parts of it). My thoughts. Kristen Ashley without a doubt truly has a way with words and totally gets playful with it. She knows that she has it and she uses it in full power. Even if the situations thrown upon the characters were scary and could certainly give readers shivers and goosebumps, she uses words to diffuse those feelings and manages to crack smiles on readers' faces. I totally enjoyed that she could do that, even highlighted/bookmarked a number of scenes where it made me cackle BUT then I find the whole book quite wordy. I don't know about you but I get the "wordy feel" when the character's thoughts gets jumbled and tangled. Then it ends up or comes out in a variety of phrasings. Towards the end part of the book, it feels like it's quite dragging already. One hurdle after another and another, gets old already by the time it hits the last page of the book. The author could've lessened the number of curveball these characters experienced in the story and should've given more focus unto my next thought which is ... I could've like this a whole lot better and even given it 5 stars if they got together months/weeks after they have rekindled their friendship and all. Some of you may be disagreeing with my sentiment and may even be saying that they've waited years already for a THEM to happen. Yes, they may have the hots and fell in love with each other years before the present time but for a decade they haven't been interacting well with each other... I can say that ten years is a long time and some things about them are bound to change in the years in between. I think, TIME is needed in that kind of situation. Though, I found it very heart-warming that they ended up with each other. Thinking of Iittle Indy having a crush on the young boy Lee and looking at them now in this book ... feels like a fairytale. All in all, I still enjoyed reading this book. If you want to laugh while reading tense action packed scenes, then this book's the one for you. Bye x

Like most kids, I went through a phase in which I read everything about Greek mythology. Had I read this book during that phase, I probably would have loved it. As I am today, it was okay. The adventure was decent. The writing was okay (though the moments Percy slipped into present tense were jarring). Okay is the word. I'm not really invested in the main character (or any of his friends) or interested in how the story continues (which, I gather, is something along the Harry Potter lines of "seemingly normal boy with daddy issues saves the world"). People/circumstances were often too convenient and the environmental/animal cruelty bits seemed a little forced. Honestly, I felt like I was reading the wrong story with the wrong main character from the moment they mentioned the pine tree. (Maybe not the "wrong" story, but one less to my liking.) Perhaps it's because I'm a girl, but Thalia sounded like a character whose story I'd enjoy much more than Percy's. My little brother has informed me that Thalia does enter the story (as a person, not a tree) down the road, but she has a limited role and Percy is still Neo. I can understand why this series has gained the acclaim and following it has. I would recommend it to younger readers looking for a new adventure series, particularly boys; however, for now, it's not one I'll continue. PS- We got a bit of North Jersey, but almost no South. What's up with that? Grover would have loved the farmland.

I've heard so much about this series for so long and I've had this particular book for ages. Took me forever to get to it, but now that I've finally read it, I'm very glad that I did and will be reading the rest of the books to get ready for book 4 later this month. Charley is an awesome heroine. I love her smartass quips. I know that can put some people off, but I just loved her for each and every one of them. It turns out that Charley is a grim reaper. The departed cross through her to reach Heaven. While Charley is sometimes annoyed with the ghosts that come to her making requests and dealing with the people-who-are-left-behing (it makes her sad, Charley is surprisingly sensitive), she doesn't seem to mind providing this service, not that she has much of a choice. She does seem to be prone to getting herself hurt, though. Still, she definitely isn't stupid and I like her a lot. Then of course, there's Reyes. This guy is an enigma up until the very end of the book. Even after we learn what we learn (shocking! ), the man is still a mystery. I'm surprised that he seems to have taken it upon himself to protect what he's protecting since it seems he's protecting more than just Charley. What made him decide to work against his father? Besides his Dutch? That scene where she seemed to obtain some of his knowledge was powerful and very enlightening. I'm wondering how to feel about this guy. I like him, but talk about dangerous. It feels a lot like liking Barrons. Not really a good guy, but pretty difficult not to like him, considering. I need to see more of him to make a real decision. I will keep him in the like column for now. I really liked the story going on as well. Charley and her Uncle did good, helping to find out who had killed those lawyers and getting an innocent man out of prison. For all that Charley isn't a real police officer (but she is a licensed PI), she actually handled herself pretty well. I'm just glad she seems willing to work with others instead of doing everything by herself. I was glad she was able to open up to Connie more than she originally had as well. It helped me to learn a lot about Charley and the kind of person she is. Hopefully, she'll be able to confide in more people as the series goes on. I really like the way Darynda Jones uses the concept of the Grim Reaper here. Much different from most grims I come across in other series. This is a very promising series.

I can't write a review right now because I'm crying so much and I've been crying since page 541 but for now all I have to say was that this reading experience was incredible and I'm glad I finally read this. *15 hours later* Ok. I've calmed down. I've decided to leave my initial reaction to this book in because I think that's what will stick with me when I think about how this novel made me feel. I can't even tell you how sceptical I was going into this book. WWII fiction is my jam, but I have to say I haven't had much luck with YA WWII fiction in the past, so I didn't have high hopes at all for this novel, especially partnered with the fact that it's still so hyped up even now. I didn't think the whole 'narrated by Death' thing was going to work, I couldn't see how a novel about a little girl that steals books in Nazi Germany was going to be interesting, and I thought I was going to be one of those people that ended up hating The Book Thief. From what I've seen, people either love this or hate this, there's very few people who just felt meh about The Book Thief. As you can tell from my rating, I ended up loving this. Having Death narrate this novel was genius. There's no other word I can use to describe that choice. It made the prose work better and it tied everything to together nicely. I enjoyed that he was basically telling us Liesel's story using her words as a base, and how he kept going off into little anecdotes when he had personally interacted with the characters, when he had seen them in person. The writing was just beautiful. The Book Thief is essentially a coming-of-age story, albeit a heartbreaking one. I loved the characters in this. I liked the representation of small German communities at the time, I liked how it was all handled by the main and side characters. I liked Death's opinion on all of it. I forgot that this was a young adult novel. Like I said originally, I started crying at page 541. Death often tells the reader what will happen, so I think the fact that it still hit me so hard is a credit to Markus Zusak's writing. I managed to keep myself in check when Liesel started shouting for her Papa. I managed to stall the tears when she kissed Rudy, when she found Rosa. Then she looked at Hans. (Side note: I'm crying again just thinking about it.) Hans Hubermann was by far my favourite character, I adored his personality and his relationship with Liesel. It was page 542 that got me the most. And I can promise you something, because it was a thing I saw many years later - a vision in the book thief herself - that as she kneeled next to Hans Hubermann, she watched him stand and play the accordion. He stood and strapped it on in the alps of broken houses. There were silver eyes. There was a cigarette slouched on his lips. He even made a mistake and laughed in lovely hindsight. The bellows breathed and the tall man played for Liesel Meminger one last time as he sky was slowly taken from the stove. Everything is still sinking in at this point, and I'll probably be thinking about this novel for a long time. I'm glad I waited to read this though, now that I think about it, because I don't think I'd have appreciated this at all when my sister first started badgering me to read this not long after it came out. All I can really say is that I think this book is important and beautiful, and I loved it.

I love graphic novel memoirs about people's childhoods in general. One about a deaf girl growing up in Virginia in the early 80s? Of course I'm gonna enjoy it. The art is lovely and clear. The choice to give every character rabbit ears is smart, since this book is all about ears. The focus on friendships and school life will make it relatable; the fact that all the teachers smoke will make it exotic! All in all, an excellent alternative to the deplorable Wonder for anybody who wants to read about growing up with a disability. 4 stars really, but a 5th from me for an excellent Helen Keller reference.

Such a beautifully tragic book. Cashore's novels are all so character driven, they come across as so real. This book was such an emotional ride, I cried at certain parts. The characters broke my heart; especially Thiel. Every time he came onto the page, I teared up for this broken, tired and gravely depressed man. And near the end, when everything came to light, I bawled like a baby for him. It wasn't just his death, it was how broken he was, how guilt stricken and how much he just wanted to protect Bitterblue from it all. To me, she should have loved him more, grieved for him more, as he was more of a father figure then Leck ever was. Bitterblue was a strong, emotional character who lost her top and lied a lot when she wanted to. For an eighteen year old queen, being kept in the dark by her trusted advisors, she had plenty on her plate and frustration is understandable. Love how it says romance on the inside flab. More romantic than Fire? Sure, Saf and Bitterblue had a little...fling dare I call it? But it felt as if Bitterblue and Giddon got along and possessed a more stable [and romantic] relationship than she and Saf ever did. And there was honesty and trust! Every relationship needs that! And Saf was rarely in the book to make this extremely subtle romance, a romance. True, Bitterblue is not a romance. But that romance was a subplot. The bridges, pretty neat! I loved them and wished there were more cheerful bridge scenes.

Sorry, no more telepathic conversations, Fitz. The worldbuilding is so amazing especially the traditions like the first day of school and the Wanderlings. While the book definitely amped up the fantasy oddness bringing in more details about genetic manipulation based on a highly intelligent animal , I did the think the picture of how creator and creation relate  was really fascinating from a Christian perspective. Elwin was fantastic as always, and if I read more it will be for more of his humor and also to find out what happens to Fitz, Wylie, and Prentice . Also, the other-worldly abilities including telepathy, telekinesis, and the powers of a unicorn-type creature  are chalked up to science but border on magical/supernatural and can get pretty intense when reading broken minds . Best quotes: "And you," Keefe said, shoving between them. "What was up with the whole Amazing Flying Foster routine?" I'm not sure I'll read the whole series, but I am interested in trying more.

I don't know why The Murder of Roger Ackroyd should have been so much more memorable to the public at large--probably because it was the first time it was done. . Her psychology is spot on here--the narrator is quite fascinating.

Good, but a little too chick-lit book-clubby for my taste. I've read a bunch of WWII books (both fiction and non) but this may be the first I've read told from the perspective of someone in the French resistance, which was interesting. But the plot was a bit too predictable, the language was unremarkable, and the tear-jerking at the end (while, again, totally expected) was a bit much. Assuming that the historical details (the way Resistance members led downed Allied pilots over the Pyrenees by foot)  were accurate, I'm generally glad I read it -- especially since it was a really quick read (see above: cliched plot and bland prose). But there are plenty of other books set in the same era (A God in Ruins always comes to mind) that are much better pieces of literature. Two and a half stars, rounded up since the subject matter was somewhat interesting.

This review was also featured on my blog. Trigger warnings for suicide, bullying, and slut-shaming. Tease definitely addresses some important issues, namely, bullying, suicide, and our society's tendency to slut-shame. The story follows Sara Wharton, a high school junior who's been criminally charged for harassment of a sophomore at her school, Emma Putnam. Sara's learning what it's like to be hated by society - she's jeered at in the grocery store, ostracised by her former friends, and her life seems totally destroyed. Between the meetings with her lawyer and her therapist, we see flashbacks to Sara's junior year, where it all began. Emma's status as a 'slut' was established soon after she transferred to Sara's school, and she starts to cosy up to Sara's boyfriend. Sara and her best friend Brielle are both furious at Emma, and guided mostly by Brielle's dogged ideas, they start off a chain of events that end in one horrific moment--Emma, found dead in her home. What's most important about this book to me is the portrayal of Sara. She's not exactly an unlikeable protagonist, but more of a realistic one, with selfish actions, a tendency to jealousy, bitterness, and teenage resentment...the whole package. In her 'war' with Emma, her own weaknesses and insecurities are exposed. The whole reason she starts picking on Emma in the first place (ignoring all the egging-on that Brielle did) was her insecurities when it came to her boyfriend Dylan. More than any malice, it's self-doubt and fear that motivated Sara's actions, and I think that was shown really well. The fact that the book itself is named for Sara's insecurity just adds on to that. It's what everyone's always saying, that the bully only attacks you because you make them feel weak, or you make their own insecurities stand out. But, Sara's portrayal is also where Tease failed. From the start of the novel Sara is unrepentant. She doesn't think she's in the wrong, because the names she called Emma were all true. In fact, she blames Emma for committing suicide and bringing all of the trouble crashing down upon them. Sara sees this as the 'weak' way out, and when everyone's hating on her, she explicitly refuses to think about suicide--because she wouldn't ever choose to be that weak. That was all very realistic, but her ideas in the beginning versus her ideas at the resolution show a drastic change that isn't properly portrayed. It's not explained why her feelings changed, it's not explained how she as a person changed, and that's where the book is lacking. The whole point of a story like this is the bully's realisation that what they did was wrong, and Tease just doesn't bring that out. Overall, it's definitely thought-provoking, moving (I cried. No surprises there. ), and a really interesting idea, but it built up to nowhere and wound up falling short. I received this book as a free ARC from NetGalley in exchange for an honest review.

2.5 Stars Overall Opinion:  This was just ok, and then it wasn't. It lost my interest completely and even though I really should've put it on my dnf shelf -- I skimmed through the last 30%. I didn't find anything really all that special about either characters, and once they developed stronger feelings it became kind of cheesy and just plain unappealing to me. I didn't hate it either. POV: This alternated between Katy and Richard's POV. Overall Pace of Story:  Not so great. I hit a wall at around 70%, and it never pulled me back in. He was a jerk at first, but he made some major changes to be a better man. He was just ok. h rating: 3 stars. Katy. She was also just ok. Nothing else really to say. Sadness level: Low. He is adamant at first that he will never fall in love, so he pushes away in a sense at first. Once they become intimate, he pursues her after she takes off. Heat level: Moderate/low. They take so long to change their relationship and become intimate that there isn't that much heat (mostly at the end where I was skimming). Descriptive sex: Yes. Safe sex: They go without protection and then have a discussion after the fact. The h is on birth control. The H mentions that he had never been without before. OW/OM drama: No Sex scene with OW or OM: No Cheating: No Separation: Yes  There is a short separation when the h runs away after they are intimate. There are no other partners during the separation. Possible Triggers: Yes  Manwhore H before agreement, virgin h, poverty, loss of parents, parental figure with Alzheimer's, and marriage of convenience. Closure: This had ok closure with a HEA ending. "It wasn't freedom she wanted. It was belief in something--a prize big enough to run for and to fight for and to keep on reaching toward no matter what." Actual rating: 3.5 stars Safiya is a Truthwitch (able to detect the truth from lies, and the first one born in the Witchlands in generations) and a Domna of Cartorra, which means she's royalty. Iseult is a Threadwitch (able to see people's emotions and their bonds to each other in the form of vividly colored threads), and she's a Nomatsi, which means she's hated, ostracized and considered disgusting by... pretty much everyone. The two of them are Threadsisters, and best friends, and together they embark on a fast-paced, breathtaking journey that shows how strong the love and the bonds between the two of them truly are. Because, ultimately, I like to think of this story as the story of their friendship. The loyalty Safi and Iz have for one another is shown at all times, and they were literally willing to risk their lives to save each other, more than once. This book won all the points with me by showing us a beautiful friendship between two teenage girls and never once trying to ruin things between them, like it so easily happens in YA books; instead, it showed how they rose above it and stood by each other, even when faced with difficulties that would break any other weaker friendship. "(...) Why does it have to be 'we'? Why not just me?" "Because 'just me' isn't who we are," Iseult hollered back. "I'll always follow you, Safi, and you'll always follow me. Threadsisters to the end." This was a strong book. It was entertaining from page 1, and there was never a dull moment. Engines were always turning, there was always action happening, and you never had a moment to catch your breath. The worldbuilding is very confusing at first. There are a lot of names thrown at us without any sort of explanation at the beggining, and it takes about 20% or 30% of the book to really understand what they all mean and to stop mistaking them for one another. But in a way, I don't think that's so bad, because if the author had chosen to do pages and pages of infodumping it would've messed with the perfectly set pace of the novel. So yeah, it's confusing, but just bear with it and you'll get the gist of it! My main issue with this book was that, by the time I was finished, it felt like I'd just read the prequel to a series. The main goal of this book is to set the story for the second one, and a lot of important questions weren't truly explained... Why does everyone hate the Nomatsis? Why do the other nations hate Nubrevna so much to the point where they'd gather together in order to really fuck them up? What's going on with the whole Cahr Awen/wells thing, when did they dry up? What's up with Aeduan's father and how did Leopold know about him? I'm fairly sure all of those will be answered in the following books, but it would've been nice to have a little more information to go on in this one. At the end, a lot has happened, but it doesn't feel like we know much more than we did at page one. The characters were great, even the ones that I didn't like very much. My favorite was Iseult, from the start. She is the rational, calculating one, a contrast to Safi's brash, short temper, and a very interesting character to read about, given her different background as a Nomatsi and the way she was forced to learn certain manners growing up because of her being a Threadwitch (even if she's not that good at that). Safi, at times, felt like a little special snowflake; Iseult was her opposite, the "normal" girl, and yet she had so much depth and character! Safi was our other protagonist (technically, both boys are main characters, but the girls were more heavily featured throughout the book so to me, they were the MCs), and it took me a while to really like her. Like I said, there was a bit of a special snowflake syndrome going on -- she was the only Truthwitch born in God knows how many years, she had such a special power, she was so beautiful and yet, she didn't know it! -- but because of the Iseult cared for her, and because of how much she was willing to sacrifice to save Iseult, she ended up growing on me. Another thing that I liked about Safiya was how she didn't make excuses for her behaviour. She was selfish and impulsive, and that led to getting her and Iseult in trouble; it would've been far to easy for her to wallow in self-pity, finding excuses for herself, but she recognizes her selfishness, and she doesn't try to sugarcoat it with bullshit. She owns up to her actions, and that's is such a rare thing to see in YA fiction! The boys, prince Merik and Aeduan, were also pretty interesting. I thought Merik was a little bland; he only seemed to get more interesting when Safi was around, which also irked me a bit, because it sounded too much like an instalove thing. I guess it's not instalove if they're bonded by Hearththreads? But then again, what if you're bonded to someone and you don't want to be? That's another concept Dennard could explore further on in the series, because I don't like how final Hearththreads seem to be so far? Aeduan, on the other hand, was an amazing antagonist. Clearly in the game for himself from the start, he revealed hidden traits and characteristics (and secrets!!) that I absolutely loved. He was definitely one of my favorites, along with Iz, and I kept looking forward to reading more chapters about them. So, to wrap this up, this book does live up to the hype. Although it failed to be a 5-star read to me, because of the couple of things that were slightly annoying, I can definitely understand why so many others would enjoy it more. At the end of the day, it's one of those it's-not-you-it's-me situations. I think that what's more important is that, despite its flaws,  Truthwitch was a very entertaining read that kept me engrossed for days, and that's what truly matters, in the end. Definitely worth checking this one out :)

Overall: 3 Stars Writing: 5 Stars Execution: 2 Stars Characters: 1 Star - Being generous Haven't we all wished we could go back in our individual lives and do it over until we get it right? This is the premise of Kate Atkinson's Life After Life with a twist. Ursula Todd keeps living, dying, living, and dying over and over. The first 100 pages were jerky in my opinion. Ms. Atkinson used short chapters and constantly drifted to different times and different lives of Ursula - the shorter her life, the shorter the chapter. It took me several hours and re-reading paragraphs to realize, I was in a different incarnation of Ursula. This made it hard to know Ursula, herself. And each life she has was sad and depressing. A few were down right vile, in my opinion. When she was raped at sixteen and underwent an illegal abortion. Or the life in which she married a misogamist and a misogynist who murdered her. Atkinson also spent too much time with Argyl Road. I just wanted Anything to happen! Let Ursula die or live, just get her out of this loop! I have to admit that I threw the book on the floor several times during this part of the book. And when Ursula finally past this time in her life, I just didn't care any more - I just wanted to finish the book. I still can't figure out which life she was supposed to live. The ending didn't help me to figure out which was Ursula's true life. And she even questions a scene, wondering if it was real. The idea of reincarnation is interesting and I loved the premise. I just didn't like the execution of it. The book could have been 75 - 100 pages shorter and the "plot" wouldn't have suffered; maybe I could have cared about Ursula more than I did. The secondary characters Pamela and Teddy seemed underdeveloped, also. And this I found odd, since her siblings played some important roles in some of her incarnations, especially in some of her major decisions. I thought the names Ursula and Teddy were wonderfully symbolic - both bears: Hibernation and Reincarnation. The writing was excellent, but I can't get beyond the execution and the lack of character development here in this novel. I feel slightly cheated that I wasted 5 days on this novel.

Annie dreams of things she should have no knowledge of, Antietam, Chancellorsville,and Gettysburg. Her dreams are horrifyingly real. Her psychiatrist believes Annie is hiding something deep in her subconsciousness. His former roommate sees it differently. He works as a historical researcher for a writer of Civil War novels. His employer is writing about Lincoln's dreams. Annie is having Robert E. Lee's dreams. Lee is restless even in death. He cannot sleep. Annie is helping him rest. Can she survive it? Willis writes gracefully of responsibility, guilt and redemption. "Lincoln's Dreams" won the John W. Campbell Memorial award for best novel in 1988.

He's growing up, though, which is nice. Part of the half star off was the revelation that Joey was in love with Ryan Dean , which I thought was kind of unnecessary because it would not have changed much if they had just been friends. Originally posted at The Secret Life of a Bookworm Copy received from Goodreads First Reads & MyKindaBook It felt like I'd been waiting forever for this book to come out. I was so desperate to to find out what was going to happen in this last book and if Helen & Lucas would ever find out the truth! So after the ending of Dreamless the Gods have been released from Olympus and are wreaking havoc. It's up to Helen to find a way to re-imprison them before they start a war. Helen was fantastic in this book. After the end of the previous book, Helen gained some extra powers and became a very powerful Scion. She was powerful and dangerous. She became a completely different person in this book, and the reason for that is revealed during the book. She was unsure of her feelings towards Orion and Lucas. She knew she shouldn't care for Lucas, but she really loves him. Lucas is just, amazing. Seriously, I love him so much. He's always trying to protect Helen and he cares deeply for her even though he shouldn't. He's just such a sweetheart. I really love Orion as well. I knew that he and Helen definitely wouldn't work because there was already someone else who loved him deeply, he just couldn't see it yet. He helped Cassandra a lot during this book. He's such a caring guy. Trust Hector to fall in love with a girl who hates him because of his face... I felt so bad for him in that moment because he genuinely liked Andy, but because he looks exactly like Apollo, Andy was terrified of him. But it all worked out in the end. I enjoyed the journey we were taken on in this one. Hades was trying to coach Helen because she's a worldbuilder and eventually she'd create a world and Zeus and the other Gods would come for her. Everyone was trying to work out who the Tyrant was (it was pretty obvious in my opinion who it was). Matt was acting weird and it turned out he was a massive part of the storyline. I learned a lot more about Orion's childhood and I felt so bad for him because he couldn't be with his mother or father. The ending was spectacular. I cried like 3 times. The first time I cried I was in shock because I just couldn't believe that had happened! I was so annoyed that Josephine Angelini had done that to one of my favourite characters that I couldn't imagine this series without! And then the second time was Lucas' decision! I mean... WHAT THE HELL, LUCAS?! Did you not even think about talking to Helen? That thought didn't cross your mind before you went off behind everyone's backs and made such a stupid decision?! Apparently it didn't. And the last time I cried was because I was so happy for Lucas and Helen. They've been through so much and Helen's bitch of a mother finally came clean. I was so glad that they finally got their happy ending (even if Lucas' decision will ruin it one day). Overall, this was a fantastic ending to the Starcrossed series. It was jam packed full of action and twists and I loved every second of it. Thank you Josephine Angelini for writing such an amazing series.

3.5 rating. This was a tough read for me. And I can't say that I enjoyed it. But I respect its place in classic literature and as a challenge for a reader, such as myself, that has a hard time with symbolism in story telling. I want to know exactly what the author meant! It makes me crazy to know that there is a swirling mist of grey area STILL by the end of the book! I realized early on, that this was not written to be taken at face value. I still struggled with the circular arguments regarding a trial and legal system that were never actually specified. Arguments to do with a symbolic "something" make my stomach turn, which may have been Kafka's intention. I read somewhere that he likened this book to or at least admired Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment and this book did give me the same feelings of unease and claustrophobia. I have come to the conclusion that Josef K. was putting himself on trial. The ravings about never being let off the hook and finding a reprieve only to be taken up again sound very much like a troubled person's emotional roller coaster. All of the people that were supposedly watching or spying on him and holding him in judgement could account for the character's self-consciousness and guilt. Bottom line: I'm glad I read it. I'm glad it's over.

That doesn't mean you absolutely have to, but if you are planning on reading the Grisha trilogy anyway, if it's on your TBR, I suggest you wait before picking up SoC. If you don't care about ever reading the main series (not judging or anything, but what's wrong with you? ), then please go ahead and start reading SoC right now. With that said. I absolutely loved this book. I had never read a heist novel before and I'm also not a fan of heist or criminal movies or TV series in general. That's the second reason for me not picking this up sooner. I wasn't expecting to love the plot because of this. I knew I would probably end up liking the characters but I thought that was going to be it. Boy was I wrong! I loved the plot! It was so intense and there were so many parts that had me on the edge of my seat like "That's it, they're done". I did not anticipate any of the twists and turns and I was flabbergasted every single time. There was just no guarantee that anyone was going to be safe and I had a hard time putting the book down for futile things like, you know, sleep or real life commitments. But like with any other book I end up loving and giving 5 stars to, the real highlight for me was the amazing cast of characters. The multiple-PoV structure was perfect to really get to know our characters with their backstory and their motives. We got only five different PoVs out of the six members of our crew, the only one missing being Wylan's, and there wasn't one PoV that wasn't interesting or one chapter that didn't add something to the character's story and personality. Each character comes from a different place on the world map and that way we get to see different belief systems and traditions (some of which we already knew a bit about from the Grisha Trilogy). Now one little thing that I think is worth mentioning is that I had to constantly remind myself that these were all teenagers. That's kind of true for any YA fantasy novel where the protagonists are doing all kind of badassery, but I can still see them as teenagers because there's usually something in their traits or mentality that still feels a little immature. This was not the case here: they all (with the exception of Wylan and, in a way, Inej) felt older. I mean like, in their thirties. I don't know if this is necessarily the author's fault, and ultimately it doesn't have a negative effect on my reading experience, and to be honest they all have their reasons to be way more mature than any of us real-world people at their age, so I don't think it should affect my rating. Now before moving on to talk a little bit more on the single characters, I want to mention that before starting reading this I went and found Bardugo's Six of Crows Spotify playlist and listened the hell out of it while reading. I don't normally listen to music while reading, especially if it's not instrumental-only, but I had the feeling that I would have needed to have some soundtrack. I don't even know why, but I can honestly say that I enjoyed it immensely. It fit so well the whole book and the single characters and I feel like I should mention it here in my review. I will write down some songs that I found fit specific characters so if you want you can go and find them if you're interested. (Songs that fit the whole feeling of the book: "Sinister kid" by The Black Keys, "Gangsta" by tUnE-yArDs, "Kiss off" by Violent Femmes, "What you do to me" by Blakroc) Kaz (Songs: "DLZ" by TV On the Radio; "Waiting room" by Fugazi) "There was no part of him that was not broken, that had not healed wrong, and there was no part of him that was not stronger or having been broken." Kaz is in a way our protagonist, although they're all main characters. He's the most mysterious of the bunch and it takes some time before getting to know his backstory, which I found absolutely heartbreaking. There is no way you're not going to fall in love with him when you read this book. Inej (Song: "Pedestrian at best" by Courtney Barnett) "She was the Wraith -the only law that applied to her was gravity, and some days she defied that, too." I loved her so much. She is such a strong, wise character and her past is also very dramatic. She is Suli and that offered us some insight on that particular region's belief system, which I found interesting, and she often gets in arguments with Kaz because of this. Nina (Song: "City in dust" by Siouxsie and the Banshees) She was probably my favorite character. She is a Grisha that was trained in the Second Army in Ravka and she drops some hints on some of the secondary characters from the Grisha Trilogy. What I loved most about her was how confident she was with her body and herself. She's described as being not-your-usual-super-thin girl and she's just perfect. Also worth mentioning is her friendship with Inej: finally a really positively portrayed female friendship!!! They genuinely care about each other and there's no jealousy between them, but only support. Their interactions were just lovely and I wish every female friendship in the YA world were like theirs. Matthias (Song: "Let her go" by Passenger) He was such an interesting character! He comes from Fjerda which is where the heist takes place. He's new to the group and has to earn their trust as well as start trusting them. It was rather frustrating to read how backwards his mentality was, and it really makes you think about similar situations in our world. "The life you live, the hate you feel -it's poison. I can drink it no longer." Jesper (Songs: "The guns of Brixton" by The Clash; "Please don't tell my lover" by Empires) He's the sharpshooter of the group, and his guns are his babies. Also, he has a gambling problem and I'm pretty sure he's an adrenaline junkie: "He gave himself a shake. What was he thinking? He needed a dose of imminent peril to get his head straight." I feel like we didn't get to know him as well as the other characters, he's our one-liner as well as being hopelessly romantic: "Maybe I liked your stupid face." Wylan He's the youngest of them all and his is also the only PoV we don't get to see, although there are reasons for that. Even so, I loved him, he's just so cute and so extremely smart. He saved the day more than once, usually by making things explode. He's also new to the group and was the object of Jesper's mockery and flirt. The romance: There's three ships in here and I'm on board all of them. There's not one I favor more than the other and I need them all to sail. Kaz and Inej: I can't wait for these two to get together! I love how Inej understood Kaz and his fears (even though she doesn't know his backstory) and she has too much respect for him and for herself to expect or demand something when it's clear it can't happen yet. Nina and Matthias: I have a thing for the hate-to-love and the killer-to-lover trope and this ship was so satisfying in every way. I'm not sure if we can call this ship as already sailed, but it's definitely the most mature of the three. Jesper and Wylan: theirs is the least mature ship as of now, but I'm completely rooting for it. They're just perfect together and I hope Wylan gets his face back, but I hope even if that doesn't happen Jesper will accept him anyway. Who would enjoy this book? Honestly, I think everybody! There's one element for every kind of reader, whether you're into romance or heavy character-development or action-packed novels.

3.5 stars After reading Co-Wrecker by Meghan Quinn, which I adored (my review can be found here), I couldn't wait to read her next book. I really liked her style of writing. Her quick witted dialogues, fast paced plots, and wonderful characters. Tucker Jameson and Emma Marks were no strangers to me. Both were supporting characters in Co-Wrecker. Emma was the best friend and Tucker the boyfriend that was left behind after the breakup. Honestly, when I realized what the storyline was about and that Tucker was going to be the hero, I wasn't sure how I would feel about it. He went through a traumatic event with Sadie and after the breakup I had the feeling he was collateral damage. Sadie moved on and Tucker stopped living. In My Best Friend's Ex he still had a hard time letting go of the past. It felt like he took all of his emotions and his true self, locked it away and threw away the key. He put on a show, but stopped living a long time ago. He went to work and slept, and that on repeat. I truly felt for him. What he went through I wouldn't wish on anyone, but the way he dealt with it didn't help with enamoring him towards me. I didn't particular connect with Emma either. Some of her actions didn't sit well with me. Even so they've been friends for a long time, I thought they were more acquaintances than friends. Of course living together changed that very quickly, I still didn't feel the chemistry or attraction that was described. I was definitely bummed that My Best Friend's Ex didn't work for me the same way Co-Wrecker did. But all in all, My Best Friend's Ex had it's cute and funny moments, and Tucker would have been an amazing and hot character - I swoon over guys that do physical labor, they are just so yummy and down to earth - except for his tendency to keep things locked up - like a fault. Otherwise Meghan Quinn did a fabulous job in writing a quick and fast paced novel. And since I really like her writing style I'm definitely looking forward reading more by her. Well, I really enjoyed this book, much more than I was expecting to. I'd read the prologue a while ago and the style threw me off a bit, so I'd put it aside, but this time I got sucked into it and read the entire book within a few days (the rest of the book isn't quite so literary and fable-like as the prologue). The story was very well-written, the characters are layered and complex, and the crime to be solved is engaging and suspenseful. Plus, it's set in and around Dublin, Ireland, which I loved being transported back to! I really appreciate that it wasn't strictly a detective story--and in fact, readers expecting a clean, tidy ending might very well be disappointed in this book--but it also dealt with themes like the fluidity of memory, the loss of innocence, and the tipping points that can unravel friendships. There was one detail that drove me crazy How did no one know about Rob's past?! Does the Murder Squad not do background checks on their detectives?!? I find that insanely hard to believe. and I had to knock a half-star for that since it was a thread throughout the whole story. But in many ways, the book is about much more than solving crimes, and I think the characters, relationships, and themes were handled beautifully. Particularly, there was something really special about the friendship between Rob and Cassie. If you like friendship stories, less-than-likeable main characters, and/or crime stories that aren't necessarily wrapped up in a pretty bow, I'd definitely check this one out. 4.5 stars.

"They say it's good to let your grudges go, but I don't know, I'm quite fond of my grudge. I tend it like a little pet." Liane Moriarty is quickly becoming one of my favorite authors. Her style is almost like Gyllian Flynn meets Sophie Kinsella, striking a perfect balance between witty humor, thoughtful commentary, and an edgy mystery. This is the story of three women--Madeline, Celeste, and Jane--who are initially connected by their children being in the same kindergarten class, but then by so much more. All three women's voices were distinct and fresh, and I found myself fully invested in each one. There are multiple mysteries wrapped up in this delicious little book: which parent is murdered at Trivia Night? Whodunit and why? Who is Ziggy's father and how is he connected to the happenings at Pirriwee Beach? And that ending. Brilliant! It was unexpected, surprising, and just so so good. I did not see the Perry White=Saxon Banks  twist coming! At first I was a little overwhelmed by the Shakespearean chorus of parents, which is interjected throughout, but once I realized I didn't need to keep track of all the names I was able to relax and enjoy the creative storytelling technique. Overall this was a wonderful book that peeled back the layers of a seemingly perfect suburban family. Can't wait for the film adaptation!

I read this awhile back and originally gave it a 4 star review. For the life of me I dont know why i gave it that added star. Maybe my reading experience has matured and grown a bit since i last read this book. But once i picked it up again, i saw some glaring things that had me a bit miffed: First, i didn't like the fact Brock was TOO Alpha male. Now, i love a good Alpha male like any other girl but the difference between a controlling prick and an Alpha male is the simple little thing called consideration. Sure he ACTS like he's putting the heroine, Tess's, opinions and well being first but after awhile you realize he's always getting his way and he always has the last say. He does what he wants, he makes her do and feel what he wants, and he could give a shit how it may or may not affect the heroine. I didn't like that. I didn't like that he acted caring but in reality he was just controlling. He was manipulative and over the top and i greatly disliked it. Second, i really didn't like how easily Tess let's him get away with shit. He says some (kinda) pretty things and flashes his butt a little and he's forgiven. There's no real big "fight", everything is resolved so neatly and so quickly that it felt unnatural and unnecessary to me. Why even fight if its just gonna last a fucking page? I wanted her to get ANGRY at him. But she didn't. She just threw a quick fit and then went on with her life. Especially when the book first begins. I felt that had the author shown those 4 months of them being together i would have felt more for the hero/heroine but instead its cut out, leaving me apathetic to Brock's "betrayal" and then subsequently skeptical that she was angry at him for the following three months. I didn't know or care about their relationship at that point to even understand how easily she could forgive him for lying to her about everything in the first place. I didn't see her slowly trust him and fall for him or vise versa. It's just BAM betrayal and the author just expects me to be okay with it. From there a bunch of annoying shit started to pop up but i'll honestly admit it was probably just being nitpicky about it. Like the fact that(like most Kirsten Ashley books) the hero would use his anger at some tiny thing that happened to beat down the heroine's anger at something huge and substantial, minimizing it so that she feels bad about being angry in the first place. A sort of "how DARE you be angry at this huge betrayal when you said that thing in passing 3 months ago????" I didn't know how i felt about that. I didnt. Is this how men feel when i woman brings up something they did way back in the day? But i digress. In the end i DID like this book to a degree and it WAS good, solid read. It had very few mistakes (i still had my old epub version so its probably been cleaned up since then) and was a complete and interesting story overall.

I find it hard to give an overall review / impression of "The Well of Ascension". The first half of the book is a totally different read than the second part. Maybe I should just review each of them separately. The First Half (3.25 stars) When comparing this book to the previous one in the series I notice a similar theme going on. Where the first book focuses on an oppressed, abused people trying to overthrow the tyrants that rule them, using some elaborate "ocean's eleven"-scheme - and the same light hearted humor used in said movie, the second book focuses for the most part on what is supposed to happen next, something that you probably wouldn't think about when you put the first book down (What I call the "Hollywood"-effect, or the "They-all-live-happily-ever-after"-effect). What do you do when you've overthrown your tyrants? The only life you have ever known, the only stability you ever had? True, your life was shit before, but at least you knew the shit you were in, you knew what to expect out of life. Now that you're left without a ruler, how do you move forward? What do you do, when your newly founded, idealistic, democratic, ... government is put under pressure by other neighboring tyrants who want to move into the current power vacuum to claim your life for themselves? This theme makes these books more a "political" read then anything else. Not that this is a bad thing, but it certainly wasn't what I had expected. What struck me though, was that in "The Last Empire" this theme was a thin red wire, running throughout an action packed, plot-twisting story with a lighthearted, almost cynical, kind of humor (coming mostly from the crew members and their stance to one another). In "The Well of Ascension" on the other hand, the thin red wire is replaced by a big fat red boat-rope. The theme is almost constantly front and center resulting in long philosophical dialog that discusses the pro's and cons of running a democracy as opposed to living under a single autocratic ruler. While I personally find these trains of though very interesting, I can't help but wish that the pace would just pick up a bit, stir some more action into the story. The occasional action scene just isn't enough to interrupt the constant pondering. Strangely enough, the book still manages to intrigue just enough to keep me invested and I haven't felt the urge to put it down. I find myself being far more drawn to the story-arc of Vin than that of Elend. Although, admittedly, Vin's constant self-loathing is getting quite repetitive and I have a much easier time to identify myself with the character of Elend and his struggles. I guess that I like Vin's arc a lot more because it appeals to the fantasy aspect of the story and NOT the political side. Overall, I liked it, but there are numerous ways this could have been improved in my opinion. General observations Where the previous book also put question marks on the religious side of a nation ruled by a god-king, the religious aspect isn't really addressed in the second part. I wonder why this is so left out? Why on earth does Sanderson constantly use the same sentence construction over and over again: - [character name] paused - it gets really repetitive over time - "bla blah", [character name] said, "bleh blaaah bleeeh" - seriously, in a conversion between two people it is NOT necessary to indicate on every sentence who is saying it, your readers aren't complete idiots that they can't figure out how a conversation works. Just using quote marks or simple indentation would do just fine. If you must insist on mentioning this in every other line of dialog, can you please use some variation in stead of constantly using the characters name? e.g he/she said (gender) / the terrisman / the kandra said (race) The Second Half (4.75 stars) The second half of the book makes me glad that I stuck through the first half. It's a constant tense, action-packed rollercoaster that has only a few brief stops for you to catch your breath. I finished it over a weekend. A lot of questions are raised, a lot are answered, and yet, when the book ends you still have questions, but just enough feeling of satisfaction that it doesn't matter. It just makes you want to jump into the last part as soon as possible. Vin finally gets over herself and starts kicking ass, so does Elend btw, which makes both characters a lot more loveable. There are some tragic moments and I felt a personal loss as some of the characters died. Especially Sazed's grief felt very real to me. . Overall, the story made a lot of sense and again I appreciate the fact that it doesn't end with "they all lived happily ever after". There is drama and there is joy, but both are in balance. The addition of several big plot twists made was very enjoyable and therefor I give the second part 4.75 stars. On average I'll rate this 4 stars, I'm inclined to rate higher, but that's just because the book ends with such a rush, that I feel like forgetting the first part entirely in favor of the second. But let's try to give a realistic rating here.

Rating: 3/5 (I received a free ecopy from the publisher, HarperFire, via Netgalley in exchange for an honest review) ***Minor spoilers*** Integrity Taylor had always been judged based on her father's actions. She is a Sidhe (Faerie, basically) and was raised awfully by a man known to the Sidhe as the bull, simply because her father was apparently a bad person. When Integrity was young, she fled from the Sidhe and a man named Taylor picked her up and introduced her to a life of thievery, which Integrity relished in being good at. Unfortunately for the Sidhe, they need Integrity. The magic is failing, and with Integrity being the last in the Adair family, a family needed to save the magic, they must get her to help them. The Sidhe have Integrity's friends arrested and Taylor threatened, and Integrity has no choice but to help the people she ran from all those years ago. This book was better than I expected it to be. While I did read it to use for a challenge, the cover is what caught my eye. While a pretty cover certainly doesn't make a good book, it definitely helps to catch my attention. I enjoy reading different takes on Fey, because everyone seems to have unique ways of writing them. As the author mentions, this was an Irish/Gaelic take on Fey, which is why the word Fey/Faerie isn't used. At first I thought Integrity was a strange name, but I got over it later. She didn't even have a name until she fled from the Sidhe, so I think she deserves to have whatever name she wants. I found the first 40% or so of the book to be quite boring, but it did serve its purpose for world-building. After that, things got more interesting but it wasn't too amazing. There were some cool dynamics that I would like to see more of if I ever get access to the second book. What bothered me most was some things just didn't make sense. You were forced to accept them and move on, which is one of my least favourite things to have to do for a fantasy book. I like things to be explained for me and have a purpose, but some things in this book happened and there was no reasoning for it. For example, there is a point in the book where they finally find what they are looking for, and somehow Integrity just "knows" how to save the magic by throwing the sphere thing (I can't remember the name) into the ray of light. How did she just know that? Overall, this was an entertaining take on Fey but it wasn't amazing. The writing is a bit iffy in places, and some of the concepts weren't explained very well. Regardless of its faults, I ended up enjoying it in the second half, although I wish it had a stronger ending. It would've been nice to get something suspenseful at the end that would have me scrambling for the next book.
