After reading After the End and being totally surprised at how entertaining it was, I was pretty excited to read the sequel. Not that I had much of a choice; After the End stopped on a cliffhanger and left me with too many unanswered questions. Naturally, I was too curious to pass up reading Until the Beginning... Here are the reasons why I didn't like this book as much as the first: While I thought the romance that gradually built between Juneau and Miles was sweet, I missed the dynamic of the first book. In the first book, what made their dynamic so entertaining was the fact that Miles believed that Juneau was crazy and delusional, and Juneau thought that Miles was unobservant and dimwitted. In this book, that dynamic was replaced by something that was a lot less entertaining: two kids that were falling in love and working toward the same goal. While it was just a natural progression of two people as their relationship moved from friends to more than friends, it made for a much less fun read. Some of the magic from the first book was lost in the second because of this. This book, with exception of the way it began, was way too similar to the first. Juneau and Miles are driving cross-country while dodging the people that are hunting Juneau. They are camping, trying to access the powers of the Yara, searching for Juneau's clan, trying to find answers...  Then Juneau is captured... again... She's confronted by Miles' dad... again... He reveals pieces of his hidden agenda... again...   I just kept getting dejavu in this book because everything that happened in it had pretty much already happened before. The big confrontation...  the battle... it was just confusing and slow. I didn't enjoy it. Maybe it was just a matter of personal taste... I don't know. But I felt like it took too long for all the conflict to blow up, then there was this huge build up of a battle where blood would be shed and people would die... according to Tallie's prophesy. And then once it all started, it didn't seem all that big of a deal. Everything just seemed too convenient and easy. Why were Miles and Juneau able to have full-blown conversations as there was a battle happening? How did the clan really escape that easily after having been held captive for months? And Miles' dad just left? Just like that, he gave up? I don't really get it... This Yara/Gaia thing got a little too trippy for me to enjoy... And is it a thing or isn't it? Was it the drugs? Was it magic? Was it divine intervention? I still don't know... Maybe I'm just being extra picky here, but I feel like this is a classic case of two books that should have only been one. I think that honestly would have solved a lot of my issues here. There just didn't seem to be enough new conflict to make two books.
Such a sweet book and a great ending  which was obvious, but surprised me anyway! :)  . It was such an enjoyable read, I started re-reading it right away.

First, I LOVE THE CHARACTERS. I follow Maggie Stiefvater's tumblr and really enjoy her posts, and I'm a fan of how she is "all about the characters". Because her characters are so well written. Ronan carried the story for me (and I'm assuming, for many other readers), he's fierce and dangerous, but also complex in his interactions and love for Gansey, Adam, and Noah. Kavinsky was an interesting one, I felt I wanted a bit more from his character as he often felt like a one-dimensional foil for Ronan. Mr. Gray was delightfully mysterious as well. The characters were written beautifully, Stiefvater really knows how to choose the perfect words to show, not tell, the truth behind her characters. Through actions instead of spelling it out for readers, we come to understand their motives, desires, fears, and beliefs. As expected, writing was great. Stiefvater-esque, which is pretty much in a category of its own. It's sharp, evocative, and fluid. Can I insert a joke about chapter 56? Okay, so what didn't work? The plot. This is a bit frustrating because I really couldn't care less about Glendower/Cabeswater. The dreams stuff was interesting, but the Welsh King stuff was just a pain to trudge through before we get back to the interactions between characters-- which is what I cared about. Like, I WANT to continue this series because I heartily adore the characters, but I hate the fact that I don't give a damn about what is essentially the overarching story to this entire series. I'm not sure of it it's just boring to me, or I no matter how clearly it's spelled out, the stakes just don't seem very high (they don't. Whatever Adam was doing at the end there, I just didn't care)... it's just a big apathatic sigh from me. In summary: loved the characters, loved the writing. Incredibly apathetic (to a point where I am angry about my apathetic reaction) about the plot. So you get what you wanted, Stiefvater, I have very strong emotions, except the caveat is that I'm experiencing both ends of the spectrum simultaneously.

Inferno is even better than Vendetta. Catherine Doyle achieved the impossible. It is even more dangerous and intense. I totally loved it. Inferno was full of crazy plot twists. The two major plot twists, which were  Sophie being a Marino   and  Sophie falling for Luca  , were really shocking. I couldn't believe what was happening! What made me really sad was the fact that I didn't like Nic anymore. He was wearing a mask. We all thought that he was sweet and kind but in reality he was a liar and manipulative. He may be a good character but he has many negatives. My opinion about Luca changed a lot and I am so surprised! I didn't expected it at all! In the previous book I didn't like him at all and now I have hope about him and Sophie. It was really surprising. I hope Mafiosa is as good as Inferno and Vendetta.

And so the Hollows series ends on a rather good note. This last installment circles around Rachel finding a way for the vampires to retain their soul, keep Landon from ruining the Ever After and magic as we know it, and deal with the crazy Elven Goddess who still wants our heroine dead. We have some semblance of the original trio that made the Hallows fun, meaning Rache, Ivy, and Jenks. There is plenty of action containing those three as they fight their way through all the plots. Initially Cormel is a big butt face and takes to attempting to off Ivy so that Rache will hurry up and find a way for the undead to keep their soul when they die. There is a lot of vampire drama in this one and it really wasn't all that bad or boring. However, I seriously got tired of all the weepy eyed hugging and what not. That seemed a bit much to me but maybe I am just an emotionally stunted robot. Surprisingly Landon is still alive.... ? I thought he had died in the last book while on the train and Rache did some sort of spell explosion but perhaps that was just wishful thinking on my part. Unfortunately that little elven douchbag is back and causing trouble for everyone! He want's the elves to rein supreme with power and still wants to get rid of the undead and anyone else who can stand up to them, like the demons. That little cookie maker just hates demons! Lastly, Rache is basically just caught in a clusterfuck of problems and has to figure it all out while dodging the psycho goddess. She has to learn how to get the vamps to keep their soulsIt is learned quickly that the surface demons in the Ever After are the souls of the undead vampires. Apparently it was the demons that made the vampires but it was the elves who decided to be even more cruel and strip their souls from them and hide them in the demon world when they died , and how to keep the keebler elf from destroying the lines all while avoiding the violet eyed mystics! Luckily our heroine has a nice safety net of friends because if she had to do it on her own she would be dead. Lets face it, Rachel is kinda pathetic by herself. When she is not making goo goo eyes at Trent and swooning over his features and how he sits with one ankle over his knee, she can get some stuff done but never makes it far without help. Queue in my favorite character ever, Al! I just adore Al! I am so glad he is back! He surprisingly and bitterly at times helps the gang kick booty and come out victorious! By far my favorite characters in this whole series has to be Al, Newt, and Kisten but we all know what happened to that last character, may he rip. After reading the last book I was upset with the fact that Rachel and Al were not going to happen because I really felt that it could have worked and it would have been great! I am glad Rachel ended up with Trent though. They are good for each other and it does work with Al being more like a saucy mentor. I do still feel that he would jump Rachel in a heart beat. There is supposedly no romantic feelings between the two but I think there could be.... Either that or I am just a rabid Al fangirl and want him to get some action! Ivy finds happiness, true happiness with her beloved NinaDuring the last encounter with Landon, Nina is critically hurt and dies in the ambulance on the way to the hospital. Ivy can't find it in her heart to kill her twice so she sucks up her soul into a bottle that will keeps it safe as opposed to going into the Ever After. Rachel later then ties Nina's soul into Ivy because she is alive and can hold it safely with love. No one knows what will happen to their souls once Ivy dies the first time but I would like to think that they go to their final resting place and be at peace . She is also the bigwig at the I.S. so that is pretty awesome! Go Ivy! Jenks is super and happy as a pestering grand daddy. Trent and Rachel are doing okay though they never married. She refused to be Mrs. Kalamack so that he could build his empire back up and lead the Dewar/enclave and help keep the peace. Towards the end things shift. After 27 years Trent wants the relationship to go his way and in doing so will change elf and demon history forever and for the better. Rachel never accepted Trent's proposals for marriage because there is a stupid rule governed by the enclave that no marriage can be blessed if the woman is barren, blah blah blah. Which is a stupid rule but it basically means that since Rachel and Trent are opposing species they can't have kids. However, since little Ray is all grown up and getting married to a demon named Keric, Trent and Al did some research and testing for three years and found a way for it to work! For the two species to have kids together! It's really quite bittersweet if you ask me. Al wanted that so bad when he was with Ceri but couldn't find a way for it to happen. Then we have Rachel who likes kids but never had the opportunity to have them until now and the fact that they only started looking into it as a gift to Ray just rubs me the wrong way. Eh... I'd like to think that Trent kept Rachel in mind as well as he wants another baby and that would be the only way for that to happen. Seems to me like he had ulterior motives if you know what I mean! Time to rev the baby maker! Let us hope that it will also help with Rachel's poor self confidence. The whole doubting herself and self worth all the time got really really old. There are some thing I am left pondering after reading this. What happened to David and the other weres? Does Jenks ever get visited by his kids? What was with the coffee shop constantly being an area of activity? Was that a joke among the book editors or something? What happened to the chrysalis? What even was the fascination with blue butterflies? What about that big bad ass group that came in one of the earlier books and scared the heck out of everyone? I would think they would have made an entrance at some point in the last book or this one but no. What of that crazy scientist lady from HAPA anyways? Why the heck did Al's long gone wife Celfnnah make the vampire curse? What drove her to make such a tormented curse? And lastly why the heck did Newt kill all the female demons? I still have no idea! In the later books the demons became less menacing and Newt became awesome so I still don't know what would prompt her to do that at all. Oh! And didn't Newt say that the goddess was a real person and that she was killed or something? How does she know that and did she have a fling with the goddess? I know they hate each other now but I am confused on many points! When all is said and done I am mostly happy with how things turned out, even if I am left hanging on some points. All the main stuff that mattered got an ending. The series as a whole I sometimes felt was stretched out for far too long but Miss Harrison wrapped up it all up nicely and I am left feeling content.

I honestly felt torn about reading the follow-up to "Bad Romeo". This was because I was left unimpressed with the hero of the story, Ethan. In the first installment, Ethan puts Cassie through the wringer and it was difficult for me to process his logic behind treating her so callously. What I found fantastic about "Broken Juliet" was how the author was able to give us an in-depth peek into Ethan's multifaceted mind which then completely changed my entire opinion. Ethan's characters was complicated and complex which made the series more interesting. He had so many issues in the beginning I thought he shouldn't have been in a relationship in the first place. When he was able to conquer his personal demons and open up to Cassie completely this is when we finally experience the extend of his feelings. I thought it was fascinating to see that beneath all those layers that he infact have a vulnerable side. "Do you feel this? This is what makes us keep coming back, despite everything we've gone through. This is why I have to change, and why despite how much I hurt you, you can't walk away. The way we sink into each other. The way I can't tell my heartbeat from yours. We have this perfect rhythm, whenever we're together, and that's the essence of us.." There were so many things about this book that kept me glued to my seat and immensely enraptured. First, was my need to find out why Ethan had a change of heart. It was always as if Cassie was far more into the relationship than Ethan. What was the turning point that made him want to become a better person for her? This time around his reasoning behind all his actions were legitimate. I can say that I was 100% satisfied with how he came to his senses. I was also eager to see how Cassie changed. She was what I would have consider weak then but as the story progressed she became the one with all the power and boy did she exploit it to the MAX. This wasn't the only think that made her amazing. I admired her for her strength and even her forgiveness. Every single time Ethan broke her down she was able to pick herself up again (of course with the help with her crude but terrific friends) and become so much more. What was beyond captivating was witnessing this all-consuming "plove" - passion and love so toxic it will drive you insane. It literally gave me goose bumps! I can not tell you how impressed I was with how the writer was able to transcribe these intense emotions into writing. Nor can I compliment her enough on how detailed she described this couples chemistry . I loved that despite having a relationship that destructive that their hearts were always in the right place. Bottom line is, "Broken Juliet" was an outstanding romance. A read that I would certainly recommend for those looking for well delivered, powerful and oh so potent second chance romance. liezelsbookblog.net

But I do solemnly swear that I am up to... good on Goodreads. ;) This is a fair and honest review of this book. Pinky promise.

I wonder what I'd have thought if I read this a decade and a half earlier. The idea of a tesseract isn't exactly new to me anymore (and just look at popular films like Interstellar now), but for a kid I'd imagine it'd be eye-opening... as are a lot of other developments in this book. It's a great read for anyone young and looking to expand their imagination. That said: - I found the characters not really all that believable, especially Calvin; at least you could get away with calling Meg and Charles precocious or something even though that's still stretching things a bit. - The explicit references to Christian ideas and quotes from the Bible felt out of place; they often got mentioned in passing without much in the way of reflection or commentary in the context of the actual story, so I found them hard to appreciate here even if I might actually agree with them. Just what are they doing here? - The final resolution was a bit too predictable. I know it's a children's book, but still, given all of the other scientific and philosophical ideas going on, finishing it all with some love wins-deus ex machina combo  is really disappointing... although ironically fitting with the narrative's tone. Basically some fascinating ideas at play, but I'm not so sure about their execution or if I should be giving it all a pass given the target audience. But honestly, I think children's lit can do (and has done) better.

1Q84 is a long, intricately-plotted novel set in a slightly-altered reality. This is the first Haruki Murakami I've read, although I've long figured that he writes the sort of cool slipstreamy fiction that I usually like. And I did like this and enjoyed the process of reading it. But I don't think I loved it. By the end I was left wondering what it really added up to, apart from an impressive stylistic workout. There are two main flaws. First, the central love affair between Aomame and Tengo is more an outline for a romance than an actual one. We're constantly being told how deep and pure their love for one another is, but since they spend basically the entire book separated from each other, we really have to take the author's word for it. I guess your reaction will depend on how romantic you find the idea of "destiny" and (moon-crossed?) lovers separated for decades. To be fair the eventual reunion (when it finally happens) does make up for it somewhat. Second, the central mystery of the Little People and the air chrysalis is really too obscure and sketchily drawn to inspire much of a reaction. It's really not entirely clear what Murakami's elaborate mythology is trying to say other than advancing the plot forward. He's clearly referencing Orwell's Big Brother, but to what end? If I had to hazard a guess, I would say that the sarin gas attacks carried out in 1995 by the Aum Shinrikyo cult left a big impression on Murakami. His non-fiction book, Underground, deals with the aftermath of the attacks, and the group clearly serves as a model for the Akebono and Sakigake cults found in 1Q84. In this reading, the Little People are a kind of an ancient, anarchic, destructive force that is periodically loosed in the world, but you don't really get that sense from actually reading the book. Their actions and motives and consequences are not really made clear in the course of the plot. Some reviewers have complained that the book is slow and repetitive, but I didn't find that to be such a problem. In certain passages Murakami achieves a kind of perfectly hypnotic and transparent clarity that the book almost seems to read itself. The ascetic personalities of Tengo and Aomame are well-adapted to this voice, but his writing style is so pervasive that it even sometimes spills over into the voices of minor characters like Ayumi, which can lead to some jarring moments. Still, a decent effort, and I do feel intrigued enough to check out some more Murakami in the future.

When I 1st started I wasn't sure I was going to enjoy this but the more I got into it I really liked it. At a very young age Prince Adam survived a horrific event that takes everything from him and left him angry, bitter and trustful of no one. He spends his life locked away from the world. Isabelle Rose is a loyal and loving daughter who cares for her ailing father. It is because of the love she has for her father she puts up with her no good, selfish step-sisters and she is betrothed to the arrogant and wicked Raphael who believes he owns her. Isabelle and her father believe that the annual merchant's fair is a way out, a way to get far away from all of the bad around them and start a new life together. But, on their way to the fair a sudden storm causes them to seek shelter. They come across and dark and eerie castle and with no other choice they must stop and ask for shelter from the storm. A tall cloaked man answers the door and attempts to turn them away but Isabelle will not take no for an answer. The man allows them to enter, the event that started it all and changed their lives forever! I liked how Rachel Demeter twisted the tale but did not destroy what makes it so beautiful!

It was alright. The book goes back and forth between our two main characters and it was clear a quarter of the way into the book that  Amy wasn't dead. There was just no way that she could have been actually killed by Nick even though some of the narrative made you wonder, it was clear that he wasn't actually a killer. The characters are both a bit rough, callous, and somewhat insane. This is a dark story that has a somewhat predictable ending when you are in the last few chapters. As a reader I was beginning to attempt to over think as much as Amy did. You could tell that she was going to blame Desi and that she was going to get pregnant with Nick's baby in the end so that she could get what she wanted all along. I don't know that I would really recommend this book to anyone but if you like dark thrillers it might be for you. Also if you don't mind a whole lot of foul language. That would be one of my bigger complaints about the book there are a whole lot of mean four letter words used to describe women and bitch is a very common word in this book.

** spoiler alert ** UPDATE 15 AUGUST 2017 I just finished this, and will have a full review tonight! 11 August 2017 MIDWAY RANT CHAPTERS 1-21 This is exactly what it claims to be: a rant. It is loosely organized and will one day transform into a review when I actually finish this book. For now, it's thoughts, notes, and general commentary (you get it) INITIAL PROS *	The "threads" and how they bind everyone is one of the reasons this reminds me so much of the mythologies. The threads are like auras, changing colors with mood or intent, and some witches, like Iseult and Safiya, can read them. These 'threadsisters' are reminiscent of the Fates, each sensing something different from the threads floating through the people around them. One particular bit I like about the threads is that neither Iseult nor Safiya can read the threads of people with which they are familiar with - example Iseult cannot read her mother's threads, but she can read the local priest's. *	[ref page 20] "...in waves that could pummel a dolphin." - I always enjoy anything that makes dolphins look bad (they are horrible) Not to mention, these two idiot girls are about to jump off a cliff into water that is LITERALLY SO INTENSE THAT A FUCKING FISH-MAMMAL MIGHT HAVE A METAPHORICAL PROBLEM IN IT. *	[ref page 164] This is the exact exchange I have been waiting for the entire time, to be completely honest. I went back-and-forth in my mind with whether or not this relationship/dynamic was something I could agree with, and the more and more I think about it (and let's be serious, this is me we are talking about) I am all for a Aeduan+Iseult situation. After this chapter concludes, these two are bound by a life debt (one of two: Aeduan also has a very mysterious life debt with another woman, and I hope this is elaborated on later). Also, it is during this altercation that Aeduan realizes he cannot sense Iseult's blood (how very Edward and Bella of them), but Iseult doesn't give a heck about Aeduan. They literally fall, tangled, through the sky, and somehow he manages to get under her to save her from CRASHING AND DYING... hmm why would he do that? I figure: he knows he will heal, and this isn't how he wants to take her out. He craves the chase and he gets a smashing one with Iseult. Anyhow, she stabs him right in the ticker before getting carried away to relative safety. At first I was in a panic. I didn't know if Aeduan had it in him to heal after (cough - he was previously mortally-if-he-was-mortal wounded by multiple arrows) falling from such a great height and then being impaled right in the heart. How savage is Iseult though, right? INITIAL CONS *	I am not a huge fan of the incessant use of the word 'witchery' as a synonym to the oft-used words of YA Fantasy like 'magic', 'ability', or 'power', and for some reason, the first few chapters had an overwhelming amount of 'witchery' going on. *	You may have to read this twice, just to make sure you read it correctly: I felt this began somewhat slow. Yes, the very first line refers to the Threadsisters getting out of trouble, but it was also a lot of running back-and-forth between the northern area of Cartorra and the southern port. It wasn't until the lighthouse scene that things began to pick up, followed quickly by the argument between Merik + Safiya on his vessel. CHARACTERS Iseult I think it's already been established that Iseult is an intense creature. As Safiya's threadwitch, Iseult is the ying to her best friends yang, and there isn't a place these two sass queens go that they won't get into trouble. Safiya fon Hasstrel Safiya reminds me of Helen of Troy, in that she is a Domna of Cartorra and she has just been willingly kidnapped by Merik; escaping a betrothal all the while secretly falling for him. CLASSIC HELEN. *	[ref pg 141] Safiya is in a stable attempting to steal a horse. She is still on the run from Aeduan, and the interaction with the stableboy proves that she is still the ruthless, knife-wielding, witch we met at the beginning. She might just kill this boy in order to secure transport out of town and escape the Bloodwitch. *	The relationship between Merik + Safiya is complicated at best. Her loyalties will always lie with Iseult, but their banter is contagious, and at times almost quite literally killer: Safiya is abovedeck after being scolded by Evrane, and an already upset Merik finds her. In short, a fight ensues. They are both wicked to each other, but like the four-step they danced, this match is no less sensual, especially when Merik flips on top of her: *	[ref pg 210] "He chuckled roughly and dipped his mouth toward her ear. His nose grazed down her cheek. 'Even without my winds,' he whispered, 'you would lose.'" AND THEN THE TEASE JUMPS UP + ORDERS HER TO BE CHAINED. Why does he sort of remind me of Tamlin right now? Merik Nihar If Safiya is Helen of Troy, then the Prince of Nubrevna and Admiral of the Nubrevnan Navy is certainly synonymous with Paris. Charming, delectable, and I bet a fabulous kisser, Merik is a cinnamon roll for sure. BUT he does get a little toasty here and there. BUT ALSO it's a bit awkward reading about a character named 'Merik', as my father's shortened name is 'Mirek' pronounced the same way, so yeah there's that. *	[ref page 44] This scene at the Doge's dinner shows Merik knows how to have a good time and joke about, and is a bit of a trickster and troublemaker himself. The clearly more charismatic and mischievous 'Prince' side is what Safiya originally saw, so later when she sees the stern 'Admiral', you would think that she would back down, BUT HECK NO. Safiya will take her blades to anyone. *	He does have an alarming and questionable temper. What will happen when he pops, I wonder? He is acting like a Big Bad Baby Wolf, LITERALLY HUFFING AND PUFFING HIS WAY AROUND TOWN [ref page 43] "With a sharp, rasping inhale, he drew the air in the room to himself. Then he huffed it out." Aeduan The Bloodwitch who is basically being added to my book harem this very second (because you know I'm trash for villain baes). He is tasked with tracking down the Truthwitch, who he believes is only Iseult at first? Until he see Safiya later on? But he is literally blood thirsty for Iseult. He is definitely my kind of villain, too. He enjoys the slow chase and tracks Iseult through Venaza City until he can't follow her any more. She crosses the now impassable canal, but from the opposite bank HE FUCKING SMIRKS AND WIGGLES HIS GODS DAMNED PHALANGES AT HER IN A WAVE. I think I fell in love with him right then. *	Plus, everything is nothing but an inconvenience to him: [ref page 13] "Aeduan allowed just the slightest fear to spike through him, Flames...bothered him." THEY JUST BOTHERED HIM Y'ALL. NO BIG DEAL, Comorant? Corlant? The Priest from the Nomatsi settlement Can you tell I'm not a fan of this man? He peeves me, but I'm also curious as heck about him. He is a type of Voidwitch, I believe, and he has the ability to suck the thread energy of those around him, and he has managed to manipulate Iseult's tribe into giving him command. I'm interested to see if he comes up more and just more about him in general, I suppose. Canon Love Interests Safiya + Merik: I am on board with this ship, or as I like to call them bakes (because reasons I won't get into here). Either way, there is some spark between these two and I want them to be a thing already. Non-Canon, Only In My Head Ships Iseult + Aeduan: I can't be certain whether or not I am for this or not, but now that it's in my head, it's staying there. If this becomes a thing I will be HAPPY Y'ALL. Miscellaneous Notes Borrows elements from: *	The Odyssey/The Iliad - Safiya is similar to Helen of Troy, making Merik the Paris figure. The multitudinous witches in this universe are similar to the various gods/goddess and minor deities the Greeks and Romans worshipped. *	The Grisha Trilogy - On that same strain as the mythological standpoint, this is also reminiscent of The Grishaverse, in the sense that each variation of witch has his/her own ability. Like the Heartrenders of Ravka, some witches, like Evrane, and Merik, can control the elements and manipulate their respective specialty to their will. Notes on the Map This universe is a squished replica of Europe and the Mediterranean region + Venaza City is between what could be the Greco-Roman peninsulas, Marstok being relative to Ottoman Empire, Nubrevna relative to Greece, Cartorra relative to Italy/Spain (large empire)

This is the 3rd book in the Beyond Series and I love the world that has been built in these books. We see a bit more of it in this book as it continues where the 2nd left off. Sector Three comes into play as Bren is asked to start getting things under control over there as the O'Kanes took over at the end of the last book. This book focuses mainly on the relationship of Bren and Six. Six was taken in by the O'Kanes in the 2nd book and it was quickly discovered she had been terribly abused. Bren was the one she latched on to and she only felt safe when he was with her. Soon he gets her complete trust but she is still fragile and it won't take much to break her heart. Both Bren and Six have a lot of baggage coming into this relationship and both are really possessive. Its difficult to be monogamous in a setting where everyone is so free with their sexuality but they manage to do just that. Overall I liked the book and love the world that is created here. As were are introduced to new characters I wondered if we would come to know more of them in books to come. An awesome series for those over 18 that enjoy dystopias as well. Can't wait til the next book in this series!

It was another fast pace book, much like the previous one. Perhaps even more brutal in the first section. Several chapter went by and it was just the first day. The reviewer who gave this book one star had made many valid points, some I disagree; Cormel's behavior was counted as severe desperation and that clouded his rationalities. Rachel was able to bested Cormel only because of the mystics. As the reviewer kept saying how useless Rachel was, I was thinking back to the first book. I felt that Rachel was never exceptionally powerful to begin with. She was, I supposed, a mid-level witch, from then on she was thrown in sink or swim situations times and times again that she had to learn to embrace her potentials or be killed. I think that reviewer forgot that Rachel was more of a lynch pin. She maybe the character who was the center of series but she was never the one with all the answers and powers. I do skim some parts because Rachel's constantly insecurities about her being with Trent was tiresome when it wasn't moving the plot along. Granted she had some legitimate concerns since her track records wasn't great in anyway shape or form. For what it was the author had manage to find ways to warp up all the loose ends. Again, a lot of the stories was mostly about how people knew the solutions and only let Rachel knew when push comes to shove. Warm Bodies was much better than I had anticipated it to be. When I first heard about it, I didn't really have much of an interest in it because I'm not that big on paranormal stories, but it has so many great reviews that I figured I'd give it a chance--I'm really glad I did. The book started off slightly awkward, I wasn't quite sure where it was going, but I wasn't exactly willing to give up reading it either. Once R meets Julie, however, it was a lot more intense. I hadn't expected that amount of suspense in the book (although it really only last a couple of pages, I still really enjoyed what was there. The ending, though, while expected, played out in a way that I hadn't expected it to. Overall, it was a really good book (as long as you see it more as a romance novel than a post-apocalyptic book). The beginning of the novel was, I felt, necessary, but not particularly enjoying to read. It established the universe that the story's based in, but lacked life in the way it was written. However, once you read through the whole novel, it is actually quite amazing. The book progressed through this lackluster life to this slow blooming to sunshine and brightness and I felt that it represented how R progressed through the novel quite amazingly. When R first meets Julie and devours her boyfriend, that was probably the part that got me hooked onto the book. I love that R is now experiencing all these feelings and how he breaks his syllable record (I felt that was a nice touch to keep in there) each day. The relationship between R and Julie is unorthodox because he's Dead and she's Living but it works in a way that is perfect. M (or perhaps I should say Marcus now) and Nora were really good secondary characters. Perhaps they were slightly cliched in the way that they were portrayed, but I felt that it worked nicely. The ending though, I was not expected that. I remember reading it and thinking, No, there's twenty pages left and it hasn't been resolved yet. What's going to happen? and when the resolution did come, it didn't happen how I was expecting it to play out. I'm not sure what I was expecting, maybe it was some half-alive-half-dead kind of thing, but it definitely wasn't R coming back to life. I think, in part, it was because R coming back to life seemed a little too... obvious for me. It was as if, Yay, he comes back to life! Happily ever after! but that isn't how it's working out. The world's still healing and I just felt like there should have been a bit more to reflect that. I do concede that that plot point is redeemed when R and Julie end up having that conversation about the future.

Sigh... I'm kind of disappointed in this one. Not completely distraught but not absolutely thrilled either. There were a lot of interesting gears turning but it just never got to ignition. I just wish it had been put together better. I found the writing to be pretty good in general but I just didn't really care for the story. I found several things to be entirely unrealistic. Mind you, most of the story takes place in a land called Algid where magic is a real thing. Even with that being the case, there were unrealistic things. For example, in the beginning Snow is in an insane asylum. However, she's been in there for 10 years because of one thing she did when she was 6 and sometimes she has a bad temper. THAT'S IT. What? I'm pretty sure they don't lock up children for their whole lives and drug them constantly for one incident where no one even got killed. Also, she never goes to school there. Snow even says there's no school and everything she knows comes from reading the encyclopedias in the library. HOW DOES SHE EVEN KNOW HOW TO READ IF SHE'S NEVER BEEN TO SCHOOL AND NO ONE TEACHES HER ANYTHING!? I could go on and on but I'll just stop there. On the bright side, one thing I actually did like was how Snow described all the different drugs she had to take by naming them after the seven dwarfs. I think the main issue here was that Snow is a genuinely insufferable character. She's just one of the most self-absorbed characters I've even seen. The whole time, the people of Algid are begging her to help them (because she's the special snowflake prophesied chosen one of course) and she's just like "O so the King is evil and kills people... Too bad! Sucks to be you! Now why don't you help me find my boyfriend and get out of here? O and I'm going to be super ungrateful the whole time too. Sound cool?" What an asshole! Why would anyone attempt to help you when you won't do anything in return for them? It's utter narcissism. The whole reason her mind starts to change and she kind of cares about Algid is because she meets her twin sister. It literally took someone who has her exact same face to get her to care about Algid. The narcissism level here is off the charts! Then she like has a romance with literally every guy she meets. Girl... aren't you there to find and save your boyfriend? I understand that she's been in an asylum and all so there weren't really a lot of options in romantic interests before now. But still... EVERY boy? Why do they even like her? It's entirely unfathomable to me. I'm willing to put up with quite a bit if I really like the characters. The problem is that I downright loathe Snow. She's just so terrible of a person/character that I don't think I would really bother to continue on with the second book whenever it comes out. Which is really unfortunate because I think this was well written enough to get me to stick with it if I had actually liked the heroine.

Cute, but kind of dull. I bet the movie was better.

3.5 stars. Okay, so here is the thing about The Nest. I liked it. I did. Except, I didn't love it, which I kind of expected to. The entire time I was reading, I was enjoying myself, and the glimpses into the lives of the Plumb children and some of the people they came into contact with, but I kept just expecting more. Part of me was thinking, the entire time, this is good, but when does it get GREAT? I really did enjoy (for lack of a better term) the dysfunction of the Plumb family -- the cold mother, the narcissist, the timid overachiever, the once-successful writer, the imposter...they were interesting and very flawed, and felt real. I think what I loved most about the Plumb siblings was how little they seemed to know about one another. These were people who grew up together, were raised by the same two parents, and lived near enough to one another even as adults, and yet they knew very little about what was really going on in one another's lives. It made me think about my own siblings, and of the secret lives they have that I know nothing about. I found it interesting to think about the secrets that we keep, and who we keep them from, and why. While I found the Plumbs interesting, I didn't find any of them particularly likable. I actually found myself gravitating more toward the peripheral characters in the story, and Stephanie in particular. I really liked Stephanie. I'd read a whole book about her I think. I just thought she was cool, and interesting because she was this super smart woman who had known Leo long enough to know what she was getting herself into. And even when things turned out differently than expected with him, she rolled with it. She was a strong woman, and his turning out to be unreliable wasn't going to derail her life or her plans. I loved her for that, and for forging ahead with her relationship with his siblings by the end. While I did enjoy those side characters and stories, though, I found myself wondering at times why they were so necessary. Admittedly, I think they all did pay off in the end -- Paul, the twins, Matilda and Vinnie, Tommy--but it seemed like a lot of build up and detail for a payoff that wasn't that mind-blowing, and sort of resolved itself very quickly? That's not to say I didn't like these characters -- for the most part I did -- but these sections often felt like short stories thrown in that tied in just enough to the main story that they seemed relevant. For example, I did love the pieces of the book about Melody's twins, when they blew off their SAT prep, and  when Nora finds herself falling in love with Simone. I found Nora's account of their time together sweet and sexy and very honest  . I actually think the strength of some of the perspectives that come through from people who are NOT the Plumb siblings themselves to be my favorite parts, and maybe that's why I'm conflicted about the book as a whole. I loved the small glimpse or two we got of how Walt felt about Melody and their family and financial situation. And the section towards the end where Walker talks about Jack revealing all of the things he has kept from him, and he has the sudden realization that this is not the life he wants, was heartbreaking and true and made me love Walker even more than I already had from his presence earlier in the book  . And maybe that was the point -- getting the perpsective of the people in the lives of the Plumb siblings gave us a better idea about who they each were, the lies they told themselves, the ways in which their own points of view were maybe not reliable or the full picture. Okay, the one thing I have not talked about is Leo. Oh, Leo, Leo....I really think this whole section needs to be spoilery.....Okay, so he's like the biggest, douchiest douche, right? I mean...there were moments where he fooled his siblings into thinking he was going to try and do the honorable thing. And there were moments where I felt like he even fooled me as the reader. But seriously, that man could not face ONE THING IN HIS LIFE, even though all of the things that went wrong were pretty much ENTIRELY HIS FAULT. And his irresponsibility combined with his charm really mind-effed everyone around him. And no one could ever really stay mad at him, because he was Leo! The wonderful, charismatic Leo! Who not only does NOT help his siblings even though he can afford to, thanks to his secret bank account, he just UP AND LEAVES, never to be heard from again. I mean, this guy was really a piece of work. Honestly. And I'm not saying his siblings were all that much more upstanding most of the time, but he really took the cake. I did appreciate how, at the end, everyone's life seemed better with him gone. It was like he was the thing wedging them all apart, and by his disappearing, his family and Stephanie were able to come together, mend, and move forward. The baby he probably never knew about was the best thing he ever did, and helped them heal and be happy  . Okay, so I think I'm coming to the end of this review. And as has happened so many times before, in writing my review I think I've found myself processing my thoughts about the book better than I did while I read it. So maybe it's a 4 star for me? Whatever --I think it's a GREAT book for discussion, because I would love to talk to other people about it and see what they thought of all the characters and the directions the story took. Definitely a worthwhile read.

This book was like a soft drink. It was great the majority of the time... I liked the progression in Eleanor and Park's relationship and it was sweet how they went from referring to each other as 'weird asian kid' or 'weird new girl' and having awkward encounters, to getting to know each other and sharing their interests...but then it fizzled out. I loved Park's family but I don't think enough time was given to Eleanor's family (besides her stepfather) to flesh them out. Eleanor really didn't seem to come in contact with them even though she lived with them. The ending was bittersweet but not at all satisfying. What happened to the rest of Eleanor's family? It's like Eleanor just ran away and they were left to deal with the aftermath (we never know what happened to them, only that Park went to hit Richie). Her postcard to Park was a hopeful touch but then it kind of showed her love for him eclipsed her love for her family...
This was a bit bleak for my taste, though not quite the soul-sucking bleak of something like Gone Girl. There was still a bit of hope, still some good characters. And it was pretty compelling.

This tale of Empress Elisabeth of Austria was kind of an uneven read for me. There were points at which I couldn't help feeling drawn into the story, particularly when Elisabeth ("Sisi") and her family first arrive at the Habsburg court. And because I got drawn into the story at the beginning, I felt deeply for Sisi over some of the early events in her marriage. From the author's note, it sounds as if some of the nightmarish mother-in-law escapades really did happen. However, the overall structure of the story seemed rather choppy. Just as readers get drawn into Sisi's initial meeting of and eventual betrothal to Emperor Franz Joseph, the pace speeds up too dramatically. Sisi settling into her new role as Empress gets short shrift, so it's almost impossible from this book to discern why the Austrian and Hungarian people so passionately adored her. In addition, Sisi's wanderings through Europe, an episode which had a deep impact on her life, gets almost entirely skipped. We see her leave for her journey and we see her return, but readers are left wondering what happened to change her. What we get isn't bad, though since I never warmed up to any of the men in Sisi's life, the romantic portions of the story left me a little cold. Speaking of which, this is definitely historical fiction and not romance. Mention is made of both Sisi and her husband committing adultery. However, I liked Sisi herself and found much of the history surrounding her earlier years quite interesting. Overall, this isn't a bad book, but it's not an amazing one either. Oh, and a note on audience - this book is published by an inspirational imprint, but if I hadn't known that, I would never have guessed that this was supposed to be even lightly inspie. There's no real inspirational content in the book. I don't say that as a positive or a negative, but just a note in case anyone is going into the book expecting something other than historical fiction.

Truthfully, the ending depicted the harsh reality of the word, one that many other authors close their eyes to and prefer not to illustrate. Steinback, however, has managed to create a truly moving story within so few pages. Lennie was a character I sympathized with to a certain degree, and George was someone I looked up to because he had taken on the role of a (somewhat) father-figure without being obliged to do so. However, the moment Candy's old dog was introduced I just connected the dots and figurerd out how the story would end. It was evident that the two were two peas in a pond that would share the same fate. That being said, when Lennie was shot at the back of the head just like the old dog was, it was a bitter-sweet moment for me.

Much as I enjoyed this book, it definitely felt like a sequel to the Mars books, except it lacked the firm grounding in a place and a landscape that made those books such a joy for me. Even the protagonists seemed a bit derived from Mars, Swan just as much an unfortunate stereotype of female emotionality as Maya was, and Wahram an equally stereotypical echo of Sax's stolid rationality (albeit a bit less clueless). That said, I'm not sure one should read KSR for his characters so much as the sense of realism and tempered hope he brings to his settings. I've heard his future fiction described as utopian but I think that's an inaccurate label for the attitude of his futures and this book in particular. Generally, just because the Mars trilogy and 2312 don't quite align with our current obsession with apocalypse doesn't mean they're blithely and unrealistically sunny in their outlook for humanity's future. If anything, 2312 is post-post-apocalyptic, the massive environmental catastrophes of ocean level rise and population-winnowing food shortages having occurred 100+ years prior, with their attendant aftermath. Earth is still pretty crappy, but things are relatively ok in space, and there are signs of terrestrial hope: coastal cities hold on in Venice-like conditions, and Earth still has it together enough to operate several space elevators. Just because horrible things happen doesn't mean everything about the world we know just winks out and we're back to the Stone Age. I like that vision. It's not all going down the crapper, it'll just suck. Sort of like the present. Some scattered thoughts: 1) I love the idea of terrariums and how they become this massive, diversified expression of human creativity. Maybe that's KSR's optimism, though. Realistically you'd think most experiments would end in disaster, something KSR only hints at with references to reactionary cults, prison terrariums, etc. 2) While not as firmly rooted in landscape as the Mars book, I thought the descriptions of Mercury were wonderful. A world of livable darkness, lethal daylight, and black-and-white chiaroscuro twilight where people walk endlessly. Lovely. 3) Somewhat let-down by the whole rise-of-the-machines thing. I feel like this is a well-trodden path and that very little consideration was given to the moral standing of the AIs. A little, to be sure, but that could (should?) have occupied the whole book. 4) Dropping megafauna from space: as fun as this was to imagine, isn't it kind of insane? Let's assume you raise the animals at 1G and that you can somehow safely drop them from space, alive, onto Earth. What do they eat? What about their gut flora? What about their diseases and parasites that keep their populations in check? Have those all been carefully cultivated in the terrariums too? I guess it's one of those shut-up-and-just-grind-your-teeth-you-niggling-biologist-you moments, but I feel like the very notion that this might be possible posits an unrealistically reductionist view of how functional ecosystems operate. 5) Hermaphrodites! I love the word "ursuline"

Definitely the best Perkins I've read yet; this time she managed to get all the pieces into the book at the right intensity. I loved how the problems are organic from who the people are, not because of external events -- it makes it less melodramatic & more realistic. Isla's confusion about herself and where she stood in relationship to Josh as an artist was so, so good -- it is a big thing, entering into relationship with someone who turns their life into art, and it is also a big thing realising that you are connecting to someone who has had an entire life before you, especially if it feels like their life is bigger & richer than yours. And that Isla discovered she could draw on her family for strength, and then we find out Josh did the same, is just so satisfying. Also, I loved that they were lovers and that it was so driven by Isla's desire -- a chance to see the man enthusiastically consenting. Plus all the art and architecture and Isla's totally understandable confusion about where she wants to go with her life and how she loves Josh but doesn't want to just be his appendage. I also loved the chance to see the characters from earlier books & hear how their lives were going.

We are the latest in a long line of strangers. Most of us are acquainted with our parents. Many of us have met at least a subset of our grandparents. But our firsthand knowledge plummets with every generation beyond that. Some of those people in the distance may have left us anecdotes or documents or china collections, but most of them only left us with genes. How many voyagers and conquerors, wearers of shackles and cloth stars, came together to bring about each of us? Could we ever know? Do we want to know? That's a question that Dana, the young black woman at the heart of Kindred, doesn't have the option of saying no to. Through involuntary journeys across a century that mirror her ancestors' involuntary journeys across an ocean, she is sent from her 1976 California home to antebellum Maryland. There, she realizes that she has a single task: save Rufus Weylin. Rufus is the son of a wealthy slave owner. He's also "destined" to have a child with one of the slaves, a child that would grow up to become Dana's ancestor. As Dana is jerked back and forth through time, a pattern emerges: she is sent to Rufus's time to save him when his life is in danger, and is returned to 1976 when her own life is threatened. She walks a tightrope, trying to keep Rufus alive long enough for him to father a child, without getting herself killed, or getting stuck in the 19th century. In the first few pages of the book, Butler's intentions are overt: this is not a book about uncovering the mechanisms of time travel, it's a book about the culture clash between times and places. Accordingly, Dana doesn't experience much bafflement about what's going on, because it's not a bafflement that Butler has any intention of allaying. Instead, Dana immediately latches on to the task that she's been given. That, I thought, was a somewhat unrealistic piece of behavior that served the purpose of getting the main plot going quickly. But once that plot got going, it wouldn't stop. When reading this book at bedtime, I would tell myself that I'd just keep reading until Dana was in a slightly less dangerous position. Each night I'd find myself awake at a more ungodly hour. Life-threatening situations are key to how the story works. They become increasingly menacing with every repetition, and are arranged in a clever cycle of water and fire that I only noticed days after I had finished the book. I often found myself trying to find little quotes to post here. Surprisingly, it was hard to do; the writing doesn't stand out because of glowing one-liners, but because of the light that bounces off one character to the next, illuminating as much as it covers in shadow. It's not a lyrical style of writing, but a spare and efficient one that I ultimately came to be grateful for. One doesn't necessarily wish to wax poetic while setting a broken bone. As I hurried up the steps, I thought of Rufus and his father, of Rufus becoming his father. It would happen some day, in at least one way. In addition to simply keeping Rufus alive through his numerous accidents and fights, Dana also wants to instill in Rufus a much-needed sense of compassion and justice; this often puts Dana in a position of opposition to Rufus's rigid and brutal father. They both leave their mark on him, although perhaps not the type of mark that either intended; he develops the devious nature endemic to the offspring of strict parents, combined with just enough open-mindedness to keep a twinge of Dana's hopes alive. Dana's position as a time traveler has many fascinating aspects, but one that I found especially striking was the way people in the past regard her as a supernatural healer - due to possession of aspirin and some basic medical knowledge from the 20th century. Rufus's father has this to say about her: "You're something different. You come out of nowhere and go back into nowhere. But you can feel pain - and you can die. Remember that and do your job. Take care of your master." It immediately reminded me of this quote from The Green Mile: "Because it's what he does. It's what God made him for," regarding John Coffey's healing abilities. There's a similar undercurrent of white characters viewing "supernatural" black characters simply as things to be used, but Kindred puts the emphasis on the fact that this apparently God-sent healer is a human in their own right. Finally, the relationship between Dana and her husband Kevin, who is white, undergoes a transformation, especially after Kevin is taken along on one of her trips. Kevin at first seems like a lazy, wishy-washy character, but eventually earned my respect through the loyalty that he demonstrates - although it's apparent that truly understanding Dana's experiences will be something that he'll have to work at over the course of his life.

I'm happy that they are all alive, don't get me wrong, but at the same time I feel like it would have added that extra piece of emotion to the story. Also, forever hate that dying-but-getting-back-to-life-trope and it happens TWICE. - The overly perfect characters and all the sappy scenes. All those 'you will bow for no one, you can make your own choices' yadieyadieya situations. It got on my nerves. Also, can we please stop those random head-conversations between Rhys and Feyre? It is rude to do so in public when you can simply use your mouth. Also, not every conversation has to be flirty/sexual. They don't all have to contain 'feasting on you' and 'have the need to feel you in me' - Still hate what she did with Tamlin's character. He is turned into such a big villain and it's ridiculous how Feyre ruins his court from the inside out, destroying an army that could have been beneficial in the end battle. Like.. how did you think this was a good idea to punish someone who, in the end, was broken and loved her TOO much for their own good? His love was definitely poisonous, but it just feels so over the top. - All. Those. Sex. Scenes. She should have called it 'A Court of Sex and Purring' because holy shit, there was a lot of them. This book could be cut in half if you leave those scenes out and most of them made me cringe. I get it, you are hungry beasts and all you can think about is 'ravishing' each other all the time, but you don't have to repeat it over and over again. - WE KNOW THAT YOU ARE MATES. WE KNOW IT. THERE IS NO QUESTION ABOUT IT. -What the fuck was her father doing on that ship, suddenly acting like a hero? Many different parties come looking around and it was definitely intense. I liked that Elain was the one to deliver the first strike on the King. Also forever sad about the Suriel, because he was such an interesting character. + Did I mention NESTA? + The writing-style is so fast and entertaining. There are many parts that doesn't add something special and the editing could have used some fine-tuning, but I always fly through her books. It was again one of those stories I couldn't lay down. Sue me. I liked it.

This is one of the books that has most affected my life. It has inspired me, it has taught me, and it has given me a glimpse of the human spirit. It is just beautiful. I wept over it. One of my favorite books of all time. ~2017 re-read~ THIS BOOK: O_O I found myself reduced to a quivering mass of humanity, drowning in tears and sobs last night as I finished it. Markus Zusak hit upon and incredibly zany, but creative way to approach this story from the perspective of death. Who would have though that it could be so amazing? THE CHARACTERS: the characters are marvelous. The way we are given such a beautiful and intimate view into the glorious souls of these humans is almost unparalleled. Hans: The man with Silver eyes of Kindness. Rosa: The Wardrobe woman who swears like a sailor, and loves with an ginormous heart. Liesel: The Book Thief and the Word Shaker Max: *sobs* The Jewish fist-fighter who stole the sky. Rudy: The boy with a heart of gold and hair like lemons. And a huge cast and a myriad of other character whose hearts are bared to the reader. THE WRITING: The word pictures in this book make it so fresh, interesting, and even humorous. The words in this book are glorious, pilling on top of eachother, wrapping around eachother and morphing into a vision in my head. Without describing things in the mundane details of the average book, everything is perfectly visible to the minds eye. THE STORY: It reads almost like an autobiography at times. There is no way when you are done that you wouldn't think that the story was real. And quite possibly, it could have been. There was so much research, reality, and even experiences that went into making this book as amazing as it was. The authors relatives were actually witness of WW2 and he used their experiences, as well as numerous others to write the book. It was a fascinating and emotional snapshot of the times. THE QUOTES: A small but noteworthy note: I've seen so many young men over the years who think they're running at othe young men. They are not. They're running at me. Five hundred souls. I carried them in my fingers, like suitcases. Or, I'd throw them over my shoulder. It was only the children I carried in my arms. Max lifted his head, with great sorrow and great astonishment. "They were stars," he said. "they burned my eyes." I have hated the words, and I have loved them. And I hope I have made them right. IN CONLUSION: This book remains a treasured piece on my bookshelf. One word of caution. There was a fair amount of profanity and swearing throughout the book. I took the liberty of editing the swears out for my own and siblings future enjoyment. But if you want to read the most amazing book ever written about WW2, you must read this book! * does contain  quite a fair bit of language (which I was not okay with) and lots of really dark things including death in many gruesome ways)

Plus, there is the confusion that David/Prodigy brings to the mix, with his surprise kisses and all. Oh, and we can't forget Billy's twin, Tommy, who has been maybe-kidnapped? Or vaporized? Of course, I'm not the one in peril.

3.5 stars I am a bit conflicted on how I feel about Lisa Kleypas' first historical romance after a 5 year hiatus. Story: Devon unexpectedly becomes an Earl after the passing of his cousin Theo. The title comes with an estate that is improvished and in the reds. He intends to sell it and enjoy the blunt. While visiting the estate he meets Theo's beautiful widow Kathleen and Theo's 3 sisters. It wasn't a story I couldn't put down. In fact in the middle of reading this book I started and finished another story before coming back to it. The writing is on-point and has LK's sharp and witty remarks and one liners, but it lacked something for me. The biggest issue was that I didn't like Kathleen, our heroine. She started off strong; she had a harsh childhood and she obviously felt when she spoke of how her husband had died. But as the story progress she became such a meddling over-critical shrew. She complains when Devon has to sacrifice 4 tenants' land so the estate can be profitable thus saving the other 200 tenants. She harps on Devon when he tries to set up one of the sisters, Helen, with a merchant friend of Devon's - before even asking Helen's opinion on if she would welcome the suit and despite the fact that Helen has no dowry and therefore little prospect marrying a peer. She later meddles again in this courtship without asking Helen. From the above, Kathleen comes across as out of touch with reality, overbearing and someone you just cannot please. Her wish to adhere to all of society's rules on proper behaviour bugs me too. Her most charming interactions seem to be with Devon's brother West. After Devon catching her in the storm, their sizzle seems to only be physical and the other times they spend together they spend arguing. As Devon once hinted during an argument with her, I can't imagine anyone wishing to spend the rest of their lives with her. Devon while not the nicest guy to start with he was at least fun to read about. And later he had his redeeming moment with taking on his responsibilities and his heroic behavior in the train incident, but I couldn't grasp what he loved about Kathleen. It all happened suddenly. And, after that  near death experience and what he said to himself as well as to her , you would think he realizes how he feels. But nope they continue on, and argue some more before breaking out their "I love yous". I was more intrigued by the secondary romance than Devon and Kathleen's. Unfortunately Helen and Rhys Winterbourne's story seems to be left for her next book Marrying Winterbourne  (to be published May 2016 -so I have to wait half a year). Cold-Hearted Rake includes an awesome excerpt from Marrying Winterbourne. I thoroughly look forward to reading more of Rhys and I am hoping this will be the book I waited 5 years for instead. I do think that it will be unfair to readers picking that book up without reading this book first since so much happens in Cold Hearted Rake. They would miss Helen nursing Rhys and the orchid gift piece of the puzzle. So there you have it. LK writes well and there were many sharp witty lines that kept me reading, some really good scenes but this ended up kind of lukewarm for me.

My first attempt at a book review! First of all, I want to preface this by saying that I came into the book prepared for greatness. I read I Am the Messenger a few years back, and was blown away by Zusak's intense and poignant voice--it takes a certain kind of beautiful soul to make the most mundane moment seem like magic. Since then, Zusak has remained near the forefront of my mind because of John Green's hearty testament "Markus Zusak is the most attractive YA writer." I can't say I disagree. All in all, I give The Book Thief 4 sobfests out of 5, because the perpetual survivor trope has been fumbled with for centuries and nothing particularly creative came out of this book on that point. One star is purely for my intense love of Rudy. The other three we can appoint to style, plot, and character. The Book Thief is one of those rare novels that leaves you feeling both full and empty. The happy in-between moments (like making a snowman in the basement and Frau Hermann leaving cookies for her intruders) make your chest swell and glow--but just like the bombs left the ribcages of the airplanes and decimated the landscape, making a Holle out of Himmel, your swollen heart is abandoned in a cratered, empty chest. A chest shaped vaguely like the box of an accordion. Something a friend pointed out to me when I suggested that Death had a crush on Rudy: "Yeah, but I like to think that Death is in love with Liesel and Rudy is a self-insert caricature embodying everything that Death loves about humanity." The idea kind of blew me away and I want to immediately reread it with that in mind. Kind of makes "One day, Liesel, you'll be dying to kiss me" even more of a punchline, eh? Said friend is also deeply of the belief that Max and Liesel were NOT married and lived happily ever after, but rather were soulmates of a different kind. I find myself agreeing. Romantic love is not the only kind of love, and I don't think that sexual relationships borne out of tragedy are usually the healthiest kind. But they were certainly meant for each other; Max pulled the words out of Liesel the same way she pushed life into him, and I like to think that they always did afterwards, too.

This book was 80% what I always wanted this series to be, totally hitting the series stride where the rules and the geography are comfortable, and the characters are familiar enough (and so awesome) that you can see how they're changing and guess what they're not saying. The other 20% felt like tidying up some things that had to be dealt with eventually, so why not now (ahem, Connor and Gillian) . No complaints about the plotting, the stakes, the new characters introduced, or the development of existing ones (and wow, it's rare that I don't have a gripe about one of those). I also really appreciated that Toby actually consumed some food and got some sleep.
