Oh man this book is awesome. I know some think it a bit dry since our astronaut Mark Watney explains what he has to do in order to survive and just how much physics and math is behind his calculations, but you're never made to feel dumb. It's actually nice that the book treats you like a rational being capable of understanding science while also entertaining you for hours. "I guess you could call it a "failure", but I prefer the term "learning experience"." I'd love if we were taught physics and math in school in a sort of space exploration project: "You've just killed your astronaut, Matty - go do that calculation again." It would feel far more useful than the usual dry way we were taught. Oh, and the professor wouldn't treat girls as incapable of understanding this stuff - women have always contributed to science, it's not my fault men buried this fact. So I loved that the commander Lewis was a strong woman and that other women on the crew contributed just as much as everyone else. In fact, there are quite a lot of amazing characters in this book. (And a fellow LOTR fan or two as well.) :D Mark Watney is my favourite, of course, and his exploits with faulty equipment, mishaps, and even catastrophic events are an inspiration to all people who feel overwhelmed with their everyday life. You just have to turn big problems into manageable chunks and tackle one at a time. It's what he does and slowly but surely he finds a way to live through another day. He may have a killer of a time when nothing works right and may even despair at ever figuring out how to solve a problem, but he always picks himself up. Of course it helps he's got a killer sense of humour which is why the book is so entertaining to read. Yes, it's a giant adventure on a foreign planet but it's so much more than that. "Actually, I was the very lowest ranked member of the crew. I would only be "in command" if I were the only remaining person." What do you know? I'm in command." The majority of the novel is told from Watney's point of view and is structured as a log report where he sometimes explains in detail what he's done and what he plans to do. Being alone, talking to himself soon becomes a habit keeping him alive and kicking. It is also his way of making sure he is never forgotten in case he doesn't make it. Soon though, as time goes by, it becomes his way of working through problems, of joking and even having imaginary conversations with his crew-members. It's almost like a podcast or a vlog. There are also reports that consist of only one sentence succinctly summing up his feelings thereby cracking you up. This is definitely one of those books, you know - written for the 'I need something positive and funny in my life right now' moments. In that way the movie has captured the spirit of the book. But it has also changed a lot of stuff in the ending and cut out a ton of material in between. Novel Watney has to struggle so much harder and deal with so much more shit than the movie version. The novel also has more believable scenarios than the Hollywood production, but that's what we all suspected anyway. "Yes, of course duct tape works in a near-vacuum. Duct tape works anywhere. Duct tape is magic and should be worshiped." There are also chapters from NASA's point of view where it jumps between people working there. You clearly see the connections between them, the different dynamic. Watney works alone and is in turn more and more self-reliant. NASA scientists and personnel have to follow rules, observe social niceties. Watney just says what he thinks; he gives a shit about political correctness or abstaining from profanity when the situation calls for it. "Me: "This is obviously a clog. How about I take it apart and check the internal tubing?" NASA: (after five hours of deliberation) "No. You'll fuck it up and die." So I took it apart." The novel moves away from the beginning format of daily entries and propels you right into the centre of action, easily switching between Watney's crew, NASA, and him. You won't be able to let go of the book at that point. Even if you saw the movie, the events differ so much by the time you reach the middle part of the book that things still surprise you. Oh, the people who read it first must have had such a wonderful experience! The underlying message of the book is summed up by Watney himself. He may be stranded on Mars but he knows he is not alone, not truly. "If a hiker gets lost in the mountains, people will coordinate a search. If a train crashes, people will line up to give blood. If an earthquake levels a city, people all over the world will send emergency supplies. This is so fundamentally human that it's found in every culture without exception. Yes, there are assholes who just don't care, but they're massively outnumbered by the people who do." So, read the book and enjoy the adventure. If you are more science inclined, this book is for you as well. Fan of exotic locales? Ditto. And if you ever think you have it bad, read this book to adjust your priorities and get inspired to do better as a person and a human being. The only problem you'll have is finding books of similar quality to devour next. Please, Andy Weir, give us another book!

2015 Reading Challenge: a book with a one-word title I adore the idea of this book. The fact that there really could be a place much like Elsewhere, where everyone ends up after they pass away and get to spend their time aging backwards until they are reborn? I absolutely love that concept. It stands to reason, therefore, that there was a good possibility I'd end up loving this book. But I didn't. In fact, I wish another writer would have thought of this idea and written a book about it. One that maybe would have reached its full potential. Because the thing is...this isn't all that well-written? The book reads more like middle grade than young adult, especially at the beginning. Actually it reads like something in between that tried to be young adult but failed. It's as if whenever something happens in the book, the characters don't actually talk about it. It gets mentioned and then there's no follow-up. I don't really know how to explain it BUT IT'S SO WEIRD. To give an example that I remember clearly because it happened towards the end: Liz decides to use the Sneaker clause and return back to earth early without telling anyone but one friend about it. She writes a note to her grandmother and leaves. But halfway back on her way to Earth, she starts regretting the decision and want to swim back to Elsewhere. The friend she told about leaving, meanwhile, informed her other friends and her grandmother and they all go look for her to see if maybe she changed her mind and is trying to get back. Her friend Owen eventually finds her on his boat and pulls her on board, and then the whole incident is basically not mentioned again. Nobody talks to her to find out why she decided not to go through with it after all, no questions the episode, nothing. In fact, the only time her grandmother makes a reference to it, Liz gives some flippant remark and the subject is dropped again. And the thing is, this is only one example. Things like this happen throughout the entire book and it bothered me to no end. Everything about the story feels so disjointed, and half the book is a succession of "Liz shrugs. "; "Liz shrugs again. "; "Liz nods." Basically, there's a lot of shrugging and nodding going on. The Afterlife, people. It's fun times. And there's many things that are never even touched upon or explored. I just. Why would you come up with a pretty great idea like this and then ruin it? I am really very disappointed. Another reason this didn't work for me, is that for 3/4 of the book, I couldn't stand Liz. I didn't care about her at all. Though I appreciated that she's not your average heroine who is always brave, and fearlessly soldiers on through whatever life (or death, in this case) throws at her. I did like the fact that she needed time to adjust and couldn't just accept everything easily. But despite all of that, she was just too one-dimensional for me. This was not at all helped by the writing, to be honest. It did pick up a little when she meets Owen. I liked Owen a lot, though not enough to redeem this in any way. I am still in love with the concept, though, but this was not at all what I had expected it to be.

Suggested by a co-worker after I had a gripe session about reading a ghastly romance. I truly enjoyed this and chalk it up to another point in her already great track record of book suggestions. It is not heavy on the Romance. It is more that it has a romantic thread in among all the others and each of the other threads were equally interesting. I did feel like some ends were left, if not open, very loosely tied. It wasn't necessary to the ending of the book, but I would have liked to see a couple of areas further developed. I'm not sure, though, if that was deliberate and opening the way for a follow up novel. Loved the time, setting, main character, and storyline. Had a bit of "Gatsby" meets "Downton Abbey" flavor to it. I liked Olivia -I felt like we were just getting to know her and...poof. I think of all the untied ends, that was the one that bothered me the most. I also felt like the romance needed, I dunno, a couple more months to develop. But, it did seem like a good fit for the Characters. Feels like it'd make a great movie.

Delicately crafted, PHANTOM LIMBS by Paula Garner is a beautiful look at grief and loss, at phantom limbs (both people and body parts), friendship, romance, and trying to move on. Otis's voice is so loud and clear with a poetic undertone (heck, they even call him Shakespeare in the book as a nickname because he loves poetry) that I am not surprised this got picked up by Candlewick. Garner has created a truly heart-wrenching book, however I docked one star because the constant "we need to talk" spiel from characters (until they finally did at 89% on the e-reader)  was a little much. I wished they'd talked sooner as the "mystery" sort of lagged on longer than I thought it needed to. I read this on my Kindle courtesy of Netgalley and the publisher and I am SO GLAD I got a chance to read this early!!! If you like Jandy Nelson's I'll Give You The Sun (loss and grief and siblings) and books by Chris Crutcher, I think you will really enjoy this one.

This one left me scratching my head. In all the books there are mentions of Anita going to church or about her religion and how she's not into premarital sex. And then by the end of this book well... All that gets thrown out the window unceremoniously. Talk about loosing all respect for the Main Female Character. Anita is... a different character in this book. She herself thinks about how she's become colder. But it's not just that, she's almost cruel in this book. Heartless. If I hadn't bought the entire series at a library book sale I'd probably stop reading here. She's no longer a character I like or enjoy reading. I find myself eagerly awaiting side characters only to wince or sigh as she treats them rudely. Richard deserves so much more than Anita and I'm not even shocked at how she decided to do Jean-Claude. Choosing him over Richard because she got a little shaken up. She just plain treats people badly and is quite arrogant about it. Someone needs to put her in her place, unfortunately with her being the MC I doubt that will happen any time soon - if ever.

"I wonder if it's possible for people to fall in love with a person one characteristic at a time, or if you fall for the entire person at once." NOTE: This is NOT Sky's story. It's NOT the same as Hopeless. This is NOT just another point of view with the same storyline. It is Holder's story and his alone. I lived through Holder vicariously. I felt his emotions (hurt, anger, self-guilt, hope, resentment) as keenly as I felt my own. This led to a plethora of emotions for me. I didn't know which feelings were my own and which feelings belonged to Holder. I was that absorbed in Losing Hope. I honestly couldn't help it.I loved every single moment. When a book with the potential to blow someone's mind away comes along, consisting of everything I've ever wanted and more, it's hard to not get totally involved. Plus I have been waiting for this book to be released for about six months now. Six. Months. It doesn't seem like a long wait compared to the time that other books take to come out. But still, Hopeless was one of the best books I've read in 2012 and I needed this book to be here a.s.a.p. But it was worth it. It was so f#!king worth it. I think the main reason is because this book is a once-in-a-lifetime type of book. It's been written exceptionally well, but then again, so has other books. It has wonderful characters I could relate to, but like the same issue as before, the same could be said for other novels. Losing Hope might be a YA/NA romance novel, about two people finding each other again but those books are a dime a dozen. I have lost count of the romance books I've seen lined up in rows and rows in book shops. But I digress. The thing that stood out to me the most was the fact that the message conveyed through the pages of Losing Hope was that people don't move on from death and destruction and the like. They suffer and a century will pass and they still will suffer. Nothing has changed except the path that people choose to take. It's very depressing but in it's own way, it's very honest. But these are just my thoughts and I've spoken to a couple other people about this, and only a few of them agree. So it differs for everyone. The other thing that I learnt was that losing hope might be the only way to find it again. And I think that that's just what Dean Holder has been trying to do all this while, even if he didn't know it. "I'm gonna go live my life now, Les. A life I'm actually able to look forward to, and I'd honestly thought I'd never be able to say that. Then again, I'd honestly thought I'd always be hopeless, but I find hope every single day."

I haven't felt this upset about finishing a book or series in a very long time. Upset in the best way. Upset because I found a series that I absolutely adore through and through and it's over. I found characters that were flawed and complex but interesting and brave and selfless. I found a series that was able to bring to life a beautiful, expansive and incredible fantasy world, while still showing the ugly sides of it, too. A series where mental illness and trauma weren't cured, but remained a part of the characters. As something they dealt with every day and worked through. Of angst and war and romance and friendship and family. Of love and hate. I don't know, maybe I'm trying to be too profound in this review. What I mean to say is this: I absolutely freaking loved everything about this, and while this book isn't perfect for everyone - it is perfect to me. So thank you, Sarah.

This review can also be found with my review for Take Me: Twelve Tales of Dark Possession on Goodreads,which is no longer available on Amazon. 3.4/5 stars It was eh. Plot: 5/5 - I love the concept of this mystery a lot. I think knowing that the murders were mirroring the 10 little soldier boys poem was exciting because you had an idea of how the next victim might die but not who it would be or when it might occur. No complaints here, super cool premise. Characters: 2/5 - I get it... there were a lot of characters and points of view to juggle in a relatively short book. BUT STILL. I feel like I could tell you 2-3 things about each character and one of those things would either be how they died or how they killed someone. I probably only know half of their names. I REGULARLY mixed up characters (especially the two female guests... there were only three women on the freaking island and I couldn't keep them straight??) and I should mention that I was listening to the audiobook, with Dan Stevens excellently performing various voices, and that didn't even help me most of the time. I just felt I wasn't given enough about who these characters were as people. I wasn't effected by a single one of their deaths and I'm not saying I expected to cry or anything, I just expected to feel something. Oh, and I totally managed to guess the killer. He was completely leading the manhunt for the killer and so I was like duh, you're making yourself seem trustworthy... I admit faking his own death was pretty clever and it threw me, but ultimately I still guessed who the killer was. Pacing: 4/5 - I think the pacing of the novel was perfect UNTIL the very end. Once everyone was dead the setting changed to two police officers going over all of the events and some possibilities and as a reader I just felt like... yeah bro, I was there. Why are we rehashing this? Then it got even LESS satisfying because we just got an entire detailed confession letter from the killer. There's no fun in that! Instead of allowing us to work things out and put pieces of the puzzle together, we just get a lecture from a long-winded, pompous murderer with every single detail of how and why his plan came together. That was super unsatisfying in my opinion, and I don't read a lot of mysteries so maybe that's commonplace but I honestly thought it was a cheap way to end the story. Writing: 3/5 - It was whatever. I didn't hate the writing, didn't find anything remarkable in it. Solid middle ground. Enjoyment: 3/5 - I was really into the mystery when it started but as it went on and on with little-to-no clues I kind of just resorted to guessing the killer based on personalities and then waited to see if I was right. The way the ending was written probably bumped this down a full star, it really irks me that much. I wouldn't discourage anyone from picking this one up (I mean, it's a classic, isn't it? ), but maybe the miniseries was better? Maybe there are better books of hers out there? I wouldn't know, and now I'm a bit hesitant to see for myself. If anyone has Agatha Christie recommendations leave them in the comments for me lol.

Damon (The Protectors, #1) by Teresa Gabelman I'm all about Amazon freebies and that's why I gave this one a shot. I normally don't set my expectations too high for novellas, but there are some that can surprise me on occasion with a very balanced and engaging story that makes the most of its page time. This one unfortunately wasn't one of them for me. Though the goal of the heroine is noble, honestly I found the plot and dialogue fairly juvenile at times and I couldn't really connect with the main pair. Though I'm not a grammar nazi, there were distracting mistakes as well that made it difficult to understand what the characters were saying and who was saying what. There are other books in this series but I probably won't be keeping up with them. *Review also posted to Amazon.

I received this ARC in exchange for my honest opinion. My thanks to the author, her publisher and Netgalley. I don't expect authors to write the same books over and over again, but I usually expect authors to remain true to a certain "style". This author did not. All of the charm and graciousness that I so much enjoyed in 'Major Pettigrew' was sadly lacking in this novel. I disliked ALL of these characters. I don't think I was supposed to, but I did. I kept thinking how petty all of these people were, especially Agatha. And I didn't understand her irrational adoration and attachment to Daniel. I found it completely over the top. We were hit over the head with instances that showed how bad Daniel was, and how much more worthy Hugh was... and how he got the shaft every time. How tiring it all became! This book did not show the English aristocracy is a very complimentary light. They were mostly portrayed as stuck up sanctimonious jerks that spend their time posturing and bleating about their own self-worth. Couldn't at least one of them have had some nobility of spirit? Beatrice and Hugh came off best in this story, and were obviously meant to be the heroine and hero. But I have a question for Hugh... do you mean to tell me that you - a certified surgeon who served in France and had dealt with every imaginable kind of horrific injury   - were not capable of delivering a baby? (Was this more manufactured drama?) This book cannot be faulted just because it was not what I expected. But it CAN be faulted on its own merits.

The perfect combination of sexy and substance! A 'must-read-right-this-second' novel. Seriously, if you haven't read it already you are missing out! Very romantic in a take-your-breath-away kinda way. Okay. SO, this was my first Mia Sheridan novel. I'm not sure about the rest, but this one had an overall slower-paced (women's fiction or old-school romance novel) feel to it. Which I enjoyed immensely. It was a nice change of pace from the last NA novel I read...which lacked real depth. But right away I could tell this novel would be full of depth, sad yet uplifting, and one of those stories that sticks without for awhile. It exceeding my expectations and then some. Bottom line. It was a great novel that can span across several genres: NA, romance, fiction, even slightly erotic. (The sex scenes were up there with the best of them!) READ IT NOW. My favorite part of the whole novel is when Archer first speaks to her! Swoon. Double swoon. He simply signs a couple words to her, after she's probably thinking 'this guy's weird and will never talk to me.' But he says three simple words and that's when I fell in love. :)

First, with the way the author was writing, I couldn't figure out the time setting for this story. I was also a bit out of my comfort zone with the werewolf sex with a human. All I can say is WOW. Cynthia Hand has successfully made her way to the top five of my favorite author's list. From start to finish, Boundless had be captivated, laughing, and crying every step of the way. As with the rest of the trilogy. I'm sad to see it finished, this whole series has definitely made an imprint on my heart and has made me really think about how I interpret  Destiny As for the question of Team Tucker or Team Christian,  I started the series on Team Tucker simply because in the general way YA books work, he was the 'underdog' of sorts. In other words, not the very first choice or romantic choice you would assume would be the way to go. (Sorry if that didnt sound right. It's 4am now and I'm tired from crying and not sleeping) I did eventually by Hallowed convert to Team Christian following the impression that they were "meant to be" and in some odd round about way they were. Just not in the way everyone was hoping for. However I am glad that Clara finally got to be with Tucker in the end. I was literally bawling by the end of the book. I liked her interpretation of  Hell  and the idea that one can leave if one chooses to, if not for the fact that they simply choose to dwell upon their sorrows or "what brought them there/here in the first place" The only idea that I had a problem with is the whole deal with Phen. I got the impression that you needed to read to understand all that consipired between him and Angela and Clara. I however do not own an e-reader and am not able to read Radiant, but it did not completely take away my experience of reading this book. Perhaps one day they will convert it into a physical book form copy and I will be able to find out what happened, just be patient... Also another thing that I picked up on was the very little more than occasional reference to current things.. for example, Richelle Mead's Vampire Academy got a little bit of a shout out, the movie Zombieland, and I'm pretty sure if not certain the dystopia Clara had been reading was one of the Hunger Games books. (i.e  three eyed mutant dog  ??) I don't know. it didnt bother me at all, just something I picked up on. Anyway, all this pretty much sums up to is that Boundless is in my opinion a successful end to the Unearthly trilogy. Cynthia Hand is a very promising author and is definitely on my prime radar for new books to read. "Four for you Cynthia Hand, you go Cynthia Hand" (Mean girls reference)

Everneath is a story about a girl, Nikki, who gets sucked in an underworld 'Everneath' for a hundred years with a 'man' named Cole, only to be released to find that barely a year has passed in the real world. Nikki is eager to spend time with her family and , importantly, readjust to her former boyfriend Jack, even though Nikki knows that in six months' time, she will be forced to go back down. 'Everneath' is a really interesting story, based on the Greek myths of Persephone, and of Eurydice and Orpheus. The three main characters were definitely interesting: Cole was a likeable bad guy (in that he isn't a total douchebag). Jack was a strong depiction of a good guy, someone who is a moral person who doesn't give up easily. Jack was definitely my favourite character. In Nikki, I found it harder to completely warm to at first. She initially seemed like a weak character who wasn't the most interesting, but she definitely came into her own. It did take me a while to really get into this book. Explanations about Nikki and what happened to her aren't forthcoming and it takes a long while before any real explanation is given, which was a little frustrating. That said, when I finally got into the book, it was brilliant and I really enjoyed the last third. There were a few things I didn't like: I felt that Nikki's reason for choosing to go with Cole initially was weak and even though the author was trying to convey her hardships, I never quite got that she'd be willing to forget about her troubles without talking it through first (to Jack or whomever.) And I also felt that Jack and Lacey not actually doing anything that night, as misconstrued by Nikki, was predictable and that when Nikki did eventually find this out, she didn't react to it in a big way, which I found odd given that was her reason for going to Cole. But then I guess she was a little preoccupied...! Also, I would have loved a bit more on Jack and Nikki's backstory. I know Nikki had a big crush on Jack. I know Jack had a crush on Nikki. Yet somehow, it took ages for them to get together. I'd love to know more about that, what bridged them etc. I know the author did tell us snippets, but I wanted more! Definitely one of my favourite things about this book is their relationship. That Jack never gave up on her is very endearing, and that he's so persistent even when she's so temperamental with him when she comes back, just speaks volumes about him. He doesn't give up on her even when any other person would have run for the hills. I knew that Jack was the 'Orpheus' of this story and that he would somehow have to sacrifice himself for Nikki. But strangely, the ending still took me for surprise. I didn't expect it to happen so soon. I actually expected Nikki to go down first and for him to somehow come after her. That he sacrificed himself first actually really excited me. It means things have been subverted and suddenly Nikki has all this determination and strength to now find *him. * I really am looking forward to that journey. I am also looking forward to finding out more about Cole. Tbh, I don't quite get why he loves Nikki. What is it about her that drew him to her? Ashton only slightly hints at this and I'd love to know if his feelings changed when they were in the underworld. And actually, what exactly both of them went through. They were cocooned together for a hundred years. What was the exact purpose of this? And was that it? Did they go through anything else? So yes, I enjoyed Everneath for the most part and am looking forward to the sequel!

After one failed attempt a few years ago, I finished the book. Prolix as all hell most of the time. This time it was serious, and that's why I got through it. I was seriousminded and all that. You can tell how the book infects a person. This book might screw up your internal monologue, or worse, your prose. Everyone will laugh at you for being a literary neophyte with Joycean pretensions. I'm not sold on the oft-winded explanation that this book is a retelling of the Odyssey. My copy even had the mythical bow imprinted on the front cover, so the allusions began extra early for me. The author himself alludes to it directly towards the end of the text, but allusions do not a retelling make. The argument can be made, however, by anyone who wants an easy B- on a graduate paper. The prose is interesting but very dense. The characters were well written, understandable, and coherent. The narratives of the book are interesting to follow, and provide what structure there is beyond the passing of time and stylistic conceit. The stream of consciousness technique I found a bit annoying at times, but I really enjoyed the Q&A chapter towards the end - something about it really struck a chord. Why did the "Q&A" chapter strike such a chord? Likely resultant of education received, receptiveness to questions all and sundry, or even the questions encountered on a daily day to which one feels hostility and impatience. Relative novelty. I have read a fair amount of books in my time, and while this was not the most pleasurable read of my life, it was one of the more obtuse books I've stumbled across. Pisser Burke, by the way, is one of the most fantastic names I've ever read. But there's not much a review can say about this book without overstating or mangling the case, and I'm the wrong person anyhow. Stephen Dedalus... we hardly knew ye.

Book: Daughter of Smoke & Bone (Daughter of Smoke and Bone, #1) Author: Laini Taylor Actual Rating: 3.5 Source: I Own It Ahh this was so cute, I loved the overall idea of 'monsters' and what creates one. We're all monsters in someone else's mind. Quote; Once upon a time, an angle lay dying in the mist. And a devil knelt over him and smiled. Characters; + Karou and her lying was a great part to the story. I love how Liani tells us that she speaks nothing but the truth, yet her little mannerisms (a quirk of the lip, a knowing smile) make it seem like she's lying. + Zuzana is my small fluffy ball of spikes. I loved the way she was depicted as not only a total badass, but someone who can laugh around with Karou and sticks with her through the total madness of the book. + Mik was so refreshing. He wasn't described as utterly gorgeous like most boys in young adult, he was real and I loved him. - Akiva didn't really have much depth to him. I get that he was meant to seem dark and mysterious, but a lot of the time he came of slightly whiny and very creepy. He didn't seem as damaged as I think the author was trying to make him. World Building; + Buying teeth from murderers. I loved this line so much because it caught Brimstone in his entirety yet it was said in such a casual way! Oh you know, the usual, murderers and such. + Cruelty is evident in everyone and everything. Shown in the contrast between Akiva and Razgut, as well as the constant descriptions of bloodied gums and broken girls. Why I'm not going to read the second book; The whole 'I'm secretly his girlfriend, and we've got a love spanning across the stars' seemed very cliche and entirely predictable. I would have been more interesting if she turned out to be his daughter from a executed lover. Although that could just be me. Basically, the last few chapters kind of ruined it for me.

I got this as a free ebook on Amazon today and am enjoying Spring Break by catching up on some reading. I put most of my review in *spoiler* mode since I don't want it to ruin it if you're NOT like me and want to be surprised. I usually read the end of a story first ;). A young French noblewoman agrees to marry an old reprobate to give her exiled family some security and better their new reduced place in society. Right after the wedding however she learns just how vile he is and runs off planning to meet up with her family later. Her escape route, enlisting in the Navy for a quick ride to London, is a shortcut fraught with complications that she could never had envisioned. The biggest hurdle is the deliciously handsome up and coming Lieutenant who's illegitimacy is constantly thrown in his face. Despite being born on the wrong side of the blanket Treynor is determined to leave her alone and maintain his honor. Too bad it's so hard to keep his hands off. What I liked about it Much of it took place at sea and she had to do normal tasks aboard the ship (okay so she didn't do much but escape from wherever Treynor told her to stay). I liked the historical aspects of it right down to the worms. I liked the relationship between Treynor and his mother and wish it could have be visited a little more (that includes the doomed romance of his parents). I also think more could have been said about his "new family" at the end and wonder if they were placed there are a tie in to a new novel. What I wish could have been different I liked the restraint (although more on his side than hers) and how he really was honor bound to leave her alone but found her reasoning a little off considering what she was running from. A few moments defied logic (mainly aboard The Tempest) and I would have liked to see her be a little more useful and a little less pigheaded always causing problems for others. But at the same time I thought she was a good, feisty heroine. Overall I found it a quick, enjoyable read and it piqued my interest for any stories about the characters introduced at the end of story.
Solid urban fantasy with a strong mystery element. It's not as humorous as The Dresden Files, but the main character is interesting.

Excuse me while I go reach for the tissues! I read Lisa Jewell's other family drama The House We Grew Up In a few years ago and was eager to read this one as well. She did not disappoint. I teared through this book so fast that at the end I was upset I finished. Sometimes books drag on and on and you can't wait for them to end...this was not the case with this one! Laurel Mack is finally beginning to move on. After the disappearance of her 15 year old daughter 10 years ago, she lost a lot more. She has met a charming and smart man named Floyd who comes into her life unexpectedly. Along with his quirky nine year old daughter Poppy, he helps Laurel learn to live again. There is one thing though...Poppy looks like her daughter Ellie did at that age. This leads Laurel to bring up the past and question what happened to Ellie. Now here's the thing with this book, it is told in 5 parts and you pretty much know who was behind Ellie's disappearance soon into the book. The characterization of everyone though...wow...that's what kept me soooo engaged. Poppy is one of the most unique characters I have come across lately and I had no clue what was going to be her story or how she would grow as a character. Man, and the villain...wow....just wow. So creepy and also someone you can meet in every day life...which made them even more terrifying. The only thing I still have a little beef about is the ending...I was just rooting for a certain couple and it didn't happen. But... amazingly atmospheric family drama that you will not want to end!!

Will Wheaton was the perfect reader & is actually mentioned by his real name in the story. If you don't know who I'm talking about, then don't bother reading the book or this review. I don't think anyone who isn't into video games or a bit of an SF nerd will get much out of this. It's probably best if you grew up in the 80's, too. Those of us who are a bit older (OK, quite a bit. My kids grew up in the 80's.) but somewhat geeky will also love it. This had it all - a dystopian world of the near future, social issues, a romance, & fantastic adventure, all set to a backdrop of an 80's geekfest. Early video games figure in prominently along with the music & movies of the decade; War Games, Rush, Star Wars, Zork, Joust, and Blade Runner. My biggest complaint with the book was redundancy. Cline was too thorough about explaining everything & if there was any chance the idiot reader might not have grasped it the first time, he told me a second time. Drove me a little crazy at times. C'mon! This was a book for nerds. Anyone who can't remember how Joust works needs to play a game again. There's an online version here: http://www.1980-games.com/us/old-game... Seriously, that's just one of the sites that comes up. Most of these old games are free online, simply google it. The book wasn't perfect. It had some issues with a variety of items & pulled off a few cheap shots in the story line. I didn't care much for the way his big infiltration was handled, for instance. Nor how H traveled around in the RV when the bus required a hit team   or some of the other tech details, but it was a fun romp. I just went with it & enjoyed. I actually kind of got several of the clues, like Captain Crunch, which made it even more fun. Overall, it had a great message, too. It is easy to get lost online & ignore the real world even today. That's just sad, but true. If I was raising a teen today, I'd probably break their phone. Thankfully for my kids, I only stomped one calculator & occasionally took away their computers. Much cheaper. Anyway, it was great fun & I highly recommend letting Will read it for you.

I finished this book several weeks ago, and it has taken me several weeks to sit down and process my thoughts into a coherent review! Pak Jun Do, who is an orphan master's son, is a citizen of North Korea. While he lives in a country that brainwashes its people into believing they are citizens of the greatest democratic nation in the world, Jun Do sees past the propoganda and recognizes that he and his fellow citizens are slaves to their leader Kim Jung Il. As Jun Do gains attention from Kim Jung Il, he begins a dangerous attempt to move into the inner circle of North Korea's government and save the woman that he loves. Like most people, I knew very little about North Korea before reading this novel. I recognize that this is a fictional story, but it does seem to be a story that is based on research and some facts, along with the author's imagination. I found it fascinating and horrifying all at the same time. And it makes me want to read and learn more about North Korea and what life is like for people in that country. I think this novel is worth reading just because it opened my eyes to a part of the world that I had never before considered. But it is also worth reading because it is just a great novel! I loved the tone of the novel. While it is about some horrible, horrible real life conditions, there is an undertone of satire and dark humor to Johnson's writing. And it worked really well in this novel. The things that are happening in North Korea are just absurd and often appear silly when read from an American perspective. It is almost laughable. Except it's not, because it is real. So while this does read like political satire, it is also a thriller and even a little bit of a love story. I read in an interview with Adam Johnson that he wanted to portray what life is like for the regular every day person in North Korea. What is it like to be a parent, a spouse, a friend in a country that controls your every movement? Through Jun Do's journey, I felt like we got a picture of all those things. I would highly recommend this novel. I give it a solid five stars!

It is, like traditional fairy tales, dark and somewhat menacing, with some beautiful moments thrown in.

3.5 Stars Since everybody and their nannies have reviewed this book, I'll add my own two pence. Honestly, I'm vacillating between screaming with glee "Queen Kleypas is back!!" to begging "For Gods' sake someone chop off the last 30 percent !" The family : I LOVED THEM!!!! Swooooon! Which other author writes such distinct, but beautiful relationships outside of the main couple.. - The bickering, but always supportive, sibling-like bond between West and Kathleen.. <3 This is the first time I've come across a HR where so much page-time is devoted to the heroine and her brother-in-law.. -Kathleen, the mother lioness to her trio of sheltered cubs - gentle Helen, and the unruly twins - Which comes down to... the Twins!! Omg.. They are so utterly hilarious and adorable and so interesting all the time.. Never change.. I would love to have another book just about their mischief and bond, and the utterly devilry they get into, now that West is by their side. I get a faint feeling that something is cooking between one of the twins and West, but only time shall tell :) On a separate note, it felt a bit incongruous that the twins are all of 19 and are still such rambunctious bandits.. Young women at 19 were strictly held to societal restrictions and were expected to be married by this age. Just shows how we generally 'gloss over' facts in order to have more age-appropriate, 25 year old heroines :) -I loved how intellectual and curious everyone (but Kathleen) was.. Helen and Winterbourne:  The talking- point of the story. Kleypas has done this in her past works - giving a prologue and context to Win and Kev's love story in her sister's book Mine Till Midnight. But instead of giving me the "this-otp-is-my-crack" feels, Helen and Winterbourne are akin to watching a car- crash in action. Winterbourne is a deeply conflicted hero.. What has hurt him in the past, that he holds the aristocracy in utter contempt; yet, now that he is his own man, makes marrying into them is objective just to 'one- up' them. He came across as domineering and careless of Helen, and I'm afraid she is going to be collateral in his quest for vengeance. And at last, we get to .. Kathleen and Devon : I loved their story! They started off as rivals, who were mean and shrewish , but somewhere along the way, they developed a deeper understanding of one another. Devon is a bit of an ass - he was childishly spiteful to Kathleen in the beginning, but he always took care of her well being. I could understand why he did so - being saddled with a huge debt and an estate crumbling around his ears and everyone's towering expectations- would not have been easy, and it humanized him in my eyes. Eventually, he took the bull by the horns and put his entire heart and soul into securing the lives of people he had just met. The formation of their tentative friendship is one of the highlights of this book..Their witty banter lit up the pages, and I found myself giggling and gleefully highlighting each and everyone of them. Nearly 60 percent into the book, an incident forces Devon to realize how deeply and irrevocably he loves Kathleen. That thought, and the agony of him not being able to grow old with her forces him to pull himself together and go home to her. That, in my mind, is the conclusion of his love story with Kathleen. I loved their story so far. I loved them both as characters, and did not mind had the major attention been drawn to their family shenanigans and how Devon manages to make the estate prosperous. Instead, we have this contrived drama where after getting Kathleen, he propositions her to be his mistress ,and very suddenly has a fear of having children. All that was good about Devon disappears, and he becomes an utterly frustrating, angry and imperious cad. This development blindsided me and left me perplexed. It, in my opinion, was a poor and ill- conceived attempt to increase the page count. I was left raging, confused and so let down to have such a beloved story turn into a complete train wreck. It does not however, negate my enjoyment of all the other parts.

This is a brilliantly written thriller. The story keeps twisting and turning, she keeps you interested and even when you predict the next turn, you are still surprised. Flynn clearly has done her research on how a psycopath sees the world. Amy is brilliant, manipulative, narcisstic, creative, can read and predict human behavior - yet she doesn't understand feelings, she just imitates. She doesn't know what happiness means but she wants it. She is always bored and is looking for a challenge - and what she is best at is pretending to be someone, and playing with other people like puppets. The action keeps you on your toes, but the real twisted delight is the unfolding of Amy and Nick's character, how they play off of each other, and how they realize that they met their match - and they like it. I love the ending. There is nothing more fitting to the perfect crime than getting away with it - and manipulating everyone into the behavior she wants - and needs. To be always amazing.

The best parts of this book were the nature writing, and the descriptions of living off the land. Very similar to some of my childhood favorites like "My Side of the Mountain" or "Hatchet" in those ways. I've always found those super independent and self-sufficient characters appealing and Margo fits right in. Unlike those children's books, Margo has adult problems and emotions, which are for the most part handled gracefully. When it comes to her family, things confused me--there are a lot of love/hate relationships going on and, out of everything in the book, I felt that they were the most heavy handed. Aside from this weaknesses, the themes of abandonment and exile at the heart of this novel were illustrated beautifully through the relationships Margo has with others. How do you survive, physically, when the people in your life habitually choose to either abandon you or exploit you? How do you survive mentally, spiritually? Those are the questions Margo needs to answer through the course of the novel. Finally, I found this book very similar to Daniel Woodrell's "Winter's Bone" and I imagine if you liked one, you'll like the other.

I read an advance readers copy of this book courtesy of a Goodreads giveaway. 80% of the book was a well-written, intriguing, suspenseful spy thriller. I enjoyed the twists and turns in the plot, and there were a few surprises along the way - which I consider to be a hallmark of a good thriller. Some of the characters - Ben Bradley, in particular - were well-developed and I would be happy to come across them again in other stories. However, I had trouble with the remaining 20% of the book. Some very graphic scenes early on in the story led me to skip a few chapters, including some that included important background on the bad guy - but I just can't read about torture. There were several parts where the supposedly-American narrator used European terminology (car park, anyone?). Although the story supposedly took place in 2002, a year after 9/11, some of the technology seemed more modern. And finally, perhaps most offensive: the ending seemed remarkably similar to  the series finale of Dexter: sailing off on a boat into a new life - WTH?? Overall, I enjoyed the story despite the inconsistencies and problems. I hope the editors take another look at the book, though, and give it some thorough editing for content before the final version is published.

Well, at the beginning I thought this book would be five stars. An intriguing premise: a great opening: beautiful evocative language that you usually don't see in a mystery. The story also had great characterisation and moved at just the right pace. Then, about 80% into the story at the time of the great revelation, everything went phut! for me. Adam "Rob" Ryan is part of the Dublin Murder Squad. He is partnered with Cassie Maddox, a resourceful female detective. Rob Ryan harbours a secret: he is Adam Ryan, one of the three children who disappeared into the woods at Knockaree twenty years ago - the only one who returned. When he came back, little Adam had no memory of the incident, and his shoes are filled with somebody else's blood. When young Katy Devlin is found murdered at the same site, the old ghosts come back to haunt Rob. He is sure that the murder is connected with his childhood trauma in some way - and the investigation becomes a journey into his past too. Don't get me wrong. This is a good mystery, with a plausible story-line and no plot holes to speak of (except one - how did Rob manage to hide his past from his department?) in addition to all the plus points I mentioned in the first paragraph. But three huge defects (IMO) pulled it down to three stars for me. One: The author cheats with the intro: while making us believe that this story is somehow connected integrally with Adam Ryan's past, we realise at the end that this was nothing but a McGuffin to end all McGuffins! The old mystery is never explained, even though tantalising snippets are provided throughout the narrative that would have us believe that the explanation is just around the corner. While this kind of open ending is admissible in a literary novel, it is totally unacceptable in a mystery. Two: The protagonist is totally unlikeable. Yeah, I know that he had a screwed up childhood, but going through such long story with only his dark thoughts for company was not an enjoyable experience to say the least. Three: I saw through the mystery - at least part of it - and I think any perceptive reader will. Rosalind's manipulative tactics were so evident that I wanted to punch Ryan in the mouth for being taken in by her wiles. Call himself a detective? However, I still think this is an enjoyable mystery worth a read.

Had it not been for the A-Z Challenge, I would've abandoned this book early on because the first 1/3 was awful -- painfully awful. Queen of Babble is an appropriate title because everything is repeated at least 3 times. Did Meg Cabot have a page threshold that she had to hit? Lizzie Nichols is meant to be adorably zany, but she just comes off annoying. She also sounds 15 years old instead 21/22. The book picks up in Part Two thanks mainly to a plot assist from Sophie Kinsella's Can You Keep a Secret. Like Emma Corrigan in Can You Keep a Secret, Lizzie ends up spilling all her secrets to a stranger on the train who, knock me over with a feather!, ends up being the owner of the chateau she's come to stay in. Not only is he rich, he's tall, dark, and handsome. And taken. But fear not, friends, because his girlfriend is a bitch. Hijinks and TEARS OVER DIET COKE (Seriously. Like, more than once. Over Diet Coke.) ensue. Lizzie and the perfect Luke de Villiers realize they're made for each other. *SWOON* Oh wait, it's only been two freakin' days since they met. I love mindlessly entertaining books, and this one had some cute moments. But unless you need to read a book that starts with "Q", your time is better served reading Sophie Kinsella books (I highly recommend Can You Keep a Secret) than the pale imitation of them that Queen of Babble is.

Are there spoilers Perhaps. It's funny how this used to be in my 'you-re-kidding-me-right' shelf and I ended up reading it out of bribery. I'm not going to lie, I would so give 50 Shades four stars... if it were written as a comedy. Alas, it is not and therefore, I'll be giving it... well, I'll get there. Basically, Fifty Shades of Grey is a lurve story between explicit (but more likable) Bella Swan and explicit Edward Cullen with less glitter and more money. Anastasia Steele is described as witty, independent, shy, clumsy and let's not forget: just plain beautiful. Furthermore, she is supposedly very well-versed with classic British literature. I say 'supposedly' because quite frankly, her vocabulary is limited to 'jeez', 'holy shit', 'damn' and 'oh my'. Not to mention the fact that she constantly referred to her some sort of alter ego as 'my subconsciousness' and 'my inner goddess'. Here are a few examples: My inner goddess is jumping up and down, clapping her hands like a five year old. Inside me! I gasp, and all the muscles deep in my belly clench. My inner goddess is doing the dance of the seven veils. My subconscious is furious, medusa-like in her anger, hair flying, her hands clenched around her face like Edvard Munch's Scream. He's naked except for those soft ripped jeans, top button casually undone. Jeez, he looks so freaking hot. My subconscious is frantically fanning herself, and my inner goddess is swaying and writhing to some primal carnal rhythm. Also, it irks me how she's so aware of Grey stalking her... yet she didn't care. At all. "How did you find me?" "I tracked your cell phone Anastasia." Oh, of course he did. How is that possible? Is it legal? Stalker, my subconscious whispers at me through the cloud of tequila that's still floating in my brain, but somehow, because it's him, I don't mind. Before I move on, I want to comment on a particular line: My mouth drops open. I am staggered by his lack of humility. Yep, yet you still 'fell in love' with said control freak two days after. Here's a word for you: dignity. Get some from eBay. To sum it all up, Anastasia is such an 'out there' character. I'm positive that there is no one in this world who thinks and acts the way she did throughout the book. Quite frankly, I think she's bipolar and completely hormone-driven which is just ridiculous considering how she supposedly had a nonexistent libido since she was never attracted to any guy... until Christian, apparently. Did that make sense? Oh whatever. Christian, on the other hand, well, I have no words for him. Aside from being more than fifty shades of fucked up, a dominant who most likely escaped from an asylum and a guy with zero tastes in girls, I really have nothing to say. Here's his best 'what-the-fuck!' line though: "No, Anastasia it doesn't. Firstly, I don't make love. I fuck... hard. Secondly, there's a lot more paperwork to do, and thirdly, you don't yet know what you're in for. You could still run for the hills. Come, I want to show you my playroom." Hold on, I lied. This is even better: "You're one challenging woman," He kisses me, forcing my lips apart with his tongue, taking no prisoners. "It's taking all my self-control not to fuck you on the hood of this car, just to show you that you're mine, and if I want to buy you a fucking car, I'll buy you a fucking car," he growls. Oops, can't forget this one, of course: "I want you sore, baby," he murmurs, and he continues his sweet, leisurely torment, backward, forward. "Every time you move tomorrow, I want you to be reminded that I've been here. Only me. You are mine." Last one: "I'm a Dominant." His eyes are a scorching gray, intense. "What does that mean?" I whisper. "It means I want you to willingly surrender yourself to me, in all things." I frown at him as I try to assimilate this idea. "Why would I do that?" "To please me," he whispers as he cocks his head to one side, and I see a ghost of a smile. Okay, quite honestly, I did not hate this book at all. It was so ridiculous, it was comedic. Seriously. I enjoyed laughing at the expense of all the characters here, Anastasia's in particular. 1 star. 09/03/12 edit! Just a couple of things I forgot to mention: In my opinion, I wouldn't consider the book as an erotica, because quite honestly, the sex material wasn't something to fawn over. The scenes weren't steamy at all, just plain gore and punishment. That aside, I found the characters underdeveloped, the plot line excruciatingly dull and the descriptions repetitive. The love story between Christian and Anastasia felt rushed and, in some parts of the book, forced. The writing style didn't sit with me well either. One thing I commend about this book though is the dialogue between the characters. I admit that I found the lines pretty amusing (see above).

3.5 Stars Ally Carter is a beautiful weirdo. "Who are you? Am I going to regret not breaking your hand? Because it's not too late. I can still totally break your hand." Embassy Row. What a great idea. The girl shrugs. "I'm Rosie. Germany. Twelve." The way she says it, I know these are the facts that matter here, the embassy-kid equivalent of name, rank, and serial number. "Grace. United States. Sixteen," I tell her. She nods as if we've bonded. A perfectly possible dystopian in the real world. I love it. "We do not go past the fence. I mean, we could. But we don't. Because none of us are superexcited about starting World War Three. So we do not go past the fence." He stares at me, as if waiting for a protest that never comes. "Say it with me, Grace. We do not go past the fence." "Noah." "Say it." "We do not go past the fence," I tell him. "Because we do not want to start World War Three." "We do not want to start World War Three," I add. "Good girl." Embassies all lined up in a row so that the German soil can be next to Canadian soil and the world is suddenly so much smaller. We were not friends. We were simply what becomes of kids who are thrust together so often that, eventually, they run out of reasons not to go play. Ally Carter is good at describing the cliche community in the most eloquent of ways. "New blood, Grace," Noah explains, his voice soft beneath the ever-stronger pulse of the music. "The sharks can smell it. Now come on. It's time for the real tour." She still does fall into plenty of other eye-rolling cliches though. A ball? Really? Do we have to do this? Grace Grace is both adroitly capable and accident prone - an interesting combination. She's scrappy and feisty. I'd rather live in a war zone with my father than with people who call me sweetie. She likes to take risks without thinking about the consequences. She's definitely a tomboy troublemaker. "That's okay," I tell her. "I don't have a home there either." For a second, she looks at me like I'm the saddest little orphan in the world, so I point at myself and say, "Army brat," as if living on ten bases in fifteen years has left me impervious to change. Ally Carter has a way with words. His English is as good as mine, but he likes to play this game. They all do. I don't play any game that I can't win. As the book goes on I became less and less impressed with Gracie. I'm a little on the fence with the mystery. It's nothing brilliant and a little disappointing because I know how clever Ally Carter is. The execution could have also been miles better. It possessed the characterisation but not the punch. Romance He nods out the window toward the Russian embassy. Because that's the thing about Embassy Row. The boy next door is probably Russian. The romance is barely there but it's lovely. I really liked it. It's been a while since I've read a will-they-won't-they and I really enjoyed how sweet and yet deep it is. "Whatever you say, Gracie." "Don't call me Gracie." "Okay." Alexei slowly nods. "It's okay. At least, I hope it's okay."

This took much longer than I thought it would take me to finish, but WOW this was good. Jack Torrance and his family are at their wits' end - Jack, the breadwinner, is unemployed, money is low and Jack is itching to start drinking again. Just as things were getting progressively worse, a friend of Jack's came to the rescue and offered him the position of the Overlook's caretaker for the winter. Just as things were starting to look up, the story begins. Don't let the 600+ page count intimidate you - it's easy to fly through the pages. Stephen King has a way of writing that engages his audience throughout these books. There was maybe one part that seemed rather dull, but it didn't last for long. More often than not, I found myself getting through 25-40ish pages (and almost missing my stop a few times) during my bus ride home because this book was too exciting to put down! Hallorann has to be my favourite character in this book - while not the star, he was portrayed to be quite selfless, caring and helped Danny navigate his powers. What was frustrating, however, was that Hallorann was so easily knocked out - I understand a mallet strike can do serious damage, but COME ON. Wendy was BATTERED and BRUISED and was STILL able to keep going. One strike and Hallorann was out? Ridiculous. One thing I hated that happened to Hallorann was that he was constantly called the "N" word. I'm not a fan of racism, so that definitely knocked some points off for me. Jack was definitely my LEAST favourite character in the book - he was the most annoying character in that book. Despite his consistent thought process, he still stayed with Wendy. He put Wendy, Danny AND himself through a tough time because he refused to divorce Wendy even though it was pretty clear the love was lost in that relationship. They seemed very dysfunctional and it was frustrating reading their scenes because their dialogues and thought processes were the exact opposite. I will say that King did a good job of trying to redeem Jack in the end when he sacrified himself to protect his child - however, Jack was still an awful character. All in all, it was a good read. If you want to get into thrillers, THIS is a good book to read. Now, to watch the movie!

Okay, for those who might be worried about it, I didn't think it was THAT dark. Kinky, and slightly dubious (in a still sexy way), but not that dark all considered. I mean Stefano was at least... polite? when poking Silvio in fascinating ways. He wasn't trying to hurt Silvio once he was well and truly smitten with him. (It does beg the question of what Silvio was actually doing in Stefano's room, but I suspect Aleks will eventually answer that.) I was happy to have figured out the reason behind Battista's decision just before it was stated. It worked well for the tone of the two stories, since they were completely different. I'm looking forward to the rest of these stories.

I was right to start reading this on a weekend because putting it down ain't easy! And can I just say how happy am I that Chosen Layla has her own story now. FINALLY!!! I don't know how it'll work out between her and that seedy new character but it'll be an interesting one, for sure. And wowza on  her and Qhuinn. I'm sure that'll be part of the story in the next book. Did not see that one coming!

Etsuko, now an old Japanese woman, has lived half her life in Japan and the other half in England. Her life in both places were filled with tragedy- she lived through the bombing of Nagasaki and lost everything, and years later her eldest daughter Keiko hanged herself alone in her flat in Manchester. When her youngest daughter comes for a visit, she starts thinking about an old friend she used know, Sachiko, and how her life used to be in post-war Japan. "A Pale View Of Hills" had a style that was familiar to me from "Never Let Me Go" - the feeling of dread starts from the first few pages and you can't help but read on to find out what is wrong with it all. You are put off by Sachiko's obviously terrible parenting, and you fear that something will happen to her daughter Mariko because of all the neglect. And it is strange how Mariko seems to be almost afraid of Etsuko. We also get to see other aspects of Etsuko's life such as her relationship with her husband who she doesn't really seem to be connecting with emotionally, and her father-in-law Ogata-San who despite seeming to care a lot for Etsuko, doesn't really think she has a bigger role to fulfill than be a good, submissive wife for his son. We see the shifting of ideas, the way that households are changing in Japan after the war and the views of both the older and the younger generations. As you are reaching the end of the book, you feel like you were cheated by Ishiguro. He had all these storylines, the fates of Sachiko and Mariko, the suicide of Keiko, how Etsuko came to leave her first husband to settle in England- and he was going to explain none of it. But then he did, and in just a single page... It takes a while to set in. You knew that Etsuko was an unreliable narrator all along. She warned you, she said that her memories may not be very exact. And she knew all along that she wasn't being very honest with you, because she spent that day on the hills with Keiko, not Mariko, and you had no idea until the last ten pages. And now you will sit and think about it for days. And there it is again, that familiar feeling you get from Ishiguro novels, of guilt over time lost. And you will never really know how much of Sachiko was Etsuko all along. Maybe the Etsuko she remembers in the past is how she feels she should have acted. Maybe if she had been that Etsuko, Keiko wouldn't have killed herself. I'm almost sad that I've finished A Pale View Of Hills. Now there is one less Ishiguro book I can read for the first time.

Dear Ari, You better live up to my name!!! FULL REVIEW: Oh, it felt so good, so personal to read my name in this story. Ari.. Ari.. Every time I read this name it filled me with joy and my heart started to beat a bit faster. It was like the book had been written just for me. Well, you can't blame me for all this excitement, because it's not like it rains all the time with characters that share my name (and if you're wondering - which you are totally not, but I don't care - "Ari" is a girl (finally! ), as I was starting to get tired and pretty much annoyed to see so many boys named like me). And now that I'm done with contemplating about my love for my own name (which might start to bore you to tears any minute now), I'll get back to the book. The Concept: The first thing that grabbed my attention - except for the character's name, that is - was the beautiful cover (because, yeah.. I choose books based on their covers. What? Don't you do the same? ), and then the synopsis really made me want to read this story. You can't just 'peek' and then not want to know more, to see what's the story really about. On the other hand, I didn't get to read many books about aliens and such, so I was eager to see how the author imagined this other world. Well, this book is more about Earth and humans and their behaviour, so don't hold your breath for too many aliens (as the cover seems to hint), but still I liked the uncertainty regarding "good" vs. "bad" in this story. I kept wondering if humans were good or bad, if the Ancients (aka. aliens) were trying to take over the world or just cohabit in peace, I wanted to understand the mystery around our alien boy and how Ari and him wanted to save both words. Sometimes you can understand a story better after you read the second book in the series, and this one seems to be like that. The story was fast-paced and action packed, but there were still many questions that haven't been answered and also there were some things that you get to understand better only near the ending. The Good: Ari's voice made me dig into this book and keep it close until the last page. I liked her strength, her courage and her need to save both worlds. The storyline was entertaining and I liked how it got to surprise me by the ending - with a few turnarounds so different than what I had in my mind. It's good to read a book that has the main characters trying to stop a war, rather than trying to fight against the system (any change in a dystopian book gives is refreshing). I was glad as well about the fact that there was no insta-love (even though it happened all a bit too quick) and there was no real love-triangle, because I was about to worry about it at some point. Also the characters were pretty great (not sure if I can say the same about the main male character - you see, I got to realize that I know nothing about him after all this time, so my connection with him was lost between the lines) and it gets more bonus point for friendship and family relation (as strange as it was it was well defined - loved the mother, by the way). "I don't know. Okay? That's the truth. It's like gravity disappears when he's around and I'm lost, no longer sure of anything." The not so good: This gets me to the things I didn't quite understand. Like how and why did Ari trust our boy Jackson and decided to help him. She didn't have many reasons to do so, and I am not telling you that she didn't make the best decision (because at this point the aliens are better than the humans in my eyes - I'll be waiting for something to make me change my mind though.. I feel it in the air), it's just that I needed her to have stronger reasons for this story to work better for me. During the book there were some things that seemed not to add up, but by the ending I got the whole picture and so they made sense. So overall, this was a good start to a new series and I am eager to see how things progress from here. Happy midnight reading! * This review can also be found at ReadingAfterMidnight.com Blog (EN) | Facebook | Twitter | Tumblr | Bloglovin' | Blog (RO)

The Favorite, I think was unique- we understood Marlee and Carter's relationship first hand. The Caning in Marlee's point of view was so beautifully written. Many vital stats of certain characters were left listed as, "Unknown." Most notably who Embry's father is!) I'm of the opinion that in a guide to a series nothing should be unknown. Even if the information never comes up in the series itself, surely the author should know, and share, these details. I also think it would have been nice if we'd been told the future of some of the characters. For example, where did the Cullens go after Forks? Was Bella just content to be Edward's wife for the rest of her life or did she go to college, take up a hobby, something? Did Renesmee grow up and just fall in line with Jacob's feelings or did she make him work for them? Did Leah ever find someone? Mostly this book could have been put together by any semi-competent fan. When I read a guide I want true insight from the author, not things I could mostly look up on the internet or infer from reading the books in the series.

Under the Empyrean Sky was a thrilling and exciting ride, full of memorable characters and memorable places. While most definitely not flawless, Under the Empyrean Sky is extremely entertaining and enjoyable. While the book wasn't especially unique, Wendig used some more commonly used tropes and elaborated on them. There were a few things that just didn't really add up in the book such as the Hunger Games-esque lottery where life couples are chosen. I've never really understood these, and in this book less so. What's the point in the government choosing your partner if it's totally random? Is it to break moral? Is it because they could? Was it the aliens? The world may never know. Also, Cael's father running a secret rebel organization was a bit out there. I like how Cael and his father had a complex relationship, instead of him being absent in the story, but how did Cael's father even have time to run a secret organization? Cael is an incredibly memorable character with a very defined personality. Though the book is in third person, I mistook it for first on more than one occasion (the POV changes were very jarring). He's not a perfect nor always likable character, but I thought he was written extremely well. His views on women were very close-minded, however. The secondary characters were, while not nearly as well developed as Cael, also enjoyable and interesting characters. Cael's two best friends were almost too similar to each other for my tastes but I liked them all the same. Pop, Cael's father, was a surprisingly well done character. It's not often that fathers - or parents in general - are given the time of day in YA and I'm always really happy when they are! Talking about women, Under the Empyrean Sky had a very misogynistic feel to it. Women were portrayed as weak and never mentioned without talking about a man. Women were docile and it often seemed like their only merits were their attractiveness. Attractiveness is a deciding factor on whether a woman is good or bad. Gwennie = attractive = good. Wanda = ugly = bad. Under the Empyrean Sky definitely does not meet the Bechdel expectations. Wendig's writing was the novel's strength. It was incredibly unique and defined. The colloquial way of writing that Wendig uses is rarely something I like but it fit very well with the themes and characters of Under the Empyrean Sky. Overall, Under the Empyrean Sky is very enjoyable and fun. While it may annoy a lot of people, I still think it's worth giving a shot. Maybe it'll surprise you!
