Twist is one of those books you don't take with you. It has no real drama, it has no loose ends, it has no "WTF" moments. It just is. And being a just is book is fine. I love Kylie Scott and I think she does an excellent job at writing a book. I just wasn't as enthralled with this book as I have been others. They aren't as memorable and the whole plot line just seems fairly far fetched, which is saying quite a bit since it's very much centered around two average Joe characters. We'll see with the next one I suppose.
This is a decent book, clearly expressed and with a positive, well-defended thesis. Memoirs aren't necessarily my thing, but I didn't consider it time wasted so that's a win!

This book is just as marvelous as all of the reviews claim, so if you like Sarah MacLean you definitely should read it. Temple is a truly loveable hero, even though he is determined to get his revenge on Mara. She, however, is an amazing heroine; we should despise her but somehow we don't. Kudos to Ms. MacLean for pulling off this difficult maneuver. Originally, I thought to rate this book at four stars, primarily because there was too much repetitive should I/shouldn't I interior monologue. I skimmed over chunks of it. But then . I read the epilogue and decided that I had to give five stars for the most astounding plot twist ever. Truly, your jaw will drop, and you'll go crazy waiting for Chase's story to arrive next year.

Eh, I'm not sure what to rate this one. Such potential, but it somehow felt very... stale? unfulfilled? disengaging? The beginning was full of action and rather intriguing, but then the plot tapered off for a while, only to be hurried up again toward the end. At first I was wondering if Bardugo was interweaving lots of hidden magic within the subtext, for a huge payoff later. But by now I don't think that's the case -- all those coincidences really were coincidences, and the romance really is that easy, and the villain really is that... dry? After a while, I've realized that it's probably because everything in this book is recycled material -- secretly pretty heroine with pretty name learns to overcome her meager place in society, find emotional and physical strength, and fulfill some sort of greater destiny, meanwhile dilly-dallying within a love triangle, struggling against a super-villain... It just wasn't unique enough for me to rave about. Plus some random sexuality is thrown in, plus the magic has unexplored potential, plus the beginning love triangle Mal is left out for the first third, only to show up just in time to save the day, then later declare his love... from then on the main romance was boring to me. Three stars for a creative universe inspired by an under appreciated culture in fantasy (albeit one that became kind of flat and old after a while). The characters were sympathetic, and I was interested enough to finish -- but not interested enough to dig up the sequel.

I am really pleased with this book. It was everything I thought and hoped it would be. It was fun and fast-paced. I really enjoyed the story and liked how the author tied everything up in the end. By now I am so used to my favourite characters in books dying (ehkem Falling Kingdoms ekhem) that I was in constant fear over everyone. And there is so many moments where you are so scared for almost every single character (because they are so likeable!) that it's just impossible to stop your heart from pounding. Or to stop reading. I still don't know how I feel about the fact that none of the more likeable characters have died. Of course, that's nice - not to be completely heartbroken after finishing a book. But still there were so many moments when someone dying would spice things up, push characters to do something they wouldn't otherwise. For example, I kinda wanted Raisa's sister to burn in this chapel. Not that I am a monster - it would be awful, of course. But I think that could add a lot to the story. I was also sure that Amon would be dead by the end of the series. Which would completely wreck me, because I adore him. But still - it could be interesting. God, I am awful

I wasn't sure what to really expect going in to this one. I'm on a current dystopian high, and have loved pretty much all of the dystopians I've read lately. So, when I initially decided to read this I was excited, then I started reading reviews of other reviewers on Goodreads who I usually agree with, and they weren't the best. Well, I went ahead and read it, and I'm glad. It wasn't the best book I've red this year, or even over the last few years, but I do think it took on a different angle of the dystopian genre. So many of which involve a war, and government oppression, where youth are disposable and looked down on. McCafferty sets up a world where teens have power, although they possibly don't even realize it. She uses the growing obsession with media and fame to demonstrate the huge impact both have on youth and how it effects what we as a society value. The contrast between Melody and Harmony was done nicely and despite an obvious lean towards showing how oppressive Harmony's life has been, there is a balance. Harmony's ideology focuses on the value of life, not just the giving of birth but also how you use your life to better that of others. Melody's is portrayed as self-indulgent and materialistic but with more freedom than Harmony's. Both girls come to realize that neither world is perfect. The alternating points of view build this wonderfully and keeps either girl from becoming too annoying. The ending was a bit unexpected although not entirely surprising. It will lead nicely into the sequel, yet even if this were the end of the girls' story I'd feel satisfied. They both learned something about themselves and what they see for their future, even if it might not be perfect. Check out more of my reviews on my blog Turning the Pages

This review was originally posted on Bedtime Bookworm Wow guys - just wow! This book completely blew me away. This book was picked for a book club with my coworkers (this was our first one!). I was excited when it was picked because I love historical fiction, especially set during the WWII time period, and I've been meaning to read more adult books. I seriously read this book in two sittings - I went to Vegas for a weekend and read half on the way drive there and half on the way back. The Plot The story is basically about two sisters during WWII, in France, and the things that they go through. I loved that this book explored a lot of the gray morality surrounding the Nazis. It shows that not all Nazis were evil people - some of the Nazis were good people who were doing bad things, but for what they thought were good reasons. The book also included Nazis who truly were bad people and it was really interesting to see that juxtaposition. I also loved that this book made me think about what I would do if I lived in this time period and was put into the situations these sisters were in. It's easy to say that we would all do "the right thing" and stand up against the Nazis. But really, when your life or your children's lives are at stake, who knows what you would do? It's also a slippery slope - you start by doing something small that is beneficial to both your family and the Nazis, and it's hard to know when to draw the line (if you even can)! The Characters I identified with Vianne right away, but not so much with Isabelle because of her obstinate personality. I felt if I was in these situations, I would have acted more like Vianne did than Isabelle did. Isabelle definitely grew as a character over time and I was attached to her by the end of the story. I wasn't a fan of the romance at first (a little on the insta-love side), but it grew on me and I was invested in that relationship by the end of the book. My poor heart broke at the end when Gaetan finally makes it back to Isabelle and she dies in his arms. So tragic! A small part of the book is written in present time from an old woman's POV and the fun part is that you don't know which sister is the old woman until the very end. I, unfortunately, assumed it was one sister from the very beginning and didn't get to enjoy this mystery throughout the book - but it was really well done and I wish I hadn't made that assumption! There were also many fantastic characters, that seemed so real, that I grew to love over the course of this book. The Writing and Setting I loved the writing style of this book - it was very atmospheric and made me feel like I was really in France. In a way, this book was educational for me because I didn't know that Germany had occupied France in this way and I definitely had NO sense of what it was like to live in an occupied country (let me tell you, it's scary!!). Reading this book has made me grateful for roof over my head, the food in my belly, and the fact that I don't have to fear for the lives of my friends and family on a day to day basis. This might sound strange, but having the present day old woman's POV juxtaposed with the POVs of the sisters when they were young really made me think about how long life can be. I kept wondering about how this old woman got from point A to point B in her life and wanting to know how she got there. I also thought about what my life looks like now, and how it could look completely different in 5-10-20+ years down the road (if I'm so lucky). In Summary I loved this book so much! The writing, setting, and characters together really made this book an emotional journey for me. I was really emotional during the second half of the book, and I probably cried (*bawled*) for about half of it - and I mean like sobbing uncontrollably (my husband was seriously concerned for me!). Despite all the heart break, I found the story very thought provoking and I loved the journey - this book has a special place in my heart. I would love to read more from Kristin Hannah. I recommend this book to anyone who enjoys historical fiction, especially of the WWII variety.

I really like this little series. It's such a messed up premise. Two teens whose memories are lost every 48hrs over the past week and they don't know why or who's doing it. Now Charlie goes missing and it's right as they wake up to another mind wipe so Silas has absolutely no idea where to look for her. It's crazy. This book always has you on the edge of your seat with anticipation of what's coming next. I like the alternating POVs because then you really get a sense of how truly lost and confused the two of them are. Silas and Charlie deal with the loss of their memories differently. They have such distinct personalities and the ways that they cope in their new lives are very interesting. They revert to their true selves not the people they had become in the few years right before the memory loss. A few more helpful tidbits were released in this installment but I would have liked more. Especially the deal with the Shrimp? I'm glad more about the scandal with Charlie's father was revealed. That gave me some satisfaction. I so hope that next/last book pulls everything together. I just want this little novella series to end on a high note. I need a nice solid ending. No cliffhangers or things open for interpretation. Just a bunch of loose ends all tied up into a nice big bow!!

Julie Kagawa doesn't disappoint in the Iron Queen. I bit my fingernails to the core as I read this fast-paced third book in the series. She is a gifted story-teller!! I CAN'T WAIT TO START ON THE NEXT! :D

This book took a lot longer to read than I thought it would. I loved reading it, but then it got put aside for other books (I'm talking about you, Chaos Walking series). I had left it for so long that I almost didn't pick it up again, BUT I'm so glad that I did. This was a book that came out when I was in college (she says muffled into her hand). I remember it being huge, but I didn't pick it up until now. The Good: This is one of those kids books that tells it like it is. Life isn't pretty and glossed over, and things don't necessarily end happily ever after. I LOVE these kinds of kid's books, especially now that my own kids are getting to the age that they can read them. I want them to see that life is at times ugly, other times beautiful and sad and ugly..... The intermingling of the two different stories was brilliant and seamless. I especially loved how  the race of Kate and Sam wasn't mentioned until later in the story. It wasn't something that mattered until the racism came into play and I thought that was well-handled by the author. The Bad: The Ugly:

You can feel that the stakes are rising for Rylee and her pack. The prophecies are becoming more clear as are the lines between friend and foe. People important to Rylee are being injured and killed, pushing everything to the edge. I have to say that  Dolan and Giselle's prediction about Liam have me broken hearted. I just hope there is a way around them.

I don't have much to say about this book, but I have to admit that it was a vast improvement from the first one. The writing flow continued to be a bit weird at times. I think the author has a problem when it comes to the big reveals. The way that the 'bad person' explains why they did what they did always comes out as a stretch for convenience sake to the storyline. The part where Lara and Mrs. Casnoff went on that speech about how their family were the original makers of Sophie's demon lineage  seemed a bit too out of left field to me. There's a difference between being shocking and being completely random. That said, the overall plot was better. I liked the introduction of Sophie's dad. Their dynamic was one of the things I liked the best. I didn't understand why Sophie was so obsessed with Archer. I just wasn't a fan of him at all. After what happened in the previous book, I had so many questions though, so it was nice to get some answers about his background. If I had to pick, I liked Cal a lot more. He didn't even say much the entire story and I still thought Sophie had better chemistry with him than she did with Archer. Also, that ending was pretty amazing. Talk about the stakes being raised. I felt so terrible when Sophie's dad got his powers taken away. There was something sad about seeing someone that was once so powerful reduced to that. I'm pretty sure that Sophie will get her powers back in the final book. I just hope it doesn't take too long . In general, I'm just interested to see where the story will lead from here, especially after that cliffhanger.

More like a 2.5. Maybe. I don't know. This book wasn't bad by any means, I just feel that it dragged on and on and on. In the same time it would take me to read 100 pages in any other book, I only read about 30 in this book. I don't know why it felt like that. I really couldn't get into the story for the first 150 or so pages. The slang was really distracting, but I find it rings pretty true as my younger brothers have made up their own swear words before. I wasn't really engaged with anything that was going on. I like Thomas, but I didn't feel attached to him or any of the other characters. Even Teresa. I kind of liked Newt and Chuck but not enough to really care. I honestly had to force myself to keep my eyes open and just read. I think this book is better read in one or two sittings. I don't recommend reading this if you can only read five minutes here, ten minutes there, etc. because if you are anything like me you will be very bored. I think the only thing that keeps me from actually disliking the book as a whole is the fact that it's being made into a movie and I saw the trailer. Had I not seen the trailer I have no idea what I would have pictured the setting to be. I know I certainly wouldn't have been as engaged as I was (even though I was already engaged very little as it is). I liked picturing all the characters as the actors (particularly Dylan O'Brien as Thomas). That helped in visualize what was happening, it gave me a better idea of what was going on. And it was actually kind of fun imagining this all play out as a movie. I think it will make for a pretty decent movie, even if I didn't totally enjoy the book. I did actually really enjoy the ending particularly when Chuck died - sad, but I really wasn't expecting it - and the epilogue. The mention of test group B really had me intrigued. If it weren't for those two events at the end I probably wouldn't even bother reading the second and third book. As it is, I do plan on reading them, but definitely not any time soon. Maybe if there's a second or third movie. Ha.

_The Story of Beautiful Girl_ by Rachel Simon (first published April 13th 2011) Added 5/12/11 - Keep in mind. On 5/12/11, I saw an ad at GR for this book. Sounded like it might be interesting. GR description: "It is 1968. Lynnie, a young white woman with a developmental disability, and Homan, an African American deaf man, are locked away in an institution, the School for the Incurable and Feebleminded, and have been left to languish, forgotten. Deeply in love, they escape, and find refuge in the farmhouse of Martha, a retired schoolteacher and widow. But the couple is not alone-Lynnie has just given birth to a baby girl. When the authorities catch up to them that same night, Homan escapes into the darkness, and Lynnie is caught. But before she is forced back into the institution, she whispers two words to Martha: "Hide her." Charles Dickens likes to beat the shit out of his main characters. It's like a form of domestic abuse! Has he beaten the crap out of another character more than poor little Nell from The Old Curiosity Shop? Certainly Pip and Oliver get theirs. But at least with them there's some sort of happy ending or comeuppance for the villains. Like Little Dorrit without the uplifting ending, Nell is flat out beat down. Time and again she is taken advantage of and there is no redemption, not in my eyes. Sure, you could say that she gets to finish out her miserable life in a better place than where she started, but then she immediately dies. . What was wrong with Dickens? Why did he like to make his characters, and by proxy us, suffer so much? Yes, pitting characters against trials is important to keep up the tension and keep the reader's eyes locked on the page, but this is different altogether. It's as if the trial is over and all we see is the punishment. No, I can not say this is one of Dickens' more successful attempts at his brand of entertainment. He wrote of, quite literally, of hard times. England was not a pleasant place for the lower classes in the 19th century, especially in the 19th century. It was a time ripe for an author keen on social commentary. In the later half of the century, England birthed an author quite keen on telling it how it was while adding in some good old fashion story-time fun in the form of adventure and outlandish characters. Good as The Old Curiosity Shop is, however, it doesn't quite work on the whole. I think it's because Dickens forgot about the fun.

At the heart of this book, there is a devastatingly relatable story of human persistence in the face of personal grief, depression, and the harshness of the real world. Unfortunately, this isn't the story of our protagonist, Quentin Coldwater, who had a magical world dropped into his lap and has been complaining about it ever since. The reason this book shines in comparison to the first Magician's book is the fact that we get a big majority of the book told to us from the perspective of Julia, Quentin ex-schoolmate and rejectee from the magical school that gave Quentin his start. I'm not sure if it's intentional on the part of Grossman, but the contrast between the two figures starkly illustrates what having a privileged start in life can give you. Julia is working from scraps and building up skills while Quentin is whining about his magical textbooks and skilled instructors. They both make it to Fillory, but it's the way they got there that color their experience of the place. Julia's story is also one of the most accurate depictions of depression (as I personally experience it) that I've ever read in fiction. Her journey in the book feels intimate and real and devastating. What happens to her along the way is also interesting, particularly the examination of local Gods and the magical scene that exists where there are no magical texts to study. For someone like me, a depressive with no connection to the Ivy League whatsoever, Julia's magical world seems so much more accessible and possible than Quentin's. The actual plot happening in the main part of the book isn't all that interesting. A rather straightforward quest uncovers a larger problem that's solved in a rather straightforward way. There are a couple hiccups along the way, but each time a problem arises, a solution or help seems to drop right into Quentin's lap. Quentin despairs and nearly gives up at each obstacle. It's chance, not his character, that allows him and the plot to continue. It's only at the end of the book that we see him making a choice of any real consequence. Maybe I should cut Quentin a bit of a break. He's not entirely unaware of the privilege he has and since The Magicians he's managed to grow up a little bit. A little. And his persistent quest for an experience that feels like a children's fantasy novel come to life (while, admittedly, living in a children's fantasy novel come to life) isn't entirely unrelatable. But I can't help wondering what this book would have looked like without him. What would have happened if Julia had brought her magical cohorts to Fillory instead of joining Quentin's crew? It's an interesting thought, but one that I doubt Grossman will ever explore.

Posting this from my phone at camp, but I did love this book. When I saw this book was set in Paris I was immediately intrigued. Paris is such a historically rich location and I was curious to see how it as a backdrop would be used in the story. One of my favorite aspects of the book, probably because it's something I love to do, is Kate exploring her arrondissement by visiting cafes to find the perfect one for her. And when she does she sits in the corner with a good book and a cup of coffee and contentedly reads the hours away. You can tell Amy is intimately familiar with France by her subtle use of the language and references to places that fleshed out the reader's idea of Paris turning it into a realistic setting rather than an overly-described Google search. The one issue I had with it was the way that Kate and Vincent started their friendship. It would make sense that they first saw each other at the cafe as that's where Kate spent the majority of her time, but the subsequent meetings were bizarre and would have freaked me out if I were Kate - you can't get out of being creepy by telling a girl she's cute. "And the girl I've seen you around the neighborhood with would be your..." "Sister," I said slowly. "Have you been spying on me?" "Two cute girls move to the area - what am I supposed to do?" (p 37) Aside from the origins of their attraction I never felt that Kate was drawing away from everyone else due to her relationship with Vincent. In fact, she often spent time with Vincent's housemates and became good friends with them - and I loved them, too! Jules in particular was my favorite housemate with his flirtatious jokes yet when someone needed him he was right there. Kate's family was fun to visit and although we didn't see enough of them as I would have liked, the reasons for Kate not being home were entirely reasonable. (Going out after being depressed and staying in her room in a funk was a good sign for her them.) When Kate was at home it was easy to get a feel for just how close she and her sister, Georgia, were with her grandparents. I don't want to give too much away by talking about what a revenant is - although if you know French you probably have an idea - or where they came from, but the idea of them was something pretty original as far as paranormal themes are concerned and played a large part in why the book was so intriguing for me. By the end of the book I was rooting for Vincent, Kate and all of her new friends. This is a book that is perfectly fine to read as a stand-alone, but there will be more coming. Hats off to Amy Plum for a great debut.

Wrath and his brothers (The Black Dagger Brotherhood) are not like Vampires of lore. Vampires in J.R. Ward's world do not feed off of humans unless they need to but rather off of each other, or more specifically the opposite sex in their race. Human blood is just a poor substitute that does not give them strength. They only need to feed every few weeks, to months, depending. They eat regular food and while they heal quickly and can live for centuries they can be mortally wounded by gunshots and other attacks. So in this world of Ms. Ward's we have Vampires that seem rather normal compared to the Vampire lore we are use to. I loved this and it made it so much easier to connect and enjoy all the characters. Beth, our heroine, was amazing. She is half human, half vamp and doesn't know it. When shitake starts hitting the fan she freaks a little as most women would but then she becomes strong, very strong, once the shock wears off. She isn't going to take crap from anyone and she is so sure of herself. She falls quickly for someone and doesn't second-guess those feelings for maybe more than a day. The love in this book is quick but done right. I could believe the instant attraction between them and I could believe the love they quickly found in each other. Wrath, the big badass mother trucker, was so easy to fall for. He isolates himself because he feels tremendous guilt for actions out of his control centuries earlier. He is an Alpha male character, which I love. It was sweet to watch his transformation as his character grew and the love that he had inside him was amazing. The supporting characters, both vampire and human alike, were well-rounded, intriguing and great comedic relief when needed. Every person in this book helped balance it out in some way. This book hooked me, and I am eager to find out more about each of the other Brothers.

I'm late to the party on this series. After a couple of tries on the first book a few years ago, I finally decided to commit and read all of City of Bones. And it was pretty okay. I didn't love this book. Which isn't necessarily a bad thing. I'm not exactly its target demographic and there's nothing wrong with that. I know this series kind of became the new Twilight, but I enjoyed this first book much more than I enjoyed that entire series. The world building is well done. Clary, like Bella, is the kind of heroine that teenage girls are meant to project themselves onto, but isn't the largely passive character that Bella ends up being. The plot was interesting, even it was a bit predictable in terms of YA paranormal romance. I am going to complain about the main love triangle: Simon/Clary/Jace. Simon is Clary's best friend and has been in love with her for years. Clary is somehow oblivious to this, but I'll give her a pass because she's 15. Clary has the hots for Jace, the mysterious bad boy who turns out to be her brother! That was a twist I don't see much in this kind of book but it was still easy to spot with the clues given. I know that Jace and Clary are somehow not actually brother and sister (I'm late to the series but I don't live under a rock) so I'm kind of interested to see how uncomfortable the Fake Sibling Sexual Tension gets. Simon. SIMON. My dude. You do NOT get to get pissed off at the girl you like for liking other boys, especially if you've waited ten years to tell her you like her. I know it sucks, but that's on you. Also I do not understand why YA romances have to do this contrived plot almost every time, but whatever, I guess. I wasn't a fan of the Clary/Isabelle antagonism. It's the whole "Girls can't be friends. These girls are cool and only have Guy Friends because they're Cool Girls. Except they can't be Cool Girl Friends because the one who isn't the main character is a bitch." They do get over it in the end, so I'm hoping they'll develop a friendship over the course of the series. Overall, I thought it was pretty okay. At some point, I'll probably read the next book to see how things go.

There were parts of this book that were really exciting and interesting. And then there was the majority of it. Adelina was two-dimensional. Like, having a scar doesn't make you less of a Mary Sue-- and I don't even throw that term around lightly. She is beautiful, except for her "marking" and missing eye...but men still want her and gazes linger, etc. Other characters talk about how she might be the most powerful of all the elites, and I'm like...what exactly has given you that impression? Her power is useful, and as the reader I can see that it might end up as something more, but it isn't the MOST powerful out of the ones described. It just seemed like I was being told how dark she was and how much potential she has and there was nothing SHOWN to really back it up. Also, let's be real here... She's so "dark" because she has "dark" thoughts...like imagining killing her father. Her abusive father. Her abusive father who feeds her these dark thoughts. Like, who wouldn't image killing their physically and mentally abusive father? Or, look, some guy being a giant dick! She's having "dark" thoughts about some guy being a massive dick! HOW SHOCKING. She doesn't actually do anything dark. She didn't even kill her father. She spooked a horse and the HORSE killed her father. Her father was strangling her, so even if she HAD killed him directly, THAT WOULDN'T BE DARK. But she didn't. The horse did. And horses are easily spooked. So, it's not even a super dark kind of death. It was an accidental death that came from actions of self-defense. So. Having "dark" thoughts about people who have wronged you really isn't that dark. That's just normal. Sorry. And it wouldn't bother me so much if it wasn't shoved down my throat that she is supposed to be a "dark" character. Moving on. The romance felt forced. I like a light/background romance. I'm surprised to see other reviewers say that the romance in this was light. It was clearly built up so that we could have the shock ending  happen. But there was no reason for Enzo to like her. Some random girl that he hardly interacts with except to pretend to kill her/use her worst fears against her to bring out her powers. Waaaaait a second. That sounds familiar. Because I was wondering why SHE would like HIM, but now it makes sense. Daddy issues. If the romance hadn't been forced into the book, I actually would have liked it way better. The characters had no chemistry or reason to like each other. I DID enjoy the scenes with Adelina and Raffaele and Adelina with her sister. We got to see more of Adelina's personality in those interactions than we did anywhere else. (Although, the whole, "I'm so jealous of my sister because she was only SLIGHTLY abused" thing was irritating. Like, she acts as if her sister got to have everything, but it's very clear that this is not the case. Her sister was always trying to help her and obviously loved her, but Adelina doesn't want to see it. That is something that is a believable character flaw, but it didn't make me like Adelina.) So, yeah. If not for the forced romance and everyone telling me how dark and scary Adelina is when she totally isn't, I would have liked the book a lot better. The last 20% was pretty interesting, but by then I had stopped caring. I've seen people say that the second book is better, so I plan on giving it a try. But Adelina better personality up, or I'm not going to finish it. Oh, and P.S. When you are a top secret organization, you probably shouldn't let new recruits have ANY access to the outside world until you are 100% sure that you can trust them. Just kidding. Never 100% trust anyone when you are a top secret organization with some big plans coming up. Just saying.

I knew you wouldn't disappoint me Caletti, I just knew it. This book...gosh I don't even have the words to express how amazing this book was. Have you ever read a book that just made so much sense and connected to you in such a way that it left you thinking about it for days later? Because that's how I felt reading this book. "It wasn't fair for a person to shove himself at you again and again when you wanted them gone. We should have the right to have someone leave when we want, to only allow those in who we want in. But the truth is, people can force their way into your life whenever they choose. If they want to remind you forevermore that they exist, they will. They can reappear in a card or a call or a "chance" meeting, they can remember your birthday or the day you met with some innocuous small note. No matter how little they matter in your new life, they can insist on being seen and recognized and remembered." Clara the main character speaks to you in a way that no other character can. She tells her story, and she really connect with the reader. The thing that I loved most about this book is how real everything was. When we read story about a couple falling love it's always the same thing: girl likes boy, boy likes girl, they fall in love, the end. But in this story we find out what happens when you fall in love, and things don't turn out the way you hoped. Clara loved Christian and a part of her always will but the big difference between her and all the other girls in novels is that she knows when things have gone to far. She realizes their relationship is not healthy and even though a big part of her wants to be with him, she knows she needs to leave. "You read all kinds of books and see all kinds of movies about the man who is obsessed and devoted, whose focus is a single solid beam, same as the lighthouse and that intense, too. It is Heathcliff with Catherine. It is a vampire with a passionate love stronger than death. We crave that kind of focus from someone else. We'd give anything to be that "loved." But that focus is not some soul-deep pinnacle of perfect devotion - it's only darkness and the tormented ghosts of darkness. It's strange, isn't it, to see a person's gaping emotional wounds, their gnawing needs, as our romance? We long for it, I don't know why, but when we have it, it is a knife at our throat on the banks of Greenlake. It is an unwanted power you'd do anything to be rid of. A power that becomes the ultimate powerlessness." Obsession is not something that should be taken lightly, and I like how in this novel it truly opened my eyes to how serious it could get. I don't know about you guys but I've read a lot of books where the guy falls in love with the girl and it's almost like he's obsessed with her because "he can't get enough"; I used to think it was so romantic how he would get incredibly jealous and want her all to himself, but now I'm seriously questioning the authors message. In Stay, Clara makes it clear from the beginning how scary and not romantic it is when you can't even look at anyone without you're boyfriend accusing you of cheating and verbally abusing you. Deb Caletti really outdid herself in this book and it's honestly got to be my favorite one from her so far! It's really a shame that she doesn't get the attention she deserves, but I know for a fact that she will keep writing amazing stories that ultimately change peoples lives. Because this book definitely changed my life, and I don't think I'll ever be the same. You have to give this book a chance, trust me you will not be sorry. And not to keep ranting on but I have yet to read one bad review about this book, and that's probably because this book is so close to perfection it's almost impossible to not like it. This review is also on my blog World of Books

Two things popped into my mind while/after reading this book: Wow, I really needed this. I'll be damned if that wasn't the last time I judged a book by its review (from my favourite book-reviewer; LOVE her, but she can be wrong sometimes, wow). WARNING BECAUSE POTENTIAL SPOILERS if you haven't already read "Me Before You". The story follows Louisa as she struggles to move on from Will's death, and frankly, she's not doing a great job at it. The fascinating thing about it is that it wonderfully captures the process of bereavement, and you don't even need to have lost someone in death to be able to sympathize. Everyone in their lives has felt loss and not necessarily of the fatal kind. Losing a prized possession, or a significant other, or even failing at certain expectations. There is grief in all of those things, and this book not only helps capture that feeling of inadequacy that comes with wondering if the loss is something you could have prevented. The beautifully constructed interweaving of other people's lives into Louisa's allow her, and the reader, to come to an acceptance of what was, what is, and gives hope to what will be. This is the story of loss and recovery, the struggles of moving on, and cherishing those around you while they're still there. TL;DR - "Me Before You" broke me, but "After You" fixed me again. "It's not the same crushing grief at first, the kind that swamps you, and makes you want to cry in the wrong places[...] It's just something you learn to accommodate. Like adapting around a hole. I don't know. It's like you become... a doughnut instead of a bun."

Rating: 4 My opinion: After having just finished the first third of Dark Lover, I wrote one big paragraph on how the Black Dagger Brotherhood wasn't that hot, and how incredibly generic this book was. And you know what? It was. It was full of stereotypes at their best. Big, powerful, careless, arrogant man meets hot, innocent girl with an uneventful life, they have sex and fall in love. At some point he struggles with becoming weak and changing because of a *gasp* woman, she gets captured/goes through some kind of torture and when he saves her he just knows he can't live without her. Him being a vampire and her a half-human aka weak was just the cherry on top. The fact that they literally fucked the first moment they saw each other doesn't really help the case. In spite of all this, it was enjoyable. At a certain point, I fell in love with each member of Brotherhood, got to like Beth, and rooted for Wrath. I don't know exactly how or when it happened, but it did. Suddenly, I got used to all those stereotypes and just appreciated all the good things they had to offer. I'm not sure why I'm so surprised, to be honest. After all, there's a reason why cliches became such, right? All those things aside, LET'S TALK ABOUT THE CHARACTER WHY THIS WHOLE BOOK IS WORTH READING. The brothers? The cops? The chicks? The bad guy? Not really. Those are okay, BUT YOU KNOW WHO IS ABSOLUTELY AWESOME Fritz, the butler. I mean, I couldn't stop grinning every single time he opened his mouth. Usually, overnice people make me want to punch babies to restore the balance of the universe. But this old man. Dude, THIS OLD MAN. I have no words to describe my love for him. I tend to be a sucker for valets and butlers for some reason, but this one takes the bigger prize. He was cuter than a kitty! So, now I get why all the fuss, whether it's my thing or not. I really hope to learn more about the Brotherhood and maybe tune down the Mr. X's parts because they slowed down the book. I'm also waiting for Butch and V's love story. *whispers* Can we get Fritz's point of view? "Welcome to the wonderful world of jealousy, he thought. For the price of admission, you get a splitting headache, a nearly irresistable urge to commit murder, and an inferiority complex." - Alive or Undead ~ 2013 -

In a dystopian near-future United States, criminals are no longer incarcerated, but instead publically shamed by having their skin color altered to shades like red (murderers), blue (child molesters), or yellow (felons). Religious conservatism has grown into a far more powerful political and social force, Roe vs. Wade has been overturned, and many states treat abortion as murder. Against this background, the author reimagines the story of Nathaniel Hawthorne's Scarlet Letter, as an evangelical Christian young women found guilty of having an abortion wakes up to find her entire body is now scarlet. This was very well-done and an enjoyable read. I liked the writing, and the characters' actions and attitudes were mostly believable. The author is great at keeping the tension and suspense high, making this a page-turner. In the course of the story, we get some musings on the nature of faith, fundamentalism, social repression and rebellion, liberalism, and God, and I felt like these musings for the most part were interesting, often insightful, and not too heavy-handed. I did have a hard time swallowing the main character's sudden jump into actions very foreign to her original belief system, which seemed like they would have required a longer psychological transition in reality (FYI, for those who are bothered by such things, there's a lesbian love scene, though as I recall it wasn't explicit and was tastefully done - personally as I say I was bothered just on believability grounds ). I'm not sure she needed to hew quite as closely to Nathaniel Hawthorne's story as she did, e.g., with the character names being so similar. But I loved the creativity of the high-concept plot.

2.5 stars. All of the 2.5 stars are for a great idea and good prose. I'm a child of the internet and I'm pretty weathered in the "things that shock me" department, so my rating isn't really a commentary on how fucked up the plot is. There were some eyebrow-raising parts, but nothing that I couldn't power through. As a primer, in Geek Love we're taken through the life and times of Olympia "Oly" Binewski, who now goes by Olympia McGurk, an albino hunchback dwarf who spent her entire childhood in a traveling circus/freak show ("fabulon" is what it's called in the book, and I apologize because I don't really know what to call it) run by her parents, Aloysius and Lily. And that's about the most basic, tame part of the whole book. It's a ride from start to finish. Oly has a number of siblings, all of whom were intentionally engineered to be born abnormally by Al and Lil, who experimented through each of Lil's many pregnancies with various combinations of drugs designed to produce unusual offspring. This can all pretty much be found in any summary of this book. Goodreads's summary also includes this information, and this is where Dunn (or the jacket copy writer) loses me: "Geek Love throws its sulfurous light on our notions of the freakish and the normal, the beautiful and the ugly, the holy and the obscene." So here's the thing. I think a book of this type really does have the potential to say something, or many things, about able bodies, societal standards of beauty, self-image, bioethics, religion, and normativity. Seriously, all of that! Yeah, it definitely does. But this book doesn't say any of it. We as readers spend pretty much no time on the ethical implications of the decisions made in this book to intentionally deform children, so much so that I assume we're not supposed to empathize with the idea. And yet... the Binewski kids love their deformities, derisively call others "norms," and emphatically believe that they would not choose to be born "normal" if given the choice. We also see Arty's church of people who willingly deform themselves, another group of people we spend a lot of time hearing about but whose choices are never empathetically justified to the reader. I struggle to see the larger picture. I want books to shine some light on dark, ugly corners of society, and to me, this book just creeps into dark, ugly corners without telling me why we're there (besides to creep me out). I also had real problems with the pacing, which is why I specified above that the prose was good but didn't say "the writing." For the first third of the book, we're keeping pace evenly with the past (time in the circus) and the future (Oly is 39 and living in "regular society" in Portland). Gradually, this goes wonky until we get a crazy long stint of past time toward the end of the book, followed by a short denouement in the present, followed by the end of the book. I was really captivated by the long stint of past time--it contains the rising action and climax--but it didn't work for me given the layout of the first part of the book, even though it did retain my attention. The climax itself, which I won't spoil, was also very briefly described and disappointing for something that's such a big deal.

I'm sorry. I'm so, so sorry... I tried, I really did try to enjoy this book. I don't think I've ever wanted to enjoy a book this badly before. Each time I read more of this book, I'd get bored and wonder why I'm even bothering, but kept going in hopes that it got better. My main issue with this book is that we're thrown into this wonderful new version of London, but we aren't told any background. We're just expected to accept this new world and everything in it. I'm sorry, but our first real experience with this new world is two freight trains battling it out to the death and we never really get any explanation as to what that was all about. Then there's the main bad guy, Reach. I still don't know if he's tangible or just an idea or what. I guess he builds these cranes all over the place that are going to destroy the city, but I just don't get what's going on. I enjoyed the minor characters so much more than the two main ones. Beth and Filius just accept each other without question. OHEY CAN I HELP YOU DEFEAT THIS BIG BAD GUY YEAH OKAY or THERE ARE THESE BIG THINGS THAT YOU'VE NEVER HEARD OF BEFORE AND WE'RE PART OF YOUR CITY YEAH THAT MAKES TOTAL SENSE LETS GO RUN AWAY TOGETHER Without. Questioning. Anything. I'd rather hear more about Pen and about Beth's father. I guess we might have learned more about them later on, but I couldn't get that far. I want to know more about how Beth's father is coping with the loss of his wife, and now with the fact that Beth has basically run away. I want to know more about Pen's life at home and how her parents are so overbearing and what exactly is going on with her and the maths teacher. I think he sexually assaulted her, but I'm not 100% sure... Hell, I would have even liked to learn more about Beth's role as a street artist. We got very little of that. Really, everything but the mystical portion of this book worked for me, which is very odd because I usually love this kind of book. I mean, I loved the idea of this new world of London, I really did. I just think we needed for background on it because it's so different. This book had so much potential and I really wish I could have finished it. I'm sure it has appeal to others, it just wasn't a book for me.

How do I feel about this book? I think I'm on neutral right now. It's interesting enough to get me through the entire book but I was looking for the  WOW  factor, and I didn't feel any. Like I said, I'm cutting the book some slack because it's only the first installment and it could get better (I hope). The story was okay but a little bit slow. The development of the story and the characters were not that noticeable. Though there were a few exciting moments like when Claire was shove into Monica's car.The scene when  Oliver and the cops were trying to break in the Glass house, which was supposed to be somewhat climatic fell a little flat for me. I was like "Oh, they were being hoarded. Some of the enemies made it in. Okay, they were running hiding a few clawing from the girls while Michael was chucking the enemies out of the house. That was it? I wished there were more. Fight scenes were a little sloppy too." *shrugs* That's just my opinion. You know what I don't understand? How come there's always a misfit plain looking transfer student, a pretty bitch bully and a dorm or boarding school in a lot of books these days, especially the YA genre. Is there a YA writing rules that the readers should know about? Are these the basic foundation of YA novels? Moving on to the characters: Eve and Michael- I really don't have anything bad to say about them. Eve's character seems very realistic. I would love to have a friend like her. Michael, the house daddy and the cool, calm responsible one is very likable. I wish he would return to normal, or at least they could do something about his situation. Claire and Shane- I like Claire's "no quitting" attitude. I'm like that too. :) So, she's supposed to be really smart right? then how come she's always doing stupid stuff like getting herself and her friends in trouble. She doesn't do what she's told even though it's for her own safety. Yeah, this is what I really hate about heroines. Doing stupid stuff and getting into shit that could have been avoided if only she listened to others. Enough of Claire, let's go to Shane. He's nice enough, "hot" enough and reliable enough. He's hero complex was a little difficult to swallow but I think he's an okay character. I didn't feel him that much, or rather I wasn't able to grasp who he really is. I hope the next book would solve that. :P Lastly, I HATE CLIFFHANGERS! WTF was that?! I was left literally dangling! What the freak happened?! I'll read the next book okay?! No need to do the shitty cliffhangers. Dammit! Not fair!

*Galley received for free from Netgalley* This was a really cute and refreshing read. The characters and circumstances felt really real and honest. I really enjoyed Sam's character. He felt like a real boy. His actions and reactions were realistic and true. I did not feel the same about Ally. For some reason, her inner self did not come across as clearly as Sam's, which was odd considering this was all in first person narrative. I would have liked to have seen more clearly into her feelings, especially as they portrayed to Sam. I never really knew what was truly going on in her head, and in first person that should be fairly obvious. Also, with as frank and as sexual as the dialogue was, I felt like the love scenes were a big let down. Not that I expected anything descriptive, I didn't. But they were all pretty much fade-to-black with not even really any of the build up present. This was a mature book, it seemed like the "mature" scenes didn't need to be completely left out. And bigger than "seeing" the subject of this entire book being played out, we don't even get a good grasp on how the characters are feeling about all this sex they're having. It's like it doesn't even matter. I mean  when Ally and San start having sex, why doesn't this seem like a big deal (at least to Ally). She doesn't seem to care at all. We don't see her really thinking about what this could mean to their lifelong friendship. She just wants him physically--along with other guys at the same time. All that just felt kind of...Blech...to me. It felt unrealistic. I needed more if the emotional stuff, because that was quite flat, to be honest. All in all, this was an enjoyable read. I would definitely recommend it to older teens and young adults.

This book left me absolutely heartbroken. All I want to do is reach out to give Conor a hug. Again, I must reiterate the point that all reviews are spoilers of varying extents. You either find out about the tone of the book, certain things others got out of the book (hence making you look out for them), about certain characters, or the reader's reaction to the book (if it made me cry, you'd expect it to be written a certain way). This is one of those books where I would rather you go in blind/fresh/clueless or just knowing very little. But because I enjoy rambling under the guise of discussion... Conor's behaviour and reaction to his circumstances gripped my heart. I felt for him, and I found myself relating to him. All of which meant I would finish a chapter and take in a deep breath, realizing I had been taking very shallow breaths (not holding my breath, obviously, I'd be dead). There are many things I wish to bring up, but I feel highly ill-equipped to do so. The symbolism of the Monster. The stories. Conor's decision. Conor's need for normalcy. Thoughts vs Action. Reading this book felt like I was expanding my capacity for sympathy for others, and more so, a personal let-it-go awakening. No, please don't sing the song to me, I've worked too hard to get it out of my head. The same with the 'bad' thoughts I've had. These are just thoughts, and there is no need to feel overly guilty about them, because at the end of the day it is my actions that count, the product of the thought(s) I choose to entertain and eventually act out. The book put the internal struggles, and coming to terms with oneself, beautifully into words. I will always hold this book dear to my heart.

I received this book for free through Goodreads First Reads giveaway and would like to thank the author Tracy Clark for this opportunity. (This is an honest review) I enjoyed this book very much and I give it a 3.5 stars. Pretty well executed book that had a good plot and was interesting enough to keep me reading more to see what would happen next albeit the romance in this novel was way too cheesy. First off, instalove? Check. Proclaiming their "love" for each other after a few meetings? Check. I let that one slide since it really was due to the fact that Finn is an Arrazi and Cora is Scintillate so he was sort of 'feeding' off her energy  Love triangle? Check. Love rival who instantly took a liking to her, supposedly just by her looks? Check. okay, I admit it was because of the both of them having silver auras and things get charged whenever they touch or are near each other But it doesn't stop there, I found it a little annoying the amount of times Cora wanted to kiss Finn throughout the book or how near the end of the book she couldn't forgive him because he was the one thing that was supposed to be her enemy yet she still claimed to love him. I hope things get cleared up between them in the next book, I really want them to end up together! Hopefully Finn doesn't die!! It was a nice change of pace to read about a main character that wasn't just plain Caucasian, like most of the books these days, but every time I read a book about the main character being half Asian/African/Hispanic or other nationality, I noticed that it's a defining factor, yes, but the authors ALWAYS mention the main character's nationality. I swear I cannot go a few pages without the main character making a reference about their roots or whatever and that just about annoys me. I can't help but think that in Scintillate, the author wanted to be different than everybody else and so they made their MC someone non-Caucasian and decided to remind us of that fact every. single. freaking. second. Like, yeah, I get it; you don't have to keep reminding me that she's different; it's bad enough that she has powers and stuff. But near the end of the book, it made sense why Cora was half Chilean. The fact that they had unique "powers", well Cora could read auras, and how it was incorporated with the Irish culture was interesting and unique. I enjoyed how the story was told but at times I wanted it to get moving, enough of the kissing and stuff, and I was glad near the end of the book with all that action that happened, plus a lot of secrets being revealed but then it left with lots of questions as it ended, which is a good thing it's a trilogy. I will definitely be looking forward to the next book in the series and seeing the characters come back and grow into their powers and destiny that they were chosen for. Especially looking forward to the interesting twists and turns and new concepts of the world Tracy Clark created. Possibly a Finn and Cora reunion, too!

After the Kate Daniels series by Ilona Andrews, the October Daye series by Seanan McGuire is probably my next favorite urban fantasy series of all time. If you are into mysteries and detective stories or like fantasy with really deep mythologies or think that putting them together is even better then this series is for you. It also has lots of Shakespeare references and there is a love interest here named Tybalt King of Cats... I mean..... I've loved all the previous books in this series and while I did really enjoy the series I had to mark it down one star for the pacing and some repetitiveness in this book. Normally most of the October Daye books has October running place to place trying to solve a crime or other mystery and it's very fast paced. It was interesting in A Red-Rose Chain that here October is sort of forced in a situation where she can't run anywhere and she just has to wait and see in what creative ways her enemies are trying to kill her and her allies. It felt somewhat frustrating, which I'm sure the author intended, but I didn't really enjoy that aspect of it. Also while I didn't mind as much at first when McGuire kept nearly killing or outright killing October several times each book it begins to really get old by book NINE. But aside from those gripes I still liked the book a lot and highly recommend the series for urban fantasy fans.

Nobody does multiple points of view like David Mitchell, and this book is another great example. It may lack the sweeping grandeur of Cloud Atlas or Ghostwritten, but it more than compensates with an absorbing, emotional and dark tale set in Japan. The first half is slow, and it does lend itself to small bites. Yet it is still engaging. As it gathers pace, the story becomes compelling, building toward a wonderful climax. As with all of Mitchell's work, it is beautifully and flawlessly written. The prose, sometimes stunning, never gets in the way of the story, as is the case with some literary authors. The flaws? I did find the naivety of Jacob de Zoet and Orito a little overplayed, and there were several occasions where they failed to pick up on hints or events that seemed blatantly obvious. Some of the plot twists, such as the true purpose of Shiranui, were easily guessed. This didn't spoil my enjoyment of the story, however. There are few authors out there at the moment who can compete with Mitchell at his best.

Where She Went is the follow-up to If I Stay, and revisits the characters of Mia and Adam three years after the conclusion of the first novel. Adam is a rock star. Mia is a cello prodigy. They have since broken up, but reunite by chance in New York City one night. For the most part, this book stayed true to character. Mia was spot on, and it was interesting to finally get into Adam's head, though he is decidedly different from his character in If I Stay. It was also believable as a story. With Mia's talent, it's plausible that she would've become such a young success, and while I thought it was a little silly to basically make Shooting Star the punk One Direction, I could still believe it. This is definitely not a standalone book (or I suspect it would be much less successful on its own)- it is a clear follow-up to If I Stay. That being said, I thought Forman developed Mia and Adam's characters quite well in a totally new setting. It was smart to jump ahead three years, making it a new story that still ties in well to the original book. The use of flashbacks was once again really successful in telling two stories at once. I was surprised by how Adam was honestly a really unpleasant character for most of the novel, though. I get that in part, he's jaded that Mia broke up with him, but I thought sometimes Forman relied a little too heavily on the "disillusioned rock star" cliche. His internal monologue was incredibly bitter after Mia said almost anything, which was a little much at points. I would've loved to see more of Adam that didn't revolve solely around Shooting Star or Mia - for example, where's his family in all this? There was also a great moment where he talked about how attached he had been to Teddy that I would've loved to have seen elucidated a little more. I'm still not totally sure how I feel about the ending of this book. I thought it would've had more emotional impetus if Adam actually let Mia go and went on with his own life. The two of them seemed unhealthily intertwined with each other, and it almost paralleled the end of If I Stay - Mia stayed because of Adam, then Adam became himself again because of Mia. It's tricky, because I think it also would've been unsatisfying in a different sense if they had just gone their separate ways, but the ending as it stood felt a little too contrived, a little too much like wrapping everything up into a nice little package. I think it would've been more successful if their relationship had still been rocky at the end, but they were working towards getting back together. Where She Went was a good read, and I think fans of If I Stay will enjoy it. It is weaker than the original story, but still a good continuation of it.

Insurgent: Like a Deflated Balloon that had Plot Diarrhoea I am sorry, dear lovelies, for actually writing this book review. I mean Roth as a writer is not as bad as I will make her out to be, and there may even be some people in the world that will love her books with a passion that would rival Genghis Khan's passion for committing horrific war crimes. But tell me readers, how am I ever going to give this book a good review if I can't even remember what happened in it? One of my friends read Divergent back in 2011, and she hadn't bothered to find Insurgent until 2014, why? Because the rest of our peers were going through the Divergent hype (because of the movie, duh! Which I still have to watch...). It just wasn't that interesting! A lot happened in Insurgent. Too freakin' much. Especially since most of the focus on the whole series was on the city when a little birdie told me that Allegiant is where the dystopia aspect hits the freaking fan. Next to nothing in Divergent and a freaking Plot Vomit in Insurgent? NO! Please. Roth, I had high expectations, and I do love this story. But I don't love the books. I think Divergent and Insurgent should have merged into one book (because a LOT is unnecessary to the story's ultimate goal) and focus more on Allegiant and what happens after Tris gets freaking -- shot! And Tris is a horrible narrator. She is a strong character yes, and I do admire her for that. But she isn't a reliable narrator (and there's no actual need for an unreliable narrator with this plot). Good Things (because it can't have been THAT bad if I'm going to read the third book!) The romance was a lot more realistic in Insurgent, and it served a purpose. There was none of that insta-love hanky panky like in Divergent. It's a WONDERFUL PLOT, and I have to commend Roth for keeping the suspense and tension on an all time high (which she doesn't know how to cap off - uhum, spoiler). I don't know why, but the world building was a lot better (I still don't get the trains), and I'm expecting good world-building in Allegiant too. And Roth deserves credit for actually making sure that stuff did happen in Insurgent, unlike the total manual-like format of Divergent - yay, she joined a faction, yay she fell in love, yay Eru-freaking-dite(! Roth isn't a bad writer, and all I'm saying is that I'd love this series all the more if some parts were tweaked here and there so it would be a better reading journey. But I love the idea, and I love how real Tris is (if I end up disliking some parts of her character and liking other parts then you know you've done something good by going for the 3D effect). I LOVE Tobias (and movie Tobias is hot - ain't gonna lie there) and cannot wait to watch the movie and put some images to these words. Can't wait to read Allegiant and finally be done with this series too, and hopefully I'll be able to fend off my dystopia addiction for a while too.

Lizzie and Diesel are after another magic stone - the one for lust. They go on a magical scavenger hunt across Boston trying to stay one step ahead of Wulf and his assistant Hatchet, and the truly evil Dierdre or does she go by Anarchy now? Carl the monkey says 'eep'. I think I read book 1 as a library borrow. Honestly I can't remember. And that's the issue with these books. They are an easy read. But I read 103 pages the first night and could not say what it was about the next morning. It just slides past. And not because it's easy reading. What was that old saying about easy reading was hard writing? Not here; it's just fluff. That's fine, if that is all you want. But do not expect anything to strain the little grey cells here. It is supposed to be a magical realism world. Lizzie is an 'unmentionable'. They each have different skills and there are some unexplainable things that they do. She met Diesel in book 1. Here, he's still around because he needs her to help him. She can tell which object is magic; that's her special skill. Diesel can find things. His cousin Wulf is the dark Diesel. Wulf's helper Hatchet is just... singularly annoying with his constant medieval speech. The agency that Diesel works for provides him with everything he needs. His car blows up, a new one is delivered. He has endless credit for shopping sprees. His assistants walk out the door carrying a large framed Van Gogh painting, a movable model and something else (I've forgotten) and they disappear within seconds. And no, they didn't get in a car because they just drove two there for Lizzie and Diesel. There's magic realism and there's handwavium. And Glo? I have no words for Glo. Even if it is magic, it has to follow the rules. The magic stones they are searching for engender each sin. I remember now that gluttony was in book 1 and it made Lizzie overeat. Here, she holds the stone of lust (transformed into the stone of true love) and it doesn't affect her. Or her friends. Evanovich has a formula and this series is the same. There's even a Grandma Masur character - an old man, Sandman, who can bend spoons. It's a 2 1/2 but sliding towards 2 stars. Wulf constantly disappears in clouds of smoke like an amateur magician. A person's magic shop gets burnt down and she just says it's okay because she was over-insured and wanted to rebuild. wtf? Hatchet slices Glo up with a knife and she still thinks he's okay. He's creepy and messed up. Even Wulf can see that. 2 stars

2 1/2 stars When I first heard Neil Peart would collaborate with author Kevin J. Anderson on a fiction project connected to the latest Rush album, I was intrigued. For about two years, since the release of the band's single "Caravan," we waited for something - anything - resembling a larger project that might necessitate a tour for support. The hardcore fan base saw that wish realized with the release of Clockwork Angels the album (which I do enjoy) and the corresponding novel of the same time, which crafts the various themes of Peart's songs into a story that blends steampunk and fantastic imagery with the humanist ideals for which the band is known. If you follow Rush religiously (sorry for the pun), you may find the former elements curious, since steampunk isn't something one would associate with them. Having browsed Anderson's bibliography, steampunk doesn't appear to be a major genre for him, and I would hesitate to place Clockwork Angels the novel solely in this category. As I read the story I didn't get a true sense of time to go with the settings - odd considering time is a primary theme. One could see this as a fantasy or dystopian adventure as well. Anderson and Peart's clockwork world is comprised of a few major continents and cities with names drawn from mythology and ancient tradition: Posiedon City, Atlantis, and Albion...an ancient name for the island of Great Britain. Here the people seem more apt to pursue manual labor, save for those who study at the Alchemy College. We are told that the country of Albion had suffered turmoil and crime before the appearance of the benevolent and enigmatic Watchmaker. For the following two hundred years through the present day, Owen's bucolic home of Barrel Arbor, the more cosmopolitan Crown City, and surrounding villages live in peace and punctuality. You can literally set your watch by everything that happens, from the distribution of national news to changes in the weather. All is for the best, as the Watchmaker is known to proclaim, and few people argue with those words. The two who do challenge this order have different motives. Owen seeks adventure and the opportunity to live out a story he can tell his grandchildren one day; the legendary Clockwork Angels who parrot the Watchmaker's maxims draw him to Crown City, and the wonder of a traveling carnival entices him to extend his journey. The story's antagonist, the Anarchist, creates havoc in hopes of waking people to the realization that the Watchmaker doesn't exactly have Albion's best interests at heart. The way he carries on, of course, makes one wonder if the Anarchist's view of the world is any better. In keeping with the story's connection to Clockwork Angels the album, an assortment of song lyrics and characters provide ample references, perhaps a bit much. A reader more familiar with Anderson's work than Rush's may be able to breeze through the book without making many connections, but I have to admit I found the Easter egg-style lines distracting at times. Anderson doesn't limit himself to the recent album, either, in this respect. A character shouts, "Presto!" and I know there's more to it than the parlor trick he's performing. What disappoints me more about this book, however, is the overall style. Between the many instances of telling instead of showing (and this is not another song reference) and repetitiveness of narrative and dialogue (more than once the author has Owen recapping his adventures and echoing lines) made it difficult for me to appreciate the story. I get the impression, too, that maybe the author hoped to attract the YA reading audience in addition to Rush's older fan base. Owen's young age and the dialogue may imply that, but I think of other books I've read in the dystopian YA genre (most notably The Hunger Games) and find them more sophisticated in style and dialogue. Clockwork Angels had the potential to deliver a thought-provoking adventure, but the writing just didn't grab me. When I think of the other Anderson/Peart collaboration, the story "Drumbeats" (reviewed on this blog), I find I enjoyed that more. For its length, "Drumbeats" is a tighter story with better dialogue - it is also in first person, which makes me wonder if Anderson had attempted Clockwork Angels in that POV would the story be improved. Will you like this book more if you're a Rush fan? You certainly don't have to be one to read it. The book hasn't changed my perception of the album, but I do know I'll revisit the songs more than the story.

I'm not sure how to do this review. It's not that I have no words for this. In fact, I have plenty but this book touches on so many debatable topics that it makes it hard to review. So I'll try to focus on characterization, setting and the other usual stuff. First of all, I recommend this for a MUCH older crowd. Like I said, many debatable topics. What I liked: -The setting was perfect. Locked elevators that needs keycards, servers that won't look the wives in the eyes, one floor for all the wives with no way out, a creepy basement and so much more eeriness. The world building was really unique. It's set in the future but humanity and science has regressed. People are dying at 20 for females and 25 for males due to a virus. -I love how the mood did a fantastic job matching the setting. This is a depressing book where all hope is lost. People are desperate for a cure and would do anything, even immoral means to discover one. I really felt that when Rose and Jenna died. Cecily will never have her baby. So if you don't want to read a depressing book then do not read this. -The characterization of the three wives: Rhine, Cecily, and Jenna. They were all very developed and defined. Each one matched their age perfectly and I love the bond between them despite their bittersweet end. What I didn't like: -The romance...ugh...seriously, somebody suggest me a book with a good romance. I really don't know what happened this week. This is the 5 review that I will be doing where the first bullet point for What I Didn't Like is about romance. Again, another book with an insta-love. Although, I am letting this book off the hook for that because of setting of the book. When you're in a world where time is so precious and life is so hopeless, the first sign of kindness will very much likely send you on a romance train. BUT I will not let it escape my notice, that the romance in this book was weird. So Rhine starts falling for one of her servants but they barely interact and he spends half of the book not being present. There's also, what I would perceive as an attempted love triangle of some sort. So Rhine is supposed to be one of Linden's wives. She despises him for being her captor but there are moments in the book where Rhine even mentions that he makes her forget that. -Linden has got to be the most gullible and easily manipulated male character I've ever read about. I didn't like that he was super emotional but I can't count that against him. He has every right to be emotional considering the fact that he only has a few years left and he has to spend it without the love of this life. I get how depressing that is but this guy does not know the first thing going on in his house. -Rhine is smart enough and manipulative enough to know what to say and gain other people's trust. She really does plan to escape and always has this optimism that really is futile to even have but I love that about her because it makes the story more real. I didn't like that she is not as observant about her surroundings and always acts at the worst possible timing. You have this character that has every great quality to achieve things but she can't put things into action because she sucks at it. That's what Rhine is like. I mean seriously, the whole damn house knew about her relationship with Gabriel except maybe the ever so gullible Linden and she doesn't see that. -The ending was laughable. The book spent so much emphasis on having that place completely inescapable that when she finally does in the end of the book, it was all to easy. I found very dissatisfying. It was a good book but I haven't decided if I'm going to continue on the series. I like the book but I'm not sure if I'm ready for another depressing book.

4.5 stars (both times I read it) Her Ladyship's Companion was the second courtesan-themed book I read in February. The irony of reading about buying love with money right around Valentine's Day does not escape me, but perhaps the real irony is that these two books have been the most romantic I have read in months. I LOVED this book. I loved the premise, so unusual in a historical - a reverse Pretty Woman, if you will and it was done well so that I believed it. I believed the characters: Isabella, lonely and isolated, estranged from her family, alone in her home in Scotland. Gideon, in his own way just as lonely as Isabella. No family to speak of, living a lifestyle that precludes friendships, saving every penny to someday escape the life and have a family of his own. The sun hung low on the horizon, streaking magenta across a sky that faded to deepest midnight. One could see nothing but open acres framed in the distance by thick woods. It was pleasing to the eye but felt secluded from the world. Now he knew why he was here. Lady Stirling was lonely. Well, at least we have something in common, he thought sardonically. But he had long ago realized physical acts could not fill the void where a family should reside. If anything, it made the emptiness reverberate with a painful echo that drove home just how alone he was in the world. Isabella's loneliness comes right off the page right from the beginning of the book. She blames herself for her arranged marriage, for her family's precarious financial situation and even for the fact that she is ostracized by her brothers. She believes herself to be unworthy and wicked, although the latter is completely unwarranted. Gideon's history was so believable, his goals so realistic and his vulnerability so appealing I fell in love with him just as Bella did. The author does a beautiful job of showing how Gideon 'works' , how attentive he is to his 'client', and how he keeps his mind separate from what he does with his body. He knows almost instinctively what she needs, and most importantly when to enforce the boundaries of their relationship. Gideon has rules. No sex without contraception. He never spends the night. He never loses control. Ever. Oh, to watch these two meet, feel their initial attraction to one another, to get to know one another, then  have lots of really, really hot sex everywhere!!!!! and finally fall in love is really well done. The obstacles to their relationship, the misunderstandings, the heartbreak, the desperation, are all SO real. How do you give your body but not your heart? How do you keep him coming back? How do you ask him to stay? How do you quit the life? What will your family say? How would you make a life together? How do you go on when you have given up everything just for a chance to see her? How do you live when you think you will never see him again? Of course, there is much more to the story than I have even mentioned here. Gideon and Bella are just the main part. How they got to where they are when we meet them, the person that brings them together, the people and circumstances that tear them apart, and how they manage to find each other and stay together made for a engrossing, compelling read that had me staying up way too late to finish, and made me want to sigh once I was done. I read this twice while I had it out from the library. While I loved the book, I don't want to say it was perfect, either. There were some things that didn't hold up completely for me. The ending was maybe a little bit convenient, and on second read I thought Bella was a little bit over-the-top . I believe the term we used back in high-school was a "fuckmonster". She's a 3 orgasm girl once she gets going, and it got to be a bit much after a while. There were other things I liked even more about the book the second time, though, and that outweighed any little things I noticed. I loved the writing. Evangeline Collins has a style I like very much. It was moody, a bit angsty, very compelling. I loved her characterizations: nuanced, with great depth and they seem very real. She lets you get to know them a bit at a time, so that you can see what each sees in the other. I loved the book. Now that I've had to give it back to the library, I'm off to hunt down my own copy for my keeper shelf. And to buy Evangeline Collin's next book. And while I'm on the subject, I need to say this about the cover: It is the prettiest I've seen in a long time. The couple on the cover resemble the couple in the book, and the pose evokes the story within in a subtle way that doesn't become really clear until you've finished the book. (I'll just say this - when Gideon first comes to Bowhill Park, it is Bella that pursues. It is she who falls first, and after I read the book, I saw that in the cover. Maybe it's just me, or maybe the person in charge of the cover actually read the book.)
Yes, I really did buy a book because of it's cover. And I adored this story.
