Every book I read in the Vorkosigan Saga just makes me love Lois McMaster Bujold more. They're just fantastic. I happened to have Komarr and A Civil Campaign with me at the same time, and the time to read them, so I read both of them in the same day. I do recommend reading them back-to-back, since they feed into each other quite well. Komarr is Miles's first job (mostly) as an official Auditor, although he's partnered with a more experienced Auditor too, and it's their job to smooth things over and find out the truth on Komarr after an incident that threatens to cause problems for Gregor's upcoming marriage to his Komarran bride, Laisa. It also adds a new point-of-view character, Ekaterin, who is just 100% fantastic. I love her so muuuuch. She's a badass, and she's kind, and I can't really say much more about her without spoilers. But suffice it to say that she is a fantastic character, who joins the myriad of other strong female characters that Bujold writes. Also, Miles definitely is coming into his own, here. He still spends a little too much time stuck in his own head, but he is growing out of that, which is good. After his crisis in Memory, he seems to have figured some stuff out.

Very unexpected book... had so much promise and such a great start, and yet, somehow, it devolved in the last 2/3rds of the book. The book is told in dual POVs of our main characters: Tasha and Dylan. My first thoughts were "finally! ", because these two characters were My first thoughts were along the lines of FINALLY, main characters who are intelligent, communicate, and don't jump to conclusions! The book is told in 1st person POV through Tasha's eyes. So yes, there is reality expressed in her inner thoughts, some self-doubt, certainly. But Dylan (our hottie Dom) is usually calm, cool, and willing to explain. Yes, events happen very quickly. Dylan spots Tasha within the first few pages, and they're connected in that "instant" way. I like that the two characters acknowledge that. And some of Dylan's nicknames are cute. Except, I agree with Tasha about the Precious nickname that he insists on using:I can't help myself. I've never been a fan of nicknames, especially ones that make me think of Gollum wandering around looking for his ring. The problems start occurring as the mystery/suspense part unfolds... while it's not tough to figure out the WHO in whodunnit, the how and why are strange. Out of nowhere, we get information about Tasha's best friend Holly that Tasha should have had a clue about if they've really been friends all that long. And you'd think that Tasha would realize her hubby was into drugs, too, especially as a dealer! Sorry, but I felt that all the wonderful potential in this book was lost to the strangeness of the motives, but also to Dylan's over-the-top Dom demeanor. I get his possessiveness of Tasha, but it doesn't take more than a look or a simple touch from another guy, even his best friend, and Dylan's punching first and asking questions later. But I do like Tommy... and the next book is about him. IF I can get that book for free or for a bargain price, I might be interested. Then again, Holly seems to be Tommy's love interest in that book... after all Holly is made out to be by the end of this book, that pairing is more than a little unusual.

Rating: 3.5 - 4ish (I'm being picky today) Life just gets creepier as the series continues. Note: I marked the summary as a spoiler from here on but it doesn't spoil anything from this book, just the previous two in the series. Alex almost led a second successful escape from the lower levels of the Furnace, but it didn't work. Now, he is caught, and the venom that destroyed Donovan is running through him. As the Warden continues his experiments and tries to turn Alex into a tool of his own, Alex is forced to battle the poison of the nectar that is being pumped through him in order to remember the one thing that can keep him connected to humanity: his name. But when his own face becomes a stranger to him, Alex has left his prison-self behind and has become one of the blacksuits he detested. This book takes you through Alex's transformation, and how his friends either life or die in the process. Most of the book is dedicated to life on the lower levels and the Warden's creepy experiments, but in part of the novel, you will get another glimpse back of what life is within the prison part of the Furnace where the inmates are still living in complete fear. This one has a little less action in it, and a lot more of the intellect behind the experiments and the larger plans that the Warden and Alfred Furnace have for the inmates. There are a couple scenes that talk about how the experiments had started as part of WWII, and explain more about what the goals of them are. Throughout the story and as Alex changes and transforms, there are sporadic scenes with more of the action, fighting, and fear but the majority of the action comes near the end (which is very cool! I had also mentioned in my last review that it was hard to get attached to some of the characters (in the last one I was mostly implying Simon) but in this one I think there is quite a bit of improvement with that. P.S. - As most books have webpages of some sort, and in the back of this book they listed it, I decided to pay it a visit. It is very creepy, and at least when I was reading I could eat a croissant and pet my cat and try to avoid complete encompassing of my mind into the terrifying world Alexander Gordon Smith creates, but once I visited the webpage I was a goner. The sounds alone scared the ba-jeeb-as out of me. But now I'm all the more motivated to keep up the series! I recommend checking it out if you decide to read the series, although I would read the first book first, because as scary as the site is I promise they are good books!

Okay. I went into this A Kiss in Time by Alex Flinn and expecting Cinder by Marissa Meyer. I would recommend to fans of  Cinder, most definitely. I am, of course, obsessed with fairy tale motifs and curious about anything that can be done with them in any setting, though my expectations for enjoyment of the scifi retellings are lower than for contemporary or typical fantasy retellings. It was good. It was really good. It was a tad too typical dystopia at the beginning for my tastes, so I was worried it was going to turn into that, but it didn't. It was almost like this book kept teasing me with any negative expectations I may have had, and then blowing them out of the water. I particularly love the way that Sheehan played with different elements of the tale. Sleeping Beauty is typically the mother of all the passive princess tales (the poor girl is literally in a coma), and Rose was very passive and submissive. It was frustrating. We were all yelling, "Tell someone that bad stuff is happening! Your problems are valuable! Stop hating yourself so much!" but then Sheehan revealed her motives and more nittygritty about her background and psychology and, oh. It was good. She had been forced into passivity by years of abuse, and once she realized that she fought it. She had simply believed all that she had been told, that she was highstrung and that was bad, that she got overexcited and that was bad, that she wasn't smart, when none of that was true. I'm excited at this look and her character and just. Oh. Yes. The shix really got real when we found out that her parents had just left her under, the timing of when they died. It was horrific, it was shocking, it was unexpected, it was everything a cureveball-plot twist desires to be in it's plottwist heart. The idea of stasis is terrifying. The idea of living a childhood like hers is terrifying. That resonates with readers because it's so freaky. The play-by-play of the entire Dark Times was a little unnecessary and I feel like it distracted from the story. But at the same time, it was telling. How much the UniCorp had to do with it, the impact on what she knew and how that was affecting her new world. I guess it wasn't too bad, it was just kind of burdensome, and that was when I was worried it was going to go onto YA dystopia "let's fall in love while I take down my corrupt post apocolyptic society" which, frankly, is just boring. I'm over it. But that didn't happen, so yay. This remained the story of one girl dealing with her life that was screwed up enough as it was. I liked the briar patch, thorny hedge, castle, princess metaphor motifs that she was playing with, I only wish it had been done either with a little more subtlety, or stronger, so it was more obvious as a recurring motif, a major theme. As it is, it feels a little like "oh, yes, look at this metaphor, but now I'm going to go back to the story" which is frustrating. Ah yes, I am Lauren, and therefore cannot let the love story go undissected. She took a page out of Debbie Viguie?? 's Beauty Sleep from the "Once Upon a Time" series. This would have annoyed me, that it was the same situation, if it hadn't been so very unexpected and well done. She put off the telling of the story with Xavier just long enough to keep us intrigued. We weren't even sure for a few chapters if Xavier was a romantic love or if he was a brother or what. Very smooth, keeping us in the dark. I liked the way the story of her and Xavier was told, even though it broke my heart. And then the shiz GOT WAY REAL for the second time in as many scenes and then it was awesome, but scary. So Xavier is alive. Why didn't he look? What, but that's so...it's creepy, but it's wonderful, but it's awful. He's still alive. And he's old and she's sixteen and it's bad. But I really really liked the way it worked out. It was always a changing relationship, and this way she had a family and by that time she had come to terms with the fact that her childhood was *not okay* and she acted. Action! No passive princess for her. I love it. The love was so wonderful, and then it was tragic, and then it was creepy, and then it was sweet. Like, much like. Many likes. Recommend to fans of scifi, a well-thought-out dystopia without the smothering social commentary, fairy tales and the many ways they can be thought about, and romance (especially if you prefer it a little less-than-straightforward). Great setting, characters that are more great than you would expect, imaginative futuristic thought, disturbing enough to make you think, but not to give you nightmares or anything. Great book, but it takes a little bit to get going. And don't hate on the protagonist until you know her story, though you may be drawn to. Enough drastic plot twists and action to keep you from being bored at all. Great.

UPDATE 6/15/12:  HA!! I was one of the lucky winners to win this book on the Goodreads giveaway!! I'm so happy! HAPPY! Actual rating: 3.5/5 stars I don't know what I was expecting with Redemption. I won this book on a Goodreads giveaway and I was excited to win something! I only saw the word "vampires" and I was sold! I didn't have any knowledge of the target audience--I automatically thought it was YA--so you can see my surprise when I discovered that this is an adult novel. Emphasis on adult. But, more on that later. Redemption is set in Penton, Alabama (A really small town; its population was 201 as of 2010), where humans have been vaccinated with a medicine that makes their blood toxic to vampires. The vampires are starving because of the lack of fresh blood and times are desperate. Aidan Murphy, our vampire protagonist, is part of a small community where vampires have unvaccinated humans to feed on, and everything seems peaceful until Aidan's brother, Owen, is killing pretty much every single one. Enter Dr. Krystal Harris, a woman who isn't vaccinated. She thought she was getting a job interview, but in reality, Aidan has plans for her . It's not every day that I get to read a book where vampires treat humans like cattle; the world was created so well, I was actually unsettled by it. And I mean that in a really good way. I liked Aidan. I don't know exactly what was it, but I liked his character. One thing, though. He and his brother kept saying "Bloody hell" a lot. Were they British or something? Aidan feigned a look of horror and fell easily into a heavy Irish brogue. "My ancestors would be hanging you from the nearest tree should they heat you sayin' that, they would." Okay, then. He is Irish. Got it. Please don't hurt me. Krystal was, in my opinion, a little bit typical: Has a terrible past (abusive dad), she doesn't have much backbone, and falls instantly for Aidan (And he fell for her as well at the same time, damn it!). Thankfully, she does become a little stronger at the end. In more ways than one. This doesn't mean that the romance didn't bother me. Okay, sure, Aidan and Krystal have a great chemistry together (which says a lot considering how romance is portrayed really poorly lately), but when I remember how they became to that point, I'm not pleased. To make it simple, Aidan KIDNAPPED Krystal because she was an unvaccinated doctor, and the vampires really needed one. And he pretty much lies to her about what he plans to do with her. "Um, yes, this is part of your interview", my ass. I can't believe Krystal was that gullible! And when Aidan confessed that he lied, she was okay with it! I repeat, SHE WAS OKAY WITH IT! What. The. Fuck. Fortunately, their relationship becomes more developed after a while. Phew. And the supporting characters were pretty cool: Owen, anyone? Remember when I said that I was surprised that this was an adult romance novel? First off, the main characters do lust after each other. I mean it. They want to take each other's clothes and Aidan does talk about his penis when Krystal is involved. And Krystal wanted to see it. Oh, my. It was unexpected for me because I thought this book was YA or at least Mature YA. But, nope! This is 100% adult. I was becoming worry that it was going to turn into erotica; although the sex scenes were sexually explicit, there was only two  of those scenes. Once again, phew. Redemption was not a bad book per se, but the climax did made me roll my eyes. Guess what happens to Krystal at the end? I'll give you a clue: Bella, Elena and many other heroines suffer this transformation. Predictability aside, the ending did make me beg for more (I whistled when I finished! The sequels don't look as interesting, but it is worth a try, right? P.S. Why is this novel classified as M/M romance? There wasn't any male "loving" in there! Unless there's a subtext I didn't figure out?

When I first read the blurb for Thumped, I was really expecting a different story, but I really like the way McCafferty took the book. In Thumped, Harmony is struggling to take on the responsibility of her pregnancy while living in a male controlled religious community. She wants to understand the laws of her religion, but every question she asks just sets her apart more. Goodside is using the publicity around the "Double Double Due Date" to promote procreation for God and as a form of responsibility the youth need to take on. Melody meanwhile has been playing a duel role. Everyone, including her parents and believe she is pregnant with Johndoe's twins, but she is really wearing a high tech fake baby bump. She and Zen are planning on a big reveal to take a stand for condoms and for non-procreating sex. But their plan is complicated when she finally meets the couple who have already paid for her "babies". I enjoyed Bumped, but for me Thumped was much better, partly because there is a solid ending that I could live with. It might sound strange considering both books are told in alternating view points between the girls, but for me Bumped was much more Melody's story and looking at how media distorts our perceptions of what is acceptable, while Thumped is Harmony's and looks at how we value life and the responsibilities a baby brings with it. Thumped is much less controversial than Bumped, probably because the world McCafferty has created is now established and not such a shock to the reader. but it's message is the same. These books are not meant to promote teen pregnancy, or make light of it. I see them as a comment on our current society and the way media and reality TV is skewing young peoples' minds into believing that teen sex and teen pregnancy are completely acceptable and desirable. Just look at the girls from all of those MTV shows, and how they are getting on the cover of magazines and on talk shows simply because they had babies in their teens. They are making money off the fact that they either weren't responsible enough to wait to have sex or that they didn't use protection. Thumped does a good job of questioning birth parent's rights, adoption, and the true value of human life. About halfway through, the ending became predictable, but it was still satisfying. ** spoiler alert ** I read a lot of the reviews for this book before I started reading it and came to the conclusion that I would either love or hate it based on what other people were saying. Knowing that I love most of what I read, I decide to give it a shot and discovered that apparently I am a rare breed when it comes to this book, because I came to the conclusion that it was just alright. Not horrible. Not amazing. Just alright. Or at least, alright when you add the sum of its parts together. What I liked: - I thought the witty banter was awesome, and it quickly drew me into the book. Both Jace and Simon had lots of sarcastic comebacks that had me smiling as I read. I saw another reviewer critique the book because many of the characters had a similar sense of humor, which is valid, but I really enjoyed that sense of humor so it didn't bother me as much as it might have someone else. -I kind of already mentioned it, but I really liked Jace's character. Some people thought he was an asshole, but personally I found him hilarious and envious of his ability to come up with a quick and witty comebacks. -The world. Honestly, I think it was the best thing about this book. Some people complained that it was a little confusing, but I didn't have this problem as I had previously read Clare's prequel trilogy, the infernal devices. I loved what she did with the world in that series, and I loved what she did with it in this book and how she worked with that same world, only in the present. -The action scenes. I know those suckers can be hard to write, especially when you have a lot of characters to keep up with, but I think Clare did a great job of pacing them and making them easy to understand. -The romance at the beginning. I am a sucker for romance. I love it. I especially love it when it's done well, but I'll even take it when it's cheesy. Action + Romance + interesting world = my kryptonite (which makes you think this book would have been 5 stars for me, but we'll get to why it wasn't in a minute). I loved how Jace and Clary began falling for each other at the beginning, and while it may have been kind of cliche and a little too fast for my taste, I loved it because like I said, I'm a sucker for romance. What I didn't like: -Ok, I have to start with the obvious. The incest thing. That bothered me. That bothered me alot. And I know that may be a personal preference, because I can deal with murder and blood and gore and violence, but I think incest just took it a step to far for me. While I like the idea of two poor tortured souls who can't be together for whatever reason, I don't like the idea that it's because they're brother and sister. And, because I personally love spoilers, I immediately googled to see how this affected things with Jace and Clary in future books, and  turns out they're not related after all. But it still bothers me immensely that they think they are, especially because they apparently share some "passionate" moments while they are still under the impression they are related. I'm sorry but no, not for me. -Valentine. I couldn't put my finger on it until another review said it, but the dude needs to get scarier. Yeah, he's evil, and he's kind of complex, but is he scary? Not really no. I mean kind of, but in a book like this the answer should be more than kind of. -Clary. Again, this is a personal preference but it bothers me when there are characters who are so obviously beautiful and yet they still can't see it. To me this usually reads as a shallow attempt to make the character (in this case Clary) seem more relatable to the "average" girl, and thus more likable. As if by not recognizing her beauty she is a morally superior (and beautiful) person. Please. In my experience, most girls who are attractive by conventional societal standards (which I know vary and isn't set in stone and such) know that they are attractive. And surprise surprise, it's possible to know you're beautiful and not be vain about it either, and on that note god forbid a woman owns their beauty and awesomeness. But perhaps I'm getting side tracked. -While we're on Clary, her general cluelessness bothered me as well. 1) It seemed so obvious that Luke was pushing her away because he wanted to keep her safe. 2) Duh, Simon liked her. That was obvious too. There were more things as well, but those stood out to me the most. -And then, of course, was that horrible chapter where Luke told the story of his past. That chapter really bothered me because it was entirely just the dialog of what he was saying to Clary. That's it. No quotation marks. No pauses where someone moved or did something or Luke paused or anything like that, which is completely unnatural because news flash, people do things while they talk. And there was no interruptions from Clary. Luke gave her a lot of information, including about the fact that she used to have a brother, and she didn't have anything to say. To me, this personally didn't read so much as a stylistic choice on Clare's part as laziness. Perhaps it was the former, but it felt like the latter. So that's my review, feel free to take it or leave it. Personally, I don't think I will be reading the other books in this series, which is a bummer because I was really excited about it considering how awesome the infernal devices was.

"If you are nothing else in this life, be wise, be compassionate, and be strong because those three are everything" **Possible Spoilers** Where do I even begin? BOOKS Tease by Amanda Maciel | Book Review December 18, 2015 Review When I initially sat down to write this review, I struggled. I apologize right now if this review makes little to no sense, or says little to nothing about the actual book. I really didn't know to feel about Tease by Amanda Maciel. Was it a good book? Was it a bad book? would I read it again? Would I recommend it to someone else? After sitting down and thinking about it for a while it came to me. Tease wasn't a good book or a bad book, it was a difficult book about a difficult topic, bullying and it's aftermath. I did enjoy this book, but not in the way that you may be thinking. It is not my favourite book of all time, it did not give me All The Feelings. *side note* The feelings it did give me were ones of overwhelming rage and disappointment. I enjoyed Tease by Amanda Maciel because it was a necessary book. Lets get one thing straight right off the bat. You are probably not going to like any of the characters in this book. Not a one of them. I mean when we first meet our main character she is in her lawyers office being questioned and she is more concerned with how 'hot' the intern is. Not those who did the bullying or even the girl who was bullied. They are all petty, and self-absorbed, and juvenile. But then again, that is the point. Bullying is petty, self-absorbed, and juvenile and it is a way of fitting in for some and attention-getting for others. The bullying in Tease was pretty severe as far as bullying goes. It was also over boys, and girls, and kids attempting to have relationships that they weren't ready for mentally or emotionally in the hopes of fitting in. I would like to say that that the bullying in Tease, while more severe, was the exception to the rule. Sadly, it's more common than any of us would like to think. I really, really look forward to a time when books like Tease are no longer necessary or at the very least serve as a testament of bad behaviour long past. But sadly, with each bullied child that takes their own life or simply suffers in silence, we seem to need books like this more and more.

As to the story itself, there is both too much going on, and not enough. There are several subplots which all tie in together, but none of which felt actually developed or all that interesting. I mean, the first half of the book barely even had the bad guys. It's mostly just Charlie and Co sitting around and talking about stuff going to happen, and waiting for things to happen. (And I didn't like Lily. Lily is no substitution for Abby. I barely even remembered Lily from before. I did, however, enjoy Wriggly Charlie.) eugh. all right. i've got a lot to say about this shit. i am, honestly, quite surprised to see this novel receive so many glowing reviews from my friends, many of whom are females. my reading of it was a feminist's nightmare. the (annoyingly unnamed) narrator is a frail, flaccid woman with no semblance of personality or existence outside of those to whom she is related. she, quite frequently, makes terrible decisions, such as: - marrying a man she had known solely from a few casual encounters, even after he called her "ignorant" and "unintelligent"; - declaring herself in love with said man (in true twilight fashion) after barely fifty pages; - hearing said man, later, confess to the murder of his ex-wife and utter dislike of her, and instead of--i don't know, running for her damn life--fixating on the fact that he did not love his ex-wife and loved her instead; - blah de blah blah i am too lazy to go get the book and dig through it some more additionally, the titular character, rebecca--(somewhat) sexually liberated, androgyne, subverter of gender norms, master of the house behind the scenes--meets a brutally murderous end. and what message does that send?? that only caricatures of women, eternally frozen in their typecast roles, are allowed to exist? and maxim's role in that murder is--of course--glossed over; it's rebecca's fault, she made him behave like this, she made him kill her. unnamed narrator (let's call her becky, i don't give a fuck)--oh, okay, actually, let's talk about that for a second. the main character doesn't have a name! ooh, so edgy. no. actually just annoying. especially when you're trying to write a paper about her. what logical function does this serve? it doesn't heighten the suspense. it doesn't heighten the "mystery." (it doesn't, as someone tried to argue in my english class, "thicken the dividing line between becky and rebecca." their differences are clear-cut enough as it is. believe me. they couldn't be more different; we already get that.) becky has a super irritating tendency to "dream"--meaning, basically, you get to read the same scene twice, once as she imagines it could happen, and once how it actually happened. one of these--arguably two--is unnecessary. (any guesses as to which?) she's also unnervingly melodramatic. she often has these aggravating swings between, "oh, everything is a failure, i must sit by the window and cry about it" and "oh! everything is grand! i am leading a life i never could have dreamed of! perfection is achievable!" there's a real sense of whiplash reading these in such close proximity. basically, what i got from this book is, women are meant to be subservient, unless they don't marry, which is weird!

"What I am telling you, before you begin my story, is this -- two things: I crave truth. And I lie." This is one of those titles that is an experience from the beginning to the end. My best friend and I both read this at the urging of a mutual friend. Said mutual friend is quite lovely and, alas, doesn't have her own Goodreads so I can appropriately credit her, and is a die-hard fan of Tana French. Since she knows that, outside of YA, I really enjoy a good thriller that will keep me up at night (literally - not just page-turning, but literally keep me up at night wondering if my closet door is opening slowly and ominously), she urged me to read this and see how it went. This actually took two attempts. The first was with a library Kindle edition. I read tediously, remembering it and demolishing a few pages, and then forgetting it again and switching to something more familiar and - as odd as it may sound - lighter, along the lines of an Agatha Christie or a regency romance. (Yes, Agatha Christie is a comfort read right alongside Courtney Milan or Jane Austen.) Recently, Book Riot had a post in their Our Reading Lives series that talked about literary no-fly zones. My literary no-fly zone is violence against women and children. Not that I literally don't fly there (see previous allusions to the Queen of Mystery, who definitely never shrank from the dead body in the library/cupboard/what have you being a woman). It's just...a very visceral, uncomfortable, even tear-inducing experience, depending on how deeply and emotionally the author weaves it. Or if it's a woman in the fridge, violence for the heck of it sort of situation. No, thank you. And particularly if it involves a kidnapped child. It's so painful. I can't even properly tell you why, though I know it has something to do with thinking about the poor child, the poor parents, the poor everyone involved - even the police officers who have to track down the responsible parties. If your no-fly zone is similar...let me tell you that Tana French does not shy away from the visceral details. I think I'm going to have the aftertaste of the grand reveal in my mind for days, juxtaposed against the sudden shift in weather from balmy to rain within the hour I was in my last class - gray skies and justice for a murdered child, but not enough to bring her back or truly set things right. And then, there is Rob. And Cassie. I fell in love with them both at the onset of the novel, and particularly with Rob as the narrator - and that made things more difficult. Like many fiction readers, I...do not do well when characters I like stumble into hard times. And Rob has a LOT of emotional baggage, seeing as he's the child left behind while his two best friends disappeared in a hazy afternoon of thick trees, leaving him behind with clotted blood in his shoes. Particularly after a Thing happens between Rob and Cassie during the plot, I was super worried and kept bugging my friend if they'd be okay at the end of the novel - not just mentally or psychologically, but with each other, because one thing that wins you over is their camaraderie when you first meet them - the late-night sleepovers and the inside jokes and how they know when to protect each other. I hated the loss of that, because it is lost, but I could not completely mourn it or feel sorry for Rob. Like I said, he has a lot of emotional baggage, and I was grateful to French for not making Cassie that type of meek female character a lot of Nice Guys (TM) would prefer who keeps making excuses, being emotionally battered and used and set aside and Puts Up With It for the sake of whatever bones he tosses her. Their friendship was real at the beginning, but as Rob unravels, you can really see how much he needs to fix within himself, and you can also see that a lot of him doesn't feel like he needs to fix it. And even if I wasn't entirely sold on the Cassie-Sam thing, I was so proud of Cassie. Rob wasn't entitled to her time, her heart or her forgiveness. And she didn't give it. She moved on. (And if you don't think Rob was entitled at the end, calling her months after the fact, drunk and aware that she was engaged to another man in the squad, please. Please.) Though, I really still wish their relationship could have stayed platonic. I'm a little tired of these stories where romance HAS to be the end game, no matter what. This story haunts. It's not just Rob's parts of it, trying to remember the events of the horrific day he seems to have blotted out for good, trying to find the lost trail of his friends as he solves a mystery on that same terrain. It's also Katy, the victim in the here and now. It's the backdrop of Irish politics and procedures, of changing atmospheres and allegiances and corruption and loyalty and at the heart of it, it's just a fascinating psychological exploration of the good, the bad and the ugly of people. The thing that sells In the Woods so well is that, for all of Rob's occasionally poetic asides and reminiscing, it is real. Horrifyingly real. I have to admit that one day, in the middle of the crowded university library, just as the friend who recommended this parted ways with me as I waited for my mother to pick me up, I had to close the book. I set it aside, and I spent a few minutes soothing my anxiety and telling myself that I was perfectly fine. It might seem a little silly. I feel a little silly admitting that. But it's a book that makes you feel uncomfortable. In the end, I'm not entirely sure how I feel about it. I took a star off because I did figure out who the killer was, and because even though I could see the Cassie-Rob trainwreck coming, I held out hope that it wouldn't be a trainwreck - and, no matter what my mom says, I can be a hopeless optimist as well as she can. I should have written this review right as soon as I finished the last page, when I had a lot of eloquent reasons why you should read it or experience it if you enjoyed thrillers and mysteries and Ireland, and not just rambling, confused thoughts and an urge to check out the next book in the series. To sum everything up: I like Tana French's writing. I like her characters. I'm confused on everything else, except that it did bother me and it was very raw and real and too close for comfort. I am probably going to read the next book in the series. I should probably write reviews as soon as I finish a book, because all of this happens. And you question my sanity. (If people didn't know that I didn't drink, I think sometimes, I would have friends asking if I was drunk rather than if I was sleepy.)

This is an absolutely wonderful retelling of East of the Sun, West of the Moon! (So if you've read ACOTAR you'll have a general idea of what to expect from the plot). This was just really well done and I adore retellings, so excuse me while I launch into an overly detailed summary (minor spoilers for what happens in general, but not HOW): The youngest daughter of a poor family (she doesn't have a name at the start) is having a difficult time making it through the winter when suddenly a prince in the form of a polar bear bursts into their house and demands that the girl go live in his ice palace with him. He can't say more or explain because he's under a curse and "She" might find out. (The girl had previously captured a white reindeer that gave her one wish + the ability to talk to animals, so she can understand Prince Polar Bear). On the way to his palace, he commands a fellow bear to sacrifice himself to a hunter in the girl's family so she'll leave knowing her family is wealthy and provided for in a fancy new home. Meanwhile, the prince lives in an awesome palace made of ice that's still magically warm and has modern plumbing. The girl can't see any servants or anyone else living there besides a faun with red hair, gold eyes, and a tragic backstory about his love being killed. When the girl can eventually see the servants they turn out to be all sorts of magical creatures like gargoyles and selkies who are killed if they answer her questions about the evil "She." The girl is told to just patiently live there for a year and not ask any questions or try to see the prince's face when he's in the form of a man. The girl still starts to piece everything together, though. She has to return home for a short time when her father's ill, but then she comes back and... long story short, she succeeds in going to "Her" castle located east of the sun and west of the moon to save everyone. The girl finds her prince sitting on a stool by the throne, staring blankly ahead while all of the trolls dance and feast. This goes on for a bit and she eventually saves the prince with her cleverness and ability to perform a task. I really liked how the story unfolded - the pacing let the whole mystery come together perfectly without ever slowing down. The writing's really good! And I loved how closely this plot followed the original story and common folktales. There were similar ideas, like how trolls can't make things and are jealous of humans who can, so the story and setting felt even more realistic/authentic (in the most fictional way? Idk how to phrase that). I also loved the characters, the gorgeous northern setting (because SNOW), and the main character's narration so much. It was just peaceful to read. I wasn't sure where the story was heading at the start, but loved the girl's relationship with her brother so much that I was already invested. And I didn't spoil any part of his story!!! Promise. So the story is way more complicated than my summary, but those were the highlights that stuck out to me. It kind of reminded me of The Golden Compass meets The Bear & the Nightingale and a bit of the original Beauty and the Beast (like where the rooms are full of weird stuff and the prince's alter-self visits the girl at night). Maybe check it out if you love retellings or if you're looking for a really cute, clean fantasy adventure!

4.5/5 stars It's over. Where am I supposed to find something this magical ever again? The Raven King is the final book of The Raven Cycle series and it's finally time for Gansey and his friends to settle things once and for all. At the end of the previous installment, something was woken up and that something is now terrorising the magical beings of Henrietta including its magical forest, Cabeswater. I'm impressed by how the plot is wrapped up. I wanted a good, satisfying ending and it certainly did not disappoint. These characters deserve a good ending after all that they've been through and as a reader, I'd rather have an ending that is beautiful and complete than one that goes out of its way to be shocking or twisted. We all know that Gansey is not going to stay dead even if he dies, and for once, I'm happy that he's alive and well. Plot aside, what this series has always been about is its characters. These characters make the story. And I'm just so glad to see all their developments throughout the series. They are all so well and fully developed by the end of it and I can't help but imagine all the adventures they will have throughout the rest of their lives, together. Also, things in the romance department happened! I think all the shippers have been waiting for these moments. I am so thankful all the ships have sailed. Both ships have their own special moments throughout the book and they were more than beautiful. I only have a minor thing that I found a bit out of place, and that was the character Henry Cheng. I'm sorry, but I don't understand the significance of his character at all. All his scenes felt really forced. It was a bit jarring to have to read about this minor character who suddenly inserts himself into the lives of the main characters. I mean, does he even go here? All in all, it was a great conclusion to a fantastic series about an interesting cast of characters who will always feel real to me. I'm sad to say goodbye. For now.

original post: http://mnonmklreviews.blogspot.com/20... Being the epilogue reader that I am, I (of course) read the last chapter and epilogue; between that and Pixie's first chapter? I knew I was going to love this book. Right from the get-go, you can feel that there's more to Pixie and Levi's story than what you are reading on their pages. Yes, the bickering and sarcasm is fun to read, but there's an underlying sense of sadness you get while reading the pages. Pixie is a hoot. I loved her from the opening sentence: If my bastard neighbor uses all the hot water again, I will suffocate him in his sleep. (No worries... later she threatens to pee on his bed) ...and all of her thoughts regarding Levi and their bickering in that first chapter? Surprise! Levi lives here too. Surprise! You'll be sleeping next door to him. Surprise! You'll be sharing a sink, a shower, and a daily dose of weird sexual tension with him. ...the giant elephant we keep sidestepping during these epic encounters of ours. There will be suffocation tonight. There will be misery and pain and a big fat pillow over Levi's big fat scruffy face. Yeah, loved them too. The majority of the book is Levi and Pixie learning to live near each other again. Once upon a time, Levi's family was her safe-haven. She met Levi and his sister when she was just an itty bitty, and she went by her given name of Sarah. After a fairy incident-almost-gone-wrong is when Sarah became Pixie to those she let in. I found it telling that even though months and an accident severed their blooming relationship, Pixie is still Pixie to Levi. Everyone else calls her Sarah, and even though there's a giant, ragged red mark between what they were and what they are, she is still Pixie and she doesn't correct him. These two really need a good fight. They need to talk and cry and be each other's shoulder to lean on, but they both harbor immense guilt. So, as Levi yells at her one day, he fights with her because it's easier. ...he later admits (at least to himself) that by fighting with her, it gave him permission to talk to her in more than grunts and hooded, averted eyes. When Pixie and Levi finally do hash it all out? Oh my goodness, bring the tissues. Be prepared for waterworks. When these two fight? They fight hard and well. Both brought good points to the table, but I would have to team up with Pixie (which, smart boy that he is, Levi teams up with her too). Side note: super pumped to read Jenna and Jack's story! ...so I went ahead and purchased e-books two and three (three being Jack and Jenna's story). And while book two seems interesting in the part that it picks up at a very interesting scene in THE BEST KIND OF BROKEN... I'm thinking I'll be nearly as enamoured with Jack and Jenna as I am with Levi and Pixie. Like your paperbacks? These two will be coming in paper form soon, too!

I definitely enjoyed this book. For a lot of the beginning I was grinning like a fool, which was quite embarrassing as I was on a bus at the time. But then the grinning stopped and I found myself huffing and rolling my eyes. There are lots of hilarious quotes from Losing It that I could pick out and share, but then you wouldn't get the pleasure that I got from them while reading. I suppose what stopped me loving this book were the main characters, Bliss and Garrick. I'll not lie, Bliss is a slightly vapid Mary-Sue. You name it, she hits every cliche. She's gorgeous and doesn't know it, gets the leading part, gets the man, and is only slightly clumsy to stop herself from being too perfect. And boy does she over think and over react about everything. You should read what she does when she lies about having a cat... I'll admit I was giggling manically but it should never have gone that far. And Garrick, love. What can I say about Garrick, love? He has this way of talking, love, which drives me mad, love. The only Englishmen I've ever heard say "love" after every sentence are creepy leery guys with a slimy look about them. It wasn't at all what I wanted to have in my mind when the supposedly gorgeous Garrick is talking, love. Overall it's a pretty good read. It wasn't quite what I was expecting, but it was good nonetheless. I received a copy of this for free via NetGalley for review purposes.

Unfortunately for me this book was just a little bit too predictable. I could see where the book was going from the beginning, so it really lost its appeal for me. It was written very well but it was really nothing out of the ordinary. I was hoping for some kind of crazy twist but there was nothing. Truth to be told, I don't know why I picked this book since my last encounter with Oliver's book didn't give me her magic again like in Delirium or Before I Fall. But it's hers though, so it was definitely compelling and it dragged me to go along with the story until the end. Vanishing Girls pretty much reminded me of Rooms. I also don't know why. Maybe the 'ghost'? The missing girl? The accident? The angst that enveloped them? Only it's written for young adult so you will find best friend-slash-love interest, broken home family, parties, and clubs. I don't understand why there were so many formats of writing. It got e-mails, flyers, prescription, texts, flashbacks, diary, and other scraps of writing found in the situation. Okay, it was unique and unusual, but also weird. I skipped some parts of the memories like Dara and Nick's childhood because it was so detail it bored me. Again, maybe I just have to re-read it. But one thing I am certain of is that this book confused me. The timeline, to be exact. We'll eventually get the answer anyway, but still there was something missing about the clues. Or maybe psychological thriller is supposed to confuse the reader, because that's why it's called psychological thriller? About the writing style, we all know Oliver--her use in metaphors and similes were creative. I spotted some allegories I couldn't relate to, because it was too strange, but most of them was okay. I certainly learn about this and the way she described something. I'm so sorry I couldn't give more than three stars, unlike Delirium and Before I Fall. It's 2.5 actually, for the whole book, but I really loved the way Oliver delivered her story with engagement so I round it up.

No question that this is a violent, terrible, yet entertaining, story! Written in 1842, and despite reflecting attitudes common to the era about women and class, it is as scary and horrific and disgusting as any modern horror novel! Baby sacrifices! Large man-eating venomous spiders! Earthquakes! Ominous lightening and thunder storms! Evil, dissipated sadistic aristocrats! Impoverished tortured serfs! Vicious servants! Pervasive smell of sulfur! Priests in combat! Quote from the book: "Christine tried to comfort herself, saying it was nothing, it would soon go away; but the pain did not let up, and imperceptibly the speck grew, and soon everyone could see it and asked about the black dot on her face. No one thought much of it, but their words were like barbs driven into her heart, awakening the heavy thoughts once more, and again and again she was forced to remember that this was the very spot where the green man had kissed her, and that the same burning pain that had flashed through all her limbs at the moment of the kiss now burned and gnawed at her without respite. Sleep abandoned her, and everything she ate tasted of fire. Agitated, she went here, went there, seeking comfort and finding none, for the pain continued to sharpen, and the black dot grew larger and blacker, isolated dark streaks radiated from it, and at the edge of the spot that was closest to her mouth a bump had risen." Cue the dark music of lost souls screaming.... Soooooooo. Grandfather decides to tell dark stories of damnation after a beautiful baptism. Why not, right? Strike while everyone is relaxed and happy and dressed up. So, after a delightfully described domestic affair of celebration, love, hope and shared bliss for the first 24 pages, the author sends the reader to a dark place of pain, death and eternal burning. In grandfather's tales, only two little orphan boys are deemed so pure of heart they alone walk untouched by the poison of spiders from hell. Nobody else escapes the mayhem. Even the babies die. As usual with many religious allegories based on older folk tales, there is so much general collateral damage, it makes it difficult for me to see the point of being a Christian. I can never figure out why religious people think the Christian god is good or just, since every religious story demonstrates exactly the opposite (as in, god will kill the baby to teach you a lesson in humility and obedience). However, even if confused mixed and horrifically unjust messages is all the comfort the living can count on from faith, praise the Lord, right? Right?!?!? In the book, grandfather tells the happy baptismal party two stories, warning of the terrifying morality and justice of god. In story #1 the entire village is screwed, no matter if the serfs were good people or sinful  (lesson - don't let strangers kiss you and all peasants are expendable),  and in horrific story #2 a household of low-class people are poisoned and changed instantly into rotting corpses (they were primarily unimportant wives and mothers-in-laws or low-life servants, so)  - the lesson to be learned is apparently the best protection from god's wrath is to be a white male of substance and leisure. The Knight von Stoffeln, tortures, maims, beats, starves and murders his peasants while enjoying a very decadent lifestyle. His serfs suffer under his torments without relief. The priests commiserate, but nonetheless, the enslaved serfs' lives are made up of unending misery and early death without justice. But then a mysterious stranger, the green man, arrives. The Knight has presented the village with the threat that he will kill the entire village if they don't stop planting food crops and plant pretty beeches for him to look at instead. He gives the villagers one month to accomplish the beech planting or else. Planting beeches will actually take them several months to do and of course, there will be no food to eat for the next year. When the magical green man (the devil) offers a temporary fix to their imminent death from overwork, aristocratic caprice or starvation, they think it over and wonder if they should accept his offer to deliver the beeches in the time specified by the wicked lord. They do not reach a decision so they return to their village. However, a spunky spoil of war, Christine ("...wife of the peasant Hornbach, who had come into possession of this female when he had followed his lord into battle.") made into (reluctant?) wife hangs around the green man and she ends up closing the deal for the entire town. The beeches are delivered as promised, and so is Satan's secret surprise of a venomous spider infestation, not immediately revealed. The priests rouse themselves for battle -at last - when they learn of the green man's deal - the beeches delivered for the offering of an unbaptized newborn. The holy men race to each birth with holy water, beating Christine in the race to claim the babes by seconds! However, soon deadly spiders are added to the peasants' woes, crawling out of Christine. The spiders hatch to bite the entire town for their breaking of the contract. (If it had been me, I'd have preferred the, admittedly terrible, hours of death by spider venom to the months of slow death by hard labor, starvation and malicious torture from the Knight and his men, acts for which the Knight is not punished by god. Instead, he is taken wholly by happenstance. When 'wicked' Christine, declared 'evil' by the author due to her uppity free-spirit ways - I think she was a spoil of war, kidnapped from her homeland, doomed to probable rape and drudgery as an unwilling wife (the ungrateful captured slave!) - shows actual leadership and curiosity and saves the entire village, she suffers the curse as much as the pious priest does, as do the enslaved serfs and their families - all of the them powerless, poor, and under threat of horrible murder/torture by the knights, and exhausted by their labors and hunger. The constantly partying Knight, who was the true source of evil, is not tortured. What does god or the devil care about justice? All people were the same to the two gods once their bloodlust got started - prey to be played with until dead In grandfather's second story, he tells of a slothful group of partying servants having too much fun after their 14-hour day slaving for their master with almost no recompense except for the rewards of servitude and serving their betters, without any economic or educational resources. To relax is declared wicked by our hero, god. This looks like another job for - the SPIDERS! Women, babies, serfs, servants - all suffer and die horribly, not from their sins, but because of the sins of the noble classes. But it's all good! Really! Somehow all of this unjust misery, mayhem and lives cut short is worth it if the lesson that god will add even more capricious pain and death gets through to the stupid trailer-trash that more mindless love and prayers for forgiveness for unknown transgressions is required! Did Gotthelf, a Swiss pastor,  unconsciously  expose the holes in Christian morality or was he consciously pointing them out, thinking fear should trump logic? The book is not a satire or a comedy, but is written as a deadly serious, if entertaining, morality tale, with familiar themes in Christian theology. However, to those of a critical and questioning turn of mind, the unintentional exposure of the logical craziness and incoherence behind the theology is screamingly apparent. Whatever. Actually, I thought the most weird element, most startling and strongly outlined as THE plot peculiarity, if ever so swiftly inserted and moved swiftly past - was the virgin orphan boys, one in each story. They are the only ones safe from evil. Why? Hmmmmm. I didn't really see in this book an instance of justice actually done - only indiscriminate pointless death of the poor and innocent. Better to be killed than to follow your own judgement, or to learn from your mistakes (even a single error) or to take responsibility for your choices and correct your course! No actual redemption or relief is possible from god's punishment if you try to avoid starvation and torture. One wrong step and you're toast. God is watching. In any case, I award points for inventive creativity, if nothing else.
A wonderful story on a long - time couple, on mutual obsession and co - dependency.

4.5 stars Alice Clayton and Nina Bocci bring us a charmingly heartwarming story of starting over and second chances in love and life. Just as Avery, you'll fall in love with the streets of Rome, devour the food, embrace the culture, and by the end you'll want nothing more than to pack your bags and catch the next flight to Rome. Our story begins when Avery walks in on her husband with another woman. Sure she's hurt, but the thing that eats at her the most is that she can't remember the last time there was that kind of passion in their own lovemaking. In the aftermath, Avery decides the best thing for her right now is to spend the summer with her best friend Daisy in Italy. Never in her wildest dreams did she think she would come face to face with Marcello-the man she loved and left behind nine years earlier. As Avery and Marcello are brought together once again, it's clear that their feelings for one another have never dissolved, and Avery is faced with the realization that it was never this good with her husband. But how can it last? She has to go home eventually, right? Of course this a love story, and I loved every aspect of Avery and Marcello's romance. But foremost, I found this to be a story of finding oneself again and being true to what's best for  YOU . I loved seeing Avery's personal growth and her complete honesty with herself. I think a lot of us lose ourselves at some point in life and it can be scary to acknowledge. I know many women, far and wide, will be able to relate to Avery's journey. My favorite thing about this book is undeniably the food. Give me some Italian all day, every day and I'll die a happy woman. I think I was hungry about 99.9% of the time but hey, I'm not complaining. The authors did an  incredible  job bringing Rome to life in these pages. I felt like I was the one walking down those cobblestones, I was the one soaking up all the art and culture, I was the one chatting about with Daisy...very very well done. All in all,  Roman Crazy  is a delightfully fun read packed with heart and humor that I know many others will enjoy as well. I can't wait to read more from the  Broads Abroad  series in the future! *ARC recieved from author in exchange for an honest review.

"You only get one life. It's actually your duty to live it as fully as possible." Wow. What a beautiful, raw, and just honest-to-the-core story. While this is declared and promoted as a romance novel, which it is in the end, it definitely is over-shadowed by the elephant in the room:  assisted suicide . I really enjoyed the way Louisa was portrayed as a normal, average and nothing over-the-top crazy about her. She's just a gal trying to find a damn job to keep her family's life afloat. Her introvertedness was so true because a lot of her initial thoughts upon entering the Traynor house were so equal to how I'd react as well. I really think that's why I read novels like this so fast- I love the genuine characterization. I definitely will be reading more Jojo Moyes novels in the near future!

Fessing up right now: I prefer the film. Still, I wouldn't have even seen the film if a high school English teacher hadn't recommended the book to me right before the release. Allow me to review the book by explaining why I enjoy the film--the movie is one of the most visually stunning things I've ever experienced. I comfort watch this movie multiple times per year, which is a big BIG deal for me. All I want to do is watch the beautiful beautiful pictures. There is a glorious marriage between the story, the culture (with a bit of artistic license taken, of course), the spoken word, the characters, and the amazing aesthetic backdrop of visuals and music. Every teeny tiny element just blends seamlessly into an end product that's hard to review beyond "Great movie." It's the exact blend I look for when I say that a book and its writing should be indistinguishable from each other. Even though the movie is long, the story keeps you interested because, while complex and rife with ups and downs, it's been pared down to the basics and doesn't feature too too much voiceover considering the title. So now the book: Sayuri has to explain/define Japanese concepts/items that might be intangible to the American audience. The movie can just show a shoe and we know "That's a shoe." Sayuri has to give the Japanese word, explain how it's different from an American shoe, and then relate an anecdote about it probably. It adds a lot of length without adding a lot of substance. The memoir style, while lovingly executed in the novel, makes Sayuri prone to tangents, sentimentality, and a lot of fluffy fluffy similes. Ye gods, the similes. Sometimes a simile/metaphor can be so illustrative, can explain better than a direct description ever could. Other times, you need to cut out the "I was as tired as an orange cat after it's run ten miles on a hot day" and just say "I was really tired." In the movie, Sayuri's voice only serves to elaborate, pass time, or explain something faster than it could otherwise be explained. In other words, the exact opposite of the function her narrative voice serves in the book. While the book is more conversational and lives up to the "Memoirs" part a lot better, it's also longer and (if you don't like the style) a little more tiresome. Now the book does top the movie in a few important ways. 1) Nobu's character is done a great disservice in the movie. He's whittled down into a very simple and unlikable character whose main function is to be an obstacle between Sayuri and the Chairman--aggressive, unpleasant, and ugly. Book Nobu, while still brusque and quick to anger, is wonderfully complex and is (this is important) actually Sayuri's friend. She feels conflicted about betraying his trust because she likes him. And Nobu, while still principled, openly desires her and (unlike Movie Nobu), bids for Sayuri's mizuage. They have meaningful conversations, their emotions towards each other vary with behavior and circumstance, you never doubt that it hurts Sayuri to choose the Chairman/freedom over Nobu/having an undesirable danna . 2) Some of the cultural details, because they'd be impossible to address without copious voiceover, are simplified or cut from the movie entirely. The example springs to mind of Pumpkin winning the prize for top-earning apprentice geisha, but at the expense of Hatsumomo permanently damaging her relationship to the teahouses where she entertains. . Because you can't just show that in a frame or two and move on, the movie axed it entirely. 3) The movie plot is much more compact, but it also simplifies Sayuri's entire life into a one-track pursuit of a virtually impossible romance. The movie is, after that initial meeting, a relentless love story. The book doesn't share this "all Chairman all the time" view, and makes Sayuri's life much richer and more realistic on the page. Still, it's hard to love the movie so much without giving the book its due. If a three-star rating is (in my system) "averagely enjoyable book", Memoirs of a Geisha is certainly above average. A four-star book and a five-star movie.

More than anything this story was chilling simply because it made me realize you never how close you can be to someone like Dahmer. What would be worse is knowing that deep down this person didn't really want to become what they did. It makes me wonder what life would have been like if Dahmer had some kind of psychological professional he could reach out to long before he became a murderer? I have mixed feelings when it comes to the author. I feel like using the word friend in the title is a bit of a stretch because it definitely seemed to me that Backderf didn't treat Dahmer much better than the rest of their peers. The only time Dahmer was included in Backderf's crowd of friends was when he served as a punchline otherwise it was outright exclusion. I'm not discounting that there was some kind of platonic emotional connection that was struck when Backderf found out about the murders but I don't believe it is as deep as the author tries to convey in his narrative. His story adds in a few personal and interesting details of what's available on Dahmer but as some people's reviews have mentioned at the same time it feels somewhat exploitative in a way. The graphic novel reminded me of how human nature baffles me sometimes particularly in terms of murderers. We don't consider it normal but these people are out there, more of them than we know. I guess it just surprises me that there are ones like Dahmer who crave some kind of normalcy but this compulsion - whatever it is and however it comes about - drives them to a path a majority would never consider let alone take. Needless to say, I liked the narrative for a new perspective on Dahmer rather than the author's story of how he was sort of friends with a would be killer.

Mare Barrow's world is divided by blood-- those with red and those with silver. Mare and her family are lowly Reds, destined to serve the Silver elite whose supernatural abilities make them nearly gods. Mare steals what she can to help her family survive, but when her best friend is conscripted into the army she gambles everything to win his freedom. A twist of fate leads her to the royal palace itself, where, in front of the king and all his nobles, she discovers a power of her own--an ability she didn't know she had. Except her blood is Red. To hide this impossibility, the king forces her into the role of a lost Silver princess and betroths her to one of his own sons. As Mare is drawn further into the Silver world, she risks her new position to aid the Scarlet Guard--the leaders of a Red rebellion. Her actions put into motion a deadly and violent dance, pitting prince against prince--and Mare against her own heart The premise of this book intrigued me. A world where the color of your blood determined your status? Definitely something I'd like to read more about. Anyway, I enjoyed this, but it kind of took me a while to really connect with the book and the characters. The book was interesting, and Victoria Aveyard did a great job of writing a story that can appeal to a wide variety of people. It was filled with action and a little suspense from start to finish. For some reason, I just didn't actually feel invested in the story until like the last 100/150 pages. And of course, with that ending, I must read the rest of the series because I have to know that things turn out ok that Mare and the Scarlet Guard are able to find the others like she and Shade, that someone gets rid of Elara and smacks Maven upside the head (I think his biggest problem is that he's a mama's boy and Elara has him wrapped around her tiny manipulative little finger), someone save Julian! I liked Mare, she was admittedly a thief, but she did it to help her family. She knew that she didn't have the skills to actually contribute like Gisa, so she did the best she could with what she had. But for some reason, I didn't actually start to warm up to her until right around her first Training. I'm really not sure why, but yeah. Cal was an interesting character too. He was clearly the boy who would be king, yet at the same time, he also saw that change was needed. I could see his reasoning in saying no when Mare begged him to become the king that stopped the segregation of Reds and Silvers, but at the same time, I think part of him was just scared to take any chances. As far as the romance goes, it wasn't exactly a triangle, but at the same time it was. Or maybe it was a square? I don't know, but there was definitely some romance and it's kind of a triangle that isn't a triangle. Is there a shape like that? Anyway, I'm going to be honest and say I'm not really sure which relationship(s) to root for. I was never really a huge shipper of Mare and Maven. I mean, I know they were both forced into that betrothal, but even as they spent more time together and she started to see that not all Silvers were evil, something was telling me that the two of them were better friends than anything of course given the fact that he was orchestrating everything just to be king, I firmly believe she should fry his sorry butt . I'm honestly really torn between shipping Mare/Kilorn or Mare/Cal. After the ending, it seems that Mare's decided Cal's out. However, they do seem to work well together. And there was Maven's comments about how Cal would always choose Mare. Granted, he was again orchestrating everything, but he clearly wasn't too far off the mark. However when Cal mentioned nearly having chosen Mare in front of the barracks, a small part of me was very excited . Then there's Kilorn. The boy that Mare has known her whole life, her best friend. There was so much flirting and teasing between the two of them. I can't figure it out. Mare is always trying to save him and he seems like he's trying to save her as well. So they could both just be really good friends, yet at the same time, especially when he gave her the earring, I think there's something more. I just don't know who to ship! Yes, that's not a huge problem, but it's something I think about! And it's something that will bother me until it's resolved. The ending though! Like I said, it took me a while to get really interested/invested in the story. But as the ending came around, I was surprised to say the least. I did see some of the reveals coming, but they came around in a way that kept me interested. And I also just have to know how things are resolved and that the characters I like come out of this for the most part ok (I won't say unscathed because I don't think that's going to happen, but I'll take ok). Can't wait to read Glass Sword!

Read This Review & More Like It On My Blog! Fun, funny, and charming, How Zoe Made Her Dreams... is a book of so much fluff, it might just float off a bookshelf. It's a fast and entertaining read, full of surprisingly developed characters, but unfortunately How Zoe Made Her Dreams (Mostly) Come True is just not on the same level as Smart Girls Get What They Want. I liked it, but it just didn't have the same impact as Strohmeyer's first. Zoe struggles with some serious issues, and I might have teared up once or twice when she confronts her issues, but the emotional pulls are few and far between. For ninety percent of the story, this is a fluffy piece, with a silly plot, operated by characters that are pretty generic, if certainly likeable. Fans of the author's other books, and epecially Smart Girls Get What They Want will find similarities between the novels, but Zoe ultimately ends up a pale copy of its predecessor. I don't mean to knock the author's newest because I was certainly entertained while reading, but anyone who has read Smart Girls before trying this will find it just not quite as good. A lot of my issues stem from the plot and the setting - the competition among the Princes and Princesses for the grant money comes across as frivolous, and often laughable. It's charming and amusing, but never really sells the competition as a serious plot device. As a result, all the drama and suspicions set up around the Dream & Do failed to make me care about its ultimate winner. Strohmeyer can certainly write a credible teenage voice, however. Zoe, through all her present struggles and past heartaches, comes across as authentic and consistently real teen girl. Her voice is strong and likeable, and the author's style works well for a silly but fun read. Zoe's relationship with her cousin is another strong point; the two girls have a real bond and love another. It's all too rare to find such real, strong friendships between teen girls in YA, but so far, in each novel, Strohmeyer has taken the time to build such remarkable and meaningful friendships for her female characters. For that alone, this novel is a winner. I wish Zoe had more female friends, maybe made during her time at Fairyland?, but I will not take her relationship with Jess for granted. For a novel of such fluff, it's heartening how well characterized Zoe (and her love interest) are shown to be. While I loved Gigi, I do think Zoe ends up being the more rounded and dimensional main character. Zoe has a lot of facets to her personality, and amazingly, who she likes doesn't define her or her actions during the novel. The romance might not be as endearing as I thought Gigi's was in Smart Girls, but I have to admit I was rooting for the two kids before the end of the novel. It's a light read, and the love interest is pretty great, but I wasn't overtly involved. I just wanted more substance and depth to the plot. If I'd had that, How Zoe Made Her Dreams (Mostly) Come True could have easily been a four-star read. If you're looking for a charming fluff read, this is a perfect fit. A "done in one day" read, Strohmeyer's capability for writing YA is evident and lends itself well here in her second YA offering. An amusing plot with a couple twists en route make for a fun few hours spent in the company of this cast of Princes and Princesses and furries. How Zoe Made Her Dreams... may not be the best book of 2013, but it's a great diversion for a few hours of pure fluff.

4.5 rating... Here with Me was one of my top reads last year but it left me hanging so I've been waiting impatiently for this second installment! I could not wait to dive in and find out which Archer brother Ryley was going to choose. Or, if she was going to choose either one... In the first book we met Evan Archer who comes home from an unusually long and secret military mission to find out that everyone had believed he was dead. In his 6 yr absence he missed the birth of his son and his fiancee Ryley was now betrothed to his twin brother Nate. The emotions were strong in book one as Ryley was battling with the sudden re-emergence of her first love against the man she grew to love when she finally decided to move on with her life. Then there was the mystery behind why this group of soldiers were declared dead only to be brought back to life 6 yrs later. Nate, his twin brother, was MIA in book one because he was away on a top secret mission... but, in book two we finally get his side of the story. Tension is high and so is mistrust as these two brothers begin the battle for Ryley's heart and search for answers behind the secrecy of the mission that has torn apart their family. Nate was definitely the more compassionate brother while Evan was more pushy, impatient and overbearing. But, they both realized that someone was going to have to make a compromise for the sake of the little boy involved. At the end of book one I was completely rooting for Evan but very quickly found myself rooting for Nate as the story evolves in this second book. There were some very emotional scenes where Nate was remembering his brother that had me all tied up in knots and questioning Evan's character. Ryley was very clearly in love with both of these men... and, choosing one or the other was an impossible choice to make. No matter who she picked, she felt like she would be losing something valuable from her life. It was a lose/lose situation and either decision would sever the relationship between two brothers who were once best friends. Somehow, the author managed to produce an interesting solution to this problem... and, even though I thought it was a little rushed... I liked how everything was resolved by the end. Most of the big questions get answered in this second installment and we are not left with a huge cliffhanger. So, I'm not entirely certain what to expect with book three. Perhaps a little more closure for the brother that doesn't get chosen?? Yep, that could be good! And, no, I'm not going to tell you which one... so, don't ask! These two books have taken me on a very suspenseful, emotional journey. A very compelling and edgy story that is sure to please fans of romantic suspense. I'm definitely looking forward to book three. Can't wait to see what else this author has up her sleeve! ARC was provided by the author for review. I'm not sure if this story is chic lit that wants to be romance or romance that wants to be chic lit. I like both genres and have liked books with a combination of both genres but this book just didn't work well for me. The book is strictly from Maggie's POV. That could be fine too but with a silent mysterious hero it was harder. I liked Maggie a lot of the time but there were moments that I found her ridiculously immature considering her age. The first part of the book was very boring for me. I kept waiting for some progress between the romantic interest but for the longest time they barely interacted. It felt like maybe the story was leaning toward focusing on Maggie's growing maturity and learning to be happy with her life but the progress with that wasn't very good either. She did finally realize she needed to be happy with what she had but it wasn't quite a featured plot. Malone was a fascinating character in the beginning and I could have loved him but (yes another but) since we are in Maggie's POV we don't get to know him. He at no point really opens up. I kept waiting to see progress in him in the romance and trusting Maggie. He didn't. Considering his silent mysterious personality I think we needed something. Actions being more careing it just seemed like he was to disconnected. I know the ending has been a big complaint but I honestly liked the ending. It just seems insufficient considering the lack of build up to the relationship throughout the book.

overall I did not like this series. there are some good points, like choosing what you want to do in life, who you want to be with and not leaving it up to 'fate'. the characters were decent but the world stopped evolving after book 1. we got very little on what was actually going on till we were there. the previous books were about a girl learning to be part angel, how to navigate the world with visions of her devine purpose, but no larger issue was brought in till the last few chapters when  she goes to hell to rescue her friend from a big baddie, who she defeats in less than one chapter It just went too fast where we could have used more explinations and then dragged on with the romance. there was some attampt to build the world with the 3/4 angels, there being only 7 at any one time and the introduction of a baddie who wants to collect all 7, but nothing was done with that other than a very quick battle and defeat. overall this series left me unsatisfied and eager to read something, anything better. If only my OCD would let me just leave series in the middle, I would have stopped after book 2, but there was just one more book so I may as well finish the series. Its not worth reading.

A deliciously quick read; a true beach book. Laugh out loud funny one moment and devastating the next. Gossipy. I enjoyed reading this book immensely, but I found myself criticizing it often... Reader beware- It is unbearably predictable. I guessed the majority of the twists and turns well ahead of time. Spoilers ahead... The matter of Jane's rape was what I found to be the most flawed aspect of the book. And yes, it was rape- despite the constant question mark associated with the event. It was difficult to tell if Moriarty's characters were simply uneducated about consent on purpose (perhaps to force the reader to examine their own ideas about rape, violence, consent culture, etc) or if Moriarty herself was hesitant to call a spade a spade. There was so much emphasis on Celeste's domestic violence situation, and I commend Moriarty for the telling of that storyline artfully. The message was crystal clear (hey, read the last line of the book!). Conversely, Jane's trauma was somehow disappointingly diminished for me. Perry hit his wife, and that point was made. But Perry was also a rapist, and it made me incredibly angry that the author danced around this fact. There was so much victim blaming, it was appalling.
