The Almond Tree is a beautifully written novel that follows the life of a Palestinian man, Ichmad, and his family. The novel is separated into four time periods: 1955, 1966, 1974, and 2009. As a novel, I give the first three Parts 5 stars. The last part I would give 2 stars. So much happened between 1974 and 2009 in the Middle East and especially in the Israeli/Palestinian conflict that was missing from the novel, and this novel was a way that the author chose to educate readers about the history of this conflict. The author is an American Jew who went to Hebrew University in the 1980s. This story had a genesis from her experiences and the people she met during this time period. The book took a sharp turn for me when it skipped from 1974 to 2009. The nature of the conflict that the author experienced in the 1980s is still how the novel presents the conflict in 2009. It totally skipped over the how the Israelis have agreed to peace treaties that the Palestinian authorities kept rejecting, including a previous offer a two-state solution. It also does not talk about how the Palestinians have treated their own people, such as: storing rockets in schools, using civilians as human shields, and misusing funds given by other countries to uplift their own people. I feel this is disingenuous. Efforts on the part of the Israelis to try to right some wrongs they committed in the past are completely overlooked. That being said, I never really understood/knew what had happened to Arabs who lived in Palestine in 1948 when the country of Israel was formed. The level to which Palestinian's were mistreated was horrible and eye opening for me. Throughout the book I kept going to resources online so that I could learn more about the actual history of the area. This novel framed issues and events into a much broader context for me, and I am grateful that I am now better aware of the history. Enough about history. The story itself (except the end) was beautifully written, the characters interesting and I really felt for all of them. It does show how individuals are able to overcome differences and learn and grow. I had a difficult time putting the book down. We follow Ichmad and his family who have their own home and possessions taken over by Jews when Israel was formed. The father becomes a political prisoner and the family has to struggle to earn money in order to survive. Accepted into Hebrew University on a scholarship, Ichmad is a rare Palestinian in the Jewish University. He is immediately judged and treated horribly by others, but when Ichmad and his Jewish peers get to know each other as people rather than someone from a certain group, the walls of hatred break down and lifelong friendships are formed. Unfortunately, not all of Ichmad's family are able or willing to let go of their hatred. The message, however, was to me the most important thing. Do you choose to try to work together toward peace or do you hold onto your hatred from your oppressors? It also shows that there are those on both sides of this complex conflict who yearn and are willing to work towards peace and reconciliation.

The latter applies to this story. There are a few scenes where magic played an important role like the Honey Cat's capture or Paks' mysterious pendant , but you don't find out how magic system(s) work, not because it can't be explained, but because the main character doesn't know herself. Paks, as a main character, as a lowly soldier in the ranks, doesn't know much of anything, let alone important things, like magic. 21/12: Won this book as a give-away today. Can't wait to receive and read it! 26/2: Finished the book, will review it later. 28/2: Time to review this book. This book covers a very important topic: the conflict between Israel and Palestine. This is a topic that many of us can't even begin to understand completely, but all I know is that the situation is terrible for both sides. For a heavy topic like this, a book can be a perfect way to raise awareness and show a human side to a conflict that we know mostly from what we see on the news. I guess this raised my expectations quite a bit. I realise this is a debut novel and as such I shouldn't be expecting too much. Let me begin by saying, as a debut novel it overall wasn't such a bad book. In this review I will judge the book as just that: a book / story. And I must say I was left a bit disappointed. For example, the book starts of with multiple terrible deaths in the first few chapters. Unfortunately the writing was too bland to get any emotion from me about the events described. This went on for most of the book, although it got a bit better near the end. The book covers the life of one person over nearly sixty years. That in itself was interesting. A side effect was that many emotional topics did not get touched upon as much as they maybe should. It felt the author was attempting to make the story more emotional but failed. Overall, I think the story told had many interesting and important aspects to it. But due to the lack of emotion, I couldn't help but roll my eyes at some events: "Seriously?" or "Not again!" Another minus is that some parts of the story were too unbelievable for me. Like winning the Nobel Prize at the end of the book after being nominated ten years in a row. This seemed to discredit a lot of the story. I can imagine other people would enjoy this book more than I did. Looking at the other reviews I see many people were very touched by the book, and I do understand and believe this. Apparently it just wasn't for me.

Temperance Dews and her brother run a foundling home in the desperately poor and dangerous London parish of St. Giles. It was established by their father and a generous patron, but now both have died and the home is struggling financially. Temperance finds a potential, if risky way out when she's approached by Lazarus Huntington, Lord Caire. Caire is searching for a murderer in St. Giles, and he's getting nowhere, as people just will not speak to him. He and Temperance make a deal: if she will act as his guide and use her connections in the area to make people a bit more forthright with him, he'll provide an introduction to respectable society events, and ensure she meets potential patrons for the foundling home. But, of course, this being a romance novel, what's supposed to be a business transaction becomes much more due to their attraction to each other. Hoyt has written some excellent books, which I've loved, but this isn't one of them. I found it very disappointing. The one element of it that I liked was the setting and atmosphere of St. Giles, which is excellently done. It's vivid and scary and feels real. Other than that? Meh. I found Caire especially problematic. Hoyt tries to write him as tortured and complex, but he just never gels, and comes across as half-baked. The perfect example of that is the big drama about how he feels pain when anyone touches him, but not when he initiates the contact. So many issues with that! 1) It's never explained why this is the case, and the whole thing seems to come and go. 2) The way it's resolved is just as mysterious and laughable. 3) The contrived way the whole thing works means he can only have sex with a woman he's tied down. This is just a cheap way of introducing some mild bondage and make reference to his dark sexual appetites, without shocking mainstream readers with actual BDSM. It was all "oh, look how tortured he is! He doesn't feel anything!". He's such a 'tortured' man that he's a complete jerk to Temperance for no reason for a lot of the book, that's how. I lost patience with him before long, and with his mission to find the murderer. That never makes any sense at all. Over and over, he keeps putting the woman he's beginning to care about in really severe danger (which he knows is so) for no reason. Caire himself acknowledges at one point that the hunt for his mistress's murderer isn't really motivated by anything other than the fact he doesn't care, but he should, which is just puzzling thinking. Temperance... well, she's supposed to be tortured as well, and have this secret pain, but really, blah. Their relationship development seems to mainly consist on sex scenes, which I found pretty boring. The plot is contrived and nonsensical, but I'm pretty sure that exact same set-up and the deal Temperance and Caire make could be made into something perfectly serviceable, even great, if only the characters' motivations were sorted out and made a bit more sense. What's just unfixable is the resolution of the case, which is ridiculous and cartoonish, with a villain who makes even less sense than the main characters. And that, I must say, is quite a feat. MY GRADE: A C-.

While I had some initial reservations about Divergent due to its rather irritating font (Filosofia... trying too hard to be cool, guys), I actually couldn't put it down once I started reading. The beginning was a little slow, of course, as beginnings are inclined to be, but I was still pretty hooked. I was fairly indifferent to Tris's character, to be perfectly honest. She was pretty irritating at parts, but most of the time I could tolerate her. I even liked her on a few occasions. I liked Four quite a bit, and his and Tris's relationship was a surprising breath of fresh air in this age of the angsty young adult lit teen love books, or whatever we're calling them. I definitely expected Four to be this raging asshole to her whenever they were in public, more so than to anybody else, so as to keep their relationship "a secret." Well, he kind of was, but he also wasn't. He just wasn't an asshole to anybody. He was a normal guy doing his job, which was being a no-nonsense initiation trainer. Yeah, there was that one time when he didn't wave back at her at lunch, but he didn't make a point of glaring or anything. He straight-up told her that it is against his job while he is her teacher to date her, because people might suspect favoritism, but after initiation it was fair game. And it totally was. I was really impressed. Once Tris was initiated, they pretty much went public with their relationship right away and it was no big deal. The ending was exciting, if a little confusing. I honestly didn't expect BOTH of her parents to die, just maybe one. I really want to read the next two, but I'll be waiting until they're out in paperback. I can't afford hardbacks anymore.

Recipe for this book: Begin with 1/2 cup of stereotypical teenage romance, wherein Emma's boyfriend Lucas is dying from cancer. Throw in 1 T. of doubt that this book is going to be any more interesting than aforementioned stereotypical teenage romances. Stir well. Add 2 cups of a sad, innocent, lonely -- but incredibly smart and adorable -- alien named Scout (who takes over Lucas' body in order to survive), and a half cup of excitement that the book is actually going to be something different than it started out seeming to be; mix thoroughly. Sprinkle in a pinch (or a bit more, depending on flavor of mixture thus far) of nagging fear that Emma is never going to get Lucas back and that Scout is never going to get home; stir well. Add 1 cup of exciting adventure and 2 cups of a happy ending that makes everyone happy. Mix well. Place in oven and bake for 6 hours. By the time 6 hours is up, the recipe should be completed. Really, really enjoyed this book (as if it's not evident by now). Scout was so sweet. The only downside is that I feel that I got to know Scout better, as he learns to navigate Earth, than I ever really knew Emma. Nevertheless, I wouldn't hesitate for a moment to recommend this book to those of my friends who like books that defy overused tropes. I look forward to see what other books Ms. McQuestion will be writing!

I wish I could rate in decimals because then Dangerous Girls would receive a whopping 4.78/5. This book was brilliant. I devoured it in one sitting. I am a fan of psychological thrillers. In the era after the hype of Gone Girl I felt like a lot of books tried too hard and fell short. I recommended this to a friend and described it as "Pretty Little Liars meets Gone Girl", and my friend replied "but you don't like either of those??? ", which is true, but for some reason, Dangerous Girls just worked for me. I haven't found myself gravitating towards many psychological thrillers recently; I haven't been in the mood for heavy-suspense-filled reading sessions. I think this falls on the "lighter" end of the genre's spectrum, which made it easier for me to read. There's not much description of ethnic/racial diversity. However, two minor characters are called Melanie Chang and Akshay Kundra who I assume to be POC. In the Elise-Anna-Tate friend group there's a pair of siblings (twins I think) called Max and Chelsea, and a guy called Lamar, I could be wrong but I don't recall any mention of these characters' last names. Melanie Chang is depicted as the submissive rule-follower, and Akshay Kundra is the spoiled son of a business mogul. Can you see how I'd have issues with the racial stereotypes? This sort of stuff has pissed me off since I realized at 13 that Aladdin (the "good" guy) had an American accent whereas Jafar (the "bad" guy) had a Middle-Eastern accent. Anyway, sorry if this comes across as a reach, this just rubbed me the wrong way, but it was more food for thought and not a total put-off. I don't want to ruin anything for anyone so be warned, but here's my 2 cents regarding the ending:  I found the ending just a little predictable (I mean, there are really only a few ways this type of story can go), but it was the ending I hoped it wouldn't be and THAT MADE ME FEEL SOME TYPE OF WAY.

Joyce Carol Oates is not in the habit of pulling her punches. She might be the only writer in the history of the world both willing and able to name a book "Rape." She's a powerful author, and I'm a big fan. This wasn't my favorite of her books. What's it all about? Fury, right? I mean, and rape. It's definitely about rape. Nothing else happens. It's short. The personalities and histories of the people in it are briefly sketched out. Mostly, there's a rape and then there's the aftermath of the rape and then it's over. The rape is unambiguous. It's about as awful as it can be. The plot is similar to the Jodi Foster movie The Accused. That movie was made in 1988, and this book was published in 2003, and it feels a little dated. Aren't we past victim blaming? Surely no one in this day and age would...oh. Never mind. Oates has picked a weird avatar for justice. This is John Dromoor, a sociopathic veteran. Oates carefully introduces him as a dangerous man. You might assume at first that he's a bad guy. He is a bad guy, as in a not good person. But after the courts fail Teena Maguire, he takes justice into his own hands, carefully murdering four of the men who raped her. You might sortof expect justice to be female, right? I'm not sure what Oates is trying to tell us here. I don't have a problem with it - it's interesting - just don't know what to make of it. There's a subtitle here, "A Love Story," and I have no idea what to make of that either. It's not a love story. There is love, I guess - Teena's 12-year-old daughter Beth has some sort of puppy love crush on Dromoor, which again fills you with dread but nothing comes of it, thank god because you've just about taken all the bad news you can get from this book  - but no story about it. It's a rape story. It's upsetting.

SO- its obvious what they would want. That being said, I AM pro-life... so I guess you can make your own decisions. I think the point was that Elysia was an anomaly now. Something that is impossible and should be revered So, overall the story line and writing was pretty awesome. But the romance was unfortunately a double case of instalove. And the realities she had to face weren't given the attention they needed. Rating: 3 stars Review by Theresa Jones on her BLOG

First off, I am a HUGE fan of Harper Fox. All of her books are extraordinarily well-written and have a serious plot line other than the obvious slash romance. That said, this was not her best, although it is a strong entry and still deserves a five-star, in my opinion, when put in context with other novels of the same genre. It's just that some of her other works, especially "A Midwinter Prince" and "Driftwood," merit more like a 10 star on my scale. "The Salisbury Key" worked more for me on the level of adventure/thriller than romance. It lacked some of the wonderful romantic angstiness of Ms. Fox's other stories. But for me, what it lacked in angst, it made up in a very interesting plot line where I really wanted to find out what was happening and what a particular character's motivation was. The romance was a bit secondary to the plot, but it was still sexy and sweet. MILD SPOILERS: Daniel is a young academic who has been living with his mentor/former professor for three years when his mentor commits suicide for no apparent reason. Daniel, not even thirty years old, takes Jason's death very hard and blames himself for it (in spite of the fact that there's no indication at all that he had anything to do with it). Trying to escape the immediate aftermath of Jason's death, Daniel presses forward with exploration of a newly demilitarized archeological site near Stonehenge (less than a week after Jason's death) and, with the help of Lieutenant Rayne, a bomb-disposal specialist, begins to explore. It doesn't take long for Daniel and Rayne to end up entangled, both emotionally and physically, a fact which gives both men pause (especially given the short time that's elapsed since Jason's death). But there's more to Jason's death than meets the eye, of course, and soon our two heroes are chasing after danger. I was on the edge of my seat towards the end of the book, rooting for both men. I am always amazed at how much Ms. Fox seems to know about her subjects - in this book, both archeology and bomb-disposal, as well as a few other little tidbits that I won't get into (don't want to spoil it). All in all, a great read as always from a great writer. If you've never read Ms. Fox before, try the two titles I've recommended above first, but don't hesitate to read this little beauty afterwards!

A great memoir that is quite like Felicia Day in real life- charming, quirky, geeky, and fun. If you know her from anything (The Guild, Dr. Horrible, Supernatural, Geek & Sundry, the Internet in general), you'll probably enjoy reading about some of her experiences through being a homeschooled violin prodigy that went to college at 16 and earned two degrees and an actress who managed to create her own webseries through favors, luck and sheer determination. But what's really memorable about her book is how honest she is about her own struggles with mental health, and her experience through the awful GamerGate fiasco. While Day does seem to gloss over or even skip large portions of her life, the topics she chooses to focus on are fascinating, honest, and informative. Her voice rings clear off the pages, and the pictures of her life help illustrate her words and endear her to the reader. After all, which ones of us haven't had some tragic wardrobe choices from our past? All in all, a great book that I totally enjoyed reading. If anything, it just makes me want to rewatch the Guild or some of her great Flog or Co-Optitude videos on YouTube. Viva Felicia Day!

This graphic novel is about the Locke family, and their adventures with keys they've found in their ancestral home. There are two teenagers and one youngster comprising the siblings that make up the family, and the main themes of the story are interspersed with and illustrated by what's happening with them at school. I liked the two romantic subplots quite a bit, and found every character compelling for a different reason. As I began to read this, I didn't really know what anyone was talking about - mention of keys seemed important, but I didn't know why. However, I was enjoying the story and the characters so much that I really stopped caring and just sank into it. The writer does a good job of getting you to want to read more so that he has time, throughout the arc, to bring you up to speed on what the titular keys are, and what they can actually do. There is a list of the keys discovered so far at the back of the book, which I thought would perhaps have been better at the start of the book, but there we are. Very early on in the story we meet Bode, who then talks to Zack, who then goes to hang out with Bode's brother and sister (Ty and Kinsey). Zack is dating Kinsey, and appears to be friends with Ty, too. Therefore, the thing that confused me was that, when Bode throws a snowball at Zack, his immediate reaction is to daydream of killing Bode and Kinsey. It eventually becomes obvious that he is a bad guy and that they are completely unaware. Whilst this is confusing initially, it's fairly clear, eventually, that he's a bad guy. And the part where people start transforming into animals is really cool. I liked the ways in which the keys have effects on the characters, especially on Kinsey, who strikes me as the one who has been most affected (for good or for ill) by the keys and their effects. I loved the drama that arises after she explores the keys with her cabal of friends at school, and I also loved the relationship that Ty attempts to strike with one of his friends. Oh, and the panels that just show the mental situations they get into every day with no commentary or text whatsoever are superbly done.

I'll update once I remember the title. [READ AT YOUR OWN PERIL] Harvard professor Robert Langdon wakes up in a hospital with a head wound and no memory of the last few days. He last remembers walking on the Harvard campus, but he quickly realizes that he is now in Florence, Italy. Dr. Sienna Brooks, one of the doctors tending to him, reveals that he is suffering from amnesia. When Vayentha, a female assassin, shows up in the hospital and kills Dr. Marconi, Brooks helps Langdon escape, and they flee to her apartment. After Brooks recounts the details of his admission to the hospital, Langdon finds a cylinder with a biohazard sign in his jacket and decides to call the U.S. consulate. He is told that they are searching for him and want his location. Per Brooks' guidance, he gives them a location across the street from her apartment to avoid getting Brooks more involved in his mysterious situation than she already is. Soon, Langdon sees Vayentha pull up to the location he gave the consulate. At this point, they both believe the U.S. government wants to kill him. Langdon then decides to open the container and finds a small medieval bone cylinder fitted with a hi-tech projector that displays a modified version of Botticelli's Map of Hell, which is based on Dante's Inferno. A trail of clues leads them toward the Old City. However, they are dismayed to find that a secretive team of soldiers, and the Florentine Carabinieri are also searching for them. They flee into a construction site near the Boboli Gardens where he examines the "Map of Hell" again, noticing several subtle changes to the layers. Langdon discovers a phrase from the painting The Battle of Marciano by Vasari, located in the Palazzo Vecchio. They manage to evade the soldiers and get into the Old City using the Vasari Corridor. At the Palazzo, a custodian sees Langdon snooping around and gets the director of the museum, Marta Alvarez. Alvarez recognizes him, having met him and Ignazio Busoni, the director of Il Duomo, the previous night. She leads them up a set of stairs by The Battle of Marciano, and Langdon realizes the top of the stairs is on the same level as the words "cerca trova" in the Battle of Marciano painting. Alvarez tells him that she showed them Dante's death mask the previous night, which sits in a room down the hall from the Battle of Marciano painting. He realizes he is retracing his own steps from the previous night. Finding the mask gone, security footage shows Langdon and Busoni stealing the mask. Fleeing the guards, they listen to a message Busoni left telling him where the mask is hidden, referring to "Paradise 25." They then escape the guards, but the soldiers arrive. They cross the attic over the Apotheosis of Cosimo I, where Brooks pushes Vayentha to her death. Langdon connects the phrase "Paradise 25" to the Florence Baptistry, where they find the Dante mask along with a riddle from its current owner, a billionaire geneticist named Bertrand Zobrist. She explains that Zobrist was a geneticist who advocated the halting of humanity's growth, due to its out of control population and that he was rumored to be working on a means to do so using an engineered disease. A man named Jonathan Ferris, with a large bruise on his chest which he hides from the two, and a severe rash on his face, claiming to be from the World Health Organization (WHO), comes and helps them escape the soldiers. They follow the riddle to Venice, where Ferris suddenly falls unconscious, with Brooks claiming he is suffering from massive internal bleeding, causing Langdon to suspect Ferris has been infected with Zobrist's plague. He is captured by a group of black-clad soldiers while she escapes. Langdon is taken to Dr. Elizabeth Sinskey, the director-general of the WHO, and is given an explanation of what is going on: Zobrist, who committed suicide the week before, was a brilliant geneticist and Dante fanatic who had supposedly developed a new biological plague that will kill off a large portion of the world's population in order to quickly solve the problem of the world's impending overpopulation, citing the Doomsday Argument. Sinskey raided Zobrist's safe deposit box, found the cylinder and flew him to Florence to follow the clues. However, he stopped communicating with Sinskey after meeting with Alvarez and Ignazio and the WHO feared he betrayed them and was working with Zobrist to unleash the plague. The soldiers were the WHO's emergency response team and never meant to kill him. Zobrist had paid a shadowy consulting group called The Consortium to protect the cylinder until a certain date. He also left a disturbing video filled with Dante imagery, which also showed a picture of the plague itself, kept in a hidden underwater location, within a slowly dissolving bag. The video claims that the world will be changed the following morning. When Sinskey took it away, they abducted Langdon and staged every event up to this point so that he would be motivated to solve it. The leader of The Consortium, having become aware of the bioterrorism plot, agrees to cooperate with the WHO. Ferris's rash was due to an allergic reaction to the spirit gum he used as part of the disguise as the doctor Vayentha "murdered." His bruises were because the squib used to simulate him being shot in the chest misfired and broke his ribs. He collapsed in Venice because he had been ordered to detain Brooks, as the Provost (Consortium head) had allied with Sinskey, with Brooks realizing and punching him in his damaged ribs. Brooks goes rogue and The Consortium realizes she was a secret supporter and lover of Zobrist. She learned where the plague was being kept after Langdon solved the riddle and acquires a private jet to get to it before everyone else. Langdon, the WHO and The Consortium team up to stop her. After watching Zobrist's video, they conclude that the bag containing the plague will be fully dissolved by the date the video specifies and that Zobrist's clues point to its location: the Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, where Enrico Dandolo is buried. He and the others find the plague is in the Cistern but discover that she is already there. The bag that held the plague had already been broken, presumably spreading through the outer world via visiting tourists. Brooks runs out of the Cistern yelling something in Turkish, which causes panic among the tourists who stampede out into the city while Langdon gives chase. It is discovered Brooks didn't puncture the bag; it was water-soluble and had dissolved one week earlier in the cistern waters, meaning that the whole world has already been infected. The date specified in Zobrist's video was the mathematical calculation of when the entire world would be infected. It is also discovered that she was trying to stop the virus herself, but didn't trust the WHO because samples of the virus would certainly find their way into the hands of governments performing weapons research. The leader of The Consortium tries to escape WHO custody with help from disguised underlings, but is caught later by Turkish police. She receives amnesty in exchange for working with the WHO to address the crisis, since she is a medical doctor and has extensive knowledge of Zobrist's research and work. The plague that Zobrist created is revealed to be a vector virus that randomly activates to employ DNA modification to cause sterility in one third of humans, thereby reducing population growth to a more stable level. Sinskey and Brooks decide not to try to reverse Zobrist's actions, Brooks pointing out that doing so would be difficult and hazardous even for someone like Zobrist and Sinskey acknowledging that Zobrist had a point about the dangers of overpopulation.

Fuck. That was definitely one of those books that was far too stressful and enticing. The whole time I was absolutely captivated--much the same kind of emotions I felt while reading anything by Gillian Flynn. The book from the get-go is dark, and steeped in pop culture media. Everything relevant to this age is mentioned: Reddit, Facebook, Kickstarter, Nyan cat, you name it. I can imagine this would be kind of baffling for people who don't have much of an online presence, because the fundamental focus of this entire narrative is social media. And boy, does social media rear its ugly head here. There's several main characters: TK: the homeless guy who just tries to do what he can to help others. Gabi: a single mom detective who is lead on the murders Layla: Gabi's 16 year old daughter, who decides to make stupid decisions Jonno: the lame wannabe journalist who forgoes basic logic to be famous Clay: a guy who has been fighting off the bad things for far too long, and finally succumbs There's some minor characters as well, characters that really are just as great as the main ones--Cas and Sparkles, namely. Basically, all of their different paths lead to one explosion of activity. Cas and Layla learn that what gets on the internet stays forever. Jonno learns that his fame rides entirely on his ability to work the internet. And Clay's dream learns that all it needs is eyeballs. Ugh. I'm getting annoyed because there's so much I want to say about this book but can't seem to articulate it. I loved the horror aspect that didn't come out until the end. I loved the steady build up of events, events that kept getting more and more rash. I loved that each character had their own issues to work through, all culminating (again) into one fabulous climax. The dream is some kind of thing that leaks into Clay and takes him over. The dream only wants to return to its own world, or bring its world out. So it starts drawing chalk doors everywhere, and creating "art" in the form of hand-sewn satyrs in the hopes of bringing that world out. When it doesn't work, it becomes increasingly determined, going bigger and bigger with its ideas. The thing is, its tendrils have started infecting others, too. Because TK is starting to see things, and Layla, and Jonno. And the more that the dream is exposed, the stronger it becomes. And stupid Jonno decides his career is more important than, you know, the world. But rest assured, Reddit users think he's nutso and with poor Sparkles serving as the door for the dream to return to its own world, there is nothing left for him to do but bemoan his lost credibility.

This book is fairly predictable and conventional, except for maybe the fact that (big spoiler about the ending under the tag)  Will does choose to die at the end, despite the power of love   but I still just devoured it because I though Moyes did such a good job in terms of character development. Perfect characters don't interest me as a reader. Lou and Will are both realistically flawed people who have complex interactions with each other, with their dysfunctional families, and with the wider world. Yet for all their foibles, Moyes did a great job of illustrating how well Lou and Will fit together and how much they need each other. I really liked how well Moyes wrote all the relationships in this book and how well she constructed Lou and Will's personal universes. They feel like authentic, three dimensional people with mostly plausible and identifiable life trajectories up until their meeting (exception: Will's great wealth is a bit of a contrivance). The development of their relationship is moving and well written. Moyes doesn't take shortcuts but skillfully sketches the gradual evolution of Will and Lou's relationship from one of animosity to cordiality to friendship to love. The supporting characters are similarly well written. I always felt like I had a good grasp of why characters felt and behaved in the way they did and I was highly emotionally invested in this story.

Awesome! Very reminiscent of Atwood's Handmaid's Tale, but this still felt fresh and relevant. It's a rare thing to read a novel that has a female character who is truly transformed through her experiences, but Hannah most certainly is. Calling this a feminist novel would be doing Jordan an injustice, particularly since "feminist" has become an almost dirty word in our "post-feminist" world, but reading this enflamed me in the same way that Atwood's book did back in my college days. it really makes you realize that women (and all of us really) hold on to our legal rights by a slim thread, and our rights are something that we need to cherish and protect at all costs. Jordan's created a believable dystopia, all the more disturbing because you could easily envision this as a possible future. The spirit of women helping other women and drawing strength from them, as well as its inverse, women sabotaging other women and drawing strength at their expense was also fascinating. This was not a chick lit let's drink overpriced coffee and indulge in retail therapy type friendship something deeper, more essential. I got so caught up in Hannah's story that I took it very personally when she  chose to try and see Aidan after Simone had trusted her to continue her journey alone . I felt betrayed and could not believe, after all she had gone through that she would  risk everything just to see him. . Upon further reflection I realized that this humanized Hannah, and gave her a chance to move on, finally. This book had heart and depth and was both discouraging and inspiring, exactly what a good book should be. Would make a great book group read.

"If I'm a monster, mademoiselle, it's because man's cruelty has made me so." Beauty of the Beast by Rachel L. Demeter is a dark, adult fairy tale retelling of Beauty and the Beast (with a teeny-tiny nod to Cinderella, too?). This edgy and historical romance is set in the 1800's in the kingdom of Demrov, France. **** Warning: this book contains mature content and dark themes, most of which are graphic. In an attempt to better her life, Isabelle Rose travels with her ailing father to the merchant's fair in LA Florin, leaving her two selfish step- sisters, Clarice and Elizabeth, and her cruel and heartless fiance, Raphael Dumont, behind. Before they were able to reach their destination, Isabelle and her father Bernard get caught in the middle of a serious snow storm and have to venture off their route to find safety. Eventually they find a decrepit castle, seemingly abandoned, and immediately seek shelter inside. What they find, however, was something way beyond what they could have imagined. The writing is filled with vivid descriptions and details, but certain things felt repetitive and that got slightly annoying. This is a stand alone book, but its also the first installment in a series of (more to come) classic fairy tale retellings with dark and realistic twists (which I'm definitely looking forward to). In some ways, this book reminded me of M.J. Haag's Beastly Tales trilogy , Depravity (mostly because of the MC's two evil step-sisters, and some similar dark themes), but Rachel L. Demeter puts her own unique twist on this fairy tale; one that's filled with strong emotion, tragedy and a slow-burning romance. I loved that there was no magic used in this story. Prince Adam Delacroix was made into a "beast" by a horrific event in his past, not cursed to be one. However, he does own an old aged "beast like" wolf-hound named Stranger (and I loved him, haha). Besides Stranger, Adam's only other friend (and only connection to the outside world until he meets Isabelle) is Sebastien, a man who served him and his family before they were horrifically attacked. Unfortunately, I felt their friendship was underdeveloped. I didn't really feel a strong connection between these characters, which was strange considering everything they've been through together. I wasn't too surprised when Sebastien ended up betraying Adam, even if he had good intentions. Although, I'll admit the lack of connection between these two characters was made up for when Sebastien helped make things right again... Sort of. Raphael Dumont, Isabelle's fiance, is handsome, rich, powerful and absolutely despicable. While I am not forgiving his actions, I was glad to know his history and learn why he became so villainous. I almost felt bad for him at times. If you're an adult who enjoys dark gothic romances, happy endings and Beauty and the Beast retellings, then this is a book for you. The pacing is great, and I had a hard time putting this book down.

This book was actually really hard for me to rate. I thought that Anna and Lola's stories were adorable, but they were a little too fluffy and rom com for me. Don't get me wrong, I loved both books. I think Stephanie Perkins' strengths are in the way she writes her characters. Her characters are all quirky and relatable. You root for them, and you want to see the happy ending. However, I always feel that she spends so much time and drama (some of it seems really unnecessary) on setting the two characters up, and then basically no time talking about them when they are together. Also, all of the books had some insta-love problems. However, this book was very different in this aspect. I think this is actually my favorite book of the series. I would have probably have given it a 5 star rating if not for the semi insta-love in the beginning. The reason why this book was different and why I liked it so much more was that it showed the characters in a relationship. It didn't mess around too much with the setting up, but rather focused on all of the things that happen in new relationships. These drama seemed more realistic. It is understandable that two people would rush right into a relationship feelings first. It is also understandable that relationships do not fix all problems, and in a lot of cases it brings these problems to the surface. I liked the individual struggles that both Josh and Isla went through to understand and accept themselves. I like how they explored these problems together and apart. I like that Isla decided to go to Dartmouth for herself. I like that she finally started to accept herself. I know some people might be annoyed to read about two introverted and insecure characters, but that didn't bother me. Maybe it is because I am shy and insecure, but I could easily relate to Isla and Josh. I could relate to Isla's inability to take risks, inability to plan a future, inability to understand why people would like her, her inability to make friends, and inability to be confident in herself. I also can relate to her love of adventure stories. However, I could also relate to Josh. I could relate to his stubbornness, his distance from his parents, and his half-ass effort in school. Essentially, I think that story was a little more serious than Anna and Lola, which I really enjoyed. However, there were defiantly some adorable moments that Perkins is known for.

Mr. Billionaire wins with a crazy high bid. She's got secrets, he's got secrets. They all come out at the end. The secrets are all extremely predictable to the reader. You won't really be surprised by any of them. In fact, I was more wondering how our heroine could NOT know some of them herself. The Hero wasn't exactly discreet at times. So the reason I can't decide on 3.5 or 4 stars- this book seemed very slow to me. Also somewhat repetitive. We often see the same scene but dressed a little differently. Example: there's at least 3 different times when the couple gets dressed up, goes to dinner, has a great time, fools around and then... doesn't have sex. A few changes in the wardrobe and places but they're all essentially the exact same thing. I also didn't like the fact that this ended up being part one of what I believe is a 3 book series that will follow our couple. I don't agree with that AT ALL. In my semi-professional-reader's opinion there should have a been an epilogue to tie up what very few loose ends there were at the end and call it a day. I don't see any good reason to keep dragging this story out. The story itself is well written and edited. I really did enjoy it. I just wish it were a bit more fast paced, less predictable and NOT part of a series- one that I doubt I'll continue to read. We'll see.

I have to preface this by saying The Gamble was the first KA I read and I LOVED it. Like, I wanted to rate it 10 stars and give out copies to everyone I know. It gave me high hopes for the rest of the series and everything else the author has written. Then I read Sweet Dreams and I really liked it but I also noticed a formula and the prose and the way the hero talked started bugging me. KA has her tics but I figured I could learn to live with some repetitiveness and awkward sentences because overall she's a great storyteller. That brings us to Lady Luck and boy did I struggle with this one. The premise hooked me from the start and the story was, again, overall interesting. But it was overly long and repetitive and the characters and plot started to feel interchangeable. The way Ty talked was almost exactly the way Tate, the hero from book 2, talked. It started to grate on my nerves. I also started skipping sections that were long, unnecessary descriptions of, say, how the living room was decorated. The hardest part, however, was the depiction of Ty, the biracial hero. It's clear KA did not do her homework beforehand. The way the characters talk about race is really strange to begin with. They all, hero included, say he's "got color." I'm not familiar with Colorado vernacular so maybe that's something they say down there but it didn't sit well. If Ry's race needs to be referenced, why can't they say he's biracial or that he's a person of color? Secondly, the stereotyping is off the charts for Ty and his POC friends. Ty's character is more one dimensional as a result and it didn't have to be that way. Imagine all the directions you could go in terms of a biracial man who grew up in a small Colorado mountain town! The sky is the limit. Instead, Ty is reduced to some antiquated ideas of how black men are. Third, while racism is at play with the crime Ty was framed for, it's treated with a heavy hand. There are clear villains and everyone else is just peachy. There's no examination of systemic racism, which tends to be more nuanced and hidden compared to the overt racists on the force. Do those people exist? Yes. But I was more interested in how the whole town collectively shrugs its shoulders at the cops' behavior (hello, privilege), even those claiming to be Ty's good friends. Plus, the part with the cabin at the end was way too over the top. The story should have ended at least 100 pages sooner. I could keep going but you get the picture. I started reading this series because a friend highly recommended the fourth book. I'm still going to read it eventually. I'll have to see if I can get over the KA formula. I'm open to being surprised. We'll see.

4.5 "Who do you Trust" Stars! Jumping right in to where the stunning conclusion of First Touch left off, Last Kiss continues the sensual and thrilling romantic suspense ride that started in the first book of this duet. Please note that First Touch must be read first and the below review contains spoilers for the first book, so please read my review for First Touch, if you have not yet started this series. Emily Wayborn's trust will be challenged to the core when she discovers herself in one of the most untenable of situations. Amber, her best friend, and boyfriend's former lover who he wanted to marry, is back from the dead. A woman she has shared men with before, but having found the one who completes and dominates her in all the right ways, she is no longer willing to share. But old habits die hard, and Amber is just as determined to win her prize. I loved how this story kept you guessing almost to the very end. Moreover the relationship both between Emily and Reeve and Emily and Amber is truly palpable and leaves you conflicted but longing for a particular resolution. Lovers of red hot passion scenes with a dominant and sub theme will definitely not want to miss this duet. Moreover Amber and Emily's complicated history and friendship further make this a unique story. Ms. Paige is a truly talented writer to be able to intermix all these themes, and I can't wait to read more of her writing. Source: Review copy provided in exchange for an honest review.

On the one hand it was far better than Voyager but on the other it was just kind of meh. It's odd, really, there was a complete story arc yet I didn't feel like much really happened. For starters there was no reason at all for it to be as long as it was. The plot didn't even appear until halfway through the book and what came before was just...there. Heck, most of what went on after the plot appeared was just there. I don't really have any feelings about Drums of Autumn either way which just feels weird. It was okay, I guess, but I don't feel like I gained anything by reading it. Going into it I didn't care about Brianna or Roger which meant I didn't much care about the plot. Did I feel bad for Brianna after she was raped and ended up pregnant by (probably) Bonnet? Yeah of course. She's still a complete idiot though and I still don't care much what happens to her. Most of her troubles are caused by her own stupidity anyway. I was more upset by Ian's fate and concerned with how Jenny would react than I was about the entire Brianna/Roger mess. I was all eager for Jamie and Brianna to meet but even that was disappointing. Jamie seemed to care more for William than he did for his only living child with his beloved wife. Like? Okay I guess? I get that he watched William grow up for several years but dude. She's your daughter. How about you care more about her well-being than your misplaced honor? By the time we hit page 800 I was silently urging the Frasers to just get back on a boat and go back to Scotland. Maybe if they had something exciting would have happened. Edit: OH MY GOD I literally just figured out (a week after finishing) that Bonnet isn't some random character he's supposed to be the notorious pirate. The real Bonnet was long dead by the time J&C wind up in the colonies but still I knew he seemed awfully familiar! If that wasn't intentional it was one heck of a screw up.

In 13-year-old Matt's world, the government imposes debt limits on families. If they exceed the debt limit, the oldest children are taken away to workhouses, to work off their parents' debt. When Matt is dragged from his home and taken to the workhouse because his parents exceeded their debt limit, he thinks he will just be there a short time -- until he finds out the truth. There is a lot more happening in the workhouse than he thought. I really liked the premise of this book, and I enjoyed the first half or so, but then it just seemed to become more and more unbelievable. Usually, when reading a dystopian novel, you take a little while to become accustomed to the new world, and then become even more immersed in the book. In this case, I found that the book just couldn't hold my interest. Many of Matt's investigational skills seem exaggerated, and the other characters in the book were very thinly drawn, so we didn't really know them. When Matt visited his sister, I just couldn't believe that she was not more upset at being in the workhouse. And in the end, I totally couldn't believe that there was a town full of parents who didn't care that their children were taken away and used as slave labor.

This book. Oh my God, you guys, THIS BOOK!!! It is absolute literary perfection. The Seven Realms series is second only to Harry Potter in my opinion (and I do NOT say that lightly! ), and the Crimson Crown is the perfect conclusion to such a stupendous series. By this point, the characters are all familiar to us - I think the only new character of note who is introduced is Char Dunedain, and her role is nothing life-changing. But the amazing thing is that the entire multitude of characters - and there are a lot! - get their due in this book. They are always squabbling and plotting, but they all have a role to play. Admittedly, some more than others - Amon's role is unfortunately way reduced in this book, and Sarie is absent entirely. There are so many layers of betrayal in this book, you have to read it with the utmost attention. Everyone has so many schemes going on at once, it's incredible anyone can keep their lies straight. The romantic question is resolved quite early on, but the whodunnit from GWT's epilogue waits until the end. Though I guessed right on the wizard killer's identity, that was through a lot of hard work - Cinda's writing is never obvious. There are two fantastic scenes in the series - one at the halfway point, the other at the climax - both dealing with fire. These scenes are magnificent. I wrote an essay analyzing all the intricacies there (link: https://sites.google.com/site/hpboy13...), but with two scenes Cinda brings the entire series full circle so beautifully, it's mind-boggling. The death toll in this book mounts quite high. (Will not actually spoil who dies, but just in case...) Just like Deathly Hallows, the main main characters survive, but other important characters die to make the war believable. The ending of this series is more perfect than anything I could have come up with. It's exquisitely elegant - all the characters get together for a joyous occasion. Plenty of them are unhappy, many are still single, and they dislike each other. Not everything is tied up in a nice little bow. But there is enough closure to leave the reader thoroughly satisfied. Most of all, I love the message here: that a new generation, willing to try new things, really can affect change and build a brighter future. There is no excuse of "they're young and stupid." There is no "adults know better." Speaker Jemson says that this current crop of teenagers will build a bright future together, and we see that they do. This is empowering, and I love this message. As usual, Cinda's writing is superb - the detailed descriptions, the unexpected humor, believable love and tension. Cinda's books have long ago achieved "must-read" status on my list, and after such a thrilling conclusion to such a great series, I am quivering with anticipation of her next treat for us. Her books have the gift of having an awful lot happen, but of never feeling long. And, I hope to one day return to the Seven Realms, because I am in love with this world and it's crazy characters.

At the beginning...it was slow and I didn't really like it. She kept complaining and I don't like to read about people complaining about their lives, but as soon as she met Will, things started to become a bit better. The things that they did are not what I would've done, but it's understandable since it does happen these days. I thank my teacher for letting me read it~

I believe I was supposed to really love this book, and I really tried, tried hard, but I just couldn't. So I guess I will be the harsh reviewer in a sea of 5 star reviews. I almost feel bad about it, but not enough to make me change my mind. After reading many reviews that explain that "this is a novel like a novel ought to be", I still wonder what it means, or maybe if I don't get the wide opinion of "what a novel ought to be". The over literary writing style is both the beauty and the weakness in this book. And as much as I love books, and books about books, and beautiful prose, the author was just so much over doing it, that it bothered me, and distracted me, and bored me, a lot! I do have to admit that in several places Zafon wrote 5 stars sentences, and that the writing is beautiful and lyrical at times. But the good parts were scattered in a really badly written book, so it doesn't add up to too much. In addition, there were too many characters. Most not memorable, and with names too similar to one another. Each character is speaking in a long long literary monolog. In many cases the characters vocalize very sexist remarks, those just pour all throughout the book (e.g. women can't do Maths). Fermin's comments bothered me the most, with his attitude that women are stupid (beautiful) objects and no more. His preaching this amazing theory to Daniel, that seem mostly to share the opinion. But maybe if the plot was good enough, if the mystery was solved in an elegant way, I could be more forgiving. But it wasn't. The mystery is being solved in a way outrages in its laziness. 30 pages of a letter unrevealing it to our protagonist. After years of search, after all the long conversations and monologs, Daniel still could not come to conclusions, and needed someone else to write a detailed long summary of the events. Lame!! The most beautiful idea in the book is the concept of the Cemetery of Forgotten Books. Unfortunately it was underdeveloped, and drowned in an avalanche of words, descriptions and similes. Contributing my 1 star, hopefully that it would not drown in a sea of other 5 stars.

Although, I think that the issues that they faced needed to be explored a lot further because they were pretty deep on Hunter's side. Honestly, I hope one day I can find a love as profound as that experienced by the three couples in this series. This last installment of the trilogy follows the same format of the previous two, with alternating chapters from two different viewpoints. The first part of the novel is devoted to telling the new story of Sophia and Gideon, though threads from the past are woven through craftily so that when it all comes together it does so seamlessly. Once again we have beautiful, flawed characters whose chemistry is a driving force through the novel, and it's written in such a way that you feel everything through them. It's the same kind of non stop action that we had in the first two, making it hard to put down, though the stakes are higher, and a conclusion imminent. It is this latter point that had me a little conflicted - whilst wanting that conclusion, I found that I liked the unpredictability of the first novel the most. Here, a lot of that is missing, and there's really only two possible conclusions - either they save the world or they don't. Still, no complaints; this is a spectacular conclusion to the series, with all threads tied and questions answered. It was particularly enjoyable to reunite with our heroes from the first and second novels, and watch them all interact together. The series is really well-written in that respect, with all links built with strong foundations meaning there's no skepticism when we realise two characters know one another. A little sad that it's over, but it's such a fantastic world that I wouldn't be surprised if it spawns a spin-off series. A worthy finish to a beautiful story.

I was pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed Falling Kingdoms. I was expecting a novel that was somewhat Game of Thrones-lite but instead the storyline was fairly complex and the setting, although not overly original, was interesting and richly detailed. The story takes place across three very different kingdoms: Limeros, Paelsia and Auranos. Limeros, the Northern kingdom, is ruled by a tyrannical King who instills fear in the populace and rules with an iron fist. Paelsia is the middle kingdom and is ruled by a chieftain who is rumoured to have magical abilities. Paelsia is a poor country and its people suffer, struggling to survive in an increasingly impoverished environment. Auranos is the Southern kingdom and is the most envied, as its denizens enjoy a life of prosperity under the more benevolent leadership of their King. There are tensions between each of these nations and violence and bloodshed will soon overtake the lands. The book follows the viewpoints of several main characters and each get their own third person point-of-view chapters. Princess Cleo is the first main character we are introduced to. Cleo and her companions are visiting Paelsia from their neighbouring kingdom of Auranos. It is during this visit that a tragic event occurs. One of her companions Aron, a young nobleman who Cleo greatly dislikes but is forced to accommodate due to him having some kind of leverage over her, has an argument with a young man from Paelsia and ends up killing him in cold blood. Cleo does nothing to stop the argument from escalating and she feels terrible guilt about this throughout the rest of the novel. This tragedy serves as a catalyst for the events which are to come. Cleo is a likeable yet somewhat naive young girl whose great beauty often allows her to get away with acting immaturely and selfishly. Cleo has very noticeable character flaws but you feel for her, especially when she is forced to endure a betrothal to the young nobleman she so thoroughly despises. Cleo shows an enormous amount of character growth throughout the novel and what she has to endure throughout the book only makes her stronger and more determined. I ended up really rooting for her towards the end, though I could not really get interested in the side-plot of her romance with her young personal guard Theon I could not really bring myself to care very much at his death either - I wish there had been a bit more development with him and his growing attachment to Cleo . Jonas is the brother of the young man who was killed and he puts the blame firmly on Princess Cleo, who stood by and let her companion drive a knife through his elder brother's throat. Jonas, filled with grief and thoughts of vengeance, vows to destroy Princess Cleo. He soon joins forces with the chieftain of Paelsia, who is determined to take down Auranos and is willing to work with the King of Limeros in order to do so. Jonas was an interesting and conflicted character. I felt sympathy for his loss and could understand why he hated Cleo but his memory of the tragedy that happened before his eyes is warped by his own misapprehensions of the situation. Jonas had very little page time in comparison to some of the other characters and I wished that he had been fleshed out a bit more. As it is he comes across a little one-sided and his thirst for revenge is a little bit tiresome I do have high hopes for him in book 2 though and I can't help but feel that he does kind of have the hots for Cleo - there are too many scenes where he describes her as being beautiful even if he views her as deadly and cunning - I think he may have a change of heart regarding the Princess in the next book . Magnus is the heir to the kingdom Limeros. In many ways I found Magnus to be the most interesting character, albeit one whose actions became increasingly hard for me to overlook. Magnus holds a shameful secret. He is deeply in love with his sister Lucia, who is the only person who has ever shown him any real affection, as his father has never much cared for him and his mother, the Queen, is a cold and distant figure in his life. To be honest, having read many fantasy novels which include incest (George R. R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire series, Katharine Kerr's Daggerspell etc.) this element never really bothered me as much as it probably should. In real-life I would most certainly not be so understanding of it mind, but in a fantasy setting it seems I can just easily accept it and move on. It is soon revealed that Magnus and Lucia are not blood-related but I can see why many people would have a problem with this part of the story as Magnus only becomes aware of this during the course of the novel and his feelings go much further back. They have been raised as brother and sister and Lucia certainly does not share her brother's feelings. Magnus starts off as a deeply troubled young man and the events in the novel only serve to make him more cold and self-loathing. He is on a dark path and the choices he makes get darker as the story progresses it is Magnus who kills Theon, earning Cleo's enmity . Magnus, somewhat in spite of himself, wants to gain his father's approval and joins with him to bring down his long-time enemy, the King of Auranos. Lucia is the only main character who I never really developed any attachment to. Although she has her own point-of-view chapters and her story may become more interesting, her character was a bit of a cypher. We are told she is destined to become a very powerful sorceress, which that is why the King took her in and raised her as his own, but her character did not have much weight for me and fell a little flat. There are a lot of familiar elements in this novel which are standard fantasy-fare: political manipulations, nations fighting each other for the throne, magic, romance, a long-awaited prophesied one, even the mysterious Watchers who have been keeping an eye on Lucia and her developing abilities are a fairly common fantasy trope. However, while this novel may not be overly original, it is a lot of fun. The plot is exciting, most of the characters are interesting and the climax leaves you anxious for the next book. I wasn't completely bowled over but I was very entertained. It was hard to get to grips with the characters at first as the book flips between the different and varied point-of-views but you did get to see every perspective of the conflict and feel sympathy for characters who will be soon pitted against each other in the forthcoming war and what follows thereafter. I am really looking forward to the next book Rebel Spring as I think the story has the potential to be even better than the first. Four stars ****

4.5 stars I put off reading this for a long time because I'm not a big fan of contemporaries. I only read it now because I needed a book by an Australian author that had a lot of points for the Scavenger Hunt and all of the ones people recommended I had already read. Walker is one of my favorite authors so I gave it a go, hoping for enough points. I'm so glad I did as I really enjoyed it (plus it did have a good amount of points! I don't have a lot to say. There wasn't much of a plot other than getting to know each other but it was good. There was a little too much sex but it was very sweet if slow moving. The whole thing was slow moving, too, not just the sex. I was also constantly wondering what this had originally been fan fiction for. Turns out that I've never even heard of the show. The art was well done in so many ways. The descriptions are beautiful, the paintings actually sound sellable and valuable, and the comprehension and understanding of the art by those who know art, was wonderfully described. I was really impressed. I recently read another story about some fantabulous painter and the art described sounded like it belonged on motel room walls. This didn't. Comments: Trent was the slowest house painter ever. Even the estimate of how long it would take was ridiculous. Trent gets in trouble for implying it was all just meaningless sex to him . I didn't get that at all from what he said. Someone was a little oversensitive. This why you don't put dogs  in the back of trucks!! Ever! At one point, I bawled my head off, tears streaming down my cheeks. Well done.The ending felt a little like a pancake ending (an expression I just read about in another book), like it should have been over chapters before because that's when the climax happened, and now they're just having breakfast together and going about their day which we don't need to hear, but it was good, and the very end was perfect. This is why she's on my favorite author's list: even contemporary, plot-less fan fiction is wonderful in her hands.

June BOTM read for Rachel E. Carter YA Book Club 4/5 stars "Sometimes we forget how good we have it until we come across someone who doesn't. I am guilty just as anyone else about comparing myself to others; this book will give you a reality check." An amazing book that deals with a really controversial subject assisted suicide . I cried several times reading this. To be perfectly honest, adult contemporary romance (although this was more like very tame NA) is not really my thing. Neither was the blurb or love story >> I read this because of the amazing movie trailer and Sam Odair (yea, well, at least I admitted it). Would I ever read this again? Nope. It's one of those books I only read once (rereads are devoted to amazing plots and romances, not sad, depressing issue books -no matter how uplifting the message or great the writing . Like I said, It wasn't really my type of book. But I did love it. Does that make sense? Like, I enjoyed the writing style and the characters but overall I'm just not a serious contemporary issues and tame romance kind of girl? I don't know how to explain my feelings for this book, other than I read it all in one night and kept hoping beyond hope I'd get a HEA . Even though I didn't, I still loved it because of the way it tackled the issues and portrayed Louisa and Will. Jojo did a ton of research -EVERYTHING felt genuine, it might as well have been a REAL love story. I actually did three years working at an agency that employed caregivers and worked with individuals like Will and I can honestly say it fit with all of my experiences. This book really made me think, and if you ever need to read something to put your self-pity to shame you should read this. Beautiful. Real. The kind of book I think everyone should read at some point in their lives because it will make you a better person.

There is a lot to like about this book- strong female characters, interesting side characters, interesting if typical magic system, and a likable main character. Persephone is a likable lead character. She's not harsh or mean. Sure she's a little shut off but she's also caring and sensitive. She's also a badass gifted with some preternatural strength. The writing is solid but a great deal of the future of the book is telegraphed, so you know what is going to happen and can even guess when and where. There are some things to not like too- riding on brooms and pointy hats during ceremonies  as well as the age old trope of weres, vamps, and witches coming out into the open and the fight for equality with humans. SIGH. I do like that the vamps are dangerous and assumed evil, even if they are sexy. One of the comments compares this to Anita Blake and the triumvirate. Yes there is a were and vamp involved in her becoming the Lustrata, the big difference is that they serve Persephone and she is not in service to them. Of course we'll see if that is the case in the later books or if Seph will go full Anita and engage in kinky three ways with her vamp and were.

Live Through This is one of those stories that will stay with me forever. I was expecting a psychological thriller about a girl who weaved a web of lies, and well, it was psychological--but not in a way that I ever would have imagined. While the jacket description is true to the story, it really doesn't prepare you for what's inside. The author's note at the beginning of the ARC did prepare me, however, and I'm glad it did. Knowing that this story involves an abusive relationship didn't ruin it for me. It made the story more real and more touching. I was still surprised along the way, and it's so hard to truly comprehend the story that I read because of how shocking it was. The characters are well done, the feelings are great, and the book has such an intense ending. It is extremely well written and I truly hope that many people will read this. I was touched by Scott's story. As great as the writing and the pacing are, however, all of this really is secondary to the message. Heartbreaking and twisted, Live Through This is a story you will never forget. It deals with an issue that is not often tackled by today's media, but deserves to be understood nonetheless. I truly hope this novel helps people like Coley to deal with their demons and understand that even though it is confusing, they are victims and nothing is their fault.

Stephanie's boss has been kidnapped. He's being held for ransom until he pays his gambling debt bill but it goes up daily and the ladies at the office don't have $750,000. Vinnie's wife and her mob father won't pay because Vinnie got snatched while he was getting some snatch from a street walker. Stephanie and Morelli are on a break and Ranger lends her cars in exchange for kisses. Lula, Connie and Stephanie come up with a plan to get the money. I finished this last night and then honestly couldn't remember the ending. Like fairy floss, it's just gone. The rob 'Peter to pay Peter' idea is nuts, as Grandma would say. Everyone knows it was them with the distinctive residue of cluck in a bucket chicken grease and eau de stink bomb courtesy of Connie. There was something about an alligator, mooner in an RV, hobbits at a con... and I don't remember. 2 stars

I binge read books 1-4 this past week and have a new favorite series to add to my list. Piper has grown a lot since the first book. Not much time has actually passed, but she has been through a lot and has become more self aware as a result. She is no longer the punk kid with an attitude that she can't back up, she is now realizing how naive she was and is trying to make changes to how she lives/thinks. This wasn't my favorite of the books, it seemed like a lot of running around and saying things need to change, but no actual follow through until the end. Piper made choices in book 3 that have come back to bite her in the ass, throwing away Ash's tracking spell for one. I do wish she would wise up about the Sahar and could see what is actually happening with that. Hopefully book 5 resolves the Sahar issue. Ash- oh Ash. I feel for the guy and his control issues. I like his character a lot and can only hope he gets his HEA with Piper. :) Thank you, thank you for his Nightmare Effect to no longer be an issue for Piper!! He was understandably angry with Piper, but still his awesome self. Lyre- I don't really understand why he would share so many secrets with Seiya in #3.5 after admitting he doesn't really trust her, but when Piper asks him what's going on he completely shuts her out and he does actually trust her. I don't see where any of that came from and it left me a little cold towards him. Not enough to hope he dies in the final battle or not get his HEA or a spin off... There are a lot of loose ends that need to be tied up in book 5 and I really hope that it is as good and better than books 1-4!
