It would be hard to think of a better name for this book, for Rachel Joyce's Perfect was, in fact, practically perfect. It was a beautifully written, evocative exploration of the power of magical thinking, the nature of friendship, and the unanticipated consequences of mistakes. The story is told in alternating chapters occurring in 1972 and today. I can't say much more without revealing a significant plot twist; suffice it to say that this structure successfully kept the tension at a steady boil until the very end. In this respect, Perfect should appeal to readers who enjoyed Gillian Flynn's Gone Girl, even though the subject matter of the two books is very different. I loved the "hook" of the added two seconds. The prologue immediately captured my attention and drew me into the lives of Byron, Diana, and James. Those considering this book will, therefore, be able to tell immediately from the sample on Amazon or Barnes & Noble whether they will enjoy it. Joyce was able to capture key aspects of each character's personality in concise visual images. Had she written only the following two lines about Byron's father, I would have known all I needed to know: "He nodded the way his father did when he was stating a fact, as if he was so correct even his own head had to agree." "If Byron ever tried to hug him, and sometimes he wished he could, the embrace ran away at the last minute and became a handshake." Can't you just see that embrace running away? Here is Byron during a conversation with James: "Every time he began a sentence he was afraid the wrong words would escape from his mouth. Consequently he had to keep examining them on their way out, as if he was checking their hands for cleanliness. It was exhausting." From these three short sentences, I learned a great deal about Byron's self-esteem, his relationship with his best friend James, and the "perfect" life led in Cranham House. My only quarrel with Joyce, and it was a minor one, was the tidy exchange at the end between Byron and James of the brass beetle key ring and the Brooke Bond tea card. It strains credulity to suggest that the staff of Besley Hill would have allowed a patient to retain such an object during his initial admission to the facility, much less through multiple admissions over almost 40 years. I did not realize before I began reading Perfect that it was written by the same author who wrote The Unlikely Pilgrimage of Harold Fry. I will certainly be seeking out that book in the near future. I received a free copy of Perfect through NetGalley in exchange for an honest review.

Disclaimer: Goodreads friends with the author. But that doesn't influence my rating one bit. This was a pretty mixed bag for me. The beginning was solid, the writing drew me in. I was rooting for Nell as she decided quite firmly to stay mum and so she wouldn't end up shackled to her clearly skeezy ne'er-do-well cousin-in-law Jack. The seduction scene was quite clever, as I assumed that it was worded so vaguely to reflect how naive and clueless Nell was about what exactly was happening. But then... that old trope of instant Maternal Instinct kicked in that set my eyes rolling. One of these days I'd like to read a heroine who actually follows through on her initial rejection of Motherhood. I'm not holding my breath, though. The only ones who do stick to their guns end up being sluts and nasty wenches. The setting of the Poor Farm was really cool. If you peruse old atlases, it seemed nearly every town had one out in the hinterlands on back roads away from sight. A very interesting and uncommon location, and as a result, we got some uncommon characters. I thought the description of daily life there was well done and gave the sneak-peek into the past that this history buff loves. I'm no fan of mystery, but the mystery in this book was pretty slight. At the first clue, I knew "whodunit" and became rather impatient as Nell slowly arrived at the obvious conclusion. I was rather surprised that at the Big Reveal, there was still almost half the book to go. The last half seemed to lose its focus, as Nell deals with her stepfather, her ailing mother, and Martin the must-be-gay bachelor. The plot started to wander aimlessly at this point, and I would go for days without picking up the book because I had started not to care how the story ended, and as I found out (because I did finish it) the conclusion was very open-ended, as the reader wonders if that was it, or there is going to be another book where Nell finds out that Martin prefers the dudes. I was also disappointed that the murderer didn't get a proper comeuppance. Slipping and falling in the river? It would totally have been awesome to have Martin blast the bastard in the back with a shotgun and that's why he went sailing into the river. There were a couple things that bugged me. The dialogue was rather stilted with a lack of contractions. It didn't sound very natural. Nell and Martin were childhood friends, but they sounded like robots talking to each other. The chapters were also really short. Like, James Patterson short. I'm not one for 20-40 page chapters, but only books the size of Gone with the Wind should have chapters into the 50s. The short chapters made the flow of the plot choppy and seemed to foster that sense of aimlessness I was getting. Was this a mystery, historical fiction, chick novel (Nell and Tess's friendship)? So it was just under 3 stars for me, but rounding it up to 3. Kudos for a total lack of obvious grammatical errors and typos. Every word meant what it was supposed to mean, and as we all know, that seems to be a major challenge among self-pubbed/indie authors, especially in the New Adult crowd.

Be prepared for some sugar-induced rambling. I first read this book when I was 12. It was my first foray into the Russian Revolution and all of the horrors it inflicted on everyone, from the gentry to the poor. This book downplayed some of the more gory experiences of the aristocrats of Russia, with Anna simply mentioning who and who died, and my young brain simply didn't quite grasp the gravity of it. Oh sure people died, how sad. Instead, I was wholly captivated by how Anna lived somewhat like a Russian Cinderella, with how noble and self-sacrificing she was. In hindsight, she might have come off a little irritating with how ridiculously mary-sue she was, but it didn't quite rub me the wrong way (I was 12, and had solely lived off enid blyton and ronald dahl, and whatever books that were deemed acceptable for children at the public library.) I greedily inhaled the book and all it's descriptions of the infamous Russian jewels, and rejoiced  when she being a countess was exposed, and 12 year old me actually teared up a little when Peter grasped Anna's hands and asked about her calluses. I will admit freely that I didn't care much for the love story, and the only parts that I so loved were descriptions of the Russian nobles, and how princes and duchesses ended up as doormans, hair dressers, and chauffeurs, all jobs all admittedly below their status, but how they clung to survival and took it all in stride! It was abit of a polished view that I had, and now, some 8 years later, I still enjoy this book, but some part of me tends to skip portions of how wonderful Anna is. This book was the book that kickstarted my interest in Russia before, during and after Revolution, and I recommend everyone to read it, but to suspend disbelief at the utter goodness of the heroine, if you tend to be cynical. (Which I am) I would have given this book 3 stars, but in lieu of the magic it brought to my mind so many years ago, I'll give it 4 for sentimentality's sake.

Tonight I will do the impossible. The Amazing Arden is a female illusionist, making a name for herself in a man's world with her famous trick of sawing a man in half. One night, she switches her saw for an ax. Later that evening, her husband is found murdered under the stage. It is up to Virgil Holt, a small-town policeman with his own secrets, to find out the truth from Arden. But during an intense night of questioning, Holt learns that Arden's tricks aren't the only things not what they seem. I found this book's depiction of the lives of illusionists in the early 20th century. I have always been fascinated by reading about travelling shows during that time period and really enjoyed that part of the book. I also liked Arden's story for the most part, coming from nothing and making something of herself. It is ultimately a coming of age story with Arden escaping the chains of her past and becoming her own person. The romance in the book felt genuine and the author does a good job of showing Arden's struggle with her feelings. My big issue with this book and other books like it, is the all-powerful antagonist. I know the book is ultimately about overcoming abuse and I respect the struggle that many abused women face when trying to escape from their abusers, but sometimes in books these abusive characters end up becoming so powerful and overwhelming to make them almost unbelievable. I mean this guy tracks Arden from Tennessee to NC to NYC to Chicago, in a time before the Internet and reliable transportation. And then she cuts his throat and leaves him bleeding out, but somehow, again in a time with substandard medical care, he magically recovers. Its seemed a bit unbelievable to me. Because of all of this, the ending feels very rushed and forced. I would recommend this book to those who enjoy stories of strong women and coming of age stories. I would also recommend it if you are someone who likes reading about travelling circuses or magic shows. There are definitely some parts where you will have to suspend your disbelief, but overall its a pretty good story.

** spoiler alert ** Gone Girl review This is the first novel turned movie that I have read in a few years. I saw the movie first and now wish that I hadn't. I wanted to hear (in my mind's ear) the character's unique voices that Flynn created but I couldn't shake off the voices of Ben and Rosey (Ben Affleck and Rosamund Pike). This isn't a movie review DUH but I thought the changes they made in the movie were good ones i.e., drip line instead of slice to the underarm. That said, Gillian Flynn is a very talented writer. The call and response of diary entries to Nick's defensive plays was great. Though I wonder why Flynn didn't use a Amy chapter to announce her return. She just kinda 'bang on the door' arrived in a Nick chapter and it wasn't much of a surprise for me. Flynn's characters were authentic and very raw. Amy's use of down and dirty cursing imprecations and locker room vulgarities were cold, crude and hard hearted and I loved that. Amy is one hard-ass control freak of a psycho bitch. Poor Nick. Poor, poor pitiful Nick. Recommended. 4 stars.
found it hard to keep interest in reading this book.

Follow You Home was very suspenseful. It kept me furiously reading, in spite of many annoyances. It didn't feel like the suspense built naturally. Instead, it felt very engineered and artificial. Daniel would be about to reveal something, and then there would be some interruption and then a change of subject. It had me rolling my eyes more than once. I was irritated with Laura's whininess by 10% into the book, and it didn't get any better from there. I don't mind disregarding plausibility for a good story, but it stretched to far on this one. After waiting so long to find out what happened that night that was too horrible to speak about, I didn't buy it. Yes, it was horrific. But there is no sane person on earth who would keep that a secret for three months. Completely unimaginable. In the end, an explanation was given for this secrecy, but I still could not fathom both of them agreeing to not report what they saw. So while I can't give it a bad rating, because it grabbed and held my attention throughout, neither can I give it a good rating.

My reviews for the other two books in this series were kind of ambivalent, but this one blew me away. N.K. Jemisin's development as a a writer practically punches you in the face here. This one is narrated by Sieh, the god(ling) of childhood and mischief. His voice is as funny, earnest, churlish, heartbreaking and variable as his nature -- I so appreciated his perspective, especially since he didn't make much of an impression on me in The Hundred Thousand Kingdoms and wasn't really present in The Broken Kingdoms. Jemisin delves without restraint into the complexity of his character, which sees MAJOR development, and as painful as that development is, it is so gratifying to go through it with him. The story is super high-stakes -- definitely higher than in the other two -- and ends on a note that feels right, even if it is gut-wrenching. After learning so much about the HunThou universe, especially from an ancient god able to add important history and context, I'm sad to leave it behind, but excited to move on to Jemisin's other works. Also, at the end there's an "extra" bit -- kind of an epilogue -- from Oree Shoth's perspective. I don't know if it's Oree's new age/wisdom or Jemisin's development as a writer, but my previous complaint that Oree's voice was too similar to Yeine's was definitely not applicable here, so if you were disappointed with The Broken Kingdoms for that reason, this is an extra reason to read this one!

I really wanted to like this book. The storyline was there: a girl playing football. I can dig it. But I felt like these characters were 12 or something. They were so immature, horny, and...they were basically cardboard-cut characters. Stereotypical. And the drama. OH THE DRAMA. WAY WAY WAY too much, man. I couldn't believe that Jordan could be over 6 feet and be "gorgeous" and yet none of the guys on her team ever liked her? That's just not possible. I hated Ty from the start. I kind of expected his mom in a wheelchair was a lie because Jordan never met her. I mean WTF?? . He was HELL ARROGANT and was all the sex really necessary in this book? I also hated Sam Henry. Their relationship was cute but sleeping around when you're in love with your best friend? Who does that? I just don't get it. And the wrap-up of the story was so lame. Sam's excuses were so damn lame. It's like the reader is expected to swoon and cry for him. PLEASE. And the way Jordan acted around the guys? It felt like she was trying too hard. And if she really wanted to be a guy, I don't think they take to heart so much on what people think of them. Who the hell cares if the bitchy cheerleader badtalks you? Key word here: BITCHY. SLUTTY. STUPID CHEERLEADER stereotype. And having two cheerleaders be "cool" to Jordan? Meh.... This whole book was just disappointing. I'll be trying Stealing Parker and Things I Can't Forget though because I got them in e-book format in a bundle so...hopefully it's better...>_>

Oh my, I don't think I can't give this a rating. So first things first - very well written and edited, no complaints on that front. It was a very enganging read and I never thought about not finishing it. Personally I would cut a few of the sex scenes but that might be just me. I just felt that some of them didn't contibute to the plot. It took me a while to realize that the MC is mentally ill, or rather to be able to get myself into that mindspace. But I did and I think it is really well narrated and (from my very limited perspective at least) - I could relate. What made me scratch my head and keeps me from giving a four star rating is the fact that almost everybody in this book is Evil - I used the capital E on purpose. Aargh, I don't think that it is necessary. I get that there are the horrors in the narrators past. Yep, might be just the reason why he is so screwed up. But - let the spoilers begin... There was no need for the encounter with the evil, evil serial killer of cute twinks? Why the callous, abusive (to say the least) customers? Why the showdown on that operatic scale? Why, why, why? I might have stumbled upon a genre thing I was not previously aware of but... Gah! It's not helping. To be fair, I'm not a huge fan of thrillers and I think I might have preferred a quieter book - not neceassarily more personal (from the narrator's point of view because that is about as personal as you can get) but, really? Mental illnesses they are just that. They happen. Sometimes because there is a traumatic event in the past but, yeah, well, sometimes not. I think here is the root of my unease. I think I might have preferred a) a straight-forward thriller with human monsters in them and a detective to root them out. And hopefully some healing for the victims. or b) the story of of somebody coping with mental illness. Period. [Though in all fairness I have to say that the painting part was written extrodinarily well. (I'm a musician, my visual imagination is for crap but the idea of capturing images in negative space was wonderful. High five for the author!)]

Memoirs of a Geisha is an incredibly, evocative and descriptive novel that had me wishing to time-travel back to that era and fully appreciate the beauty of Japan. I found it hard not to empathise with the protagonist, Sayuri, and her deeply moving narration just absolutely destroyed me. Sure there were too many similes and metaphors splattered all throughout the novel, enough to make me aim the book across the far wall but after a while, even that added to the hypnotising effect this novel has on you. I did feel that the characters were just cardboard cut-outs though, and felt oddly detached to them. I really wish Arthur Golden had built a more sturdy foundation under the characters. I wanted to feel close to them, to relate to them. Still, this was amazing and whenever I find that I have spare time on my hands, Memoirs of a Geisha will be one of the first book that I'll pick up.

Lock In worked as a great science fiction story, but only an okay mystery. On the SF side, the concept of a new minority created by a disease that kills a lot of people, but leaves some trapped in a 'locked in' state. They are called Haydens, since one of the early victims was President Hayden's wife. This has led to the development of various technologies (online life, Surrogates style artificial bodies, and riding the minds of people called Integrators who survived without being locked it). These technologies are funded by the government, but a new bill is cutting off that funding. Some things that were missing from the world-building, though, was any hint of labour shortages due to the number of people who died, and information about how other countries are dealing with the Haydens (what happens in third-world countries, for example). The mystery revolves around a Hayden, Chris Shane, who is on his first day as an FBI agent. Chris's father is very rich and running for the Senate, and Chris grew up as the poster child for Haydens. On the first day, though, Chris is paired with a surly older agent, and immediately thrown into the mystery of a murder (?) committed by an Integrator (?). There's also a cop with a hate for the older agent, who once was an Integrator but left after an incident. The mystery was interesting, but there was little in the way of twists to it. No false paths, no alternate theories. They focus in pretty fast on who did it and why. One element that was pointed out to me that I found intriguing is the main character. The novel is written in first person by Agent Chris Shane, and there wasn't a single hint that I could remember to what gender Chris was. For some reason I read the character as male, but it would be interesting to figure out if there are any trends on what kind of readers saw Chris as male or female. I would definitely read a sequel, but the mystery definitely needed some work.

Hmm... 4.5? I liked this book so, so, so much. It has a deep and solid world-building (I could just dwell on it, it's so colorful and there's SO much to see! ), well-shaped characters and a lot of political intrigue, this book is so worth it! The relationship between Safiya and Iseult melted my heart. It was so deep and true and I just cRY when I read the way they get along! Also, thanks goodness, there was no lnsta-love. Oh, and don't get me started on how much I loved Evrane, she's my beautiful cinnamon roll and I'll cry and fight if anything ever happens to her! Can't wait for the next book!

This was a very short read about the joys, sorrows, trials and triumphs of love in dictionary form. Telling a story through definitions of words is, for me, very effective. Sometimes the words and the "definitions" that followed were self-explanatory, other times they were ironic, and sometimes they were sad. A great read about a not-so-perfect love story.

It starts with the king's son venturing into Elfland to win the heart of the king of Elfland's daughter, but mostly tells the story of what happens after their "happily ever after" (which is not as happy as you might have expected). While a bit slow in the middle, it is nonetheless fascinating with some rather unexpected twists along the way. It also deals extensively with the magic coming back to the small realm of Erl and some of the most fascinating passages are devoted to the ways ordinary men deal with the strange and alien that creep into their peaceful, ordinary lives. In this aspect it reveals a lot about even today's people attitudes towards everything that is Other. Written in a beautiful, poetic 19th century prose, this book most likely provided a huge amount of inspiration and is the predecessor of some of the most beloved contemporary fantasy novels, i.e. Neil Gaiman's "Stardust" and Susanna Clarke's "Jonathan Strange & Mr. Norrell". If you like fairy-tale-like fantasy, you should most definitely read "The King of Elfland's Daughter".

Blood Song is one of my favourite fantasy novels, and I'm very much looking forward to the (hopefully) final volume, but ... ... if it wouldn't be for my positive attitude and an affection for some of the characters, I would have given Tower Lord just three stars. It has pacing issues, occasionally serious ones at that, and would have benefited from cutting some 100 pages. I think calling the typical 'middle book' of the trilogy sums it up best - assuming the third one will be brilliant again of course.

I liked this book. I didn't love it but I also didn't hate it. It kept me entertained for the 350 pages, but it's not one I'd go out recommending to my friends either. I really liked the first chapter, I was sort of disappointed when it changed into first person. I had taken an unintentional break from reading Young Adult novels and just started reading them again this year. I've noticed this continuous pattern of always having to be written in first person through the eyes of a self-described ugly (but really pretty) teenage girl. Looking through the reviews there were a lot of complaints about Alina and her lack of self confidence. I really didn't have an issue with that. I was actually excited because I saw a glimpse of confidence at the beginning of the novel (notated in my updates) when Alina stated she was going to hold up her head and ignore the stares because she had worse. Unfortunately, I didn't see much more of that same confidence continued throughout and I was hoping to see that growth. Yet, that wasn't the issue that really bothered me. What did bother me was the confusion I felt about The Fold and the history of the current and previous wars. Since this was a new world to me I would have loved to get more of a background. It felt like a lot of this story was going through the motions getting Alina from Part A to Part B and leaving out many details that could have made this story really stand out. Onto more positives, I really loved the plot twist. There was quite a bit of foreshadowing, but I still thought "woah" when I read it. To recap, like I said at the beginning, not a book to die for, but an enjoyable read that was easy to finish.

I started reading this book after watching a few episodes of TV adaptation. I really don't understand why they changed anything in the book, because none of the change makes sense to me. The suspense in the TV episodes was successful for maybe 2-3 episodes, but after that it's completely ruined due to the change they made. Following are the changes I observe and my comments: The fact Ethan was integrated for the third time and Teresa and Ben had lived in Pines for 5 years. I personally like the chapter about Teresa watching Ethan running from afar her house before the truth is revealed to Ethan. When the whole story was explained to Ethan, suddenly it all made sense. And the fact that Ethan wasn't allowed to tell Teresa the truth even after he took the position of Sheriff also feels quite good, as it adds to the depressing atmosphere and drama of untrusting in their relationship. But all these dynamics are missing in TV adaptation. Also, setting Ben to be 13 right away makes it a bit absurd to see him coerced by school teachers right away. The age of Kate In the novel, Kate had been living in Pines for decades, while in TV it's just one decade and she didn't change much other than growing hair and some wrinkles. I imagine it's because the production team of TV adaptation were hoping there might be some change of doing make-out scenes of Ethan and Kate, but it really is not necessary, because compared with this potentially juicy scene, the shock Ethan experienced when facing the old Kate is much better, and it's truly a pity this is missing in TV adaptation. Pope's image and death I don't see why they'd removed stereotyped image of sheriff, a mid-aged white with blond hair. Also, his death in novel is a successful tool of illustration showing the character of Pilcher. In TV, the scene in which Pope got run over by Ethan seems ridiculous compared with the original work. Nurse Pam I rather like the image of her in the original work, a pretty and young psychopath who's enjoying her job of manipulating the whole town. But I suspect she'd want to rule some time later in the series. In TV, on the other hand, Pam is much more boring, being an old lady seeming crazy. Pilcher I really like the untrusting partnership full of sarcasasm between Ethan and Pilcher, because it's very unsettling in a way I think good for suspense novel. But to my disappointment, Pilcher becomes a amiable small prophet in TV. I do see an attempt of describing the process he fell less and less humane with a broken heart, but it's really nothing like Pilcher in novel, who's a cold and calculating dictator. But I do agree the endless memory of being tortured is best deleted. It made the story go painfully slow, but the drama it created does not create much effect.

Solid and interesting angel mythology? Check and check. I love how this book lays a solid foundation for the mythology and manages to do so in a way that is so deftly woven into the storytelling that you don't feel bogged down by it. The author has clearly done her research and added her own spin to it. I'm all for fantasy and creativity and for me, the strongest stories have come from authors who clearly know what came before and use that knowledge (directly or indirectly). One minute you're a happy fourteen-year-old--good at everything you try, popular, fun--the next you're a freak with wings. Clara appears to be a normal 16-year-old, just a little stronger, faster... you get the picture ... than her peers. However, along with the usual teenage issues, she's struggling to balance "appearing" normal, waiting for her purpose (something that as an angel, even a quarter-angel like she is, she will receive and must complete). And she really does have wings. I decided to leave out most of the wing refs I noted -- though I had to include a few here -- it highlighted how more "other" this made Clara, her brother, Jeffrey, and her mother appear than I'm used to finding in the angel books I've read so far. They are physically a part of her body, like another limb. The handling of this type of detail just added to the number of elements I appreciated about this story. The book had a slow pace at the start, but then before I knew it, I was heavily invested in Clara's relationships and journey. I think the birds in the area are dying laughing watching me try not to crash. Clara certainly has her struggles, and those make her very relatable. I love the way we get to experience the relationships in her life (brother, mom, new friends, Christian, and Tucker.) I especially love how we see her friendship develop with Tucker. Ah, Tucker and Christian. There are two boys. I will say up front that while I really do hate the whole love triangle angle, I can appreciate the challenge the author has created by introducing two equally attractive love interests. (I'm team Tucker, just saying that right now.) I'm flying! Of course, I'm not flying so much as coasting over the treetops like a hang glider or a freakishly large flying squirrel. There is humor. There are layers. And there are very definitely secrets. The author dangled many juicy tidbits throughout the story and I'm very interested in learning more. I mentioned the book had a slow-feeling start, but by the end of the book, I appreciated the author laying a solid foundation. I'll also say right now...I don't trust Angela. I'm worried about Jeffrey. The writing flowed well and I appreciated the flashes of humor throughout. And did I say yet how much I love her brother, Jeffrey? I'm very much looking forward to Hallowed, however, I will likely wait to read it a little closer to the release of Boundless.

I've talked about the starfish thing, the alien toilet and the time that the Animorphs were force to infiltrate a slaughterhouse. Yet this book - THIS book - somehow manages to be worse than all of these things. For one thing, there really is nothing to this story. It's constant action, with Rachel "leading" the Animorph into battle after battle, destroying shops, putting Andalite's on live TV and (somehow) stealing a plane and flying it into a building. Just, what am I reading? Is this still Mean Rachel from The Separation? Rachel can be gung-ho, but she's never had such a casual disregard for human life before. This ghostwriter doesn't seem to understand the subtleties of Rachel's character. This Rachel bullies her way into leadership, won't listen to her friends, and berates and insults them when they voice their worries. And yet the still follow her, for some reason, even when she has them doing stupid and dangerous things. The one good thing about this book was the final chapter, where Rachel finally addresses the fact that she caused the death of an innocent bystander and talks to Jake about leadership, but this is really only in the last five pages. Of all the Animorphs books that I've read so far, this one is truly missable.

4.5 Stars I have wanted to read Kerrelyn Sparks for YEARS and even have a few of the Love at Stake books. But I just never find the time to make the commitment to start a series already with so many books in it. When HOW TO TAME A BEAST IN SEVEN DAYS landed in my hands, I thought it would be perfect. Try a new to me author, and read something completely different in a new fantasy world. Win-win! I really went in with no expectations and this book quickly swept me off my feet. One of those that I just had to read every spare moment I had until I finished it. Lets talk about the world building first. Ms. Sparks does an amazing job at exploring this intricate world with us in a way that never felt heavy. The concept behind this series is really lots of fun. This has so many elements from Medieval times, which I think worked perfectly with the different Kingdoms in this world and gave the story a historical romance feel to it. Then the paranormal elements... the powers, the curses, the creatures, the magic even. The Embraced are born with special gifts and powers and the Kingdoms can't let these creatures exist. The Beast is one of the few Embraced alive because to be born Embraced means a death sentence he was spared because his cousin is the King. Luciana, on the other hand, is one of the few Embraced that was saved by exile at birth. Her family sent her to live in an orphanage on the Isle of Moon until now it's time she comes back to her rightful place. Each of them have a different gift. Luciana sees ghosts and Leo harnesses the power of lightning in his body. Obviously his is a deadlier skill and that's why he's been named The Beast. He cannot touch another without frying them with the shocks from any part of his skin. Both of them are so young and that also comes through in this story and makes it such a sweet and endearing tale. The mix of the innocence of their characters amongst this setting was a nice complement and softened this story. I think it's really one of the things that makes it such a breeze to read. It's so cute you just have to have more. The plot in this story is full of intrigue, lies and politics along with a simple romance between two people that were thrust together against their initial will but all along following fates' plan. I hope you let this story sweep you to another world. I think this is paranormal romance done in a new refreshing way but also that brings forth all the elements that I've loved in the genre for years. I was taken by surprise by how much I really loved it. I couldn't get enough of this and I am dying to read more!

Book on CD narrated by Heather Henderson From the book jacket One day in 2009, twenty-four-year-old Susannah Cahalan woke up alone in a strange hospital room, strapped to her bed, under guard, and unable to move or speak. A wristband marked her as a "flight risk," and her medical records - chronicling a month-long hospital stay - showed hallucinations, violence, and dangerous instability. Only weeks earlier, Susannah had been ... a healthy, ambitious college grad a few months into her first serious relationship and a promising career as a cub reporter at a major New York newspaper. Who was the stranger who had taken over her body? What was happening to her mind? My reactions This was a fascinating memoir - drawn partly from interviews with friends, relations, colleagues and medical personnel, her journal writings during the period, and her medical records - of a time period when Cahalan was nearly completely lost. It was luck that caused her diagnosis to come early enough in her disease process to not only correct the problem, but minimize the brain damage she might otherwise have suffered. For the cause of her apparent mental illness (some physicians felt her symptoms pointed to alcohol withdrawal, other drug use, and/or schizophrenia) was actually a little-known form of encephalitis. The fact that she had a major seizure brought her to the attention of neurologists, rather than psychiatrists, and one neurologist in particular who followed a hunch and suggested a brain biopsy which the autoimmune disorder which was causing her brain to swell. As she recovered, Cahalan was encouraged to write about her experience, and the first article (published by her employer, The Post) gained world-wide attention, and resulted in timely intervention for many other patients as well. Her training as a journalist is evident here. She includes much background information on the research into the disorder - anti-NDMA-receptor encephalitis - and the history of mental illness (including "demonic possession") and autism. I was engaged and interested from beginning to end, though I did feel it was a bit repetitive. Heather Henderson does a fabulous job reading the audio book. Her performance really brought to life the deterioration Cahalan experienced, as well as how anxious and confused she felt. Henderson's skill as a voice artist also allowed her to give the other people in the book unique voices, making it easy to distinguish who was speaking. The only thing missing from the audio, of course, are the illustrations - pages from Cahalan's journals at the time, or slides of her brain scans, etc. - but this did not materially affect my understanding or enjoyment of the book.

5 Stars (Orginally read on 5/10/2014) 4.5 Stars (Re-Read on 11/15/2016) Overall Opinion:  If you follow my reviews you know that suspenseful romances are not my favorite, so for one to be in my favorites shelf I think says a lot about how I felt about it. I did lower my rating, but I will be keeping it on my shelf because I do think that it is still one of my favorites. The reason for my lower rating is the ending. I needed more! I wanted a jump ahead epilogue where we get to see them happy and safe down the line! BUT, there were still a few aspects of the story that make it a winner for me -- First, the h being a fighter and not being broken even though she is in an environment where many do. I loved that she was so strong (even though she did cry a good bit)! And second, the humor. I loved the banter between the h and H and witty personality of the H. It made the story well balanced between romance and suspense, which is where I often struggle with in these types of stories. Would recommend this one, but it does have some intense situations and rape Brief Summary of the Storyline:  This is Reagan and Daniel's story. Reagan has been kidnapped and sold into sex slavery. Daniel has been looking for his sister who is in the same situation as Regan, and he comes across her and saves her from the brothel she is in. There is a good bit of obstacles that they have to get through to get themselves as well as Daniel's sister safely back home, and they really only have each other to rely on. They fall in love and do get a HFN ending. POV: This alternated between Reagan and Daniel's POV. Overall Pace of Story:  Good. I never skimmed, and I thought it flowed well. Instalove: Yes. They've only known each other for a short period of time, so feelings are developing really quick. It felt understandable to me, especially because of the circumstances they were in. H rating: 5 stars. Daniel. I loved him. He was witty, sarcastic, bad a$s, hot, and sweet! I don't think the h could have asked for a better guy in this situation. h rating: 4 stars. Reagan. I liked her. I only wish she didn't cry so much. It makes me feel kind of mean to say that though, because the girl had been through some pretty horrific things and I would've probably been a blubbering mess... Sadness level: Low. No tissues needed. Push/Pull: A little  The h has been traumatized, so it (understandably) takes her a while to come around to trusting the H. Heat level: Moderate. They take a little while to become intimate, but then they have a good bit of scenes. I wouldn't say it was so much that it took away from the storyline though. Descriptive sex: Yes Safe sex: Yes and no. Mentions of condoms and STD status, but they do go without protection a few times. I don't remember any mention of previous practices. OW/OM drama: Really mild The h has a boyfriend when she is kidnapped. She ends up calling him when she is with H, and she also confronts him when she gets back home. This does cause some mild jealousy with H, but not much drama. Sex scene with OW or OM: No Cheating: No Separation: No Possible Triggers: Yes  Rape, human trafficking, abuse, and violence/murder. Closure:  This is my only complaint. I felt like the ending was a little too abrupt, and I wanted a HEA! I really wanted a jump ahead epilogue so we could see them as a happy and functioning couple!! I would call this one a HFN ending. How I got it: I had gotten this originally with my scribed subscription, but it is no longer available on there. I ended up borrowing it from my local library this time. Safety: I'd say that this one is probably Safe with exception for most readers. - Does Not have cheating - Does Not have a descriptive sex scene with OW/OM -  Does Not have the H or h pushing away -  Does Not have a separation between the h and H -  Does  have sexual abuse -  Does Not have OTT sad parts - Does Not have a HEA ending.

Oh yeah, I was on a three hour plane ride while I bawled my way through this book. Embarrassed, I had to keep looking up from the book to stare at the headrest in front of me while I tried to think happy thoughts so I could keep the tears at bay. Pretty humiliating...but worth it! With themes on loss, mourning, moving on, and the consequences of holding back, Winter Longing by Tricia Mills is a story to read. Mills created characters who felt exceedingly real; I laughed with them, cried with them, sympathized with them and when their hearts broke, my heart broke. I also appreciate how Mills showed Winter struggling and grieving for an extended period of time versus three pages later having her happy and free (WOW that sounds mean) but this, especially, kept the story genuine. I gave Winter Longing 4 STARS. I was very pleased with this emotional, bittersweet tale, and I strongly recommend for others to read it. -XOXO Reading, Eating & Dreaming

A great classic tale at sea set during World War II! 5 shining stars! Herman Wouk won the Pulitzer Prize for this masterpiece in 1952 and it is a wonderful story! I first read and loved this as a high school sophomore and really enjoyed revisiting it! It was even better the second time around! Don't be intimidated by the military setting as there are so many elements to enjoy about the story even if war or the navy is not your thing. Why I liked it: 1) Brilliant and well-developed characters * Willie Keith evolves over the course of the novel from a spoiled rich kid to a capable young man * May comes from a different part of New York and initially kept Willie at a distance. She is strong and practical. * Captain Queeg takes the award for the most colorful character. I expect that he is the epitome of what NOT to be in a leader. I can envision him playing with those little metal balls. * Keefer the novelist who is a better sailor than a friend. * Maryk the sailor who is competent and respected  I wish he would have taken his log to a superior and avoided these charges all together which ruined his military career... * Willie's Mom who is over-indulgent and lonely. * Greenwald who doesn't initially want to be involved in the court martial  and who does a great job of defending Maryk, but then repudiates him at the dinner party thrown by Keefer 2) Descriptively written Just the right amount of detail. The Navy regulations for an officer relieving a Captain for mental impairment. The descriptions of the ship and the various crew members. The background on Willie's piano playing and May's singing. The rescue of the various members of another ship in the typhoon. 3) Funny at points I loved reading about Captain Queeg's various exploits and his inability to let go of the small details even to the detriment of the larger picture. * The strawberry debacle was hilarious. * The ship cuts its tow line while Queeg is admonishing a crew member for not tucking in his shirt tails. Then, Queeg isn't honest about the tow line. * The liquor incident.... * The water "shortage"... Maybe this point is all around the hilarity of Queeg! 4)  The ending is left open for the reader to imagine whether Willie and May got married or not. I tend to think that he blew his chance, but you never know... Favorite quote: "Remember this, if you can--there is nothing, nothing more precious than time. You probably feel you have a measureless supply of it, but you haven't. Wasted hours destroy your life just as surely at the beginning as at the end--only in the end it becomes more obvious." I highly recommend The Caine Mutiny to all readers of classics and historical fiction! I can't wait to delve into some of Wouk's other works!

In general, I liked the stories and didn't like the essays. The essays were best when they were separate from the stories, in my opinion, and not trying to provide a review of the stories, which made them feel... inauthentic. The stories varied in quality for me, of course, but I think the best ones walked the line between being too jokey before a big! twist! and the ones that took themselves a little too seriously the whole time. Regarding spoilers below, there may be some, and I'll try to have them officially marked as spoilers but by going below this line, you understand that there may be spoilers. Also, the ratings are for the stories not the essays, but the essays as a whole do bring down the rating of the collection. The Blood of Imuriv by Renee Ahdieh  and  The Evil Vaccine: Keep the Darkness At Bay by Christine Riccio I thought that this was one of the stories that benefited from its scope, being really only one scene. I wish that the world around these characters could've been built up a little bit more (the whole matriarchal dictatorship is a great jumping off point that I would've loved to hear more about.) I also think that the... kind of rage spirals that the main character tends to get into could use a little more explanation (that's basically my feeling on the ending as well.) So, as a scene I think this was really well done with great dialogue and good characterization, but I don't think that the world surrounding the scene was great. I thought that the essay was one of the best- it was its own entity and was fun to read. 2/5 Jack by Ameriie  and  Giants and Tyrants by Tina Burke This one was just kind of weird. The idea is kind of cool, but ending really came out of absolutely nowhere, and also seemed really poorly planned. I feel like we had no inclination that she was going to kill him, and then he just kind of puts himself into the bull by himself, and it just felt really odd to me. Like, I kind of get the motivation re: facing your fears, but I do think that came out of nowhere. The characters were fine, but the mood switched too frequently for me (too light at the beginning/ most of the way through, heavy at the end.) I thought the "Giants and Tyrants" premise of the essay was good, but it was quickly abandoned for the same kind of... analysis, I guess, as in the other essays. I wanted more of a history lesson and comparison, less of a run through of the metaphors etc. Gwen and Art and Lance by Soman Chainani  and  The Bad Girl Hall of Fame by Samantha Lane So this was certainly a fun time. I think that often stories told this way don't end up reading quite as easily as this story did, and when I look back at the collection as a whole this story stands out to me. I would say that it doesn't really read quite like a story about villainy, and the villain of the story doesn't seem... super evil, just kind of misguided and pressured. But, that does mean you understand her motivations and reasoning, which was a plus. It was a happy, light departure from some of the other stories and it was one of the only ones that kept me wanting to read all the way through, because I was both intrigued and enjoying it. Again, I liked the premise of the essay, kind of going through the "bad girls" of literature, but I think that sticking to that idea all the way through would've been better than, again, descending into a kind of meta, critical thinking situation. 3/5 Shirley & Jim by Susan Dennard  and  Dear Sasha, The 411 For Villains by Sasha Alsberg So something that I noticed in a lot of these stories, not just in this one, is that we get the story, get to know the characters, and then at the very end we learn what kind of evil thing the villain did. That's a fine set-up for a story, it's entertaining and delivers, but I think it's much more difficult and interesting to show us a villain who is doing villainous things, and still have the reader understand and empathize. Anyway, clearly I digress. This read like a romance for the vast majority of it. And the romance was sweet, don't get me wrong, but nothing all that great. I thought the chess stuff was cute, and I liked the idea that they made up their own rules, but only when both were aware of the rules. I do think that the ending was very abrupt, and we had no way of seeing it coming, or, really, or having Jim's actions rationalized. We're not in his head. I think this essay was one of the best, it's a cute idea and fairly well executed. I would've gotten rid of the last one from "Moriarty" but it's fine. The Blessing of Little Wants by Sarah Enni  and  Will the Real Villain Please Stand Up by Sophia Lee Wow, another one with that surprise villainy at the end! The ending was also REALLY confusing, like I have zero clue what happened, how did this work, what's going on, etc etc. I also just wasn't really compelled by the story as a whole, it was just kind of ehh... Essay was ehh. Not the worst, has at least a kind of gimicky thing with the questions, but I didn't love it. The Sea Witch by Marissa Meyer  and  Villain or Hero? You Decide by Zoe Herdt So this rating is kind of just based on my enjoyment, because I really liked this. I think that the character is really well developed, and that the progression of the story makes sense (ie. the insta-love makes sense to me, just because of her inexperience.) It's the one that feels the most like a longer story, I think, it feels substantial in my memory. Anyway. I think that the villainy in this one relies upon our understanding of the sea witch (or Ursula, from the Disney version), instead of her demonstrating  actual  villainy within the story. Like, there are other characters that do way worse things. So. But I think the quality of the writing and storytelling in this one was great, I just don't think it was the best re: villainy. Didn't like the essay. It tried to have a thing with the quiz but the options were so clear one way or the other and it kind of simplifies villainy in a way the entire anthology is trying to prevent. Beautiful Venom by Cindy Pon  and  Without the Evil in the World, How Do We See the Good by Benjamin Alderson I am  here  for feminist Medusa. The themes in this one are A+, the characterization is really good, and it's one that isn't quite as fantastical as the others at the beginning, which I like. I also like (I mean, not like, but think is really useful and interesting in this instance) that  she  is blamed for what the god did to her, because that's what happens to many victims of sexual assault in real life. (I also like that she was kind of into it at the beginning, because sex isn't a terrible thing,  rape  is a terrible thing.) This was one of my least favorite essays, honestly. It felt condescending and I really like that the story speaks for itself. Death Knell by Victoria Schwab  and  Dear Death by Jesse George This was good! It's really well written, though it takes itself a *little* seriously. The characters are interesting, and the setting is very different from the others. I think it's also interesting that the mood of the prompt feels kind of silly and this is a much more serious-toned story. It was atmospheric, it was well-written, the characters were interesting! The villainy was debatable, but that's okay. One of the better essays. It's interesting, and some of it is serious etc., but I think the tone can be a little bit off. 4.5/5 Marigold by Samantha Shannon  and  Evil Revealed by Regan Perusse More feminism! In this one, I think it would've been interesting to hear from George, who does seem to be the more actually evil of the two of the villains. Anyway. This is interesting because it's not a villain who is just trying to get by, this is a guy who is trying to do what he thinks is the right thing, who learns that it is very much not. I very much liked it for that. Didn't love the essay. I think that there's great humor in the subtitles used throughout, but not really in the actual content of the essay. It was fine, though. You, You, It's All About You by Adam Silvera  and  Behind the Villain's Mask by Catriona Reeney This wasn't very memorable (like I had to basically reread the whole thing to remember it.) I also don't get why it was addressed to "you." I liked the main character, I think her fake relationship is really interesting in terms of why she would create that situation, but it just wasn't totally for me (which is weird, because it feels like it should be.) I did think that the magic potions type things were cool. Didn't love the essay. Julian Breaks Every Rule by Andrew Smith  and  Julian Powell: Teen Psycho Extraordinaire by Raeleen Lemay I loved the voice in this story, and I think that it's written in a really interesting way. It's all real-world, which I like, and there is a lot of ambiguity in it. I also like the ending, because it kind of cements the main character as a villain and not as a kind of nice guy who weird things keep happening to. Y'know? The essay was fine, I just think they needed to give the booktubers a better thing to do, honestly. Indigo and Shade by April Genevieve Tucholke  and  Glamorized Recovery: Expectations vs. Reality by Whitney Atkinson Okay, so once I realized our narrator was Gaston I was really interested, but I didn't think that we saw the Gaston that I really wanted. I wanted to see from the Gaston who is, like, in the animated Disney movie and is obsessed with himself and wants to "save" Belle, and force her into marriage. (Kind of like Marigold, now that I think about it.) It was fine, it just wasn't what I wanted and I didn't think it was super well executed. Yes, this is where I basically stopped reading the essays. Sera by Nicola Yoon  and  The Bad Girls' Guide to Villainy by Steph Sinclair This one was pretty cool too! I liked the set-up of it, and it was maybe the best for characterization of the characters? Like, I feel like the family relationships in this one were amazing, and the development was really interesting and it was well done and interesting. I actually did read this essay, and it was one of the better ones. Had a sense of humor and a purpose, pretty good. Fin! Ups and downs, liked the stories and didn't like the essays: 85%

DNF'ed at about two hundred pages and I skimmed the last fifty. I always feel guilty disliking such popular books, especially ones that get five stars galore but I just did not care for this. The parts that were interesting, such as The Cemetery of Forgotten Books was pathetically underdeveloped and forgotten to make room for Daniel's love life which I just didn't care for. I picked up this book expecting mystery and intrigue. Instead I basically got a love story. If I had known it was a love story and if it had been marketed as a love story, that'd be different. But it's marketed as mystery and slightly spooky. It's not. It's overly long, boring, and dry. The characters are horribly flat. The mystery of the author tends to be put aside and when it does come back around Daniel really doesn't have to do much work to find the answers he wants, which was seriously disappointing. My biggest issue however was the homophobia and sexism. I get it, it takes place in the fifties but that still doesn't make it okay. All the female characters are basically just sex objects for the male characters, especially Fermin, who I could not stand. Maybe if he wasn't in the book I could have gotten farther into it but he really ruined it for me. I was expecting so much more. The hype really did not help. Overall, really disappointing.

Was my edition 50 pages short? Did I somehow glaze over all of this world-building and explanations? Which, hey, is sort of monotonous and awful to read sometimes, I get it, but this felt like Dennard expected us to walk in knowing certain things--I still have no clue what makes a Threadsister a Threadsister and the different kids of witches and what country has which element and what that even all means and what the heck cleaving is? Bite Me, Your Grace was a disappointment on a couple of levels. I was expecting a fun wallpaper historical romance with vampires, a smart heroine and humor (kind of like Minda Webber's books), which I guess was my first mistake. This is by no means a bad book, its just...Angelica is so annoying. She's an utter harridan! ***SPOILERS BEYOND THIS POINT*** This was kind of how things went: Mother: Angelica! You need to behave! Angelica: I refuse to behave as a lady must! I will RUIN MYSELF! :flings self into ruination: Ian: This damn female...I should marry her and maybe possibly get these people off my back about being a vampire...ho young lady! I shall save you! You shall be awesomely celebrated! Also lots of passion! Angelica: Married to a vampire? Never! I will show you how smart I am! And difficult! And political! And strongly against women being marginalized! Mother: Oh my smelling salts! Ian: All you are doing is proving how different you are and how right I was. Angelica: I'd rather be poor and destitute! As long as I can write it doesn't matter! Ian: :shows Angelica the poor and destitute lifestyle: Angelica: :immediately horrified by the stench: Maybe I will marry you I mean it can't possibly be as bad as all that right? I mean I can still do whatever I want... So on and so forth. The book is literally one idiotic notion of Angelica's after another as she attempts to either a) get Ian to not marry her, b) get Ian to tell her more about his vampire lifestyle for her Gothic writing or c) both at once. After they marry it only gets worse because she then falls into the 'Oh the sex is so good! Why does he not love me?' angst. I don't know Angelica, considering you spent half the book trying to convince him you shouldn't marry? Or maybe because you're idea of communication is to say how strong and independent you are and then run off doing something stupid? She gets drunk at Almack's and kicked out just to prove she shouldn't get married for pity's sake! I realize she was meant to be a 'strong' and 'socially progressive' woman, but instead it seemed like she was a child having a tantrum because no one would listen. Why did she have to be a Women's Rights Activist AND a gothic romance author AND cross dress AND not want to be married or have children AND hate everything about the ton AND be virtually friendless? Mind you she's also an immensely wealthy heiress who's apparently gorgeous. Meanwhile Ian, who's a couple centuries old and has not apparently ever fallen for a mortal before, finds her simply refreshing. Personally I think he just likes having to save her. Oh he's Lord of London and is super powerful and super wealthy and super this and super that, but for a guy who's ready to take some poor writer's head off for writing a satirical novel (that may or may not be about his vampire self) he's awfully jolly about sharing everything with Angelica. Only to wonder why his gothic romance obsessed wife would try to write a gothic romance about it. Ian you knew what you were marrying when you married her, don't acted surprised when the crazy woman who broke into your house (for research!) ends up, well, being crazy even after you marry her. Honestly it sounds like I dislike the book and really I only disliked Angelica. She just...no. Every time she spoke I was taken out of the story. Yeah I can see why folk want her dead. Your mileage may vary though, so take this as a cautious recommendation.

Original post at One More Page I remember talking to my friend who's the biggest C.S. Lewis fan, asking him if there will be a next Narnia movie. I caught The Voyage of the Dawn Treader on the plane on my way to Europe last August, and as usual, I shed some tears with Repicheep's scene and whenever Aslan comes out. To my dismay, he told me it might take a while years before the next movie will be made because the license expired. And that just made me sad. But that doesn't really excuse me from continuing my Narnia adventures, so when I was already feeling too full of contemporary stuff while writing my NaNoWriMo novel, I decided to pick up some simple and familiar middle grade fantasy and what better book to read than a Narnia one, right? The Silver Chair introduces different characters from what I have been used to, save for Aslan and Caspian and Eustace, who I first got to know in the previous book. In this book, I was introduced to Jill Pole, Eustace's school mate and a bully target. One day, while she was hiding from the bullies in their school, Eustace finds her and tells her about the magical place he had been in with his cousins that changed him. The bullies arrived, and Eustace and Jill scramble away, going to a door on a wall that led them to Narnia. Or what looked like Narnia. Jill was surprised and scared, so much that she ends up pushing Eustace off a tall cliff. But Aslan comes to the rescue and saves him, and then gave Jill a mission with specific signs. Aslan warned Jill that she must remember these instructions and repeat them and put them in her heart, especially since it was different there in the mountain where they landed and in Narnia where they have to fulfill their mission. Aslan sends her away and she finds herself in the Narnia that Eustace also knows, and off they go to follow Aslan's instructions, not knowing the adventures and troubles that would await them. The Silver Chair had that same vibe that The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe had, in the sense that it was also an adventure book where our heroes and heroines have a mission to fulfill. While it didn't feel as magical as the first book in the series, there was still that sense of the unknown and the various charming and fearsome creatures that mean them good and bad. I liked how it feels like it's a different Narnia from what I know from the first three books I've read. Eustace is loads better in this book, even if I can't stop imagining him the same way as how the actor who played him spoke and acted. He still had that annoying know-it-all tendencies, but it was not as annoying as it was before. On the other side, there is Jill. Oh Jill. How much you reminded me of myself! I always thought I would be an Edmund (and in a lot of ways, I still am), but Jill. I saw so much of myself in Jill Pole that it felt uncomfortable. At the start of the story, I kind of wanted to strangle Jill for being so stubborn -- as a reader I could see where she would go wrong from a mile away, and I knew that it's all going to bite her back. But then as I think about it...don't I do the same thing, too? Aren't I just as stupid and as shortsighted as Jill was, trading quick, temporary comforts for the things that really matter? But I kind of have a feeling Aslan knew that Jill would mess up, hence the warning (also one of my favorite quotes in the book): But, first, remember, remember, remember the signs. Say them to yourself when you wake in the morning and when you lie down at night, and when you wake in the middle of the night. And whatever strange things may happen to you, let nothing turn your mind from following the signs. And secondly, I give you a warning. Here on the mountain I have spoken to you clearly: I will not often do so down in Narnia. Here on the mountain, the air is clear and your mind is clear; as you drop down into Narnia, the air will thicken. Take great care that it does not confuse your mind. And the signs which you have learned here will not look at all as you expect them to look, when you meet them there. That is why it is so important to know them by heart and pay no attention to appearances. Remember the signs and believe the signs. Nothing else matters. (p.27) There was more of Aslan in this book, but one of my favorite scenes in the book was actually one without Aslan. I liked how the kids and Puddleglum got through the encounter with an enemy without Aslan's direct interference, but just plain belief in him. I wasn't expecting to like The Silver Chair that much, really, but I'm glad to say it's one of the books that surprised me. I think The Silver Chair is that book for people who's already found the faith and is in need to strengthen that faith they found. I think it's a book that teaches how it is to follow, how it is to live and keep the faith even in the face of adversity, and how Aslan is victorious even with the slightest, smallest concerns that we have.

An absorbing novel that holds attention from beginning to end, a fine example of alternative history that makes its skewed (from our perspective) world feel real. Part of what makes the novel so successful is the way Harris is sparing with details, giving just enough to create atmosphere and satisfy readers' curiosity about what things would have been like if Germany had won the war, resisting the temptation to over-explain that would unnecessarily slow narrative flow and dissipate tension. The scenario depicted by Harris in the novel is believable. The Cold War is between the US and Germany, following America's defeat of Japan after use of atomic bombs as in our history but a year later which meant the Nazis had time to develop nuclear capability. With celebrations approaching for the Fuhrer's seventy-fifth birthday, there are moves in favour of Detente. Though the Nazis control most of Europe, Germany's ongoing war of attrition with the Soviet Union isn't going too well so the upcoming visit of American President Kennedy must be handled carefully. Not a good time, therefore, for dark secrets to be revealed, which Xavier March stumbles upon in the course of his investigations, aided by a beautiful and resourceful American journalist with a thing for father figures. The characters are well developed and the love interest handled in a way that did not annoy me, which is not easy, believe me. Harris paints a chilling picture of life in a Totalitarian police state in which people are told what to think, trained to follow blindly and to inform on anyone who deviates, with children turning in their parents, always under the watchful eye of the Gestapo. I really liked Xavier March, the Berlin policeman with SS officer rank tasked with investigating the discovery of a man's body in a river. A WWII U-boat veteran, divorced with a young son, March is a good cop and decent man troubled by doubts and questions regarding the regime still led by Hitler. "A police state is a country run by criminals" and they don't much like police officers who fail at total faith and obedience to the Fatherland, so March is on a very sticky wicket indeed even before he becomes embroiled in a complicated political case involving top level Nazis, corruption, treachery, and the truth about what happened to Europe's Jews. One quibble I will put under spoiler tags because it reveals plot details so do not proceed unless you have read the book. I have some issues with the ending. I don't mind its ambiguity because it works in context, and is realistic, but the way he sets the scene I can't help feeling Harris felt obliged for Xavier March to atone with his life for wearing the uniform he frequently says he hates simply because he's SS therefore cannot be allowed escape to freedom. I could be wrong. As I said, the ending isn't clear on what happens, though I am fairly convinced my interpretation is correct, i.e. either he shoots himself or is shot by his pursuers. I just can't see it any other way. I suppose there's a small chance Charlie isn't where March thinks she is and somehow has mounted a rescue, but that seems most unlikely, and too neat. Other readers might disagree, about either the author's intent or my take on the closing scene. I would be happy to read another novel set in Harris' alternate world. The cracks in the Nazi regime, with an ageing leadership and internal power struggles, war weariness, terrorism, etc. offer interesting possibilities.

SPOILERS. Such a wonderful book in so many ways. It has a very controversial point of contention for the protagonists. It has a fairly predictable plot that stays captivating the whole way through. It has characters that read real to me. And that, ladies and gents, is why I cried. I think this book gives voice to all of those dashed hopes and dreams that come with a severe accident such as Will's. WIll went from literally being on top of the world (or at least, top of Africa), top at his career, and always on a new adventure to bottoming out. He hit rock bottom so hard he couldn't see the light from the bottom of the well he was lying in. I would imagine that having to restructure your life in such a dramatic fashion is hard enough living a regular lifestyle, let alone the jet-setting one Will employed. New countries, new physical activities, no shortage of women wanting attention. All that is gone in an instant. Will, understandably in my opinion, gets very depressed about this. He tries very hard to kill himself, and fails only because someone found him in time. It is that kind of determination in Will that sets the tone for the whole book. He is determined to have his final nuggets of freedom, and he will not relinquish. So he plans to do physician-assisted suicide. This was a particularly interesting book for me because I have written several college papers on the subject. We were always told to write about something controversial, and I wanted to do something not really found in the limelight. And predictably, there is a fairly large chasm between the two opposing parties for this. On the one hand: murder is murder, it should not be allowed. On the other hand: if they are of sound mind, they can make their own decisions. It is these two opinions that ultimately make up the book. Will wants to exercise the only freedom he has left, and everyone else is trying to convince him not to do it. Honestly? They all have really great points. Every single one of the characters have great reasons to back up their own personal opinions. I think that is why I appreciated this so much, because the constant ping-ponging from denial to acceptance for these characters seems so realistic. Knowingly sending someone to their death is not nearly so easy as it may seem. Louisa and Will's attraction for one another felt organic, which equally made this an attractive read. I loved how they both adopted each other to be their pet projects. Louisa was hellbent on getting him to change his mind about killing himself, and Will was hellbent on forcing Louisa to actually spread her wings and explore beyond her little town. They influenced one another for the better, and I loved that it was an improvement on both of them. The story is predictable. If a man with no mobility from his nipples down wants to commit suicide, and is wealthy enough to leave the girl protagonist well off, what do you think will happen? Right. He goes through with it (after lots of soul searching on Louisa's part) and leaves her a nice chunk of change to pursue her newly found interests in her career. There was no other way this could have ended, and I knew that going in. It was no big surprise, and yet I was desperate to keep reading. I wanted to feel what Will felt. I wanted to feel what Louisa felt. It's a love story, sure. But I think more than anything it is just a story about growth, and I love that so much more. Louisa grew, and Will grew. Will's mother grew, Louisa's sister grew. I would not have had it any other way.

Work buddy book club read. Hear me out. It's a bestseller. Made into a movie. That doesn't suck. Hang on to your hats! What I heard from everyone (Literally. Everyone.) was that the book was an easy read, it was good, and it was nearly impossible to put down. This has been confirmed. The Girl on the Train is honestly a well-constructed thriller/mystery. Hawkins plays fair with the clues, she has you both rooting for Rachel and becoming wary of her. You alternate between how you feel about the people around her. It's a perfect air of uncertainty until the end. Well played, Hawkins. For all the ambiguity and complexity of character, I think we can all agree that Tom sucks a big bag of dicks. It was easy to hate him for cheating on Rachel, but there's a point when Hawkins has us imagining that Rachel has spun the story in her head one way, and that Tom is not ALL BAD. This was up until Tom bought Anna lingerie for her birthday, and Anna talks about how she wants everything perfect for TOM on HER BIRTHDAY. That's when we feel something is... not right. Scattered thoughts. -My favorite thing to do with books is to reread the middle of the book and look for significance in that scene, a habit out of my obsession with ring cycle writing. Wouldn't you know it, but p.163, Megan is thinking "I need to get to the end of my story." Hm hm hm. Also, the beginning of the book is Rachel riding on the train, the big ending and reveal is with the train passing (and not one witness looking up!) Heavy Sylvia Plath influence, more or less intentional Some of the inner thoughts of the characters reminds me of Plath, like Megan thinking "I never got to the crux of it" and "I need to learn to lose better." Of course, direct mention of Plath and Hughes and Assia. Feminist Theme -Potential nod to "The Yellow Wallpaper" when Megan thinks "The last thing I need is rest." specifically when men tell women to relax, not worry their pretty lil heads - I kept writing "HOUSEWIFE SYNDROME" with Anna's and Megan's sections. They're restless, the men in their lives have little patience for them, they're told to keep doing their wifely duties, but they dream about doing something a little MORE. -"Women are still only really valued for two things - their looks and their roles as mothers." - Rachel, 79 -In the end, none of the men are redeemable. Motherhood Theme I don't know how to approach this one, because I've never had kids, nor do I want to, but the theme is important. Rachel is unable to conceive and partially slips because of it. Megan's big story involves the accidental death of her baby; later, when she becomes pregnant, her resolution to come clean and fix her life. Anna struggles with wanting to be someone outside the home (back when she was out and desired, single) and her role as a mother. Admittedly, the struggle is not too strong, because she feels that being a mother is the OBVIOUSLY the best possible thing you can be. In either case, in the strong feminist theme (and anti-man theme, possibly), motherhood is never condemned, but regarded as important in women's lives. So, hey, another feminist thing. Observer/Participant -"I'm connected, I am no longer just a girl on the train" -The idle observers on the train -What do we really know about the strangers around us and their struggles, what do we know about the people closest to us (OO! Shivers!) -Anna's observation that Rachel didn't feel real to her (233) when she was being a homewrecker. More Scattered Thoughts -This is the second book I've read that has used trains as a motif (or whatever that fancy word is), the first being Haruki Murakami's Colorless Tsukuru Tazaki and His Years of Pilgrimage. Both have to deal with being unsettled, someone in constant motion/liminality. Life goes on, but terrible things happen, even mere feet away as you whiz on by. -Despite the terrible things that happened on that street, I really had warm feelings for it, like I wanted to be there, that I could love a cozy life with a train that passes by. -My heart hurts. "She's just a sad little liar with no life.,""Fat Rachel," "It's impossible to resist the kindness of strangers" Yep, go ahead and twist that knife in further.
Just enough plot to make you curious what's next... but still, barely any plot and too many questions.

I almost gave up on this book a few pages in. The narrative has no quotation marks, and seems to switch between run on sentences and stream of consciousness at the drop of a hat. But, since it's less than 200 pages, I decided to stick it out and read it anyway. And I'm very glad I did. The story was fantastic, I devoured the entire book in just a couple of hours. The only thing keeping this book from a five star rating is the narrative style, although that did grow on me the longer I read, and did, in some ways, help me slip into Daisy's mind in ways other books never have.

This was my first McEwan, and it will almost certainly be my last. I usually read Amazon reviews prior to purchasing but for some reason didn't in this case. This cost me numerous hours and nearly PS9 that I'd have preferred to have donated to charity; I won't forget again! PS8.84 is a rip-off for a good book in Kindle format. Paying that for complete nonsense has left me more than a little annoyed, especially when I noticed at least two typos - and I'm no proof-reader. I admit I rushed this book, as I wasn't enjoying it and had a nasty feeling I was wasting my time. When I reached the end I didn't know what to think. I felt cheated - and slightly confused. Was I missing something? I decided to read some reviews to see if, perhaps, I'd failed to understand the point. But it seems there was no real point - just a 'clever' literary device and a love story in disguise - though I'm not quite sure what as. The idea of literature being a powerful political tool was certainly touched upon, though it might have been better exemplified in a different story altogether; and while deceit certainly appears to have been the main theme, it seemed to me that nothing meaningful was said or shown regarding this. I like to feel I've learned something or gained a deeper understanding of myself or the world around me through the fiction I read, but I didn't feel I gained anything from this book - not even general entertainment. Even the obviously well-crafted sentences didn't seem genuine or meaningful, just an exercise in how to write well-crafted sentences. There was no real emotion or passion, no authenticity to anyone or anything. I had no image in mind of anyone or anything I read about and I couldn't have cared less what happened to any of the non-characters. The main character in particular was completely unbelievable. She didn't feel like a woman, never mind a woman in the given time period. At one point, when still in her early twenties - and having made a pass at virtually every male she'd met - she was outraged at someone pinching her bottom at a party! This was back when Benny Hill was in full force and women were (legally) raped by their husbands. Do me a favour! Also, I can't believe someone who supposedly attended Cambridge could be so dull and average. She wasn't intelligent or funny and didn't really examine her own or anyone else's behaviour, other than to question whether people fancied her (or were otherwise homosexual). I imagine the 'clever' twist at the end of the book was merely a trick to disguise the poor quality of the text preceding it. I can only imagine someone told Mr McEwan how terrible it was, and that he, unprepared to sacrifice months/hours(?) of 'hard work,' decided to excuse the poorly-drawn protagonist by attributing the writing to her almost as poorly-drawn lover.
