I love mermaids. I really, really do. I think they're criminally underrated when it comes to magical creatures. They're beautiful, they're deadly, they're dangerous... This book is none of those things. And, to be honest, I didn't really enjoy it that much. Our hero, Sam, is one of the weirder characters I've ever read. He's overly concerned with his penis. (I seem to remember there being a passage where he talks about walking around with "a heaviness in my dick" or something to that effect while at the beach.) He's trying to become a man, and becoming a man means getting laid, right? And there are a lot of strange, gorgeous blonde chicks crawling around this beach, ogling him and wanting to be with him. Sounds like a veritable dream come true. Trouble is, Sam doesn't exactly have the best ideas regarding women. His previous experience with girls involve groping one through a "deliberately slutty" costume, then he decided she was "annoying" and just... kind of left her. His mother left the family after she discovered Facebook and went off to "Women's Land" (I kid you not) and Sam thinks her feminist thought is a load of hooey. She returns to the family and her return is weird, because she's accepted back in, but she also feels kind of like a non-entity, but that's another problem. I spent the entire book hoping, HOPING DESPERATELY, that Sam would wake up and change his ideas about women. That "becoming a man" would mean realizing women are actually people and not just sex machines. (Sam's brother, Jeff, is probably worse on this scale, but let's not go there.) There wasn't really enough character development in Sam, though, and certainly none of the, "Wait! Maybe I was wrong!" type. He befriends a couple mermaids, and then it turns out there's a curse on the mermaids. The only way to break the curse for the mermaids is to have sex with a male virgin, which is why Sam is so desirable. Which was just... I am not really one for reducing people to their sexual capabilities in the first place, but also, this felt like, "Wow! I can be the hero of this tale! Because I AM A TEENAGE MALE VIRGIN WHICH IS ABOUT AS RARE AS A UNICORN." Unhealthily spreads the idea that All Teenage Boys Have Wild Crazy Sex Always (not true by any stretch of the imagination) and was also uncomfortably a way of making Sam a saviour for one of the girls. Sam helps out as best he can, but... by the end of it, it doesn't really feel like he has any new ideas regarding women, or that he's learnt anything about himself. It felt like a cop-out ending. Oh yeah. Let's discuss the mermaids in this book, okay? I don't know how you can make mermaids boring but Madison did a great job of that. They're all beautiful, perky-boobed and blonde, all totally into him, big into partying, etc. The only one who gets any real character development is DeeDee, and even then, I didn't really feel like I knew her that well. Everyone seemed to be a Manic Pixie Dream Mermaid on Sam's journey into manhood, and... I don't know. There are alternating chapters from the mermaids' perspective, but they got a bit repetitive (Our mother is the blab blah, our father is blah blah, our brothers are Speed and Calm...). I also didn't really like the fact that they stole their names from brands. Which is a bit of a weird point to pick, but I'm not sure anyone would take girls named Olay, Tresemme, Activia, L'Oreal, etc. seriously. I wanted fantastically named, wild mermaids with names that meant so much to the sea; that's not what I got. There were a lot of times when I wondered why this story in particular was worth telling. Sam didn't strike me as a memorable narrator, nor his story an intriguing one. I didn't find it eerie or romantic, and several times I wanted to throw the book across the room. (The worst offense was when Sam and DeeDee are in a cove full of stolen treasures, and she literally says, "Look at this stuff. Isn't it neat?" You can't throw a Little Mermaid reference as large as that one in there and not expect it to feel a little cheap.) The writing itself wasn't really that bad, and when I sat down with the book I got through a lot fast, but I really had to push myself, which I don't think is the sign of a good story. I've heard Tides is supposed to be better, so I'll put that one on my to-read list. Edit. Okay, some of the other (more positive) reviews have pointed out that Sam DOES experience some character change overall--he finally sees DeeDee as her own person, not as another faceless blonde chick who wants to have sex with him. At the same time, it's so subtly done that I feel like I missed that passage. Even then, I still don't really feel like Sam gets enough of an arc--it's more like a straight line that curves up very slightly at the end.

"He smelled of salt and blood, and only when his mouth came close to her ear did she understand what he is saying, what he had been whispering before, and it was the simplest litany of all: her name, just her name." Okay, so first things first, City of Bones is about a world where demons, vampires, werewolves, and the like exist. There are also Shadowhunters who are dedicated to ridding the earth of demons, and keeping the balance in line. While I was reading the book, I couldn't help but find some similarities between Cassandra Clare's City of Bones, and JK Rowling's Harry Potter. Maybe to make myself clear, I'll note the three (yes, only three) similarities I observed: 1) Valentine and Voldemort (Though according to City of Bones that Valentine wasn't really dead, and Voldemort on the other hand rose from the dead, still I can't help but find similarities between them. Maybe because they are both villains--the irritating, wearisome, and vexing type of villains! And I like that. I despised Voldemort in HP, and after reading City of Bones, I think I'll be hating on Valentine more than I hate him now.) 2) The Circle and the Death Eaters (In City of Bones, Valentine formed his own cult which was called the Circle. The members were at first in support of his ideals, but later on some backed-out or left. In HP, Voldemort also had followers, the Death Eaters, but unlike Valentine's, most of his people stayed loyal to him until the final battle. But in City of Bones, I noted that there were still some loyal members of Valentine. AND I CAN'T WAIT FOR SOME MORE ACTION TO KICK-IN IN THE NEXT BOOKS!) 3) Mundane and Muggle (In City of Bones, those who do not belong in the Shadow World are called mundanes. In HP, those who do not belong in the magical world are called muggles.) ...And the similarities stop there. I must congratulate Cassandra Clare for being able to think and to write about a world like that. It's one of the worlds I like to live in (but because I'm too chicken, I'd rather be a mundane. Hahaha.) In the first few parts of the book, I was being introduced to the Shadow World, just like Clary. There were parts where I was having a hard time to keep up because of some terms and side stories I couldn't catch, and it felt like I was having information overload. But as I reached the mid-part of the book, I became so hooked with the world which Cassandra Clare carved, that I didn't want to pull away anymore. There were lots of twists and turns in this book which made it so exciting. My favorite chapter was "Chapter 17: The Midnight Flower". I was like smiling like an idiot because of Jace and Clary, and that chapter was just light which made it outstanding. I liked Jace's sarcasm and over-confidence, and I liked how Clary could make him different. Clary could make him do things he never thought he could for other people. He really cared for her and I was starting to ship them. Then the real excitement started at Chapter 22, and went onwards. That was where the questions, confusion, and excitement started to mix up and mess with my brain. After reading Chapter 22, I was like "Wait, what the?! I think I know where this will be going..." And then I continued reading chapter 23, and after I finished it I was like gasping for breath. I didn't know which was true and which wasn't anymore. It made me want to keep on reading and finish the book, and move on to City of Ashes already! Those chapters from Chapter 22 until the end were total mind fuck. There was this twist in the end which made me flabbergasted and heartbroken at the same time. I think those parts made the book really good. Anyway, when I get home tonight, I'll start reading City of Ashes already. :) I'm excited for the movie adaptation, too.

While the crimes are ingenious, I read Rex Stout's work for the characters and their incredibly distinct voices. Nero Wolfe, Archie Goodwin and Fritz make an odd threesome, but they are a perfectly rendered bachelor household. The New York brownstone is a peculiar Peter Pan world where exotic flowers bloom in the rooftop gardens, luxurious meals are concocted in the kitchens, beer and milk flow freely, and a safe full of money and firearms sits in the office, ready to finance any lucrative adventure with a twist of genuine mystery behind it. The fat genius is just one component of this ensemble cast. It's Archie who tells you the story, who shares his frustrations in being left in the dark by his employer, who imparts his own suspicions, methods of collecting evidence and testimony, and "phenomena". Fraught with some of the same problems that haunt modern readers approaching Dashiell Hammett, like casual racism, sexism and violence, these are books reflective of a certain era of America's past and should be read with a grain of salt. An absorbing mystery and a great read - recommended.

[3.5/5 stars] After hearing all of the hype surrounding this book before and after its release I was pretty hesitant to pick it up, since I tend to be disappointed with extremely popular books. But after seeing many people who have similar reading tastes, read and love this book, I was willing to give it a chance. And I have to say after reading the book I feel like it lived up to most of the hype, however, it wasn't as mind-blowing or epic, as many people had made it out to be. It was excellent at many points, but ultimately I felt like something was missing after finishing the book. When I first started this book I went into it knowing only that one of the characters was a slave and that the other was a soldier, so I had no idea what kind of adventure they would be going on or how they would meet. I was intrigued in the first few chapters but I was not completely sucked in either, I was mostly just trying to figure out how the two characters would eventually cross paths. Another aspect that kept me from getting into the story right away was the confusion about Scholars and Martials. I wasn't sure whether Martials were a group of people or soldiers and what differentiated them from the Scholars. Most of this had to do with the way they were named; it wasn't until a few hundred pages in that this was cleared up. But the physical differences between the two are still not completely clear to me, as they weren't clearly outlined. I was also surprised to learn that magic was real in this book, maybe it was because I went in knowing very little about the story or because both Elias and Laia kept mentioning the fact that Jinns etc. weren't real and the fact that Augurs were frauds. So that threw me off a bit, but it wasn't completely out of place because Laia was seeing things early on. I also wish that there had been a little bit more world building in this book because aside from the information given to the reader in the beginning there wasn't too much time spent on explaining the world and where it was, if there are any other countries or empires etc . After finishing this book I found that I came out of it not really knowing too much about the world overall. With regards to the characters I can't say that I particularly disliked any of the characters, even the Commandant (I was more curious about how she came to be the way she was), though I did find their actions annoying at times. Most of the characters were pretty well developed, aside from a few side characters who didn't really play a part in the story. I was surprised to hear that many people disliked Laia and found her extremely weak, but I have to say I actually liked her and preferred her most of the time to Elias (who annoyed me through a big chunk of the book). And even though she was weak at first, I found it to be quite realistic. Many people would have run as well when faced with the same circumstances, it's sad but true, and it's not what she did then that matters, but what she did afterwards. Even though she acted selfishly at that moment it was probably for the best because both her and Darian would have been killed, had she stayed, ruining any chance she had to save them both. It also gave her the chance to experience hardship and grow from it. That being said I did find it annoying when she constantly berated herself and compared herself to her mother, but once again it slightly realistic as most people are hard on themselves and compare themselves to those they consider to be better. I also found her blind faith in the Resistance annoying and the fact that it took her so long to become suspicious, even after Cook's and even Keenan's warnings, was frustrating. Though I did enjoy the book and found it very intense and action packed, I also felt that there were a few things missing or unanswered that kept me from completely loving it. Like the fact that throughout most of the book I felt like we needed to see Helene's perspective, especially when she and Elias' were fighting. I felt like we got a very one side view of her because we were only seeing her through Elias' eyes and I feel like that was a shame since she seemed like such a complex character. I would have loved to find out what she really thought of the treatment of Scholar slaves, because at times she seemed almost sympathetic, but at other points she came off as cold and uncaring. Additionally I wanted to see where the story would go with Helene's magical abilities, but it wasn't mentioned again after she healed Laia. Some other things that weren't completely explained as well were, the Nightbringer's plan, who the traitor in the Resistance was, and how the Augur's magic worked etc. With all these questions I'm really glad that there's going to be another book. Overall I really enjoyed this book and I'm looking forward to the next book. Though I did have some problems with the plot, I found the writing to be quite beautiful, so much so, that I actually wrote down a few of my favourite quotes, which is a first for me, so I included them here. Favourite quotes: "Life is made of so many moments that mean nothing. Then one day, a single moment comes along to define every second that comes after." "There are two kinds of guilt. The kind that's a burden and the kind that gives you purpose. Let your guilt be your fuel. Let it remind you of who you want to be. Draw a line in your mind. Never cross it again. You have a soul. It's damaged but it's there. Don't let them take it from you. "You are an ember in the ashes, Elias Veturius. You will spark and burn, ravage and destroy. You cannot change it. You cannot stop it. "You are full, Laia. Full of life and dark and strength and spirit. You are in our dreams. You will burn, for you are an ember in the ashes."

I didn't like Shadow and Bone. Two things that made Shadow and Bone reading close to bearable: One. I was conned by the Darkling. I was rooting for him, then well, you know... let's just say Leigh Bardugo has a mean streak in Darkling's character. Two. The action scene in the Fold at the end of the book. I admit it was cool. Other than that, Shadow and Bone is one big disappointment for a fantasy lover. Little and so few action scenes. Such a downer. Alina has self-esteem issues. I cannot understand why almost 2/3 of the book is dedicated to Alina being conscious about her looks! What a useless heroine. She spent half the time swooning over the Darkling when she should've been training rigorously as a Grisha! Alina is annoying, irritating, and always in need of someone to help. Is this the kind of fantasy heroine I want? NO! The plot was unique but it was poorly executed. And while i read some of the not-so-glowing reviews, I agree that the research behind the story was poor, as well. Shadow and Bone = a lot of eyeroll = palpable distaste.

Why I picked it up: I really liked Smile and I suspected Drama would be on the "Great Graphic Novels for Teens" list this year. I was right, plus it was on several other lists. I lettered in Drama in high school, but I was only on stage for one play. Instead, I did mostly behind-the-scenes (and under the stage) stuff, including running the box office for two years. But the stage crew kids don't usually get much notice. It was super awesome, then, to see the stage crew get most of the spotlight in Drama. The characters were fun, believable, and age-appropriate. I enjoyed the characters and watching each of them do their thing, and I really admired Callie for her determination to get the cannon right. (My favorite scene is when they go to the cafeteria and do a scene and the cannon goes off, then all the students eating lunch immediately leave and get in line to buy tickets.) I read an ARC and while I suspect the content remained the same for the final book, mine had only one chapter in color. This didn't bother me, and in fact I didn't really notice it until I finished. But I checked out the published edition and confirmed that the actual book does indeed have color illustrations all the way through. This is a personal five stars for me, but I dropped it to four because while it may fulfill by daily addiction of paranormal romance, there were a few things that I have to point out in the spoiler section. First: Charlie was a very admirable and witty, does-what-she-wants woman who had better standards for herself than letting society dictate her further actions as an individual. Hard thing to do in the 1800s, I think, which made it even more appealing. However, the moment they found out she was a female, they changed towards her. I expected this. What I didn't, was her changing. She let what she was used to overcome the way she acted. Charlie became an alter ego. While I don't mind a complicated situation, I was still expecting her to be a little more challenging for Lincoln. Instead she fell for him and became an infatuated woman (the type I'm sure he's more than annoyed in dealing with). As for Lincoln himself, I love him. He's got questionable intentions and the way he goes about getting things done. But he's not the worse monster out there, or a monster at all, really. Can't fault a guy for being grouchy and silent, and though his one mistake was almost getting Charlie raped, he did nothing to defend himself. Merely told her that he was a dangerous type of man whom she had to choose to be with (the establishment, not him personally.) With that said, I absolutely LOVE necromancers and seemingly cold-hearted alphas. Lincoln was such a man, because he's had to keep himself to a certain lifestyle in order to do the things he was bred to do. Charlie is a fresh breeze for him and the people in his home. I adore the way she got to Seth and Gus, and vise versa. It was a little too good to be true, or I just didn't see them warming up to her so quickly, but it was still fun. Loved more that it was a full story and not one of those cliffhangers. The surprise was nice! Won't spoil it, but the 'surprise' did fall a little for me. It's like... THE SURPRISE. Maybe I was just expecting something bigger. Otherwise this is my personal perfection and can't wait to read the second novel. Definite recommend.

So I finally read what everyone calls "The White American Woman's Bible." All about yoga and food and traveling and sex, right? I am aghast at the reviewers who hate this book; my heart sank right into my stomach. I mean the hatred is absolutely tangible. From what I gather, most hate for this book comes from the fact that this woman is privileged, white, and gets to travel around the world carelessly as money is no object. Also, since it's a memoir/autobiography, it's all about her all day. Therefore she should be disallowed from placing pen to paper recounting her journey and talking so much about her life. Who is she to talk about how much fun she's having when everyone else is suffering? The nerve of this woman! But wait. Is that really what we're judging books on these days? Everyone wishes they could travel where they wanted without a care in the world. But... does that make this a bad book? I beg to differ, at least in this case. Usually, I would not read any such book about a woman who is unaware of the privilege she has. But that is not this woman. I was hesitant to read this book for the reasons above from hearsay. I've dreaded it, scoffed at it, rolled my eyes at it. But I saw it on the thrift store shelf, and said what the hell. What I found was a something that I'd been looking for and wasn't at all expecting: a story about a woman who is reinvigorating her Christian faith in an unconventional way by exploring different cultures. I needed something like that. Elizabeth Gilbert seems to be very aware of the fact that she is a privileged white woman. She expresses this repeatedly. She is at ease discussing other people, and she speaks of different people of all ethnicities and races and cultures with respect, honesty, ease, and good-natured humor. In appearances, she is exactly not like me in any way (I'm a young black girl with little money, never traveled out of the country, amongst other contrasts...) and yet... I was intrigued by her search for faith. She writes with a frankness and honesty that is refreshing. Nothing purple in these parts, thank goodness. Eat Pray Love is the story of a woman who has made a name for herself as a writer. She went from living on a farm to being an accomplished author and writer. She finds that she doesn't love her husband all that much anymore, and in a moment of clarity, finds herself searching for God's voice again. On the bathroom floor of her house she asks for God's help, and her journey begins from there: Following the frightful divorce, and the diminishing of her self, she says "fuck it" and goes across the world to re-find herself. I had a lot of fun traveling with her. I really grew to like her. She has a good heart, and seems like a lovely woman who's a lot of fun. She has some interesting views on religion and spirituality, that reminded me of Caroline Myss in Anatomy of the Spirit. Perhaps it was my having read that book that allowed me to see this book in a different light. Let me end this by saying that I am kinda sad that so many people hate this book because their experience is so different from hers. I liked the book myself, although who knows about next week? If there's anyone's writing I hate for the aforementioned reasons, it's David Sedaris, who really doesn't seem to see or care about the privilege he has, talks to and about people from other cultures in an ignorant and dumb fashion, and is self righteous. I gather this from reading his later works, and cannot tolerate it. TL;DR This is a great book written in a frank matter from a self-aware woman who does whatever the fuck she wants with her money and fixes herself rather than complain about her problems. She's self-made and religious, and goes on a journey to reaffirm and revaluate her relationship with her Christianity and God. There is food, prayer and love. And hardly any sex at all, but there be a little bit. Go in with an open mind, and make your own opinion on this book.

I have been rereading this for the umpteeth time and am as completely enthralled, obsessed and consumed by The Bronze Horseman as ever. What is it? TBH is a novel set around the harrowing siege of Leningrad during WW2 (the Germans besieged the city, which refused to surrender, and in the resulting siege, which lasted for two-and-a-half years, over 1,500,000 people died). If you are looking for a panoramic take on the siege and WW2 in the Soviet Union, you are better off reading non-fiction, to be honest. What TBH is - is an amazingly passionate and tender character study and love story. The characters who are being explored are Tatiana* Metanova, a 17-yr-old factory worker, eventual nurse, and Alexander Belov, a 22-yr-old officer in the Soviet Army. We are almost constantly in their heads (though the focus is primarily on Tanya) but I did not feel constrained by that focus - instead I couldn't get enough. * I wonder if she's named Tatiana because of Tatiana Savicheva, a young girl who died of starvation and whose harrowing diary of Leningrad siege, was so famous. The novel starts on June 21, 1941 - the day Hitler invaded USSR. It is also the day before Tanya's 17th birthday. She's part of a close, loving, though sometimes too constricting family, and as she is waiting to catch a bus, her gaze crosses with that of a young officer. They feel drawn to each other from that very first moment, and the novel's strength is convincing me of their unshakeable, unkillable bond - despite family complications, despite a secret of Alexander's past (not to spoil anything, but let's say a Soviet military tribunal would probably shoot him on the spot if they knew) and, of course, despite the horrors of war - the bombings, the starvation, the front line (Alexander fighting on it and Tanya being a nurse on the same). And despite their characters - they might love each other more than breathing but both are very strong and stubborn individuals who often cannot give an inch. Tanya starts the book as a shy, naive and very sheltered teen, a little solipsistic about her world and Alexander is overly contained and burned-out, but by the end of the book they have been transformed by their love and loss and horrors of war and Tanya becomes an amazing woman, making her own way, alone, across the frozen parts of Finland, while Alexander finds both hope and humanity. I have a confession - I usually cannot stand fiction about Russia written by non-Russians because it rings false. Yet I did not feel that sense of frustration at all here and was shocked, until I found out Ms. Simons was born and brought up in Leningrad and later immigrated with her family. That background informs a lot of the book - from familiarity with Leningrad streets, to the feel of Soviet reality, to the correct use of diminutives (you have no idea how happy I was to see the heroine, Tatiana, being addressed as Tanya, Tatya, Tanyushka etc and Alexander is often referred to as Shura). There are a few things that stick out a bit but they can be attributable to creating dramatic tension and are minor (e.g. I cannot imagine Tanya having her own hospital room when she broke her leg, but I can fanwank it as hospital being pretty empty due to evacuation and it's necessary for the scene that follows). I wonder if this book works for me so well because it's basically about my grandparents' generation - all of whom either fought in the war or were involved in the war effort (one of my great-uncles was one of the Soviet soldiers who took Berlin with his tank brigade). Maybe that is why I don't find the story far-fetched - I know some much more incredible than that. But what works for me the most in the book is that it manages to convince me that Tanya and Shura's love really is that strong, that amazing, that desperate, that much greater than death. I can fully believe that she cannot breathe without him and that he would die for her without a second's hesitation. You have no idea how rare that is.

Meg Corbyn is a blood prophet. A special human being that when their skin is cut, is able to see into the future. When Meg escapes the compound where she is hidden to attempt to live her life, Meg finds a haven with a group of Others as a human liason between species. Unfortunately this seemingly wondrous new life is not exactly what it seems when Meg learns that more than one person is after her and her very valuable skin. I did not really enjoy the beginning of this book, it moved too slowly for me and I couldn't get past the fact that I didn't really like Meg as a character. She was extremely weak and always so scared. Granted, I understand that Meg is an adult with the mind of a child given the fact that she was in a compound for the majority of her life. But I still couldn't shake my annoyance towards her habits. At first I also didn't care for Simon and his hard ways but with time I grew to really care for the characters in this story. I truly hated Asia Crane. Her character was completely despicable and I found myself attempting to read as quickly as I could through her chapters. This was not because of the wonderful writing style but mostly because of the fact that Bishop wrote such a detestable character. The last 200 pages or so were what really hooked me. I could not get enough of the book and need to read as much as I could. I loved the characters all the way to the end. Specifically, Sam, Simon, Meg, Erebus, Vlad, Henry, Winter, and Tess. I CAN NOT wait to continue with the trilogy and see where it takes me. I would rate this book at more of a 4.5 out of 5 stars simply because of the fact that I didn't particularly enjoy the beginning but I loved it enough that I didn't feel right only giving the story a 4 star rating. Highly recommend and will be continuing.

I enjoyed how the author divided each part and the way breaks were laid out, but I'm unsure about how I feel about the writing style. It tended to be VERY (flowerly) descriptive , even in parts where we didn't really need it. Did I enjoy this one? Yes. I've never read a book centering around a cult, and besides that aspect, I liked being alongside Evie as she deals with her fragmented family life and growing up. Do I think this book deserves ALL the hype? Not really.

I'd only read this if you're interested in early SF / horror. Relative to 2014, this is a 1 or 2 star story. The Day of the Triffids probably deserves a higher rating based on its influence and that, apparently, it was the first of its kind. I can't see how this book would be praised outside of its historical context. The writing is pretty good but it is a first person narrator with a "telling" summary style of relating events. The story is somewhat interesting but with the synopsis format it's difficult to get engaged by it. The Day of the Triffids has 3 major elements to it: The Triffids, a bioengineered plant that can be fatal to humans. "Comet dust" that blinds nearly everyone alive. And a post-apocalyptic setting. The Triffids only become a threat after people have been blinded, even though they have nothing to do with the "comet dust." Surviving in this post-apocalyptic setting is pretty dull but the Triffids provide small doses of excitement. The ending is disappointing. There isn't any solution to the Triffid problem. There isn't a clever idea or SF development to close the story. I was interested in this book because of its popularity and praise. I'm glad I've read it because it will be easier for me to pass on older books that sound ridiculous but have quotes such as Hailed as the greatest science-fiction masterpiece of our time and most terrifying. If it hadn't been a short book, I'd be pissed.

Much as I really, really wanted to enjoy this book, and having heard loads of rave reviews about it, I was just really disappointed. And worse, /bored/ most of the book through. I literally kept reading at points for the fact that it had gotten such good reviews, I don't like to leave books hanging, and I hoped that it might pick up a bit. It didn't. I was disappointed. There were a lot of things that disappointed me, in hindsight. There were things, of course, that had made me interested in the first place; this isn't my normal genre, it's narrated by death, and has lots of quirky stylistic bits with side notes and such littered the whole way through. These, I did enjoy. The rest of the book just didn't hold any interest for me however. The plot is simple; the story of a young girl in Nazi Germany. Her family shelters a jew, various other events occur. She steals some books, but not really because actually the woman who she steals books from doesn't mind at all and leaves open her window purposefully for Liesel . Some bits were vaguely amusing and sweet, but a lot of it was just wholly either boring, slow or depressing. Especially the end, when everyone just dies. Like that. Disappointed. So, for me, dull, dull, dull. The characters had barely any life in them. Perhaps I can say it a little ironically, when Death was the only one who seemed to have a personality. They all felt very flat, with events happening to them all, but none ever taking ahold of their own stories. There's barely any spark, and I can't really think of a defining trait for any of the characters apart from perhaps Hans and Rosa; 'perfect' and 'harsh but loving'. Frustrating. I feel like I /want/ to like Liesel, but most of the time she just vaguely irritated me. Max was quite interesting, but the style just sucked out any life and soul out of all the characters. It's telling, not showing, the whole way through- and it just bored me. Which brings me onto Death, and the narration. Spoilers ahoy- literally. There's absolutely no suspense or intrigue to keep reading, because the moment things start to roll, our much-too-helpful narrator decides each time to announce exactly what will happen and who is the unfortunate to die next. By the end, I didn't feel like I was being robbed of interesting events any more, merely that I was ploughing on to the end to move onto a book less boring. I tried really hard to like this, but it just did absolutely nothing for me.

I struggled through a lot of this book. There were about 80 pages in the middle that almost made me give up on it. The first part is interesting and dramatic enough. Frank and Mamah fall in love and the ensuing drama is interesting enough, even if their decisions make me roll my eyes a little bit- mostly because Frank Lloyd Wright feels like the biggest liar in the universe. I just assumed he was using her. By the end you figure out that he isn't. Part of the theme of this book is the question of a woman's personal happiness and how that may impact her family and whether she has the right to be happy if she makes some wrong decisions in her life. I understood that, but that doesn't make the situation any harder. I can see the argument for showing your children that living in unhappiness doesn't make for a positive role model. However, Mamah has to abandon her family for two years in order to get a divorce . The most boring bit is when Mamah stays in Germany by herself. There are a TON of "oh woe is me" moments that I had very little sympathy for. Mamah made a very conscious decision to leave her family. She has two choices: to go back and ask forgiveness or to continue on. All the hemming and hawing made me really dislike her, probably because of her feminist intuitions. A woman who would choose personal happiness is going to sacrifice her family a bit- particularly pre-WWI. The fact that she didn't realize this annoyed me to no end. I digress, the ending bit is the part that really gets you. You feel like things are heading to an ultimate end (I have no knowledge of Frank Lloyd Wright and his life) and then it takes a sharp right turn. It left me a little numb inside. I was just beginning to like Mamah again. She was making efforts to think of people outside of herself and Frank again. Then...well, I won't spoil it, but it was awful. I think it is even worse because it actually happened. I think my heart hurts the most because her kids were pulled into it. That's what feels the most unfair about it. So, it is probably a book worth reading, but it really drags in the middle. Still, I won't forget it for some time.

I thought Falling Under was awesome and this sequel didn't disappoint! The thing that strikes me the most about this book is how beautiful the writing is. They Hayes can describe feelings and emotions and especially Under just blows my mind. That being said I also love the way the romance plays out. This is not a heroine who just sits back and lets her prince save the day. She is a doer, and in this book, as she discovers her power, she really can fend for herself. Unfortunately she does fall into the category of the girl who pushes her friends away. But in this book her friends and boyfriend actually CONFRONT her and she realizes she made a mistake and move on. This really makes me just LOVE Theia. She makes mistakes but she owns up to them. She falls hopelessly in love, but she doesn't lose herself. And Haden is just the perfect romeo. He is supportive and understanding, has a life but still lets his world revolve around Theia. There are so many frustrating YA paranormal romances out there but THIS IS NOT ONE OF THEM!! This book is straightforward in plot and characters. I also love how Hayes twists in different perspectives, even though the majority of the book is from Theia's perspective. I don't want to give away the plot, but it was a really great adventure and such a good complement to the first book. I can't tell if there will be a sequel, the book did kinda wrap up but I can see how there could be another one, but I hope there is because I would love to spend more time with Theia, Haden, and all their friends! This is really a great read and if you haven't read Falling Under yet, read it!

This book was everything and nothing I was expecting it to be! It fell short when it came to the Miniaturist story line. It feels like Burton began the book with this story in mind and as she continued to write forgot what it was she was supposed to be talking about and so began a new story and then was reminded right at the end of her original plot and lazily bought it all together. I'm not normally a fan of books set from years ago, but the plot of this mysterious miniaturist intrigued me. As I went through I began to realise this story line was being forgotten and thought that maybe I would begin to grow bored of the story however I was extremely mistaken. I was so involved in the characters lives that I almost forgot about the miniaturist myself! Burton pulls at heart strings with her characters and I can admit I did have a little cry to myself over this book. I fell in love Johannes, he was a good man who was trying his best to keep his unconventional family going and he did not deserve the fate that was brought to him. I'd recommend this book to those who enjoy a long and fufilling read.

Such a creative form of writing that you won't ever be bored when you read this book. Stories are presented along with a vocabulary related to one and only, wretched and bitter thing that is love:) There are many kinds of tales, but this book contain mostly sad-tales about domesticity, moving in, real love, gloomy pasts, and perhaps a hinted adultery? All written in the most beautiful way possible, inferring that love doesn't have to be gendered, or only exclusive to a certain sexuality. Some drabbles still reverberate like echo in my heart. Especially the story for the word reverberate, so simple yet imply so much meaning. And also if my partner were to ask me that, I'd be taken aback and probably burst in quiet tears  . 4 out of 5 stars.

I really wanted to love this book. I thought I did, back when I first started it. However, the further along I got through this story the more I found myself questioning whether it's really all that good. I even question my 3 star rating now. Okay, holy sexism batman. I can't count the number of times I got angry at how weak all of the women were (with one exception- Bruna, I'm looking at you). Not the mention the fact that all women are valued for is how quickly they can pop babies out (but only once married- sleep around before that and get labelled the town whore by everyone, while the men get called heroes. I understand how that is a reflection on the sexism still apparent in today's society but come on dude. Calm it down a notch. A woman's virginity is not her 'greatest gift that should be treasured'. Ugh.) By the end of the book if I had to hear any more about how a woman is nothing until she's had children I was going to burn the thing in a bonfire. Also: I'm not a fan of gratuitous rape. And I especially do not like (nay, I f*cking hated) that:  Only a day or 2 after Leesha was GANG RAPED (after being a virgin no less) she's suddenly craving sex with someone she has just met? Um, author, do you have no understanding of how traumatic getting freaking gang raped is? Why was there no development of her character after that? Why did it do nothing to her other than make her cry for 5 minutes and then be desperate to bang the next guy she sees? HORRIBLE STORYTELLING. GTFO NOW.) I found the character development to be incredibly lazy. Skipping years ahead and having the characters become different people without much of an explanation is just lazy. It made the characters (the main one, especially) unrelatable, and unrealistic. The demons were interesting. For the first part of the book. Then, we only learn one thing about them they like to dance and listen to music? Wtf? and we have no clue about anything else to do with them. They became flat, one dimensional 'baddies' with zero motives and frankly, they bored me. As I said, I enjoyed the first part of the book. It was headed towards a solid 4.5. By the end, I couldn't wait to finish it just so I didn't have to read the goddamn thing anymore and the rating had dropped to a 1.5. Calling it 3 to be fair. *- EDIT- changing to a 1-1.5 because thinking about this months months down the line is still making me mad* I wouldn't really recommend this book, and I have doubts that I'll continue this series.

4.5 Stars The plot. After a volcra attack that almost killed her and her bestfiend, Alina's life changed tremendously. She's no longer the mapmaker girl who grew up in an orphanage. Turns out, she's a Grisha, one gifted with ability, and a very special and powerful at that. She's the Sun Summoner, the only hope to destroy the Shadow Fold that weakens the Ravka, and finds herself under the Darkling's protection. Alina Starkov Honestly, it took me a while to like her. She has the tendency to be pessimistic and that sort of put me off a little. She irks me when she goes all "woe is me". Like, say, when she keeps insisting to the Darkling that she's not a Grisha when, in fact, her "glowing like sun" ability makes that crystal clear that she certainly is. Eventually, though, she sucked it up and embraced what she is and I might have loved her a little bit. Then, in the last quarter of the book, she was so awesome and a bit of a badass. The romance in Shadow and Bone is predictable. NOT! There is a love triangle in this book. Kinda. Alina has been secretly in love with her bestfriend, Mal , and had to suffer through watching him flirt with other girls. I felt really sorry for her. You guys, unrequited love SUCKS! Then, they were taken apart, came in the mysterious and powerful Darkling, and Alina couldn't help but be drawn to him. I can't say much about the Darkling because you know, spoilers and all. All I can say though is he's dangerous. In the "I can tear you in half with just a sway of my hand" kind of way. Scaryyyy. He's also ridiculously good-looking, commands the dark, and wears all black. Need I say more? Alina fears him but at the same time, a part of her wants to please him. Oh, and there were some really sizzling hot moments between them. Mal, who? Holy crappola, this book is evil! Just when I thought I knew where the plot is going, I was rendered speechless by the twist. A real game-changer, I tell you. I was, like, "I SHOULD'VE SEEN THAT COMING!! The Darkling is E.V.I.L.! Mal is amazing! I just have to say I was rooting for Mal in the beginning because I love "friends-turned-lovers" relationship but thought it was a lost cause what with the intimate moments Alina and the Darkling shared. Although, after the twist was revealed about the Darkling's real dark plans, I was sorry for Alina at the same time my heart soared. Mal is back in the game. Woot! Woot! "I missed you every hour. And you know what the worst part was? It caught me completely by surprise. I'd caught myself walking around to find you, not for any reason, just out of habit, because I'd seen something I wanted to tell you about or because I wanted to hear your voice. And then I'd realized that you weren't there anymore, and every time, every single time, it was like having the wind knocked out of me. I've risked my life for you. I've walked half the length of Ravka for you, and I'd do it again and again and again just to be with you, just to starve with you and freeze with you and hear you complain about hard cheese every day. So don't tell me we don't belong together. I'm sorry it took me so long to see you, Alina. But I see you now. "I don't care if you danced naked in the roof of the Little Palace with him. I love you, Alina. Even the part of you that loved him. Just not to spoil, I'm team happy ever after for the boy and the girl.

This review is going to be a little bit unconventional for me, much like The Book Thief is itself. Usually, in the first part of my review I write a little summary of the plot in my own words, then I move on to breaking down what I liked and didn't like, summing up my overall opinion at the end. That won't work for The Book Thief because I literally can't find a fault with it. I was recommended this book by so many different people and none of them had a bad word to say about it. Usually, that kind of situation leaves me feeling a bit cynical and reluctant because I'm sure the book can't live up to the hype but The Book Thief lived up to it and then trumped it a couple of times too. Written from the perspective of Death, the narrative voice is poetic, full of vivid imagery, harsh honesty and wrapped up with an engaging sense of humour. I don't think a single word or sentence was placed in this book that wasn't thoroughly thought out, which is only fitting for a story that hinges on the power of words. The Book Thief didn't tell me anything about the Second World War or the Holocaust that I didn't already know but it did make me think about it all over again and, more importantly, feel it. I hardly ever cry at books but this one had me tearful on a number of occasions and an absolute wreck by the finale. That isn't to say that this is a depressing book, it has it's moments of fun, it's characters that are full of love and kindness and bravery but unfortunately that is what ultimately broke my heart. After all, if I didn't care for the characters, the events would not have hit me so hard. The foreshadowing of Rudy's death, who was already my favourite character up to that point, undid me. Every endearing thing he did tasted bitter-sweet but it was a very clever idea - it made me home in completely on the preciousness of the life that was to be lost. I was surprised when I heard that this book is sometimes marketed as YA but now I have read it, I actually think that's a wonderful thing. If I had read this when I was a teenager I know it would have not only blown me away, it would have opened my mind.

We serial killers are your sons, we are your husbands, we are everywhere. And there will be more of your children dead tomorrow. What are the chances of a ex-policewoman turned journalist working on a story about random murders taking place in the country actually having worked at close quarters with the same serial killer in a crisis centre? That's a pretty unique position to be in and Ann Rule was unfortunate enough to be on the spot. She had bonded with Ted over months of saving people's lives together and never in her wildest dreams did she realise that the same Ted was also murdering young women all over the place at the same time that he was saving people from committing suicide. This is a fascinating and frightening book that focuses on how psychopaths are in our midst and we don't recognise them. Rule struggles to accept the truth as gradually one by one, the evidence piles up against Bundy. Vacillating from fear to tenderness, from friendship to hate, from a desire to get Bundy receive the help he badly needed to a need to tell the victim's stories, Rule has written a comprehensive and insightful book about this case. Her emotions come through in the book and for this, I can forgive the average writing and the author getting in the way of the narrative at times. The book starts off with several clarifications and a FAQ for people who keep writing to Rule asking the same things over and over again. The actual 'story' starts with Ted's escape from prison and then moves back and forth. The author follows the different murders and disappearances one by one and keeps the knowledge of the culprit or the end result from the reader for the first half of the book. It is almost like you are following the case for several years in exactly the same way as the investigators did. The descriptions of the trials take up a good chunk of the latter half of the book. While I generally find this section pretty boring in most true crime books, it was not the case with this one. I don't know whether it was the skill of the author in involving me so deep into the events of the time, or Bundy's shenanigans in court. But I was interested till the end. Rule and Bundy corresponded over a long period, and she shared some of his letters in the book, which I found rather enlightening. The author might have been friends with a serial killer but she also shows respect and sympathy for the murdered women and their families. Almost every woman was given a short biography, and the subject was dealt with very delicately. Rule makes the point again and again that these women did nothing wrong, and there was simply no way they could have escaped, except by a stroke of luck. It is indeed true. There was no way anyone could have suspected Ted Bundy to be a murderer, with his good looks and charm. Rule also retains enough sympathy for Bundy and wonders what could have been done to prevent his turning into a monster. A man with so much promise, knowledge and intellect ending up as a common criminal is a waste of not just his life, but that of all the smart and intelligent women he murdered. Bundy put the blame for his murder spree on pornography. It is anyone's guess if this is the case, but I personally think that if pornography had an effect on Bundy, it was only to enhance what had already been created inside him. I certainly don't believe the monster was created because of a rejection by a woman. I personally think that his maternal grandfather, Samuel Cowell, abuser and bigot extraordinnaire, abused Bundy when he was a child. The very fact that Bundy talks of this horrible man as loving and wonderful is a red flag since no one else thinks so! Rule appears to agree with me. We get to see Bundy through the eyes of a person who had known him under ordinary circumstances as an ordinary person. And that is why this book is so creepy and disturbing. A seemingly ordinary man with oodles of charm goes about murdering women without anyone realising it at all! It shows how vulnerable we really are in the face of a maniacal and intelligent killer. And now I am off to double-check that the doors and windows are locked ...

3.5 stars Kate's parents have just died, and she's moved from New York to Paris. She's basically a living dead person (Hehehe...c what I did there?) until she meets Vincent. But there's something different about him and his friends. And Kate will stop at nothing to find out what. Everything about this book was average. Average writing, average characters, average romance, and an average plot line. The writing would have gotten me a three by my english teacher. Which isn't bad. It's just grade level, or average. And honestly, if a book is published, shouldn't the writing be a bit better than average? The characters were nice and everything, but they're not memorable. The author doesn't give us enough character building for us to have a sense of who they really are. But there's enough for the characters to act while making sense. We just don't really know the details of their existence. Like, for example, Kate. First person book and everything, and yet she never gives us any details for her past except that her parents died. She's always telling Vincent about her past but it's never stated directly so that I, the reader, understand who she used to be and how she became who she is now. The romance was nice. That's it. It was nice to read about and everything, but it wasn't a romance to where every time they looked at each other I got like excited with anticipation of what that look could mean. But I still enjoyed how the story played out; just not to a heart wrenching, "I will not sleep until I finish" level. I did however like the take on zombies being sexy and everything. The one element of this book that was anything but average was the cover. It is drop dead gorgeous! It's what originally intrigued me about the book, and every time I look at it I get wistful. I mean, she's in a beautiful dress, the Eiffel Tower is in the background, and those designs around the title are equally as beautiful! This book isn't a waste of time or anything, but it's not a must read. It really just depend on what other books you have inline to read...

Cover Blurb: Yes or No? I'm a little divided about the cover. The title is mostly what caught my attention, and while the dominoes now make more sense than they did before reading the book, I still don't quite get why it was chosen for the cover art. Hmmm. Characters: Death as a character is a concept that doesn't always work, but I liked him quite a bit in The Book Thief. He made for a very interesting and surprisingly good narrator, and I enjoyed his odd sense of humor. While never truly a direct character in the story, he was perfect for seeing the events through his eyes. Hans Hubermann, Liesel's foster father, was my favorite character. I loved his easy, quiet manner and gentle teasing. If I could have an ideal uncle, I'd want Hans Hubermann. Rosa, on the other hand, took me a while to get used to. Verbally abusive, rude, and sour, I didn't much care for her form of affection, though in the end I did come to like her a bit. I loved Max and Rudy and of course Liesel. Rudy had a defiant streak and Liesel was spunky. She didn't always behave well, but she always felt horrible afterward; it was hard not to forgive her. The Romance: Rudy and Liesel have a bit of a childhood crush on one another, though neither would ever admit it. With so much going on in this book, it never takes forefront. Plot: This is a character-driven book. Many things do happen, but there isn't a main plot. When Max arrives at the Hubermann home, it is definitely a turning point in the story, but it is only one of many in Liesel's life. The Book Thief goes from 1939 to 1945, and follows Liesel's time in a little town outside of Munich. We meet the people who influence her life, witness the events that change it, all through the eyes of Death, who takes an uncanny interest in Liesel for many reasons. Liesel is forced to leave her home and her mother when her father is arrested for being a Kommunist, and when her little brother dies on their way to Himmel Street, where they are to live with the Hubermanns, Liesel turns to book thieving for comfort. She can't read, but there is something about books that she cannot resist. Life with the Hubermanns isn't easy. They are barely able to feed themselves, and Hans Hubermann isn't exactly in agreement with the Nazi Party. But Liesel likes her foster father and she makes friends with a neighboring boy, Rudy. But every once in a while, she still feels the need to steal books, and she soon finds herself taking them from the bonfires and the mayor's house. When a Jewish man shows up at Himmel Street one night, seeking refuge with the Hubermanns, Liesel discovers someone she can share her books with. But Max can't stay forever - not with the war looming ever closer to Himmel Street. Despite the lack of definite plot (because again, Max and even the book thieving is only a small part of the story), I couldn't help but be drawn into The Book Thief. The characters are interesting, I love the era, and the narration style is just so unique and emotional. This is a feels book, and I definitely had a lot of feelings going through me as I read - sometimes laughing, but mostly sad. Believability: Nothing to complain about. Writing Style: First person, past tense. Though every once in a while, Death would kind of start talking in present tense. The narration took me a little while to get used to. It comes across as choppy at first; Death doesn't have a linear way of thinking. He will jump around quite a bit from one event to another, and sometimes this event has happened before that other event. But in about 50 pages, I got used to it, and was able to follow Death's thought process. And I must admit that I really enjoyed it. His dry, dark sense of humor and sometimes bizarre metaphors and similes added an extra layer of bleakness and emotion to a topic that is already very bleak and emotional. Content: 15 s-words, 8 g--damns Conclusion: The Reader will see the end coming fairly well in advance, because Death keeps dropping hints. But it still hit me very hard when I finally read it. I was a little stunned, and for a moment I debated whether or not it completely ruined the book. What was the point, after all, if that was just going to happen? But I honestly liked it, though I cannot exactly say why. I just did. I first tried to read The Book Thief when it initially came out. A story about a young girl who steals books during Nazi Germany sounded like the sort of thing I would love. But I couldn't get into the narration and I thought it was a little too weird, so I didn't pick it up again until recently. The movie is being releases soon, after all, and I hate seeing movies without reading the book first. Now that I'm older, I was able to enjoy The Book Thief a whole lot more. It is a little odd because of Death's narration, and it can feel a tiny bit slow. But I honestly didn't want to put it down, it captivated me so thoroughly. And what exactly it was that captivated me, I'm still not entirely certain. The characters were good, the era was good, the narration was very interesting, and it was an extremely emotional read. But I can't say that the characters were my absolute favorites, or that this was even the best WWII novel I've ever read - or even the most emotional read I've encountered. And yet, there was something about it that just stuck with me. The opening lines and the ending lines will always stay with me. Recommended Audience: Girl-and-guy read, better for teens seventeen and up, and adults. Anyone younger than seventeen probably won't stick with it for long just due to interest level. Fans of WWII, Holocaust, and emotional novels will like this.

I finished this yesterday and yet it feels like weeks since I've read it. Not sure what that means. First of all, I'd have given this book four stars if Putney knew how to write anything realistically--which she does not. Granted, it is partly my own fault, because I know from past experience that I don't generally enjoy books by her with tortured heroes, simply because the heroes aren't actually tortured. The characters in the book claim the hero is tortured, and so does the hero himself, but this is not displayed at all in the actual story. I have no problem with non-tortured heroes, but if you're going to write a TH, then at least do it right. I am reminded of Ian from another Putney book. He spent years in dungeon which was literally a hole dug into the ground. When he was freed, he was in perfect health. Mildly underweight, but otherwise in tip top shape. We are told he is claustrophobic, but he doesn't exhibit as much. Perhaps he thinks, Damn, this darkness kinda sucks-- oh well! - It's not that I wanted him to suffer, but how am I supposed to get into his character when he feels so unreal? Same thing happened with Grey. Imprisoned in solitary confinement for TEN years. Despite this, he is in pique physical condition-- he is slightly underweight, but only by a few pounds or so, and is in stunningly perfect health. Yes, I want him healthy, but not at the cost of accuracy. I'm supposed to believe he spent ten years in a French dungeon and can just pop out back into society totally healthy mentally and physically? Oh, sure, he claims he's insane, but is there any proof? No. Supposedly, his temper is the proof. Okay. Also, he has a mild distaste for crowds now. Whatever that means. It just felt like his character post-prison was just slapped together at random. Oh, gee, he should be scarred. Let's see...how about he wants to beat up a few people and gets a bit irritated in crowds! Perfect! On a high note, I found Cassie a pretty likable heroine. I found it refreshing how she wasn't the typical naive virgin - not to mention the fact that she could kick major butt. Plus, she actually showed affection to her hero-- I know, you'd think romances are full of that, but really it's mostly the heroes drooling and caressing the heroines. I like some equality myself. As for Grey, nothing new or special here. He felt like a generic hero to me. I did however enjoy the fact that he readily admitted to needing Cassie and to wanting her around. He knew what he wanted from the beginning, HER, and he wasn't afraid to tell her so. He actually asked for her to go places with him because he wanted her support. It's fairly typical for the heroes to defend the heroine's name, but it's rarer to find the alternative. Cassie, for me, is that. I loved how she wouldn't let anyone badmouth Grey, not even his own mother. She respected him and cared about him as a person, and he did the same for her. In fact, the best part about this book was that the H/h liked each other--and ADMITTED to it. Low points include: The reunions. Grey and Kirkland...meh. It was okay. Grey and his family...below average. I just didn't feel the emotion at all. It felt distant. Not to mention that his brother immediately did the whole  boohoohoo my bro's back from the dead, now I can't be the heir! thing, which is just dumb. I'm getting bored of the "crappy family members care more about titles than loved ones" scenario. Especially in this case, since  his brother didn't even want the title! He wanted to be an actor! And of course immediately after Grey says he'll support Peter in his acting career, Petey Boy is all glad Big Bro is alive again. Whatta guy. Also, the male friendships here should be a major point, but they came off as weak. For a guy who spent years trying to find his friend, Kirkland's reaction to his return was ho-hum. I get that they're men, but come on.

Seventeen-year-old Ezra Faulkner believes that everyone will experience their own personal tragedy. For Ezra, the junior class president and captain of the tennis team, this comes in the form of a careless driver slamming into his car; shattering his knee, his tennis dreams and his seemingly perfect life. Ezra no longer feels like he is part of his popular crowd of friends or the life he was living before the accident. When he returns to school he finds himself falling back into a friendship with Toby Ellicott, the boy, who up until his own personal tragedy age twelve, used to be Ezra's best friend. Through his friendship with Toby, Ezra finds himself signed up to the debate team, hanging out with Toby's eccentric friends and getting to know the mysterious new girl, Cassidy Thorpe. Soon Ezra is beginning to see that maybe his accident didn't destroy his life but actually helped to really start it. I loved this book. L.O.V.E.D it! To the point where I really just want to be able to scream that at people but I'm not sure that's appropriate. I was actually really excited when I received this book at work because when I had read the back I thought it sounded ridiculously interesting. So I was happy to find that this book didn't leave me disappointed and actually made me fall in love with it! Now I am really trying to do a review of this book that doesn't just have me screaming at you all through the blogosphere READ IT!!! Even if that is all my brain is telling me to do right now. So I shall at least try to coherently right down some of my thoughts and feelings on this book; because I really do have a lot of them. I have to start off by saying that thanks to this book I now have a new author to look out for. As soon as Robyn Schneider releases another book I will be buying it. So I guess I will be virtually stalking her in order to catch any mention of a new book. The cover of the book shows part of a review from Publishers Weekly that says "I couldn't help but think of John Green's novels - I think his fans will eat this up.". As a fan of John Green I do have to agree with that, I did eat it up. I loved the fact I found another author who manges to write characters that actually make me laugh out loud (even if this does get you odd looks from people on public transport). This book had me laughing right from the beginning. The story of how Toby met his moment of tragedy was so hilarious to me that I choked on the juice I was drinking and almost spurted it out of my nose. I wish this were not true, and my poor burning nostrils at the time also really wished it wasn't true but it was. I think I was guaranteed to love Toby after that, and I did, I really did. I think that was one of the reasons I loved this so much; it gave me so many characters to love. Which is something I really adore in a book, I mean it's part of the reason I will always hold Harry Potter so dear to my heart. While we are talking about loving characters I must say: Cassidy Thorpe, I love thee. Cassidy Thorpe had me as a fan the minute she turned up to the debate tournament in a Hogwarts uniform. I could picture it so clearly and I adored her for it. I think the debate group as a whole was one of my favourite things about this book. I enjoyed all their back and forth, their quick witted jokes and the crazy things they got up to. I am jealous that I don't get to go to the Floating Movie Theatre, which are film screenings that are held in secret in different locations of their school. As I was reading it I was just thinking that it sounded ridiculously epic and that I wished I could go. If I had to say one thing I didn't like about it, it would probably be the end. I saw the revelation coming and it just didn't end how I wanted it to. I guess I was left feeling dissatisfied with it. I think it's partly to do with the fact I am still reeling from the Dexter finale and I just want something, anything, to end how I want it to end! This book had everything that I needed and the fact it didn't end the way I wanted it to didn't make me love it any less. I would highly recommend it and urge you to all go out and read it. I loved the fact the characters had me laughing from beginning to end, they all had such individual personalities which most books I have read lately have been seriously lacking. If you read or have read it I would love to hear what you thought. 4/5 Stars P.s. I must admit to over thinking some things way too much when reading a book. Ezra has a poodle named Cooper who he got from his aunt when he was nine and the dog was eight. Now at age sixteen the dog is still running about, chasing rabbits and this bothered me. I'm sitting there thinking that poodles average twelve years and that it is highly unlikely it would be so fit and healthy. This actually bothered me for about another three chapters and I suddenly realised: I THINK TOO MUCH! Check out my blog to see my other reviews at: http://reviewsfromabookworm.blogspot.... .

The 12th book of the Women's Murder Club has a different feel from the previous books in the series. 12th of Never focuses less on the members of the club and more on the cases. The story jumps around from the cases to Lindsay's personal life. Also, this is another book without chapters from the killer's point of view, but unlike 10th Anniversary the other aspects of the book made this barely noticeable. The book still has the traditional court case but with Yuki litigating a sleazier-than-normal perp (in my opinion, the best Yuki story/case of the series). Claire faces her biggest challenge as an ME. Cindy has a minor role. And Lindsay is adjusting to life as a mom, going back to work early from maternity leave, balancing cop with family, and of course, catching the bad guy. There were a few twists in the stories that I didn't foresee (always a plus, I like when a book can surprise me). The different stories intertwined nicely and had unsuspected connections. When I finished the epilogue, I was left hanging & am hopeful for a 13th book in the series.

Whether you want to go all the way and change your lifestyle, or you just want to get some tips on how to keep your household clean a little easier, this book will have answers. Kondo talks a lot about her own experiences and how she's come to the clean lifestyle she leads now. She also gives enough concrete information for the reader to apply the 'Konmari way' to their own life. I would honestly recommend everyone to read this book. It's a really quick and easy read and I think anyone could benefit from it.

Why is everything I'm picking up lately disappointing me so much?? I haven't read a good college romance I loved since The Hook Up and wanted to give this one a try. Despite the cover and title, this story has nothing to do with a love triangle, but is more about a reformed party girl trying to get her life back on track and starts to hook up with a popular manwhore from school. And though the blurb makes it sound like Nora has some big scandalous secret, it was revealed within the first chapter and wasn't really scandalous or remarkable at all. In fact. NOTHING REALLY HAPPENS. Maybe the author was going for a low drama type of story, which is fine. But something needs to keep the reader engaged and keep the story interesting, and sadly nothing in this did. I just couldn't connect with this. The heroine was dull and pretty annoying at times, the conversations and dialogue were boring and I didn't find them humorous though I can see that's what the author was going for. And there were just some really random things thrown in here that didn't add to the story at all : The manwhore turning out to be a magician? Um ok. Was that supposed to make him original? Something to make him stand out? Because it didn't work and instead was a weird addition to the overall plot. The heroine starts out with a huge crush on her roommate. When he asks her to dinner and stands her up she basically cries in a corner and is extremely angry with him. 2 chapters later she's completely over it and it's just never brought up again. By him or her. I found it odd there was no resolution to that situation. I started to skim about 50% in, which is just a red flag for me to stop. I found it overall to be an unemotional an uninspiring read. Find Me On: Instagram  FB Page  FB Blog  Blog

Gosh I read this in July, and obviously meant to come back and review it before it came out, but now I am three weeks late! And of course since then, I have read another heap of books, and my memory is what it used to be. I remember loving get up again in the lives of these two curse-ridden characters. I remember being satisfied with the way the author dealt with the time-travel paradoxes. I found the ending realistic, if not altogether happy-ever-after. This is YA romance with a twist of twisty plot and time travel. It's very good. Copy provided by publisher via Netgalley, and received with thanks.

This book was well written and for the most part I liked the style. I wasn't surprised at the part that was probably supposed to be surprising, as I guessed it much earlier on. The characters were unlikable, but with Anna I eventually liked unliking her. While this book was pretty good, I don't feel like it lived up to the hype.

This is the first in the series and sets the style and pace for books to come.. Not only do we get the feline pride's alpha Callen, finding his mate.. we have a perfect storyline set up for Sherra and hints that feline DNA was not the only one used to in the Council's experiments to create the perfect solider.

I was just looking for some YA titles to read- something that didn't involve vampires or fallen angels when I came across this trilogy. I saw good reviews for it so decided it to try it anyway. I think the book is more like 3.5 stars than 4- but never mind. I decided to round it off to four. What I liked about this book was that was pretty good paced and a very quick read. The action pretty much started in the first few pages. The writing was easy and there wasn't much to understand in the novel. I had no expectations from this novel, so I am not going to criticize it any way. This is one of those books which are meant for entertainment and there is hardly anything in them to be taken seriously or get offended about. It's not that dark- it's a somewhat cheerful book compared to today's painful YA novels like Twilight, Fallen or Hush, Hush. It is about Sophie Mercer, who is a witch and gets sent to a reform school for Prodigium (that's the term for faeries, shapeshifters, werewolves and witches). Of course, she is an awkward girl who has trouble "fitting in". Her roommate is Jenna who is the only vampire on the campus- and they are both unpopular. But there is a lot about her true identity that Sophie doesn't know. She has powers beyond her imagination and she discovers the truth of who she is and what her parents kept from her all their life. On the romance front, she spends the whole book crushing on the resident bad boy Archer. Although I did like him, he seemed sweet to me rather than a bad boy. Apart from his occasional rudeness there was hardly anything "bad" about him. And then there is the hot groundskeeper Cal and I sensed some attraction between him and Sophie. Since Archer  goes missing in the end  maybe she and Cal become a thing in the other books. All in all, I enjoyed this book and would recommend it to anyone who enjoys witchcraft and Harry Potter. This book reminded me a lot of Harry Potter except that the main character here is a girl and the whole book is girly. It's a fun, quick read and I am going to read the other two in the series as well. I would tell you read this during the summer by the pool. It's a relaxing read and the humor is dry, but Sophie can make you laugh at times. She's probably one of the best YA female characters I have come across in a long time. She is not complicated and doesn't seem to spend all her time moping around. She makes mistakes but otherwise she is frank, loving and a loyal friend. I think girls should look up to characters like Sophie rather than Bella Swan or Lucinda Price.

3.5 stars This isn't a really low grade in my book; I'm trying to stick to the "did not like it/it was okay/liked it/really liked it/loved it" scale that Goodreads already has in place. When I first started reading this book, I was at a rehearsal for a musical I'm in. I was trying to pay attention to the book during a scene I wasn't in; I think that instance set the tone for more than half the book. The tone I'm talking about is reading but not reading -- physically reading the book but not really remembering or caring subconsciously. That, I think, is why I only liked it, not really liked it or loved it. The second half-ish of the book I found really good, for obvious reasons. I might have to reread this in the near future. The style of writing for this book is something that I had to grow used to, but began to love. The whole "it's a small world/the universe makes everyone meet everyone" theme is evident in this book and the enormously popular the Instalove(tm) (term coined by fellow Goodreader Ben Ace) novel The Sun Is Also a Star. I honestly preferred it in The Nest because it was more realistic and not as forced as The Sun Is Also a Star (read my strange review for that here). I just loved seeing how in The Nest, all of the characters lives began to intertwine. It was super cool to see that, and it was something I really enjoyed. For that alone, I'm giving this rating another half star (crazy, I know). I hope this stays a stand-alone novel because I really liked the note it left off on. I'm actually kind of glad Leo left the Plumb's life. I think he needed it as much as the other Plumbs did; he was always messing things up and manipulating people. I never liked Leo throughout the book. Including that fact, the ending of the book was honestly perfect. Everyone ended up with who they needed to end up with (Matilda and Vinnie! Yay!) and everyone left with the self-realization that they needed. The total epiphany approach for the ending was honestly the best part of the entire book. I'd recommend this for mature readers (it's adult fiction for a reason) who are able to actually absorb words (instead of reading them and having them immediately go out the other ear; something I am working on). Also: that third paragraph might have way too many links. Will I fix it? No

I was pulled in from the first page. Knowing it was about a couple's relationship on the rocks, I expected a lot of the usual tropes, but I was pleasantly surprised by Rainbow's depiction of Georgie and her well defined and acknowledged love for her family. Rowell knows how to write characters. They are always flawed but loveable. I definitely have a few twinges of nostalgia when reading about Georgie's flashbacks and remembering my own young love all over again.
