This was an odd book. I found it readable enough, and the descriptions of General Lee's Civil War were interesting, but I kept thinking (while I was sporadically reading it - there was no impetus ever to rush to the end) that it was surely leading up to some truly cool ending where all the many threads of her plot would be pulled together in some amazing way. Um, no. Not so much. She had some potential here, but she didn't seem to have a clue what to do with it. Actually, I think I should probably give this 2 stars, but I'm still feeling fond of her for writing "Passage".

I probably shouldn't have read this book right after I read Something, Maybe, as the same sorts of problems I encountered with that one showed up in this one. The dad was the same as in that one - a grown man who refuses to deal with negative emotions, who thinks only of himself, and who has practically zero redeeming qualities. There's also a main character who's so oblivious to the world around her that I have a hard time finding the plot believable at times. I did like this book more than the previous one. I found myself relating to Kate more than I would care to admit. I wanted to hate her for jumping to (obviously false) conclusions and cutting Will off before he even got to finish a sentence, but that still sounds like something I would do: be so afraid of rejection and humiliation that you hurry to reject the other person first. It's stupid, but I can definitely look back and see when I did that, so I guess it's realistic. I didn't find Kate's father all that realistic, but maybe I'm just lucky and haven't come across someone like that. I just found him so infuriating, and I ended up hating everyone else in the family for not yelling at him, for continuing to make excuses for him as he throws their savings down the drain so he can follow his "dream" of selling vitamins, even though he was constantly leaving the kiosk to go to the movies or get food or buy video games. He was just so selfish and irresponsible, and it takes forever until someone besides their grandmother finally noticed. I mean, seriously - they lose their house, and still no one yells at him. I almost set the book down right then. Obviously I kept reading, and I'm fairly glad I did, but still...I just wanted to scream at all of these people. Really, the only character I really liked (besides Will) was the grandmother, whom everyone else seemed to hate. I get that she can be a bit judgmental at times, but she obviously cares about them, and she's right about most everything (except for the bright purple shoes), and it was annoying to watch everyone else side with the father when she would put him down, when clearly she was the one who was right. It sounds like I hated this book, but I didn't. I found Kate rather immature at times, and she was kind of annoying, but I could still mostly understand her, and I was looking forward to the moment when she would finally stop getting in her own way and just be able to get along with Will. He was cute and amusing. I don't really understand why he put up with her, but my boyfriend puts up with me, so I guess it's at least realistic. I loved their "10 second rule," which is pretty much how my boyfriend and I correspond most of the time. Overall, this book was rather infuriating, but it wasn't horrible. And I got the ending I was hoping for, so it was mostly worth it in the end.

This was a very cute read! Watching Annabel gain confidence in herself as she loses weight and falls in love was awesome... I love to see teenage girls come into their confidence and feel good about themselves - She was mature and classy instead of the typical mean girl way. She was already a smart, funny, beautiful girl but that confidence made her that much more. It wasn't about losing the weight, it was about feeling good about herself. Tegan was just a doll... he saw Annabel for who she was and not what she looked like, even though he thought she was beautiful anyway. He admired her for who she was because of a few choices she made and her determination when she wanted something. He had a lot going on in his own life  and while it was heartbreaking to see him end their relationship because of what happened with his Mom and Brother, it made their reconnection that much sweeter. He obviously had to come to terms with what his dad did and what exactly his responsibilities were before he could fully commit to Annabel. . I love Nyrae Dawn's writing style and can not wait to read more of her heartwarming sweet stories!

Before reading: Looking at the back of this book yesterday, it occurred to me that the author, Erik Larson, is also the author of Issac's Storm, a book about the 1900 Galveston hurricane which has also been on my to-read list for a while. After reading: I can;t decide if I liked this book or not. I was engrossed in the story and I kept reading because I was trying to make it through the chapters about Burnham to make it to the chapters about Holmes. Looking back, I just find I wasn't that interested in the minute details about the fair's inception. A few things annoyed me about the book too. Larson starts by alternating chapters, one short chapter about Burnham then one short chapter about Holmes. It's easy reading, even though there are tons of names and details and dates to keep straight. But halfway through the book Larson changes this pattern, so you end up wading through more and more pages to get to the salacious details of the book. Larson has done extensive research into the story, and the fair details I found most fascinating where not the numbers of visitors of the hours of work that went into the design, but the little details -- the creation of Shredded Wheat, for example, and the epic introduction of the world's first Ferris Wheel. I can't say I didn't enjoy the book because I burned through it's nearly 400 pages pretty quickly, but when I consider now picking up "Isaac's Storm" from the library it sounds like the last thing I could possibly want to read right now.

The Bazaar of Bad Dreams is a collection of short stories by Stephen King. Some of these stories have been told before, and some of them have never been published. True to form, Stephen King delivers his normal brand of horror with a few twists to remind the reader that nothing is really as it seems. Although I was disappointed at re-reading a few of the stories, overall, the book was a hit!

1.5 stars I had low expectations for this one, yet it managed to be worse than I was expecting. This retelling/twist on Disney's "Beauty and the Beast" had promise in its premise - it's much darker and closes some plot holes from the movie - but butchers the lovable heroine that makes the film so enjoyable. Seriously, let's talk about Belle. For a character who repeatedly thinks about how smart and superior to the villagers she is, this version of Belle is kind of dumb. She sees an image of herself as a baby in an apartment and then marvels (more than once) about how she can't remember the apartment, and isn't that weird? No. It's not weird. You were a baby. Nobody retains memories from infancy. Why is this so shocking? She also has a habit of thinking about how the dumb heroines of gothic romances would do something AND THEN PROCEEDS TO DO THE SAME THING< usually after thinking she's not an idiot like them. No, Belle. You are. She's also kind of self-absorbed. After  speeding up the curse and shattering the rose  , it takes her a long time to think about the impact on the innocent servants. Or, even after learning that the Beast is actually a prince (I'm not putting a spoiler tag here because who doesn't know this? ), she still proceeds to call him "Beast" to his face. Like, it doesn't even occur to her to ask him his name. Rude AF. (To be fair to the author, she put herself in a tough position. A lot of people my age have strong opinions about Belle. She's a beloved Disney princess that appeals to those of us who grew up lost in a book and feeling a little bit different. Write the character differently and it feels like butchering, fair assessment or not.) There were a few things I did like. The politics of the kingdom were interesting, and I enjoyed the story of Belle's parents. But the poor character development, slow plot, and fizzle of an ending  (the Beast is still a beast and has to go searching for people to turn him into a prince, there's no kiss or even any love declaration between Belle and the Beast, etc) , this book doesn't work even on a guilty pleasure level. Pass.

Short Review An okay standalone in the Discworld universe that you'll likely enjoy more if you're a big fan of classic old-timey Hollywood. The humor throughout is chuckle worthy, but a little short of what you get in many of the other Discworld novels. Good if you really like Discworld, but if some of the other books have left you unimpressed I'd bet this one will too. Long Review A long parody of the 'golden age' of Hollywood by way of Discworld's equivalent, Holy Wood. While there are some deeper undertones of questioning the role of over-escapism and retreating too far into the fantasy worlds of film, it's mostly just a parody. This is Discworld after all. There are a lot of new interesting characters - I enjoyed Victor's scheming to be a lifelong student, I enjoyed Ginger's cynicism, and both the type-casting issues and romantic advances of the trolls (romancing of the stones?). The only one I didn't really click with was Gaspode, and that might've just been me since I can't put a hard finger down on why exactly. C.M.O.T. Dibbler's involvement fit perfectly in the role he stepped into, the Bursar and Arch-chancellor make a great comedic duo as always, and the Librarian was great - particularly the reverse King Kong business that goes down at the finale. It's fascinating to me that in a book that isn't really about them, Ridcully and Stibbens pop up here in essentially their first roles to then go on to be major players - and really interesting characters - in their own rights in later books. They were a bright spot here, but one that I think you would appreciate more if you had actually read their other later books first, rather than getting them in the 'proper' order. All in all, like the pop-up on the stars there says, I thought it was okay. I enjoyed it, but not a ton. I didn't dislike it, but it wasn't all that great either. In my opinion all Pratchett books are better than average, but among all those other better than average books, this one just fell a little flat for me.

My Southern Lit professor suggested Sherman Alexie's The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian way back during my sophomore year of college. I put off reading it, afraid that - like so many other highly-recommended books - it would fall short of the hype. Five years later I picked it up looking for that ever-elusive well-written YA novel. It did not disappoint! Alexie's protagonist - Junior - is an earnest character that gives the reader a pragmatic and sometimes desperate view of life "on the rez". There is no grand narrative here, and it's no The Catcher in the Rye; you won't find prolonged periods of reflection or pages where the narrator waxes poetic about the plight of Native Indians. Junior does not - and should not - have the capacity to truly grapple with the alcoholism, depression and poverty that is endemic to his reservation. Junior's reactions to death, violence and other Big Issues seem authentic: he is a 14-year-old living in a world where these things are commonplace. It would be out of character if he suddenly launched into a monologue about institutionalized racism. The only criticism I have is that Junior's character progression once at Riordan seems "easy". Junior is viewed as an absolute loser by his peers at the onset of the novel. He is weak and weird, and is constantly bullied as a result. After a few months at Riordan, he is one of the most popular kids in school: a star basketball player dating the prettiest girl. This progression highlights the divide between life on Spokane and life at Riordan. It allows Alexie to paint a more nuanced picture of the racism and avoid the All Whites Suck narrative. However, it also seems to give credence to the idea that Native Indians perpetuate their circumstances. Life becomes so easy for Junior at Riordan: he experiences far less racism than I expected and succeeds easily. Meanwhile, everyone else remains on the reservation. Alexie touches on this briefly throughout the novel, but since this is a YA book and is thus limited in scope, he cannot explore it in the way the topic really deserves. I have not read his other works, but perhaps the complexity I am looking for can be found there. Overall, great book. I would definitely recommend it as an introduction to Native Indian issues for teenagers or young adults.

3.5/5 - At 400+ pages this is not a quick read, but it's a compelling mystery that doesn't leave you struggling to keep interest. French's lovely prose was unusual for this genre but I thought it worked. Rob Ryan, a detective on the Dublin Murder Squad, and his partner and best friend Cassie Maddox are assigned to the investigation of a twelve-year-old girl's murder. Katy's body, found near the woods on an archaeological dig site, seems to have appeared with no clues as to who her killer was. Ryan assures Cassie he can handle working on this case - for the time being, she's the only one aware there might be a conflict of interest. Over twenty years before, when he was a kid, Ryan had been playing in those same woods with two friends. He was found hours later in a panic, clawing a tree with blood on his shoes, but he was alone. His friends had disappeared, were never found, and he couldn't remember a thing. To avoid attention from this case as an adult, he uses his middle name (Adam being his first name) and his superiors don't realize until later he's working a case with possible connections to his own. Cassie and Ryan struggle to find a lead. They question Katy's family, the workers of the dig, they both have their suspicions and assurances of innocence even while feeling local political pressure to get this case solved. Through it all, Ryan secretly hopes - and dreads - that Katy's case is related to his own and that he will find answers. He struggles to remember events he has blocked out for twenty years, but for every clue they gain, they hit a dead end and get more and more frustrated. Finally, when visiting the archaeological dig where Katy was found, Ryan comes to a sudden moment of realization and the mystery begins to unravel. Ryan and Cassie's relationship has become strained by this point, but they work together to solve the murder before drifting apart. The best part of this novel was Cassie and Ryan's relationship. I was considerably less interested after they had a best-friend-breakup-fight. Ryan was THE biggest baby in that whole thing and I was so frustrated with how he handled both his work and personal relationships with her. He overreacted to one incident big time and all I wanted was for him to grow up, be an adult about it, and realize he didn't need to push Cassie away. At the end of the novel, Ryan told the reader "She fooled you too," speaking of [insert character who will remain nameless so I don't spoil too much]. I was already irritated with him over Cassie at that point, so when I read that I rolled my eyes. I hadn't trusted this character from the start and I knew something was up with her, though I didn't predict exactly what it was. She was dramatic, flirty, and obvious in her need for attention. Maybe I'm supposed to assume that Ryan fell for her act because he's a man, but I really hope male detectives out there in the world aren't that easily fooled. This doesn't mean I didn't find Ryan a compelling or believable character, though. The novel's pace was solid, except for about 50 pages near the end. It started dragging and even though I intended to see the story through I got a little bored, right before the part where the mystery (well, part of it) was solved. That Ah-ha! moment seemed to come about way too easily, when I read the ending I was confused about how they didn't at least investigate this particular location more thoroughly at the beginning. Overall, French's story was intriguing and I'll probably give her work another go at some point. I'm still curious about what happened to young Rob Ryan (although I'm not sure he's a character in her next novels, I believe they all stand alone).

Oh my goodness. This...I'm speechless. I have no words to write about how wonderful this is. It's one of the most magical books I've ever read. Where to start? I liked this better than  Where the Mountain Meets the Moon, believe it or not. And let me tell you, I love that book. But this is even better! If I could give this 6 stars instead of a mere 5, I'd do it in a heartbeat. I loved everyone so much: Rendi, Peiyi, Mr. Shen, Master Chao...but Madame Cheng especially. They felt so realistic, and I could identify with every single one of them. They felt like my friends, and that rarely happens to me when I read, even if a book is great and I really like the characters. I'm not kidding you, they seriously felt like my friends. I cried when they cried, I cried when they felt alone, I cried during their letdowns and disappointments (especially sweet little Peiyi's! Oh my word tHE TEARSSSS), I cried when Madame Cheng comforted them during that time of sadness with the phrase, "Every night of your life, I will be there for you." I cried when they felt joy. I'M VERY EMOTIONAL, OK? *clears throat and grabs Kleenex* If anyone knows how to connect the reader with characters, Grace Lin is one of those people. It takes pure talent to do that. Bless you, Grace Lin. To say you're a brilliant writer is an understatement. Like WTMMTM, the story is delightfully unpredictable. Just when I thought I had something figured out, the story surprised me with something I wouldn't have guessed. However, I figured out Madame Cheng was the Moon Lady by chapter 38. The book has 45 chapters. Took me long enough lol. The pacing was perfect, the plot was perfect, the little stories told throughout were perfect... Shall I go on? Can I just take a moment to comment on how much I ADORED the whole Moon Lady thing? One of my favorite childhood books was  The Moon Lady. (Highly recommended if you like books like this!) I've always thought the concept of the Moon Lady was fascinating and mysterious, so I really loved reading more about the Moon Lady here and finding out more about her. While I do still love The Moon Lady, you don't know a lot about her other than she grants secret wishes, was separated from her husband, and seems to like helping lost children find their way home. In this, you get a wonderful picture of her personality, and you actually grow to love HER, as a person. I just loved it so very much. To summarize this whole thing into a few short sentences, I give this book 6 out of 5, and I cried. I cried a lot. As soon as I closed the book and picked up my phone to write this, I had an all-consuming desire to read it again!

A-/B+ As a Kindle freebie, I didn't have high expectations for this book, and so I was happy to be pleasantly surprised at its quality Thoroughbreds and Trailer Trash is a solid contemporary romance with well-developed characters, an interesting layered plot, and complex character interactions. It's funny, poignant and honest. The characters are flawed and sometimes make decisions I don't agree with, but those decisions were always "in character" and therefor understandable. There wasn't too much internal musing by the characters, and the dialogues sounded natural. I was honestly impressed by the complexity of the plot and the characters. Unfortunately, I think the very end is weak, and was the only time characters seem to act out-of-character. I do not think Burke would have ducked Jenna's calls like that. And the whole "mail carrier" thing was silly. Very rom-com movie. But overall this is a winner! and I've already downloaded another of Pettersen's books.

Guys. This is so hard. I want to love this book. I really do. But I just can't. Half the time I read it I was enjoying it and the other half I was squirming in my seat. Which is why I've settled on a 3 rating as I flipped back and forth between 2 and 4 stars. Why did I flop so hard between these ratings? Because this book had nuggets of genius but also flopped a lot from overkill to underwhelming. It's unfortunate because I think this book had the power to be the best book in the series but for me it isn't because of some writing choices. But first! Let's talk about what I did like: Lucien. Lucien stole the show for me. His character development was the most interesting in my opinion and it's unfortunate he sort of slips from the story about halfway through. Realistic portrayals of a traumatized or abused person. This was my favorite aspects of ACOMAF and it carried over into this book. PTSD is real. Abusive relationships, whether physically, verbally or emotionally, stay with people, leave them feeling broken. I will always appreciate that this series took lengths to show that. And also show that you can put yourself back together again. Nesta and Cassian. I ship it. More of the other courts. I was happy we got to see the rest of the High Lords and travel to new places. The political maneuverings were interesting. Some more background on Amren, The Bone Carver, and the Weaver. Even if it's all pretty ambiguous. Despite a lot of things I disliked about the book, I still have to give the author props. I read the whole thing in one sitting. There's no doubt that she's a talented storyteller. Now onto what I didn't like. Just fair warning, it's a much larger list. And general spoilers ahead. Bigger or more specific ones will be blacked out. If you love this book or Sarah J. Maas, you may not want to continue. This is not a personal attack on anyone. You can like what you like. But these aspects of the story didn't work for me. And without further ado, here are my unpopular opinions haha. For all the stuff going on a lot of things still boil down to the love confusion between Rhys/Feyre/Tamlin. A certain meeting for instance that started off awesome quickly turned into a Rhys/Feyre/Tamlin drama fest and it all became quite childish. The problem I've always had with this series is that the romance elements always seem to overshadow everything else. Overuse of ellipses. Like what the heck? Was it this bad in every book and I just didn't notice? I don't think a single page didn't have one and it distracted me. One page I seriously counted 9 of them. These should be used sparingly in my not so humble opinion otherwise they lose all impact. And while I'm nitpicking on this, I also spotted 2 typos. The villains are not compelling. The King of Hybern isn't scary or a strong presence. Tamlin is childish and still makes everything about Feyre. The Queens are absent through the story. And Jurian's role is undermind. Lots and lots of unnecessary hanky pank. Seriously these scenes just make me roll my eyes and want to throw up. They're not steamy as much as ridiculous and there is less emotional weight to them at this point in the story. We get it. Feyre and Rhysand like to have sex. At this point it just comes off as fan fictiony and makes their relationship seem shallow to me as it's the majority of the action between the two of them. As opposed to the last book when they actually did stuff. Like Rhysand teaching Feyre to read. Overuse of deus ex machina. I felt that there was a lot of this going on. More so than the other books. Powerful characters show up at the most convenient times, magic is doing stuff it had never done before. It was just all over the place. This story borrows a lot of lines from other beloved stories and popular fandoms. "Like calls to like." "Always." "I am yours and you are mine." "Even the most unlikely person can change the course of the future." I don't know quite how to explain this one so bear with me. The author seems to have a pretty single view of what a strong female character should be: sassy, bold, flippant, and prone to making vulgar gestures. Now I am not saying it's bad to be those things but I feel like in every Sarah J. Maas book the strong females are the same. They are also portrayed as the most desirable, the pinnacles of perfection; Feyre, Morrigan, Amren, they're all fairly similar and don't even get me started on Caleana Sardothien. Their flaws are generally romanticized, even when they're chucking books at people's heads. The other females with softer or more lady like personalities are portrayed as lesser and are more prone to being criticized. Being a soft female fae in this world can basically reduce you to being property of a male. Elain's softeness basically reduces her to a crazed damsel in distress. Nesta is viewed as strong but also as prudish, cold, and unapproachable. Not many of the main characters have positive things to say about her. Ianthe is a villain with no redeeming qualities. Something about it just rubs me the wrong way. I guess I just wish authors would branch out in their definitions of what a strong/desirable female character is. Rhysand. Sigh. I adore Rhysand so this is painful to write, but I think Sarah J. Maas loves Rhysand a little too much. I felt in this book Rhysand transformed from the tragic and roguish hero into a martyred saint who can do no wrong and gets a gold star for everything he does. Feyre basically supports all his actions, he is always justified, and both Feyre and the author constantly goes out of their way to tell us how wonderful he is over and over. I felt like his role in the previous books were so dynamic where in this book it's very one note for me. His portrayal felt like less of a real person to me in this book and more like a sexual fantasy. I just don't really enjoy 700 pages of swooning. Which brings me to the thing I really cannot stand the most: the author is way too enamored with her own characters to ever put them in peril. And boy did she have me fooled between these three books. Shame on me. I suppose I should've seen it coming with Feyre's resurrection in the first book but with the set up of ACOMAF I totally didn't. I thought for sure someone was gonna die. But alas, nay. This book reminded me a lot of Breaking Dawn in the Twilight series actually. They both set you up for death and gore in one final ultimate battle only for both to end in sunshine and rainbows  with allies conveniently appearing right and left when all seems lost. It's bothersome to me because I felt that this book so desperately wanted to portray the realities of war. It told us over and over again how destructive and harrowing war is. And yet, while all of our characters go forward to sacrifice themselves bravely for the cause, they all are miraculously saved. Not one but two characters are essentially brought back to life. If an author wants me to take their portrayal of war and death seriously, then they have to be willing to kill their darlings. And last but not least, we have a never-ending ending. You know the kind where the book was over 20 pages ago and yet it keeps going. I felt like I was sitting through the last 40 minutes of Peter Jackson's Return of the King. I think Sarah J. Maas and I just need to break up. Again, I have no doubt at her innate talent at story telling. But as much as I try really hard to make it work and want to enjoy her writing, something about her books just aren't for me. I have basically DNFed the Throne of Glass series. While I enjoyed ACOTAR and gave it a high rating, something about it put me off. I loved ACOMAF and still love Mr. Rhysand but now I just don't know if I can continue reading these books. I do not find these characters as compelling as I did nor do I believe any of these characters are ever going to be in real danger. If I read the next book, it is purely to see where Nesta, Elain, and Lucien go. First Response Upon Book Completion: I don't even know how to rate this. Part of me wants to give it a 4 and the other a 1. Some of it I really loved, parts of it I really hated. And I can't even begin to count the amount of times I rolled my eyes, and yet I read the whole thing I one sitting. I need some time to sort myself out. Review to come. We'll see about a rating.

Perhaps 4.5 stars would be more accurate, but a high rating is warranted by the fact that I felt so compelled to keep reading straight through the book and that I now feel slightly bereft, knowing that I've reached the end of what has been published in this series to date. Who knows how long we will have to wait for the next installment to be ready? We learned long ago that no character is safe, but I was a little shocked by one (apparent) death in the final chapters. (No spoilers here!) It would seem to leave us without an important point of view on the unfolding events. Disappointed not to have many chapters from Arya's point of view, but I suppose I should be pleased that she hadn't met some gruesome death by the end. Will just have to hope for a bigger role next time. With a series as sprawling as this, it can be hard to keep track of all the characters and events that have preceded the current volume. I heartily endorse the excellent wiki at westeros.org for timely reminders of where exactly you last saw what character and what they were doing at the time. Ready for the next one now please, George!

I'm currently a jumble of thoughts and the most prominent one is... wow. When Clara leaves her old life behind, it's to escape Christian--who is quite literally crazy about Clara. He calls her, texts her, and e-mails her too. Finally, her father decides that enough is enough and along with Clara they escape their old life and start anew at a seaside town. There, she meets Finn who is the opposite of Christian. He's confident and she doesn't have to worry about what not to say around him. Things take a turn when Christian contacts Clara again and she'll be forced to confront him one last time. Where do I begin? Most of the time, I loved Clara's character and I felt like I could identify with her--not due to Christian, but due to her shy nature. However, there were times in which she annoyed me (namely when she gave in to Christian and tried not to "hurt his feelings"). Christian and Finn were as different as night and day and to be honest, I loved watching Clara and Finn's relationship evolve. Then, on a minor note, there was Chloe (Finn's sister) whom I loved as well as her seagull stalker. Yes, you heard me right, she has a seagull that follows her to work and home again--whom she named Gulliver. Deb Caletti has done a wonderful job with Clara's voice and she's created a great cast of characters in Stay. If contemporary (YA) romance is your particular cup of tea--or if the plot has you intrigued--I'd definitely suggest picking up a copy of Stay to read. I feel like I should mention that although my review focuses on the main plot, it is not the plot in its entirety--however, I feel that I shouldn't give too much away and so I shall say no more than that.

On the subject I couldn't help but wonder what I would do with so little time... I'm as lost as I was when I was 18 trying to decide wether I should study chemistry or sea animals. (done neither) And we so should consider the excellent characters DeStefano created. Rhine (the leading)is the one trying to escape at all expense, 'cause the situation and marriage it's not "real". Jenna  is dead inside and she might as well go in style. Cecily (the brat)knew no better,so she's ready to believe anything and do anything to remain exactly where she is. The top one is where are we going with so much genetic engineering not only in humans but plants and animals that end up in our system anyway. But there are so many more. After an endless wait for the audio version of this book to come to my library, I finally gave up and just ordered it from Amazon. It was money well spent. This is a wonderful book. I listen to virtually all the books I read. That said, I get to hear voice actors and narrators do all the accents that would otherwise bother me if I were to read them in print. This is the case here. Once in awhile you get a boring narrator - but for the most part, books like this are even better coming from a voice actor. So on to the actual story - I was never bored, not for a second. I loved Saba - she frustrated me at times, scared me at others. But overall, I loved her. She was so fierce and brave and vulnerable - and just like a real person would be in some situations. She was awkward at times. She'd be self-assured and then doubt herself and get embarrassed and react with anger. She's a kick-ass heroine. I like her. I hated the bad guys, I was filled with dread when she  was captured and had her head shaved  . The Free Hawks - I didn't love them, but I didn't have to love them. They did their job as far as the plot goes. I loved Jack. The end. This is every bit the great read that everyone has said it is. You will have a blast with it.

Mercy is recovering from the events of book 3. She finds herself closer than ever to Adam, the alpha over the back fence but the pack aren't keen on a coyote shifter being his mate. She's still friendly with her house mate Samuel, but now she's front page news everyone shows up to either commiserate (which she can't deal with) or to ask her for something. High on that list is Amber, her old college friend. Amber says her house is haunted; can Mercy come investigate? Marsilia, the local Vampire Queen, sends Stefan as the equivalent of a vampire hand grenade - starved and desperate for blood - but the pack are there to stick their arms in his mouth instead of Mercy whom he would have drained in his desperation. Her mother shows up as well - always a fun time. Mercy needs a break from town - the vampires have literally painted a mark on her garage - so she takes Amber's job. I nearly DNF'd this book in five pages. It starts with the MC staring at herself in a mirror. Really? And then the big story line is that she's recovering from a rape. I swear, I threw it away. Today it was so hot I lay on my bed and read... So Mercy is a coyote shifter, a walker, can see ghosts, has some fae magic (a brownie stick keeps following her around), is blood bound to a vampire, gets blood bound to another, and is so attractive to werewolves that I assume she has had two alphas fighting over her for three books, and has finally chosen Adam. Oh, and she speaks Welsh. Although Adam made that decision for her by shoving part of his flesh down her throat while she was having a panic attack... without asking either her OR the pack. *frowns* Given she's supposed to be recovering from a rape days ago that seems a whole lot heavy handed. Especially when you get that he didn't know she was having a PTSD panic attack, but he thought she was under thrall by Stefan and Adam was staking his claim. *frowns harder* And really? With her wicked shifter and magic skills she didn't notice that Amber was dead? No heartbeat, no body warmth, no breathing, and she smelt dead... shake my head. That offer even stank before she noticed the dead people. And Mercy knew it. Why go? There was a lot here that just felt ... idk... too contrived. I mean... she explains to the deaf boy that the only way you can kill a vampire is with a stick, and OH... here's one now... I can't explain today. Maybe because I'm just so tired of rape being a story line for female MC's? Sighs... 2 stars

I liked two stories and the other three were just kind of meh. I knew I would like the In Death story (Taken in Death) - it is why I got the book. It was interesting to see Eve concentrating on finding kids alive instead of the dead. Good take on Hansel & Gretel. Beauty, Sleeping by Elaine Fox was intriguing. Definitely different than expected and enjoyed seeing it all come together. Stroke of Midnight by R.C. Ryan I really liked until the end. Cullen had to have the painting measured to make sure it was an exact match before he was willing to marry her? Love wasn't enough? And the whole keeping her in the dark was annoying. If Wishes Were Horses by Mary Blaney - I just didn't care about any of the characters. Although I must say I rarely read historicals. The Christmas Comet by Mary Kay McComas - I didn't like Natalie. She just seemed to only be concerned with helping others no matter the cost (be it safety or the law or anything else). ** spoiler alert ** The final book in the "Shades of Magic" trilogy was...incredible. I was worried because trilogies tend to fall flat on their faces by the third book, but Schwab stayed true to the characters and didn't slow down from page 1. So much happened in this book. Within the first 30 pages I thought we were already reaching the climax of the story. Not only were we holding on to our seats the whole way, we were given backgrounds of some of the characters. I thought it was an interesting choice of characters to provide this for, but it was actually very brilliant. It added more color and complexity to those characters, rather than just putting them in the "good" and "bad" categories, while also shedding some light on main characters of Kel and Lila, without actually giving their backgrounds. I thought the plot device of "we must find this magical object to stop the bad guy" was kind of lame at first, but it wasn't even about the object as much as it was the journey to get there and what they also found along the way. There were definite sacrifices in the book, which I can always appreciate when an author commits to a story rather than trying to make it all feel good in the end. Overall, great book, great series.

http://theprettygoodgatsby.wordpress.... Sometimes I need a push to read a book. Whether it's because I've had an iffy experience with the author/similar novels in the past or I simply have too much on my plate already, there have been numerous books widely loved that I just haven't managed to get to yet. Shadow and Bone is one of those novels. For over a year I've been hearing absolutely GLOWING reviews and the current buzz over the third (and final?! I HOPE NOT!) installment coming in the spring has brought this series to my attention once again. Earlier in December, I posted about Epic Recs, a book club of sorts founded by Judith and Amber. What makes this book club different is that you have a partner and you recommend books to each other. You can read more about it in my post - including what book I recommended to Lillian! As for Lillian, she wasted no time in recommending Shadow and Bone and I immediately grabbed a copy from my library. Russia (or, in this case, Russia-inspired), high fantasy, mythology - these are things that IMMEDIATELY appeal to me. I dove right in and, much to my delight, was not disappointed one bit! Shadow and Bone tells the story of Alina and Mal, two orphans who were taken in by a Duke and raised together. When they were children they were visited by Grisha, people who possess magical abilities. Every child in Ravka undergoes testing to determine Grisha talents, but neither Alina nor Mal presented abilities and that was it. Ten years later, however, things have changed. Mal is a tracker in the First Army and Alina is a passable mapmaker. On an expedition to the Shadow Fold, a darkness home to creatures seemingly plucked from nightmares, Alina risks her life to save Mal's and soon the entire kingdom hails the coming of their Sun Summoner. Suddenly Alina is thrown into the world of the Grisha, a world with magic, fine clothes, and people so utterly breathtaking they can't possibly be real (and I won't say anything further on that!). As a Sun Summoner Alina ranks among the most powerful Grisha - comparable to the Darkling, a man who has taken quite an interest in this once-ordinary girl. Alina's put to the test - physically, mentally, and emotionally. She's desperate for a friendly face, she misses the bond she shared with Mal, and struggles to perform her magic. The pressure of being Ravka's savior weighs heavy on her shoulders and the complete lack of word from Mal cuts deep. Could this pale, scrawny, lonely orphan really be the answer to Ravka's prayers? Could Alina truly be the person to banish the Fold? Just like with The Raven Boys, I dreaded the thought of writing a review for Shadow and Bone. I loved this book, absolutely ADORED it, and nothing I could possibly type could ever do it justice. Leigh Bardugo thoroughly won me over, not just with the Russian-esque setting, but with her gorgeous writing, fantastic characters, and beautiful story. I was completely enchanted and had to make the hard decision of reading the entire book in one go (I definitely didn't want to stop!) or take my time to live and breathe this world. Ultimately the latter choice won - though it was certainly a hard decision to make! - and I spent four glorious days immersed in the world of Grisha. It's extremely rare for me to jump right into the next book in a series, but my library currently has a copy of Siege and Storm and, well, I've never been very good at controlling temptation..

3.5 STARS. I don't read shape-shifter books (yet) or alien love stories (yet). Some readers' comments re Black Lies suggest suspending common sense when reading this book. The most far fetched part- is the ever used Gorgeous, hunky, genius billionaire. Don't say that this is the only book that does this BILLIONAIRE romance story (with a twist!) I really got into the story. It did drag in the middle- kind of stalled. The writing was OK but a couple of things pulled me out of the story: like the sun rising over the Pacific (?). Layana said that she was "scared of.." Wouldn't an upper class society girl say "afraid"? Little things. I don't want to be in a contest to see who figured out the secret first. Reading a book is a solitary thing- then I can talk about it later. I have to admit that I was tempted to stop reading, but my curiosity kept me going. This is fiction people! Novels, romance, fiction, fantasy- nothing to be ashamed of! I don't regret reading it. I enjoyed it...Before I read the book-- I was caught in the hype, the buzz. After reading Black Lies: Originality-- 4.5 IMHO. Good escape-reading. Maybe they can make a movie out of this & they can have midnight showings & we can throw toast at the movie screen ^_~ In other words, enjoy yourself.
Never stop fighting, but know when to fight.. and whom.

4 Stars Overall Opinion: This was better than I expected! I am always super hesitant to read any book that is so late in a series, and for some reason I get intimidated when I see something like "#8" in the title...but I'm glad I gave it a shot! It was full of fun love/hate witty banter that was perfect for what I was in the mood for. My biggest issue? Sex. They had such great tension and chemistry that I felt a big "waa waa" when we finally got to the super vague and non-descriptive sex scenes. This couple could've set my iPad on fire for the tension and chemistry they had! Too bad. Brief Summary of the Storyline:  This is Piper and Cooper's story. Piper is a private investigator, and they meet when she gets caught trailing Cooper. Cooper ends up hiring her to help with his club, and they start an odd friendship that is of the hate/love variety. There is someone sabotaging Cooper, some odd jobs Piper is caught up in, some strong and unwanted feelings being developed, and some past baggage they have to deal with...but they do get a HEA ending. POV: This alternated between focusing on Piper and Cooper in 3rd person narrative. Overall Pace of Story:  Good for the most part. It did take a little bit for me to get into the story, but when I did I had no further problems and I never skimmed. Instalove: No, more like a love-hate thing going on. H rating: 4 stars. Cooper. I liked him. He came off as a douchey kind of guy at first, but I came around to actually like that about him later on. h rating: 4 stars. Piper. I liked her strength and her sassiness, but I did want her to a little more open with the H. Sadness level: Low, no tissues needed Push/Pull: Yes  The h pushes away a good bit, and I would say the H is the main pursuer of the relationship. Heat level: Low. They have great tension and chemistry, but the scenes felt extremely lacking to me (probably because of the great tension and chemistry) Descriptive sex: Kind of. I wouldn't say it was full on fade-to-black, but it was really close in that it wasn't descriptive. OW/OM drama: Yes Both the h and H have people interested in them that causes some jealousy, but it was pretty mild. Sex scene with OW or OM: No Cheating:  No Separation: Yes They are separated shortly (~2 weeks), but there was no mention or suggestion of other partners during this time. Possible Triggers: Yes  Loss of parents (both h and H - off page), emotional abuse (h's dad to her - off page), slavery/trafficking (side character - on page), and violence/attempted murder (on page) Closure:  This had good closure with a cute epilogue and a HEA ending. How I got it: I got it on loan through my public library and Amazon. Safety: This one should be Safe for most safety gang readers - Does Not have cheating - Does Not have a descriptive sex scene with OW/OM -  Does have the h pushing the H away -  Does have a short separation between the h and H -  Does Not have abuse by mcs -  Does Not have OTT sad parts - Does  have a HEA ending

Jen gave me this lovely book for Christmas, and it was the perfect way to start off the reading year. You're likely to hear the 'timeless children's book' descriptor a lot, and with good reason. It's timeless in the sense that it's a non-specified date in the past (early 1900s? Later 1800s?) when women were not cellists and were not supposed to wear trousers, but when it also feels perfectly right for a delightful man like Charles to rescue a baby, take her home and raise her, without bothering either of them with stupid things like school. It's also timeless in that same way because it could be a Noel Streatfield if he got in a Nanny to help out. Mostly, though, it made me think of A Little Princess, with a very different sense of social justice: no romanticizing of the diamond mines into something out of The Arabian Nights; no meek and grateful poor children, and no patient suffering. Sophie is a wonderful character, the rooftoppers she meets are heartbreaking and yet so strong, and I fell head over heels with Charles. It's whimsical and funny, too, which I don't think of A Little Princess as being, and yet ... that rooftop feast, for hungry Matteo (and Sophie, though hers was a voluntary hunger! ), had the same emotional payoff as the one from the earlier book. My only concern was that a bit of me wanted the ending tied up with a series of weatherproof (and not from pigeon fat) bows. So. There is now an epilogue in which Sophie's mother produces her birth cert, thereby clearing Charles, his scholarly work can be done perfectly well in Paris, and they set up a proper home for all the children together - one so free and with such perfect access to the rooftops that even Matteo feels safe there. I will not countenance Charles going back to London alone.

MY OPINION: ***** So this book was meh at first and then OOH by the end. I loved it. Anyways, this book was about a girl named Ellie; honestly, I completely forgot that was her name until someone said it, which was pretty rare. Ellie is the stepdaughter of a TV star and she's used to people trying to be her friend just for the sake of saying that they met her stepdad, etc. But her two best friends are home and she feels pretty good. She is in her senior year and she's ready to apply to colleges. She has one college in mind, though she could have made it into an Ivy League college. She has a tutor, George, who I basically adored from the start. Except for his name. Honestly, I don't have anything against the name George but there is someone at my school with the name George that I can't stand and when I read about a character named George, my mental image of that character is that kid at school. So basically, I loved the ending. The ending was really beautiful and romantic and amazing. But the beginning and about the first half of the middle was either very rushed or very slow... What I didn't like about this book was the fact that Ellie was so self-centered and spoiled. I completely agree with George! 4.5 "Elly May & Lawn bum are fantastic" Stars I don't know why I'm surprised since the last time I read a Kristen Callihan book I loved it, but I didn't expect to fall this hard for Idol, the first book in her VIP series. The thing is, I didn't only fall in love with the two main characters... I want more of the world Kristen created and all the characters in it. I'm dying for Mr. Scott's story (coming next). For Brenna and Rye's story. Jax, OMG, Jax's story is going to be phenomenal, I can already tell. I want them all. So, yeah... this book and this VIP world won me over. In a way, Idol reminded me of a rock-star-falls-for-normal-girl book I read a while ago called A Million Miles Away by Elizabeth Corva (a series that definitely deserves more attention). Like AMMA, Idol felt legit. I could relate to the music/celebrity world Kristen explored. I could understand the problems that she presented. I felt the pain the characters were dealing with. I understood what was happening and could get behind it because everything made sense. It may not look like it, but making the famous/celebrity world real in books isn't an easy task. It's too easy to dive into cliches, but I didn't feel like Kristen did that at all. But yeah, the main star hear is the romance, as it's supposed to be. The love story between Liberty, a.k.a Libby or Libs (a recluse living on her own after her parent's death), and Killian (the lead singer of the bigger rock band in the world who's broken because of his closest friend's suicide attempt) is so perfect and beautiful and raw you won't be able to look away until you read the last page. Don't worry, you'll get your well-deserved HEA. Before you get there, though, you'll get to meet these two amazing people. Learn about what makes them special--their kind hearts and love for music. Watch them rediscover their passion for life after tragedy took or almost took the people they loved away. Fall in love with them as they fall for each other. Hurt when life throws them apart. Keep your fingers crossed that they come together sooner than later. Well, I felt everything, and I blame it on Kristen's writing! The characters were so ridiculously relatable that I didn't even know what to do with myself as I fell hard for them. They were flawed, but so good on the inside that I couldn't help but love them no matter what. They had a great sense of loyalty and an even better sense of humor. The freaking chemistry when they were together? Ha. Just ridiculous. And don't get me started on the pacing. In this book, it was close to perfect. Everything happened as it was supposed to. Nothing felt rushed. Nothing dragged. In fact, I didn't want it to end. I wanted more and more, and that teaser with Mr. Scott's story was pure torture because I'm on hold on the library and the line to get this book is so stupidly long. *cries* Speaking of crying, while Idol didn't bring tears of sadness, it brought some of joy because this book was so freaking funny. Libs and Killian had the best chemistry--not just sexually, but that, too--and that means we got some pretty spectacular moments with them interacting, teasing each other and making me laugh. I can stress enough how great this book was. Just go read it, please. Then come thank me later. Meanwhile, I'll be here, slowly dying until I can get my hands on Managed, the second book in the series, featuring too-hot-for-this-world Mr. Scott. Can someone wake me up when I'm next in line?

4 STARS FOR "APPRENTICE" BY RACHEL E. CARTER "I told you not to trust a wolf," he continued. His words dripped like honeyed venom. "Because it would only ever want to break you." Darren let out a small, harsh laugh. "Haven't you figured it out yet? I'm the wolf, Ryiah. I guess what I really should have told you was to never trust a prince, but that's not quite as memorable." What's that I hear? Oh, sounds like Darren swooping in and capturing my heart once again! Seriously, I get really gushy when it comes to these books. It's only two books into a four part series, but I get really excited about its characters and the characters found within it. While sequels usually fall short to its predecessor, Apprentice held its own and was pretty darn great. I got to see more sides to the characters as they continue along in their apprenticeship. Since they've all grown since their first year at the Academy, it was really nice to see the developments made because of their previous experiences. Alex really matured in his approach to a potential relationship with Ella, realizing that he would just have to man up and stop playing the jealousy game if he wants to be with her. It may have worked to push Ella to realize her feelings for him, but it won't prevent pushing her away once she's done so. I could also tell the subtle changes that Ryiah goes through as the story progresses. It really hit me how far she's come already when she was an important piece in all the mock battle plannings. Whether it was her as an important piece in their plans, or her coming up with the plans themselves, she was putting herself forward with a ton more confidence than she had in the beginning of the series. She's a lot more comfortable and confident with her abilities, even if she still has a lot more work to do to impress her Combat master. And seeing Ryiah's friendship with Darren? Them teaming up instead of always antagonizing each other? Darren admitting that she's been his first ever true friend? Darren growing up and taking responsibility for when he hurts his friends - whether he meant to or not? DARREN COMING TO TERMS WITH HIS FEELINGS FOR RYIAH? I love Darren so much, y'all. He definitely had those moments in this book where I was like "yikes, don't make me revoke my Darren-fanclub membership" but he shows so much growth! We see him really valuing Ryiah as a friend and individual, not just as a potential girlfriend. And he's so much more open about his friendship with her, too. He knows she can defend herself against Priscilla, but I loved those moments where he'd show his protectiveness and tell Priscilla to back off. I had the pleasure of seeing the raven-haired beauty turn an unattractive shade of red. "I-I'll tell Byron she attacked me!" "Priscilla." Darren's patience was growing thin. "If you do I will tell him the truth... We may be betrothed but Ryiah is my friend. I try to stay out of your disagreements, but if you do this I will take her side. I just really liked those small moments of protectiveness, where he wasn't afraid to claim her as someone important to him. And one of my absolute favourite parts of the whole book was when he took the blame for hurting Ryiah, even if his intentions (well, most of them) were good and battle-focused: "-And while I know I was right, I still find myself thinking I was wrong. Because of you, Ryiah." His gaze fell away and he was staring at the back of his hands. "I hurt you by hurting him, and for that I'm sorry." And their chemistry. His endearing cockiness in knowing exactly how she feels about him, even if she's not willing to admit it aloud. Like when Darren casts his lightning by imagining their kiss? And while he was willing to fight for her, I did like that he backed off a bit when she "chose" (and I put that in quotations because I think we all knew her true choice was with Darren) Ian. I loved that Darren was just so open in general to her, that he showed her more of his life back home and introducing her to the people he knew he could trust with their secret. And while I always knew deep down that Darren would never just give up on their HEA despite the obstacles thrown their way, I cheered Ry on when she said that she would never be Darren's mistress. It was either his heart and attention fully, or nothing. As much as she loved Darren, she wasn't going to live the rest of her life knowing he was married to Priscilla. You go girl! And while I despise love triangles, and I found it a little odd that both guys were so willing to stick around when there was another guy in the picture, I loved both men involved. Ry and Darren belong together, but even I felt bad for Ian in the end. He was sweet and funny. There was no question why Ry liked him at first. Ry really did end up doing him dirty, being with him when she knew deep down she still loved Darren. While the flip-flopping did bother and irritate me a bit, I understand that it was an important piece to Ry's individual journey and deciding what she wanted for herself and her life. I was worried that Ry would just jump back into it with Ian once Darren broke it off with her, but I was pleasantly surprised to find them coming to a mature decision to acknowledge their mistakes and how they've hurt each other. Let's cross our fingers that they work it out and become friends again. I think they would be really cute as friends only. I didn't really get a lot of payoff when Ry and Darren got back together in the end, but I'm willing to forgive it since I know we'll get another whole book of them finally being a couple. Thankfully the love triangle issue is over and done with now too. Their feelings for each other are out there. They're solid. Let's just continue with that, please. (Can you tell I've been burned before with love triangles in YA?) Other quick thoughts: - I liked that Darren and Ry's bickering affected the people around them. When Eve was elected because Ry and Darren couldn't stop arguing? Perfect. - Darren's brother needs to get his karma. I don't like him having to be around Ry, either. He's a gross person. - Speaking of gross, does anyone other than Alex know how Ry discovered her power? - Who else did Ry do dirty? Ian's girlfriend. Asking him to dance when she was right there? Not cool, girl, not cool. - Chapter twelve in Darren's bedroom. Swoon. - The Ry and Darren shipper in me is screaming, but I did appreciate that Darren was prioritizing his country above his romance with her. It showed maturity, even if it was at the expense of our (and their!) hearts. - I loved Priscilla and Ry teaming up even if for just a second and to cover their own butts in a mock battle.

I could clearly see throughout the book how Alex was struggling with the loss of Caleb, death of the Pure guard on her hands, Seth's growing uncaring manner and everything else in her crazy life as the second Apollyon. Which made me want to give her big bear hugs. Her choices in Deity were also much more reasonable than those she made before. Now, this is the part where I start fangirling and if you have not read Deity & don't want a spoiler, skip the part below please. AIDEX HAPPENED. IT FREAKING HAPPENED. AHHHH!! Ok, I'm better now. Anyway, as for the romance in the story... lets just leave it as me being very happy with the way things turned out. Does that count as a spoiler? Nevermind. So I finally got around to reading this, a few years after the rest of the world. Early in the book, I described it as a compulsive read, and that opinion stayed until the end. If you were to graph it in terms of intensity, it stays pretty high up on the chart the whole time, so it's hard to find the right point to finish up reading for a while and put it down. I very much admire authors who can do this, and I think this is a very clever book. I don't know that I liked it an enormous amount, but I enjoyed the escapist experience of reading it, just as I do with authors like Dan Brown. I think my opinions are necessarily clouded by the fact that I did read this long after it was all over everything and therefore I don't know whether I would have predicted so much about the plot if I hadn't already known that the book was full of twists. I thought Amy's diary was fake from very early in the piece and knew Nick was cheating and she was setting him up. But, as I said, I was expecting twists, so I was probably looking for them. On the downside, I hated almost every character in the book. I liked Go, and I appreciated Boney, and that was it. The rest of them are loathsome. "The only way to clamp down on my energy is to erase my emotions, and so I them each away, one by one. My sorrow turns to anger, then ice-cold fury. My soul curls in on itself in defense. I am gone. I am truly gone. I am not sorry." Can I get a fuck yeah? Reading this was an entertaining ride. It wasn't full-blown perfection or anything, far from it, but it explores how a character may choose to veer off the path of goodness. Most of all, it was fun. In The Young Elites, Marie Lu creates a world where malfettos, survivors of the blood fever who are marked with imperfections, are considered to be abominations. Amongst these malfettos, there are those who inherited powers as an effect of the blood fever and they are known as the elites. Adelina Amouteru is one of them. Sentenced to death for committing a crime, she was saved by a band of elites known as The Dagger Society, who intend to recruit Adelina and her powers into their fold for a larger mission. Sick of being banished and treated like worthless defects, the elites wish to take over the kingdom and establish a better world for malfettos. Can Adelina help them or does her power have other things in store for her? For once, we have a character who chooses to go down that dark path instead of fighting it. I've been so sick of characters who choose to stay on that honourable path just because it's "right". At first, I was a bit sceptical about Adelina's character. At the beginning, she's often scared and confused about the darkness that dwells within her while toeing the line between good and bad. I just wasn't convinced about her past to consider it be dark or whatever. But after going through the tribulations since her recruitment into the Daggers, I finally see it. I see how she finally welcomes the darkness with open arms and this time, I was won over by her motivations and started rooting for it. One of the things I loved about this is how there were barely any good or righteous characters. There were no saints, no heroes, no martyrs. There is certainly none of that "good trumps evil" bullshit that most typical stories seem to shove into our throats. Anything goes here. We have other characters like Enzo Valenciano who is bent on seizing the throne after being stripped of his birthright, and Teren Santoro who is on some quest of his own to wipe the kingdom clean of malfettos because he believes that that is his calling by God. And do they use the "right" way to get what they want? Fuck no. Plot-wise, I can say that it was enjoyable (it was unputdownable) although it did get a bit trope-y at certain parts. Things did heat up towards the end and I was actually caught by surprise when Enzo was killed off. Provided he doesn't get revived in the next book . It was great. I like it when the author doesn't take the safe route when it comes to storytelling. It keeps things unpredictable and fresh. Overall, an exciting first installment to what could potentially be a spectacular series about the making of a villain. I hope the author was just scratching the surface of Adelina's character because I'd be down for some more darkness wherever it's at.

I had to read this for school, and for my first Margaret Atwood novel, it was pretty good. Summary of the Story Snowman is the last human left alive on earth, with only a new species of humans called the "Crakers" for company. Told in alternating snippets of flashbacks and the present, we find out about the the futuristic world in which Snowman used to live, and what exactly led to his current predicament. Snowman was called Jimmy originally, and he lived with his parents in a community of scientists. In this world, science is highly valued and the arts have little relevance (much like our own society unfortunately, if you ask me). Jimmy's father is involved in a project where pigs are given parts of human DNA to make them larger and grow additional organs, which are called Pigoons. Other genetically modified animals are the rakunk (domesticated raccoon-skunks that make ideal pets) and the snat (rat snake -- and you think the animals we have are scary???? His mother starts to think the work they're doing is wrong and flees, and later in Jimmy's life he finds out she was executed for her protesting. He meets Crake, who's real name is Glenn, in high school. They become best friends, playing video games like Exthinctathon and watching the many kiddie porn and murder sites available to them. That's when Jimmy first sees Oryx, on a porn website. He instantly feels connected to her, and when he meets her -- or the woman he believes to have been the child from the video -- he is in love. Jimmy and Crake go their separate ways in University, but Crake invites him to start working for him years later. He is working on many projects, including the creation of a new human species called the "Crakers," who are all beautiful, come in different colours, and only eat foliage. Crake is also developing a pill for increased sexual pleasure which secretly renders its takers infertile, to help with overpopulation. But really, the pill actually starts a plague that kills the entire world. Jimmy realizes too late, and Oryx has just left to pick up their food. Crake calls, promising to arrive back at the lab soon. When he does, he brings Oryx with him, slits her throat, and is shot by Jimmy, who understands Crake wanted to die too, leaving Jimmy to take care of the "Crakers." Back in the present, Snowman arrives back from his journey in search for food and supplies, and finds the "Crakers" singing his name, awaiting his return. When he gets back, they tell him they saw three people who looked like Snowman. He isn't the last human alive. What I Thought This book was a surprisingly easy read. I mean, the ideas are so complex and well thought out, it just caught me off guard that the vocabulary would be so simple. My only specific comment would be that the only moment I found myself actually feeling any sort of emotion other than Crake and Oryx dying, was when Jimmy's mom wrote in the letter that she took Killer (Jimmy's pet rakunk) with her. I just kept thinking how if my mom ran away and took my pet with her I would hunt her down to the ends of the earth to get it back, because that is so uncool! I loved how Jimmy felt the same way too. He didn't really care much for his mother, so he read the letter and was just like, "HOW DARE YOU STEAL KILLER!" I will eventually get around to reading the other two books in the trilogy, but probably not anytime soon.

I really enjoyed the characters (two sisters as major characters, the fantastic Lightsong, and quirky forces all around them), plot (and twists), background, history and most of the book. The only thing that made me like this less than The Emperor's Soul (the first Sanderson I read), was the magic system. The way it was introduced and used was a little too system-y for my liking. I did like the creativity required to use it in action, and the discussions/theorizing about how things developed historically. But this would all make for very good and clear RPG rules. When I was younger I probably would have loved that aspect, but I found The Emperor's Soul far more elegant in every way. All that being said, I really enjoyed the book and applaud the author for the amazing window he provided into his creative process with how he released it in the public view from the early stages. And my respect for him, and interest in reading more of his books, only grows.

This is great. I don't know why people sometimes label this as ugly and boring but seriously, it's not! I admire how Luce and Daniel's love went through different complicated things and then there's Cam. But I'm Team Daniel all the way

Before I get into why I disliked this book so much, I feel compelled to point out that the premise of the book is completely different than the summary listed on the back of the book. "Isleen Walker has long since given up hope of escape from the nightmare of captivity and torture that is draining her life, her mind, and her soul. Except...there is the man in her feverish dreams, a strangely beautiful man who beckons her to freedom. And when he comes, if he comes, it will take all their combined fury and faith to overcome a madman bent on fulfilling a deadly prophecy." In actuality, this plot line is resolved within probably the first 25-30 pages of the book. At this point, I'd try to give you an accurate summary of this book, but I honestly don't even know where to start, which maybe explains why the book's back doesn't even try. I guess it's about Isleen exploring her dreams about others, and being hunted by a killer, and the relationship between her and Xander. You know, I can handle paranormal/sci-fi/fantasy/supernatural, completely whacked out powers (in fact, the idea of being able to "hear" people's thoughts is pretty dang cool); I could even handle the really odd and random "mythology" that's just kind of thrown in there to somehow magically support everything. But what I absolutely could not get over in this book was the complete lack of humanity in the characters in this book. If you want to make a complete fantasy world, fine. Completely fantasy characters? Fine. But having human characters with fantasy emotions? Absolutely ridiculous. Isleen's held captive and tortured for eight years, and her biggest concern after she wakes up is that the man who rescued her and she's insanely attracted to is her uncle? She comes home three days after her rescue, and the first thing she wants to do is lose her virginity to a guy she just met (oh wait, they must "Once Upon a Dream", like Sleeping Beauty)? Even if you can get over the complete insta-love, there is NO WAY IN HELL a person who succumbed to years of torture like that comes out completely unaffected. Just...I can't...there are no words. Plus, then I read the author's bio and find out that she's a mental health therapist! If anyone should be familiar with real human emotions, it should be her. So frustrating. Really interesting premise with such potential, but just so unrealistic emotionally that it's just laughable and torturous to finish. Save yourself the frustration and stay away.

I struggled to get into this novel, assuming it would transform from "Girl from colonized India struggles to fit into proper society" (a bit like the Secret Garden but with soirees) but instead, it took a quick left turn and became a glorious Horatio Hornblower riff, complete with gritty details of ship life. The book suffers from two minor flaws. First, the authorial voice tries too "demmed" (or "d----d") hard to be cutesy and periodesque. Second, it is written quite politically as a lesson about anti-colonialism, both on Earth and Mars. This second bit bit into the story too much and was pretty heavy-handed, especially given the lack of honorable traits among any of the British and the ethical clarity of the Martians. Despite that, the heroine has a grand adventure. The world building was delightful. The notion of the airships and the Napoleonic threats encountered felt fresh. (More than the His Majesty's Dragons, which I also enjoyed.) But this best part was limited to the middle of the book and the two bookends that began and ended the story didn't live up to that marvelous center. I particularly hated the trope that the captain basically got injured (and later her brother)  so Arabella could take over the story. That's lazy writing. Her value and capabilities could have easily grown without the senseless mutiny  sequence. The French were a sufficient threat to carry the narrative without that. In summary: the middle part (the majority of the book really) was really really good. The two end bits that set up the adventure and then create a silly distraction to eliminate the cousin  and force Arabella's hand in marriage  did the book no favors. Four Goodread stars for the middle, two for the start and end, and bonus star credit for the magic and wonder of inter-planetary air ships and automata, no matter how ridiculous they look. Can't wait for the movie.
