"Finding a best friend is like finding a true love: when you meet yours, you just know." I thoroughly enjoyed this one. I had considerably low expectations for it- thinking it was going to be a re-hashed 13 Reasons Why or Dark Places. A lot of people went into this book expecting that- and for the first half, that's what it sounds like. Our main character, June, goes around asking the same questions after her enigmatic friend, Delia, commits suicide. Of course, a mystery opens up. But then....well, there's an exciting twist. I liked the first half- don't get me wrong-but I had read that kind of story before- many times. When the book came to a close, I was left with us a sense of contentment, strictly because the story had gone in a completely different direction. "The world is only as fair as you make it." I'll be frank here- this book is not about suicide. It's about what happens when friendship gets toxic- and how it can corrupt the relationships we have with each other and those we hold closest to us. June and her friend Delia's relationship- told in flashbacks throughout the novel- is the most interesting and complex part of the story. It's the sort of friendship that goes deep, to almost dangerous levels. However, their relationship suffers because Delia is not as well fleshed out. She is an enigma and not a real person. It's obvious that she's a girl made to consume all that she sets her eyes on- human affection, attention, hate, etc. but we never find out why. June, on the other hand, appears to be meek and mild but slowly develops a backbone. I wish that was explore more- because Delia is June's equal- and if Delia was crazy, June wasn't shouldn't have been that far behind. "The messed-up thing is how so many people think your body is their business, especially if you're a girl." I do not think this book was good because of it's writing style or because of the ending. I enjoyed this book because it had had so much potential. It went so many places and I wish there was a second book to see where everything left off. There was murder, rape, conspiracy, drugs, theft, animal-porn- it put Pretty Little Liars to shame. I suppose because it was a standalone it didn't come off as a campy romp through trope-land. I loved the rest of the "Suicide/Murder Squad"...I wanted to know more about Evan, Sebastian, and Ashling. I wish they were explored more. Sebastian and June's relationship should've been explored in greater depth and I wish Ashling had more nuance to her. She just came off as the crazy love-sick lesbian and that didn't seem right. I wanted to know where they would go next- despite their crazy nature and all. Would they rob a bank? Go to South America? Fix an election? Lord knows.... Overall, I really enjoyed this book. I felt like it had some really awesome moments and lived up to it's Gillian Flynn-esque nature. Sure, Delia and June needed fleshing out, but it was a worthwhile, enthralling read. If you do decide to read Suicide Notes from Beautiful Girls, I recommend you do it during the winter. It helps with the whole "atmosphere" of the novel.

Annalisa Townsend's father's ship was robbed by pirates one year ago. Anna was on board during the time and one of the pirate's stole something very, very valuable from her. .a kiss. Now Anna's father is in jail since he ship was very important to the king and she is very determined to find this nasty pirate who was the cause of her father's demise. So what would a strong young woman do? She would but a ship, forge a letter of marque to look for the pirate and then catch him. But when Anna tries to do all that, she gets much more than she bargained for. To Catch a Pirate was a great, fun read that I loved! When we meet Anna on the ship you immediately love her and I did. She was a headstrong, extremely brave and was good with a knife. She was one of the best characters and I think it would be cool if she was actually alive. Don't we all wish that characters from books were alive?. .especially the boys! The pirate, James Sterling was great too and I think he and Anna were a great match, even though neither really wanted to admit that! The plot was good and full of action and adventure and the characters really spiced things up a lot. I mean who wouldn't love a book that had pirates and was historical fiction!!? I love books like this one! I especially liked the ending and I thought it was a perfect ending to the story! I wish there was a sequel but sadly I don't think there will ever be! Also Jade Parker is a pen name, I think that authors real name is Rachael Hawthorne! Go check it out and on the way pick up this book!

I held off reading this for a long time because the name of the book coupled with the cover of a sweet young man made me think this was about a couple who come together because they both really care about a developmentally disabled kid. Nope. This book had almost no substance. The plot was definitely an excuse for the romance. The promised thriller aspect was lame. The fact that the two have been in love and best friends for five years with Nic telling Lucas all the time that he doesn't care about the scars   and yet Lucas still has no self-esteem and thinks he is unattractive so he won't have a sexual relationship , is just ridiculous, especially when Nic sees pictures of Lucas's back This is my complete synopsis of the book in 20 short lines: Evil guy: I hate Lucas because I loved him. Nic: I love you Lucas. Lucas: Let's just be friends. Nic: I love you Lucas. Lucas: It can never be more. Evil guy: I will kill you Lucas and make you suffer. But I will hurt your boy first. Lucas: I love you Nic. Nic: I love you Lucas. Lucas: I love you, too, but we can't have more. Nic: I love you Lucas. Lucas: Okay. Let's fuck. Nic: I will go and leave you all alone so I can deal with what is most likely a distraction. Evil guy: Lucas you will now die. Lucas: No. Evil guy: Then I will hurt Nic. Lucas: No. Lame fight scene. Nic: I love you Lucas. Lucas: I love you, too.

enjoyed this. at times the characters could be frustrating, but/yet they were consistent in word and action. sometimes the prose was a little dramatic, but it was a very dramatic time so again - it fit.

Based on Pride and Prejudice.. and since we can never really get enough of Bride and Prejudice.. it's always a welcome to see it in another setting. It has very funny scenes.. awkward ones.. and you can't help but picture Angelina Jolie as Derek's mother =D. I liked reading it.. but don't feel strongly about anything about it to comment at it *sorry*

What a great story - had a big smile on my face for most of it. Well written, great characters - especially Grandma Nadine !!! Loved the humour between the brothers and the table banter with the whole family present is priceless. Jake Titus and Kacey Jacobs are childhood best friends who grew apart 5 yrs earlier after an incident that changed their friendship dynamics forever - also the day Kacey lost both her parents in a car accident. Jake now finds himself in a bit of a bind with the Titus Industries board in his quest to become CEO as they aren't too pleased with his stripper bedmates and philandering ways. And his beloved grandmother who recently suffered a stroke has been asking to see Kacey. Jake therefore approaches Kacey with a plan to pretend they're engaged to appease both the board and his grandma. So they head for a weekend at his family estate in Portland to play out the ruse. Enter Travis Titus - aka Satan - Kacey's arch enemy from childhood who teased her relentlessly but out of love never hate. The one girl that got away is back and he's not about to lose her again - so let the seduction begin. First read by this author and I just loved her writing style and her use of humour throughout. Great book and have already downloaded Jake's story. Only wish this was a trilogy or more !! *4.5 Stars*

Wil Wheaton nailed the narration of this hilarious and geeky thrill ride. There was a bit of a lull in the middle when some boring romantic exposition intruded  but mostly it was a brilliant, laugh-out-loud, mega-world-building joy.

Quick read, awesome audio version by Wil Wheaton! I recommend it for light reading, VERY amusing, but avoid the codas! They lay there like a dead dog, trust me. Best read during a re-watch of the classic Star Trek series. I was confused by the whole Hanson thing. I could have done with the book ending at chapter 22 myself. That said, I listened to the audio WITH someone else. We had it going with the digital version up on the computer like subtitles. Why subtitles, you ask? We were laughing out loud. We were also yelling out loud ("NO...FINN!"). What I'm saying, is really, I didn't read or listen to the book...we experienced it in a group imagining. We got as close as you could to watching it as a tv show, and I am telling you, any other complaint I've made, I THOUGHT IT WAS GREAT! This book was fun, if that is what you were looking to get out of it. It was no SG:U, sometimes it felt like a fifteen year old wrote it ("owe ya a blowjob"...really? ), but I had fun, which is what I was looking for.

Word count: about 130 000? or something... Rating: I really need all three swords It ate my review! I had one and it ate it! *huddles in a corner crying* Goodreads hates me... ARC provided by NetGalley Were up all night to the sun Were up all night to get some Were up all night for good fun Were up all night, I got lucky! Were up all night - I got lucky! Were up all night - I got lucky! Were up all night - I got lucky! Were up all night - I got lucky! (*Yes, I've changed the lyrics a bit. No, I don't need you to tell me I got it wrong.) I really hate writing it again. I truly do. Tomorrow on the news... *a young woman... Bodies were found... police couldn't stop...* I badly needed to read a good fantasy book (there's only so much mindless, repetitive romance for teen twats I can take). And I found it *gasp*! This was my first encounter with Sullivan's writing, and I WANT MORE! Since new books published today are like a minefields, I got lucky with it. Really lucky. It was just lying there to be taken! No pending requests necessary. I was fully prepared for this book to suck, and was pleasantly disappointed. Writing was good. Language nice, pretty, graphic, but to the point. You know you're reading a good book, when sword fights suck you in and have you all pumped up. It was impressive. Not once felt I lost or were overwhelmed by excessive amount of details slowing down the action. Props to the author. I also enjoyed the fact, that characters had diverse personalities. And I don't mean main characters - I mean an entire fictional world. You know how in books people are either nice, good-natured with a few rotten apples here and there? Or the world is a cold, dark place where everyone's out to get you? In this case... Neither. There are all kinds of people in Sullivan's world - good, bad, kind, brave, cowardly, selfish, selfless, dedicated, scheming, straightforward, lying, cheating, honest, strong, weak... I liked it. There's just a right mix of crooks and lawfuls. Not all sunshine and rainbows, but not enough to kill your faith in humanity. This book was predictable (much), but execution of a concept was perfect. I'm a sucker for a good story about genius/talented/deadly/special characters that save the day, win against the odds, overcome all sorts of impossible obstacles. I had a blast reading it. Sue me.

It was a good conclusion to the trilogy. The author left a lot of room for further books if she decides to, but they aren't necessary to complete the story. The prophecy comes full circle and it is up to the players to accept or defy their roles as the Fates have set them. Helen finds herself with a collection of new powers. Lines are drawn and a battle is inevitable. Each character embraces their essence in the cycle. I liked how Helen experienced the memories of former Helen's and was able to learn from them. I was sad when people died, but that's war. After finding out what Daphne had been up to all along, I just felt sorry for her. She is kind of pitiful. I'm glad that Helen and Lucas finally discover they aren't cousins and can be together. I love that Lucas vowed to replace Hades. This book had more of the gods in it and I enjoyed that. I kind of wished there was more of a battle between Helen and Zeus, but I liked the way she beat him. By giving up her world it also keeps her in check. She can't give powers to people or herself and she can't grant immortality to anyone else either. I'm interested to know how long the gods will behave before Helen will have to deal with them again. .

I had only read Dick-as-Batman as background for other story arcs (like Steph's run as Batgirl) and so I finally picked this up to get a better picture. I really liked the portrayal of Dick's struggle to play this role, and his interactions with Damian. The rest of the story fell a little flat for me, but that might be in part because I'm not as familiar with Jason's backstory. This really does make me want to read more Dick!Batman, though.

Ah, I've really come to adore Jane. The fire underneath her timid demeanor, her apt perceptions of those around her, her resilience and resolve. The plot of Jane's story has its weak points, but I have to give it five stars for her.

This book made me laugh, it made me cry. It made me feel all the feelings and honestly I couldn't put it down. I really did enjoy it and love it and not want this book to end. The only reason it has gotten 4 stars rather than 5 is because I desperately wanted to know what happened to Hazel in the end!!!

Fish Girl is a cute, but not particularly amazing graphic novel for kids. The main character is a mermaid who is held captive in an aquarium by a man that she thinks is Neptune. She is only allowed to show glimpses of herself, but one day a girl spots her and befriends her. And Fish Girl decides she wants more than the tiny house and the mean man. It gets a bit weird at that point. There's a fascinating story buried in this, but the age bracket this is aimed at means the narrative is much less powerful than it could be. Beautiful art though!

I loved it so much, the book was much more than a pretty cover with an exciting synopsis. It was love story, reality, unbelievable awesome fiction and unique characters all rolled into one. In the book, all of the new generations are dying early, the girls die at 20 while the guys die at 25. This all happened when the first generation did an experiment that made them live longer, but the result was the cut of the lifespan of their children. Rhine Ellery was one of the chosen wives for Linden, with her stunning face and unique eyes, she easily became first wife, and also her husband's favorite. For months she does everything to make a plan, a plan for escape. But she finds herself trapped on her goal of escaping, she can't leave her sister wives, she can't leave Gabriel, she isn't sure if she can't leave Linden too. Plus, she found out that her father-in-law is doing vile experiments on dead bodies of  Linden's wife and his son  . Can she save not just herself, but those who needs saving as well? It was BAVAVING BABAVAAA~!, hahaha, it was a whirlwind of adventure, I am enthralled by the plot and simply put, I love it and I recommend that others read it as well

For all of us who suffered through the Sookie Stackhouse ending debacle, can I just say: Bravo, Ms. Frost!! For ending this series on a high note. We all know that she could have milked the love that people have for Cat and Bones until we couldn't stand the sight of them, but she didn't. Now.... please write a book starring Ian and I will become you're fan-girl.

*3.5 stars* I was head-over-heels in love with Daughter of Smoke and Bone, but I didn't feel the same way about the sequel. Karou is now aware that she is Madrigal and she makes her way to Eretz. She starts assembling new chimaera for the White Wolf - even though she doesn't trust him, he is acting completely different than he did before. He is kind to her and gentle. Akiva is in a bad place because Karou found out what the angels did to her race and he is now her enemy. This book was quite slow for a good chunk - about midway through it picked up and I was hooked. Zuzanna takes more of a primary character status and part of the story is told from her point of view. I really love her personality and sections of the book. Most of all, Issa is back!!! I am so so glad that Karou gets a piece of her family back. Issa is such an incredible character anyways! Looking forward to what will happen in the third installment.

"Choosing to be with you isn't a difficult decision, Jacqueline," he breathed, pulling back one final time to stare into my eyes. "It's easy. Incredibly easy. "Oh man, it was so good. Really good. So why the heck did I gave it 3.5 and I didn't even have the heart to round it up to four stars? I don't know why, but something's off with my ratings today. I just can't force myself to raise it, even just a tiny notch. I will feel a little dishonest if I did. I have soft spot for Ms. Webber's books. I fell in love with her Between the Line series (though I haven't finished it yet, I wasn't really that amped to read Reid's story. But I'll it read...soon (hopefully, not never). Interesting though, I was a little disappointed that there's only one MC for this book. Jacqueline was hardly impressive but that said I liked her. If only the book was written in dual POVs I would have enjoyed it more. There are some things I want to know about Lucas in a more personal level. His past, his story was obviously more interesting than Jacqueline's (disclaimer: at least for me). But I get her story was relevant too but I'm more connected with Lucas (and not because he's a guy). It was just shocking, the trauma this guy experienced was the one that speaks to me the most. Connected to me in an emotional level. I liked the romance. It was really deliciously (and oh so hotly!) written. I liked that they were developed, connected in different things, and not just the physical. I like London, the tutor and I loved the email exchanges. It was fun, it was like synch of minds in kinda (somewhat) nonchalant way. I also the bad boy image, (though I don't normally like tats, me approves of the ink. I like the reason why he did it.). But like I said earlier, the broken guy was the one the truly captivated me. The one that pushed me to go on, and on, and on. Because I want to know why. I want him to move on. I want him to be whole again. And I thank Jackie for that. What have you told me, over and over? It wasn't your fault. You need to talk to someone, and figure out how to forgive yourself for responsibility your mother never would have wanted you to accept. Will you try? Please?" He brushed my tears from my face. "How did I find you?" I shook my head. "Maybe I'm exactly where I should be after all. "Here's a confession, I struggled to write a review for this one. While I rated it average, it was only because I'm slightly (ok, not really slight but really) dissatisfied that there were a little of Lucas than what I wanted. There. As simple as that. So ignore my rating. This one's good.

I love this book. I really, really do. If you've read Where the Mountain Meets the Moon, then you'll absolutely love sorting through this tale, recognizing bits and pieces of what you've read before. If this is your first time reading either book, then this one will give you a great insight into the next! I think my only questions are: if Jiming and MeiLan are Minli's parents, and they eventually live near Fruitless Mountain, then why does Minli's adventure seem so hopeless to her mother? Don't they remember the events of the past with the Moon Lady and the Spirit of the Mountain? Or have generations gone by, and no one remembers? That's the only bit of inconsistency I found and would like to know (unless I've missed something). I adore the characters, especially the three-legged toad. Oh, my heart went out to that creature. Just. Love love love. Love. Love.

I read this in Monterey during a terrific storm... hotel-bound, I read by flashes of lightning... I'm exaggerating a bit, but there was enough suspense to completely hold my interest. I guessed the ending beforehand, though... but it was still pretty smart.

Just... wow. As many have said before, this isn't just a light romance story. It's heavy, intense, emotional, and a story with so many different layers that are important to discuss. If you can, avoid reading too many reviews or seeing spoilers - I think it's better going into this without knowing much about it. But, I think it's important to note there are certain aspects of the story that can be Triggers to some: domestic abuse and attempted rape . Though I wasn't a huge fan of Hoover's writing style in this one - something about it took a while for me to get into - I liked the story and the characters. Actually, I was kind of nervous about the choices Lily would make at the end and was so conflicted right along with her. I really connected with her and that's always something I like in a story. One last thing - I didn't cry during the story itself. I felt a lot of things and it was a rollercoaster, but I shed no tears. The Author's Note, though? I cried - a lot. Definitely read it and definitely read it after the story.

Actual: 2.5 stars I really tried to love this book but everything just felt wrong. The manner of storytelling didn't work for me. I couldn't relate to the characters. What do I care about Tariq, Harry and Craig, Peter and Neil, Avery and Ryan, and Cooper? Everything felt so surreal... in a negative way. I felt so detached that even though it's a relatively short book, I felt like I've read a 500-page book that contained boring essays about philosophy. Le sigh.

I honestly think this one was so much better than Twilight. I do not have a review of Twilight up, nor do I plan on putting one up, but in comparison I feel like this was an improvement. I don't really know what the general opinion about this one is (not majorly a part of the fandom), but I do know that many people get annoyed with Bella in this one. People, she is annoying 24/7; however, I feel like her reactions in this book were described very acutely in a way that I feel like not many people can necessarily relate to or they are uncomfortable with, resulting in them degrading her character for it. For those who have read the book, you probably know what I'm talking about (more details later), and for those of you who haven't, it isn't bad, it's just honest and people don't like that honesty.PLOT: Nothing major happens in the plot in this one--- I feel like it's more setup. Although, I really liked what was going on during the setup. It was exploratory of human nature and there were some really fun scenes.CHARACTERS: Bella- Honey, grow up. You're not ten anymore. That being said, people say her actions and reactions are exaggerations, but you have to put in into perspective. It is a paranormal situation.... I think it's fairly safe to say non-normal reaction are the new normal. Edward- Get over yourself. Dumb***. Jacob- I fell in love with Jacob in this book. I don't ship them. I think they're better as friends. But I'd ship him with me .... :) Nobody else is a main player in this one I don't think..... WORLD: I really liked how we got to hang out around La Push more. That was a really interesting development of where Bells lives and I feel like it filled in the picture more- it added some more colors to it. The Volturi I thought were really interesting. Especially Aro and Jane. It brought to the surface the dangers of vampires that was mentioned in Twilight, but we weren't really exposed to before. The whole thing with the Treaty is brought up too and we get some interesting info on the wolf-y ones as well. SPOILER TIME PLOT: I liked the plot!! Like I said, not much happens, but we get to hang out with Jacob and it seems like there was more doing instead of talking. We get Bella talking so much and her adjusting in the first book- which is fine- but in this one, we see her develop more indirectly, which made her character more relatable while making the plot and events more fun and interesting at the same time. We got to see a lot of really fun things, like motorcycle riding and cliff diving. And then later on we get an almost-death when Alice, Bella, and Edward are in Italy, which is always something that keeps us on our feet. CHARACTERS: (I'm not going to do everybody) Jacob- We really get to know Jacob and his personality in this book. One of this things that I love about him is that he won't stop trying to get Bella to go out with him. This was sooooo cute to me. She even admits it to him at one point that she isn't ready to date, and he's just like, "Eh. I'll just keep it up 'til you say yes". It is just so boyishly charming that it made me love him so much more. Aro- The contrast between his authority and how he behaves and speaks is hilarious. Granted, there is nothing funny about the situation they're in when we meet him, but he seems like he's trying so hard to make everything less tense in the room. This makes me think that he isn't really that bad of a vamp. Bella- Ok. Previous to reading this, I had heard so many negative things about her depression and how the pages only had months on them, but when I was reading it, I couldn't see anything bad with it. If anything, it was very strongly accurate to depression and what that feels like. I'm not sure why people got so annoyed by that. If anything, it should have made them more aware of anyone around them who seemed "numb". I actually thought the whole month-on-a-page thing was really creative. And you shouldn't have had to have ever been depressed or know anyone depressed to see that- it was obvious that that was what she was feeling. WORLD: Nothing really spoiler-y to say here. Jake becomes a werewolf, so they are introduced. Adds another element to the series. And like I stated previously, the Volturi come into play, and I think they are really interesting. Thanks for reading!

An interesting little novella that touches on the interplay of technology and memory - if you're connected 24/7 and can review anything you've seen or said at the touch of a button, do you really have to remember anything? What happens when you're disconnected after a lifetime of never being alone? I'm torn between 3 and 4 stars for this one - I want to give it 4 for the premise and the questions it raises, but at the same time, that's like praising a chef for assembling gourmet ingredients in the kitchen before they've actually cooked anything. I really wish this was an actual novel - 85 pages is not long enough to develop the character or premise. And as proof of this, everyone seems to discuss the questions about memory, recollection, authenticity, etc., raised by this book; but the ACTUAL conflict  (some kind of eco/tech terrorism? Some shadowy AI or corporation that's infecting deer herds with some kind of spreadable/communicable internet-blocking "virus"? WTF?!) gets almost no mention. And it's because there's just no time for it in this book! This really needed to be longer. But if you've got 45 minutes, I recommend reading this. It's certainly worth the minimal time investment. If this author ever expands this into a novel, I'm on board! 2016 reading challenge: a book under 100 pages long

I have to wait 24 hours for the next book, and it is AGONY, I tell you! The Hunt is everything it should be, a stellar second installment in Kade's trilogy, living up to the skyrocketing standard she continues to set. It picks up right where The Rules left off, and follows Ariane and Zane as they go on the run. It's a textbook example of how to do a middle book right: up the stakes, change the setting, introduce exciting new characters, have an action-filled climax, and leave on the cruelest of cliffhangers. I loved the expansion of Ariane's world, the rival corporations and other hybrids. It makes perfect sense, and in no way cheapens anything that came before. We leave Wingate behind for the suburbs of Chicago, where we get to meet Zane's mom. I loved what Kade did with Zane's mom - instead of a saintly woman fleeing her abuser, we get a flawed and fascinating character whom I never knew whether to sympathize with or not. I also thought the hybrids were very intriguing, and felt really awful after what happened in the climax. What came across so incredibly well was just how out of their depth Ariane and Zane were. There was no "safe at home base," no clear plan that would fix everything, no way to win at the game. I remarked on how well Kade did this in Ghost and the Goth, but it bears repeating: her characters are wonderfully intelligent. They do their due diligence, thoroughly analyzing things to make decisions. I was so happy I was reaching some of the same conclusions they were, because they were the logical conclusions. They also have the wherewithal to analyze moral dilemmas, and debate Ariane's question of identity, human or alien. I feel like that could lead to some excellent late-night discussions with fellow fans. Kade also made the most of her two POVs, allowing the reader to see situations from Zane and Ariane's disparate world views. It also drove home how difficult it must be to have a telepath in a relationship. Every time Zane was thinking something awkward (which, like most people, is quite often), I just kept worrying that Ariane was reading those thoughts. It made me appreciate just how difficult that invasion of privacy was, and Zane gets many brownie points for not getting mad about it (since Ariane couldn't control it). And since we also get Ariane's side, and the pain that reading thoughts brings to her, I am able to fully empathize with both of them. While I can usually take or leave romance, Ariane and Zane's romance leaves me breathless. It's such a fantastic relationship, and it's great seeing them work at it. If only they were not always getting cockblocked - the instance around page 230 actually made me growl in frustration. Is it too much to ask for some happy romantic fluff?! (Yes, I realize it is too much to ask, but still...) That's part of what makes the end so tragic, and left me feeling like I was sucker punched in the feels. That ending!!! It's like the ultimate Greek tragedy, where all the characters are doing things that are right in their minds, but are missing a crucial piece of information! And then when Zane dies... I was shocked, but I actually believed Kade would go through with it. And just when I had numbly accepted Zane's death, we get the stinger with Emerson St. John. It's literally the only thing that could make The Trials more painful than Zane actually dying... I can already tell that book will destroy me! Yet it makes so much sense, and was so cleverly set up with foreshadowing throughout the book. I really must applaud Stacey Kade for that, even though it hurts.

I loved so much of this book. Robinson's sense of wonder and beauty are very lovely to read, but unfortunately the story got in the way and ruined all of that. I feel a little robbed, because it started out slow, but gorgeous, and just kept unraveling as the book went on. Why I didn't love it: gaping plot holes, the strangely explained gender issues, preachiness, the overstretched Mercurial/Saturnine contrast between Swan and Wahram, the extracts and lists, the lack of resolution, the unrealistic epilogue, the "love" story. Robinson handed me a mystery in an interesting backdrop of future space colonization, and then as a resolution, gives me next to no resolution, but tells me all the things I've already figured out, and then marries off the two main characters that could never, ever live a life together because they don't even want to live in the same planet. But hey, they sort of think they love each other, and he has a teeny vagina and she has an angry inch, in addition to their regular parts, so obviously they're the perfect match. It's like opposites attract. Woah. So disappointing!

Probably my favorite contemporary fiction I've read this year. The Rosie Project is a charming, warm, laugh-out-loud funny romance about a 40-year-old genetics professor (with likely undiagnosed Asperger's Syndrome) looking for a wife. I gobbled it up and along the way fell in love with Don and Rosie and their quirky, unlikely romance. It's not saccharine, it's not earth-shattering and unpredictable (although, I would argue that it *is* original) - it's just a good old-fashioned rom-com done very, very well. And did you know it's going to be a movie? With Jennifer Lawrence (as Rosie, obvs)? I didn't, until now. So excited.

4 don't you know all creative types have a VIVID imagination stars. The first book in the series is where we meet Cujo as Trent's best friend and partner at Second Circle Tattoos. He's cocky, loyal, fun-loving, and protective. We also meet Drea in the first book as she's Harper's best friend.While Harper and Trent are on the fast track to marriage, Drea and Cujo are responsible for putting together their engagement party and sparks do fly. Drea didn't have time to go to college because she was stuck taking care of her mother and providing a roof over both of their heads. She works multiple jobs in order to live. She's hardworking, honest, loyal, sweet and in serious need of love and care. She can't help but be attracted to Cujo but knows she should stay away from him. Cujo loves his life but there are parts of it that led him to be who he was including a  run in with cancer in his teens and his mother taking off  . He works hard, is loyal to those he cares about, and is extremely sexual. It is really easy to like Cujo and even more so when he goes out of his way to help and take care of Drea. The two struggle with their attraction, being together and all the other things life throws at them. The story is about learning to forgive, learning to accept help and learning to let others love you and give love. The novel is decently paced, there's no rush to the finish line but there's also no dragging. I liked Cujo from the first book and am glad to really see him in this one. The way he lives his life makes sense given what he has dealt with and gone through. I remember Drea vaguely and really enjoyed seeing all her sides and shades.

*takes a few deep breaths, wears wampa cap on* You can do this Brenda. Okay, let me tell you one thing about Krista and Becca's novels: they always go so smoothly, the pacing is always on point. This being said, i loved Amour Amour. I loved it in so many levels that my mind has been in a spin ever since i finished it. I never write reviews telling how the story proceeds and how i reacted to each chapter. That's not how reviews work for me. I'd much rather tell you how it felt, which impact the characters left on me. So here we go. Amour Amour was utterly encouraging. Thora's tone was very different from any of the addicted series' character tones. She was funny, brave and dreamy. Her optimism affected me so much that when something bad happened, i couldn't totally believe it. I cheered for her from the very first pages, i never doubted she could go far. It was very refreshing, you see, because despite the complications she never lasted too long crying on self-pity. Then we have Nikolai. God did i love Nikolai. There's another thing about Krista and Becca's novels... they never centrate too much in one particular moment from their characters pasts. How many novels have we read with male protagonists with a dark past that still affects the character's present? More than that, it always almost seems that it is the girl who has to fix it. Well, this never happens in their novels. And in this particular case, i just really appreciated it. This way, Nikolai maybe seemed a little too perfect (he does have his flaws, but nothing we went too much into), but this lead us to centrate a lot more on Thora's story, and hey, it's her book after all, right? Also, i can't stop thinking about how many awful and abusive male characters are out there in other books. Before Becca and Krista's novels i'd say that i hated alpha male characters. Well, when it comes to these girl's novels, i have no complaints. Nikolai is very masculine, and i loved him. He certainly has a presence and power, but he never put strains on Thora, neither pressured her, he always let her learn and decide what her limits were. (THANK YOU KRISTA AND BECCA, FOR UNDERSTANDING THE IMPORTANCE OF THIS.) So, we can now go on to discuss about this: their novels are never centered on the romance, but yet, you end up believing in the relationships. There's never unnecesary drama, but yes realistic problems. And maybe even more importantly, you can always believe in them as individuals. C'mon, have i not sold the book to you already? If not, i can still tell you that this book wasn't what i was expecting. I had all my trust put on it, of course, i do not mean that i doubted i'd enjoy it. What i mean is that i pictured it on a totally different way. Reading it i was so sure of where it was leading. I was wrong. It took a very different path, a funny and interesting one. We could meet some amazing side characters, that hopefully maybe we'll know more about in the future. So yeah, consider my soul sold to Becca and Krista, those twins surely have talent, and are also very interactive with the fans. I can't thank enough the series of decisions that lead me to start reading their books.

Like many readers, I had mixed feelings about this book (which I read as an audiobook). In fact, I'm pretty sure that those mixed feelings were what Hamilton intended to invoke with her writing. One thing I did like about Hamilton's writing was the way I reacted to and envisioned things from her descriptions: the house she grew up in, her kitchen at Prune, the crumbling Italian villa she stayed in. There are other descriptions of things she's felt or experienced that definitely dragged me along with her emotionally (her account of attending a CIA conference, especially the early morning I left my sleeping child for this? musings)... She's also, at least in her middle age, an over-thinker of her thoughts and experiences, which I identify with. And again, she drags us along with her, in her emotional choices about relationships with her mother, with her spouse, with her family. She's brutally honest, but she keeps us on the edge of our seats wondering what will happen next. Now, that's a blessing and a curse. I now feel like I know Too Damn Much about Hamilton's inner life. About her opinions and all the things she's a complete bastard about. As a teenager, she made some really dodgy decisions that tripped my [well I came from a screwed up family and I never did that crap] judgy prude circuit in; as an adult, she describes her choices in her major adult relationship in a way that makes me want to scream both "What were you thinking?!" and "O my god you wrote this down and published it, someday your kids will hate you forever!" There's a hell of a lot about that relationship, too, and exactly how and why it's effed up. And you may notice that my review is about emotions, not about cooking. This is no Bourdain memoir, how-I-got-to-be-a-chef. This is a memoir about how-my-fucked-up-relationship-with-cooking-and-cooking-for-others-led-me-to-be-a-chef. I have no doubt she's a good chef; if she wasn't, her restaurant Prune wouldn't still be around. I can go online and read her menus, and read what she says about what she cooks, and be pretty sure I'd like her food. I read her description of working the egg station at brunch and have a visceral notion of what that's like; I can read her description of running a restaurant-while-38-weeks-pregnant and have a much clearer image of that than either BOURDAIN ANTHONY or Heat: An Amateur's Adventures as Kitchen Slave, Line Cook, Pasta-Maker, and Apprentice to a Dante-Quoting Butcher in Tuscany give me. But still, it's mostly about what's in her head. And that made this book fascinating, and also a pain. It wasn't the self-conscious boy-was-I-dumb-then of The Pioneer Woman: Black Heels to Tractor Wheels but I'm not sure I would ever want to sit next to this woman on a train, or be her friend. Sit around on the back stoop of a cooking gig smoking cigarettes and listening to people bullshit-- okay, I could do that. But if I met her in real life, I'd figure she was judging me as inadequate to her own screwed up standards; and if I were her friend, I'd want to punch her half the time. So, yeah. This book drew me in and made me react. And it had lots of good mentions of food, even though there was too much lamb. And I half sympathized/identified with and half judged the author. What else can I say? I didn't fall in love with this memoir. I'm not sure I'll ever re-read it. but I will never, ever forget it, and some of the scenes are now part of the furniture of my mind.
I even think this is a 2.5, I'm done with this series or now, they're a lot of characters I wold like to know more about, but honestly I can't go on.

Cover Blurb: Yes or No? It's not enough that the cover is shiny - there is still a shirtless man on the front. I'm not down with that; sorry. It's embarrassing to walk around in public with this book. Characters: I was a little surprised at how okay I was with all of the characters. I wasn't super attached to anyone, but I didn't hate any of them and I was all right with accepting them as my "team" for the book. Having seen the movie before reading the book, I couldn't help but make comparisons. I did like Clary better in the movie, but she was all right in this as well. She was a normal girl who had been thrust into dangerous circumstances, and everyone she had known her whole life weren't who she thought they were. Her emotional trauma and flying off the handle made absolute sense. I didn't think Jace was a jerk. He was confident - or at least pretended confidence when he didn't feel it - and he was also very sarcastic. Both are traits that I can relate to. Alec was okay; I definitely liked him better in the book than the movie. His reasons for disliking Clary were annoying, but I liked his quieter personality - and I could understand his not wanting to let an outsider into the group. Especially one that yes, could get them killed. I was also pretty okay with Isabelle. Her personality was straight forward; she didn't hide who she was or what she thought. Simon was better in the movie - less whining - but I also understood his complaints in both cases. If I was especially attached to anyone, though, it was Luke. He was pretty awesome. Valentine was an all right villain; he didn't especially intimidate me, nor was he just a silly villain. He was somewhere in between, and he did have style and the ability to control the situation. He's a villain that I think can grow as the series continues. So we'll see. The Romance: It's probably easy to guess that affection blooms between Jace and Clary. To make things a bit more complicated, Simon has had a lifelong crush on Clary, and Alec happens to like Jace (yes, Alec is gay). The romance is a hard thing to really decide what I thought of it. I dislike love triangles, and I couldn't believe it took Clary so bloody long to realize that Simon liked her. Alec's main initial dislike for Clary is because he has a crush on Jace, and Clary is kind of shoving in, which is why I thought it was annoying. But surprisingly, the romance is balanced pretty well with the action. It isn't focused on too heavily, and it also isn't in the background. It gets even more awkward, of course, when Clary finds something out about Jace he's her brother . So I do have to give the Author some props for having some original twists in the romance. Plot: Clary has been a regular fifteen-year-old girl, hanging out with friends and going to clubs, until the day she witnesses a murder by people that no one else can see. Suddenly, Clary is thrust into the world of Shadowhunters - or Nephilim, as they are known in legend - and their legacy of hunting demons. It's an accident that Clary stumbles into their world, but it opens up a whole lot of secrets about her mom's past that she didn't know about. When Clary's mom disappears and Clary is attacked by a demon, it becomes obvious that Clary must know something. But Clary's mom wiped her memory, and they have to find someone who can lift the spell so they can find what the enemy is after before they do - the legendary Mortal Cup. The cup that originally created the Shadowhunters. I would never call The Mortal Instruments literature, or even good fiction. But the storyline and the world are all very entertaining - mindless entertainment, but entertaining nonetheless. And while I maintain that reading is about more than entertainment, there's nothing wrong with having some books that are just that and not much else. The Author has created a strangely addicting world that, as the Reader, you do want to learn more about, despite yourself. There's plenty of action in City of Bones to keep things exciting, and when our heroes aren't fighting demons and vampires and other Downworlders, we're learning about the background of the Shadowhunters and exploring the mundane world through Shadowhunter eyes. Like I said, this isn't a book that requires you to think at all; you just sit back and enjoy the ride. Believability: Not applicable. Writing Style: Third person, past tense. I'm really glad it was in third person; I didn't mind Clary, but if I had to be locked up in her head the entire time, I think I would have grown to hate her. The style itself is nothing special, but it worked for the book. Content: 1 g--damn. Alec is gay, Magnus Bane - the High Warlock of Brooklyn - is gay, there's lots of blood and freaky demons. Conclusion: I do wish I hadn't seen the movie first, because all of the twists at the end of the book were ruined for me. I knew what was coming - in general - so the surprise was totally lost on me. Oh well. City of Bones is an entertaining read, and not as bad as I was expecting. Of course, this is only the first book, and many have told me that it's after Book #3 it gets frustrating. However, I've also heard that the last book makes it all worth it. So we'll see. It's the summer and I'm willing to stick with this series to get some entertainment out of it. Recommended Audience: Girl-read, seventeen-and-up, fans of well-developed supernatural and paranormal worlds will like this. So long as you don't mind some complicated romance.

*Disclaimer* For whatever reason, I thought that this was a Printz Honor book this year. Not working at a library anymore, I am totally out of the loop with books now, which is sad in some ways and freeing in others. I no longer feel that undeniable pull to read ALL THE BOOKS, therefore freeing me to do other hobbies, sleep, and work more. But sad too, as I know I'm missing out on that little bit of emotion that books insert into my life. I kinda feel like an android now, and I don't mean the phone. So, this book was one I thought I had put on hold very recently after the Printz awards were announced. I was just waiting, and waiting and waiting for the BIG SOMETHING that usually sets an award winning book apart from the rest. This book didn't really have that for me, but that doesn't mean it wasn't good or interesting. It was. It is. It's good. It's interesting, and a little bit unique (hard to say that about any YA book nowadays) and it scratched an itch you didn't know you had. It was just so dang short. But, it didn't have MANY, if not ALL the hallmarks of a typical YA book. And for that, the author deserves a round of applause. I am still not sure if this is not a book that is a straight up allegory about coming out of the closet and eating disorders. That's not a bad thing at all. If I'm correct, it was deftly done a la Neal Shusterman and the underlying sentiments of Unwind. And by that I mean that you feel like the author is saying something deep, but he/she is leaving it up to you to decide how you feel about it. Sentimentality is left out. I look forward to future books in this series, and a new author to obsess over.

OH MY GOSH!! I...LOVED... THIS...BOOK!!!!! This was the first that I've read from the author, but if this book was any indication of her skills I will be hunting down more by her!!! I loved, loved, loved this story; girl from the "right" side of town meets boy from the "wrong" side and an amazing story that covers almost 2 decades ensues!!! I loved how the author wrote the story, in first person, so it was actually like we were listening to Alix tell the story in her words, of how her and Nick first officially met at the age of 8 and 10 respectively, and how for the next decade things developed and their lives changed as different events affected them both. When I say I read this book in one sitting, I did! I couldn't put it down, so I finished it in less than a day, at 1:30 this morning to be exact! It was just THAT enjoyable, full of that fun summer love in the South that tends to happen when you are young and you don't have a clue about anything outside your little world. I loved how we learned about all the family that surrounded Alix, her mother, her grandfather, and her two aunts, one named Darla too, just like me, so I really got a hoot out of her stuffy character!! LOL!!! The book was separated into two parts, the 1st was during the early years, and served as a build up of life in Morganville, Ark. for Alix and Nick; the 2nd part entailed the events that took place 15 years from the start of the book, and filled in things that happened that we'd previously hadn't been privy to. Again, all I can say is I LOVED THIS BOOK!!! I laughed, I cried, I got aggravated and upset; there was a whole plethora of emotions reading this book. If you are looking for a lovely, sweet, enjoyable, you-can't-put-the-book-down read, then I strongly, STRONGLY suggest you pick it up or download it! It only cost me like a buck and change, and for that price I wasn't expecting much, but boy was I wrong, and happily so!!! This was just what I needed to get me out of my serious good book drought! Kudos to Katherine Allred, this book was a beautiful GEM!!! It is one that will resonate with me for a long time!

If it was me, I'd back-stab every Silver I met, none of them deserved the decency Mare was so apt to show. Finally Maven,  saw it coming from the beginning. I never liked that guy.

3.5 I give it a 3.5, my 5 year old and 7 year old give it a 5. This story has grown on me from the last story. The friendships are more developed. I loved Tyson and I saw the Rick Riordan humor in this story that everyone talks about (I didn't find book one to be very funny). December 2016 Review: This was an incredible read. I love the Sullivans series. The writing and the characters are so amazing and I just love reading this series every year. I loved Lori and Grayson's story. This is a typical love story. A cowboy meets city girl, they are antagonistic towards each other then fall in love with each other. Lori is a member of the San Francisco Sullivans who is a dancer and choreographer. Grayson is a Farmer who operates a CSA (he offers the community fruits and crops). They have amazing chemistry. This book proves that the special person in your life may be closer than expected. I can't wait to read Book 9 - Kissing Under The Mistletoe. Overall, an amazing read. December 2015 Review: This was another fantastic read by Bella Andre. She knows how to draw her audience in. Lori and Grayson's love story is no different than the other books in the series. This was my second favourite in the series actually. For me, Sophie and Lori's love stories were my favourite. It was brilliant and it proves that a big, close-knit family of brothers and sisters can demonstrate their love each other and the loves of their lives. Grayson is a farmer. He is a cowboy, sexy, and smart. He falls for Lori, the Naughty Sullivan. Lori is a dancer and a choreographer. She has a great passion for dance. She is talented, smart, and sexy as well. Also, she is not afraid to take risks. Even when she fails, she redeems herself in the task over and over again. She is a sassy, strong, and sweet heroine of this story. This was a unbelievable story. It was filled with passion, love and steamy scenes. Lori and Grayson are perfect for each other. I am glad that they found their happily ever after. Can't wait to read Jack and Mary's love story in book 9 of the Sullivans series, Kissing Under the Mistletoe. Overall, an amazing read.

I've loved Mary Kubica's other books and was super excited about this one. The book had a lot of potential and started off really strong, but I felt like the big "reveal" and the ending were too messy and rushed and hard to follow. A bit disappointing.

Meaghan Spooner and Amie Kaufman wowed us with their first two volumes, THESE BROKEN STARS and THIS SHATTERED WORLD. Now, they're back to wrap up the trilogy and THEIR FRACTURED LIGHT, and boy do they deliver! I enjoyed both Gideon and Sofia's characters from the outset, something that had taken me longer for the main characters in the previous books (though I, of course, loved all the couples by the end). Gideon's wise-cracking hacker was particularly appealing, and a great way to keep the harder elements of sci-fi and science tech at the fore. Sofia, on the other hand, is street smart by necessity and scarred by the running she's been forced into over the last few years. Throughout the series, Kaufman and Spooner have set up a "lovers from different worlds" theme, and it works again in this installment. Sofia and Gideon have two extremely different life perspectives...and yet, not so different after all. I really loved seeing how all three couples come together in this one and how the final "victory" isn't as centered in revenge as we all might think given that Roderic La Roux was shaping up to be a pretty horrific villain. The group's sacrifices for each other and their decisions when everything is falling apart are what make this trilogy special, and it shines at its brightest here. I still have a special place in my heart for Lilac and Tarver, and OH MY THE FEELS IN THIS BOOK!!!! As much as I enjoyed Finn and Jubilee, they can't really hold a candle in this one. Gideon and Sofia come close because they're the POV characters, but for all you Lilac and Tarver fans out there, hold on to your hearts...the light isn't the only thing that gets fractured in the book. The pace rollicks right along, with a fun cast of supporting characters too. We see cameos from some of the cast from past books, and overall the supporting characters felt more fully fleshed out in this one than in past volumes. As usual, the between-chapter sections with the whispers are utterly fascinating. In each book, these sections are written in an entirely different tone than the rest - far more literary and elegant in a way that is sometimes terrifying. I give Kaufman and Spooner a lot of credit for weaving a breathtaking and haunting plot from these glimpses. It is almost solely what drives the final showdown. Beautifully done! I can't wait to see what these ladies tackle next!

Listen. Why on earth did it take me so long to read this? This series been has on my list for over a year now and I am ashamed with myself for putting it off. This book has everything I love about fantastical storytelling, a great intriguing plot, a vividly imaginative world, great, well developed characters, and a heartbreaking romance. I'll admit that it's bit a different style wise than I've ever read and it took me a while to get used to the strangeness and flow of the writing, but after finishing it, I see how much the style contributed to the affect of the story itself. Laini Taylor's prose and vivid descriptions are breathtaking - every line seems to be worthy of quoting - and the semi omniscient POV from which its told really gives you the board scope you need to appreciate this story. I understand this type of story might not be for everyone. There is a strangeness to it and there is a lot thrown at you at once, once you get to the second half, but this is the kind of story I love to dive into, one that transports you somewhere during the time you spend between the pages. If you're a fan of Sarah J Maas' ACOTAR series, this is definitely something you should consider reading. The style is bit a different in terms of storytelling but the similarities and inspiration SJM obviously took from this book is astounding, but not in the way that suggests she ripped the story off, more like nods to a story that gave life to elements in her own books I've always been a fan of stories full of other worldly, deadly but alluring creatures and Daughter of Smoke and Bone is no exception. The blurred line between light and dark, good and evil, is such an intriguing concept and placing a forbidden romance right in the middle of it, creates the perfect mixture of elements I enjoy in my fantasy. I can't wait to see how it continues in the second and third book. Hopefully, it keeps getting better. Now just for a few little spoilery opinions... Brimstone: I was so wrong do dislike you and I'm sorry. I thought you were a creepy devil, hoarding you're human teeth and were hiding Karou away for your own selfish purpose. You were protecting her and trying to give her the better that she'd dreamed about. I'm sorry you had to die, and I was sadder than I expected when I read about it. Though, something tells me you might not be dead. Who knows with fantasy. Zuzana: Thank you for blessing this story with your so utterly mortal, teenage girl humor. I laughed out loud at your conversation about mating. Thiago: You're an ass. You're this series Tamlin and I hope you get what's coming for you, you entitled, hypocritical piece of shit. Karou/Madrigal: You're so beautiful and brave and such a badass. I loved you in both forms but I hope somehow you get back your bat wings (the horns and the ram feet can stay away though. I'm sorry I couldn't imagine you in a sexy dress with them, it was impossible). I'm also very sorry that the only family you've ever really known, got burned alive because of the actions of the one person you love more than anything else. I'm also sorry you're sisters a bitch. But you did NOT need to walk away from Akiva like that! He thought you were dead! That you'd been betrayed by your own people and was angry and wanted revenge! He didn't know Brimstone was the one who saved you! How could he have known that!? If you don't forgive him in book 2, I'm coming for you. Akiva: Sweet, broken, angel of fire and darkness. You didn't deserve everything that's been done to you. You took an act of kindness and let it change the twisted way of thinking you'd been taught since you were a child and you dreamed of a better world. I'm sorry you're father is an ass and the girl you love and thought was dead left you because of a mistake you made in your ignorance and I hope you don't let it break you again. Also, there are so many elements of this story that parallel the ACOTAR series, its almost absurd. Dreaming of a better world of coexistence, burdened, most handsome male lead with dark features and wings, eyes on the palms, bat wings for Karou... I love it, though. I love that she took something that inspired her and made it something of her own. I'm not sure if I'll regret reading this as my first read after ACOWAR, but we'll see.

I feel like I'm the only person who reads ya and hasn't read this wonderful, little book yet. And that's good. "Be kinder than is necessary. Because it's not enough to be kind. One should be kinder than needed." Wonder really is something special. It's about a young boy, named August who was born with a misformed face, he was home schooled his whole life. The book is about Augusts journey when he starts going to a real school. So, now you know what this book is about and you are probably going to think that August life in school is going to feel like hell to him. But that's not what this book is about. Of course it wasn't easy but in the end you'll gain faith in humanity and friendship and kindness. I loved that this book had many points of views. I especially liked the chapters that were told from Olivia, Augusts older sister because they made me understand August more. It's never easy for a sibling of someone with special needs and I enjoyed reading about her journey and her great character development. I enjoyed the book a lot, it also made me cry a few tears. I rarely cry when I read but when a beloved dog dies  I just can't hold my tears in. If you haven't read Wonder yet do yourself a favor and do so.

I had heard so many great things about this novel so when my book club added it to a list of fall reads, I finally picked it up. Set in biblical times, we follow the life of Dinah, from birth through death. She is the only daughter of Jacob who is a wealthy shepherd. Jacob's four wives all take strong mothering roles for Dinah and impart different gifts and talents to her. She is invited into the Red Tent each month long before her puberty but there she learns to love the women of her life. We get a glimpse into the transient shepherding life and Dinah's training as a midwife. Eventually she finds love, loses it, loses her family and goes on to live a depressing life among strangers, always pining for the comfort of the Red Tent. After decades of moping around, she finally rediscovers her talent for midwifery, goes on to find new love and seeks out her long lost family. I quickly found that it just isn't my cup of tea. The whole midwifery descriptions were over the top and unnecessary. The endless broods that women would have made them no different than dogs and the men treated them no better. Dinah goes through her entire life without ever speaking to her father although he lives with them and leads their family. She also has no relationships with any of her brothers (around a dozen!) except for one. Even when she is summoned to go to her father on his death bed, she is not invited in to see him and none of her brothers even recognize her - not that they even bothered to look her way. I put it down about halfway through but finally finished it. If you get to the point where you are struggling with the endless account of Dinah's childhood, my advice is to skip forward to chapter 6 and you will find that the story finally starts moving forward again.

The long wait is almost over! I can't believe it's been more than four years since we've heard anything from the American-born Faerie Princess Meredith NicEssus. I am thrilled to say that it was well worth the wait. Just like we expected we observe Merry in a whole different light. We've seen her as a resourceful private detective, as an agreeable niece to the faerie queen, as a compelling negotiator, a fearless adversary , a good friend and most especially a more than passionate lover. What we have never seen in the previous eight books is Merry in the role as a fierce protector and devoted mother. Yes, you've read that right! In "A Shiver of Light" we witness the birth of the most awaited triplets. And while her pregnancy wasn't all rainbows and unicorns , catching the first glimpse of the newborns in all their splendor and glory was well worth all the distress. It was defintely moving and beautiful to witness the reaction of her men during that entire process. Since it was mentioned in the previous book who the suspected fathers were we aren't too surprised who among her numerous lovers are featured in this book. However, what was unexpected was discovering the unique elements that each one of the babies inherited from the fathers. At birth, they already begin exhibiting powers of their own and I am excited to see where LKH eventually takes this. Being that these children are the first royals in centuries they receive large amounts of attention. Some of which is largely unwarranted. As the story moves along, we learn of one particular delusional person that attempts to capitalize on the entire situation which leaves everyone around Merry in danger. As always the goddess remains at Merry's side as she battles against these forces and while she remains protected not everyone is spared. She unexpectedly loses one of her beloved which was beyond heart breaking. Did I enjoy the book? I did on so many levels. To be honest, it has to be one of my favorites in the entire series. Since it has been years since the last book, I did appreciate how each of the pertinent characters was described in the very beginning. The way that aspect was delivered was terrific. It felt like I was reuniting with old friends. I also appreciated how the last few moments of Merry's pregnancy was narrated. The aches and pains she experienced during and after made it feel more real and portrayed Merry in a much more human light. I won't fail to mention that since Merry just gave birth we don't see as much carnal and erotic scenes that we expect in any LKH book and while that would be discouraging for most, for me I thought it was a breath of fresh air. I thought it provided a rare opportunity to showcase the deeper side of Merry's relationships. Don't you worry even if the sex is toned down, the over all content is overwhelmingly sufficient. The story remains just as dramatic, action filled and intense as the previous books. There truly is never a dull moment. I loved the ninth installment to the Merry Gentry series and although we do read some finality in different aspects of the story I'm hoping that that the series continues on whether it be Merry's story or a spin-off revolving around her heirs I'm certain it will be just as magnificent. liezelsbookblog.net eARC provided by Berkley via Netgalley

Death is now my favorite narrator thanks to this wonderful book right here. The way Markus Zusak wrote this book was beautiful and unique. Someday in the future, like 2100, when we have to choose a new list of classic books that show that our generation had at least some geniuses, I vote The Book Thief to be one of them. If you are looking for a good, by good i mean heart wrenchingly beautiful, book I give you The Book Thief. Even if you aren't looking for that kind of book read it anyways because like I said this book will be a classic someday and will be in all the AP English test. You will look back when you 100 years old and think gee I should have read The Book Thief what was I thinking. Don't be that person read the book. Trust me when I say that you will see everything differently after this book and the sky will become more than the color blue. Okay time for spoilers people. I loved this book obviously but can I just point out how horrible the ending was. Well actually the ending was good but was it really necessary to kill off everyone. All you left us with that we actually cared about was Liesel and Max. You killed off all of Heavens Street except Liesel. Why?! I guess an ending in a World War 2 book where everybody lives happily ever after is too much to ask for but I don't care. It was better in the book though I thought Rudy death in the movie was just dumb. I like how Zusak exlored all the ways people died though it was really cool. I especially loved how he described how war was more like a boss than a friend to death. I also liked Liesel's character development because she went from a scared kid to one that wanted to punch Hitler in the face, helped hide a Jew, and kissed Rudy. So what if she kissed him when he was dead it counts. Her friendship with Max was cute and now thanks to them my morning routine includes describing the weather the Liesel Meminger way. It was nice to see her go from illiterate to a skilled writer who could paint pictures with her words. I think all good strive to do that. The way he interpreted the colors of the Nazi flag into the color of the sky was super cool. Hans death was pretty sad too though because he just survived the war and came home guys I mean come on. I still can't believe they burned books so it was nice to see Liesel saving one from the flames. I want a library like the one the Mayor's wife has or like the one Belle has in Beauty and the Beast. We book nerds all want a library that big.
