Entwined With You: If you are a Crossfire fan please read the book before reading this review. Contains Spoilers!!!!! You have been warned. Yes! I was all twisted waiting for another dose of Gideon & Eva (would they be Eveon or Gideva in celeb circles?). I read the teaser sample posted before the publishing date and it merely served to whet my appetite further. I gasped with pleasure when it popped onto my screen and immediately got stuck in. I have given it 5/5 because it is so bloody brilliant in all obsessive things G&E but I also have a moan. A major one. Sell-out! The original concept of Crossfire was as a trilogy and this has been bumped up to five books. Now, I do not wish to cast false allegations but I personally believe the publishers have been salivating at the idea of more books=more money and as BTY and RIY were such great money-spinners why not ride the gravy train a little longer. It is not in the style of Eragon's final book split (that completely made sense to me and was beautifully handled). Normally the idea of more Gideon and Eva would not be something I'd ever moan about. Instead I'd be whoop-de-whooping and eagerly scouring the interweb for any snippets of info on release dates and teasers. Not this time and I shall tell you why. Ready? I think the original plot is still visible as a golden thread that has been unteased into several strands and wound round a thick bundle of 'what about' and 'have you considered' and...you get the idea. Picture it: the publishing team sat Ms Day in a velvet room and tried to sell her on the idea of the Crossfire series. When she politely told them where they could stuff it they charmed and smarmed and proffered little canapes and flutes of champagne and wheeled in their arsenal of ideas. Ideas that she could easily write in to help extend the plot and turn the trilogy into a series. Then, and this is the killer, they displayed the virtual truckload of 'More, please' emails and requests and said, 'how could you possibly disappoint all these fans?' Okay, I'm making the publishers out to be mercenary bastards - perhaps they are and perhaps they aren't, but this is what I felt, because: First - additional characters. Yep, you heard me. Mr Giroux and Deanna. Let's focus on Deanna. Why does she exist in the book at all? What possible reason could she have to turn up? It is just a little too much like a sidecar - easily removable and will make a huge difference to the journey. In several instances I thought, 'er, okay, but what's the point?' I offer two examples out of the many; the 'buy her a glass of wine' scenario and the bit where she is sitting in Eva's seat at the charity do. Next - that isosceles triangle rearing up from her BFF, Cary, with his two lovers Tatiana and Trey. That triangle has developed a seriously cumbersome 'bump' at one corner. Again - why? It is quite possible this was always going to be on the cards and Cary would have ended up resolving the issue in one form or another. However it is just a little too clunky. Very unCrossfire. Next, Brett. Lovely, self-obsessed Brett. That little nail should have been well and truly hammered in halfway through the book yet he still protrudes like a well-placed annoyance just waiting to snag your tights. What's with the coincidental trip to SoCal ? He doesn't call her/keep in touch yet tells her he can't wait to 'feel her round him again'. She says she just wants to be friends and ensures that they have dinner in one of Gideon's restaurants so he can't try anything on...then contrarily invites him into her flat for a coffee and says, 'are you going?' What's with the smiley text she just sends on a whim? Nope, not working for me. The sex video - just slotted in there at the end and primed us for revelations in book 4. Got to keep that gravy train fuelled. The Mob? Gangsterville? Okay, I bought that, totally, especially with the bracelet, but that one tiny, little sentence brought the whole thing storming back into paddedville: 'who is protecting him?' Anne (green dress, red hair a the charity function) getting it on with Cary - yep, that was totally going to be in the book because it sets up for the all elusive who, what and why of Gideon's abuse that Eva is going to crack and 'save him' as he saved/protected her. The way she keeps things from Cary - don't get it. Angus knows everything and Cary is her Angus. She would have told him. If not about Gideon being her secret romance then at least about the wedding. She would! Yet, it is being strung out and the reason - her insecurity. That just doesn't gel with me. Her seesaw of I trust him implicitly and want to spend the rest of my life with him vs trust issues, jealousy and marriage is too big a step. Please. I wanted to smack her upside the head. Monsieur Giroux, Corinne and le bebe. I'm rolling my eyes because that is just so obviously a fill-in. Corinne should have been kicked to the kerb within the first three chapters. Magdalene, on the other hand.... There's more but I shan't bore you with minor annoyances. I hope you can see why my jaw dropped when I got to the end of EWY. 50% intoxicated on G&E and 50% fuming and feeling like a shmuck. It really did feel like one of those holidays you've been told you've won...except you have to pay for your flight back...and meals...and there's a service charge...pool use not included.... Hmm, I do sound a little bitter, don't I? My apologies. If you're a Crossfire fan then you will get lots of yummy G&E. I did. Will I continue flying the Crossfire flag? You bet. Only it won't be flown quite as high or as vigorously.

This book is 10+++ stars. No question. At first, from the premise and even the first few pages, I was worried that this was mostly erotica and glorifying prostitution but it is soooo not. Don't get me wrong, there is a lot of sex in it- a LOT and it's hot! But, there is a super strong underlying message to the entire story about self worth, shaming women, and loving yourself. I loved that this wasn't the typical damsel in distress saved by the white knight story either. As much of a role as Sebby had in changing Ysa's life.... she saved herself. Only after she created the life she wanted do they even have a chance. This book gives you a major book hangover because when you read it, you physically feel the emotions. My heart actually physically hurt in my chest. You watch these characters in gray situations, not sure what you would do if you were them because no matter what they do, there isn't a right answer. The author created real life dilemmas and situations that made you hate and love each character, but be moved by the book. Utterly moved by the things they learned, the tragedies they experienced, and who they discovered- themselves. It's something that will leave you thinking about yourself for days. This book is deceptively deep and heart wrenching, it leaves a message with each and every reader. You are loved. You are worthy.

China Mieville has quickly become my favorite sci-fi/fantasy author, and of all his books I have read, this is the one where he puts it all together. Here he gives us his best, most fully-realized character, more glorious urban sociography, loads of bizarre conceptual nuggets, and a cracker-jack plot with a great ending. A loose sequel to Perdido Street Station, The Scar replicates many of that book's virtues and manages to avoid the third act doldrums that sapped PSS's manic energy. (Admittedly, I should probably re-read PSS to see if my initial criticisms have held up.) Bellis Coldwine is fleeing New Crobuzon when her ship is taken by pirates and all passengers are press-ganged into Armada, a giant floating city built out of captured ships. A renowned linguist, Bellis is given a job in the city library where she stumbles upon a book that allows Armada's rulers to set in motion a bizarre plan for world domination. Bellis is a reserved and introverted person with an amazing poker-face, but with an unrealized romantic streak underlying her standoffish exterior. She's a great character and an unconventional heroine. But once again, the heart of the book lies in Mieville's world-building. Armada is like a remixed, nautical mirror to the New Crobuzon of PSS, and Mieville takes great joy in detailing the complex sociological interplay between the species and factions and neighborhoods found there. While New Crobuzon is an authoritarian state limited only by the fundamental chaos and ungovernability of the city itself, Armada is portrayed as a generally tolerant, anarchist confederation, home to a variety of forms of government. Notably the Remade are allowed to live as equal citizens in Armada. The great diversity of species found in the world of Bas-Lag is further expanded here to include the anophelii (mosquito-people), scabmettlers, grindylow, vampir and the avanc. Mieville remains an intense writer with a $6 million vocabulary. Several scenes in the book veer toward horror and might not be for everyone. Some of the words I had to look up include: benthic, puissant, chitin, eidolon, purulent, corium, trireme, prognathous, paradoses, strath, shinnery.

I tend to be super wary of YA fantasy books - actually I'm wary about fantasy in general. When it's good, it's good, but when it's bad it's poison to my soul. No poison here - hooray! Bardugo did good here. I mean, I always have something to nit pick but overall I really enjoyed this. I like the flavor of the setting. I've heard some criticism of the Russian/Not Russian of this and to all those poeple I lovingly flip the bird. This is fantasy, folks, and as much as you might disagree that means the author can do *~*~anything she wants*~*~ to her setting (so long as it's consistent and works with plot and all of that, of course). It's beautiful magic. If you're going to moan about the improper use of Russian words, you should probably also be concerned with the fact that magic doesn't exist in real life. Just sayin'. Sorry for that side track - let me start over. I like the flavor of the setting. I love the back and forth between suspense and life. I like our main character and how we get deep but not too deep. I like the conflicting romance and, even more, I like what took me by surprise. Characters evolved in great ways. Bardugo had my hand quivering at a page turn because I didn't want to see what would happen next because I was so sure it shouldn't happen but everything was just going wrong... anyway, that's enough of that before I have to hide this in a spoiler. Like I said, I have some nit-picky. Teenage girls are annoying with their wallowing, sulking, and cattiness and I would rather not read about it, but so it is. I have high hopes for this series moving forward. Once, just once I want to be totally satisfied with a YA series when I'm done with it. I've given a lot of them a chance (The Hunger Games, Twilight, Divergent) and by the end they all sucked. Come on Bardugo. I am rooting for you here.

This review is for the entire series as a whole (books 1-4) because the cohesiveness of the plot is very tight and feels like one epic story told in 4 parts. It's been a while since I've read a Young adult fantasy series that was written so well that it could easily have passed off for a direct competitor in the adult fantasy genre. There's always been a sense of naivety in characters and plot when it comes to YA Fantasy and while I do love the simplicity of action motivations and the black and whiteness of the characters, sometimes I do like my books to be a little bit grey and just a tad bit on the complicated side. I haven't seen a YA book tackle general fantasy in a way that was mature yet still absolutely at its heart YA since Finnikin of the Rock. Absolutely riveting, the story of the seven realms can be pretty complicated. It's like a untying a knot in a ball of yarn. Just when you think you've undone one string, another string comes in blocking your way to cause more tangles. So just when you think one plot point has come into conclusion, another plot gets tangled with it creating this delicious web of truth and lies becoming very organic and alive. I love the fact that the plotting is well thought out and hints of things to come from the first book come to fruition in the last. As for characters, they are absolutely amazing. The growth they experience is tremendous and my favorite part about YA is the transformation of characters from young adult to adult and this book demonstrates it for most of the YA characters. I also love the fact that they feel real! It also takes some fantastic character building to make antagonists work together with the main characters for the greater good of the kingdom (or for their own personal agendas) which just adds more to the web of deception. I love the fact that everyone (in some form of fashion) is grey and not the usual black or white. They will take actions that will surprise you (whether 'good' characters doing 'bad' things or 'bad' characters doing 'good' things) but when examining their motivations it actually makes a lot of sense. Just like in all YA, there's romance in the plot but what I appreciate is the fact that it takes romance in a very realistic manner. All the characters take their time exploring different kind of relationships with one another which to me sounds more realistic than the usual "omg trueee loovveeee" type. Yes warning there's some sort of a love triangle but it's quite integral to the story and it's part of 'growing up' and there's some important lessons to be learnt from the experience for all those involved  Well it's not /really/ a love triangle....... I honestly think the second romance would never had happened if the first one did not end as final as it did and my heart was honestly broken because I was quite attached to the first romance since the attraction was built so well =. Actually screw that I was really attach to the first romance and was so close to throwing my kindle out the window when things ended so finally between them. The pacing is done excellently well. I have to admit, the beginning parts a little bit of a slow burn (esp book 2) but this is a necessary evil as it sets the stage for books 3 and 4. And yes at 500 pages on average per book, this series is a lot longer than a typical YA series but it didn't feel long at all and there was really no wasted parts. I was hooked to the story and totally engaged for all 2000 pages. As for the ending, it was immensely satisfying and it ends very neatly with no lose ends in terms of plot points. However it does feel a little bit rushed. I think another chapter or two would have wrapped the story up a little better. I cannot stop recommending this series to anyone who loves high fantasy. The characters are amazing and the plot absolutely engaging. Even if you don't really like YA as a genre, fans of fantasy will absolutely enjoy this. As for fans of YA, this series may be a bit of slow burn since it's very long and the politicking at the end might tire out some.

Better writing than the previous books. Less strained metaphors. The ones that were there were actually nice. Quality over quantity. I like the 'twist' (could see that coming from early in the book) and the ending (which was inevitable, but the method surprising). I don't see how unleashing Asmodeus/Rafi on the world is really Felix' fault. I mean, it wasn't as if he had any choice. Not using Asmo would have let Mark grow. It was merely a choice between demons . It was nice to delve into Felix' past and personality. There is even a little character development going on, which is always nice (and long overdue). I don't understand why Basquiet (sp? I listened to the audiobook) treats him like that and refused to believe him. After all, he had proven to her what he did and knew and on whose side he was in the second book. By the end of that one they were on a better understanding. This was just... incongruous. "We need a disbelieving blocking cop because that's mandatory in the noir genre" or something. On the same note, there were many little plot/story errors. Which is just sloppy editing. But the story is entertaining. It is still far from Jim Butcher's, as we compare his book 4 with this book 4. I must admit that Dresden Files 1-3 were very rough and choppy and hardly polished writing as well, but the were a lot more smooth and well-built. Not mysteries though, and that I like. So, 3.5 stars out of 5.

I really, really loved this. It's exactly what I think is the best kind of fantasy: using magic and fantasy tropes to explore real-world problems - in this case, recovering and healing after surviving abuse. This book picks up nine years after the first Graceling book. Bitterblue, daughter of King Leck, is still trying to pick up the broken pieces of her kingdom. Leck had used his mind control powers on pretty much everyone for 35 years and committed horrible acts, and the people of Monsea were deeply damaged by Leck's reign. Bitterblue needs to sort out truth from lies and dig into the kingdom's painful past in order to help her people find closure and an honest path forward. The underlying trauma felt realistic, and characters responded to it in different ways. At the plot level, the story was entertaining, with a few different interwoven mysteries, and Bitterblue is a smart, funny heroine. Trigger warning for sexual and domestic violence and general atrocity, but if you can make it past the haunted memories, the message of survival and healing is a good one. Recommended (but I'd only consider this "YA" for 16+).

I read this book because I was curious what all the hullabaloo was about. Why is there a run on grey neckties in New York City department stores? Why are women claiming that this book has put some pizzaz back in the bedroom? Mommy porn? I am still curious, but not so curious that I am going to read the remaining books in the series. Personally I like how the first book ended. The only thing I would change is that it would have ended this way soon after chapter 1. Ana would have run away after the first peek into the playroom or that ridiculous contract. At this juncture, I am delighted with the ending of the first book, so why read books 2 and 3 and get angry again? "Oh this is not my normal read, I am just curious." Oh bullshit! I have nothing against a good hot sex scene with details, and crude language doesn't bother me...if it did I would be speechless. Romance is not my genre, but I like a little romance in a normal read. So let's dispel the idea that I am some nice old man who fell into this book by accident. I will say however that I did read this out of curiosity--what is it that has all the ladies at our book club chirping about the naughtiness? So what is with this book? Well it is a Cinderella story with a lot of good hot sex, then again it is perhaps Beauty and the Beast with a lot of good hot sex. I am not sure. There are plenty of books out there that turn an archetype fable into a modern romance with good hot sex. So why is this one causing a shortage of grey neckties? Why in a world of a zillion erotic romances does this one go viral? My guess is that it is not just because it has good hot sex, but because it dips one's toes into the taboo of BDSM without wallowing in it. Prince Charming is very charming indeed, a billionaire, cultivated, handsome, young, educated, refined, sexy and for the most part he allows Ana to introduce him to normal vanilla sex. So most of the sex scenes are not employing spiked black leather collars and leg shackles in a sweaty dungeon with whips and chains. No, the BDSM occurs in a relatively civilized "playroom." There are only three trips into the playroom and as far as BDSM goes, I imagine that it is fairly tame. Most of the sex is just the good old fun kind, free of pain, with a slightly veiled authoritarian threat in the background. On the other hand Prince Charming is a damaged beast. He becomes sexually aroused by humiliating and hurting women. So no matter how gorgeous and refined he may be, and no matter how many cars, clothes, and computers that he may shower on Ana, the fact remains that he gets off by causing Ana to suffer pain. He becomes highly excited and aroused by hitting and hurting women. I don't believe that this book is about BDSM, if it was I doubt that it would attain mainstream popularity. I think the book uses the taboo of BDSM as a metaphor. In trying to understand what the big whoop is about, I have read several articles that compares Fifty Shades of Grey to the Twilight phenomenon. I was a bit befuddled by popularity of Twilight also. I read someplace that the drop dead gorgeous Edward's potential bite in Twilight was an exaggerated metaphor for the old time tension of desire for sexual union off set by the fear and the cultural taboo of losing one's virginity. In our cool worldly modern times, the loss of one's virginity is no big deal. All the cool beautiful kids shed it with glee and talk about it on Facebook. Yet somehow I suspect that to many young people, the not so cool kids like you and I, who still lead examined lives, and who question the role of love and sex and their place in it, the gift of one's virginity remains a very big deal, especially for girls for whom sex remains risky business. Yet in the popular imagination, the loss of one's virginity has become commonplace--no big deal. Hence the strange appeal of being bit by a vampire to teenage girls, and to be bit by one that looks like Robert Pattinson, oh my! Alright, that makes sense in a pop psych sort of way. But what exactly is the metaphor that the BDSM represents in Fifty Shades of Grey? Why does it appeal to mature and sexually experienced women? Is it also simply an exaggerated metaphor for the loss of one's virginity? Or is there a bigger issue? Is the BDSM a kinky exaggerated metaphor for a fear of the subjugation of marriage and perhaps the angst of the marriage bed? For 10,000 years women have been trapped in often loveless marriages, where they were nothing but chattel whom had no legal rights, had to obey their husbands, and were often raped, savagely beaten, and disciplined. In the past two centuries, women's rights within marriages have gradually improved. In the past 50 years women's rights both within marriage and within society have drastically improved. Yet at this time, women still often get the poopey end of the stick in both marriage and the wider social milieu. So is the metaphor of the BDSM in Fifty Shades of Grey for the fear of a damaged marriage and sexual boredom? Is Ana going to become a heroine by curing Christian of his sadism through a woman's strength, wisdom, tenderness and love? Will they ride off into the sunset, making love, and convert the playroom into a nursery? To be quite honest, I have no idea what exactly the appeal of this book is. While the BDSM is tame compared to how it could be, I still found the episodes of where Christian physically assaulted Ana to be revolting. Book 1 ends with Ana leaving the sadistic bastard. Good. The book ended the way I wanted it to. Ana leaves him. There is no need for any additional books. Ana go find a nice man who loves you without hitting you and live happily ever after. Somehow I doubt that occurs in books 2 or 3. When considering social effects, there is one way in which Twilight differs significantly from Fifty Shades of Grey. After reading Twilight, no one has to worry about getting bit by a vampire. But at the risk of being overly melodramatic, is there not a reasonable concern about the possible aftermath of a book that somewhat romanticizes and moves BDSM to the mainstream? Being loosely tied up with a grey necktie and getting a playful slap on the butt may be deliciously kinky, may put some zing back in the bedroom, and is harmless. However, as thrilling as that tender moment with the riding crop in the playroom may have been, in the hands of an inexperienced, too exuberant, or somewhat inebriated lover, a riding crop could wreak some real devastation, not to mention what some over excited dominant feeling his macho oats could do. Some how I think BDSM is best left to a knowledgeable and skilled subculture. I just hope that there is no run on the emergency rooms like there was on those grey neckties. Aside from the BDSM, which I thoroughly despised, the book was fairly well written. However, I was disappointed in Ana's character. She was a very intelligent and capable young woman whom I liked and could easily regard as a daughter. Yet she maintained an internal mental litany of a 13 year old. "Holy crap! Her muscles clenched in her belly with desire, but her scalp prickled with apprehension, while her inner goddess did somersaults for joy" at the mere sight of Christian...over and over. As a another reviewer mentioned I wanted to punch her stupid internal goddess in the face. A spanking in the stars for you Ms. James for displeasing me. EDIT 4-19-2012: I ran into this blog post on Fifty Shades: http://open.salon.com/blog/sbynoe/201... Aha! Some insight into the reason for the popularity: "Now, to its credit, there are moments when the book is kind of hot. It's pretty hard to read a book with so much sex and not get turned on. I lost count but I think there's  at least 15 sex scenes, compared to 3  in other romance novels I've read. The downside is that it's so completely unbelievable you're thrown right out of the story. How they hope to make a movie out of this, I don't know. Then again, people liked Twilight. " Emphasis mine. Me and my metaphors! This is what happens when you read a review by a guy that lives under a rock regarding pop culture. I have over analyzed this thing. This is not great literature, there are no metaphors. The reason this is popular? Its a good buy, an erotic bodice ripper with a lots of erotic and not a whole lot of bodice. It is a fairy tale with a lot of bang for the buck and just enough kinky to give it some pizazz without grossing one out. The bad boy is a perhaps a bit farfetched...but billionaires and sadists exist...vampires, no matter how dashing, don't. Indeed it is beauty and the beast in the buff and the beast brandishing a riding crop instead of fangs. Don't look for metaphors, just suspend your normal sense of belief, and read how the beautiful young maiden turns a frog into handsome prince with a lot of hot vanilla sex.

Rachel is such an annoying character. She's a 30-something English woman who travels into London every day on a commuter train. Her husband has left her for another woman due to her severe problem with alcohol. Everyday, Rachel's train passes by the home of a couple who seem perfect. Rachel comes up with names and invents a fantasy life for them. Rachel's life thus consists of three preoccupations: alcohol, her ex-husband Tom, and the couple. Nothing much happens until gasp! the wife of the perfect couple ends up missing and Rachel is determined to help solve the mystery of the woman's disappearance. Yawn. A friend from work encouraged me to read Paula Hawkins' newest novel Into the Water and even lent me her copy, so I guess I'm going to give this author another shot...

Reading this in the ebook version, I actually got to make specific notes as I went along and have a bunch to say about it. The cover of the book is beautiful, and the story started out intriguing and I was hopeful. Sigh. The story could have been good. It could have been juicy, wonderful and exciting but instead it was so meek, feeble and routine. About Henry: Everything about Henry, Kate, and Henry & Kate together was... dead (no pun intended, really. Really) Everything felt so calculated and cold. Their first kiss was a completely no chemistry kiss. If the story wasn't told from Kate's point of view, I would have thought she was actually some neutral character that no one cared about, lol. I didn't understand when and why (and how) she started to care for Henry enough to kiss him and make him a blanket like I swear they only talked like 3 times so far, and those conversations weren't even anything remotely meaningful. About the Gods: The whole idea of "Gods" was so underplayed! Henry, a millennium old god, was portrayed more as a tortured teenager. A teenager. A teen- okay, you get it. Every other god was the same. Greek gods, I'm pretty sure, were especially cruel and didn't care about puny humans. But these ones, these ones goddamn cared about every little stupid thing that even I wouldn't care about. They didn't have a presence at all. Gods? more like Blobs. Heh. Hehheh. About the attacks: If I was the target of some unknown assassin that had killed 11 girls before me, I would probably be really suspicious of everything and everyone. Now I realize she didn't really have to, because the attacks were so lame, I almost laughed one time. Kate was extremely bad at this suspicious thing, and it annoyed me to no end when she banished Ava and then started to think she was the culprit of the attacks. If you can doubt a person so quickly like that, you have to question if you ever really considered then a friend. Which brings me to the assumption that Kate just can't handle the idea that people die (Surprise!!) and that made her even stupider in my eyes. She was living in the underworld, for god's sake. She is stuck on staying alive no matter what, she is stuck on keeping her mother alive no matter what, she is stuck on saving Ava, who I doubt she even cared that much about. Or, once again, I just failed to see the "chemistry" between Ava and Kate. About the Tests: They were such. A. Disappointment. This is pretty much where the book almost made me cry with boredom/frustration. A lot of spoilers coming up!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! Okay first of all, eating my general three meals a day is not something I would consider gluttony at all. I, like other sometimes eat even when I'm not hungry, because- well, food. And I don't think this is wrong at all, unless you are costing someone else their meal. Damn, it's not like Kate is hogging all the underworld food and leaving all her maids and other underworld poor people staving and dying. Now that is gluttony. Second, the humility test- wtf? Say I'm Kate. I tried my fricking hardest to win the test, and someone spiked me and I accidentally had sex- with someone I love, mind you, I'm not just gonna sit there and accept that I failed the test. I did nothing wrong and I sure as hell would yell until they admitted it. It's like saying rape happens because the girl has no humility. I do not get how accepting that I'm a failure when I'm clearly not will give me passing marks. I wish there had been at least one fight, or anything otherwise... exciting related to the tests, and that they weren't all just about dresses and eating and mundane stuff like that- I mean, the story is set in the underworld, and there couldn't have been anything more interesting happening? Kate has only been given poison once in the whole book, and she didn't even eat it. /Eternal sigh/

I am not going to compare this to the Hunger Games, that's just a good way to be let down. I don't understand when people try to compare two completely different things and are let down...DUH!!! Anyway, what I liked about this book is that you know as much as everyone else in the book (thus far). This is a great strategy to keep readers interested. If I wanted to read a book worthy of being called great literature, I would pull out Faulkner, Joyce, Kafka, Tolestoy, etc; however, where this book lacks in the classical literature department, it makes up in the hole story department. I always forget that people don't seem to understand that the reason classical literature is so good in sentence structure, word choice and what I like to call "pretty prose" because classical literature deals with everyday life. Modern literature doesn't have to compensate because the story itself is what brings the reading alive. Sometimes I just get a little annoyed when people are comparing potatoes to trees... I give this book a 4 for keeping guessing, for not letting me give up, and eventhough I could see the ending from a far distance, this book made me realize that a closer glance my prediction was not as acurret as I thought. And God knows I like being in the wrong, if it's done right!

I really enjoyed Dimitri in the previous Guild Hunter books and was always interested in finding out more about him. So we knew Dimitri didn't like people being victimised and I loved how that was played out by him helping Honor take revenge. I thought that the revenge was dealt with incredibly well. He didn't go off an secretly kill people for her, as male leads often do in vampire books when they love a mortal and she didn't go overboard or be irritatingly forgiving. I really liked Honor as well, her transition from feeling like a victim to being a survivor was incredibly deftly handled. My only issue was the reincarnation, I didn't mind it in the beginning, her being drawn to him before she knew him, even being drawn to the field, but remembering so much of her previous life, even though she said she was Honor and not Ingrede, towards the end it felt too much like Ingrede was taking over. Maybe if they have another story centered on them and she remembered other lives, and it became something of interest outside just her suitability to be with him, or there where lives where she was near him in some way but they didn't connect. With it as it is, it seemed more a plot device to enable her to get him to talk about what happened to his children and to stop him from feeling guilty about loving someone else.

This is such a sweet story, I just love it. I really feel for the characters and I hurt when they hurt. I think Michael is a bit over the top with his compassion and that would drive me crazy in real life, but he's adorable and his relationship with James is more real. They're hilarous with one other, sarcastic and silly. Plus I have so much in common with James (except I can walk most of the time) that I would love to hang out with him. Michael would intimidate me at first, but he would win me over pretty quickly. The story doesn't have a lot of plot, but it has lots of angst and that works for me. The author gave an accurate portray of Seattle, which was refreshing. Some other things I noticed: Calling Tommy "champ" is so condescending. The whole scene made Tommy sound like he was developmentally disabled. Way too many metaphors. It was a black and white photo he had seen but now he says the hair is a lighter brown than in the photo, more of a chestnut. Um... He thinks he has a shot because the guy is in a wheelchair? Oh, that's offensive on so many levels. Odd to have a sex thereapist use the euphism "do the dirty." Michael thinks sex is beautiful and necessary. Ticket to Ride is a great game. The Doomsday Book is my second favorite book of all time, and Snow Crash is up near the top too. I would totally love hsnging out with these guys. He was 28 earlier and now he's 29 without any mention of a birthday. James mentioned Goodreads! Woo hoo! It's funny that the excerpts from James's books aren't nearly as well written as the actual story even though he's supposed to be an amazing writer. I know it makes me a horrible person, but I don't think I could date a sex surrogate. I'm too insecure. Emotional cheating is worse than physical cheating to me and the tenderness and caring the sex surrogate has with his/her clients would be way too hard for me to deal with. That makes me like James even more. If I read the ending to the trilogy James's wrote that everyone is impressed by, I would be furious and heartbroken. Wild Ginger is a fantastic restaurant. If you're ever in Seattle and can afford it, go. Much, much better than the previous ones even though I liked them, too, and quite different. This was wonderful.

This was a book that took me a while to warm to, and this is more like a 3.5 than a 4 for me. I'm still not into the first person present tense narrative style (mostly because the present tense just doesn't seem necessary), but I suddenly loved the novel about 2/3 of the way in after Stack dies, and Derlock & Emerald take off in the cap . That, to me, is when things get really great. I particularly loved the reveal about Penn Slabilis and the overriding media interest thing . Okay, maybe loved isn't quite the right word--it pissed me off and made me want to reach through the pages to choke the life out of Penn Slabilis. I spent 2/3 of the book not really liking most of the characters (and being tempted to bail on the book) and the last 1/3 wanting to hug them, so I'm not sure what that says. The Notes for the Interested thing . I'm undecided about those. Certain notes were necessary to, as Barnes indicates, avoid infodump. At the same time, I skimmed/barely read 95% of them. The final third of this novel was fantastic and redeemed the entire endeavor. I'm glad I hung in there.

Loved this installment! Jane kicks ass as usual, but we see more development of the relationships with those she claims as hers and coming to terms with her role. I've never liked Rick and am glad she's finally realized what a royal ass he is and promised herself she won't be going back there. She doesn't know it, but we know Bruiser's problems with Leo are because he's been putting Jane first, culminating in being kicked out. I really hope she gives him a real chance in the next book - all obstacles are now out of the way, except her lingering feelings for Rick. I also love that since others now know of Beast, if not the details, she can let her free in public and they have a better partnership. "Sparring" with Leo, was a great demonstration of their ability to lean on one another and use the strengths each possess.
